fields.Text:
Which histone type is not a part of the octomer during the formation of a nucleosome?

{{c1::H1}} type
fields.Back Extra: It binds the nucleosome and the linker DNA to stabilize the chromatin structure.

fields.Text:
What structures are indicated by the E and H in the electron microscopic image of the eukaryotic nucleus provided here?



E = {{c1::Euchromatin}}
H = {{c1::Heterochromatin}}

Where may Barr bodies be seen on electron microscopy?

{{c1::Periphery}} of the {{c1::nucleus}}
fields.Back Extra: Barr bodies are inactive X chromosomes.

fields.Text:
What two histone modifications decrease DNA transcription?

{{c1::Methylation}}
{{c1::Deacetylation}}

How does histone acetylation increase transcription?

Acetylation removes the histone's {{c1::positive::positive/negative}} charge → Relaxation of DNA coiling → Increased transcription

What amino acids give histones their positive charge?

{{c1::Lysine}}
{{c1::Arginine}}

What is the result of methylation of CpG islands within the promotor region?

{{c1::Repression}} of gene transcription

What makes up a nucleosome?

{{c1::2::Number}} loops of DNA around a {{c1::histone octomer}}
fields.Back Extra:
A histone octomer consists of 2 copies of 4 core histone proteins:

H2A
H2B
H3
H4

fields.Text:
What DNA modifications are implicated in fragile X syndrome and Huntington disease?

Fragile X syndrome → Dysregulated DNA {{c1::methylation}}
Huntington disease → Histone {{c1::deacetylation}}

What is the less condensed form of chromatin that is transcriptionally active called?

{{c1::Euchromatin}}

During which phase of the cell cycle does synthesis of DNA and histones occur?

{{c1::S}} phase

Which part of DNA makes it negatively charged?

{{c1::Phosphate}} groups

What is the transcriptionally inactive, condensed form of chromatin called?

{{c1::Heterochromatin}}

How does mitochondrial DNA differ structurally from nuclear DNA?

{{c1::Circular::Shape}}
Does not utilize {{c1::histones}}

What DNA modification is implicated in genomic imprinting, carcinogenesis, transposable element repression, inactivation of the X chromosome, and aging?

DNA {{c1::methylation}}

What process changes the expression of a DNA segment without changing the sequence?

DNA {{c1::methylation}}

How does histone deacetylation decrease transcription?

Removal of {{c1::acetyl}} groups → Tightened DNA coiling → Decreased transcription

If DNA1 consists of 60% C-G bonds and DNA2 consists of 70% A-T bonds, then which DNA would have a higher boiling point?

{{c1::DNA1}}
fields.Back Extra: C-G bonds have 3 hydrogen bonds, whereas A-T bonds have only 2 hydrogen bonds.

fields.Text:
What is the end product of uracil methylation?

{{c1::Thymine}}

What chemical groups are attached to the 5' and 3' ends of a phosphodiester bond?

{{c1::Triphosphate}} group at the 5' end
{{c1::Hydroxyl}} group at the 3' end

Name the products formed after deamination of guanine and 5-methylcytosine.

{{c1::Xanthine}} is formed after deamination of guanine
{{c1::Thymine}} is formed after deamination of 5-methylcytosine

Which amino acids are necessary for purine synthesis?

{{c1::Glycine}}
{{c1::Aspartate}}
{{c1::Glutamine}}

Which type of bond links nucleotides?

{{c1::3}}'-{{c1::5}}' {{c1::phosphodiester}} bond

Which type of nucleic acid will uracil and thymine be found in?

Uracil is found in {{c1::RNA}}
Thymine is found in {{c1::DNA}}

What differentiates nucleosides from nucleotides?

{{c1::Phosphate}} group
fields.Back Extra:
Nucleoside = Base + Ribose/Deoxyribose

Nucleotide = Base + Ribose/Deoxyribose + Phosphate

fields.Text:
Name the bases formed after deamination of cytosine and adenine.

{{c1::Uracil}} is formed after deamination of cytosine
{{c1::Hypoxanthine}} is formed after deamination of adenine

Name the three pyrimidine bases.

{{c1::Cytosine}}
{{c1::Uracil}}
{{c1::Thymine}}

Name the two purine bases.

{{c1::Adenine}}
{{c1::Guanine}}

What serves as the energy source to form the phosphodiester bond between nucleotides?

The {{c1::5}}' end of the incoming nucleotide since it has a {{c1::triphosphate}} group

What enzyme is affected in orotic aciduria?

{{c1::UMP synthase}}

What enzyme do mycophenolate and ribavirin inhibit?

{{c1::IMP dehydrogenase}}
fields.Back Extra: This is in the purine synthesis pathway.

fields.Text:
What drug inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase?

{{c1::Leflunomide}}

Dihydrofolic acid is converted to tetrahydrofolic acid by which enzyme?

{{c1::Dihydrofolate reductase}}

How do azathioprine and xanthine oxidase inhibitors interact?

Azathioprine is metabolized by the {{c1::purine::purine/pyrimidine}} degradation pathway
Xanthine oxidase inhibitors {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} the plasma levels of azathioprine, resulting in {{c1::immunosuppression}}

What is the mechanism of action of the anticancer drug 6-mercaptopurine and its prodrug, azathioprine?

It inhibits {{c1::de novo purine}} synthesis by inhibiting the conversion of {{c1::PRPP}} to {{c1::IMP}}

What cofactor is required for the synthesis of dTMP by thymidylate synthase?

{{c1::N5, N10-methylene tetrahydrofolate}}

What enzyme does hydroxyurea inhibit?

{{c1::Ribonucleotide reductase}}

dUMP is converted to dTMP by which enzyme?

{{c1::Thymidylate synthase}}

What enzyme converts UDP to dUDP?

{{c1::Ribonucleotide reductase}}

What enzyme is inhibited by 5-fluorouracil and its prodrug, capecitabine?

{{c1::Thymidylate synthase}}

In de novo nucleotide synthesis, which nucleotides are made from orotic acid, with the addition of PRPP?

{{c1::dUMP}}
{{c1::dTMP}}
{{c1::CTP}}

In de novo nucleotide synthesis, which nucleotides are made from IMP precursors?

{{c1::AMP}}
{{c1::GMP}}

What drugs inhibit the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase in humans, bacteria, and protozoa?

{{c1::Methotrexate}} in humans
{{c1::Trimethoprim}} in bacteria
{{c1::Pyrimethamine}} in protozoa

What enzyme converts glutamine and carbon dioxide into carbamoyl phosphate for the synthesis of pyrimidine bases?

{{c1::Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II}}

Most drugs that inhibit nucleotide synthesis typically fall into what three categories?

{{c1::Antineoplastics}}
{{c1::Antibiotics}}
{{c1::Immunosuppressants}}

Name the key intermediate that is common to the de novo synthesis pathway of both purines and pyrimidines.

{{c1::PRPP}}

What is the inheritance pattern of SCID when it is due to adenosine deaminase deficiency?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

How does rasburicase, a recombinant version of urate oxidase, help with uric acid excretion?

By converting uric acid to soluble {{c1::allantoin}}

What enzyme does allopurinol and febuxostat inhibit?

{{c1::Xanthine oxidase}}

What is the classic presentation of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?

{{c1::Hyperuricemia::Hyperuricemia/Hypouricemia}}
{{c1::Gout}}
{{c1::Pissed off}}
{{c1::Retardation}}
{{c1::Tense}} muscles

The activity of which two enzymatic pathways is responsible for increased uric acid in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?

{{c1::Uric acid}} production
{{c1::De novo purine}} synthesis
fields.Back Extra:
Uric acid production occurs via xanthine oxidase.

De novo purine synthesis occurs via PRPP amidotransferase.

fields.Text:
Name the two drugs that are used in the treatment of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

{{c1::Allopurinol}} (1st line)
{{c1::Febuxostat}} (2nd line)

How does adenosine deaminase deficiency result in SCID?

Decrease in adenosine deaminase → Increase in {{c1::dATP}} → Decrease in {{c1::ribonucleotide reductase}} activity → Decrease in {{c1::DNA}} precursors in cells → Decrease in lymphocytes

A deficiency of which purine salvage enzyme may result in SCID?

{{c1::Adenosine deaminase}}

Which enzyme catalyzes the formation of AMP from adenine and PRPP?

{{c1::APRT}}

Which enzyme in the purine salvage pathway catalyzes the conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid?

{{c1::Xanthine oxidase}}

Which enzyme catalyzes the conversion of guanine to GMP and hypoxanthine to IMP?

{{c1::HGPRT}}

Which pathway is uric acid the final product of?

{{c1::Purine salvage}} pathway

What is the function of adenosine deaminase?

It catalyzes the conversion of adenosine to {{c1::inosine}}

What is the inheritance pattern of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

What enzyme is deficient in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?

{{c1::HGPRT}}
fields.Back Extra: This leads to a defect in the purine salvage pathway.

fields.Text:
How do wobble-codons code for the same tRNA or amino acid?

Codons that differ in the {{c1::3rd}} ("wobble") position may code for the same tRNA or amino acid
fields.Back Extra: Specific base pairing is usually required only in the first 2 nucleotide positions of a mRNA codon.

fields.Text:
What is the one noteworthy exception to the rule, in humans, which says the genetic code is conserved throughout evolution?

{{c1::mtDNA}}

What does a commaless, nonoverlapping genetic code mean?

The entire genome is read from a {{c1::fixed}} starting point as a {{c1::continuous}} sequence of bases

What is the exception for a commaless, nonoverlapping genetic code?

Some {{c1::viruses}}

How is the genetic code unambiguous and yet redundant?

Although each codon specifies a {{c1::single}} amino acid (unambiguous), an amino acid can be encoded by {{c1::multiple}} codons (redundant)

Name the two amino acids that are encoded by a single codon.

{{c1::Tryptophan}}
{{c1::Methionine}}
fields.Back Extra:
Tryptophan is encoded by UGG.

Methionine is encoded by AUG.

fields.Text:
What DNA sequence does telomerase add to the 3' ends of chromosomes?

{{c1::TTAGGG}}

Name the proteins responsible for preventing parent strands from reannealing during DNA replication.

{{c1::Single-stranded binding}} proteins

Which enzyme unwinds the DNA template at the replication fork?

{{c1::Helicase}}

What is the name of the Y-shaped region where leading and lagging strands are formed?

{{c1::Replication fork}}

DNA polymerases I and III are enzymes only found in what class of organisms?

{{c1::Prokaryotes}}

What are the discontinuous DNA segments formed on the lagging strand called?

{{c1::Okazaki fragments}}

What is the function of telomerase?

Adds {{c1::DNA nucleotides}} to the {{c1::3}}' ends of chromosomes
fields.Back Extra: This is to prevent loss of genetic material with every duplication in eukaryotes.

fields.Text:
What drugs inhibit eukaryotic topoisomerase I?

{{c1::Irinotecan}}
{{c1::Topotecan}}

What drugs inhibit eukaryotic topoisomerase II?

{{c1::Etoposide}}
{{c1::Teniposide}}

Which class of drugs inhibits prokaryotic topoisomerase II (DNA gyrase) and topoisomerase IV?

{{c1::Fluoroquinolones}}

Where does DNA replication begin in the genome?

In {{c1::AT}}-rich sequences
fields.Back Extra: These can be found in promoters and origins of replication.

fields.Text:
When does DNA polymerase III stop adding deoxynucleotides to the lagging strand?

When it reaches the {{c1::primer}} of the preceding fragment

What is the mechanism by which drugs that block DNA replication cause chain termination?

They have a modified {{c1::3}}' {{c1::hydroxyl}} group that prevents the addition of the next DNA nucleotide
fields.Back Extra: This disrupts the growth of the DNA strand.

fields.Text:
To which end of the newly synthesized DNA molecule does DNA polymerase III add the next deoxynucleotide?

The {{c1::3}}' end

Which enzyme degrades the RNA primer and replaces it with DNA during prokaryotic DNA replication?

{{c1::DNA polymerase I}}

What does DNA polymerase III require to initiate replication?

{{c1::RNA primer}}

Which prokaryotic enzyme elongates the leading strand by adding deoxynucleotides to the RNA primer?

{{c1::DNA polymerase III}}

What activity of DNA polymerases allows for proofreading during DNA replication?

{{c1::3}}' → {{c1::5}}' {{c1::exonuclease}} activity

What is the function of DNA topoisomerase?

To add or remove {{c1::supercoils}} by creating breaks in the DNA helix
fields.Back Extra:
Topoisomerase I causes a single-stranded break.

Topoisomerase II causes a double-stranded break.

fields.Text:
What characteristics of DNA replication are shared by both prokaryotes and eukaryotes?

The process is {{c1::semiconservative}}
Occurs in the {{c1::5}}' → {{c1::3}}' direction
Involves {{c1::continuous}} and {{c1::discontinuous}} synthesis

What syndrome results from a deficiency of helicase enzyme?

{{c1::Bloom}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This syndrome has a BLM gene mutation.

fields.Text:
Name the eukaryotic enzyme involved in DNA replication that has reverse transcriptase activity.

{{c1::Telomerase}}
fields.Back Extra: Reverse transcriptase is also known as RNA-dependent DNA polymerase.

fields.Text:
Which enzyme of DNA replication is often upregulated in progenitor cells and tumor cells and downregulated in aging and progeria?

{{c1::Telomerase}}

What enzyme joins the Okazaki fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds between strands during replication?

{{c1::DNA ligase}}

In DNA replication, how many origins of replication do prokaryotes and eukaryotes have?

Prokaryotes → {{c1::Single}}
Eukaryotes → {{c1::Multiple}}

What are the five key enzymes involved in base excision repair?

Base-specific {{c1::glycosylase}}
{{c1::AP-endonuclease}}
{{c1::AP-lyase}}
{{c1::DNA polymerase-β}}
{{c1::DNA ligase}}

In which phase of the cell cycle does base excision repair occur?

It occurs {{c1::throughout}} the cell cycle

How does nucleotide excision repair remove damaged bases such as pyrimidine dimers?

Specific {{c1::endonucleases}} excise {{c1::oligonucleotides}} that contain damaged bases

How does DNA mismatch repair occur?

Mismatched nucleotides are {{c1::removed}} from a newly synthesized strand of DNA
fields.Back Extra: The gap is then filled and resealed.

fields.Text:
Which DNA repair methods address double-stranded breaks?

{{c1::Nonhomologous end joining}}
{{c1::Homologous recombination}}

Which type of DNA repair mechanism addresses spontaneous/toxic deamination?

{{c1::Base excision}} repair

Which DNA repair mechanism is defective in hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, also known as Lynch syndrome?

{{c1::Mismatch}} repair

In which phase of the cell cycle does nucleotide excision repair occur?

{{c1::G1}} phase

What is the role of AP-endonuclease and AP-lyase in base excision repair?

AP-endonuclease removes one or more nucleotides by cleaving the {{c1::5}}' end
AP-lyase removes one or more nucleotides by cleaving the {{c1::3}}' end

What is the first step in base excision repair of damaged DNA?

A base-specific {{c1::glycosylase}} recognizes and removes a single damaged base to create an {{c1::AP site}}

Which type of DNA repair mechanism is defective in a child with dry skin, photosensitivity, and increased risk of skin cancer?

{{c1::Nucleotide excision}} repair
fields.Back Extra:
This prevents excision of pyrimidine dimers caused by ultraviolet exposure.

The child has xeroderma pigmentosum.

fields.Text:
What mechanism is used to repair bulky helix-distorting lesions in DNA?

{{c1::Nucleotide excision}} repair

What are the two key differences between homologous recombination and nonhomologous end joining?

Homologous recombination → Homology {{c1::is::is/is not}} required, but {{c1::no}} DNA is lost
Nonhomologous end joining → Homology {{c1::is not::is/is not}} required, but {{c1::some}} DNA is lost

Which DNA repair method is defective in ataxia-telangiectasia?

{{c1::Nonhomologous end joining}}

Which DNA repair pathway is defective in Fanconi anemia and BRCA1/BRCA2-induced breast/ovarian cancers?

{{c1::Homologous recombination}}

In which phase of the cell cycle does mismatch repair occur?

{{c1::S}} phase

Which enzymes fill and reseal the gap during nucleotide excision repair?

{{c1::DNA polymerase-β}} fills the gap
{{c1::DNA ligase}} seals the gap

What type of mutation would ensue from a change in a codon from UGC to UGA?

{{c1::Nonsense}} mutation
fields.Back Extra: UGA, UAA, and UAG are all stop codons.

fields.Text:
What is a transversion mutation?

A change from {{c1::purine}} to {{c1::pyrimidine}} or vice versa

When adenine is replaced by guanine or cytosine is replaced by thymidine, what type of point mutation has occurred?

{{c1::Transition}} mutation
fields.Back Extra: In this mutation, a purine is converted to a different purine or a pyrimidine is converted to a different pyrimidine.

fields.Text:
What type of mutation can result in a shorter or longer protein with altered function?

{{c1::Frameshift}} mutation

Which DNA mutation results from an insertion or a deletion of nucleotides that is not divisible by three?

{{c1::Frameshift}} mutation
fields.Back Extra: All nucleotides downstream from this mutation are misread.

fields.Text:
Silent mutations typically result from a base change in which position of the codon?

{{c1::3rd}} position of the codon
fields.Back Extra: This is due to tRNA wobbling.

fields.Text:
Which type of DNA mutation results in no change in the amino acid sequence?

{{c1::Silent}} mutation

Which type of mutation results in a retained intron in the mRNA that leads to the formation of a protein with impaired or altered function?

{{c1::Splice site}} mutation

Rank the following types of mutations from most to least severe:

Missense mutation
Frameshift mutation
Silent mutation
Nonsense mutation

{{c1::Frameshift}} mutation > {{c1::Nonsense}} mutation > {{c1::Missense}} mutation > {{c1::Silent}} mutation

What type of mutation causes sickle cell disease, where glutamate is replaced with valine?

{{c1::Missense}} mutation
fields.Back Extra: This is a type of single nucleotide substitution.

fields.Text:
Name the three types of single nucleotide substitution mutations.

{{c1::Silent}} mutation
{{c1::Missense}} mutation
{{c1::Nonsense}} mutation

What type of DNA mutation is seen with Duchenne muscular dystrophy and Tay-Sachs disease?

{{c1::Frameshift}} mutation

What type of mutation is implicated in diseases such as dementia, epilepsy, Gaucher disease, Marfan syndrome, and some types of β-thalassemia?

{{c1::Splice site}} mutation

In the absence of glucose, what protein is activated that acts as an inducer of the lac operon?

{{c1::Catabolite activator}} protein

In a high-lactose environment, what mechanism results in increased transcription of the lac operon gene?

The repressor protein unbinds from the {{c1::operator}} site and binds to {{c1::lactose}} to form an inactivated repressor

What is the mechanism for having high levels of lac operon genes in a low-glucose environment?

Increased activity of {{c1::adenylate cyclase}} → Greater production of {{c1::cAMP}} from ATP → Activation of {{c1::catabolite activator}} protein
fields.Back Extra: This results in increased levels of transcription.

fields.Text:
Describe the state of glucose and lactose in Escherichia coli if both the catabolite activator protein site and the operator site are unbound by their respective proteins.

{{c1::High::High/Low}} levels of glucose via unbinding of the catabolite activator protein
{{c1::High::High/Low}} levels of lactose via unbinding of the repressor protein

What prevents the lac operon genes from being expressed in the absence of lactose, regardless of the level of glucose?

The {{c1::repressor}} protein binding to the operator site

What happens to the expression of the lac operon genes when bacteria are exposed to a low-glucose, but high-lactose environment?

The lac operon genes are {{c1::strongly}} expressed

What is the genetic response of Escherichia coli in the absence of glucose and the presence of lactose?

The {{c1::lac operon}} is activated, and a switch to {{c1::lactose}} metabolism occurs

Are the lac genes expressed when lactose is unavailable, regardless of whether the glucose level is high or low?

The lac operon genes {{c1::are not::are/are not}} expressed in either of these conditions
fields.Back Extra: Both conditions result in binding of the repressor protein to the operator site, which prevents gene expression.

fields.Text:
What is the region following the stop codon called, where the polyadenylation signal is found?

{{c1::3}}' {{c1::untranslated region}}

What is the stretch of DNA/RNA between the transcription start site and the start codon called?

{{c1::5}}' {{c1::untranslated region}}

During transcription, in what direction is mRNA synthesized?

{{c1::5}}' to {{c1::3}}'

In eukaryotic genes, what does the open reading frame consist of?

{{c1::Introns}}
{{c1::Exons}}

In which region are sequences such as the TATA box and CAAT box found in a eukaryotic gene?

{{c1::Promoter}} region

Where might enhancers and silencers be located relative to the gene being regulated?

{{c1::Far from}} the gene itself
{{c1::Close to}} the gene itself
{{c1::Within}} the gene itself

Name the DNA loci to which activator proteins bind to increase gene expression.

{{c1::Enhancers}}

What is the result of mutations in the promoter region?

A marked {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} in the level of gene transcription

What are the DNA sequences that negative regulators ("repressors") bind to in order to decrease gene expression called?

{{c1::Silencers}}

Is the promoter region upstream or downstream of its gene locus?

{{c1::Upstream}}

What characteristic elements make up a gene's promoter region?

An {{c1::AT}}-rich sequence with {{c1::TATA}} and {{c1::CAAT}} boxes
fields.Back Extra: These boxes differ between eukaryotes and prokaryotes.

fields.Text:
Name the DNA region that RNA polymerase II and transcription factors bind to in order to initiate transcription.

{{c1::Promoter}} region

What nucleotide sequence is added to the 5' end of hnRNA as part of the capping process?

{{c1::7-methylguanosine}}

What function does the sequence AAUAAA serve in eukaryotes?

{{c1::Polyadenylation}} signal

What is the role of cytoplasmic processing bodies in RNA processing?

{{c1::Quality control}}
fields.Back Extra: mRNAs can be degraded or stored with the help of exonucleases, decapping enzymes, and miRNAs for future translations.

fields.Text:
What is the term for the initial (unprocessed) RNA transcript in eukaryotes?

{{c1::hnRNA}}

What are the three modifications involved in eukaryotic processing?

{{c1::Capping}} of the 5' end
{{c1::Polyadenylation}} of the 3' end
{{c1::Splicing out}} of introns

Where in the eukaryotic cell does RNA processing and translation take place?

RNA processing occurs in the {{c1::nucleus}}
RNA translation occurs in the {{c1::cytoplasm}}

Which class of drugs inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase in prokaryotes?

{{c1::Rifamycins}}

Where does RNA polymerase II open DNA?

{{c1::Promoter}} site

In prokaryotes, which enzyme makes rRNA, mRNA, and tRNA?

{{c1::RNA polymerase}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a single multisubunit complex.

fields.Text:
Which RNA types are the largest, the most abundant, and the smallest, respectively?

Largest = {{c1::mRNA}}
Most abundant = {{c1::rRNA}}
Smallest = {{c1::tRNA}}

In eukaryotes, which polymerases make tRNA, mRNA, and rRNA, respectively?

tRNA = RNA polymerase {{c1::III}}
mRNA = RNA polymerase {{c1::II}}
rRNA = RNA polymerase {{c1::I}}

Inhibition of which enzyme by α-amanitin, found in certain mushroom species, leads to cytotoxicity, dysentery, and hepatic failure?

{{c1::RNA polymerase II}}

What function do RNA polymerases in eukaryotes lack?

{{c1::Proofreading}}

Which RNA polymerase is only present in the nucleolus?

RNA polymerase {{c1::I}}

What is the mechanism of action of dactinomycin?

Inhibition of {{c1::RNA polymerase}} in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes

Which RNA types are synthesized by RNA polymerase II?

{{c1::miRNA}}
{{c1::snRNA}}
{{c1::mRNA}}

What is the final step in the removal of an intron?

{{c1::Clevage}} at the {{c1::3}}' splice site
fields.Back Extra: This allows for the release of the lariat (containing the intron) from the pre-mRNA.

fields.Text:
What occurs after the formation of the spliceosome before the removal of an intron?

{{c1::snRNPs}} cleave at the {{c1::5}}' splice site

What is formed when pre-mRNA binds to a snRNP particle with other proteins?

{{c1::Spliceosome}}

What is the pathophysiology of spinal muscular atrophy?

Defect in {{c1::snRNP}} assembly secondary to decreased {{c1::survival motor neuron}} protein → Congenital degradation of the {{c1::anterior horns}} of the spinal cord

What diseases are commonly associated with anti-U1 snRNP antibodies?

{{c1::SLE}}
{{c1::Mixed connective tissue}} disease
Other {{c1::rheumatic}} diseases

What cellular process allows for a single gene transcript to result in the production of multiple different proteins?

{{c1::Alternative splicing}}

What is the name of the intervening segments of DNA within a gene that does not code for protein, but have a role in regulating gene expression?

{{c1::Introns}}

What parts of the gene contain the actual genetic information for coding proteins or functional RNA?

{{c1::Exons}}

Provide examples that exhibit alternative splicing.

Brain → {{c1::Dopamine}} receptors
Muscle → {{c1::Tropomyosin}} variants
Blood → {{c1::Transmembrane immunoglobulin}} versus {{c1::secreted immunoglobulin}}
Tumor cells → {{c1::Host defense evasion}}

In the tRNA molecule shown in the image, identify the pink (left), blue (right), and green (bottom) segments.



Pink = {{c1::T-arm}}
Blue = {{c1::D-arm}}
Green = {{c1::Anticodon loop}}

What is the function of the D-arm?

Ensures {{c1::identification}} of tRNA by the correct {{c1::aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase}}, as it contains {{c1::dihydrouridine}} residues

What is the function of the T-arm in the tRNA molecule?

It is necessary for {{c1::tRNA}}-{{c1::ribosome}} binding

What is the function of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase?

Catalyzes {{c1::aminoacylation}} of the tRNA with a high level of {{c1::accuracy}}
fields.Back Extra: It attaches tRNA to its appropriate amino acid.

fields.Text:
What are the three substrates required for the reaction catalyzed by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase?

{{c1::Uncharged::Charged/Uncharged}} tRNA
Appropriate {{c1::amino acid}}
{{c1::ATP}}

What does the anticodon from 5' to 3' read if the codon in mRNA reads 5'-AUG-3'?

5'-{{c1::CAU}}-3'

Does charging a tRNA molecule with an amino acid require energy?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Specifically, the conversion of ATP to AMP occurs.

fields.Text:
Where on a tRNA does the amino acid that will be incorporated into the protein bind?

At the {{c1::3}}' end, which has the sequence {{c1::CCA}}

What base sequence is present at the 3' end of both eukaryotic and prokaryotic tRNAs?

{{c1::CCA}}

What is the role of IF2 in tRNA charging?

It is responsible for facilitating {{c1::codon}}-{{c1::anticodon}} pairing

What happens if a tRNA is mischarged?

The tRNA reads the usual codon, but inserts the wrong {{c1::amino acid}}

What two factors determine whether an amino acid is accurately selected by the tRNA?

{{c1::Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase}}
Binding of {{c1::charged::charged/uncharged}} tRNA to the codon

How many charging enzymes are there per amino acid?

{{c1::1}} unique enzyme (aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase) per respective amino acid

What unique nucleotide sequence is found in the T-arm of a tRNA?

{{c1::TΨC}}
fields.Back Extra:
T symbolizes ribothymidine.

Ψ symbolizes pseudouridine.

C symbolizes cytidine.

fields.Text:
If AUG is the start codon in eukaryotes, is methionine always the first amino acid of the protein after translation?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because methionine may be removed before translation is completed.

fields.Text:
What are the three stop codons?

{{c1::UGA}}
{{c1::UAA}}
{{c1::UAG}}

Which prokaryotic amino acid stimulates neutrophil chemotaxis?

{{c1::N-formylmethionine}}

Name the common mRNA start codon.

{{c1::AUG}}

Which amino acids does AUG code for in prokaryotes and eukaryotes?

{{c1::N-formylmethionine}} in prokaryotes
{{c1::Methionine}} in eukaryotes

During protein synthesis, what is targeted by bacterial toxins from Diphtheria and Pseudomonas?

{{c1::Elongation}} factors

What is the function of eukaryotic release factors?

They recognize the {{c1::stop codon}} and release the translated protein from the ribosome

In protein synthesis, what are the three steps of protein elongation?

1.) {{c1::Aminoacyl-tRNA}} binds to the A site
2.) Transfer of growing {{c1::peptide chain}} to the amino acid at the A site
3.) Moving {{c1::peptidyl-tRNA}} to the P site

What is the order of the positions within the ribosome that the tRNA occupies during translation?

{{c1::A}} site
{{c1::P}} site
{{c1::E}} site

When the ribosome shifts after the formation of a peptidyl bond, where is the uncharged tRNA found?

{{c1::E}} site

Which molecule provides the energy for the charging of tRNA?

{{c1::ATP}}

What catalyzes the formation of the peptide bond during protein synthesis in the ribosome?

{{c1::rRNA}}

What serves as the energy source for both the assembly of the ribosomal 60S subunit with mRNA and the translocation of ribosome along mRNA?

{{c1::GTP}}

In which direction, relative to mRNA, does the ribosome shift after the formation of a peptidyl bond?

{{c1::3::Number}} nucleotides toward the {{c1::3}}' end of the mRNA

Name the protein molecules responsible for assembling the 40S subunit with the initiator tRNA.

{{c1::Eukaryotic::Prokaryotic/Eukaryotic}} {{c1::initiation}} factors

In what direction does protein synthesis occur?

{{c1::N}}-terminus to {{c1::C}}-terminus

What is the purpose of the P site of the ribosome?

Accommodates the growing {{c1::peptide chain}}

What is unique about the binding site for the initiator methionine tRNA?

It binds to the {{c1::P}} site
fields.Back Extra: All other aminoacyl-tRNAs bind to the A site.

fields.Text:
What are the two subunits of the eukaryotic ribosome?

{{c1::40S}} subunit
{{c1::60S}} subunit

Which organisms have ribosomes with 30S and 50S subunits?

{{c1::Prokaryotes}}

What part of the mRNA do eukaryotic initiation factors recognize?

The {{c1::5}}' {{c1::cap}}

What is the role of eukaryotic initiation factors during protein synthesis?

They assist in assembling the {{c1::40S}} subunit with the {{c1::initiator tRNA}} and are released when the {{c1::60S}} subunit and the {{c1::mRNA}} are assembled with the complex

During protein synthesis, does the process of termination require energy?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}

What is the function of the Shine-Dalgarno sequence in prokaryotic protein synthesis?

It serves as a ribosomal {{c1::binding site}} in prokaryotic mRNA
fields.Back Extra: It aligns the ribosome with the start codon so that the codon is read correctly.

fields.Text:
Name six examples of posttranslational covalent alterations.

{{c1::Acetylation}}
{{c1::Glycosylation}}
{{c1::Hydroxylation}}
{{c1::Methylation}}
{{c1::Phosphorylation}}
{{c1::Ubiquitination}}

The conversion of trypsinogen to trypsin is an example of what type of posttranslational modification?

{{c1::Trimming}}
fields.Back Extra: In trimming, the N-terminal and C-terminal propeptides are removed to form mature protein.

fields.Text:
What intracellular proteins are responsible for facilitating and maintaining protein folding?

{{c1::Chaperone}} proteins

Name the special class of chaperone proteins that prevents protein denaturation at high temperatures in yeast.

{{c1::Heat shock}} proteins
fields.Back Extra: This prevents denaturing/misfolding with high temperatures, acidic pH, and hypoxia.

fields.Text:
In the diagram of the cell cycle shown in the image, impairment at which point is responsible for the pathophysiology of Li-Fraumeni syndrome and cervical cancer?



The {{c1::G1}}-{{c1::S}} checkpoint

What are cyclins?

{{c1::Regulatory}} proteins that activate {{c1::CDKs}} at appropriate times in the cell cycle when stimulated by {{c1::growth}} factors

List the five phases of mitosis, in order.

{{c1::Prophase}}
{{c1::Prometaphase}}
{{c1::Metaphase}}
{{c1::Anaphase}}
{{c1::Telophase}}

List the three components of interphase.

{{c1::G1}} phase
{{c1::S}} phase
{{c1::G2}} phase

Which type of cells divide rapidly with a short G1 phase, never enter G0 phase, and are most affected by chemotherapy?

{{c1::Labile}} cells
fields.Back Extra: This can include hair follicles, skin, bone marrow, gut epithelium, and germ cells.

fields.Text:
What cell type, as classified by cell cycle regulation, can enter the G1 phase of the cell cycle from the G0 phase when stimulated?

{{c1::Stable}} cells
fields.Back Extra: Examples include hepatocytes, periosteal cells, proximal convuluted tubule cells, and lymphocytes.

fields.Text:
Permanent cells such as neurons, red blood cells, skeletal myocytes, and cardiac myocytes are arrested in which phase of the cell cycle?

{{c1::G0}} phase

Which phase of the cell cycle has a variable duration?

{{c1::G1}} phase

Which phase of the cell cycle is usually the shortest?

{{c1::M}} phase

During which phase of the cell cycle can a cell enter the G0 phase?

{{c1::G1}} phase
fields.Back Extra: This is a subset of interphase.

fields.Text:
When does DNA synthesis occur in the cell cycle?

{{c1::S}} phase
fields.Back Extra: This is after the G1 phase and before the G2 phase in the cell cycle.

fields.Text:
What two processes occur during the M phase?

{{c1::Mitosis}}
{{c1::Cytokinesis}}
fields.Back Extra:
Mitosis is the splitting of the nucleus.

Cytokinesis is the splitting of the cytoplasm.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism by which the p53 protein inhibits the progression of the cell cycle from the G1 phase to the S phase?

Damaged DNA → p53 induces {{c1::p21}} → Inhibits {{c1::CDK}} → Hypophosphorylates (activates) {{c1::retinoblastoma}} protein → Inhibits progression from G1 phase to S phase

How do growth factors promote the transition of a cell from the G1 phase to the S phase?

By binding to {{c1::tyrosine kinase}} receptors

Where are cytosolic, peroxisomal, and mitochondrial proteins synthesized?

{{c1::Free ribosomes}}

What is the histologic term for the rough endoplasmic reticulum in neurons?

{{c1::Nissl bodies}}

Name two cell types that would be rich in the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

{{c1::Goblet}} cells
{{c1::Plasma}} cells
fields.Back Extra:
Goblet cells secrete mucus.

Plasma cells secrete antibodies.

fields.Text:
Which organelle synthesizes secretory proteins and adds N-linked oligosaccharides to proteins?

{{c1::Rough endoplasmic reticulum}}

Where are proteins within Golgi bodies, lysosomes, and the endoplasmic reticulum synthesized?

{{c1::Rough endoplasmic reticulum}}

What two cell types are rich in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum?

{{c1::Steroid hormone-producing}} cells
{{c1::Hepatocytes}}
fields.Back Extra: The steroid hormone-producing cells are located in the adrenal cortex and gonads.

fields.Text:
Which organelle is resposible for steroid synthesis and detoxification of poisons and drugs?

{{c1::Smooth endoplasmic reticulum}}

Which organelle found in the rough endoplasmic reticulum is missing from the smooth endoplasmic reticulum?

{{c1::Surface ribosomes}}

Name the enzyme involved in both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis that is found in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum.

{{c1::Glucose-6-phosphatase}}

What is the result of having a dysfunctional signal recognition particle in the cell?

Accumulation of {{c1::protein}} in the cytosol

Endosomes act as sorting centers for molecules that are destined for what two purposes?

Sending it to lysosomes for {{c1::degradation}}
Sending it back to the plasma membrane or Golgi apparatus for {{c1::further}} use

What is the role of COPII in vesicular trafficking?

{{c1::Anterograde}} transport from the endoplasmic reticulum to the {{c1::cis}}-Golgi apparatus

Which vesicular protein is involved in the trafficking of molecules taken into the cell via receptor-mediated endocytosis?

{{c1::Clathrin}}

In the Golgi apparatus, the addition of what carbohydrate to proteins makes them a target for lysosomes?

{{c1::Mannose-6-phosphate}}

What is the role of COPI in vesicular trafficking?

{{c1::Retrograde}} transport from the Golgi apparatus to the Golgi apparatus or from the {{c1::cis}}-Golgi apparatus to the endoplasmic reticulum

What is the prognosis for a child with symptoms similar to but more severe than those of Hurler syndrome, who has elevated plasma lysosomal enzymes?

The condition is usually {{c1::fatal}} in childhood

A boy has coarse facial features, gingival hyperplasia, corneal clouding, claw hand, kyphoscoliosis, and high levels of lysosomal enzymes. What is the inheritance pattern?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What enzyme is defective in inclusion-cell disease?

{{c1::N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase}}

What are the three posttranslational modifications that occur in the Golgi apparatus?

Modification of {{c1::N-oligosaccharides}} on asparagine
Addition of {{c1::O-oligosaccharides}} on serine and threonine
Addition of {{c1::mannose-6-phosphate}} to proteins

Clathrin functions to transport vesicles from the trans-Golgi apparatus to which organelle?

{{c1::Lysosome}}

List three locations to which the Golgi apparatus sends proteins and lipids.

{{c1::Plasma membrane}}
{{c1::Lysosomes}}
{{c1::Secretory vesicles}}

The Golgi apparatus acts as a distribution center for what macromolecules?

{{c1::Proteins}}
{{c1::Lipids}}
fields.Back Extra: This is specifically from the endoplasmic reticulum to the vesicles and plasma membrane.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiology of inclusion-cell disease?

Inability of Golgi apparatus to phosphorylate {{c1::mannose}} on glycoproteins → Extracellular secretion of {{c1::lysosomal}} enzymes → Lack of {{c1::digestive}} enzymes → Inclusion bodies

What is the function of a signal recognition particle?

Traffics a {{c1::polypeptide}}-{{c1::ribosome}} complex from the cytosol to the rough endoplasmic reticulum

What disease is also referred to as mucolipidosis type II?

{{c1::Inclusion-cell}} disease
fields.Back Extra: This is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder.

fields.Text:
Which metabolic process is affected in a patient with ataxia, scaly skin, long-standing night blindness, and shortened 4th toes?

{{c1::α-oxidation}} of {{c1::branched-chain fatty acids}} in {{c1::peroxisomes}} is impaired → Buildup of phytanic acid

What are three important clinical manifestations of Zellweger syndrome?

{{c1::Hepatomegaly}}
{{c1::Hypotonia::Hypertonia/Hypotonia}}
{{c1::Seizures}}

What is synthesized in peroxisomes?

{{c1::Bile acids}}
{{c1::Plasmalogens}}

What organelle is responsible for the catabolism of ethanol and amino acids?

{{c1::Peroxisome}}

Which organelle is responsible for the breakdown of very-long-chain fatty acids via β-oxidation?

{{c1::Peroxisome}}

What two metabolic processes occur strictly in peroxisomes?

{{c1::α-oxidation}} of {{c2::branched-chain fatty acids}}
{{c1::β-oxidation}} of {{c2::very-long-chain fatty acids}}

What is the mode of inheritance of Refsum disease?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of Zellweger syndrome?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What are the treatment options for Refsum disease?

{{c1::Dietary}} modification
{{c1::Plasmapheresis}}

What are plasmalogens?

Important membrane phospholipids necessary for the {{c1::white matter}} of the central nervous system

A mutation in which gene is implicated in Zellweger syndrome?

{{c1::PEX}} gene

What organs are primarily affected by the accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids in adrenoleukodystrophy?

{{c1::Testes}}
{{c1::Adrenal}} glands
{{c1::White matter}} of the brain

What X-linked inherited disease is caused by a mutation resulting in defective β-oxidation in peroxisomes?

{{c1::Adrenoleukodystrophy}}

What are the long-term consequences of adrenoleukodystrophy?

{{c1::Adrenal}} gland crisis
Progressive loss of {{c1::neurologic}} function
{{c1::Death}}

A mutation in which gene is associated with adrenoleukodystrophy?

{{c1::ABCD1}} gene

Refsum disease results from overaccumulation of which fatty acid?

{{c1::Phytanic acid}}
fields.Back Extra: This cannot be metabolized to pristanic acid.

fields.Text:
Defects in the ubiquitin-proteasome system have been linked to which neurologic disease?

{{c1::Parkinson}} disease

Which barrel-shaped protein complex degrades damaged or ubiquitin-tagged proteins?

{{c1::Proteasome}}

Name two cytoskeletal elements that are described as microfilaments.

{{c1::Actin}}
{{c1::Microvilli}}

What is the major function of intermediate filaments?

Maintain cell {{c1::structure}}

Cilia, flagella, mitotic spindles, and centrioles are examples of which type of cytoskeletal element?

{{c1::Microtubules}}

What are the three major types of cytoskeletal elements?

{{c1::Microfilaments}}
{{c1::Intermediate filaments}}
{{c1::Microtubules}}

What type of cytoskeleton filament is involved in muscle contraction and cytokinesis?

{{c1::Microfilaments}}
fields.Back Extra: An example of this is actin.

fields.Text:
Cytokeratin, desmin, GFAP, lamins, neurofilaments, and vimentin are examples of what type of cytoskeletal element?

{{c1::Intermediate filaments}}

Which type of cytoskeletal element functions to move a cell and assists in cell division?

{{c1::Microtubules}}

HSV, poliovirus, and rabies virus use which molecular motor protein for retrograde transport to reach the cell body?

{{c1::Dynein}}

How many GTP molecules are bound to each microtubule heterodimer?

{{c1::2}}

What are microtubules composed of?

Polymerized heterodimers of {{c1::α-tubulin}} and {{c1::β-tubulin}} proteins

What motor protein is responsible for anterograde transport of cargo on microtubules?

{{c1::Kinesin}}

Name the antifungal agent that targets microtubules.

{{c1::Griseofulvin}}

Vinca alkaloids, which are used as anticancer drugs, act on what cytoskeletal element?

{{c1::Microtubules}}

Name the antigout drug that targets microtubules.

{{c1::Colchicine}}

Name the antihelminthic drug that targets the structure shown below.



{{c1::Mebendazole}}
fields.Back Extra: The structure shown is a microtubule.

fields.Text:
Which cytoskeletal elements are involved in slow axoplasmic transport in neurons?

{{c1::Microtubules}}

Clostridium tetani uses dynein to move in which direction on a microtubule?

From the {{c1::positive}} end to the {{c1::negative}} end
fields.Back Extra: This is known as retrograde transport.

fields.Text:
Which cellular structure is shown?



{{c1::Cilia}}
fields.Back Extra: These consist of microtubules arranged in 9 doublets around 2 central singlets.

fields.Text:
Which cellular structure is shown in the image below?



{{c1::Basal body}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is located at the base of the cilium, below the cell membrane.

This consists of 9 microtubule triplets without any central microtubules.

fields.Text:
What screening test can be used to identify patients with primary ciliary dyskinesia?

{{c1::Nasal nitric oxide}}
fields.Back Extra: This would be decreased in primary ciliary dyskinesia.

fields.Text:
Why would a patient with the finding in the chest X-ray shown be at an increased risk for hearing loss?



{{c1::Cilia}} of the {{c1::eustachian tube}} is dysfunctional
fields.Back Extra:
The X-ray shows situs inversus due to impaired migration and orientation.

This is primary ciliary dyskinesia.

fields.Text:
Why are patients with primary ciliary dyskinesia likely to be infertile or develop recurrent ectopic pregnancy?

Dysfunctional cilia of the {{c1::fallopian tube}} in females
Immotile {{c1::spermatozoa}} in males

What ATPase protein links the peripheral nine doublets and allows for bending of the cilia by differential sliding of the doublets?

{{c1::Axonemal dynein}}

What leads to dysfunctional cilia in patients with primary ciliary dyskinesia?

Defect in the {{c1::dynein arm}} → Immotile cilia

What cell junctions allow for coordinated movement of cilia?

{{c1::Gap}} junctions

Why do patients with primary ciliary dyskinesia develop recurrent infections of the respiratory tract?

Impaired {{c1::mucociliary clearance}} of debris and pathogens → Sinusitis, ear infections, and bronchiectasis

What is the mode of inheritance of primary ciliary dyskinesia?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

For each ATP consumed, Na+/K+-ATPase transports how many Na+ and K+ molecules, and in what direction?

{{c1::3}} Na+ molecules {{c1::out::in/out}}
{{c1::2}} K+ molecules {{c1::in::in/out}}

The ATP binding site of Na+/K+-ATPase is located on which side of the plasma membrane?

{{c1::Cytosolic}} side

What is the mechanism of action of cardiac glycosides?

{{c1::Na+/K+-ATPase}} blockade → Decreased activity of {{c1::Na+/Ca2+}} antiporter → Increased [{{c1::Ca2+}}] intracellularly → Increase in cardiac contractility

What covalent change occurs in Na+/K+-ATPase when K+ is transported into the cell?

The pump is {{c1::dephosphorylated}}

What type of collagen is defective in Alport syndrome?

Type {{c1::IV}} collagen

Which collagen type production is impaired in osteogenesis imperfecta?

Type {{c1::I}} collagen

In what structures can the most abundant type of collagen be found?

{{c1::Bone}}
{{c1::Skin}}
{{c1::Tendon}}
{{c1::Fascia}}
{{c1::Cornea}}
{{c1::Dentin}}
Areas undergoing {{c1::late::early/late}} wound repair

What five structures are composed of reticulin fibers?

{{c1::Blood vessels}}
{{c1::Skin}}
{{c1::Uterus}}
{{c1::Fetal}} tissue
Areas undergoing {{c1::early::early/late}} wound repair

What structures are composed of type II collagen?

{{c1::Cartilage}}
{{c1::Nucleus pulposus}}
{{c1::Vitreous body}}

In what structures can type IV collagen be found?

{{c1::Basement membrane}}
{{c1::Lens}}

What is the basic role of collagen in the body?

{{c1::Strength}} and {{c1::organization}} to the extracellular matrix

Name the most abundant protein in the body, which undergoes extensive posttranslational modification.

{{c1::Collagen}}

Which type of collagen is deficient in the vascular type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome?

Type {{c1::III}} collagen

What type of collagen is targeted by autoantibodies in Goodpasture syndrome?

Type {{c1::IV}} collagen
fields.Back Extra: This makes up the basement membrane.

fields.Text:
Which type of collagen makes up reticulin?

Type {{c1::III}} collagen

What cells are responsible for secretion of type IV collagen and wound contraction?

{{c1::Myofibroblasts}}

Osteogenesis imperfecta results from a defect in what step of collagen formation?

Formation of the collagen {{c1::triple helix}}

What disease results from a defect in the process shown in the image below?



{{c1::Menkes}} disease
fields.Back Extra: In this disease, there would be a defect in cross-linking.

fields.Text:
One-third of collagen is composed of which amino acid?

{{c1::Glycine}}
fields.Back Extra: Its content is less variable than that of proline and lysine.

fields.Text:
Which enzyme catalyzes the covalent cross-linking of lysine and hydroxylysine residues to make collagen fibrils?

{{c1::Lysyl oxidase}}

Cleavage of the terminal disulfide-rich regions from procollagen results in the formation of what collagen derivative?

{{c1::Tropocollagen}}

What cofactor is required for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in collagen?

Vitamin {{c1::C}}

In which cellular space is tropocollagen formed?

{{c1::Extracellular space}}

Where does collagen synthesis mainly occur inside the cell?

{{c1::Rough endoplasmic reticulum}}

Individual collagen α chains are also referred to as what?

{{c1::Preprocollagen}}

What is the structure of procollagen?

{{c1::Triple helix}} of {{c1::3::number}} collagen {{c1::α chains}} with {{c1::hydrogen}}/{{c1::disulfide}} bonds

Which amino acid residue is glycosylated in collagen synthesis?

{{c1::Hydroxylysine}}

What two amino acids undergo hydroxylation in collagen synthesis?

{{c1::Proline}}
{{c1::Lysine}}

Which collagen precursor is exocytosed from the cell into the extracellular space during collagen production?

{{c1::Procollagen}}

What step in collagen synthesis is impaired in patients with scurvy?

{{c1::Hydroxylation}}

What changes in the cross-linking of collagen occur with aging?

Cross-linking of collagen {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} with age

What is the pathophysiology of a disease in a child with poor dentition, blue sclerae, and fractures and bone deformities after minimal trauma as shown in the image?



Decreased production of type {{c1::I}} collagen

What is the cause of conductive hearing loss in a child with recurrent fractures and blue sclerae as shown in the image below?



Abnormal {{c1::ossicles}}

What is the pathophysiology behind opalescent teeth in patients with osteogenesis imperfecta?

Lack of {{c1::dentin}} → Teeth that become worn out easily

How is the most common form of osteogenesis imperfecta inherited?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}
fields.Back Extra: The most common form consists of a decrease in production of otherwise normal type I collagen.

fields.Text:
What medication can help reduce the incidence of fractures in patients with osteogenesis imperfecta?

{{c1::Bisphosphonates}}

What are the manifestations of osteogenesis imperfecta?

Multiple {{c1::fractures}}
{{c1::Blue::Color}} sclerae
{{c1::Dental}} imperfections
{{c1::Hearing}} loss

What are the most common genetic mutations involved in osteogenesis imperfecta?

{{c1::COL1A1}}
{{c1::COL1A2}}

What causes blue sclerae in osteogenesis imperfecta?

{{c1::Translucent}} connective tissue overlying {{c1::choroidal}} veins

Which type of collagen is affected in the vascular type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome?

Type {{c1::III}} collagen
fields.Back Extra: This results in fragile vessels and organs.

fields.Text:
What is the most common type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome?

{{c1::Hypermobility}} type
fields.Back Extra: Joint instability is the most common finding.

fields.Text:
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is transmitted through what inheritance patterns?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}
{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}
fields.Back Extra: The mode of inheritance and severity can vary.

fields.Text:
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is due to a defect in what process?

{{c1::Collagen}} synthesis

What types of aneurysms are commonly associated with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome?

{{c1::Berry}} aneurysms
{{c1::Aortic}} aneurysms

What type of specific collagen is affected in a patient with easy bruising and findings as shown in the image below?



Type {{c1::V}} collagen
fields.Back Extra:
This is the classical type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

This is due to mutations caused by COL5A1 and COL5A2.

fields.Text:
Which type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome has fragile vessels, muscles, and organs prone to rupture?

{{c1::Vascular}} type
fields.Back Extra: There is a mutation in type III collagen caused by COL3A1.

fields.Text:
The activity of what enzyme is decreased in Menkes disease?

{{c1::Lysyl oxidase}}

What connective tissue disease is the result of a mutation in the ATP7A gene?

{{c1::Menkes}} disease

What is the diagnosis for a child who has brittle, "kinky" hair, hypotonia, delays in growth and development, and an increased risk for cerebral aneurysms?

{{c1::Menkes}} disease

Impaired copper metabolism in Menkes disease ultimately results in a defective production of what protein?

{{c1::Collagen}}

How do serum copper levels differ in Menkes disease when compared with Wilson disease?

Copper levels are {{c1::low::high/low}} in Menkes disease
Copper levels are {{c1::high::high/low}} in Wilson disease

What is the most common enzyme deficiency that leads to homocystinuria?

{{c1::Cystathionine synthase}} deficiency

Elastin is rich in which three amino acids?

{{c1::Proline}}
{{c1::Glycine}}
{{c1::Lysine}}
fields.Back Extra: Unlike in collagen, these are nonhydroxylated residues.

fields.Text:
What is the function of fibrillin-1?

It is a glycoprotein that forms a sheath around {{c1::elastin}} and sequesters {{c1::TGF-β}}

What enzyme is inhibited by α1-antitrypsin?

{{c1::Elastase}}

In which cellular compartment does cross-linking of elastin by lysyl oxidase occur?

{{c1::Extracellular space}}

Name two aortic/vascular pathologies associated with Marfan syndrome.

Aortic root {{c1::aneurysm rupture}} or {{c1::dissection}}
{{c1::Cystic medial necrosis}} of the aorta

What is arachnodactyly?

{{c1::Long::Long/Short}}, {{c1::tapering}} fingers and toes
fields.Back Extra: This is seen in patients with Marfan syndrome or homocystinuria.

fields.Text:
What valvular abnormality is most commonly associated with Marfan syndrome?

{{c1::Mitral valve prolapse}}

How is lens dislocation in Marfan syndrome different from that in homocystinuria?

Lens dislocate {{c1::upward::upward/downward}} and {{c1::temporal}} in Marfan syndrome
Lens dislocate {{c1::downward::upward/downward}} and {{c1::nasal}} in homocystinuria

How does Marfan syndrome affect the intellect of a patient?

Intellect is {{c1::normal}}

What lung disease can be caused by a deficiency of α1-antitrypsin?

{{c1::Chronic obstructive pulmonary}} disease
fields.Back Extra: This results in unopposed elastase activity.

fields.Text:
A mutation in what gene is responsible for a tall child presenting with arachnodactyly, hypermobile joints, and the deformity in the image?



A mutation in {{c1::FBN1}} on chromosome {{c1::15}}
fields.Back Extra:
The diagnosis is Marfan syndrome.

The deformity shown is pectus excavatum.

fields.Text:
What is the inheritance pattern of Marfan syndrome?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What protein is abundantly found in the vocal cords, epiglottis, lungs, large arteries, elastic ligaments, skin, and ligamenta flava?

{{c1::Elastin}}

What is the most common cause of sudden death in a patient with Marfan syndrome?

Aortic root {{c1::dissection}}
Aortic root {{c1::aneurysm rupture}}

Which disease presents with an increased arm to height ratio, pectus deformity, skin hyperelasticity, arachnodactyly, and scoliosis similar to Marfan syndrome?

{{c1::Homocystinuria}}

State, in order, the three steps of the polymerase chain reaction.

{{c1::Denaturation}}
{{c1::Annealing}}
{{c1::Elongation}}

In the polymerase chain reaction, what added enzyme is responsible for the process shown in the image?



Heat-{{c1::stable::stable/labile}} {{c1::DNA polymerase}}

During the annealing step of the polymerase chain reaction, what is used to recognize and bind to the DNA fragment of interest?

{{c1::DNA primers}}

How is DNA separated into two strands during a polymerase chain reaction?

DNA is heated to about {{c1::95}}°C with the addition of the DNA template strand, a heat-stable DNA polymerase, DNA primers, and dNTPs

What is the purpose of the polymerase chain reaction?

To {{c1::amplify}} the number of copies of a specific {{c1::DNA fragment}}
fields.Back Extra: This is useful as a diagnostic tool.

fields.Text:
During which step of the polymerase chain reaction does DNA polymerase attach dNTPs to the DNA template strand to replicate the sequence after each DNA primer?

{{c1::Elongation}}

Which genome editing tool is used to create "knock-out" or "knock-in" DNA mutations?

{{c1::CRISPR/Cas9}}

What is the function of the enzyme Cas9 in the CRISPR/Cas9 technique?

It is an {{c1::endonuclease}} that creates single-stranded or double-stranded {{c1::breaks}} at the target site of the DNA sequence

Which molecule recognizes and binds to the target DNA sequence in the CRISPR/Cas9 technique?

{{c1::gRNA}}
fields.Back Extra: This is complementary to the target DNA sequence.

fields.Text:
In the CRISPR/Cas9 technique, how is DNA altered to create a frameshift mutation of a gene?

Imperfect repair of cut segments by {{c1::nonhomologous end joining}} → Accidental frameshift mutation
fields.Back Extra: This is known as a "knock-out" DNA mutation.

fields.Text:
By what cellular mechanism can new or donor DNA be added to a target site in CRISPR/Cas9?

{{c1::Homology-directed repair}}

Name three potential clinical applications of CRISPR/Cas9.

Replacement of {{c1::disease}}-causing alleles of genes with healthy variants
Removal of {{c1::virulence factors}} from pathogens
Specific targeting of {{c1::tumor}} cells

Which blotting technique detects splicing errors?

{{c1::Northern}} blot

How is the DNA of interest isolated and visualized in a Southern blot?

DNA sample is enzymatically cleaved → Separated via {{c1::gel electrophoresis}} → Transferred to a membrane → Exposed to a labeled {{c1::DNA probe}} that anneals to its complementary strand → Visualized on exposure to film or digital imager

Which blotting technique is used to measure the level of gene expression in a sample?

{{c1::Northern}} blot
fields.Back Extra: This can identify mRNA, which is indicative of gene expression.

fields.Text:
Which blotting technique can be used to identify DNA-binding proteins?

{{c1::Southwestern}} blot

Which technique separates the DNA samples in a Southern blot, the RNA samples in a Northern blot, and protein in a Western blot?

{{c1::Gel electrophoresis}}

What does the labeled DNA probe in a Northern blot bind to?

{{c1::RNA::DNA/RNA}} sample

Which blotting technique is used to detect DNA sequences in a sample?

{{c1::Southern}} blot

Which blotting technique is used to identify and seperate proteins?

{{c1::Western}} blot

What is used as a probe in a Southwestern blot?

Labeled {{c1::double::single/double}}-stranded {{c1::DNA::DNA/RNA}}

Which blotting technique uses a labeled antibody to isolate the molecule of interest?

{{c1::Western}} blot

On the flow cytometry scatter plot shown in the image, T cells positive for both CD3 and CD8 are represented in which quadrant?



{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::upper::upper/lower}} quadrant

How are the tagged cell samples analyzed in flow cytometry?

Cell-specific antibodies are tagged with a unique {{c1::fluorescent dye}} → {{c1::Laser}} is focused on each cell → Light scatters → Intensity of fluorescence is determined

What laboratory technique is used to count CD4+ cells in patients with HIV infection?

{{c1::Flow cytometry}}
fields.Back Extra: This is commonly used in testing for hematologic abnormalities and immunodeficiencies.

fields.Text:
Which technique can be used to determine the immunophenotype of individual cells in a sample?

{{c1::Flow cytometry}}

How are flow cytometry data commonly represented?

One measure → {{c1::Histogram}}
Two measures → {{c1::Scatter plot}}

On the flow cytometry scatter plot shown in the image, what does the right lower quadrant correspond to?



Cells that are positive for {{c1::CD8}}
Cells that are negative for {{c1::CD3}}
fields.Back Extra: In this example, the quadrant is empty because all cells that express CD8 also express CD3.

fields.Text:
On the flow cytometry scatter plot shown in the image, what does the left lower quadrant correspond to?



Cells that are {{c1::negative::positive/negative}} for both CD8 and CD3

What characteristics of a cell are assessed by flow cytometry?

{{c1::Granularity}}
{{c1::Size}}
{{c1::Protein}} expression

What lab technique can be used to compare the relative transcription of genes in two RNA samples?

{{c1::Microarrays}}
fields.Back Extra: It can also detect single nucleotide polymorphisms and copy number variants.

fields.Text:
How do microarrays reflect the relative expression of genes and the relative amount of hybridization in two samples of DNA or RNA?

Determines the ratio of the {{c1::fluorescence signal}} at a particular DNA oligonucleotide

In microarrays, what does an array consist of?

Thousands of {{c1::DNA oilgonucleotides}} in a grid on a silicon or glass chip

Name some of the clinical applications of microarray analysis.

{{c1::Cancer mutation}} analysis
Clinical {{c1::genetic}} testing
{{c1::Forensic}} analysis
{{c1::Genetic linkage}} analysis
{{c1::Genotyping}}

Which immunologic test is commonly used to screen for HIV infection?

{{c1::ELISA}}

How does the specificity of an ELISA compare with that of a Western blot?

ELISA is {{c1::less::more/less}} specific than a Western blot

What is an ELISA used to detect?

Specific {{c1::antigens}} or {{c1::antibodies}} in a blood sample

How is a detectable signal produced in an ELISA?

An {{c1::antibody}} linked to an enzyme reacts with an added {{c1::substrate}} to produce the detectable signal
fields.Back Extra: There is usually a high sensitivity and specificity.

fields.Text:
Which tissues and bodily fluids can be sampled for karyotype analysis?

{{c1::Amniotic}} fluid
{{c1::Placental}} tissue
{{c1::Blood}}
{{c1::Bone marrow}}

Karyotyping can be used to identify which abnormalities?

Chromosomal {{c1::imbalances}}
fields.Back Extra: Examples include sex chromosome disorders and autosomal trisomies.

fields.Text:
In karyotyping, how are chromosomes ordered and numbered?

{{c1::Morphology}}
{{c1::Size}}
{{c1::Arm}} to {{c1::length}} ratio
{{c1::Banding}} pattern

Results of a genetic test are shown in the image. What type of test is this?



{{c1::Karyotype}} analysis

In karyotyping, colchicine is added to halt chromosomes in which phase of the cell cycle?

{{c1::Metaphase}}

How are the chromosomes visualized by fluorescence in situ hybridization?

A fluorescent DNA/RNA probe binds to a particular {{c1::gene}} or another site on chromosomes

What is fluorescence in situ hybridization basically used for?

Specific {{c1::gene}} localization
Direct identification of {{c1::chromosomal}} abnormalities at the molecular level

What type of chromosomal anomaly is shown by fluorescence in situ hybridization below?



{{c1::Duplication}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows a tetrasomy of chromosome 8.

fields.Text:
Name three chromosomal anomalies that can be identified by fluorescence in situ hybridization.

{{c1::Microdeletions}}
{{c1::Translocations}}
{{c1::Duplications}}

What chromosomal abnormality is indicated by the double white arrows shown in the image below?



{{c1::Translocation}}
fields.Back Extra: The fragments of chromosome 17 have been translocated to chromosome 19.

fields.Text:
How does fluorescence in situ hybridization demonstrate a translocation?

Fluorescence signal corresponding to one chromosome is seen in a {{c1::different::similar/different}} chromosome

What distinguishes cDNA from nuclear dsDNA?

cDNA lacks {{c1::introns}}

In molecular cloning, cDNA fragments are inserted into bacterial plasmids. What gene do these bacterial plasmids contain?

{{c1::Antibiotic resistance}} gene

What enzyme is used to synthesize cDNA from mRNA in molecular cloning?

{{c1::Reverse transcriptase}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase.

fields.Text:
What is molecular cloning?

A technique for producing a {{c1::recombinant DNA}} molecule in a bacterial host
fields.Back Extra: It can be used to produce human proteins in bacteria.

fields.Text:
List, in order, the five steps involved in molecular cloning.

Isolate {{c1::mRNA}} → Add {{c1::reverse transcriptase}} → Insert {{c1::cDNA}} on bacterial plasmids → Transform recombinant plasmid into bacteria → Grow bacteria on an {{c1::antibiotic}} medium to produce cloned DNA

Give an example of how abnormal expression of miRNA can contribute to the development of certain malignancies.

By silencing {{c1::mRNA}} from a tumor suppressor gene

What characteristic of miRNA allows for broader targeting of related mRNA molecules?

miRNA forms {{c1::loose}} nucleotide pairs with the mRNA

What is a small non-coding RNA molecule with a hairpin structure that blocks translation of mRNA and accelerates its degradation?

{{c1::miRNA}}

What is a small non-coding RNA molecule that is derived from an exogenous dsRNA source and causes cleavage of its target mRNA before translation?

{{c1::siRNA}}

What is meant by "knock-out" and "knock-in" in mice?

Knock-out = {{c1::Removal}} of a gene from a host genome
Knock-in = {{c1::Insertion}} of a gene from a host genome

Which transgenic strategy in mice is facilitated by homologous recombination?

Targeted {{c1::insertion}} or {{c1::deletion}} of a gene into the genome of a mouse

Random insertion of a gene into a mouse genome results in what type of gene expression?

{{c1::Constitutive}} expression

Targeted insertion of a gene into a mouse genome results in what type of gene expression?

{{c1::Conditional}} expression

What characteristic of siRNA allows for specific mRNA targeting?

siRNA requires {{c1::complete}} nucleotide pairing

What is RNA interference?

A process by which {{c1::small::large/small}} {{c1::non-coding::coding/non-coding}} RNA molecules target mRNAs to {{c1::inhibit::stimulate/inhibit}} gene expression

How are siRNAs produced for gene “knockdown” experiments?

{{c1::Chemical}} synthesis
{{c1::Transcription}}

What is the term for different mutations in the same locus that result in the same disease?

{{c1::Allelic heterogeneity}}

What term is used to describe a group of individuals with a mutated gene in which only some members express the phenotype resulting from the mutation?

{{c1::Incomplete penetrance}}

What term describes the presence of both normal and mutated mtDNA in offsprings who have varying expressions of mitochondrial disease?

{{c1::Heteroplasmy}}

What genetic term is used when mutations at different loci result in the same phenotype?

{{c1::Locus heterogeneity}}

Describe aneuploidy.

An abnormal number of chromosomes caused by chromosomal {{c1::nondisjunction}} during meiosis or mitosis

Describe epistasis.

The allele of one gene influences the {{c1::phenotypic}} expression of alleles in a {{c1::different::similar/different}} gene

What term is used when both alleles of a heterozygote contribute to a phenotype?

{{c1::Codominance}}

How do most occurrences of uniparental disomy manifest phenotypically?

As {{c1::normal}} phenotypes

What are three malignancies that are commonly associated with loss of heterozygosity?

{{c1::Lynch}} syndrome
{{c1::Retinoblastoma}}
{{c1::Li-Fraumeni}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: Lynch syndrome is also known as hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer.

fields.Text:
What term is used when a mitotic error mutation occurs after fertilization and manifests in multiple tissues and organs in the same individual?

{{c1::Somatic mosaicism}}

What term is used when the two alleles in close proximity on a chromosome associate more or less often than expected by chance in a population?

{{c1::Linkage disequilibrium}}

What is the cause of isodisomy?

Error in {{c1::meiosis II}}
Postzygotic chromosomal {{c1::duplication}} of one of a pair of chromosomes and {{c1::loss}} of the other of the original pair of chromosomes

What term is used when a mutated gene creates nonfunctional proteins and stops a normal gene product from functioning as expected?

{{c1::Dominant negative mutation}}

A young girl presents with unilateral café-au-lait spots with ragged edges, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, and precocious puberty. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::McCune-Albright}} syndrome

Heterodisomy results from a defect in what phase of meiosis?

Meiosis {{c1::I::I/II}}

What term is used when there is an increase in the severity of a genetic disease in future generations?

{{c1::Anticipation}}

What mutation leads to McCune-Albright syndrome?

{{c1::Gs}}-protein activating mutation

Is the loss of heterozygosity in an oncogene required for cancer to develop?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Unlike tumor suppressor genes, oncogenes do not require a deletion or mutation of the complementary allele.

fields.Text:
What term is used when a genetic mutation only exists in an individual's egg or sperm cells?

{{c1::Germline mosaicism}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as gonadal mosaicism.

fields.Text:
What term is used when a single gene influences several different phenotypic effects?

{{c1::Pleiotropy}}

What term is used when a child receives two chromosome copies from one parent and no chromosome copies from the other?

{{c1::Uniparental disomy}}

What term is used when two parents have the same genotype but different phenotypes?

{{c1::Variable expressivity}}

If an individual has a mutation in a tumor suppressor gene, what must also occur in the gene for cancer to develop?

The wild type allele must be {{c1::eliminated}}, {{c1::deleted}}, or {{c1::mutated}}
fields.Back Extra: This is known as loss of heterozygosity.

fields.Text:
In a disease with incomplete penetrance, what equation can be used to quantify the risk of disease expression?

{{c1::Percent penetrance}} × {{c1::Probability of inheriting genotype}} = Risk of expressing phenotype

What histologic findings would be seen in a bone biopsy specimen obtained from a patient with McCune-Albright syndrome?

Bone replaced by {{c1::collagen}} and {{c1::fibroblasts}}

mtDNA is transmitted through which parent?

{{c1::Mother}}

What are the five assumptions of Hardy-Weinberg population genetics?

No {{c1::mutation}} occuring at the locus
No {{c1::natural selection}}
{{c1::Random}} mating
No {{c1::net migration}}
{{c1::Large::Large/Small}} population

What does 2pq represent in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?

Frequency of {{c1::heterozygosity}}

What does p2 and q2 represent in Hardy-Weinberg population genetics?

Frequencies of {{c1::homozygosity}} for 2 seperate alleles of a gene

What is the frequency of an X-linked recessive disease in males and females according to Hardy-Weinberg population genetics?

Males = {{c1::q}}
Females = {{c1::q2}}

What does p and q represent in Hardy-Weinberg population genetics?

Frequency of 2 {{c1::alleles}}

Assuming a population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of a dominant allele is 0.8. What is the frequency of homozygous recessive individuals?

{{c1::0.04}}

An individual presents with severe intellectual disability, laughter at inappropriate times, seizures, and ataxia. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Angelman}} syndrome

What is genetic imprinting?

One gene copy is {{c1::expressed}} while the other is {{c1::silenced}} by methylation → Parent-of-origin effects
fields.Back Extra: The expressed copy may be mutated, unexpressed, or deleted.

fields.Text:
An individual presents with hyperphagia, intellectual disability, hypogonadism, hypotonia, and obesity. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Prader-Willi}} syndrome

What syndrome results from paternal silencing of UBE3A on chromosome 15 while the maternal allele is deleted or mutated?

{{c1::Angelman}} syndrome

What are two syndromes commonly attributed to genetic imprinting?

{{c1::Prader-Willi}} syndrome
{{c1::Angelman}} syndrome

Which modes of inheritance exhibit no father-to-son transmission?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}
{{c1::X-linked dominant}}
{{c1::Mitochondrial inheritance}}

Disorders of which inheritance pattern are often pleiotropic and variably expressed?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

Offsprings in consanguineous families have an increased risk of developing diseases with what inheritance pattern?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What is the chance that two heterozygous carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder will have an affected offspring?

{{c1::25}}%

What mode of inheritance is shown in the given family tree?



{{c1::X-linked dominant}}

Why are X-linked recessive diseases more commonly seen in males?

Males only need {{c1::one}} copy of the mutant allele
Females need to be {{c1::homozygous::homozygous/heterozygous}} to be affected

What is the likelihood that a female carrier of an X-linked recessive disease will have an affected son?

{{c1::50}}%

How does the severity of autosomal recessive disorders compare to that of autosomal dominant disorders?

Autosomal recessive disorders tend to be {{c1::more::more/less}} severe and present in {{c1::childhood}}

What inherited condition could lead to phosphate wasting at the proximal tubule leading to a rickets-like presentation?

{{c1::Hypophosphatemic rickets}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also called X-linked hypophosphatemia.

fields.Text:
What mode of inheritance is shown in the given family tree?



{{c1::Mitochondrial inheritance}}

In X-linked dominant disorders, what percentage of daughters of affected fathers will have the disorder?

{{c1::100}}%

What is the likelihood that a pregnant patient with an X-linked dominant disease will transmit the disease to her child?

{{c1::50}}%

Defects in structural genes are often associated with what inheritance pattern?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What is the probability that an unaffected individual with an affected sibling is a carrier of an autosomal recessive disease?

{{c1::2}}/{{c1::3}}

What mode of inheritance is shown in the given family tree?



{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance in the image below?



{{c1::X-linked dominant}}

What is the mode of inheritance of the multiple endocrine neoplasias?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What is the mode of inheritance of Marfan syndrome?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What is the mode of inheritance of hereditary spherocytosis?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What is the mode of inheritance of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome.

fields.Text:
What is the mode of inheritance of familial hypercholesterolemia?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What is the mode of inheritance of familial adenomatous polyposis?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What is the mode of inheritance of von Hippel-Lindau disease?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What is the mode of inheritance of tuberous sclerosis?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What is the mode of inheritance of neurofibromatosis type 1?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as von Recklinghausen disease.

fields.Text:
What is the mode of inheritance of neurofibromatosis type 2?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What is the mode of inheritance of achondroplasia?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What is the mode of inheritance of myotonic muscular dystrophy?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What is the mode of inheritance of Li-Fraumeni syndrome?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What is the mode of inheritance of Huntington disease?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

Which of the sphingolipidoses is not autosomal recessive?

{{c1::Fabry}} disease

What is the mode of inheritance of the thalassemias?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of sickle cell disease?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of phenylketouria?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of mucopolysaccharidoses, excluding Hunter syndrome?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of Kartagener syndrome?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of glycogen storage diseases?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of oculocutaneous albinism?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of Wilson disease?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of Friedreich ataxia?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of the polycystic kidney disease that most commonly manifests at a younger age?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of hemochromatosis?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What findings may be present on a CT scan of the sinuses in a patient with cystic fibrosis?

{{c1::Opacification}} of the sinuses

Which medication slows the progression of cystic fibrosis?

{{c1::Ibuprofen}}

What is the benefit of prescribing azithromycin for patients with cystic fibrosis?

{{c1::Anti-inflammatory}} activity

What is the function of aerosolized dornase alfa, albuterol, inhaled hypertonic saline, and chest physiotherapy in the treatment of cystic fibrosis?

Facilitates {{c1::mucus}} clearance

What is the earliest manifestation of cystic fibrosis in a newborn?

{{c1::Meconium ileus}}

What is the reason for subfertility in females with cystic fibrosis?

{{c1::Amenorrhea}}
Abnormally {{c1::thick::thick/thin}} cervical mucus

What is the cause of infertility in males with cystic fibrosis?

Absence of {{c1::vas deferens}}

What complications occur in the gastrointestinal tract as a result of pancreatic insufficiency and biliary cirrhosis in patients with cystic fibrosis?

Deficiencies of {{c1::fat}}-soluble vitamins
{{c1::Malabsorption}} with {{c1::steatorrhea}}
fields.Back Extra:
The fat-soluble vitamins includes the following:

Vitamin A
Vitamin D
Vitamin E
Vitamin K

fields.Text:
What diagnosis is suggested if a newborn screening test reveals increased immunoreactive trypsinogen?

{{c1::Cystic fibrosis}}

Which pathogens commonly cause recurrent pulmonary infections in infants/children versus adults with cystic fibrosis?

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} in infants and children
{{c1::Pseudomonas aeruginosa}} in adults

What might be seen on a chest X-ray obtained from a patient with cystic fibrosis?

{{c1::Reticulonodular}} pattern
fields.Back Extra: This is due to chronic bronchitis and bronchiectasis.

fields.Text:
Which metabolic disorders may be present in patients with cystic fibrosis?

{{c1::Hypokalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
Contraction {{c1::alkalosis::acidosis/alkalosis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to extracellular fluid H2O/Na+ loss via sweating and concomitant renal K+/H+ wasting.

fields.Text:
A child has steatorrhea, nasal polyps, chronic bronchitis, and nail clubbing. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Cystic fibrosis}}

How does the transepithelial potential differ in patients with cystic fibrosis?

It is more {{c1::negative::positive/negative}} due to high {{c1::Na+}} reabsorption

In patients with cystic fibrosis, how does a decrease in Cl- secretion cause thick mucus production in the lungs and gastrointestinal tract?

Low Cl- secretion → {{c1::High::High/Low}} intracellular Cl- → Compensatory {{c1::Na+}} reabsorption via {{c1::ENaC}} → Increase in {{c1::H2O}} reabsorption → Abnormally thick mucus in lungs and gastrointestinal tract

What is the diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis?

{{c1::Pilocarpine-induced sweat}} test
fields.Back Extra: This would reveal increased chloride concentration.

fields.Text:
What does the CFTR gene code for?

An {{c1::ATP}}-gated {{c1::Cl-}} channel that secretes {{c1::Cl-}} into the lungs and gastrointestinal tract while reabsorbing {{c1::Cl-}} in sweat glands

What genetic defect causes cystic fibrosis?

{{c1::Phe508}} deletion → Defect in the {{c1::CFTR}} gene on chromosome {{c1::7}}

A patient presents with recurrent pulmonary infections, pancreatic insufficiency, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Cystic fibrosis}}

What is the sequelae of a Phe508 deletion in patients with cystic fibrosis?

A {{c1::misfolded}} protein that is retained in the rough endoplasmic reticulum
fields.Back Extra: Thus, it is not transported to the cell membrane.

fields.Text:
In patients with cystic fibrosis, what medication functions to reduce symptoms by opening chloride channels leading to improved chloride transport?

{{c1::Ivacaftor}}

What is the mechanism of action of lumacaftor or tezacaftor in patients with cystic fibrosis?

Corrects the {{c1::misfolding}} of proteins caused by the {{c1::Phe508}} deletion
fields.Back Extra: This improves the transport of proteins to the cell membrane.

fields.Text:
A patient with cystic fibrosis has severe malnutrition and steatorrhea. What is the treatment?

{{c1::Pancreatic}} enzyme replacement

Fungi are detected in a lung biopsy specimen obtained from a patient with cystic fibrosis and recurrent pneumonia. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis}}

What are some late-stage complications of cystic fibrosis?

{{c1::Endocrine}} dysfunction
{{c1::Biliary cirrhosis}}
{{c1::Liver::Organ}} disease

A combination of which two medications corrects misfolded proteins and improves their transport to the cell surface in cystic fibrosis?

A combination of either {{c1::lumacaftor}} or {{c1::tezacaftor}} with {{c1::ivacaftor}}
