Why are female carriers of X-linked recessive disorders variably affected?

There are variations in the pattern of {{c1::inactivation}} of the {{c1::X}} chromosome carrying the mutant gene

What is the pattern of inheritance of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

What is the pattern of inheritance of Fabry disease?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of Duchenne muscular dystrophy?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of Becker muscular dystrophy?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of Bruton agammaglobulinemia?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

Why are females with Turner syndrome more likely to have an X-linked recessive disorder?

They only have 1 {{c1::X}} chromosome

What is the term for the process in which one of the two X chromosomes is deactivated and becomes a Barr body?

{{c1::X-inactivation}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as lyonization.

fields.Text:
What is the mode of inheritance of hemophilia A?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of hemophilia B?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of Hunter syndrome?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of Lesch-Nyham syndrome?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of ocular albinism?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

What is the mode of inheritance of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

A patient with muscular dystrophy uses the upper extremities to stand up. What is the name of this sign?



{{c1::Gowers}} sign

What is the disease mechanism of myotonic dystrophy?

{{c1::CTG}} trinucleotide repeat expansion in the {{c1::DMPK}} gene → Abnormal expression of {{c1::myotonin protein kinase}}

What is the inheritance pattern of myotonic dystrophy?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What is the genetic mechanism that causes Becker muscular dystrophy?

{{c1::Non-frameshift}} deletion in the {{c1::dystrophin}} gene
fields.Back Extra: This leads to a partially functioning dystrophin gene.

fields.Text:
The findings shown in this calf muscle biopsy specimen from a 4-year-old boy suggest what diagnosis?



{{c1::Duchenne muscular dystrophy}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows fibrofatty replacement of muscle.

fields.Text:
How is the diagnosis of Duchenne muscular dystrophy confirmed?

{{c1::Genetic}} testing

Which two enzymes are elevated in patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy?

{{c1::Creatine kinase}}
{{c1::Aldolase}}

At what age does Becker muscular dystrophy present?

{{c1::Adolescence}}
{{c1::Early::Early/Late}} adulthood

What is the most common cause of death in patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy?

{{c1::Dilated cardiomyopathy}}

At what age do patients typically present with Duchenne muscular dystrophy?

Before the age of {{c1::5}} years

What is the function of dystrophin protein?

Dystrophin {{c1::anchors}} muscle fibers to the {{c1::extracellular::intracelluar/extracellular}} matrix
fields.Back Extra: This is particularly in skeletal and cardiac muscle.

fields.Text:
What unique characteristic of the dystrophin gene makes it particularly susceptible to mutations?

It is the {{c1::largest::largest/smallest}} protein-coding human gene
fields.Back Extra: This allows for a high rate of spontaneous mutations.

fields.Text:
In patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, weakness first presents in which group of muscles before progressing superiorly?

{{c1::Pelvic girdle}} muscles

A 3-year-old boy has pelvic girdle muscle weakness, pseudohypertrophy of the calves, and a waddling gait. What gene is most likely mutated?

{{c1::Dystrophin}} gene

A frameshift deletion occurs in the dystrophin gene. This leads to a truncated/deleted dystrophin gene and myofibrillar damage. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Duchenne muscular dystrophy}}

What is the pathophysiology of Duchenne muscular dystrophy?

Loss of {{c1::dystrophin}} protein → {{c1::Myonecrosis}}

A male at 25 years of age presents with gonadal atrophy, early balding, cataracts, and muscle wasting. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Myotonic dystrophy}}

A patient between ages 1 and 4 presents with stereotypical hand-wringing, seizures, intellectual disability, and regression in verbal, cognitive, and motor skills. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Rett}} syndrome

The mother of a child with Rett syndrome is pregnant with another child and inquires about the inheritance of the disease. How would you respond?

Rett syndrome is a {{c1::sporadic}} disorder
fields.Back Extra: This is due to a de novo mutation.

fields.Text:
Why is Rett syndrome almost exclusively seen in females?

Affected males {{c1::die}} in utero or shortly after birth

Between what ages does Rett syndrome usually manifest?

Between ages {{c1::1}} and {{c1::4}}

What are the clinical manifestations of Rett syndrome?

{{c1::Ataxia}}
{{c1::Seizures}}
{{c1::Growth}} deceleration
Characteristic {{c1::hand-wringing}}
{{c1::Regression}} of motor, verbal, and cognitive skills

What is the underlying mutation in Rett syndrome?

{{c1::De novo}} mutation of {{c1::MECP2}} on the {{c1::X}} chromosome

What is the most common heritable cause of intellectual disability?

{{c1::Fragile X}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: Down syndrome is the most common genetic cause of intellectual disability.

fields.Text:
What is the underlying genetic cause of fragile X syndrome?

Trinucleotide repeats in the {{c1::FMR1}} gene

What heart defect is most likely present in patients with fragile X syndrome?

{{c1::Mitral valve prolapse}}

During embryonic development, when does the trinucleotide repeat expansion that leads to fragile X syndrome occur?

{{c1::Oogenesis}}

How does the trinucleotide expansion in fragile X syndrome affect gene expression?

Trinucleotide repeats in the {{c1::FMR1}} gene causes hypermethylation of {{c1::cytosine}} residues → Decreased expression

What is the mode of inheritance of fragile X syndrome?

{{c1::X-linked dominant}}

What are the clinical manifestations of fragile X syndrome when there is a full mutation?

{{c1::Long::Long/Short}} face
{{c1::Large::Large/Small}} jaw
{{c1::Large::Large/Small}}, {{c1::everted::inverted/everted}} ears
{{c1::Mitral valve prolapse::Heart defect}}
{{c1::Hypermobile::Hypermobile/Hypomobile}} joints
{{c1::Autism}}
Postpubertal {{c1::macroorchidism}}

What disease is caused by a trinucleotide repeat expansion of GAA?

{{c1::Friedreich ataxia}}

What disease is caused by a trinucleotide repeat expansion of CAG?

{{c1::Huntington}} disease

What does anticipation refer to in genetic disease?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} disease severity in successive generations
{{c1::Earlier::Earlier/Later}} age of onset in successive generations

What disease is caused by a trinucleotide repeat expansion of CGG?

{{c1::Fragile X}} syndrome

What are the reproductive manifestations of myotonic dystrophy?

Gonadal {{c1::atrophy}} in men
Reduced {{c1::fertility}} in women

How many normal gametes are produced during gametogenesis if nondisjunction occurs during meiosis II?

{{c1::2}}

How many normal gametes are produced during gametogenesis if nondisjunction occurs during meiosis I?

{{c1::0}}

Which two trisomy disorders may present with severe intellectual disability, rocker-bottom feet, and congenital heart disease?

{{c1::Edwards}} syndrome
{{c1::Patau}} syndrome

What disease is suspected if a newborn with evidence of Down syndrome on prenatal screening does not pass meconium after birth but is not vomiting?

{{c1::Hirschsprung}} disease

Prenatal screening markers show low β-hCG and low PAPP-A. What are the possible diagnoses?

{{c1::Edwards}} syndrome
{{c1::Patau}} syndrome

What changes may be noted in hCG, inhibin A, estriol, and α-fetoprotein levels if a fetus is suspected to have Edwards syndrome?

{{c1::Low::High/Low}} hCG levels
{{c1::Low::High/Low}} inhibin A levels
{{c1::Low::High/Low}} estriol levels
{{c1::Low::High/Low}} α-fetoprotein levels

A hypoplastic nasal bone and an increase in nuchal translucency is present on a fetal ultrasound exam. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Down}} syndrome

What is the life expectancy of a child born with either trisomy 13 or trisomy 18?

Death usually occurs by age {{c1::1}}

What autosomal trisomy is associated with Patau syndrome?

Trisomy {{c1::13}}

What autosomal trisomy is associated with Edwards syndrome?

Trisomy {{c1::18}}

What autosomal trisomy is associated with Down syndrome?

Trisomy {{c1::21}}

What are the prenatal screening markers for Down syndrome?

{{c1::High::High/Low}} hCG levels
{{c1::High::High/Low}} inhibin A levels
{{c1::Low::High/Low}} estriol levels
{{c1::Low::High/Low}} α-fetoprotein levels

Females of which age group are at an increased risk of having a child with Down syndrome?

Females of {{c1::advanced}} maternal age

What is the most common viable autosomal trisomy disorder?

{{c1::Down}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This is also the most common cause of genetic intellectual disability.

fields.Text:
A newborn has exam findings of a single palmar crease, incurved fifth finger, a gap between the first two toes, flat facies, and prominent epicanthal folds. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Down}} syndrome

Impairment of what embryonic process results in the midline defects seen in Patau syndrome?

Impairment in the fusion of the {{c1::prechordal mesoderm}}

What hematologic malignancies are associated with Down syndrome?

{{c1::ALL}} (> 5 years of age)
{{c1::AML}} (< 5 years of age)

What are two causes of Down syndrome that occur less commonly than meiotic nondisjunction?

{{c1::Unbalanced Robertsonian translocation}}
Postfertilization {{c1::mitotic}} error
fields.Back Extra: Unbalanced Robertsonian translocation usually occurs between chromosomes 14 and 21.

fields.Text:
What ophthalmologic finding may be present in a patient with Down syndrome?

{{c1::Brushfield}} spots
fields.Back Extra: These are whitish spots at the margin of the iris.

fields.Text:
What are the five A's of Down syndrome?

{{c1::Advanced}} maternal age
{{c1::Atresia}}
{{c1::Atrioventricular septal}} defect
{{c1::Alzheimer}} disease
{{c1::AML/ALL}}

Down syndrome is most frequently caused by a defect in the process shown in the image below. What is this defect called?



{{c1::Meiotic nondisjunction}}

What are the major signs and symptoms of Edwards syndrome?

{{c1::Prominent}} occiput
{{c1::Rocker-bottom}} feet
{{c1::Intellectual}} disability
{{c1::Nondisjunction}}
{{c1::Clenched}} fists with {{c1::overlapping}} fingers
{{c1::Ears}} that are low-set

Which chromosome is affected in Edwards syndrome?

Chromosome {{c1::18}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation for Prader-Willi syndrome?

Chromosome {{c1::15}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation for von Hippel-Lindau disease?

Chromosome {{c1::3}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1?

Chromosome {{c1::11}}

Which chromosome carries the BRCA1 mutation and the mutations that result in Li-Fraumeni syndrome and neurofibromatosis type 1?

Chromosome {{c1::17}}

Which chromosome is affected in Wilms tumor?

Chromosome {{c1::11}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation for α-thalassemia and other α-globin gene defects?

Chromosome {{c1::16}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation for Marfan syndrome?

Chromosome {{c1::15}}

Which chromosome carries the BRCA2 mutation?

Chromosome {{c1::13}}

Hemochromatosis is a disorder caused by a mutation in which chromosome?

Chromosome {{c1::6}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation for Huntington disease?

Chromosome {{c1::4}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation that predisposes a person to renal cell carcinoma?

Chromosome {{c1::3}}

Which chromosome mutation is associated with familial adenomatous polyposis?

Chromosome {{c1::5}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation for cri-du-chat syndrome?

Chromosome {{c1::5}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation for cystic fibrosis?

Chromosome {{c1::7}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation for Williams syndrome?

Chromosome {{c1::7}}

Which chromosome is affected in Patau syndrome?

Chromosome {{c1::13}}

Duplication of which chromosome results in Klinefelter syndrome?

Chromosome {{c1::X}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation for Friedreich ataxia?

Chromosome {{c1::9}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation for Wilson disease?

Chromosome {{c1::13}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation for Angelman syndrome?

Chromosome {{c1::15}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation for neurofibromatosis type 2?

Chromosome {{c1::22}}

Which chromosome carries the defect that is responsible for achondroplasia?

Chromosome {{c1::4}}

A defect in which chromosome leads to Down syndrome?

Chromosome {{c1::21}}

A patient has a chromosomal defect that results in large, bilateral cystic kidneys. Which genes might be affected?

{{c1::PKD1}} on chromosome 16
{{c1::PKD2}} on chromosome 4
fields.Back Extra: This is autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.

fields.Text:
Which chromosome carries the mutation for DiGeorge syndrome?

Chromosome {{c1::22}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation for agammaglobulinemia?

Chromosome {{c1::X}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation for β-globin defects?

Chromosome {{c1::11}}

Which chromosome carries the mutation for retinoblastoma?

Chromosome {{c1::13}}

Which two chromosome mutations are associated with each type of tuberous sclerosis?

TSC1 is associated with chromosome {{c1::9}}
TSC2 is associated with chromosome {{c1::16}}

Genetic testing performed for a patient with tuberous sclerosis reveals an abnormal TSC1 gene. What chromosome is most likely mutated in this patient?

Chromosome {{c1::9}}

Karotype analysis reveals a balanced translocation between chromosomes 14 and 21. How will this affect the individual's phenotype?

The individual will be {{c1::unaffected}}
fields.Back Extra:
Balanced translocations, unlike unbalanced translocations, do not cause abnormal phenotypes.

There will be no gain or loss of genetic material.

fields.Text:
What feature of chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22 predisposes them to Robertsonian translocations?

They are {{c1::acrocentric}} chromosomes
fields.Back Extra: They have centromeres near their ends.

fields.Text:
What are acrocentric chromosomes?

Chromosomes with centromeres near their {{c1::ends}}

What is a Robertsonian translocation?

Fusion of the {{c1::long::long/short}} arms of two {{c1::acrocentric}} chromosomes at the centromeres
fields.Back Extra: This results in the loss of two short arms and ultimately a single, large chromosome.

fields.Text:
What is the underlying cause of cri-du-chat syndrome?

{{c1::Short::Long/Short}} arm deletion on chromosome {{c1::5}}

What is the genetic syndrome associated with high-pitched crying, microcephaly, epicanthal folds, cardiac abnormalities, and intellectual disability?

{{c1::Cri-du-chat}} syndrome

Despite their intellectual disability, patients with Williams syndrome are typically advanced in which skill set?

{{c1::Verbal}} skills

What is the probable diagnosis of a child with “elfin” facies, intellectual disability, notable friendliness with strangers, hypercalcemia, and cardiovascular problems?

{{c1::Williams}} syndrome

Which connective tissue gene is deleted in Williams syndrome?

{{c1::Elastin}} gene

What chromosomal abnormality is the cause of Williams syndrome?

{{c1::Microdeletion}} of the {{c1::long::long/short}} arm of chromosome {{c1::7}}

Name two cardiovascular conditions that may be present in patients with Williams syndrome.

{{c1::Supravalvular aortic stenosis}}
{{c1::Renal artery stenosis}}

Name two essential polyunsaturated fatty acids.

{{c1::Linoleic acid}}
{{c1::Linolenic acid}}

What two products are created from the metabolism of linoleic acid?

{{c1::Leukotrienes}}
{{c1::Prostaglandins}}
fields.Back Extra: Linoleic acid is metabolized to arachidonic acid, which serves as the precursor to leukotrienes and prostaglandins.

fields.Text:
Which polyunsaturated fatty acid has been shown to have antihyperlipidemic and cardioprotective effects?

{{c1::Linolenic acid}}

What three factors alter absorption of fat-soluble vitamins?

Bile {{c1::emulsification}}
{{c1::Pancreatic}} secretions
Presence of intact {{c1::ileum}}

Why is toxicity more common with fat-soluble vitamins than with water-soluble vitamins?

Fat-soluble vitamins {{c1::accumulate}} in fat
fields.Back Extra: Water-soluble vitamins are eliminated more rapidly.

fields.Text:
Malabsorption syndromes, often presenting with chronic steatorrhea, can lead to deficiency of which vitamins?

{{c1::Fat}}-soluble vitamins

Approximately how long is vitamin B9 stored in the liver?

3 to 4 {{c1::months::months/years}}

Approximately how long is vitamin B12 stored in the liver?

3 to 4 {{c1::years::months/years}}

Which three symptoms are most often associated with all the vitamin B deficiencies?

{{c1::Glossitis}}
{{c1::Dermatitis}}
{{c1::Diarrhea}}

Although most water-soluble vitamins are cleared from the body quickly, which two remain stored?

Vitamin {{c1::B12}}
Vitamin {{c1::B9}}

Which vitamins are water soluble?

Vitamin {{c1::B1}}
Vitamin {{c1::B2}}
Vitamin {{c1::B3}}
Vitamin {{c1::B5}}
Vitamin {{c1::B6}}
Vitamin {{c1::B7}}
Vitamin {{c1::B9}}
Vitamin {{c1::B12}}
Vitamin {{c1::C}}

What is the alternative name for vitamin B7?

{{c1::Biotin}}

What is the alternative name for vitamin B9?

{{c1::Folate}}

What is the alternative name for vitamin B12?

{{c1::Cobalamin}}

What is the alternative name for vitamin C?

{{c1::Ascorbic acid}}

What is the main molecular derivative of vitamin B1?

{{c1::Thiamine pyrophosphate}}

What are the two main molecular derivatives of vitamin B2?

{{c1::FAD}}
{{c1::FMN}}

What is the main molecular derivative of vitamin B3?

{{c1::NAD+}}

What is the main molecular derivative of pantothenic acid?

{{c1::CoA}}

What is the main molecular derivative of vitamin B6?

{{c1::Pyridoxal phosphate}}

What vitamin deficiency causes the ocular manifestation shown in the image?



Vitamin {{c1::A}} deficiency
fields.Back Extra: The image shows Bitot spots on the conjunctiva.

fields.Text:
Which vitamin is essential for the differentiation of epithelial cells into specialized tissue?

Vitamin {{c1::A}}

All-trans retinoic acid is a treatment for which malignancy?

{{c1::Acute promyelocytic}} leukemia

Which vitamin prevents squamous metaplasia?

Vitamin {{c1::A}}

What requirements must be met before prescribing isotretinoin to a female of childbearing age?

A pregnancy test result must be {{c1::negative::positive/negative}}
The patient must use two forms of contraception because of isotretinoin's {{c1::teratogenic}} properties

What are the teratogenic effects of vitamin A?

{{c1::Cleft palate}}
{{c1::Cardiac}} abnormalities

What are the symptoms of acute vitamin A toxicity?

{{c1::Nausea}}
{{c1::Vomiting}}
{{c1::Vertigo}}
{{c1::Blurred}} vision due to increased intracranial pressure

What is the diagnosis for a person who eats a lot of spinach and liver, presenting with hair loss, dry skin, joint pain, hepatomegaly and intracranial hypertension?

Chronic vitamin {{c1::A}} toxicity

What vitamin A derivative is a component of visual pigments?

{{c1::Retinal}}

What two dietary sources are rich in vitamin A?

{{c1::Liver::Organ}}
{{c1::Leafy vegetables}}

What is another name for vitamin A?

{{c1::Retinol}}

Name two topical uses of vitamin A.

{{c1::Wrinkles}}
{{c1::Acne}}

Supplementation of which vitamin may be helpful in the treatment of measles?

Vitamin {{c1::A}}

What are the symptoms of vitamin A deficiency?

{{c1::Night blindness}}
Skin that is {{c1::dry}}/{{c1::scaly}}
{{c1::Dry}} eyes
Corneal squamous metaplasia → {{c1::Bitot spots}}
{{c1::Corneal}} degeneration
{{c1::Immunosuppression}}

How can you confirm a diagnosis of vitamin B1 deficiency?

Increased RBC {{c1::transketolase}} activity following vitamin B1 administration

In the emergency department, a man with a history of alcoholism requests a drink and receives orange juice. He is later found in an obtunded state. What is the cause of the change in status?

Impaired {{c1::glucose}} breakdown → ATP depletion that is exacerbated by {{c1::glucose}} infusion

Which regions of the brain are damaged in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome as a result of vitamin B1 deficiency?

{{c1::Mammillary bodies}}
{{c1::Medial dorsal nucleus}} of the {{c1::thalamus}}

Why are the heart and brain particularly susceptible to injury in patients with thiamine deficiency?

Highly {{c1::aerobic}} cells require more ATP to function
fields.Back Extra: Thiamine is required for the breakdown of glucose and the production of ATP.

fields.Text:
A male patient who is a heavy drinker reports difficulty walking because of decreased sensation and muscle wasting in his legs. Which vitamin deficiency might he have?

Vitamin {{c1::B1}} deficiency
fields.Back Extra: Dry beriberi is characterized by polyneuropathy and symmetric muscle wasting.

fields.Text:
What is a major complication of wet beriberi caused by vitamin B1 deficiency?

{{c1::High::High/Low}}-output {{c1::cardiac}} failure
fields.Back Extra: This often presents with dyspnea, fatigue, and edema.

fields.Text:
What is the role of thiamine in the TCA cycle?

It is a cofactor for {{c1::α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase}}

Vitamin B1 is the precursor to what metabolic cofactor?

{{c1::TPP}}

What are the symptoms of Wernicke encephalopathy?

{{c1::Confusion}}
{{c1::Ophthalmoplegia}}
{{c1::Nystagmus}}
{{c1::Ataxia}}

Deficiency of which vitamin causes beriberi?

Vitamin {{c1::B1}}

What 4 dehydrogenase enzymes require TPP as a cofactor?

{{c1::Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase}}
{{c1::α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase}}
{{c1::Pyruvate dehydrogenase}}
{{c1::Transketolase}}

What 3 signs indicate a diagnosis of Korsakoff syndrome in a patient with a history of chronic alcoholism?

{{c1::Personality}} changes
{{c1::Confabulation}}
{{c1::Irreversible::Reversible/Irreversible}} memory loss

What vitamin deficiency causes Wernicke encephalopathy?

Vitamin {{c1::B1}} deficiency

Vitamin B2 deficiency can lead to the deficiency of which two cofactors in the tricarboxylic acid cycle?

{{c1::FAD}}
{{c1::FMN}}

What is the role of FAD and FMN?

Cofactors in {{c1::redox}} reactions

What are the signs that indicate riboflavin deficiency?

{{c1::Cheilosis}}
{{c1::Corneal}} vascularization
"{{c1::Magenta}}" tongue

Excess of which vitamin can precipitate gout?

Vitamin {{c1::B3}}
fields.Back Extra: This causes hyperuricemia and can be used to treat dyslipidemia.

fields.Text:
What is the treatment for Hartnup disease?

High-{{c1::protein}} diet to increase serum tryptophan
Vitamin {{c1::B3}}

For what reason might patients with diabetes mellitus be discouraged from taking niacin supplements?

Niacin can cause {{c1::hyperglycemia}} as a side effect

Niacin is derived from which amino acid?

{{c1::Tryptophan}}

How can the facial flushing associated with use of niacin be prevented?

By taking {{c1::aspirin}} along with niacin
fields.Back Extra: This is because the flushing is caused by prostaglandin release.

fields.Text:
Which vitamin deficiency causes diarrhea, a "broad collar" rash, dementia, and hallucinations?

Vitamin {{c1::B3}} deficiency

What is the cause of numbness and pellagra-like symptoms in a patient taking antitubercular drugs?

Isoniazid depletes vitamin {{c1::B6}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is required for the conversion of tryptophan to niacin.

Vitamin B6 and niacin deficiencies cause neuropathy and pellagra.

fields.Text:
How does malignant carcinoid syndrome cause pellagra?

Tryptophan is shunted primarily toward the synthesis of {{c1::serotonin}}
fields.Back Extra: Less tryptophan to synthesize niacin → Pellagra-like symptoms

fields.Text:
How does Hartnup disease lead to pellagra?

Deficiency of {{c1::neutral amino acid}} transporters in proximal renal tubular cells and enterocytes → Impaired absorption → Decreased {{c1::tryptophan}} → Decreased niacin → Pellagra

What are the two components of the dermatitis observed in vitamin B3 deficiency?

A circumferential "{{c1::broad collar}}" rash in the C3 to C4 dermatomes
{{c1::Hyperpigmentation::Hyperpigmentation/Hypopigmentation}} of sun-exposed skin
fields.Back Extra: The "broad collar" rash in the C3 to C4 dermatomes is also known as a Casal necklace.

fields.Text:
What are the effects of niacin on serum lipid levels?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} HDL
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} VLDL

Which two vitamins are involved in the synthesis of niacin from tryptophan?

Vitamin {{c1::B2}}
Vitamin {{c1::B6}}

What might urinalysis show in a patient with Hartnup disease?

{{c1::Neutral aminoaciduria}}

Which vitamin is a component of CoA and fatty acid synthase?

Vitamin {{c1::B5}}

What are four key signs/symptoms of vitamin B5 deficiency?

{{c1::Alopecia}}
{{c1::Dermatitis}}
{{c1::Enteritis}}
{{c1::Burning}} sensation in feet

Which 5 major neurotransmitters require vitamin B6 for synthesis?

{{c1::Epinephrine}}
{{c1::Norepinephrine}}
{{c1::Serotonin}}
{{c1::Dopamine}}
{{c1::GABA}}

What is the pathophysiology behind sideroblastic anemia caused by vitamin B6 deficiency?

Vitamin B6 deficiency leads to impaired {{c1::hemoglobin}} synthesis and {{c1::iron}} excess

What 3 types of reactions does PLP take part in?

{{c1::Glycogen phosphorylation}}
{{c1::Transamination}}
{{c1::Decarboxylation}}

Vitamin B6 is the precursor to which cofactor?

{{c1::PLP}}

Which 2 medications can induce a vitamin B6 deficiency?

{{c1::OCPs}}
{{c1::Isoniazid}}

Vitamin B6 is required for the synthesis of what other vitamin?

Vitamin {{c1::B3}}

What are the 4 signs/symptoms of vitamin B6 deficiency?

{{c1::Hyperirritability}}
{{c1::Peripheral}} neuropathy
{{c1::Convulsions}}
{{c1::Sideroblastic}} anemia

What are the 3 main manifestations of vitamin B7 deficiency?

{{c1::Dermatitis}}
{{c1::Alopecia}}
{{c1::Enteritis}}

How does long-term consumption of raw egg whites lead to a vitamin B7 deficiency?

{{c1::Avidin}} found in egg whites binds to vitamin B7
fields.Back Extra: Avidin in egg whites avidly binds to biotin.

fields.Text:
What are the 2 main causes of vitamin B7 deficiency?

Long-term {{c1::antibiotic}} therapy
Excessive consumption of raw {{c1::egg whites}}

Vitamin B7 is a cofactor for which type of enzymes?

{{c1::Carboxylation}} enzymes

What vitamin is required for the synthesis of tetrahydrofolic acid?

Vitamin {{c1::B9}}

A blood smear from a patient with a history of alcoholism shows macrocytosis. Labs show increased serum homocysteine levels and normal serum methylmalonic acid levels. What vitamin should be supplemented?

Vitamin {{c1::B9}}

How can folate deficiency be differentiated from colbalamin deficiency?

Patients with folate deficiency have {{c1::normal}} serum methylmalonic acid levels
Patients with cobalamin deficiency have {{c1::increased}} serum methylmalonic acid levels
fields.Back Extra: Patients with cobalamin deficiency can also present with neurologic symptoms.

fields.Text:
What are the 3 drugs that cause folate deficiency?

{{c1::Methotrexate}}
{{c1::Phenytoin}}
{{c1::Sulfonamides}}

Why is folate supplementation necessary throughout pregnancy?

Folate reduces the risk of {{c1::neural tube}} defects

Why do symptoms of folate deficiency manifest more quickly than symptoms of cobalamin deficiency?

Folate is stored in the liver for 3 to 4 {{c1::months}}
Cobalamin is stored in the liver for 3 to 4 {{c1::years}}

Where is folate absorbed in the body?

{{c1::Jejunum}}

What type of food is a good source of folate?

{{c1::Leafy green vegetables}}

What is the function of tetrahydrofolate?

It is a coenzyme for {{c1::1-carbon}} metabolism and {{c1::methylation}} reactions
fields.Back Extra: It is important for the synthesis of nitrogenous bases in DNA and RNA.

fields.Text:
What might you expect to see in a peripheral blood smear of a patient with folate deficiency?

{{c1::Macrocytic}}, {{c1::megaloblastic}} anemia
{{c1::Hypersegmented polymorphonuclear}} cells

Which vitamin deficiencies are most commonly associated with chronic alcohol use?

Vitamin {{c1::B9}} deficiency
Vitamin {{c1::B12}} deficiency

Although found in animal products, vitamin B12 can only be synthesized by what in the body?

Intestinal {{c1::microbiota}}

Why does vitamin B12 deficiency cause decreased levels of serum S-adenosylmethionine?

S-adenosylmethionine is derived from {{c1::methionine}}, which is made by {{c1::methionine synthase}}

What is the effect of vitamin B12 deficiency on homocysteine and methionine levels?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} homocysteine levels
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} methionine levels

What is the effect of vitamin B12 deficiency on tricarboxylic acid cycle activity and heme synthesis?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} tricarboxylic acid cycle activity
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} heme synthesis

Which fatty acids and amino acids will increase in individuals with reduced methylmalonyl-CoA activity?

{{c1::Odd}}-chain fatty acids
{{c1::Branched}}-chain amino acids

Are neurologic manifestations of prolonged cobalamin deficiency reversible?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Prolonged deficiency of cobalamin leads to irreversible nervous system damage.

fields.Text:
Which vitamin deficiency causes subacute combined degenerative disease?

Vitamin {{c1::B12}} deficiency

What factors predispose an individual to develop vitamin B12 deficiency?

Absence of {{c1::terminal ileum}}
{{c1::Malabsorption}}
Lack of {{c1::intrinsic factor}}
{{c1::Medications}}
Insufficient {{c1::intake}}

Resection of the terminal ileum predisposes patients to the development of which vitamin deficiency?

Vitamin {{c1::B12}} deficiency
fields.Back Extra: This is because it is absorbed in the terminal ileum.

fields.Text:
Infection with which parasite can lead to a vitamin B12 deficiency?

{{c1::Diphyllobothrium latum}}

How does pernicious anemia lead to vitamin B12 deficiency?

Formation of {{c1::anti-intrinsic factor}} antibodies → Decrease in {{c1::intrinsic factor}} levels → Decrease in vitamin B12
fields.Back Extra: Intrinsic factor is needed for the absorption of vitamin B12.

fields.Text:
What should be recommended for a patient presenting with fatigue and paresthesia whose blood smear shows hypersegmented polymorphonuclear neutrophils and macrocytosis?

Vitamin {{c1::B12}} supplementation
Increased intake of {{c1::animal}} products
fields.Back Extra: The patient has macrocytic anemia with neurologic symptoms.

fields.Text:
In which organ is vitamin B12 primarily stored?

{{c1::Liver}}

How does vitamin B12 deficiency lead to secondary folate deficiency?

Vitamin B12 is a required cofactor for {{c1::methionine synthase}}
fields.Back Extra: It is dependent on the conversion of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, which is the active form of folate.

fields.Text:
Why might high succinyl-CoA levels still be noted after treatment of anemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency?

The patient may have low levels of vitamin {{c1::B6}}
fields.Back Extra: This is required for the conversion of succinyl-CoA to heme.

fields.Text:
Blockade of which biochemical reaction causes an increase in methylmalonic acid?

Conversion of {{c1::homocysteine}} to {{c1::methionine}}

What will happen to symptoms like fatigue and paresthesias in a patient treated with folic acid only if both vitamin B12 and B9 deficiencies are present?

Fatigue will {{c1::decrease}}
Paresthesia will {{c1::remain}}
fields.Back Extra: Folate will not resolve neurologic symptoms in a patient with vitamin B12 deficiency.

fields.Text:
Which drug, used in the treatment of diabetes mellitus and polycystic ovary syndrome, may cause vitamin B12 deficiency?

{{c1::Metformin}}

Where does the methyl group methionine synthase receives come from?

{{c1::5-methyltetrahydrofolate}}

Which vitamin acts as a cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase?

Vitamin {{c1::B12}}
fields.Back Extra:
It transfers methyl groups as methylcobalamin for methionine synthase.

Vitamin B12 deficiency disrupts DNA synthesis, causing anemia.

fields.Text:
Excessive consumption of which vitamin can cause recurrent calcium oxalate renal stones?

Vitamin {{c1::C}}

What vitamin can aid in reversing an amyl nitrite overdose?

Vitamin {{c1::C}}
fields.Back Extra: Vitamin C can be used to treat methemoglobinemia by reducing Fe3+ to Fe2+.

fields.Text:
What enzyme uses ascorbic acid to convert dopamine to norepinephrine?

{{c1::Dopamine β-hydroxylase}}

What are the main dietary sources of vitamin C?

{{c1::Fruits}}
{{c1::Vegetables}}

Vitamin C is required for the synthesis of which neurotransmitter?

{{c1::Norepinephrine}}

How does vitamin C promote the absorption of iron?

By reducing {{c1::Fe3+}} to {{c1::Fe2+}}

What is the role of vitamin C in collagen synthesis?

{{c1::Hydroxylation}} of {{c1::lysine}} and {{c1::proline}} residues

A patient with scurvy would be at risk for which two specific types of hemorrhages?

{{c1::Perifollicular}} hemorrhages
{{c1::Subperiosteal}} hemorrhages

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient who has swollen gums, anemia, corkscrew hair who reports poor wound healing, recurrent infections, and easy bruising?

Vitamin {{c1::C}} deficiency
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as scurvy.

fields.Text:
A 2-year-old boy born at 32 weeks gestation presents with bony deformities as shown on the X-ray. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Rickets}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is caused by a deficiency in vitamin D.

This may also present with deformities such as genu varum.

fields.Text:
What two factors predispose to the development of a vitamin D deficiency?

{{c1::Dark::Light/Dark}} skin
{{c1::Premature}} birth

What preventative measure can be taken to decrease the risk of developing rickets in an exclusively breastfed infant?

Oral vitamin {{c1::D}} supplementation
fields.Back Extra: This is because breast milk is deficient in vitamin D3.

fields.Text:
What conditions are attributed to vitamin D deficiency?

{{c1::Rickets}} in children
{{c1::Osteomalacia}} in adults
Hypocalcemic {{c1::tetany}}

What causes hypercalcemia in patients with sarcoidosis?

Increased activation of vitamin {{c1::D}} by {{c1::epithelioid macrophages}} in {{c1::granulomas}}

What is the function of vitamin D at high and low levels in the bones?

At higher levels, vitamin D increases bone {{c1::resorption}}
At lower levels, vitamin D increases bone {{c1::mineralization}}

Deficiency of vitamin D may lead to what two electrolyte abnormalities?

{{c1::Hypocalcemia::Hypercalcemia/Hypocalcemia}}
{{c1::Hypophosphatemia::Hyperphosphatemia/Hypophosphatemia}}
fields.Back Extra: Vitamin D increases intestinal absorption of Ca2+ and PO43-.

fields.Text:
What is the storage form of vitamin D?

{{c1::25-OH D3}}
fields.Back Extra: Vitamin D2 and D3 are converted to 25-OH D3 and stored in the liver.

fields.Text:
What are the four main sources of vitamin D3?

Exposure of skin (stratum basale) to the {{c1::sun}}
{{c1::Milk}}
{{c1::Fish}}
{{c1::Plants}}

What are the three main dietary sources of vitamin D2?

{{c1::Plants}}
{{c1::Fungi}}
{{c1::Yeasts}}

What is the active form of vitamin D?

{{c1::1,25-(OH)2 D3}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as calcitriol.

fields.Text:
What are the four regulating factors detected in blood that might increase the production of 1,25-(OH)2 D3?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PTH
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} calcium
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} phosphate
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} 1,25-(OH)2 D3

What are five common causes of vitamin D deficiency in adults?

{{c1::Malabsorption}}
Insufficient {{c1::sun}} exposure
Poor {{c1::diet}}
Chronic {{c1::kidney::organ}} disease
Advanced {{c1::liver::organ}} disease

Why does primary hyperparathyroidism cause hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia?

It increases {{c1::calcium}} reabsorption
It decreases {{c1::phosphate}} reabsorption

An excess of what vitamin may cause hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, appetite loss, and stupor?

Vitamin {{c1::D}}

Which layer of skin is responsible for the production of vitamin D3 from exposure to the sun?

Stratum {{c1::basale}}

Where in the body is 25-OH D3 converted to its active form?

{{c1::Kidneys::Organ}}
fields.Back Extra: It is converted from 25-OH D3 to 1,25-(OH)2 D3.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiology behind the neurologic findings in vitamin E deficiency?

Demyelination of the posterior columns causes decreased {{c1::proprioception}} and decreased sensation of {{c1::vibration}}
Demyelination of the spinocerebellar tracts causes {{c1::ataxia}}

How does vitamin E protect neuronal membranes and red blood cells?

Vitamin E acts as an {{c1::antioxidant}}
fields.Back Extra: This is protective against free radical damage.

fields.Text:
How can vitamin E and vitamin B12 deficiency be distinguished when a patient presents with ataxia and decreased vibration sensation and proprioception?

In contrast to vitamin B12 deficiency, vitamin E deficiency will present with the following:

No {{c1::megaloblastic}} anemia
No {{c1::hypersegmented}} neutrophils
No elevated serum {{c1::methylmalonic acid}} levels

What is the likely cause of a hemorrhagic stroke in a patient being treated with warfarin who takes a vitamin E supplement?

Excess vitamin E alters the metabolism of vitamin {{c1::K}} → Enhanced {{c1::anticoagulant}} effects of warfarin → Increased risk of bleeding

What is a possible complication of excessive vitamin E supplementation in infants?

{{c1::Enterocolitis}}

What are the names of the two main forms of vitamin E?

{{c1::Tocopherol}}
{{c1::Tocotrienol}}

How may vitamin E deficiency present clinically?

{{c1::Acanthocytosis}}
{{c1::Hemolytic}} anemia
{{c1::Muscle}} weakness
Decreased {{c1::proprioception}}
Decreased {{c1::vibration}} sensation
{{c1::Ataxia}}

By what biochemical mechanism does vitamin K promote synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X?

Through {{c1::γ-carboxylation}} of {{c1::glutamic acid}} residues

Why might a patient develop vitamin K deficiency after prolonged antibiotic use?

Due to destruction of {{c1::intestinal microbiota}}
fields.Back Extra: Vitamin K is synthesized by intestinal microbiota.

fields.Text:
What is the main source of vitamin K in humans?

Synthesis by {{c1::intestinal bacteria}}

Which six clotting factors and proteins depend on vitamin K?

Clotting factors {{c1::II}}, {{c1::VII}}, {{c1::IX}}, and {{c1::X}}
Proteins {{c1::C}} and {{c1::S}}

A male neonate born at home has a spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage. What intervention could likely have prevented this problem?

Injection of vitamin {{c1::K}}
fields.Back Extra: This is not found in breast milk.

fields.Text:
What changes might be seen in the PT, aPTT, and bleeding time in a neonatal hemorrhage due to vitamin K deficiency?

{{c1::Increased}} PT
{{c1::Increased}} aPTT
{{c1::Normal}} bleeding time

Breastfed neonates are deficient in vitamin K for what two physiologic reasons?

{{c1::Breast milk}} does not contain vitamin K
Neonates have {{c1::sterile}} intestines

What are the key functions of zinc in the human body?

Involved in the activity of {{c1::100+::number}} enzymes
Important in the formation of {{c1::zinc fingers}}

Deficiency of which micronutrient can predispose an individual to alcoholic cirrhosis?

{{c1::Zinc}}

What symptoms are associated with a zinc deficiency?

Delayed {{c1::wound healing}}
{{c1::Hypogonadism::Hypergonadism/Hypogonadism}}
Reduced adult {{c1::hair}} growth
{{c1::Dysgeusia}}
{{c1::Anosmia}}

What is the diagnosis of the condition shown in the image in a malnourished patient with poor wound healing and impaired taste sensation?



{{c1::Zinc}} deficiency
fields.Back Extra: The image shows acrodermatitis enteropathica, which is caused by a defect in intestinal absorption of zinc.

fields.Text:
Why might a patient with zinc deficiency develop recurrent bacterial and fungal infections?

Zinc deficiency can cause {{c1::immunosuppression}}

What dermatologic condition is associated with impaired intestinal absorption of zinc?

{{c1::Acrodermatitis enteropathica}}

What is the mechanism for edema formation in a patient with kwashiorkor?

{{c1::Protein}} malnutrition → Decreased serum {{c1::albumin}} → Decreased plasma oncotic pressure → Edema

What condition results from caloric deficiency in the diet with no particular nutrients being absent?

{{c1::Marasmus}}

What condition does a protein deficiency in the diet cause?

{{c1::Kwashiorkor}}

What is the reason for fatty change seen in a liver biopsy specimen from a child with kwashiorkor?

Decreased {{c1::apolipoprotein}} synthesis secondary to {{c1::protein}} malnutrition → Fat deposition in the liver

What macronutrient is deficient in the diet of the child shown in the image?



{{c1::Protein}}

What is deficient in the diet of the child shown in the image?



{{c1::Calories}}

What are the primary findings in a patient with kwashiorkor?

{{c1::Malnutrition}}
{{c1::Edema}}
{{c1::Anemia}}
{{c1::Fatty}} liver
{{c1::Skin}} lesions

Fomepizole can be used to treat overdoses of which two toxic agents?

{{c1::Methanol}}
{{c1::Ethylene glycol}}

Disulfiram causes the accumulation of what molecule in ethanol metabolism, resulting in hangover-like symptoms?

{{c1::Acetaldehyde}}
fields.Back Extra: Disulfiram inhibits acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, leading to increased acetaldehyde.

fields.Text:
What happens to the rate of ethanol metabolism by alcohol dehydrogenase as more ethanol is consumed?

{{c1::No}} change in the rate of ethanol metabolism
fields.Back Extra: This is due to zero-order kinetics.

fields.Text:
What is the role of ethanol in antifreeze poisoning?

Alcohol dehydrogenase has a greater {{c1::affinity}} for ethanol than for ethylene glycol or methanol
fields.Back Extra: Hence, it can be used as a competitive inhibitor for ethylene glycol or methanol poisoning.

fields.Text:
What is the limiting reagent in alcohol metabolism?

{{c1::NAD+}}

What enzyme does fomepizole block to inhibit ethanol metabolism, and where in the cell does it act?

Fomepizole inhibits {{c1::alcohol dehydrogenase}} in the {{c1::cytosol}}

The breakdown of ethanol into acetate results in the generation of how many molecules of NADH?

{{c1::2}}

What is the final product of ethanol metabolism?

{{c1::Acetate}}
fields.Back Extra: This is produced in the mitochondria.

fields.Text:
What product is ethanol converted to in the cytosol?

{{c1::Acetaldehyde}}

What will measurements of reactive oxygen species and NADP+ levels show when ethanol is given to a subject with high CYP2E1 activity?

{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in reactive oxygen species
{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in NADP+
fields.Back Extra: CYP2E1 in microsomes converts ethanol into acetaldehyde, creating reactive oxygen species and NADP+ as byproducts.

fields.Text:
What happens to alcohol's rate of metabolism as a result of blocking catalase and administering ethanol?

It is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because catalase converts ethanol to acetaldehyde.

fields.Text:
In ethanol toxicity, the overproduction of lactic acid causes what metabolic disorder evident on lab findings?

{{c1::High anion gap metabolic acidosis}}

The high NADH/NAD+ ratio after ethanol ingestion causes shunting of pyruvate, oxaloacetic acid, acetyl-CoA, and dihydroxyacetone phosphate toward which biochemical products?

Pyruvate → {{c1::Lactate}}
Oxaloacetic acid → {{c1::Malate}}
Acetyl-CoA → {{c1::Ketoacids}} and {{c1::fatty acids}}
Dihydroxyacetone phosphate → {{c1::Glycerol-3-phosphate}}

What is the mechanism underlying hypoglycemia in chronic alcoholism?

Decrease in {{c1::oxaloacetic acid}} → Decrease in gluconeogenesis
fields.Back Extra: Ethanol metabolism leads to an increased NADH/NAD+ ratio in the liver, shunting oxaloacetic acid to malate.

fields.Text:
What enzyme does disulfiram act on to inhibit ethanol metabolism?

Disulfiram inhibits {{c1::acetaldehyde dehydrogenase}} in the mitochondria

What is the mechanism underlying hepatosteatosis in a patient with chronic alcoholism?

Increase in {{c1::NADH}}/{{c1::NAD+}} ratio → Increase in {{c1::glycerol-3-phosphate}} and {{c1::fatty acids}}, which combine to make triglycerides → Hepatosteatosis

In alcoholism, what is the mechanism for development of lactic acidosis?

Increase in {{c1::NADH}}/{{c1::NAD+}} ratio → Increase in conversion of pyruvate to lactate

What three physiologic reasons cause females to be more susceptible to the effects of alcohol than males?

{{c1::Smaller::Larger/Smaller}} body size
Lower percentage of {{c1::water}} in body weight
Less activity of gastric {{c1::alcohol dehydrogenase}}

Name the three enzymes involved in the conversion of ethanol to acetaldehyde and their respective locations within the cell.

CYP2E1 → {{c1::Microsome::Location}}
Alcohol dehydrogenase → {{c1::Cytosol::Location}}
Catalase → {{c1::Peroxisome::Location}}

Which enzyme category adds a hydroxyl group to a substrate?

{{c1::Hydroxylases}}

Which enzyme category relocates a functional group within a molecule?

{{c1::Mutases}}

Which enzyme category transfers carboxyl groups using biotin as a cofactor?

{{c1::Carboxylases}}

Dehydrogenases catalyze which type of reaction?

{{c1::Oxidation-reduction}} reactions

Which enzyme category removes a phosphate group from a substrate?

{{c1::Phosphatases}}

Which enzyme category adds an inorganic phosphate to a substrate without using ATP?

{{c1::Phosphorylases}}

Kinases catalyze what enzymatic process?

The transfer of a {{c1::phosphate}} group from a {{c1::high::high/low}}-energy molecule to a substrate

Which enzyme categories joins two molecules using a source of energy?

{{c1::Synthase}}
{{c1::Synthetase}}

What is the rate-limiting enzyme of fatty acid synthesis?

{{c1::Acetyl-CoA carboxylase}}

What is the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle?

{{c1::Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I}}

What are the important upregulators and downregulators of HMG-CoA reductase in cholesterol synthesis?

{{c1::Upregulators}} → Insulin, thyroxine, and estrogen
{{c1::Downregulators}} → Glucagon and cholesterol

What is the rate-limiting enzyme of ketogenesis?

{{c1::HMG-CoA synthase}}

What is the rate-limiting enzyme of fatty acid oxidation?

{{c1::Carnitine acyltransferase I}}

What is the rate-limiting enzyme of the hexose monophosphate shunt?

{{c1::Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase}}

What are the important upregulators and downregulators of the enzyme glycogen phosphorylase?

{{c1::Upregulators}} → AMP, epinephrine, and glucagon
{{c1::Downregulators}} → Glucose-6-phosphate, insulin, and ATP

What are the important reaction upregulators and downregulators of glycogenesis?

{{c1::Upregulators}} → Glucose-6-phosphate, insulin, and cortisol
{{c1::Downregulators}} → Epinephrine and glucagon

What is the rate-limiting enzyme of the tricarboxylic acid cycle?

{{c1::Isocitrate dehydrogenase}}

What is the rate-limiting enzyme of gluconeogenesis?

{{c1::Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1}}

What are the important reaction upregulators and downregulators of glycolysis?

{{c1::Upregulators}} → AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate
{{c1::Downregulators}} → ATP and citrate

What is the rate-limiting enzyme of de novo purine synthesis?

{{c1::Glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase}}

What is the rate-limiting enzyme of de novo pyrimidine synthesis?

{{c1::Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II}}

What is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis?

{{c1::Phosphofructokinase-1}}

What are the important reaction downregulators of the enzyme fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1 in gluconeogenesis?

{{c1::AMP}}
{{c1::Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate}}

What are the important reaction upregulators and downregulators of the enzyme isocitrate dehydrogenase in the tricarboxylic acid cycle?

{{c1::Upregulators}} → ADP
{{c1::Downregulators}} → ATP and NADH

What is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogenesis?

{{c1::Glycogen synthase}}

What are the important reaction upregulator and downregulator of the enzyme glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase in the hexose monophosphate shunt?

{{c1::Upregulator}} → NADP+
{{c1::Downregulator}} → NADPH

What are the important reaction upregulators and downregulators of the enzyme carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II in de novo pyrimidine synthesis?

{{c1::Upregulators}} → ATP and PRPP
{{c1::Downregulator}} → UTP

What are the important reaction downregulators of the enzyme glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase in de novo purine synthesis?

{{c1::AMP}}
{{c1::IMP}}
{{c1::GMP}}

What is the important reaction upregulator of the enzyme carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the urea cycle?

{{c1::N-acetylglutamate}}

What are the important reaction upregulators and downregulators of the enzyme acetyl-CoA carboxylase in fatty acid synthesis?

{{c1::Upregulators}} → Insulin and citrate
{{c1::Downregulators}} → Glucagon and palmitoyl-CoA

What is the important reaction downregulator of the enzyme carnitine acyltransferase I in fatty acid oxidation?

{{c1::Malonyl-CoA}}

What is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis?

{{c1::HMG-CoA reductase}}

What is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogenolysis?

{{c1::Glycogen phosphorylase}}

Where in the cell does ketogenesis occur?

{{c1::Mitochondria}}

Where in the cell does oxidative phosphorylation occur?

{{c1::Mitochondria}}

Where in the cell does cholesterol synthesis occur?

{{c1::Cytoplasm}}
fields.Back Extra: It utilizes the smooth endoplasmic reticulum.

fields.Text:
Name the three cellular reactions that occur in both the mitochondria and cytoplasm.

{{c1::Heme}} synthesis
{{c1::Urea}} cycle
{{c1::Gluconeogenesis}}

Where does protein synthesis occur in the cell?

{{c1::Cytoplasm}}
fields.Back Extra: It utilizes the rough endoplasmic reticulum and free ribosomes.

fields.Text:
Where in the cell are the enzymes of the hexose monophosphate shunt located?

{{c1::Cytoplasm}}

In which cellular locations does fatty acid oxidation and fatty acid synthesis occur?

Fatty acid oxidation occurs in the {{c1::mitochondria}}
Fatty acid synthesis occurs in the {{c1::cytoplasm}}

Where in the cell are the enzymes of the tricarboxylic acid cycle located?

{{c1::Mitochondria}}

Where in the cell does nucleotide synthesis take place?

{{c1::Cytoplasm}}

Where does acetyl-CoA production occur in the cell?

{{c1::Mitochondria}}

What enzyme converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate in cholesterol synthesis?

{{c1::HMG-CoA reductase}}

Propionyl-CoA can be synthesized from what four substrates?

{{c1::Threonine}}
{{c1::Methonine}}
{{c1::Odd}}-chain fatty acids
{{c1::Branched}}-chain amino acids

What cofactor is required for the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA?

Vitamin {{c1::B12}}

Which enzyme is responsible for converting propionyl-CoA into methylmalonyl-CoA?

{{c1::Propionyl-CoA carboxylase}}

Starting with CO2 and NH3, outline all the steps within the urea cycle.

CO2 and NH3 → {{c1::Carbamoyl phosphate}} → {{c1::Citrulline}}, which requires ornithine → {{c1::Argininosuccinate}}, which requires aspartate→ {{c1::Arginine}} or fumarate → {{c1::Ornithine}} → Urea, which requires water

Argininosuccinate produced in the urea cycle can be converted into which intermediate of the tricarboxylic acid cycle?

{{c1::Fumarate}}

The conversion of citrulline into argininosuccinate in the urea cycle requires what additional molecule, other than ATP?

{{c1::Aspartate}}

What molecule is produced as a byproduct of the conversion of arginine to ornithine in the urea cycle?

{{c1::Urea}}

An enzyme sequesters CO2 and NH3 within a cell. Why would production of citrulline within that cell decrease?

Conversion of ornithine to citrulline requires {{c1::carbamoyl phosphate}}
fields.Back Extra: This is synthesized from CO2 and NH3 via carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I.

fields.Text:
Which enzyme converts fructose-1-phosphate to dihydroxyacetone phosphate in the liver?

{{c1::Aldolase B}}

Which enzymes require TPP as a cofactor in the glycolysis, tricarboxylic acid cycle, hexose-monophosphate shunt, and lipid metabolism pathways?

{{c1::Transketolase}}
{{c1::Pyruvate dehydrogenase}}
{{c1::α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase}}

In the tricarboxylic acid cycle, what enzyme is responsible for converting isocitrate into α-ketoglutarate?

{{c1::Isocitrate dehydrogenase}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an important, irreversible point of regulation in the tricarboxylic acid cycle.

fields.Text:
Which enzyme converts α-ketoglutarate into succinyl-CoA in the citric acid cycle?

{{c1::α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase}}

Which enzyme converts oxaloacetate into citrate in the tricarboxylic acid cycle?

{{c1::Citrate synthase}}

Which enzyme converts phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate in glycolysis?

{{c1::Pyruvate kinase}}

Which enzyme converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA?

{{c1::Pyruvate dehydrogenase}}

What enzyme converts fructose-6-phosphate into fructose-1,6-bisphosphate in glycolysis?

{{c1::Phosphofructokinase-1}}

What two enzymes convert glucose into glucose-6-phosphate?

{{c1::Hexokinase}}
{{c1::Glucokinase}}

What enzyme drives glucose-6-phosphate into the hexose-monophosphate shunt by converting it into 6-phosphogluconolactone?

{{c1::Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase}}

A new anti-lipid agent secondarily increases both HMG-CoA and β-hydroxybutyrate levels. What enzyme might this novel agent inhibit?

{{c1::HMG-CoA reductase}}
fields.Back Extra: This prevents production of mevalonate and shunts it towards β-hydroxybutyrate production.

fields.Text:
Glycerol, the end product of lipid metabolism, is converted to what molecule that can become either glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate or fructose-1,6-bisphosphate?

{{c1::Dihydroxyacetone phosphate}}

What enzyme deficiency is responsible for severe galactosemia?

{{c1::Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase}} deficiency

Outline the steps by which glucose-6-phosphate may be converted to glycogen.

Glucose-6-phosphate → {{c1::Glucose-1-phosphate}} → {{c1::UDP-glucose}} → Glycogen

Which two enzymes are responsible for ultimately converting galactose to glucose-1-phosphate?

{{c1::Galactokinase}}
{{c1::Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase}}

The irreversible conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6,-bisphosphate is mediated by which enzyme?

{{c1::Phosphofructokinase-1}}

Fructose can enter glycolysis by two pathways. Outline them.

Fructose → {{c1::Fructose-1-phosphate}} → Either {{c1::dihydroxyacetone phosphate}} or {{c1::glyceraldehyde}} → Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate

Outline the steps that ultimately convert glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate into pyruvate in glycolysis.

Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate → {{c1::1,3-bisphosphoglycerate}} → {{c1::3-phosphoglycerate}} → {{c1::2-phosphoglycerate}} → {{c1::Phosphoenolpyruvate}} → Pyruvate

What are the two fates of oxaloacetate after it is generated?

Enters the {{c1::tricarboxylic acid}} cycle for oxidative phosphorylation
Converted to {{c1::phosphoenolpyruvate}} for gluconeogenesis

What enzymes serve as irreversible points of regulation in the conversion of pyruvate to phosphoenolpyruvate?

{{c1::Pyruvate carboxylase}}
{{c1::Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase}}

What are the three intermediates in the conversion of acetyl-CoA into β-hydroxybutyrate?

{{c1::Acetoacetyl-CoA}}
{{c1::HMG-CoA}}
{{c1::Acetoacetate}}

In the tricarboxylic acid cycle, the enzyme citrate synthase produces citrate from acetyl-CoA and what other substrate?

{{c1::Oxaloacetate}}

Glucose-6-phosphate is converted into what product to enter the hexose-monophosphate shunt?

{{c1::6-phosphogluconolactone}}

Glucose-6-phosphate is converted into what product to proceed with glycolysis?

{{c1::Fructose-6-phosphate}}

Glucose-6-phosphate is converted into what product to proceed with glycogenesis?

{{c1::Glucose-1-phosphate}}

What enzyme is impaired in fructose intolerance?

{{c1::Aldolase B}}

What enzyme converts glucose-6-phosphate into glucose?

{{c1::Glucose-6-phosphatase}}

What enzyme converts fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into fructose-6-phosphate?

{{c1::Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1}}

Which enzyme converts fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to dihydroxyacetone phosphate in muscle?

{{c1::Aldolase A}}

Argininosuccinate can be converted into both fumarate and what other product found in the urea cycle?

{{c1::Arginine}}

What enzyme is impaired in essential fructosuria?

{{c1::Fructokinase}}

In the urea cycle, what is the key regulatory enzyme that converts ornithine to citrulline?

{{c1::Ornithine transcarbamylase}}

What enzyme deficiency is associated with mild galactosemia?

{{c1::Galactokinase}} deficiency

Which three enzymes require biotin as a cofactor in general metabolic processes?

{{c1::Pyruvate carboxylase}}
{{c1::Acetyl-CoA carboxylase}}
{{c1::Propionyl-CoA carboxylase}}

What is the net gain in ATP molecules from anaerobic glycolysis in a single glucose molecule?

{{c1::2}}
fields.Back Extra: NADH cannot be used to generate energy without oxygen.

fields.Text:
A male with garlic breath is noted to have arsenic poisoning from groundwater. How many ATP molecules will he produce via glycolysis?

{{c1::0}}
fields.Back Extra: Arsenic causes glycolysis to produce 0 net ATP molecules.

fields.Text:
What supplies the energy to turn substrate into product in energetically unfavorable reactions?

{{c1::ATP hydrolysis}}

How many ATP molecules are produced per 1 glucose molecule via the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle?

{{c1::30}} ATP molecules

How many ATP molecules are produced per 1 glucose molecule via the malate-aspartate shuttle pathway?

{{c1::32}} ATP molecules

What organ tissues utilize the malate-aspartate shuttle during aerobic metabolism?

{{c1::Heart}}
{{c1::Liver}}

What organ tissue utilizes the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle pathway during glucose metabolism?

{{c1::Muscle}}

What compounds are used as single-carbon donors in various reactions?

{{c1::Tetrahydrofolates}}

Acyl groups are carried in the active form by what two carrier molecules?

{{c1::CoA}}
{{c1::Lipoamide}}

Which activated carrier molecule donates aldehyde groups?

{{c1::TPP}}
fields.Back Extra: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is the active form of thiamine.

fields.Text:
What is the activated carrier molecule for methyl groups?

{{c1::S-adenosylmethionine}}

What is the activated carrier for phosphoryl groups?

{{c1::ATP}}

What are the carrier molecules for electrons?

{{c1::NADH}}
{{c1::NADPH}}
{{c1::FADH2}}

What chemical compound does biotin carry?

{{c1::CO2}}

The flavin nucleotide FAD is derived from what vitamin?

Vitamin {{c1::B2}}

What is the function of NAD+ in catabolic processes?

Functions as an {{c1::electron acceptor}} to carry reducing equivalents away as {{c1::NADH}}

In which four metabolic processes is NADPH consumed?

{{c1::Anabolic::Anabolic/Catabolic}} processes
{{c1::Respiratory burst}}
{{c1::Cytochrome P-450}} system
{{c1::Glutathione reductase}}

What is a byproduct of the hexose-monophosphate shunt that is used in anabolic processes in the body?

{{c1::NADPH}}

The nicotinamides NAD+ and NADP+ are derived from what vitamin?

Vitamin {{c1::B3}}

What enzyme sequesters glucose in the peripheral tissues, even at low blood glucose concentrations?

{{c1::Hexokinase}}

How does insulin affect the action of hexokinase and glucokinase?

Insulin induces {{c1::glucokinase}}, but not {{c1::hexokinase}}

Does glucokinase or hexokinase have a greater capacity to convert glucose to glucose-6-phoshate?

{{c1::Glucokinase}}

Which glucose-phosphorylating enzyme is feedback-inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate?

{{c1::Hexokinase}}

Does glucokinase or hexokinase have a higher Km?

{{c1::Glucokinase}}

In which organs/tissues is glucokinase expressed?

{{c1::Liver}}
{{c1::β}} cells of the {{c1::pancreas}}

What enzymatic reaction is catalyzed by the enzymes hexokinase and glucokinase?

Glucose → {{c1::Glucose-6-phosphate}}

In which organs/tissues is hexokinase found?

Hexokinase is found in {{c1::most}} tissues
fields.Back Extra: Exceptions include the liver and the β cells of the pancreas.

fields.Text:
What disease states are associated with glucokinase deficiency?

{{c1::Gestational diabetes}}
{{c1::Maturity onset diabetes of the young}}

Glucokinase is influenced by feedback inhibition of what substrate of glycolysis?

{{c1::Fructose-6-phosphate}}

In glycolysis, which two reactions generate ATP?

1,3-bisphosphoglycerate → {{c1::3-phosphoglycerate}}
Phosphoenolpyruvate → {{c1::Pyruvate}}

In glycolysis, the conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate is irreversibly catalyzed by which enzyme?

{{c1::Pyruvate kinase}}

What enzyme catalyzes the only reversible reaction in glycolysis that produces ATP?

{{c1::Phosphoglycerate kinase}}

What compounds inhibit the reaction catalyzed by phosphofructokinase-1?

{{c1::ATP}}
{{c1::Citrate}}

Which compounds inhibit the reaction catalyzed by pyruvate kinase?

{{c1::ATP}}
{{c1::Alanine}}
{{c1::Glucagon}}

What enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step in glycolysis?

{{c1::Phosphofructokinase-1}}

What are the two steps in glycolysis that require ATP?

Glucose → {{c1::Glucose-6-phosphate}}
Fructose-6-phosphate → {{c1::Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate}}

What are the net products of glycolysis?

2 {{c1::pyruvate}}
2 {{c1::ATP}}
2 {{c1::NADH}}
2 {{c1::H+}}
2 {{c1::H2O}}

Where in the cell does glycolysis occur?

{{c1::Cytoplasm}}

What compounds inhibit the conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate?

{{c1::Glucose-6-phosphate}} inhibits hexokinase
{{c1::Fructose-6-phosphate}} inhibits glucokinase

What compounds promote the reaction catalyzed by phosphofructokinase-1?

{{c1::AMP}}
{{c1::Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate}}

How does fasting affect the action of fructose bisphosphatase-2 and phosphofructokinase-2?

Increase in {{c1::glucagon}} → Increase in {{c1::cAMP}} → Increase in {{c1::protein kinase A}} activity → {{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in fructose bisphosphatase-2 activity and {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} in phosphofructokinase-2 activity → Decrease in glycolysis and increase in gluconeogenesis

How does insulin affect the action of fructose bisphosphatase-2 and phosphofructokinase-2?

Insulin → {{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in cAMP → {{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in protein kinase A activity → {{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in fructose bisphosphatase-2 activity and {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} in phosphofructokinase-2 activity → Increase in glycolysis and decrease in gluconeogenesis

Which enzyme that regulates the level of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is active in the fasting state?

{{c1::Fructose bisphosphatase-2}}
fields.Back Extra: This increases gluconeogenesis and decreases glycolysis.

fields.Text:
The fed state is associated with increased activity of which enzyme that regulates the level of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate?

{{c1::Phosphofructokinase-2}}

What reaction is catalyzed by fructose bisphosphatase-2?

{{c1::Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate}} → {{c1::Fructose-6-phosphate}}

In gluconeogenesis, what enzyme catalyzes fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to fructose-6-phosphate?

{{c1::Fructose bisphosphatase-1}}

The enzyme phosphofructokinase-2 catalyzes which reaction?

{{c1::Fructose-6-phosphate}} → {{c1::Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate}}

What are the names of the 2 components of the bifunctional enzyme involved in fructose-2,6-bisphosphate metabolism?

{{c1::Fructose bisphosphatase-2}}
{{c1::Phosphofructokinase-2}}

What compound promotes the activity of phosphofructokinase-1?

{{c1::Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate}}

Which enzyme catalyzes the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate?

{{c1::Phosphofructokinase-1}}

What enzyme reverses directionality of the bifunctional enzyme involved in fructose-2,6-bisphosphate metabolism?

{{c1::Protein kinase A}}

In a patient with arsenic poisoning, what changes are typically seen on an ECG?

{{c1::QT prolongation}}

Pyruvate dehydrogenase is active in which metabolic state?

It is active in the {{c1::fed::fed/fasting}} state

What are the similarities of the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex and the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?

α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase uses the same {{c1::cofactors}} with a similar substrate and action

Which 5 cofactors are required for the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?

{{c1::TPP}}
{{c1::Lipoic acid}}
{{c1::CoA}}
{{c1::FAD}}
{{c1::NAD+}}

What is the mechanism of arsenic poisoning?

Inhibits {{c1::lipoic acid}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a cofactor for the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.

fields.Text:
Where is the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex found in the cell?

{{c1::Mitochondria}}

The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex links what 2 metabolic processes?

{{c1::Glycolysis}}
{{c1::TCA}} cycle

The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is activated by what factors?

Increased {{c1::ADP}}
Increased {{c1::Ca2+}}
Increased {{c1::NAD+}}/{{c1::NADH}} ratio

What is the reaction of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?

{{c1::Pyruvate}} + {{c1::NAD+}} + {{c1::CoA}} → {{c1::Acetyl-CoA}} + {{c1::CO2}} + {{c1::NADH}}

What are the clinical findings of arsenic poisoning?

{{c1::Pigmentary skin}} changes
{{c1::Skin}} cancer
{{c1::Vomiting}}
{{c1::Diarrhea}}
{{c1::QT prolongation}}

What is the treatment for pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency?

Increased consumption of {{c1::ketogenic}} foods
fields.Back Extra: This includes foods rich in lysine and leucine, or with high fat content.

fields.Text:
In pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency, the excess pyruvate is metabolized into what byproducts?

{{c1::Lactate}}
{{c1::Alanine}}

What are the 3 major clinical findings of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency?

Increased serum {{c1::alanine}} beginning in infancy
{{c1::Lactic acidosis}}
{{c1::Neurologic}} defects

What is the pattern of inheritance for pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency?

{{c1::X-linked}}

Where in the cell do pyruvate dehydrogenase and pyruvate carboxylase act?

{{c1::Mitochondria}}
fields.Back Extra: The effects of alanine aminotransferase and lactate dehydrogenase occur in the cytosol.

fields.Text:
During pyruvate metabolism, which enzyme produces CO2 as a byproduct?

{{c1::Pyruvate dehydrogenase}}

Pyruvate is converted into which 2 molecules that enter the TCA cycle?

{{c1::Acetyl-CoA}}
{{c1::Oxaloacetate}}

In anaerobic glycolysis, pyruvate is converted to lactate by which enzyme?

{{c1::Lactate dehydrogenase}}

Of the 4 pyruvate metabolic pathyways, which requires ATP and CO2?

{{c1::Pyruvate carboxylase}}

What is the end product of the pyruvate carboxylase pathway that can be used to replenish the TCA cycle or be used in gluconeogenesis?

{{c1::Oxaloacetate}}

What enzyme catalyzes the conversion of pyruvate to alanine?

{{c1::Alanine aminotransferase}}

Which amino acid carries amino groups from muscle to the liver?

{{c1::Alanine}}

There are 4 primary pathways of pyruvate metabolism. What products are ultimately produced from each pathway?

{{c1::Alanine}}
{{c1::Oxaloacetate}}
{{c1::Acetyl-CoA}}
{{c1::Lactate}}

Lactate dehydrogenase is a major active enzyme in what organs and cells?

{{c1::Kidney medulla}}
{{c1::Testes}}
{{c1::Lens}}
{{c1::Cornea}}
{{c1::Red blood}} cells
{{c1::White blood}} cells

A patient has vitamin B3 deficiency. What enzymes of pyruvate metabolism will be affected in this patient?

{{c1::Lactate dehydrogenase}}
{{c1::Pyruvate dehydrogenase}}

Of the 4 pyruvate metabolic pathways, which requires NADH?

{{c1::Lactate dehydrogenase}}

Of the 4 pyruvate metabolic pathways, which requires NAD+?

{{c1::Pyruvate dehydrogenase}}

What are the associated cofactors of alanine aminotransferase, pyruvate carboxylase, and lactic acid dehydrogenase?

Alanine aminotransferase = Vitamin {{c1::B6}}
Pyruvate carboxylase = Vitamin {{c1::B7}}
Lactic acid dehydrogenase = Vitamin {{c1::B3}}

Which enzyme facilitates the end of anaerobic glycolysis?

{{c1::Lactate dehydrogenase}}

Name the TCA cycle intermediate between fumarate and oxaloacetate.

{{c1::Malate}}

Citrate enters the TCA cycle and eventually transforms into a product that inhibits α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Name this product.

{{c1::Succinyl-CoA}}

What is the order of substrates of the TCA cycle after acetyl-CoA enters?

{{c1::Citrate}}
{{c1::Isocitrate}}
{{c1::α-ketoglutarate}}
{{c1::Succinyl-CoA}}
{{c1::Succinate}}
{{c1::Fumarate}}
{{c1::Malate}}
{{c1::Oxaloacetate}}

Where in the cell does the TCA cycle take place?

{{c1::Mitochondria}}

What intermediate of the TCA cycle provides negative feedback to α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase to inhibit its function?

{{c1::Succinyl-CoA}}

Which cofactors are required by the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex?

{{c1::Lipoic acid}}
Vitamin {{c1::B1}}
Vitamin {{c1::B2}}
Vitamin {{c1::B3}}
Vitamin {{c1::B5}}

At which steps in the TCA cycle is NADH produced?

{{c1::Isocitrate}} → {{c1::α-ketoglutarate}}
{{c1::α-ketoglutarate}} → {{c1::Succinyl-CoA}}
{{c1::Malate}} → {{c1::Oxaloacetate}}

In the TCA cycle, ATP inhibits which 3 enzymes?

{{c1::Citrate synthase}}
{{c1::Isocitrate dehydrogenase}}
{{c1::α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase}}

In the TCA cycle, which steps produce CO2?

{{c1::Isocitrate}} → {{c1::α-ketoglutarate}}
{{c1::α-ketoglutarate}} → {{c1::Succinyl-CoA}}

How many ATP molecules are produced during 1 turn of the TCA cycle?

{{c1::10}} ATP for each acetyl-CoA

In the TCA cycle, which compounds inhibit isocitrate dehydrogenase?

{{c1::ATP}}
{{c1::NADH}}

How many NADH molecules are produced during one turn of the TCA cycle?

{{c1::3}}

Which 3 enzymes in the TCA cycle are irreversible?

{{c1::Citrate synthase}}
{{c1::Isocitrate dehydrogenase}}
{{c1::α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase}}

How many FADH2 molecules are produced during 1 turn of the TCA cycle?

{{c1::1}}

How many CO2 molecules are produced during 1 turn of the TCA cycle?

{{c1::2}}

In the TCA cycle, which compound activates isocitrate dehydrogenase?

{{c1::ADP}}

How many ATP molecules are produced from one glucose molecule in the TCA cycle?

{{c1::20}} ATP

At which step in the TCA cycle is GTP produced?

{{c1::Succinyl-CoA}} → {{c1::Succinate}}

At which step in the TCA cycle is FADH2 produced?

{{c1::Succinate}} → {{c1::Fumarate}}

What 3 compounds inhibit the activity of pyruvate dehydrogenase?

{{c1::ATP}}
{{c1::Acetyl-CoA}}
{{c1::NADH}}

How much GTP is produced in the TCA cycle?

{{c1::1}} GTP

What are the products of the enzymatic activity of pyruvate dehydrogenase on pyruvate?

{{c1::Acetyl-CoA}} (2)
{{c1::CO2}} (1)
{{c1::NADH}} (1)

To lose weight, a man takes 2,4-dinitrophenol. He is hospitalized with hyperthermia. What is the mechanism of his hyperthermia?

2,4-dinitrophenol causes {{c1::H+}} ions to leak back into the matrix → {{c1::ATP}} production becomes inefficient
O2 consumption increases, but {{c1::ATP}} synthesis ceases → Creates heat

What physiologic change is observed as a direct consequence of aspirin's effect on the electron transport chain?

{{c1::Hyperthermia}}
fields.Back Extra: Aspirin is an uncoupling agent that produces heat due to continued electron transport, although ATP synthesis has stopped.

fields.Text:
What is the common mechanism by which 2,4-dinitrophenol and aspirin overdose affect ATP production?

Both inhibit ATP synthesis by {{c1::increasing::increasing/decreasing}} mitochondrial membrane permeability → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} proton gradient and {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} O2 consumption

How does oligomycin affect ATP production in the electron transport chain?

Inhibits mitochondrial {{c1::ATP synthase}}
fields.Back Extra: This stops the electron transport chain and results in an increased proton gradient.

fields.Text:
What are the 3 direct electron transport inhibitors of complex IV?

{{c1::Cyanide}}
{{c1::Carbon monoxide}}
{{c1::Azide}}

How does cyanide poisoning affect ATP production in the electron transport chain?

Cyanide inhibits electron transport at complex {{c1::IV}} → {{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} the proton gradient → Blocks ATP synthesis

How does the passage of electrons from NADH and FADH2 produce ATP?

It results in a {{c1::proton gradient}} through which oxidative phosphorylation produces ATP

Why does FADH2 produce fewer molecules of ATP than NADH?

FADH2 enters the electron transport chain at a {{c1::lower::higher/lower}} energy level

How many ATP molecules are produced from 1 NADH molecule during oxidative phosphorylation?

{{c1::2.5}} ATP molecules

Electrons carried by NADH created in glycolysis enter the mitochondria via which 2 shuttles?

{{c1::Malate-aspartate}} shuttle
{{c1::Glycerol-3-phosphate}} shuttle

How many ATP molecules can be produced from one FADH2 molecule during oxidative phosphorylation?

{{c1::1.5}} ATP molecules

What compound directly inhibits complex I?

{{c1::Rotenone}}

Which compound directly inhibits complex III?

{{c1::Antimycin A}}

What role does thermogenin play in white and brown fat?

Thermogenin can act as an {{c1::uncoupling}} agent and produce {{c1::heat}}
fields.Back Extra: Brown fat has more mitochondria and therefore produces more heat than white fat.

fields.Text:
List the 6 most common inhibitors of the electron transport chain.

{{c1::2,4-dinitrophenol}}
{{c1::Rotenone}}
{{c1::Antimycin A}}
{{c1::Cyanide}}
{{c1::Carbon monoxide}}
{{c1::Oligomycin}}

What enzyme produces ATP as the end product of oxidative phosphorylation?

{{c1::ATP synthase}}

What are the inhibitors of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1?

{{c1::Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate}}
{{c1::AMP}}

Name the 4 enzymes in gluconeogenesis whose actions are irreversible.

{{c1::Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1}}
{{c1::Glucose-6-phosphatase}}
{{c1::Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase}}
{{c1::Pyruvate carboxylase}}

Why are even-chain fatty acids unable to produce new glucose?

Their metabolism yields only {{c1::acetyl-CoA}} equivalents

What is the role of odd-chain fatty acids in gluconeogenesis?

The metabolism of odd-chain fatty acids produces one {{c1::propionyl-CoA}}
fields.Back Extra: This can enter the TCA cycle as succinyl-CoA and undergo gluconeogenesis.

fields.Text:
What 2 organs or tissues, other than the liver, contain gluconeogenic enzymes?

{{c1::Kidneys}}
{{c1::Intestinal}} epithelium

A 3-year-old boy has a genetic deficiency of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase. What is his primary symptom?

{{c1::Hypoglycemia}}

Why is muscle unable to participate in gluconeogenesis?

Muscle lacks {{c1::glucose-6-phosphatase}}

In which organ does gluconeogenesis primarily occur?

{{c1::Liver}}

In gluconeogenesis, the production of glucose occurs via an enzyme found in which cellular organelle?

{{c1::Endoplasmic reticulum}}

In gluconeogenesis, which enzyme reaction is activated by acetyl-CoA?

{{c1::Pyruvate}} → {{c1::Oxaloacetate}}
fields.Back Extra: The enzyme involved is pyruvate carboxylase.

fields.Text:
In gluconeogenesis, which reaction requires GTP?

{{c1::Oxaloacetate}} → {{c1::Phosphoenolpyruvate}}

Which 2 irreversible steps of gluconeogenesis occur in the cytosol?

{{c1::Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate}} → {{c1::Fructose-6-phosphate}}
{{c1::Oxaloacetate}} → {{c1::Phosphoenolpyruvate}}

The conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate requires which 2 cofactors?

{{c1::ATP}}
{{c1::Biotin}}

In which organelle is pyruvate carboxylase found?

{{c1::Mitochondria}}

A patient is taking primaquine and dapsone, which both increase oxidative stress. Where will the pentose phosphate pathway be upregulated in response?

{{c1::Red blood}} cells

Besides the liver and adrenal cortex, what other site of fatty acid or steroid synthesis has high pentose phosphate pathway activity?

{{c1::Lactating mammary}} glands

What is the function of NADPH in RBCs?

It reduces {{c1::glutathione}}

In what phase of the HMP shunt are phosphopentose isomerase and transketolase used?

{{c1::Nonoxidative}} phase

What vitamin is required as a cofactor in the pentose phosphate pathway and in which phase?

Vitamin {{c1::B1}} in the {{c1::nonoxidative}} phase

How many ATP molecules are used and produced by the HMP shunt?

{{c1::0}} ATP molecules

What is the rate-limiting enzyme in the HMP shunt?

{{c1::Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase}}

What are the 2 phases of the HMP shunt?

Irreversible {{c1::oxidative}} phase
Reversible {{c1::nonoxidative}} phase

Which substrate initiates the oxidative reaction in the pentose phosphate pathway?

{{c1::Glucose-6-phosphate}}

What molecule acts as an inhibitor of the oxidative phase of the HMP shunt?

{{c1::NADPH}}

The pentose phosphate pathway is the major source of which 2 molecules required for cellular processes?

{{c1::NADPH}}
{{c1::Ribose}}

Where does each phase of the HMP shunt occur?

Oxidative phase occurs in the {{c1::cytoplasm}}
Nonoxidative phase occurs in the {{c1::cytoplasm}}

What are the 3 products of the nonoxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway?

{{c1::Ribose-5-phosphate}}
{{c1::Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate}}
{{c1::Fructose-6-phosphate}}

What is the most common cause of hemolysis in a patient with underlying glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency?

{{c1::Infection}}

What enzyme catalyzes the conversion of peroxide to water?

{{c1::Glutathione peroxidase}}

In a patient with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency who underwent a splenectomy, how might the appearance of a blood smear change?

More {{c1::Heinz bodies}}
Fewer {{c1::bite}} cells

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase changes glucose-6-phosphate into which substrate?

{{c1::6-phosphogluconolactone}}

What form of inheritance does glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency follow?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

Peripheral blood smear obtained from a patient with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is likely to show what features?

{{c1::Heinz bodies}}
{{c1::Bite}} cells

Which enzyme deficiency is most common in humans?

{{c1::Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase}} deficiency

Why may patients become anemic after ingesting oxidizing agents such as fava beans, sulfonamide drugs, nitrofurantoin, primaquine/chloroquine, or antituberculosis drugs?

Patients with a {{c1::glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase}} deficiency have a poor ability to neutralize oxidizing agents due to an inability to create {{c1::NADPH}}

Which substance detoxifies free radicals and peroxides in the cell?

{{c1::Glutathione}}

What are Heinz bodies composed of?

{{c1::Denatured globin chains}}
fields.Back Extra: These subsequently precipitate within RBCs undergoing oxidative stress.

fields.Text:
The enzyme glutathione reductase uses which substrate to reduce glutathione?

{{c1::NADPH}}

Could a child have essential fructosuria if neither of the parents do?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Essential fructosuria has an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.

fields.Text:
Can urine tests be used to definitively diagnose hereditary fructose intolerance?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: The urine dipstick will be negative as it detects only glucose.

fields.Text:
What enzyme pathway becomes primary for converting fructose to fructose-6-phosphate in essential fructosuria?

{{c1::Hexokinase}}

What is the treatment for aldolase B deficiency?

Decreased intake of {{c1::fructose}}
Decreased intake of {{c1::sucrose}}
Decreased intake of {{c1::sorbitol}}

What enzyme is defective in essential fructosuria?

{{c1::Fructokinase}}

Is essential fructosuria or hereditary fructose intolerance more clinically significant?

{{c1::Hereditary fructose intolerance}}
fields.Back Extra: Fructose is not trapped in essential fructosuria.

fields.Text:
What enzyme is deficient in hereditary fructose intolerance?

{{c1::Aldolase B}}

Hereditary fructose intolerance shows what form of inheritance?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}
