In a patient with hereditary fructose intolerance, the accumulation of what substrate results in decreased available phosphate?

{{c1::Fructose-1-phosphate}}

What two metabolic pathways are inhibited in patients with hereditary fructose intolerance as a result of depletion of available phosphate?

{{c1::Glycogenolysis}}
{{c1::Gluconeogenesis}}

What intermediate in fructose metabolism directly feeds into glycolysis, thereby bypassing the rate-limiting step of phosphofructokinase?

{{c1::Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate}}

What enzyme converts dihydroxyacetone phosphate to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate?

{{c1::Triose phosphate isomerase}}

What enzyme converts glyceraldehyde to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate?

{{c1::Triose kinase}}

Which disease results from deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase?

{{c1::Classic galactosemia}}

What enzyme catalyzes production of galactitol?

{{c1::Aldose reductase}}

What two milestone abnormalities might be present in a toddler with recently diagnosed galactokinase deficiency?

Failure to {{c1::track}} objects
Failure to develop a {{c1::social smile}}

What cofactor is required for the conversion of galactose-1-phosphate to glucose-1-phosphate?

{{c1::UDP-glucose}}

Severe galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency results in the depletion of which molecule?

{{c1::Phosphate}}

What symptoms are associated with classic galactosemia?

Failure to {{c1::thrive}}
{{c1::Jaundice}}
{{c1::Hepatomegaly}}
{{c1::Cataracts}}
{{c1::Intellectual}} disability when infant begins feeding
Risk for neonatal {{c1::Escherichia coli}} sepsis is increased

What is the treatment for classic galactosemia?

Exclusion of {{c1::galactose}} and {{c1::lactose}} from the diet

In galactose metabolism, a block in the conversion of galactose to galactose-1-phosphate is caused by what disease?

{{c1::Galactokinase}} deficiency

In galactose metabolism, galactose-1-phosphate is converted to glucose-1-phosphate by which enzyme?

{{c1::Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase}}

What is the inheritance pattern of galactokinase deficiency and classic galactosemia?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}
fields.Back Extra: This is like most enzymatic disorders.

fields.Text:
In classic galactosemia, the buildup of which substance causes damage to organs, especially the lens of the eye?

{{c1::Galactitol}}

What infantile enzyme deficiency results in cataracts and galactose in both the blood and urine?

{{c1::Galactokinase}} deficiency

Does classic galactosemia or galactokinase deficiency have milder symptoms?

{{c1::Galactokinase deficiency}}

Which enzyme regenerates UDP-glucose from UDP-galactose?

{{c1::4-epimerase}}

When would you expect the features of classic galactosemia to manifest in an infant?

Once the infant starts {{c1::feeding}}
fields.Back Extra: Both breast milk and routine formula contain lactose.

fields.Text:
Besides glucose, what other sugar is also converted to its respective osmotically active alcohol form via aldose reductase?

{{c1::Galactose}}

What cofactor is used by aldose reductase?

{{c1::NADPH}}

Why does excess blood glucose damage the eyes, nerves, and kidneys, but not other organs such as the liver, ovaries, and seminal vesicles?

The retinas, kidneys, and nerves lack {{c1::sorbitol dehydrogenase}}
fields.Back Extra: Hence, the trapped sorbitol builds up, causing osmotic damage.

fields.Text:
How is sorbitol cleared from cells in some tissues?

Conversion of sorbitol to {{c1::fructose}} by {{c1::sorbitol dehydrogenase}}

Glucose is converted to sorbitol, its alcohol counterpart, via what enzyme?

{{c1::Aldose reductase}}

What is the cofactor used by the enzyme sorbitol dehydrogenase?

{{c1::NAD+}}

What three tissues have both aldolase reductase and sorbitol dehydrogenase?

{{c1::Liver}}
{{c1::Ovaries}}
{{c1::Seminal vesicles}}

Which enzyme is primarily involved in sorbitol metabolism in the lens?

{{c1::Aldose reductase}}

Cells in what three tissues have only aldose reductase?

{{c1::Retina}}
{{c1::Kidney}}
{{c1::Schwann}} cells

Where does lactase function in the gastrointestinal tract?

Intestinal {{c1::brush border}}

What might be noted on testing of a stool sample obtained from a patient with lactase deficiency?

Decreased stool {{c1::pH}}

What are the causes of secondary lactase deficiency?

Loss of intestinal brush border caused by {{c1::gastroenteritis}}
{{c1::Autoimmune}} disease

What would an intestinal biopsy specimen from a patient with hereditary lactose intolerance show?

{{c1::Normal}} mucosa

What are the clinical features of lactase deficiency?

{{c1::Flatulence}}
{{c1::Bloating}}
{{c1::Cramps}}
{{c1::Osmotic}} diarrhea

What is the treatment for lactase deficiency?

Dietary avoidance of {{c1::lactose}}-containing products
Replacement of lactase in {{c1::pills}}

Which groups of people tend to be lactase deficient in adulthood because of the absence of a lactase-persistent allele?

{{c1::Asians}}
{{c1::Africans}}
{{c1::Native Americans}}

Lactase breaks down lactose into which monosaccharides?

{{c1::Galactose}}
{{c1::Glucose}}

What finding is expected on hydrogen breath testing in a patient with lactase deficiency?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} hydrogen levels
fields.Back Extra: This is due to increased fermentation of undigested lactose by colonic bacteria.

fields.Text:
Which amino acid is most basic?

{{c1::Arginine}}

Which basic amino acid has no charge at body pH?

{{c1::Histidine}}

Name the four essential amino acids that are both glucogenic and ketogenic.

{{c1::Isoleucine}}
{{c1::Phenylalanine}}
{{c1::Threonine}}
{{c1::Tryptophan}}

Name the amino acids that are basic.

{{c1::Histidine}}
{{c1::Lysine}}
{{c1::Arginine}}

Which two acidic amino acids are both negatively charged at body pH?

{{c1::Aspartic acid}}
{{c1::Glutamic acid}}

Which two amino acids are increased in histones?

{{c1::Arginine}}
{{c1::Lysine}}

Which two amino acids are additionally essential for a growing child?

{{c1::Arginine}}
{{c1::Histidine}}

Name three essential glucogenic amino acids.

{{c1::Methionine}}
{{c1::Histidine}}
{{c1::Valine}}

Name the nine essential amino acids.

{{c1::Phenylalanine}}
{{c1::Valine}}
{{c1::Tryptophan}}
{{c1::Threonine}}
{{c1::Isoleucine}}
{{c1::Methionine}}
{{c1::Histidine}}
{{c1::Leucine}}
{{c1::Lysine}}

Which amino acid isomer is found in the human body?

{{c1::L}}-amino acids

Name the two purely ketogenic amino acids.

{{c1::Leucine}}
{{c1::Lysine}}

What are the sources for the amino groups in urea?

{{c1::Aspartate}}
{{c1::NH3}}

What two precursors are converted by argininosuccinate synthetase into argininosuccinate?

{{c1::Citrulline}}
{{c1::Aspartate}}

In the urea cycle, ornithine combines with carbamoyl phosphate to form which compound?

{{c1::Citrulline}}

What two compounds are formed by the action of argininosuccinate lyase on argininosuccinate in the urea cycle?

{{c1::Arginine}}
{{c1::Fumarate}}

In what organ does the urea cycle occur?

{{c1::Liver}}

What are the two energy-requiring steps in the urea cycle, and how many ATP molecules does each step require?

CO2 + NH3 → {{c1::Carbamoyl phosphate}} (2 ATP molecules)
Aspartate + Citrulline → {{c1::Argininosuccinate}} (1 ATP molecule)

What is the allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I?

{{c1::N-acetylglutamate}}

Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step in the urea cycle?

{{c1::Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I}}

The urea cycle removes which element that is generated by amino acid catabolism?

{{c1::Nitrogen}}

What are the byproducts of amino acid catabolism?

{{c1::Urea}}
{{c1::Fumarate}}

Where does the urea cycle occur in the cell?

{{c1::Mitochondria}}, which involves carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and ornithine transcarbamylase
{{c1::Cytosol}}, which involves all other enzymes

What happens to gluconeogenesis when conversion of alanine to pyruvate is blocked in the liver?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}}

What links the Cori cycle to the transport of ammonia, allowing it to enter the Cahill cycle?

Conversion of {{c1::pyruvate}} to {{c1::alanine}} in muscles

Amino acids derived from muscle catabolism can transfer their NH3 group to α-ketoglutarate, forming which amino acid?

{{c1::Glutamate}}

Glutamate in muscle donates its NH3 group to pyruvate to form which amino acid?

{{c1::Alanine}}

What is the name of the cycle in which excess ammonia in muscles is transferred for urea cycle processing in the liver?

{{c1::Cahill}} cycle

Which two compounds in the Cahill cycle are able to move freely between muscle and liver?

{{c1::Alanine}}
{{c1::Glucose}}

What process must pyruvate undergo to be transported from the liver back to muscle via the Cahill cycle?

{{c1::Gluconeogenesis}}

Which two compounds in the Cori cycle are able to move freely between the muscle and liver?

{{c1::Glucose}}
{{c1::Lactate}}

Which metabolite excess may lead to the findings shown in the image below?



{{c1::Ammonia}}

How does lactulose promote excretion of ammonia?

Lactulose {{c1::acidifies}} the gastrointestinal tract → Traps {{c1::NH4+}} for excretion

How do benzoate, phenylbutyrate, and phenylacetate promote excretion of ammonia?

They react with {{c1::glutamine}} or {{c1::glycine}} and form products that are excreted in the urine

What is the best-long term treatment for a patient with hyperammonemia due to liver disease?

Limit {{c1::protein}} in the diet

How does the presence of excess ammonia result in inhibition of the tricarboxylic acid cycle?

Hyperammonemia depletes stores of {{c1::α-ketoglutarate}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a key tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediate.

fields.Text:
How would a defect in one of the urea cycle enzymes affect serum ammonia level?

Serum ammonia would be {{c1::high::high/low}}
fields.Back Extra: Hyperammonemia can be hereditary, as in urea cycle disorders.

fields.Text:
What is the diagnosis for a patient with alcoholic cirrhosis who presents with asterixis and altered mental status?

{{c1::Hyperammonemia::Hyperammonemia/Hypoammonemia}} secondary to liver disease

In hyperammonemia, what key amino acid is depleted?

{{c1::Glutamate}}

What antibiotic that decreases ammoniagenic bacteria in the colon is commonly used in hyperammonemia treatment?

{{c1::Rifaximin}}

What sign of hyperammonemia might be seen on a brain MRI?

Cerebral {{c1::edema}}
fields.Back Extra: This results from an osmotic shift.

fields.Text:
How are levels of GABA and α-ketoglutarate altered in patients with  hyperammonemia presenting with central nervous system toxicity?

GABA is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}
α-ketoglutarate is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}

What changes are due to excess glutamine in patients with hyperammonemia?

Central nervous system toxicity with decreased {{c1::GABA}}
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} α-ketoglutarate
Cerebral {{c1::edema}}
{{c1::Tricarboxylic acid}} cycle inhibition

What peripheral blood smear finding differentiates ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency from orotic aciduria?

Lack of {{c1::megaloblasts}}
fields.Back Extra: Orotic aciduria is associated with megaloblastic anemia.

fields.Text:
Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency causes increased blood and urine levels of what substance?

{{c1::Orotic acid}}
{{c1::Ammonia}}

What enzyme deficiency in the urea cycle does not have an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance?

{{c1::Ornithine transcarbamylase}}

Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency interferes with the body's ability to carry out which important metabolic process?

Elimination of {{c1::ammonia}}

The excess orotic acid resulting from ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency contributes to the synthesis of which DNA molecule?

{{c1::Pyrimidine}}

What biochemical anomaly explains reduced blood pressure in a patient with scurvy?

Decreased {{c1::catecholamine}} synthesis due to vitamin {{c1::C}} deficiency
fields.Back Extra: Vitamin C is required to convert dopamine to norepinephrine.

fields.Text:
NAD+ and NADP+ are derived from which amino acid?

{{c1::Tryptophan}}

Which amino acid and vitamin produces histamine?

{{c1::Histidine}}
Vitamin {{c1::B6}}

What amino acid and cofactor are required to produce porphyrin, the precursor to heme?

{{c1::Glycine}}
Vitamin {{c1::B6}}

What amino acid can be used to synthesize creatinine, urea, and nitric oxide?

{{c1::Arginine}}

The conversions of phenylalanine to tyrosine and tyrosine to dopa require what cofactor?

{{c1::BH4}}

Thyroxine is derived from which amino acid?

{{c1::Tyrosine}}

Melanin is derived from which compound?

{{c1::Dopa}}

The conversion of dopa to dopamine requires what cofactor?

Vitamin {{c1::B6}}

Norepinephrine is converted into epinephrine via a methyl group provided by what cofactor?

{{c1::S-adenosylmethionine}}

What two cofactors are needed to produce NAD+ and NADP+ from tryptophan?

Vitamin {{c1::B2}}
Vitamin {{c1::B6}}

What two cofactors are needed to produce melatonin from tryptophan?

{{c1::BH4}}
Vitamin {{c1::B6}}

What neurotransmitter is produced from glutamate? Mention the required cofactor.

{{c1::GABA}}
Vitamin {{c1::B6}} is the cofactor

A baby with phenylketonuria has normal phenylalanine hydroxylase activity with an abnormally low dopamine level. What is the cause?

Lack of {{c1::BH4}}
fields.Back Extra: This is needed to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine and tyrosine to DOPA.

fields.Text:
Which two enzymes require BH4 in catecholamine synthesis?

{{c1::Phenylalanine hydroxylase}}
{{c1::Tyrosine hydroxylase}}

What enzyme does carbidopa inhibit?

{{c1::DOPA decarboxylase}}

Which three reactions in the catecholamine synthesis pathway, starting with DOPA, require cofactors?

DOPA → {{c1::Dopamine}} → {{c1::Norepinephrine}} → {{c1::Epinephrine}}

What compound causes increased production of epinephrine and eventually metanephrine?

{{c1::Cortisol}}

What byproduct is dopamine broken down to for excretion?

{{c1::Homovanillic acid}}

What enzyme catalyzes the breakdown of norepinephrine to normetanephrine?

{{c1::Catechol-O-methyltransferase}}

A deficiency in the enzyme tyrosine can result in what disease?

{{c1::Albinism}}

What pigment compound is not being adequately produced in a patient with albinism?

{{c1::Melanin}}

What enzyme is responsible for the conversion of dopamine to norepinephrine?

{{c1::Dopamine-β-hydroxylase}}

What enzyme is responsible for the conversion of norepinephrine to epinephrine?

{{c1::Phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase}}

What causes the musty odor in phenylketonuria?

Disorder of {{c1::aromatic}} amino acid metabolism

Name two possible deficiencies that can cause phenylketonuria.

Decreased {{c1::phenylalanine hydroxylase}}
Decreased {{c1::BH4}} cofactor

Why should a patient with phenylketonuria avoid most artificial sweetners?

Phenylalanine is found in {{c1::aspartame}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an ingredient of artificial sweetners.

fields.Text:
Why are newborns screened for phenylketonuria at 2 to 3 days of age and not earlier?

The result is always normal at birth due to the presence of {{c1::maternal enzymes}}

What is the treatment for phenylketonuria?

Decrease dietary {{c1::phenylalanine}}
Increase dietary {{c1::tyrosine}}
Provide {{c1::BH4}} supplementation

Which nonessential amino acid becomes essential for patients with phenylketonuria?

{{c1::Tyrosine}}

An increase in phenylalanine levels due to phenylketonuria leads to the presence of what class of metabolites in urine?

{{c1::Phenyl ketones}}

What skin condition, apart from decreased pigmentation, can be seen with phenylketonuria?

{{c1::Eczema}}

Phenylketonuria exhibits what pattern of inheritance?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}
fields.Back Extra: This is like most enzyme deficiencies.

fields.Text:
What findings would be present in a patient who was born to a mother with maternal phenylketonuria?

{{c1::Microcephaly::Macrocephaly/Microcephaly}}
{{c1::Intellectual}} disability
{{c1::Growth}} retardation
Congenital {{c1::heart::organ}} defects

Why is BH4 deficiency also responsible for phenylketonuria?

BH4 is a cofactor for {{c1::phenylalanine hydroxylase}}
fields.Back Extra: Hence, its deficiency can lead to the accumulation of phenylalanine and subsequent conversion to phenyl ketones.

fields.Text:
The enzyme deficient in maple syrup urine disease is dependent on which vitamin to function?

Vitamin {{c1::B1}}

What molecule levels increase in the blood in maple syrup urine disease?

{{c1::α-ketoacids}}, especially those derived from {{c1::leucine}}

What is the treatment for maple syrup urine disease?

Restrict {{c1::isoleucine}}, {{c1::leucine}}, and {{c1::valine}} in the diet
Provide {{c1::thiamine}} supplementation

What is the inheritance pattern of maple syrup urine disease?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

Which amino acids cannot be degraded in maple syrup urine disease?

{{c1::Leucine}}
{{c1::Isoleucine}}
{{c1::Valine}}

What condition should be suspected when a urine sample obtained from a lethargic child smells like burnt sugar?

{{c1::Maple syrup urine}} disease
fields.Back Extra: This is due to a deficiency in α-ketoacid dehydrogenase.

fields.Text:
What is the inheritance pattern of alkaptonuria?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What causes joint pain in a patient with alkaptonuria?

Buildup of {{c1::homogentisic acid}}

Which benign enzyme deficiency causes arthralgias, darkened sclerae and connective tissues, and urine that turns black on air exposure?

{{c1::Homogentisate oxidase}} deficiency

What metabolic pathway is affected in alkaptonuria?

Degradation of {{c1::tyrosine}} to {{c1::fumarate}}

What is the treatment for homocystinuria caused by a deficiency of methionine synthase?

Increased intake of {{c1::methionine}}

What is the treatment for homocystinuria due to cystathione synthase deficiency?

Increased intake of {{c1::cysteine}}, vitamin {{c1::B6}}, vitamin {{c1::B12}}, and {{c1::folate}}
Decreased intake of {{c1::methionine}}

What ocular changes can be observed in a patient with homocystinuria?

{{c1::Downward::Upward/Downward}} and {{c1::inward::inward/outward}} lens subluxation

Why is serum homocysteine elevated in vitamin B12 deficiency?

Vitamin B12 (methylated) is the cofactor for {{c1::homocysteine methyltransferase}}

What is the inheritance pattern for the four forms of homocystinuria?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What enzyme converts homocysteine to cystathionine?

{{c1::Cystathionine synthase}}

What enzyme converts homocysteine to methionine?

{{c1::Methionine synthase}}

If cystathionine synthase deficiency is left untreated, what laboratory and clinical findings might develop?

Increased {{c1::homocysteine}} in urine
{{c1::Osteoporosis}}
{{c1::Marfanoid}} habitus
Lens {{c1::subluxation}}
{{c1::Thrombosis}}
{{c1::Atherosclerosis}}
{{c1::Kyphosis}}
{{c1::Intellectual}} disability
{{c1::Hypopigmented::Hyperpigmented/Hypopigmented}} skin

What is the treatment for homocystinuria caused by a decreased affinity of cystathionine synthase for pyridoxal phosphate?

Increase in dietary {{c1::cysteine}}
Increase in vitamin {{c1::B6}}

What are the four possible causes of homocystinuria?

{{c1::Cystathionine synthase}} deficiency
Decreased affinity of cystathionine synthase for vitamin {{c1::B6}}
{{c1::Methionine synthase}} deficiency
{{c1::MTHFR}} deficiency

What amino acid and cofactor are required for the conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine?

{{c1::Serine}}
Vitamin {{c1::B6}}

What is the treatment for homocystinuria due to MTHFR deficiency?

Increase of {{c1::folate}} in the diet

What tests can be used to confirm the diagnosis in a patient who has recurring kidney stones, with urinalysis showing the findings in the image?



{{c1::Cyanide-nitroprusside}} test
{{c1::1H-NMR spectroscopy}} of urine

What is the inheritance pattern of cystinuria?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What type of crystals are seen when kidney stones passed by a patient with cystinuria are analyzed?

{{c1::Hexagonal}} crystals

What is the treatment for cystinuria?

{{c1::Hydration}}
Urinary {{c1::alkalinization}}
Chelation with agents that increase stone {{c1::solubility}}
Diet low in {{c1::methionine}}

The amino acid transporter affected in cystinuria transports which four amino acids?

{{c1::Cystine}}
{{c1::Ornithine}}
{{c1::Lysine}}
{{c1::Arginine}}

Where is the transporter affected in cystinuria located?

{{c1::Intestines}}
{{c1::Proximal convoluted tubules}} of the kidneys

What kind of chemical bond is found in cystine?

{{c1::Disulfide}} bond

In deficiency of propionyl-CoA carboxylase, what two metabolic products are affected?

{{c1::Propionyl-CoA}}
{{c1::Methylmalonic acid}}
fields.Back Extra: Propionyl-CoA is increased and methylmalonic acid is decreased.

fields.Text:
What are common clinical features seen in infants with organic acidemias?

Poor {{c1::feeding}}
{{c1::Vomiting}}
{{c1::Hypotonia::Hypertonia/Hypotonia}}
{{c1::Hepatomegaly}}
{{c1::High anion gap metabolic acidosis}}
{{c1::Seizures}}

What is the treatment for propionic acidemia?

Low-protein diet limited in substances that are converted to propionyl-CoA including the following:

{{c1::Valine}}
{{c1::Odd}}-chain fatty acids
{{c1::Methionine}}
{{c1::Isoleucine}}
{{c1::Threonine}}

What are the two potential causes of methylmalonic acidemia?

Deficiency of {{c1::methylmalonyl-CoA mutase}}
Deficiency of vitamin {{c1::B12}}

What is the mechanism by which organic acidemias can produce high anion gap metabolic acidosis?

Inhibition of {{c1::gluconeogenesis}} → Reduced blood {{c1::glucose}} → Increased ketone production → High anion gap metabolic acidosis

What is the laboratory finding that results from urea cycle inhibition in patients with organic acidemias?

{{c1::Hyperammonemia::Hyperammonemia/Hypoammonemia}}

What is the mechanism by which cAMP promotes glycogenolysis induced by glucagon?

cAMP → Increase in {{c1::protein kinase A}} → Increase in {{c1::glycogen phosphorylase kinase}} → Increase in {{c1::glycogen phosphorylase}} → Increase in glycogenolysis

What organ does glucagon act on to stimulate the breakdown of glycogen?

{{c1::Liver}}

What enzyme do calcium and the calcium-calmodulin complex both directly stimulate during the conversion of glycogen to glucose?

{{c1::Glycogen phosphorylase kinase}}

What receptor does insulin bind to in liver and muscle cells?

{{c1::Tyrosine kinase dimer}} receptor

Which enzyme converts glucose to glycogen?

{{c1::Glycogen synthase}}

What protein in muscle activates glycogen phosphorylase kinase to coordinate glycogenolysis with muscle activity?

{{c1::Calcium-calmodulin}}

What receptor does epinephrine bind to in the liver to release calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum during glycogen breakdown?

{{c1::α}}-receptor

What are the 2 pathways by which epinephrine can induce glycogen breakdown?

{{c1::α}}-receptors
{{c1::β}}-receptors

Glycogen is broken down to glucose by what enzyme?

{{c1::Glycogen phosphorylase}}

Glucagon stimulates the breakdown of glycogen by which second-messenger system?

{{c1::cAMP}}

What 3 substances stimulate the enzyme glycogen phosphorylase kinase during glycogenolysis?

{{c1::Calcium}}
{{c1::Calcium}}-{{c1::calmodulin}} complex
{{c1::Protein kinase A}}

When insulin binds to tyrosine kinase receptors, which 2 enzymes are stimulated to promote glycogen synthesis?

{{c1::Glycogen synthase}}
{{c1::Protein phosphatase}}

What is the effect of protein phosphatase in the insulin signaling pathway?

Activates {{c1::glycogen synthase}}
Inhibits {{c1::glycogen phosphorylase}}

Most of the glucose released from glycogenolysis is in the form of glucose-1-phosphate, but a small amount of free glucose is still produced. How?

Clevage of {{c1::limit dextrin}} by {{c1::α-1,6-glucosidase}} yields free glucose

During glycogenolysis, which enzyme cleaves off the last glucose-1-phosphate residue from branched glycogen?

{{c1::α-1,6-glucosidase}}

A glycogen molecule branch undergoing glycogenolysis has only limit dextrins remaining. What happens next?

A {{c1::debranching}} enzyme moves {{c1::3}} of the 4 remaining glucose units from the branch to the linkage

What is the immediate product of glycogen breakdown by glycogen phosphorylase?

{{c1::Glucose-1-phosphate}}

What is a limit dextrin in glycogen storage?

{{c1::2}} to {{c1::4}} residues remaining on a glycogen branch after it has been shortened by {{c1::glycogen phosphorylase}}

What must glucose-1-phosphate first be converted to during glycogenolysis to be converted to glucose?

{{c1::Glucose-6-phosphate}}

What molecule is the end product of glycogenolysis?

{{c1::Glucose-6-phosphate}}

In patients with defects in both debranching enzyme and glycogen phosphorylase, small amounts of glycogen are still broken down. How?

By {{c1::lysosomes}} via {{c1::α-1,4-glucosidase}}

In which part of the body does glycogen undergo rapid glycogenolysis during exercise?

{{c1::Skeletal muscle}}

What type of bond is found at glycogen branch points?

{{c1::α-(1,6)}} bond

What type of bond is found at side-by-side linkages of glucose in glycogen?

{{c1::α-(1,4)}} bond

What is the second-wind phenomenom seen in patients with type V glycogen storage disease?

A sudden burst of {{c1::energy}} after profound {{c1::weakness}}
fields.Back Extra: This arises from increased blood flow to muscles.

fields.Text:
What abnormalities can be seen in lab tests done for a patient with von Gierke disease?

{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in fasting glucose levels
{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in blood lactate levels
{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in triglycerides levels
{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in uric acid levels

What would measurement of blood glucose show in a patient with McArdle disease who reports painful muscle cramps during intense exercise?

{{c1::Normal}} blood glucose levels

Which enzyme is deficient in Pompe disease?

{{c1::Lysosomal acid α-1,4-glucosidase}}

Periodic acid-Schiff staining of hepatocytes from a patient shows accumulation of limit dextrin-like structures in the cytosol. Which glycogen storage disease would you suspect?

{{c1::Cori}} disease

What stain is best used to visualize glycogen within cells?

{{c1::Periodic acid-Schiff}} stain

A patient with myophosphorylase deficiency has ventricular tachycardia during exercise. What is the cause of the arrhythmia?

Predisposition to {{c1::electrolyte}} abnormalities

Which 3 organ systems are affected in Pompe disease?

{{c1::Muscle}}
{{c1::Heart}}
{{c1::Liver}}

What is the treatment for von Gierke disease?

Frequent consumption of {{c1::glucose}} and {{c1::cornstarch}}
Avoidance of {{c1::galactose}} and {{c1::fructose}}

A patient with McArdle disease has red urine, but urinalysis is negative for red blood cells. Why?

The red urine is due to {{c1::myoglobinuria}}, not hematuria

What are the 2 debranching enzymes deficient in Cori disease?

{{c1::α-1,6-glucosidase}}
{{c1::4-α-D-glucanotransferase}}

What enzyme is deficient in von Gierke disease?

{{c1::Glucose-6-phosphatase}}

What is the other name for lysosomal acid α-1,4-glucosidase?

{{c1::Acid maltase}}

What would you expect to see in a muscle biopsy specimen obtained from a patient with McArdle disease?

Increased amount of {{c1::glycogen}}

What enzyme is deficient in McArdle disease?

Skeletal muscle {{c1::glycogen phosphorylase}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as myophosphorylase.

fields.Text:
How does Cori disease differ from von Gierke disease in its clinical manifestation?

Cori disease is {{c1::milder}} in presentation with {{c1::normal}} blood lactate levels

A 4-year-old boy with known glycogen storage disease has cardiomegaly, hypotonia, and exercise intolerance. What is his prognosis?

{{c1::Poor}}

What are the inheritance patterns of the glycogen storage diseases, types I to V?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

How do lactate and ammonia levels change after exercise in patients with McArdle disease?

Ammonia level {{c1::increases}}
Lactate level remains {{c1::stable}}

What is the pathophysiology shared by all glycogen storage diseases?

Abnormal {{c1::metabolism}} of glycogen → {{c1::Accumulation}} of glycogen within cells

Which glycogen storage disorder presents with infantile hepatosplenomegaly, cirrhosis, hypotonia, and cardiomyopathy?

{{c1::Anderson}} disease
fields.Back Extra: There is a deficiency of branching enzyme.

fields.Text:
A man with a known lysosomal storage disease has pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, avascular necrosis of the femur, and recurrent bone crisis. What will a blood smear show?

{{c1::Gaucher}} cells
fields.Back Extra: Gaucher cells are macrophages that look like crumpled tissue paper.

fields.Text:
A blockade at which numbered step in the image leads to Krabbe disease?



Step {{c1::4}}

A blockade at which numbered step in the image leads to metachromatic leukodystrophy?



Step {{c1::3}}
fields.Back Extra: The deficient enzyme is arylsulfatase A.

fields.Text:
A blockade at which numbered step in the image leads to Fabry disease?



Step {{c1::2}}
fields.Back Extra: The deficient enzyme is α-galactosidase A.

fields.Text:
A blockade of which step in the image leads to Niemann-Pick disease?



Step {{c1::6}}

A blockade of which step in the image leads to Gaucher disease?



Step {{c1::5}}

What late-stage complications may occur in Fabry disease?

{{c1::Cardiovascular}} disease
Progressive {{c1::kidney::organ}} failure

Which enzyme is deficient in a patient with Tay-Sachs disease?

{{c1::Hexosaminidase A}}

What is the treatment for Gaucher disease?

Recombinant {{c1::glucocerebrosidase}}

A patient is suspected of having one of the sphingolipidoses. Biopsy reveals foam cells. What substrate is accumulated in this disease?



{{c1::Sphingomyelin}}

A girl has progressive neurodegeneration, hepatosplenomegaly, and a cherry-red spot on her macula. What enzyme is deficient?



{{c1::Sphingomyelinase}}

A boy has episodic peripheral neuropathy, angiokeratomas, and hypohidrosis. Name the deficient enzyme.



{{c1::α-galactosidase A}}

Which 2 lysosomal storage diseases do not have an autosomal recessive type of inheritance?

{{c1::Fabry}} disease
{{c1::Hunter}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: The inheritance pattern for both of these diseases is X-linked recessive.

fields.Text:
Increased incidence of which 3 lysosomal storage diseases has been found in Ashkenazi Jews?

{{c1::Tay-Sachs}} disease
{{c1::Niemann-Pick}} disease
{{c1::Gaucher}} disease (some forms)

A child has mild symptoms similar to those of Hurler syndrome, but has no corneal clouding. What behavioral problem might he exhibit?

{{c1::Aggression}}

Name the deficient enzyme in Hunter syndrome.

{{c1::Iduronate-2-sulfatase}}

Which enzyme deficiency causes Hurler syndrome?

{{c1::α-L-iduronidase}} deficiency

Which is the most common lysosomal storage disease?

{{c1::Gaucher}} disease

Name the deficient enzyme in Gaucher disease.

{{c1::Glucocerebrosidase}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as β-glucosidase.

fields.Text:
What cellular changes are seen in the CNS in Krabbe disease?

Loss of {{c1::oligodendrocytes}}
Presence of {{c1::globoid}} cells
fields.Back Extra: This may lead to developmental delay.

fields.Text:
Which enzyme is deficient in Krabbe disease?

{{c1::Galactocerebrosidase}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as galactosylceramidase.

fields.Text:
Name the enzyme deficient in metachromatic leukodystrophy.

{{c1::Arylsulfatase A}}

Name 2 lysosomal storage diseases that may present with a cherry-red spot on the macula.

{{c1::Niemann-Pick}} disease
{{c1::Tay-Sachs}} disease

A 2-year-old boy has a "cherry-red" spot on his macula, onion skin lysosomes, and a normal liver. What excess substrate has accumulated in his cells?

{{c1::GM2 ganglioside}}

What substrate accumulates in metachromatic leukodystrophy?

{{c1::Cerebroside sulfate}}

What is the accumulated substrate in the only X-linked recessive inherited sphingolipidosis?

{{c1::Ceramide trihexoside}}

What substrates accumulate in Krabbe disease?

{{c1::Psychosine}}
{{c1::Galactocerebroside}}

What is the accumulated substrate in Gaucher disease?

{{c1::Glucocerebroside}}

Hunter syndrome and Hurler syndrome are both examples of what kind of lysosomal storage diseases?

{{c1::Mucopolysaccharidoses}}

Name the accumulated substrates in the mucopolysaccharidoses.

{{c1::Dermatan sulfate}}
{{c1::Heparan sulfate}}

What clinical finding distinguishes Niemann-Pick disease from Tay-Sachs disease?

{{c1::Hepatosplenomegaly}}
fields.Back Extra: This is seen in Niemann-Pick disease, but not in Tay-Sachs disease.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiology of medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency?

Decrease in the ability to break down fatty acids into {{c1::acetyl-CoA}} → Accumulation of {{c1::fatty acyl carnitines}} in the blood with {{c1::hypoketotic hypoglycemia}}

An infant presents with vomiting, lethargy, and seizures. Lab reports show liver dysfunction, hypoglycemia, and hyperammonemia. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

Diagnosis → {{c1::Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase}} deficiency
Treatment → Avoidance of {{c1::fasting}}

In what 3 organs/tissues does fatty acid synthesis predominantly occur in the body?

{{c1::Liver}}
{{c1::Lactating mammary}} glands
{{c1::Adipose}} tissue

Name the process fatty acyl-CoA undergoes in the mitochondria to be converted to acetyl-CoA.

{{c1::β-oxidation}}

What molecule regulates the carnitine shuttle in fatty acid degradation?

{{c1::Malonyl-CoA}}

What is the first step in fatty acid degradation?

Formation of {{c1::fatty acyl-CoA}}
fields.Back Extra: This is via acyl-CoA synthetase in the cytoplasm.

fields.Text:
What is the name of the 16C fatty acid produced in fatty acid synthesis?

{{c1::Palmitate}}

A patient with an enzyme deficiency has weakness, hypotonia, dilated cardiomyopathy, and hypoketotic hypoglycemia, but no vomiting or seizures. What causes these symptoms?

{{c1::Systemic primary carnitine}} deficiency
fields.Back Extra: There is a toxic accumulation of long-chain fatty acids in the cytosol due to a lack of transport of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria.

fields.Text:
Which step of fatty acid synthesis is most likely impaired in a patient with biotin deficiency?

{{c1::Acetyl-CoA}} → {{c1::Malonyl-CoA}}

Where does fatty acid degradation occur?

{{c1::Mitochondrial matrix}}

What biochemical "shuttle" do the building blocks of fatty acids use to get into the cytoplasm from the mitochondria?

{{c1::Citrate}} shuttle

In what cellular compartment does fatty acid synthesis occur?

{{c1::Cytoplasm}}

Long-chain fatty acid degradation requires what biochemical shuttle to be transported into the mitochondrial matrix?

{{c1::Carnitine}} shuttle

What is the potential fate of acetyl-CoA made from β-oxidation of fatty acyl-CoA?

Enters the {{c1::TCA}} cycle
Converted into {{c1::ketone bodies}}

What enzyme converts citrate into acetyl-CoA inside the cytoplasm?

{{c1::ATP citrate lyase}}

In which organ are fatty acids and amino acids metabolized to ketone bodies?

{{c1::Liver}}

What is the mechanism for ketone production in a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis or prolonged starvation?

{{c1::Oxaloacetate}} is depleted for gluconeogenesis → {{c1::Acetyl-CoA}} accumulates → Ketone production

How does chronic alcoholic use increase ketone body formation?

Overuse of alcohol results in increased {{c1::NADH}} state → Accumulation of {{c1::oxaloacetate}} → Shunted to {{c1::malate}} → Buildup of {{c1::acetyl-CoA}} → Production of ketones

Which of the three ketone bodies do not appear on a standard urinalysis?

{{c1::β-hydroxybutyrate}}
{{c1::Acetone}}
fields.Back Extra: Acetone is secreted via the respiratory system.

fields.Text:
Which organs can use ketone bodies as their source of energy?

{{c1::Muscle}}
{{c1::Brain}}

Which cells cannot utilize ketone bodies?

{{c1::Red blood}} cells
fields.Back Extra: Red blood cells can only use glucose as an energy source.

fields.Text:
What is the key enzyme in the process of ketogenesis?

{{c1::HMG-CoA lyase}}

Which ketone gives the fruity smell to the breath of a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis?

{{c1::Acetone}}

How does the action of epinephrine and glucagon on adipocytes increase triglyceride breakdown during the fasted state?

Increased {{c1::ATP}} to {{c1::cAMP}} conversion → Increased {{c1::protein kinase A}} activity → Activation of {{c1::hormone-sensitive lipase}} to breakdown triglyceride → Increased free fatty acids and glycerol

How do triglyceride molecules enter adipocytes during the fed state?

Apolipoprotein {{c1::CII}} molecules of triglycerides bind to {{c1::lipoprotein lipase}} → Triglycerides break down to {{c1::free fatty acids}} → Transported to adipocytes

What hormone influences glucose and triglyceride uptake in adipocytes in the fed state?

{{c1::Insulin}}

What hormones act on adipocytes during the fasted state to break down triglycerides?

{{c1::Epinephrine}}
{{c1::Glucagon}}

Name the enzyme activated in adipocytes during the fasted state that breaks down triglycerides into free fatty acids and glycerol.

{{c1::Hormone-sensitive lipase}}

On the graph shown, identify the energy sources represented by individual lines.



Red → Stored {{c1::ATP}}
Green → {{c1::Creatinine phosphate}}
Orange → {{c1::Anaerobic::Aerobic/Anaerobic}} metabolism
Light blue → {{c1::Aerobic::Aerobic/Anaerobic}} metabolism
Purple → {{c1::Overall performance}}

What is the primary process of energy generation during a full exercise session?

{{c1::Aerobic::Aerobic/Anaerobic}} metabolism

What three processes or reserves provide sources of energy within the first minute of the onset of exercise?

Stored {{c1::ATP}} (2 seconds)
{{c1::Creatinine phosphate}} (10 seconds)
{{c1::Anaerobic::Aerobic/Anaerobic}} metabolism (1 minute)

What type of cells are unable to use ketone bodies as a fuel source and why?

{{c1::Red blood}} cells because of their lack of {{c1::mitochondria}}

How long do glycogen reserves last?

{{c1::1}} day(s)

What determines the length of survival after three days of starvation?

Amount of excess {{c1::adipose}} stored

What is the primary source of energy for vital organs after three days of starvation?

{{c1::Ketones}}
fields.Back Extra: These are synthesized from the breakdown of adipose stores.

fields.Text:
Which two hormones stimulate the use of fuel reserves in between meals?

{{c1::Glucagon}}
{{c1::Epinephrine}}

What metabolic processes are used as major and minor sources of fuel between meals?

Major source → Hepatic {{c1::glycogenolysis}}
Minor sources → Hepatic {{c1::gluconeogenesis}} and adipose tissue release of {{c1::free fatty acids}}

What is the role of insulin in the fed state?

Stimulates storage of {{c1::glycogen}}, {{c1::lipids}}, and {{c1::proteins}}

What metabolic processes are used for fuel in the fed state?

{{c1::Glycolysis}}
{{c1::Aerobic::Aerobic/Anaerobic}} respiration

What are the metabolic sources of hepatic gluconeogenesis during the first three days of starvation?

{{c1::Peripheral}} tissues → Supplies lactate and alanine
{{c1::Adipose}} tissues → Supplies glycerol and propionyl-CoA

During the first three days of fasting, which four processes maintain blood glucose levels?

Hepatic {{c1::glycogenolysis}}
Hepatic {{c1::gluconeogenesis}}
Adipose {{c1::free fatty acid}} release
Muscle and liver {{c1::free fatty acid}} use

1 gram of protein or carbohydrate equals how many kilocalories of energy?

{{c1::4}} kilocalories

1 gram of fatty acid equals how many kilocalories of energy?

{{c1::9}} kilocalories

1 gram of alcohol equals how many kilocalories of energy?

{{c1::7}} kilocalories

After absorption of dietary fat and cholesterol in intestinal cells, where are lipids distributed next?

{{c1::Lymphatics}}

Which two apolipoproteins are transferred from HDL to chylomicrons and VLDL in circulation?

Apolipoprotein {{c1::CII}}
Apolipoprotein {{c1::E}}

Apolipoprotein CII is critical in the activation of which enzyme?

{{c1::Lipoprotein lipase}}

A chylomicron remnant binds to a hepatocyte utilizing which apolipoprotein and receptor?

Apolipoprotein {{c1::E}} on chylomicrons binds to apolipoprotein {{c1::E}} receptors on hepatocytes

Chylomicron remnants are broken down by hepatocytes into cholesterol and triglycerides. What is the next step in lipid transport?

Cholesterol and triglycerides are released into {{c1::circulation}} from hepatocytes as {{c1::VLDL}}

After lipid breakdown via lipoprotein lipase, chylomicrons and VLDL become what respective lipoprotein forms?

Chylomicrons become {{c1::chylomicron remnants}}
VLDL becomes {{c1::IDL}}

When IDL is delivered to hepatocytes via apolipoprotein E and apolipoprotein E receptors, what lipoprotein is then released from hepatocytes?

{{c1::LDL}}

In the final step of lipid transport, LDL particles are taken up by peripheral cells with the help of which apolipoprotein and receptor?

Apolipoprotein {{c1::B100}} on LDL binds to {{c1::LDL}} receptors on peripheral cells

What are the two major sources of HDL in the body?

{{c1::Liver}}
{{c1::Small intestine}}

What is the function of cholesterol ester transfer protein?

Assists in the transfer of {{c1::cholesterol esters}} to other {{c1::lipoprotein}} particles

What is the function of hormone-sensitive lipase in lipid transport?

Degrades {{c1::triglycerides}} in adipocytes
Releases {{c1::glycerol}}

What is the function of hepatic lipase in lipid transport?

Degrades {{c1::triglycerides}} still present in {{c1::IDL}} and {{c1::chylomicron remnants}}

What enzyme degrades triglycerides present in circulating chylomicrons and VLDL?

{{c1::Lipoprotein lipase}}

What is the function of pancreatic lipase in lipid transport?

Degrades {{c1::triglycerides}} obtained from the diet in the {{c1::small intestine}}

What enzyme catalyzes the esterification of the majority of plasma cholesterol and converts nascent HDL to mature HDL?

{{c1::Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase}}

What is the function of PCSK9 in lipid metabolsim?

Promotes degradation of {{c1::LDL}} receptors
fields.Back Extra: This would increase the serum LDL levels.

fields.Text:
If a drug inhibits PCSK9, how will this affect serum LDL levels?

It will {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} serum LDL levels

Which apolipoprotein mediates secretion of chylomicrons from the small intestine to the lymphatics?

Apolipoprotein {{c1::B48}}

Which apolipoprotein functions as a lipoprotein lipase cofactor?

Apolipoprotein {{c1::CII}}

Which apolipoprotein mediates remnant uptake?

Apolipoprotein {{c1::E}}

Which apolipoproteins binds to LDL receptors?

Apolipoprotein {{c1::B100}}

What is the function of the apolipoprotein found only in HDL?

It activates {{c1::lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase}}

In which types of lipoproteins is apolipoprotein CII found?

{{c1::Chylomicrons}}
{{c1::VLDL}}
{{c1::IDL}}
{{c1::HDL}}

In which lipoproteins is apolipoprotein B100 found?

{{c1::VLDL}}
{{c1::IDL}}
{{c1::LDL}}

In which lipoproteins is apolipoprotein B48 found?

{{c1::Chylomicrons}}
{{c1::Chylomicron remnants}}

Which apolipoprotein is present in all forms of cholesterol except LDL?

Apolipoprotein {{c1::E}}

Apolipoprotein B48 is found only on particles orginating from which organ?

{{c1::Intestines}}

Apolipoprotein B100 is found only on particles originating from which organ?

{{c1::Liver}}

Synthesis of which lipoprotein is increased by alcohol consumption?

{{c1::HDL}}

Where and how is LDL formed?

LDL is formed in the {{c1::liver::organ}} and peripheral tissues via modification of {{c1::IDL}} by {{c1::hepatic lipase}}

What is the role of VLDL in circulation?

Delivery of triglycerides from the {{c1::liver::organ}} to the {{c1::peripheral}} tissues

What is the primary function of chylomicrons?

Delivery of dietary {{c1::triglycerides}} to {{c1::peripheral}} tissue

Which lipoprotein is formed by degradation of VLDL and functions to deliver triglycerides and cholesterol to the liver?

{{c1::IDL}}

Which lipoprotein acts as a repository for apolipoproteins C and E?

{{c1::HDL}}
fields.Back Extra: These apolipoproteins are needed for chylomicron and VLDL metabolism.

fields.Text:
Which lipoproteins carry the most cholesterol?

{{c1::LDL}}
{{c1::HDL}}

What are lipoproteins composed of?

{{c1::Triglycerides}}
{{c1::Cholesterol}}
{{c1::Phospholipids}}
{{c1::Proteins}}

What precursor is common to the synthesis of bile acids, steroid hormones, and vitamin D?

{{c1::Cholesterol}}

What is the role of cholesterol in the plasma membrane?

Maintains plasma membrane {{c1::integrity}}

How is cholesterol stored in LDL delivered to the peripheral tissues?

{{c1::Receptor-mediated endocytosis}}

What fat absorption disorder can lead to steatorrhea, failure to thrive during infancy, retinitis pigmentosa, progressive ataxia, and acanthocytosis?

{{c1::Abetalipoproteinemia}}

What three lipoproteins are absent in apolipoprotein B48 and B100 deficiency?

{{c1::Chylomicrons}}
{{c1::LDL}}
{{c1::VLDL}}

A patient with abetalipoproteinemia is treated with large doses of oral vitamin E to prevent which complication?

{{c1::Spinocerebellar degeneration}}

What is the inheritance pattern of abetalipoproteinemia?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What is the treatment for apolipoprotein B48 and B100 deficiency?

Restricted consumption of {{c1::long}}-chain fatty acids
Large doses of oral vitamin {{c1::E}}

A mutation in what gene results in abetalipoproteinemia?

{{c1::MTP}} gene

What is the likely finding in an intestinal biopsy specimen obtained from an infant with abetalipoproteinemia?

{{c1::Lipid-laden enterocytes}}

Which two familial dyslipidemias are inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern?

Type {{c1::I}} familial dyslipidemia
Type {{c1::III}} familial dyslipidemia

A 25-year-old man with an autosomal dominant familial dyslipidemia presents with acute pancreatitis. Which disease does he likely have?

Type {{c1::IV}} familial dyslipidemia
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by hepatic overproduction of VLDL.

fields.Text:
What is the causative defect in patients with dysbetalipoproteinemia?

Defective {{c1::apolipoprotein E}}

A 40-year-old man has angina. You observe palmar xanthomas and tuberoeruptive xanthomas on his knees. What dyslipidemia does he most likely have?

Type {{c1::III}} familial dyslipidemia
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as dysbetalipoproteinemia, which presents with premature atherosclerosis.

fields.Text:
What cardiovascular event is pertinent to a patient with type II familial dyslipidemia?

{{c1::Myocardial infarcation}}
fields.Back Extra: This may occur before the age of 20.

fields.Text:
What abnormal lipid panel findings are comparable for familial hypercholesterolemia type IIa and IIb?

Familial hypercholesterolemia type IIa and IIb have an increase in {{c1::LDL}} and {{c1::cholesterol}}
Familial hypercholesterolemia type IIb has an increase in {{c1::VLDL}} as well

Compare the average cholesterol level of a patient who is heterozygous for familial hypercholesterolemia with one who is homozygous.

Heterozygote → {{c1::300}} mg/dL
Homozygote → {{c1::700+}} mg/dL

Which two familial dyslipidemias are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern?

Type {{c1::II}} familial dyslipidemia
Type {{c1::IV}} familial dyslipidemia

Deficiency of which two proteins in lipid transport contributes to the pathogenesis of type I familial dyslipidemia?

{{c1::Lipoprotein lipase}}
{{c1::Apolipoprotein CII}}

What gross finding in a blood sample is associated with hyperchylomicronemia?

{{c1::Creamy supernatant}} layer

What is the defect in familial hypercholesterolemia?

Defective {{c1::apolipoprotein B100}}
Absent/defective {{c1::LDL}} receptors

Hypertriglyceridemia is related to which endocrine disorder?

{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because it is associated with insulin resistance.

fields.Text:
In type I familial dyslipidemia, which lipoproteins are elevated?

{{c1::Chylomicrons}}
{{c1::Triglycerides}}
{{c1::Cholesterol}}

What is the pathogenesis of type IV familial dyslipidemia?

Overproduction of {{c1::VLDL}} by the liver

What is the function of the secondary immune system organs?

Allowing interaction of immune cells with {{c1::antigens}}

Are the spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, and Peyer patches a part of primary or secondary immune system organs?

{{c1::Secondary::Primary/Secondary}} immune system organs

What is the primary immune function of the thymus?

{{c1::Maturation}} of {{c1::T}} cells

What are the two primary immune functions of the bone marrow?

Production of {{c1::immune}} cells
{{c1::Maturation}} of {{c1::B}} cells

What are the two primary immune system organs?

{{c1::Bone marrow}}
{{c1::Thymus}}

What region of the lymph nodes is likely underdeveloped in a patient with DiGeorge syndrome?

{{c1::Paracortex}}

In which section of the lymph node are T cells located?

{{c1::Paracortex}}

How do T cells and B cells enter the paracortex of a lymph node from blood?

Through {{c1::high::high/low}} {{c1::endothelial venules}}

Where can the paracortex be found within a lymph node?

Between the {{c1::follicles}} and {{c1::medulla}}

What two types of cells are found in the medullary sinus of the lymph node?

{{c1::Macrophages}}
{{c1::Reticular}} cells

Which two types of immune cells make up the medullary cords?

{{c1::Lymphocytes}}
{{c1::Plasma}} cells

What are the types of follicles in the outer cortex of the lymph node?

{{c1::Primary}} follicles
{{c1::Secondary}} follicles

What is the site of B-cell localization and proliferation in a lymph node?

{{c1::Follicle}}

What are the three main functions of a lymph node?

Nonspecific {{c1::filtration}} of lymph by {{c1::macrophages}}
Circulation of {{c1::B}} cells and {{c1::T}} cells
Activation of {{c1::immune}} responses

How does lymphadenopathy occur in patients with a viral infection?

Through {{c1::paracortical hyperplasia}}
fields.Back Extra: The paracortex enlarges in extreme cellular immune responses to viral pathogens.

fields.Text:
Where are follicles found within a lymph node?

{{c1::Outer cortex}} of the lymph node

Which area of the lymph node communicates with the efferent lymphatics?

{{c1::Medullary sinuses}}

Which part of the lymph node consists of sinuses and cords?

{{c1::Medulla}}

Which major lymphatic duct carries drainage from the area of the body highlighted in blue in the image?



{{c1::Right}} lymphatic duct

Where does the right lymphatic duct drain into the venous system?

At the junction of the {{c1::right::left/right}} {{c1::subclavian}} vein and the {{c1::right::left/right}} {{c1::internal jugular}} vein

Which lymph node clusters may be enlarged in association with mesenteric lymphadenitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and celiac disease?

{{c1::Celiac}} cluster
{{c1::Superior mesenteric}} cluster
{{c1::Inferior mesenteric}} cluster

Which lymph nodes are likely to become enlarged in a patient with lateral foot or leg cellulitis?

{{c1::Popliteal}} lymph nodes

Which lymph nodes are likely to become enlarged in a patient with medial foot or leg cellulitis?

{{c1::Superficial inguinal}} lymph nodes

Where should the physical exam be focused to find the cause of enlarged superficial inguinal lymph nodes?

{{c1::Scrotum}}/{{c1::vulva}}
Anal canal {{c1::below::above/below}} the pectinate line
{{c1::Subumbilical}} skin except for the {{c1::popliteal}} area

Which lymph node cluster should be assessed for evidence of metastases from the testes, ovaries, kidneys, and fallopian tubes?

{{c1::Para-aortic}} cluster

Which lymph node cluster is likely to be enlarged in a patient with mastitis or metastasis from breast cancer?

{{c1::Axillary}} cluster

Which lymph nodes drain the lower rectum to the anal canal (above the pectinate line), bladder, middle third of the vagina, cervix, and prostate?

{{c1::Internal iliac}} lymph nodes

Which lymph nodes drain the cervix, upper third of the vagina, superior part of the bladder, and body of the uterus?

{{c1::External iliac}} lymph nodes

Which area of the body is drained by deep cervical lymph nodes?

{{c1::Head}}
{{c1::Neck}}
{{c1::Oropharynx}}

Which lymph nodes are enlarged in association with upper respiratory tract infections, infectious mononucleosis, Kawasaki disease, and malignancy of the head/neck/oropharynx?

{{c1::Deep cervical}} lymph nodes

Which four common pathologic conditions are associated primarily with hilar lymphadenopathy?

Pulmonary {{c1::tuberculosis}}
{{c1::Sarcoidosis}}
{{c1::Lung::Organ}} cancer
{{c1::Granulomatous}} disease

Which three lymph node clusters may exhibit pathologic involvement in sexually transmitted infections?

{{c1::External iliac}} lymph node cluster
{{c1::Internal iliac}} lymph node cluster
{{c1::Superficial inguinal}} lymph node cluster

What abdominal organs drain into the celiac cluster, superior mesenteric cluster, and inferior mesenteric cluster of lymph nodes?

{{c1::Celiac}} cluster → Liver, stomach, spleen, pancreas, and upper duodenum
{{c1::Superior mesenteric}} cluster → Lower duodenum, jejunum, ileum, and colon to splenic flexure
{{c1::Inferior mesenteric}} cluster → Rest of colon to upper rectum

What body area is drained by the thoracic duct?

Area {{c1::below::above/below}} the diaphragm
{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} hemithorax
{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::upper::upper/lower}} limb
{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} head

Which lymph node is likely to be enlarged in association with a malignancy in the left hemithorax, abdomen, or pelvis?

{{c1::Supraclavicular}} lymph node

Which superficial lymph node in the trunk is likely to be enlarged in a patient with gastric cancer?

{{c1::Periumbilical}} lymph node

Which disease is indicated by epitrochlear lymphadenopathy?

{{c1::Secondary syphilis}}

Which lymph node clusters are enlarged in association with a malignancy of the oral cavity, anterior tongue, and lower lip?

{{c1::Submandibular}} lymph node cluster
{{c1::Submental}} lymph node cluster

What type of vaccines should patients who have undergone splenectomy and those with splenic dysfunction due to sickle cell disease receive?

Vaccines that target {{c1::encapsulated}} bacteria
fields.Back Extra: The notable ones include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Neisseria meningitidis.

fields.Text:
Name four hematologic findings in a patient who has undergone splenectomy.

{{c1::Target}} cells
{{c1::Howell-Jolly bodies}}
{{c1::Thrombocytosis}}
{{c1::Lymphocytosis}}

How does splenic dysfunction lead to increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms?

Decreased Ig{{c1::M}} → Decreased {{c1::complement}} activation → Decreased {{c1::C3b opsonization}}

In which histologic section of the spleen do the antigen-presenting cells capture blood-borne antigens for later recognition by lymphocytes?

{{c1::Marginal}} zone

In which section of the splenic white pulp can B cells be found?

{{c1::Follicles}}

In which section of the splenic white pulp can T cells be found?

{{c1::Periarteriolar lymphatic sheath}}

Where is the spleen located?

Under the {{c1::9th}} to {{c1::11th}} ribs
{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::upper::upper/lower}} quadrant of the abdomen
fields.Back Extra: This is anterolateral to the left kidney.

fields.Text:
Which zone is located between the red and white pulp?

{{c1::Marginal}} zone

Which cells are found in the marginal zone of the spleen?

{{c1::Macrophages}}
Specialized {{c1::B}} cells

What four complications are classically associated with thymomas?

{{c1::Superior vena cava}} syndrome
{{c1::Myasthenia gravis}}
{{c1::Pure red cell aplasia}}
{{c1::Good}} syndrome

Which two immunodeficiency syndromes are commonly associated with a hypoplastic thymus or absent thymic shadow?

{{c1::DiGeorge}} syndrome
{{c1::Severe combined immunodeficiency}}

Which histologic region of the thymus contains mature T cells and epithelial reticular cells?

{{c1::Medulla}}
fields.Back Extra: The Hassall corpuscles in the medulla contain epithelial reticular cells.

fields.Text:
Which histologic section of the thymus contains immature T cells?

{{c1::Cortex}}

In what region of the mediastinum is the thymus found?

{{c1::Anterosuperior}} mediastinum

What is the main immunologic function of the thymus?

{{c1::T}}-cell {{c1::differentiation}} and {{c1::maturation}}

From which pharyngeal pouch is the thymic epithelium derived?

{{c1::3rd}} pharyngeal pouch

What is the highlighted finding on this chest X-ray obtained from a neonate?



{{c1::Thymus}}
fields.Back Extra: This has a characterisitic "sail-shape" on a chest X-ray.

fields.Text:
From which embryonic germ layer are thymic lymphocytes derived?

{{c1::Mesoderm}}

By what age does the characteristic radiologic finding of a normal neonatal thymus involute?

Age {{c1::3}}
fields.Back Extra: This would be "sail-shaped" on a chest X-ray.

fields.Text:
Why does the adaptive immune response to previously encountered antigens become stronger and quicker on repeat exposure?

Formation of {{c1::memory}} cells after activation by an antigen during intial exposure → Quicker recognition and response on subsequent exposure

List three characteristics of the adaptive immune response.

Highly {{c1::specific}}
Develops over a {{c1::longer::longer/shorter}} time
Has a {{c1::faster::faster/slower}} and more {{c1::robust}} memory system

Through which mechanism does the adaptive immune system develop a highly specific defense against pathogens?

{{c1::V(D)J recombination}} during lymphocyte development

What are the three components responsible for adaptive immunity?

{{c1::B}} cells
{{c1::T}} cells
Circulating {{c1::antibodies}}

Give an example of a pathogen-associated molecular pattern for viruses and for bacteria.

Viruses → {{c1::Nucleic acids}}
Bacteria → {{c1::Lipopolysaccharides}} and {{c1::flagellin}}

In an innate immune response to a pathogen, which receptors are activated?

{{c1::Toll-like}} receptors

What five types of protein are secreted in an innate immune response?

{{c1::Lysozyme}}
{{c1::Complement}}
{{c1::C-reactive}} protein
{{c1::Cytokines}}
{{c1::Defensins}}

What is the benefit of germline-encoded target antigen recognition in the innate immune response?

It allows innate immunity to be both {{c1::fast::fast/slow}} and {{c1::nonspecific::specific/nonspecific}}

Name eight components of the innate immune system.

{{c1::Neutrophils}}
{{c1::Monocytes}}
{{c1::Macrophages}}
{{c1::Dendritic}} cells
{{c1::Natural killer}} cells
{{c1::Complement}}
Secreted {{c1::enzymes}}
Physical {{c1::epithelial}} barriers

Toll-like receptor activation via pathogen-associated molecular patterns leads to activation of what cellular protein complex?

{{c1::NF-κB}}
fields.Back Extra: This functions as a transcription factor.

fields.Text:
What two types of proteins are secreted in an adaptive immune response?

{{c1::Cytokines}}
{{c1::Immunoglobulins}}

What happens when there is a release of an invariant chain in an acidified endosome?

The bacterial antigens are loaded onto an MHC {{c1::II::I/II}} molecule

Which MHC molecule presents exogenous antigens to CD4+ helper T cells?

MHC {{c1::II::I/II}}

Which three HLA loci encode for MHC II in antigen-presenting cells?

HLA-{{c1::DP}}
HLA-{{c1::DQ}}
HLA-{{c1::DR}}

Which cells express MHC II?

{{c1::Antigen-presenting}} cells

What transporter in the rough endoplasmic reticulum is involved in loading of viral antigens onto an MHC I molecule?

{{c1::TAP}}
fields.Back Extra:
TAP stands for transporter associated with antigen processing.

This delivers the antigen to the rough endoplasmic reticulum for loading onto the MHC I protein.

fields.Text:
Which MHC class presents endogenous antigens to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells?

MHC {{c1::I::I/II}}

Which cells do not express MHC I on their surface?

{{c1::Red blood}} cells

Which three HLA loci encode for MHC class I?

HLA-{{c1::A}}
HLA-{{c1::B}}
HLA-{{c1::C}}

Name the structural protein associated with MHC II.

{{c1::Invariant chain}}

Name the structural protein associated with MHC I.

{{c1::β2-microglobulin}}

How do MHC I and MHC II differ from each other structurally?

MHC I has {{c1::1::number}} long and {{c1::1::number}} short chain
MHC II has {{c1::2::number}} equal chains
fields.Back Extra: MHC II has 2 α and 2 β chains.

fields.Text:
What receptor do all MHC molecules bind to on T cells?

{{c1::T-cell}} receptor
fields.Back Extra: CD4 and CD8 may also be binded to depending on the MHC class.

fields.Text:
What genes encode MHC receptors?

{{c1::HLA}} genes

What is the function of MHC receptors?

Present {{c1::antigen fragments}} to {{c1::T}} cells for recognition of foreign particles
Bind to {{c1::T-cell}} receptors to initiate an immune response

Which disorders are associated HLA-DR3?

{{c1::Systemic lupus erythematosus}}
{{c1::Addison}} disease
{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}} type {{c1::1}}
{{c1::Hashimoto thyroiditis}}
{{c1::Graves}} disease

Which HLA subtype is most commonly associated with rheumatoid arthritis?

HLA-{{c1::DR4}}

Which two HLA subtypes are associated with celiac disease?

HLA-{{c1::DQ2}}
HLA-{{c1::DQ8}}

Which two diseases are associated with both HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 subtypes?

{{c1::Addison}} disease
{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}} type {{c1::1}}

Which four diseases are most commonly associated with the HLA-B27 subtype?

{{c1::Psoriatic arthritis}}
{{c1::Ankylosing spondylitis}}
{{c1::Inflammatory bowel}} disease-associated {{c1::arthritis}}
{{c1::Reactive arthritis}}

Which HLA subtype is associated with abacavir hypersensitivity?

HLA-{{c1::B57}}

Name the surface receptor of natural killer cells that is involved in antibody-dependent cytotoxicity.

{{c1::CD16}}
fields.Back Extra: This binds to the Fc region of IgG bound to target cells, thereby activating natural killer cells.

fields.Text:
Which two signals allow natural killer cells to recognize and kill target cells?

Absence of an {{c1::inhibitory}} signal on the target cell surface
Exposure to a {{c1::nonspecific::specific/nonspecific}} activation signal on the target cell

Which two molecules are released by natural killer cells, inducing apoptosis of tumor cells and virus-infected cells?

{{c1::Granzymes}}
{{c1::Perforin}}

Which four cytokines enhance the activity of natural killer cells?

{{c1::IFN-α}}
{{c1::IFN-β}}
{{c1::IL-2}}
{{c1::IL-12}}

Which type of lymphocyte belongs to the innate immune system?

{{c1::Natural killer}} cells

What is the rule of 8 regarding T cells and MHC binding?

MHC I × CD{{c1::8}} = 8
MHC II × CD{{c1::4}} = 8

Which types of organ graft rejections are mediated by T cells?

{{c1::Acute cellular}} organ rejection
{{c1::Chronic cellular}} organ rejection

Which cells of the immune system mediate a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction?

{{c1::T}} cells

What is the primary function of Tc cells?

Killing {{c1::virus}}-infected cells and {{c1::tumor}} cells via {{c1::perforin}} and {{c1::granzymes}}

What are the primary functions of Th cells?

Assist {{c1::B}} cells in forming antibodies
Produce {{c1::cytokines}} to recruit phagocytes and activate other leukocytes

What is the function of memory B cells?

{{c1::Accelerate}} future immune responses to specific antigens

Why do B cells undergo somatic hypermutation in an antigenic response?

To optimize antigen {{c1::specificity}}

What are the three functions of B cells?

{{c1::Antigen}} recognition and presentation
{{c1::Antibody}} production
Maintenance of immunologic {{c1::memory}}

What types of immunity are mediated by B cells and T cells?

B cells mediate {{c1::humoral}} immunity
T cells mediate {{c1::cell-mediated}} immunity

Why do B cells differentiate into plasma cells in an antigenic response?

To secrete specific {{c1::immunoglobulins}}

Deficiency of which transcription factor involved in negative T-cell selection can lead to autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome-1?

{{c1::Autoimmune regulator}}

The action of which protein allows self-antigens to be expressed in the thymus for appropriate negative selection?

{{c1::Autoimmune regulator}}

How do T cells undergo negative selection at the thymic medulla?

T cells that have T-cell receptors with a high affinity for self-{{c1::antigens}} will become Treg cells or undergo apoptosis

How do T cells undergo positive selection at the thymic cortex?

T cells with T-cell receptors that are able to bind to self-{{c1::MHC}} on cortical epithelial cells will survive

During the process of T-cell differentiation, what are the locations of positive and negative selection within the thymus?

Thymic {{c1::cortex}} for positive selection
Thymic {{c1::medulla}} for negative selection

Which cytokines function to drive differentiation of Th cells into Th2 cells?

{{c1::IL-2}}
{{c1::IL-4}}

In which organ do T-cell differentiation and maturation occur?

{{c1::Thymus}}

Which cytokines induce differentiation of Th cells to Th17 cells?

{{c1::TFG-β}}
{{c1::IL-1}}
{{c1::IL-6}}

Which four types of T helper cells differentiate from CD4+ T cells?

{{c1::Th1}} cells
{{c1::Th2}} cells
{{c1::Th17}} cells
{{c1::Treg}} cells

Which cytokines from Th2 cells inhibits the action of Th1 cells?

{{c1::IL-4}}
{{c1::IL-10}}

What cytokines do Th2 cells secrete?

{{c1::IL-4}}
{{c1::IL-5}}
{{c1::IL-6}}
{{c1::IL-10}}
{{c1::IL-13}}

Which cytokines work to induce differentiation of Th cells to Th1 cells?

{{c1::IFN-γ}}
{{c1::IL-12}}

What are the two functions of IFN-γ and IL-2 secreted by Th1 cells?

Activation of {{c1::macrophages}}
Activation of {{c1::Tc}} cells

Which cytokines function to drive differentiation of Th cells into Treg cells?

{{c1::TGF-β}}
{{c1::IL-2}}

What is the function of Th2 cells?

Activate {{c1::eosinophils}}
Promote Ig{{c1::E}} production

What cytokines do Th17 cells secrete?

{{c1::IL-17}}
{{c1::IL-21}}
{{c1::IL-22}}

What is the function of Th17 cells?

They stimulate mobilization of {{c1::neutrophils}} in the inflammation process

Which cytokines inhibit the differentiation of Th17 cells?

{{c1::IFN-γ}}
{{c1::IL-4}}

What cytokines do Treg cells secrete?

{{c1::TGF-β}}
{{c1::IL-10}}
{{c1::IL-35}}

What is the function of Treg cells?

Maintain tolerance to self-{{c1::antigens}} to prevent {{c1::autoimmunity}}

Which cytokine inhibits the differentiation of Treg cells?

{{c1::IL-6}}

Name four diseases associated with autoimmune regulator deficiency.

{{c1::Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis}}
{{c1::Hypoparathyroidism::Hyperparathyroidism/Hypoparathyroidism}}
{{c1::Adrenal}} insufficiency
Recurrent {{c1::Candida}} infections

Which cytokine secreted by Th1 cells enhances monocyte/macrophage killing of ingested microbes?

{{c1::IFN-γ}}

What cell surface receptor molecule and cell ligand interact on macrophages to enhance microbial killing ability?

Cellular marker → {{c1::CD40}}
Cell ligand → {{c1::CD40L}}

In the cytotoxic granules released by T cells, what induces apoptosis in target cells?

{{c1::Preformed}} proteins
fields.Back Extra: Examples of preformed proteins include granzyme B and perforin.

fields.Text:
How do cytotoxic T cells kill virus-infected, neoplastic, and donor graft cells?

{{c1::Apoptosis}}

What receptor does CD8 on cytotoxic T cells bind to on virus-infected cells?

MHC {{c1::I::I/II}}

What endocrine disorder is associated with IPEX syndrome in male infants?

{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}

What syndrome is associated with genetic deficiency of FOXP3?

{{c1::IPEX}} syndrome

Expression of which four proteins helps in identifying Treg cells?

{{c1::FOXP3}}
{{c1::CD3}}
{{c1::CD4}}
{{c1::CD25}}

How do Treg cells maintain specific immune tolerance?

By suppressing CD{{c1::4}}+ and CD{{c1::8}}+ T-cell effector responses

Name two anti-inflammatory cytokines produced by activated Treg cells.

{{c1::IL-10}}
{{c1::TGF-β}}

What two processes can activated B cells that produce IgM undergo?

{{c1::Class switching}}
{{c1::Affinity}} maturation

What determines immunoglobulin class switching of B cells?

{{c1::Cytokines}}
fields.Back Extra: This is secreted by Th cells.

fields.Text:
Activation of which cell type is required for B-cell activation?

Activation of {{c1::Th}} cells

After T-cell activation, what is the function of Th and Tc cells, respectively?

Th cells produce {{c1::cytokines}}
Tc cells recognize and kill {{c1::virus}}-infected cells

What is the purpose of each of the two signals in T-cell activation?

Signal 1 presents {{c1::antigen}} for T-cell activation
Signal 2 induces {{c1::proliferation}} and {{c1::survival}}

What is the secondary or costimulatory signal in the process of B-cell activation?

Binding of {{c1::CD40}} receptor on the B cell to {{c1::CD40L}} on the Th cell

After receptor-mediated endocytosis by B cells, how is the antigen processed?

Exogenous antigen is presented on MHC {{c1::II::I/II}} and recognized by {{c1::T-cell}} receptors on {{c1::Th}} cells

What two receptors interact between T cells and antigen-presenting cells to stimulate the costimulatory signal?

{{c1::CD28}}
{{c1::B7}}

What serves as the primary signal for naive Tc cell activation?

An {{c1::endogenous::endogenous/exogenous}} or {{c1::cross-presented}} antigen is presented on MHC {{c1::I::I/II}} to Tc cells

What serves as the primary signal for naive Th cell activation?

An {{c1::exogenous::endogenous/exogenous}} antigen is presented on MHC {{c1::II::I/II}} and recognized by T-cell receptors on Th cells

Name the four antigen-presenting cells.

{{c1::Macrophages}}
{{c1::B}} cells
{{c1::Dendritic}} cells
{{c1::Langerhans}} cells

What are the three ways by which antibody-mediated pathogen elimination occurs?

{{c1::Opsonization}}
{{c1::Neutralization}}
{{c1::Complement}} activation

How does antibody specificity occur?

{{c1::Somatic hypermutation}} and {{c1::affinity}} maturation for the variable region
{{c1::Isotype switching}} for the constant region

Name the three methods by which antibody diversity is established.

Random recombination of {{c1::VJ}} or {{c1::V(D)J}} genes
{{c1::Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase}} inserts random nucleotides into DNA during recombination
Random combination of {{c1::light chains}} and {{c1::heavy chains}}

In antibody generation, which steps are antigen independent and which steps are antigen dependent?

Generation of antibody {{c1::diversity}} is antigen independent
Generation of antibody {{c1::specificity}} is antigen dependent

What are the properties of the Fc fragment of an antibody?

{{c1::Constant}} region
{{c1::Carboxy}} terminal
{{c1::Complement}} binding
{{c1::Carbohydrate}} side chains
{{c1::Confers}} isotype

How do the Fab and Fc regions determine the type of antibody that will be produced?

Fab determines the {{c1::idiotype}}
Fc determines the {{c1::isotype}}

Antibodies are made up of the Fab and Fc regions. What is the function of each region in immunity?

Fab region recognizes {{c1::antigens}}
Fc region fixes to {{c1::complement}}

What are the four domains that comprise the Fab region of an antibody?

{{c1::Variable light}} region
{{c1::Constant light}} region
{{c1::Variable heavy}} region
{{c1::Constant heavy 1}} region

The hinge region of an antibody connects which two domains?

The {{c1::Fab}} region of the heavy chain and the {{c1::Fc}} region

What unique chemical bond is found within the hinge region of an antibody molecule?

{{c1::Disulfide}} bond

What is the process by which an antibody prevents bacterial adherence?

{{c1::Neutralization}}

What is the process by which an antibody promotes phagocytosis?

{{c1::Opsonization}}

What structure helps antibodies to activate a complement and enhance opsonization and lysis?

{{c1::Membrane attack complex}}

Where can IgD be found?

Surface of many {{c1::B}} cells
{{c1::Serum}}

Which immunoglobulin isotype contributes to immunity against parasites by activating eosinophils?

Ig{{c1::E}}

Which antibody isotype facilitates an immediate, type I hypersensitivity reaction?

Ig{{c1::E}}
fields.Back Extra: It cross-links when exposed to an allergen and mediates the release of inflammatory mediators.

fields.Text:
What benefit is conferred by IgM assuming a pentameric configuration?

Increased ability to {{c1::trap}} free antigens out of tissue while the humoral response is evolving

In which structural form is IgM secreted?

{{c1::Pentameric}} form
fields.Back Extra: This is associated with J chains.

fields.Text:
Which immunoglobulin isotype is produced in the primary, immediate response to an antigen?

Ig{{c1::M}}

How does IgA protect itself from breakdown by luminal proteases?

It picks up a {{c1::secretory}} component from epithelial cells, thereby shielding its {{c1::Fc}} portion from luminal proteases

What do affinity and avidity of an immunoglobulin signify?

Affinity → Refers to the {{c1::individual}} antibody-antigen interaction
Avidity → Refers to the cumulative {{c1::binding strength}} of all antibody-antigen interactions in a {{c1::multivalent}} molecule

Which is the most abundantly produced immunoglobulin?

Ig{{c1::A}}
fields.Back Extra: It is produced in the gastrointestinal tract.

fields.Text:
In which structural form is IgA secreted?

{{c1::Dimeric}} form
fields.Back Extra:
This is with a J chain when it is secreted.

The monomeric form is only found in the serum.

fields.Text:
Which immunoglobin isotype provides infants with passive immunity through breast milk?

Ig{{c1::A}}

Which immunoglobulin isotype protects mucous membranes from invading pathogens?

Ig{{c1::A}}

What two immunoglobulin isotypes are involved in fixation of complement?

Ig{{c1::G}}
Ig{{c1::M}}

List the four main functions of IgG.

Fixation of {{c1::complement}}
{{c1::Opsonization}} of bacteria
{{c1::Neutralization}} of bacterial toxins and viruses
Provision of {{c1::passive}} immunity to infants via the {{c1::placenta}}

Which antibody isotype is the most abundant in the serum?

Ig{{c1::G}}

Which antibody isotype acts as the main antibody in the secondary, delayed response to an antigen?

Ig{{c1::G}}

Before activation, mature, and naïve B cells express what immunoglobulin isotypes on their surfaces?

Ig{{c1::M}}
Ig{{c1::D}}

Which immunoglobulin isotypes are secreted by plasma cells?

Ig{{c1::A}}
Ig{{c1::G}}
Ig{{c1::E}}

All immunoglobulin isotypes can exist in which structural form?

{{c1::Monomers}}

Which immunoglobulin, passed from mother to infant, is responsible for passive immunity after birth?

Ig{{c1::G}}

Immunoglobulin isotypes differentiate in germinal centers of lymph nodes by which mechanism?

{{c1::Isotype switching}} into {{c1::plasma}} cells

Name two molecules that induce gene rearrangement and/or isotype switching.

{{c1::Cytokines}}
{{c1::CD40L}}

Which immunoglobulin isotypes are associated with cold and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia?

Cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia → Ig{{c1::M}}
Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia → Ig{{c1::G}}

By which process does IgA cross epithelial cells?

{{c1::Transcytosis}}

Which immunoglobulin isotype protects against gut infections?

Ig{{c1::A}}

Which two immunologic phenomena are caused by thymus-dependent antigens?

{{c1::Class switching}}
Immunologic {{c1::memory}} formation
fields.Back Extra: This is due to the interaction of B cells and Th cells.

fields.Text:
Why are thymus-independent antigens weakly immunogenic?

They lack a {{c1::peptide}} component
fields.Back Extra: Therefore, MHC-mediated presentation to T cells cannot occur.

fields.Text:
What kind of antigens are lipopolysaccharides on gram-negative bacteria, with relation to thymus activation?

Thymus-{{c1::independent::independent/dependent}} antigens that lack a {{c1::peptide}} component

Why are thymus-dependent antigens often strongly immunogenic?

They contain a {{c1::protein}} component
fields.Back Extra: Hence, they can be presented by MHC to T cells.

fields.Text:
Which type of vaccine often requires boosters and adjuvants?

Vaccines that contain thymus-{{c1::independent::independent/dependent}} antigens with no {{c1::peptide}} component

How is the alternative pathway of the complement system activated?

{{c1::Spontaneously}}
Microbial {{c1::surface}} molecules

Trace the alternative pathway from C3 all the way to the cleavage of C5.

C3 is cleaved into C3b → C3b + {{c1::Bb}} → {{c1::C3bBb}}, which cleaves C3 into C3a/C3b → {{c1::C3bBb}} + C3b → {{c1::C3bBb3b}}, which cleaves C5 into C5a/C5b

Describe the lectin pathway all the way to C5 cleaving into C5a/C5b.

Microbial surfaces → {{c1::C1}}-like complex → Cleaves C4 into C4a/C4b → C4b + {{c1::C2b}} → {{c1::C4b2b}}, which cleaves C3 into C3a/C3b → Increase in {{c1::C4b2b3b}} activity cleaves C5 into C5a/C5b

How is the classic complement pathway activated?

Ig{{c1::G}}
Ig{{c1::M}}

Name two proteins that prevent complement activation on self cells.

{{c1::Decay-accelerating}} factor
{{c1::C1 esterase}} inhibitor

Name the two molecules that act as primary opsonins to defend against bacteral infections.

{{c1::C3b}}
Ig{{c1::G}}

Which complement proteins combine to form the membrane attack complex to mediate cytolysis?

{{c1::C5b}}
{{c1::C6}}
{{c1::C7}}
{{c1::C8}}
{{c1::C9}}

Which complement protein attracts neutrophils to the site of inflammation?

{{c1::C5a}}

Which three complement proteins are responsible for anaphylaxis?

{{c1::C3a}}
{{c1::C4a}}
{{c1::C5a}}

The membrane attack complex is important for protection against what type of organisms?

Gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} bacteria
fields.Back Extra: An example of this is the Neisseria species.

fields.Text:
How is the lectin pathway of the complement system activated?

By {{c1::mannose}} or other {{c1::sugars}} found on microbial {{c1::surfaces}}

What are the two primary functions of C3b?

{{c1::Opsonization}}
Clearance of {{c1::immune}} complexes

What component on the bacterial surface does C3b bind in order to opsonize the pathogen?

{{c1::Lipopolysaccharides}}

What is the result of activation of the membrane attack complex?

{{c1::Cytolysis}}
{{c1::Cytotoxicity}}

Name two processes in which complement proteins play a role.

{{c1::Innante}} immunity
{{c1::Inflammation}}

What is the test that is used to screen for activation of the classical complement pathway?

{{c1::CH50}} test

Which class of medication is contraindicated for patients with C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency?

{{c1::ACE}} inhibitors

How does hereditary angioedema occur in C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency?

Unregulated activation of {{c1::kallikrein}} → Increased {{c1::bradykinin}} levels

Which complement disorder increases the susceptibility to recurrent Neisseria bacteremia?

{{c1::Terminal::Early/Terminal}} complement deficiencies

Which complement disorder is associated with recurrent pyogenic sinus and respiratory tract infections?

{{c1::Early::Early/Terminal}} complement deficiencies

Early complement deficiencies are associated with an increased risk of which autoimmune disease?

{{c1::Systemic lupus erythematosus}}

A defect in what gene prevents anchoring of complement inhibitors in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?

{{c1::PIGA}} gene

What lab findings might be seen in patients with C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency?

Decreased {{c1::C4}} levels

What type of hemolysis is associated with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?

{{c1::Complement}}-mediated {{c1::intravascular::intravascular/extravascular}} hemolysis
fields.Back Extra: This presents with low haptoglobin and dark urine.

fields.Text:
Name the disease that is implicated with defects in anchoring of complement inhibitors, such as decay-accelerating factor (CD55) and membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis (CD59).

{{c1::Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria}}

How do early complement deficiencies increase the risk of systemic lupus erythematosus?

Reduced clearance of {{c1::antigen}}-{{c1::antibody}} complexes due to lack of {{c1::C3b}}

Name four examples of atypical venous thrombosis that can occur in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?

{{c1::Budd-Chiari}} syndrome
