{{c1::Portal vein}} thrombosis
{{c1::Cerebral}} thrombosis
{{c1::Dermal}} thrombosis

Which cytokines are involved in the induction, facilitation, and maintenance of granulomas in tuberculosis?

{{c1::IFN-γ}} → Activates macrophages to induce granuloma formation
{{c1::IL-12}} → Facilitates granuloma formation
{{c1::TNF-α}} → Maintains granuloma

Which two cytokines have the same attenuating effect on the immune system?

{{c1::TGF-β}}
{{c1::IL-10}}

Which three cytokines secreted by macrophages may contribute to the development of fever and sepsis?

{{c1::IL-1}}
{{c1::IL-6}}
{{c1::TNF-α}}

Which cytokine is known to promote cachexia in malignancy?

{{c1::TNF-α}}

What are the three main functions of TNF-α?

Activation of {{c1::endothelium}}
Recruitment of {{c1::white blood}} cells
Promotion of vascular {{c1::leak}}

Which cytokine induces IgG isotype switching in B cells and increases MHC expression and antigen presentation?

{{c1::IFN-γ}}

Which cytokine is secreted by natural killer cells and Th1 cells to stimulate macrophages to destroy phagocytosed pathogens and inhibit Th2 differentiation?

{{c1::IFN-γ}}

What are the two main functions of IL-12?

Activates {{c1::natural killer}} cells
Induces differentiation of T cells to {{c1::Th1}} cells

Which two types of immune cells secrete IL-10?

{{c1::Th2}} cells
{{c1::Treg}} cells

How does IL-10 attenuate the inflammatory response?

It decreases expression of MHC {{c1::II::I/II}} cytokines and {{c1::Th1}} cell cytokines
It inhibits active {{c1::macrophages}} and {{c1::dendritic}} cells

What is the main function of IL-8?

Promotes {{c1::neutrophil chemotaxis}} to clear infections

Which cytokines are secreted by macrophages?

{{c1::IL-1}}
{{c1::IL-6}}
{{c1::IL-8}}
{{c1::IL-12}}
{{c1::TNF-α}}

Which interleukin is responsible for mediating fever and stimulating acute-phase protein production?

{{c1::IL-6}}

What are the three main functions of IL-5?

Promotes growth and differentiation of {{c1::B}} cells
Enhances class switching to Ig{{c1::A}}
Stimulates growth and differentiation of {{c1::eosinophils}}

What are the three main functions of IL-4?

Induces differentiation of T cells into {{c1::Th2}} cells
Promotes growth of {{c1::B}} cells
Enhances class switching to Ig{{c1::E}} and Ig{{c1::G}}

Which cells secrete IL-2 and IL-3?

{{c1::T}} cells

What is the function of IL-3?

Functions like {{c1::GM-CSF}}
Supports the growth and differentiation of {{c1::stem}} cells in the bone marrow

What is the main function of IL-2?

Stimulates the growth of {{c1::Th}} cells, {{c1::Tc}} cells, {{c1::Treg}} cells, and {{c1::natural killer}} cells

What are the main functions of IL-1?

Induces {{c1::fever}} and acute {{c1::inflammation}}
Activates {{c1::endothelium}} to express adhesion molecules
Induces {{c1::chemokine}} secretion to recruit white blood cells
Activates {{c1::osteoclasts}}

What is another name for IL-1?

{{c1::Osteoclast-activating}} factor

Which two cytokines function in the recruitment of immune cells after the initial phase of acute inflammation?

{{c1::IL-8}}
{{c1::IL-12}}

A patient with longstanding severe rheumatoid arthritis is diagnosed with osteoporosis. Which cytokine may have mediated the development of this condition?

{{c1::IL-1}}
fields.Back Extra:
This may have been upregulated by chronic inflammation.

IL-1 causes activation of osteoclasts, which can increase bone resorption.

fields.Text:
What are two important functions of IL-13?

Promotes Ig{{c1::E}} production by {{c1::B}} cells
Induces alternative activation of {{c1::macrophages}}

In what part of the phagocyte does respiratory burst occur?

{{c1::Phagolysosome}}

Which enzyme catalyzes the conversion of oxygen to superoxide in the first step of respiratory burst?

{{c1::NADPH oxidase}}

Which molecular cofactor is required for both the creation and neutralization of reactive oxygen species?

{{c1::NADPH}}

What end product of oxygen-dependent respiratory burst is used to kill bacteria in the phagolysosome?

{{c1::Hypochlorite}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as bleach.

fields.Text:
To prevent cell lysis, which form of glutathione must be readily available in the cell to remove reactive oxygen species?

{{c1::Reduced::Oxidized/Reduced}} form

To kill competing bacteria, Pseudomonas aeruginosa cultures can use high levels of reactive oxygen species. How does this occur?

Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces {{c1::pyocyanin}}, which produces reactive oxygen species to kill competing microbes

A patient with bronchiectasis produces blue-green sputum when she coughs. Which enzyme in neutrophils gives the sputum its color?

{{c1::Myeloperoxidase}}

Why do cells like neutrophils and monocytes have high concentrations of NADPH oxidase?

To rapidly release {{c1::reactive oxygen species}}

What are the two cells that utilize the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex?

{{c1::Neutrophils}}
{{c1::Monocytes}}

What protein found in secretory fluids and neutrophils inhibits microbial growth via iron chelation?

{{c1::Lactoferrin}}

The phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex utilizes what molecule as a substrate?

{{c1::Oxygen}}

What enzyme catalyzes the conversion of superoxide into hydrogen peroxide in the second step of respiratory burst?

{{c1::Superoxide dismutase}}

The bacterial catalase enzyme converts H2O2 generated from oxidative burst into what two products?

{{c1::Water}}
{{c1::Oxygen}}

What enzyme is responsible for the incorporation of chloride into hydrogen peroxide to form hypochlorite radicals?

{{c1::Myeloperoxidase}}

The phagocytes of patients with chronic granulomatous disease can still make reactive oxygen species from what compound provided by invading organisms?

{{c1::H2O2}}
fields.Back Extra: However, catalase-positive organisms can neutralize their own H2O2, thus circumventing this mechanism.

fields.Text:
Why are patients with chronic granulomatous disease susceptible to catalase-positive organisms?

Catalase-positive species can neutralize their own {{c1::H2O2}}
fields.Back Extra: This leaves the phagocytes of patients with chronic granulomatous disease incapable of producing reactive oxygen species to fight infections.

fields.Text:
Which enzyme is involved in the regeneration of NADPH from NADP+?

{{c1::Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase}}

Deficiency of which enzyme can cause chronic granulomatous disease?

{{c1::NADPH oxidase}}

Interferons are effective in the immune response against which type of pathogens?

{{c1::Viruses}}
fields.Back Extra: This is for both RNA and DNA viruses.

fields.Text:
What are the five major adverse effects of interferons?

{{c1::Myopathy}}
{{c1::Neutropenia}}
{{c1::Flu}}-like symptoms
{{c1::Depression}}
{{c1::Autoimmune}} reactions

What four types of neoplasms are treated with interferons?

{{c1::Renal cell}} carcinoma
Malignant {{c1::melanoma}}
{{c1::Kaposi}} sarcoma
{{c1::Hairy cell}} leukemia

When do cells generally synthesize interferons?

When infected by {{c1::viruses}}

Interferons can prime local cells for self-defense against viruses by inducing downregulation of what process?

{{c1::Protein}} synthesis
fields.Back Extra: This is to resist potential viral replication.

fields.Text:
Interferons can prime local cells for self-defense against viruses by inducing upregulation of what process?

{{c1::MHC}} expression
fields.Back Extra: This is to facilitate the recognition of infected cells.

fields.Text:
Which two viral infections are commonly treated with interferons?

Chronic hepatitis {{c1::B}} virus
{{c1::Condyloma acuminatum}}

Which immunodeficiency syndrome is commonly treated with interferons?

{{c1::Chronic granulomatous}} disease

What are the three major types of interferons?

{{c1::IFN-α}}
{{c1::IFN-β}}
{{c1::IFN-γ}}

Detection of which cell surface protein indicates hematopoietic stem cells?

{{c1::CD34}}

Which cell surface protein on B cells binds antigens?

{{c1::Immunoglobulin}}

Which two cell surface proteins are suggestive of natural killer cell lineage?

{{c1::CD16}}
{{c1::CD56}}

How does Epstein-Barr virus invade B cells?

Epstein-Barr virus binds to {{c1::CD21}} on the surface of B cells

Which cell surface proteins are common to all B cells?

{{c1::Immunoglobulin}}
{{c1::CD19}}
{{c1::CD20}}
{{c1::CD21}}
{{c1::CD40}}
MHC {{c1::II::I/II}}
{{c1::B7}}

Besides typical T-cell surface proteins, which two additional cell surface proteins do Treg cells have?

{{c1::CD4}}
{{c1::CD25}}

Which cell surface protein is unique to Tc cells?

{{c1::CD8}}

Which cell surface receptors does HIV use to infect its target host cells?

{{c1::CXCR4}}
{{c1::CCR5}}
fields.Back Extra: These serve as coreceptors on Th cells.

fields.Text:
Which three cell surface proteins are common to all T cells?

{{c1::CD3}}
{{c1::CD28}}
{{c1::T-cell}} receptors

Which cell surface proteins are found on macrophages?

{{c1::CD14}}
{{c1::CD40}}
{{c1::CCR5}}
MHC {{c1::II::I/II}}
{{c1::B7}}
Receptors for {{c1::Fc}}
Receptors for {{c1::C3b}}

What cell surface protein found on macrophages acts as a receptor for pathogen-associated molecular patterns, such as lipopolysaccharides?

{{c1::CD14}}

The presence of which two receptors on macrophages enhances their phagocytic activity?

{{c1::Fc}} receptors
{{c1::C3b}} receptors

Which receptor found on natural killer cells binds to the Fc region of IgG?

{{c1::CD16}}

Besides typical T-cell surface proteins, which three cell surface proteins are found on Th cells?

{{c1::CD4}}
{{c1::CD40L}}
{{c1::CXCR4}}/{{c1::CCR5}}

Which mechanism can be adopted by immune cells to promote self-tolerance to self-antigens?

A state of {{c1::anergy}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a state in which activation of a cell by exposure to its antigen is not possible.

fields.Text:
In what situation do T cells and B cells become anergic?

When they do not receive a {{c1::costimulatory}} signal on exposure to an antigen

After exposure to which six agents are unvaccinated patients administered preformed antibodies as a part of postexposure prophylaxis?

{{c1::Tetanus}} toxin
Hepatitis {{c1::B}} virus
{{c1::Varicella zoster virus}}
{{c1::Rabies virus}}
{{c1::Botlinum}} toxin
{{c1::Diphtheria}} toxin

How does a person acquire passive immunity?

By getting {{c1::preformed}} antibodies

How does a person acquire active immunity?

By exposure to {{c1::exogenous}} antigens

What is the temporal onset and duration of passive immunity?

{{c1::Rapid::Rapid/Slow}} onset, but {{c1::short::long/short}} duration of antibody protection

What is the temporal onset and duration of active immunity?

{{c1::Slow::Rapid/Slow}} onset, but {{c1::long::long/short}}-lasting immune protection

What are two clinical examples of passive immunity being used as treatment?

{{c1::Antitoxins}}
{{c1::Humanized monoclonal}} antibodies

Which antibody do infants receive via breastfeeding to acquire passive immunity?

Ig{{c1::A}}

What are the three means by which one can acquire active immunity to an antigen?

{{c1::Natural}} infection
{{c1::Toxoid}} exposure
{{c1::Vaccination}}

Exposure to which two viruses requires combined active and passive immunization?

Hepatitis {{c1::B}} virus
{{c1::Rabies virus}}

What are ten key examples of live vaccines?

{{c1::Adenovirus}} vaccine
{{c1::Typhoid}} vaccine
{{c1::Polio (Sabin)}} vaccine
{{c1::Varicella}} vaccine
{{c1::Smallpox}} vaccine
{{c1::BCG}} vaccine
{{c1::Yellow fever}} vaccine
{{c1::Influenza}} vaccine
{{c1::MMR}} vaccine
{{c1::Rotavirus}} vaccine

What are hepatitis A, typhoid, rabies, influenza, and polio (Salk) vaccines examples of?

{{c1::Inactivated}}/{{c1::killed}} vaccines

What is the main drawback of receiving the annual injected influenza vaccine?

Because it is an {{c1::inactivated}} vaccine, the immune response is {{c1::weaker}}

What are the common and rare adverse effects associated with mRNA vaccines?

Common → Local and transient {{c1::systemic}} reactions
Rare → {{c1::Pericarditis}} or {{c1::myocarditis}}, especially in young males

What two live attenuated vaccines can be given to patients with HIV infection and a CD4+ cell count of ≥ 200 cells/mm3?

{{c1::MMR}} vaccine
{{c1::Varicella}} vaccine

Why should patients with immunodeficiency and pregnant patients avoid receiving live attenuated vaccines?

Because the microorganism in live attenuated vaccines may revert to a {{c1::virulent}} form

Which type of vaccines often induce strong, lifelong immunity?

{{c1::Live attenuated}} vaccines

Which live nonattenuated viral vaccine is only given to military recruits?

{{c1::Adenovirus}} vaccine

What two types of vaccines can activate both a cellular and a humoral response?

{{c1::Live attenuated}} vaccines
{{c1::mRNA}} vaccines

What are the two key disadvantages of subunit vaccines?

{{c1::Expensive}}
Induce a {{c1::weaker}} immune response

List seven examples of subunit vaccines.

Hepatitis {{c1::B}} virus
{{c1::HPV}}
{{c1::Acellular pertussis}}
{{c1::Neisseria meningitidis}}
{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae type b}}
{{c1::Herpes zoster}}

What type of vaccine is composed of a denatured bacterial toxin with an intact receptor binding site?

{{c1::Toxoid}} vaccine
fields.Back Extra: This is protective against bacterial toxins.

fields.Text:
What is the main drawback associated with toxoid vaccines?

They stimulate the production of antitoxins, but levels {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} with time

What are two key examples of bacterial toxoid vaccines?

{{c1::Diphtheria}} toxoid
{{c1::Tetanus}} toxoid

Which typhoid vaccine is capable of producing a stronger immune response?

{{c1::Ty21a}} typhoid vaccine
fields.Back Extra: This is a live attenuated vaccine.

fields.Text:
Which typhoid vaccine against Salmonella typhi poses a lower risk of causing infection?

The intramuscular {{c1::Vi polysaccharide}} typhoid vaccine

What is the mechanism through which mRNA vaccines work?

A lipid {{c1::nanoparticle}} transports mRNA into the cell, which is later used by the cell to synthesize foreign {{c1::protein}}

Which hepatitis B virus antigen does the recombinant subunit hepatitis B virus vaccine contain?

{{c1::HBsAg}}

How is a killed vaccine prepared?

The pathogen is inactivated with {{c1::heat}} or {{c1::chemicals}} before administration
fields.Back Extra: This leaves the epitope structure on surface antigens intact.

fields.Text:
What does a live attenuated vaccine contain?

A microorganism that has been modified to lose its {{c1::pathogenicity}}
fields.Back Extra: However, it retains the capacity for transient growth within the host.

fields.Text:
Which type of vaccine stimulates antibody production without the potential for causing disease?

{{c1::Toxoid}} vaccine

What types of vaccines include specific antigens that best elicit an immune response?

{{c1::Subunit}} vaccines
{{c1::Recombinant}} vaccines
{{c1::Polysaccharide}} vaccines
{{c1::Conjugate}} vaccines

What type of active immune response is triggered by inactivated or killed vaccines?

{{c1::Humoral}} response

What are the common mechanisms of a type II hypersensitivity reaction?

Antibodies bind to cell surface antigens → Cellular {{c1::destruction}}, {{c1::inflammation}}, {{c1::dysfunction}}

How does the immediate phase of type I hypersensitivity reaction take place?

Antigen crosslinks Ig{{c1::E}} on the surface of presensitized cells → Immediate {{c1::degranulation}} → Release of histamine, tryptase, and leukotrienes

A child develops wheezing and hives after consuming peanuts. How would you test for the responsible hypersensitivity reaction?

{{c1::Skin}} test
{{c1::Blood}} test
fields.Back Extra: This is to test for an allergen-specific IgE in a type I hypersensitivity reaction.

fields.Text:
The Arthus reaction is what type of hypersensitivity reaction?

Type {{c1::III}} hypersensitivity reaction

What are the four "T's" associated with type IV hypersensitivity reactions?

{{c1::T}} cells
{{c1::Transplant rejections}}
{{c1::Tuberculosis}} skin tests
{{c1::Touching}}

Allergic asthma and anaphylaxis are what type of hypersensitivity reaction?

Type {{c1::I}} hypersensitivity reaction

A patient develops worsening edema and necrosis at the site of recent tetanus vaccination. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Arthus}} reaction
fields.Back Extra: Preformed antibodies attack injected antigen → Immune complexes form in the skin → Complement activation

fields.Text:
Which hypersensitivity reaction has a delayed response and does not involve antibodies?

Type {{c1::IV}} hypersensitivity reaction

What are the four types of hypersensitivity reactions?

Type I hypersensitivity reaction → {{c1::Anaphylactic}} and {{c1::atopic}}
Type II hypersensitivity reaction → {{c1::Antibody}}-mediated
Type III hypersensitivity reaction → {{c1::Immune}} complex
Type IV hypersensitivity reaction → {{c1::Delayed}}

Reaction to the PDD skin test is what type of hypersensitivity reaction?

Type {{c1::IV}} hypersensitivity reaction

Goodpasture syndrome, rheumatic fever, and hyperacute transplant rejection exemplify what type II hypersensitivity mechanism?

{{c1::Inflammation}}

Name two examples of type IV hypersensitivity reaction.

{{c1::Graft-versus-host}} disease
{{c1::Contact dermatitis}}

What hypersensitivity reaction is associated with vasculitis and systemic manifestations?

Type {{c1::III}} hypersensitivity reaction

What is the mechanism of the type III hypersensitivity reaction?

Antigen-antibody complexes activate {{c1::complement}} → Neutrophil {{c1::chemotaxis}} → Neutrophils release {{c1::lysosomal}} enzymes

What are the common causes of serum sickness-like reactions?

Drugs such as {{c1::penicillin}} and {{c1::monoclonal::monoclonal/polyclonal}} antibodies
Infections such as {{c1::hepatitis B}}

How does type II hypersensitivity mediate cellular destruction?

Cells are {{c1::opsonized}} → Phagocytosis with/without {{c1::complement}} system activation or killed by {{c1::natural killer}} cells

What type of hypersensitivity reaction is serum sickness?

Type {{c1::III}} hypersensitivity reaction

Describe the mechanism of the late phase of a type I hypersensitivity reaction.

{{c1::Mast}} cell degranulation → {{c1::Chemokines}} attract inflammatory cells and other mediators from {{c1::mast}} cells → Inflammation and tissue damage

Describe the mechanism by which type II hypersensitivity reactions causes cellular dysfunction.

Antibodies bind to cell-surface receptors → Abnormal {{c1::blockade}} or {{c1::activation}} of downstream processes

Myasthenia gravis, Graves disease, and pemphigus vulgaris are examples of what type II hypersensitivity mechanism?

Cellular {{c1::dysfunction}}

What immunoglobulin isotype most commonly forms the immune complexes implicated in type III hypersensitivity reactions?

Ig{{c1::G}}

Describe the mechanism of serum sickness.

Antibodies to foreign proteins are produced → 1 to 2 weeks later, {{c1::antibody}}-{{c1::antigen}} complexes are formed and deposited in tissue → {{c1::Complement}} activation → Inflammation and tissue damage

List eight examples of type III hypersensitivity reactions.

{{c1::Serum sickness}}
{{c2::Arthus}} reaction
{{c3::Systemic lupus erythematosus}}
{{c4::Polyarteritis nodosa}}
{{c5::Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis}}
{{c6::Rheumatoid arthritis}}
{{c7::Reactive arthritis}}
{{c8::IgA vasculitis}}

How does inflammation occur in type IV hypersensitivity reactions?

Effector CD{{c1::4}}+ {{c1::T}} cells detect antigen and release {{c1::cytokines}} that induce inflammation

Describe the mechanism of direct cell cytotoxicity in type IV hypersensitivity reactions.

Targeted cells are killed by CD{{c1::8}}+ {{c1::Tc}} cells

What test is used to determine T-cell immune function via a type IV hypersensitivity-mediated reaction?

{{c1::Candida skin}} test

Name four important examples of type II hypersensitivity reaction due to cellular destruction.

{{c1::Autoimmune hemolytic}} anemia
{{c1::Immune thrombocytopenia}}
{{c1::Transfusion}} reactions
{{c1::Hemolytic}} disease of the newborn

How does a type II hypersensitivity reaction mediate inflammation?

Binding of antibodies to cell surfaces → Activation of {{c1::complement}} system and {{c1::Fc}} receptor-mediated inflammation

What are the two phases of type I hypersensitivity reaction?

{{c1::Immediate}}
{{c1::Late}}

What is the marker of mast cell activation during a type I hypersensitivity reaction?

Release of {{c1::tryptase}} following mast cell degranulation

What is the cause of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema within minutes to hours of receiving blood products?

{{c1::Transfusion}}-related acute lung injury

What type of hypersensitivity reaction is acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?

Type {{c1::II}} hypersensitivity reaction
fields.Back Extra: This is mediated by antibodies to donor red blood cell surface antigens.

fields.Text:
How could febrile nonhemolytic reactions be prevented in previously affected patients?

By using {{c1::leukoreduced}} blood

Why does intravascular hemolysis occur in acute hemolytic transfusion reactions?

ABO blood group {{c1::incompatibility}}

What could be causing hives, wheezing, and shock within minutes of receiving a blood transfusion?

Type {{c1::I}} hypersensitivity reaction against {{c1::plasma}} proteins in the transfused blood

What is the 2-hit mechanism of injury in transfusion-related acute lung injury?

Sequestered {{c1::neutrophils}} are primed in pulmonary vessels → Activated in transfused blood → Release {{c1::inflammatory}} mediators → Increased capillary {{c1::permeability}} → Pulmonary edema

What is the pathogenesis of a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction?

An {{c1::anamnestic}} response to a foreign {{c1::antigen}} on the donor red blood cells

Why does a delayed hemolytic reaction usually take 1 to 2 weeks to develop?

{{c1::Slow::Fast/Slow}} destruction of the red blood cells in the {{c1::reticuloendothelial}} system

Which blood transfusion reaction is clinically silent, but may present with mild fever and hyperbilirubinemia, and is usually self-limited?

{{c1::Delayed hemolytic}} transfusion reaction

Why does an allergic reaction to a blood product occur within minutes to hours of transfusion?

{{c1::Preformed}} inflammatory mediators are released from degranulating {{c1::mast}} cells

Why can an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction occur during transfusion?

{{c1::Preformed}} antibodies attack when {{c1::ABO}}-incompatible blood is transfused

Which type of blood transfusion reaction may exhibit fevere, headache, chills, and flushing in children?

{{c1::Febrile nonhemolytic}} transfusion reaction
fields.Back Extra: This is due to buildup of preformed cytokines, which are released by donor white blood cells when blood is stored.

fields.Text:
What type of hemolysis usually occurs in delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction?

{{c1::Extravascular::Intravascular/Extravascular}} hemolysis
fields.Back Extra: Intravascular hemolysis usually occurs in the acute hemolytic transfusion reactions.

fields.Text:
What specific precautions should be taken for an IgA-deficient person before they get a blood transfusion?

They should be given blood products {{c1::without::with/without}} IgA

Which autoantibodies are associated with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome?

Anti-{{c1::presynaptic::presynaptic/postsynaptic}} {{c1::voltage}}-gated {{c1::calcium}} channel autoantibodies

Rheumatoid factor, often positive in rheumatoid arthritis, is an autoantibody targeting which immunoglobulin?

It is an Ig{{c1::M}} antibody against the {{c1::Fc}} region of Ig{{c1::G}}

Which autoantibodies are more specific to rheumatoid arthritis?

{{c1::Anti-CCP}} autoantibodies

What autoantibodies are associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis?

{{c1::PR3-ANCA}} autoantibodies
{{c1::c-ANCA}} autoantibodies

MPO-ANCA and p-ANCA autoantibodies are associated with which four disorders?

{{c1::Ulcerative colitis}}
{{c1::Microscopic polyangiitis}}
{{c1::Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis}}
{{c1::Primary sclerosing cholangitis}}

Name the three autoantibodies associated with celiac disease.

IgA and IgG {{c1::deamidated gliadin peptide}} autoantibodies
IgA {{c1::anti-endomysial}} autoantibodies
IgA {{c1::anti-tissue transglutaminase}} autoantibodies

Anti-U1 RNP autoantibodies are associated with which disorder?

{{c1::Mixed connective tissue}} disease

What autoantibodies are found in association with Graves disease?

{{c1::Anti-TSH receptor}} autoantibodies

What autoantibodies are associated with Sjögren syndrome?

{{c1::Anti-Ro}}/{{c1::SSA}} autoantibodies
{{c1::Anti-La}}/{{c1::SSB}} autoantibodies

What autoantibodies are associated with autoimmune hepatitis?

{{c1::Anti-smooth muscle}} autoantibodies
{{c1::Anti-liver/kidney microsomal-1}} autoantibodies

What autoantibodies are associated with diffuse scleroderma?

{{c1::Anti-Scl-70}} autoantibodies

Name the two autoantibodies associated with pernicious anemia.

{{c1::Antiparital cell}} autoantibodies
{{c1::Anti-intrinsic factor}} autoantibodies

Which disease is associated with antimitochondrial autoantibodies?

{{c1::Primary biliary cholangitis}}

Name the two primary autoantibodies associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis.

{{c1::Antithyroglobulin}} autoantibodies
{{c1::Antithyroid peroxidase}} autoantibodies
fields.Back Extra: Antithyroid peroxidase autoantibodies are also known as antimicrosomal autoantibodies.

fields.Text:
Name the autoantibodies associated with dermatomyositis and polymyositis.

{{c1::Antisynthetase}} autoantibodies
{{c1::Anti-SRP}} autoantibodies
{{c1::Anti-helicase}} autoantibodies

What autoantibodies are found in association with drug-induced lupus?

{{c1::Antihistone}} autoantibodies

Which disease is associated with anti-hemidesmosome autoantibodies?

{{c1::Bullous pemphigoid}}

Which two autoantibodies are associated with type 1 diabetes mellitus?

{{c1::Islet cell cytoplasmic}} autoantibodies
{{c1::Anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase}} autoantibodies

Which five autoantibodies are associated with systemic lupus erythematosus?

{{c1::Anti-dsDNA}} autoantibodies
{{c1::Anti-Smith}} autoantibodies
{{c1::Anticardiolipin}} autoantibodies
{{c1::Lupus anticoagulant}} autoantibodies
{{c1::Antinuclear}} autoantibodies

What autoantibodies are present in patients with pemphigus vulgaris?

{{c1::Anti-desmosome}} autoantibodies

What autoantibodies are associated with limited scleroderma (CREST syndrome)?

{{c1::Anticentromere}} autoantibodies

Which two disorders are associated with both anticardiolipin and lupus anticoagulant autoantibodies?

{{c1::Systemic lupus erythematosus}}
{{c1::Antiphospholipid}} syndrome

Anti-glomerular basement membrane autoantibodies are associated with which disorder?

{{c1::Goodpasture}} syndrome

Which autoantibody is associated with myasthenia gravis?

Anti-{{c1::postsynaptic::presynaptic/postsynaptic}} {{c1::acetylcholine}} receptor autoantibodies

What autoantibodies are associated with antiphospholipid syndrome?

{{c1::Anti-β2 glycoprotein I}} autoantibodies
{{c1::Lupus anticoagulant}} autoantibodies
{{c1::Anticardiolipin}} autoantibodies

Anti-phospholipase A2 receptor autoantibodies are associated with which disorder?

{{c1::Primary membranous nephropathy}}

Which immunodeficiency can cause a false-negative celiac disease test result?

{{c1::Selective IgA}} deficiency
fields.Back Extra:
This is the most common primary immunodeficiency.

The cause is unknown.

fields.Text:
List the six clinical features of hyper-IgE syndrome.

{{c1::Noninflamed::Inflamed/Noninflamed}} {{c1::staphylococcal abscesses}}
Retained {{c1::baby teeth}}
{{c1::Coarse}} facies
{{c1::Dermatologic}} problems
High Ig{{c1::E}}
{{c1::Fractures}} from minor trauma
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as Job syndrome.

fields.Text:
Defect in which gene impairs the phagosome-lysosome fusion in Chédiak-Higashi syndrome?

{{c1::LYST}} gene
fields.Back Extra: This leads to microtubule dysfunction, impairing phagosome-lysosome fusion.

fields.Text:
What gene mutation leads to autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome?

{{c1::STAT3}} gene mutation
fields.Back Extra: This leads to Th17 deficiency, resulting in impaired neutrophil recruitment to infection sites.

fields.Text:
The response of which leukocyte and cytokine are decreased in patients with IL-12 receptor deficiency?

{{c1::Th1}} cells with {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} IFN-γ

Name the five immunodeficiency disorders that follow autosomal recessive inheritance patterns.

{{c1::IL-12 receptor}} deficiency
{{c1::Adenonsine deaminase}} deficiency
{{c1::Ataxia-telangiectasia}}
{{c1::Leukocyte adhesion}} deficiency type {{c1::1}}
{{c1::Chédiak-Higashi}} syndrome

Risk for what conditions get increased in patients with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?

{{c1::Malignancy}}
{{c1::Autoimmune}} diseases

What genetic defect causes thymic aplasia?

{{c1::22q11}} microdeletion

What three symptoms are seen in patients with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?

{{c1::Thrombocytopenia}}
{{c1::Eczema}}
{{c1::Recurrent}} infections

What are the classic findings of X-linked agammaglobulinemia?

Absent {{c1::B}} cells in peripheral blood
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in immunoglobulin of all classes
{{c1::Scanty}} tonsils/lymph nodes

What are the characteristic lab findings in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?

Decreased or normal Ig{{c1::G}} and Ig{{c1::M}}
Increased Ig{{c1::A}} and Ig{{c1::E}}
{{c1::Thrombocytopenia}} with {{c1::microsized}} platelets

A defect in which gene causes Bruton agammaglobulinemia?

{{c1::BTK}} gene
fields.Back Extra:
This leads to absent B-cell maturation.

The risk is increased in boys.

fields.Text:
How does a defective ATM gene lead to the accumulation of mutations in ataxia-telangiectasia?

ATM gene defects → Failure to detect {{c1::DNA}} damage and to halt the progression of the {{c1::cell cycle}} → Mutations accumulate

Patients with hyper-IgM syndrome are more susceptible to infection by which type of organisms?

{{c1::Cytomegalovirus}}
{{c1::Cryptosporidium}}
{{c1::Pneumocystis}}

What is the classic triad of presentation seen in ataxia telangiectasia?

{{c1::Ataxia}}
{{c1::Spider angiomas}}
Ig{{c1::A}} deficiency

Thymic aplasia, IL-12 receptor deficiency, Job syndrome, and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis feature dysfunction of which cell type?

{{c1::T}} cells

Name five inherited immunodeficiencies that are X-linked recessive and thus more common in boys.

{{c1::Hyper-IgM}} syndrome
{{c1::Wiskott-Aldrich}} syndrome
{{c1::Chronic granulomatous}} disease
{{c1::Bruton agammaglobulinemia}}
Some types of {{c1::severe combined immunodeficiency}}

X-linked agammaglobulinemia, selective IgA deficiency, and common variable immunodeficiency are disorders of which type of leukocyte?

{{c1::B}} cells

What characteristic findings are seen in chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis?

Lack of {{c1::cutaneous}} reaction to Candida antigens
Absence of in vitro {{c1::T}}-cell proliferation in response to Candida antigens

What is the most common cause of hyper-IgM syndrome?

Defective {{c1::CD40L}} on {{c1::Th}} cells → {{c1::Class switching}} defect

Describe the levels of immunoglobulins that characterize selective IgA deficiency.

Decreased Ig{{c1::A}} level
Normal Ig{{c1::G}} and Ig{{c1::M}} levels

A child has recurrent bacterial skin infections with absence of pus and impaired wound healing. What lab findings might confirm the diagnosis?

Increased serum {{c1::neutrophil}} levels
Lack of {{c1::neutrophils}} at infection sites
fields.Back Extra: This is leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1.

fields.Text:
A 2-year-old child with recurrent severe pyogenic bacterial infections has high IgM levels and low levels of all other immunoglobulins. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Hyper-IgM}} syndrome

Increased risk of what four types of conditions are found in patients with common variable immunodeficiency?

{{c1::Autoimmune}} diseases
{{c1::Bronchiectasis}}
{{c1::Lymphoma}}
{{c1::Sinopulmonary}} infections

What can be observed on chest X-ray, flow cytometry, and lymph node biopsy from a patient with severe combined immunodeficiency?

No {{c1::thymic shadow}} on chest X-ray
Lack of {{c1::T}} cells on flow cytometry
No {{c1::germinal centers}} in lymph nodes

Which immunodeficiency is due to a defect in B-cell differentiation resulting in decreased plasma cell levels?

{{c1::Common variable immunodeficiency}}

What are the common presenting findings of selective IgA deficiency?

{{c1::Asymptomatic::Symptomatic/Asymptomatic}}
{{c1::Airway}} and {{c1::gastrointestinal}} infections
{{c1::Autoimmune}} disease
{{c1::Atopy}}
{{c1::Anaphylaxis}} to IgA-containing blood products

What are three possible causes of severe combined immunodeficiency

{{c1::Adenosine deaminase}} deficiency
Defective {{c1::IL-2R gamma chain}}
{{c1::RAG}} mutation → Defects in VDJ recombination

Which two tests confirm the diagnosis of chronic granulomatous disease?

{{c1::Dihydrorhodamine}} test
{{c1::Nitroblue tetrazolium dye reduction}} test

Deficiency of which immune cells can cause hyper-IgE syndrome?

{{c1::Th17}} cells

How does a defective NADPH oxidase enzyme cause chronic granulomatous disease?

Defective NADPH oxidase → Decrease in {{c1::reactive oxygen species}} and {{c1::oxidative burst}} in neutrophils → Increased susceptibility to catalase-positive organisms, recurrent infections, and granulomas

A patient has recurrent fungal infections of the skin and mucous membranes due to a defect in the AIRE gene. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis}}

What types of infections are commonly seen in patients with X-linked agammaglobulinemia?

Recurrent {{c1::bacterial}} and {{c1::enteroviral}} infections after {{c1::6}} months of life
fields.Back Extra: This is as maternal IgG starts to decrease.

fields.Text:
What type of vaccine is contraindicated in patients with X-linked agammaglobulinemia?

{{c1::Live}} vaccines

Which immunodeficiency disorder results in low T-cell counts, low PTH, and low calcium?

{{c1::Thymic aplasia}}

Selective IgA deficiency increases the risk for which parasitic infection?

{{c1::Giardiasis}}

Thymic aplasia results from a failure in the development of what pharyngeal pouches?

{{c1::3rd}} and {{c1::4th}} pharyngeal pouches

What three organs have a defect in patients with DiGeorge syndrome?

{{c1::Thymus}}
{{c1::Parathyroid}} glands
{{c1::Heart}}

Which immunodeficiency syndrome is the most common cause of Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial diseases?

{{c1::IL-12 receptor}} deficiency

Which condition caused by T-cell dysfunction presents with persistent noninvasive Candida infection?

{{c1::Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis}}

What is the pathogenesis of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?

{{c1::WAS}} gene mutation prevents leukocytes and platelets from reorganizing {{c1::actin}} cytoskeleton → Defective antigen presentation

What five classical clinical presentations are associated with thymic aplasia?

{{c1::Cardiac}} defects
Abnormal {{c1::facies}}
Absent {{c1::thymic shadow}} on chest X-ray
{{c1::Cleft palate}}
{{c1::Hypocalcemia::Hypercalcemia/Hypocalcemia}}

Patients with ataxia-telangiectasia are at an increased risk for which malignancies?

{{c1::Lymphomas}}
{{c1::Leukemias}}

What is the pathophysiologic process of leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 leading to impaired migration and chemotaxis?

Lack of {{c1::LFA-1 integrin}} on phagocytes → Impaired migration and chemotaxis

What are the five manifestations of Chédiak-Higashi syndrome?

Progressive {{c1::neurodegeneration}}
{{c1::Lymphohistiocytosis}}
{{c1::Albinism}}
Recurrent {{c1::pyogenic}} infections
{{c1::Peripheral::Central/Peripheral}} neuropathy

What characteristic finding associated with Chédiak-Higashi syndrome is shown in the image?



{{c1::Giant}} granules within granulocytes and platelets

Which three structures/organs have defects in velocardiofacial syndrome?

{{c1::Face}}
{{c1::Palate}}
{{c1::Heart}}

A patient with ataxia-telangiectasia has the skin findings shown. What precautions must be taken for this patient?



Limit {{c1::X-ray}} exposure because patient has increased sensitivity to {{c1::radiation}}

Which is the most common primary immunodeficiency disorder?

{{c1::Selective IgA}} deficiency

Name two immunodeficiency disorders where the thymic shadow is absent on chest X-ray.

{{c1::Thymic aplasia}}
{{c1::Severe combined immunodeficiency}}

Which immunodeficiency syndrome is associated with lymphopenia, high α-fetoprotein levels, low IgA, IgG, and IgE levels, and cerebellar atrophy?

{{c1::Ataxia-telangiectasia}}

Name four immunodeficiency syndromes associated with B and T cell dysfunction.

{{c1::Severe combined immunodeficiency}}
{{c1::Ataxia-telangiectasia}}
{{c1::Hyper-IgM}} syndrome
{{c1::Wiskott-Aldrich}} syndrome

Levels of which molecule is used as part of newborn screening for severe combined immunodeficiency?

{{c1::T}}-cell receptor {{c1::excision circles}}
fields.Back Extra: They would be decreased in severe combined immunodeficiency.

fields.Text:
What are the common lab findings of common variable immunodeficiency?

Decrease in {{c1::plasma}} cells
Decrease in {{c1::immunoglobulins}}

Which immunodeficiency syndrome may cause disseminated mycobacterial and fungal infections?

{{c1::IL-12 receptor}} deficiency

Which immunodeficiency syndrome is associated with late separation of umbilical cord, absence of pus, and dysfunctional neutrophils?

{{c1::Leukocyte adhesion}} deficiency type {{c1::1}}

What are the common clinical findings of severe combined immunodeficiency?

Failure to {{c1::thrive}}
Chronic {{c1::diarrhea}}
{{c1::Thrush}}
{{c1::Recurrent}} infections

What type of cell deficiency is associated with local Candida infections, Cryptococcus infections, and Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia?

{{c1::T}} cell

Patients with complement deficiencies are susceptible to which bacteria?

Patients with early complement deficiencies are susceptible to {{c1::encapsulated}} species
Patients with late complement deficiencies are susceptible to {{c1::Neisseria}} species

B-cell immunodeficiency results in predisposition to which two type of viruses?

{{c1::Poliovirus}}
{{c1::Enteroviral encephalitis}}

Patients with granulocyte immunodeficiencies are susceptible to which five bacteria?

{{c1::Staphylococcus}}
{{c1::Burkholderia cepacia}}
{{c1::Pseudomonas aeruginosa}}
{{c1::Nocardia}}
{{c1::Serratia}}

Deficiency of what type of cell is associated with gastrointestinal giardiasis?

{{c1::B}}-cell deficiency without Ig{{c1::A}} production

What type of vaccines are contraindicated for patients with B-cell immunodeficiencies?

{{c1::Live attenuated}} vaccines

What is the general difference between infections commonly associated with T-cell and B-cell immunodeficiencies?

T-cell deficiencies tend to produce recurrent {{c1::viral}}/{{c1::fungal}} infections
B-cell deficiencies tend to produce recurrent {{c1::bacterial}} infections

What effect can a T-cell deficiency have on bacterial infection?

Increased risk of {{c1::sepsis}} due to rapid {{c1::dissemination}} of organisms

A diagnosis of Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia can indicate deficiency of what cell type?

{{c1::T}} cells

Deficiency of T cells can result in which viral infections?

{{c1::Epstein-Barr virus}}
{{c1::Cytomegalovirus}}
{{c1::JC}} virus
{{c1::Varicella-zoster virus}}
Chronic infections with other {{c1::respiratory}} and {{c1::gastrointestinal}} viruses

Infections with which type of bacteria are more common in patients with B-cell deficiencies?

{{c1::Encapsulated}} bacteria

When is graft-versus-host disease potentially beneficial?

When a bone marrow transplant is done to treat {{c1::leukemia}}

What is the mechanism of chronic transplant rejection?

{{c1::T}} cells react to recipient {{c1::antigen-presenting}} cells presenting donor peptides and allogeneic MHC → Activates a cellular and humoral response

What pathogenic mechanism drives the development of graft-versus-host disease?

Immunocompetent {{c1::T}} cells from graft proliferate in the immunocompromised host and reject cells with "{{c1::foreign}}" proteins

Graft-versus-host disease usually occurs with which two types of transplants?

{{c1::Bone marrow}} transplants
{{c1::Liver::Organ}} transplants

What are the common histologic manifestations of chronic rejection of transplant in the liver, kidney, heart, and lungs?

Liver → {{c1::Vanishing bile duct}} syndrome
Kidney → Chronic {{c1::allograft nephropathy}}
Heart → Accelerated {{c1::atherosclerosis}}
Lungs → {{c1::Bronchiolitis obliterans}}

How can acute transplant rejection be prevented or reversed?

With the use of {{c1::immunosuppressants}}

What type of transplant rejection will feature vasculitis of graft vessels with an interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate?

{{c1::Acute}} rejection

What is the pathogenetic mechanism of hyperacute transplant rejection?

Pre-existing recipient antibodies react to donor {{c1::antigens}} → Activates {{c1::complement}} → Thrombosis of graft vessels and necrosis

How does the humoral type of acute rejection differ from hyperacute rejection in its pathophysiology?

Antibodies against graft donor antigens develop {{c1::after::before/after}} transplantation in acute rejection

Mention four typical clinical signs found on a patient presenting with graft-versus-host disease.

{{c1::Jaundice}}
{{c1::Maculopapular rash}}
{{c1::Diarrhea}}
{{c1::Hepatosplenomegaly}}

What are the cellular and humoral pathogenic mechanisms underlying acute transplant rejection?

Cellular → {{c1::T}} cells are activated against donor MHCs
Humoral → {{c1::Antibodies}} develop against donor antigens

What three HLA mismatches are most importantly associated with increased risk for graft-versus-host disease?

HLA-{{c1::A}}
HLA-{{c1::B}}
HLA-{{c1::DR}}

What type of transplant rejection is characterized by the histologic finding evident in this image?



{{c1::Chronic}} rejection

How rapidly does acute transplant rejection develop?

Within {{c1::weeks}} to {{c1::months}} of transplantation

How rapidly does chronic transplant rejection develop?

Within {{c1::months}} to {{c1::years}} of transplantation

What type of hypersensitivity reaction is involved in graft-versus-host disease?

Type {{c1::IV}} hypersensitivity reaction

How are blood products prepared before transfusion for immunocompromised patients?

Blood products must be {{c1::irradiated}} before transfusion
fields.Back Extra: This is to prevent graft-versus-host disease in immunocompromised patients.

fields.Text:
What is the treatment for hyperacute transplant rejections?

Removal of {{c1::graft}}

What type of rejection is characterized by the histologic finding in this image?



{{c1::Acute}} rejection

Which type of transplant rejection is characterized by the histologic findings shown?



{{c1::Hyperacute}} rejection

What is the mechanism of action of mycophenolate mofetil?

Mycophenolate mofetil reversibly inhibits {{c1::IMP dehydrogenase}} → Prevents {{c1::purine}} synthesis in T cells and B cells

What is the mechanism of action of tacrolimus?

FK506 binds to {{c1::FK506-binding}} protein → Inhibits {{c1::calcineurin}} → Prevents {{c1::IL-2}} transcription → Inhibits T-cell activation

What is the mechanism of action of cyclosporine?

Cyclosporine inhibits {{c1::calcineurin}} and binds to {{c1::cyclophilin}} → Prevents {{c1::IL-2}} transcription → Blocks T-cell activation

What are the two monoclonal antibodies that bind to and inhibit the IL-2 receptor?

{{c1::Daclizumab}}
{{c1::Basiliximab}}

What is the mechanism of action of sirolimus?

Sirolimus inhibits {{c1::mTOR}} → Inhibits the cellular response to {{c1::IL-2}} → Blocks T-cell activation and B-cell differentiation
fields.Back Extra: Sirolimus is also known as rapamycin.

fields.Text:
Which messenger, directly downstream from the T-cell receptor, is activated to promote inflammatory cytokine gene transcription?

{{c1::NFAT}}
fields.Back Extra: NFAT is generated from NFAT-P by calcineurin-mediated dephosphorylation.

fields.Text:
How does the inhibition of NF-κB by steroids lead to immune system suppression?

NF-κB inhibition decreases {{c1::cytokine}} transcription → Suppresses B cell and T cell function while inducing T-cell {{c1::apoptosis}}

Which immunosuppressant drug class can cause a buffalo hump, hyperglycemia, striae, and acne?

{{c1::Glucocorticoids}}

What are three toxicities associated with basiliximab?

{{c1::Edema}}
{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Tremor}}

What immunosuppressant is associated with increased toxicity when combined with allopurinol?

{{c1::Azathioprine}}
fields.Back Extra: Its metabolite, 6-mercaptopurine, is metabolized by xanthine oxidase, which is inhibited by allopurinol.

fields.Text:
Apart from transplant rejection prophylaxis, what are the three main clinical indications for azathioprine?

{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}
{{c1::Glomerulonephritis}}
{{c1::Crohn}} disease

For which antimetabolite is azathioprine a precursor?

{{c1::6-mercaptopurine}}

Which immunosuppressant is often found in drug-eluting stents?

{{c1::Sirolimus}}

Which three toxicities are associated with sirolimus?

{{c1::Pancytopenia}}
{{c1::Insulin}} resistance
{{c1::Hyperlipidemia::Hyperlipidemia/Hypolipidemia}}

Which immunosuppressant medication is synergistic with cyclosporine?

{{c1::Sirolimus}}

Which two immunosupressants are specifically preferred for kidney transplant rejection prophylaxis?

{{c1::Sirolimus}}
{{c1::Basiliximab}}

Which immunosuppressant used for psoriasis can cause gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism?

{{c1::Cyclosporine}}

Which two immunosupressants are commonly associated with drug-induced kidney failure?

{{c1::Cyclosporine}}
{{c1::Tacrolimus}}

Apart from transplant rejection, what are the two main clinical indications for cyclosporine?

{{c1::Psoriasis}}
{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}

Long-term use of immunosuppressants increases the risk of which two conditions?

{{c1::Cancers}}
{{c1::Infections}}

What is the clinical advantage of combining different immunosuppressants?

Combining immunosupressants increases their net {{c1::efficacy}} while minimizing their individual {{c1::toxicities}}

What is the most common and concerning adverse effects of cyclosporine?

{{c1::Nephrotoxicity}}

What are the two adverse effects that are more pronounced with use of tacrolimus compared with use of cyclosporine?

{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}
{{c1::Neurotoxicity}}

What is beneficial about the side-effect profile of mycophenolate mofetil?

Less {{c1::nephrotoxic}} and {{c1::neurotoxic}} than other immunosuppressants

Which viral infection is associated with mycophenolate mofetil?

{{c1::Cytomegalovirus}}

Glucocorticoids inhibit the transcription of what two types of genes?

{{c1::NF-κB}}
{{c1::Inflammatory}} cytokine genes

Which two hematologic malignancies are glucocorticoids often used to treat?

{{c1::Non-Hodgkin}} lymphoma
{{c1::CLL}}

What mechanism causes artificial leukocytosis in patients taking glucocorticoids?

Glucocorticoids cause {{c1::demargination}} of white blood cells in the vasculature

mTOR is responsible for driving the transcription of what types of genes?

{{c1::Proliferation}} genes

What complication can result if a patient abruptly stops taking a glucocorticoid after long-term use?

{{c1::Adrenal}} insufficiency

Which two factors can amplify the nephrotoxicity of calcineurin inhibitors?

Administration at {{c1::higher::higher/lower}} doses
Poor baseline {{c1::renal}} function

Which two recombinant cytokines can be used to treat renal cell carcinoma?

{{c1::Aldesleukin}}
{{c1::IFN-α}}

Which two recombinant cytokines may be useful in treating autoimmune thrombocytopenia by acting as platelet stimulators?

{{c1::Romiplostim}}
{{c1::Eltrombopag}}

Which recombinant cytokine may be used to treat multiple sclerosis?

{{c1::IFN-β}}

What are the three clinical indications for treatment with IFN-α?

Chronic {{c1::hepatitis B}}
Chronic {{c1::hepatitis C}} (not preferred)
{{c1::Renal cell}} carcinoma

Which two recombinant cytokines could be used to treat leukopenia?

{{c1::Filgrastim}}
{{c1::Sargramostim}}
fields.Back Extra: These aid in the recovery of granulocyte and monocyte counts.

fields.Text:
Which recombinant cytokine can be used to treat chronic granulomatous disease?

{{c1::IFN-γ}}

What bone marrow-stimulating agent can be used to treat renal failure-associated anemias?

{{c1::Epoetin alfa}}

Aldesleukin is a recombinant form of which cytokine?

{{c1::IL-2}}

Which two types of cancer can recombinant IL-2 be used to treat?

{{c1::Renal cell}} carcinoma
Metastatic {{c1::melanoma}}

What risk is associated with eculizumab therapy?

Increased risk of {{c1::meningococcal}} infection

What immunosuppressive antibody targeting α4-integrin can be used in the treatment of multiple sclerosis and Crohn disease?

{{c1::Natalizumab}}

Which therapeutic antibody would help to reduce the fracture risk in patients with osteoporosis?

{{c1::Denosumab}}

What molecule does the antibody omalizumab target?

Ig{{c1::E}}

Which monclonal antibody may be given to infants at high risk for respiratory syncytial virus infection to prevent it?

{{c1::Palivizumab}}

What are four clinical indications for treatment with adalimumab and infliximab?

{{c1::Inflammatory bowel}} disease
{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}
{{c1::Psoriasis}}
{{c1::Ankylosing spondylitis}}

What two recombinant antibodies have been developed to treat autoimmune diseases by targeting soluble TNF-α?

{{c1::Infliximab}}
{{c1::Adalimumab}}

What drug is a decoy TNF-α receptor?

{{c1::Etanercept}}

What serious adverse infection can result from use of natalizumab?

{{c1::Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy}}
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by the JC virus.

fields.Text:
What are the two molecular targets of ustekinumab?

{{c1::IL-12}}
{{c1::IL-23}}

What is the molecular target of denosumab?

{{c1::RANKL}}

What are the two main indications for treatment with ustekinumab?

{{c1::Psoriasis}}
{{c1::Psoriatic arthritis}}

What is the molecular target of eculizumab in the treatment of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinruria?

Complement protein {{c1::C5}}

Which two monoclonal antibody treatments target IL-17A?

{{c1::Ixekizumab}}
{{c1::Secukinumab}}

Which monoclonal antibody may be used to treat refractory allergic asthma?

{{c1::Omalizumab}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a recombinant antibody targeting IgE.

fields.Text:
Which six monoclonal antibodies can be used to treat psoriasis, as shown in the image?



Ixekizumab and secukinumab → {{c1::IL-17A}} inhibitors
Ustekinumab → {{c1::IL-12}}/{{c1::IL-23}} inhibitors
Adalimumab and infliximab → {{c1::TNF-α}} inhibitors
Guselkumab → {{c1::IL-23}} inhibtiors

What is the mechanism of the α4-integrin antibody vedolizumab in the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease?

Inhibition of this gut-specific integrin prevents migration of {{c1::leukocytes}} to the gastrointestinal tract

Screening for what six infections is necessary when beginning treatment with adalimumab or infliximab?

{{c1::Cytomegalovirus}}
{{c1::Epstein-Barr virus}}
{{c1::Hepatitis B}}
{{c1::Hepatitis C}}
{{c1::Tuberculosis}}
{{c1::Varicella zoster virus}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to risk of reactivation.

fields.Text:
Which therapeutic antibody mimics factor VIII in the treatment of hemophilia A?

{{c1::Emicizumab}}

What disease can be treated with the therapeutic antibody emicizumab, which targets factors IXa and X?

{{c1::Hemophilia A}}

A gram-positive bacterium produces a structure containing a special keratin-like coat, dipicolinic acid, peptidoglycan, and DNA. What is the purpose of this structure?

{{c1::Survival}}
fields.Back Extra: The structure is an endospore resistant to chemicals, heat, and dehydration.

fields.Text:
Which bacterial structural appendage composed of protein is known to help provide motility?

{{c1::Flagellum}}

Which glycoprotein-derived structures allows bacteria to adhere to the cell surface, such as during conjugation?

{{c1::Fimbria}}
{{c1::Pilus}}
fields.Back Extra: The sex pilus forms during conjugation.

fields.Text:
What is the function of the peptidoglycan cell wall?

Protects against {{c1::osmotic pressure}} damage
Provides cell {{c1::rigidity}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to the mesh-like structure of peptidoglycan.

fields.Text:
A pharmaceutical company wishes to target β-lactamases. In which compartment of the bacteria are they located?

{{c1::Periplasmic}} space
fields.Back Extra: This is the space between the cytoplasmic membrane and the outer membrane in gram-negative bacteria.

fields.Text:
Where is endotoxin located in gram-negative bacteria?

{{c1::Outer::Inner/Outer}} leaflet of the {{c1::outer::inner/outer}} membrane

What component of the cell envelope extends from the membrane to the exterior and induces TNF-α and IL-1 on gram-positive bacteria?

{{c1::Lipoteichoic acid}}

What component of the cell envelope induces TNF on gram-negative bacteria?

{{c1::Lipid A}}
fields.Back Extra:
Lipid A also induces IL-1.

Lipid A is an antigenic O polysaccharide component.

fields.Text:
What components of the cell envelope are found only in gram-negative bacteria?

{{c1::Outer::Inner/Outer}} membrane that incorporates {{c2::porin}} and {{c2::endotoxin}}
{{c1::Outer membrane}} proteins that are {{c2::antigenic}}

What is the function of the bacterial capsule of the cell envelope?

Discrete layer of polysaccharides that protects against {{c1::phagocytosis}}

The inner leaflet of the outer membrane of a bacterium is composed of what molecules?

{{c1::Phospholipids}}

Where in the cell of gram-negative bacteria are β-lactamases located?

{{c1::Periplasmic}} space

How do the cell envelopes of gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria compare?

Gram-positive bacteria → {{c1::Thick::Thick/Thin}} peptidoglycan layer and {{c2::lipoteichoic acid}}
Gram-negative bacteria → {{c1::Thin::Thick/Thin}} peptidoglycan layer, {{c2::porin}}, {{c2::endotoxin}}, {{c2::lipopolysaccharide}}, and {{c2::periplasmic}} space

What component of the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane is unique to gram-positive bacteria?

{{c1::Lipoteichoic acid}}

What five cell wall structures do gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria have in common?

{{c1::Flagella}}
{{c1::Pili}}
{{c1::Capsules}}
{{c1::Peptidoglycans}}
{{c1::Cytoplasmic}} membrane

Which bacteria can be identified with a Giemsa stain?

{{c1::Chlamydia}}
{{c1::Rickettsia}}
{{c1::Trypanosomes}}
{{c1::Borrelia}}
{{c1::Helicobacter pylori}}
{{c1::Plasmodium}}

What fungi are shown with a silver stain in the image?



{{c1::Coccidiodes}}

A Giemsa stain of a stool specimen obtained from a patient with recurring fever and somnolence is shown in the image. What is the pathogen?



{{c1::Trypanosomes}}

Which acid-fast bacteria can be visualized with a Ziehl-Neelsen stain?

{{c1::Mycobacteria}}
{{c1::Nocardia}}

What is a common fluorescent antibody stain used to confirm syphilis infection?

{{c1::FTA-ABS}} stain

Which pathogen can be visualized using India ink or mucicarmine?

{{c1::Cryptococcus neoformans}}
fields.Back Extra: It has a thick polysaccharide capsule that stains red with mucicarmine.

fields.Text:
Why don't Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma Gram stain well?

These species do not have {{c1::cell walls}}

Why wouldn't Treponema and Leptospira be visualized with Gram staining?

They are too {{c1::thin::thick/thin}} to be visualized on Gram staining

What component of the outer layer of Mycobacteria is stained with the Ziehl-Neelsen stain?

{{c1::Mycolic acid}}

What organism can be diagnosed with periodic acid-Schiff stain?

{{c1::Tropheryma whipplei}}

Which dye is retained by the thick peptidoglycan layer of gram-positive bacteria?

{{c1::Crystal violet}}

Bacteria with thin peptidoglycan layers turn what colors with counterstain on Gram staining?

{{c1::Red}}
{{c1::Pink}}
fields.Back Extra: This indicates that they are gram-negative.

fields.Text:
Chlamydia do not Gram stain well because they are intracellular and have low levels of what acid in their cell wall?

{{c1::Muramic acid}}
fields.Back Extra: This results in suboptimal staining of peptidoglycan.

fields.Text:
Legionella, Rickettsia, Chlamydia, Bartonella, Anaplasma, and Ehrlichia all share what property that makes them suboptimal for Gram staining?

They are all primarily {{c1::intracellular::intracellular/extracellular}} bacteria

What cheaper and more sensitive stain is used in place of the Ziehl-Neelsen stain to screen for acid-fast bacteria?

{{c1::Auramine-rhodamine}} stain

Two plates grow the same lactose-fermenting bacteria. Colonies on plate A appear pink and colonies on plate B appear metallic green. What medium was used on each plate?

Plate A → {{c1::MacConkey}} agar
Plate B → {{c1::Eosin-methylene blue}} agar

What medium is used to culture Mycoplasma pneumoniae?

{{c1::Eaton}} agar

In the microbiology lab, there are growing microorganisms in a Sabouraud agar. What is likely growing?

{{c1::Fungi}}

What medium is used to culture Brucella, Francisella, Legionella, and Pasteurella?

{{c1::Charcoal yeast extract}} agar buffered with {{c1::cysteine}} and {{c1::iron}}

What medium causes lactose-fermenting colonies to turn pink?

{{c1::MacConkey}} agar
fields.Back Extra: This is used to identify lactose-fermenting enterics.

fields.Text:
What mediums should be used to culture Mycobacterium tuberculosis?

{{c1::Löwenstein-Jensen}} agar
{{c1::Middlebrook}} medium
{{c1::Rapid automated broth}} cultures

What medium should be used to culture Corynebacterium diphtheriae?

{{c1::Tellurite}} agar
{{c1::Löffler}} medium

What organism is cultured on the Bordet-Gengou agar?

{{c1::Bordetella pertussis}}
fields.Back Extra: Bordetella pertusis can also be applied on a Regan-Lowe medium.

fields.Text:
What is the media used for Neisseria gonorrhea culture?

{{c1::Thayer-Martin}} agar
fields.Back Extra: This is a selective medium containing vancomycin, trimethoprim, colistin, and nystatin.

fields.Text:
What is the media used for Haemophilus influenzae culture?

{{c1::Chocolate}} agar
fields.Back Extra: This contains factors V and X.

fields.Text:
Can facultative anaerobes use pathways other than those requiring oxygen as a terminal electron receptor to generate ATP?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: They can use fermentation and other metabolic pathways that do not require oxygen.

fields.Text:
Which class of antibiotics is not effective against anaerobes?

{{c1::Aminoglycosides}}
fields.Back Extra: They require oxygen to enter a bacterial cell.

fields.Text:
Although anaerobes are pathogenic in most tissues, where are they most commonly part of the microflora?

{{c1::Gastrointestinal}} tract

Why do anaerobes have increased susceptibility to oxidative damage?

They lack the enzymes {{c1::superoxide dismutase}} and/or {{c1::catalase}}

What properties with regard to oxygen use do Clostridium, Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, and Actinomyces israelii share?

They are all {{c1::anaerobes::aerobes/anaerobes}}
They cannot survive in oxygen-{{c1::rich::rich/poor}} environments

Name the common obligate intracellular bacteria.

{{c1::Rickettsia}}
{{c1::Chlamydia}}
{{c1::Coxiella}}

How do obligate intracellular bacteria obtain energy?

They obtain ATP from {{c1::host}} cells

Which virulence feature provides the capsule of Streptococcus pneumoniae?

{{c1::Antiphagocytic}} virulence factor

Which bacterial vaccines are necessary in a patient with asplenia?

{{c1::Neiserria meningitis}}
{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae}}

What are the two components of the antigen in a conjugate vaccine?

{{c1::Capsular}} polysaccharide
{{c1::Protein}} conjugate

How does the bacterial capsule, as shown in the image, increase virulence?



The capsule is {{c1::antiphagocytic}}

What are the commonly encountered encapsulated bacteria?

{{c1::Pseudomonas aeruginosa}}
{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae type b}}
{{c1::Neiserria meningitidis}}
{{c1::Escherichia coli}}
{{c1::Salmonella}}
{{c1::Klebsiella pneumoniae}}
Group {{c1::B}} Streptococci

What is the underlying biochemical reaction that leads to struvite stone formation in the presence of urease-positive bacteria?

Urease hydrolyzes urea → Release of {{c1::ammonia}} and {{c1::CO2}} → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} urine pH
fields.Back Extra: This is conducive to the formation of ammonium magnesium phosphate stones.

fields.Text:
By what mechanism do urease-positive bacteria increase pH?

Urease hydrolyzes urea → Release of {{c1::ammonia}} and {{c1::CO2}} → {{c1::Ammonia}} reacts with the medium to increase pH

An unmarked bacterial plate is producing urease. Name the organisms that could be growing on the plate.

{{c1::Proteus}}
{{c1::Crytptococcus}}
{{c1::Helicobacter pylori}}
{{c1::Ureaplasma}}
{{c1::Nocardia}}
{{c1::Klebsiella}}
{{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}}
{{c1::Staphylococcus saprophyticus}}

How does the catalase enzyme make bacteria more pathogenic?

Catalase degrades {{c1::H2O2}} to {{c1::H2O}} and {{c1::O2}} before myeloperoxidase can convert it to microbicidal products

What disease leads to increased susceptibility to infections with catalase-positive bacteria?

{{c1::Chronic granulomatous}} disease
fields.Back Extra: There is a deficiency in NADPH oxidase.

fields.Text:
Staphylococcus aureus is noted to produce bubbles when treated with H2O2 in an artifical medium, as shown in the image. What causes this?



{{c1::Catalase}} degrades H2O2 into H2O and O2

What color pigment does Serratia marcescens produce?

{{c1::Red}}

In the microbiology lab, there are bacteria that produce yellow "sulfur" granules. Which bacterium is it?

{{c1::Actinomyces israelii}}

What color pigment does Staphylococcus aureus produce?

{{c1::Golden yellow}}

What color pigment does Pseudomonas aeruginosa produce?

{{c1::Blue-green}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to pyocyanin and pyoverdin.

fields.Text:
Which biofilm-producing bacteria can cause otitis media?

Nontypeable {{c1::Haemophilus influenzae}}

Which biofilm-producing bacteria causes contact lens–associated keratitis and ventilator-associated pneumonia?

{{c1::Pseudomonas aeruginosa}}

Which biofilm-producing bacteria commonly colonize the respiratory tree and are associated with cystic fibrosis?

{{c1::Pseudomonas aeruginosa}}

Which biofilm-producing bacteria are associated with dental plaque and infective endocarditis?

{{c1::Streptococcus mutans}}
{{c1::Streptococcus sanguinis}}

Which in vivo biofilm-producing bacteria grows on catheters and prosthetic devices?

{{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}}

In what situations do some gram-positive bacteria typically form spores?



{{c1::Nutrient}}-poor settings

What compound found in the core of a bacterial spore is responsible for heat resistance?

{{c1::Dipicolinic acid}}

When autoclaving surgical equipment, what temperature and time setting should be used to eliminate bacterial spores?

Equipment must be autoclaved for {{c1::15}} minutes at {{c1::121}}°C
fields.Back Extra: This is because bacterial spores are highly resistant to heat and chemicals.

fields.Text:
What is the purpose of autoclaving surgical equipment?

To eliminate bacterial {{c1::spores}}

What two chemical solutions are sporicidal?

{{c1::Hydrogen peroxide}}
{{c1::Iodine}}-based agents

In a patient with acute rheumatic fever, what bacterial virulence factor may be responsible for the autoimmune response?

{{c1::M protein}} by group {{c1::A}} streptococci
fields.Back Extra: It has epitopes similar to those of human cellular proteins, a phenomenon known as molecular mimicry.

fields.Text:
Describe the mechanism of action of IgA protease.

IgA protease cleaves Ig{{c1::A}} → Bacteria adheres to {{c1::mucous}} membranes

IgA protease is secreted by which three bacterial species?

{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae type b}}
{{c1::Neisseria}}
fields.Back Extra: These normally colonize the respiratory mucosa.

fields.Text:
Name five bacterial toxins coded for in a lysogenic phage.

Group {{c1::A}} streptococcus erythrogenic toxin
{{c1::Botulinum}} toxin
{{c1::Chlorea}} toxin
{{c1::Diphtheria}} toxin
{{c1::Shiga}} toxin

Describe the mechanism of bacterial transposition.

A transposon DNA segment {{c1::excises}} itself and "jumps" to a new location on the same {{c1::chromosome}} or on an exogenous {{c1::DNA}} molecule
fields.Back Extra: This is critical in conferring antibiotic resistance genes.

fields.Text:
Describe how a phage helps a toxin gene undergo transduction.

A lysogenic phage infects bacteria and inserts viral DNA into {{c1::chromosomes}} → Viral DNA are excised into a {{c1::phage capsid}} that can infect other bacteria

Which process of transduction involves infection of a bacterium by a lysogenic phage and incorporation of viral DNA into the bacterial chromosome, as shown below?



{{c1::Specialized}} transduction

Which process of transduction involves infection of a bacterium by a lytic phage, leading to cleavage of bacterial DNA, as shown below?



{{c1::Generalized}} transduction

An F+ bacterium and an F- bacterium participate in high-frequency recombination. What is the result for the F- bacterium?

The F- bacterium has received {{c1::plasmid DNA}} from the F+ bacterium, but remains as F- bacterium

What is the name of the process of incorporating an F+ plasmid into the bacteria's own chromosomal DNA?

{{c1::High-frequency recombination}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a subtype of conjugation.

fields.Text:
How can conjugation not involve the transfer of chromosomes?

In F+ to F- conjugation, plasmids are transferred from the {{c1::F+}} cell through a {{c1::conjugal bridge}}

Which three bacteria often take up naked DNA from the environment?

{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae}}
{{c1::Neisseria}}

Which process of gene transfer among bacteria will be halted by deoxyribonuclease?

{{c1::Transformation}}
fields.Back Extra: Deoxyribonuclease lyses the naked DNA, thus preventing transformation.

fields.Text:
What is the process of transfer of a plasmid from one bacterium to another called?

{{c1::Conjugation}}

Which type of transduction does not incorporate viral DNA into host DNA?

{{c1::Generalized}} transduction

In which type of transduction is viral DNA incorporated into the host DNA?

{{c1::Specialized}} transduction

Bacteria are able to import short pieces of naked bacterial DNA from bacterial cell lysis, as shown in the image. What process is this?



{{c1::Transformation}}

What differentiates F+ × F- conjugation from high-frequency recombination × F- conjugation?

F+ × F- conjugation involves transfer of {{c1::plasmid DNA}}
High-frequency recombination × F- conjugation involves direct transfer of {{c1::genes}} located on the bacterial {{c1::chromosome}}

In generalized transduction, what happens after a lytic phage infects a bacterium?

{{c1::Cleavage}} of bacterial DNA → DNA segments may be packed in a {{c1::phage capsid}}
fields.Back Extra: When the phage infects other bacteria, the genes are transferred.

fields.Text:
Describe how specialized transduction takes place.

A lysogenic phage infects a bacterium → Viral DNA is {{c1::incorporated}} into bacterial DNA → On excision, bacterial DNA can be excised with phage DNA and packaged into a {{c1::phage capsid}}

Name four bacterial diseases that are typically caused by exotoxins.

{{c1::Cholera}}
{{c1::Tetanus}}
{{c1::Botulism}}
{{c1::Diphtheria}}

What are the two notable bacterial exotoxins that are typically stable at 60°C?

{{c1::Staphylococcal}} enterotoxin
{{c1::Escherichia coli}} heat-stable toxin

What type of bacterial toxin are typically heat-stable?

{{c1::Endotoxins::Endotoxins/Exotoxins}}
fields.Back Extra: These are stable at 100°C for 1 hour.

fields.Text:
Why can vaccines be created for exotoxins, but not endotoxins?

Exotoxins are highly {{c1::antigenic}}
fields.Back Extra: They are able to induce antibody production and their toxoids can be used to make vaccines.

fields.Text:
What are endotoxins composed of?

The {{c1::lipid A}} component of a lipopolysaccharide

What are exotoxins composed of?

{{c1::Polypeptides}}

Where are genes coding for the exotoxin of bacteria located?

{{c1::Plasmid}}
{{c1::Bacteriophage}}

Where are genes coding for the endotoxin of bacteria located?

Bacterial {{c1::chromosome}}

Which three main cytokines are induced by the outer cell membrane of gram-negative bacteria to cause septic shock?

{{c1::TNF}}
{{c1::IL-1}}
{{c1::IL-6}}

Name two bacterial diseases that are typically caused by endotoxins.

{{c1::Sepsis}} caused by gram-negative rods
{{c1::Meningococcemia}}

Low activity of which neurotransmitters results in the spastic paralysis, risus sardonicus, trismus, and opisthotonos caused by tetanospasmin?

{{c1::Glycine}}
{{c1::GABA}}
fields.Back Extra: The toxin prevents release of these neurotransmitters from Renshaw cells in the spinal cord.

fields.Text:
How does the heat-stable toxin of enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli cause watery diarrhea?

By decreasing the ability of the gut to reabsorb {{c1::NaCl}} and {{c1::H2O}} secondary to overactivation of guanylate cyclase

Identify the exotoxin responsible for persistent cough for 3 months in a teacher who teaches students not currently fully vaccinated.

{{c1::Pertussis}} toxin
fields.Back Extra: This is produced by Bordetella pertussis, which can cause a "100-day cough" in adults.

fields.Text:
Which bacteria have exotoxin A, which inactivates EF-2 to trigger host cell death?

{{c1::Pseudomonas aeruginosa}}

Name the functions of the A and B components of ADP ribosylating AB toxins found in Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

The A component is {{c1::active}}
The B component binds and triggers {{c1::endocytosis}}

In a patient with scarlet fever caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, what specific toxin is to blame for the symptoms?

{{c1::Erythrogenic exotoxin A}}

Name three toxins produced by Staphylcoccus aureus and their associated symptoms.

{{c1::Toxic shock syndrome}} toxin → Rash, fever, and shock
{{c1::Exfoliative}} toxin → Scalded-skin syndrome
{{c1::Enterotoxin}} → Diarrhea and vomiting

What is the mechanism of anthrax toxin, released by Bacillus anthracis?

Mimics {{c1::adenylate cyclase}} → Edematous borders of {{c1::black::color}} {{c1::eschar}}

What is the mechanism by which the Shiga toxin causes damage to the gastrointestinal mucosa and dysentery?

Removes {{c1::adenine}} from rRNA → Inactivation of the {{c1::60S}} ribosomal subunit

What is the mechanism by which streptolysin O toxin leads to hemolysis?

Streptolysin O degrades red blood cell {{c1::membranes}} → {{c1::β}}-hemolysis

What is the mechanism of botulinum toxin?

Botulinum toxin inhibits release of {{c1::acetylcholine}} at the neuromuscular junction by cleaving {{c1::SNARE}} proteins

What is the mechanism of action of the alpha toxin of Clostridium perfringens?

Alpha toxin is a phospholipase that degrades {{c1::phospholipids}} → {{c1::Myonecrosis}} and {{c1::hemolysis}}

What is the mechanism of the offending toxin of Bordetella pertussis?

The pertussis toxin disables the {{c1::Gi}} protein

Why does Clostridium perfringens lead to hemolysis when cultured in a blood agar?

This is due to the {{c1::alpha}} toxin→ Forms a {{c1::double}} zone of hemolysis on blood agar

What is the mechanism of the heat-labile toxin of enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli?

{{c1::Adenylate cyclase}} is activated causing greater secretion of Cl- and H2O in the gut

Name two common gram-positive bacteria that can cause a rash and septic shock.

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
{{c1::Streptococcus pyogenes}}

How does the AB toxin in Vibrio cholerae cause water diarrhea?

AB toxin permanently activates {{c1::Gs}} protein → Stimulates {{c1::adenylate cyclase}} → Increases Cl- and H2O secreted in the gut

What is the mechanism by which superantigens cause toxic shock syndrome?

Superantigens binds to {{c1::MHC II}} molecules and {{c1::T-cell}} receptors → Overwhelming release of {{c1::cytokines}}

What is the mechanism of the diphtheria toxin?

Inactivates {{c1::EF-2}} via {{c1::ADP ribosylation}} → Pseudomembranous pharyngitis, bull neck, and myocarditis

Which bacteria causes "rice-water" diarrhea via an ADP-ribosylating AB toxin?

{{c1::Vibrio cholerae}}

The diagnostic test for rhematic fever uses antibodies against what part of the causative agent?

Antibodies against {{c1::Streptococcus}} toxin, specifically {{c1::streptolysin O}}

Which four bacteria have exotoxins that increase cAMP?

{{c1::Vibrio Cholerae}}
{{c1::Bacillus anthracis}}
{{c1::Bordetella pertussis}}
{{c1::Escherichia coli}}

How is endotoxin released from cells?

Cell {{c1::lysis}}
Detaching {{c1::blebs}} from the outer surface membrane of living cells

What are the components of lipopolysaccharide?

{{c1::O-antigen}}
{{c1::Lipid A}}
Core {{c1::polysaccharide}}

A man with an Escherichia coli infection has significant fever, hypotension, and edema. What component of the bacteria is responsible for his symptoms?

{{c1::Lipopolysaccharide}}
fields.Back Extra: It leads to macrophage actiavation, complement activation, and tissue factor activation.

fields.Text:
What are the effects and characteristics of an endotoxin?

{{c1::Edema}}
{{c2::Nitric oxide}}
{{c3::Disseminated intravascular coagulation}}
{{c4::Outer::Inner/Outer}} membrane
{{c5::TNF-α}}
{{c6::O-antigen}}
Extremely heat-{{c7::stable::stable/labile}}
{{c8::IL-1}}/{{c8::IL-6}}
Neutrophil {{c9::chemotaxis}}
{{c10::Shock}}

Which cytokines cause fever and hypotension secondary to macrophage activation by endotoxins?

Fever → {{c1::IL-1}} and {{c1::IL-6}}
Fever and hypotension → {{c1::TNF-α}}

What replaces lipopolysaccharides in the cell wall of Neisseria species?

{{c1::Lipooligosaccharides}}

What factor causes endotoxins to activate the coagulation cascade leading to disseminated intravascular coagulopathy?

{{c1::Tissue}} factor

In an endotoxin-based complement activation, which complement promotes neutrophil chemotaxis?

{{c1::C5a}}

In an endotoxin-based complement activation, which complements cause hypotension and histamine release?

{{c1::C3a}}
{{c1::C5a}}

What are the main immune effects of endotoxin?

Activation of {{c1::macrophages}}
Activation of {{c1::complement}}
Activation of {{c1::tissue}} factor

What is the primary toxic component of an endotoxin?

{{c1::Lipid A}}

Where is endotoxin located in bacteria cells?

{{c1::Outer::Inner/Outer}} membrane of gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} bacteria

What is the chemical composition of an endotoxin?

{{c1::Lipopolysaccharide}}

Endotoxin activation of macrophages causes release of which hypotensive intermediates?

{{c1::Nitric oxide}}
{{c1::TNF-α}}

Which gram-positive spherical bacteria appear in clusters?

{{c1::Staphylococcus}} species

Which β-hemolytic bacteria are catalase-negative, bacitracin-resistant, gram-positive cocci?

{{c1::Streptococcus agalactiae}}

Which gram-positive bacteria may be either α-hemolytic or γ-hemolytic?

{{c1::Enterococcus}} species

In the lab, how can nonenterococcus species be differentiated from enterococcus species?

Nonenterococcus species {{c1::cannot::can/cannot}} grow in 6.5% NaCl and are PYR {{c1::negative::positive/negative}}
Enterococcus species {{c1::can::can/cannot}} grow in 6.5% NaCl and are PYR {{c1::positive::positive/negative}}

In the lab, how can Streptococcus species exhibiting complete hemolysis be further differentiated?

Streptococcus pyogenes is bacitracin {{c1::sensitive::sensitive/resistant}} and PYR {{c1::positive::positive/negative}}
Streptococcus agalactiae is bacitracin {{c1::resistant::sensitive/resistant}} and PYR {{c1::negative::positive/negative}}

In the lab, how can Streptococcus species with partial hemolysis be differentiated?

Viridans streptococci is optochin {{c1::resistant::sensitive/resistant}} and bile {{c1::insoluble::soluble/insoluble}}
Streptococcus pneumoniae is optochin {{c1::sensitive::sensitive/resistant}} and bile {{c1::soluble::soluble/insoluble}}

Describe the appearance of α, β, and γ hemolysis on agar.

α-hemolysis → {{c1::Partial}}
β-hemolysis → {{c1::Complete}}
γ-hemolysis → {{c1::Absent}}

What is the hemolysis pattern of Streptococcus pneumoniae?

{{c1::Green::Color}}, {{c1::partial}} hemolysis

In the lab, how can you differentiate staphylococci from streptococci?

Staphylococcus species are catalase-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}} and grow in {{c1::clusters}}
Streptococcus species are catalase-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} and grow in {{c1::chains}}

Name an aerobic, gram-positive, acid-fast branching filament.

{{c1::Nocardia}}

How can catalase-positive cocci be differentiated?

Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}}
Staphylococcus epidermidis and Staphylococcus saprophyticus are coagulase-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}}

Name three common pathogenic aerobic gram-positive bacilli.

{{c1::Corynebacterium}}
{{c1::Listeria}}
{{c1::Bacillus}}

Which two gram-positive bacilli can survive without oxygen?

{{c1::Cutibacterium}}
{{c1::Clostridium}}

Which catalase-positive Staphylococcus species is novobiocin resistant?

Staphylococcus {{c1::saprophyticus}}

What type of hemolysis is seen on blood agar with the organism shown in the image?



{{c1::β}}-hemolysis

Staphylococcus aureus most commonly colonizes which parts of the body?

{{c1::Nares}}
{{c1::Ears}}
{{c1::Axillae}}
{{c1::Groin}}

Which three abnormal values will you see on labs in a patient with staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome?

Increased {{c1::bilirubin}}
Increased {{c1::AST}}
Increased {{c1::ALT}}

How would the presentation be different if a patient had Staphylococcus aureus toxic shock syndrome versus Streptococcus pyogenes toxic shock syndrome?

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} toxic shock syndrome → Fever, vomiting, shock, desquamation, rash, and end-organ failure
{{c1::Streptococcus pyogenes}} toxic shock syndrome → Painful skin infection with ARDS

How does coagulase positivity contribute to the pathogenicity of Staphylococcus aureus?

It allows the organism to form a {{c1::fibrin clot}} around itself, leading to {{c1::abscess}} formation

How long after exposure to Staphylococcus aureus toxin will patients typically experience nonbloody diarrhea and emesis?

Preformed staphylococcal enterotoxins that cause food poisoning have a {{c1::short}} incubation period of {{c1::2}} to {{c1::6}} hours

What is the mechanism by which Staphylococcus aureus infection cause toxic shock syndrome?

{{c1::TSST-1}}, a superantigen produced by Staphylococcus aureus, binds to {{c1::MHC II}} and {{c1::T-cell}} receptors → {{c1::Polyclonal T-cell}} activation and {{c1::cytokine}} release

What is the mechanism of action of Staphylococcus aureus protein A?

It binds to the {{c1::Fc}} region of Ig{{c1::G}}, inhibiting {{c1::complement}} activation and {{c1::phagocytosis}}

Name six inflammatory diseases that can result from infection with Staphylococcus aureus.

{{c1::Skin}} infection
{{c1::Infective endocarditis}}
{{c1::Pneumonia}}
Organ {{c1::abscess}}
{{c1::Septic arthritis}}
{{c1::Osteomyelitis}}

Name the three toxins produced by Staphylococcus aureus and their associated effects.

TSST-1 → {{c1::Toxic shock}} syndrome
Exofoliative toxin → {{c1::Scalded skin}} syndrome
Enterotoxin → {{c1::Rapid-onset food poisoning}}

Which gene from the staphylococcal chromosomal cassette is involved in penicillin resistance?

{{c1::mecA}} gene

What two risk factors are associated with staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome?

Prolonged use of {{c1::vaginal tampons}} or {{c1::nasal packing}}

Which form of Staphylococcal aureus is an important cause of serious nosocomial and community-acquired infections?

{{c1::Methicillin}}-resistant Staphylococcus aureus

How does Staphylococcus epidermidis ferment mannitol?
