{{c1::It does not}}

What property of Staphylococcus epidermidis allows it to easily infect prosthetic devices and intravenous catheters?

Production of adherent {{c1::biofilm}}

What novobiocin-sensitive bacterium found in normal skin flora commonly contaminates blood cultures?

{{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}}

What normal skin bacteria are gram-positive, catalase-positive, coagulase-negative, urease-positive, appear as cocci in clusters, and are sensitive to novobiocin?

{{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}}

Where is Staphylococcus saprophyticus normally found in the human body?

Female {{c1::genital}} tract
Female {{c1::perineum}}

What histologic findings are expected when Staphylococcus saprophyticus is grown in culture?

Gram-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}}
Catalase-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}}
Coagulase-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}}
Urease-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}}
Cocci in {{c1::clusters}}

What organism is the second most common cause of uncomplicated urinary tract infections in young women?

{{c1::Staphylococcus saprophyticus}}

Is Staphylococcus saprophyticus sensitive or resistant to novobiocin?

{{c1::Resistant}} to novobiocin

What determines the virulence of Streptococcus pneumoniae?

{{c1::Capsule}}
fields.Back Extra: The virulence is lost in its absence.

fields.Text:
The bacteria shown in the image below are gram-positive, α-hemolytic, lancet-shaped diplococci. They are isolated from a patient's sputum sample. What color is the sputum expected to be?



"{{c1::Rusty}}" appearance

What two patient populations are susceptible to Streptococcus pneumoniae sepsis?

Patients with {{c1::sickle cell}} disease
Patients with {{c1::asplenia}}

Name the four illnesses most commonly caused by infection with Streptococcus pneumoniae.

{{c1::Meningitis}}
{{c1::Otitis media}} in children
{{c1::Sinusitis}}
{{c1::Pneumonia}}

What features help in isolating Streptococcus pneumoniae from a culture medium?

Gram-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}}
{{c1::α}}-hemolytic
{{c1::Lancet}}-shaped diplococci
Optochin-{{c1::sensitive::sensitive/resistant}}
Bile-{{c1::soluble::soluble/insoluble}}

What are the two virulence factors of Streptococcus pneumoniae?

{{c1::IgA protease}}
{{c1::Capsule}}

Explain the mechanism through which viridans group streptococci cause infective endocarditis.

Streptococcus {{c1::sanguinis}} produces {{c1::dextrans}} → Binds to {{c1::fibrin-platelet}} aggregates on damaged {{c1::heart valves}} → Infective endocarditis

Which two optochin-resistant bacteria, that are part of the normal oropharyngeal flora, cause dental caries?

{{c1::Streptococcus mutans}}
{{c1::Streptococcus mitis}}

Describe the gram staining, hemolysis, and unique antibiotic resistance patterns of viridans group streptococci.

Gram-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}}
{{c1::α}}-hemolytic
Optochin-{{c1::resistant::sensitive/resistant}}
Bile-{{c1::insoluble::soluble/insoluble}}

Where do viridans group streptococci commonly colonize in the human body?

{{c1::Oropharynx}}

Antibodies to which virulent component of Streptococcus pyogenes can give rise to rheumatic fever?

{{c1::M protein}}

What two characteristics of Streptococcus pyogenes prevent phagocytosis by the host?

{{c1::Hyaluronic acid}} capsule
{{c1::M protein}}

Which pyogenic infection by Streptococcus pyogenes most commonly precedes glomerulonephritis?

{{c1::Impetigo}}

Which toxin is responsible for the toxigenic diseases caused by Streptococcus pyogenes?

{{c1::Erythrogenic}} toxin

What two immunologic diseases result from Streptococcus pyogenes?

{{c1::Rheumatic fever}}
{{c1::Glomerulonephritis}}

What three toxigenic diseases result from infection with Streptococcus pyogenes?

{{c1::Scarlet fever}}
{{c1::Necrotizing fasciitis}}
{{c1::Toxic shock-like}} syndrome

What four pyogenic illnesses are caused by Streptococcus pyogenes?

{{c1::Pharyngitis}}
{{c1::Erysipelas}}
{{c1::Impetigo}}
{{c1::Cellulitis}}

Describe the laboratory properties of Streptococcus pyogenes.

Gram-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}}
{{c1::β}}-hemolytic
Bacitracin-{{c1::sensitive::sensitive/resistant}}
PYR-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}}
Cocci in {{c1::chains}}

Results of which two lab tests can indicate a recent Streptococcus pyogenes infection?

{{c1::ASO}} titer
{{c1::Anti-DNase B}} antibodies

Identify the organism shown in the image.



{{c1::Streptococcus pyogenes}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows gram-positive cocci in chains.

fields.Text:
Streptococcus agalactiae is added to a culture of Staphylococcus aureus, which enlarges the area of hemolysis. What bacterial substance causes this finding?

{{c1::CAMP}} factor made by Streptococcus agalactiae

Name three possible diseases that may develop in an infant after delivery as a result of maternal colonization with Streptococcus agalactiae.

{{c1::Meningitis}}
{{c1::Pneumonia}}
{{c1::Sepsis}}

A woman who is colonized with Streptococcus agalactiae is in labor. What medication should be administered as prophylaxis?

{{c1::Penicillin}} or {{c1::ampicillin}}

In a pregnant woman, what common bacterium is screened for in the weeks before expected delivery?

{{c1::Streptococcus agalactiae}}
fields.Back Extra: This is at 35 to 37 weeks of gestation with rectal and vaginal swabs.

fields.Text:
Name the bacteria that are hippurate test positive, PYR negative, bacitracin resistant, and β-hemolytic.

{{c1::Streptococcus agalactiae}}

Increase in incidence of what disease is associated with Streptococcus gallolyticus endocarditis?

{{c1::Colon cancer}}

What two immediate complications are possible if a patient contracts an infection with Streptococcus gallolyticus?

{{c1::Bacteremia}}
{{c1::Infective endocarditis}}

What part of the body does Streptococcus gallolyticus typically colonize?

{{c1::Gut}}

Name three infections that are caused by enterococci.

{{c1::Urinary}} tract infections
{{c1::Biliary}} tract infections
{{c1::Infective endocarditis}}

What does testing with catalase and PYR yield for enterococci?

Catalase-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}}
PYR {{c1::positive::positive/negative}}

What antibiotic are the bacteria Enterococcus faecalis normally resistant to?

{{c1::Penicillin G}}

What type of hemolysis is induced by Enterococcus species?

{{c1::Variable}} hemolysis

What lab test can differentiate enterococci from streptococci bacteria?

Enterococci grows in {{c1::6.5}}% {{c1::NaCl}} and {{c1::bile}}

What is the likely healthcare-associated cause of infective endocarditis after gastrointestinal and genitourinary procedures?

{{c1::Enterococci}}

Infections caused by enterococci in hospitalized patients are commonly resistant to which antibiotic?

{{c1::Vancomycin}}
fields.Back Extra: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci are a major cause of healthcare-associated infections.

fields.Text:
Describe the symptoms seen in pulmonary anthrax most commonly due to inhalation of spores from contaminated animals or animal products.

{{c1::Flu}}-like symptoms
Rapid progression to {{c1::fever}}
{{c1::Mediastinitis}}
Pulmonary {{c1::hemorrhage}}
{{c1::Shock}}

What is the composition of the capsule of Bacillus anthracis?

A polypeptide capsule of {{c1::poly D-glutamate}}

What are the two modes of transmission of Bacillus anthracis?

{{c1::Cutaneous}} exposure
{{c1::Inhalation}}

What gram-positive spore-forming organism causes painless, ulcerating lesions with black eschar, as shown in the image?



{{c1::Bacillus anthracis}}

What is woolsorter's disease?

{{c1::Bacillus anthracis}} infection leading to {{c1::mediastinitis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is seen as mediastinal widening on chest X-ray.

fields.Text:
Name the toxin produced by Bacillus anthracis and its components.

{{c1::Anthrax}} toxin, which consists of {{c1::protective}} antigen, {{c1::edema}} factor, and {{c1::lethal}} factor

What symptoms and incubation period are associated with the diarrheal type of Bacillus cereus infection?

{{c1::Nonbloody::Bloody/Nonbloody}}, {{c1::watery}} diarrhea
{{c1::Gastrointestinal}} pain that arises {{c1::8}} to {{c1::18}} hours after ingestion of contaminated foods

What are the two types of presentations with Bacillus cereus infection?

{{c1::Diarrheal}} type
{{c1::Emetic}} type

What bacterial toxin causes vomiting 1 to 5 hours after consumption of reheated rice?

{{c1::Cereulide}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the preformed toxin in Bacillus cereus.

fields.Text:
Explain how Bacillus cereus survives heating.

Spores survive cooking rice → Rewarming the rice promotes {{c1::germination}} of spores and {{c1::enterotoxin}} formation

What is the management strategy for a Bacillus cereus infection?

{{c1::Supportive care}}

Which antibiotics commonly cause Clostridium difficile infection?



{{c1::Ampicillin}}
{{c1::Clindamycin}}
{{c1::Cephalosporins}}
{{c1::Fluoroquinolones}}

What treatment is recommended for a patient with recurrent Clostridium difficile infections to prevent relapse?

Repeat courses of oral {{c1::vancomycin}} or {{c1::fidaxomicin}}
fields.Back Extra: For refractory cases, a fecal microbiota transplant can be performed.

fields.Text:
How do you diagnose disease in a patient with suspected Clostridium difficile infection?

{{c1::PCR}}
Antigen detection of {{c1::toxin A}} and/or {{c1::toxin B}} in stool

What are the effects of toxins A and B produced by Clostridium difficile?

Toxins A and B damage {{c1::enterocytes}} → {{c1::Watery}} diarrhea and {{c1::pseudomembranous colitis}}

What is the treatment for diarrhea caused by Clostridium difficile?

Oral {{c1::vancomycin}} or {{c1::fidaxomicin}}

What is the mechanism of the heat-labile toxin produced by Clostridium botulinum?

Inhibition of {{c1::acetylcholine}} release at the {{c1::neuromuscular junction}}

How can tetanus be prevented?

{{c1::Tetanus vaccine}}
fields.Back Extra: Most cases occur in unvaccinated individuals.

fields.Text:
What are the four classic symptoms caused by tetanospasmin produced by Clostridium tetani?

{{c1::Spastic}} paralysis
{{c1::Risus sardonicus}}
{{c1::Trismus}}
{{c1::Opisthotonos}}

Explain the mechanism of tetanospasmin, the exotoxin produced by Clostridium tetani.

Cleavage of {{c1::SNARE}} proteins → Blocks release of {{c1::glycine}} and {{c1::GABA}}

Name four Clostridium species that produce exotoxins.

Clostridium {{c1::perfringens}}
Clostridium {{c1::botulinum}}
Clostridium {{c1::tetani}}
Clostridium {{c1::difficile}}

Which bacterial species appears as gram-positive, spore-forming, obligate anaerobic bacilli?

{{c1::Clostridium}}

Name four conditions that are treated using local botulinum toxin A?

Muscle {{c1::spasms}}
{{c1::Focal dystonia}}
{{c1::Hyperhidrosis}}
Facial {{c1::wrinkles}}

Ingestion of what substance classically causes floppy baby syndrome due to Clostridium botulinum spores?

{{c1::Honey}}

What are the five major symptoms of infection with Clostridium botulinum?

{{c1::Diplopia}}
{{c1::Dysarthria}}
{{c1::Dysphagia}}
{{c1::Dyspnea}}
{{c1::Descending::Ascending/Descending}} flaccid paralysis

What is the cause of spontaneous gas gangrene seen in association with colonic malignancy?

{{c1::Clostridium septicum}}
fields.Back Extra: This is caused via hematogenous seeding.

fields.Text:
What is the treatment for botulism?

{{c1::Human botulinum immunoglobulin}}

What is the mechanism by which α-toxin, produced by Clostridium perfringens, leads to the condition shown in the image?



α-toxin is a {{c1::lecithinase}}, which causes {{c1::myonecrosis}} and {{c1::hemolysis}}

What is the life-threatening complication that can occur in a patient with Clostridium difficile diarrhea?

{{c1::Toxic megacolon}}

Describe how food poisoning can arise from food contaminated with Clostridium perfringens spores.

Spores germinate when food is left standing at less than {{c1::60}}°C → Gives rise to vegetative bacteria that produce heat-{{c1::labile::stable/labile}} enterotoxin → Food poisoning symptoms

After ingestion of food contaminated with Clostridium perfringens spores, when do symptoms of food poisoning arise and how long do they last?

Symptoms occur within {{c1::10}} to {{c1::12}} hours and resolve in {{c1::24}} hours

What organism causes the findings shown in the image and appears as metachromatic granules with a positive Elek test result?



{{c1::Corynebacterium diphtheriae}}

How is Corynebacterium diphtheriae transmitted?

Via {{c1::respiratory droplets}}

Explain the mechanism of the exotoxin produced by Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

Exotoxin blocks {{c1::protein}} synthesis via {{c1::ADP-ribosylation}} of {{c1::EF-2}}

What color colony will Corynebacterium diphtheriae produce when cultured?

{{c1::Cystine-tellurite}} agar will grow {{c1::black::color}} colonies of this bacterium

What is the treatment for Corynebacterium diphtheriae?

{{c1::Diphtheria antitoxin}} alone or with {{c1::penicillin}}/{{c1::erythromycin}}

What are three conditions that can result from toxin dissemination in a patient with diphtheria?

{{c1::Arrythmias}}
{{c1::Myocarditis}}
{{c1::Neuropathies}}

What help does the virulence factor listeriolysin provide to Listeria?

Generates {{c1::pores}} in phagosomes → Allows it to escape into the {{c1::cytoplasm}}

What characteristic finding can you see while examining Listeria monocytogenes under the microscope in broth?

{{c1::Tumbling}} motility

How does Listeria monocytogenes avoid the immune system?

It forms "{{c1::rocket tails}}" by means of {{c1::actin polymerization}} → Allows movement through cell membranes while avoiding host antibodies

How is an infection of Listeria monocytogenes commonly contracted?

Ingestion of {{c1::unpasteurized dairy}} products and {{c1::cold deli meats}}
{{c1::Transplacental}} transmission

What facultative intracellular gram-positive rod is acquired by ingestion of unpasteurized dairy products?

{{c1::Listeria monocytogenes}}

In which three populations can Listeria monocytogenes infection lead to meningitis?

{{c1::Neonates}}
{{c1::Immunocompromised}} patients
{{c1::Older::Older/Younger}} adults

What are three complications due to maternal infection with Listeria monocytogenes during pregnancy?

{{c1::Amnionitis}}
{{c1::Septicemia}}
{{c1::Spontaneous abortion}}

How does Listeria monocytogenes infection commonly present in a healthy individual?

As mild, self-limited {{c1::gastroenteritis}}

What are two complications of infection with Listeria monocytogenes that can occur in infants?

{{c1::Granulomatosis infantiseptica}}
Neonatal {{c1::meningitis}}

What is the treatment for infection with Listeria monocytogenes?

{{c1::Ampicillin}}

What gram-positive rod shown in the image resembles fungi and responds best to sulfonamides?



{{c1::Nocardia}}

What gram-positive rod shown in the image forms long, branching filaments resembling fungi and responds well to penicillin?



{{c1::Actinomyces}}

What condition is a female with an intrauterine device at risk for if she has a confirmed Actinomyces infection?

{{c1::Pelvic inflammatory}} disease

Where is Actinomyces found?

{{c1::Oral}} microbiota
{{c1::Reproductive}} microbiota
{{c1::Gastrointestinal}} microbiota

How do you treat each patient if one patient has an Actinomyces infection while another has a Nocardia infection?

Nocardia is treated with {{c1::sulfonamides}}
Actinomyces is treated with {{c1::penicillin}}

Describe the typical lesions caused by Actinomyces.

Oral/facial {{c1::abscesses}} draining through sinus tracts containing {{c1::yellow::color}} "{{c1::sulfur granules}}"
fields.Back Extra: This is often associated with dental caries/extraction and other maxillofacial trauma.

fields.Text:
Which bacterium is a gram-positive, filamentous, weakly acid-fast aerobe usually found in soil and mostly affects immunocompromised hosts?

{{c1::Nocardia}}

What is the treatment for severe Nocardia infection?

{{c1::TMP-SMX}}

What two characteristics differentiate Actinomyces from Nocardia?

Actinomyces are {{c1::anaerobes::aerobes/anaerobes}} and {{c1::are not::are/are not}} acid fast
Nocardia are {{c1::aerobes::aerobes/anaerobes}} and {{c1::are::are/are not}} acid fast

Which gram-positive filamentous and weakly acid-fast bacteria can spread to the central nervous system and cause cerebral abscess?

{{c1::Nocardia}}

Which Mycobacterium species causes cervical lymphadenitis in children?

Mycobacterium {{c1::scrofulaceum}}

What component of virulent Mycobacterium tuberculosis induces release of TNF-α?

{{c1::Cord}} factor

How is Mycobacterium marinum acquired?

Through {{c1::aquatic}} exposure
fields.Back Extra: This is likely through aquarium handling.

fields.Text:
What are the five classical symptoms of tuberculosis?

{{c1::Night sweats}}
Weight {{c1::loss::gain/loss}}
{{c1::Fever}}
{{c1::Hemoptysis}}
{{c1::Cough}}

In a patient with virulent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, what specific bacterial factor activates macrophages?

{{c1::Cord}} factor
fields.Back Extra:
This causes a "serpentine cord" appearance in virulent strains.

The activation of macrophages promotes formation of granulomas.

fields.Text:
Which two mycobacterial species are usually resistant to multiple drugs?

Mycobacterium {{c1::tuberculosis}}
Mycobacterium {{c1::avium-intracellulare}}

Name four clinically important mycobacteria that cause tuberculosis-like illnesses.

Mycobacterium {{c1::tuberculosis}}
Mycobacterium {{c1::scrofulaceum}}
Mycobacterium {{c1::avium-intracellulare}}
Mycobacterium {{c1::marinum}}

What staining property do all mycobacteria have in common?

All are {{c1::acid-fast}} rods

In a patient with virulent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, what inhibits phagolysosome fusion?

{{c1::Sulfatides}}

Describe the histologic findings of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, as seen in the image.



{{c1::Pink::Color}} {{c1::rods::shape}}

What is the most appropriate tuberculosis screening test to order for a patient who has had the bacille Calmette-Guérin vaccine?

{{c1::Interferon-γ release assay}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a more specific test that yields fewer false-positive results than purified protein derivative.

fields.Text:
Name three possible scenarios in which a positive PPD test result may be observed.

Current {{c1::tuberculosis}} infection
Previous exposure to {{c1::tuberculosis}}
{{c1::Bacille Calmette-Guérin}} vaccination

Why does a reactivation of tuberculosis have a predilection for the apices of the lung?

Because the bacteria is highly {{c1::aerobic::aerobic/anaerobic}}

What condition may bring about a false-negative PPD test result?

{{c1::Immunocompromised}} patients
fields.Back Extra: This is especially seen in patients with a low CD4+ count.

fields.Text:
Name seven extrapulmonary sites potentially affected by tuberculosis.

{{c1::Vertebrae}}
{{c2::Meninges}}
{{c3::Lymph nodes}}
{{c4::Liver}}
{{c5::Spleen}}
{{c6::Adrenal}} glands
{{c7::Joints}} and {{c7::long::long/short}} bones

Following severe bacteremia caused by tuberculosis, what might be seen on examination of histopathology slides from various organs?

Small, widespread {{c1::granulomas}} in multiple organs

What two potential outcomes could be expected after a primary tuberculosis infection?

{{c1::Recovery}} (>90%)
{{c1::Progressive primary tuberculosis}} (<10%)

What type of lesion is seen on a chest X-ray obtained from a patient with secondary tuberculosis?

A {{c1::fibrocaseous cavitary}} lesion in the {{c1::upper::upper/lower}} lobe

What specific finding on an X-ray of the chest confirms primary tuberculosis?

{{c1::Ghon complex}}

What gross findings differentiate primary Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection from secondary infection?

Primary tuberculosis presents with a {{c1::Ghon complex}}
Secondary tuberculosis presents with {{c1::fibrocaseous cavitary}} lesions

What structural changes might result from local tissue destruction by secondary tuberculosis?

{{c1::Cavitation}}
{{c1::Caseation}}
{{c1::Scar}} formation

What typical histological finding is seen in a lesion of secondary tuberculosis?



{{c1::Caseating::Caseating/Noncaseating}} granuloma with central {{c1::necrosis}} and {{c1::Langhans giant}} cell

Why is lepromatous leprosy, as shown in the image, so dangerous?



It is highly {{c1::communicable}}
fields.Back Extra: It presents with a high bacterial load and low cell-mediated immunity.

fields.Text:
Which animals serve as reservoirs of Mycobacterium leprae in the United States?

{{c1::Aramadillos}}

Which form of leprosy presents with hypoesthetic, hairless skin nodules?

{{c1::Tuberculoid}} leprosy

Which form of leprosy presents with diffuse, communicable skin lesions and leonine facies?

{{c1::Lepromatous}} leprosy

How do you confirm a Mycobacterium leprae infection?

Tissue {{c1::PCR}}
Skin {{c1::biopsy}}
fields.Back Extra: It cannot be grown in vitro.

fields.Text:
Compare T-cell responses associated with lepromatous leprosy and tuberculoid leprosy.

Lepromatous leprosy causes a {{c1::Th2}} response
Tuberculoid leprosy causes a {{c1::Th1}}-type response

Infection with which mycobacterium leads to a "glove and stocking" loss of sensation?

Mycobacterium {{c1::leprae}}
fields.Back Extra: It likes cool temperatures and therefore affects the skin and superficial nerves.

fields.Text:
What three medications would be used to treat the lepromatous form of leprosy?

{{c1::Dapsone}}
{{c1::Rifampin}}
{{c1::Clofazimine}}

What two drugs are used to treat a patient with tuberculoid leprosy?

{{c1::Dapsone}}
{{c1::Rifampin}}

What organism causes Hansen disease?

{{c1::Mycobacterium leprae}}
fields.Back Extra: Hansen disease is another name for leprosy.

fields.Text:
What shape and gram stain group do Campylobacter, Vibrio, and Helicobacter belong to?

Gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}}
{{c1::Curved rods::Shape}}

Which two bacteria can be identified as gram-negative diplococci?

{{c1::Neisseria}} species
{{c1::Moraxella}} species

Besides Neisseria gonorrhoeae, which gram-negative aerobic diplococci does not use maltose?

{{c1::Moraxella}}

Which agar can be used to differentiate bacteria based on H2S production?

{{c1::Triple sugar iron}} agar

Which oxidase-positive, comma-shaped, gram-negative bacterium can grow at 42°C?

{{c1::Campylobacter jejuni}}

Among lactose nonfermenters, which four gram-negative bacilli are oxidase-negative?

{{c1::Shigella}}
{{c1::Salmonella}}
{{c1::Proteus}}
{{c1::Yersinia}}

Which lactose-nonfermenting, gram-negative bacilli are oxidase-positive?

{{c1::Pseudomonas}}
{{c1::Burkholderia}}

Which comma-shaped, gram-negative organism that grows in alkaline media is oxidase-positive?

{{c1::Vibrio cholerae}}

Which two common pathogenic bacteria are slow lactose-fermenting gram-negative bacilli?

{{c1::Citrobacter}}
{{c1::Serratia}}

Which three common pathogenic bacteria are fast lactose-fermenting gram-negative bacilli?

{{c1::Klebsiella}}
{{c1::Escherichia coli}}
{{c1::Enterobacter}}

Gram-negative bacilli are differentiated by their ability to ferment what substance?

{{c1::Lactose}}

How can you distinguish between Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae based on their metabolism?

Neisseria meningitidis {{c1::does::does/does not}} ferment maltose
Neisseria gonorrhoeae {{c1::does not::does/does not}} ferment maltose

Which curved, gram-negative bacterium is urease-positive and oxidase-positive?

{{c1::Helicobacter pylori}}

Name six common pathogenic organisms that are gram-negative coccobacilli.

{{c1::Acinetobacter baumannii}}
{{c1::Bordetella pertussis}}
{{c1::Brucella}}
{{c1::Francisella tularensis}}
{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae}}
{{c1::Pasteurella}}

What four shapes are most gram-negative organisms classified as?

{{c1::Diplococci}}
{{c1::Coccobacilli}}
{{c1::Bacilli}}
{{c1::Curved rods}}

Which bacteria produce H2S on triple sugar iron agar?

{{c1::Salmonella}}
{{c1::Proteus}}

What gram-negative intracellular diplococci, as shown in image, causes pelvic inflammatory disease?



{{c1::Neisseria gonorrhoeae}}

What three prophylactic medications can be offered to individuals after exposure to Neisseria meningitidis?

{{c1::Ciprofloxacin}}
{{c1::Ceftriaxone}}
{{c1::Rifampin}}

What are the modes of transmission of Neisseria meningitidis?

{{c1::Respiratory}} secretions
{{c1::Oral}} secretions

What is the treatment of choice for a patient with petechiae and toe gangrene that develop as a result of meningococcemia?



{{c1::Ceftriaxone}}
{{c1::Penicillin G}}

What three clinical conditions usually follow Neisseria meningitidis infection?

{{c1::Meningococcemia}}
{{c1::Meningitis}}
{{c1::Waterhouse-Friderichsen}} syndrome

What two features differentiate gonococcus from meningococcus?

Neisseria gonorrhoeae {{c1::lacks::has/lacks}} a polysaccharide capsule and {{c1::does not::does/does not}} ferment maltose
Neisseria meningitidis {{c1::has::has/lacks}} a polysaccharide capsule and {{c1::does::does/does not}} ferment maltose

What five disease states might Neisseria gonorrhoeae present as?

{{c1::Gonorrhea}}
{{c1::Pelvic inflammatory}} disease
{{c1::Septic arthritis}}
{{c1::Fitz-Hugh-Curtis}} syndrome
Neonatal {{c1::conjunctivitis}}

What virulence factor causes the severe inflammatory response from Neisseria diplococci?

{{c1::Lipooligosaccharides}}
fields.Back Extra: They have a potent endotoxin activity.

fields.Text:
Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae both ferment what type of sugar?

{{c1::Glucose}}

For which Neisseria species is a vaccine available?

Neisseria {{c1::meningitidis}}

What are the modes of transmission of Neisseria gonorrhoeae?

{{c1::Sexual intercourse}}
{{c1::Maternal}}-{{c1::fetal}} transmission during delivery

How would you prevent disease transmission of Neisseria gonorrhoeae?

{{c1::Condoms}} decrease sexual transmission
{{c1::Erythromycin}} ointment prevents neonatal blindness

What is the treatment for gonococcal infection?

Single dose IM {{c1::ceftriaxone}}
fields.Back Extra: If Chlamydia infection has not been ruled out by molecular testing, doxycycline is also added.

fields.Text:
Why does Neisseria gonorrhoeae not have a vaccine?

Because of the {{c1::antigenic variation}} of pilus proteins

How are gonococcal and meningococcal infections diagnosed?

Gonococcus is diagnosed with {{c1::NAAT}}
Meningococcus is diagnosed with {{c1::culture}}-based tests or {{c1::PCR}}

When does neonatal conjunctivitis due to Neisseria gonorrhoeae present?

{{c1::2}} to {{c1::5}} days after birth

What is the route of spread of Haemophilus infection?

{{c1::Aerosol}} transmission

What is the treatment for the condition shown in the image?



{{c1::Amoxicillin}} alone or in combination with {{c1::clavulanate}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows a "thumb sign" of epliglottitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae.

fields.Text:
What can be used to prevent the condition shown in the image?



{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows an endoscopic appearance of epiglottitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae.

fields.Text:
Describe the vaccine used against Haemophilus influenzae.

The vaccine consists of a {{c1::type b capsular polysaccharide}} conjugated to a {{c1::diphtheria toxoid}} or another protein

What is the most likely causative agent in an unvaccinated boy who has a "cherry red" epiglottis and a lateral X-ray of the neck showing "thumb sign"?

{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae}}

The Haemophilus influenzae vaccine is typically given to which age group?

Infants that are {{c1::2}} to {{c1::18}} months of age

What medium is used to culture Haemophilus influenzae?

{{c1::Chocolate}} agar with factors {{c1::V}} and {{c1::X}}
fields.Back Extra: It can also be grown with Staphylococcus aureus, which provides factor V via red blood cell hemolysis.

fields.Text:
What virulence factor is produced by Haemophilus influenzae?

{{c1::IgA protease}}

Which strain of Haemophilus influenzae most commonly causes the mucosal and invasive disease?

{{c1::Nontypeable}} strains

Name four diseases caused by Haemophilus influenzae.

{{c1::Epiglottitis}}
{{c1::Meningitis}}
{{c1::Otitis media}}
{{c1::Pneumonia}}

What can be used to treat meningitis due to Haemophilus influenzae?

{{c1::Ceftriaxone}}
fields.Back Extra: Individuals that have close contact should receive rifampin as prophylaxis.

fields.Text:
What is the shape of Haemophilus influenza?

{{c1::Coccobacillary}}

Infection with which gram-negative bacilli is a relative contraindication to lung transplantation?

{{c1::Burkholderia cepacia}}

Describe the type of infection caused by Burkholderia cepacia and its mode of transmission.

It causes {{c1::pneumonia}} in patients with {{c1::cystic fibrosis}} and can be transmitted between them

Why might a bacterial infection in a patient with whooping cough be mistaken for a viral infection?

The immune response to {{c1::Bordetella pertussis}} generates a {{c1::lymphocytic}} infiltrate

What vaccinations can prevent whooping cough?

{{c1::Tdap}} vaccine
{{c1::DTaP}} vaccine

What are the three virulence factors of Bordetella pertussis?

{{c1::Tracheal}} cytotoxin
{{c1::Pertussis}} toxin
{{c1::Adenylate cyclase}} toxin

What symptoms are seen in the catarrhal phase of Bordetella pertussis infection?

{{c1::Coryza}}
{{c1::Low::High/Low}}-grade fevers

What symptoms are seen in the paroxysmal phase of Bordetella pertussis infection?

Paroxysms of intense cough followed by an inspiratory "{{c1::whoop}}"
Posttussive {{c1::vomiting}}

What is the last clinical stage of an infection caused by Bordetella pertussis?

{{c1::Convalescent}} stage
fields.Back Extra: Here, there would be a gradual recovery from chronic cough.

fields.Text:
What class of antibiotics could be used for the treatment of Bordetella pertussis?

{{c1::Macrolides}}
fields.Back Extra: If a patient is allergic to macrolides, TMP-SMX should be used instead.

fields.Text:
What gram-negative bacteria causes undulating fevers, night sweats, and arthralgias after consumption of unpasteurized milk?

{{c1::Brucella}}

What histologic finding is characteristic of the lesions associated with Brucella infection?

{{c1::Noncaseating::Caseating/Noncaseating}} granulomas

What is the treatment for a patient infected with Brucella?

{{c1::Doxycycline}} with {{c1::streptomycin}}/{{c1::rifampin}}

What cell type does Brucella reside in?

{{c1::Macrophages}} of the {{c1::reticuloendothelial}} system

What stain can be used to identify Legionella?

{{c1::Silver}} stain

What infection presents as fever, diarrhea, and headache with initial lab results indicating hyponatremia?



{{c1::Legionnaires'}} disease
fields.Back Extra: The image shows unilateral and lobar pneumonia.

fields.Text:
What populations are at an increased risk for Legionella pneumophila infection?

{{c1::Smokers}}
Patients with chronic {{c1::lung::organ}} disease
{{c1::Older::Older/Younger}} adults

Differentiate Legionnaires' disease from Pontiac fever.

{{c1::Pontiac fever}} causes a mild, flu-like syndrome
{{c1::Legionnaires' disease}} causes severe pneumonia, fever, and and central nervous system and gastrointestinal symptoms

What two clinical syndromes are caused by Legionella?

{{c1::Legionnaires'}} disease
{{c1::Pontiac fever}}

What type of laboratory sample is tested to diagnose Legionella infection?

{{c1::Urine}} is used to detect the presence of an antigen

How is the bacteria Legionella pneumophila transmitted?

{{c1::Aerosol}} transmission from an environmental {{c1::water}} source

What bacteria grows well in a charcoal yeast extract medium with iron and cysteine?

{{c1::Legionella}}

What is the treatment for Legionnaires' disease?

{{c1::Macrolides}} or {{c1::quinolones}}

What blue-green pigment-producing organism can cause a rapidly progressing necrotic skin lesion like that shown in the image?



{{c1::Pseudomonas aeruginosa}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows ecthyma gangrenosum, seen mostly in immunocompromised states.

fields.Text:
Which drugs of the penicillin class are appropriate for the treatment of Pseudomonas infection?

{{c1::Antipseudomonal}} penicillins combined with a {{c1::β-lactamase}} inhibitor

What three treatment options are available for Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection resistant to antipseudomonal penicillins and cephalosporins?

{{c1::Fluoroquinolones}}
{{c1::Monobactams}}
{{c1::Carbapenems}}

Which cephalosporins can be used to treat a Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection?

{{c1::Third}}-generation cephalosporins
{{c1::Fourth}}-generation cephalosporins

What are the laboratory characteristics of Pseudomonas aeruginosa?

{{c1::Aerobic::Aerobic/Anaerobic}}
{{c1::Motile::Motile/Non-motile}}
Catalase-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}}
Oxidase-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}}
Gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} rod with a {{c1::grape}}-like odor

What organism is the likely pathogen if osteomyelitis develops following a puncture wound, especially in patients with diabetes?

{{c1::Pseudomonas aeruginosa}}

The following common clinical conditions are associated with what bacterial infection?

Pneumonia
Sepsis
Ecthyma gangrenosum
Urinary tract infections
Osteomyelitis
Otitis externa
Healthcare-associated infections
Skin infections
Diabetics and people who use injectable drugs

{{c1::Pseudomonas}}

How would you differentiate Pseudomonas from other nonlactose fermenters?

It is oxidase-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}}

Which organism is likely responsible for corneal ulcers?

{{c1::Pseudomonas aeruginosa}}

What type of Pseudomonas toxin produces symptoms of sepsis?

{{c1::Endotoxin}}

What are the common sources of infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa?

{{c1::Water}} from sources such as {{c1::swimming pools}} and {{c1::hot tubs}}
fields.Back Extra: Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes swimmer's ear and hot tub folliculitis.

fields.Text:
Which nonlactose-fermenting, gram-negative rod is commonly associated with wound infections in patients with burn injuries?

{{c1::Pseudomonas aeruginosa}}

What property of Pseudomonas may contribute to chronic pneumonia in patients with cystic fibrosis?

{{c1::Mucoid polysaccharide capsule}}

Pseudomonas aeruginosa exotoxin A shares a mechanism with which pseudomembrane-forming pathogen?

{{c1::Corynebacterium diphtheriae}}
fields.Back Extra: Exotoxin A from Pseudomonas aeruginosa and diphtheria toxin from Corynebacterium diphtheriae both inhibit EF-2.

fields.Text:
What product of Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes degradation of cell membranes?

{{c1::Phospholipase C}}

Which gram-negative organism is the most likely cause of pneumonia in individuals with cystic fibrosis?

{{c1::Pseudomonas aeruginosa}}

What are the virulence factors produced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa?

{{c1::Phospholipase C}}
{{c1::Endotoxin}}
{{c1::Exotoxin A}}
{{c1::Pyoverdine}}
{{c1::Pyocyanin}}

What two pigments are produced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa to give it the appearance shown here?



{{c1::Pyoverdine}}
{{c1::Pyocyanin}}

What do patients with Salmonella and Shigella have in common with their clinical presentation?

Both Salmonella and Shigella often cause {{c1::bloody diarrhea}}

How does Salmonella spread through the body as compared to Shigella?

Salmonella spreads {{c1::hematogenously}}
Shigella spreads from {{c1::cell}} to {{c1::cell}}

What are the reservoirs for Shigella and Salmonella?

All strains of Salmonella except Salmonella typhi have {{c1::human}} and {{c1::animal}} reservoirs
Shigella and Salmonella typhi have {{c1::human}} reservoirs only

Do Salmonella and Shigella both have flagella?

Only {{c1::Salmonella}} have flagella
fields.Back Extra: This enables hematogenous dissemination, also known as salmon swim.

fields.Text:
How do antibiotics affect fecal excretion of Salmonella when compared with Shigella?

Antibiotics {{c1::prolong::prolong/shorten}} the duration of fecal excretion of Salmonella
Antibiotics {{c1::shorten::prolong/shorten}} the duration of fecal excretion of Shigella

Name the virulence factor of Salmonella.

{{c1::Endotoxin}}
fields.Back Extra: Salmonella typhi has an additional virulence factor known as the Vi capsule.

fields.Text:
Compare the infectious dose (ID50) of Salmonella to that of Shigella.

{{c1::Salmonella}} has a high ID50
{{c1::Shigella}} has a low ID50

Describe the immune response to Salmonella or Shigella species.

Both Salmonella and Shigella promote response by {{c1::polymorphonuclear leukocytes}}, except for Salmonella typhi, which has a {{c1::monocytic}} response

In what four ways can Shigella be transmitted between humans?

{{c1::Fingers}}
{{c1::Flies}}
{{c1::Food}}
{{c1::Feces}}

What two vaccination options are available to prevent Salmonella typhi infection?

Oral vaccine with {{c1::live attenuated}} Salmonella typhi
Intramuscular vaccine with {{c1::Vi capsular polysaccharide}}

How do levels of Shiga toxin in Shigella boydii, Shigella sonnei, Shigella dysenteriae, and Shigella flexneri compare?

Shigella {{c1::dysenteriae}} > Shigella {{c1::flexneri}} > Shigella {{c1::boydii}} > Shigella {{c1::sonnei}}

Name the possible sources of infection with Salmonella species.

{{c1::Eggs}}
{{c1::Poultry}}
{{c1::Turtles}}
{{c1::Pets}}

What organ does Salmonella typhi colonize?

{{c1::Gallbladder}}

A patient presents with fever, abdominal pain, constipation, and rose-colored spots on his abdomen. What is the causative agent?

{{c1::Salmonella typhi}}

What antibiotics are used to treat infection with Salmonella typhi and other Salmonella species?

Salmonella typhi is treated with {{c1::ceftriaxone}} or a {{c1::fluoroquinolone}}
Salmonella species {{c1::are not::are/are not}} treated with antibiotics

What similarities are there in laboratory characteristics and pathogenicity of Salmonella and Shigella?

Gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} rods
Oxidase-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}}
{{c1::Non-lactose::Lactose/Non-lactose}} fermenters
Can invade the gastrointestinal tract via {{c1::M}} cells of the {{c1::Peyer patches}}

What are the two virulence factors of Shigella species?

{{c1::Endotoxin}}
{{c1::Shiga}} toxin

How do Salmonella and Shigella compare with regard to the production of H2S gas?

{{c1::Salmonella}} produces H2S
{{c1::Shigella}} does not produce H2S

Why does infection with Yersinia enterocolitica often present in a manner similar to appendicitis?

The bacterium causes {{c1::mesenteric adenitis}} and/or {{c1::terminal ileitis}}
fields.Back Extra: This produces right lower quadrant abdominal pain.

fields.Text:
In what three ways is Yersinia enterocolitica typically transferred to humans?

Pet {{c1::feces}}
{{c1::Pork}}
Contaminated {{c1::milk}}

What three illnesses does Yersinia enterocolitica typically cause?

Acute {{c1::bloody diarrhea}}
{{c1::Pseudoappendicitis}}
{{c1::Reactive arthritis}} (adults)

What is the gram stain and morphology of Yersinia enterocolitica?

Gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} pleomorphic {{c1::rod}}/{{c1::coccobacillus}}

Bacteria with what property grow pink colonies on MacConkey agar?

{{c1::Lactose}} fermenters

What two colors do colonies of lactose-fermenting bacteria exhibit on eosin-methylene blue agar?

{{c1::Purple}}
{{c1::Black}}
fields.Back Extra: Escherichia coli organisms grow with a green sheen.

fields.Text:
A risk of enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli contamination is typically associated with what foods?

{{c1::Undercooked meats}}
{{c1::Raw leafy vegetables}}

How can you distinguish enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli from other strains using a culture?

Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli does not ferment {{c1::sorbitol}}, whereas other strains do

How does hemolytic-uremic syndrome develop following an infection with enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli?

Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli releases {{c1::Shiga}}-like toxin → Formation of {{c1::microthrombi}} on damaged endothelium → {{c1::Schistocytes}}, {{c1::platelet}} consumption, and {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} renal blood flow

What is the triad of hemolytic-uremic syndrome?

{{c1::Anemia}}
{{c1::Thrombocytopenia}}
Acute {{c1::kidney::organ}} injury

What population is typically affected by enteropathogenic Escherichia coli infections?

{{c1::Children}}

How does enteropathogenic Escherichia coli cause diarrhea?

It adheres to the {{c1::apical}} surface → {{c1::Flattens}} villi → Decreases absorption

What toxins are responsible for traveler's diarrhea?

Heat-{{c1::labile}} enterotoxin of {{c1::enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli}}
Heat-{{c1::stable}} enterotoxin of {{c1::enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli}}

How does enteroinvasive Escherichia coli cause dysentery?

Enteroinvasive Escherichia coli invades the {{c1::mucosa}} of the intestine → {{c1::Necrosis}} and {{c1::inflammation}} → Dysentery

What Escherichia coli virulence factor is responsible for the development of septic shock?

{{c1::Lipopolysaccharide}} endotoxin

What Escherichia coli virulence factor is responsible for the development of pneumonia and neonatal meningitis?

{{c1::K capsule}}

What Escherichia coli virulence factor is responsible for the development of cystitis and pyelonephritis?

{{c1::Fimbriae}}
fields.Back Extra: The P pili is specifically for pyelonephritis.

fields.Text:
What is the most common serotype of enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli in the United States?

{{c1::O157:H7}}

What give Klebsiella pneumoniae colonies their mucoid appearance?



Presence of numerous {{c1::polysaccharide capsules}}

What illnesses can Klebsiella cause?

{{c1::Lobar pneumonia}} in patients with heavy alcohol use or with impaired host defenses
Healthcare-associated {{c1::urinary}} tract infections

Describe the gram stain and morphology of Klebsiella.

Gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} {{c1::rod::shape}}

What bacteria may cause an aspiration pneumonia productive of "currant jelly" sputum?

{{c1::Klebsiella}}

A pig farmer has bloody diarrhea. He later reports dysuria and sore red knees. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Reactive arthritis}} from {{c1::Campylobacter jejuni}} infection
fields.Back Extra: This was most likely contracted from infected farm animals.

fields.Text:
What findings help identify Campylobacter jejuni as a cause of infection?

{{c1::Comma}} or "{{c1::S}}" shaped with {{c1::polar::polar/nonpolar}} flagella
Oxidase-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}}
Grows at {{c1::42}}°C

What are two possible sequelae of Campylobacter jejuni infection?

{{c1::Reactive arthritis}}
{{c1::Guillain-Barré}} syndrome

What are two common modes of transmission for Campylobacter jejuni?

{{c1::Fecal}}-{{c1::oral}}
Ingestion of {{c1::unpasteurized milk}} or {{c1::undercooked meat}}
fields.Back Extra: The risk is increased with contact with infected animals.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism leading to profuse rice-water diarrhea caused by Vibrio cholerae?



Enterotoxin permanently activates {{c1::Gs}} → Increase in {{c1::cAMP}}

How is Vibrio cholerae transmitted?

Consumption of contaminated {{c1::water}}
Consumption of {{c1::undercooked seafood}}

Why is a patient at higher risk for Vibrio cholerae infection when gastric acidity is reduced?

Vibrio cholerae is {{c1::sensitive}} to stomach acid and typically requires a {{c1::large::large/small}} inoculum
fields.Back Extra: If gastric acidity is reduced, a lower inoculum is needed.

fields.Text:
What are the laboratory characteristics of Vibrio cholerae?

Gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}}
{{c1::Comma}}-shaped
{{c1::Flagellated::Flagellated/Non-flagellated}}
Oxidase-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}}
Grows in {{c1::alkaline::acidic/alkaline}} media
Sensitive to {{c1::stomach acid}}

How would you treat a patient with profuse rice-water diarrhea caused by gram-negative flagellated bacteria?

{{c1::Oral rehydration}} therapy
fields.Back Extra: The patient is infected with Vibrio cholerae.

fields.Text:
What gram-negative bacillus found in marine environments can cause cellulitis that progresses to necrotizing fasciitis?

{{c1::Vibrio vulnificus}}

What procedural treatment may be necessary for severe wound infections caused by Vibrio vulnificus?

{{c1::Surgical debridement}}

Where do Helicobacter pylori typically colonize?

{{c1::Antrum}} of the {{c1::stomach}}

What two tests can be used to diagnose an infection with Helicobacter pylori?

{{c1::Urea breath}} test
{{c1::Fecal antigen}} test

Helicobacter pylori is positive for what three enzymes?

{{c1::Catalase}}
{{c1::Oxidase}}
{{c1::Urease}}

A patient with Helicobacter pylori has an increased risk for which two cancers?

{{c1::Gastric}} adenocarcinoma
{{c1::MALT}} lymphoma

In a patient with peptic ulcers caused by Helicobacter pylori, how are the bacteria able to thrive in the stomach's acidic mucosa?

Helicobacter pylori is urease-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}} and can produce {{c1::ammonia}}, thus creating an alkaline environment

Infection with Helicobacter pylori increases the risk of what three pathologic conditions in the gastrointestinal tract?

{{c1::Peptic ulcer}} disease
{{c1::Gastric}} adenocarcinoma
{{c1::MALT}} lymphoma

What is the most common initial treatment for a Helicobacter pylori infection?

Triple therapy → {{c1::Amoxicillin}} + {{c1::Clarithromycin}} + {{c1::Proton pump}} inhibitor
fields.Back Extra: If the patient is allergic to penicillin, metronidazole is given instead of amoxicillin.

fields.Text:
What is the treatment for macrolide-resistant Helicobacter pylori?

{{c1::Bismuth}}-based quadruple therapy

Describe the morphology and gram staining pattern of Helicobacter pylori.

{{c1::Curved::Shape}}
{{c1::Flagellated::Flagellated/Non-flagellated}}
Gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} rod

What is the general morphology of spirochetes?



{{c1::Spiral}}-shaped
{{c1::Axial}} filaments

What two techniques are used to visualize Treponema?

{{c1::DFA}} microscopy
{{c1::Dark-field}} microscopy

What spirochete can be visualized on light microscopy using aniline dyes?

{{c1::Borrelia}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to its size.

fields.Text:
What are the three medically important spirochete bacterial species?

{{c1::Leptospira}}
{{c1::Treponema}}
{{c1::Borrelia}}

What medications are used to treat the pathology associated with the examination finding shown?



{{c1::Doxycycline}} (first-line)
{{c1::Amoxicillin}} for children under the age of 8 and pregnant patients
{{c1::Ceftriaxone}} for severe illness requiring IV administration

What three pathogens are carried by the vector pictured?



{{c1::Borrelia burgdorferi}}
{{c1::Anaplasma}}
{{c1::Babesia}}

What are the three common manifestations of Lyme disease's third stage?

{{c1::Encephalopathy}}
{{c1::Peripheral::Central/Peripheral}} neuropathy
Chronic {{c1::arthritis}}

What are the five common manifestations of Lyme disease's second stage?

Secondary {{c1::lesions}}
{{c1::Migratory myalgias}}/{{c1::transient arthritis}}
{{c1::Bell palsy}}
{{c1::Atrioventricular block}}
{{c1::Carditis}}

What are the two common manifestations of Lyme disease's first stage?

{{c1::Erythema migrans}}
{{c1::Flu}}-like symptoms

In what region of the United States is Lyme disease common?

{{c1::Northeastern}} United States

Borrelia burgdorferi, which causes Lyme disease, relies on what two animals to replicate and spread?

{{c1::Mice}}
{{c1::Deer}}

What bacterium causes Lyme disease?

{{c1::Borrelia burgdorferi}}

What infectious organism is associated with bilateral facial nerve palsy?

{{c1::Borrelia burgdorferi}}

Which spirochete causes fever, fatigue, body aches, photophobia, and conjunctival suffusion after swimming in contaminated water?

{{c1::Leptospira interrogans}}

How would a patient with Weil disease typically present?

{{c1::Fever}}
{{c1::Hemorrhage}}
{{c1::Anemia}}
{{c1::Jaundice}} and {{c1::azotemia}} due to liver and kidney dysfunction

What is the typical source of Leptospira interrogans infection?

{{c1::Water}} contaminated with {{c1::animal urine}}
fields.Back Extra: The disease is particularly prevalent in the tropics and among surfers.

fields.Text:
What is the typical morphology of Leptospira interrogans?

{{c1::Spirochete}} with {{c1::hook}}-shaped ends

How could maternal transmission of syphilis to a neonate be prevented?

By treating the mother with {{c1::penicillin}} early in pregnancy
fields.Back Extra: This is because placental transmission of syphilis usually occurs after the first trimester.

fields.Text:
What is the name of the chronic granulomas caused by tertiary syphilis shown in the image?



{{c1::Gummas}}

What are the cutaneous manifestations of secondary syphilis shown in the image?



{{c1::Condylomata lata}}

What treatment can be offered to a patient with syphilis and the maculopapular rash on the palms shown in the image?



{{c1::Penicillin G}}
fields.Back Extra: This is used to treat all stages of syphilis.

fields.Text:
What stage of syphilis presents with the finding shown in the image?



{{c1::Primary}} syphilis
fields.Back Extra: The image shows a painless chancre.

fields.Text:
What do the red and black arrows on the image of a patient with congenital syphilis indicate?



Black arrow → {{c1::Rhagades}}
Red arrow → {{c1::Snuffles}}

In what stage of syphilis would a patient note lymphadenopathy and patchy hair loss?

{{c1::Secondary}} syphilis

Tabes dorsalis with general paresis may present in which stage of syphilis?

{{c1::Tertiary}} syphilis

What is the most likely diagnosis in a newborn with snuffles, saddle nose deformity, mulberry molars, and notched teeth?

Congenital {{c1::syphilis}}

What spirochete causes destruction of the vasa vasorum of the aorta?

{{c1::Treponema pallidum}}
fields.Back Extra: This can cause aortitis in tertiary syphilis.

fields.Text:
What three tests can confirm the diagnosis of neurosyphilis?

Testing of spinal fluid with {{c1::VDRL}} test
{{c1::FTA-ABS}} test
{{c1::PCR}}

What is latent syphilis characterized by?

{{c1::Positive::Positive/Negative}} serology {{c1::without::with/without}} symptoms

What pathogen is visualized on dark-field microscopy of sample from a chancre?



{{c1::Treponema pallidum}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the causative agent of syphilis.

fields.Text:
What is the definition of an Argyll Robertson pupil?

A pupil that {{c1::constricts::dilates/constricts}} with {{c1::accommodation}}, but {{c1::is not::is/is not}} reactive to light
fields.Back Extra: This is seen in association with tertiary syphilis.

fields.Text:
What percentage of patients with primary syphilis will be VDRL positive?

{{c1::80}}%

What does the presence of constitutional symptoms in a patient with syphilis indicate?

{{c1::Disseminated}} disease

Why do you confirm a positive VDRL result with a FTA-ABS test when testing for syphilis?

An FTA-ABS test is more {{c1::specific::specific/sensitive}} for syphilis
A VDRL test is more {{c1::sensitive::specific/sensitive}} for syphilis

How is the VDRL test typically used in the workup for syphilis?

As an {{c1::initial screening}} test
fields.Back Extra: The VDRL test is considered to be sensitive, not specific.

fields.Text:
The VDRL test detects antibodies that have formed against which molecule?

{{c1::Beef cardiolipin}}

What are two serologic tests that are specific for treponemal infections?

{{c1::FTA-ABS}} test
{{c1::TPPA}} assay

What are two nonspecific serologic tests used to screen for syphilis?

{{c1::VDRL}} test
{{c1::RPR}} test

What are two ways to directly test for syphilis?

{{c1::Dark-field}} microscopy
{{c1::PCR}}

What can yield false-positive results on the VDRL test?

{{c1::Pregnancy}}
{{c1::Viral}} infection
{{c1::Drugs}}
{{c1::Rheumatic fever}} (rare)
{{c1::Lupus}}
{{c1::Leprosy}}

What ocular infection is shown in the image?



Follicular adult {{c1::conjunctivitis}}

In patients with Chlamydia infection, why is azithromycin the favored treatment?

It is a {{c1::one-time}} treatment
fields.Back Extra: Doxycycline, in contrast, requires several doses.

fields.Text:
Why are Chlamydia species obligate intracellular organisms?

They cannot make their own {{c1::ATP}}

What unique property of chlamydial cell walls make β-lactam antibiotics ineffective?

Chlamydial cell walls lack classic {{c1::peptidoglycan}}
fields.Back Extra: Hence, they would contain less muramic acid.

fields.Text:
How do you treat a chlamydial infection?

{{c1::Azithromycin}} (single dose)
{{c1::Doxycycline}}
fields.Back Extra: Ceftriaxone may be added for possible concomitant gonorrhea.

fields.Text:
What two stains can be used to visualize chlamydiae?

{{c1::Giemsa}} stain
{{c1::Fluorescent antibody}} stain
fields.Back Extra: Both of these will show cytoplasmic inclusions.

fields.Text:
Which species of chlamydiae that causes an atypical pneumonia is associated with exposure to birds?

Chlamydophila {{c1::psittaci}}

Which two species of chlamydiae are transmitted through the air and cause atypical pneumonia?

Chlamydophila {{c1::psittaci}}
Chlamydophila {{c1::pneumoniae}}

What are the two forms of chlamydiae?

Elementary body enters the cell by {{c1::endocytosis}} → Turns into reticulate body
Reticulate body replicates in the cell by {{c1::fission}} → Reorganizes into elementary body

What four diseases are caused by Chlamydia trachomatis?

{{c1::Nongonococcal urethritis}}
{{c1::Pelvic inflammatory}} disease
Neonatal and follicular adult {{c1::conjunctivitis}}
{{c1::Reactive arthritis}}

Which two lab methods are used to diagnose a chlamydial infection?

{{c1::NAAT}}
{{c1::PCR}}
fields.Back Extra: It can also be visualized on Giemsa and fluorescent antibody stains.

fields.Text:
Which chlamydial serotype causes neonatal pneumonia with eosinophilia?

Chlamydia {{c1::trachomatis}}, types {{c1::D}} to {{c1::K}}

What is the treatment for lymphogranuloma venereum caused by Chlamydia trachomatis?

{{c1::Doxycycline}}

How is neonatal disease due to Chlamydia acquired?

As the infant passes through an infected {{c1::birth canal}}

Which Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes cause lymphogranuloma venereum?

{{c1::L1}}
{{c1::L2}}
{{c1::L3}}

Which Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes cause urethritis, pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy, neonatal pneumonia with eosinophilia, and neonatal conjunctivitis?

{{c1::D}} to {{c1::K}}

Blindness due to follicular conjunctivitis by Chlamydia trachomatis is often seen in what type of area?

{{c1::Resource-limited}} areas

How long after birth does neonatal conjunctivitis caused by Chlamydia present?

{{c1::1}} to {{c1::2}} weeks after birth

What is the typical presentation for Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes A, B, and C?

Follicular {{c1::conjunctivitis}} causing {{c1::blindness}}

What is the treatment for an infection caused by the organism shown in the image?



{{c1::Metronidazole}}
{{c1::Clindamycin}}

Overgrowth of what type of bacteria occurs in the vagina of a patient with bacterial vaginosis?

{{c1::Anaerobic::Aerobic/Anareobic}} bacteria
fields.Back Extra: This includes the pleomorphic, gram-variable Gardnerella vaginalis.

fields.Text:
What is an amine whiff test?

Mixing {{c1::vaginal}} discharge with {{c1::10}}% {{c1::KOH}} solution
fields.Back Extra: This is to enhance the fishy odor of Gardnerella vaginalis.

fields.Text:
What is seen on a wet prep of Gardnerella vaginalis?

{{c1::Clue}} cells with {{c1::stippled}} outer margins

A sexually active patient develops a Gardnerella vaginalis infection, but her partner does not. What is the reason?

Gardnerella vaginalis is not transmitted {{c1::sexually}}

Describe the clinical presentation associated with Gardnerella vaginalis infections.

{{c1::Gray::Color}} discharge with a {{c1::fishy}} odor
{{c1::Nonpainful::Painful/Nonpainful}}

How is Pasteurella multocida transmitted?

Via {{c1::bites}} from {{c1::animals}}
fields.Back Extra: Particularly, it is from dogs and cats.

fields.Text:
What bacterium is transmitted by fleas and causes plague in humans?

{{c1::Yersinia pestis}}

What animal reservoirs are the source of disease in those with a diagnosis of plague?

{{c1::Rats}}
{{c1::Prairie dogs}}
fields.Back Extra: These animals are reservoirs of fleas that transmit Yersinia pestis.

fields.Text:
What is the vector for the pathogen causing endemic typhus?

{{c1::Fleas}}

What is the vector causing Rocky Mountain spotted fever?

{{c1::Dermacentor}}
fields.Back Extra:
These transmit Rickettsia rickettsii.

They are also known as the dog tick.

fields.Text:
What disease does Rickettsia prowazekii cause?

{{c1::Epidemic typhus}}

Where do humans acquire Mycobacterium leprae?

Mainly from infected {{c1::humans}}
fields.Back Extra: Rarely, it can be acquired from armadillos.

fields.Text:
What bacteria is found in animal urine and often contaminates public recreational water supplies?

{{c1::Leptospira}} species

What are three vectors for tularemia?

{{c1::Rabbits}}
{{c1::Deer flies}}
{{c1::Ticks}}

What is the vector of ehrlichiosis?

{{c1::Lone Star tick}}

How is Campylobacter jejuni transmitted?

{{c1::Fecal-oral}} transmission

What zoonotic pathogen is found in unpasteurized dairy products and can cause recurrent rising and falling fevers?

{{c1::Brucella}} species

What is responsible for the recurrent nature of the fever in Borrelia recurrentis infections?

Variations in bacterial {{c1::surface antigens}}

A louse is a vector for which bacterial species?

{{c1::Borrelia recurrentis}}

How are Anaplasma and Borrelia burgdorferi transmitted?

{{c1::Ixodes ticks}}
fields.Back Extra: These live on mice and deer.

fields.Text:
What two diseases are associated with Bartonella infections in patients who are immunocompromised?

{{c1::Bacillary angiomatosis}}
{{c1::Cat scratch}} disease

What is the definition of zoonosis?

The transmission of an infectious disease between {{c1::animals}} and {{c1::humans}}

Which zoonotic bacteria, transmitted by reptiles and poultry, cause bloody diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, and fever?

{{c1::Salmonella}} species

Which disease is spread by parrots and other birds?

{{c1::Psittacosis}}

How are Bartonella species transmitted?

{{c1::Cat scratches}}

How is Coxiella burnetti, the causative organism behind Q fever, transmitted?

Via the {{c1::aerosols}} of {{c1::cattle}}/{{c1::sheep}} {{c1::amniotic fluid}}

What disease demonstrates morulae in monocytes?



{{c1::Ehrlichiosis}}

The image shows a granulocyte infected with a rickettsial organism. What finding is indicated by the arrow?



A {{c1::morula}} in the cytoplasm
fields.Back Extra: This is observed in infections caused by Anaplasma.

fields.Text:
What treatment do you typically use for rickettsial diseases and vector-borne illnesses?

{{c1::Doxycycline}}

What vector is responsible for the transmission of ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis?

{{c1::Ticks}}

What differentiates Q fever from the diseases of the Rickettsia genus, to which it is closely related?

Q fever, caused by {{c1::Coxiella burnetii}}, can survive in the {{c1::endospore}} form
Q fever does not have a {{c1::rash}} or {{c1::vector}}

What illness caused by Coxiella burnetii presents as headache, cough, flu-like symptoms, pneumonia, and possibly hepatitis?

{{c1::Q fever}}
fields.Back Extra: This may also present as culture-negative endocarditis.

fields.Text:
How is Q fever transmitted?

By inhalation of {{c1::aerosols}} from the {{c1::amniotic fluid}} of {{c1::sheep}}/{{c1::cattle}} infected with Coxiella burnetii
fields.Back Extra: Coxiella burnetii is the organism that causes Q fever.

fields.Text:
In which host cell type do bacterial microcolonies form when a patient has anaplasmosis?

{{c1::Granulocytes}}

How does the rash in epidemic and endemic typhus spread?

Starts {{c1::centrally::centrally/peripherally}} and spreads {{c1::out::in/out}}
Spares the {{c1::palms}} and {{c1::soles}}

What three diseases start with a rash on the palms and soles?

{{c1::Coxsackievirus A}} infection
{{c1::Rocky Mountain spotted fever}}
{{c1::Secondary syphilis}}

What is the classic triad of symptoms of Rocky Mountain spotted fever?

{{c1::Fever}}
{{c1::Headache}}
{{c1::Rash}}

How does the rash caused by Rickettsia rickettsii spread on the body?

Starts at {{c1::ankles}} and {{c1::wrists}}
Spreads to {{c1::trunk}}, {{c1::palms}}, and {{c1::soles}}

Which bacteria are responsible for endemic typhus and epidemic typhus?

Endemic typhus is caused by {{c1::Rickettsia typhi}}
Epidemic typhus is caused by {{c1::Rickettsia prowazekii}}

In what states is Rocky Mountain spotted fever commonly found?

{{c1::South Atlantic}} states, especially {{c1::North Carolina}}

What pathogen is responsible for Rocky Mountain spotted fever?

{{c1::Rickettsia rickettsii}}

Which bacteria that frequently causes atypical pneumonia can cause an atypical variant of Stevens-Johnson syndrome in children and adolescents?

{{c1::Mycoplasma pneumoniae}}

How would you describe the morphology of Mycoplasma as shown in the image?



{{c1::Pleomorphic}}

What populations are most likely to experience a Mycoplasma pneumoniae outbreak?

Individuals under {{c1::30}} years of age
{{c1::Military}} recruits
{{c1::College}} students
Those in {{c1::prison}}

What stabilizes the membrane of Mycoplasma pneumoniae?

{{c1::Sterols}} in the bacterial membranes

Why can't Mycoplasma pneumoniae be observed on a Gram stain?

Mycoplasma pneumoniae lack {{c1::cell walls}}

In what culture medium does Mycoplasma pneumoniae grow?

{{c1::Eaton}} agar

What hematologic finding may help confirm Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection?

A high titer of {{c1::cold agglutinins}}, which can {{c1::agglutinate}} red blood cells

What bacteria causes an atypical "walking pneumonia" with diffuse interstitial infiltrates seen on chest X-ray?

{{c1::Mycoplasma pneumoniae}}

Why is penicillin ineffective as a therapy option for Mycoplasma pneumoniae?

Mycoplasma pneumoniae lack {{c1::cell walls}}
fields.Back Extra: This allows it to be resistant to penicillin.

fields.Text:
In a patient with Mycoplasma pneumoniae, how does the chest X-ray finding compare to the severity of clinical illness?

X-ray usually looks {{c1::worse}} than the patient's clinical presentation

What three antibiotics or antibiotic class are helpful to treat atypical pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae?

{{c1::Doxycycline}}
{{c1::Fluoroquinolones}}
{{c1::Macrolides}}

What systemic mycosis is indicated by the histopathologic findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Histoplasmosis}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows a macrophage filled with Histoplasma.

fields.Text:
What systemic mycosis is indicated by the findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Paracoccidioidomycosis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the characteristic "captain's wheel" of Paracoccidioides.

fields.Text:
What systemic mycosis is characterized by the histopathologic findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Blastomycosis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the characteristic "broad-based budding" of Blastomyces.

fields.Text:
In what regions is blastomycosis endemic in the United States?

{{c1::Eastern}} United States
{{c1::Central}} United States
{{c1::Great Lakes}}

How do tuberculosis and the systemic mycoses differ in transmission?

{{c1::Tuberculosis}} can be transmitted from person-to-person
{{c1::Systemic mycosis}} cannot be transmitted from person-to-person

How do Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides, and Paracoccidioides organisms compare in terms of size to red blood cells?

Histoplasma organisms → {{c1::Smaller}}
Blastomyces organisms → {{c1::Same}}
Coccidioides organisms → {{c1::Larger}}
Paracoccidioides organisms → {{c1::Larger}}

All systemic mycoses can primarily cause what type of illness?

{{c1::Pneumonia}}
fields.Back Extra: These all can disseminate as well.

fields.Text:
Where is paracoccidioidomycosis endemic?

{{c1::Latin America}}

What physical exam findings can be noted in a patient with coccidioidomycosis?

{{c1::Erythema nodosum}}
{{c1::Erythema multiforme}}
{{c1::Arthralgias}}
{{c1::Meningeal}} signs if {{c1::meningitis}} is present

What systemic mycosis can present with meningitis and pneumonia?



{{c1::Coccidioidomycosis}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows spherule filled with endospores of Coccidioides.

fields.Text:
How is Coccidioides distinguished from all other dimorphic fungi?

It is a {{c1::spherule}} in tissue at 37°C

Which systemic mycosis presents with pneumonia and verrucous skin lesions?

{{c1::Blastomycosis}}

Where is histoplasmosis endemic in the United States?

{{c1::Ohio River Valley}}
{{c1::Mississippi River Valley}}

Which systemic fungi are dimorphic?

{{c1::Histoplasma}}
{{c1::Blastomyces}}
{{c1::Coccidioides}}
{{c1::Paracoccidioides}}

Pathologically, how are systemic mycoses and tuberculosis similar?

Both can form {{c1::granulomas}}

What systemic mycoses can cause the skin manifestation shown?



{{c1::Blastomycosis}}

What exposure is most strongly associated with coccidioidomycosis?

{{c1::Dust}} exposure in endemic areas

How is histoplasmosis generally acquired?

Inhalation from {{c1::bird}}/{{c1::bat}} {{c1::droppings}}

In what regions is coccidioidomycosis endemic in the United States?

{{c1::Southwestern}} United States
{{c1::California::State}}

How do you treat local infections caused by dimorphic fungi?

{{c1::Itraconazole}}
{{c1::Fluconazole}}

What is the treatment for disseminated systemic mycoses?

{{c1::Amphotericin B}}

Which systemic mycoses can present with erythema nodosum?

{{c1::Histoplasmosis}}
{{c1::Coccidioidomycosis}}

What signs/symptoms can be seen in a patient with histoplasmosis?

Tongue/palatal {{c1::ulcers}}
{{c1::Erythema nodosum}}
{{c1::Pancytopenia}}
{{c1::Splenomegaly}}

To what tissues/organs can blastomycosis disseminate?

{{c1::Bone}}
{{c1::Skin}}
fields.Back Extra: This can mimic squamous cell carcinoma.

fields.Text:
Is paracoccidioidomycosis more common in males or females?

{{c1::Males::Males/Females}}

What test is used to diagnose histoplasmosis?

{{c1::Urine}}/{{c1::serum}} antigen

Which opportunistic fungus is shown in the image?



{{c1::Aspergillus fumigatus}}

What disease features oral white plaques as shown in the image?



{{c1::Oral thrush}} from {{c1::Candida albicans}}

What organism is revealed by light microscopy at 37°C as shown in the image?



{{c1::Candida albicans}}

Which patient populations are most susceptible to the fungal infection that corresponds with the culture shown?



Patients with {{c1::diabetic ketoacidosis}}
Patients with {{c1::neutropenia}}

What might be seen on brain imaging of a patient with cryptococcal meningitis?

"{{c1::Soap bubbles}}" lesions

Name the three presentations of aspergillosis.

{{c1::Allergic bronchopulmonary}} aspergillosis
{{c1::Lung cavity}} aspergillosis
{{c1::Invasive}} aspergillosis

Where is the central nervous system pathology that is caused by Mucor and Rhizopus infections?

{{c1::Rhinocerebral}} lobe abscess
{{c1::Frontal}} lobe abscess
{{c1::Cavernous}} sinus thrombosis

What opportunistic fungus is a cause of infective endocarditis in persons who use injectable drugs?

{{c1::Candida albicans}}

How does Aspergillus fumigatus appear on culture media at 37°C?

{{c1::45}}° branching {{c1::septate hyphae}}

What is the most sensitive and specific test to confirm an infection with Crytococcus neoformans?

{{c1::Latex agglutination}} test
fields.Back Extra: This can detect the polysaccharide capsular antigen.

fields.Text:
Identify the growing fungi with these characteristics:

Broad
Irregular
Nonseptate hyphae that branch at wide angles

{{c1::Mucor}} species
{{c1::Rhizopus}} species

Which two groups of patients are most likely to develop allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis?

Patients with {{c1::asthma}}
Patients with {{c1::cystic fibrosis}}

What fungal pulmonary infection are patients with tuberculosis likely to develop?

{{c1::Aspergillus fumigatus}}
fields.Back Extra: This may cause aspergillomas in pre-existing lung cavities, especially those due to tuberculosis.

fields.Text:
What pathology is associated with Aspergillus aflatoxins?

{{c1::Hepatocellular}} carcinoma

What is the treatment for cryptococcal meningitis?

Induction therapy with {{c1::amphotericin B}} and {{c1::flucytosine}}, followed by maintenance therapy with {{c1::fluconazole}}

What is the treatment for mucormycosis?

{{c1::Surgical}} debridement
{{c1::Amphotericin B}}
{{c1::Isavuconazole}}

You culture Cryptococcus neoformans at 25°C in plate A and at 37°C in plate B. What morphology do you note in each plate?

{{c1::Yeast}} formation in both plates

What is observed when Candida albicans is grown at 20°C and at 37°C?

Formation of {{c1::pseudohyphae}} and {{c1::budding}} yeast at 20°C
Formation of {{c1::germ tube}} at 37°C

What is the treatment for oral thrush?

{{c1::Nystatin}}
{{c1::Azoles}}
{{c1::Echinocandins}} (rarely)

What three medications can treat systemic candidiasis?

{{c1::Amphotericin B}}
{{c1::Fluconazole}}
{{c1::Echinocandins}}

How do Mucor and Rhizopus invade and cause infection?

Fungi spores are inhaled → Proliferation in {{c1::blood vessels}} → Penetrates the brain via the {{c1::cribriform plate}}

How is cryptococcosis acquired?

Through {{c1::hematogenous dissemination}}
fields.Back Extra: This is after inhalation from soil/pigeon droppings.

fields.Text:
What heavily encapsulated, nondimorphic yeast that stains PAS-positive commonly infects immunocompromised patients?

{{c1::Cryptococcus neoformans}}

How can cryptococcosis manifest in a patient?

{{c1::Meningitis}}
{{c1::Pneumonia}}
{{c1::Encephalitis}}

What populations are at high risk for oral/esophageal thrush?

{{c1::Immunocompromised}} patients

Patients with neutropenia or dysfunctional neutrophils are highly susceptible to which two opportunistic fungal infections?

{{c1::Candida albicans}}
{{c1::Aspergillus}}

What is the pathophysiology of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis?

A {{c1::hypersensitivity}} response to Aspergillus colonization in the lung mucus

What are the treatment options for Aspergillus infections?

{{c1::Voriconazole}}
{{c1::Echinocandins}} (second-line)

What two stains are used to diagnose Cryptococcus neoformans?

{{c1::India ink}} stain
{{c1::Mucicarmine}} stain

Which population has an increased risk of developing vulvovaginitis due to Candida albicans?

Patients with {{c1::diabetes}}
Patients using {{c1::antibiotics}}

What is the treatment for vaginal candidiasis?

Oral {{c1::fluconazole}}
Topical {{c1::azoles}}

A patient who is HIV-positive is diagnosed with fungal pneumonia. Initial X-ray is shown. What stain should be used to confirm the pathogen on lung biopsy?



{{c1::Methenamine}} stain
fields.Back Extra:
A fluorescent antibody may be used as well.

The X-ray shows Pneumocystis pneumonia.

fields.Text:
What is the appearance of Pneumocystis pneumonia on chest imaging?

{{c1::Diffuse}}, {{c1::bilateral::unilateral/bilateral}} {{c1::ground-glass opacities}} with {{c1::pneumatoceles}}

At what CD4+ count should patients who are HIV-positive begin to receive prophylaxis against Pneumocystis pneumonia?

Below {{c1::200}} cells/mm3

How is Pneumocystis pneumonia diagnosed?

{{c1::Bronchoalveolar lavage}}
Lung {{c1::biopsy}}

Which group of hosts would be symptomatic if infected with Pneumocystis?

{{c1::Immunocompromised}} patients

What agents can be used for treatment or prophylaxis of Pneumocystis pneumonia?

{{c1::TMP-SMX}}
{{c1::Dapsone}}
{{c1::Pentamidine}}
{{c1::Atovaquone}}

How does Pneumocystis pneumonia appear on methenamine silver-stained samples?

{{c1::Disc}}-shaped yeasts

What disease is caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii?

{{c1::Pneumocystis pneumonia}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a diffuse interstitial pneumonia.

fields.Text:
A gardener has an arm pustule with ascending lymphangitis. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Sporotrichosis}}

What two medications can treat sporotrichosis?

{{c1::Itraconazole}}
{{c1::Potassium iodide}}
fields.Back Extra: This is only for cutaneous/lymphocutaneous disease.

fields.Text:
How does Sporothrix schenckii exist in the human body and in the soil?

{{c1::Cigar}}-shaped yeast in the human body at {{c1::37}}°C
{{c1::Hyphae}} with {{c1::spores}} in soil

How is sporotrichosis transmitted?

Introduction of fungal {{c1::spores}} into the {{c1::skin}} after an injury
fields.Back Extra: This is often caused by thorns.

fields.Text:
What dimorphic fungus presents as a pustule and multiple nodules tracing upward along draining lymphatics?

{{c1::Sporothrix schenckii}}

You find this microorganism in a blood sample. Describe the structures the arrows are pointing to.



A {{c1::trophozoite}} with engulfed {{c1::red blood}} cells in the cytoplasm

You find the following microorganism in a stool sample. What is the treatment for this disease?



{{c1::Metronidazole}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a cyst of Entamoeba histolytica.

fields.Text:
How can Cryptosporidium infection be prevented?

{{c1::Water filtration}}

Which gastrointestinal infection causes fatty, foul-smelling diarrhea and is pictured below?



{{c1::Giardiasis}}

How is an Entamoeba histolytica infection diagnosed from a stool sample?

Presence of {{c1::trophozoites}} with engulfed {{c1::red blood}} cells or {{c1::cysts}} with up to {{c1::4}} nuclei

What are the findings on colon biopsy of Entamoeba histolytica infection?

{{c1::Flask}}-shaped {{c1::ulcers}}

What protozoan infection is characterized by bloody diarrhea, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and liver abscesses?

{{c1::Entamoeba histolytica}} infection

How does Cryptosporidium present in immunocompromised hosts?

Severe {{c1::diarrhea}}

What acid-fast organism causes watery diarrhea in healthy patients?

{{c1::Cryptosporidium}}

What methods can be used to diagnose an Entamoeba histolytica infection in a blood sample?

{{c1::Serology}}
Serum {{c1::antigen}} testing

You find the following microorganism in a blood sample. You identify multinucleated trophozoites as shown. What disease is caused by this microorganism?



{{c1::Giardiasis}}

How is Entamoeba histolytica transmitted?

Via {{c1::cysts}} in {{c1::water}}

How does treatment of amebiasis differ between symptomatic and asymptomatic patients?

Symptomatic patients will be given {{c1::metronidazole}}
Asymptomatic patients will be given {{c1::paromomycin}} or {{c1::iodoquinol}}

How is Cryptosporidium diarrhea treated in immunocompetent patients?

{{c1::Nitazoxanide}}
fields.Back Extra: Otherwise, it is prevented by water filtration.

fields.Text:
How does Cryptosporidium present in immunocompetent hosts?

{{c1::Mild}} disease, presenting with {{c1::watery::watery/bloody}} diarrhea

What drug can be used to treat infection with Giardia lamblia?

{{c1::Metronidazole}}

What is the pathophysiology of recurrent fevers caused by Trypanosoma brucei, shown in the blood smear?



{{c1::Antigenic variation}}

What is the treatment for toxoplasmosis?

{{c1::Sulfadiazine}} + {{c1::Pyrimethamine}}

How is African sleeping sickness transmitted?

Trypomastigotes are transmitted through the bite of a {{c1::tsetse fly}}

What is the most appropriate treatment for the protozoa shown, which usually leads to rapidly fatal meningoencephalitis?



{{c1::Amphotericin B}}

What diagnostic tests can confirm Toxoplasma infection?

{{c1::Serology}}
{{c1::Biopsy}}
{{c1::PCR}} test of amniotic fluid

How is Toxoplasma gondii acquired?

Ingesting {{c1::meat}} infected with cysts
Exposure to oocysts in {{c1::cat feces}}

What is noted in the blood smear of patients with African sleeping sickness?

{{c1::Trypomastigotes}}

What is the treatment of choice for African sleeping sickness with involvement of the central nervous system?

{{c1::Melarsoprol}}

What is the treatment of choice for a blood-borne Trypanosoma brucei infection?

{{c1::Suramin}}

How is Naegleria fowleri transmitted?

Acquired from {{c1::warm freshwater}} → Invades the central nervous system through the {{c1::cribriform plate}}

What is the classic triad of congenital toxoplasmosis?

{{c1::Chorioretinitis}}
{{c1::Hydrocephalus}}
Intracranial {{c1::calcifications}}

Why should pregnant women avoid cat litter boxes?

Cat feces may contain {{c1::Toxoplasma}} oocysts
fields.Back Extra: These can cross the placenta and cause birth defects.

fields.Text:
What is the most appropriate diagnostic test for Naegleria fowleri?

Test for {{c1::amoebas}} in the {{c1::cerebrospinal fluid}}

Toxoplasma causes severe disease in what two patient populations?

Patients with {{c1::AIDS}} → Reactivation
{{c1::Neonates}} → Congenital toxoplasmosis

How does toxoplasmosis present in immunocompetent adults?

As a {{c1::mononucleosis}}-like syndrome with {{c1::negative::positive/negative}} heterophile antibodies

How does African sleeping sickness present?

Recurrent {{c1::fevers}}
{{c1::Somnolence}}
{{c1::Coma}}
{{c1::Lymphadenopathy}}

What protozoa can cause a ring form or "Maltese cross" on a blood smear, as shown?



{{c1::Babesia}}

What is the structure shown in the blood smear below?



{{c1::Trophozoite ring}} of {{c1::Plasmodium malariae}}

How can you diagnose babesiosis?

{{c1::Blood smear}}
{{c1::PCR}}

What group of people are at risk for severe infections of babesiosis?

Patients with {{c1::asplenia}}
fields.Back Extra: Infected red blood cells do not get cleared effectively.

fields.Text:
In what region of the world is Babesia infection most common?

{{c1::Northeastern}} United States
{{c1::North central}} United States

How is Babesia transmitted?

{{c1::Ixodes ticks}}

In patients with Plasmodium falciparum infections, red blood cells tend to occlude capillaries in which three organs?

{{c1::Kidneys}}
{{c1::Lungs}}
{{c1::Brain}}

Which two species of Plasmodium form dormant hypnozoites in the liver, leading to relapsing malaria?

Plasmodium {{c1::vivax}}
Plasmodium {{c1::ovale}}

What findings on blood smear confirm a diagnosis of malaria?

{{c1::Trophozoite ring}} forms within red blood cells

What is the mode of transmission of the Plasmodium species that cause malaria?

Bite of the {{c1::Anopheles mosquito}}

What is the specific treatment for the dormant form of malaria?

{{c1::Primaquine}}

Before using chloroquine to treat malaria, what should be verified about the patient's particular strain of malaria?

{{c1::Sensitivity}} to chloroquine
fields.Back Extra: Some patients have developed resistance to this drug.

fields.Text:
What infection is most commonly associated with the findings of the blood smear in the image?



{{c1::Plasmodium vivax}}
{{c1::Plasmodium ovale}}
fields.Back Extra: The blood smear shows Schüffner stippling.

fields.Text:
How does the fever pattern differ in malaria caused by Plasmodium vivax, Plasmodium ovale, Plasmodium falciparum, and Plasmodium malariae?

Plasmodium malariae → {{c1::72}} hours
Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale → {{c1::48}} hours
Plasmodium falciparum → {{c1::Irregular}}

With which antimalarial agents is it important to screen for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency prior to use?

{{c1::Quinidine}}
{{c1::Artesunate}}

What two treatments are used in life-threatening forms of malaria?

Intravenous {{c1::quinidine}}
Intravenous {{c1::artesunate}}

How is babesiosis treated?

{{c1::Atovaquone}} + {{c1::Azithromycin}}

Ixodes tick is the vector for which three diseases?

{{c1::Babesiosis}}
{{c1::Lyme}} disease
{{c1::Anaplasmosis}}

Wet mounts results from a vaginal culture are shown below. What is the likely infectious entity?



{{c1::Trichomonas vaginalis}}

A blood smear is shown from a patient diagnosed with visceral leishmaniasis. Describe the findings.



{{c1::Amastigotes}} within a {{c1::macrophage}}

What does this blood smear from a recently migrated South American with unilateral periorbital swelling show?



{{c1::Trypomastigote}}
fields.Back Extra: This is characteristic of a Trypanosoma cruzi infection.

fields.Text:
How is Trypanosoma cruzi transmitted?

{{c1::Fecal}} transmission from a {{c1::triatomine insect}} that bites and defacates near the {{c1::mouth}} or {{c1::eyes}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as the "kissing bug".

fields.Text:
