A patient who recently returned from an international trip developed the ulcerated rash shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?



{{c1::Cutaneous leishmaniasis}}

How is Trichomonas vaginalis transmitted?

{{c1::Sexually}}
fields.Back Extra: Trichomonas vaginalis exists only in the human body due to the inability to form cysts.

fields.Text:
What vaginal infection is characterized by a foul-smelling, itching, burning vaginitis with green discharge?

{{c1::Trichomoniasis}}

A man is bitten by a sandfly and develops spiking fevers, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia. What is the likely diagnosis?

{{c1::Visceral leishmaniasis}}

A patient has unilateral, nontender periorbital swelling after recently traveling to Bolivia. What is the likely diagnosis?

Acute {{c1::Chagas}} disease
fields.Back Extra: The patient presents with the Romaña sign.

fields.Text:
How is Chagas disease treated?

{{c1::Benznidazole}}
{{c1::Nifurtimox}}

What are the key aspects of treating Trichomonas vaginalis infections?

{{c1::Metronidazole}} should be given to both the patient and the sexual partner for prophylaxis
Screen for {{c1::sexually transmitted}} infections

What are two diagnostic findings of Trichomonas vaginalis infection?

{{c1::Motile trophozoites}} on wet mount
"{{c1::Strawberry cervix}}"

What are the typical presentations of Chagas disease?

{{c1::Dilated}} cardiomyopathy with {{c1::apical}} atrophy
{{c1::Megaesophagus}}
{{c1::Megacolon}}

What is the treatment for leishmaniasis?

{{c1::Amphotericin B}}
{{c1::Sodium stibogluconate}}

On what continent is Chagas disease predominantly found?

{{c1::South America}}

Infection by what parasite is associated with Chagas disease?

{{c1::Trypanosoma cruzi}}

Which three nematodes are transmitted cutaneously?

{{c1::Strongyloides}}
{{c1::Ancylostoma}}
{{c1::Necator}}

Which three nematodes are transmitted through bites?

{{c1::Loa loa}}
{{c1::Onchocerca volvulus}}
{{c1::Wuchereria bancrofti}}

Which five nematodes are transmitted by fecal-oral route?

{{c1::Enterobius}}
{{c1::Ascaris}}
{{c1::Toxocara}}
{{c1::Trichinella}}
{{c1::Trichuris}}

What is the treatment of choice for elephantiasis?

{{c1::Diethylcarbamazine}}

A man moved to a rural, swampy area with poor health care access. A year later, he presents with the findings shown. Which organism causes this presentation?



{{c1::Wuchereria bancrofti}}
{{c1::Brugia malayi}}

This egg was found on the anal canal of a child complaining of anal pruritus. Which organism is this?



{{c1::Enterobius vermicularis}}

What are two other classic findings associated with the infection causing river blindness?

{{c1::Skin}} changes
Loss of {{c1::elastic fibers}}

What are the commonly seen symptoms in patients infected with Toxocara canis?

{{c1::Myocarditis}}
{{c1::Hepatitis}}
{{c1::Visual}} impairment
{{c1::Seizures}}
{{c1::Coma}}
fields.Back Extra:
These are features of visceral larva migrans.

The patient is often asymptomatic.

fields.Text:
A recent visitor to Mexico develops fever, vomiting, perioribital edema, and muscle pain. A muscle biopsy is shown. What organism has he been infected by?



{{c1::Trichinella spiralis}} nematodes

How does Trichinella spiralis cause muscle inflammation?

Larvae enter the {{c1::bloodstream}} and encyst in {{c1::striated muscle}} cells

How is Toxocara canis transmitted?

{{c1::Fecal-oral}} route

What is the pathogenesis of lymphatic filariasis?

Worms invade the {{c1::lymph nodes}} → {{c1::Inflammation}} → Lymphedema

What is the treatment for Loa loa infection?

{{c1::Diethylcarbamazine}}

What is the appropriate treatment for visceral larva migrans caused by Toxocara canis infection?

{{c1::Bendazoles}}

A woman lives near a stable. She presents with new-onset skin swelling and conjunctival worms. What is the most likely causative organism?

{{c1::Loa loa}} nematode

A man bitten by a black fly experiences skin changes and blindness. What is the most likely diagnosis?

{{c1::Onchocerca volvulus}} infection

A patient develops the pruritic rash after walking barefoot at a beach. Which parasite is likely responsible?



{{c1::Hookworm}}
fields.Back Extra: The diagnosis is cutaneous larva migrans.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of anemia in hookworm infestations?

The worms suck blood through the {{c1::intestinal walls}} → Microcytic anemia

What is the common name for Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus?

{{c1::Hookworms}}

What form of the nematode is excreted in the stool of an individual infected with Strongyloides stercoralis?

{{c1::Rhabditiform larvae}}

How do you treat an infection with Strongyloides stercoralis?

{{c1::Ivermectin}}
{{c1::Bendazoles}}

A patient presents with cough, gallstones, and abdominal pain. The stool sample results are shown. What organism is most likely responsible?



{{c1::Ascaris lumbricoides}}
fields.Back Extra: These are characterized by "knobby-coated" eggs visible in feces under a microscope.

fields.Text:
What are three possible intestinal complications associated with Ascaris lumbricoides infections?

{{c1::Ileocecal valve}} obstruction
Intestinal {{c1::perforation}}
{{c1::Biliary}} obstruction

What is the common name for Ascaris lumbricoides?

{{c1::Giant roundworm}}

How is an Enterobius vermicularis infection diagnosed?

{{c1::Tape}} test
fields.Back Extra: This test will look for the presence of eggs stuck to the tape.

fields.Text:
What is the common name for Enterobius vermicularis?

{{c1::Pinworm}}

What is the treatment for pinworm and hookworm infections?

{{c1::Pyrantel pamoate}}
{{c1::Bendazoles}}

What are the characteristics of a clinically significant infection with Trichuris trichiura?

{{c1::Loose}} stools
Rectal {{c1::prolapse}} (usually in children)
{{c1::Anemia}}

What are the commonly encountered intestinal nematodes?

{{c1::Enterobius}}
{{c1::Ascaris}}
{{c1::Strongyloides}}
{{c1::Ancylostoma}}/{{c1::Necator}}
{{c1::Trichinella}}
{{c1::Trichuris}}

What are the commonly encountered tissue nematodes?

{{c1::Toxcara}}
{{c1::Onchocerca}}
{{c1::Loa loa}}
{{c1::Wuchereria bancrofti}}/{{c1::Brugria malayi}}

How do you treat Onchocerca volvulus infections?

{{c1::Ivermectin}}

How is Enterobius vermicularis transmitted?

{{c1::Fecal-oral}} route

How is Ascaris lumbricoides transmitted?

{{c1::Fecal-oral}} route

How is Strongyloides stercoralis transmitted?

Larvae from {{c1::soil}} penetrate {{c1::skin}}

How are Necator americanus and Ancylostoma species transmitted?

Larvae enter through the {{c1::skin}}

How is Trichinella spiralis transmitted?

More commonly → Ingestion of {{c1::undercooked meat}}, especially {{c1::pork}}
Less commonly → {{c1::Fecal-oral}} route

How is Trichuris trichiura transmitted?

{{c1::Fecal-oral}} route

How is Loa loa transmitted?

{{c1::Flies}}
fields.Back Extra: Specifically, it may be from a deer fly, horse fly, or mango fly.

fields.Text:
How is Wuchereria bancrofti/Brugia malayi transmitted?

{{c1::Female::Male/Female}} {{c1::mosquito}} bite

How does hyperinfection syndrome occur with Strongyloides stercoralis?

Via {{c1::autoinfection}} by larvae entering the {{c1::bloodstream}}
fields.Back Extra: This is especially in patients who are immunocompromised.

fields.Text:
What are common symptoms of Strongyloides stercoralis infection?

{{c1::Duodenitis}}
{{c1::Dry}} cough
{{c1::Hemoptysis}}
{{c1::Cutaneous}} symptoms

All intestinal nematodes can be treated with which medication?

{{c1::Bendazoles}}

A sheepherder presents with the CT scan of the abdomen findings shown. He then develops acute-onset anaphylaxis. What is the causal organism?



{{c1::Echinococcus granulosus}}
fields.Back Extra:
The image shows eggshell calcifications, characteristic for hydatid cysts in the liver.

Sheeps are intermediate hosts for the tapeworm.

fields.Text:
A patient ingests an organism after handling dog feces. What disease does the causative agent shown cause?



{{c1::Hydatid cysts}} in the {{c1::liver::organ}}

What is the mode of transmission of Diphyllobothrium latum?

Consumption of larvae present in {{c1::raw freshwater fish}}

What is the treatment for Diphyllobothrium latum?

{{c1::Praziquantel}}
{{c1::Niclosamide}}

A patient has an intestinal infection with the tapeworm shown in the image. What is the treatment?



{{c1::Praziquantel}}
fields.Back Extra: The patient has a Taenia solium infection.

fields.Text:
What is the mode of transmission of intestinal Taenia solium?

Consumption of {{c1::undercooked pork}} containing encysted larvae

Taenia solium, Diphyllobothrium latum, and Echinococcus granulosus are examples of what type of organism?

{{c1::Cestodes}}

How is cysticercosis transmitted?

By ingestion of food contaminated with {{c1::human feces}} containing {{c1::Taenia solium}} eggs

How does an infection with Diphyllobothrium latum cause megaloblastic anemia?

The tapeworm competes for vitamin {{c1::B12}} in the intestines

A sheep farmer is found to have cysts in his liver. One such cyst is shown. What is the treatment for the most likely causative agent?



{{c1::Albendazole}}
{{c1::Surgical}} excision for complicated cysts

A 40-year-old man has new-onset seizures and is found to have cystic brain lesions. What is the most likely diagnosis?



{{c1::Neurocysticercosis}}

What additional drug is used in the treatment of neurocysticerosis, other than praziquantel?

{{c1::Albendazole}}

A patient presents with chronic pulmonary hypertension. What is the most likely diagnosis based on the microscopy image below?



{{c1::Schistosoma haematobium}} infection

What is the organism shown in the image?



{{c1::Schistosoma mansoni}}

How are infections with Clonorchis sinensis treated?

{{c1::Praziquantel}}

Which fluke is transmitted in undercooked fish?

{{c1::Clonorchis sinensis}}

A patient with a past medical history of a trematode infection presents with painless hematuria. What complication could he be experiencing?

Chronic {{c1::Schistosoma haematobium}} infection is associated with {{c1::squamous cell}} carcinoma of the bladder

How is Schistosoma transmitted to humans?

Through penetration of the skin by {{c1::cercariae}} upon contact with contaminated {{c1::freshwater}}

What is the intermediate host of Schistosoma flukes?

{{c1::Snails}}

What malignant complication is associated with Clonorchis sinensis infection?

{{c1::Cholangiocarcinoma}}

What are the characteristics of a Clonorchis sinensis infection?

{{c1::Biliary tract}} infection leading to {{c1::pigmented}} gallstones

What characteristic features may be noted in a patient with intestinal schistosomiasis?

{{c1::Diarrhea}}
{{c1::Abdominal}} pain
{{c1::Iron deficiency}} anemia

How can you distinguish Schistosoma mansoni from Schistosoma haematobium?

Schistosoma mansoni → Egg with a {{c1::lateral}} spine
Schistosoma haematobium → Egg with a {{c1::terminal}} spine

How is an infection with Schistosoma species treated?

{{c1::Praziquantel}}

What symptoms are associated with infection by Schistosoma mansoni?

Liver and spleen {{c1::enlargement}}
{{c1::Fibrosis}}
{{c1::Inflammation}}
Portal {{c1::hypertension::hypertension/hypotension}}

How does Sarcoptes scabiei invade the host and cause pruritus?

Mites burrow into the {{c1::stratum corneum}} → Pruritus

In what population is scabies common?

{{c1::Children}}
{{c1::Prison inmates}}
{{c1::Nursing home}} residents

Where on the body are Pediculus humanus and Phthirus pubis commonly found?

{{c1::Scalp}}/{{c1::neck}} (head lice)
{{c1::Waistline}}/{{c1::axillae}} (body lice)
{{c1::Pubic}}/{{c1::perianal}} regions (pubic lice)

What three microorganisms can body lice transmit to humans?

{{c1::Rickettsia prowazekii}}
{{c1::Borrelia recurrentis}}
{{c1::Bartonella quintana}}

What methods can be used to treat Sarcoptes scabiei infestation?

{{c1::Permethrin}} cream
Oral {{c1::ivermectin}}
{{c1::Laundering}} of all bedding and clothing
Treating {{c1::close contacts}}

A child presents with intense pruritus that is worse at night and a rash on the hand. How is the causative infestation transmitted?



{{c1::Skin-to-skin}} contact
Via {{c1::fomites}}

What parasites can lead to following macroscopic findings in the scalp or hairy regions like axilla or pubis?



{{c1::Pediculus humanus}}
{{c1::Phthirus pubis}}

What is the treatment for lice infection?

{{c1::Pyrethroids}}
{{c1::Malathion}}
{{c1::Ivermectin}} lotion
{{c1::Nit combing}}

What organism causes scabies?

{{c1::Sarcoptes scabiei}}

For school-aged children who are diagnosed with lice, how is their school attendance generally affected?

{{c1::Minimally}}
fields.Back Extra: Children with head lice can continue to attend school while receiving treatment at home.

fields.Text:
What are the presenting signs and symptoms of Pediculus humanus and Phthirus pubis infections?

Severe {{c1::pruritus}}
{{c1::Excoriations}} on the head, torso, or pubic regions

Name the helminth that causes nocturnal perianal pruritus.

{{c1::Enterobius}}

Name the two helminths that classically cause microcytic anemia.

{{c1::Ancylostoma}}
{{c1::Necator}}

Name the two helminths that can cause portal hypertension.

{{c1::Schistosoma mansoni}}
{{c1::Schistosoma japonicum}}

Which helminth causes biliary tract disease and is associated with cholangiocarcinoma?

{{c1::Clonorchis sinensis}}

Name the helminth that causes vitamin B12 deficiency.

{{c1::Diphyllobothrium latum}}

Name the parasite that is associated with the development of hematuria and squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

{{c1::Schistosoma haematobium}}

Name the parasite that commonly leads to formation of hydatid cysts.

{{c1::Echinococcus granulosus}}

What parasite causes brain cysts and seizures?

{{c1::Taenia solium}}

What parasite causes myalgias and periorbital edema?

{{c1::Trichinella spiralis}}

Describe the type of virus shown in the image based on the presence of the envelope and capsid type.



{{c1::Enveloped::Enveloped/Nonenveloped}} virus with an {{c1::icosahedral}} capsid

Describe the type of virus shown in the image based on the presence of the envelope and capsid type.



{{c1::Nonenveloped::Enveloped/Nonenveloped}} virus with {{c1::icosahedral}} capsid

Describe the type of virus shown in the image.



{{c1::Bacteriophage}}

Two segmented viruses undergo reassortment and produce a new, highly virulent strain. What is this mechanism called?

{{c1::Antigenic shift}}

Hepatitis D virus infection needs coinfection with hepatitis B to supply the envelope protein for hepatitis D virus. What is this mechanism called?

{{c1::Complementation}}

What is a pseudovirion?

The {{c1::genetic}} material of one virus coated by the {{c1::surface}} proteins of a different virus

Viruses A and B infect a cell. Virus A mutates and becomes nonfunctional, while virus B expresses a protein that serves both A and B. What is this mechanism called?

{{c1::Complementation}}

What type of viral genome structure is necessary for viral genome reassortment?

{{c1::Segmented}} genome

What is the mechanism behind phenotypic mixing?

Two viruses coinfect a cell → Virus A becomes {{c1::coated}} with virus B {{c1::proteins}} → Progeny have type A {{c1::genome}} and {{c1::coat}}

In viral genetics, what is the definition of reassortment?

The exchange of genetic material among viruses with {{c1::segmented}} genomes

What is the definition of viral genetic recombination?

Gene exchange between two {{c1::chromosomes}} via {{c1::crossing over}} within regions of {{c1::homologous}} base sequences

In phenotypic mixing, what determines the tropism of a progeny virus?

The {{c1::protein coat}} of the hybrid virus

All DNA viruses are linear with the exception of which DNA virus families?

{{c1::Papillomaviruses}}
{{c1::Polyomaviruses}}
{{c1::Hepadnaviruses}} (circular genomes)

All DNA viruses have double-stranded DNA genomes with that exception?

{{c1::Parvoviridae}}

As an exception to most other enveloped viruses, from what cellular structure in their hosts do the herpesviruses acquire their envelopes?

{{c1::Nuclear membrane}}

From what source do enveloped viruses generally obtain their envelopes?

From the {{c1::plasma membrane}} as they {{c1::exit::enter/exit}} the cell
fields.Back Extra: The exception to this is herpesvirus.

fields.Text:
Name eight nonenveloped viruses.

{{c1::Calicivirus}}
{{c1::Picornavirus}}
{{c1::Reovirus}}
{{c1::Parvovirus}}
{{c1::Adenovirus}}
{{c1::Papillomavirus}}
{{c1::Polyomavirus}}
{{c1::Hepevirus}}

Name three commonly encountered pathogenic enveloped DNA viruses.

{{c1::Herpesvirus}}
{{c1::Hepadnavirus}}
{{c1::Poxvirus}}

Besides febrile pharyngitis, what other signs or symptoms could adenovirus be responsible for?

Acute {{c1::hemorrhagic cystitis}}
{{c1::Pneumonia}}
{{c1::Conjunctivitis}}
{{c1::Gastroenteritis}}
{{c1::Myocarditis}}

Which disease caused by a DNA virus has been eradicated through the use of a live-attenuated vaccine?

{{c1::Smallpox}}

Which DNA viruses have the smallest and largest structures?

{{c1::Parvovirus}} is the smallest
{{c1::Poxvirus}} is the largest

In immunocompromised patients, what virus can cause progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy?

{{c1::Polyomavirus}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as JC virus.

fields.Text:
Which HPV serotypes are associated with warts?

Serotype {{c1::1}}
Serotype {{c1::2}}
Serotype {{c1::6}}
Serotype {{c1::11}}

Describe the DNA structure of papillomavirus.

{{c1::Double}}-stranded
{{c1::Circular}} DNA
{{c1::Nonenveloped::Enveloped/Nonenveloped}}

What DNA virus in adults can cause pure red blood cell aplasia and rheumatoid arthritis-like symptoms?

{{c1::Parvovirus B19}}

What complications may occur to a fetus exposed to parvovirus B19?

{{c1::Hydrops fetalis}}
Fetal {{c1::death}}

Describe the DNA structure of adenovirus.

{{c1::Double}}-stranded
{{c1::Linear}} DNA
{{c1::Nonenveloped::Enveloped/Nonenveloped}}

Which DNA virus contains the reverse transcriptase enzyme in order to replicate its genome?

{{c1::Hepadnavirus}}

To what viral family does hepatitis B virus belong?

{{c1::Hepadnaviridae}}

Describe the DNA structure of herpesviruses.

{{c1::Double}}-stranded
{{c1::Linear}} DNA

{{c1::Healthcare}}-associated infection

What is the incubation period for Ebola?

Up to {{c1::21}} days

What are initial symptoms of Ebola?

Abrupt onset of {{c1::flu}}-like symptoms
{{c1::High::High/Low}} fever
{{c1::Diarrhea}}/{{c1::vomiting}}
{{c1::Myalgia}}

What virus family does Ebola belong to?

{{c1::Filovirus}}

This virus was isolated from a health care worker volunteering in Sub-Saharan Africa. With which virus is the patient infected?



{{c1::Ebola virus}}

Given the high mortality rate, what steps should be taken to prevent transmission of the Ebola virus?

{{c1::Vaccinations}}
{{c1::Barrier}} practices for health care workers
Strict {{c1::isolation}} of infected individuals

What is the genomic structure of SARS-CoV-2?

{{c1::Enveloped::Enveloped/Nonenveloped}}
{{c1::Positive}}-sense
{{c1::Single}}-stranded RNA
{{c1::Helical}} capisd

What is the primary route of transmission for SARS-CoV-2?

{{c1::Respiratory droplets}}
{{c1::Aerosols}}

How does SARS-CoV-2 gain entry into host cells?

Attachment of {{c1::viral spike}} protein to {{c1::ACE2}} receptor on cell membranes
fields.Back Extra: Antispike protein antibodies confer immunity to host.

fields.Text:
What are the typical symptoms of infection by SARS-CoV-2?

{{c1::Fever}}
{{c1::Dry}} cough
{{c1::Shortness of breath}}
{{c1::Fatigue}}

What two sensory changes may occur with infection by SARS-CoV-2?

{{c1::Anosmia}}
{{c1::Dysgeusia}}

What are potential complications of infection by SARS-CoV-2?

{{c1::Acute respiratory distress}} syndrome
{{c1::Hypercoagulability::Hypercoagulability/Hypocoagulability}}
{{c1::Shock}}
{{c1::Organ}} failure
{{c1::Death}}

What are six significant risk factors for severe illness or death secondary to infection by SARS-CoV-2.

Increasing {{c1::age}}
{{c1::Obesity}}
{{c1::Diabetes}}
{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
Chronic {{c1::kidney::organ}} disease
Severe {{c1::cardiopulmonary}} illness

What is the most common diagnostic test used to determine infection by SARS-CoV-2?

{{c1::RT-PCR}}
fields.Back Extra: Antigen and antibody tests are also available.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of vaccination against SARS-CoV-2?

Induces {{c1::humoral}} and {{c1::cellular}} immunity → Decreased risk of contracting or transmitting the virus → Prevents serious disease, hospitalization, and death

What is the function of the hepatitis B DNA polymerase?

Has {{c1::DNA}}-dependent and {{c1::RNA}}-dependent activities
Enters nucleus → Completes {{c1::partially double}}-stranded DNA and {{c1::reverse transcribes}} viral RNA → DNA for progeny genome synthesis

Why are hepatitis B, C, and D viruses unable to spread via the fecal-oral route?

They are {{c1::enveloped::enveloped/nonenveloped}} viruses that are killed in the {{c1::gut}}
fields.Back Extra: Hepatitis A and E are nonenveloped viruses that are not destroyed in the gastrointestinal tract.

fields.Text:
What signs and symptoms are characteristic of acute viral hepatitis?

{{c1::Fever}}
{{c1::Jaundice}}
Increased {{c1::ALT}}
Increased {{c1::AST}}

What patient population has a high mortality rate if infected with hepatitis E virus?

{{c1::Pregnant}} {{c1::women::men/women}}

Which types of hepatitis can have a carrier state?

Hepatitis {{c1::B}}
Hepatitis {{c1::C}}

Which of the hepatitis viruses has DNA genome?

Hepatitis {{c1::B}} virus

What characteristic liver biopsy findings are seen in hepatitis C?

{{c1::Lymphoid aggregates}} with {{c1::focal macrovesicular steatosis}}

What mediates the granular eosinophilic "ground glass" appearance found on a liver biopsy specimen of hepatitis B?

Accumulation of {{c1::surface antigen}} in infected hepatocytes and {{c1::cytotoxic T-cell}}-mediated damage

Which hepatitis types can be transmitted by blood?

Hepatitis {{c1::B}}
Hepatitis {{c1::C}}
Hepatitis {{c1::D}}

Which hepatitis virus is most likely to progress to cirrhosis or carcinoma?

Hepatitis {{c1::C}} virus

How is hepatitis B transmitted?

{{c1::Parenteral}} transmission
{{c1::Sexual}} transmission
{{c1::Perinatal}} transmission

Name the family of each of the hepatitis viruses.

Hepatitis A virus → RNA {{c1::picornavirus}}
Hepatitis B virus → DNA {{c1::hepadnavirus}}
Hepatitis C virus → RNA {{c1::flavivirus}}
Hepatitis D virus → RNA {{c1::deltavirus}}
Hepatitis E virus → RNA {{c1::hepevirus}}

What molecular characterisitic allows the hepatitis C virus to evade host antibodies?

Antigenic variation due to lack of {{c1::3}}'-{{c1::5}}' {{c1::exonuclease}} activity → Production of new mutant strains faster than host antibody production

What is the route of transmission for hepatitis A?

{{c1::Fecal-oral}} transmission
fields.Back Extra: This is via contaminated shellfish, exposure during travel, or in daycare centers.

fields.Text:
What would you see on the liver biopsy of a patient infected with hepatitis A?

Hepatocyte {{c1::swelling}}
{{c1::Monocyte}} infiltration
{{c1::Councilman bodies}}

What is the clinical course of a patient infected with hepatitis A virus?

{{c1::Acute::Acute/Chronic}} and {{c1::self-limiting}} in adults
{{c1::Asymptomatic}} in children

What is the mode of transmission for hepatitis C virus?

Primarily {{c1::blood}} transmission

Why can hepatitis D infection only occur in conjunction with hepatitis B infection?

Hepatitis D virus depends on hepatitis B virus {{c1::HBsAg coat}} for entry into hepatocytes

How can hepatitis E be acquired?

Via the {{c1::fecal-oral}} route, especially from {{c1::waterborne}} sources

What hepatitis virus can initially present like serum sickness?

Hepatitis {{c1::B}} virus

What is the prognosis for hepatitis B in adults and neonates?

Adults → Mostly a {{c1::full resolution}}
Neonates → {{c1::Worse}} prognosis

Which hepatitis viruses are transmitted fecal-orally?

Hepatitis {{c1::A}} virus
Hepatitis {{c1::E}} virus

In what part of the world is hepatitis E infection most common?

{{c1::Asia}}
{{c1::Africa}}
{{c1::Middle East}}

For hepatitis D virus and hepatitis B virus, would superinfection or coinfection have worse prognosis?

{{c1::Superinfection}}

What are the most common endocrine manifestations of hepatitis C?

Increased risk of {{c1::diabetes mellitus}}
Autoimmune {{c1::hypothyroidism::hyperthyroidism/hypothyroidism}}

What dermatological conditions can be seen in patients with hepatitis C?

Sporadic {{c1::porphyria cutanea tarda}}
{{c1::Lichen planus}}

What are the two most common renal manifestations of hepatitis viruses?

{{c1::Membranous glomerulonephritis}} (more common)
{{c1::Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis}}

Hepatitis B is associated with what hematologic abnormality?

{{c1::Aplastic anemia}}

What three hematologic manifestations can occur in hepatitis C infection?

{{c1::Essential mixed cryoglobulinemia}}
{{c1::Idiopathoc thrombocytopenic purpura}}
{{c1::Autoimmune hemolytic anemia}}

What hepatitis virus is associated with polyarteritis nodosa?

Hepatitis {{c1::B}} virus

What vascular pathology can occur with hepatitis C?

{{c1::Leukocytoclastic vasculitis}}

Hepatitis C infection confers increased risk for which hematological cancer?

{{c1::B-cell non-Hodgkin}} lymphoma

What serologic markers would you expect in a patient immunized against hepatitis B?

Positive for {{c1::anti-HBs}}
fields.Back Extra: All other hepatitis B markers are negative.

fields.Text:
What serologic marker may be positive during the window period of the hepatitis B virus?

{{c1::Anti-Hbc IgM}}

The presence of which serologic markers indicate a recovery from hepatitis B infection?

{{c1::Anti-HBs}}
{{c1::Anti-HBe}}
{{c1::Anti-HBc IgG}}

What positive markers are expected in a chronic hepatitis B virus infection with high infectivity?

{{c1::HbsAg}}
{{c1::HBeAg}}
{{c1::Anti-HBc IgG}}

What positive markers would you expect during the acute stage of infection with hepatitis B?

{{c1::HBsAg}}
{{c1::HBeAg}}
{{c1::Anti-HBc IgM}}

What is the difference in likely transmissibility between testing positive for HBeAg compared to anti-HBe?

HBeAg indicates {{c1::high::high/low}} transmissibility and {{c1::poorer}} prognosis
Anti-HBe indicates {{c1::low::high/low}} transmissibility

What is the difference between anti-HBc IgM and anti-HBc IgG?

IgM is a marker for {{c1::acute::acute/chronic}} or {{c1::recent}} infection
IgG is a marker for {{c1::prior exposure}} or {{c1::chronic::acute/chronic}} infection

What antigen is associated with the core of hepatitis B virus?

{{c1::HBcAg}}

Which antibody is protective against hepatitis B infection acquired after recovery from an infection or vaccination?

{{c1::Anti-HBs}}

What does a positive test for HBsAg indicate?

{{c1::Active}} hepatitis B infection

Which serologic marker indicates prior infection with hepatitis A and protects against reinfection?

{{c1::Anti-HAV IgG}}

What serological marker is best to detect acute hepatitis A?

{{c1::Anti-HAV IgM}}

What is the source of HBeAg found in the serum of a patient infected with hepatitis B?

{{c1::Secretion}} by infected hepatocytes into the {{c1::circulation}}
fields.Back Extra: It is not part of the mature hepatitis B virus virion.

fields.Text:
What do IgG antibodies to HBcAg signify?

{{c1::Chronic::Acute/Chronic}} infection of hepatitis B
{{c1::Prior exposure}} to hepatitis B

What does the window period found during infection with hepatitis B refer to?

The period where serum {{c1::HBsAg}} drops to undetectable levels, while serum {{c1::anti-HBs}} begin to form 5 to 6 months post-infection

What does a heterozygous CCR5 gene mutation indicate for the disease course in a patient with HIV?

{{c1::Slower::Faster/Slower}} disease course

What gene mutation can cause immunity to HIV?

{{c1::Homozygous::Homozygous/Heterozygous}} {{c1::CCR5}} mutation

Name two coreceptors in immune cells to which HIV binds in different stages of infection.

{{c1::CCR5}}
{{c1::CXCR4}}

How does HIV integrate its genome into the host DNA?

{{c1::Reverse transcriptase}} converts HIV viral RNA to double-stranded DNA → Integrates into host DNA

What is the function of the two envelope proteins on the surface of HIV?

{{c1::gp120}} helps HIV adhere to CD4+ T cells
{{c1::gp41}} facilitates HIV fusion/entry

What is the function of the env gene of HIV?

Encodes {{c1::gp160}} precursor that is cleaved into {{c1::gp120}} and {{c1::gp41}}

Which HIV proteins are encoded from the gag gene and located in the matrix and capsid?

Matrix → {{c1::p17}}
Capsid → {{c1::p24}}

What is the ploidy of the HIV genome?

{{c1::Diploid::Haploid/Diploid}} RNA

Name the proteins for which each of these HIV genes code.

env → {{c1::gp120}} and {{c1::gp41}}
gag → {{c1::p24}} and {{c1::p17}}
pol → {{c1::Reverse transcriptase}}, {{c1::integrase}}, and {{c1::protease}}

How are HIV envelope proteins acquired?

Via {{c1::budding}} from the host cell {{c1::plasma membrane}}

What are the criteria for the diagnosis of AIDS?

CD4+ count ≤ {{c1::200}} cells/mm3
{{c1::HIV}}-positive with an AIDS-defining illness

How do you evaluate the response to an antiretroviral therapy for HIV?

Test the amount of viral {{c1::RNA}} in plasma

What is the test of choice for determining maternal HIV transmission to a newborn child?

HIV {{c1::viral load}} in the newborn

Why is HIV-1/2 Ag/Ab testing not recommended in babies with suspected HIV?

Results are confounded due to maternally transferred HIV {{c1::antibodies}}

What does the HIV-1/2 Ag/Ab immunoassay detect?

Viral {{c1::p24 capsid}} protein antigen
Ig{{c1::G}} antibodies to HIV-1/2

When are immunoassays unreliable to evaluate HIV infection?

During the first {{c1::2}} weeks

What test can be performed in the setting of an indeterminate HIV-1/2 differentiation immunoassay?

HIV-{{c1::1::1/2}} {{c1::nucleic acid amplification}} test

What is a patient's HIV status if the nucleic acid amplification test is negative following a positive HIV-1/2 Ag/AB immunoassay?

HIV-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}}

Which test determines appropriate antiretroviral therapy in HIV-positive patients?

HIV {{c1::genotype}} testing

Which test is no longer recommended for confirmatory testing for HIV?

{{c1::Western blot}}

What is considered the normal range of CD4+ cell count?

{{c1::500}} to {{c1::1,500}} cells/mm3

Infections with which organisms are possible when the CD4+ count is < 200 cells/mm3?

{{c1::JC virus}} reactivation
{{c1::Pneumocystis jirovecii}}
{{c1::HIV}} infection
{{c1::Histoplasma capsulatum}}

What CD4+ count is associated with Toxoplasma gondii infection in patients with HIV?

CD4+ count < {{c1::100}} cells/mm3

What infection in a patient with a CD4+ count < 100 cells/mm3 presents with nonspecific systemic symptoms and lymphadenitis?

{{c1::Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare}} infection
{{c1::Mycobacterium avium complex}} infection

What biopsy findings are associated with a Histoplasma capsulatum infection in patients with CD4+ count < 200 cells/mm3?

{{c1::Macrophages}} containing {{c1::oval yeast}} cells

How does central nervous system lymphoma differ from a Toxoplasma gondii infection on a brain MRI of a patient who has a CD4+ count < 100 cells/mm3?

A {{c1::solitary ring-enhancing}} lesion is usually seen in central nervous system lymphoma
{{c1::Multiple}} lesions are usually found in a Toxoplasma gondii infection

Epstein-Barr virus is associated with what medical complication in patients with a CD4+ count < 100 cells/mm3?

{{c1::B-cell}} lymphoma

What is seen on biopsy of tissues infected with cytomegalovirus?

Cells with {{c1::intranuclear inclusion bodies}}

What presentation might cytomegalovirus infection have in a patient with a CD4+ count < 100 cells/mm3?

{{c1::Colitis}}
{{c1::Retinitis}}
{{c1::Encephalitis}}
{{c1::Esophagitis}}
{{c1::Pneumonitis}}

What endoscopic and biopsy findings are seen in Candida albicans esophagitis?

{{c1::White plaques}} on endoscopy
Biopsy shows {{c1::yeast}} and {{c1::pseudohyphae}}

What are the tests of choice for cryptococcal meningitis infection?

Positive {{c1::capsular antigen}}
{{c1::India ink}} stain to reveal encapsulated yeast

What infection in patients with a CD4+ count < 200 cells/mm3 presents with bilateral ground-glass opacities on chest X-ray?

{{c1::Pneumocystis pneumonia}}

What infection presents with non-enchancing areas of demyelination on MRI in a patient with a CD4+ count < 200 cells/mm3?

{{c1::Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to JC virus reactivation.

fields.Text:
What malignancy is associated with HPV infection in the population with HIV/AIDS?

{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma of the {{c1::anus}}, {{c1::cervix}}, and {{c1::oropharynx}}

What is the test of choice for cryptosporidium infection in patients with chronic, watery diarrhea and a CD4+ count < 200 cells/mm3?

An {{c1::acid-fast}} stain of the stool sample
fields.Back Extra: This is to show acid-fast oocysts.

fields.Text:
What is expected on a biopsy of multiple purple nodules in a patient who is HIV-positive?

{{c1::Neutrophilic inflammation}} caused by {{c1::Bartonella}} species

What kind of infections are HIV-positive patients generally at risk for as the CD4+ cell count drops?

{{c1::Reactivation}} of past infections
{{c1::Non-Hodgkin}} lymphoma
{{c1::Dissemination}} of bacterial/fungal infections

What disease process should you consider in a patient with a CD4+ count < 200 cells/mm3, progressive memory loss, and an otherwise negative infectious work-up?

{{c1::HIV dementia}}

What disease presents with esophagitis and linear ulcerations on esophagogastroduodenoscopy in a patient with a CD4+ count < 100 cells/mm3?

{{c1::Cytomegalovirus esophagitis}}

How does cytomegalovirus infection present on fundoscopy?

{{c1::Cotton-wool}} spots

What common diseases are possible in the population with HIV/AIDS when the CD4+ count is < 500 cells/mm3, but > 200 cells/mm3?

{{c1::Oral thrush}}
{{c1::Oral leukoplakia}}
{{c1::Kaposi}} sarcoma
{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma

What findings would you expect on neuroimaging in a patient with HIV dementia with a CD4+ count < 200 cells/mm3?

{{c1::Cerebral atrophy}}

What central nervous system infections are associated with HIV?

{{c1::Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy}}
{{c1::Central nervous system}} lymphoma
{{c1::Toxoplasma gondii}} brain abscesses
{{c1::HIV dementia}}

What are the physical findings of Kaposi sarcoma associated with HHV-8 infection with a CD4+ count < 500 cells/mm3?

Invading {{c1::perivascular spindle}} cells that form {{c1::vascular}} tumors visible on histology

What infection is associated with a CD4+ count < 200 cells/mm3, fever, fatigue, weight loss, cough, nausea, vomiting, dyspnea, and diarrhea?

{{c1::Histoplasma capsulatum}} infection

What is the most salient clinical difference between opportunistic infections of Candida albicans and Epstein-Barr virus?

Candidia albicans → White plaques are {{c1::scrapable}} in {{c1::oral thrush}}
Epstein-Barr virus → White plaques of {{c1::oral hair leukoplakia}} are {{c1::unscrapable}}

What prion disease is notable in tribal populations practicing human cannibalism?

{{c1::Kuru}}

What prion disease causes typically sporadic, rapidly progressive dementia?

{{c1::Creutzfeldt-Jakob}} disease

What five clinical manifestations does PrPSC accumulation cause?

{{c1::Spongiform encephalopathy}}
{{c1::Dementia}}
{{c1::Ataxia}}
{{c1::Startle myoclonus}}
{{c1::Death}}

What is the pathophysiology of prion disease?

Converts {{c1::PrPC}} to {{c1::PrPSC}} → Resists {{c1::proteases}} to facilitate further conversion

What are the possible means of transmission for PrPSC?

Via infected {{c1::central nervous system}} tissue
Via food contaminated by {{c1::bovine spongiform encephalopathy}}

To what common sterilization procedure are prion diseases known to be resistant?

{{c1::Standard autoclaving}}

What is the disease condition also named "mad cow disease"?

{{c1::Bovine spongiform encephalopathy}}

Is a neonate delivered via cesarean section colonized with bacteria at the time of birth?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra:
Neonates delivered by cesarean section are born without any flora, but are colonized quickly after birth.

They have microbiota enriched in skin commensals.

fields.Text:
What bacteria are considered normal flora in the vagina?

{{c1::Lactobacillus}}
{{c1::Escherichia coli}}
Group {{c1::B}} streptococcus

Which two bacteria are considered part of the normal flora in the colon?

{{c1::Bacteroides fragilis}}
{{c1::Escherichia coli}} (lesser extent)

What bacteria are typically found in dental plaque?

{{c1::Streptococcus mutans}}

In which part of the body are viridans streptococci considered normal flora?

{{c1::Oropharynx}}

What part of the body does Staphylococcus aureus normally colonize?

{{c1::Nose}}

Staphylococcus epidermidis is part of the normal flora of what two parts of the body?

{{c1::Skin}}
{{c1::Nose}}

What microorganism may cause wound infections from contact with contaminated shellfish or water?

{{c1::Vibrio vulnificus}}

What microorganisms are associated with a food-borne illness from raw and undercooked seafood?

{{c1::Vibrio parahaemolyticus}}
{{c1::Vibrio vulnificus}}

Why does Staphylococcus aureus cause food poisoning quickly?

The toxins that cause the food poisoning are {{c1::preformed}}

What microorganism is associated with a food-borne illness from meats, mayonnaise, and custards?

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}

What microorganism is associated with a food-borne illness from poultry, meat, and eggs?

{{c1::Salmonella}}

What microorganism is associated with a food-borne illness from undercooked meat?

{{c1::Escherichia coli O157:H7}}

What microorganism is associated with a food-borne illness from reheated meat?

{{c1::Clostridium perfringens}}

What two microorganisms are associated with a quick onset and a quick resolution of food poisoning?

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
{{c1::Bacillus cereus}}

What microorganism is associated with food poisoning from reheated rice?

{{c1::Bacillus cereus}}

Which components of Clostridium botulinum are associated with a food-borne illness from consumption of improperly canned foods versus raw honey?

Improperly canned foods → {{c1::Toxins}} of Clostridium botulinum
Raw honey → {{c1::Spores}} of Clostridium botulinum

What microorganism is associated with a food-borne illness from deli meats or soft cheeses?

{{c1::Listeria monocytogenes}}

What organism causes both watery diarrhea and gas gangrene?

{{c1::Clostridium perfringens}}

What protozoa can cause both bloody diarrhea and liver abscesses?

{{c1::Entamoeba histolytica}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a protozoan that causes amebic dysentery.

fields.Text:
Which comma-shaped or S-shaped organism grows at 42°C and causes bloody diarrhea?

{{c1::Campylobacter}}

What is the most common source of Vibrio cholerae diarrhea?

Infected {{c1::seafood}}

Which comma-shaped organisms cause rice-water stools?

{{c1::Vibrio cholerae}}

What two protozoa are most likely to cause watery diarrhea?

{{c1::Giardia}}
{{c1::Cryptosporidium}}

Which three viruses cause watery diarrhea?

{{c1::Rotavirus}}
Enteric {{c1::adenovirus}}
{{c1::Norovirus}}

What two toxins are produced by enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli?

{{c1::Heat-labile}} toxin
{{c1::Heat-stable}} toxin

Name two classes of drugs that are associated with a Clostridium difficile infection.

{{c1::Antibiotics}}
{{c1::Proton pump}} inhibitors

What organism is associated with pseudomembranous colitis and watery diarrhea?

{{c1::Clostridium difficile}}

Name the four common bacterial organisms that can cause watery diarrhea.

{{c1::Clostridium difficile}}
{{c1::Clostridium perfringens}}
{{c1::Enterotoxigenic}} Escherichia coli
{{c1::Vibrio cholerae}}

What organism is associated with bloody diarrhea and pseudoappendicitis?

{{c1::Yersinia enterocolitica}}

What are the reservoirs associated with Shigella versus Salmonella?

Shigella → {{c1::Human}} reservoir only
Salmonella → {{c1::Animal}} reservoirs

What lactose-negative bacterium with a low median infective dose is associated with bloody diarrhea?

{{c1::Shigella}}

What food sources are commonly associated with a Salmonella infection?

{{c1::Poultry}}
{{c1::Eggs}}

What is the most common cause of diarrhea in developed countries?

{{c1::Norovirus}}

What is the cause of decreased incidence of rotavirus infections in developed countries?

{{c1::Vaccination}}

What organisms are associated with postviral causes of pneumonia?

{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae}}

What organisms are associated with healthcare-associated pneumonia?

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
{{c1::Pseudomonas}}
Enteric gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} {{c1::rods::shape}}

What infectious agents are the most common causes of pneumonia in the immunocompromised?

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
{{c1::Pneumocystis jirovecii}}
Enteric gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} {{c1::rods::shape}}
{{c1::Fungi}}
{{c1::Viruses}}

Which organisms cause pneumonia in patients with cystic fibrosis?

{{c1::Pseudomonas}}
{{c1::Burkholderia cepacia}}
{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}

What pathogens are associated with atypical pneumonia?

{{c1::Chlamydophila}}
{{c1::Mycoplasma}}
{{c1::Legionella}}
{{c1::Viruses}}

What causes of pneumonia are associated with injection drug use?

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}

What causes of pneumoniae are associated with alcohol overuse?

{{c1::Klebsiella}}
{{c1::Anaerobes::Aerobes/Anaerobes}} secondary to {{c1::aspiration}}

What are the most likely causes of pneumonia in the elderly population?

{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Influenza virus}}
{{c1::Anaerobes::Aerobes/Anaerobes}}
{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae}}
Gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} {{c1::rods::shape}}

Name the most common causes of pneumoniae in adults 40 to 65 years of age.

{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae}}
{{c1::Mycoplasma}}
{{c1::Anaerobes::Aerobes/Anaerobes}}
{{c1::Viruses}}

Name the most common causes of pneumonia in adults 18 to 40 years of age.

{{c1::Mycoplasma}}
{{c1::Chlamydia pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Viruses}}

Which species of Chlamydia causes pneumonia in children younger than 3 years of age, and which causes it in school-aged children?

Chlamydia {{c1::trachomatis}} in children younger than 3 years of age
Chlamydia {{c1::pneumoniae}} in school-aged children

Name the most common causes of pneumonia in patients who are 4 weeks to 18 years of age.

{{c1::Viruses}}
{{c1::Mycoplasma}}
{{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}}
{{c1::Chlamydia pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}

Which two organisms are common causes of pneumonia in neonates?

Group {{c1::B}} streptococci
{{c1::Escherichia coli}}

Which organisms commonly cause pneumonia in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?

{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae}}
{{c1::Moraxella catarrhalis}}
{{c1::Pseudomonas}}

How has the incidence of meningitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae changed over time?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the result of conjugate Haemophilus influenzae vaccinations.

fields.Text:
What fungal organisms cause meningitis and are associated with HIV?

{{c1::Cryptococcus}} species

Name five viral causes of meningitis.

{{c1::Enteroviruses}}
{{c1::HSV-2}}
{{c1::HIV}}
{{c1::West Nile virus}}
{{c1::Varicella-zoster virus}}

What are the initial steps in treatment of a patient with suspected meningitis?

{{c1::Ceftriaxone}} and {{c1::vancomycin}} are empirically given

What are the most likely causes of meningitis in patients older than 60 years?

{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Neisseria meningitidis}}
{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae type b}}
Group {{c1::B}} Streptococcus
{{c1::Listeria}}

What organisms are the most likely causes of meningitis in patients aged 6 to 60 years?

{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Neisseria meningitidis}}
{{c1::Enteroviruses}}
{{c1::HSV}}

What are the most likely causes of meningitis in children 6 months to 6 years of age?

{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Neisseria meningitidis}}
{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae type b}}
Group {{c1::B}} Streptococcus
{{c1::Enteroviruses}}

What organisms most commonly cause meningitis in newborns and infants up to 6 months of age?

Group {{c1::B}} Streptococcus
{{c1::Escherichia coli}}
{{c1::Listeria}}

Why has the incidence of group B streptococcal meningitis decreased in neonates?

Because of {{c1::screening}} and {{c1::antibiotic prophylaxis}} during pregnancy

Which white blood cell type predominates in the cerebrospinal fluid in bacterial, fungal, and viral meningitis?

{{c1::Polymorphonuclear}} leukocytes in bacterial meningitis
{{c1::Lymphocytes}} in fungal and viral meningitis

What are the protein levels in cerebrospinal fluid in bacterial, fungal, and viral meningitis?

{{c1::Increased}} in bacterial and fungal meningitis
{{c1::Normal}} to {{c1::increased}} in viral meningitis

What are the glucose levels in cerebrospinal fluid in bacterial, fungal, and viral meningitis?

{{c1::Decreased}} in bacterial and fungal meningitis
{{c1::Normal}} in viral meningitis

When preforming lumbar puncture, what are the opening pressure levels expected in bacterial, fungal, and viral meningitis, respectively?

{{c1::Increased}} in bacterial and fungal meningitis
{{c1::Normal}} or {{c1::increased}} in viral meningitis

When analyzing cerebrospinal fluid, what are the findings associated with fungal/tuberculosis infection?

{{c1::Low::High/Low}} glucose levels
{{c1::Lymphocytosis}}
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} opening pressure
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} protein levels

What organism is likely responsible for a brain abscess in a patient with AIDS and a CD4+ count < 100 cells/mm3?

{{c1::Toxoplasma}}

Where in the central nervous system does an abscess due to sinusitis or a dental infection typically present?

{{c1::Frontal}} lobe

Where in the central nervous system does an abscess resulting from otitis media or mastoiditis typically present?

{{c1::Temporal}} lobe
{{c1::Cerebellum}}

What causes of brain abscesses are associated with preceding dental infection or extraction?

Oral {{c1::anaerobes::aerobes/anaerobes}}

Infection by which two organisms is most likely commonly linked to brain abscesses?

{{c1::Viridans streptococci}}
{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}

Why is MRI better than X-rays for the diagnosis of osteomyelitis?

MRI detects {{c1::acute::acute/chronic}} infection and details {{c1::anatomic}} involvement

What is the test of choice for the diagnosis of acute osteomyelitis?

{{c1::MRI}}

What organisms commonly cause osteomyelitis associated with intravenous drug use?

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} (most common)
{{c1::Pseudomonas}}
{{c1::Candida}}

Osteomyelitis from cat or dog bites is most frequently caused by which organism?

{{c1::Pasteurella multocida}}

Vertebral osteomyelitis can be uniquely caused by which organisms?

{{c1::Mycobacterium tuberculosis}} in Pott disease
{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}

Which two organisms are likely causes of osteomyelitis in patients with prosthetic joint replacements?

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
{{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}}

What two organisms commonly cause osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell disease?

{{c1::Salmonella}}
{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}

In sexually active individuals, which pathogen commonly causes septic arthritis and rarely causes osteomyelitis?

{{c1::Neisseria gonorrhoeae}}

What organism is the most common cause of osteomyelitis?

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
fields.Back Extra: Assume this is the cause if information is limited.

fields.Text:
How sensitive and specific are ESR and C-reactive protein laboratory assays in the workup for osteomyelitis?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} values are sensitive, but not specific for osteomyelitis

What diagnostic test is used to identify the organisms in osteomyelitis?

Culture of specimen obtained via {{c1::biopsy}} or {{c1::aspiration}}

What is a life-threatening fetal complication caused by exposure to parovirus B19 during pregnancy?

{{c1::Hydrops fetalis}}

What childhood rash presents with a vesicular rash that begins on the trunk beforee spreading to the face and extremities with lesions in different stages?



{{c1::Chickenpox}}
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by the varicella-zoster virus.

fields.Text:
What childhood rash presents with pink macules and papules that start on the head and spread to the body and postauricular lymph nodes?

{{c1::Rubella}}

What is the cutaneous manifestation of erythema infectiosum?

The classic "{{c1::slapped cheek}}" rash that appears on the {{c1::face}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a parvovirus B19 infection.

fields.Text:
What childhood rash presents with cough, conjunctivitis, coryza, and bluish spots on the buccal mucosa followed by a descending confluent rash?

{{c1::Measles}}
fields.Back Extra: The blue-white spots on the buccal mucosa are known as Koplik spots.

fields.Text:
What childhood rash presents with a high fever for several days followed by diffuse rose-colored macules?

{{c1::Roseloa}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is caused by HHV-6 infection.

This may be present with febrile seizures.

fields.Text:
What childhood rash presents with vesicles and ulcers in the oral mucosa and oval-shaped vesicles on the palms and soles as shown in the image?



{{c1::Hand-foot-mouth}} disease
fields.Back Extra: The vesicles and ulcers in the oral mucosa are referred to as herpangina.

fields.Text:
A child, who has had a fever and sore throat, now exhibits a sandpaper-like rash that is also seen on the trunk and extremities. What bacteria are responsible for these findings?



{{c1::Streptococcus pyogenes}}

Why are urinary tract infections 10 times more common in females than in males?

Females have {{c1::shorter::shorter/longer}} urethras
fields.Back Extra: This can be colonized by fecal microbiota.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiology behind pyelonephritis?

Ascension of bacteria to the {{c1::kidneys}} from the {{c1::bladder}}

What is the most common route of transmission for microbes that cause urinary tract infections?

Bacteria from urethra {{c1::ascends::ascends/descends}} to the {{c1::bladder}}

What are the common signs and symptoms of cystitis?

{{c1::Dysuria}}
{{c1::Suprapubic}} pain
Urinary {{c1::frequency}} and {{c1::urgency}}
Urinalysis positive for {{c1::white blood}} cells

Which diagnostic marker of urinary tract infections indicates evidence of white blood cell activity?

{{c1::Leukocyte esterase}}

What organism that causes urinary tract infections is associated with a fruity odor and blue-green tint?

{{c1::Pseudomonas aeruginosa}}

What organism that causes urinary tract infection is associated with the formation of struvite stones?

{{c1::Proteus mirabilis}}

What aspects of Enterococcus infections make them particularly difficult to treat?

{{c1::Drug resistant}}

Which organism that causes urinary tract infections is characterized by production of a red pigment?

{{c1::Serratia marcescens}}

When will a urease test result be positive for a patient with a urinary tract infection?

When the infection is due to a {{c1::urease}}-producing organism

What organism is the second most common cause of urinary tract infections in sexually active females?

{{c1::Staphylococcus saprophyticus}}

What species of bacteria that causes urinary tract infections grows with strong, pink lactose fermentation on MacConkey agar?

{{c1::Escherichia coli}}

What species of bacteria is the leading cause of urinary tract infections?

{{c1::Escherichia coli}}

Name some of the common predisposing factors for urinary tract infections.

{{c1::Female::Male/Female}} sex
{{c1::Obstruction}}
{{c1::Catheterization}}
{{c1::Kidney::Organ}} surgery
Congenital {{c1::genitourinary}} malformation
{{c1::Pregnancy}}
{{c1::Diabetes}}

What does a positive urine nitrite test result indicate?

Reduction of nitrates in urine by gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} bacteria

What organism that causes urinary tract infections is associated with a large mucoid capsule and viscous colonies?

{{c1::Klebsiella pneumoniae}}

What organism that causes urinary tract infections is associated with "swarming" on agar due to motility?

{{c1::Proteus mirabilis}}

What are the common signs and symptoms of pyelonephritis?

{{c1::Fevers}}
{{c1::Chills}}
{{c1::Costovertebral angle}} tenderness
{{c1::Flank}} pain
{{c1::Hematuria}}

What finding on urinalysis can help to distinguish a urinary tract infection from pyelonephritis?

Detection of {{c1::white blood}} cell {{c1::casts}}

What is the treatment of choice for a patient with the microscopic findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Metronidazole}} for both the patient and partners
fields.Back Extra: The motile, pear-shaped trichomonads indicate a Trichomonas infection.

fields.Text:
What microscopic findings are seen with Candida vulvovaginitis?

{{c1::Pseudohyphae}}

What microscopic findings are seen with Trichomonas vaginitis?

{{c1::Motile::Motile/Immotile}} {{c1::trichomonads}}

What characteristic microscopic finding is associated with bacterial vaginosis?

{{c1::Clue}} cells

What common vaginal infection presents without inflammation?

{{c1::Bacterial vaginosis}}

What is the treatment of choice for bacterial vaginosis?

{{c1::Metronidazole}}
{{c1::Clindamycin}}

What group of drugs is used in the treatment of Candida vulvovaginitis?

{{c1::Azoles}}

What vaginal infection presents with a "strawberry cervix" and frothy, foul-smelling, green-yellow discharge?

{{c1::Trichomonas vaginitis}}

You examine the vagina of a woman with vaginal discomfort and note thin, white discharge with fishy odor. The KOH whiff test is positive What is your diagnosis?



{{c1::Bacterial vaginosis}}

Which vaginal infections present with a vaginal pH > 4.5?

{{c1::Bacterial vaginosis}}
{{c1::Trichomonas vaginitis}}

What is the vaginal pH in Candida vulvovaginitis?

{{c1::4.0}} to {{c1::4.5}}

A young woman presents with vaginal inflammation and a thick, white, cottage cheese-like discharge. What is your diagnosis?



{{c1::Candida vulvovaginitis}}

What sexually transmitted infection presents with vaginitis and a strawberry-colored cervix?

{{c1::Trichomoniasis}}

What are the characteristics of tertiary syphilis?

{{c1::Gummas}}
{{c1::Tabes dorsalis}}
{{c1::Aortitis}}
General {{c1::paresis}}
{{c1::Argyll Robertson}} pupil

Which stage of syphilis presents with fever, skin rashes, lymphadenopathy, and condyloma lata?

{{c1::Secondary}} syphilis

Which stage of syphilis presents with a painless chancre?

{{c1::Primary}} syphilis

What is the pathophysiology of lymphogranuloma venereum?

Infection of the {{c1::lymphatics}} caused by {{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is specifically with serotypes L1 to L3.

fields.Text:
What sexually transmitted infection presents with painful inguinal lymphadenopathy and painless genital ulcers, as shown in the image?



{{c1::Lymphogranuloma venereum}}

What sexually transmitted infection may result in jaundice?

{{c1::Hepatitis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by hepatitis B virus.

fields.Text:
What microscopic findings are associated with the ulcer shown in the image, which bleeds readily on contact?



Cytoplasmic {{c1::Donovan bodies}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is granuloma inguinale.

The infectious agent is Klebsiella.

fields.Text:
What sexually transmitted infection presents with a painless, beefy red ulcerative genital lesion that bleeds on contact?

{{c1::Donovanosis}}

What sexually transmitted infection may present with urethritis, cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, creamy purulent discharge, prostatitis, epididymitis, or arthritis?

{{c1::Gonorrhea}}

In addition to painful genital lesions, herpes genitalis causes what systemic symptoms?

{{c1::Headaches}}
{{c1::Fevers}}
{{c1::Myalgia}}

What organisms cause condyloma acuminata and condyloma lata, respectively?

{{c1::HPV-6}} and {{c1::HPV-11}} cause condyloma acuminata
{{c1::Treponema pallidum}} causes condyloma lata

What sexually transmitted infection may present with conjunctivitis, urethritis, cervicitis, epididymitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and reactive arthritis?

{{c1::Chlamydia}}

What sexually transmitted infection presents with exudative, painful genital ulcers and inguinal lymphadenopathy?

{{c1::Chancroid}}

What sexually transmitted infection has a high risk for oppotunistic infections, Kaposi sarcoma, and lymphoma?

{{c1::HIV}}

How does genital herpes present?

Painful penile, vulvar, or cervical {{c1::ulcers}} and {{c1::vesicles}}

What is seen on a wet prep performed for a patient with trichomoniasis?

{{c1::Motile::Motile/Immotile}} {{c::trichomonads}}

What sexually transmitted infection is characterized by genital warts and koilocytes?

{{c1::Condyloma acuminata}}

What are two causes of painful genital ulcers?

Chancroid caused by {{c1::Haemophilus ducreyi}}
Genital herpes caused by {{c1::HSV-2}}

What congenital infection presents with the CT findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Cytomegalovirus}} infection

Which of the TORCH infections often results in stillbirth or hydrops fetalis?

{{c1::Syphilis}}

When a pregnant patient contracts syphilis, which stages of the illness are likely to cause fetal infection?

{{c1::Primary}} stage
{{c1::Secondary}} stage

What complications may be seen with a congenital HSV-2 infection?

{{c1::Meningoencephalitis}}
Herpetic {{c1::vesicular}} lesions

What is the mechanism of transmission of HSV-2?

Contact with {{c1::skin}}
Contact with {{c1::mucous membranes}}

What are the three congenitally acquired TORCH infections in which the pregnant patient is usually asymptomatic?

{{c1::Toxoplasma gondii}}
{{c1::Cytomegalovirus}}
{{c1::HSV-2}}

The newborn of a mother with poor prenatal care has a rash. Which three infectious agents are in your differential diagnosis?



{{c1::Toxoplasma gondii}}
{{c1::Rubella}}
{{c1::Cytomegalovirus}}

What constellation of findings may be seen in a congenital rubella infection?

{{c1::Eye}} abnormalities
{{c1::Ear}} issues
Congenital {{c1::heart::organ}} disease
fields.Back Extra: There may or may not be a "blueberry muffin" rash.

fields.Text:
How does a rubella infection typically present in a pregnant patient?

{{c1::Rash}}
{{c1::Polyarthritis}}
{{c1::Polyarthralgia}}
{{c1::Lymphadenopathy}}

What clinical features are seen in the mother of an infant with Toxoplasma gondii infection?

The mother is usually {{c1::asymptomatic::symptomatic/asymptomatic}} and rarely has {{c1::lymphadenopathy}}

In a child with a Toxoplasma gondii infection, what finding in addition to the classic triad of manifestations might be observed?

"{{c1::Blueberry muffin}}" rash
fields.Back Extra: The classic triad of manifestations include hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, and intracranial calcifications.

fields.Text:
Name the six organisms that cause the TORCH infections.

{{c1::Toxoplasma gondii}}
{{c1::Rubella}}
{{c1::Cytomegalovirus}}
{{c1::HIV}}
{{c1::HSV-2}}
{{c1::Syphilis}}

What is the mode of transmission of a TORCH infection?

Transmission of a microbe from {{c1::mother}} to {{c1::fetus}}
fields.Back Extra: This is usually transplacental, but it can also occur during vaginal delivery.

fields.Text:
How does cytomegalovirus infection present in a pregnant patient?

{{c1::Asymptomatic::Symptomatic/Asymptomatic}} (usually)
{{c1::Mononucleosis}}-like symptoms (rare)

What is the mechanism of cytomegalovirus transmission?

{{c1::Sexual}} contact
Organ {{c1::transplantation}}

What constellation of findings is seen in patients with congenital cytomegalovirus infection?

{{c1::Hearing}} loss
{{c1::Seizures}}
{{c1::Chorioretinitis}}
"{{c1::Blueberry muffin}}" rash
{{c1::Petechial}} rash
{{c1::Periventricular calcifications}}

How is Toxoplasma gondii characteristically transmitted?

{{c1::Cat feces}}
{{c1::Undercooked meat}}

How is rubella typically acquired?

{{c1::Respiratory droplets}}

How does congenital HIV infection present?

{{c1::Recurrent}} infections
Chronic {{c1::diarrhea}}

How does maternal HSV-2 infection present?

{{c1::Asymptomatic::Symptomatic/Asymptomatic}}
{{c1::Vesicular}} lesions

How does congenital syphilis infection present if the baby survives?

{{c1::Facial}} abnormalities
Cranial nerve {{c1::VIII}} {{c1::deafness}}
{{c1::Saber}} shins

The newborn of a mother with poor prenatal care has the eye findings shown in the image, and you note a continous heart murmur on auscultation. What infection do you suspect?



Congenital {{c1::rubella}}
fields.Back Extra: This can cause both cataracts and congenital heart disease such as patent ductus arteriosus.

fields.Text:
What are the nonspecific signs common to many ToRCHHeS infections?

{{c1::Hepatosplenomegaly}}
{{c1::Thrombocytopenia}}
{{c1::Jaundice}}
{{c1::Growth}} retardation

What microbes, other than ToRCHHeS, can be causes of neonatal infection or hydrops fetalis?

{{c1::Streptococcus agalactiae}}, {{c1::Escherichia coli}}, and {{c1::Listeria monocytogenes}} can cause meningitis in neonates
{{c1::Parvovirus B19}} can lead to hydrops fetalis

Findings on a laparoscopy of a 42-year-old patient with a history of untreated sexually transmitted infections are shown. Parietal peritoneum adhesions to her liver are noted. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Fitz-Hugh-Curtis}} syndrome

A patient presents with purulent cervical discharge, adnexal tenderness, and cervical motion tenderness. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Pelvic inflammatory}} disease

What are some of the complications of salpingitis?

{{c1::Adhesions}}
{{c1::Ectopic}} pregnancy
{{c1::Infertility}}
Chronic {{c1::pelvic}} pain

Name the four types of infectious processes that make up pelvic inflammatory disease.

{{c1::Salpingitis}}
{{c1::Endometritis}}
{{c1::Hydrosalpinx}}
{{c1::Tubo-ovarian}} abscess

Pelvic inflammatory disease is most often caused by which two organisms?

{{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}}
{{c1::Neisseria gonorrhoeae}}

What pathogen is associated with infection related to water aerosols?

{{c1::Legionella}}

What pathogens are associated with infection related to urinary catheterization?

{{c1::Proteus}} species
{{c1::Escherichia coli}}
{{c1::Klebsiella}}

A patient in the intensive care unit who has been intubated for 1 week shows increased sputum production on suctioning. A chest X-ray shows new infiltrates. What is the likely diagnosis?

{{c1::Ventilator}}-associated {{c1::pneumonia}}
fields.Back Extra: This is from Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella, Acinetobacter, or Staphylococcus aureus.

fields.Text:
What pathogens are associated with infections related to mechanical ventilation or endotracheal intubation?

{{c1::Pseudomonas aeruginosa}}
{{c1::Klebsiella}}
{{c1::Acinetobacter}}
{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}

What pathogens are likely responsible for infections related to intravascular catheters?

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
{{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}} (long-term use)

What pathogens are likely responsible for nosocomial infections associated with decubitus ulcers, surgical wounds, or drains?

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
Gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} {{c1::anaerobes::aerobes/anaerobes}}

What characteristic X-ray findings may be seen after aspiration?

Infiltrates in the {{c1::right::left/right}} {{c1::lower::upper/lower}} lobe
fields.Back Extra: If the patient is recumbent, the infiltrates may be in the right upper or middle lobe.

fields.Text:
Which microorganisms are associated with aspiration pneumonia?

{{c1::Polymicrobial}}, gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} bacteria

What risk factors predispose a patient to Clostridium difficile infection?

Recent {{c1::antibiotic}} use
{{c1::Hospitalization}}

Whihc risk factors are associated with hepatitis B and hepatitis C nosocomial infections?

Renal {{c1::dialysis}} provided in a {{c1::dialysis}} unit
{{c1::Needlestick}}

What are the two most common causes of nosocomial infections?

{{c1::Escherichia coli}} (urinary tract infections)
{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} (wound infections)

What is the character of the sputum produced by patients with aspiration pneumonia?

{{c1::Purulent}}
{{c1::Malodorous}}

What features are seen in infection caused by mechanical ventilation or endotracheal intubation?

New {{c1::infiltrate}} on chest X-ray
Increased {{c1::sputum}} production
fields.Back Extra: There may be a sweet odor if the infection is due to Pseudomonas.

fields.Text:
What are the most common symptom and laboratory finding seen with Clostridium difficile infection?

{{c1::Watery}} diarrhea
{{c1::Leukocytosis}}

What are some signs and symptoms commonly seen in Legionella infection?

{{c1::Pneumonia}}
{{c1::Neurologic}} abnormalities
{{c1::Gastrointestinal}} symptoms

What pathogen is higher risk in unvaccinated individuals and presents with pharyngitis and grayish pseudomembranes that may cause airway obstruction?

{{c1::Corynebacterium diphtheriae}}

What pathogen is higher risk in unvaccinated individuals and presents with fever, drooling, dysphagia, and difficulty breathing due to edema?

{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae tybe b}}

What pathogen is higher risk in unvaccinated individuals and presents with meningitis, myalgia, and paralysis?

{{c1::Poliovirus}}

What pathogen redsides in the nasopharynx and causes meningitis in unvaccinated children?

{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae type b}}

What pathogen is higher risk in unvaccinated individuals and presents with cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis, a diffuse rash, and blue-white spots in the mouth?

{{c1::Measles virus}}
fields.Back Extra: The mouth lesions are called Koplik spots.

fields.Text:
What pathogen is higher risk in unvaccinated individuals and presents with postauricular lymphadenopathy and a descending rash?

{{c1::Rubella virus}}

What pathogen is higher risk in unvaccinated individuals and presents with low-grade fever and coryza progressing to cough and posttussive emesis?

{{c1::Bordetella pertussis}}

What are some of the ways that the spastic paralysis of Clostridium tetani infection may present?

{{c1::Lockjaw}}
{{c1::Opisthotonus}}

What pathogen is higher risk in unvaccinated individuals and presents with muscle spasms and spastic paralysis?

{{c1::Clostridium tetani}}

Name two antibiotics that work by blocking peptidoglycan synthesis.

{{c1::Bacitracin}}
{{c1::Vancomycin}}

Which group of antimicrobials does aztreonam belong to?

{{c1::Monobactams}}

Which antibiotic class do doripenem, ertapenem, imipenem, and meropenem belong to?

{{c1::Carbapenem}}

Name the antibiotics that inhibit peptidoglycan cross-linking and are penicillinase resistant.

{{c1::Oxacillin}}
{{c1::Nafcillin}}
{{c1::Dicloxacillin}}

How do penicillins, antipseudomonals, cephalosporins, carbapenems, and monobactams work?

They block {{c1::cell wall}} synthesis by inhibiting {{c1::cross-linking}} of {{c1::peptidoglycans}}

Name three classes of antibiotics that work by binding to the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit.

{{c1::Aminoglycosides}}
{{c1::Glycylcycline}}
{{c1::Tetracyclines}}

Name five antibiotics/antibiotic classes that work by binding to the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunits and blocking protein synthesis.

{{c1::Chloramphenicol}}
{{c1::Clindamycin}}
{{c1::Linezolid}}
{{c1::Streptogramins}}
{{c1::Macrolides}}

Which process does rifampin block to exert antimicrobial effects?

The synthesis of bacterial {{c1::mRNA}} via inhibiting {{c1::RNA polymerase}}

Through inhibition of which enzyme do fluoroquinolones and quinolones exert their antibacterial effects?

{{c1::DNA gyrase}} inhibition

Which processes do sulfonamides and trimethoprim affect to exert their antibacterial effects?

Sulfonamides inhibit conversion of {{c1::PABA}} to {{c1::dihydrofolate}}
Trimethoprim inhibits conversion of {{c1::dihydrofolate}} to {{c1::tetrahydrofolate}}
fields.Back Extra: This affects folic acid synthesis and reduction.

fields.Text:
What antimicrobial effect is the mechanism of action of metronidazole?

{{c1::Free radical}}-induced damage to {{c1::DNA::DNA/RNA}} integrity

Which two antimicrobials act by disrupting membrane integrity?

{{c1::Daptomycin}}
{{c1::Polymyxins}}

Name the antibiotics that inhibit peptidoglycan cross-linking and are penicillinase sensitive.

{{c1::Penicillin G}}
{{c1::Penicillin V}}
{{c1::Ampicillin}}
{{c1::Amoxicillin}}

How do bacteria develop resistance to penicillin?

By producing a {{c1::β-lactamase}}, which cleaves the {{c1::β-lactom ring}}
By mutations in {{c1::penicillin-binding proteins}}

What are the common adverse effects of penicillin?

{{c1::Hypersensitivity}} reactions
Drug-induced {{c1::interstitial nephritis}}
Positive {{c1::direct Coombs}} test

Against which classes of bacteria do penicillins exhibit bactericidal activity?

Gram-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}} {{c1::cocci::shape}}
Gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} {{c1::cocci::shape}}
Gram-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}} {{c1::rods::shape}}
{{c1::Spirochetes}}

What is the mechanism of action of penicillin?

As a {{c1::D-Ala-D-Ala}} structural analog, it binds to {{c1::penicillin-binding proteins}} and inhibits transpeptidase cross-linking of {{c1::peptidoglycan}} in cell walls

Compare the modes of administration for penicillin G and penicillin V.

Penicillin G → {{c1::Intravenous}} or {{c1::intramuscular}}
Penicillin V → {{c1::Oral}}

What is the mechanism of resistance to ampicillin and amoxicillin?

Bacterial {{c1::penicillinase}} cleaves the {{c1::β-lactam ring}}

What are the major adverse effects of ampicillin and amoxicillin?

{{c1::Rash}}
{{c1::Hypersensitivity}} reaction
{{c1::Pseudomembranous colitis}}

What organisms do ampicillin and amoxicillin cover that penicillin does not?

{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae}}
{{c1::Helicobacter pylori}}
{{c1::Escherichia coli}}
{{c1::Enterococci}}
{{c1::Listeria monocytogenes}}
{{c1::Proteus mirabilis}}
{{c1::Salmonella}}
{{c1::Shigella}}

Which of the two aminopenicillins has a greater oral bioavailability?

{{c1::Amoxicillin}}

Which agent, when given with amoxicillin, protects against β-lactamases?

{{c1::Clavulanic acid}}

What is the mechanism of action of ampicillin and amoxicillin?

They bind to {{c1::penicillin-binding}} proteins and block {{c1::cross-linking}} of {{c1::peptidoglycan}} in bacterial cell walls

Name the penicillin-type antibiotics that are sensitive to penicillinase.

{{c1::Amoxicillin}}
{{c1::Ampicillin}}

Name the narrow-spectrum, penicillinase-resistant antibiotics.

{{c1::Nafcillin}}
{{c1::Oxacillin}}
{{c1::Dicloxacillin}}

What are some adverse effects of penicillinase-resistant penicillins?

{{c1::Interstitial nephritis}}
{{c1::Hypersensitivity}} reactions

Against which organism are dicloxacillin, nafcillin, and oxacillin useful?

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}

What aspect of nafcillin, dicloxacillin, and oxacillin makes them resistant to degradation by the bacterial enzyme β-lactamase?

{{c1::Bulky R}} groups in these drugs blocks access of β-lactamase to β-lactam ring

What is the mechanism of action of dicloxacillin, nafcillin, and oxacillin?

Inhibition of peptidoglycan {{c1::cross-linking}} in bacterial cell walls

What biochemical variation in methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus makes nafcillin ineffective?

Alteration of the {{c1::penicillin-binding}} protein target site

Which bacterial species are targeted by piperacillin?

{{c1::Pseudomonas}} species
Gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} {{c1::rods::shape}}

What is the mechanism of action of the antipseudomonal penicillins?

They inhibit peptidoglycan {{c1::cross-linking}} in bacterial cell walls
fields.Back Extra: This is the same as penicillin.

fields.Text:
To overcome bacterial resistance, what drug must be administered with extended-spectrum β-lactams for pseudomonal infection?

{{c1::β-lactamase}} inhibitors
fields.Back Extra: This is because of the sensitivity of Pseudomonas species to penicillinase.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of resistance to cephalosporins?

Via inactivation of the drug by {{c1::cephalosporinases}}
Via structural changes in the {{c1::penicillin-binding}} proteins

A patient with sepsis receiving an aminoglycoside is also prescribed a cephalosporin. What adverse effect could occur?

When combined with aminoglycosides, cephalosporins increase the potential for {{c1::nephrotoxicity}}

Are patients with penicillin allergies likely to be allergic to cephalosporins?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Cephalosporins have a low rate of cross-reactivity even in patients with penicillin allergy.

fields.Text:
What adverse effects are associated with cephalosporin use?

{{c1::Disulfiram}}-like reaction
{{c1::Autoimmune hemolytic}} anemia
{{c1::Hypersensitivity}} reaction
Vitamin {{c1::K}} deficiency

What could lead to prolongation of prothrombin time in a patient taking a drug from the cephalosporin group?

Cephalosporin use can cause vitamin {{c1::K}} deficiency → Decrease in {{c1::clotting}} factors

Ceftaroline is active against which organisms?

Gram-positive organisms, such as {{c1::methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus}} and {{c1::Enterococcus faecalis}}
Gram-negative organisms
fields.Back Extra: There is no coverage of Pseudomonas species.

fields.Text:
Cefepime has increased activity against which organisms?

{{c1::Pseudomonas}}
Gram-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}} organisms

Name the fourth-generation cephalosporin.

{{c1::Cefepime}}

Which third-generation cephalosporin is effective against Pseudomonas species?

{{c1::Ceftazidime}}

Which drug is effective in treatment of both disseminated Lyme disease and gonorrhea?

{{c1::Ceftriaxone}}

Which cephalosporins work particularly well in the treatment of meningitis and why?

{{c1::Third}}-generation cephalosporins because they can cross the {{c1::blood-brain barrier}}

What generation of cephalosporins is used for severe gram-negative infections resistant to previously prescribed β-lactams?

{{c1::Third}}-generation cephalosporins

Name five cephalosporins from the third-generation.

{{c1::Ceftriaxone}}
{{c1::Cefotaxime}}
{{c1::Ceftazidime}}
{{c1::Cefpodoxime}}
{{c1::Cefixime}}

Which organisms do second-generation cephalosporins cover?

Gram-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}} {{c1::cocci::shape}}
{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae}}
{{c1::Enterobacter aerogenes}}
{{c1::Neisseria}} species
{{c1::Serratia marcescens}}
{{c1::Proteus mirabilis}}
{{c1::Escherichia coli}}
{{c1::Klebsiella pneumoniae}}

Name four commonly used examples of second-generation cephalosporins.

{{c1::Cefaclor}}
{{c1::Cefoxitin}}
{{c1::Cefuroxime}}
{{c1::Cefotetan}}

Which organisms are covered by the first-generation cephalosporins?

Gram-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}} {{c1::cocci::shape}}
{{c1::Proteus mirabilis}}
{{c1::Escherichia coli}}
{{c1::Klebsiella pneumoniae}}

Name two commonly used examples of first-generation cephalosporins.

{{c1::Cefazolin}}
{{c1::Cephalexin}}

Which organisms are typically not covered by the first four generations of cephalosporins?

{{c1::Listeria}}
{{c1::Atypicals}}
{{c1::Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus}}
{{c1::Enterococci}}

Compared with other β-lactams, cephalosporins are more resistant to what bacterial enzyme?

{{c1::Penicillinase}}

What is the mechanism of action of cephalosporin antibiotics?

They are bactericidal {{c1::β-lactams}} that inhibit {{c1::cell wall}} synthesis

Which antibiotic is most commonly used preoperatively to protect against Staphylococcus aureus wound infections?

{{c1::Cefazolin}}

Name a fifth-generation cephalosporin.

{{c1::Ceftaroline}}

Name four drugs that can be given with penicillin antibiotics to prevent degradation by β-lactamase.

{{c1::Clavulanic acid}}
{{c1::Avibactam}}
{{c1::Sulbactam}}
{{c1::Tazobactam}}

Name four combinations of penicillin antibiotics with β-lactamase inhibitors commonly used to treat bacterial infections.

Amoxicillin-{{c1::clavulanate}}
Ampicillin-{{c1::sulbactam}}
Ceftazidime-{{c1::avibactam}}
Piperacillin-{{c1::tazobactam}}

What is the mechanism by which bacteria develop resistance to carbapenems?

Via {{c1::carbapenemases}}

What are the possible adverse effects of the carbapenem class of antibiotics?

Skin {{c1::rashes}}
{{c1::Gastrointestinal}} distress
{{c1::Central nervous system}} toxicity

Which of the carbapenem antibiotics has a lower risk of seizures?

{{c1::Meropenem}}

At what point during disease progression are carbapenem antibiotics considered?

They are used when other medications have {{c1::failed}} or when an infection is {{c1::life-threatening}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because of their significant adverse effects.

fields.Text:
Carbapenems are used to treat infections with which three types of organisms?

{{c1::Anaerobes::Aerobes/Anaerobes}}
Gram-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}} {{c1::cocci}}
Gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} {{c1::rods}}

Which carbapenem has limited Pseudomonas coverge?

{{c1::Ertapenem}}

Name the carbepenem that is resistant to β-lactamase and is prescribed with cilastatin to prevent inactivation by the kidneys.

{{c1::Imipenem}}

Name the commonly used carbapenem antibiotics.

{{c1::Doripenem}}
{{c1::Imipenem}}
{{c1::Meropenem}}
{{c1::Ertapenem}}

How does cilastatin work to decrease inactivation of carbepenem antibiotics?

Its an inhibitor of {{c1::renal dehydropeptidase I}}

Which of the carbapenem antibiotics is not affected by renal dehydropeptidase I?

{{c1::Meropenem}}

Aztreonam is active against which group of organisms?

Gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} {{c1::rods::shape}}

Would aztreonam induce a reaction in a patient allergic to penicillin?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Aztreonam has no cross-sensitivity to penicillins.

fields.Text:
Aztreonam is synergistic with which class of antibiotics?

{{c1::Aminoglycosides}}

Aztreonam inhibits peptidoglycan cross-linking by binding to which protein?

{{c1::Penicillin-binding protein 3}}

A patient treated with vancomycin develops diffuse flushing. How could this have been prevented?



Pretreatment with {{c1::antihistamines}}
fields.Back Extra: This is red man syndrome, which is seen in vancomycin toxicity.

fields.Text:
How do bacteria develop resistance to vancomycin?

Conversion of {{c1::D-Ala-D-Ala}} to {{c1::D-Ala-D-Lac}}

What are some adverse reactions associated with vancomycin?

{{c1::DRESS}} syndrome
{{c1::Nephrotoxicity}}
{{c1::Ototoxicity}}
{{c1::Thrombophlebitis}}
{{c1::Red man}} syndrome

Which types of organisms are treated with vancomycin?

Gram-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}} organisms
fields.Back Extra: Vancomycin may also be used to treat serious, multidrug-resistant organisms, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Enterococcus species, and Clostridium difficile.

fields.Text:
β-lactamase inhibitors are used to protect antibiotics from bacterial penicillinases. Would you use these with vancomycin?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because vancomycin is resistant to β-lactamases.

fields.Text:
Vancomycin is bactericidal except against which bacteria?

{{c1::Clostridium difficile}}

What is the mechanism of action of vancomycin?

It binds to the {{c1::D-Ala-D-Ala}} part of {{c1::cell wall}} precursors, inhibiting the formation of peptidoglycan {{c1::cell wall}}
fields.Back Extra: This is bactericidal against most bacteria.

fields.Text:
Which two systemic reactions accompanied by diffuse rash can be seen with vancomycin toxicity?

{{c1::Red man}} syndrome
{{c1::DRESS}} syndrome

Which antibiotics inhibit bacterial translocation?
