{{c1::Macrolides}}
{{c1::Clindamycin}}

You add a bacteriostatic antibiotic to bacteria and notice that the A-site tRNA binding is reduced. Which ribosomal subunit is inhibited?

{{c1::30S}}
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by tetracycline antibiotics.

fields.Text:
Which 50S-inhibiting antibiotic inhibits peptidyl transferase activity?

{{c1::Chloramphenicol}}

Addition of a certain bactericidal antibiotic leads to misreading of the mRNA by inhibition of which ribosomal subunit?

{{c1::30S}} ribosomal subunit
fields.Back Extra: This is blocked by aminoglycosides and can cause midreading of mRNA.

fields.Text:
Which protein synthesis-inhibiting antibiotics are bacteriostatic?

{{c1::Tetracyclines}}
{{c1::Chloramphenicol}}
{{c1::Clindamycin}}
{{c1::Erythromycin}}
fields.Back Extra: Linezolid can be either bacteriostatic or bactericidal.

fields.Text:
Which protein synthesis-inhibiting antibiotics are bactericidal?

{{c1::Aminoglycosides}}
fields.Back Extra: Linezolid can be either bacteriostatic or bactericidal.

fields.Text:
List the antibiotics that inhibit the 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome.

{{c1::Aminoglycosides}}
{{c1::Tetracyclines}}

Why do antibiotics that inhibit protein synthesis generally not affect human cells?

They target bacterial ribosome {{c1::70S}}, which is {{c1::smaller::larger/smaller}} than the human ribosome {{c1::80S}}

List the antibiotics that inhibit the 50S subunit of the bacterial ribosome.

{{c1::Chloramphenicol}}
{{c1::Clindamycin}}
{{c1::Erythromycin}}
{{c1::Linezolid}}

Which adverse effects are associated with aminoglycosides?

{{c1::Nephrotoxicity}}
{{c1::Neuromuscular}} blockade
{{c1::Ototoxicity}} (combined with loop diuretics)
{{c1::Teratogenitcity}}

Which antibiotic targeting bacterial protein synthesis can be given prophylactically before bowel surgery?

{{c1::Neomycin}}

What is the mechanism by which bacteria develop resistance to aminoglycosides?

{{c1::Transferase}} enzymes in bacteria cause inactivation of the drug via {{c1::acetylation}}, {{c1::phosphorylation}}, or {{c1::adenylation}}

Aminoglycosides are synergistic with which class of antibiotics?

{{c1::β-lactams}}

What organisms are aminoglycosides used against?

Gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} {{c1::rods::shape}}
fields.Back Extra: This is particularly in cases of severe infection.

fields.Text:
Can aminoglycosides kill anaerobic bacteria?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because they require oxygen for uptake.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides?

They are {{c1::bactericidal::bactericidal/bacteriostatic}} antibiotics that {{c1::irreversibly::reversibly/irreversibly}} inhibit the initiation complex by binding to {{c1::30S}} → Blocks {{c1::translocation}} → Misreading of mRNA

Name five antibiotics that belong to the aminoglycoside class of antibiotics.

{{c1::Gentamicin}}
{{c1::Neomycin}}
{{c1::Amikacin}}
{{c1::Tobramycin}}
{{c1::Streptomycin}}

Use of aminoglycoside antibiotics is absolutely contraindicated for patients with what neuromuscular disorder?

{{c1::Myasthenia gravis}}

What is the mechanism of resistance against tetracyclines?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} uptake into bacterial cells
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} efflux out of cells by {{c1::plasmid}}-encoded {{c1::transport pumps}}

What dermatologic adverse effect results from use of tetracyclines?

{{c1::Photosensitivity}}

A child presents with discolored teeth, inhibited bone growth, and gastrointestinal distress secondary to antibiotic treatment. What antibiotic was used?

{{c1::Tetracycline}}

Which feature of tetracyclines makes them effective against Rickettsia and Chlamydia infections?

Their ability to {{c1::accumulate}} intracellularly

Name the bacterial infections that can be treated with tetracycline antibiotics.

{{c1::Mycoplasma pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Chlamydia}}
{{c1::Borrelia burgdorferi}}
{{c1::Rickettsia}}
Community-acquired {{c1::methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus}} (doxycycline)

What diet modifications must a patient taking a tetracycline follow?

Avoid {{c1::milk}}
Avoid {{c1::antacids}}
Avoid {{c1::iron}}-containing preparations
fields.Back Extra: This is because divalent cations inhibit tetracycline absorption in the gut.

fields.Text:
A patient with renal failure needs a tetracycline for treatment of a Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection. What do you prescribe and why?

{{c1::Doxycyline}}, it is eliminated {{c1::fecally}}

What is the mechanism of action of tetracyclines?

They are {{c1::bacteriostatic::bactericidal/bacteriostatic}}, binding to {{c1::30S}} and preventing the attachment of {{c1::aminoacyl-tRNA}}

Name three antibiotics that belong to the tetracycline class of antibiotics.

{{c1::Doxycycline}}
{{c1::Minocycline}}
{{c1::Tetracycline}}

Why are tetracycline antibiotics not a good choice for infections of the central nervous system?

They have limited central nervous system {{c1::penetration}}

Name a skin condition that can be treated with tetracycline antibiotics.

{{c1::Acne}}

What organisms does tigecycline cover?

{{c1::Anaerobic::Aerobic/Anaerobic}}
Gram-positive organisms
Gram-negative organisms
{{c1::Multidrug}}-resistant organisms

What is the mechanism of action of tigecycline?

It binds to the {{c1::30S}} ribosome subunit to inhibit bacterial {{c1::protein}} synthesis
It is {{c1::bacteriostatic::bacteriostatic/bactericidal}}

What is the mechanism by which bacteria develop resistance to chloramphenicol?

By acquiring a {{c1::plasmid}}-encoded {{c1::acetyltransferase}} that inactivates the drug

Lack of which enzyme is to blame for premature infants developing gray baby syndrome after receiving chloramphenicol?

{{c1::UDP-glucuronosyltransferase}}

What is the mechanism of action of the antibiotic chloramphenicol?

Inhibits {{c1::peptidyltransferase}} activity in the {{c1::50S}} subunit of the ribosome

How does adjusting the dose of the antibiotic chloramphenicol influence its risk of causing pancytopenia?

{{c1::No effect}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because aplastic anemia is a dose-independent adverse effect of chloramphenicol.

fields.Text:
What are the most common uses for chloramphenicol?

{{c1::Rickettsial}} diseases
{{c1::Meningitis}}

What is the major reason for the limited use of chloramphenicol in the United States?

High level of {{c1::toxicity}}
fields.Back Extra: It is still widely used in some countries because of its low cost.

fields.Text:
How does adjusting the dose of the antibiotic chloramphenicol influence its risk of causing anemia?

Lowering the dose will {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} the risk of anemia
fields.Back Extra: This is because chloramphenicol-induced anemia is a dose-dependent adverse effect of the drug.

fields.Text:
When would you consider using clindamycin over metronidazole to treat an anaerobic infection?

Clindamycin is useful for anaerobic infections {{c1::above::above/below}} the diaphragm
Metronidazole is useful for anaerobic infections {{c1::below::above/below}} the diaphargm

What organisms are targeted by clindamycin?

Organisms causing {{c1::anaerobic::aerobic/anaerobic}} {{c1::lung::organ}} infections
Group {{c1::A}} streptococcal infections

What is the mechanism of action of clindamycin?

It is a {{c1::bacteriostatic::bacteriostatic/bactericidal}} antibiotic that inhibits {{c1::peptide}} transfer at the {{c1::50S}} ribosomal subunit

A patient being treated with clindamycin for pneumonia develops fever and loose stools. What is the bacterial culprit?

{{c1::Clostridium difficile}} overgrowth in the colon

What infectious processes are commonly treated using clindamycin?

{{c1::Aspiration pneumonia}}
Lung {{c1::abscesses}}
{{c1::Oral}} infections involving {{c1::anaerobic::aerobic/anaerobic}} organisms

A patient taking an antidepressant is prescribed linezolid for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia. Which serious adverse effect might you worry about?

{{c1::Serotonin}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This is more likely to occur if a patient is also taking a SSRI.

fields.Text:
How would an organism become resistant to linezolid?

{{c1::Point}} mutation of {{c1::rRNA}}

What is the mechanism of action of the antibiotic linezolid?

Binds to the {{c1::50S}} subunit and blocks the formation of the {{c1::initiation}} complex → Inhibits protein synthesis

What are the common adverse effects of linezolid?

{{c1::Peripheral::Central/Peripheral}} neuropathy
{{c1::Myelosuppression}}
{{c1::Serotonin}} syndrome

Which organisms would you consider using a linezolid against?

Gram-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}} organisms

What is the mechanism by which bacteria develop resistance to macrolide antibiotics?

By {{c1::methylation}} of the {{c1::23S}} {{c1::rRNA}}-binding site, which prevents the drug from binding to it

Which macrolide antibiotics inhibit cytochrome P-450 enzymes?

{{c1::Erythromycin}}
{{c1::Clarithromycin}}

A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and a recent episode of pneumonia has increased serum levels of theophylline. Which antibiotic is this patient likely taking?

{{c1::Macrolide}}

What is the most common electrical cardiac abnormality seen with erythromycin?

{{c1::Prolonged QT interval}}

What are the common major adverse effects caused by macrolides?

Gastrointestinal {{c1::motility}} issues
{{c1::Arrhythmia}}
Acute {{c1::cholestatic hepatitis}}
{{c1::Rash}}
{{c1::Eosinophilia}}

What types of infections are macrolides used to treat?

{{c1::Sexually transmitted}} infections
{{c1::Atypical pneumonias}}
Gram-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}} {{c1::cocci::shape}}
{{c1::Bordetella pertussis}}

Describe the mechanism of action of the bacteriostatic macrolide antibiotics.

They inhibit {{c1::protein}} synthesis by binding to the {{c1::23S}} rRNA of the {{c1::50S}} subunit → Prevents translocation

Name three examples of macrolide antibiotics.

{{c1::Erythromycin}}
{{c1::Azithromycin}}
{{c1::Clarithromycin}}

A patient is taking warfarin because of a recent pulmonary embolism. What complication could arise if a macrolide is prescribed for newly diagnosed pneumonia?

Increased risk of {{c1::bleeding}}

Name the two antibiotics that belong to the polymyxin class.

{{c1::Colistin}}
{{c1::Polymyxin B}}

What is the mechanism of action of polymyxin antibiotics?

{{c1::Cation::Cation/Anion}} polypeptides bind to phospholipids on cell membranes of gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} bacteria → Disruption of cell membrane {{c1::integrity}} → Leakage of cellular components and cell death

What are the common major adverse effects of the drugs belonging to the polymyxin class?

{{c1::Nephrotoxicity}}
{{c1::Neurotoxicity}}
{{c1::Respiratory}} failure

A patient is given a triple antibiotic ointment for a superficial skin infection. Which antibiotic in the topical therapy is a cationic polypeptide?

{{c1::Polymyxin B}}

Polymyxins are used to treat which types of infections?

Last resort treatment for {{c1::multidrug}}-resistant gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} bacterial infections
Topical treatment for {{c1::superficial skin}} infections

What are the three different mechanisms by which bacteria develop resistance against sulfonamides?

Alteration in bacterial {{c1::dihydropteroate synthase}}
Decreased {{c1::uptake}}
Increased synthesis of {{c1::PABA}}

A patient receiving warfarin therapy begins taking a sulfonamide for an infection and soon notes easy bruising and dark tarry stools. What mechanism causes this adverse effect?

The sulfonamide {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} the plasma concentration of warfarin by displacing it from {{c1::albumin}}

What neurologic injury can sulfonamides cause in infants?

{{c1::Kernicterus}}

What are two dermatologic manifestations of sulfonamide toxicity?

{{c1::Photosensitivity}}
{{c1::Stevens-Johnson}} syndrome

What is the common renal manifestation of sulfonamide toxicity?

{{c1::Tubulointerstitial nephritis}}

A patient presents with low hemoglobin soon after initiation of treatment with sulfadiazine. Which underlying enzyme deficiency does this patient likely have?

{{c1::Glucose-6-phosphate-dehydrogenase}} deficiency

Sulfonamides are active against which organisms?

Gram-positive organisms
Gram-negative organisms
{{c1::Nocardia}}

Sulfonamides are bacteriostatic when used alone, but addition of which antibiotic can cause sulfonamides to be bactericidal?

{{c1::Trimethoprim}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor.

fields.Text:
Describe the mechanism of action for sulfonamide antibiotics.

They prevent {{c1::folate}} synthesis by inhibiting {{c1::dihydropteroate synthase}}

Name the three drugs that belong to the sulfonamide class.

{{c1::Sulfamethoxazole}}
{{c1::Sulfadiazine}}
{{c1::Sulfisoxazole}}

Hemolysis may occur as an adverse effect in which patients taking dapsone?

Patients who are {{c1::glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase}} deficient

What two diseases is dapsone indicated to treat?

{{c1::Leprosy}}
{{c1::Pneumocystis jirovecii}} (if used with trimethoprim)

What is the mechanism of action of dapsone?

It inhibits {{c1::dihydropteroate synthase}}, impairing bacterial {{c1::folate}} synthesis

What are the major adverse effects of dapsone?

{{c1::Hemolysis}} in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
{{c1::Methemoglobinemia}}
{{c1::Agranulocytosis}}

Dapsone is used for prophylaxis against infection with which organism?

{{c1::Pneumocystis jirovecii}}

How can megaloblastic anemia seen in trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole be avoided?

By coadministration of {{c1::leucovorin}}

Trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole are used to treat which types of infections?

{{c1::Urinary}} tract infections
{{c1::Shigella}}
{{c1::Salmonella}}
{{c1::Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia}}

Why are trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole used in combination?

To synergistically inhibit {{c1::folate}} metabolism and thus {{c1::DNA}} synthesis
fields.Back Extra: This allows it to become bactericidal instead of bacteriostatic.

fields.Text:
Describe the mechanism of action of trimethoprim.

It blocks {{c1::dihydrofolate reductase}} → Prevents bacterial {{c1::replication}}

What are the common adverse effects of trimethoprim?

{{c1::Hyperkalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
{{c1::Leukopenia}}
{{c1::Granulocytopenia}}
{{c1::Megaloblastic}} anemia

By what three mechanisms can bacteria develop resistance to a fluoroquinolone antibiotic?

Chromosome-encoded mutation in the bacterial {{c1::DNA gyrase}}
{{c1::Efflux}} pumps
Resistance mediated by {{c1::plasmids}}

Why should fluoroquinolones be avoided in patients older than 60 years of age?

Fluroquinolones may cause {{c1::tendinitis}} and/or {{c1::tendon rupture}} in people older than 60 years of age

Why are fluoroquinolones contraindicated for women who are pregnant or breastfeeding and for children younger than 18 years of age?

Possibility of {{c1::cartilage}} damage

What are the common central nervous system adverse effects of fluoroquinolones?

{{c1::Headaches}}
{{c1::Dizziness}}

What are the clinical uses of fluoroquinolones?

Gram-negative rods causing {{c1::urinary}} tract infections and {{c1::gastrointestinal}} tract infections
Some gram-positive organisms
{{c1::Otitis externa}}

What drug class should not be taken with fluoroquinolones?

{{c1::Antacids}}

What is the mechanism of action of fluoroquinolones?

Inhibition of prokaryotic {{c1::topoisomerase II}}
Inhibition of prokaryotic {{c1::topoisomerase IV}}

Name the four nonrespiratory fluoroquinolones.

{{c1::Ciprofloxacin}}
{{c1::Norfloxacin}}
{{c1::Ofloxacin}}
{{c1::Enoxacin}}

Name the three respiratory fluoroquinolones.

{{c1::Levofloxacin}}
{{c1::Monifloxacin}}
{{c1::Gemifloxacin}}

What is the effect of ciprofloxacin on cytochrome P-450?

{{c1::Inhibits}} cytochrome P-450

What abnormality might be seen on an ECG in a patient being treated with a fluoroquinolone?

{{c1::Prolonged QT interval}}

What are two potential adverse effects of daptomycin?

{{c1::Rhabdomyolysis}}
{{c1::Myopathy}}

Why is daptomycin ineffective against pneumonia?

Daptomycin binds to and is inactivated by {{c1::surfactant}} before acting on the lungs

Daptomycin is used to treat what types of infections?

{{c1::Vancomycin-resistant enterococcus}}
{{c1::Bacteremia}}
{{c1::Endocarditis}}
Skin infections with {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}

What is the mechanism of action of daptomycin?

Lipopeptide disrupts gram-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}} {{c1::cocci::shape}} cell membranes by creating {{c1::transmembrane}} channels

Why should you advise the patient to avoid alcohol use when prescribing metronidazole?

Metronidazole with alcohol causes a {{c1::disulfiram}}-like reaction

What two common adverse effects of metronidazole are NOT associated with alcohol use?

{{c1::Headache}}
{{c1::Metallic}} taste

Which antimicrobials are used to treat anaerobic infections below and above the diaphragm?

{{c1::Metronidazole}} treats anaerobic infections below the diaphragm
{{c1::Clindamycin}} treats anaerobic infections above the diaphragm

You want to prescribe a triple therapy regimen for a patient with Helicobacter pylori, but she has a penicillin allergy. How do you alter your treatment plan?

Replace amoxicillin with {{c1::metronidazole}}
fields.Back Extra: The triple therapy also includes a proton pump inhibitor and clarithromycin.

fields.Text:
List the organisms that can be treated with metronidazole.

{{c1::Giardia}}
{{c1::Entamoeba}}
{{c1::Trichomonas}}
{{c1::Gardnerella vaginalis}}
{{c1::Anaerobes::Aerobes/Anaerobes}}
{{c1::Helicobacter pylori}}

What is the mechanism of action of metronidazole?

Forms {{c1::free radical}} metabolites that damage bacterial {{c1::DNA}}, leading to cell death

What is the four-drug regimen commonly used to treat tuberculosis?

{{c1::Rifampin}}
{{c1::Isoniazid}}
{{c1::Pyrazinamide}}
{{c1::Ethambutol}}

What is the treatment for lepromatous leprosy?

Long-term regimen of {{c1::dapsone}}, {{c1::rifampin}}, and {{c1::clofazimine}}

What is the treatment for tuberculoid leprosy?

Long-term regimen of {{c1::dapsone}} and {{c1::rifampin}}

What drug regimen can you use to treat a Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare infection?

{{c1::Azithromycin}} or {{c1::clarithromycin}} + {{c1::Ethambutol}}
fields.Back Extra: Rifabutin or ciprofloxacin can be added.

fields.Text:
Which two antibiotics would you prescribe as prophylaxis against Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare infection?

{{c1::Azithromycin}}
{{c1::Rifabutin}}

What drug is used for Mycobacterium tuberculosis prophylaxis?

{{c1::Rifamycin}}-based regimen for 3 to 4 months

What is the mechanism of action of isoniazid?

Decreases {{c1::mycolic acid}} synthesis

What is the mechanism of action of pyrazinamide?

{{c1::Unclear}}
fields.Back Extra: It acts via an unknown mechanism intracellularly.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of resistance of the rifamycins, particularly with monotherapy?

Mutations decrease the drug's ability to bind to {{c1::RNA polymerase}}

A patient with HIV contracts tuberculosis. Why would rifabutin be favored over rifampin for this patient?

Less {{c1::cytochrome P-450}} stimulation

A patient develops minor hepatotoxicity and red secretions after starting treatment for tuberculosis. What class of medications is the most likely cause?

{{c1::Rifamycins}}

What is the consequence of treating latent tuberculosis solely with rifamycins?

Development of rapid {{c1::resistance}}

Besides treatment of mycobacterial infections, what are two other uses for rifamycins?

Meningococcal prophylaxis and chemoprophylaxis for contacts of children with {{c1::Haemophilus influenzae type b}}

What is the benefit of utilizing rifampin in the treatment of Mycobacterium leprae?

It delays resistance to {{c1::dapsone}}

What is the mechanism of action of the rifamycin class?

Inhibition of {{c1::DNA-dependent RNA polymerase}}

Which three medications belong to the rifamycin class of antibiotics?

{{c1::Rifampin}}
{{c1::Rifapentine}}
{{c1::Rifabutin}}

What are the four "R's" of rifampin?

{{c1::RNA polymerase}} inhibitor
Ramps up microsomal {{c1::cytochrome P-450}}
{{c1::Red}}/{{c1::orange}} body fluids
Rapid {{c1::resistance}} when used alone

What is the mechanism of resistance of isoniazid?

Mutations resulting in the underexpression of {{c1::KatG}}, which encodes bacterial {{c1::catalse-peroxidase}}

A patient is found to have drug-induced systemic lupus erythematosus after completing prophylaxis for tuberculosis. Which drug is the most likely cause?

{{c1::Isoniazid}}

A patient presents with peripheral neuropathy and sideroblastic anemia after being treated with tuberculosis. What medication is the most likely cause?

{{c1::Isoniazid}}

How can you prevent peripheral neuropathy in a patient being treated for tuberculosis with isoniazid?

By coadministering {{c1::pyridoxine}} to prevent vitamin {{c1::B6}} deficiency induced by isoniazid

Why do patients require different dosages of isoniazid?

People are either slow or fast {{c1::acetylators}}
fields.Back Extra: The half-life of isoniazid differs depending on the individual rate of acetylation.

fields.Text:
Which bacterial enzyme is needed to activate isoniazid?

{{c1::Catalase-peroxidase}}

A patient requests prophylaxis against Mycobacterium tuberculosis before travel. What is the one drug that can be used as solo prophylaxis?

{{c1::Isoniazid}}

How does isoniazid affect cytochrome P-450?

{{c1::Inhibits}} cytochrome P-450

What is unique regarding seizures induced by isoniazid toxicity?

Seizures caused by isoniazid toxicity are refractory to {{c1::benzodiazepines}}

A patient receiving single-agent therapy for latent tuberculosis has abnormal liver function test results. Which medication is the most likely cause?

{{c1::Isoniazid}}

A patient develops an anion gap metabolic acidosis after being treated for tuberculosis. What is the most likely causal medication?

{{c1::Isoniazid}}

At what pH does pyrazinamide work best?

{{c1::Acidic}} pH

What are the two most common adverse effects of pyrazinamide?

{{c1::Hepatotoxicity}}
{{c1::Hyperuricemia}}

What is the major toxicity associated with ethambutol?

{{c1::Optic neuropathy}}
fields.Back Extra: This commonly manifests as red-green color blindness and is usually reversible.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of ethambutol?

Inhibition of {{c1::arabinosyltransferase}}
fields.Back Extra: This prevents carbohydrate polymerization of mycobacterial cell walls.

fields.Text:
Ethambutol is used to treat which bacterial infection?

{{c1::Mycobacterium tuberculosis}}

What antibiotic do you prescribe as prophylaxis against streptococcal pharyngitis for a child with a history of rheumatic fever?

Oral {{c1::penicillin V}}
{{c1::Benzathine penicillin G}}

Which two antibiotics can be used as prophylaxis against postsurgical Staphylococcus aureus infection?

{{c1::Cefazolin}}
{{c1::Vancomycin}} for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infections

Which antibiotic ointment is applied to prevent gonococcal conjunctivitis in newborns?

Opthalmic {{c1::erythromycin}}

Which two antibiotics can be administered prophylactically for pregnant women with group B streptococcal colonization?

{{c1::Ampicillin}}
{{c1::Penicillin G}}

Which three antibiotics can be administered prophylactically for meningococcal meningitis exposure?

{{c1::Rifampin}}
{{c1::Ceftriaxone}}
{{c1::Ciprofloxacin}}

Which antibiotic is administered prophylactically for women with recurrent urinary tract infections?

{{c1::Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole}}

Patients undergoing which procedures should receive prophylactic amoxicillin?

Patients at high risk for {{c1::endocarditis}} who are undergoing {{c1::surgical}} or {{c1::dental}} procedures

What five medications can be given to a person traveling to an area in which malaria is endemic?

{{c1::Atovaquone-proguanil}}
{{c1::Doxycycline}}
{{c1::Mefloquine}}
{{c1::Primaquine}}
{{c1::Chloroquine}}

An HIV-positive patient has a CD4+ count of < 100 cells/mm3 and must receive prophylactic therapy for Pneumocystis pneumonia and toxoplasmosis. Which medication is indicated?

{{c1::Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole}}

An HIV-positive patient has a CD4+ count of < 200 cells/mm3 and must be treated with prophylaxis for Pneumocystis pneumonia. What medication is indicated?

{{c1::Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole}}

What is the mechanism of action of the polyenes?

Creates membrane {{c1::pores}} to disrupt cell membrane integrity

Which antifungal agent inhibits nucleic acid synthesis?

{{c1::Flucytosine}}

What is the mechanism of action of echinocandins?

Inhibition of {{c1::cell wall}} synthesis

The use of azoles in the treatment of fungal infections targets which fungal cell structure?

{{c1::Cell membrane}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to the inhibition of intracellular 14-α-demethylase, which reduces ergosterol synthesis.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of azoles?

Decreased {{c1::ergosterol}} synthesis from {{c1::lanosterol}} via the inhibition of {{c1::14-α-demethylase}}

What is the mechanism of action of terbinafine?

It inhibits {{c1::squalene epoxidase}}, which inhibits synthesis of the {{c1::cell membrane}}

What are two methods for reducing amphotericin B toxicity?

Using the {{c1::liposomal}} formulation of the drug
{{c1::Hydrate}} the patient to prevent nephrotoxicity

What are the major adverse effects of amphotericin B?

{{c1::Anemia}}
{{c1::Arrhythmias}}
{{c1::Fevers}}
{{c1::Chills}}
{{c1::Neprotoxicity}}
{{c1::Hypotension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
Intravenous {{c1::phlebitis}}

Which two electrolytes must be supplemented when amphotericin B is prescribed?

{{c1::Potassium}}
{{c1::Magnesium}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to altered renal tubule permeability.

fields.Text:
Intrathecal administration of amphotericin B is indicated for the treatment of which fungal meningitis?

Meningitis caused by {{c1::Coccidioides}}

Amphotericin B is used to treat which serious, systemic fungal infections?

{{c1::Blastomyces}}
{{c1::Candida}}
{{c1::Coccidioides}}
{{c1::Cryptococcus}}
{{c1::Histoplasma}}
{{c1::Mucor}}

What is the mechanism of action of amphotericin B?

Amphotericin B binds to {{c1::ergosterol}} and forms membrane {{c1::pores}}, allowing leakage of {{c1::electrolytes}}

What second agent can be administered with amphotericin B to treat cryptococcal meningitis?

{{c1::Flucytosine}}

A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease being treated with inhaled steroids develops oral candidiasis. Which antifungal medication is indicated for this patient?

{{c1::Nystatin}}

What is the mechanism of action of nystatin?

It forms membrane {{c1::pores}} on fungi, allowing {{c1::electrolytes}} to leak

What are two indications for topical nystatin?

Vaginal {{c1::candidiasis}}
{{c1::Diaper rash}}

Which antifungal agent acts like amphotericin B, but is only available in topical formulations because of systemic toxicity?

{{c1::Nystatin}}
fields.Back Extra: It has the same mechanism of action as amphotericin B.

fields.Text:
What is the most serious adverse effect of flucytosine?

{{c1::Myelosuppression}}

What is the mechanism of action of flucytosine?

Flucytosine is converted to {{c1::5-fluorouracil}} by {{c1::cytosine deaminase}} → {{c1::5-fluorouracil}} inhibits {{c1::DNA}} and {{c1::RNA}} synthesis

In combination with amphotericin B, flucytosine is indicated in the treatment of what condition?

{{c1::Systemic}} fungal infections
fields.Back Extra: This is especially with meningitis caused by Cryptococcus.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action that leads to liver dysfunction when azoles are used in the treatment of fungal infections?

Inhibition of {{c1::cytochrome P-450}}

A patient being treated for systemic mycoses develops gynecomastia. What is the most likely causal agent?

{{c1::Ketoconazole}}
fields.Back Extra: This is secondary to the inhibition of testosterone synthesis.

fields.Text:
Isavuconazole is indicated for which two fungal infections?

Serious {{c1::Mucor}} infection
Serious {{c1::Aspergillus}} infection

Which azole antifungal medication is indicated for Aspergillus and some Candida infections?

{{c1::Voriconazole}}

Which two azoles are commonly used to treat topical fungal infections?

{{c1::Miconazole}}
{{c1::Clotrimazole}}

Itraconazole is indicated for which four fungal infections?

{{c1::Histoplasma}}
{{c1::Blastomyces}}
{{c1::Coccidioides}}
{{c1::Sporothrix schenckii}}

In patients with HIV, what is the indication for use of fluconazole?

Long-term suppression of {{c1::cryptococcal meningitis}}

Localized or less serious systemic mycoses are an indication for which class of antifungal agents?

{{c1::Azoles}}

What is the mechanism of action of azoles?

They block fungal synthesis of sterols by inhibiting {{c1::cytochrome P-450}} enzymes from converting {{c1::lanosterol}} to {{c1::ergosterol}}

Fluconazole is indicated for the treatment of which common fungal infection?

{{c1::Candidal}} infections of all types
fields.Back Extra: This can also be used for the suppression of cryptococcal meningitis in patients with HIV.

fields.Text:
What are the four most common adverse effects of terbinafine therapy?

Gastrointestinal {{c1::upset}}
{{c1::Headache}}
{{c1::Taste}} disturbances
{{c1::Hepatotoxicity}}

Which antifungal agent is primarily used to treat dermatophytoses, especially onychomycosis?

{{c1::Terbinafine}}

What is the mechanism of action of terbinafine?

Inhibits {{c1::squalene epoxidase}} in fungal cells

What are the two most common adverse effects of echinocandins?

Gastrointestinal {{c1::upset}}
{{c1::Flushing}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to the release of histamine.

fields.Text:
Which two infections are the echinocandins used to treat?

Invasive {{c1::aspergillosis}}
{{c1::Candida}} infections

What is the mechanism of action of the echinocandins?

Inhibition of {{c1::β-glucan}} synthesis, which disrupts {{c1::cell wall}} synthesis

What are the three medications classified as echinocandins?

{{c1::Anidulafungin}}
{{c1::Caspofungin}}
{{c1::Micafungin}}

What is the mechanism by which echinocandins cause flushing?

Release of {{c1::histamine}}

A young female presents for treatment of tinea corporis. What do you need to remember when considering the antifungal griseofulvin for her?

It is {{c1::teratogenic}} and contraindicated in {{c1::pregnancy}}
fields.Back Extra: A pregnancy test should be performed before starting therapy.

fields.Text:
What is the effect of griseofulvin on warfarin metabolism?

It {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} warfarin metabolism because it is a {{c1::cytochrome P-450}} inducer

What are two clinical uses of griseofulvin?

{{c1::Superficial}} infections
{{c1::Dermatophytoses}}

Which antifungal agent deposits into keratin-containing tissues, thus making it effective against dermatophyte infections?

{{c1::Griseofulvin}}

What is the mechanism of action of griseofulvin?

Inhibition of {{c1::microtubule}} function, thereby disrupting {{c1::mitosis}}

A patient being treated for ringworm experiences flushing, tachycardia, and hypotension after a bachelor party. What drug interaction occurred?

{{c1::Alcohol}} and {{c1::griseofulvin}} caused a {{c1::disulfiram}}-like reaction

What antiprotozoal agent is used to treat leishmaniasis?

{{c1::Sodium stibogluconate}}

What antiprotozoal agent is used to treat Trypanosoma cruzi infection?

{{c1::Nifurtimox}}

What two antiprotozoal agents are used to treat Trypanosoma brucei infection?

{{c1::Suramin}}
{{c1::Melarsoprol}}

What antiprotozoal agent is used to treat toxoplasmosis?

{{c1::Pyrimethamine}}

Which three anti-mite/louse agents may be used to treat an infection with scabies or lice?

{{c1::Permethrin}}
{{c1::Malathion}}
{{c1::Ivermectin}}

What is the mechanism of action of malathion?

It inhibits {{c1::mite}}/{{c1::louse}} {{c1::acetylcholinesterases}}

A patient reports blurry vision after being treated for malaria. What is the most likely cause?

{{c1::Chloroquine}}-induced retinopathy

Which three antimalarial agents can be administered to a patient with a life-threatening malaria infection?

{{c1::Quinidine}} in the United States
{{c1::Quinine}} outside the United States
{{c1::Artesunate}}

Which two combinations of medications are indicated for a patient with malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum?

{{c1::Artemether}} + {{c1::Lumefantrine}}
{{c1::Atovaquone}} + {{c1::Proguanil}}

What is the mechanism of resistance of Plasmodium falciparum to chloroquine?

{{c1::Membrane pumps}} decrease intracellular concentrations of the drug

What is the mechanism of action of chloroquine?

Stops the detoxification of {{c1::heme}} into {{c1::hemozoin}} → Accumulation of {{c1::heme}}, which is toxic to plasmodia

Which medication is indicated in the treatment of plasmodia malaria (not including Plasmodium falciparum)?

{{c1::Chloroquine}}

What adverse effect is more commonly seen in dark-skinned individuals taking chloroquine?

{{c1::Pruritus}}

Which five agents can be used to treat helminthic infections?

{{c1::Pyrantel pamoate}}
{{c1::Ivermectin}}
{{c1::Mebendazole}}
{{c1::Praziquantel}}
{{c1::Diethylcarbamazine}}

What is the mechanism of action of mebendazole?

Inhibition of {{c1::microtubules}}

What is the mechanism of action of praziquantel?

It increases {{c1::Ca2+}} permeability and vacuolization

Which drug class stops viral particle budding and release in HIV-infected cells and allows HIV proteins to remain within cells?

{{c1::Protease}} inhibitors

What is a common suffix for the protease inhibitor class?

{{c1::-navir}}

What is the mechanism of action of an integrase inhibitor?

{{c1::Reversibly::Reversibly::Irreversibly}} blocks viral {{c1::DNA}} integration into the host cell genome for {{c1::transcription}}

What are the two NNRTIs that are commonly used to treat HIV?

{{c1::Efavirenz}}
{{c1::Nevirapine}}

Which two classes of HIV antiviral drugs act by inhibiting reverse transcriptase?

{{c1::NRTIs}}
{{c1::NNRTIs}}

Enfuvirtide blocks which genetic processes immediately downstream of penetration?

{{c1::Uncoating}}
{{c1::Reverse transcription}}

What is the mechanism of action of oseltamivir and zanamivir?

Inhibition of {{c1::neuraminidase}} → Blocks the release of progeny virus from the cell

Ribavarin is used to treat an infection with which two viruses?

{{c1::Respiratory syncytial virus}}
{{c1::Hepatitis C virus}}

What viruses are targeted by the antiviral medications, acyclovir and ganciclovir?

Acyclovir targets {{c1::HSV}} and {{c1::varicella zoster virus}}
Ganciclovir targets {{c1::cytomegalovirus}}

Which antiviral medications are inhibitors of viral DNA polymerase?

{{c1::Cidofovir}}
{{c1::Foscarnet}}

What is the mechanism of action of the antiviral medications acyclovir and ganciclovir?

They are {{c1::guanosine}} analogs that inhibit DNA {{c1::replication}}

Which antiviral medication prevents HIV virions from attaching to host cells?

{{c1::Maraviroc}}

Neuraminidase inhibitors are used to treat which viral infections?

{{c1::Influenza A}} infections
{{c1::Influenza B}} infections
fields.Back Extra: The two neuraminidase inhibitors are oseltamivir and zanamivir.

fields.Text:
How soon after the onset of influenza symptoms should treatment with oseltamivir or zanamivir be initiated?

Within {{c1::48}} hours of symptom onset

What is the shared mechanism of action of oseltamivir and zanamivir?

Inhibition of viral {{c1::neuraminidase}}, which blocks the release of viral progeny

Which strains of influenza are oseltamivir and zanamivir effective against?

{{c1::Influenza A}} infection
{{c1::Influenza B}} infection
fields.Back Extra: This is for both treatment and prevention.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of baloxavir?

It decreases viral replication by inhibiting the "{{c1::cap snatching}}" {{c1::endonuclease}} activity of influenza virus {{c1::RNA polymerase}}

What is the clinical use of baloxavir?

Decreases the duration of illness due to {{c1::influenza virus}} if taken within {{c1::48}} hours of symptom onset

What is the clinical use for remdesivir?

Treatment of patients with {{c1::COVID-19}} who require hospitalization

What is the mechanism of action of remdesivir?

It inhibits viral {{c1::RNA-dependent RNA polymerase}}
It evades proofreading by viral {{c1::exoribonuclease}}
fields.Back Extra:
Hence, it decreases production of viral RNA.

It is a prodrug of an ATP analog.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of resistance for valacyclovir?

Mutation in viral {{c1::thymidine kinase}}

What are two major adverse effects of acyclovir, famciclovir, and valacyclovir?

Acute {{c1::kidney::organ}} injury
{{c1::Obstructive crystalline nephropathy}}
fields.Back Extra: This is in association with inadequate hydration.

fields.Text:
Which antiviral medication is most appropriate for treating herpes zoster?

{{c1::Famciclovir}}

What is the advantage of using valacyclovir over acyclovir?

Valacyclovir is a prodrug of acyclovir with better oral {{c1::bioavailability}}

What is the activity of acyclovir, famciclovir, or valacyclovir against latent varicella-zoster virus and HSV?

{{c1::None}}

Why are acyclovir and valacyclovir not useful against cytomegalovirus?

The virus lacks {{c1::thymidine kinase}}
fields.Back Extra: This is required to activate the guanosine analogs.

fields.Text:
Acyclovir, famciclovir, and valacyclovir are guanosine analogs that inhibit which viral enzyme?

Viral {{c1::DNA polymerase}}

Why does acyclovir interfere with viral DNA synthesis and not human DNA synthesis?

It requires {{c1::monophosphorylation}} by the {{c1::thymidine kinase}} of HSV or varicella-zoster virus
Inactive in uninfected cells

What are the three first-line antiviral agents used to treat HSV and varicella-zoster virus infections?

{{c1::Valacyclovir}}
{{c1::Famciclovir}}
{{c1::Acyclovir}}

What are three indications for acyclovir, famciclovir, and valacyclovir?

{{c1::HSV}}-induced {{c1::oral}}/{{c1::genital}} lesions
{{c1::HSV}}-induced {{c1::encephalitis}}
Prophylaxis against {{c1::HSV}} for immunocompromised individuals or immunocompetent patients with severe/recurrent infections

What is the mechanism of resistance of ganciclovir?

Mutation of viral {{c1::kinase}}

What are two adverse effects of taking ganciclovir?

{{c1::Myelosuppression}}
{{c1::Renal}} toxicity

What advantage does valganciclovir have over ganciclovir?

Valganciclovir has better oral {{c1::bioavailability}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because it is a prodrug of ganciclovir.

fields.Text:
Which antiviral medication is indicated for an immunocompromised patient with a cytomegalovirus infection?

{{c1::Ganciclovir}}

Ganciclovir inhibits which viral enzyme?

Viral {{c1::DNA polymerase}}

What is the mechanism of action of ganciclovir?

{{c1::Guanosine}} analog that inhibits viral {{c1::DNA polymerase}}

What is the mechanism of resistance of foscarnet?

{{c1::DNA polymerase}} mutation

What are the adverse effects of foscarnet therapy?

{{c1::Electrolyte}} abnormalities → Seizures
{{c1::Nephrotoxicity}}

Which antiviral agent should be considered for a patient with acyclovir-resistant HSV?

{{c1::Foscarnet}}

Which antiviral agent should be considered for an immunocompromised patient that has cytomegalovirus retinitis refractory to ganciclovir?

{{c1::Foscarnet}}

Where does foscarnet bind on viruses?

The {{c1::pyrophosphate}}-binding site of either viral DNA/RNA polymerase or HIV reverse transcriptase

What is the major adverse effect of cidofovir and how can it be minimized?

The major adverse effect is {{c1::nephrotoxicity}}
The major adverse effect can be minimized with {{c1::probenecid}} and intravenous {{c1::saline}} solution

What is the mechanism of action of cidofovir?

Inhibits viral {{c1::DNA polymerase}}

What are the two major indications for use of cidofovir?

{{c1::Cytomegalovirus retinitis}} in immunocompromised patients
{{c1::Acyclovir}}-resistant {{c1::HSV}} infections

What is the mechanism of action of maraviroc?

Inhibits viral attachment by binding to {{c1::CCR-5}} on T-cells and monocytes → Prevents {{c1::CCR-5}} interaction with {{c1::gp120}}

A patient receiving a new HIV drug regimen has had several skin reactions at the site of injection. What drug was she prescribed?

{{c1::Enfuvirtide}}

Which class of HIV medication binds to the gp41 protein?

{{c1::Entry}} inhibitors
fields.Back Extra: This is enfuvirtide, which inhibits fusion.

fields.Text:
A patient being treated for HIV is noted to have an elevated creatine kinase level and weight gain. Which class of drugs is the most likely cause?

{{c1::Integrase}} inhibitor

What is the mechanism of action of elvitegravir?

As an {{c1::integrase}} inhibitor, elvitegravir stops {{c1::HIV}} genome {{c1::integration}} into the host cell {{c1::DNA}}

A patient with active tuberculosis is found to be HIV-positive. How must the treatment regimen for either diagnosis be modified?

Rifampin causes potent {{c1::CYP}}/{{c1::UGT}} induction that decreases {{c1::protease}} inhibitor levels; it should be replaced with {{c1::rifabutin}}

A patient receiving antiretroviral therapy for HIV has nausea, diarrhea, lipodystrophy, and episodes of hyperglycemia. Which class of drugs is the patient likely taking?

An HIV {{c1::protease}} inhibitor

Is ritonavir a cytochrome P-450 inhibitor or inducer?

{{c1::Inhibitor}}

What is the function of the HIV-1 protease from the pol gene?

Cleaves {{c1::polypeptides}} made from HIV {{c1::mRNA}} into functional components
fields.Back Extra: Therefore, protease inhibitors prevent the maturation of new viruses.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of protease inhibitors?

They stop viral {{c1::maturation}} by preventing the formation of {{c1::polypeptide}} products

What are two common adverse effects of efavirenz?

{{c1::Central nervous system}} symptoms
{{c1::Vivid}} dreams

What are two common adverse effects of all NNRTIs?

{{c1::Rash}}
{{c1::Hepatotoxicity}}

Which drug is contraindicated in a patient who has HIV and an HLA-B*5701 mutation?

{{c1::Abacavir}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because of increased risk of hypersensitivity.

fields.Text:
Anion gap metabolic acidosis develops in a patient being treated for HIV. What is the most likely cause?

{{c1::NRTI}}-induced {{c1::lactic acidosis}}

Which drugs are indicated for counteracting myelosuppression secondary to HIV treatment?

{{c1::G-CSF}}
{{c1::Erythropoietin}}
fields.Back Extra: This is to combat bone marrow suppression.

fields.Text:
Which NRTI is indicated for a pregnant patient who is HIV-positive?

{{c1::Zidovudine}}
fields.Back Extra: This can reduce the risk of vertical transmission and is also used for general prophylaxis.

fields.Text:
Which NRTI used for HIV does not require intracellular phosphorylation?

{{c1::Tenofovir}}
fields.Back Extra: This is already a nucleotide; all other NRTIs require phosphorylation.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of NRTIs?

Inhibits nucleotide binding to {{c1::reverse transcriptase}} due to the lack of {{c1::3}}' {{c1::OH}} group, thus stopping {{c1::DNA}} synthesis
fields.Back Extra: NRTIs must be phosphorylated to be activated.

fields.Text:
What is the recommended combination of antiretroviral therapy medication classes in HIV therapy?

Two {{c1::NRTIs}} and a third agent
fields.Back Extra: For the third agent, integrase inhibitors are preferred.

fields.Text:
What are three strong indications for initiation of antiretroviral therapy for HIV?

High viral {{c1::load}}
CD4+ cell count <{{c1::500}} cells/mm3
Presence of {{c1::AIDS}}-defining illness

Which class of antiretroviral drugs are not effective against both HIV-1 and HIV-2?

{{c1::NNRTIs}} and {{c1::enfuvirtide}} are only effective against HIV-{{c1::1}}

What is the mechanism of action of NNRTIs?

Binding of {{c1::reverse transcriptase}} at different locations than {{c1::NRTIs}}
fields.Back Extra: NNRTIs do not require phosphorylation or completion with nucleotides to be activated.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of the anti-hepatitis C virus drugs simeprevir and grazoprevir?

Inhibition of hepatitis C virus {{c1::protease}}
fields.Back Extra:
Hence, this will prevent viral replication.

This is specifically NS3/4A.

fields.Text:
What are the two most common adverse effects of the NS5B inhibitors, sofosbuvir and dasabuvir?

{{c1::Headache}}
{{c1::Fatigue}}

What is the mechanism of action of sofosbuvir and dasabuvir?

Inhibition of {{c1::NS5B}}, an {{c1::RNA-dependent RNA polymerase}} that serves as a chain {{c1::terminator}} → Prevents viral replication

What is a major hematologic adverse effect of ribavirin?

{{c1::Hemolytic}} anemia

What is the mechanism of action of ribavirin?

Competitive inhibition of {{c1::IMP dehydrogenase}} → Inhibits synthesis of {{c1::guanine}} nucleotides

What is the mechanism of action of ledipasvir, ombitasvir, and velpatasvir?

{{c1::NS5A}} inhibition → Prevents {{c1::RNA}} replication

What are the two most common adverse effects of grazoprevir?

{{c1::Headache}}
{{c1::Fatigue}}

A patient with hepatitis C refractory to newer therapies is in need of which medication adjunct?

{{c1::Ribavirin}}

Combinations of which three drug classes can be used to treat chronic hepatitis C infections?

{{c1::NS5A}} inhibitors
{{c1::NS5B}} inhibitors
{{c1::NS3/4A}} inhibitors

What are the two most common adverse effects of NS5A inhibitors?

{{c1::Diarrhea}}
{{c1::Headache}}

What are the two most common dermatologic adverse effects of simeprevir?

{{c1::Photosensitivity}}
{{c1::Rash}}

When selecting appropriate treatment of hepatitis C infection in pregnant women, which medication should be avoided?

{{c1::Ribavirin}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because of severe teratogenicity.

fields.Text:
How do iodine and iodophores work to control infection?

{{c1::Halogenation}} of proteins, DNA, and RNA

What is the mechanism of action of hydrogen peroxide in infection control?

Induction of {{c1::free radical oxidation}}

Which two infection control techniques disrupt cell membranes?

{{c1::Alcohols}}
{{c1::Chlorhexidine}}

What is autoclaving?

An infection control technique that involves the use of {{c1::pressurized steam}} at temperatures > {{c1::120}}°C

What is the difference between disinfection and sterilization?

Disinfection reduces the number of of pathogenic organisms to a {{c1::safe}} level
Sterilization inactivates {{c1::all}} microbes

The autoclave is not reliably successful against what pathologic agents?

{{c1::Prions}}

What is the mechanism of action of chlorine in infection control?

{{c1::Oxidizes}} and {{c1::denatures}} proteins

What is the mechanism of action of quaternary amines on microbes?

Impairment of cell membrane {{c1::permeability}}

What is the mechanism of action of ethylene oxide in infection control?

{{c1::Alkylation}}

Which two commonly used disinfection and sterilization techniques are not sporicidal?

{{c1::Alcohols}}
{{c1::Quaternary amines}}

Which six disinfection and sterilization techniques are sporicidal?

{{c1::Autoclaving}}
{{c1::Chlorine}}
{{c1::Ethylene oxide}}
{{c1::Hydrogen peroxide}}
{{c1::Iodine}}
{{c1::Iodophors}}

How does chlorhexidine affect the intracellular components of pathologic agents in infection control?

{{c1::Coagulates}} intracellular components

Why should chloramphenicol not be prescribed for pregnant patients?

It can cause {{c1::gray baby}} syndrome

In a pregnant patient taking a tetracycline, what adverse effect would be expected in the fetus?

{{c1::Discolored}} teeth
Inhibited {{c1::bone}} growth

In a pregnant patient taking a fluoroquinolone, what adverse effect would be expected in the fetus?

{{c1::Cartilage}} damage

In a pregnant patient taking an aminoglycoside, what adverse effect would be expected in the fetus?

{{c1::Ototoxicity}}

In a pregnant patient taking a sulfonamide, what adverse effect would be expected in the fetus?

{{c1::Kernicterus}}

Which antibiotics should be avoided in pregnancy?

{{c1::Sulfonamides}}
{{c1::Aminoglycosides}}
{{c1::Fluoroquinolones}}
{{c1::Clarithromycin}}
{{c1::Tetracyclines}}
{{c1::Ribavirin}}
{{c1::Griseofulvin}}
{{c1::Chloramphenicol}}

How does Barrett esophagus affect the risk of developing esophageal adenocarcinoma?

A patient with Barret esophagus is at {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} risk because {{c1::metaplasia}} may progress to {{c1::dysplasia}} and {{c1::neoplasia}} with persistent exposure to the insult
fields.Back Extra: Gastric acid is the insult in this case.

fields.Text:
What changes would be seen on upper endoscopic biopsy that would confirm a diagnosis of Barrett esophagus in a patient with long-standing gastroesophageal reflux disease?

{{c1::Columnar::Squamous/Cuboidal/Columnar}} epithelium is replaced by {{c1::squamous::squamous/cuboidal/columnar}} epithelium

What is hyperplasia?

{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in cell {{c1::number}} due to controlled {{c1::proliferation}} of cells

What are three cellular mechanisms that result in atrophy?

Increrased {{c1::cytoskeleton}} degradation
Decreased {{c1::protein}} synthesis
{{c1::Apoptosis}}

What cellular injury would result from traumatic injury to the median nerve?

{{c1::Atrophy}} secondary to denervation

What cellular changes result in hypertrophy?

{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in {{c1::structural}} proteins and organelles → {{c1::Larger::Larger/Smaller}} cell size

What two pathologic processes usually precede dysplasia?

Persistent {{c1::metaplasia}}
Pathologic {{c1::hyperplasia::hyperplasia/hypoplasia}}

What are the two main differences between mild dysplasia and severe dysplasia?

Mild/moderate dysplasia → {{c1::Reversible::Reversible/Irreversible}}, only involves part of the {{c1::epithelium}}
Severe dysplasia → {{c1::Irreversible::Reversible/Irreversible}}, progresses to {{c1::carcinoma in situ}}

Define cellular dysplasia.

{{c1::Disordered}} or {{c1::precancerous}} growth of epithelial cells

Define cellular atrophy.

Decrease in tissue {{c1::mass}} caused by decreased cell {{c1::size}} and/or reduced cell {{c1::number}}

What cellular adaptation response can you expect in the respiratory epithelium of patient with a long history of tobacco smoking?

{{c1::Metaplasia}}
fields.Back Extra: Ciliated columnar epithelium has been replaced by stratified squamous epithelium as a result of recurrent exposure to cigarette smoke.

fields.Text:
Briefly explain the mechanism of metaplasia.

{{c1::Reprogramming}} of {{c1::stem}} cells → {{c1::Replacement}} of one cell type with another that is better suited to handle the new {{c1::stress}}

What is the major difference between metaplasia and dysplasia?

Metaplasia is a change in cell {{c1::type}}
Dysplasia is a change in cell {{c1::structure}}

Endometrial ultrasonography of a 29-year-old pregnant patient shows uterine enlargement. What type of cellular adaptation has occurred?

Physiologic {{c1::hypertrophy::hypertrophy/hypotrophy}}

What are five possible causes of atrophy?

Poor {{c1::nutrition}}
{{c1::Denervation}}
{{c1::Disuse}}
Loss of {{c1::blood supply}}
Loss of {{c1::hormonal}} stimulation

What three molecular and cellular changes are characteristic of cellular dysplasia?

Abnormal {{c1::nuclear}} changes
{{c1::Pleomorphisim}}
Loss of tissue {{c1::orientation}}

What is a type of metaplasia that can occur after trauma?

{{c1::Myositis ossificans}}

During irreversible cell injury, what are the consequences of the breakdown of the plasma membrane?

Leakage of cytosolic {{c1::enzymes}} into the blood
Influx of {{c1::calcium}}
fields.Back Extra: This results in the activation of degradative enzymes.

fields.Text:
A tissue biopsy specimen shows membrane blebbing and clumping of chromatin after a period of hypoxia. What type of cell injury did the tissue sustain based on the findings?

{{c1::Reversible::Reversible/Irreversible}} cell injury

Mitochondrial permeability and loss of the electron transport chain correspond with what type of generalized cell injury?

{{c1::Irreversible::Reversible/Irreversible}} cell injury

Ribosomal detachment and decreased protein synthesis correspond with what type of generalized cell injury?

{{c1::Reversible::Reversible/Irreversible}} cell injury

What is the earliest morphologic manifestation of reversible cell injury?

Cell {{c1::swelling}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to low ATP levels resulting in reduced activity of Ca2+ and Na+/K+ pumps.

fields.Text:
What are three nuclear changes seen in irreversible cell injury?

{{c1::Pyknosis}} → Nuclear condensation
{{c1::Karyorrhexis}} → Nuclear fragmentation
{{c1::Karolysis}} → Nuclear dissolution

What process leads to the nucleus being disintegrated by karyorrhexis?

Cleavage by {{c1::endonucleases}}

Lysosomal rupture corresponds with what type of generalized cell injury?

{{c1::Irreversible::Reversible/Irreversible}} cell injury

Rapid loss of cell function is seen in which type of cell injury?

{{c1::Reversible::Reversible/Irreversible}} cell injury

An elevation in serum troponin levels after myocardial ischemia corresponds with what type of generalized cell injury?

{{c1::Irreversible::Reversible/Irreversible}} cell injury
fields.Back Extra: There is leakage of cytosolic proteins after membrane damage.

fields.Text:
Noncontractile myocardial cells being noted within minutes of myocardial ischemia corresponds with what type of generalized cell injury?

{{c1::Reversible::Reversible/Irreversible}} cell injury
fields.Back Extra: There is rapid loss of cellular function.

fields.Text:
Myelin figures correspond with what type of generalized cell injury?

{{c1::Reversible::Reversible/Irreversible}} cell injury

Amorphic densities seen within mitochondria indicate which type of cell injury?

{{c1::Irreversible::Reversible/Irreversible}} cell injury

What is the final common target of the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways of apoptosis?

Activation of {{c1::caspases}}

What two seperate mechanisms trigger the extrinsic apoptotic pathway?

{{c1::Ligand}}-receptor interactions
Tc cells releasing {{c1::granzyme B}} and {{c1::perforin}}

What happens to apoptotic bodies after they are formed?

They are {{c1::phagocytosed}}

What are some of the histologic features seen in cells undergoing apoptosis?

{{c1::Eosinophilic}} cytoplasm
Cell {{c1::shrinkage}}
{{c1::Basophilic}} nucleus
{{c1::Pyknosis}}
Membrane {{c1::blebbing}}
Nuclear {{c1::fragmentation}}

What is energy-dependent programmed cell death called?

{{c1::Apoptosis}}

What might be seen on DNA gel electrophoresis of a sample containing genetic material from apoptotic cells?

DNA {{c1::laddering}}
fields.Back Extra: The fragments are in multiples of 180 base pairs.

fields.Text:
Under what two conditions does intrinsic apoptosis occur?

Tissue {{c1::remodeling}} during embryogenesis
Exposure to {{c1::noxious}} stimuli

What are the two proapoptotic proteins and two antiapoptotic proteins involved in the intrinsic pathway?

Proapoptotic → {{c1::BAX}} and {{c1::BAK}}
Antiapoptotic → {{c1::Bcl-2}} and {{c1::Bcl-xL}}

How does apoptosis differ from necrosis?

In apoptosis, the cell membrane remains relatively intact and significant inflammation {{c1::does not::does/does not}} occur

A defect in which apoptotic pathway results in autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome?

{{c1::Extrinsic::Intrinsic/Extrinsic}} pathway
fields.Back Extra: This is due to defective Fas/FasL interactions.

fields.Text:
What is the consequence of defective Fas-FasL interaction in regard to negative selection in the thymus?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} number of self-reacting lymphocytes due to failure of {{c1::clonal deletion}}

Which cytokine mediates resolution of an immunologic reaction leading to apoptosis of the involved effector cells?

A decrease in {{c1::IL-2}} after a completed immunologic reaction causes apoptosis of proliferating effector cells
fields.Back Extra: This is via the intrinsic pathway.

fields.Text:
Describe the mechanism of action of the proapoptotic factors BAX and BAK.

BAX and BAK form {{c1::pores}} in the mitochondrial membrane → Release of {{c1::cytochrome C}} in the cytoplasm → Activation of {{c1::caspases}}

Describe the mechanism of action of antiapoptotic factor Bcl-2.

Bcl-2 prevents the release of {{c1::cytochrome C}} by keeping the mitochondrial membrane {{c1::impermeable}}

What is the mechanism of tumorigenesis in follicular lymphoma?

{{c1::Bcl-2}} overexpression → Decreased {{c1::caspase}} activation → Tumorigenesis

A patient in the ICU requiring multiple pressors for cardiogenic shock has the findings shown in the image. What is the cause of this?



Limb {{c1::ischemia}} secondary to long-term pressor use

What is the difference between dry gangrene and wet gangrene?

Dry gangrene is due to {{c1::ischemia}}
Wet gangrene is due to {{c1::superinfection}}

What is the mechanism that leads to fibrinoid necrosis?

{{c1::Immune complex}} deposition
Leakage of {{c1::plasma}} proteins from a damaged vessel

What histologic features are seen in the type of necrosis shown in the image?



Fragmented cells and debris surrounded by {{c1::lymphocytes}} and {{c1::macrophages}}

What type of necrosis is shown in the image?



{{c1::Coagulative}} necrosis

What are the histologic features of fat necrosis?

Outlines of dead fat cells {{c1::without::with/without}} peripheral nuclei
{{c1::Dark blue::Color}} appearance of {{c1::saponified}} fat on H&E stain

What type of necrosis occurs in tuberculosis, systemic mycoses, and Nocardia infections?

{{c1::Caseous}} necrosis

A man with a history of alcoholism has recurrent bouts of acute pancreatitis. What is the cause of the findings seen in the biopsy specimen shown in the image?



Damaged pancreatic cells release {{c1::lipase}} → {{c1::Lipase}} breaks down triglycerides → Free fatty acids bind to {{c1::calcium}} → Saponification
fields.Back Extra: This appears dark blue on an H&E stain.

fields.Text:
What are the early and late changes associated with liquefactive necrosis in the brain?

Early changes → Cell {{c1::debris}} and {{c1::macrophages}}
Late changes → Formation of {{c1::cavities}} and {{c1::cystic}} spaces

What is the mechanism of caseous necrosis?

{{c1::Macrophages}} wall off the infecting microorganism → {{c1::Granular}} debris

What histologic features are seen in coagulative necrosis?

Increased cytoplasmic binding of {{c1::eosin}} dye
Loss of {{c1::nuclei}}
Preserved cell {{c1::outlines}} with absence of {{c1::nuclei}}

What type of necrosis can be seen in the artery biopsy specimen shown in the image?



{{c1::Fibrinoid}} necrosis
fields.Back Extra: The vessel walls are thick and pink, containing proteinaceous material.

fields.Text:
What two conditions present with fibrinoid necrosis?

{{c1::Immune}} vascular reactions
{{c1::Nonimmune}} vascular reactions

What is the mechanism of the necrosis shown in the image?



{{c1::Neutrophils}} release {{c1::lysosomal}} enzymes that digest tissue
fields.Back Extra: This is liquefactive necrosis in the brain.

fields.Text:
A patient has a lung abscess secondary to a staphylococcal infection. What type of necrosis might be seen on microscopic analysis?

{{c1::Liquefactive}} necrosis
fields.Back Extra: This is seen with bacterial abscesses.

fields.Text:
Which type of necrosis most commonly occurs in the limbs and the gastrointestinal tract secondary to chronic ischemia?

{{c1::Gangrenous}} necrosis

When is coagulative necrosis usually seen?

After the occurance of {{c1::ischemia}} or {{c1::infarction}} in most tissues
fields.Back Extra: The exception to this is in the brain.

fields.Text:
What is the major difference between necrosis and apoptosis?

Necrosis is associated with local {{c1::inflammation}} and breakdown of the cellular {{c1::membrane}}

What is the mechanism by which an exogenous injury to a tissue results in necrosis?

Plasma membrane damage → Enzymatic degradation and protein breakdown within cells → {{c1::Leakage}} of intracellular components → Local inflammation

What are the two conditions in which fat necrosis is seen?

Acute {{c1::pancreatitis}}
{{c1::Trauma}}

What parts of the nephron are most susceptible to ischemic injury?

{{c1::Thick::Thick/Thin}} {{c1::ascending::ascending/descending}} limb
Straight segment of the {{c1::proximal::proximal/distal}} tubule
fields.Back Extra: These are both in the medulla of the kidney.

fields.Text:
Which region of the heart is most susceptible to ischemia?

{{c1::Subendocardial}} tissue
fields.Back Extra: This is especially in the left ventricle because it lies farthest from the arterial supply.

fields.Text:
What is the definition of a watershed area?

Area with {{c1::low::high/low}} blood supply due to its distance from the {{c1::distal::proximal/distal}} branches of arteries

Which parts of the brain are most susceptible to hypoxia?

{{c1::Anterior cerebral}} artery boundary area
{{c1::Middle cerebral}} artery boundary area
{{c1::Posterior cerebral}} artery boundary area
fields.Back Extra: This is because they are watershed areas.

fields.Text:
Which neurons are primarily affected by hypoxic-ischemic insults?

{{c1::Pyramidal}} cells of the neocortex and hippocampus
{{c1::Purkinje}} cells of the cerebellum
fields.Back Extra: In the neocortex, zones 3, 5, and 6 are involved.

fields.Text:
An elderly patient has ischemic colitis after an episode of profound shock. What areas of the gastrointestinal tract are likely affected?

{{c1::Rectosigmoid}} junction
{{c1::Splenic}} flexure
fields.Back Extra: These are both watershed areas of the colon.

fields.Text:
The hepatic lobule is seperated into three histological zones based on oxygen supply. Which zone is most susceptible to ischemia?

Zone {{c1::III}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the area around the central vein.

fields.Text:
How does atherosclerotic disease increase susceptibility to ischemia?

By decreasing arterial {{c1::perfusion}}

What is the cause of ischemia in a patient with Budd-Chiari syndrome or testicular torsion?

Decreased venous {{c1::drainage}}

The specimen shown is a prime example of which type of infarct?



{{c1::Red}} infarct
fields.Back Extra: This is in a lung, which has multiple blood supplies.

fields.Text:
The specimen shown is a prime example of which type of infarct?



{{c1::Pale}} infarct
fields.Back Extra: This is in a kidney, which has an end-arterial blood supply.

fields.Text:
What type of infarct usually occurs in the heart and kidneys?

{{c1::Pale}} infarct
fields.Back Extra: This is due to a single, end-arterial blood supply.

fields.Text:
In which instances do pale infarcts occur?

They occur in organs with an {{c1::end-arterial}} blood supply

In three which instances do red infarcts occur?

Venous {{c1::occlusion}}
{{c1::Reperfusion}} injury
Tissues with {{c1::multiple}} blood supplies

What type of infarct may be seen in the intestine, liver, lungs, and testes?

{{c1::Red}} infarct
fields.Back Extra: This is due to venous occlusion and multiple blood supplies.

fields.Text:
A patient has a rising troponin level with persistent ST changes on ECG shortly after emergent angioplasty. What is a possible explanation for the findings?

{{c1::Reperfusion}} injury from {{c1::free radical}} damage

Which two metal storage diseases can result in free radical injury?

{{c1::Wilson}} disease
{{c1::Hemochromatosis}}

Free radical damage by carbon tetrachloride leads to what pathologic processes?

{{c1::Fatty}} changes in the liver
{{c1::Centrilobular necrosis}} in the liver

What type of free radical injury is of greatest concern in a patient who has recently undergone thrombolysis for acute limb ischemia?

{{c1::Reperfusion}} injury

Free radical injury can be induced by exposure to what six substances and processes?

{{c1::Radiation}}
{{c1::Drug}} metabolism
{{c1::Transition}} metals
{{c1::Redox}} reactions
{{c1::Nitric oxide}}
Leukocyte {{c1::oxidative burst}}

Name three vitamins with antioxidant properties involved in removal of free radicals.

Vitamin {{c1::A}}
Vitamin {{c1::C}}
Vitamin {{c1::E}}

Name three scavenging enzymes responsible for degradation of free radicals.

{{c1::Catalase}}
{{c1::Glutathione peroxidase}}
{{c1::Superoxide dismutase}}

An infant born at 22 weeks develops blindness and respiratory distress after receiving oxygen therapy. Abnormal vascularization is noted on fundoscopic exam. What is the mechanism of injury?

Oxygen-mediated {{c1::free radical}} injury → Retinopathy of prematurity and bronchopulmonary dysplasia

Name four processes by which free radicals are eliminated.

{{c1::Scavenging}} enzymes
{{c1::Antioxidants}}
{{c1::Metal carrier}} proteins
Spontaneous {{c1::decay}}

Free radicals damage cells by which three main mechanisms?

DNA {{c1::breakage}}
Membrane lipid {{c1::peroxidation}}
Protein {{c1::modification}}

How does ionizing radiation induce cellular and DNA damage?

By production of {{c1::free radicals}}
fields.Back Extra: This is through direct and indirect manners.

fields.Text:
Why does radiotherapy damage cancer cells more than healthy cells?

Cancer cells have impaired {{c1::DNA repair}} mechanisms making them prone to damage in addition to {{c1::high::high/low}} replicative rates

Which type of tissues are most susceptible to injury?

Rapidly {{c1::regenerating}} tissues

Name the skin manifestations of acute radiation syndrome.

{{c1::Hair}} loss
{{c1::Erythema}}
{{c1::Ulcers}}
{{c1::Necrosis}}

What is the common hematopoietic manifestation of acute radiation syndrome?

{{c1::Myelosuppression}}

What are three organs that might be affected by acute local toxicity secondary to ionizing radiation?

{{c1::Skin}}
{{c1::Gonads}}
{{c1::Eyes}}

H&E stain of a lung tissue specimen from a patient with tuberculosis is shown in the image. What is indicated by the yellow star?



{{c1::Calcium}} deposits
fields.Back Extra: This appears basophilic on the H&E stain.

fields.Text:
Name three disorders that lead to metastatic calcification.

{{c1::Sarcoidosis}}
{{c1::Hyperparathyriodism::Hyperparathyriodism/Hypoparathyriodism}}
{{c1::Hypervitaminosis D}}

Name three common sites of metastatic calcification.

{{c1::Interstitial}} tissues of the lungs
{{c1::Kidneys::Organ}}
{{c1::Gastric}} mucosa

What would you expect serum Ca2+ levels to be in an elderly patient with a calcified aortic valve?

{{c1::Normal}}

Differentiate dystrophic and metastatic calcification based on extent of calcification.

Dystrophic clacification → {{c1::Localized::Localized/Widespread}} Ca2+ deposition in {{c1::abnormal::normal/abnormal}} tissues after injury
Metastatic calcification → {{c1::Widespread::Localized/Widespread}} Ca2+ deposition in {{c1::normal::normal/abnormal}} tissues

What type of calcification is present in granulomatous infections, infarcts and thrombi, congenital cytomegalovirus, and CREST syndrome?

{{c1::Dystrophic}} calcification

What renal disorders might develop from metastatic calcification seen in nephrocalcinosis of the collecting ducts?

{{c1::Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus}}
{{c1::Renal}} failure

A tissue specimen obtained at autopsy of an elderly woman is shown. What molecular mechanism explains the findings shown?



The yellow-brown pigments, called {{c1::lipofuscin}}, are due to lipid {{c1::peroxidation}} of polyunsaturated lipids of subcellular membranes

Autopsy of an elderly man revealed yellow-brown pigments in most tissues, including the heart, colon, kidneys, and liver. What is the significance of these findings?

Accumulation of {{c1::lipofuscin}} pigments in various organs is part of the normal aging process
fields.Back Extra: This is the expected "wear and tear".

fields.Text:
What is lipofuscin composed of?

Polymers of {{c1::lipids}} and {{c1::phospholipids}} complexed with {{c1::protein}}

A 35-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has chronic renal failure. Kidney biopsy reveals abnormal findings as shown. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Secondary amyloidosis}}

What phenomenon associated with multiple myeloma is shown in the image?



{{c1::Apple-green::Color}} {{c1::birefringence}} on exposure to polarized light

Deposition of which amyloid protein is seen in medullary thyroid cancer?

{{c1::Calcitonin}}

Which type of amyloidosis is seen in patients with multiple myeloma?

{{c1::Primary}} amyloidosis

Describe the amyloidosis seen in type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Deposition of {{c1::islet amyloid polypeptide}} in the pancreatic islets

Describe the pathophysiology of amyloidosis in Alzheimer disease.

Depletion of {{c1::β-amyloid}} protein cleaved from {{c1::amyloid precursor}} protein

What is the abnormal protein in secondary amyloidosis derived from?

{{c1::AA}} fibrils
fields.Back Extra: These are composed of serum amyloid A.

fields.Text:
What is the abnormal protein in primary amyloidosis derived from?

{{c1::AL}} fibrils
fields.Back Extra: These are dervied from immunoglobulin light chains.

fields.Text:
What stains can be used to visualize amyloid deposits?

{{c1::Congo red}} staining
{{c1::H&E}} staining

Name three amyloid diseases that have systemic manifestations.

{{c1::Primary}} amyloidosis
{{c1::Secondary}} amyloidosis
{{c1::Dialysis}}-related amyloidosis

What genetic mutation is responsible for the hereditary form of amyloidosis?

{{c1::Transthyretin}} gene mutation

An 80-year-old man with no significant medical history has gradual decline in cardiac function due to restrictive cardiomyopathy. What is the likely diagnosis?

{{c1::Systemic senile amyloidosis}}

A patient with end-stage renal disease receiving hemodialysis has neuropathy and restrictive cardiomyopathy. What fibril protein will be found in the patient's myocardial tissues?

{{c1::β2-microglobulin}}

What is the underlying pathogenesis of amyloidosis?

Abnormal protein aggregation into {{c1::β-pleated sheets}} → {{c1::Insoluble::Soluble/Insoluble}} fibers → Cell damage and apoptosis

What are the cardiac sequelae of amyloidosis?

Cardiac → {{c1::Restrictive}} cardiomyopathy

What are the two primary types of familial amyloidosis?

Familial amyloid {{c1::cardiomyopathy}}
Familial amyloid {{c1::polyneuropathies}}

What arrhythmia is associated with isolated atrial amyloidosis?

{{c1::Atrial fibrillation}}

What protein is deposited in a patient with isolated atrial amyloidosis?

The protein deposited is {{c1::ANP}}
fields.Back Extra: The patient has an increased risk for development of atrial fibrillation.

fields.Text:
What diseases are commonly associated with secondary amyloidosis?

{{c1::Familial Mediterranean}} fever
{{c1::Inflammatory bowel}} disease
{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}

Deposition of amyloid protein in which layer of the heart increases the risk of arrhythmias and results in restrictive cardiomyopathy?

{{c1::Ventricular::Atrial/Ventricular}} {{c1::endomyocardium}}

Which cytokine is particularly responsible for mediating production of acute-phase proteins?

{{c1::IL-6}}

Which prostaglandin is involved in the development of fever during inflammation?

{{c1::PGE2}} increases the temperature set point

What are the five cardinal signs of inflammation?

{{c1::Rubor}}
{{c1::Dolor}}
{{c1::Calor}}
{{c1::Tumor}}
{{c1::Functio laesa}}

What physiologic changes manifest as the redness and warmth associated with acute inflammation?

{{c1::Relaxation::Contraction/Relaxation}} of arteriolar smooth muscle → Vasodilation and increased blood flow

What is the pathophysiology of the swelling associated with acute inflammation?

Increased vascular {{c1::permeability}} due to {{c1::endothelial}} damage → Leakage of {{c1::protein}}-rich fluid from the venules into the interstitium → Edema and increased oncotic pressure

Which three types of mediators are associated with endothelial contraction and edema during inflammation?

{{c1::Leukotrienes}}
{{c1::Histamine}}
{{c1::Serotonin}}

Name three factors that mediate pain in inflammation.

{{c1::Bradykinin}}
{{c1::PGE2}}
{{c1::Histamine}}

A man with cellulitis in his right hand is unable to flex or extend his fingers. What cardinal sign of acute inflammation does this represent?

{{c1::Functio laesa}}

What are the three functions of inflammation?

{{c1::Eliminate}} the initial cause of injury
Initiate tissue {{c1::repair}}
Remove {{c1::necrotic}} cells

Name the four factors that mediate redness and warmth seen in acute inflammation.

{{c1::Bradykinin}}
{{c1::Histamine}}
{{c1::Prostaglandins}}
{{c1::Nitric oxide}}

List three examples where the inflammatory response can be harmful to the host.

{{c1::Prolonged}} immune response
{{c1::Excessive}} immune response
{{c1::Inappropriate}} immune response

Which two acute phase reactants are down-regulated to conserve amino acids for positive reactants?

{{c1::Albumin}}
{{c1::Transthyretin}}

What can be a complication of prolonged elevation of serum amyloid A levels?

{{c1::Amyloidosis}}

What is the role of acute-phase reactants in anemia of chronic disease?

{{c1::Hepcidin}} decreases iron absorption by degrading {{c1::ferroportin}}

Which coagulation factor is increased in inflammation, aids in endothelial repair, and correlates with the ESR?

{{c1::Fibrinogen}}

How do ferritin and transferrin function as acute-phase reactant proteins?

They both sequester {{c1::iron}} within {{c1::macrophages}}

What is the function of haptoglobin as an acute phase reactant?

Binds to extracellular {{c1::hemoglobin}} → Protects against oxidative stress

How does C-reactive protein help mediate immunity during an active infection?

It acts as an {{c1::opsonin}}, fixing {{c1::complement}} and promoting {{c1::phagocytosis}}

Which seven acute-phase reactants are up-regulated during inflammation?

{{c1::Ferritin}}
{{c1::Fibrinogen}}
Serum {{c1::amyloid A}}
{{c1::Hepcidin}}
{{c1::Haptoglobin}}
{{c1::Procalcitonin}}
{{c1::C-reactive}} protein

Which acute phase reactant increases in response to bacterial infection and remains normal during viral infection?

{{c1::Procalcitonin}}

What does ESR measure?

The rate at which {{c1::red blood}} cells coated with products of {{c1::inflammation}} aggregate

Why does ESR increase in states of inflammation?

Coating of red blood cells by products of inflammation decreases their {{c1::negative::positive/negative}} charge → Aggregation (sedimentation)
fields.Back Extra: Dense red blood cell aggregates fall at a faster rate.

fields.Text:
A medical student is concerned that a pregnant patient has an active infection based on an elevated ESR. How do you interpret the result?

ESR is normally {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} in pregnancy

How is the ESR affected in most types of anemia, pregnancy, infections, temporal arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, renal disease, and multiple myeloma?

The ESR is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}

List five conditions that present with lower than expected ESR.

{{c1::Sickle cell}} anemia
{{c1::Polycythemia}}
{{c1::Hypofibrinogenemia::Hyperfibrinogenemia/Hypofibrinogenemia}}
{{c1::Heart::Organ}} failure
{{c1::Microcytosis::Macrocytosis/Normocytosis/Microcytosis}}

Which is a more specific marker for inflammation?

{{c1::C-reactive protein::C-reactive protein/ESR}}

What are five possible outcomes of an acute inflammatory episode?

{{c1::Complete::Complete/Incomplete}} resolution and healing
{{c1::Persistent}} acute inflammation
{{c1::Abscess}} formation
Progression to {{c1::chronic}} inflammation
{{c1::Scarring}}

Which clotting factor is involved in acute inflammation?

{{c1::Hageman}} factor
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as factor XII.

fields.Text:
Which type of inflammation is characterized by rapid onset within seconds to minutes, short duration, and neutrophils in tissue?

{{c1::Acute::Acute/Chronic}} inflammation

What four stimuli can commonly trigger acute inflammation?

{{c1::Trauma}}
{{c1::Infection}}
{{c1::Foreign bodies}}
{{c1::Necrosis}}

What is an inflammasome and what is its role in acute inflammation?

A protein complex that recognizes {{c1::microbial}} products, {{c1::crystals}}, and products of {{c1::dead}} cells to induce inflammation

What vascular changes happen as a result of acute inflammation?

{{c1::Vasodilation::Vasoconstriction/Vasodilation}}
Increased endothelial {{c1::permeability}} → Delivery of cells and proteins to the site of infection/injury

How do leukocytes reach the site of acute inflammation?

Leukocytes {{c1::extravasate}} from {{c1::postcapillary venules}} and accumulate at the area of injury

Name two growth factors and/or cytokines that help in resolution and healing following acute inflammation.

{{c1::TGF-β}}
{{c1::IL-10}}

Which cytokine is increased in persistent acute inflammation?

{{c1::IL-8}}

What cell type peaks at 2 to 3 days after onset of acute inflammation?

{{c1::Macrophages}}

Through what mechanism does acute inflammation transition into chronic inflammation?

{{c1::Macrophages}} and other {{c1::antigen-presenting}} cells present antigens that result in the activation of CD{{c1::4}}+ {{c1::Th}} cells

A 12-year-old boy injured his foot a day ago and now has edema. You aspirate fluid from the foot and do microscopic analysis. What cells do you note in the fluid?



{{c1::Neutrophils}}
fields.Back Extra: These are important mediators of acute inflammation and are typically associated with edema.

fields.Text:
What two inflammatory factors are primarily responsible for E-selectin upregulation?

{{c1::TNF}}
{{c1::IL-1}}

A patient has a defect in the Sialyl-LewisX receptor. What step in leukocyte extravasion will be affected?

{{c1::Margination and rolling}}
fields.Back Extra: The patient has leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 2.

fields.Text:
Describe the process of migration during leukocyte extravasation.

Cells travel via the {{c1::interstitium}} to the site of infection or injury with the guidance of {{c1::chemotactic}} signals

In which step of leukocyte extravasation do bacterial products, C5a, IL-8, LTB4, kallikrein, 5-HETE, platelet-activating factor, and N-formylmethionyl peptides play a role?

{{c1::Migration}}

In which step of leukocyte extravasation do ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 play a role?

{{c1::Tight binding}}

In which step of leukocyte extravasation do E-selectin, P-selectin, GlyCAM-1, and CD34 play a role?

{{c1::Margination and rolling}}

P-selectin is released primarily from which endothelium-derived structure?

{{c1::Weibel-Palade bodies}}

In which step of extravasation does a decrease in CD18 integrin subunits on leukocytes lead to a defect?

{{c1::Tight binding}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is a result of the inability to attach to ICAM-1.

This is leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1.

fields.Text:
Describe the process of diapedesis during leukocyte extravasation.

Leukocytes use {{c1::PECAM-1}} to migrate between {{c1::endothelial}} cells and exit the blood vessel

In which step of leukocyte extravasation does PECAM-1 play a role?

{{c1::Diapedesis}}

Name the four steps involved in leukocyte extravasation.

{{c1::Margination and rolling}}
{{c1::Tight binding}}
{{c1::Diapedesis}}
{{c1::Migration}}

What is the primary site of leukocyte extravasation?

{{c1::Postcapillary venules}}

Which type of inflammation is characterized by simultaneous destruction and repair of tissue, associated with blood vessel proliferation and fibrosis?

{{c1::Chronic::Acute/Chronic}} inflammation

Which immune cells mediate chronic inflammation?

{{c1::Mononuclear}} cells

What are the three possible outcomes of chronic inflammation?

{{c1::Scarring}}
{{c1::Amyloidosis}}
{{c1::Neoplastic}} transformation

What type of hypersensitivity reaction occurs in patients with persistent infections resulting in chronic inflammation?

Type {{c1::IV}} hypersensitivity reaction

Persistent infections, autoimmune diseases, foreign bodies, and prolonged exposure to toxic agents can lead to what type of inflammation?
