{{c1::Chronic::Acute/Chronic}} inflammation

Which proinflammatory cytokine is secreted by Th1 cells to promote macrophage activation?

{{c1::IFN-γ}}

Which T lymphocytes are involved in the mediation of anti-inflammatory and repair processes by alternative activation of macrophages in chronic inflammation?

{{c1::Th2}} cells
fields.Back Extra: This is via the secretion of IL-4 and IL-13.

fields.Text:
What is the difference between the classical and alternative macrophage activation pathways?

The classical activation pathway is {{c1::proinflammatory}}
The alternative activation pathway is {{c1::anti-inflammatory}} and promotes {{c1::repair}}

Name the dominant leukocytes involved in chronic inflammation.

{{c1::Macrophages}}

Interaction of macrophages with which inflammatory cell leads to chronic inflammation?

{{c1::T}} cells

Which one vitamin and one mineral deficiency can impede the proliferative phase of wound healing?

Vitamin {{c1::C}}
{{c1::Copper}} deficiency

What two mineral deficiencies are associated with delayed wound healing?

{{c1::Zinc}} deficiency
{{c1::Copper}} deficiency

What is the role of collagenases in the remodeling phase of wound healing?

They break down type {{c1::III}} collagen

What is the role of tissue mediator metalloproteinases?

Tissue {{c1::remodeling}}

In wound healing, which tissue mediator induces vascular remodeling and smooth muscle cell migration along with stimulation of fibroblasts for collagen synthesis?

{{c1::PDGF}}

During wound healing, which tissue mediator promotes cell growth via tyrosine kinases?

{{c1::EGF}}

What is the role of TGF-β in wound healing?

Promotes {{c1::angiogenesis}} and {{c1::fibrosis}}

Name the three wound healing mediators that promote angiogenesis.

{{c1::FGF}}
{{c1::TGF-β}}
{{c1::VEGF}}

What is the function of myofibroblasts in wound healing?

Wound {{c1::contraction::contraction/relaxation}}

Why does the remodeling phase of wound healing involve the replacement of type III collagen with type I collagen?

To increase the {{c1::tensile strength}} of the tissue

What phase of wound healing involves deposition of type III collagen?

{{c1::Proliferative}} phase
fields.Back Extra: Type III collagen is formed along with granulation tissue.

fields.Text:
In which phase of wound healing do collagen deposition, angiogenesis, clot dissolution, epithelial cell proliferation, and wound contraction occur?

{{c1::Proliferative}} phase

Which type of cell is the effector during the remodeling process of wound healing?

{{c1::Fibroblasts}}

Which phase of wound healing includes infiltration of fibroblasts, myofibroblasts, endothelial cells, and keratinocytes at the site of injury?

{{c1::Proliferative}} phase

Which phase of wound healing is characterized by infiltration of platelets, neutrophils, and macrophages at the site of injury?

{{c1::Inflammatory}} phase

What are the different cell types that make up the structure shown in the image?



{{c1::Epitheloid}} cells
{{c1::Multinucleated giant}} cells
{{c1::Lymphocytes}}

What is the histologic difference between granulomas seen in tuberculosis and those seen in sarcoidosis?

Tuberculosis involves {{c1::caseating::caseating/noncaseating}} granulomas
Sarcoidosis presents with {{c1::noncaseating::caseating/noncaseating}} granulomas

A 30-year-old woman has a chronic cough, hilar lymphadenopathy, and noncaseating granulomas detected by lung biopsy. Why might her serum calcium level be elevated?

Hypercalcemia would be due to increased activation of vitamin {{c1::D}} by {{c1::1α-hydroxylase}} from the {{c1::macrophages}} in the granulomas

Name four immune-mediated causes of granulomatous diseases.

{{c1::Crohn}} disease
{{c1::Primary biliary cholangitis}}
{{c1::Sarcoidosis}}
{{c1::Subacute thyroiditis}}

Name some infectious causes of granulomatous diseases.

{{c1::Bacteria}}
{{c1::Fungi}}
{{c1::Parasites}}

Why is it important to test for latent tuberculosis before initiating anti-TNF therapy?

Anti-TNF drugs can lead to the breakdown of {{c1::granulomas}} via inhibition of TNF → Disseminated disease

What is the role of Th1 cells in the formation of epithelioid macrophages and giant cells?

Th1 cells secrete {{c1::IFN-γ}} → Activation of macrophages → Increased secretion of {{c1::cytokines}} → Formation of epithelioid macrophages and giant cells

Name the four vasculitides that present with granulomas.

{{c1::Giant cell arteritis}}
{{c1::Takayasu arteritis}}
{{c1::Granulomatosis with polyangiitis}}
{{c1::Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis}}

What are two noninfectious causes of granulomatous disease other than immune-mediated and vasculitis?

Presence of foreign material as in {{c1::berylliosis}} or {{c1::talcosis}}
{{c1::Hypersensitivity pneumonitis}}

Which disease is associated with granuloma formation when infected with catalase-positive species?

{{c1::Chronic granulomatous}} disease

What is the role of granuloma formation in controlling persistent infections?

Granulomas function to wall off a {{c1::resistant}} stimulus without completely degrading or eradicating it

A patient wishes to undergo surgical resection of the scar shown. What is the likelihood of recurrence of the scar tissue?



{{c1::High::High/Low}}

A patient has a scar after sustaining a laceration. What type of collagen organization is found in the scar?



{{c1::Parallel}}

Which collagen types are seen with keloid and hypertrophic scar formation?

Keloid scars → Type {{c1::I}} and {{c1::III}} collagen
Hypertrophic scars → Predominantly type {{c1::III}} collagen

Which type of scar extends beyond the borders of the original wound?

{{c1::Keloid}} scar

How do collagen synthesis and organization differ in hypertrophic and keloid scars?

Keloid scars have a much {{c1::higher::higher/lower}} level of collagen synthesis in a {{c1::disorganized}} fashion
Hypertrophic scars have collagen organized in a {{c1::parallel}} fashion

Which group of people are associated with an increased incidence of keloid scar formation after a wound?

Individuals with {{c1::darker::lighter/darker}} skin

What is the pathophysiology of scar formation?

Cell regeneration is {{c1::inadequate}} to achieve repair → Cells that are not regenerated are replaced by {{c1::connective}} tissue

An excess amount of which cytokine is associated with scar formation?

{{c1::TGF-β}}

Via what two routes do metastases typically spread to distant organs?

{{c1::Blood}}
{{c1::Lymphatics}}

What are the five general stages of neoplastic progression of a malignant tumor?

Normal tissue → {{c1::Dysplasia}} → {{c1::Carcinoma in situ}} → {{c1::Invasive carcinoma}} → Metastasis

How does decreased E-cadherin expression relate to tumor development?

Decreased expression of E-cadherin causes {{c1::cell}}-{{c1::cell}} contacts to be lost, allowing a tumor to invade local tissues

Which two types of enzymes are upregulated by neoplastic epithelial cells to invade the basement membrane?

{{c1::Collagenases}}
{{c1::Hydrolases}}

What are three key changes that occur in dysplasia?

Loss of {{c1::uniformity}} in shape and size of cells
Loss of tissue {{c1::orientation}}
{{c1::Nuclear}} changes

What stage in neoplastic progression is shown in the image?



{{c1::Invasive carcinoma}}
fields.Back Extra: It invades the basement membrane, but does not spread to distant organs.

fields.Text:
What stage in neoplastic progression is shown in the image?



{{c1::Metastasis}}

What is the uncontrolled monoclonal proliferation of cells, which may be benign or malignant?

{{c1::Neoplasia}}

What are the two components of any neoplastic growth?

{{c1::Parenchyma}}
Supporting {{c1::stroma}}

What stage in neoplastic progression is shown in the image?



{{c1::Carcinoma in situ}}
fields.Back Extra: This involves the entire epithelium, but does not penetrate the basement membrane.

fields.Text:
What stage in neoplastic progression is shown in the image?



{{c1::Dysplasia}}
fields.Back Extra: There is loss of cellular uniformity and loss of tissue orientation.

fields.Text:
What is the difference between leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma?

Leiomyoma is {{c1::benign::benign/malignant}}
Leiomyosarcoma is {{c1::malignant::benign/malignant}}
fields.Back Extra: Both are derived from smooth muscle.

fields.Text:
What is the difference between rhabdomyoma and rhabdomyosarcoma?

Rhabdomyoma is {{c1::benign::benign/malignant}}
Rhabdomyosarcoma is {{c1::malignant::benign/malignant}}
fields.Back Extra: Both are derived from striated muscle.

fields.Text:
Name two benign epithelial tumors.

{{c1::Adenoma}}
{{c1::Papilloma}}

What type of tumor is an osteoma?

{{c1::Benign::Benign/Malignant}} bone tumor

What are the five main features of malignant tumors?

{{c1::Poor::Well/Poorly}}-differentiated
{{c1::Erratic}} growth
{{c1::Local}} invasion
{{c1::Metastasis}}
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} apoptosis

What are the five main features of benign tumors?

{{c1::Well::Well/Poorly}}-differentiated
{{c1::Well::Well/Poorly}}-demarcated
{{c1::Low::High/Low}} mitotic activity
No {{c1::metastases}}
No {{c1::necrosis}}

What type of tissue do adenocarcinomas and papillary carcinomas arise from?

{{c1::Epithelial}} tissue

What would you call a malignant tumor originating from a blood vessel?

{{c1::Angiosarcoma}}

Liposarcoma is a malignant tumor of what tissue?

{{c1::Fat}}

What type of tumor is a lipoma?

{{c1::Benign::Benign/Malignant}} fat tumor

Osteoma is a benign tumor of what tissue?

{{c1::Bone}}

Fibroma is a benign tumor of what tissue?

{{c1::Connective}} tissue

Hemangioma is a benign tumor of what tissue?

{{c1::Blood vessels}}

What are malignancies of blood cells called?

{{c1::Leukemias}}
{{c1::Lymphomas}}

What type of cells do sarcomas originate from?

{{c1::Mesenchymal}} cells

What type of cells do carcinomas originate from?

{{c1::Epithelial}} cells

What is the term for a benign neoplasm of melanocytes?

{{c1::Nevus}}

What is the term for a malignant neoplasm of melanocytes?

{{c1::Melanoma}}

What is a malignant tumor of connective tissue called?

{{c1::Fibrosarcoma}}

What term is used to describe disorganized overgrowth of non-neoplastic tissue in its native location?

{{c1::Hamartoma}}

What term is used to describe normal overgrowth of non-neoplastic tissue in an ectopic location?

{{c1::Choristoma}}

What term describes the degree to which neoplastic cells resemble their tissue of origin?

{{c1::Differentiation}}

What term describes the lack of differentiation of neoplastic cells?

{{c1::Anaplasia}}

In the TNM staging system for neoplasia, which two factors usually have the greatest prognostic importance?

{{c1::M}} factor (most important)
{{c1::N}} factor
fields.Back Extra: These indicate the degree to which the tumor has spread to distant sites.

fields.Text:
What term describes the degree of spread and invasion of neoplastic cells?

Tumor {{c1::stage::grade/stage}}

Which three factors are considered when a stage is assigned to a tumor?

Primary tumor {{c1::size}}/{{c1::invasiveness}}
Regional {{c1::lymph node}} involvement
Presence or absence of {{c1::metastasis}}

With respect to neoplastic growth, what term describes the degree of cellular differentiation and mitotic activity of cells?

Tumor {{c1::grade::grade/stage}}

What are the key traits of a well-differentiated tumor?

{{c1::Close::Close/Lacks}} resemblance to cells of origin

What are the key traits of a poorly differentiated tumor?

{{c1::Lacks::Close/Lacks}} resemblance to cells of origin

Histology of a tumor shows the following. What is the grade of this tumor?



{{c1::High::High/Low}} grade

What kind of molecule does the MYC gene encode?

A {{c1::transcription}} factor, which causes {{c1::growth}} signal self-sufficiency

Name two examples of cell cycle regulators that may be altered to produce growth signal self-sufficiency in cancer cells.

{{c1::Cyclins}}
{{c1::CDKs}}

What kind of molecule is coded for by the Rb gene?

{{c1::Tumor suppressor}} gene
fields.Back Extra: When mutated, it allows the tumor cell to develop anti-growth signal insensitivity.

fields.Text:
What molecule is made dysfunctional by an NF2 mutation resulting in anti-growth signal insensitivity?

{{c1::E-cadherin}}
fields.Back Extra: Loss of E-cadherin leads to loss of contact inhibition.

fields.Text:
Loss of E-cadherin function promotes tumor cells through which two cancer hallmarks?

Antigrowth signal {{c1::insensitivity}}
Tissue {{c1::invasion}}

What would you expect the apoptotic index to be in a patient with follicular B-cell lymphoma?

{{c1::Low::High/Low}}
fields.Back Extra: The cells of follicular B-cell lymphoma evade apoptosis via mutations in genes that regulate apoptosis.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism through which malignant cells develop limitless replicative potential?

Reactivation of {{c1::telomerase}}

How might a cancer drug that targets VEGF inhibit tumor growth?

VEGF is a {{c1::pro-angiogenic}} factor that may be upregulated by tumor cells to produce sustained {{c1::angiogenesis}}

What is the process whereby cells migrate through the degraded extracellular matrix to reach blood vessels in cancer tissue invasion?

{{c1::Locomotion}}

Name the process by which tumor cells or emboli move through lymph or blood, adhere to endothelium, and extravasate and home to a new site.

{{c1::Metastasis}}

What is the main predictor of the first site of tumor metastatsis?

Location of the {{c1::primary}} tumor
fields.Back Extra: The target organ is often the first encountered capillary bed.

fields.Text:
Lung cancers are known to metastasize preferentially to the adrenals. What is the name for this phenomenon?

{{c1::Organ tropism}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the tendency for certain cancers to metastasize to certain sites more frequently.

fields.Text:
Describe the Warburg effect.

Metabolism of {{c1::glucose}} shifts away from mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation to {{c1::glycolysis}} → Provides cancer cells with {{c1::carbon}} required for creation of cellular structures

In cancer hallmarks, which five types of gene encoding mutations result in the presentation of growth signal self-sufficiency?

{{c1::Growth factor}} receptors
{{c1::Signaling}} molecules
{{c1::Proto-oncogenes}}
{{c1::Transcription}} factors
{{c1::Cell cycle}} regulators

How does a mutation in the HER2/neu gene drive tumor growth?

It is a {{c1::growth factor}} receptor that causes {{c1::constitutive}} signaling

By what process do cancer cells promote generation of vessels from existing capillaries?

{{c1::Neoangiogenesis}}

What is the process by which cancer cells form vessels from the recruitment of endothelial cells from bone marrow?

{{c1::Vasculogenesis}}

What are three mechanisms used by tumor cells to evade the immune system?

Decreased MHC {{c1::I::I/II}} expression
Downregulation of {{c1::immune}} response
Regulation of {{c1::immune checkpoint}} molecules

What ability is conferred to cancer cells by mutations in TP53 and BCL2 genes?

Their ability to avoid {{c1::apoptosis}}

During the process of tissue invasion, tumor cells often attach to two extracellular matrix proteins. Name the two proteins.

{{c1::Laminin}}
{{c1::Fibronectin}}

Decreased expression of MHC I leads to decreased tumor cell recognition by which immune cells?

{{c1::Tc}} cells

Upregulation of immune checkpoint molecules by cancer cells helps them to evade the immune system by what mechanism?

Inhibition of the {{c1::immune}} response

What receptors on tumor cells interacts with PD-1 on T cells to cause T-cell dysfunction?

{{c1::PD-L1}}
{{c1::PD-L2}}

What role do immune checkpoint molecules play in evasion of the immune system by a tumor?

Immune checkpoint molecules modulate {{c1::T}}-cell activation and function

What immune checkpoint molecule is targeted by cemiplimab, pembrolizumab, and nivolumab?

{{c1::PD-1}}

What immune checkpoint molecule is targeted by atezolizumab, durvalumab, and avelumab?

{{c1::PD-L1}}
fields.Back Extra: This is on tumor cells or immune cells.

fields.Text:
Which receptor on antigen-presenting cells does CTLA-4 compete with to cause a loss of T-cell costimulatory signaling?

{{c1::CD28}} for {{c1::B7}} on antigen-presenting cells

What immune checkpoint molecule is targeted by ipilimumab?

{{c1::CTLA-4}}

Which three cancers have the highest incidence and highest mortality among children?

{{c1::Leukemia}}
Cancers of the {{c1::central nervous system}}
{{c1::Neuroblastoma}}

Which three cancers lead to the most deaths in women?

1 → {{c1::Lung}} cancer
2 → {{c1::Breast}} cancer
3 → {{c1::Colorectal}} cancer

Which three cancers have the highest incidence among women?

1 → {{c1::Breast}} cancer
2 → {{c1::Lung}} cancer
3 → {{c1::Colorectal}} cancer

What is the most common type of cancer in the general population?

{{c1::Skin}} cancer

What are the two leading causes of death in the United States?

{{c1::Heart::Organ}} disease
{{c1::Cancer}}

Which three cancers cause the most death in men?

1 → {{c1::Lung}} cancer
2 → {{c1::Prostate}} cancer
3 → {{c1::Colorectal}} cancer

Which three cancers have the highest incidence among men?

1 → {{c1::Prostate}} cancer
2 → {{c1::Lung}} cancer
3 → {{c1::Colorectal}} cancer

A brain cancer presents as multiple brain tumors, as shown in the image. Is it a primary tumor or metastases?



{{c1::Metastases}}
fields.Back Extra: These often appear as multiple well-circumscribed tumors.

fields.Text:
How likely is a brain tumor to be a primary tumor?

About {{c1::50}}% of all brain tumors are primary tumors

What are the three primary tumors that metastasize most commonly to the liver?

{{c1::Colon}} (most common)
{{c1::Stomach}}
{{c1::Pancreas}} (least common)

Which five cancers commonly metastasize to bone?

{{c1::Prostate}} cancer
{{c1::Breast}} cancer
{{c1::Kidney}} cancer
{{c1::Thyroid}} cancer
{{c1::Lung}} cancer

What type of bone metastatic lesion is seen with thyroid cancer, kidney cancer, and non–small cell lung cancer?

{{c1::Lytic}} lesion

What are the five primary tumors that commonly metastasize to the brain?

{{c1::Lung}}
{{c1::Breast}}
{{c1::Melanoma}}
{{c1::Colon}}
{{c1::Kidney}}

Statistically, what are the three most common sites of metastasis?

Regional {{c1::lymph nodes}}
{{c1::Liver}}
{{c1::Lungs}}

List the four carcinomas that spread hematogenously rather than via lymphatics.

{{c1::Follicular}} thyroid carcinoma
{{c1::Choriocarcinoma}}
{{c1::Renal cell}} carcinoma
{{c1::Hepatocellular}} carcinoma

How common are metastatic lesions to the bone relative to primary bone tumors?

Metastatic lesions to the bone are {{c1::more::more/less}} common than primary bone tumors

What type of bony metastatic lesions are associated with breast cancer?

{{c1::Mixed}} lesions

Which two cancers are associated with blastic metastatic lesions within bones?

{{c1::Small cell}} cancer of the lung
{{c1::Prostate}} cancer

By what route do most carcinomas metastasize?

Via {{c1::lymphatic}} spread

Which part of the skeleton is most commonly affected by metastases to bone?

{{c1::Axial}} skeleton

By what route do most sarcomas metastasize?

Via {{c1::hematogenous}} spread

What general type of gene product do BCR-ABL and JAK2 encode?

{{c1::Non-receptor::Receptor/Non-receptor}} {{c1::tyrosine kinase}}

Mutations of which two oncogenes are associated with papillary thyroid carcinoma?

{{c1::RET}}
{{c1::BRAF}}

What five cancer types can result from a mutation in the BRAF genes that encode serine/threonine kinase?

{{c1::Melanoma}}
{{c1::Non-Hodgkin}} lymphoma
{{c1::Colorectal}} carcinoma
{{c1::Papillary}} thyroid carcinoma
{{c1::Hairy cell}} leukemia

What type of molecule do MYCC and MYCN encode?

{{c1::Transcription}} factors

How many mutations (in alleles) must be acquired to convert a proto-oncogene to an oncogene?

{{c1::1}}

Gastrointestinal stromal tumors and mastocytosis are associated with upregulation of which type of receptor?

{{c1::Cytokine}} receptors
fields.Back Extra: This is the result of increased c-KIT activity.

fields.Text:
A patient with a RET gene mutation has an increased risk for development of which cancers and syndromes?

{{c1::Pheochromocytoma}}
{{c1::Medullary}} thyroid carcinoma
{{c1::Papillary}} thyroid carcinoma
{{c1::MEN}} type {{c1::2A}}
{{c1::MEN}} type {{c1::2B}}

Which genetic mutation is associated with neuroblastoma?

{{c1::MYCN}} gene

Which oncogene should show increased activity in Burkitt lymphoma?

{{c1::MYCC}} gene

Which three cancer types are associated with the KRAS oncogene?

{{c1::Colon}} cancer
{{c1::Lung}} cancer
{{c1::Pancreatic}} cancer

How does an oncogene generally increase cancer risk?

Via {{c1::gain-of-function}} mutation of a normal {{c1::proto-oncogene}}

Which two malignancies are associated with the HER2 oncogene?

{{c1::Breast}} carcinoma
{{c1::Gastric}} carcinoma

What general type of gene product do HER2, ALK, EGFR, and RET genes encode?

{{c1::Receptor::Receptor/Non-receptor}} {{c1::tyrosine kinase}}
fields.Back Extra: This is most often seen with breast and gastric carcinomas.

fields.Text:
What two subtypes of lymphoma are associated with BCL-2 oncogene mutations?

{{c1::Follicular}} lymphoma
{{c1::Diffuse large B-cell}} lymphoma

Which two malignancies are associated with the BCR-ABL oncogene?

{{c1::ALL}}
{{c1::CML}}

What kind of cancer are ALK and EGFR oncogenes associated with?

{{c1::Lung}} adenocarcinoma

What kind of gene product is associated with myeloproliferative neoplasms?

{{c1::Non-receptor::Receptor/Non-receptor}} {{c1::tyrosine kinase}}

What kind of gene product is encoded by the KRAS oncogene?

{{c1::RAS GTPase}}

What is the function of the gene product of the PTEN tumor suppressor gene?

It negatively regulates the {{c1::PI3k/AKT}} pathway

Melanomas have a tumor suppressor gene mutation at CDKN2A. What protein does this gene typically encode?

{{c1::p16}}
fields.Back Extra: This blocks cell progression from the G1 phase to S phase.

fields.Text:
What function does the product of TP53 normally perform?

p53 is a transcription factor for {{c1::p21}} → Blocks the transition from {{c1::G1}} phase to {{c1::S}} phase

Which cancer is related to mutations in DCC and APC genes?

{{c1::Colorectal}} cancer

Which cancers are related to mutations of SMAD4 (DPC4) tumor suppressor gene?

{{c1::Pancreatic}} cancer
{{c1::Colorectal}} cancer

What is the role of the protein encoded by the VHL tumor suppressor gene?

Inhibition of {{c1::hypoxia-inducible factor 1a}}

What syndrome does a patient with a defective menin protein likely have?

{{c1::MEN}} type {{c1::1}}
fields.Back Extra: This is associated with a defective menin protein encoded by the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene.

fields.Text:
BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations increase the risk for developing which four cancers?

{{c1::Breast}} cancer
{{c1::Ovarian}} cancer
{{c1::Prostate}} cancer
{{c1::Pancreatic}} cancer

What syndrome/cancers are associated with a mutation in TP53, a tumor suppressor gene?

{{c1::Li-Fraumeni}} syndrome

What is the function of the protein encoded by the tumor suppressor gene mutated in familial retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma?

The {{c1::RB1}} tumor suppressor gene results in inhibition of {{c1::E2F}} → Blocks transition from {{c1::G1}} phase to {{c1::S}} phase

What protein is typically produced by the NF2 tumor suppressor gene?

{{c1::Merlin}} protein
fields.Back Extra:
This is also known as schwannomin protein.

This is defective in neurofibromatosis type 2.

fields.Text:
What protein is typically produced by the NF1 tumor suppressor gene?

{{c1::Neurofibromin}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a Ras GTPase activating protein that is defective in neurofibromatosis type 1.

fields.Text:
Mutation of which tumor suppressor gene is associated with the development of nephroblastoma?

{{c1::WT1}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as Wilms tumor.

fields.Text:
Which three cancers are associated with an inherited PTEN mutation?

{{c1::Prostate}} cancer
{{c1::Breast}} cancer
{{c1::Endometrial}} cancer

How many alleles of a tumor suppressor gene must be mutated to express oncologic disease?

{{c1::2}}

What is the normal function of the gene product of the APC tumor suppressor gene?

A negative regulator of the {{c1::β-catenin/WNT}} pathway

What protein is encoded by the TSC2 tumor suppressor gene?

{{c1::Tuberin}} protein

What protein is encoded by the TSC1 tumor suppressor gene?

{{c1::Hamartin}} protein

What disease is associated with mutations on VHL tumor suppressor gene?

{{c1::Von Hippel-Lindau}} disease

Arsenic exposure from herbicides and metal smelting is associated with which three types of cancer?

{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma of the skin
{{c1::Lung::Organ}} cancer
{{c1::Hepatic}} angiosarcoma

Long-term exposure to asbestos can predispose an individual to which two cancers?

{{c1::Bronchogenic}} carcinoma
{{c1::Mesothelioma}}

A patient with long-term exposure to an aflatoxin-producing strain of Aspergillus is at risk for developing what type of carcinoma?

{{c1::Hepatocellular}} carcinoma

Excessive alcohol intake increases the risk for which three types of cancer?

{{c1::Hepatocellular}} carcinoma
{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma of the esophagus
{{c1::Breast}} cancer

Treatment with an alkylating agent increases the risk of developing which two malignancies?

{{c1::Leukemias}}
{{c1::Lymphomas}}

What type of toxic chemical is classically associated with transition cell carcinoma of the bladder?

{{c1::2-naphthylamine}} in cigarette smoke
{{c1::2-naphthylamine}} and {{c1::benzidine}} in caustic dyes

Nitrosamines present in smoked food products are associated with development of which cancer?

{{c1::Gastric}} cancer

Environmental exposure to which carcinogen increases the likelihood of hepatic angiosarcoma in a plumber?

{{c1::Vinyl chloride}}
fields.Back Extra: This is used to make PVC pipes.

fields.Text:
Exposure to ionizing radiation increases the risk for which two types of cancer?

{{c1::Papillary}} thyroid carcinoma
{{c1::Leukemia}}

What cancer is most commonly associated with radon exposure?

{{c1::Lung::Organ}} cancer
fields.Back Extra: Radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer after tobacco smoke.

fields.Text:
What two types of lung cancer are classically associated with cigarette smoking?

{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma
{{c1::Small cell}} carcinoma

Occupational exposure to nickel, chromium, beryllium, and silica increase the risk for which type of cancer?

{{c1::Lung::Organ}} cancer

What carcinogen are shipyard workers most likely to be exposed to?

{{c1::Asbestos}}

Patients with a history of Schistosoma haematobium infection are at an increased risk for which type of cancer?

{{c1::Squamous cell}} cancer of the bladder

Which two cancers are associated with Helicobacter pylori infection?

{{c1::MALT}} lymphoma
{{c1::Gastric}} adenocarcinoma

A patient with AIDS who is infected with Epstein-Barr virus has an espcially increased risk of developing which malignancy?

{{c1::Primary central nervous system}} lymphoma

Which oncogenic virus is associated with Kaposi sarcoma?

{{c1::HHV-8}}

Epstein-Barr virus is most commonly associated with which four malignancies?

{{c1::Nasopharyngeal}} carcinoma
{{c1::Burkitt}} lymphoma
{{c1::Hodgkin}} lymphoma
{{c1::Primary central nervous system}} lymphoma

Which type of cancer is a complication of infection with Clonorchis sinensis?

{{c1::Cholangiocarcinoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as the Chinese liver fluke.

fields.Text:
What four sites may be prone to cancer development in patients infected with oncogenic HPV strains?

{{c1::Cervix}}
{{c1::Penis}}
{{c1::Anus}}
{{c1::Head}} and {{c1::neck}}

Which two oncogenic viruses are associated with hepatocellular carcinoma?

Hepatitis {{c1::B}} virus
Hapatitis {{c1::C}} virus

Adult T-cell leukemia is associated with which oncogenic virus?

{{c1::HTLV-1}}

Which two types of HPV are associated with carcinoma of the penis, anus, and cervix?

HPV type {{c1::16}}
HPV type {{c1::18}}

What three conditions may be on the differential when the serum PSA level is elevated?

{{c1::Benign prostatic hyperplasia}}
{{c1::Prostatitis}}
{{c1::Prostate}} cancer

What three nonhepatic diseases are associated with an elevated ALP level?

Metastases to {{c1::liver::organ}} or {{c1::bone::organ}}
{{c1::Seminoma}}
{{c1::Paget disease of bone}}

Which tumor marker can be normally produced by a fetus and is increased in the presence of an abdominal wall or neural tube defect?

{{c1::α-fetoprotein}}

Which two tumor markers are associated with neuroendocrine tumors?

{{c1::Chromogranin}}
{{c1::Neuron}}-specific {{c1::enolase}}

Apart from in utero conditions, increased α-fetoprotein levels are associated with what five diseases?

{{c1::Yolk sac}} tumor
{{c1::Hepatocellular}} carcinoma
{{c1::Mixed germ cell}} tumor
{{c1::Ataxia-telangiectasia}}
{{c1::Neural tube}} defects

What type of cancer is associated with elevated CA 15-3 or CA 27-29?

{{c1::Breast}} cancer

Which tumor marker may be elevated in association with isolated medullary thyroid carcinoma and MEN type 2A or 2B?

{{c1::Calcitonin}}

What are two clinical uses for tumor markers?

To monitor for tumor {{c1::recurrence}}
Response to {{c1::therapy}}
fields.Back Extra: Tumor markers are not used to screen or diagnose, as definitive diagnosis is made via biopsy.

fields.Text:
Which tumor marker is specifically associated with pancreatic adenocarcinoma?

{{c1::CA 19-9}}

What tumor marker is associated with epithelial ovarian cancer?

{{c1::CA 125}}

Which four pathologies are associated with an elevated hCG level?

{{c1::Hydatidiform moles}}
{{c1::Choriocarcinomas}}
{{c1::Testicular}} cancer
{{c1::Mixed germ cell}} tumors

Which two cancers can be monitored with CEA levels?

{{c1::Colorectal}} cancer
{{c1::Pancreatic}} cancer

Which marker can be used to monitor for the recurrence of prostate cancer?

{{c1::PSA}}

What role do serum PSA measurements play in terms of screening for prostate cancer in patients with no symptoms?

They have a {{c1::questionable}} risk/benefit ratio for screening

Which genetic syndrome is associated with low levels of α-fetoprotein?

{{c1::Down}} syndrome

With elevated ALP level, which two tests can aid in the exclusion of hepatic origin?

{{c1::Liver::Organ}} function tests
{{c1::GGT}} levels

Which two types of cancer are most commonly associated with elevations in lactate dehydrogenase?

{{c1::Testicular germ cell}} tumors
{{c1::Ovarian dysgerminoma}}

Which cells within the placenta are responsible for producing hCG?

{{c1::Syncytiotrophoblasts}}

Besides colorectal and pancreatic cancers, what three other cancers are associated with elevated levels of CEA?

{{c1::Gastric}} cancer
{{c1::Breast}} cancer
{{c1::Medullary}} thyroid carcinomas

What tumor marker might be measured to check for recurrence of seminoma?

{{c1::PLAP}}

What are four tumors that might stain positively with vimentin?

{{c1::Mesenchymal}} tumors
{{c1::Endometrial}} carcinoma
{{c1::Meningioma}}
{{c1::Renal cell}} carcinoma

If the immunohistochemical staining of a tumor specimen is positive for GFAP, what does this indicate about the likely primary tumor?

The primary tumor is likely of {{c1::neuroglial}} origin
fields.Back Extra: GFAP is positive in astrocytes, Schwann cells, and oligodendrocytes.

fields.Text:
Which tumors stain positively with cytokeratin?

{{c1::Epithelial}} tumors

What immunohistochemical stain might be helpful in establishing the diagnosis of a rhabdomyosarcoma?

{{c1::Desmin}}
fields.Back Extra: This may be positive in tumors of muscular origin.

fields.Text:
What type of tissue is targeted by the vimentin stain?

{{c1::Mesenchymal}} tissue

What cells are targeted by the S-100 stain?

{{c1::Neural crest}} cells

Immunohistochemical staining of which three primary neoplasms will be S-100 positive?

{{c1::Schwannoma}}
{{c1::Melanoma}}
{{c1::Langerhans cell histiocytosis}}

What stain may be helpful in establishing the diagnosis of glioblastoma and astrocytoma?

{{c1::GFAP}}
fields.Back Extra: This is helpful for identifying tumors of neuroglial origin.

fields.Text:
What type of cell is targeted by the neurofilament stain?

{{c1::Neurons}}

What tissue may show a positive neurofilament stain?

{{c1::Neurons}}
fields.Back Extra: This can be noted in diseases like neuroblastoma.

fields.Text:
What type of tissue is the target of the PSA stain?

{{c1::Prostatic}} epithelium

What is the molecular target of the TRAP stain?

{{c1::Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase}}

What stain may be helpful in establishing the diagnosis of hairy cell leukemia?

{{c1::TRAP}}

What type of cell is targeted by the chromogranin and synaptophysin stains?

{{c1::Neuroendocrine}} cells

Small cell carcinoma of the lung, carcinoid tumor, and neuroblastoma can be identified with which two immunohistochemical stains?

{{c1::Chromogranin}}
{{c1::Synaptophysin}}

Which malignancy is classically associated with increased expression of P-glycoprotein?

{{c1::Adrenocortical}} carcinoma
fields.Back Extra: P-glycoprotein can also be expressed by colon or liver cancer cells.

fields.Text:
What is the alternate name for multidrug resistance protein 1?

{{c1::P-glycoprotein}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an ATP-dependent efflux pump.

fields.Text:
How does P-glycoprotein contribute to tumor cell resistance to chemotherapy?

P-glycoprotein pumps {{c1::out::in/out}} toxins
fields.Back Extra: This includes chemotherapeutic agents, which increases resistance to treatment.

fields.Text:
What notable histologic finding is shown in the image?



{{c1::Psammoma body}}

What histologic finding can be described as a laminated, concentric spherule with dystrophic calcification?

{{c1::Psammoma body}}

In which five malignancies are psammoma bodies commonly seen?

{{c1::Papillary}} thyroid carcinoma
{{c1::Meningioma}}
{{c1::Serous ovarian}} carcinoma
{{c1::Mesothelioma}}
{{c1::Prolactinoma}}

Which four inflammatory markers are responsible for mediating cachexia?

{{c1::TNF-α}}
{{c1::IFN-γ}}
{{c1::IL-1}}
{{c1::IL-6}}

What term describes weight loss, muscle atrophy, and fatigue in the setting of chronic or terminal illness?

{{c1::Cachexia}}

Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is a paraneoplastic syndrome associated with which malignancy?

{{c1::Ovarian teratoma}}

Which neuromuscular paraneoplastic syndrome may be associated with a thymoma?

{{c1::Myasthenia gravis}}

What four types of cancer are associated with paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration?

{{c1::Small cell}} cancer of the lung
{{c1::Gynecologic}} cancers
{{c1::Breast}} cancers
{{c1::Hodgkin}} lymphoma

What two paraneoplastic syndromes are especially associated with pancreatic adenocarcinoma?

{{c1::Trousseau}} syndrome
{{c1::Nonbacterial::Bacterial/Nonbacterial}} {{c1::thrombotic endocarditis}}

Which two hematologic paraneoplastic syndromes are associated with thymoma?

{{c1::Pure red cell aplasia}}
{{c1::Good}} syndrome

Which cancer is related to the paraneoplastic increase in ACTH and ADH?

{{c1::Small cell lung}} cancer
fields.Back Extra: This produces ectopic ACTH that causes Cushing syndrome and ectopic ADH that causes hyponatremia (SIADH).

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism underlying hypercalcemia of malignancy in lymphoma?

Increase in {{c1::calcitriol}}

What five underlying malignancies may be associated with abnormally elevated erythropoietin?

{{c1::Pheochromocytoma}}
{{c1::Renal cell}} carcinoma
{{c1::Hepatocellular}} carcinoma
{{c1::Hemangioblastoma}}
{{c1::Leiomyoma}}

Acanthosis nigricans is associated with which underlying malignancies?

{{c1::Gastric}} adenocarcinoma
Other {{c1::visceral}} malignancies

What is the mechanism underlying Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome?

Antibodies against {{c1::presynaptic::presynaptic/postsynaptic}} {{c1::Ca2+}} channels at {{c1::neuromuscular junctions}}
fields.Back Extra: This is associated with small cell lung cancer.

fields.Text:
What tumors are commonly associated with sudden onset of numerous seborrheic keratoses?

{{c1::Gastric}} adenocarcinoma
Other {{c1::visceral}} malignancies
fields.Back Extra: This can present with the sign of Leser-Trélat, which are multiple seborrheic kertoses.

fields.Text:
Which paraneoplastic syndrome is associated with pediatric neuroblastoma?

{{c1::Opsoclonus-myoclonus ataxia}} syndrome

What are five cancers associated with hypercalcemia due to the production of PTHrP?

{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinomas
{{c1::Bladder}} carcinomas
{{c1::Breast}} cancers
{{c1::Ovarian}} cancers
{{c1::Renal}} cancers

What is the mechanism underlying hyponatremia associated with small cell lung cancer?

Ectopically produced {{c1::ADH}} by small cell lung cancer

What cancer is highly associated with hypertrophic osteoarthropathy?

{{c1::Adenocarcinoma}} of the {{c1::lung::organ}}

Which paraneoplastic syndrome has the constellation of heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, and weakness of the thighs and shoulders?

{{c1::Dermatomyositis}}

Which three antibodies against Purkinje cells are associated with paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration?

{{c1::Anti-Hu}} antibodies → Small cell lung cancer
{{c1::Anti-Yo}} antibodies → Gynecologic and breast cancers
{{c1::Anti-Tr}} antibodies → Hodgkin lymphoma

What are the six paraneoplastic syndromes associated with small cell lung cancer?

{{c1::SIADH}}
Paraneoplastic {{c1::cerebellar degeneration}}
Paraneoplastic {{c1::encephalomyelitis}}
{{c1::Opsoclonus-myoclonus ataxia}} syndrome
{{c1::Lambert-Eaton myasthenic}} syndrome
{{c1::Cushing}} syndrome

Which paraneoplastic syndrome is associated with autonomic instability, seizures, memory deficits, dyskinesias, language dysfunction, and psychiatric disturbance?

{{c1::Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis}}

Which paraneoplastic syndrome is associated with abnormal proliferation of skin and bone at distal extremities?

{{c1::Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy}}

The Michaelis-Menten kinetics graph for an uninhibited drug is shown in red. Which line represents addition of a competitive inhibitor?



{{c1::Green}} curve
fields.Back Extra: The Vmax stays the same, but it takes a larger [S] to reach it.

fields.Text:
The Michaelis-Menten kinetics graph for an uninhibited drug is shown in red. Which line represents addition of a noncompetitive inhibitor?



{{c1::Blue}} curve
fields.Back Extra: The Vmax is lower regardless of the [S].

fields.Text:
What happens to the line in the Lineweaver-Burk plot shown in the image when a competitive inhibitor is added?



Slope → {{c1::Increased}}
x-intercept → {{c1::Increased}}
y-intercept → {{c1::Unchanged}}

What happens to the line in the Lineweaver-Burk plot shown in the image when a noncompetitive inhibitor is added?



Slope → {{c1::Increased}}
x-intercept → {{c1::Unchanged}}
y-intercept → {{c1::Increased}}

Given the y-intercept of the Lineweaver-Burk plot, what happens to the Vmax when the y-intercept is moved up?



Vmax {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
fields.Back Extra: The closer to 0 on the y-axis, the higher the Vmax.

fields.Text:
Indicate which inhibitors resembles its substrate.

Reversible competitive inhibitor → {{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}
Irreversible competitive inhibitor → {{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}
Noncompetitive inhibitor → {{c1::No::Yes/No}}

Indicate which inhibitors can be overcome by an increase in substrate.

Reversible competitive inhibitor → {{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}
Irreversible competitive inhibitor → {{c1::No::Yes/No}}
Noncompetitive inhibitor → {{c1::No::Yes/No}}

Indicate which inhibitors bind to an active site.

Reversible competitive inhibitor → {{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}
Irreversible competitive inhibitor → {{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}
Noncompetitive inhibitor → {{c1::No::Yes/No}}

Describe the effect of each inhibitor on the pharmacodynamics of potency and/or efficacy.

Reversible competitive inhibitor → Decreases {{c1::potency::potency/efficacy}}
Irreversible competitive inhibitor → Decreases {{c1::efficacy::potency/efficacy}}
Noncompetitive inhibitor → Decreases {{c1::efficacy::potency/efficacy}}

Describe the effect of each inhibitor on Vmax.

Reversible competitive inhibitor → Vmax is {{c1::unchanged}}
Irreversible competitive inhibitor → Vmax is {{c1::decreased}}
Noncompetitive inhibitor → Vmax is {{c1::decreased}}

Describe the effect of each inhibitor on Km.

Reversible competitive inhibitor → Km is {{c1::increased}}
Irreversible competitive inhibitor → Km is {{c1::unchanged}}
Noncompetitive inhibitor → Km is {{c1::unchanged}}

How is Vmax related to enzyme concentration?

{{c1::Directly::Directly/Indirectly}} proportional
fields.Back Extra: An increase in enzyme concentration will lead to an increase in Vmax.

fields.Text:
How is Km related to the affinity of an enzyme for its substrate?

{{c1::Inversely}} related
fields.Back Extra: A decrease in Km leads to an increase in enzyme affinity.

fields.Text:
What is the velocity of the reaction when the concentration of the substrate is equal to Km?

The reaction velocity is at {{c1::50}}% of the maximum

How do pharmacokinetic curves differ in shape for drugs that follow Michaelis-Menten kinetics versus those that follow cooperative kinetics?

Michaelis-Menten kinetics → {{c1::Hyperbolic}} curve
Cooperative kinetics → {{c1::Sigmoidal}} curve

A Lineweaver-Burk plot is shown by a red line for an uninhibited drug. Indicate what type of inhibitors are represented by the green and blue lines.



Green line → {{c1::Competitive}} inhibitor
Blue line → {{c1::Noncompetitive}} inhibitor

Where is a drug with small lipophilic molecules typically distributed?

{{c1::Tissues}}
fields.Back Extra:
This distribution also includes fat.

Small lipophilic molecules have a high volume of distribution, especially when bound to tissue protein.

fields.Text:
Where is a drug made of large charged molecules or plasma protein-bound molecules typically distributed?

{{c1::Intravascular::Intravascular/Extravascular}} compartment
fields.Back Extra:
Anything large will likely stay in that compartment, especially if it is charged.

The volume of distribution is low for large charged molecules.

fields.Text:
Where is a small hydrophilic drug with a medium volume of distribution typically distributed?

{{c1::Extracellular fluid}}

After 3 half-lives, what percentage of a drug remains if it was given as a single-dose IV bolus?

{{c1::12.5}}% of its original concentration

Why is the bioavailability of a drug taken orally less than 100%?

Incomplete {{c1::absorption}} of the drug
{{c1::First-pass}} metabolism
fields.Back Extra: In comparison, bioavailability of IV drugs is 100%.

fields.Text:
After 1 half-life, given constant IV infusion of a drug, how close to steady state is the concentration of the drug?

{{c1::50}}% of steady state concentration

You administer a drug with a volume of distribution of 30 L and a clearance rate of 1.05 L/min. What is the half-life of this drug?

{{c1::20}} minutes

You administer a drug with a 2-hour half-life to a patient by constant infusion. How long will it take to reach steady state?

{{c1::8}} to {{c1::10}} hours
fields.Back Extra: In first-order kinetics, a drug infused at a constant rate takes 4 to 5 half-lives to reach steady state.

fields.Text:
What is the definition of the half-life of a drug?

The time required to change the amount of drug in the body by {{c1::half}} as elimination occurs
fields.Back Extra: It is a property of first-order elimination.

fields.Text:
Disease in which three organs could impair drug clearance?

{{c1::Heart}}
{{c1::Kidney}}
{{c1::Liver}}

The half-life of a drug that follows first-order kinetics is 4 hours. How long after discontinuation of the drug until 6.25% of the drug remains?

{{c1::16}} hours

What does clearance of a drug measure and how is it calculated?

Volume of {{c1::plasma}} cleared of drug per unit time
CL = {{c1::Vd}} × {{c1::Ke}}

How is the half-life of a drug calculated in first-order elimination in relation to the volume of distribution and the clearance of drug?

t1/2 = ( {{c1::0.7}} × {{c1::Vd}} ) / {{c1::CL}}

How many half-lives does a drug, infused at a steady rate, take to reach steady state if it follows first-order kinetics?

{{c1::4}} to {{c1::5}} half-lives

Damage to which two organs can alter the volume of distribution of plasma protein-bound drugs?

{{c1::Liver}} disease
{{c1::Kidney}} disease
fields.Back Extra: A decrease in protein binding leads to an increase in volume of distribution.

fields.Text:
How is the volume of distribution related to the amount of drug in the body and plasma drug concentration?

Vd = {{c1::Amount of drug in the body}} / {{c1::Plasma drug concentration}}

Define bioavailability.

The {{c1::fraction}} of administered drug that reaches the {{c1::systemic}} circulation unchanged
fields.Back Extra: For an IV dose, the bioavailability is 100%.

fields.Text:
You give 50 mg of drug A to a patient. The initial plasma drug concentration is 2.5 mg/L. What is the volume of distribution of drug A?

{{c1::20}} L
fields.Back Extra: Vd = Amount of drug in the body / Plasma drug concentration

fields.Text:
For a drug that is infused at a constant rate, how many half-lives does it take to reach 90% of the steady state level?

{{c1::3.3}} half-lives

After 2 half-lives, what percentage of a drug remains if it was given as a single-dose IV bolus?

{{c1::25}}% of its original concentration

What is the state of dynamic equilibrium called in which the rate of drug elimination is equal to the rate of drug ingestion?

{{c1::Steady}} state

How does the volume of distribution of a drug affect the efficacy of hemodialysis of that same drug?

Drugs with a low volume of distribution are {{c1::more::more/less}} effectively removed via hemodialysis

Name the variable on which time to steady state depends.

{{c1::Half-life}}
fields.Back Extra: It is independent of dose and dosing frequency.

fields.Text:
In patients with cirrhosis and renal failure, how do you modify the loading and maintenance doses of a given drug?

Loading dose is {{c1::unchanged}}
Maintenance dose is {{c1::decreased}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because drug clearance is impaired.

fields.Text:
What is the formula for calculating the maintenance dose of a drug?

Maintenance dose = ( {{c1::Cp}} × {{c1::CL}} × {{c1::τ}} ) / {{c1::F}}

What is the formula for the loading dose of a drug?

Loading dose  = ( {{c1::Cp}} × {{c1::Vd}} ) / {{c1::F}}

How does being a slow acetylator affect a patient's adverse effect burden compared with someone with normal acetylation power?

{{c1::Greater::Greater/Less}} adverse effect burden due to {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} rate of metabolism
fields.Back Extra: An example of this is isoniazid.

fields.Text:
How do drugs change after undergoing phase II drug metabolism?

They become very {{c1::polar::polar/nonpolar}}
fields.Back Extra: The exception to this is acetylated metabolites.

fields.Text:
Which enzyme system mediates phase I metabolism of drugs in the body?

{{c1::CYP450}}

Which three types of biochemical reactions are involved in phase I metabolism of drugs?

{{c1::Reduction}}
{{c1::Oxidation}}
{{c1::Hydrolysis}}

Which four types of conjugation reactions are involved in phase II metabolism of drugs?

{{c1::Methylation}}
{{c1::Glucuronidation}}
{{c1::Acetylation}}
{{c1::Sulfation}}

How do drugs change after undergoing phase I drug metabolism?

They become slightly {{c1::polar::polar/nonpolar}}
May either be {{c1::active}} or {{c1::inactive}}

Which phase of drug metabolism do geriatric patients lose first?

Phase {{c1::I::I/II}}

What order of elimination is depicted in the drug clearance graph?



{{c1::Zero-order}}

What order of elimination is depicted in the drug clearance graph?



{{c1::First-order}}

In first-order elimination kinetics, what is the relationship between rate of elimination and drug concentration?

Rate of elimination is {{c1::directly::directly/indirectly}} proportional to the concentration of the drug
fields.Back Extra: A constant fraction of drug is eliminated per unit time.

fields.Text:
Phenytoin, ethanol, and high-concentration aspirin display what order of elimination kinetics?

{{c1::Zero-order}} elimination
fields.Back Extra: They are eliminated linearly with time.

fields.Text:
In zero-order elimination kinetics, what is the relationship between rate of elimination and drug concentration?

{{c1::None}}
fields.Back Extra: The rate of elimination is constant, regardless of drug concentration.

fields.Text:
Zero-order elimination is also known by what other name?

{{c1::Capacity-limited}} elimination

First-order elimination is also known by what other name?

{{c1::Flow-dependent}} elimination

What order of elimination is typical for most drugs?

{{c1::First-order}} elimination

Which substance would enhance the renal clearance of weakly basic drugs such as amphetamines or TCAs?

{{c1::Ammonium chloride}}
fields.Back Extra: An acidic environment ionizes weakly basic drugs, which are then trapped in the urine and cleared.

fields.Text:
What substance is given to enhance the renal clearance of weakly acidic drugs such as phenobarbital, methotrexate, and salicylates?

{{c1::Sodium bicarbonate}}
fields.Back Extra: A basic environment ionizes weakly acidic drugs, which are then trapped in the urine and cleared.

fields.Text:
In which acid-base environment is a weak acid most likely to become trapped?

{{c1::Basic::Acidic/Basic}} environment

In which acid-base environment is a weak base most likely to become trapped?

{{c1::Acidic::Acidic/Basic}} environment

Why is tricyclic antidepressant toxicity treated with sodium bicarbonate rather than a weak acid even though tricyclic antidepressants are weakly basic?

Sodium bicarbonate is used to prevent tricyclic antidepressants from blocking {{c1::sodium}} channels rather than accelerating drug {{c1::elimination}}

Differentiate between the clearance of ionized versus neutral species in the urine.

{{c1::Ionized::Ionized/Neutral}} species are trapped in the urine, allowing them to be cleared quickly
{{c1::Neutral::Ionized/Neutral}} species can be reabsorbed

Define pKa.

The pH at which a weak acid or base is 50% {{c1::ionized}} and 50% {{c1::nonionized}}
fields.Back Extra: It represents the strength of a weak acid or base.

fields.Text:
You measure the effects of two drugs at different dosages. Which drug is more potent?



Drug {{c1::A}}
fields.Back Extra: Drugs that are more potent have a lower effective concentration.

fields.Text:
You measure the effects of two drugs at different dosages. Which drug is the partial agonist?



Drug {{c1::B}}
fields.Back Extra: Partial agonists are less efficacious than full agonists.

fields.Text:
By increasing drug efficacy, what happens to potency?

{{c1::Nothing}}
fields.Back Extra: These factors are unrelated and independent of one another.

fields.Text:
If 50 mg of drug A is needed to achieve an effect, but 100 mg of drug B is needed for the same effect, which drug is is more potent?

Drug {{c1::A}}

What is the definition of drug potency?

The amount of drug needed to produce a given {{c1::effect}}
fields.Back Extra: It is represented by the x-value (EC50).

fields.Text:
What is the definition of drug efficacy?

The {{c1::maximal}} effect that a particular drug can produce
fields.Back Extra: It is represented by the y-value (Vmax).

fields.Text:
If changes in norepinephrine binding are shown, the addition of phenoxybenzamine will cause what type of inhibition on α-receptors?



Potency → {{c1::Unchanged}}
Efficacy → {{c1::Decreased}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows an agonist with a noncompetitive antagonist.

fields.Text:
If the black curve denotes diazepam, the addition of flumazenil will cause what type of binding on GABAA receptors?



Potency → {{c1::Decreased}}
Efficacy → {{c1::Unchanged}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows an agonist with a competitive antagonist.

fields.Text:
How does the potency of a partial agonist relate to the potency of a full agonist of the same receptor?

A partial agonist may be {{c1::more}} potent than, {{c1::less}} potent than, or {{c1::just as}} potent as a full agonist

How does the efficacy of a partial agonist relate to the efficacy of a full agonist of the same receptor?

A partial agonist has a(n) {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} in maximal efficacy
fields.Back Extra: Potency is a separate, independent variable.

fields.Text:
In pharmacodynamics, what happens to the efficacy of an agonist in the presence of a noncompetitive antagonist?

Efficacy is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} and cannot be overcome by {{c1::increasing::increasing/decreasing}} the agonist substrate concentration

What happens to efficacy of an agonist when a competitive antagonist is given?

Efficacy is {{c1::unchanged}}
fields.Back Extra: A competitive antagonist is overcome with an increase in agonist concentration.

fields.Text:
What type of antagonist is phenoxybenzamine, which decreases the efficacy of norepinephrine on α-receptors?

{{c1::Noncompetitive::Competitive/Noncompetitive}} antagonist

What value replaces median toxic dose for animal studies?

{{c1::Lethal median dose}}

What is the range of concentrations of a drug that can treat disease safely and effectively called?

{{c1::Therapeutic window}}

Drug A has a therapeutic index of 5, whereas drug B has a therapeutic index of 30. Which drug is safer for your patient?

Drug {{c1::B}}
fields.Back Extra: Safer drugs have higher therapeutic indices.

fields.Text:
What is the formula that describes the therapeutic index of a drug?

TI = {{c1::TD50}} / {{c1::ED50}}

Which property of a drug is determined by its therapeutic index?

{{c1::Safety}}
fields.Back Extra: Drugs with higher therapeutic indices are less likely to cause toxicity.

fields.Text:
Name five common drugs and/or drug classes that have a low therapeutic index and require frequent monitoring.

{{c1::Warfarin}}
{{c1::Theophylline}}
{{c1::Digoxin}}
{{c1::Antiepileptics}}
{{c1::Lithium}}

Define a synergistic drug interaction.

The total effect of drug A and drug B taken together is {{c1::greater::greater/less}} than the sum of their individual effects
fields.Back Extra: An example of this is clopidogrel and aspirin taken together.

fields.Text:
Define a permissive drug interaction.

Drug A is {{c1::required}} to see the {{c1::full}} effect of drug B
fields.Back Extra: An example of this is cortisol on catecholamine responsiveness.

fields.Text:
Define an additive drug interaction.

The effect of drug A and drug B taken together is {{c1::equal}} to the sum of their individual effects
fields.Back Extra: An example of this is aspirin and acetaminophen taken together.

fields.Text:
Define a tachyphylactic drug interaction.

An acute {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} in response to a drug following initial or repeated administration
fields.Back Extra: Repeated use of oxymetazoline decreases its response and causes rebound congestion.

fields.Text:
Define an antagonistic drug interaction.

Effect of drug A and drug B together is {{c1::less::greater/less}} than the sum of their individual effects
fields.Back Extra: An example of this is an ethanol antidote for methanol toxicity.

fields.Text:
Define potentiation in terms of drug interactions.

Drug B has no therapeutic action, but it {{c1::enhances}} the therapeutic action of drug A
fields.Back Extra: An example of this can be seen when carbidopa only blocks an enzyme that prevents peripheral conversion of levodopa.

fields.Text:
Which two cell types are part of the sympathetic pathway but are innervated by cholinergic fibers?

{{c1::Adrenal medulla}}
{{c1::Sweat}} glands

How many synapses are involved in activation of the adrenal medulla?

{{c1::1}}
fields.Back Extra: The adrenal medulla is directly innervated by preganglionic sympathetic fibers.

fields.Text:
Which two substances are released into the blood from the adrenal medulla after the activation of the sympathetic nervous system?

{{c1::Epinephrine}}
{{c1::Norepinephrine}}

Which neurotransmitter and neurotransmitter receptor mediates sympathetic tone in the smooth muscles of the renal vasculature?

{{c1::Dopamine}}, which acts on the {{c1::D1}} receptor

Which neurotransmitter and receptors mediate sympathetic tone in cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, glandular cells, and nerve terminals?

{{c1::Norepinephrine}} via {{c1::α}}-receptors and {{c1::β}}-receptors

Sweat glands are unique in that they receive sympathetic input through which receptors?

{{c1::Muscarinic acetylcholine}} receptors

Which neurotransmitter is present at the paravertebral ganglia, and what type of receptor does it act on?

{{c1::Acetylcholine}} is present at the paravertebral ganglia and acts on {{c1::nicotinic}} receptors, specifically the {{c1::N}}-type

Where do preganglionic sympathetic neurons synapse?

{{c1::Paravertebral ganglia}}
fields.Back Extra: This is at the sympathetic chain ganglia.

fields.Text:
How many neurons are involved in sympathetic transmission from the spinal cord to the target organ?

{{c1::2}} with the exception of the {{c1::adrenal medulla}}

Which neurotransmitter receptors on skeletal muscle receive input from somatic nerves arising in the the spinal cord?

{{c1::Nicotinic acetylcholine}} receptors, specifically the {{c1::M}}-type

Which neurotransmitter receptors mediate sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system function at the peripheral ganglia?

{{c1::Nicotinic acetylcholine}} receptors, specifically the {{c1::N}}-type

Which neurotransmitter mediates parasympathetic nervous system function?

{{c1::Acetylcholine}}
fields.Back Extra: This is at both postganglionic neurons and target cells.

fields.Text:
Describe the two neurons in the parasympathetic nervous system.

The preganglionic neuron originates in the {{c1::brainstem}} or the {{c1::sacral}} nerve roots with a {{c1::long::short/long}} axon
The postganglionic neuron is near the {{c1::destination}} with a {{c1::short::short/long}} axon

Which neurotransmitter receptors mediate parasympathetic tone in cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, gland cells, and nerve terminals?

{{c1::Muscarinic acetylcholine}} receptors

Which types of nerves arise from the spinal cord and directly innervate skeletal muscle?

{{c1::Somatic}} nerves

Which nerves are responsible for providing parasympathetic innervation to viscera in the abdomen and pelvic regions?

{{c1::Pelvic splanchnic}} nerves

Which cranial nerves are part of the parasympathetic nervous system?

Cranial nerve {{c1::III}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::VII}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::IX}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::X}}

How many subtypes of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are there?

{{c1::5}}

Where are the subtypes of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors found?

{{c1::Heart::Organ}}
{{c1::Smooth}} muscle
{{c1::Brain::Organ}}
{{c1::Exocrine}} glands
{{c1::Sweat}} glands

In what two locations is the NN subtype of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor found?

{{c1::Adrenal medulla}}
{{c1::Autonomic}} ganglia

What type of receptors are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors?

{{c1::G-protein–coupled}} receptors that act via {{c1::secondary messengers}}

What type of receptors are nicotinic acetylcholine receptors?

{{c1::Ligand}}-gated channels that allow for an influx of either {{c1::Na+}} or {{c1::Ca2+}} and an efflux of {{c1::K+}}

In what location is the NM subtype of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor found?

{{c1::Neuromuscular junctions}} of {{c1::skeletal}} muscle

Which part of the brain regulates micturition and how is it regulated?

The {{c1::pons}}, which contains the micturition center that regulates {{c1::involuntary::voluntary/involuntary}} function of the bladder

Activation of which part of the autonomic nervous system results in urinary retention?

{{c1::Sympathetic::Sympathetic/Parasympathetic}} nervous system

Which arm of the autonomic nervous system helps us void?

{{c1::Parasympathetic::Sympathetic/Parasympathetic}} nervous system

Which drug classes would be useful in treating urge incontinence?

{{c1::Muscarinic}} antagonists
{{c1::Sympathomimetics}}

What is the mechanism of action of oxybutynin in the treatment of urgency incontinence?

As a {{c1::muscarinic}} antagonist, it inhibits the {{c1::M3}}-receptor, causing {{c1::relaxation::contraction/relaxation}} and {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} overactivity of the detrusor smooth muscle

Which drug class would be useful in treating urinary retention?

{{c1::Muscarinic}} agonists

What is the mechanism of action of bethanechol in the treatment of urinary retention?

Activation of the {{c1::M3}}-receptor, causing {{c1::contraction::contraction/relaxation}} of the detrusor smooth muscle and improved bladder emptying

What is the mechanism of action of mirabegron in the treatment of urgency incontinence?

Activatation of {{c1::β3}}-adrenergic receptors, leading to {{c1::relaxation::contraction/relaxation}} of the detrusor smooth muscle and increased bladder capacity

A 65-year-old male who is unable to sleep well at night comes to the clinic for evaluation of worsening nocturia and a weak stream of urine. What is the medication of choice?

{{c1::Tamsulosin}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an α1-receptor blocker used for benign prostatic hyperplasia.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of tamsulosin?

As an {{c1::α1}}-blocker, it {{c1::relaxes::contracts/relaxes}} the detrusor smooth muscle at the {{c1::bladder neck}} and {{c1::prostate}}
fields.Back Extra: It is used for treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia.

fields.Text:
Which two tissues contain β1-adrenergic receptors and what happens when they are activated?

{{c1::Heart}} → {{c2::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} heart rate
{{c1::Kidney}} → {{c2::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} renin secretion

Which two tissues contain α1-adrenergic receptors and what happens when they are activated?

{{c1::Vascular}} smooth muscle → {{c2::Vasoconstriction::Vasodilation/Vasoconstriction}}
{{c1::Visceral}} smooth muscle → Smooth muscle {{c2::contraction::contraction/relaxation}}

Which three tissues contain α2-adrenergic receptors and what happens when they are activated?

{{c1::Pancreas}}
{{c1::Presynaptic::Presynaptic/Postsynaptic}} terminals
{{c1::Salivary}} glands

Activation of these tissues causes inhibition of {{c2::neurotransmitter}} release

Which four tissues contain β2-adrenergic receptors and what happens when they are activated?

{{c1::Liver}} → Inhibition of {{c2::insulin}} secretion
{{c1::Bronchioles}} → {{c2::Bronchodilation::Bronchodilation/Bronchoconstriction}}
{{c1::Cardiac}} muscles → {{c2::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} heart rate
{{c1::Visceral}} smooth muscles → {{c2::Vasodilation::Vasodilation/Vasoconstriction}}

Which tissue contain β3-adrenergic receptors and what happens when they are activated?

{{c1::Adipose}} tissue → {{c2::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} lipolysis

What is the effect of a V1-receptor agonist on vascular smooth muscle?

{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in vascular smooth muscle contraction

What is the effect of H2-receptor activation in the gastrointestinal system?

{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in gastric acid production

Activation of which receptors would lead to pruritus, pain, increased nasal and bronchial mucus production, increased vascular permeability, and bronchoconstriction?

Activation of {{c1::H1}}-receptors

What is the primary effect of D2-receptor activation?

{{c1::Modulation}} of neurotransmitter release, especially in the {{c1::brain}}

How does activation of D1-receptors affect the renal vasculature?

{{c1::Relaxes::Contracts/Relaxes}} the renal vascular smooth muscle

Which enzyme is directly activated when Gq-linked receptors are activated?

{{c1::Phospholipase C}}

What are the three effects of M3-receptor activation on the eye?

{{c1::Miosis::Mydriasis/Miosis}}
{{c1::Accommodation}}
{{c1::Lacrimation}}

What is the effect of M3-receptor activation on the bowels and bladder?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} gut peristalsis
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} bladder contractions

How do M2-receptors regulate cardiac function?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} heart rate
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} atrial contractility

Which cholinergic receptor mediates higher cognitive function and stimulates the enteric nervous system?

{{c1::M1}}-receptor
fields.Back Extra: This is by activating the receptor.

fields.Text:
What enzyme is directly stimulated or inhibited by the activation of Gs-coupled or Gi-coupled receptors?

{{c1::Adenylate cyclase}}

What are the three major effects of β3-receptor activation in adipocytes, the urinary bladder, and skeletal muscles?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} lipolysis
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} bladder relaxation
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} thermogenesis in skeletal muscle

What is the effect of β2-receptor activation on respiration?

Promotes {{c1::bronchodilation::bronchodilation/bronchoconstriction}}

What is the effect of β2-receptor activation on vascular tone?

{{c1::Vasodilation::Vasodilation/Vasoconstriction}}

What effect is seen in the uterus with β2-receptor activation?

{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in uterine tone
fields.Back Extra: β2-agonists may be used as tocolytics to slow down labor.

fields.Text:
What are the major functions of β1-receptor activation in the heart, adipocytes, and kidneys?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} cardiac contractility
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} lipolysis
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} renin release

Name the G-protein classes of the following histamine receptors.

H1-receptor → {{c1::Gq}}
H2-receptor → {{c1::Gs}}

What are the major effects of α2-receptor activation on lipolysis and insulin release?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} lipolysis
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} insulin release

How does M3-receptor activation affect insulin release?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} insulin release

What two main effects does activation of protein kinase A have?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} intracellular calcium in the heart
{{c1::Relaxes::Contracts/Relaxes}} smooth muscle

Binding of which receptors would lead to increased production of aqueous humor, increased cellular K+ uptake, tocolysis, vasodilation, and relaxation of ciliary muscles?

{{c1::β2}}-receptors

What role does DAG play in the cascade of reactions that occur after phospholipase activation?

Activation of {{c1::protein kinase C}}

What two molecules result from the reaction of phospholipase C with the membrane lipid PIP2?

{{c1::IP3}}
{{c1::DAG}}

What is the final effector enzyme influenced in pathways linked to Gs and Gi proteins?

{{c1::Protein kinase A}}

What reaction does adenylate cyclase catalyze?

Adenylate cyclase catalyzes the conversion of {{c1::ATP}} to {{c1::cAMP}}

What are the three types of receptors coupled to Gi proteins?

{{c1::M2}}-receptor
{{c1::α2}}-receptor
{{c1::D2}}-receptor

What are the six types of receptors coupled to Gs proteins?

{{c1::β1}}-receptor
{{c1::β2}}-receptor
{{c1::β3}}-receptor
{{c1::D1}}-receptor
{{c1::H2}}-receptor
{{c1::V2}}-receptor

What are the five types of receptors coupled to Gq proteins?

{{c1::H1}}-receptor
{{c1::α1}}-receptor
{{c1::V1}}-receptor
{{c1::M1}}-receptor
{{c1::M3}}-receptor

What is the major effect of V2-receptor activation on the kidney?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} water reabsorption
fields.Back Extra: This is by upregulation of aquaporin-2 in the collecting tubules.

fields.Text:
Is protein kinase A upregulated or downregulated by a Gs protein?

{{c1::Upregulated}}

Is protein kinase A upregulated or downregulated by a Gi protein?

{{c1::Downregulated}}

What is the major effect of α2-receptor activation on platelets?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} platelet aggregation

Activation of which receptors leads to mydriasis, vascular smooth muscle contraction, and intestinal and bladder sphincter muscle contraction?

{{c1::α1}}-receptors

What are the major effects of α2-receptor activation on overall sympathetic tone?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} sympathetic tone
fields.Back Extra: This is via inhibition of adrenergic outflow.

fields.Text:
How do D1-receptors and D2-receptors behave in the striatum?

D1-receptors {{c1::activate::activate/inhibit}} the {{c1::direct::direct/indirect}} pathway
D2-receptors {{c1::inhibit::activate/inhibit}} the {{c1::indirect::direct/indirect}} pathway

What is the effect of M3-receptor activation on the respiratory system?

{{c1::Bronchoconstriction::Bronchodilation/Bronchoconstriction}}

What role does cAMP play in the cascade of reactions that occurs after activation of adenylate cyclase?

Adenylate cyclase converts ATP into cAMP, leading to the {{c1::downstream::upstream/downstream}} activation of {{c1::protein kinase A}}

How does V2-receptor activation assist in hemostasis?

Via {{c1::increasing::increasing/decreasing}} vWF release

What is the effect of M3-receptor activation on vascular tone?

Promotes endothelium-mediated {{c1::vasodilation::vasodilation/vasoconstriction}}

What two adrenergic receptors are involved in the regulation of aqueous humor production?

{{c1::α2}}-receptors decrease aqueous humor production
{{c1::β2}}-receptors increase aqueous humor production

Why are β-agonists sometimes used in the treatment of hyperkalemia?

β2-receptor activation promotes cellular {{c1::uptake}} of K+

Where in the synapse does a drug inhibiting acetylcholinesterase act?

{{c1::Postsynaptic::Presynaptic/Postsynaptic}} membrane

What are the steps by which amphetamines gain access to neurosecretory vesicles in presynaptic neurons?

Amphetamines use {{c1::NETs}} to enter presynaptic terminals; then they enter vesicles via {{c1::VMATs}}

A drug company designs a drug that reduces acetylcholine synthesis by blocking the uptake of its substrate. Which substrate is this?

{{c1::Choline}}

By what steps do amphetamines promote norepinephrine release into the synapse?

Amphetamines displace norepinephrine from {{c1::neurosecretory}} vesicles

How does pyridostigmine affect synaptic choline and acetate levels?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} choline level
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} acetate level
fields.Back Extra: This is due to the inhibition of acetylcholine breakdown.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiology of botulism?

Botulinum toxin blocks {{c1::acetylcholine}} release from the {{c1::presynaptic::presynaptic/postsynaptic}} vesicles, producing {{c1::flaccid}} paralysis

What two drugs promote the release of norepinephrine from presynaptic vessels into the synapse?

{{c1::Amphetamine}}
{{c1::Ephedrine}}

How does reserpine affect presynaptic norepinephrine release?

Blocks neurotransmitter packaging into vesicles by inhibiting {{c1::VMAT}}
fields.Back Extra: This decreases the release of norepinephrine into the synapse.

fields.Text:
What three important drugs inhibit the reuptake of norepinephrine from the synapse?

{{c1::Cocaine}}
{{c1::TCAs}}
{{c1::Amphetamines}}

Norepinephrine-mediated activation of α2-receptors on presynaptic sympathetic nerve terminals is an example of what type of feedback?

{{c1::Negative::Positive/Negative}} feedback

What would be the effect of clonidine, a selective α2-receptor agonist, on the presynaptic release of norepinephrine?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} norepinephrine release

Which two receptors modulate the presynaptic release of norepinephrine?

Promotes release → {{c1::Angiotensin II}} receptors
Inhibits release → {{c1::α2}}-receptors

Which three mechanisms are used to clear norepinephrine from the synaptic cleft?

{{c1::Diffusion}}
{{c1::Metabolism}}
{{c1::Reuptake}}

Where in the neuron is dopamine converted to norepinephrine?

Within {{c1::presynaptic::presynaptic/postsynaptic}} vesicles

What amino acid is the precursor in the synthesis of dopamine?

{{c1::Tyrosine}}

What amino acid is the precursor to norepinephrine?

{{c1::Tyrosine}}

What enzyme breaks down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft?

{{c1::Acetylcholinesterase}}

Influx of which ion into the nerve terminal promotes presynaptic acetylcholine release?

{{c1::Ca2+}}

What enzyme is responsible for the formation of acetylcholine?

{{c1::Choline acetyltransferase}}

What are the two substrates of choline acetyltransferase?

{{c1::Acetyl-CoA}}
{{c1::Choline}}

What two products result from the breakdown of acetylcholine by acetylcholinesterase?

{{c1::Choline}}
{{c1::Acetate}}

How will losartan, an angiotensin II receptor antagonist, affect presynaptic release of norepinephrine?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} release of norepinephrine

What molecules are responsible for the packaging of dopamine into neurosecretory vesicles?

{{c1::VMATs}}

Which three direct cholinomimetic drugs are resistant to degradation by acetylcholinesterase?

{{c1::Bethanechol}}
{{c1::Carbachol}}
{{c1::Pilocarpine}}

How does methacholine work in the airway challenge test for asthma?

Causes {{c1::bronchoconstriction::bronchodilation/bronchoconstriction}} via stimulation of {{c1::muscarinic}} receptors in the airway

Which direct cholinomimetic drug is used in the airway challenge test for the diagnosis of asthma?

{{c1::Methacholine}}

What action of pilocarpine makes it useful in the treatment of open-angle glaucoma?

{{c1::Contraction::Contraction/Relaxation}} of the {{c1::ciliary}} muscle

Which two cholinomimetic drugs can be used in the treatment of glaucoma?

{{c1::Carbachol}}
{{c1::Pilocarpine}}

How does bethanechol treat urinary retention?

By {{c1::activation::activation/inhibition}} of bladder smooth muscle

What is the mechanism of action of bethanechol, carbachol, pilocarpine, and methacholine?

{{c1::Direct::Direct/Indirect}} {{c1::cholinergic}} agonism

What structural property of anticholinesterases determines whether they can act on the central nervous system?

They are {{c1::tertiary amines}}
fields.Back Extra: They can cross the blood-brain barrier and enter the central nervous system.

fields.Text:
Why is pilocarpine useful in the treatment of patients with dry eyes and dry mouth?

It is a potent stimulator of sweat, tears, and saliva production via {{c1::parasympathomimetic::sympathomimetic/parasympathomimetic}} action on muscarinic receptors and smooth muscles

How does neostigmine work in the reversal of a neuromuscular blockade?

Increases synaptic {{c1::acetylcholine}} levels by inhibiting {{c1::acetylcholinesterase}}

What action of pilocarpine makes it useful in the treatment of closed-angle glaucoma?

{{c1::Contraction::Contraction/Relaxation}} of the {{c1::pupillary sphincter}} muscle

How does pyridostigmine help in the treatment of myasthenia gravis?

It increases {{c1::acetylcholine}} levels → Improves muscle strength

What three cholinomimetic drugs are used as the first-line therapy in the treatment of Alzheimer disease?

{{c1::Donepezil}}
{{c1::Galantamine}}
{{c1::Rivastigmine}}

Which direct cholinomimetic is used to treat xerostomia commonly associated with Sjögren syndrome?

{{c1::Pilocarpine}}

What three medical conditions can be exacerbated by cholinomimetic agents in susceptible patients?

{{c1::Chronic obstructive pulmonary}} disease
{{c1::Asthma}}
{{c1::Peptic ulcer}} disease

What effect does neostigmine have on the central nervous system?

{{c1::None}}
fields.Back Extra: It does not penetrate the blood-brain barrier.

fields.Text:
What properties of pyridostigmine make it particularly useful in the treatment of myasthenia gravis compared with other anticholinesterases?

{{c1::Long::Short/Long}} acting
Does not cross the {{c1::blood-brain barrier}}
Acts on the {{c1::peripheral}} acetylcholinergic synapses

What enzyme is inhibited by indirect cholinergic agonists?

{{c1::Acetylcholinesterase}}

Which anticholinesterase drug is used as an antidote for atropine poisoning?

{{c1::Physostigmine}}

Which acetylcholinesterase inhibitor was historically used to diagnose myasthenia gravis?

{{c1::Edrophonium}}

Which cholinomimetic can be used to treat postoperative and neurogenic ileus, urinary retention, and myasthenia gravis?

{{c1::Neostigmine}}

What direct cholinomimetic drug is typically used for open-angle glaucoma, but not for closed-angle glaucoma?

{{c1::Carbachol}}

To what drug class do edrophonium, donepezil, and galantamine belong?

{{c1::Indirect::Direct/Indirect}} {{c1::cholinomimetics}}

Why doesn't bethanechol cause contraction of skeletal muscle?

Lacks {{c1::nicotinic acetylcholine}} receptor activity

What serologic test has replaced the use of edrophonium in the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis?

{{c1::Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody}} test

How does carbachol work in the treatment of open-angle glaucoma?

{{c1::Contracts::Contracts/Relaxes}} the pupil

Which cholinomimetic can be used in the treatment of both open-angle and closed-angle glaucoma?

{{c1::Pilocarpine}}

Why is physostigmine the drug of choice for treatment of anticholinergic toxicity?

As a {{c1::tertiary amine}}, it can freely cross the {{c1::blood-brain barrier}}

Which three drugs can be administered along with pyridostigmine to minimize its adverse effects?

{{c1::Glycopyrrolate}}
{{c1::Hyoscyamine}}
{{c1::Propantheline}}

What is the mechanism of action of pralidoxime?

Regenerates {{c1::acetylcholinestrase}} by {{c1::dephosphorylation}}

What are the treatments for organophosphate poisoning?

{{c1::Atropine}}
{{c1::Pralidoxime}}

What enzyme does an organophosphate irreversibly inhibit?

{{c1::Acetylcholinesterase}}

What are the characteristic muscarinic symptoms/signs seen with acetylcholinesterase inhibitor toxicity?

{{c1::Diarrhea}}
{{c2::Urination}}
{{c3::Miosis::Mydriasis/Miosis}}
{{c4::Bronchospasm}}
{{c5::Bradycardia::Tachycardia/Bradycardia}}
{{c6::Emesis}}
{{c7::Lacrimation}}
{{c8::Sweating}}
{{c9::Salivation}}

What effect does organophosphate poisoning produce through its action on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors?

{{c1::Neuromuscular}} blockade

What potential central nervous system effects can occur with anticholinesterase poisoning?

{{c1::Lethargy}}
{{c1::Respiratory}} depression
{{c1::Seizures}}
{{c1::Coma}}

Why are farmers at higher risk of organophosphate poisoning?

Organophosphates are commonly used as {{c1::insecticides}}

Which of the two antidotes used for organophosphate poisoning can reverse the muscarinic and central nervous system effects?

{{c1::Atropine}}

Which of the two antidotes for organophosphate poisoning can help relieve the nicotinic effects?

{{c1::Pralidoxime}}
fields.Back Extra: This is effective if given early.

fields.Text:
Why is pralidoxime not effective for the treatment of central nervous system toxicity seen with anticholinesterase poisoning?

Pralidoxime does not cross the {{c1::blood-brain barrier}} because it is a {{c1::quaternary amine}}

What are the clinical uses of the antimuscarinic drugs hyoscyamine and dicyclomine?

They act as {{c1::antispasmodics}} in {{c1::irritable bowel}} syndrome

What are the two antimuscarinic agents that can be used for acute dystonia in a patient with schizophrenia who is taking haloperidol?

{{c1::Benztropine}}
{{c1::Trihexyphenidyl}}

Which antimuscarinic drug is used for the treatment of motion sickness?

{{c1::Scopolamine}}

Name the four muscarinic antagonists used to treat overactive bladder symptoms.

{{c1::Oxybutynin}}
{{c1::Tolterodine}}
{{c1::Solifenacin}}
{{c1::Flavoxate}}

Which antimuscarinic agent is typically used intravenously to reduce airway secretions in the perioperative setting?

{{c1::Glycopyrrolate}}

Which two muscarinic antagonists are used in the treatment of asthma and COPD?

{{c1::Ipratropium}}
{{c1::Tiotropium}}

What are the two clinical indications for benztropine use?

Acute {{c1::dystonia}}
{{c1::Cholinergic}} symptoms of {{c1::Parkinson}} disease

What are the two main uses of oral glycopyrrolate?
