Reduce {{c1::drooling}}
Treat {{c1::peptic ulcer}} disease

On which organ system do trihexiphenidyl and benztropine exert their effect?

{{c1::Central nervous}} system

What are the two effects of muscarinic antagonists on the eye?

{{c1::Mydriasis::Mydriasis/Miosis}}
{{c1::Cycloplegia}}

Why might an ophthalmologist administer atropine eyedrops before performing an eye exam?

Atropin causes {{c1::mydriasis::mydriasis/miosis}} and {{c1::cycloplegia}}
fields.Back Extra: This allows for easier examination of the eye, especially the retina.

fields.Text:
What adverse effect of atropine is most likely to arise in infants?

{{c1::Hyperthermia::Hyperthermia/Hypothermia}}

What are two common indications for use of atropine?

{{c1::Bradycardia::Tachycardia/Bradycardia}}
{{c1::Ophthalmic}} applications

A patient arrives in the emergency department with disorientation, flushing, and mydriasis after working in the garden. What environmental exposure should be suspected?

{{c1::Plant alkaloids}}

What are the two cutaneous effects of atropine?

{{c1::Dryness}}
{{c1::Flushing}}

What cardiovascular effect is seen with administration of atropine?

{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in heart rate

An elderly patient reports sudden onset of severe ocular pain and blurry vision in the right eye after receiving a drug for symptomatic bradycardia. What should be suspected?

Acute {{c1::closed-angle glaucoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a known adverse effect of atropine use, especially in the elderly.

fields.Text:
Why does atropine cause hyperthermia?

Decreases {{c1::sweating}}

What is the effect of atropine on the bladder?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} urinary urgency

What effect does atropine produce in the gut?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} motility

What is the effect of atropine on the stomach?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} acid secretion

What are the two effects of atropine on the airway?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} secretions
Causes {{c1::bronchodilation::bronchodilation/bronchoconstriction}}

What are the central nervous system manifestations of atropine toxicity?

{{c1::Disorientation}}
{{c1::Confusion}}

What is a major concern with atropine use in males with benign prostatic hyperplasia?

Urinary {{c1::retention}}

What symptoms associated with organophosphate poisoning will atropine fail to reverse?

Weakness due to {{c1::neuromuscular}} blockade

What is the mechanism of action of atropine?

Antagonism of {{c1::muscarinic acetylcholine}} receptors

What direct sympathomimetic is used in the treatment of overactive bladder and urinary urgency or incontinence?

{{c1::Mirabegron}}

What are two indications for midodrine administration?

{{c1::Postural hypotension}}
{{c1::Autonomic}} insufficiency

What adverse effect might be seen with midodrine use?

Exacerbation of {{c1::supine hypertension}}

What are two clinical indications for norepinephrine?

{{c1::Septic shock}}
{{c1::Hypotension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}

What antihypertensives should you consider avoiding when treating cocaine intoxication?

{{c1::β-blockers}}

What four adverse effects may be seen with the use of fenoldopam?

{{c1::Hypotension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Reflex tachycardia}}
{{c1::Flushing}}
{{c1::Headache}}

How does fenoldopam lower blood pressure?

{{c1::D1}} direct agonism → Vasodilation
Promotion of {{c1::natriuresis}}

How does cocaine produce its sympathomimetic effects?

It acts as a(n) {{c1::indirect::direct/indirect}} general agonist by inhibiting reuptake of {{c1::catecholamines}}

What are three clinical indications for ephedrine?

Urinary {{c1::incontinence}}
{{c1::Hypotension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
Nasal {{c1::congestion}}

How does ephedrine produce its sympathomimetic effects?

Stimulates release of stored {{c1::catecholamines}}

What indirect sympathomimetic is indicated in the treatment of narcolepsy?

{{c1::Amphetamine}}

How do amphetamines produce their sympathomimetic effects?

Stimulates the release of stored {{c1::catecholamines}} and inhibits their {{c1::reuptake}}

What is the pharmacologic class of amphetamine, cocaine, and ephedrine?

{{c1::Indirect::Direct/Indirect}} {{c1::sympathomimetics}}

What is the difference between albuterol and salmeterol?

Albuterol is used for {{c1::acute}} treatment of asthma and COPD
Salmeterol is used for {{c1::serial}} treatment of asthma and COPD

What are four clinical indications for phenylephrine?

{{c1::Ocular}} procedures
{{c1::Hypotension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Rhinitis}}
{{c1::Ischemic priapism}}

What are two clinical indications for dobutamine?

Acute decompensated {{c1::heart}} failure with {{c1::cardiogenic shock}}
{{c1::Cardiac stress}} testing

What are two clinical indications for dopamine?

{{c1::Shock}}
Unstable {{c1::bradycardia::tachycardia/bradycardia}}

What is the sympathomimetic effect of dopamine at high doses?

{{c1::Vasoconstriction::Vasodilation/Vasoconstriction}}
fields.Back Extra: This would raise the blood pressure.

fields.Text:
What drug is used in the electrophysiologic study of tachyarrhythmias?

{{c1::Isoproterenol}}

Apart from being used as a pressor, what are the three clinical indications for epinephrine?

{{c1::Anaphylaxis}}
{{c1::Open-angle glaucoma}}
{{c1::Asthma}}

Sympathomimetic agents such as albuterol, salmeterol, and terbutaline act on what adrenergic receptors?

{{c1::β2}} > {{c1::β1}}

Which types of receptors are activated by dopamine?

{{c1::D1}} = {{c1::D2}} > {{c1::β}} > {{c1::α}}

What adrenergic receptors does isoproterenol act on?

{{c1::β1}} = {{c1::β2}}

For what adrenergic receptors does norepinephrine have more affinity?

{{c1::α1}} > {{c1::α2}} > {{c1::β1}}

For what adrenergic receptors does epinephrine have more affinity?

{{c1::β}} > {{c1::α}}

Which types of receptors are activated by dobutamine?

{{c1::β1}} > {{c1::β2}}
{{c1::α}}

What receptors does phenylephrine act on?

{{c1::α1}}-receptors
{{c1::α2}}-receptors

What dose of dopamine would cause increased cardiac contractility and heart rate?

{{c1::Low}} dose

What are the common indications for use of terbutaline?

{{c1::Tocolysis}}
Acute {{c1::bronchospasm}} in asthma

What are three clinical indications for amphetamine use?

{{c1::ADHD}}
{{c1::Narcolepsy}}
{{c1::Obesity}}

What drug can be used to relieve painful penile erection in a patient with sickle cell anemia?

{{c1::Phenylephrine}}

Which adrenergic receptor activity predominates at higher doses of epinephrine?

{{c1::α}}-receptor activity

Which of the endogenous catecholamines has the greatest effect on β2-receptors?

{{c1::Epinephrine}}

What is a major concern with isoproterenol use?

Worsening of {{c1::cardiac ischemia}}

Which types of receptors does midodrine act on?

{{c1::α1}}-receptors

Which types of receptors does mirabegron act on?

{{c1::β3}}-receptors

What effect does isoproterenol have on α-receptors?

{{c1::Negligible}} effect

Which two direct sympathomimetics might reduce cardiac output by decreasing the heart rate?

{{c1::Phenylephrine}}
{{c1::Midodrine}}

Most direct sympathomimetics cause an increase in blood pressure and concomitant increase in heart rate and cardiac output. What are the three exceptions that decrease blood pressure?

{{c1::Dobutamine}}
{{c1::Fenoldopam}}
{{c1::Isoproterenol}}

How will an α-blocker influence the agonist effects of isoproterenol?

{{c1::Minimally}}
fields.Back Extra: Isoproterenol has very little α activity.

fields.Text:
What are the effects of isoproterenol on systolic and diastolic blood pressure, pulse pressure, and heart rate?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} systolic pressure
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} diastolic pressure
{{c1::Widens::Widens/Narrows}} pulse pressure
{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} heart rate

What are the effects of norepinephrine on blood pressure, pulse pressure, and heart rate?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} blood pressure
{{c1::Widens::Widens/Narrows}} pulse pressure
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} heart rate

How does the agonist effect of isoproterenol on β-receptors compare to its effect on α-receptors?

It agonizes β-receptors {{c1::more::more/less}} than α-receptors

A patient's blood pressure over time after receiving norepinephrine is shown in the image. What response will you see in the patient's heart rate?



{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in heart rate
fields.Back Extra: This is due to reflex bradycardia.

fields.Text:
A patient's blood pressure over time after receiving isoproterenol is shown in the image. What response will you see in the patient's heart rate?



{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in heart rate
fields.Back Extra: This is due to combined reflex tachycardia and β1-mediated positive chronotropy.

fields.Text:
A patient's peripheral vascular resistance after a dose of epinephrine is shown in the image. What response will you see in the patient's mean arterial pressure?



Mean arterial pressure will {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} slightly

A patient's heart rate after receiving epinephrine is shown in the image below. What would be the expected peripheral vascular resistance in this patient?



{{c1::Lower::Higher/Lower}}

A patient's heart rate after administration of norepinephrine is shown in the image below. What response will you see in the patient's mean arterial pressure?



It will {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}}
fields.Back Extra: This is from unopposed α1 activity.

fields.Text:
Among isoproterenol, epinephrine, and norepinephrine, which of the following has the greatest impact on the cardiac output?

{{c1::Isoproterenol}} > {{c1::Epinephrine}} > {{c1::Norepinephrine}}

What is the effect of norepinephrine on cardiac output, heart rate, mean arterial pressure, and pulse pressure?

Cardiac output → {{c1::Unchanged}}
Heart rate → {{c1::Decreased}}
Mean arterial pressure → {{c1::Increased}}
Pulse pressure → {{c1::Increased}}

What is the effect of epinephrine on cardiac output, heart rate, mean arterial pressure, and pulse pressure?

Cardiac output → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}}
Heart rate → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}}
Mean arterial pressure → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}}
Pulse pressure → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}}

What is the effect of isoproterenol on cardiac output, heart rate, mean arterial pressure, and pulse pressure?

Cardiac output → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}}
Heart rate → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}}
Mean arterial pressure → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}}
Pulse pressure → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}}

What adverse effect might a patient experience if he stops taking clonidine or guanfacine suddenly?

{{c1::Rebound hypertension}}

What are the three adverse effects associated with α-methyldopa?

Positive {{c1::direct Coombs}} test
{{c1::Hyperprolactinemia::Hyperprolactinemia/Hypoprolactinemia}}
Drug-induced {{c1::lupus}}
fields.Back Extra: A positive direct Coombs test is associated with hemolytic anemia.

fields.Text:
What are four clinical indications for the use of clonidine and guanfacine?

{{c1::ADHD}}
{{c1::Hypertensive urgency}} (limited situations)
{{c1::Tourette}} syndrome
Control of {{c1::opioid}} withdrawal symptoms

What sympatholytic drug can be used to treat hypertension during pregnancy?

{{c1::α-methyldopa}}

What are three possible adverse effects of tizanidine?

{{c1::Weakness}}
{{c1::Hypotension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Xerostomia}}

What is the main clinical indication for tizanidine?

Relief of {{c1::spasticity}}

What are the four commonly used sympatholytic agents?

{{c1::Guanfacine}}
{{c1::Clonidine}}
{{c1::Tizanidine}}
{{c1::α-methyldopa}}

A patient taking a new medication for depression reports weight gain and sedation. Routine lab work shows new increase in serum cholesterol. Which drug might account for these findings?

{{c1::Mirtazapine}}

What is the mechanism of action of mirtazapine?

Selective blockade of {{c1::α2}}-adrenergic receptors

A 75-year-old man with hypertension has a new diagnosis of benign prostatic hyperplasia. Of the α1-selective blockers, which is least effective in treating both conditions?

{{c1::Tamsulosin}}

What are the three main adverse effects of α1-selective blockers?

{{c1::Orthostatic hypotension}} after the first dose
{{c1::Headache}}
{{c1::Dizziness}}

What are the two adverse effects associated with nonselective α-blockers?

{{c1::Reflex tachycardia}}
{{c1::Orthostatic hypotension}}

A patient taking phenelzine is brought to the emergency department after consuming wine and cheese. Blood pressure is 220/111 mmHg. What drug should be administered?

{{c1::Phentolamine}}
fields.Back Extra: This is used to treat a tyramine-induced hypertensive crisis in patients taking MAO inhibitors.

fields.Text:
Which drug should be given preoperatively for resection of a pheochromocytoma?

{{c1::Phenoxybenzamine}}

A patient with PTSD reports feeling dizzy when standing up after taking his first dose of prazosin. Why might this be?

Prazosin causes {{c1::orthostatic hypotension}} with the first dose

A patient with cancer-related cachexia presents with anhedonia, depression, and sleep difficulties. What medication may be most effective for the treatment of his mood disorder?

{{c1::Mirtazapine}}

A patient presents with severe hypertension after cocaine use. Blood pressure remains at 215/134 mmHg after multiple doses of lorazepam. What drug may be administered next?

{{c1::Phentolamine}}

How do β-blockers effectively terminate supraventricular tachycardias?

By decreasing {{c1::atrioventricular conduction velocity}}

Which three β-blockers are commonly used to treat patients with variceal bleeding?

{{c1::Nadolol}}
{{c1::Propranolol}}
{{c1::Carvedilol}}

What is the mechanism by which β-blockers help control esophageal variceal bleeding?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} hepatic venous pressure gradient
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} portal hypertension

What is the theoretical risk associated with prescribing β-blockers for treatment of cocaine-associated chest pain?

Risk of unopposed {{c1::α}}-adrenergic receptor agonist activity

What unique β-receptor activity does nebivolol have?

Blocks {{c1::β1}}-receptors
Stimulates {{c1::β3}}-receptors

What is the concern related to prescribing a nonselective β-blocker for patients with asthma?

Causes exacerbation of {{c1::reactive airway}} diseases by preventing {{c1::bronchodilation::bronchodilation/bronchoconstriction}}
Interferes with the action of {{c1::β}}-agonists

What sexual adverse effect is associated with β-blocker use?

{{c1::Erectile}} dysfunction

What are three adverse cardiovascular effects seen with β-blocker toxicity?

{{c1::Bradycardia::Tachycardia/Bradycardia}}
{{c1::Atrioventricular block}}
{{c1::Heart::Organ}} failure

How does propranolol help control symptoms in a patient with hyperthyroidism or thyroid storm?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} heart rate
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} tremor

What are the two nonselective α-antagonists and β-antagonists?

{{c1::Carvedilol}}
{{c1::Labetalol}}

Which two β-blockers are partial agonists?

{{c1::Acebutolol}}
{{c1::Pindolol}}

What are the six β1-selective blockers?

{{c1::Acebutolol}} (partial agonist)
{{c1::Atenolol}}
{{c1::Betaxolol}}
{{c1::Bisoprolol}}
{{c1::Esmolol}}
{{c1::Metoprolol}}

Name the four nonselective β-blockers.

{{c1::Nadolol}}
{{c1::Pindolol}} (partial agonist)
{{c1::Propranolol}}
{{c1::Timolol}}

What is the effect of β3‑receptor stimulation by nebivolol?

It activates {{c1::nitric oxide synthase}} in the vasculature, thus {{c1::decreasing::increasing/decreasing}} systemic vascular resistance

What are the two mechanisms by which β-blockers help reduce blood pressure in patients with hypertension?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} cardiac output
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} renin secretion

Which three β-blockers have been shown to reduce mortality in patients with congestive heart failure?

{{c1::Bisoprolol}}
{{c1::Carvedilol}}
{{c1::Metoprolol}}

How do β-blockers help in patients with angina pectoris?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} heart rate
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} contractility

What β-blocker is frequently used to treat glaucoma by reducing the synthesis of aqueous humor?

{{c1::Timolol}}

What is the major risk in prescribing β-blockers for patients with insulin-dependent diabetes?

They mask the symptoms of {{c1::hypoglycemia}}

What is the long-term benefit of treating patients who have had a myocardial infarction with β-blockers?

β-blockers decrease {{c1::mortality}} after a myocardial infarction

How do β-blockers help patients who have hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} heart rate
fields.Back Extra: This allows for greater diastolic filling time and thus relief of outflow obstruction.

fields.Text:
What are the central nervous system side effects of β-blockers?

{{c1::Sleep}} alterations
{{c1::Seizures}}

How do β-blockers decrease mortality in patients with heart failure?

By blocking {{c1::neurohormonal stress}}, leading to prevention of deleterious cardiac {{c1::remodeling}}

What is the short-term benefit of treating patients who have had a myocardial infarction with β-blockers?

Reduced {{c1::oxygen}} demand

Which two β-blockers are especially useful in the treatment of supraventricular tachycardias?

{{c1::Esmolol}}
{{c1::Metoprolol}}

Which β-blocker is associated with dyslipidemia?

{{c1::Metoprolol}}

How do PDE-5 inhibitors help treat pulmonary hypertension?

Inhibition of PDE-5 → Decreased hydrolysis of {{c1::cGMP}} → Increased intracellular {{c1::cGMP}} levels → Increased smooth muscle relaxation by enhancing {{c1::nitric oxide}} activity → Pulmonary vasodilation

How does sildenafil cause cyanopia?

It inhibits {{c1::PDE-6}} in the retina

What are three main clinical uses of PDE-5 inhibitors?

{{c1::Erectile}} dysfunction
Pulmonary {{c1::hypertension::hypertension/hypotension}}
{{c1::Benign prostatic hyperplasia}} (tadalafil only)

How does sildenafil cause penile erection?

Inhibits {{c1::PDE-5}} → Decreased hydrolysis of {{c1::cGMP}} → Increased intracellular {{c1::cGMP}} levels → Increased smooth muscle relaxation by {{c1::nitric oxide}} activity → Increased blood flow in the corpus cavernosum

A 70-year-old man with uncontrolled hypertension presents with severe hypotension after taking sildenafil. What other medication is he likely taking?

{{c1::Nitrates}}

An older man reports sudden onset of flushing, heartburn, and headache during intercourse. Hypotension is observed on exam. What drug is the likely cause?

{{c1::PDE-5}} inhibitor

What are three adverse effects of milrinone?

{{c1::Ventricular arrhythmias}}
{{c1::Tachycardia::Tachycardia/Bradycardia}}
{{c1::Hypotension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}

What isoform of the PDE enzyme does milrinone inhibit?

It is a selective {{c1::PDE-3}} inhibitor

What is the mechanism of action of milrinone in vascular smooth muscle?

Increased {{c1::cAMP}} → {{c1::MLCK}} inhibition → {{c1::Vasodilation::Vasodilation/Vasoconstriction}} → Decreased preload and afterload

What is the mechanism by which milrinone increases inotropy and chronotropy in cardiomyocytes?

Inhibits {{c1::PDE-3}} → Increased {{c1::cAMP}} → {{c1::Ca2+}} influx → Increased inotropy/chronotropy

Platelet-inhibiting agents such as cilostazol and dipyridamole are used in the prevention of what two medical conditions?

{{c1::Transient ischemic attack}} or {{c1::stroke}} (with aspirin)
{{c1::Coronary stent restenosis}}

Platelet-inhibiting agents such as cilostazol and dipyridamole are used in the treatment of what medical condition?

{{c1::Intermittent claudication}}

What are five adverse effects associated with cilostazol and dipyridamole?

{{c1::Nausea}}
{{c1::Abdominal}} pain
{{c1::Headache}}
Facial {{c1::flushing}}
{{c1::Hypotension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}

What is the most common indication for milrinone use?

Acute decompensated {{c1::heart}} failure with {{c1::cardiogenic shock}}

Which PDE inhibitor is used in cardiac stress testing?

{{c1::Dipyridamole}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because it causes coronary vasodilation, which shunts blood away from atherosclerotic vessels that are already maximally dilated, resulting in hypoperfusion.

fields.Text:
Which isoform of the PDE enzyme is inhibited by cilostazol?

{{c1::PDE-3}}

What is the mechanism by which dipyridamole causes coronary vasodilation?

Inhibits {{c1::PDE}} in platelets → Decreased {{c1::adenosine}} reuptake by platelets → Increased extracellular {{c1::adenosine}} → Vasodilation

The PDE-4 inhibitor roflumilast is used in the treatment of what disease?

Severe {{c1::COPD}}

What five adverse effects are associated with roflumilast?

{{c1::Abdominal}} pain
Weight {{c1::loss::gain/loss}}
{{c1::Insomnia}}
{{c1::Depression}}
{{c1::Anxiety}}

Roflumilast functions by increasing the cAMP levels in which three types of cells?

{{c1::Neutrophils}}
{{c1::Granulocytes}}
{{c1::Bronchial}} epithelium

What is the function of the PDE enzyme?

To hydrolyze {{c1::cAMP}} and/or {{c1::cGMP}}

What are the side effects of theophylline?

{{c1::Abdominal}} pain
{{c1::Cardiotoxicity}}
{{c1::Neurotoxicity}}

Although theophylline is rarely used in clinical practice today, what two medical conditions might it be used to treat?

{{c1::Asthma}}
{{c1::Chronic obstructive pulmonary}} disease

What is the mechanism of action of the nonspecific PDE inhibitor theophylline?

Increased intracellular {{c1::cAMP}} → Bronchial smooth muscle {{c1::relaxation::contraction/relaxation}} → Bronchodilation

What is the effect of cilostazol and dipyridamole on platelet activity?

They inhibit platelet {{c1::aggregation}} by increasing {{c1::cAMP}} levels

If left untreated, what are the grave consequences of scombroid poisoning?

{{c1::Bronchospasm}}
{{c1::Angioedema}}
{{c1::Hypotension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}

What is scombroid poisoning often misdiagnosed as?

{{c1::Fish allergy}}
fields.Back Extra: Scombroid poisoning is actually caused by excess histamine in spoiled dark-meat fish.

fields.Text:
What are the acute symptoms associated with scombroid poisoning?

{{c1::Burning}} sensation in the mouth
{{c1::Flushing}}
{{c1::Erythema}}
{{c1::Urticaria}}
{{c1::Itching}}

What is the treatment for scombroid poisoning?

{{c1::Antihistamines}}
fields.Back Extra: Albuterol and epinephrine can be used if needed.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action in scombroid poisoning?

{{c1::Histidine}} is converted to {{c1::histamine}} by bacterial {{c1::histidine decarboxylase}} → Symptoms similar to those observed with anaphlyaxis

What is the treatment for ciguatoxin poisoning?

{{c1::Supportive care}}

What is the mechanism of action of ciguatoxin?

It causes opening of {{c1::Na+}} channels → {{c1::Depolarization}}

Which ingested seafood can cause weakness, dizziness, paresthesias, and loss of reflexes?

{{c1::Tetrodotoxin}}

Which ingested seafood toxin can cause perioral numbness, hypotension, heart block, bradycardia, and reversal of hot and cold sensation?

{{c1::Ciguatoxin}}

What is the treatment for tetrodotoxin poisoning?

{{c1::Supportive care}}

What is the mechanism of action of tetrodotoxin?

Binds to fast {{c1::voltage}}-gated {{c1::Na+}} channels in nerve tissue → Prevents {{c1::depolarization}}

What are the general mechanisms of scombroid, tetrodotoxin, and ciguatoxin poisoning?

Scombroid → {{c1::Histamine}} release
Tetrodotoxin → Total blockage of {{c1::Na+}} channels
Ciguatoxin → Opening of {{c1::Na+}} channels causing {{c1::depolarization}}

Tetrodotoxin is mainly found in what organism?

{{c1::Pufferfish}}

What types of fish produce ciguatoxin?

{{c1::Reef}} fish
fields.Back Extra: Examples include the barracuda, moray eel, and snapper.

fields.Text:
What is the common cause of scombroid poisoning?

Consumption of spoiled {{c1::dark-meat fish}}
fields.Back Extra: Examples include the tuna, mahi-mahi, bonito, or mackerel.

fields.Text:
What is a unique symptom of ciguatoxin poisoning?

{{c1::Temperature}}-related {{c1::dysesthesias}}

What three hepatic changes in the elderly may affect the pharmacokinetics of drug metabolism in the body?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} hepatic mass
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} hepatic blood flow
Decreased phase {{c1::I::I/II}} metabolism

What changes in the elderly may affect distribution of drugs in the body?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} body fat content
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} total body water

What changes in the elderly may affect elimination of drugs from the body?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} GFR
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} renal mass

Which phase of hepatic metabolism of drugs is lost first with aging?

Phase {{c1::I::I/II}}
fields.Back Extra: Therefore, drugs metabolized in phase II are safer than the ones metabolized in phase I.

fields.Text:
What two drugs may be useful in treating a patient with arsenic poisoning?

{{c1::Dimercaprol}}
{{c1::Succimer}}

A patient with Wilson disease presents with encephalopathy secondary to copper toxicity. What two therapies may be used?

{{c1::Penicillamine}}
{{c1::Trientine}}

A patient taking warfarin has a large intracranial bleed requiring immediate reversal of warfarin to minimize further bleeding. What are the two treatment options?

{{c1::Prothrombin complex concentrate}}
{{c1::Fresh frozen plasma}}

Protamine sulfate is used as a reversal agent for which drug?

{{c1::Heparin}}

How does sodium bicarbonate help in the treatment of TCA toxicity?

It stabilizes the cardiac {{c1::cell membrane}} to prevent cardiotoxicity

What antidote should be given immediately to a patient with suspected heroin overdose?

{{c1::Naloxone}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an opioid receptor antagonist.

fields.Text:
A child comes to the emergency department after drinking a whole jug of antifreeze. What are the three treatments of choice?

{{c1::Fomepizole}} (preferred)
{{c1::Ethanol}}
{{c1::Dialysis}}
fields.Back Extra: Both ethylene glycol (antifreeze) and methanol toxicity are treated with fomepizole, ethanol, or dialysis.

fields.Text:
A child in respiratory distress is brought in after a house fire. Blood analysis reveals elevated carboxyhemoglobin levels. What is the immediate treatment?

{{c1::100}}% {{c1::O2}}
{{c1::Hyperbaric O2}}

What two antidotes can reverse methemoglobinemia?

{{c1::Methylene blue}}
Vitamin {{c1::C}}

What are the treatments for cyanide toxicity?

{{c1::Hydroxocobalamin}}
{{c1::Nitrites}} + {{c1::Sodium thiosulfate}}

What are two possible treatments for mercury posioning?

{{c1::Dimercaprol}}
{{c1::Succimer}}

What are the four treatment options for lead poisoning?

{{c1::Calcium disodium EDTA}}
{{c1::Dimercaprol}}
{{c1::Succimer}}
{{c1::Penicillamine}}

A patient presents with hemochromatosis after receiving frequent transfusions for β-thalassemia over several years. What is the treatment?

{{c1::Deferoxamine}}
{{c1::Deferasirox}}
{{c1::Deferiprone}}
fields.Back Extra: These are used to chelate iron in iron toxicity.

fields.Text:
What is the treatment for digitalis toxicity?

{{c1::Digoxin}}-specific {{c1::antibody fragments}}

What are three treatment options for β-blocker toxicity?

{{c1::Atropine}}
{{c1::Glucagon}}
{{c1::Saline}} infusion

What drug can be used to treat antimuscarinic agent–induced toxicity?

{{c1::Physostigmine}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that can cross the blood-brain barrier.

fields.Text:
What drugs can be used to treat organophosphate poisoning?

{{c1::Atropine}} (preferred)
{{c1::Pralidoxime}}

What are the two treatments for salicylate toxicity?

{{c1::Sodium bicarbonate}}
{{c1::Dialysis}}

What is the mechanism of action of the antidote used for acetaminophen toxicity?

{{c1::N-acetylcysteine}} replenishes {{c1::glutathione}} that is depleted in acetaminophen toxicity

What drug can be used to reverse dabigatran toxicity?

{{c1::Idarucizumab}}

What can be used to reverse the effect of warfarin in a patient requiring surgery in the next two days?

Vitamin {{c1::K}}

A patient experiences apnea after receiving five times the prescribed dose of midazolam due to a medication error. What antidote should he receive?

{{c1::Flumazenil}}

What is the treatment for methotrexate toxicity?

{{c1::Leucovorin}}

A 72-year-old female patient who has been receiving long-term apixaban therapy for anticoagulation presents with an acute intracranial bleed. What is the treatment?

{{c1::Andexanet alfa}}
fields.Back Extra: This is used for direct factor Xa inhibitors.

fields.Text:
What effect do macrolides, fluoroquinolones, and fluconazole have on cardiac electrophysiology, and what condition may result?

Prolongs the {{c1::QT}} interval → Increased risk for {{c1::torsades de pointes}}

Which chemotherapeutic agents can cause dilated cardiomyopathy?

{{c1::Trastuzumab}}
{{c1::Anthracyclines}}

Name six pharmacologic agents that are commonly associated with cutaneous flushing.

{{c1::Vancomycin}}
{{c1::Adenosine}}
{{c1::Niacin}}
{{c1::Calcium}} channel blockers
{{c1::Echinocandins}}
{{c1::Nitrates}}

What four drugs are associated with coronary vasospasm?

{{c1::Cocaine}}
{{c1::Amphetamines}}

fields.Text:
Does a cross-sectional study prove causality?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Cross-sectional studies demonstrate associations of risk factors with disease, but do not prove causality.

fields.Text:
What type of study can be used to study the incidence of gastric bleeding in patients taking ibuprofen?

{{c1::Cohort}} study
fields.Back Extra: This compares exposed and nonexposed groups to yield a relative risk.

fields.Text:
What type of study can show that patients with diabetes are more likely to have a history of obesity than those without diabetes?

{{c1::Case-control}} study
fields.Back Extra: This compares individuals with disease to those without disease to determine risk factors.

fields.Text:
Which study compares the frequency of development of the same disease in monozygotic twins and dizygotic twins?

{{c1::Twin concordance}} study

A study conducted in 2020 determined the prevalence of COPD in the United States in 2010. What type of study was conducted?

{{c1::Cross-sectional}} study
fields.Back Extra: This assesses the frequency of disease and risk factors in a population to determine prevalence.

fields.Text:
A study compares the frequency with which adopted and nonadopted siblings develop a trait or disease. What does this study type measure?

The influence of {{c1::genes}} and {{c1::environment}} on the development of traits and diseases

{{c1::Heritability}} of a disease

{{c1::Prospective}} cohort study
{{c1::Retrospective}} cohort study
fields.Back Extra: The risk factor being studied must occur prior to disease onset.

fields.Text:
Whom does safety culture inspire to bring up safety concerns in an organization?

{{c1::Everyone}}
fields.Back Extra: Safety culture provides an organizational environment for everyone to bring up safety concerns without fear of penalty.

fields.Text:

{{c1::Simplification}}
fields.Back Extra: It is intended to reduce wasteful activities.

fields.Text:
What is the benefit of a forcing function in human factors design?

Forcing functions are the interventions most effective in preventing {{c1::undesirable}} actions

How does deficient design impact safety features?

Hinders {{c1::workflow}}
Leads to staff {{c1::workarounds}} that bypass safety features

What is the PDSA cycle's primary objective within clinical settings?



To process {{c1::improvement}} models to test changes

What does the "Plan" stage of the PDSA cycle entail?

Defining the {{c1::problem}} and {{c1::solution}}

What does the "Do" stage of the PDSA cycle entail?

{{c1::Testing}} a new process

What does the "Study" stage of the PDSA cycle entail?

{{c1::Measuring}} and {{c1::analyzing}} data

What does the "Act" stage of the PDSA cycle entail?

{{c1::Integrating}} the new process into the workflow

fields.Text:

fields.Text:

What is the "Swiss cheese" model?

fields.Back Extra: Harm may still occurs if flaws in processes and systems align.

fields.Text:
From the image below, when does patient harm occur despite multiple safeguards?



Patient harm occurs when the flaws in systems and conditions {{c1::line up}}

What type of medical error occurs if different types of IV pumps are used within the same hospital?

This occurs in processes indirect from the operator, but still affects patient care.

It is an accident waiting to happen.

fields.Text:
What type of medical error occurs when a nurse programs the wrong IV pump dose for a patient's medication?

{{c1::Active}} error
fields.Back Extra: This occurs at the level of frontline operators and has an immediate impact.

fields.Text:
What is a never event that led to death, permanent harm, or severe temporary harm called?

{{c1::Sentinel event}}

What type of medical error occurs if a scalpel is found inside the patient's abdomen after surgery?

{{c1::Never event}}
fields.Back Extra: It is a major error that should never occur because it is identifiable, serious, and typically preventable.

fields.Text:
What type of medical error occurs when a pharmacist recognizes a medication interaction and cancels the order?

{{c1::Near miss}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an unplanned event that does not result in harm, but could do so.

fields.Text:
Compare medical errors made when a provider is burnt out versus when a provider experiences fatigue.

Burnout causes medical errors due to reduced professional {{c1::efficacy}}
Fatigue causes medical errors due to {{c1::cognitive}} impairment

Describe the symptoms of healthcare worker burnout and how it starts.

Excessive, prolonged {{c1::stress}} → Reduced efficacy at work

Describe the symptoms of health care worker fatigue and how it starts.

{{c1::Sleep}} deprivation → Decreased energy/motivation and cognitive impairment

What type of medical error analysis occurs when a hospital uses records and participant interviews to identify all the underlying problems that led to an error?

{{c1::Root cause}} analysis
fields.Back Extra: This is a retrospective approach that is applied after a failure event to prevent a recurrence.

fields.Text:
What type of medical error analysis is defined as applied inductive reasoning to determine how a process might fail and prioritization of those issues by likelihood of occurrence?

{{c1::Failure mode and effects}} analysis
fields.Back Extra: A forward-looking approach is initiated before process implementation to prevent failure occurrence.

fields.Text:
What is the level of disease prevention when a patient with lung cancer is given chemotherapy?

{{c1::Tertiary}} disease prevention

Pap smear for cervical cancer is what level of disease prevention?

{{c1::Secondary}} disease prevention

HPV vaccination is an example of what level of disease prevention?

{{c1::Primary}} disease prevention

Avoiding unnecessary imaging studies is what level of disease prevention?

{{c1::Quaternary}} disease prevention

Optimizing medication to reduce polypharmacy is what level of disease prevention?

{{c1::Quaternary}} disease prevention

Which insurance plans require referral from a primary care physician to see a specialist?

{{c1::Health maintenance organization}} plan
{{c1::Point of service}} plan

In an exclusive provider organization plan, describe the limitations related to seeing providers outside of the network.

Except in {{c1::emergencies}}, patients are restricted to a {{c1::limited}} panel of providers

In a health maintenance organization plan, describe the limitations related to seeing providers outside of the network.

Except in {{c1::emergencies}}, patients are restricted to a {{c1::limited}} panel of providers who are in the network

What is a common drawback of point of service and preferred provider organization plans?

Higher {{c1::deductibles}}
Higher {{c1::copays}}

In which organizations are patients not restricted to a limited panel of providers and hospitals?

{{c1::Point of service}} plan
{{c1::Preferred provider organization}} plan

Which medical insurance plans do not require referral from a primary care physician to see a specialist?

{{c1::Exclusive provider organization}} plan
{{c1::Preferred provider organization}} plan

In which medical insurance plans are patients restricted to a limited panel of providers and hospitals?

{{c1::Exclusive provider organization}} plan
{{c1::Health maintenance organization}} plan

In an accountable care organization, what type of insurance typically covers the costs of services?

{{c1::Medicare}}

What organization has providers who voluntarily enroll to give care to their Medicare patients?

{{c1::Accountable care}} organization

In what healthcare payment model does an insurer pay for each service at a predetermined discounted rate?

{{c1::Discounted fee-for-service}}

In what healthcare payment model does a physician receive a set amount per patient for a particular period of time, regardless of how much the patient uses the healthcare system?

{{c1::Capitation}}
fields.Back Extra: This is generally used by some health maintenance organizations.

fields.Text:
In what healthcare payment model does a healthcare organization receive a set amount per service, regardless of ultimate cost?

{{c1::Bundled}} payment
fields.Back Extra: The amount is divided among all providers/facilities involved.

fields.Text:
In what healthcare payment model does an insurer and/or patient pay all the costs associated with a single incident of care with a single payment?

{{c1::Global}} payment
fields.Back Extra: This is commonly used during elective surgeries as it covers the cost of surgery and all preoperative and postoperative charges.

fields.Text:
In what type of healthcare payment model does a patient/insurer pay for each service individually?

{{c1::Fee-for-service}}

Which part of Medicare provides prescribed drugs?

Part {{c1::D}}

Medicare is available to what group of patients?

Patients ≥ {{c1::65}} years old
Patients < {{c1::65}} years old with certain disabilities
Patients with {{c1::end-stage renal}} disease

Medicaid is available to what group of patients?

People with limited {{c1::income}} or {{c1::resources}}

What are the two federal social healthcare programs that originated from amendments to the Social Security Act?

{{c1::Medicare}}
{{c1::Medicaid}}

What services do part A of Medicare give?

{{c1::Hospital admissions}}

What services does part B of Medicare provide?

Basic {{c1::medical bills}}

What services does part C of Medicare provide?

{{c1::Hospital admissions}}
Basic {{c1::medical bills}}
fields.Back Extra: This is delivered by approved private companies.

fields.Text:
What kind of medical care aims at improving quality of life in patients with serious illnesses despite their prognosis and is often given with curative treatment?

{{c1::Palliative}} care

What should be the life expectancy of the patients to be eligible for hospice care?

Less than {{c1::6}} months

Which type of medical care focuses on providing comfort and palliation instead of a definitive cure in patients with a prognosis of < 6 months?

{{c1::Hospice}} care

What are the top three causes of death in children < 1 year of age in order?

1 → Congenital {{c1::malformations}}
2 → {{c1::Preterm}} birth
3 → Sudden unexpected infant {{c1::death}}

List the top three causes of death in people > 65 years of age in order.

1 → {{c1::Heart}} disease
2 → {{c1::Cancer}}
3 → Chronic {{c1::lower respiratory}} disease

What are the top three causes of death in people aged 45 to 64 years?

1 → {{c1::Cancer}}
2 → {{c1::Heart}} disease
3 → {{c1::Unintentional}} injury

List the top three causes of death in people aged 35 to 44 years.

1 → {{c1::Unintentional}} injury
2 → {{c1::Cancer}}
3 → {{c1::Heart}} disease

What are the top three causes of death in children aged 1 to 14 years?

1 → {{c1::Unintentional}} injury
2 → {{c1::Cancer}}
3 → Congenital {{c1::malformations}}

What are the top three causes of death in people aged 15 to 34 years?

1 → {{c1::Unintentional}} injury
2 → {{c1::Suicide}}
3 → {{c1::Homicide}}

List six important components of patient-centered interviewing techniques.

{{c1::Introduction}}
{{c1::Agenda}} setting
{{c1::Reflection}}
{{c1::Validation}}
{{c1::Recapitulation}}
{{c1::Facilitation}}

How is the agenda preferably set in a patient-centered interview?

Identifying {{c1::concerns}} and setting {{c1::goals}} by developing a joint agenda between patient and physician

What actions can you perform to practice facilitation in patient-centered interviewing techniques?

Encourage patients to speak {{c1::freely}} and ask {{c1::questions}} throughout the interview

What is validation in patient-centered interview techniques?

{{c1::Legitimizing}} a patient's views

How do you recapitulate in a patient-centered interview?

{{c1::Summarizing}} what the patient said to ensure accurate interpretation

How should you perform reflection in patient-centered interviewing techniques?

Actively {{c1::listening}} and synthesizing {{c1::information}} provided by a patient, particularly with respect to {{c1::primary}} concerns

List the six important components of expressing empathy to a patient.

{{c1::Partnership}}
{{c1::Empathy}}
{{c1::Apology}}
{{c1::Respect}}
{{c1::Legitimization}}
{{c1::Support}}

How do you develop a partnership with a patient while establishing rapport?

{{c1::Work}} with the patient to identify primary concerns
{{c1::Discuss}} preferred options for solutions

How do you display empathy for patients while establishing rapport?

Acknowledging the {{c1::emotions}}
Demonstrating that you {{c1::understand}} why the patient is feeling that way

How do you display your support while establishing rapport?

Assure patients that you will work {{c1::together}}
Provide them with {{c1::resources}} during challenging times

How do you demonstrate respect for patients when establishing rapport?

Commending the patient for {{c1::constructive}} behaviors

How do you engage in legitimization while establishing rapport?

{{c1::Reassure}} the patient that having an emotional response is understandable

When should you provide an apology when establishing rapport with a patient?

Assume {{c1::personal responsibility}} when it is appropriate

What are the six steps for delivering bad news?

{{c1::Setting}}
{{c1::Perception}}
{{c1::Invitation}}
{{c1::Knowledge}}
{{c1::Emotions}}
{{c1::Strategy}}

How do you create the setting to deliver bad news to a patient?

Offering {{c1::support}} to patients in advance
Removing {{c1::distractions}}
Ensuring {{c1::privacy}}
{{c1::Sitting down}} with the patient during the conversation

What does the component "perception" of delivering bad news mean?

Evaluating the patient's {{c1::understanding}} and {{c1::expectations}}

What does the component "invitation" of delivering bad news mean?

Obtain {{c1::permission}} to disclose the news
Clarify what level of {{c1::detail}} the patient desires

How do you share information with a patient according to the "knowledge" component of delivering bad news?

Share the information in {{c1::small::large/small}} pieces without medical {{c1::jargon}}
fields.Back Extra: This will allow time to process and assess the patient's understanding.

fields.Text:
How do you appropriately react to a patient's emotions while delivering bad news?

Allow the patient to {{c1::express}} emotions
Listen and acknowledge the emotions with {{c1::empathetic}} responses

What should be your strategy if the patient finally feels ready for more information after you have delivered bad news?

Discuss {{c1::goals}} of care and {{c1::options}} for treatment
Provide an {{c1::agenda}} for the patient's next appointment

What assumptions are preferably avoided in gender-inclusive and sexuality-inclusive history?

Gender {{c1::identity}}
Gender {{c1::expression}}
Sexual {{c1::orientation}}
{{c1::Behavior}}

How is a patient's husband or wife preferably referred to when a history is taken?

As a {{c1::partner}}

How would you address your patient regarding their gender and sexual identity?

Ask patients how they would like to be addressed and the {{c1::pronouns}} they use in reference to themselves

Would you ask about gender when a gender-nonconforming patient is seeking treatment for a hand laceration?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Do not bring up gender or sexuality if it is not relevant to the visit.

fields.Text:
How would you try to make a patient comfortable if you know that the patient may not be open about sexual orientation or gender identity to others?

By reassuring them about the {{c1::confidentiality}} of their appointments
Being {{c1::sensitive}} to their choices related to disclosure of sexual orientation or gender identity

What assumption about a patient's gender identity can be made from the patient's sex assigned at birth?

{{c1::None}}
fields.Back Extra: Sex assigned at birth and gender identity may differ.

fields.Text:
What is motivational interviewing?

A technique used in counseling to facilitate {{c1::modification}} of behavior by assisting patients to overcome {{c1::ambivalence}} about change

When are motivational interviewing techniques helpful?

When a patient wants to make a {{c1::change}}, but is not yet {{c1::committed}} to making it

What do you want to ask patients and what should you assess during motivational interviewing?

Ask patients how their behavior affects their {{c1::life}} and {{c1::why}} they want to change it
Assess {{c1::obstacles}} to change

What are the characteristics of physician-suggested goals in motivational interviewing?

{{c1::Specific}}
{{c1::Measurable}}
{{c1::Achievable}}
{{c1::Relevant}}
{{c1::Time}} bound

What screening should a patient with a history of psychological trauma receive?

Thorough {{c1::behavioral health}} screening
fields.Back Extra:
This includes assessment of mood, suicide risk, substance use, and social support.

Ask the patient for permission before screening.

fields.Text:
What are the four "Rs" of trauma-informed care?

{{c1::Realize}}
{{c1::Recognize}}
{{c1::Respond}}
Resist {{c1::retraumatization}}

Assessments of patients with history of psychological trauma should be focused on what type of trauma-related symptoms?

Symptoms that interfere with {{c1::occupational}} and {{c1::social}} function

What type of questions should be avoided when speaking to a patient with a history of psychological trauma?

{{c1::Invasive}} questions that require detailed description of the trauma

How would you prepare a patient who has a history of psychological trauma for a physical exam?

Reassure patient that they can signal an {{c1::end}} to the exam if they are experiencing discomfort
Offer to have other staff members present for {{c1::support}}

Should you omit parts of the physical exam if the exam is challenging because of a patient's disability?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Do not omit relevant aspects of the physical exam, even if the exam is challenging because of the patient's disability.

fields.Text:
When a disabled patient is accompanied by a caregiver, whom should you address?

Address the {{c1::patient}} directly in most situations
fields.Back Extra: Do not assume that nonverbal patients do not understand.

fields.Text:
Name three tools you can use to effectively communicate with patients who have difficulty speaking.

Allow extra {{c1::time}} during the visit
Consider asking them to {{c1::write down}} or {{c1::rephrase}} what they have said
{{c1::Repeat}} information they provide to ensure you understand it correctly

Name four tools you can use to communicate with a patient with cognitive impairment.

Ask {{c1::simple}} questions with concrete, specific language
Eliminate {{c1::distractions}}
Use {{c1::gestures}}
Do not assume the patient can {{c1::read}}

How should you communicate with patients who are deaf or have a hearing impairment?

Ask them how they {{c1::prefer}} to commmunicate
For patients who speak and lipread, reduce {{c1::noise}} and {{c1::face}} them, but don't change mode of speech
Get attention by {{c1::waving}} or {{c1::light}} touch

Would you ask about disability if a patient seeks treatment for a condition unrelated to the disability?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}

When should a professionally trained medical interpreter be employed during a visit with a patient?

When a patient speaks {{c1::little}} or {{c1::no}} English
fields.Back Extra: An exception can be made if the physician is also fluent in the patient's preferred language.

fields.Text:
By what means can interpretation services be provided?

{{c1::In person}}
{{c1::Video call}}
{{c1::Telephone}}

What should you do if a patient prefers to have a family member serve as an interpreter?

{{c1::Record}} the preference in the patient's chart

How would you determine a patient's preferred language?

By {{c1::asking}} the patient
fields.Back Extra: Do not assume that a patient does not speak English well on the basis of accent, name, or skin tone.

fields.Text:
How should a physician speak to a patient in the presence of an interpreter?

The physician should make eye contact with the {{c1::patient}} and speak to them directly, without referring to them in the third person

Where should an interpreter ideally be positioned for in-person spoken and sign language interpretation, respectively?

Spoken language → Next to or slightly behind the {{c1::patient}}
Sign language → Next to or slightly behind the {{c1::physician}}

What do you do if both a woman and her 13-year-old daughter require a blood transfusion in an emergency, but the father refuses to give consent, saying both are Jehovah’s Witnesses?

Transfuse the {{c1::daughter}}
Do not transfuse the {{c1::mother}}
fields.Back Extra: A healthcare proxy can refuse emergency treatment for an adult patient, but not for a minor, on the basis of religious beliefs.

fields.Text:
Should you accept a sponsorship offered by a drug company in exchange for advertising a new drug?

The offer must be {{c1::rejected::accepted/rejected}}
fields.Back Extra: In general, all such gifts (with a few exceptions) should be declined to avoid a conflict of interest.

fields.Text:
How do you respond when a brain-dead patient's family insists that life support be maintained because the patient is still moving when touched?

Gently inform the family that involuntary movement is caused by {{c1::spinal reflexes}} and that brain death is equivalent to {{c1::death}}
Inform the {{c1::ethics board}}

What should you do when a physician colleague arrives at work in an impaired state?

You are ethically and legally obliged to {{c1::report}} impaired colleagues
fields.Back Extra: Seek guidance in making the report because applicable laws and requirements vary by state and institution.

fields.Text:
How should you respond if your patient wants to try alternative or holistic medicine?

Find out {{c1::why}} the patient wants this
Inform the patient about known {{c1::benefits}} and {{c1::risks}}
fields.Back Extra:
Be supportive and nonjudgemental.

You may refer the patient to a naturopath.

fields.Text:
What should you do if you find out that your patient is experiencing physical abuse from an intimate partner?

Ensure that patient is {{c1::safe}} and has an {{c1::emergency}} plan
Ask {{c1::open-ended}} questions
Provide {{c1::summary}} of answers in response
Do not push patient to take a step unless required by {{c1::law}}

What do you do if a patient requires a treatment not covered by insurance?

Discuss {{c1::all}} options
fields.Back Extra:
Do not limit treatment because of financial or time constraints.

Provide information about financial assistance programs.

fields.Text:
What is the best approach when a 7-year-old boy feels responsible for his older sister's death from cancer?

Use {{c1::concrete}} terms in discussing his sister's death
{{c1::Reassure}} him that it was not his fault
Identify/normalize {{c1::fears}} and {{c1::feelings}}
Encourage healthy {{c1::coping}} strategies

How should you respond when a 15-year-old pregnant patient wants to keep the baby, but the patient's parents want you to tell her to give the baby up for adoption?

The {{c1::patient}} has the right to make choices regarding the baby
fields.Back Extra: Physicians should discuss infant care and adoption as needed and encourage open family discussion.

fields.Text:
What is an appropriate response if an invasive test is performed on the wrong patient?

Regardless of the result, the physician is obligated to {{c1::tell}} the patient about the mistake

What is an appropriate response if a woman who had a mastectomy says she now feels ugly?

Find out more about {{c1::why}} the patient feels this way without offering {{c1::falsely}} reassuring statements

What is the most appropriate next step when a patient is suicidal and has a plan?

Suggest voluntary {{c1::hospitalization}}
fields.Back Extra: If necessary, the patient can be hospitalized involuntarily.

fields.Text:
A patient’s son asks you not to tell his mother the results of a test if the prognosis is poor because she won't be able to cope with it. How do you respond?

Explore his {{c1::reasoning}}
Explain that if a patient wants information, you must {{c1::provide}} it
If you believe the patient might harm herself or others, you can {{c1::withhold}} it

How would you help a patient if the patient has difficulty taking medication?

Provide {{c1::written}} instructions
{{c1::Simplify}} the regimen
Use the {{c1::teach-back}} method

How can you help a patient if the patient is not adherent?

Discuss any {{c1::logistical}} or {{c1::financial}} obstacles to adherence
Schedule regular {{c1::follow-ups}}
Avoid {{c1::coercion}} and {{c1::referrals}} to other physicians

What is an appropriate response if a patient is upset with the treatment provided by another physician?

Advise the patient to talk {{c1::directly}} to that physician
fields.Back Extra: If the problem is with a staff member in your office, tell the patient that you will speak to the person.

fields.Text:
What is an appropriate response if a patient is angry about the amount of time spent in the waiting room?

{{c1::Apologize}} for any inconvenience and {{c1::acknowledge}} the patient's anger
{{c1::Thank}} the patient for being patient, but {{c1::avoid}} explaining why the delay occurred

What is an appropriate response if a patient wants an unnecessary procedure?

Discuss the patient's {{c1::concerns}} and {{c1::reasons}} for requesting the procedure
Avoid unwarranted procedures
Do not {{c1::discharge}} or {{c1::refer}} the patient to another provider

What is an appropriate response if a patient flirts with you and asks you out on a date?

Explain that romantic relationships with patients are {{c1::never::always/never}} appropriate
Employ a {{c1::chaperone}}
fields.Back Extra: It may be necessary to transfer the patient to another physician.

fields.Text:
How do you respond if a terminally ill patient requests physician-assisted dying?

In most states, this is {{c1::prohibited}}
fields.Back Extra: However, physicians may prescribe certain analgesics that happen to shorten the patient's life.

fields.Text:
What is the appropriate response if a pregnant 17-year-old patient requests an abortion?

Certain states require {{c1::parental consent}} for minors to undergo abortion
fields.Back Extra: Unless there are medical concerns, physicians should not attempt to influence the patient's decision.

fields.Text:
How do you proceed when a family member wants information about a patient's prognosis?

Unless the patient gives {{c1::permission}}, you {{c1::should not::should/should not}} give the information to family members

What do you do when standard vaccinations are recommended for a pediatric patient, but the child's parent refuses to provide consent for adminstration?

Address any {{c1::concerns}}
Explain {{c1::risks}} and {{c1::benefits}} and why vaccinations are recommended
Do not administer routine vaccinations without the parent's {{c1::consent}}

What should be done when a dependent patient presents with injuries inconsistent with the caregiver's account?

{{c1::Record}} detailed history and exam findings
{{c1::Interview}} patient alone if feasible
Contact {{c1::authorities}} for assessment
{{c1::Inform}} caregiver of your duty to report suspected abuse
fields.Back Extra: Physicians are required by law to report suspected abuse.

fields.Text:
How should you proceed if a patient requests a nonemergent treatment option that is against your personal beliefs?

Provide {{c1::accurate}} and {{c1::unbiased::biased/unbiased}} information, so the patient can make an informed decision
Explain that you do not perform the procedure, but offer to {{c1::refer}} them to another physician

What ethical principle has been balanced against beneficence when a patient with cancer is treated with drugs causing multiple adverse effects?

{{c1::Nonmaleficence}}
fields.Back Extra:
In many cases, treatment may harm the patient, but benefits outweigh the risks.

The patient can make an informed choice to proceed.

fields.Text:
The principle of "do no harm" describes what ethical term?

{{c1::Nonmaleficence}}

What ethical responsibility is being displayed when a physician acts in a patient's best interest in providing treatment choices?

{{c1::Beneficence}}
fields.Back Extra: The physician has a fiduciary duty to the patient.

fields.Text:
Which core ethical principle of medicine dictates that all patients must be treated fairly and equitably?

{{c1::Justice}}

Which core ethical principle allows a patient with cancer who has decision-making capacity to refuse life-prolonging treatment?

{{c1::Autonomy}}

What ethical principle is defined as an obligation to respect patients as individuals, ensure they provide informed consent, and honor their preferences in medical care?

{{c1::Autonomy}}

What are the four core ethical principles of medicine?

{{c1::Autonomy}}
{{c1::Beneficence}}
{{c1::Nonmaleficence}}
{{c1::Justice}}

Does the core principle of justice dictate that all patients always be treated equally?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Patients sometimes need to be triaged according to disease severity.

fields.Text:
What core ethical principle traditionally supersedes beneficence when a patient has decision-making capacity?

{{c1::Autonomy}}

Who has the power to determine a patient's legal competence to make an informed healthcare-related decision?

{{c1::Judge}}

Who determines a patient's capacity to make an informed healthcare-related decision?

{{c1::Physician}}

If a patient loses capacity, can the previous decisions made with full capacity be revoked?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Decisions made with capacity cannot be revoked if the patient later loses capacity.

fields.Text:
Are intellectual disabilities and mental illness exclusion criteria for informed decision-making?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: The exception is if the condition presently impairs the ability to make healthcare decisions.

fields.Text:
With regard to age, how do you determine decision-making capacity?

Age ≥ {{c1::18}} years
Legally {{c1::emancipated}}

What are the major components of decision-making capacity?

{{c1::Understanding}}
{{c1::Appreciation}}
{{c1::Reasoning}}
Expressing a {{c1::choice}}

What are the four exceptions to informed consent?

{{c1::Waiver}} of informed consent
Legal {{c1::incompetence}}
{{c1::Therapeutic}} privilege
{{c1::Emergency}} situations

Do patients have the right to revoke their written consent at any time?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}

What are the four requirements for obtaining informed consent?

{{c1::Disclosure}} of information
Patient {{c1::understanding}}
Patient {{c1::capacity}}
{{c1::Voluntariness}}

What three aspects of an intervention must a patient understand to properly grant informed consent?

The {{c1::diagnosis}}
The risks/benefits of the proposed {{c1::intervention}}
The risks/benefits of the {{c1::alternatives}}

How is consent for treatment obtained when a patient is considered legally incompetent?

Consent should be obtained from the patient's legal {{c1::surrogate}}

Is it ethical to perform a life-saving operation when a person injured in a motor vehicle accident is rushed to the emergency department without first obtaining informed consent?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: In emergency situations consent is considered to be implied.

fields.Text:
Is a minor's assent necessary even if their consent is not?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}

What circumstances make a minor legally emancipated?

{{c1::Married}}
{{c1::Self-supporting}}
In the {{c1::military}}

Under what special circumstances is parental notification not required for care of a minor < 18 years of age?

Treatment of {{c1::sexually transmitted}} infections
{{c1::Prenatal}} care
{{c1::Contraception}}
Treatment related to {{c1::drug abuse}}
{{c1::Emergencies}}
The minor is legally {{c1::emancipated}}

What measures are prohibited under the DNR order?

Performing {{c1::CPR}}
fields.Back Extra: Patients may still consider other life-sustaining measures.

fields.Text:
How can problems arise in an oral advance directive?

Arise from {{c1::variance}} in interpretation

What is an advance directive?

Oral or written instructions given by a patient in anticipation of a need to make important medical {{c1::decisions}}
fields.Back Extra: Legal requirements vary depending on state laws.

fields.Text:
What is a written advance directive?

A document that details specific {{c1::interventions}} the patient is willing to accept or reject while receiving treatment for a critical or life-threatening illness

Which type of advance directive has more flexibility than a living will?

{{c1::Medical power of attorney}}
fields.Back Extra: This may be revoked by a patient if decision-making capacity is intact.

fields.Text:
What is medical power of attorney?

Designation of someone by the patient as legally authorized to make medical {{c1::decisions}} if the patient loses {{c1::decision-making}} capacity

Name the three methods by which patients can establish advance directives.

{{c1::Oral}} advance directive
{{c1::Written}} advance directive
{{c1::Medical power of attorney}}

What four factors would make an oral advance directive more valid?

The patient was {{c1::informed}}
The directive was {{c1::specific}}
The patient made a {{c1::choice}}
The decision was {{c1::repeated}} over time to multiple people

What is the priority ranking of surrogates for a patient without an advance directive?

{{c1::Spouse}} → {{c1::Adult children}} → {{c1::Parents}} → {{c1::Siblings}} → Other {{c1::relatives}}

When is a surrogate decision-maker sought on behalf of a patient?

When a patient loses {{c1::decision-making}} capacity and does not have an {{c1::advance directive}} on file

What are five notable exceptions to patient confidentiality?

Patients with {{c1::suicidal}}/{{c1::homicidal}} ideation
{{c1::Abuse}}
Duty to {{c1::protect}}
Patients with {{c1::epilepsy}} and other impaired {{c1::automobile drivers}}
{{c1::Reportable}} diseases

Should confidentiality be maintained when a working bus driver is given a new diagnosis of epilepsy?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: A physician must break confidentiality to report an impaired driver.

fields.Text:
Should a physician maintain confidentiality when child abuse is suspected?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: A physician must break confidentiality and alert appropriate authorities in any case of suspected abuse.

fields.Text:
What are the general principles that guide exceptions to patient confidentiality?

Potential of {{c1::harm}} to self or others is imminent and serious
Alternative means to {{c1::warn}} or {{c1::protect}} those at risk is not possible
Steps can be taken to prevent {{c1::harm}}

In what common situation may a patient voluntarily waive the right to confidentiality?

To comply with {{c1::insurance company}} requests

Which patients are included in a per-protocol analysis?

Only patients who {{c1::complete}} their original randomly assigned study treatment

What three sources of bias are potentially avoided in intention-to-treat analysis?

{{c1::Crossover}}
{{c1::Attrition}}
{{c1::Nonrandom::Random/Nonrandom}} noncompliance

In what three ways can the quality of a clinical trial be enhanced?

{{c1::Randomizing}}
{{c1::Controlling}}
{{c1::Double}}-blinding

How is a clinical trial triple-blinded?

The {{c1::subjects}}, researchers {{c1::conducting}} the study, and researchers {{c1::analyzing}} the data do not know to which group each subject has been assigned

A researcher wants to assess the rare or long-term adverse effects of a drug. Which phase of a clinical trial is best for this?

Phase {{c1::IV}}
fields.Back Extra: This is when postmarketing surveillance occurs.

fields.Text:
What is the purpose of a phase III clinical trial?

To assess {{c1::effectiveness}} of a new treatment compared with standard of care in a large number of individuals with the disease

What kind of study compares two or more treatments or treatment versus placebo in humans?

{{c1::Clinical trial}}

In what kind of population is a phase I clinical trial typically performed?

A {{c1::small::large/small}} number of {{c1::healthy}} volunteers or patients {{c1::with::with/without}} the disease of interest

In what kind of population is a phase II clinical trial typically performed?

A {{c1::moderate}} number of individuals with the disease of interest

Which phase of a clinical trial determines efficacy and short-term adverse effects of a drug?

Phase {{c1::II}}

Which phase of a clinical trial assesses drug safety via dose escalation and identifies a maximum tolerated dose?

Phase {{c1::I}}

What is the purpose of phase 0 in a clinical trial?

Initial assessment of a drug's {{c1::pharmacodynamics}} and {{c1::pharmacokinetics}} by means of microdosing

In which type of clinical trial do participants serve as their own controls?

{{c1::Crossover}} study

Briefly describe how a crossover study is conducted.

It compares the effect of two or more treatments on participants, with treatments provided in a {{c1::random}} order and separated by a {{c1::washout period}}

What is an intention-to-treat analysis in a clinical trial?

Subjects are evaluated based on original {{c1::random}} assignments and no subjects are {{c1::excluded}} from analysis
fields.Back Extra: Actual effects of intervention being studied may be diluted.

fields.Text:
What are Bradford Hill criteria?

Principles that provide {{c1::limited}} support in establishing evidence of a presumed {{c1::causal}} relationship

"Smoking 1 cigarette/day for 40 years can lead to lung cancer, but smoking 2 packs/day for 40 years is more likely to lead to lung cancer" describes which Bradford Hill criterion?

{{c1::Strength}}
fields.Back Extra: This criterion implies that a strong association is more likely to be a cause, rather than just an association.

fields.Text:
Lisinopril has been shown to decrease chronic kidney disease progression in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus in multiple studies. This is an example of which Bradford Hill criterion?

{{c1::Consistency}}
fields.Back Extra: Repeated observations of findings are reported for multiple distinct samples.

fields.Text:
Insulin lowers blood glucose levels consistently. This is an example of which Bradford Hill criterion?

{{c1::Specificity}}
fields.Back Extra: There is strong evidence of causation of low blood glucose after insulin use.

fields.Text:
Which Bradford Hill criterion states that there is more evidence for causation when the presumed cause occurs an expected amount of time before the effect?

{{c1::Temporality}}

Which Bradford Hill criterion states that there is more evidence for causation when a dose-response relationship exists between a presumed cause and effect?

{{c1::Biological gradient}}

Insulin promotes uptake of glucose in skeletal muscle cells. This has been shown in biological models. This is an example of which Bradford Hill criterion?

{{c1::Plausibility}}
fields.Back Extra: In this example, a mechanism exists whereby a cause may lead to the effect.

fields.Text:
Insulin lowering blood glucose is consistent with currently established medical knowledge. This is an example of which Bradford Hill criterion?

{{c1::Coherence}}
fields.Back Extra: In this example, it is a well known and established fact in medical literature that insulin decreases the blood glucose level.

fields.Text:
Multiple animal models in basic science research have proven that insulin decreases blood glucose levels. This is an example of which Bradford Hill criterion?

{{c1::Experiment}}
fields.Back Extra: Evidence from basic science research supports the presumed cause and effect.

fields.Text:
Sulfonylureas decrease blood glucose levels in a way similar to insulin administration. This is an example of which Bradford Hill criterion?

{{c1::Analogy}}
fields.Back Extra: The presumed cause and effect are comparable to a similar cause and effect that have already been established.

fields.Text:
What is the formula for odds ratio based on a 2 × 2 contingency table?

OR = ( {{c1::a}} / {{c1::c}} ) / ( {{c1::b}} / {{c1::d}} )
OR = ( {{c1::a}} × {{c1::d}} ) / ( {{c1::b}} × {{c1::c}} )

What does it mean if a new drug has a lower value for number needed to treat?

The new drug is a {{c1::safer}} treatment

What measurement approximates the relative risk of a rare disease?

{{c1::Odds ratio}}
fields.Back Extra: This approximates the relative risk for diseases with a low prevalence.

fields.Text:
What is the formula for attributable risk based on a 2 × 2 contingency table?

AR = ( {{c1::a}} / [ {{c1::a}} + {{c1::b}} ] ) - ( {{c1::c}} / [ {{c1::c}} + {{c1::d}} ] )

What measure describes the risk difference between exposed and unexposed groups?

{{c1::Attributable risk}}

How do you calculate the number of patients who need to be treated for 1 patient to benefit?

NNT = {{c1::1}} / {{c1::ARR}}
fields.Back Extra: A lower number means better treatment.

fields.Text:
What does it mean if the relative risk is > 1 in a cohort study?

The exposure is associated with a(n) {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} risk of disease

What is the attributable risk if a study shows that a disease develops in 21% of people with a given exposure versus 1% of people without that exposure?

AR = {{c1::20}}%
fields.Back Extra: This is the proportion of disease attributable to an exposure.

fields.Text:
Which measure describes the proportion of risk reduction that can be attributed to the intervention as compared with the control?

{{c1::Relative risk reduction}}

What type of study typically calculates an odds ratio?

{{c1::Case-control}} studies

What type of study typically calculates and reports a relative risk?

{{c1::Cohort}} study

What does it mean to have a relative risk of 1 in a cohort study?

{{c1::No}} association between the exposure and the disease

What does it mean if the relative risk is < 1 in a cohort study?

Exposure is associated with {{c1::lower::higher/lower}} disease occurrence

What is the calculation for relative risk based on a 2 × 2 contingency table?

RR = ( {{c1::a}} / [ {{c1::a}} + {{c1::b}} ] ) / ( {{c1::c}} / [ {{c1::c}} + {{c1::d}} ] )

What is the calculation for absolute risk reduction based on a 2 × 2 contingency table?

ARR = ( {{c1::c}} / [ {{c1::c}} + {{c1::d}} ] ) - ( {{c1::a}} / [ {{c1::a}} + {{c1::b}} ] )

What is the formula used to calculate attributable risk percentage without using a contingency table?

AR% = ( [ {{c1::RR}} - {{c1::1}} ] / {{c1::RR}} ) × {{c1::100}}

What is the meaning of an odds ratio = 1?

Odds of exposure are {{c1::equal}} in cases and in controls

What term describes the number of deaths within a population over a specific period, usually scaled to deaths per 1,000 individuals per year?

{{c1::Mortality rate}}

What measure describes the risk difference attributable to an intervention compared with the control?

{{c1::Absolute risk reduction}}

What is the negative likelihood ratio if a test's true-negative rate is 95% and its false-negative rate is 5%?

{{c1::0.05}}
fields.Back Extra:
LR- = FN rate / TN rate

In this case, LR- < 0.1, so the test is highly sensitive.

fields.Text:
What is the positive likelihood ratio if a test's true-positive rate is 90% and its false-positive rate is 20%?

{{c1::4.5}}
fields.Back Extra:
LR+ = TP rate / FP rate

In this case, LR+ < 10, so the test is not highly specific.

fields.Text:
A test has 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity. What is the positive likelihood ratio?

{{c1::18}}
fields.Back Extra:
LR+ = Sensitivity / [ 1 - Specificity ]

In this case, LR+ > 10, so the test is specific.

fields.Text:
What positive likelihood ratio indicates a highly specific test?

> {{c1::10}}

What negative likelihood ratio indicates a highly sensitive test?

< {{c1::0.1}}

What is the definition of the negative likelihood ratio?

The likelihood of a {{c1::negative::positive/negative}} test result in a patient with a disease versus the likelihood of a {{c1::negative::positive/negative}} test result in a patient without the disease

What happens to the test's sensitivity and specificity if a researcher changes the cutoff for diagnosis from point B to point C?



Sensitivity {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
Specificity {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}

What do points A, B, and C represent in the image shown?



A = 100% {{c1::sensitivity}} cutoff value
B = Reasonable compromise between {{c1::sensitivity}} and {{c1::specificity}}
C = 100% {{c1::specificity}} cutoff value

What characteristic of a test describes the proportion of people without a disease who test negative for the disease?

{{c1::Specificity::Sensitivity/Specificity}}

How is the specificity of a test determined from the 2 × 2 table shown?



Specificity = {{c1::TN}} / ( {{c1::TN}} + {{c1::FP}} )

What characteristic of a test describes the proportion of people with a disease who test positive for the disease?

{{c1::Sensitivity::Sensitivity/Specificity}}

What is implied about the false-negative rate if the test is highly sensitive?

False-negative rate is {{c1::low::high/low}}

What happens to the test's sensitivity and specificity if a researcher changes the cutoff for diagnosis from point B to point A in the image?



Sensitivity {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}
Specificity {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}

What is implied about the false-positive rate if a test is highly specific?

False-positive rate is {{c1::low::high/low}}

How would prevalence affect the positive predictive value of a test?

The PPV of a test is {{c1::directly::directly/indirectly}} proportionate to the prevalence

If the result of a highly sensitive test is positive for a particular disease, what is the desired specificity to confirm the diagnosis?

Tests with {{c1::high::high/low}} specificity are ideal to confirm a diagnosis
fields.Back Extra: This can rule in the disease when it is positive.

fields.Text:
What is the desirable sensitivity of a test used for screening?

{{c1::High::High/Low}} sensitivity tests
fields.Back Extra: This can rule out the disease when it is negative.

fields.Text:
How is the sensitivity of a test determined from the 2 × 2 table shown?



Sensitivity = {{c1::TP}} / ( {{c1::TP}} + {{c1::FN}} )

How is the specificity of a test calculated using only the false-positive rate?

Specificity = {{c1::1}} - {{c1::FP rate}}

How is the positive predictive value of a test determined from the 2 × 2 table shown?



PPV = {{c1::TP}} / ( {{c1::TP}} + {{c1::FP}} )

How is the negative predictive value of a test determined from the 2 × 2 table shown?



NPV = {{c1::TN}} / ( {{c1::TN}} + {{c1::FN}} )

How is the prevalence of a disease determined from the 2 × 2 table shown?



Prevalence = ( {{c1::TP}} + {{c1::FN}} ) / ( {{c1::TP}} + {{c1::FN}} + {{c1::FP}} + {{c1::TN}} )

How is negative predictive value related to prevalence?

Negative predictive value is {{c1::inversely}} related to prevalence

How is the sensitivity of a test calculated using only the false-negative rate?

Sensitivity = {{c1::1}} - {{c1::FN rate}}

What is the definition of positive predictive value?

It represents the probability that a person with a {{c1::positive::positive/negative}} test result actually has the disease

What is the definition of negative predictive value?

It represents the probability that a person with a {{c1::negative::positive/negative}} test result actually does not have the disease

What do the two axes in a receiver operating characteristic curve represent?



The vertical axis represents the {{c1::TP rate}}
The horizontal axis represents the {{c1::FP rate}}

In a receiver operating characteristic curve, how do you determine which test has better performance?



The test with better performance will have a {{c1::higher::higher/lower}} area under the curve, and the curve will be positioned to the {{c1::upper::upper/lower}} {{c1::left::left/right}} corner

What is a receiver operating characteristic curve used to demonstrate?

It is used to show how well a {{c1::diagnostic}} test can {{c1::differentiate}} between 2 groups

Describe the test's accuracy and precision in the image where the blue dots are a test's results and the bull's-eye is the actual result.



{{c1::Is not::Is/Is not}} precise
{{c1::Is not::Is/Is not}} accurate

Describe the test's accuracy and precision in the image where the blue dots are a test's results and the bull's-eye is the actual result.



{{c1::Is::Is/Is not}} precise
{{c1::Is not::Is/Is not}} accurate

Describe the test's accuracy and precision in the image where the blue dots are a test's results and the bull's-eye is the actual result.



{{c1::Is not::Is/Is not}} precise
{{c1::Is::Is/Is not}} accurate

Describe the test's accuracy and precision in the image where the blue dots are a test's results and the bull's-eye is the actual result.



{{c1::Is::Is/Is not}} precise
{{c1::Is::Is/Is not}} accurate

What happens to statistical power when precision increases?

Statistical power {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}

What kind of error reduces a test's accuracy?

{{c1::Systematic}} error
fields.Back Extra: Accuracy means that there is little systematic error or bias in a test.

fields.Text:
What measurement describes the consistency and reproducibility of a test?

{{c1::Precision::Precision/Accuracy}}

How is the precision of a test related to the standard deviation found when that test is applied?

{{c1::Inverse}} relationship
fields.Back Extra: Increased precision means decreased standard deviation.

fields.Text:
What measurement describes the trueness of a test's measurements?

{{c1::Accuracy::Precision/Accuracy}}

What kind of error reduces a test's precision?

{{c1::Random}} error
fields.Back Extra: Precision means that there is little random error in a test.

fields.Text:
What two disease outcomes might reduce the prevalence of a disease?

{{c1::Mortality}}
{{c1::Cure}}

In cases of the common cold, is the prevalence equal to the incidence?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: This is for diseases of short duration.

fields.Text:
In cases of chronic diseases, is the prevalence greater than or less than the incidence?

Prevalence is much {{c1::greater::greater/less}} than incidence
fields.Back Extra: This is because of the long duration of the disease.

fields.Text:
What measure describes the number of new cases of a disease in the total population at risk for a given time?

{{c1::Incidence}}
fields.Back Extra: Incidence = New cases / Number of people at risk
