fields.Text:
What is the mathematical relationship between incidence and prevalence?

Prevalence / ( {{c1::1}} - Prevalence ) = Incidence × {{c1::Average duration of disease}}

What measure describes the number of existing cases of a disease in the total population at one point in time?

{{c1::Prevalence}}
fields.Back Extra: Prevalence = Number of existing cases / Total population

fields.Text:
How does the prevalence of a disease influence the pretest probability of a patient having that disease?

Prevalence is {{c1::directly}} proportional to the pretest probability
Prevalence is {{c1::directly}} proportional to the positive predictive value
Prevalence is {{c1::inversely}} proportional to the negative predictive value

How does decreased contact between patients with and without an airborne infectious disease affect prevalence and incidence?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} prevalence
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} incidence

How does decreased contact between patients with and without noninfectious diseases affect prevalence and incidence?

{{c1::Unchanged}} prevalence
{{c1::Unchanged}} incidence

How would increased survival time affect incidence and prevalence?

{{c1::Increased}} prevalence
{{c1::Unchanged}} incidence

How does increased diagnostic sensitivity affect incidence and prevalence?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} prevalence
{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} incidence

How does faster recovery time affect incidence and prevalence?

{{c1::Decreased}} prevalence
{{c1::Unchanged}} incidence

How does extensive vaccine administration affect incidence and prevalence?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} incidence
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} prevalence

How does a decrease in risk factors affect incidence and prevalence?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} incidence
{{c1::Decreases::Increasas/Decreases}} prevalence

How can recall bias be reduced?

{{c1::Decreasing::Increasing/Decreasing}} time from exposure to follow-up
Using information collected from {{c1::medical records}}

What kind of bias might be present in a study where a researcher studying college athletes adds all of his basketball players to the control group?

{{c1::Selection}} bias
fields.Back Extra: Basketball players were nonrandomly assigned to one group over the other.

fields.Text:
What are two research strategies or study designs that can help to eliminate confounding bias?

Performing {{c1::multiple}} or {{c1::repeated}} studies
Performing a {{c1::crossover}} study in which each subject acts as his or her own control

What type of bias might be present in a study in which patients lost to follow-up have different outcomes than those who remain in the study?

{{c1::Attrition}} bias
fields.Back Extra: This is a type of selection bias.

fields.Text:
What type of bias is present in a study in which a factor related to the exposure and outcome influences the effect of the exposure on the outcome?

{{c1::Confounding}} bias

What specific type of bias might be present when a sample is taken from a hospital with a different exposure rate than the general population?

{{c1::Berkson}} bias
fields.Back Extra: Hospitalized patients are less healthy and have different exposures.

fields.Text:
List two strategies to reduce the selection bias in a study.

{{c1::Randomization}}
{{c1::Appropriate}} choice of comparison/reference group

What are two strategies to reduce measurement bias?

{{c1::Standardized}}, {{c1::objective}}, and previously {{c1::tested}} data collection methods that are planned ahead of time
Using a {{c1::placebo}} group

If a screening test appears to exaggerate survival time because of early diagnosis, how can it be reduced?

By measuring {{c1::"back-end" survival}}

What type of bias is likely present if an observer with a strong belief in a treatment records more positive results?

{{c1::Observer-expectancy}} bias
fields.Back Extra: This is known as the Pygmalion effect.

fields.Text:
What type of bias might be present in a study in which information is collected with a systematically distorted method?

{{c1::Measurement}} bias

What type of bias is present when early detection of a disease is confused with increased survival despite no changes in disease course?

{{c1::Lead-time}} bias

How can the bias in a study in which patient groups are treated differently be limited?

{{c1::Blinding}}
Using a {{c1::placebo}} group

What type of bias might be present in a study that asks patients known to have a disease about prior exposures?

{{c1::Recall}} bias

What type of studies are most likely to introduce recall bias?

{{c1::Retrospective}} studies

If the researcher's belief in the efficacy of a treatment is likely to influence the outcome of a trial, how can it be reduced?

{{c1::Blinding}}
Using a {{c1::placebo}} group

What type of bias is present in a study in which participants change behavior when they become aware they are being observed?

{{c1::Hawthorne effect}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a type of measurement bias.

fields.Text:
What is the strategy to reduce the confounding bias where patients with similar characteristics are selected in both treatment and control groups?

{{c1::Matching}}

What type of bias might be present when a screening test identifies diseases with a long latency period, while diseases with a short latency period produce symptoms earlier?

{{c1::Length-time}} bias

What type of study can be used to reduce length-time bias?

{{c1::Randomized controlled trial}}
fields.Back Extra: The subjects will be either assigned to screening or no screening.

fields.Text:
What type of bias might be present in a study in which participant groups are treated differently?

{{c1::Procedure}} bias

Which measure of central tendency is least affected by outliers?

{{c1::Mode}}

What is the calculation for standard error based on the sample size and standard deviation?

SE = {{c1::σ}} / √ {{c1::n}}

What is a standard deviation?

An estimate of the amount of {{c1::variability}} from the {{c1::mean}} in a given set of values

What is the relationship between the mean, median, and mode in a negatively skewed distribution?

Mean {{c1::<}} Median {{c1::<}} Mode

What is the relationship between the mean, median, and mode in a positively skewed distribution?

Mean {{c1::>}} Median {{c1::>}} Mode

What is the standard error?

Estimate of the amount of {{c1::variability}} in a theoretical set of sample {{c1::means}} around the true {{c1::mean}} of the population

How is the standard error of a study related to the sample size of the study?

Standard error {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} as sample size increases

What are the three key measures of central tendency in a set of data?

{{c1::Mean}}
{{c1::Median}}
{{c1::Mode}}

What are the two key measures of dispersion in a set of data?

{{c1::Standard deviation}}
{{c1::Standard error}}

What is the definition of the mean?

The {{c1::average}}
fields.Back Extra: It is calculated as the sum of values divided by the total number of values.

fields.Text:
What is the definition of the median?

The {{c1::middle}} value in a list of data sorted from least to greatest
fields.Back Extra: If the list of values is an even number, the median is the average of the two values in the middle.

fields.Text:
What is the definition of the mode?

The {{c1::most::most/least}} common value in a list of data

Which measure of central tendency is most affected by outliers?

{{c1::Mean}}

What is the relationship between the mean, median, and mode in a normal distribution?

Mean {{c1::=}} Median {{c1::=}} Mode

What percentage of values in a normal distribution fall within 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations of the mean?

1 standard deviation = {{c1::68}}%
2 standard deviations = {{c1::95}}%
3 standard deviations = {{c1::99.7}}%

What is the relationship between standard variance and standard deviation?

Standard variance = ( σ ) {{c1::2}}

What is a bimodal distribution?

{{c1::Nonnormal::Normal/Nonnormal}} distribution suggesting 2 {{c1::different::similar/different}} populations

What is the best measure of central tendency for normal distribution?

{{c1::Mean}}

Which hypothesis posits that there is some difference or relationship between groups being compared?

{{c1::Alternative}} hypothesis

Which hypothesis posits that there is no difference between groups being compared?

{{c1::Null}} hypothesis

What is p-value in hypothesis testing?

The probability that the test results will be at least as {{c1::extreme}} as the results actually observed, assuming the null hypothesis is {{c1::correct::correct/incorrect}}
fields.Back Extra: It is usually set to a value of 0.05.

fields.Text:
What type of error is made when results of a research study indicate no difference when there truly was a difference?

Type {{c1::II}} error
fields.Back Extra: This is also called the false-negative error.

fields.Text:
What statistical term refers to the probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis?

{{c1::Statistical power}}

What does α represent, and what value of α is often used in hypothesis testing?

α represents the probability of making a type {{c1::I::I/II}} error
α is usually set to a value of {{c1::0.05}}

Is a statistically significant study always significant clinically?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}

What are three ways that the power of a study can be increased?

Increased {{c1::sample}} size
Increased expected {{c1::effect}} size
Increased {{c1::precision}} of measurement

What type of statistical error is made when the study's null hypothesis is mistakenly rejected?

Type {{c1::I}} error
fields.Back Extra: This is also called a false-positive error.

fields.Text:
What type of statistical error is made when a study's null hypothesis is not rejected when it should have been?

Type {{c1::II}} error
fields.Back Extra: This is also called a false-negative error.

fields.Text:
What does it mean in terms of statistical power if the β value of a study is 20%?

The study has an {{c1::80}}% chance of {{c1::rejecting::accepting/rejecting}} the null hypothesis when it is {{c1::false::true/false}}

What does it mean if the p-value is less than α, assuming H0 is true?

The probability of getting the test results is {{c1::lower::higher/lower}} than the probability of making a type {{c1::I::I/II}} error

Is it possible to definitively prove that the alternative hypothesis is correct?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: However, the null hypothesis can be rejected as being highly unlikely.

fields.Text:
What three conditions must be met by confidence intervals to reject the null hypothesis?

A 95% confidence interval for the mean difference excludes {{c1::0}}
A 95% confidence interval for either the odds ratio or relative risk excludes {{c1::1}}
The confidence intervals between 2 groups are not {{c1::overlapping}}

What is the value of Z in a study in which a 95% confidence interval is reported?

Z = {{c1::1.96}}

What is the definition of confidence interval?

Range of values within which a population's true {{c1::mean}} is expected to fall, with a specified probability
fields.Back Extra: A 95% confidence interval is commonly used.

fields.Text:
What is the value of Z in a study in which a 99% confidence interval is reported?

Z = {{c1::2.58}}

What is the mathematical relationship between the confidence interval and the standard error?

CI = {{c1::x̄}} ± {{c1::Z}} ({{c1::SE}})

What happens to the confidence interval as the sample size increases?

It {{c1::narrows::widens/narrows}}

What two factors can limit the findings of a meta-analysis?

{{c1::Quality}} of the individual studies chosen
{{c1::Bias}} in the study selection

What are the benefits of performing a meta-analysis?

Increased {{c1::power}}
Increased {{c1::generalizability}}
Increased strength of {{c1::evidence}}

What is a meta-analysis?

Statistical analysis that pools data from {{c1::multiple}} studies to produce a more {{c1::precise}} measurement of the size of an effect
fields.Back Extra: It also estimates heterogeneity of effect sizes between studies.

fields.Text:
Which statistical test is used to compare differences in proportions of categorical outcomes in two or more groups with large sample sizes?

{{c1::Chi-square}}

What statistical test is used for comparing differences between the means of two groups?

{{c1::t-test}}

Which statistical test is used to compare differences between means of three or more groups?

{{c1::ANOVA}}

Which statistical test is used to compare differences in proportions of categorical outcomes in two or more groups with small sample sizes?

{{c1::Fisher's exact}} test

What can you say about the correlation in the graph below showing data with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0?



{{c1::No}} correlation

What can you say about the correlation in the graph below showing data with a Pearson correlation coefficient of -0.4?



{{c1::Weak::Strong/Weak}} {{c1::negative::positive/negative}} correlation

What can you say about the correlation in the graph below showing data with a Pearson correlation coefficient of +0.8?



{{c1::Strong::Strong/Weak}} {{c1::positive::positive/negative}} correlation

What can you say about the correlation in the graph below showing data with a Pearson correlation coefficient of +0.4?



{{c1::Weak::Strong/Weak}} {{c1::positive::positive/negative}} correlation

What can you say about the correlation in the graph below showing data with a Pearson correlation coefficient of -0.8?



{{c1::Strong::Strong/Weak}} {{c1::negative::positive/negative}} correlation

In biostatistics, how is the coefficient of determination calculated from the Pearson correlation coefficient?

Coefficient of determination = r {{c1::2}}

Define the coefficient of determination.

The amount of {{c1::variance}} in 1 variable that can be determined by the {{c1::variance}} in another variable

What determines how much a measured value differs from the average value in a given data set?

The {{c1::variance}} of the data set

Which statistical term's absolute value indicates the strength of the linear correlation between two variables?

{{c1::Pearson correlation coefficient}}

What is the numeric range of the Pearson correlation coefficient?

{{c1::-1}} to {{c1::+1}}

What absolute value of r indicates that a correlation is stronger?

The correlation gets stronger as the absolute value of r approaches {{c1::1}}

Growth of what structures separate the atria from ventricles?

{{c1::Endocardial cushions}}

What structure will form after rotation of the structure indicated by the arrow in the image?



{{c1::Membranous interventricular septum}}
fields.Back Extra: The aorticopulmonary septum rotates and fuses with the muscular ventricular septum to form it.

fields.Text:
What is the structure forming in between the ventricles in the embryonic heart shown in the image?



{{c1::Muscular interventricular septum}}
fields.Back Extra: An opening called the interventricular foramen is formed as well.

fields.Text:
What residual foramen is shown in the embryonic heart in the image?



{{c1::Foramen ovale}}
fields.Back Extra: The septum secundum has expanded and covered most of the foramen secundum.

fields.Text:
What structure forms the one-way valve of the foramen shown in the image?



{{c1::Septum primum}}

What structure is indicated by the black arrow in the image of an embryonic heart shown here?



{{c1::Ostium primum}}

The truncal and bulbar ridges are formed from what two types of cellular precursors?

{{c1::Neural crest}} cells
{{c1::Endocardial}} cells

Which two heart valves are derived from fused endocardial cushions of the atrioventricular canal?

{{c1::Mitral}} valve
{{c1::Tricuspid}} valve

Which two heart valves are derived from the endocardial cushions of the outflow tract?

{{c1::Aortic}} valve
{{c1::Pulmonary}} valve

What is the most common congenital cardiac anomaly?

{{c1::Ventricular septal}} defect
fields.Back Extra: This most commonly occurs in the membranous septum.

fields.Text:
What three structures may fail to form as a result of defective endocardial cushion formation?

{{c1::Membranous interventricular septum}}
{{c1::Atrial septum}}
{{c1::Heart valves}}

A failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to rotate and fuse with the muscular ventricular septum would result in what defect?

{{c1::Ventricular septal}} defect
fields.Back Extra: This is from persistence of the interventricular foramen in the membranous interventricular septum.

fields.Text:
If neural crest cells fail to migrate during embryonic heart development, what three conotruncal abnormalities may occur?

{{c1::Transposition of great arteries}}
{{c1::Tetralogy of Fallot}}
{{c1::Persistent truncus arteriosus}}

Which two cardiac structures of the outflow tract will be affected if a fetus has defects in neural crest migration?

{{c1::Ascending aorta}}
{{c1::Pulmonary trunk}}
fields.Back Extra: These develop from the truncus arteriosus.

fields.Text:
What are the four main types of valvular anomalies?

{{c1::Stenotic}}
{{c1::Regurgitant}}
{{c1::Atretic}}
{{c1::Displaced}}

What are paradoxical emboli?

{{c1::Venous::Arterial/Venous}} thromboemboli that enter the systemic circulation through the {{c1::right}}-to-{{c1::left}} shunt
fields.Back Extra: They occur with an atrial septal defect.

fields.Text:
What is the final event in the septation of the atrial chambers?

The {{c1::septum secundum}} and {{c1::septum primum}} fuse during infancy or early childhood

How does the foramen ovale close in the sixth step of fetal atrial septation?

{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in left atrial pressure and {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} in right atrial pressure after birth → {{c1::Septum primum}} closes against the {{c1::septum secundum}} → Closure of the foramen ovale

How is the foramen ovale formed from the ostium secundum?

{{c1::Septum secundum}} expands and covers most of ostium secundum → The residual foramen is the foramen ovale

During the third step of fetal atrial septation, which foramen is essential in maintaining normal fetal hemodynamics?

{{c1::Ostium secundum}}
fields.Back Extra: This maintains a right-to-left shunt for blood to bypass the developing lungs.

fields.Text:
In fetal atrial septation, what does the septum primum develop into as it grows toward the endocardial cushions?

{{c1::Ostium secundum}}
fields.Back Extra: This forms in the septum primum as the ostium primum disappears.

fields.Text:
What is the first step of fetal atrial septation?

The {{c1::septum primum}} grows toward endocardial cushions, narrowing the {{c1::ostium primum}}

What molecular defect is responsible for dextrocardia, as seen in Kartagener syndrome?

A defect in {{c1::dynein}}

What is the first functional organ in vertebrate embryos?

{{c1::Heart}}
fields.Back Extra: The heart beats spontaneously by the 4th week of development.

fields.Text:
During which week of gestation does the primary heart tube begin to establish left-right polarity?

{{c1::4th}} week of gestation

During which week of gestation does the heart start to beat spontaneously?

{{c1::4th}} week of gestation

Embryologically, the 6th aortic arch gives rise to what important systemic shunt on the left side of the body?

{{c1::Ductus arteriosus}}

Embryologically, the 6th aortic arch gives rise to what structure on both sides?

{{c1::Proximal::Proximal/Distal}} part of the {{c1::pulmonary}} arteries

Embryologically, the 4th aortic arch on the right gives rise to what structure?

The {{c1::proximal::proximal/distal}} part of the right {{c1::subclavian}} artery

Embryologically, the 4th aortic arch on the left gives rise to what structure?

{{c1::Aortic arch}}

Embryologically, the 3rd aortic arch gives rise to which two arteries?

{{c1::Common carotid}} artery
{{c1::Proximal::Proximal/Distal}} part of the {{c1::internal carotid}} artery

Embryologically, the 2nd aortic arch gives rise to what two arteries?

{{c1::Stapedial}} artery
{{c1::Hyoid}} artery

Embryologically, the 1st aortic arch gives rise to part of what artery?

The {{c1::maxillary}} artery
fields.Back Extra: This is a branch of the external carotid artery.

fields.Text:
Which structure loops around the right subclavian artery during aortic arch development?

Right {{c1::recurrent laryngeal}} nerve

Which structure loops around the aortic arch distal to the structure marked "X" during aortic arch development?



Left {{c1::recurrent laryngeal}} nerve

The superior vena cava is derived from what embryonic structures?

Right {{c1::common cardinal}} vein
Right {{c1::anterior cardinal}} vein

The right horn of the sinus venosus gives rise to what structure?

The {{c1::smooth}} part of the {{c1::right::left/right}} {{c1::atrium}}

Which embryonic structure gives rise to the coronary sinus?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} horn of {{c1::sinus venosus}}

The primitive pulmonary vein gives rise to what structure?

The {{c1::smooth}} part of the {{c1::left::left/right}} {{c1::atrium}}

Which structures does the primitive ventricle give rise to?

The {{c1::trabeculated}} part of the left and right {{c1::ventricles}}

Which structures does the primitive atrium give rise to?

The {{c1::trabeculated}} part of the left and right {{c1::atria}}

What structures do the endocardial cushions give rise to?

{{c1::Atrial septum}}
{{c1::Membranous interventricular septum}}
{{c1::Atrioventricular valve}}
{{c1::Semilunar valve}}

Which structures does the truncus arteriosus give rise to?

{{c1::Ascending aorta}}
{{c1::Pulmonary trunk}}

Which structures does the bulbus cordis give rise to?

The {{c1::smooth}} parts of the right and left {{c1::ventricles}}

The posterior, subcardinal, and supracardinal veins together give rise to which blood vessel?

{{c1::Inferior vena cava}}

What treatment would keep the patent ductus arteriosus open?

{{c1::Prostaglandin E1}}
{{c1::Prostaglandin E2}}

How does high pulmonary artery resistance affect fetal circulation?

Blood entering the main pulmonary artery is preferentially shunted to the {{c1::descending aorta}} via the {{c1::ductus arteriosus}}

Describe the pathway by which deoxygenated blood travels from the superior vena cava to the placenta, including the shunts.

Superior vena cava → {{c1::Right atrium}} → {{c1::Right ventricle}} → {{c1::Pulmonary artery}} → {{c1::Ductus arteriosus::Shunt}} → {{c1::Descending aorta}} → {{c1::Internal iliac}} arteries → {{c1::Umbilical}} arteries → Placenta

Describe the path of oxygen-rich blood from the umbilical vein to systemic circulation in the fetus.

Umbilical vein → {{c1::Ductus venosus}} → {{c1::Inferior vena cava}} → {{c1::Right atrium}} → {{c1::Foramen ovale}} → {{c1::Left atrium}} → {{c1::Left ventricle}} → Aorta

What is the purpose of the ductus venosus in fetal circulation?

It transports blood from the {{c1::umbilical}} vein to the {{c1::inferior vena cava}}
fields.Back Extra: This allows it to bypass the liver.

fields.Text:
What is the medical treatment for patent ductus arteriosus?

{{c1::Indomethacin}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an NSAID that decreases prostaglandin production.

fields.Text:
What changes are responsible for the closure of the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus, respectively?

{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in left atrial pressure causes the foramen ovale to close
{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in O2 and {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} in prostaglandins cause the ductus arteriosus to close

What happens to pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary venous oxygen saturation after a neonate takes the first breath?

Pulmonary vascular resistance {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
Pulmonary venous oxygen saturation {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}

In the fetal heart, which atrium has the higher pressure and how does this pressure dynamic change after birth?

Pressure in the {{c1::right::left/right}} atrium is higher in the fetus
At birth, the pressure in the {{c1::left::left/right}} atrium becomes higher

In fetal circulation, most of the highly oxygenated blood that reaches the heart passes through which structure on its way to the left atrium?

{{c1::Foramen ovale}}

In fetal circulation, most deoxygenated blood reaching the heart via the superior vena cava passes through which shunt on its way to the aorta?

{{c1::Ductus arteriosus}}

What is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus?

{{c1::Ligamentum arteriosum}}

What are three important shunts present in fetal circulation?

{{c1::Ductus venosus}}
{{c1::Foramen ovale}}
{{c1::Ductus arteriosus}}

What is the postnatal derivative of the ductus venosus?

{{c1::Ligamentum venosum}}

After birth, a neonate's foramen ovale closes and becomes what structure?

{{c1::Fossa ovalis}}

From what prenatal structures are the medial umbilical ligaments derived?

{{c1::Umbilical}} arteries

What is the prenatal precursor of the ligamentum teres hepatis, which is contained in the falciform ligament?

{{c1::Umbilical}} vein

What structure derived from the allantois lies between the bladder and umbilicus?

{{c1::Urachus}}

From what prenatal structure is the median umbilical ligament derived?

{{c1::Allantois}}

What is the postnatal derivative of the ductus arteriosus and what clinically significant structure lies near it?

{{c1::Ligamentum arteriosum}}, where the left {{c1::recurrent laryngeal}} nerve lies near it

Infarction in which coronary artery territory may cause nodal dysfunction?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} coronary artery
fields.Back Extra: This supplies the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes via its branches.

fields.Text:
Enlargement of which labeled structure in the image is most likely to cause Ortner syndrome?



{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::atrium::atrium/ventricle}}

To which areas of the body is pain referred in a patient with pericarditis?

{{c1::Neck}}
{{c1::Arms}}
{{c1::Shoulders}}
fields.Back Extra: The left shoulder is often involved.

fields.Text:
The pericardial space is located between which two layers of the pericardium?

{{c1::Parietal}} pericardium
{{c1::Epicardium}}

What are the three layers of the pericardium, from outermost to innermost?

{{c1::Fibrous}} pericardium
↓
{{c1::Parietal}} pericardium
↓
{{c1::Epicardium}}

Which artery supplies the following?

Posterior 1/3 of the interventricular septum
Posterior 2/3 of the ventricular walls
Posteromedial papillary muscle

{{c1::Posterior descending}} artery

What structure is supplied by the right marginal artery?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::ventricle::atrium/ventricle}}

Which coronary artery gives rise to the posterior descending artery in most people?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} coronary artery

In which phase of the cardiac cycle does coronary blood flow to the left ventricle and intraventricular septum peak?

{{c1::Early diastole}}

What three areas of the heart are supplied by the left anterior descending artery?

Anterior surface of the {{c1::left::left/right}} {{c1::ventricle::atrium/ventricle}}
Anterolateral {{c1::papillary}} muscle
Anterior 2/3 of the {{c1::interventricular septum}}

What is the most posterior chamber of the heart?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::atrium::atruim/ventricle}}

Which coronary artery gives rise to the posterior descending artery in left dominant circulation?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::circumflex}} artery

Which chamber of the heart is most commonly injured in trauma?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::ventricle::atrium/ventricle}}

Which nerve innervates the pericardium?

{{c1::Phrenic}} nerve

Which coronary artery is most commonly occluded?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::anterior descending}} artery

What two symptoms can enlargement of the left atrium cause as a result of compression of related structures?

{{c1::Dysphagia}} from compression of the esophagus
{{c1::Hoarseness}} from compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve

In what two ways does activated protein kinase A act to increase contractility and stroke volume after β1 stimulation?

{{c1::Ca2+ channel phosphorylation}} → Increased Ca2+ entry → Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release
{{c1::Phospholamban phosphorylation}} → Active Ca2+ ATPase → Increased sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ storage

How does the stroke volume change during the first trimester of pregnancy?

It {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}
fields.Back Extra: This is secondary to an increase in preload.

fields.Text:
How does anxiety or exercise affect stroke volume?

Anxiety or exercise {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} contractility, thus {{c1::increasing::increasing/decreasing}} stroke volume

What classes of drugs used to treat heart failure decrease both preload and afterload?

{{c1::ACE}} inhibitors
{{c1::Angiotensin}} receptor blockers

How does hydralazine affect afterload?

It {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} afterload

How does nitroglycerin affect preload?

It {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} preload

In a patient with chronic hypertension, how does the left ventricle compensate for increased afterload?

Left ventricular wall {{c1::hypertrophies::hypertrophies/hypotrophies}} to decrease wall stress

What four cardiac variables affect cardiac oxygen demand?

{{c1::Contractility}}
{{c1::Afterload}}
{{c1::Heart rate}}
{{c1::Diameter}} of the ventricle

How do non-dihydropyridine Ca2+ channel blockers affect contractility and stroke volume?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} contractility
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} stroke volume

How does acidosis affect heart contractility?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} contractility

How do β1-receptor antagonists affect contractility and stroke volume?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} contractility
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} stroke volume
fields.Back Extra: This is because β1-receptor antagonists decrease cAMP.

fields.Text:
How would an increase in intracellular calcium affect the stroke volume and contractility of the heart?

Contractility would {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}}
Stroke volume would {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}}

How does a decrease in extracellular sodium affect stroke volume?

It decreases the activity of the {{c1::Na+}}/{{c1::Ca2+}} exchanger → {{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} contractility and stroke volume

What three variables affect stroke volume?

{{c1::Contractility}}
{{c1::Afterload}}
{{c1::Preload}}

What measurement best approximates preload?

{{c1::Ventricular EDV}}

What two parameters does preload depend on?

{{c1::Venous tone}}
{{c1::Circulating blood volume}}

What measurement best approximates afterload?

{{c1::Mean arterial pressure}}
fields.Back Extra: Increased wall tension → Increased pressure → Increased afterload

fields.Text:
How would a decrease in afterload affect stroke volume?

Stroke volume would {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}}

How does digitalis increase heart contractility?

Digitalis blocks {{c1::Na+}}/{{c1::K+}} pump → Increased intracellular {{c1::Na+}} → Decreased {{c1::Na+}}/{{c1::Ca2+}} exchanger activity → Increased intracellular {{c1::Ca2+}} → Increased contractility

What are the equations used to calculate wall stress and wall tension of a chamber of the heart?

Wall stress = ( {{c1::Pressure}} × {{c1::Radius}} ) ÷ ( {{c1::2}} × {{c1::Wall thickness}} )
Wall tension = {{c1::Pressure}} × {{c1::Radius}}

How does tachycardia lead to decreased cardiac output?

Increased heart rate → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} diastolic filling time → Ventricles are unable to fill completely → {{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in stroke volume → Decrease in cardiac output

How does pulse pressure change with advanced heart failure, aortic stenosis, cardiogenic shock, and cardiac tamponade?

All 4 conditions cause a {{c1::narrow::widened/narrow}} pulse pressure

What two factors maintain cardiac output during exercise?

During the early stages of exercise, both {{c1::stroke volume}} and {{c1::heart rate}} maintain cardiac output
During the late stages of exercise, only {{c1::heart rate}} maintains cardiac output

How does stroke volume relate to end-diastolic volume and end-systolic volume?

Stroke volume = {{c1::End-diastolic volume}} – {{c1::End-systolic volume}}

How is pulse pressure calculated and how is it related to stroke volume and arterial compliance?

Pulse pressure = {{c1::Systolic blood pressure}} - {{c1::Diastolic blood pressure}}
Pulse pressure is {{c1::proportional}} to stroke volume
Pulse pressure is {{c1::inversely proportional}} to arterial compliance

What are three equations used to calculate mean arterial pressure?

Mean arterial pressure = {{c1::Cardiac output}} × {{c1::Total peripheral resistance}}
Mean arterial pressure = 1/3 {{c1::Systolic blood pressure}} + 2/3 {{c1::Diastolic blood pressure}}
Mean arterial pressure = {{c1::Diastolic blood pressure}} + 1/3 {{c1::Pulse pressure}}

How do you calculate cardiac output according to the Fick principle?

Cardiac output = Rate of {{c1::O2}} consumption ÷ ( {{c1::Arterial O2}} content - {{c1::Venous O2}} content )

How are cardiac output, stroke volume, and heart rate related?

Cardiac output = {{c1::Stroke volume}} × {{c1::Heart rate}}

What common effect do anemia, exercise, hyperthyroidism, aortic regurgitation, aortic stiffening, and obstructive sleep apnea have on pulse pressure?

All 6 conditions cause a {{c1::widened::widened/narrow}} pulse pressure

What is cardiac ejection fraction and how would you calculate it?

The ejection fraction is an index of {{c1::ventricular contractility}}
Ejection fraction = {{c1::Stroke volume}} ÷ {{c1::End-diastolic volume}}
Ejection fraction = ( {{c1::End-diastolic volume}} – {{c1::End-systolic volume}} ) ÷ {{c1::End-diastolic volume}}

What are the changes in the ejection fraction in systolic and diastolic heart failure?

The ejection fraction is {{c1::decreased}} in systolic heart failure
The ejection fraction is {{c1::normal}} in diastolic heart failure

How does digoxin affect myocardial contractility?

It {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} contractility

What condition causes right and downward shift of the Starling curve due to loss of functional myocardium?

{{c1::Myocardial infarction}}

The force of cardiac contraction is proportional to what cardiac parameter?

{{c1::End-diastolic length}} of cardiac muscle fiber
fields.Back Extra: This is in relation to the preload.

fields.Text:
How do β-blockers and nondihydropyridine Ca2+ channel blockers affect cardiac contractility?

They {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} contractility

In what direction is the Starling curve shifted during exercise?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}}
fields.Back Extra: This leads to increased stroke volume.

fields.Text:
What will happen to this curve in response to heart failure?



It will shift {{c1::downward::upward/downward}} and {{c1::rightward::leftward/rightward}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because contractility is lost secondary to cardiomyopathy.

fields.Text:
What will happen to this curve in response to exercise?



It will shift {{c1::upward::upward/downward}} and {{c1::leftward::leftward/rightward}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because contractility increases secondary to exercise.

fields.Text:
How do catcholamines, exercise, digoxin, milrinone, and dobutamine affect inotropy?

They {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} inotropy

How does sympathetic activity and fluid infusion affect venous return?

They {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} venous return

How do acute hemorrhage and spinal anesthesia affect venous return?

They {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} venous return

How is total peripheral resistance affected by use of vasopressors?

It {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}

What causes a decrease in total peripheral resistance?

{{c1::Exercise}}
{{c1::Arteriovenous shunt}}

Which type of blood vessels have the lowest flow velocity?

{{c1::Capillaries}}

How does blood viscosity change with anemia?

Blood viscosity {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
fields.Back Extra: This is primarily due to the decrease in hematocrit.

fields.Text:
Which type of blood vessel has the highest storage capacity for blood?

{{c1::Veins}}

What equation relates volumetric flow rate, flow velocity, and cross-sectional area?

Q = {{c1::v}} × {{c1::A}}

Which type of blood vessels account for most of the total peripheral resistance in the body?

{{c1::Arterioles}}

Blood flows in what direction across the pressure gradient?

{{c1::High::High/Low}} pressure → {{c1::Low::High/Low}} pressure

What lab value primarily determines viscosity of blood?

{{c1::Hematocrit}}

What is the equation for the total resistance of blood vessels in parallel?

1 ÷ RT = ( 1 ÷ {{c1::R1}} ) + ( 1 ÷ {{c1::R2}} ) + ( 1 ÷ {{c1::R3}} ) + ...

What is the equation for the total resistance of blood vessels in series?

RT = {{c1::R1}} + {{c1::R2}} + {{c1::R3}} + ...

By what factor does resistance increase in a vessel whose diameter is reduced by half?

{{c1::16}} times
fields.Back Extra: Resistance is inversely proportional to the radius to the 4th power.

fields.Text:
What are two equations for blood vessel resistance?

Resistance = {{c1::ΔP}} ÷ {{c1::Q}}
Resistance = ( {{c1::8}} × {{c1::η}} × {{c1::Length}} ) ÷ ( {{c1::π}} × {{c1::r4}} )

What two disease states can increase the viscosity of blood?

{{c1::Hyperproteinemic::Hyperproteinemic/Hypoproteinemic}} states
{{c1::Polycythemia}}

Which type of blood vessels have the highest total cross-sectional area?

{{c1::Capillaries}}

Which of the dotted curves represents the change expected with spinal anesthesia or acute hemorrhage?



Curve {{c1::4}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to a decrease in venous tone and volume.

fields.Text:
A patient has an arteriovenous fistula surgically created for hemodialysis. Which curve shift on the image best represents the changes expected with total peripheral resistance?



Curve {{c1::6}}
fields.Back Extra: This represents a decrease in total peripheral resistance.

fields.Text:
What does a shift in the blue line from curve 4 to curve 3 in the image represent?



Increase in {{c1::volume}}
Increase in {{c1::venous tone}}
fields.Back Extra: This leads to an increase in right atrial pressure, which increases systolic volume and cardiac output.

fields.Text:
How does treatment with catecholamines, dobutamine, milrinone, or digoxin increase cardiac output?

It increases {{c1::contractility}}, so cardiac output increases for any given right atrial pressure

How is sympathetic activity related to right atrial pressure?

An increase in sympathetic activity {{c1::increases}} right atrial pressure through an {{c1::increase}} in preload

How is cardiac output affected by an overdose of narcotics?

It is {{c1::decreased}}

The findings of heart failure and a reduced ejection fraction correspond to which curve on the graph shown?



The curve {{c1::closer}} to the x-axis and {{c1::farther}} from the y-axis
fields.Back Extra: This represents a decrease in inotropy.

fields.Text:
How does exercise affect cardiac output, and why?

It {{c1::increases}} cardiac output due to an increase in {{c1::heart rate}} and decrease in {{c1::total peripheral resistance}}

How will the cardiac function curve change with opioid administration?



This will result in a change from normal inotropy to {{c1::negative}} inotropy

How is cardiac output maintained in heart failure?

Decrease in inotropy leads to {{c1::fluid retention}} → Increased {{c1::preload}} maintains cardiac output

What does the intersection of the cardiac function curve and vascular function curve represent?



{{c1::Operating point}} of the heart

Which phase of the cardiac cycle does number 5 on the image represent?



{{c1::Reduced filling}}

Which phase of the cardiac cycle does number 4 on the image represent?



{{c1::Rapid filling}}

Which phase of the cardiac cycle does number 3 on the image represent?



{{c1::Isovolumetric relaxation}}

Which phase of the cardiac cycle does number 2 on the image represent?



{{c1::Systolic ejection}}

Which phase of the cardiac cycle does number 1 on the image represent?



{{c1::Isovolumetric contraction}}

During which phase of the cardiac cycle is oxygen consumption the highest?

{{c1::Isovolumetric contraction}}

In which condition is the a wave of the jugular venous pulse absent?

{{c1::Atrial fibrillation}}

On the jugular venous pulse, what does the y descent represent?

{{c1::Right}} atrium {{c1::emptying}} into the {{c1::right}} ventricle

The a and c waves of the jugular venous pulse are associated with which physiologic events?

a wave → {{c1::Atrial contraction}}
c wave → {{c1::Right ventricular contraction}}

In tricuspid regurgitation, which portion of the jugular venous pulse is absent?

{{c1::x descent}}
fields.Back Extra: It is also absent in right heart failure and is caused by reduced pressure gradients in both cases.

fields.Text:
During which phase of the cardiac cycle is ventricular volume the highest?

{{c1::Isovolumetric contraction}} of ventricles

What causes an S4 heart sound ("atrial kick") and in which area is it best heard?

An S4 sound is caused by the left atrium pushing blood against a {{c1::stiff}} left ventricular wall in a patient with ventricular {{c1::noncompliance}}
An S4 sound is best heard at {{c1::apex}} with patient in {{c1::left lateral decubitus}} position

In what populations can an S3 heart sound be a normal finding?

{{c1::Children}}
{{c1::Young adults}}
{{c1::Pregnant}} patients
{{c1::Athletes}}

What causes an S3 heart sound and in which area is it best heard?

An S3 heart sound is caused by {{c1::increased}} filling pressures in {{c1::early}} diastole during rapid ventricular filling phase
An S3 heart sound is best heard at {{c1::apex}} with patient in {{c1::left lateral decubitus}} position

What causes an S2 heart sound and in which area is it best heard?

An S2 heart sound is caused by an {{c1::aortic}} and {{c1::pulmonary}} valve closure
An S2 heart sound is best heard at {{c1::left upper sternal border}}

What causes an S1 heart sound and in which area is it best heard?

An S1 heart sound is caused by {{c1::mitral}} and {{c1::tricuspid}} valve closure
An S1 heart sound is best heard in the {{c1::mitral}} area

What does the v wave represent on a jugular venous pressure curve?

Increased {{c1::right atrial pressure}}
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by increased volume against a closed tricuspid valve.

fields.Text:
During which phase of the cardiac cycle is ventricular volume the lowest?

{{c1::Isovolumetric relaxation}}

What conditions cause a pathologic S3 heart sound?

Conditions leading to increased {{c1::filling pressures}} or {{c1::dilated}} ventricles

On the jugular venous pulse, what does the x descent represent?

{{c1::Downward}} displacement and {{c1::atrial relaxation}} of the closed {{c1::tricuspid}} valve during the rapid ventricular ejection phase

What component of the jugular venous pulse is prominent in constrictive pericarditis but absent in cardiac tamponade?

{{c1::y descent}}

How does increased contractility affect stroke volume, ejection fraction, and end-systolic volume?

{{c1::Increases}} stroke volume
{{c1::Increases}} ejection fraction
{{c1::Decreases}} end-systolic volume

How does increased afterload affect aortic pressure, stroke volume, and end-systolic volume?

{{c1::Increases}} aortic pressure
{{c1::Decreases}} stroke volume
{{c1::Increases}} end-systolic volume

What changes are seen in end-diastolic volume in a patient with mitral regurgitation?

{{c1::Increased}} end-diastolic volume
fields.Back Extra: This is due to increased left atrial volume/pressure from regurgitation, which leads to increased ventricular filling.

fields.Text:
Which valvular pathology causes a significant increase in the pulse pressure?

{{c1::Aortic regurgitation}}

What 2 heart murmurs have no true isovolumetric phases?

{{c1::Aortic regurgitation}}
{{c1::Mitral regurgitation}}

How do the end-diastolic volume and end-diastolic pressure change in aortic stenosis?

End-diastolic volume is {{c1::unchanged}}
End-diastolic pressure is {{c1::increased}}

What is the pathophysiology underlying the end-systolic volume changes seen with mitral regurgitation?

The end-systolic volume decreases due to {{c1::decreased}} resistance and {{c1::increased}} regurgitation into the left atrium during systole

How does ventricular hypertrophy caused by aortic stenosis affect ventricular compliance?

It causes ventricular compliance to {{c1::decrease}}

Which valvular pathology causes a significant increase in left ventricular pressure?

{{c1::Aortic stenosis}}

What is the pathophysiology underlying changes in end-diastolic volume seen with mitral stenosis?

End-diastolic volume {{c1::decreases}}
fields.Back Extra: This is as a result of impaired ventricular filling.

fields.Text:
Identify the valvular pathology that corresponds to the pressure-volume loop shown in red in the image.



{{c1::Aortic stenosis}}

Identify the valvular pathology that corresponds to the pressure-volume loop shown in green in the image.



{{c1::Mitral regurgitation}}

Identify the valvular pathology that corresponds to the pressure-volume loop shown in red in the image.



{{c1::Aortic regurgitation}}

Identify the valvular pathology that corresponds to the pressure-volume loop shown in green in the image.



{{c1::Mitral stenosis}}

What happens to the stroke volume in aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation, aortic regurgitation, and mitral stenosis?

Aortic stenosis → {{c1::Decreases}}
Mitral regurgitation → {{c1::Increases}}
Aortic regurgitation → {{c1::Increases}}
Mitral stenosis → {{c1::Decreases}}

What happens to the end-systolic volume in aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis?

Aortic stenosis → {{c1::Increases}}
Mitral regurgitation → {{c1::Decreases}}
Mitral stenosis → {{c1::Decreases}}

What happens to the end-diastolic volume in aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation, aortic regurgitation, and mitral stenosis?

Aortic stenosis → {{c1::Unchanged}}
Mitral regurgitation → {{c1::Increases}}
Aortic regurgitation → {{c1::Increases}}
Mitral stenosis → {{c1::Decreases}}

Which valvular pathology causes a significant increase in left atrial pressure?

{{c1::Mitral stenosis}}

The graph shown here correlates to which valvular pathology?



{{c1::Aortic stenosis}}

The graph shown here correlates to which valvular pathology?



{{c1::Mitral regurgitation}}

The graph shown here correlates to which valvular pathology?



{{c1::Aortic regurgitation}}

The graph shown here correlates to which valvular pathology?



{{c1::Mitral stenosis}}

What splitting pattern is shown in the image?



{{c1::Physiologic}} splitting

What splitting pattern is shown in the image?



{{c1::Paradoxical}} splitting

What splitting pattern is shown in the image?



{{c1::Wide}} splitting

What type of splitting pattern occurs in an individual with an atrial septal defect?

{{c1::Fixed}} splitting

What type of splitting is seen in conditions that delay right ventricle emptying?

{{c1::Wide}} splitting
fields.Back Extra: The delayed right ventricular emptying causes the delayed pulmonic sound, especially on inspiration.

fields.Text:
Describe the mechanism by which inspiration leads to splitting of S2.

Inspiration → {{c1::Decreased}} intrathoracic pressure → {{c1::Increased}} venous return → {{c1::Increased}} right ventricle filling, stroke volume, and ejection time → Delayed pulmonic valve closure

How does the time between pulmonic and aortic valvular closure change during inspiration in aortic stenosis?

It {{c1::decreases}}
fields.Back Extra: P2 closes later and moves closer to A2, "paradoxically" eliminating the split.

fields.Text:
What is the name of the phenomenon that occurs when P2 precedes A2 in S2?

{{c1::Paradoxical}} splitting

Which valvular stenosis is associated with wide splitting of S2?

{{c1::Pulmonary}} stenosis
fields.Back Extra: This causes delayed right ventricular emptying and therefore a delayed pulmonic sound.

fields.Text:
What is the underlying pathophysiology of fixed splitting of the S2 heart sound in a patient with an atrial septal defect?

{{c1::Left-to-right}} shunt → {{c1::Increased}} volume of right atrial/ventricular volumes → {{c1::Increased}} flow through pulmonic valve → Delayed pulmonic valve closure that is independent of respiration

During which phase of the breathing cycle does physiologic splitting of S2 occur?

{{c1::Inspiration}}

What cardiac pathology can cause paradoxical splitting of S2?

Conditions that delay {{c1::aortic}} valve closure

What splitting pattern is shown in the image?



{{c1::Fixed}} splitting

How is the murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy affected during the following maneuvers?

Valsalva maneuver → {{c1::Increased}}
Squatting and hand grip → {{c1::Decreased}}

How does squatting affect the murmur of mitral valve prolapse?

It {{c1::decreases}} the murmur and {{c1::delays}} the onset of the midsystolic click

How does the Valsalva maneuver affect the murmur of mitral valve prolapse?

{{c1::Increases}} murmur and causes {{c1::earlier}} midsystolic click

An increase in afterload will cause which 3 murmurs to increase in intensity?

{{c1::Mitral regurgitation}}
{{c1::Aortic regurgitation}}
{{c1::Ventricular septal defect}}

What maneuvers decrease the intensity of the murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?

Rapid {{c1::squatting}}
Passive {{c1::leg raising}}
{{c1::Hand grip}}

How is the murmur of most left-sided murmurs affected by the hand-grip maneuver?

It {{c1::increases}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to an increase in systemic vascular resistance and thus afterload.

fields.Text:
Which 4 murmurs are heard during diastole?

{{c1::Aortic regurgitation}}
{{c1::Pulmonic regurgitation}}
{{c1::Mitral stenosis}}
{{c1::Tricuspid stenosis}}

Which anatomical landmarks help to locate the region where the murmur of tricuspid stenosis is best heard?

{{c1::Left sternal border}} at {{c1::4th intercostal space}}

Which anatomical landmarks help to locate the region where the murmur of pulmonic stenosis is best heard?

{{c1::Left sternal border}} at {{c1::2nd intercostal space}}

Which anatomical landmarks help to locate the region where the murmur of aortic stenosis is best heard?

{{c1::Right sternal border}} at {{c1::2nd intercostal space}}

What happens to preload during the Valsalva maneuver?

{{c1::Decreases}}

What physiologic cardiovascular changes occur with squatting?

{{c1::Increased}} preload
{{c1::Increased}} afterload
{{c1::Increased}} left ventricular volume

Which 2 physical maneuvers increase afterload?

{{c1::Hand grip}}
{{c1::Squatting}}

Where is the murmur of aortic regurgitation best heard?

{{c1::Left sternal border}}

Where is the murmur of pulmonic regurgitation best heard?

{{c1::Left sternal border}}

How do right-sided cardiac murmurs change with inspiration?

{{c1::Intensify}} with inspiration

Which systolic murmurs are best heard in the aortic area?

{{c1::Flow murmurs}}
{{c1::Aortic stenosis}}
{{c1::Aortic valve sclerosis}}

Which diastolic and systolic murmurs are best heard at the left sternal border?

Diastolic → {{c1::Aortic regurgitation}} and {{c1::pulmonary regurgitation}}
Systolic → {{c1::Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy}}

Which systolic murmurs are best heard in the pulmonic area?

{{c1::Atrial septal defect}}
{{c1::Pulmonary stenosis}}
{{c1::Flow murmurs}}

Which systolic and diastolic murmurs are best heard in the tricuspid area?

Systolic → {{c1::Ventricular septal defects}} and {{c1::tricuspid regurgitation}}
Diastolic → {{c1::Tricuspid stenosis}}

Which systolic and diastolic murmurs are best heard in the mitral area?

Systolic → {{c1::Mitral valve prolapse}} and {{c1::mitral regurgitation}}
Diastolic → {{c1::Mitral stenosis}}

How does inspiration increase the intensity of right-sided heart sounds?

Via increased {{c1::venous return}} to the {{c1::right atrium}}

Most murmurs increase in intensity with passive leg raise and squatting. Which 2 murmurs decrease in intensity with these maneuvers?

{{c1::Mitral valve prolapse}}
{{c1::Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy}}

Most murmurs decrease in intensity with the strain phase of the Valsalva maneuver. Which 2 murmurs increase in intensity with this maneuver?

{{c1::Mitral valve prolapse}}
{{c1::Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy}}

Why does hand gripping cause a decrease in the intensity of an aortic stenosis murmur?

It causes a decrease in the {{c1::transaortic valve pressure gradient}}

What are 2 causes of a patent ductus arteriosus in a newborn?

{{c1::Prematurity}}
Congenital {{c1::rubella}}

What physical exam findings are associated with aortic regurgitation?

{{c1::Hyperdynamic}} pulse
Long {{c1::diastolic}} murmur
{{c1::Head bobbing}} when it is chronic or severe

What connective tissue diseases can be associated with mitral valve prolapse?

{{c1::Ehlers-Danlos}} syndrome
{{c1::Marfan}} syndrome

In a newborn, what cardiac abnormality is the likely cause of a harsh holosystolic murmur that is loudest at the left sternal border of the 5th intercostal space?

{{c1::Ventricular septal defect}}
fields.Back Extra: This is loudest in the tricuspid area.

fields.Text:
What is the relationship between left atrial pressure and left ventricular pressure during diastole in a patient with mitral stenosis?

In mitral stenosis, left atrial pressure greatly {{c1::exceeds}} left ventricular pressure during diastole

In mitral stenosis, how does the interval between S2 and the opening snap sound correlate with severity?

{{c1::Decreased}} interval correlates with increased severity of mitral stenosis

What valvular abnormalities can be sequelae of rheumatic fever?

{{c1::Mitral stenosis}}
{{c1::Aortic regurgitation}}
{{c1::Mitral valve prolapse}}
{{c1::Mitral regurgitation}}
{{c1::Tricuspid regurgitation}}

What are 4 pathologic processes that can cause aortic regurgitation?

{{c1::Bicuspid aortic valve}}
{{c1::Endocarditis}}
{{c1::Aortic root dilation}}
{{c1::Rheumatic fever}}

What is the most common valvular lesion that can be associated with myxomatous degeneration?

{{c1::Mitral valve prolapse}}

What symptoms are commonly associated with aortic stenosis?

{{c1::Syncope}}
{{c1::Angina}}
{{c1::Dyspnea}} on exertion

Which cardiac murmur is characteristically associated with "pulsus parvus et tardus"?

{{c1::Aortic stenosis}}
fields.Back Extra: It is associated with a weak pulse that occurs late after S1.

fields.Text:
How is the pressure different in the left ventricle of a patient with aortic stenosis versus a healthy patient?

The left ventricular pressure is {{c1::increased}} compared with that of a healthy patient

What is the murmur associated with holosystolic blowing that is loudest at the left sternal border of the 4th intercostal space?

{{c1::Tricuspid regurgitation}}

Which 2 heart murmurs are described as holosystolic, high-pitched, and blowing?

{{c1::Mitral regurgitation}}
{{c1::Tricuspid regurgitation}}

Where is the continuous machine-like murmur of a patent ductus arteriosus heard best on a neonate?

{{c1::Left infraclavicular}} area

How can mitral stenosis cause dysphagia?

Dysphagia can be caused by esophageal {{c1::compression}} from left atrial {{c1::dilation}} caused by mitral stenosis

Which heart murmur is associated with hoarseness?

{{c1::Mitral stenosis}}
fields.Back Extra: Left atrial dilatation leads to hoarseness due to compression of the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

fields.Text:
What murmur is associated with the sound pattern shown in the image?



{{c1::Aortic regurgitation}}

What heart murmur is associated with a mid-late diastolic rumble following an opening snap?



{{c1::Mitral stenosis}}

What murmur is associated with the sound pattern shown in the image?



{{c1::Mitral valve prolapse}}

What murmur is associated with the sound pattern shown in the image?



{{c1::Patent ductus arteriosus}}

What murmur is associated with the crescendo-decrescendo pattern shown in the image?



{{c1::Aortic stenosis}}

Describe the anatomic mechanism that results in the classic murmur of mitral valve prolapse.

There is sudden {{c1::tensing}} of the {{c1::chordae tendinae}} while mitral leaflets prolapse into the left atrium

How does the size of a ventricular septal defect alter the sound of its murmur?

Small ventricular septal defects have {{c1::higher}} intensity murmurs than larger ones, which are {{c1::quieter}}

What are 3 pathophysiologic sequelae of chronic mitral stenosis?

{{c1::Pulmonary congestion}}
{{c1::Pulmonary hypertension}}
{{c1::Left atrial dilation}}

What 2 disorders may develop in a patient with chronic mitral stenosis?

{{c1::Atrial fibrillation}}
{{c1::Ortner}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: Both are mostly secondary to pulmonary hypertension.

fields.Text:
Which populations are most at risk for the development of aortic stenosis?

Patients older than {{c1::65}} years because of age-related {{c1::calcification}}
Younger patients who have early-onset {{c1::calcification}} of the {{c1::bicuspid aortic}} valve

During which phase of the cardiac myocyte action potential does extracellular calcium enter the cell?

Phase {{c1::2}}

At each phase of the myocardial action potential, list the ions that enter and exit cells through the cellular membranes.

Phase 0 → {{c1::Na+}} in
Phase 1 → {{c1::Na+}} in and {{c1::K+}} out
Phase 2 → {{c1::Ca2+}} in and {{c1::K+}} out
Phase 3 → {{c1::Ca2+}} in and {{c1::K+}} out
Phase 4 → {{c1::K+}} out

How is the resting potential of a ventricular myocyte maintained?

The resting potential is maintained by high {{c1::K+}} permeability through {{c1::K+}} channels

What cellular adaptation allows cardiac myocytes to be electrically coupled?

{{c1::Gap junctions}}

What 3 key features distinguish cardiac muscle action potentials from skeletal muscle action potentials?

{{c1::Ca2+/K+}}-mediated plateau
{{c1::Ca2+}}-induced Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
{{c1::Gap junctions}} for coupling

What occurs during phase 3 of the myocardial action potential?

Opening of {{c1::K+}} channels
Closing of {{c1::Ca2+}} channels

Which cardiac cells demonstrate a myocardial action potential?

All cardiac {{c1::myocytes}}, except for cells in the {{c1::SA node}} and {{c1::AV node}}

What happens during phase 4 of the myocardial action potential?

This is the phase of resting potential at {{c1::-85}} mV, with high {{c1::K+}} permeability through {{c1::K+}} channels

What phases make up the effective refractory period during the myocardial action potential, and what is the typical duration of this period?

Phase {{c1::0}}
Phase {{c1::3}}

What happens during phase 0 of the myocardial action potential?

Rapid {{c1::upstroke}}
{{c1::Depolarization}}
{{c1::Voltage}}-gated {{c1::Na+}} channels open

What happens during phase 1 of the myocardial action potential?

Inactivation of {{c1::voltage}}-gated {{c1::Na+}} channels
{{c1::Voltage}}-gated {{c1::K+}} channels begin to open

What happens during phase 2 of the myocardial action potential?

{{c1::Ca2+}} influx through {{c1::voltage}}-gated {{c1::Ca2+}} channels

What happens during phase 3 of the myocardial action potential?

Rapid {{c1::repolarization}}
Massive {{c1::K+}} efflux caused by opening of {{c1::voltage}}-gated slow {{c1::K+}} channels
Closure of {{c1::voltage}}-gated {{c1::Ca2+}} channels

The influx of which ion is required for cardiac muscle contractions?

Influx of {{c1::Ca2+}} from the extracellular fluid
fields.Back Extra: This will induce release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

fields.Text:
What neurotransmitters increase and decrease heart rate?

{{c1::Catecholamines}} increase heart rate
{{c1::Acetylcholine}} and {{c1::adenosine}} decrease heart rate

How does sympathetic stimulation affect the If channels?

It {{c1::increases}} the likelihood that If channels will be open
fields.Back Extra: This causes the pacemaker cell to depolarize more frequently and leads to an increased heart rate.

fields.Text:
How does phase 4 of the cardiac action potential create automaticity of the pacemaker nodes?

The If channels conduct {{c1::Na+}} and {{c1::K+}}, which causes spontaneous {{c1::depolarization}}

The slope of which phase in the sinoatrial node determines the heart rate?

Phase {{c1::4}}

During which phase of the pacemaker action potential are K+ channels activated?

Phase {{c1::3}}

Compared with the myocardial action potential, which phases are absent from the pacemaker action potential?

Phase {{c1::1}}
Phase {{c1::2}}

What effect does the resting potential of the pacemaker cell have on the speed of conduction?

The less negative resting potential leads to permanent {{c1::inactivation}} of the fast {{c1::voltage}}-gated {{c1::Na+}} channels
fields.Back Extra: This results in a slow conduction velocity through the AV node.

fields.Text:
In which locations do cardiac myocytes have pacemaker action potentials?

{{c1::SA node}}
{{c1::AV node}}

What channels are open during the upstroke of cardiac pacemaker action potential?

{{c1::Voltage}}-gated {{c1::Ca2+}} channels

An ECG tracing is shown in the image. What does the PR interval represent?



Time from the beginning of {{c1::atrial depolarization}} to the beginning of {{c1::ventricular depolarization}}

An ECG tracing is shown in the image. What pathology does the presence of the U wave indicate?



{{c1::Hypokalemia}}
{{c1::Bradycardia}}

An ECG tracing is shown in the image. What does the ST segment indicate?



That the ventricles are {{c1::depolarized}}

An ECG tracing is shown in the image. What does the J point represent?



{{c1::Junction}} between the end of QRS complex and start of the ST segment

An ECG tracing is shown in the image. What does the T wave represent?



{{c1::Ventricular repolarization}}

An ECG tracing is shown in the image. What does the Q-T interval represent?



Ventricular {{c1::depolarization}} → Mechanical {{c1::contraction}} of the ventricles → Ventricular {{c1::repolarization}}

An ECG tracing is shown in the image. What does the QRS complex represent?



{{c1::Ventricular depolarization}}

An ECG tracing is shown in the image. What does the P wave represent?



{{c1::Atrial depolarization}}

Which pacemaker would take over if the SA node stopped functioning?

The {{c1::AV node}}

Enlarged P waves on an electrocardiogram may indicate pathology in which part of the heart?

The {{c1::atrium}}

Which segment of an electrocardiogram do you expect to change with a drug that slows AV nodal conduction?

The {{c1::PR interval}}
fields.Back Extra: This represents the time from start of atrial depolarization to start of ventricular depolarization.

fields.Text:
What may inverted T waves represent in a patient who had chest pain recently?

{{c1::Cardiac ischemia}}
Recent {{c1::myocardial infarction}}

How long are the normal PR interval and QRS complex?

PR interval → {{c1::120}} to {{c1::200}} milliseconds
QRS complex → < {{c1::100}} milliseconds

Outline the conduction pathway starting from the SA node and ending with the ventricles.

SA node → {{c1::Atria}} → {{c1::AV node}} → {{c1::Bundle of His}} → Right and left {{c1::bundle branches}} → Left anterior and posterior {{c1::fascicles}} → {{c1::Purkinje fibers}} → Ventricles

Arrange the AV node, atria, bundle of His, Purkinje fibers, and ventricles in order from fastest to slowest conduction.

{{c1::Bundle of His}} = {{c1::Purkinje fibers}} > {{c1::Atria}} > {{c1::Ventricles}} > {{c1::AV node}}

Rank the bundle of His, Purkinje fibers, ventricles, SA node, and AV node in order from fastest to slowest heart rate.

{{c1::SA node}} > {{c1::AV node}} > {{c1::Bundle of His}} = {{c1::Purkinje fibers}} = {{c1::Ventricles}}

What is the purpose of the atrioventricular delay in the context of cardiac blood flow?

The delay allows time for the {{c1::ventricles}} to {{c1::fill}} with blood

In the heart, what is the role of the Bachmann bundle in the conduction system?

It conducts electrical impulses from the {{c1::SA node}} to the {{c1::left atrium}}

What is the effect of atrial natriuretic peptide on the renal collecting tubule?

Promotes {{c1::vasodilation}}
Decreases the reabsorption of {{c1::Na+}} at the renal collecting tubule

How is the "aldosterone escape" mechanism mediated by atrial natriuretic peptide?

Activation of atrial natriuretic peptide → {{c1::cGMP}}-mediated {{c1::dilation}} of the afferent arteriole and {{c1::constriction}} of the efferent arteriole → Promotes diuresis and counteracts the effects of aldosterone

What stimulates release of atrial natriuretic peptide?

Increased {{c1::blood volume}}
Increased {{c1::atrial pressure}}

What cells release atrial natriuretic peptide?

{{c1::Atrial myocytes}}

What drug used in the treatment of heart failure is a recombinant form of BNP?

{{c1::Nesiritide}}

What statistical relevance does the level of BNP have in the diagnosis of heart failure?

BNP has a {{c1::good negative}} predictive value
fields.Back Extra: So a patient with a normal BNP likely does not have heart failure.

fields.Text:
What stimulates release of BNP?

Increased {{c1::ventricular tension}}

Which cells release BNP?

{{c1::Ventricular myocytes}}

What three major blood parameters do peripheral chemoreceptors respond to?

{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in PO2
{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in PCO2
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in blood pH

What is the mechanism that leads to the physiologic response of patients to hypotension?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} arterial pressure and stretch → Decreased baroreceptor firing → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} sympathetic tone and {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} parasympathetic tone → Increased heart rate, blood pressure, and contractility

How does a carotid massage reduce heart rate?

Increased pressure on carotid sinus → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} arterial stretch and baroreceptor firing → {{c1::Longer::Longer/Shorter}} AV node refractory period → Decreased heart rate and cardiac output

Which type of receptor is most important in responding to hypotension?

{{c1::Baroreceptors}}

What is the mechanism of action behind bradycardia and hypertension seen in Cushing reflex?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} intracranial pressure constricts arterioles → Cerebral ischemia → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} pCO2 and {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} pH → Central reflex sympathetic {{c1::increase::increased/decreased}} in perfusion pressure → Increased stretch → Peripheral reflex bradycardia

What are the three components of the Cushing reflex?

{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Bradycardia::Tachycardia/Bradycardia}}
Respiratory {{c1::depression}}

What two main parameters do central chemoreceptors respond to?

{{c1::pH}}
{{c1::PCO2}}
fields.Back Extra: These are influenced by arterial CO2.

fields.Text:
How is blood pressure related to the transmission of signals from carotid sinus receptors to the brain?

Baroreceptor afferents near dilated regions at the carotid bifurcation travel via the {{c1::glossopharyngeal}} nerve to the {{c1::solitary nucleus}} of the medulla

How is blood pressure related to the transmission of impulses from the aortic arch receptors to the brain?

Aortic arch baroreceptor afferents travel via the {{c1::vagus}} nerve to the {{c1::solitary nucleus}} of the medulla

How would mitral stenosis affect pulmonary capillary wedge pressure as compared with left ventricular end-diastolic pressure?

Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure would be {{c1::greater::greater/less}} than left ventricular end-diastolic pressure

What is the normal pressure for the aorta during systole and diastole?

Systole → {{c1::120}} mmHg
Diastole → {{c1::80}} mmHg

What is the normal pressure for the pulmonary artery during systole and diastole?

Systole → {{c1::25}} mmHg
Diastole → {{c1::8}} mmHg

What is the normal pressure for the left ventricle during systole and diastole?

Systole → {{c1::120}} mmHg
Diastole → < {{c1::12}} mmHg

What is the normal pressure for the right ventricle during systole and diastole?

Systole → {{c1::25}} mmHg
Diastole → < {{c1::5}} mmHg

What measure, obtained with a Swan-Ganz catheter, estimates left atrial pressure?

{{c1::Pulmonary capillary wedge}} pressure

What are the normal pressures for the right and left atria?

Right atrium → < {{c1::5}} mmHg
Left atrium → < {{c1::12}} mmHg

How does hypoxia affect pulmonary vessels, and how may it benefit a patient with chronic hypoxia?

Hypoxia causes {{c1::vasoconstriction::vasoconstriction/vasodilation}} → Allows for only well-{{c1::ventilated}} areas to remain perfused → Optimizes gas exchange

What is the definition of autoregulation?

Maintaining {{c1::constant}} blood flow to an organ over a {{c1::wide::wide/narrow}} range of perfusion pressures

What factor primarily governs the autoregulation of the vasculature of the skin?

{{c1::Sympathetic::Sympathetic/Parasympathetic}} {{c1::vasoconstriction::vasoconstriction/vasodilation}} controls temperature of the skin

What primarily governs the autoregulation of perfusion in skeletal muscles at rest?

Arterial {{c1::sympathetic::sympathetic/parasympathetic}} tone

What two factors primarily govern the autoregulation of perfusion of the kidneys?

{{c1::Myogenic}} feedback
{{c1::Tubuloglomerular}} feedback

Which local metabolite autoregulates perfusion of the brain by vasodilation?

{{c1::CO2}}

Which three local metabolites autoregulate the perfusion of the heart?

{{c1::CO2}}
{{c1::NO}}
Decreased {{c1::O2}}

In which organ does hypoxia cause vasoconstriction?

{{c1::Lungs}}

Which five metabolites primarily govern the autoregulation of skeletal muscle perfusion during exercise?

{{c1::CO2}}
{{c1::H+}}
{{c1::Adenosine}}
{{c1::Lactate}}
{{c1::K+}}

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism leading to edema in lymphatic obstruction?

Lymphatic obstruction causes {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} interstitial colloid osmotic pressure → Causes fluid to move from the {{c1::capillaries}} into the {{c1::interstitium}}

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism by which toxins, infections, and burns can cause edema?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} capillary permeability causes an increase in {{c1::Kf}} → Leakage into the interstitium

How do nephrotic syndromes affect Starling forces leading to edema?

Loss of plasma proteins {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} plasma colloid oncotic pressure → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} pull of fluids into the capillaries → Edema

How does cirrhosis affect Starling forces leading to the development of peripheral edema and ascites?

Cirrhosis {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} plasma protein content → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} plasma oncotic pressure → Fluid moves from the capillaries into the interstitium

How does heart failure affect Starling forces resulting in peripheral edema?

Heart failure {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} capillary pressure → Drives fluid out of capillaries and into the interstitium

Which two Starling forces, when increased, have a tendency to cause fluid to move from tissues into capillaries?

{{c1::Interstitial hydrostatic}} pressure
{{c1::Plasma colloid osmotic}} pressure

What two Starling forces, when increased, would promote fluid to move from capillaries into tissues?

{{c1::Capillary hydrostatic}} pressure
{{c1::Interstitial fluid colloid osmotic}} pressure

What is the equation to calculate net fluid flow?

Jv = {{c1::Kf}} × [ ( {{c1::Pc}} − {{c1::Pi}} ) − {{c1::σ}} ( {{c1::πc}} − {{c1::πi}} ) ]
fields.Back Extra:
Pc → Capillary pressure
Pi → Interstitial fluid pressure
πc → Plasma colloid osmotic pressure
πi → Interstitial colloid osmotic pressure
Kf → Capillary fluid permeability
σ → Reflection coefficient

fields.Text:
A newborn has cyanotic spells. Chest X-ray is shown. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Tetralogy of Fallot}}

Cardiac MRI of a newborn reveals the pathology shown in the image. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Patent ductus arteriosis}}

What is the structural difference between an atrial septal defect and a patent foramen ovale?

Atrial septal defect → The septal tissues are {{c1::missing}}
Patent foramen ovale → The septal tissues are {{c1::present}} but {{c1::unfused}}

At least 1 of 3 other cardiac defects must be present for survival of a baby with D-transposition of the great arteries. List these 3 cardiac defects.

{{c1::Ventricular septal defect}}
{{c1::Patent ductus arteriosus}}
{{c1::Patent foramen ovale}}
fields.Back Extra: One of these shunts is required to allow mixing of blood.

fields.Text:
What drug when taken during pregnancy can cause tricuspid regurgitation and atrialization of the right ventricle in a newborn?

{{c1::Lithium}}
fields.Back Extra: This is often used to treat bipolar disorder and can cause the Ebstein anomaly.

fields.Text:
Timing-wise, what is the pattern of cyanosis seen with left-to-right cardiac shunts?

{{c1::Late}} cyanosis
fields.Back Extra: Cyanosis does not occur until increased pulmonary pressure becomes significant.

fields.Text:
What is the most common cause of cyanotic heart disease in very young children?

{{c1::Tetralogy of Fallot}}

What is the most common atrial septal defect?

An {{c1::ostium secundum}} defect
fields.Back Extra: An ostium primum defects is rarer but is usually accompanied by other cardiac anomalies.

fields.Text:
What is the common finding on chest X-ray for infants with D-transposition of great arteries?

"{{c1::Egg on a string}}" appearance due to failure of the {{c1::aorticopulmonary septum}} to spiral
fields.Back Extra: Death occurs within the first few months of life if the condition remains uncorrected.

fields.Text:
Name the 4 congenital heart defects that comprise tetralogy of Fallot.

{{c1::Pulmonary infundibular stenosis}}
{{c1::Right ventricular hypertrophy}}
{{c1::Overriding aorta}}
{{c1::Ventricular septal defect}}

What drug is necessary for an infant with transposition of the great vessels and a continuous machine-like murmur detected on examination?

{{c1::Prostaglandin E}}
fields.Back Extra: This is used to maintain a patent ductus arteriosus until transposition is corrected.

fields.Text:
How does squatting relieve cyanosis in a patient with tetralogy of Fallot?

Increased {{c1::systemic vascular resistance}} decreases {{c1::right-to-left}} shunting

What 2 factors contribute to patency of the ductus arteriosus?

{{c1::Prostaglandin E}} synthesis
Low {{c1::oxygen}} tension

In patients with tetralogy of Fallot, how does a "tet spell" occur?

Exacerbation of {{c1::pulmonary stenosis}} causes blood to shunt through the {{c1::ventricular septal defect}}, resulting in {{c1::right ventricular hypertrophy}}

Name a congenital heart disease and a genetic disease associated with coarctation of the aorta.

Congenital heart disease → {{c1::Bicuspid aortic valve}}
Genetic disease → {{c1::Turner}} syndrome

What is the most important determinant of prognosis for a patient with tetralogy of Fallot?

{{c1::Pulmonary infundibular stenosis}}

What chest X-ray finding is associated with coarctation of the aorta?

{{c1::Notched ribs}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to collateral circulation enlarging the intercostal arteries and eroding the ribs.

fields.Text:
What congenital heart disease causes hypertension in the upper extremities and weak pulses in the lower extremities?

{{c1::Coarctation of the aorta}}

Tetralogy of Fallot is caused by the displacement of which structure during embryogenesis?

{{c1::Infundibular septum}}
fields.Back Extra: It is displaced anteriorly and superiorly.

fields.Text:
Describe total anomalous pulmonary venous return.

Pulmonary veins drain into {{c1::right}} heart circulation instead of {{c1::left}} heart circulation

How can an uncorrected left-to-right shunt lead to Eisenmenger syndrome?

Pathologic vasculature changes lead to {{c1::pulmonary hypertension}} and resultant {{c1::right ventricular hypertrophy}}, causing a new-onset right-to-left shunt

What 2 other heart anomalies must exist for a newborn with tricuspid atresia to survive?

{{c1::Atrial septal defect}}
{{c1::Ventricular septal defect}}

What congenital heart defect presents with a wide, fixed split S2 on cardiac exam?

{{c1::Atrial septal defect}}

What are the 3 congenital heart diseases that result in a left-to-right cardiac shunt?

{{c1::Ventricular septal defect}}
{{c1::Atrial septal defect}}
{{c1::Patent ductus arteriosus}}

What are the 5 congenital heart diseases that result in a right-to-left cardiac shunt?

{{c1::Truncus arteriosus}}
{{c1::D-transposition of great arteries}}
{{c1::Tricuspid atresia}}
{{c1::Tetralogy of Fallot}}
{{c1::Total anomalous pulmonary venous return}}

Which congenital heart disease results when formation of the aorticopulmonary septum fails to occur?

{{c1::Persistent truncus arteriosus}}

What 3 pathologic findings are associated with the Ebstein anomaly?

{{c1::Tricuspid regurgitation}}
{{c1::Accessory conduction pathways}}
{{c1::Right}}-sided heart failure

A child has the findings shown in the image. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Ventricular septal defect}}

A patient presents with the findings shown in the image. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Coarctation of the aorta}}

Describe the progression of the majority of small ventricular septal defects in children.

Most are {{c1::asymptomatic}} at birth and may manifest {{c1::weeks}} later or remain {{c1::asymptomatic}}
The majority will eventually {{c1::self-resolve}}

What distinct difference in O2 saturation exists in atrial septal defects and not in ventricular septal defects?

{{c1::Atrial}} septal defects increase O2 saturation in the right atrium, right ventricle, and pulmonary artery
{{c1::Ventricular}} septal defects increase O2 saturation in the right ventricle and pulmonary artery

What heart defect is associated with Down syndrome?

{{c1::Atrial septal defect}}
fields.Back Extra: This can cause paradoxical emboli to bypass the lungs and enter the systemic circulation.

fields.Text:
What congenital abnormality associated with tetralogy of Fallot is characterized by frequent infections, developmental delay, and cleft palate?

{{c1::DiGeorge}} syndrome

Why is total anomalous pulmonary venous return associated with atrial septal defect and patent ductus arteriosus?

They result in {{c1::right-to-left}} shunting
fields.Back Extra: This allows the heart to maintain cardiac output.

fields.Text:
What complications may arise in patients who have a large ventricular septal defect?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} ventricular {{c1::overload}}
{{c1::Heart failure}}

What are 4 potential complications of coarctation of the aorta?

{{c1::Heart failure}}
Increased risk of {{c1::cerebral hemorrhage}}
Aortic {{c1::rupture}}
Possible {{c1::endocarditis}}

What congenital cardiac defect is associated with Williams syndrome?

{{c1::Supravalvular aortic stenosis}}

Prenatal lithium exposure can result in what cardiac defect?

{{c1::Ebstein anomaly}}

What 4 congenital cardiac defects are associated with fetal alcohol syndrome?

{{c1::Ventricular septal defect}}
{{c1::Atrial septal defect}}
{{c1::Patent ductus arteriosus}}
{{c1::Tetralogy of Fallot}}

What 2 congenital cardiac defects are associated with maternal diabetes during pregnancy?

{{c1::Transposition of great vessels}}
{{c1::Ventricular septal defect}}

What 3 congenital cardiac defects are associated with Marfan syndrome?

{{c1::Mitral valve prolapse}}
{{c1::Aortic regurgitation}}
Thoracic aortic {{c1::aneurysm}} and {{c1::dissection}}

What 3 congenital cardiac defects are associated with congenital rubella?

{{c1::Septal}} defects
{{c1::Patent ductus arteriosus}}
{{c1::Pulmonary artery stenosis}}

What 3 congenital cardiac defects are associated with Down syndrome?

{{c1::Atrial}} defect
{{c1::Ventricular}} defect
{{c1::Atrioventricular}} septal defect
