What 2 congenital cardiac defects are associated with 22q11 syndromes?

{{c1::Tetralogy of Fallot}}
{{c1::Truncus arteriosus}}

What 2 congenital cardiac defects are associated with Turner syndrome?

{{c1::Coarctation of aorta}}
{{c1::Bicuspid aortic valve}}

A renal angiogram obtained from a 30-year-old woman with hypertension is shown. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Fibromuscular dysplasia}}
fields.Back Extra:
Note the "string of beads" appearance of the renal artery.

This causes hypertension and is usually found in women of child-bearing age.

fields.Text:
What 3 fundoscopic findings might be seen in a patient with hypertensive emergency?

{{c1::Papilledema}}
Retinal {{c1::hemorrhages}}
Retinal {{c1::exudates}}

What is the difference between hypertensive urgency and hypertensive emergency?

Hypertensive urgency → Severe hypertension {{c1::without}} evidence of acute end-organ damage
Hypertensive emergency → Severe hypertension {{c1::with}} evidence of acute end-organ damage

What are 3 noncardiac conditions to which individuals with hypertension are predisposed?

{{c1::Chronic kidney}} disease
{{c1::Retinopathy}}
{{c1::Stroke}}

What are 5 possible cardiac sequelae of uncontrolled hypertension?

{{c1::Coronary artery}} disease
{{c1::Left ventricular hypertrophy}}
{{c1::Heart failure}}
Aortic {{c1::dissection}}/{{c1::aneurysm}}
{{c1::Atrial fibrillation}}

What are the 2 mechanisms underlying essential hypertension?

Increased {{c1::cardiac output}}
Increased {{c1::total peripheral resistance}}

What are 6 modifiable and 3 nonmodifiable risk factors for hypertension?

Modifiable → {{c1::Physical}} inactivity
Modifiable → {{c1::Cigarette smoking}}
Modifiable → {{c1::Obesity}}
Modifiable → {{c1::Diabetes}}
Modifiable → Excess {{c1::salt}} intake
Modifiable → Excess {{c1::alcohol}} intake
Nonmodifiable → Increased {{c1::age}}
Nonmodifiable → {{c1::Family history}}
Nonmodifiable → {{c1::Race}}

What are the major causes of secondary hypertension?

{{c1::Renal}}/{{c1::renovascular}} diseases
{{c1::Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis}}
{{c1::Primary hyperaldosteronism}}

What is the definition of hypertension in an adult?

Persistent blood pressure of at least {{c1::130}} mmHg systolic and/or at least {{c1::80}} mmHg diastolic

What histologic findings are associated with the lesions shown in the image?



{{c1::Lipid-laden histiocytes}}

What is the name of this lesion associated with hyperlipidemia?



{{c1::Arcus senilis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a corneal lipid deposit that is common in the elderly or younger patients with hypercholesterolemia.

fields.Text:
A patient with a high cholesterol level has this finding on his hands. Name these lesions.



{{c1::Tendinous xanthomas}}

Name the lesions in the image that are associated with elevated cholesterol.



{{c1::Xanthelasma}}

A 55-year-old man with hyperlipidemia notices a painless nodule on his Achilles tendon. What is this finding called?

{{c1::Tendinous xanthoma}}

A patient with poorly controlled diabetes has a biopsy performed. The image shows tissue obtained from the small arteries. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Hyaline arteriosclerosis}}

Describe the histologic finding shown, which is associated with uncontrolled severe hypertension.



"{{c1::Onion skinning}}" of vessel walls
Proliferation of {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells

What finding is shown in this X-ray obtained from a patient with hypertension?



"{{c1::Pipestem}}" appearance due to calcification of the {{c1::internal elastic lamina}} and {{c1::media}} of arteries, which leads to vascular stiffening without obstruction

Arteries of what size are affected by Mönckeberg sclerosis?

{{c1::Medium}}-sized arteries

What pathologic finding may be seen in the small arteries and arterioles of a patient with diabetes or essential hypertension?

{{c1::Hyaline arteriolosclerosis}}

What is the underlying mechanism of hyaline-type arteriolosclerosis?

{{c1::Plasma protein}} leakage into the {{c1::endothelium}}
fields.Back Extra: This is typically associated with hypertension and diabetes mellitus.

fields.Text:
What are the 2 main types of arteriolosclerosis?

{{c1::Hyperplastic}} arteriolosclerosis
{{c1::Hyaline}} arteriolosclerosis

What is the underlying mechanism of hyperplastic-type arteriolosclerosis?

Proliferation of {{c1::smooth muscle}} cells in response to severe hypertension

What is the mechanism by which atherosclerotic plaques form?

{{c1::Endothelial}} cell dysfunction leads to {{c1::macrophage}}-mediated plaque formation via {{c1::foam}} cell formation
fields.Back Extra: Fatty streaks and smooth muscle proliferation contribute to fibrous plaques.

fields.Text:
What are the 5 vessels most commonly affected by atherosclerosis?

{{c1::Abdominal aorta}} > {{c1::Coronary artery}} > {{c1::Popliteal artery}} > {{c1::Carotid artery}} > {{c1::Circle of Willis}}

What are 4 modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis?

{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}
{{c1::Dyslipidemia}}
{{c1::Hypertension}}
{{c1::Smoking}}

How does menopause affect atherosclerosis?

Risk increases after menopause because {{c1::estrogen}} is protective against atherosclerosis

How does a patient's risk of atherosclerosis change with increases in HDL and LDL?

High {{c1::HDL}} is protective and decreases atherosclerotic risk
High {{c1::LDL}} increases atherosclerotic risk

What are 3 nonmodifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis?

{{c1::Family history}}
{{c1::Age}}
{{c1::Sex}}

What condition is shown in the CT scan?



{{c1::Abdominal aortic aneurysm}}
fields.Back Extra: There is an outer dilated calcified aortic wall.

fields.Text:
Pain in which 2 parts of the body may be a sign of leaking, dissection, or imminent rupture of an aortic aneurysm?

{{c1::Back}}
{{c1::Abdomen}}

What is a congenital condition that increases the risk for development of thoracic aortic aneurysms?

{{c1::Connective tissue}} disease

An elderly man with a long smoking history has abdominal pain and a pulsatile abdominal mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?

{{c1::Abdominal aortic aneurysm}}

What might cause a patient with a thoracic aortic aneurysm to develop a murmur?

{{c1::Aortic root dilatation}}
fields.Back Extra: This may lead to an aortic regurgitation.

fields.Text:
What pathologic process is typically associated with formation of an abdominal aortic aneurysm?

{{c1::Atherosclerotic}} disease

What pathologic process is typically associated with formation of a thoracic aortic aneurysm?

{{c1::Cystic medial degeneration}}

Syphillis increases the risk of development of what vascular disease?

{{c1::Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to tertiary syphilis and may cause a thoracic aortic aneurysm.

fields.Text:
What are 4 risk factors for development of an abdominal aortic aneurysm?

{{c1::Male}} sex
Increased {{c1::age}}
{{c1::Smoking}}
{{c1::Family history}}

Which congenital heart condition increases the risk of development of a thoracic aortic aneurysm?

{{c1::Bicuspid aortic valve}}

What acquired condition is an important risk factor for development of a thoracic aortic aneurysm?

{{c1::Hypertension}}

What part of the aorta is most likely to rupture due to trauma or a deceleration injury?

{{c1::Aortic isthmus}}

What are 2 common causes of traumatic aortic rupture?

{{c1::Deceleration}} injury
{{c1::Trauma}}

A widened mediastinum on a chest X-ray raises concern for what pathology?

Aortic {{c1::rupture}}/{{c1::dissection}}

A patient presents with sudden, tearing chest pain. A CT angiogram of the chest is shown. What is your diagnosis?



{{c1::Aortic dissection}}

What is the treatment for an aortic dissection extending from the ascending aorta to the aortic arch?

{{c1::Surgery}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a Stanford type A aortic dissection.

fields.Text:
What is the treatment for an aortic dissection confined to the descending aorta?

{{c1::β-blockers}}, then {{c1::vasodilators}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a Stanford type B aortic dissection.

fields.Text:
What are 3 conditions associated with aortic dissection?

Inherited {{c1::connective tissue}} disorders
{{c1::Hypertension}}
{{c1::Bicuspid aortic valve}}

What are 3 complications that may result from an aortic dissection?

Aortic {{c1::rupture}}
Organ {{c1::ischemia}}
{{c1::Death}}

What are 2 cardiac complications from a proximal Stanford type A aortic dissection?

{{c1::Cardiac tamponade}}
{{c1::Acute aortic regurgitation}}

What is an aortic dissection?

A {{c1::longitudinal intimal}} tear, which forms a {{c1::false lumen}} within the aorta

What chest X-ray finding do you expect in a patient with aortic dissection?

{{c1::Widened mediastinum}}

What are 3 conditions associated with subclavian steal syndrome?

{{c1::Takayasu arteritis}}
{{c1::Arteriolosclerosis}}
{{c1::Heart surgery}}

Define subclavian steal syndrome.

{{c1::Stenosis}} of subclavian artery near origin of vertebral artery → {{c1::Reversed}} blood flow in {{c1::ipsilateral}} vertebral artery → Reduced {{c1::cerebral perfusion}} on exertion of affected arm

What symptoms would you expect in a patient with subclavian steal syndrome?

Arm {{c1::ischemia}}
{{c1::Pain}}
{{c1::Paresthesia}}
{{c1::Vertebrobasilar insufficiency}}

What developmental abnormality of the lungs results from errors during the embryonic stage?

{{c1::Tracheoesophageal fistula}} formation

At what gestational age does respiration become possible?

{{c1::25}} weeks at the end of the {{c1::canalicular}} stage

By what age are lungs fully developed?

{{c1::8}} years of age

Describe the difference in vascular resistance between the respiratory system in utero and at birth.

In utero, "breathing" occurs by means of aspiration/expulsion of amniotic fluid, {{c1::increasing::increasing/decreasing}} vascular resistance
At birth, replacement of fluid with air {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} vascular resistance

Which gestational weeks does the saccular stage of lung development encompass?

Week {{c1::24}} to {{c1::birth}}

Which gestational weeks does the canalicular stage of lung development encompass?

Week {{c1::16}} to week {{c1::25}}

When do pneumocytes begin developing?

During the {{c1::canalicular}} stage, at week {{c1::20}}

In which gestational week does the alveolar stage of lung development begin?

Week {{c1::36}}

Which gestational weeks does the pseudoglandular stage of lung development encompass?

Week {{c1::5}} to week {{c1::17}}

What happens during the saccular stage of lung development?

Alveolar ducts become {{c1::terminal sacs}}, which are separated by {{c1::primary septae}}

What structural changes occur during the pseudoglandular stage of lung development?

Endodermal tubules become {{c1::terminal}} bronchioles, which are surrounded by a modest {{c1::capillary}} network

What structural changes occur during the alveolar stage of lung development?

Terminal sacs become {{c1::adult alveoli}} due to {{c1::secondary septation}}

What structures are developed during the embryonic stage of lung development?

Bronchial buds → {{c1::Mainstem}} bronchi → {{c1::Lobar}} bronchi → {{c1::Segmental}} bronchi

During which week of embryonic development does lung development start?

Week {{c1::4}}

Name all the stages of lung development, in order.

{{c1::Embryonic}}
{{c1::Pseudoglandular}}
{{c1::Canalicular}}
{{c1::Saccular}}
{{c1::Alveolar}}

What structural changes occur during the canalicular stage of lung development?

Terminal bronchioles become {{c1::respiratory}} bronchioles, which form the {{c1::alveolar ducts}}

During what two stages of lung development is respiration not possible?

{{c1::Embryonic}} stage
{{c1::Pseudoglandular}} stage

What symptoms may be seen with bronchogenic cysts?

They can drain poorly, causing {{c1::compression}} of airways and/or recurrent {{c1::respiratory}} tract infections
fields.Back Extra: Bronchogenic cysts usually produce no symptoms.

fields.Text:
What congenital lung malformation demonstrates discrete, round, sharply defined, fluid-filled densities on a chest X-ray?

{{c1::Bronchogenic cysts}}

Pulmonary hypoplasia is related to which two developmental abnormalities?

{{c1::Bilateral::Unilateral/Bilateral}} renal {{c1::agenesis}}
Congenital {{c1::diaphragmatic hernias}}

What congenital lung malformation may be caused by abnormal budding of the foregut as well as dilation of the terminal bronchi or large bronchi?

{{c1::Bronchogenic cysts}}

What are the three functions of club cells?

They secrete a constituent of {{c1::surfactant}}
Degrade toxins through {{c1::cytochrome P-450}}
Act as {{c1::progenitor}} cells for ciliated and club cells

What cells are histologically described as nonciliated, low-columnar, or cuboidal cells containing secretory granules and found in the bronchioles?

{{c1::Club}} cells

What are two functions of alveolar macrophages?

{{c1::Phagocytose}} foreign materials
Release {{c1::cytokines}} and alveolar {{c1::proteases}}

Describe the mechanism of action of surfactant.

Surfactant reduces alveolar {{c1::surface tension}} → Prevents {{c1::collapse}} of alveoli → {{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} lung recoil → {{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} compliance

What is the main lecithin in surfactant?

{{c1::DPPC}}

Explain how the law of Laplace affects the collapsing pressure.

Alveoli have a(n) {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} tendency to collapse on expiration as radius decreases

What are two important functions of type II pneumocytes?

Secrete {{c1::surfactant}} from lamellar bodies
Serve as {{c1::precursors}} to type I and other type II pneumocytes

What is the function of type I pneumocytes?

{{c1::Gas exchange}}

Which type of alveolar cell is cuboidal and clustered on histology?

{{c1::Type II pneumocytes}}

Which type of alveolar cell appears as a thin squamous cell lining alveoli on histology?

{{c1::Type I pneumocytes}}

In what two settings might hemosiderin-laden macrophages be seen?

Pulmonary {{c1::edema}}
Alveolar {{c1::hemorrhage}}

What exogenous substance can be given to help with lung development and production of surfactant?

{{c1::Glucocorticoids}}

When does surfactant synthesis start and when are mature levels reached?

Surfactant synthesis starts at {{c1::20}} weeks of gestation and does not reach mature levels until {{c1::35}} weeks of gestation

What is the function of lamellar bodies in type II pneumocytes?



They secrete {{c1::surfactant}}

What chest X-ray findings are seen in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?

{{c1::Ground-glass opacities}} in the lung fields

What are three screening tests for fetal lung maturity?

{{c1::Lecithin}}-{{c1::sphingomyelin}} ratio
{{c1::Foam stability index}} test
{{c1::Surfactant}}-{{c1::albumin}} ratio

Why is cesarean delivery a risk factor for neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?

Decreased release of fetal {{c1::glucocorticoids}} → Decreased {{c1::surfactant}} production

How does maternal diabetes lead to increased risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?

Increased level of fetal {{c1::insulin}} → Decreased {{c1::surfactant}}

What three complications may develop as a result of use of supplemental oxygen to treat neonatal respiratory distress?

{{c1::Retinopathy}} of prematurity
Intraventricular {{c1::hemorrhage}}
Bronchopulmonary {{c1::dysplasia}}

What are three major risk factors for neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?

{{c1::Prematurity}}
Maternal {{c1::diabetes}}
{{c1::C-section}} delivery

What vascular pathology is associated with persistently low oxygen tension due to neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?

{{c1::Patent ductus arteriosus}}

What is the pathophysiology of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?

Surfactant deficiency leads to an increase in {{c1::surface tension}} → {{c1::Collapse}} of alveoli

How is neonatal respiratory distress syndrome treated?



Administration of {{c1::glucocorticoids}} to the pregnant patient before delivery
Administration of exogenous {{c1::surfactant}} to the infant

In measuring lung maturity prenatally, what lecithin-sphingomyelin values are expected in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?

A lecithin-sphingomyelin ratio in amniotic fluid of < {{c1::1.5}}
fields.Back Extra: A lecithin-sphingomyelin ratio in amniotic fluid of ≥ 2 is healthy.

fields.Text:
What is the main clinical indication for second-generation H1 blockers?

{{c1::Allergies}}

Why are second-generation antihistamines far less sedating than first-generation antihistamines?

Second-generation antihistamines have decreased {{c1::central nervous system}} penetration

Is the action of H1 blockers reversible?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}

What are the four most commonly used first-generation H1 blockers?

{{c1::Diphenhydramine}}
{{c1::Dimenhydrinate}}
{{c1::Chlorpheniramine}}
{{c1::Doxylamine}}

What are the four most commony used second-generation H1 blockers?

{{c1::Loratadine}}
{{c1::Fexofenadine}}
{{c1::Cetirizine}}
{{c1::Desloratadine}}

What are the main clinical indications for first-generation H1 blockers?

{{c1::Allergies}}
{{c1::Motion sickness}}
{{c1::Insomnia}}
{{c1::Vomiting}} in pregnancy

What are the most common adverse effects associated with first-generation H1 blockers?

{{c1::Sedation}}
{{c1::Antimuscarinic}} effects
Anti-{{c1::α}}-adrenergic effects

Why would diphenhydramine be a poor choice for allergy relief for a truck driver?

First-generation antihistamines are highly {{c1::sedating}} and would pose a risk for a patient who operates heavy machinery

What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient who takes dextromethorphan while also taking citalopram and presents with hyperthermia, tachycardia, diaphoresis, and tremors?

{{c1::Serotonin}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This is seen when dextromethorphan is combined with other serotonergic agents.

fields.Text:
What drug can be used to treat a dextromethorphan overdose?

{{c1::Naloxone}}

Dextromethorphan is a synthetic analog of what drug?

{{c1::Codeine}}

By what mechanism does dextromethorphan suppress a cough?

It antagonizes {{c1::NMDA glutamate}} receptors

Why does dextromethorphan, a commonly used antitussive, have a mild abuse potential?

Dextromethorphan is a synthetic {{c1::codeine}} analog that produces mild {{c1::opioid}} effects

What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient who had taken phenylephrine for a viral upper respiratory infection for 10 days and now has worsening congestion?

{{c1::Rebound congestion}}
fields.Back Extra: This is observed when α-agonists are used for more than 4 to 6 days.

fields.Text:
What are the main clinical indications for pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine?

Nasal {{c1::congestion}}
{{c1::Hyperemia::Hyperemia/Hypoemia}}
{{c1::Edema}}
Used to open obstructed {{c1::Eustachian tubes}}

What is the mechanism of action of pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine?

As {{c1::α}}-adrenergic agonists, they cause local {{c1::vasoconstriction::vasodilation/vasoconstriction}} in the nasal mucosa

What are the key adverse effects of pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine?

{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Central nervous system}} stimulation (particularly with pseudoephedrine)
{{c1::Rebound congestion}} if taken longer than 4 to 6 days

What over-the-counter nasal medication can lead to presentation with new-onset anxiety?

{{c1::Pseudoephedrine}}
fields.Back Extra: This can cause central nervous system stimulation and anxiety when used in excess.

fields.Text:
What three classes of drugs are commonly used to treat pulmonary hypertension?

{{c1::Endothelin}} receptor antagonists
{{c1::Prostacyclin}} analogs
{{c1::PDE-5}} inhibitors

What are two key prostacyclin analogs used to treat pulmonary hypertension?

{{c1::Epoprostenol}}
{{c1::Iloprost}}

A patient with both pulmonary hypertension and erectile dysfunction might benefit most from which medication?

{{c1::Sildenafil}}
fields.Back Extra: This can be used to treat erectile dysfunction, as well as pulmonary hypertension.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of sildenafil?

Inhibition of {{c1::PDE-5}} → Increased {{c1::cGMP}} → Prolonged {{c1::vasodilation::vasodilation/vasoconstriction}} due to nitric oxide

What lab value must be monitored for patients taking endothelin receptor antagonists?

{{c1::Liver::Organ}} enzyme levels
fields.Back Extra: Endothelin-1 receptor antagonists prescribed for pulmonary hypertension can cause hepatotoxicity.

fields.Text:
What are two common adverse effects of prostacyclin analogs?

{{c1::Flushing}}
{{c1::Jaw}} pain

What is the mechanism of action of bosentan?

Competitive antagonism of {{c1::endothelin-1}} receptors → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} pulmonary vascular resistance
fields.Back Extra: This is used to treat pulmonary hypertension.

fields.Text:
What drug class should be avoided for patients taking PDE-5 inhibitors?

{{c1::Nitroglycerin}} and other {{c1::nitrates}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to the risk of severe hypotension.

fields.Text:
What are the two main mechanisms of action of epoprostenol and iloprost?

Direct {{c1::vasodilation::vasodilation/vasoconstriction}} of pulmonary and systemic arterial beds
Inhibition of platelet {{c1::aggregation}}

In the pathogenesis of asthma, the binding of antigens to IgE on mast cells results in what effect?

The release of mediators such as {{c1::leukotrienes}} and {{c1::histamine}} from mast cells

What are the two main adverse effects of theophylline?

{{c1::Cardiotoxicity}}
{{c1::Neurotoxicity}}
fields.Back Extra: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index.

fields.Text:
About which key adverse effect should patients taking budesonide or fluticasone be counseled?

{{c1::Oral thrush}}

What are the two likely mechanisms of action of theophylline?

Inhibition of {{c1::phosphodiesterase}} → Increased {{c1::cAMP}} levels
{{c1::Bronchodilation::Bronchodilation/Bronchoconstriction}} via {{c1::adenosine}} blockade

What is the mechanism of action of omalizumab?

It is a monoclonal anti-Ig{{c1::E}} antibody that binds unbound Ig{{c1::E}} and blocks {{c1::FcεRI}} binding

What medication is used to treat allergic asthma resistant to inhaled corticosteroids and β2-agonists?

{{c1::Omalizumab}}

Ipratropium and tiotropium belong to what class of asthma drugs?

{{c1::Muscarinic}} antagonists

What class of drugs is considered first-line therapy for control of chronic asthma?

Inhaled {{c1::corticosteroids}}

NF-κB induces the production of what major inflammatory factor critical in the pathophysiology of asthma?

{{c1::TNF-α}}
fields.Back Extra: It is also involved in the production of other inflammatory agents.

fields.Text:
Inhaled corticosteroids, such as fluticasone or budesonide, are useful in treating asthma due to their ability to inactivate what transcription factor?

{{c1::NF-κB}}

What are two inhaled corticosteroids commonly prescribed for the treatment of asthma?

{{c1::Fluticasone}}
{{c1::Budesonide}}

What are two common adverse effects of albuterol, salmeterol, and formoterol?

{{c1::Tremor}}
{{c1::Arrhythmias}}

What are the two long-acting β2-agonists most commonly used in the treatment of asthma?

{{c1::Salmeterol}}
{{c1::Formoterol}}

What is the main indication for albuterol in the treatment of asthma?

{{c1::Relief}} of symptoms during {{c1::acute::acute/chronic}} asthma exacerbations

What two general pathways mediating bronchoconstriction are targeted by drugs used to treat patients with asthma?

{{c1::Parasympathetic::Sympathetic/Parasympathetic}} tone
{{c1::Inflammatory}} processes

What is the mechanism of action of albuterol?

Relaxes bronchial smooth muscle through its short-acting agonism of {{c1::β2}}-adrenergic receptors

What two drug classes help directly reduce the late inflammatory response that causes bronchial hyperreactivity in asthma?

{{c1::Steroids}}
{{c1::Antileukotrienes}}

How can PDE-4 inhibitors like roflumilast decrease exacerbations of bronchoconstrictive diseases?

Increases {{c1::cAMP}} → Bronchodilation and decreases airway inflammation
fields.Back Extra: This is used mostly for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbations.

fields.Text:
What are two common methods that can be used to decrease the risk of oral thrush in patients using inhaled corticosteroids for treatment of asthma?

Use of a {{c1::spacer}}
{{c1::Rinsing}} the mouth after use of the inhaler

What is the mechanism of action of tiotropium and ipratropium in the treatment of asthma?

Blocks {{c1::muscarinic}} receptors competitively → Prevents {{c1::bronchoconstriction::bronchodilation/bronchoconstriction}}

In addition to the treatment of asthma, what is a key indication for the use of tiotropium and ipratropium?

{{c1::Chronic obstructive pulmonary}} disease

What is the main difference between tiotropium and ipratropium?

Tiotropium is {{c1::long}}-acting
Ipratropium is {{c1::short}}-acting

What are three key examples of antileukotriene drugs?

{{c1::Zileuton}}
{{c1::Zafirlukast}}
{{c1::Montelukast}}

What is the mechanism of action of zileuton?

Inhibition of the {{c1::5-lipoxygenase}} pathway → Blocks conversion of {{c1::arachidonic acid}} to {{c1::leukotrienes}}

What is the main adverse effect of zileuton?

{{c1::Hepatotoxicity}}

What is the mechanism of action of montelukast and zafirlukast?

Blockage of {{c1::leukotriene}} receptors

For what two types of asthma are montelukast and zafirlukast especially useful?

{{c1::Aspirin}}-induced asthma
{{c1::Exercise}}-induced asthma

What drug likely leads to palpitations and confusion in a patient with persistent asthma after consumption of grapefruit juice?

{{c1::Theophylline}}

Why is there likely minimal response to adenosine in a patient with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia who is being treated for asthma?

The patient is likely being treated with {{c1::theophylline}}, which blocks the actions of adenosine

What is the mechanism of action of the chromones in the treatment of asthma?

Prevents release of {{c1::inflammatory}} mediators from {{c1::mast}} cells
Prevents {{c1::acute::acute/chronic}} asthma symptoms

What three drug classes help directly reduce the early response that causes bronchoconstriction in asthma?

{{c1::β}}-agonists
{{c1::Methylxanthines}}
{{c1::Muscarinic}} antagonists

What are the three agents used as anti-IL-5 monoclonal therapy in asthma?

{{c1::Mepolizumab}}
{{c1::Reslizumab}}
{{c1::Benralizumab}}

What are the downstream biologic effects of anti-IL-5 monoclonal therapy?

It prevents {{c1::eosinophil}} differentiation, maturation, activation, and survival mediated by IL-5 stimulation

What is the mechanism of benralizumab?

Targeted against the {{c1::α chain}} of the {{c1::IL-5}} receptor → Blocks activation of the {{c1::IL-5}} receptor

What is the mechanism of mepolizumab and reslizumab?

Blockage of {{c1::IL-5}}

What is anti-IL-5 monoclonal therapy used for?

It is used as {{c1::maintenance}} therapy for patients with severe {{c1::eosinophillic asthma}}

What is the most common cause of rhinosinusitis?

{{c1::Viral}} upper respiratory tract infection

What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient with fever, facial pain, and the CT findings shown?



{{c1::Rhinosinusitis}}
fields.Back Extra: Note the fluid-filled right maxillary sinus indicated by the red arrow.

fields.Text:
What are the three most common bacterial pathogens leading to a superimposed infection in patients with rhinosinusitis?

{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae}}
{{c1::Moraxella catarrhalis}}

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism leading to the typical symptoms of rhinosinusitis?

{{c1::Obstruction}} of sinus {{c1::drainage}} into the nasal cavity
fields.Back Extra: This produces pain and inflammation over the affected area.

fields.Text:
What is the reason that the maxillary sinuses are most commonly affected in rhinosinusitis?

The maxillary sinuses drain against {{c1::gravity}}

What is the major reason infections in the sphenoid and ethmoid sinuses typically cause severe complications?

These infections can extend to the {{c1::cavernous}} sinus, {{c1::orbits}}, and {{c1::brain::organ}}
fields.Back Extra: Complications include cavernous sinus syndrome, orbital cellulitis, and meningitis.

fields.Text:
What opacified cavity is indicated by the red arrow on the CT scan obtained from a patient with rhinosinusitis?



{{c1::Maxillary}} sinus

Which nasal meatus drains the nasolacrimal duct?

{{c1::Inferior}} meatus

Which sinuses does the superior meatus drain?

{{c1::Posterior ethmoid}} sinus

Which sinuses does the middle meatus drain?

{{c1::Frontal}} sinus
{{c1::Maxillary}} sinus
{{c1::Anterior ethmoid}} sinus

What three complications are commonly associated with paranasal sinus infections?

{{c1::Cavernous sinus}} syndrome
Orbital {{c1::cellulitis}}
{{c1::Meningitis}}

What is a common cause of epistaxis in an adolescent male?

Nasal {{c1::angiofibromas}}

Which artery is often involved in life-threatening posterior nosebleeds?

{{c1::Sphenopalatine}} artery
fields.Back Extra: This is a branch of the maxillary artery.

fields.Text:
What is the most common location of bleeding in a patient with epistaxis?

The {{c1::anterior::anterior/posterior}} segment of the nostril

What are the four main arteries that contribute to the formation of the Kiesselbach plexus?

{{c1::Superior labial}} artery
Anterior and posterior {{c1::ethmoidal}} arteries
{{c1::Greater palatine}} artery
{{c1::Sphenopalatine}} artery

What is field cancerization?

A carcinogen causes damage to a large {{c1::mucosal}} area, resulting in {{c1::independent::dependent/independent}} development of multiple tumors after exposure

What are the two major modifiable risk factors associated with the development of head and neck cancer?

{{c1::Alcohol}} use
{{c1::Tobacco}} use

What type of cancer most often occurs in the head and neck region?

{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma

What virus is responsible for the majority of oropharyngeal cancers?

{{c1::HPV-16}}

What virus is responsible for most nasopharyngeal cancers?

{{c1::Epstein-Barr virus}}

What are the three most common presenting signs and symptoms of nasopharyngeal carcinoma?

{{c1::Epistaxis}}
{{c1::Unilateral::Unilateral/Bilateral}} nasal obstruction
Nasal {{c1::discharge}}

What two clinical conditions are typically seen as a result of Eustachian tube obstruction?

{{c1::Otitis media}}
{{c1::Hearing}} loss

What general medication is used for long-term prevention or treatment of deep vein thrombosis?

Oral direct {{c1::anticoagulants}}

What is the drug of choice for the acute management of deep vein thrombosis?

{{c1::Unfractionated heparin}}
{{c1::Low-molecular-weight heparin}}
fields.Back Extra: These can also be used for prophylaxis.

fields.Text:
Where do the majority of pulmonary emboli arise from?

{{c1::Proximal::Proximal/Distal}} deep veins of the {{c1::lower::upper/lower}} extremity

What three circumstances may lead to increased hypercoaguability?

Genetic defect in {{c1::coagulation cascade}} proteins
{{c1::Pregnancy}}
{{c1::Oral contraceptive pill}} use

What three major factors that predispose patients to thrombosis are described by the Virchow triad?

{{c1::Stasis}}
{{c1::Hypercoagulability::Hypercoagulability/Hypocoagulability}}
{{c1::Endothelial}} damage

What pathophysiologic mechanism explains how endothelial damage leads to the formation of a clot?

Exposed {{c1::collagen}} triggers the clotting cascade

What laboratory test is typically used to rule out deep vein thrombosis in a patient at low or moderate risk of developing deep vein thrombosis?

{{c1::D-dimer}} test
fields.Back Extra: This test has a high sensitivity, but low specificity.

fields.Text:
What is the diagnostic test of choice for a patient who has been confined to bed for an extended period and has the physical examination findings shown?



{{c1::Compression ultrasonography}} with {{c1::Doppler ultrasound}} of lower leg veins
fields.Back Extra: The most likely diagnosis is new deep vein thrombosis in the right lower extremity.

fields.Text:
What circumstance typically increases venous stasis in a patient?

Prolonged {{c1::inactivity}}

What imaging modality is the preferred method of diagnosing a pulmonary embolism?

{{c1::CT pulmonary angiography}}
fields.Back Extra: This allows detection of a filling defect from a clot.

fields.Text:
What is the typical treatment of a deep-sea diver who ascended too quickly and now reports joint pain and dyspnea?

Administration of {{c1::hyperbaric oxygen}}
fields.Back Extra: The patient likely has an air embolus.

fields.Text:
What dangerous hematologic condition can result from an amniotic fluid embolus?

{{c1::Disseminated intravascular coagulation}}

What comprise the classical triad of symptoms seen in a patient with a fat embolism?

{{c1::Hypoxemia}}
{{c1::Neurologic}} abnormalities
{{c1::Petechial}} rash

What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient with a V/Q mismatch and sudden-onset dyspnea several hours after a femur fracture?

{{c1::Fat embolus}}
fields.Back Extra: Fat embolism syndrome can occur with long bone fractures and liposuction.

fields.Text:
What are the classic types of pulmonary emboli?

{{c1::Fat}} embolism
{{c1::Air}} embolism
{{c1::Thrombus}}
{{c1::Bacterial}} embolism
{{c1::Amniotic fluid}} embolism
{{c1::Tumor}} embolism

What are the classic findings of acute pulmonary embolism?

Sudden-onset {{c1::shortness of breath}}
{{c1::Pleuritic}} chest pain
{{c1::Tachycardia::Tachycardia/Bradycardia}}
{{c1::Tachypnea::Tachypnea/Bradypnea}}
{{c1::Respiratory alkalosis}}

What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient with sudden-onset chest pain, dyspnea, tachypnea, and the CT findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Pulmonary embolus}}

When did the finding shown in the image occur in relation to the patient's death?



{{c1::Before::Before/After}} death, as the premortem thrombi have {{c1::lines of Zahn}}

What are the two most common causes of air embolism?

Precipitation of {{c1::nitrogen}} bubbles in ascending divers
{{c1::Iatrogenic}} air introduction

What treatment options are available for treating pulmonary emboli?

{{c1::Anticoagulants}}
{{c1::Inferior vena cava filter}}

What kind of V/Q defect is seen in patients with a pulmonary embolism?

V/Q {{c1::mismatch}}
fields.Back Extra: This is chiefly due to defects in perfusion from obstruction of the pulmonary arteries.

fields.Text:
What kind of acid-base abnormality is most commonly seen in patients with an acute pulmonary embolism?

{{c1::Respiratory alkalosis}}

What classic ECG finding is relatively specific for acute pulmonary embolism?

{{c1::S1Q3T3}} abnormality

What was the cause of death in a patient with pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, an episode of arrest with pulseless electrical activity, and the autopsy findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Saddle pulmonary embolus}}
fields.Back Extra: This is likely causing electromechanical dissociation of the heart.

fields.Text:
When is an amniotic fluid embolism most likely to occur?

During {{c1::labor}}
{{c1::Postpartum}} period
fields.Back Extra: An embolism can also be a result of uterine trauma.

fields.Text:
In which mediastinal compartment will esophageal carcinoma arise?

The {{c1::middle}} mediastinal compartment
fields.Back Extra: Metastases, hiatal hernia, and bronchogenic cysts can also be found.

fields.Text:
Which two pathologies are commonly found in the posterior mediastinal compartment?

{{c1::Neurogenic}} tumors
{{c1::Multiple myeloma}}

Contiguous spread of infection from which two broad anatomic locations can lead to mediastinitis?

{{c1::Teeth}}
{{c1::Retropharyngeal}} region

What infection can lead to chronic mediastinitis?

Infection with {{c1::Histoplasma capsulatum}}

What are the two primary classifications of the pathologic finding shown in this X-ray of the chest?



Pneumomediastinum can be either {{c1::spontaneous}} or {{c1::secondary}}

What is the most likely radiographic finding in a patient with crepitus heard on cardiac auscultation?

{{c1::Pneumomediastinum}}
fields.Back Extra: Crepitus on cardiac auscultation is known as a positive Hamman sign, which supports the diagnosis of pneumomediastinum.

fields.Text:
What are the common etiologies of an anterior mediastinal mass?

Substernal {{c1::goiter}}
{{c1::Thymic}} neoplasm
{{c1::Teratoma}}
"Terrible" {{c1::lymphoma}}

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient presenting with fever, chest pain, leukocytosis, and sternal wound drainage 11 days after a cardiothoracic surgical procedure?

{{c1::Mediastinitis}}
fields.Back Extra: This often occurs ≤ 14 days after cardiothoracic surgery.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism associated with the formation of pneumomediastinum?

Ruptured alveoli allow air to {{c1::enter::enter/leave}} the mediastinum via {{c1::peribronchial}} and {{c1::perivascular}} sheaths

How do FEV1 and FVC change in a patient with restrictive lung disease when compared with normal values?

FEV1 would be {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}
FVC would be {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}

How do TLC, FRC, and RV change in a patient with obstructive lung disease when compared with a healthy individual?

TLC is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}
FRC is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}
RV is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}

How do FEV1 and FVC change in a patient with obstructive lung disease when compared with normal values?

FEV1 is greatly {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}
FVC is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}

How does the FEV1/FVC ratio change in a patient with obstructive lung disease when compared with normal values?

The FEV1/FVC would be {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because FEV1 is decreased more than FVC.

fields.Text:
How do TLC, FRC, and RV change in a patient with restrictive lung disease when compared with normal values?

TLC is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}
FRC is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}
RV is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}

How does the FEV1/FVC ratio change in a patient with restrictive lung disease when compared with normal values?

It remains {{c1::normal}} or {{c1::increases}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because FEV1 and FVC are proportionally decreased.

fields.Text:
What type of lung disease presents with the flow-volume loop shown in green in the image?



{{c1::Obstructive::Obstructive/Restrictive}} lung disease

What type of lung disease presents with the flow-volume loop shown in blue in the image?



{{c1::Restrictive::Obstructive/Restrictive}} lung disease

What two tests are commonly used for the diagnosis of asthma?

{{c1::Spirometry}}
{{c1::Methacholine challenge}} test

What are the common triggers leading to bronchial hyper-responsiveness in patients with asthma?

Environmental {{c1::allergens}}
{{c1::Viral}} upper respiratory tract infections
{{c1::Emotional}} stress

What three histologic findings do you expect in a lung biopsy specimen from a patient with asthma?

{{c1::Curschmann spirals}}
Smooth muscle {{c1::hypertrophy::hypertrophy/hypotrophy}}/{{c1::hyperplasia::hyperplasia/hypoplasia}}
{{c1::Charcot-Leydon crystals}}

How is asthma differentiated from other obstructive lung diseases?

The bronchoconstriction associated with asthma is {{c1::reversible::reversible/irreversible}}

What part of the pulmonary system becomes hyper-responsive in patients with asthma?

{{c1::Bronchi}}
fields.Back Extra: The bronchi constricts readily in response to triggers.

fields.Text:
How do you distinguish between centriacinar emphysema and panacinar emphysema based on location in the lungs?

Centriacinar emphysema is associated with smoking and is usually in the {{c1::upper}} lobes
Panacinar emphysema is usually in the {{c1::lower}} lobes

Which type of emphysema is associated with smoking?

{{c1::Centriacinar}} emphysema

What enzyme deficiency is associated with panacinar emphysema?

{{c1::α1-antitrypsin}} deficiency

What are the two main subtypes of emphysema?

{{c1::Centriacinar}} emphysema
{{c1::Panacinar}} emphysema

How does breathing through pursed lips help a patient with emphysema?

It {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} airway pressure
Helps prevent airway {{c1::collapse}}

What happens to compliance, the DLCO, elastic recoil, and blood volume in pulmonary capillaries in patients with emphysema?

Compliance {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}
DLCO {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
Elastic recoil {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
Blood volume in pulmonary capillaries {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}

Which two genetic diseases are associated with bronchiectasis?

{{c1::Cystic fibrosis}}
{{c1::Kartagener}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: Both of these diseases impair lung clearance of pathogens.

fields.Text:
What conditions are commonly associated with bronchiectasis?

Bronchial {{c1::obstruction}}
Poor ciliary {{c1::motility}}
{{c1::Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis}}
{{c1::Cystic fibrosis}}
Pulmonary {{c1::infections}}

What is the Reid index in chronic bronchitis?

Ratio of the thickness of the {{c1::gland}} layer to the total thickness of the {{c1::bronchial wall}} between epithelium and cartilage

What are classic signs and symptoms of bronchiectasis?

Digital {{c1::clubbing}}
{{c1::Purulent}} sputum
{{c1::Hemoptysis}}
{{c1::Recurrent}} infections

What are the criteria for the diagnosis of chronic bronchitis?

{{c1::Productive}} cough for more than {{c1::3}} months in a year for more than {{c1::2}} consecutive years

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism leading to the development of bronchiectasis?

Chronic {{c1::necrotizing}} infection or {{c1::obstruction}} of the bronchi resulting in permanently {{c1::dilated::dilated/constricted}} airways

What are the four main types of obstructive lung disease?

{{c1::Chronic bronchitis}}
{{c1::Emphysema}}
{{c1::Asthma}}
{{c1::Bronchiectasis}}

What cardiac complication can result from chronic obstructive lung disease?

{{c1::Cor pulmonale}}

What is the hallmark pulmonary function test finding in patients with obstructive lung disease?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} FEV1/FVC ratio
fields.Back Extra: The decrease in FEV1 is greater than the decrease in FVC.

fields.Text:
How does FVC change in obstructive lung disease?

FVC is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}

How does an obstructive lung disease affect FRC, RV, and TLC?

FRC is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}
RV is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}
TLC is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}

What is the definition of an obstructive lung disease?

Obstruction to airflow leads to air {{c1::trapping}} → Airways close {{c1::prematurely}} at high volumes → {{c1::V/Q mismatch}}

What type of obstructive lung disease is associated with the findings in the gross specimen shown?



{{c1::Bronchiectasis}}
fields.Back Extra: In this case, it is due to cystic fibrosis.

fields.Text:
What is the histologic finding shown called?



{{c1::Curschmann spirals}}
fields.Back Extra:
This consist of shed epithelium that forms whorled mucous plugs.

This is characteristic of asthma.

fields.Text:
What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient with a barrel-shaped chest who consistently breathes through pursed lips and has the chest X-ray shown?



{{c1::Emphysema}}

What two common physical exam findings may be seen in a patient with emphysema?

{{c1::Barrel}}-shaped chest
{{c1::Pursed-lip}} breathing

What are the four typical physical exam findings and two lab findings associated with chronic bronchitis?

{{c1::Crackles}} (physical)
{{c1::Wheezing}} (physical)
{{c1::Cyanosis}} (physical)
{{c1::Dyspnea}} (physical)
{{c1::CO2::Gas}} retention (lab)
{{c1::Secondary polycythemia}} (lab)

What is the effect of chronic bronchitis on DLCO?

{{c1::None}}

How does hematocrit change in a patient with chronic bronchitis?

It {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}
fields.Back Extra: Secondary polycythemia is common in patients with long-standing hypoxemia due to chronic bronchitis.

fields.Text:
What are the three most common radiographic findings in a patient with emphysema?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} AP diameter
{{c1::Flattened}} diaphragm
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} lung field lucency

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism that leads to cyanosis in a patient with chronic bronchitis?

{{c1::Shunting}} due to airway {{c1::obstruction}} → Hypoxemia

What two conditions classically impair ciliary motility and may lead to bronchiectasis?

Chronic {{c1::smoking}}
{{c1::Kartagener}} syndrome

What is the classic phenotype of a patient with chronic bronchitis?

A {{c1::blue bloater}} phenotype

What is the classic phenotype of a patient with emphysema?

A {{c1::pink puffer}} phenotype

What happens to the inspiratory/expiratory ratio in a patient with an asthma exacerbation?

It {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
fields.Back Extra: Expiration is prolonged due to airflow obstruction.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism underlying NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease?

Inhibition of the {{c1::COX}} pathway by NSAIDs → {{c1::Leukotriene}} overproduction → Airway constriction

What is the classic triad seen in a patient with NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease?

Chronic {{c1::sinusitis}}
Nasal {{c1::polyps}}
{{c1::Asthma}} symptoms
fields.Back Extra: This was previously referred to as aspirin-induced asthma.

fields.Text:
What type of hypersensitivity reaction is implicated in the pathogenesis of asthma?

Type {{c1::I}} hypersensitivity reaction

How does the DLCO change in asthma?

DLCO is {{c1::normal}} or {{c1::increased}}
fields.Back Extra: It is increased because of pulmonary vascular congestion.

fields.Text:
What is the sputum finding shown called?



{{c1::Charcot-Leyden crystals}}

What obstructive lung disease presents with the histologic findings shown?



{{c1::Emphysema}}
fields.Back Extra: The image reveals destruction of alveolar walls.

fields.Text:
How might systolic blood pressure vary with breathing in a patient presenting with sudden wheezing and the biopsy findings shown?



{{c1::Asthma}} exacerbation → Systolic blood pressure decreases by > {{c1::10}} mmHg on inspiration
fields.Back Extra: The image shows mucous plugging, which is characteristic of asthma.

fields.Text:
What is the likely pattern of alveolar damage in a smoker with a barrel-shaped chest and the autopsy specimen shown?



{{c1::Centriacinar emphysema}}

What enzyme is likely overactive in the lungs of a patient who is a smoker with prolonged expiration and the CT findings shown?



{{c1::Elastase}}
fields.Back Extra:
Increased elastase activity leads to loss of elastic fibers and an increase in lung compliance.

The CT scan of the chest shows centriacinar emphysema.

fields.Text:
The following signs and symptoms are commonly seen in a patient with which obstructive lung disease?

Coughing
Wheezing
Tachypnea
Dyspnea
Hypoxia
Pulsus paradoxus

{{c1::Asthma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is usually triggered by stress, an allergen, or a viral upper respiratory infection.

fields.Text:
Which subtype of emphysema affects both respiratory bronchioles and alveoli?

{{c1::Panacinar}} emphysema

How does centriacinar emphysema affect the respiratory bronchioles and the distal alveoli?

{{c1::Damages}} the respiratory bronchioles
{{c1::Spares}} the distal alveoli

Which subtype of emphysema is shown in the diagram?



{{c1::Centriacinar}} emphysema
fields.Back Extra: This affects the respiratory bronchioles yet spares distal alveoli.

fields.Text:
Which subtype of emphysema is shown in the diagram?



{{c1::Panacinar}} emphysema
fields.Back Extra: This affects both the respiratory bronchioles and distal alveoli.

fields.Text:
What will a chest X-ray likely show in a patient with progressive dyspnea, arthritis, and elevated serum ACE and Ca2+ levels?

{{c1::Bilateral::Unilateral/Bilateral}} {{c1::hilar lymphadenopathy}}

What would you expect the DLCO and A-a gradient to be in a patient with Langerhans cell histiocytosis?

DLCO will be {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}
A-a gradient will be {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}

Which small-vessel to medium-vessel vasculitis causes restrictive lung disease?

{{c1::Granulomatosis with polyangiitis}}
fields.Back Extra: This was formerly known as Wegener granulomatosis.

fields.Text:
What are four drug toxicities that most commonly cause interstitial lung disease?

{{c1::Bleomycin}}
{{c1::Busulfan}}
{{c1::Methotrexate}}
{{c1::Amiodarone}}

What type of lung disease is present in a patient presenting with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, noncaseating granulomas, and hypercalcemia?

{{c1::Sarcoidosis}}
fields.Back Extra: It is an interstitial lung disease that will show a restrictive pattern.

fields.Text:
Which category of lung disease typically leads to restrictive lung disease?

{{c1::Pneumoconioses}}

Severe obesity can lead to what type of lung disease?

{{c1::Restrictive::Obstructive/Restrictive}} lung disease

What disease affecting the neuromuscular junction causes a restrictive lung disease?

{{c1::Myasthenia gravis}}

What viral illness classically leads to restrictive lung disease?

{{c1::Poliomyelitis}}

How is restrictive lung disease due to poor mechanics differentiated from those due to interstitial lung disease?

Poor mechanics → A-a gradient and DLCO are {{c1::normal}}
Interstitial lung disease → A-a gradient is {{c1::increased}} and DLCO is {{c1::decreased}}

What are the two general types of restrictive lung disease?

Altered respiratory {{c1::mechanics}}
{{c1::Interstitial}} lung diseases

What typically happens to the FEV1/FVC ratio in the setting of restrictive lung disease?

The ratio is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}

Which two lung volumes are decreased in most patients with restrictive lung disease?

{{c1::FVC}}
{{c1::TLC}}

What are the two general subtypes of restrictive lung disease caused by altered breathing mechanics?

Respiratory {{c1::muscle}} weakness
{{c1::Chest wall}} abnormalities

What two laboratory values are characteristic of a patient with sarcoidosis?

Elevated soluble {{c1::ACE}} levels
{{c1::Hypercalcemia::Hypercalcemia/Hypocalcemia}}

What type of lung pathology pattern is seen in acute respiratory distress syndrome?

{{c1::Restrictive::Obstructive/Restrictive}} pattern

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism associated with the formation of radiation-induced lung injury?

Release of {{c1::proinflammatory cytokines}}
fields.Back Extra: These are TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6.

fields.Text:
What type of lung pathology pattern is seen in radiation-induced lung injury?

{{c1::Restrictive::Obstructive/Restrictive}} pattern

When does acute radiation pneumonitis typically present?

{{c1::3}} to {{c1::12}} weeks after radiation exposure

When does radiation fibrosis typically present?

{{c1::6}} to {{c1::12}} months after radiation exposure

What are the most common symptoms seen in patients with radiation-induced lung injury?

{{c1::Dry}} cough
{{c1::Dyspnea}}
{{c1::Low::High/Low}}-grade fever

What are the three most common risk factors associated with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?

Exposure to environmental {{c1::pollutants}}
{{c1::Smoking}}
{{c1::Genetic}} defects

What is the common radiographic appearance of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?

{{c1::Peripheral::Central/Peripheral}} {{c1::reticular opacities}} with {{c1::traction bronchiectasis}}

What histologic pattern is seen in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?

Usual {{c1::interstitial pneumonia}}

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with a CT scan of the chest showing peripheral reticular opacities with traction bronchiectasis?

{{c1::Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis}}

What are the four most common findings of a patient with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?

Progressive {{c1::dyspnea}}
{{c1::Dry}} cough
Digital {{c1::clubbing}}
{{c1::Crackles}} on chest auscultation

What are the major potential complications of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?

{{c1::Right::Let/Right}} heart failure
{{c1::Coronary artery}} disease
{{c1::Arrhythmias}}
Pulmonary {{c1::hypertension::hypertension/hypotension}}
Respiratory {{c1::failure}}
Lung {{c1::cancer}}

What vessel is likely blocked in a patient presenting with a left lung mass, headaches, dizziness, and a berry aneurysm on angiography?

{{c1::Superior vena cava}}
fields.Back Extra: This is superior vena cava syndrome.

fields.Text:
Superior vena cava syndrome puts a patient at risk for rupture of which arteries?

{{c1::Intracranial}} arteries
fields.Back Extra: These arteries may burst as a result of elevated intracranial pressure.

fields.Text:
What has likely occurred in a patient with superior vena cava syndrome who has developed rapid-onset confusion, loss of sensation, and hemiparesis?

Critically {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} intracranial pressure → Intracranial bleed
fields.Back Extra: This is either from a ruptured aneurysm or an intracranial artery.

fields.Text:
What are the two most common causes of superior vena cava syndrome?

{{c1::Malignancy}}
{{c1::Thrombosis}} from indwelling catheters

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with a known lung malignancy presenting with jugular venous distention and the skin finding shown?



{{c1::Superior vena cava}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: Shown is blanching after fingertip pressure, which is characteristic of facial plethora.

fields.Text:
How urgently should a patient with an indwelling venous catheter, facial edema, and the CT findings shown be treated?



Treat {{c1::emergently}}
fields.Back Extra: This patient has superior vena cava syndrome, which is a medical emergency.

fields.Text:
What type of hypersensitivity reaction leads to hypersensitivity pneumonitis?

Mixed type {{c1::III}} and {{c1::IV}} hypersensitivity reaction

What two occupations are at most risk for the development of hypersensitivity pneumonitis?

{{c1::Farmers}}
{{c1::Bird}}-fanciers

What three major pathologic changes to the lungs occur over the long term in patients with hypersensitivity pneumonitis?

{{c1::Fibrosis}} with {{c1::noncaseating::caseating/noncaseating}} granulomas
{{c1::Thickening::Thickening/Thinning}} of the alveolar septum
{{c1::Traction bronchiectasis}}

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism seen in patients with sarcoidosis?

{{c1::Immune}}-mediated, {{c1::noncaseating::caseating/noncaseating}} granulomatous inflammation spread throughout multiple organs

What is the classic bronchoalveolar lavage finding in a patient with sarcoidosis?

Elevated {{c1::CD4}}/{{c1::CD8}} ratio

What patient population does sarcoidosis most commonly affect?

{{c1::Black::Ethnicity}} {{c1::women::men/women}}

What is the most common presentation of sarcoidosis?

Clinically {{c1::asymptomatic::symptomatic/asymptomatic}} with {{c1::lymphadenopathy}} on exam

What two histologic features are commonly present in the noncaseating epithelioid granulomas of sarcoidosis?

{{c1::Schaumann bodies}}
{{c1::Asteroid bodies}}

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism that causes hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis?

Increased {{c1::1α-hydroxylase}} activity in macrophages → Vitamin D activation

What is the preferred treatment for symptomatic sarcoidosis?

{{c1::Glucocorticoids}}

What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient with unilateral facial nerve palsy, episodic uveitis, joint pain, granulomas on lymph node biopsy, and the CT findings shown?



{{c1::Sarcoidosis}}
fields.Back Extra: CT of the chest shows extensive hilar and mediastinal adenopathy.

fields.Text:
What is the likely diagnosis for a woman with long-standing dyspnea, erythematous nodules on her shins, and the chest X-ray findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Sacroidosis}}
fields.Back Extra: Note the bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with coarse reticular opacities.

fields.Text:
The following classic clinical and laboratory findings are seen in a patient with what disease?

Bell palsy
Granulomas
Lupus pernio
Uveitis
Erythema nodosum
Interstitial fibrosis
Rheumatoid arthritis–like arthropathy
Hypercalcemia

{{c1::Sarcoidosis}}

What serum marker is often elevated in patients with sarcoidosis?

{{c1::ACE}} levels

What is the likely diagnosis of a patient presenting with worsening dyspnea, bilateral arthralgia, and the lymph node biopsy findings shown?



{{c1::Sarcoidosis}}
fields.Back Extra: The lymph node biopsy shows a noncaseating granuloma.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism leading to inhalation injury?

Inhalation of a {{c1::noxious}} stimulus
Particulates < {{c1::1}} µm in diameter
{{c1::Irritants}}
{{c1::Heat}}

What two physical exam findings are highly suggestive of inhalation injury?

{{c1::Soot}} in the oropharynx
{{c1::Singed}} nasal hairs

What other bronchoscopic findings may be seen in a patient with the bronchoscopic finding shown?



Bronchial {{c1::congestion}}
Severe {{c1::edema}}
Deposits of {{c1::soot}}

What diagnoses are typically associated with inhalation injuries?

{{c1::Carbon monoxide}} exposure
{{c1::Burns}}
{{c1::Cyanide}} poisoning
{{c1::Arsenic}} poisoning

When can resolution of an inhalation injury be expected?

Resolution should occur {{c1::11}} days after injury
fields.Back Extra: This is assuming that there is no additional exposure to noxious stimuli.

fields.Text:
What pathologic findings in the respiratory system are often seen in those with an inhalation injury?

Airway {{c1::edema}}
{{c1::Tracheobronchitis}}
{{c1::Pneumonia}}
{{c1::Acute respiratory distress}} syndrome

What study would confirm the likely diagnosis for a patient who works as a shipbuilder with "ivory white" supradiaphragmatic and pleural plaques found on imaging?

{{c1::Bronchoalveolar lavage}} with {{c1::Prussian blue}} stain
fields.Back Extra:
This will demonstrate fusiform/dumbbell rods in alveolar sputum.

This is asbestosis.

fields.Text:
How does silicosis increase a patient's susceptibility to developing tuberculosis?

Silica impairs {{c1::macrophages}} and {{c1::phagolysosomes}}
fields.Back Extra: This affects their ability to effectively kill microbes.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism associated with the development of silicosis?

{{c1::Macrophages}} respond to silica exposure by releasing {{c1::fibrogenic}} factors → Fibrosis of the lungs

Which lobes of the lung are more commonly affected in patients with berylliosis?

{{c1::Upper}} lobes

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism seen in the development of coal worker's pneumoconiosis?

Prolonged exposure to coal dust → Deposition of {{c1::carbon}} in macrophages → Inflammation and fibrosis in the lungs
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as black lung disease.

fields.Text:
What is the preferred treatment for berylliosis?

{{c1::Glucocorticoids}}
fields.Back Extra: Granulomatous inflammation in berylliosis may respond to anti-inflammatory therapy.

fields.Text:
What occupational exposure increases the risk of development of berylliosis?

{{c1::Aerospace}} industry
{{c1::Manufacturing}} industry

Which lobes of the lungs are most commonly affected in patients with asbestosis?

{{c1::Lower}} lobes

What substance are patients working in shipbuilding, roofing, or plumbing at increased risk of being exposed to?

{{c1::Asbestos}}

What four conditions do patients with silicosis have a higher risk of developing?

{{c1::Tuberculosis}}
{{c1::Cor pulmonale}}
{{c1::Cancer}}
{{c1::Caplan}} syndrome

What is the classic pathologic finding seen in the autopsy specimen obtained from the diaphragm of a patient who was employed as a plumber?



{{c1::Calcified supradiaphragmatic plaques}}

What was the patient with the sputum sample findings shown likely exposed to?



{{c1::Asbestos}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows dumbbell-shaped golden-brown fusiform rods called asbestos or ferruginous bodies.

fields.Text:
What is the likely diagnosis for a roofer with dyspnea, cough, and the CT findings shown?



{{c1::Asbestosis}}
fields.Back Extra: CT scan of the chest shows pleural plaques, which are pathognomonic.

fields.Text:
Which lobes of the lungs are most affected by silicosis and coal workers' pneumoconiosis?

{{c1::Upper}} lobes

What two conditions are patients with berylliosis at increased risk of developing?

{{c1::Cancer}}
{{c1::Cor pulmonale}}

How does the presentation of anthracosis differ from that of coal workers' pneumoconiosis?

Anthracosis is {{c1::asymptomatic}}

What three occupations are commonly associated with the development of silicosis?

{{c1::Sandblasting}}
{{c1::Foundries}}
{{c1::Mines}}

What type of intrathoracic malignancy is most common in patients with asbestosis?

{{c1::Bronchogenic}} carcinoma
fields.Back Extra: The risk of bronchogenic carcinoma is greater than the risk of mesothelioma.

fields.Text:
What are the radiographic findings commonly seen in patients with silicosis?

"{{c1::Eggshell}}" calcifications of hilar lymph nodes on X-ray of the chest

What two nonmalignant complications are most commonly associated with asbestosis?

Pleural {{c1::effusions}}
{{c1::Caplan}} syndrome

What is the most likely diagnosis of the patient with the lung biopsy findings shown?



{{c1::Berylliosis}}
fields.Back Extra: Shown are the noncaseating granulomas typical of significant beryllium exposure.

fields.Text:
What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with rheumatoid arthritis and intrapulmonary nodules?

{{c1::Caplan}} syndrome

What classic histologic finding is commonly seen in patients with mesothelioma?

{{c1::Psammoma bodies}}

What effect does a history of smoking have on a patient's risk for the development of mesothelioma?

{{c1::None}}
fields.Back Extra: Smoking is not a risk factor for mesothelioma.

fields.Text:
What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient who worked as a plumber whose autopsy specimen is shown?



{{c1::Mesothelioma}}
fields.Back Extra: Pleural thickening can be seen in the specimen.

fields.Text:
What type of immunohistochemical staining is positive in mesothelioma?

{{c1::Calretinin}}
{{c1::Cytokeratin 5}}
{{c1::Cytokeratin 6}}

What are the two classic presentations of mesothelioma?

{{c1::Exudative::Transudative/Exudative}} pleural effusion
Pleural {{c1::thickening::thickening/thinning}}

What occupational/environmental exposure is associated with mesothelioma?

{{c1::Asbestos}}

What is the most common cause of acute respiratory distress syndrome?

{{c1::Sepsis}}

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism leading to the development of acute respiratory distress syndrome after alveolar insult?

Cytokines and toxic mediators → Capillary {{c1::endothelial}} damage → Leakage of {{c1::protein}}-rich fluid → Intra-alveolar {{c1::hyaline}} membrane formation and pulmonary {{c1::edema}} → Hypoxic vasoconstriction → Increased pulmonary vascular resistance

What is the typical pulmonary capillary wedge pressure in acute respiratory distress syndrome?

{{c1::Normal}}

What is the preferred mechanical ventilation strategy used in a patient with acute respiratory distress syndrome?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} tidal volume
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} positive end-expiratory pressure

What are the two key pathophysiologic mechanisms involved in the alveolar damage and collapse seen in acute respiratory distress syndrome?

Acute {{c1::inflammation}}
Loss of {{c1::surfactant}}

What are the four diagnostic criteria for acute respiratory distress syndrome?

Abnormal {{c1::chest X-ray}}
Respiratory failure within {{c1::1}} week(s) of insult
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} PaO2/FIO2
Symptoms not due to {{c1::heart::organ}} failure or {{c1::fluid}} overload

What are the two key pathophysiologic mechanisms that lead to the hypoxemia seen in acute respiratory distress syndrome?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} lung compliance
{{c1::V/Q mismatch}}
fields.Back Extra: This leads to increased intrapulmonary shunting and hypoxia.

fields.Text:
What are the three pathophysiologic consequences of acute respiratory distress syndrome?

Impaired {{c1::gas exchange}}
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} lung compliance
Pulmonary {{c1::hypertension::hypertension/hypotension}}

What is the likely diagnosis of a mechanically ventilated patient with acute pancreatitis presenting with the X-ray of the chest shown?



{{c1::Acute respiratory distress}} syndrome secondary to pancreatitis

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with sepsis, a normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, and the lung biopsy findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Acute respiratory distress}} syndrome secondary to sepsis
fields.Back Extra: The image shows intra-alveolar hyaline membranes.

fields.Text:
What is the likely diagnosis of an obese patient presenting with snoring, disrupted sleep, reduced PaO2, and increased PaCO2?

{{c1::Obesity hypoventilation}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as Pickwickian syndrome.

fields.Text:
What is the first-line treatment for central sleep apnea?

{{c1::Positive::Positive/Negative}} airway pressure

What test confirms the suspected diagnosis in an obese patient presenting with daytime somnolence, disrupted sleep, and loud snoring?

{{c1::Sleep}} study

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism that leads to a high hematocrit in a patient with daytime somnolence, disrupted sleep, and loud snoring?

Increased {{c1::erythropoietin}} release secondary to hypoxia → Increased erythropoiesis

What anatomic abnormality is commonly associated with obstructive sleep apnea in adults?

Excess {{c1::parapharyngeal}} tissue

What anatomic abnormality is commonly associated with obstructive sleep apnea in children?

{{c1::Adenotonsillar}} {{c1::hypertrophy::hypertrophy/hypotrophy}}

What are the two preferred treatment options for obesity hypoventilation syndrome?

Weight {{c1::loss::gain/loss}}
{{c1::Positive::Positive/Negative}} airway pressure

What is the major difference in the etiology of central sleep apnea compared to obstructive sleep apnea?

Central sleep apnea is due to {{c1::central nervous system}}-driven impairment in respiratory effort
Obstructive sleep apnea is due to respiratory efforts against airway {{c1::obstruction}}

What severe complications are commonly seen due to nocturnal hypoxia in sleep apnea?

{{c1::Arrhythmias}}
Systemic/pulmonary {{c1::hypertension::hypertension/hypotension}}
Sudden {{c1::death}}

What would you expect the daytime PaO2 to be in a patient with sleep apnea?

{{c1::Normal}}

What three findings are classically associated with obstructive sleep apnea?

{{c1::Obesity}}
Loud {{c1::snoring}}
Daytime {{c1::sleepiness}}

What happens to a patient's PaCO2 in the setting of obesity hypoventilation syndrome?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PaCO2 is seen during waking and sleeping hours

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism whereby sleep apnea leads to sleep disruption?

Repeated {{c1::cessation}} of breathing during sleep → Sleep disruption

What are the three most common causes of central sleep apnea?

{{c1::Opioid}} use
{{c1::Central nervous system}} injury/toxicity
{{c1::Heart::Organ}} failure

What type of sleep apnea can cause a patient with advanced heart failure to oscillate between apnea and hyperpnea during sleep?

{{c1::Central::Central/Obstructive}} sleep apnea
fields.Back Extra: This is associated with Cheyne-Stokes respirations in some patients, as well as congestive heart failure and central nervous system toxicity.

fields.Text:
What two drugs that are commonly abused are associated with the development of pulmonary hypertension?

{{c1::Cocaine}}
{{c1::Amphetamine}}

How do recurrent microemboli typically lead to the development of pulmonary hypertension?

Microemboli decreases the total {{c1::cross-sectional area}} of the pulmonary vascular bed → Increases pulmonary arterial pressures

How does obstructive sleep apnea or living at high altitudes lead to the development of pulmonary hypertension?

Obstructive sleep apnea and living at high altitudes can cause {{c1::hypoxia}} → Chronic pulmonary {{c1::vasoconstriction::vasodilation/vasoconstriction}} → Pulmonary hypertension

What pathophysiologic mechanism is associated with interstitial lung disease leading to pulmonary hypertension?

Via lung {{c1::inflammation}}/{{c1::fibrosis}}

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism that ultimately leads to development of pulmonary hypertension in patients with a chronic history of emphysema?

By destruction of lung {{c1::parenchyma}}

What are the most common causes of pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease?

{{c1::Systolic}}/{{c1::diastolic}} left ventricular dysfunction
{{c1::Valvular}} disease

What is the prognosis for a patient diagnosed with idiopathic or heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension?

{{c1::Poor}}

What is the most common underlying genetic cause of heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension?

An inactivating mutation in the {{c1::BMPR2}} gene
fields.Back Extra: This normally inhibits vascular smooth muscle proliferation.

fields.Text:
What are the five main etiologic categories of pulmonary hypertension?

Pulmonary {{c1::arterial}} hypertension
Chronic {{c1::thromboembolic}} pulmonary hypertension
{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} heart disease
{{c1::Hypoxia}}
{{c1::Multifactorial}}

What pathologic changes in the vasculature are commonly caused by pulmonary hypertension?

Medial {{c1::hypertrophy::hypertrophy/hypotrophy}}
{{c1::Arteriosclerosis}}
{{c1::Intimal fibrosis}} of the pulmonary arteries
{{c1::Plexiform}} lesions

What is the pulmonary artery pressure value needed for diagnosing pulmonary hypertension?

Greater than {{c1::20}} mmHg during rest

What is a particularly common cause of death related to long-standing pulmonary hypertension?

{{c1::Cor pulmonale}}

What disorders commonly lead to multifactorial pulmonary hypertension?

Pulmonary vasculature compression caused by a {{c1::tumor}}
{{c1::Hematologic}} disorder
{{c1::Systemic}} disorder
{{c1::Metabolic}} disorder

What happens to the levels of vasoconstrictors in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension?

They {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to endothelial dysfunction in the pulmonary vasculature.

fields.Text:
What happens to the levels of vasodilators in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension?

They {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to endothelial dysfunction in the pulmonary vasculature.

fields.Text:
What are three general conditions that typically lead to pulmonary hypertension due to lung disease?

Lung {{c1::parenchymal}} destruction
Hypoxemic {{c1::vasoconstriction::vasodilation/vasoconstriction}}
Lung {{c1::inflammation}}/{{c1::fibrosis}}

If a patient with a history of abusing injectable drugs presents with cytomegalovirus retinitis, what type of pulmonary pathology are they at risk of developing?

Pulmonary arterial {{c1::hypertension::hypertension/hypotension}}
fields.Back Extra: This may be caused by HIV infection.

fields.Text:
What type of rheumatologic disease is associated with the development of pulmonary hypertension?

{{c1::Connective tissue}} disease

What parasitic infection is typically associated with the development of pulmonary hypertension?

{{c1::Schistosomiasis}}

To which side would the trachea be expected to deviate in both tension pneumothorax and a large pleural effusion?

{{c1::Away}} from the side of the lesion

What findings on auscultation are commonly seen in a patient with lung consolidation?

{{c1::Bronchial}} breath sounds
{{c1::Crackles}} during late inspiration
{{c1::Egophony}}
{{c1::Whispered pectoriloquy}}

What lung condition presents with bronchial breath sounds, dullness to percussion, and increased tactile fremitus without tracheal deviation on physical examination?

Lung {{c1::consolidation}}
fields.Back Extra: This is possibly secondary to lobar pneumonia or pulmonary edema.

fields.Text:
What lung condition presents with absent right-sided breath sounds, hyperresonance to percussion, decreased tactile fremitus, and tracheal deviation to the left side on physical examination?

{{c1::Tension pneumothorax}}
fields.Back Extra: This would be on the right side.

fields.Text:
What lung condition presents with decreased breath sounds and tactile fremitus on the left with hyperresonance to percussion and no tracheal deviation on physical examination?

{{c1::Simple pneumothorax}}
fields.Back Extra: This would be on the left.

fields.Text:
What lung condition presents with decreased breath sounds on the right side with dullness to percussion, decreased tactile fremitus, and tracheal deviation to the left side on physical examination?

Large {{c1::right::left/right}}-sided {{c1::pleural effusion}}

What lung condition is associated with decreased right-sided breath sounds, dullness to percussion, decreased tactile fremitus, and no tracheal deviation on physical examination?

{{c1::Pleural effusion}}

What physical findings may be indicative of atelectasis?

Presence of {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} breath sounds
{{c1::Dullness}} to percussion
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} tactile fremitus on the side of lesion
{{c1::Tracheal deviation}} to the side of lesion

What examination finding is shown in the image?



Digital {{c1::clubbing}}

What is the proposed pathophysiologic mechanism leading to digital clubbing?

Intrapulmonary shunt is present → {{c1::Megakaryocytes}} and {{c1::platelets}} lodge in vessels of the digits → Release of {{c1::PDGF}} and {{c1::VEGF}}

What are the two respiratory conditions not typically associated with digital clubbing?

{{c1::Asthma}}
{{c1::Chronic obstructive pulmonary}} disease

What are the four major subtypes of atelectasis?

{{c1::Adhesive}} atelectasis
{{c1::Compressive}} atelectasis
{{c1::Contraction}} atelectasis
{{c1::Obstructive}} atelectasis

What is the underlying cause of atelectasis in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?

Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is atelectasis with an {{c1::adhesive}} etiology due to a lack of {{c1::surfactant}}

What is the mechanism of atelectasis typically seen in a patient with sarcoidosis?

Distortion of {{c1::alveoli}}
fields.Back Extra: This can be caused by contraction or scarring of lung parenchyma.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism that causes airway obstruction to lead to atelectasis?

Airway obstruction keeps new air from getting to the {{c1::distal::proximal/distal}} airways → Old air is {{c1::resorbed}}

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism that causes external compression of the lung to lead to atelectasis?

External compression of the lung {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} the volume of the lung

What is the preferred treatment of a pleural effusion?

{{c1::Thoracocentesis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is to remove or reduce the built-up fluid.

fields.Text:
What is the definition of a pleural effusion?

{{c1::Fluid}} accumulation between the {{c1::visceral}} pleura and {{c1::parietal}} pleura
fields.Back Extra: This results in limited lung expansion during inspiration.

fields.Text:
What is the typical cause of a lymphatic pleural effusion?

{{c1::Thoracic duct}} injury
fields.Back Extra: This can be either from a trauma or malignancy.

fields.Text:
What type of pleural effusion would be present if the fluid had a milky appearance and high triglyceride levels?

{{c1::Lymphatic}}

How does the protein content in a transudate differ from the protein content in an exudate?

A transudate contains {{c1::less::more/less}} protein than an exudate

What is the common pathophysiologic mechanism associated with the development of exudative pleural effusions?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} vascular permeability

What are the two major pathophysiologic mechanisms associated with the development of transudative pleural effusions?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} hydrostatic pressure
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} oncotic pressure

What would you expect the cellularity and protein content of the pleural fluid to be in a patient with cirrhosis and bilateral pleural effusions?

{{c1::Hypocellular::Hypercellular/Hypocellular}}
{{c1::Low::High/Low}} protein content

What is the expected protein level in a pleural fluid sample from a patient with active tuberculosis?

Protein-{{c1::rich::rich/poor}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an exudative effusion due to infection.

fields.Text:
What are the classic characteristics of an exudative pleural effusion?

{{c1::Cellular}} fluid
Protein-{{c1::rich::rich/poor}}
LDH-{{c1::rich::rich/poor}}

Why does an exudative pleural effusion require prompt drainage?

Exudates are associated with a significant risk of {{c1::infection}}

What is the finding indicated by the red arrows in the image?



{{c1::Pleural effusion}}

What is the likely diagnosis in a patient with the CT scan shown?



{{c1::Pleural effusion}}

What is the definition of a pneumothorax?

Accumulation of {{c1::air}} in the {{c1::pleural}} space

What is the first-line treatment of a tension pneumothorax?

Immediate {{c1::needle decompression}} followed by {{c1::chest tube}} placement

What is the most likely diagnosis of a patient with left-sided chest pain, diminished breath sounds on the left side, and decreased tactile fremitus after falling from a roof?

{{c1::Traumatic pneumothorax}}

What are the main etiologies of secondary spontaneous pneumothorax?

{{c1::Lung::Organ}} disease
{{c1::Barotrauma}}

What are the four major types of pneumothorax?

{{c1::Primary spontaneous}} pneumothorax
{{c1::Secondary spontaneous}} pneumothorax
{{c1::Traumatic}} pneumothorax
{{c1::Tension}} pneumothorax

What exam findings are common in all types of pneumothorax?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} tactile fremitus
{{c1::Hyperresonance::Hyperresonance/Hyporesonance}} on percussion
{{c1::Diminished}} breath sounds on the affected side

What is the likely cause of the pathology seen in a young and tall male patient who presents with pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and uneven chest expansion?

Rupture of an {{c1::apical bleb}} or {{c1::cyst}}
fields.Back Extra: This patient likely has a primary spontaneous pneumothorax.

fields.Text:
What patient populations are most susceptible to the development of a primary spontaneous pneumothorax?

{{c1::Tall::Tall/Short}}, {{c1::thin::thick/thin}} young {{c1::males::males/females}}
{{c1::Smokers}}

What is the most likely diagnosis for a mechanically ventilated patient who suddenly develops unilateral hyperresonance and diminished breath sounds?

{{c1::Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to barotrauma caused by the high pressure of the ventilator.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism associated with tension pneumothorax causing reduction in cardiac output?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} intrathoracic pressure → Mediastinal {{c1::displacement}} and {{c1::kinking}} of the inferior vena cava  → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} venous return → Decreased cardiac output

Can a primary spontaneous pneumothorax evolve into a tension pneumothorax?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}

How does a tension pneumothorax develop?

{{c1::Air}} enters {{c1::pleural}} space but cannot exit → Increased amount of trapped {{c1::air}}

What direction does the tracheal deviate in the setting of a tension pneumothorax?

{{c1::Away}} from the affected side

What is the definition of cryptogenic organizing pneumonia?

A type of {{c1::noninfectious::infectious/noninfectious}} pneumonia featuring {{c1::inflammation}} of bronchioles and surrounding structures

What pathologic finding is typically seen in interstitial pneumonia?

{{c1::Diffuse patchy inflammation}} localized to interstitial areas at the alveolar walls
fields.Back Extra: A chest X-ray will show bilateral multifocal opacities.

fields.Text:
Which type of pneumonia typically develops slowly over time compared with other types of pneumonia?
