{{c1::Interstitial}} pneumonia
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as atypical pneumonia.

fields.Text:
What are the five most common bacteria associated with pathology represented by the X-ray findings in the image?



{{c1::Mycoplasma}}
{{c1::Legionella}}
{{c1::Coxiella burnetii}}
{{c1::Chlamydophila pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Chlamydophila psittaci}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an interstitial pneumonia, evidenced by bilateral multifocal opacities.

fields.Text:
What is the characteristic histologic appearance of the type of pneumonia shown?



Acute {{c1::inflammatory infiltrates}} of the bronchioles and adjacent alveoli

What are the four most common viral causes of interstitial pneumonia?

{{c1::RSV}}
{{c1::CMV}}
{{c1::Influenza}}
{{c1::Adenovirus}}

What is the response of cryptogenic organizing pneumonia to antibiotics?

{{c1::No}} response

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with poorly controlled lupus, subacute cough, fever, and negative cultures?

{{c1::Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia}}

What four bacterial organisms are most commonly associated with bronchopneumonia?

{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
{{c1::Haemophilus influenzae}}
{{c1::Klebsiella}}

How many lobes can be involved in the type of pneumonia indicated by the biopsy findings shown?



{{c1::1}} or more

What three pathogens are the most common causes of the disease type indicated by the autopsy specimen shown?



{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Legionella}}
{{c1::Klebsiella}}

What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient with a productive cough, fever, leukocytosis, and the chest X-ray shown?



{{c1::Lobar pneumonia}}

What are the four main stages in the natural history of lobar pneumonia?

{{c1::Congestion}}
{{c1::Red hepatization}}
{{c1::Gray hepatization}}
{{c1::Resolution}}

How many days from onset of lobar pneumonia does red hepatization occur?

{{c1::3}} to {{c1::4}} days

What are the gross pathologic features of lobar pneumonia at the red hepatization phase?

{{c1::Red-brown::Color}} {{c1::consolidation}} of the lung

What are the histologic features of the exudate of lobar pneumonia at the red hepatization phase?

The exudate contains {{c1::fibrin}}, {{c1::bacteria}}, {{c1::red blood}} cells, and {{c1::white blood}} cells

How many days from onset of lobar pneumonia does gray hepatization occur?

{{c1::5}} to {{c1::7}} days

What are the gross pathologic features of lobar pneumonia at the gray hepatization phase?

Uniformly {{c1::gray::color}} {{c1::parenchyma}}

What are the histologic features of the exudate of lobar pneumonia at the gray hepatization phase?

The exudate contains lysed {{c1::red blood}} cells, {{c1::white blood}} cells, and {{c1::fibrin}}

How many days from onset of lobar pneumonia does congestion occur?

{{c1::1}} to {{c1::2}} days

What are the gross pathologic features of lobar pneumonia at the congestion phase?

{{c1::Red-purple::Color}}, partially {{c1::consolidated}} lung parenchyma

What are the histologic features of the exudate of lobar pneumonia during the congestion phase?

The exudate contains mostly {{c1::bacteria}}

How many days from onset of lobar pneumonia does resolution occur?

{{c1::8}} or more days

What are the histologic features of the exudate of lobar pneumonia at the resolution phase?

{{c1::Macrophagic}} enzymes digest components of the exudate

What are the two common types of pathogens that cause lung abscesses?

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
{{c1::Anaerobes::Aerobes/Anaerobes}}

What finding on an X-ray of the chest is highly suggestive of a lung abscess?

{{c1::Air-fluid}} levels

What are the two conditions that commonly predispose a patient to lung abscess formation?

Bronchial {{c1::obstruction}}
Oropharyngeal content {{c1::aspiration}}

What is the definition of a lung abscess?

A localized collection of {{c1::pus}} within the lung parenchyma

Which individuals are predisposed to developing the pathologic finding shown in the absence of preexisting pulmonary disease?



Individuals prone to {{c1::aspiration}} of oropharyngeal contents
fields.Back Extra: The image shows a lung abscess.

fields.Text:
Which lung is more likely to be affected by abscess formation due to aspiration?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} lung

What are the three possible treatment options for a lung abscess?

{{c1::Antibiotics}}
{{c1::Surgery}}
{{c1::Drainage}}

What is the main determinant of the location of lung abscess formation after aspiration?

The patient's {{c1::position}} during aspiration

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with a history of myoclonic epilepsy who has a productive cough, fever, and the chest X-ray findings shown?



Lung {{c1::abscess}}
fields.Back Extra: This is likely secondary to aspiration in a patient predisposed to seizures and aspiration.

fields.Text:
In which lobe of the right lung does an abscess typically form if a patient is upright during an aspiration episode?

{{c1::Lower}} lobe

In which lobes of the right lung does an abscess typically form if a patient is recumbent during an aspiration episode?

{{c1::Upper}} lobe
{{c1::Middle}} lobe

What classic histologic finding is associated with a bronchial carcinoid tumor?

Nests of {{c1::neuroendocrine}} cells that are {{c1::chromogranin A}} positive

What two types of lung cancer have generally favorable prognoses?

{{c1::Bronchial}} carcinoid tumor
{{c1::Bronchioloalveolar}} subtype of adenocarcinoma

What is the likely diagnosis given the biopsy findings shown?



{{c1::Large cell}} carcinoma of the lung
fields.Back Extra: The image shows pleomorphic giant cells.

fields.Text:
What peripherally located bronchogenic carcinoma is classically anaplastic and undifferentiated?

{{c1::Large cell}} carcinoma
fields.Back Extra: It therefore carries a poor prognosis.

fields.Text:
What features are associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the lungs?

{{c1::Cavitation}}
{{c1::Cigarettes}}
{{c1::Hypercalcemia::Hypercalcemia/Hypocalcemia}}
{{c1::Central}} location

What benign lung disease has similar X-ray findings as the bronchoalveolar subtype of adenocarcinoma?

{{c1::Pneumonia}}

What lung cancer is associated with hypertrophic osteoarthropathy?

{{c1::Adenocarcinoma}}

What is the likely diagnosis given the biopsy findings shown?



{{c1::Adenocarcinoma}} of the lung

What is the most common type of lung cancer in nonsmokers and overall?

{{c1::Adenocarcinoma}}

Which four lung cancers are considered non-small cell tumors?

{{c1::Adenocarcinoma}}
{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma
{{c1::Large cell}} carcinoma
{{c1::Bronchial}} carcinoid tumor

What paraneoplastic syndrome associated with lung cancer presents as muscle weakness that improves with activity?

{{c1::Lambert-Eaton myasthenic}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra:
This is a paraneoplastic syndrome due to antibodies against presynaptic Ca2+ channels.

This is associated with small cell carcinoma.

fields.Text:
What is the likely diagnosis given the biopsy findings shown?



{{c1::Small cell}} carcinoma

What are the common main risk factors for developing lung cancer?

{{c1::Asbestos}} exposure
{{c1::Family history}} of lung cancer
{{c1::Radon}} exposure
{{c1::Radiation}} exposure
{{c1::Smoking}}
Exposure to {{c1::secondhand smoke}}
Pulmonary {{c1::fibrosis}}

What two lung tumors most often arise in the periphery of the lung?

{{c1::Adenocarcinoma}}
{{c1::Large cell}} carcinoma

Which two body cavities typically harbor effusions as a result of lung cancer?

{{c1::Pleural}} space
{{c1::Pericardial}} space

What are the most common complications of lung cancer?

{{c1::Superior vena cava}}/{{c1::thoracic outlet}} syndromes
{{c1::Pancoast}} tumor
{{c1::Horner}} syndrome
{{c1::Endocrine}} effects
{{c1::Recurrent laryngeal}} nerve compression
{{c1::Effusions}}

What are the four most common primary sites of cancer that metastasize to the lung?

{{c1::Breast}}
{{c1::Colon}}
{{c1::Prostate}}
{{c1::Bladder}}

What is the most common malignant cause of lung masses?

{{c1::Metastases}}

What finding suggests bone metastases in a patient with primary lung cancer?

Pathologic {{c1::fractures}}

What are the four most common sites of metastases from primary lung cancer?

{{c1::Liver}}
{{c1::Adrenal}} glands
{{c1::Bone}}
{{c1::Brain}}

What are the two most common presenting X-ray findings in patients with lung cancer?

Pneumonic "{{c1::coin}}" lesions on chest X-ray
{{c1::Noncalcified::Calcified/Noncalcified}} nodules on CT of the chest

What is the likely diagnosis in a current smoker presenting with cough, wheezing, occasional hemoptysis, and a right upper lobe nodule on X-ray of the chest?

Right-sided lung {{c1::cancer}}

What type of cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States?

{{c1::Lung}} cancer

What two findings on the physical exam suggest liver metastases in a patient with lung cancer?

{{c1::Jaundice}}
{{c1::Hepatomegaly}}

How can metastases to the lung be differentiated from primary lung cancers on imaging?

Metastases often appear as {{c1::multiple::single/multiple}} lesions

How can lung cancer cause changes in a patient's voice?

Growth of tumor may result in compression of the {{c1::recurrent laryngeal}} nerve

What are the two subtypes of lung cancer associated with smoking that present with the chest X-ray findings shown?



{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma
{{c1::Small cell}} carcinoma

What is the mainstay of therapy for small cell lung cancer?

{{c1::Chemotherapy}} with or without {{c1::radiation}}
fields.Back Extra: This type of aggressive cancer is inoperable.

fields.Text:
From what type of cell is small cell carcinoma derived?

Neuroendocrine {{c1::Kulchitsky}} cells

What paraneoplastic syndrome may present with hyponatremia in a patient with lung cancer?

{{c1::SIADH}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to ectopic production of ADH by a small cell carcinoma.

fields.Text:
What paraneoplastic syndrome is typically associated with large cell lung carcinoma?

{{c1::Gynecomastia}}

How does the bronchioloalveolar subtype of adenocarcinoma appear histologically?

{{c1::Tall::Tall/Short}}, {{c1::columnar::squamous/cuboidal/columnar}} {{c1::mucus}}-containing cells growing along alveolar septa with apparent wall "{{c1::thickening}}"

How strongly is large cell carcinoma associated with smoking?

{{c1::Strongly::Strongly/Weakly}}
fields.Back Extra: Smoking is a key risk factor.

fields.Text:
What are the two main causes of symptoms in patients with a bronchial carcinoid tumor?

{{c1::Mass}} effect
{{c1::Carcinoid}} syndrome

What is a common mutation associated with the development of small cell carcinoma?

Amplification of {{c1::myc}} oncogenes

What three histologic stains are positive in small cell lung cancer?

{{c1::Chromogranin A}}
{{c1::Neuron}}-specific {{c1::enolase}}
{{c1::Synaptophysin}}

What two histologic features are seen in squamous cell carcinoma?

{{c1::Keratin pearls}}
{{c1::Intercellular bridges}}

What is the likely diagnosis given the biopsy findings shown?



{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma

What histologic features are seen in adenocarcinoma?

{{c1::Glandular}} pattern on histology that stains positive for {{c1::mucin}}

What special stain is positive in bronchial carcinoid tumor?

{{c1::Chromogranin A}}

What lung cancer is associated with Cushing syndrome?

{{c1::Small cell}} lung cancer
fields.Back Extra: This is because it may produce ACTH.

fields.Text:
What lung cancer is associated with hypercalcemia?

{{c1::Squamous cell}} lung cancer
fields.Back Extra: This is because it can produce PTHrP.

fields.Text:
What histologic findings indicate large cell carcinoma of the lung?

{{c1::Pleomorphic giant}} cells

What paraneoplastic syndromes are commonly seen in a patient with small cell lung cancer?

{{c1::Cushing}} syndrome
{{c1::SIADH}}
{{c1::Lambert-Eaton myasthenic}} syndrome
Paraneoplastic {{c1::myelitis}}
{{c1::Encephalitis}}
{{c1::Subacute cerebellar}} degeneration

What three mutations are commonly associated with adenocarcinoma of the lung?

{{c1::ALK}}
{{c1::EGFR}}
{{c1::KRAS}}

What is the most likely treatment for large cell carcinoma of the lung?

{{c1::Surgical removal}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because of a poor response to chemotherapy.

fields.Text:
How can a Pancoast tumor cause sensorimotor deficits in the upper extremity?

By compression of the {{c1::brachial plexus}}

How can a Pancoast tumor cause hoarseness?

By compression of the {{c1::recurrent laryngeal}} nerve

What three symptoms are typically seen if a Pancoast tumor disrupts the cervical sympathetic plexus at the stellate ganglion?

Ipsilateral {{c1::ptosis}}
{{c1::Miosis}}
{{c1::Anhidrosis}}

What three neurologic structures are commonly compressed by a Pancoast tumor?

{{c1::Recurrent laryngeal}} nerve
{{c1::Stellate}} ganglion
{{c1::Brachial plexus}}

What two vascular structures are commonly compressed by a Pancoast tumor?

{{c1::Superior vena cava}}
{{c1::Brachiocephalic}} vein

How can a Pancoast tumor cause unilateral congestion of the upper arm, neck, and face?

By compression of a {{c1::brachiocephalic}} vein

How can a Pancoast tumor cause plethora, venous distention, and edema of the bilateral upper extremities, head, and neck?

By compression of the {{c1::superior vena cava}}

What is the likely diagnosis given the CT scan findings shown?



{{c1::Pancoast}} tumor
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as a also known as a superior sulcus tumor.

fields.Text:
Why might a patient with Pancoast tumor have hemidiaphragm elevation on a chest X-ray?

The tumor is compressing the {{c1::phrenic}} nerve

Which three lung volumes and/or capacities cannot be measured by spirometry?

{{c1::RV}}
{{c1::FRC}}
{{c1::TLC}}

What is the definition of a capacity in the lung?

The {{c1::sum}} of 2 or more physiologic lung volumes

What term is used to define the volume of air present in the lungs after maximal inspiration?

{{c1::Total lung capacity}}

What is the term for the maximum volume of air that can be expired after maximum inspiration?

{{c1::Vital capacity}}

What is the formula for vital capacity?

{{c1::VT}} + {{c1::IRV}} + {{c1::ERV}}

What is inspiratory capacity?

The volume of gas that can be {{c1::inhaled}} after a normal exhalation

What is functional residual capacity?

The volume of gas in the lungs after normal {{c1::expiration}}

What is the term for the volume of air that remains in the lungs after maximal expiration?

{{c1::Residual volume}}

Can residual volume be measured by spirometry?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}

What is the term for the volume of air that can still be breathed out after a normal expiration?

{{c1::Expiratory reserve volume}}

What is the term for the volume of air that is breathed in during each "quiet" inspiration?

{{c1::Tidal volume}}

What is the term for the volume of air that can be breathed after a normal inspiration?

{{c1::Inspiratory reserve volume}}

On the graph provided, which lung volumes comprise total lung capacity?



{{c1::IRV}} + {{c1::VT}} + {{c1::ERV}} + {{c1::RV}}

On the graph provided, which lung volumes comprise vital capacity?



{{c1::IRV}} + {{c1::VT}} + {{c1::ERV}}

On the graph provided, which lung volumes comprise functional residual capacity?



{{c1::ERV}} + {{c1::RV}}

On the graph provided, which lung volumes comprise inspiratory capacity?



{{c1::IRV}} + {{c1::VT}}

What can contribute to a greater physiologic dead space compared to the anatomic dead space?

Lung diseases with {{c1::V/Q mismatch}}

What is the equation for determining the volume of dead space in the lungs?

VD = {{c1::VT}} × ( [ {{c1::PaCO2}} - {{c1::PECO2}} ] ÷ {{c1::PaCO2}} )

What parts of the airway contribute to the physiologic dead space?

{{c1::Anatomic}} dead space of conducting airways
{{c1::Alveolar}} dead space
fields.Back Extra: It is the inspired air volume that does not participate in gas exchange.

fields.Text:
Which region of the normal lung contributes most to physiologic alveolar dead space?

The {{c1::apex}} of the healthy lung
fields.Back Extra: This is where perfusion is lowest.

fields.Text:
A patient in the emergency department reports headache and dizziness. His skin is cherry red. He was found in his car with the engine running. What is the treatment?

{{c1::100}}% {{c1::O2}}
{{c1::Hyperbaric O2}} (severe)

Does carbon monoxide or oxygen have a greater affinity for hemoglobin?

{{c1::Carbon monoxide}}

When carbon monoxide binds to hemoglobin in place of oxygen, what are the effects on hemoglobin's oxygen-binding capacity?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} oxygen-binding capacity
fields.Back Extra: There will be a left shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, resulting in decreased unloading of O2 at the tissues.

fields.Text:
What metabolic finding is seen in a patient with cyanide poisoning?

{{c1::Anion gap metabolic acidosis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to elevated lactate.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism by which carbon monoxide and cyanide cause hypoxia?

Inhibition of {{c1::aerobic::aerobic/anaerobic}} metabolism by inhibiting complex {{c1::IV}} → Hypoxia with increased {{c1::anaerobic::aerobic/anaerobic}} metabolism
fields.Back Extra: The hypoxia is unresponsive to supplemental O2.

fields.Text:
What are the clinical manifestations common to both carbon monoxide poisoning and cyanide poisoning?

{{c1::Cherry red}} or {{c1::pink}} skin
{{c1::Headache}}
{{c1::Coma}}

Other than the direct consumption of cyanide, what are three common sources of cyanide poisoning?

Burning of {{c1::synthetic}} products
{{c1::Amygdalin}} in {{c1::apricot}} seeds
{{c1::Fire}} exposure

What is the treatment for cyanide poisoning?

{{c1::Decontamination}}
{{c1::Nitrites}}
{{c1::Hydroxocobalamin}}
{{c1::Sodium thiosulfate}}

Exposure to what toxin is classically associated with the MRI findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Carbon monoxide}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows bilateral globus pallidus lesions.

fields.Text:
What are three common sources of carbon monoxide poisoning?

{{c1::Car exhaust}}
{{c1::Gas heaters}}
{{c1::Fire}} exposure

How does hydroxocobalamin treat cyanide poisoning?

Hydroxocobalamin binds to cyanide → Formation of {{c1::cyanocobalamin}} → Renal excretion

How do nitrites treat cyanide poisoning?

Nitrites {{c1::oxidize}} hemoglobin → {{c1::Methemoglobin}} formation → Binds to cyanide → Converts to {{c1::cyanomethemoglobin}} → Reduced toxicity

How does sodium thiosulfate treat cyanide toxicity?

Increases conversion of cyanide to {{c1::thiocyanate}} → Renal excretion

What is the mechanism by which dapsone, nitrites, and benzocaine cause poisoning?

By oxidizing {{c1::Fe2+}} to {{c1::Fe3+}}, resulting in methemoglobinemia

A cyanotic patient is found to have chocolate-colored blood. What is the appropriate treatment?

{{c1::Methylene blue}}
Vitamin {{c1::C}}

What is the difference between hemoglobin and methemoglobin?

Iron in hemoglobin is in its {{c1::reduced}} form
Iron in methemoglobin is in its {{c1::oxidized}} form

In what ionization state is iron in hemoglobin normally found?

{{c1::Reduced::Oxidized/Reduced}}

Does ferric or ferrous iron have a greater affinity for oxygen?

{{c1::Ferrous}} iron

What three exposures classically cause methemoglobinemia?

{{c1::Dapsone}}
{{c1::Nitrites}}
{{c1::Benzocaine}}

In response to exercise, what happens to the venous CO2 and venous O2 content?

Venous CO2 {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}
Venous O2 {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}

What happens to PaO2 and PaCO2 in response to exercise?

{{c1::Stays the same}}
fields.Back Extra: They are maintained by homeostatic mechanisms.

fields.Text:
During exercise, does pulmonary blood flow increase, decrease, or stay the same?

{{c1::Increase}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to increased cardiac output.

fields.Text:
During exercise, what effects does increased cellular respiration have on CO2 production and tissue pH?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} CO2 production
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} pH

During exercise, what happens to the rate of ventilation?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}}
fields.Back Extra: This is to meet O2 demand and remove CO2 excess.

fields.Text:
During exercise, what happens to the V/Q ratio throughout the lungs?

The ratio {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} and becomes more uniform from base to apex

During exercise, what alterations can be seen in heart rate, stroke volume, and cardiac output?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} heart rate
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} stroke volume
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} cardiac output

What shift of the oxygen dissociation curve occurs in response to exercise?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} shift

The increased renal excretion of bicarbonate that is seen in response to high altitude can be augmented by using which drug?

{{c1::Acetazolamide}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used to treat altitude sickness.

fields.Text:
Increased renal excretion of what substance occurs in response to high altitudes?

Renal excretion of {{c1::bicarbonate}} increases
fields.Back Extra: This is to compensate for respiratory alkalosis.

fields.Text:
Which cellular organelles in healthy human tissues increase in quantity at high altitudes?

{{c1::Mitochondria}}
fields.Back Extra: This is to promote greater aerobic efficiency.

fields.Text:
Mention five symptoms that patients with altitude sickness can present with.

{{c1::Nausea}}
{{c1::Fatigue}}
{{c1::Headaches}}
{{c1::Lightheadedness}}
{{c1::Sleep}} disturbance

What happens to 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate during high-altitude exposure?

It {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}
fields.Back Extra: This results in a right shift in the oxyhemoglobin-dissociation curve.

fields.Text:
What happens to erythropoetin levels in response to high altitude?

Erythropoietin levels are {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to chronic hypoxia.

fields.Text:
At high altitude where there is low atmospheric oxygen, what happens to ventilation, PaO2, and PaCO2?

Ventilation {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}
PaO2 {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
PaCO2 {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
fields.Back Extra: This leads to respiratory alkalosis and can result in altitude sickness.

fields.Text:
What is the primary acid-base disturbance characterizing altitude sickness?

{{c1::Respiratory alkalosis}}

What are two long-term effects on the cardiopulmonary system resulting from living at extremely high altitudes?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::ventricular::atrial/ventricular}} {{c1::hypertrophy::hypertrophy/hypotrophy}}
Pulmonary {{c1::hypertension::hypertension/hypotension}}

What parts of a neuron are seen with Nissl staining and why?

{{c1::Cell bodies}} and {{c1::dendrites}} are stained because they contain {{c1::rough endoplasmic reticulum}}

Identify the parts of a neuron that receive input and send output.

{{c1::Dendrites}} receive input
{{c1::Axons}} transmit output

What is the cell division potential of a fully mature neuron?

They are {{c1::permanent}} cells and do not divide in {{c1::adulthood}}

What markers are associated with neurons?

{{c1::Synaptophysin}}
{{c1::Neurofilament}} protein

How does the cell shown in the image classically respond to neural injury?



{{c1::Reactive gliosis}}

From what germinal layer do astrocytes arise?

{{c1::Neuroectoderm}}

Which glial cell type is the most common in the central nervous system, with functions such as support, repair, and contributing to the blood-brain barrier?

{{c1::Astrocytes}}

What marker is associated with astrocytes?

{{c1::GFAP}}

What is the main function of the glial cell shown in the image?



{{c1::Phagocytosis}}
Release of {{c1::inflammatory}} mediators in the setting of tissue damage in the central nervous system

What is the embryologic origin of microglia?

{{c1::Mesoderm}}

Which brain cells act as the phagocytic scavenger cells of the central nervous system?

{{c1::Microglia}}
fields.Back Extra: They become large phagocytic cells when activated.

fields.Text:
How do HIV-infected microglia cells appear histologically in patients with HIV-associated dementia?

{{c1::Multinucleated giant}} cells

What two structures in the central nervous system are lined by ependymal cells?

{{c1::Ventricles}}
{{c1::Central canal}} of the spinal cord

What are the respective functions of cilia and microvilli in ependymal cells?

{{c1::Cilia}} → Circulate cerebrospinal fluid
{{c1::Microvilli}} → Assist with cerebrospinal fluid absorption

Histologically, how do ependymal cells appear?

{{c1::Ciliated::Ciliated/Nonciliated}} {{c1::simple::simple/stratified}} {{c1::columnar::squamous/cuboidal/columnar}} cells

What cell type in the brain is responsible for the production of cerebrospinal fluid?

Specialized {{c1::ependymal}} cells in the choroid plexus

What is indicated by the red arrow in the electron micrograph showing an axon in cross-section?



{{c1::Myelin}}

What cell types produce myelin in the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system?

Central nervous system → {{c1::Oligodendrocytes}}
Peripheral nervous system → {{c1::Schwann}} cells

What does myelin do to an axon's space constant, conduction velocity, membrane resistance, and membrane capacitance?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} space constant
{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} conduction velocity
{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} membrane resistance
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} membrane capacitance

What role does myelin play in neuronal activity?

Myelin forms an {{c1::insulating}} sheath around a neuron's axon to {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} conduction velocity of action potentials

How does myelin increase conduction velocity down an axon?

It promotes {{c1::saltatory}} conduction at the {{c1::nodes of Ranvier}} where concentrations of {{c1::Na+}} channels are high

Which cranial nerves are myelinated as part of the central nervous system and peripheral nervous system?

Central nervous system → Cranial nerve {{c1::II}}
Peripheral nervous system → Cranial nerves {{c1::III}} to {{c1::XII}}

What is the embryologic origin of Schwann cells?

{{c1::Neural crest}}

What are the two main functions of Schwann cells?

{{c1::Myelination}} of axons in the peripheral nervous system
Promotion of axonal {{c1::regeneration}} after injury

Which component in the image is injured in Guillain-Barré syndrome?



{{c1::Schwann}} cell

How many axons does each Schwann cell myelinate?

{{c1::1}} peripheral nervous system axon

What is the cell marker for Schwann cells?

{{c1::S100}}

What part of the body is covered by the L4 dermatome?

{{c1::Kneecaps}}

What dermatome represents the area of pain that is experienced early on in appendicitis?

{{c1::T10}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to dull pain referred to the umbilicus.

fields.Text:
Which nerve roots are involved in the sensation from the penile regions?

{{c1::S2}} to {{c1::S4}}

Which nerve root innervates the dermatome at the level of the xiphoid process?

{{c1::T7}}

What area of the body is covered by the T4 dermatome?

{{c1::Nipples}}

Which dermatome relays sensation from the thumb?

{{c1::C6}}

What nerve root provides sensory innervation in the neck in the distribution of a high turtleneck shirt?

{{c1::C3}}

Which nerve root provides sensory innervation along the edge of the jaw and over the mastoid and back of the head?

{{c1::C2}}

Serotonin, dopamine, and neurokinin receptor antagonists are used to treat vomiting induced by what kind of treatment?

{{c1::Chemotherapy}}

Antagonists to which 2 receptors can treat motion sickness?

{{c1::Muscarinic}} receptors
{{c1::Histamine}} receptors

Antagonists to which receptors are used to treat hyperemesis gravidarum?

{{c1::Histamine}} receptors

In addition to repeated nighttime and early morning awakenings, how does depression affect sleep? Specify its effects on REM and N3 stages of sleep.

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} duration of REM sleep
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} REM latency
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} duration of stage N3

What hormone is likely deficient in a patient who lacks a pineal gland?

{{c1::Melatonin}}
fields.Back Extra: This is released by the pineal gland in response to norepinephrine from the suprachiasmatic nucleus.

fields.Text:
The circadian rhythm controls the nocturnal release of what 4 hormones?

{{c1::ACTH}}
{{c1::Melatonin}}
{{c1::Norepinephrine}}
{{c1::Prolactin}}

What environmental stimulus regulates the suprachiasmatic nucleus?

{{c1::Light}}

Which nucleus of the hypothalamus drives circadian rhythm?

The {{c1::suprachiasmatic nucleus}} of the hypothalamus

Describe the changes in physiology with REM sleep, including the effects on the heart, acetylcholine levels, brain oxygen use, and sex organs.

{{c1::Increased}} and {{c1::variable}} heart rate and blood pressure
{{c1::Increased}} acetylcholine levels
{{c1::Increased}} brain oxygen use
{{c1::Increased}} penile/clitoral tumescence

What is a possible treatment for night terrors, and what is the mechanism?

{{c1::Benzodiazepines}}, which can reduce the duration of {{c1::slow-wave}} sleep

Which brain area is responsible for the rapid eye movements of REM sleep?

{{c1::Paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF)}}

How does norepinephrine affect melatonin release and the sleep cycle?

It {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} secretion of melatonin in response to stimulus from the {{c1::suprachiasmatic nucleus}}, but {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} REM sleep

How do alcohol, benzodiazepines, and barbiturates interfere with sleep?

By {{c1::decreasing::increasing/decreasing}} REM and delta wave sleep, thus {{c1::lowering}} sleep quality

What EEG waveform would you expect to see in a man meditating with his eyes closed?

{{c1::Alpha}} waves

During what stage of sleep do loss of motor tone and vivid dreams usually occur?

{{c1::REM}} sleep

During what stage of sleep do sleepwalking, night terrors, and bedwetting typically occur?

Stage {{c1::N3}}

A 23-year-old woman grinds her teeth while sleeping. During what stage of sleep does this usually occur?

Stage {{c1::N2}}

Assuming a 20-year-old man has perfect sleep habits, what percentage of time is spent in N1, N2, N3, and REM sleep?

N1 → {{c1::5}}%
N2 → {{c1::45}}%
N3 → {{c1::25}}%
REM → {{c1::25}}%

What are the EEG waveforms associated with the following stages of sleep?

Awake state (eyes open) → {{c1::Beta}}
Awake state (eyes closed) → {{c1::Alpha}}
N1 → {{c1::Theta}}
N2 → {{c1::Sleep spindles}} and {{c1::K complexes}}
N3 → {{c1::Delta}}
REM → {{c1::Beta}}

How does the duration of REM sleep change through the night?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} with each sleep cycle

How often do REM sleep cycles occur?

Every {{c1::90}} minutes

What 4 changes to the sleep stages can be seen in an elderly patient?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} duration of REM sleep
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} duration of stage N3
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} sleep latency
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} early awakenings

How does narcolepsy affect REM sleep?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} REM latency

What transports ADH and oxytocin from the hypothalamus to the posterior pituitary, where these hormones are stored and released?

{{c1::Neurophysins}}

Where in the hypothalamus are the hormones ADH and oxytocin produced?

ADH is produced in the {{c1::supraoptic}} nucleus
Oxytocin is produced in the {{c1::paraventricular}} nucleus

What are the 7 major functions of the hypothalamus?

{{c1::Thirst}}
{{c1::Adenohypophysis}}
{{c1::Neurohypophysis}}
{{c1::Hunger}}
{{c1::Autonomic::Somatic/Autonomic}} nervous system
{{c1::Temperature}}
{{c1::Sexual}} urges

Which region of the hypothalamus regulates parasympathetic activity and induces you to cool off?

{{c1::Anterior}} nucleus

Which part of the hypothalamus regulates sleep and the circadian rhythm?

{{c1::Suprachiasmatic}} nucleus

How might a hypothalamic mass compressing the ventromedial nucleus present in a young patient?

{{c1::Hyperphagia}}

Which part of the hypothalamus regulates sympathetic activity and makes you to feel warm?

{{c1::Posterior nucleus}}

What hormone regulates the ventromedial nucleus's function?

{{c1::Leptin}} stimulates it

What area of the hypothalamus induces the sensation of satiety?

{{c1::Ventromedial}} nucleus

An infant is born with hypoplastic lateral hypothalamic nuclei. How does this condition manifest?

Failure to {{c1::thrive}}

What 2 hormones regulate the lateral nucleus of the hypothalamus?

{{c1::Ghrelin}} stimulates
{{c1::Leptin}} inhibits

What area of the hypothalamus mediates hunger by stimulating the appetite?

{{c1::Lateral}} nucleus

Name the 2 inputs to the hypothalamus.

{{c1::Area postrema}}
{{c1::Organum vasculosum lamina terminalis (OVLT)}}

What are the 3 functions of the preoptic nucleus in the hypothalamus?

Release of {{c1::GnRH}}
{{c1::Sexual}} behavior
{{c1::Thermoregulation}}

What is Kallman syndrome?

A form of {{c1::hypogonadotropic hypogonadism}} due to the failure of {{c1::GnRH}}-producing neurons to migrate from the olfactory pit to the preoptic nucleus

Which areas supplying input to the hypothalamus lack protection from the blood-brain barrier?

{{c1::Organum vasculosum lamina terminalis (OVLT)}}
{{c1::Area postrema}}

What are the functions of the organum vasculosum lamina terminalis (OVLT) and area postrema with relation to the hypothalamus?

OVLT senses changes in {{c1::osmolarity}}
Area postrema responds to {{c1::emetics}}

To what structure do axons from the ventral anterior nuclei and ventral lateral nuclei of the thalamus project?

{{c1::Motor cortices}}

From what 2 structures do the ventral anterior nuclei and ventral lateral nuclei of the thalamus receive inputs?

{{c1::Basal ganglia}}
{{c1::Cerebellum}}

What sense is relayed by the ventral anterior nuclei and ventral lateral nuclei of the thalamus?

{{c1::Motor}}

To what structure do axons from the ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus project?

{{c1::Primary somatosensory cortex}}

From what 2 pathways does the ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus receive input?

{{c1::Trigeminal}} pathway
{{c1::Gustatory}} pathway

What sensory information is relayed by the ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus?

{{c1::Face}} sensation
{{c1::Taste}}

What 2 structures provide input to the ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus?

{{c1::Spinothalamic}} tract
{{c1::Dorsal column}}/{{c1::medial lemniscus}}

What sensory information is relayed by the ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus?

{{c1::Vibration}}
{{c1::Pain}}
{{c1::Pressure}}
{{c1::Proprioception}}
{{c1::Light}} touch
{{c1::Temperature}}

To what structures do axons of the medial geniculate nucleus project?

{{c1::Primary auditory cortex}}

From what 2 structures does the medial geniculate nucleus receive input?

{{c1::Superior olive}}
{{c1::Inferior colliculus of tectum}}

What sensory information is relayed by the medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus?

{{c1::Hearing}}

The thalamus relays all ascending sensory information to the cortex except for what?

{{c1::Olfaction}}

To what structures do axons from the lateral geniculate nucleus project?

Axons project to the {{c1::primary visual cortex}}

From what structures does the lateral geniculate nucleus receive input?

Cranial nerve {{c1::II}} → {{c1::Optic chiasm}} → {{c1::Optic tracts}} → Thalamus

What sensory information is relayed by the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus?

{{c1::Vision}}

In the image, identify the structures indicated by the red and yellow arrows.



Red arrows mark the {{c1::hippocampus}}
Yellow arrows mark the {{c1::cingulate gyri}}

What are the 5 functions of the limbic system?

{{c1::Feeding}}
{{c1::Fleeing}}
{{c1::Fighting}}
{{c1::Feeling}}
{{c1::Sex}}

The hippocampus, amygdalae, anterior thalamic nuclei, mammillary bodies, cingulate gyrus, and entorhinal cortex make up what system?

{{c1::Limbic}} system

Altered activity of what dopaminergic pathway can lead to gynecomastia in males?

{{c1::Tuberoinfundibular}} pathway

What is the major dopaminergic pathway in the brain?

{{c1::Nigrostriatal}} pathway

Why do antipsychotics often cause galactorrhea and decreased libido?

They block the {{c1::tuberoinfundibular}} pathway, which leads to increased release of prolactin and decreased libido

Which dopaminergic pathway is responsible for hormonal symptoms such as decreased libido and galactorrhea?

{{c1::Tuberoinfundibular}} pathway

What is the function of the nigrostriatal dopaminergic pathway?

Control of {{c1::movement}}

Which dopaminergic pathway is responsible for parkinsonism and other major movement disorders?

{{c1::Nigrostriatal}} pathway

What dopaminergic pathway and symptoms are most resistant to antipsychotic drugs?

{{c1::Mesocortical}} pathway

What is the desired effect of antipsychotic drugs in the mesolimbic pathway?

Inhibition of the pathway to block "{{c1::positive}}" symptoms

What dopaminergic pathway is the primary therapeutic target of antipsychotic drugs?

{{c1::Mesolimbic}} pathway

Which dopaminergic pathway leads to "positive" symptoms, and how?

{{c1::Mesolimbic}} pathway, through {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} dopamine activity

Which dopaminergic pathway leads to "negative" symptoms, and how?

{{c1::Mesocortical}} pathway, through {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} dopamine activity

What are the names of the 4 dopaminergic pathways in the brain?

{{c1::Mesocortical}} pathway
{{c1::Mesolimbic}} pathway
{{c1::Nigrostriatal}} pathway
{{c1::Tuberoinfundibular}} pathway

What are the downstream consequences of decreasing dopamine activity in the nigrostriatal dopaminergic pathway?

{{c1::Extrapyramidal}} symptoms

From lateral to medial, what are the 4 deep nuclei of the cerebellum?

{{c1::Dentate}}
{{c1::Emboliform}}
{{c1::Globose}}
{{c1::Fastigial}}

A patient has head tilting, wide gait, and nystagmus. Where in the cerebellum is the lesion likely to be?

{{c1::Medial::Medial/Lateral}} cerebellum

Ipsilateral proprioceptive information is sent to what structure of the cerebellum?

{{c1::Inferior cerebellar peduncle}}

Describe the path of outputting information from the cerebellar cortex to the contralateral motor cortex.

Cerebellar cortex via {{c1::Purkinje}} cells → {{c1::Deep cerebellar nuclei}} → {{c1::Superior cerebellar peduncle}} → Contralateral motor cortex

Voluntary movements are relayed to the cerebullum by the contralateral cortex via what structure?

{{c1::Middle cerebellar peduncle}}

To what brain structures do the Purkinje cells of the cerebellum project?

{{c1::Deep cerebellar nuclei}}

What are the output neurons of the cerebellar cortex?

{{c1::Purkinje}} cells

Recurrent falls to the left side indicate a lesion in which location of the cerebellum?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::lateral::medial/lateral}} cerebellum

An active subthalamic nucleus will directly stimulate which structure? Does this ultimately promote or decrease movement?

The {{c1::globus pallidus interna}}, which {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} movement
fields.Back Extra: This is via increased inhibitory output to the thalamus.

fields.Text:
An active globus pallidus externa will directly inhibit which structure? Does this ultimately promote or decrease movement?

The {{c1::subthalamic nucleus}}, which {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} movement
fields.Back Extra: This is via reduced stimulatory output to the globus pallidus interna.

fields.Text:
An active globus pallidus interna will directly inhibit which structure? Does this ultimately promote or decrease movement?

The {{c1::thalamus}}, which {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} movement
fields.Back Extra: This is via reduced stimulatory output to the cortex.

fields.Text:
Dopamine unbinds from D2 receptors in the striatum. What happens within the indirect pathway to decrease movement?

Striatal {{c1::GABA}} increases → {{c1::Globus pallidus externus}} inhibited → {{c1::Subthalamic nucleus}} disinhibited → {{c1::Globus pallidus internus}} stimulated → {{c1::Thalamus}} and {{c1::cortex}} inhibited → Movement decreases

Dopamine binds to D2 receptors in the striatum. What happens downstream in the indirect pathway to promote movement?

Striatal {{c1::GABA}} decreases → {{c1::Globus pallidus externus}} disinhibited → {{c1::Subthalamic nucleus}} inhibited → {{c1::Globus pallidus internus}} inactivated → {{c1::Thalamus}} disinhibited → {{c1::Cortex}} stimulated → Movement promoted

Dopamine binds to D1 receptors in the striatum. What happens downstream in the direct pathway to promote movement?

Striatum inhibits the {{c1::globus pallidus interna}} → Disinhibition of the {{c1::thalamus}} → Stimulation of the {{c1::cortex}} → Promotion of movement

If the subthalamic nucleus is stimulated, what happens to the thalamus and cortex? What happens to movement?

Subthalamic nucleus stimulates the {{c1::globus pallidus interna}} → {{c1::Inhibition::Stimulation/Inhibition}} of the thalamus and cortex → {{c1::Prevention}} of movement

If the globus pallidus internus is stimulated, what happens to the thalamus and cortex? What happens to movement?

Stimulation of the globus pallidus internus → {{c1::Inhibition::Stimulation/Inhibition}} of the thalamus and cortex → {{c1::Prevention}} of movement

Where in the basal ganglia are D2 receptors chiefly found?

{{c1::Striatum}}
fields.Back Extra: They function to disinhibit movement when acted on by nigrostriatal dopamine.

fields.Text:
Dopamine from which area binds D2 receptors in the striatum? Does this stimulate or inhibit movement? Specify direct or indirect pathway.

The {{c1::substantia nigra pars compacta}}, which {{c1::stimulates::stimulates/inhibits}} movement via inhibition of the {{c1::indirect::direct/indirect}} pathway

Where in the basal ganglia are D1 receptors chiefly found?

{{c1::Striatum}}
fields.Back Extra: They function to stimulate movement when acted on by nigrostriatal dopamine.

fields.Text:
Dopamine from which area binds D1 receptors in the striatum? Does this stimulate or inhibit movement? Specify direct or indirect pathway.

The {{c1::substantia nigra pars compacta}}, which {{c1::stimulates::stimulates/inhibits}} movement via the {{c1::direct::direct/indirect}} pathway

How does the cortex modulate the striatum in the indirect pathway to stop movements?

The cortex {{c1::stimulates::stimulates/inhibits}} the striatum

How does the cortex modulate the direct dopaminergic pathway to initiate movement?

The cortex stimulates the {{c1::striatum}} → Inhibition of the {{c1::globus pallidus interna}} → Disinhibition of the {{c1::thalamus}} → Generation of movement

What neurotransmitter is used by the substantia nigra pars compacta to modulate the direct and indirect pathways in the basal ganglia?

{{c1::Dopamine}}

What neurotransmitter is released by the striatum to inhibit the globus pallidus interna or globus pallidus externa?

{{c1::GABA}}

What do the putamen and globus pallidus make up?

{{c1::Lentiform nucleus}}

What are the 2 areas of the striatum, and how does each function in movement and cognition?

The {{c1::caudate nucleus}} is involved in cognitive aspects of motion
The {{c1::putamen}} guides motor learning and performance

Which brain area is important in voluntary movement and postural adjustments?

{{c1::Basal ganglia}}

If the globus pallidus externus is stimulated, what happens to the thalamus and cortex? What happens to movement?

Stimulation of globus pallidus externus inhibits the {{c1::subthalamic nucleus}} → Prevents {{c1::globus pallidus interna}} stimulation → {{c1::Stimulates::Stimulates/Inhibits}} the thalamus and cortex → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} movement

What effect does the striatum have on the globus pallidus externa in the indirect pathway?

The striatum {{c1::inhibits::stimulates/inhibits}} the globus pallidus externa

In the indirect pathway, what happens to the subthalamic nucleus when the striatum inhibits the globus pallidus externa?

Globus pallidus externa {{c1::disinhibits}} the subthalamic nucleus → Stimulation of the {{c1::globus pallidus interna}}

Where in the brain is the primary visual cortex found?

{{c1::Occipital}} lobe

A patient has a large lesion affecting the primary auditory cortex. What adjacent language processing area may also be affected?

{{c1::Wernicke}} area

A stroke affecting the most anterior part of the temporal lobe will lead to dysfunction in which area?

{{c1::Limbic association}} area

A patient with a parietal lobe stroke cannot repeat a phrase. Why might a stroke affecting the parietal lobe lead to aphasia?

The {{c1::arcuate fasciculus}} passes through the parietal lobe

What parietal lobe cortex is found directly posterior to the primary somatosensory cortex?

{{c1::Somatosensory association}} cortex

What are the 2 cortical areas linked by the arcuate fasciculus? What are their functions?

{{c1::Wernicke}} area → Language comprehension
{{c1::Broca}} area → Speech production

What lobes are associated with the premotor cortex, primary motor cortex, frontal eye fields, and Broca area, respectively?

All are found in the {{c1::frontal}} lobe

In what lobes are the primary visual cortex, primary auditory cortex, primary sensory cortex, and frontal eye fields found, respectively?

{{c1::Occipital}} lobe → Primary visual cortex
{{c1::Temporal}} lobe → Primary auditory cortex
{{c1::Parietal}} lobe → Primary sensory cortex
{{c1::Frontal}} lobe → Frontal eye fields

What frontal lobe cortex is found directly anterior to the primary motor cortex?

{{c1::Premotor}} cortex

Which 2 lobes are separated by the Sylvian fissure?

{{c1::Frontal}} lobe
{{c1::Temporal}} lobe

Which 2 lobes are separated by the central sulcus?

{{c1::Frontal}} lobe
{{c1::Parietal}} lobe

A patient with multiple sclerosis has left-sided nystagmus and right-sided failure of eye adduction on looking left. Where is the lesion?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::medial longitudinal fasciculus}}

What three underlying conditions can cause Parinaud syndrome?

{{c1::Hydrocephalus}}
{{c1::Stroke}}
{{c1::Pineal gland}} tumors

A patient presents with an inability to look up with both eyes. What brain region is likely damaged?

{{c1::Dorsal midbrain}}

A patient with headaches, hostility, and poor decision making and concentration has bilateral Babinski signs. Where is the lesion?

{{c1::Frontal}} lobe
fields.Back Extra: This governs executive function and inhibits primitive reflexes.

fields.Text:
What brain lesion causes sudden hyperoral, hypersexual, and uninhibited behavior with a positive cerebrospinal fluid polymerase chain reaction for HSV-1?

{{c1::Bilateral amygdala}} lesions
fields.Back Extra: The patient has Klüver-Bucy syndrome, which is associated with HSV-1 encephalitis.

fields.Text:
What is the most likely cause of confabulation, nystagmus, and gait disturbance in an alcoholic?

{{c1::Wernicke-Korsakoff}} syndrome

In what direction will the eyes deviate in a patient with a left-sided paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) lesion?

To the {{c1::right::left/right}}

A patient has a lesion in the left frontal eye fields. Where do his eyes look in relation to the lesion?

Toward the {{c1::left::left/right}}

A patient loses the ability to make new memories. Where is the brain lesion?

{{c1::Hippocampus}}

Where is the lesion in a patient who repetitively flails his left arm and leg when he tries to move either of them?

{{c1::Hemiballismus}} due to a lesion in the {{c1::right::left/right}} {{c1::subthalamic nucleus}}

In a patient with a long history of alcohol abuse, what pathologic cerebellar symptoms would be expected?

{{c1::Truncal ataxia}}
{{c1::Nystagmus}}
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by degeneration of the cerebellar vermis.

fields.Text:
Damage to what part of the brain causes a wide-based gait and slurred speech?

{{c1::Cerebellar vermis}}

On which side of the body are the deficits in tumor of the right cerebellar hemisphere?

{{c1::Right}} side

Lesion in what part of the brain causes left-sided intention tremor and limb ataxia?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::cerebellar hemisphere}}

What three disorders are classically related to dysfunction of the basal ganglia?

{{c1::Parkinson}} disease and related {{c1::parkinsonian}} syndromes
{{c1::Huntington}} disease
{{c1::Wilson}} disease

Lesion in what part of the brain causes chorea and athetosis?

{{c1::Basal ganglia}}

A coma due to a brainstem stroke has most likely affected what specific region of the brain?

{{c1::Reticular activating}} system

What is the syndrome and where is the brain lesion that causes left-right disorientation, finger agnosia, acalculia, and agraphia?

{{c1::Gerstmann}} syndrome, which is due to a lesion in the {{c1::dominant parietal cortex}}

Name the syndrome and site of the brain lesion that causes agnosia of the left side of the world.

{{c1::Hemispatial neglect}} syndrome, which is due to a lesion in the {{c1::nondominant parietal cortex}}

Where is the lesion in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome?

{{c1::Mammillary bodies}}

What are the features of Parinaud syndrome?

Pupillary {{c1::light-near dissociation}}
Lid {{c1::retraction}}
{{c1::Vertical}} gaze palsy
{{c1::Convergence-retraction}} nystagmus

A patient with a stroke involving the motor tracts in the cortex will show what type of posturing on the contralateral side?

{{c1::Decorticate}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because the lesion is above the red nucleus.

fields.Text:
Where is the lesion in a patient with decorticate posturing?

{{c1::Above}} the {{c1::red nucleus}}

How does decorticate posturing present?

{{c1::Flexion::Flexion/Extension}} of upper extremities
{{c1::Extension::Flexion/Extension}} of lower extremities

Where is the lesion in a patient with decerebrate posturing?

{{c1::Below}} the {{c1::red nucleus}}

How does decerebrate posturing present?

{{c1::Extension::Flexion/Extension}} of upper extremities
{{c1::Extension::Flexion/Extension}} of lower extremities

What two treatments may be offered to a patient with hyperacusis, diminished taste sensation, and facial paralysis as shown?



{{c1::Glucocorticoids}} with or without {{c1::acyclovir}}

What is the pathologic cause of a facial nerve palsy?

Complete destruction of the {{c1::facial nucleus}} or its {{c1::branchial efferent}} fibers

What syndrome describes unilateral facial paralysis and vesicles on the face after reactivation of herpes zoster infection?

{{c1::Ramsay Hunt}} syndrome

Name five common causes of cranial nerve VII palsy.

{{c1::Lyme}} disease
{{c1::Sarcoidosis}}
{{c1::Ramsay Hunt}} syndrome
{{c1::Tumors}}
{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}

In Bell palsy, where do the facial symptoms arise relative to the location of the lesion?

The facial findings occur on the side {{c1::ipsilateral}} to the lesion

A patient has left lower facial paralysis but can raise his eyebrows bilaterally. Where is the lesion causing these findings?

This is an {{c1::upper motor neuron}} lesion
fields.Back Extra: This affects either the right motor cortex or a connection between the cortex and the facial nucleus in the pons.

fields.Text:
A patient has facial drooping that affects the right side of the forehead and cheek. Where is the lesion causing these findings?

This is a {{c1::lower motor neuron}} lesion of the {{c1::right::left/right}} {{c1::facial}} nerve

Facial expression of the upper face is controlled by the facial nerve. What area of the cerebral cortex sends upper motor neuron signaling to the right upper face?

The {{c1::ipsilateral}} and {{c1::contralateral}} areas of the cerebral cortex

What is the most common variant of peripheral facial palsy?

{{c1::Bell palsy}}

How does Bell palsy most commonly occur?

Usually due to {{c1::HSV}} reactivation

What is the prognosis for a patient with Bell palsy?

Most patients {{c1::recover}} function {{c1::gradually}}

The forehead is involved in which types of lesions of the facial nerve?

{{c1::Lower motor neuron}} facial nerve lesions
fields.Back Extra: The forehead is spared with upper motor neuron lesions due to bilateral upper motor neuron innervation.

fields.Text:
Which side of the face is affected by upper motor neuron and lower motor neuron lesions of the facial nerve, respectively?

Upper motor neuron lesions affect the {{c1::contralateral}} side
Lower motor neuron lesions affect the {{c1::ipsilateral}} side

Why do dry eyes and corneal ulceration occur in a patient with a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve?

Incomplete eye {{c1::closure}}

In addition to facial findings, what other symptoms do patients with lower motor neuron facial palsies often report?

Loss of {{c1::taste}} in the {{c1::anterior}} tongue
{{c1::Hyperacusis}}

Which muscles are involved in an upper motor neuron lesion of facial nerve?

Contralateral {{c1::lower}} muscles of {{c1::facial expression}}

Which muscles are involved in a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve?

Ipsilateral {{c1::upper}} and {{c1::lower}} muscles of {{c1::facial expression}}

In which type of conditioning is a natural response elicited by a conditioned stimulus, which was previously presented with an unconditioned stimulus?

{{c1::Classical}} conditioning

In Pavlov's classical conditioning experiment, when you ring a bell, a dog salivates. What is the unconditioned stimulus?

{{c1::Food}}

In Pavlov's classical conditioning experiment, when you ring a bell, a dog salivates. What is the learned/conditioned stimulus?

{{c1::Bell}}

How do classical and operant conditioning differ with respect to voluntariness to complete the action involved?

Classical conditioning is usually {{c1::involuntary::voluntary/involuntary}}
Operant conditioning is usually {{c1::voluntary::voluntary/involuntary}}

What is the effect in which removal of positive reinforcement eventually leads to elimination of behavior?

{{c1::Extinction}}

How do positive punishment and negative reinforcement differ in operant conditioning?

Applying an aversive stimulus to {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} behavior is positive punishment
Removing an aversive stimulus to {{c1::encourage::encourage/discourage}} behavior is negative reinforcement

What type of operant conditioning leads to repeat injection of a drug that produces euphoria in the user?

{{c1::Positive reinforcement}}

What is operant conditioning?

{{c1::Learning}} in which a specific action is elicited because it leads to a {{c1::reward}} or {{c1::punishment}}

What term describes the behavior of a physician projecting feelings about a formative or other important individual, such as a younger sibling, onto a patient?

{{c1::Countertransference}}

What term describes the behavior of a patient projecting feelings about a formative or other important individual, such as a parent, onto a physician?

{{c1::Transference}}

A man with cancer constantly reminds his family about his rate of survival and chances of successful treatment. Define this ego defense.

{{c1::Intellectualization}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an immature ego defense in which one uses facts and logic to achieve emotional distance from a stressful situation.

fields.Text:
What ego defense is believing that people are either all good or all bad at different times?

{{c1::Splitting}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an immature ego defense.

fields.Text:
In what ego defense is there a subconscious method of coping with stress or conflict in which actions take the place of reflection or expression of feelings?

{{c1::Acting out}}

Define the ego defense known as projection.

A(n) {{c1::immature::mature/immature}} ego defense in which one's own unacceptable feelings or beliefs are attributed to {{c1::someone}} or {{c1::something else}}

What are the four mature ego defenses?

{{c1::Sublimation}}
{{c1::Altruism}}
{{c1::Suppression}}
{{c1::Humor}}

What mature ego defense is evoked when an individual voluntarily blocks an idea or feeling from their own awareness?

{{c1::Suppression}}

Differentiate between sublimation and reaction formation.

Sublimation → {{c1::Redirecting}} feelings into similar but socially acceptable actions
Reaction formation → {{c1::Replacing}} a feeling deemed unacceptable with actions emphasizing its opposite

Define the ego defense of sublimation.

A(n) {{c1::mature::mature/immature}} ego defense in which an unacceptable desire is addressed by behavior that channels the desire in a {{c1::socially acceptable}} way

Describe humor as an ego defense.

A(n) {{c1::mature::mature/immature}} ego defense in which {{c1::amusement}} in an anxiety-provoking situation is used to diffuse the pressure

What personality disorder is the ego defense splitting associated with?

{{c1::Borderline}} personality disorder

Describe the ego defense altruism. Is it considered mature or immature?

A(n) {{c1::mature::mature/immature}} defense where negative emotions are alleviated through acts of {{c1::unsolicited generosity}} toward others, leading to {{c1::gratification}}

In terms of voluntariness and maturity, how does repression differ from suppression?

Repression is {{c1::involuntary::voluntary/involuntary}} and {{c1::immature::mature/immature}}
Suppression is {{c1::voluntary::voluntary/involuntary}}, intentional, and {{c1::mature::mature/immature}}

Define the ego defense known as reaction formation.

A(n) {{c1::immature::mature/immature}} ego defense in which a warded-off idea or feeling is replaced with an emphasis on the {{c1::opposite}} idea or feeling

Which ego defense is a largely unconscious, immature ego defense in which one assumes traits or qualities of another person or group?

{{c1::Identification}}

Define the ego defense isolation of affect.

{{c1::Immature::Mature/Immature}} defense in which the memory of an unacceptable act is {{c1::separated}} from the emotion associated with it

Is asserting plausible explanations for events that occurred for other reasons a mature or immature ego defense?

{{c1::Immature::Mature/Immature}} ego defense

Differentiate between fixation and regression as ego defenses.

Fixation is partially remaining at a more {{c1::childish}} level of development
Regression is involuntarily returning to less {{c1::mature}} behavior in {{c1::stressful}} situations

What type of ego defense is an immature ego defense in which someone expresses very positive thoughts about self and others but ignores negative thoughts?

{{c1::Idealization}}

Define fixation as an ego defense and indicate whether it is a mature or immature defense.

A(n) {{c1::immature::mature/immature}} ego defense wherein a person partially remains at a more {{c1::childish}} level of development

What ego defense is avoiding awareness of some painful reality?

{{c1::Denial}}

Define displacement as an ego defense.

The {{c1::redirection}} of impulses or feelings toward an {{c1::object}} or {{c1::person}} unrelated to an inciting event

What ego defense is an indirect show of opposition by failing to meet expectations?

{{c1::Passive aggression}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an immature ego defense.

fields.Text:
What is an ego defense?

An involuntary or voluntary {{c1::behavior}} or {{c1::mental}} process used to resolve conflict and prevent unpleasant feelings

Which ego defense involves emulating the behavior of another person or group, and is it immature or mature?

{{c1::Identification}}, which is a(n) {{c1::immature::mature/immature}} ego defense

What are the five stages of grief a person will likely go through according to the Kübler-Ross model?

{{c1::Denial}}
{{c1::Anger}}
{{c1::Bargaining}}
{{c1::Depression}}
{{c1::Acceptance}}
fields.Back Extra: These stages may occur in any order.

fields.Text:
A boy hears his mother's voice during the year after her death. He has no depressive or psychotic symptoms. Does he have a disorder?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Hallucinations can occur in the context of normal bereavement.

fields.Text:
Since his wife died 2 years ago, a man has been severely depressed. He has not been eating or bathing regularly and has not kept up with household tasks. Is this grief normal?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: This is persistent complex bereavement disorder.

fields.Text:
By what age is a child expected to take first steps?

{{c1::12}} months

By what age should a child be able to kick a ball?

{{c1::24}} months

By what age should an infant be able to use a pincer grasp?

{{c1::10}} months

By what age should an infant begin to roll and sit?

{{c1::6}} months

At approximately what age is core gender identity formed?

{{c1::36}} months

A toddler plays alongside, but not with, another toddler. How old is this toddler?

{{c1::24}} to {{c1::36}} months
fields.Back Extra: This is known as parallel play.

fields.Text:
At what age should children be able to self-groom, button buttons, zip zippers, and brush their own teeth?

{{c1::5}} years

What is rapprochement?

When a child is {{c1::comfortable}} moving away and then returning to their {{c1::mother}}

What is the approximate age at which an infant will turn toward a voice?

{{c1::4}} months

By what age does a child usually begin to stand?

{{c1::10}} months

How many words are expected to be included in a 2-year-old's vocabulary?

{{c1::50}} to {{c1::200}} words

By what age should a child be able to understand approximately 1000 words?

{{c1::3}} years

When might a child begin to develop a social smile?

{{c1::2}} months

By what age should a child be able to climb stairs?

{{c1::18}} months

By what age should a child begin pointing to objects?

{{c1::12}} months

At what age might a child have an imaginary friend?

{{c1::4}} years

By what age should a child be able to use a tricycle?

{{c1::3}} years

By what age should an infant be responding to names and gestures?

{{c1::9}} months

By what age should an infant start to hold his or her head up in a prone position?

{{c1::1}} month(s)

By what age should a child be able to hop on 1 foot?

{{c1::4}} years

By what age should a child be able to draw stick figures and copy lines or circles?

{{c1::4}} years

By what age should a child be able to build a tower of blocks with other children of the same age?

{{c1::4}} years
fields.Back Extra: This is known as cooperative play.

fields.Text:
By what age should children be able to feed themselves with a fork and spoon?

{{c1::20}} months

At what age does a child typically show evidence of anxiety on contact with strangers?

{{c1::6}} months

By what age should a child begin to use prepositions and complete sentences, as well as tell detailed stories?

{{c1::4}} years

By what age should a child be able to comfortably spend some time away from their mother?

{{c1::3}} years

By 2 years of age, how many blocks should a child be able to stack?

{{c1::6}} blocks
fields.Back Extra: Number of blocks stacked = Age in years × 3

fields.Text:
By what age should a child begin to say "dada" and "mama"?

{{c1::10}} months

By what age does an infant usually begin to crawl?

{{c1::8}} months

By what age does a child usually pass a toy from one hand to the other?

{{c1::6}} months

How many words are expected to be included in a 3-year-old's vocabulary?

More than {{c1::300}} words

What is the likely underlying cause of gonorrhea in a 5-year-old girl with 2-week history of vaginal discharge?

{{c1::Sexual abuse}}

The peak incidence of sexual abuse of children occurs in what age range?

{{c1::9}} to {{c1::12}} years

What evidence from an eye exam might indicate physical child abuse?

{{c1::Retinal hemorrhages}}
fields.Back Extra: This is suggestive of shaken baby syndrome.

fields.Text:
What type of child abuse presents with lack of bond with caregiver but increased affection with less familiar adults?

{{c1::Emotional}} abuse

What symptoms usually indicate emotional abuse in older children?

Frequent {{c1::anger}} outbursts
{{c1::Distancing}} themselves from caregivers and other children
Emotional {{c1::lability}}
{{c1::Somatic}} symptoms for which no physical cause can be found

What evidence may indicate sexual abuse in children?

{{c1::Sexually transmitted}} infections
{{c1::Urinary}} tract infections
{{c1::Genital}} trauma
{{c1::Anal}} trauma
{{c1::Oral}} trauma
Exhibition of sexual {{c1::knowledge}} or {{c1::behavior}} incongruent with age

In the setting of physical abuse of a child, what signs may caregivers exhibit?

{{c1::Delay}} of medical care
Provide explanations that do not fit the child's {{c1::age}} or {{c1::injury}} patterns
Change their {{c1::stories}} over time

What outcome can be expected in young adult victims of child emotional abuse by the age of 21?

Most of them may meet one or more criteria for diagnosis of a {{c1::psychiatric}} illness by this age

What is the next step after evidence of child neglect has been found in a patient?

{{c1::Report}} the findings to local {{c1::child protective}} services

What are the signs of child neglect?

Failure to {{c1::thrive}}
{{c1::Malnutrition}}
Poor {{c1::hygiene}}
{{c1::Withdrawal}}
Impaired {{c1::social}} or {{c1::emotional}} development

What is the definition of child neglect?

{{c1::Failure}} to meet a child's need for adequate supervision, shelter, food, education, affection, or any combination of these needs

What are two consequences of vulnerable child syndrome?

The child may miss {{c1::school}}
The child may have excessive {{c1::medical}} visits
fields.Back Extra: This is due to parents' worry that the child is more susceptible to illness or injury.

fields.Text:
What is vulnerable child syndrome?

Parents think their child is more susceptible to {{c1::illness}} or {{c1::injury}}
fields.Back Extra: This often occurs after a major illness or life-threatening event.

fields.Text:
What additional disorder do patients with selective mutism usually have?

{{c1::Social anxiety}} disorder

Selective mutism interferes with performance of what kinds of tasks?

{{c1::Academic}} tasks
{{c1::Social}} tasks
{{c1::Occupational}} tasks

What is selective mutism?

{{c1::Anxiety}} disorder that involves refraining from {{c1::speech}} in specific situations for ≥ {{c1::1}} month in a child < {{c1::5}} years who has no impairment in speech/language development

How do you distinguish between conduct disorder and oppositional defiant disorder?

In {{c1::conduct}} disorder, the basic rights of others or social norms are violated
In {{c1::oppositional defiant}} disorder, the basic rights of others or social norms are not violated

An episode of separation anxiety in older children must last how long for it to be considered a disorder?

{{c1::4}} weeks or more

What classes of drugs are used to treat disruptive mood dysregulation disorder?

{{c1::Stimulants}}
{{c1::Antipsychotics}}

What modalities are used to treat intractable tics in a patient with Tourette syndrome?

High-potency {{c1::antipsychotics}}
{{c1::α2}}-agonists
{{c1::Tetrabenazine}}

What is the first-line therapy for Tourette syndrome?

{{c1::Behavioral}} therapy
{{c1::Psychoeducation}}

How long do symptoms need to be present for Tourette syndrome to be diagnosed?

More than {{c1::1}} year(s)

What three traits characterize attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder?

{{c1::Inattention}}
{{c1::Impulsivity}}
{{c1::Hyperactivity::Hyperactivity/Hypoactivity}}
fields.Back Extra: This is in two or more settings.

fields.Text:
What are the treatment options for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder?

{{c1::Stimulants}} with or without {{c1::cognitive behavioral}} therapy
{{c1::Stimulant}} alternatives

You suspect that a child who does poorly in school has attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. Does this disorder affect intelligence?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Intelligence is normal, but the child may experience difficulties in school due to symptoms.

fields.Text:
How does disruptive mood dysregulation disorder present?

Severe, recurrent {{c1::temper}} outbursts incongruent to situation

A child is diagnosed with autism. When does this disorder present, and is it more common in girls or boys?

Autism must present in {{c1::early::early/late}} childhood and is more common in {{c1::boys::boys/girls}}

At what age would you diagnose a patient with conduct disorder?

Before the age of {{c1::18}} years
fields.Back Extra: After age 18, it is reclassified as antisocial personality disorder.

fields.Text:
Which childhood disorder is characterized by poor social interactions, communication deficits, ritualized or repetitive behavior, and restricted interests?

{{c1::Autism spectrum}} disorder

Persistent symptoms of limited attention span and/or poor impulse control must be present for ≥ 6 months and in ≥ 2 settings signify which childhood behavioral disorder?

{{c1::Attention-deficit hyperactivity}} disorder

What features and associated disorders may be seen in a patient with Tourette syndrome?

Vocal and motor {{c1::tics}}
{{c1::Coprolalia}}
{{c1::Obsessive-compulsive}} disorder
{{c1::Attention-deficit hyperactivity}} disorder

What is intellectual disability?

{{c1::Global}} cognitive deficits that affect memory, reasoning, judgment, abstract thinking, language, and learning

Why do patients with intellectual disability have difficulties in socialization, education, employment, and independence?

{{c1::Adaptive}} functioning is impaired due to {{c1::global}} cognitive deficits
fields.Back Extra: This affects the ability to learn, remember, reason, use language, think in abstract terms, and make judgments.

fields.Text:
How do you treat a patient with intellectual disability?

By providing {{c1::multidisciplinary}} support to improve {{c1::global}} functioning

Tourette syndrome presents with what symptoms and at what age?

Sudden, rapid, recurrent, {{c1::nonrhythmic::rhythmic/nonrhythmic}} stereotyped vocal and motor {{c1::tics}} that are present  > {{c1::1}} year(s) before the age of {{c1::18}} years

A child is unable to read near the level of proficiency for his or her age even after working with a tutor 7 months. What is the most likely diagnosis?

{{c1::Specific learning}} disorder

How do intellect and head/brain size in a child with a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder compare with those of a child who does not have this disorder?

A child with autism may have an {{c1::intellectual}} disability or {{c1::exceptional}} abilities or specific skills
Size of head and/or brain may be {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}

What happens to general functioning and intelligence in an individual with specific learning disorder?

They are usually {{c1::normal}}

How do you treat a patient with specific learning disorder?

{{c1::Academic}} support
{{c1::Counseling}}
{{c1::Extracurricular}} activities

How do you treat selective mutism?

{{c1::Behavioral}}, {{c1::family}}, and {{c1::play}} therapies with or without {{c1::SSRIs}}

Up to what age is separation anxiety considered a normal phenomenon?

{{c1::3}} to {{c1::4}} years

What can be used to treat a child with separation anxiety disorder?

{{c1::Cognitive behavioral}} therapy
{{c1::Play}} therapy
{{c1::Family}} therapy

What is the treatment for conduct disorder?

{{c1::Psychotherapy}}

How do you treat a child with oppositional defiant disorder?

{{c1::Psychotherapy}}

List the order in which a person loses his or her components of orientation.

First → {{c1::Time}}
Second → {{c1::Place}}
Third → {{c1::Person}}

What is orientation in the context of the psychiatric exam?

An individual’s ability to know {{c1::who}} he/she is, {{c1::where}} he/she is, and the {{c1::date}} and {{c1::time}}

What are the common causes of loss of orientation?

{{c1::Head}} injury
Fluid/electrolyte {{c1::imbalance}}
{{c1::Drugs}}
{{c1::Alcohol}}
{{c1::Hypoglycemia::Hyperglycemia/Hypoglycemia}}
{{c1::Hypoxia}}
{{c1::Infection}}
{{c1::Nutritional}} deficiencies

What is the likely diagnosis for an adult with a history of chronic alcohol consumption who is exhibiting anterograde amnesia and confabulation in the emergency department?

{{c1::Korsakoff}} syndrome

What syndrome would be present in a patient with destruction of the mammillary bodies and anterior thalamus?

{{c1::Korsakoff}} syndrome

What type of amnesia is present in a patient who sustained a head injury and is unable to recall anything that occurred from the time that the injury occurred?

{{c1::Anterograde}} amnesia

What type of amnesia is present in a patient who cannot recall anything that occurred before they sustained a head injury but can still make new memories?

{{c1::Retrograde}} amnesia

Korsakoff syndrome is a late neuropsychiatric manifestation of what disease?

{{c1::Wernicke encephalopathy}}

What treatment can be helpful in preventing Korsakoff syndrome in a patient with a long-standing history of alcohol use?

Vitamin {{c1::B1}} therapy

Name six psychiatric conditions associated with dissociative identity disorder.

{{c1::Post-traumatic stress}} disorder
{{c1::Depression}}
{{c1::Borderline}} personality disorder
{{c1::Substance use}} disorder
{{c1::Somatoform}} disorders
History of {{c1::sexual abuse}}

Dissociative identity disorder is more common in which sex?

{{c1::Female::Male/Female}}

What is the difference between depersonalization and derealization?

Depersonalization → Feelings of detachment/estrangement from one's {{c1::self}}
Derealization → Feelings of detachment/estrangement from one's {{c1::environment}}

A man often feels estranged from his surroundings and from himself, almost as if he is merely an observer. What could this condition be?

{{c1::Depersonalization/derealization}} disorder

If a patient has two or more distinct personality states or identities, what is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Dissociative identity}} disorder

Due to the severe trauma of child abuse, a woman is unable to recall her date of birth. What type of amnesia is this?

{{c1::Dissociative}} amnesia

A man abruptly travels to the other side of the country and is found wandering on the streets there. What is the most likely diagnosis?

{{c1::Dissociative fugue}}
fields.Back Extra: This occurs during a period of dissociative amnesia, which is often associated with traumatic circumstances.

fields.Text:
How do you treat delirium?

Treatment of delirium is aimed at identifying and addressing the {{c1::underlying condition}}
fields.Back Extra: Antipsychotics may be used as needed for acute episodes.

fields.Text:
What classes of medication should be avoided in the treatment of delirium?

{{c1::Benzodiazepines}}
{{c1::Anticholinergics}}
{{c1::Opioids}}

What could be the cause of sudden waning of consciousness in hospitalized older patients?

{{c1::Delirium}}

You suspect that your patient with altered mental status has delirium. What test may help to confirm the diagnosis?

{{c1::EEG}}
fields.Back Extra: It may reveal diffuse background rhythm slowing, a finding associated with delirium.

fields.Text:
Define delirium.

Acute, {{c1::reversible::reversible/irreversible}}, onset of waxing/waning {{c1::consciousness}} with rapidly decreasing {{c1::attention}} span and level of {{c1::arousal}}

How do you begin management of delirium before considering medication?

Identifying/treating {{c1::underlying condition}}
Providing {{c1::cognitive}} stimulation
Keeping a clock or calendar nearby for {{c1::orientation}} purposes
Reducing {{c1::sleep}} disturbances

What condition is associated with gustatory hallucinations?

{{c1::Epilepsy}}

What type of hallucination is associated with waking from sleep?

{{c1::Hypnopompic}}

What two substances, which are frequently abused, are associated with tactile hallucination?

{{c1::Alcohol}}
{{c1::Stimulants}}

What type of hallucination is associated with falling asleep?

{{c1::Hypnagogic}}

What two conditions are associated with olfactory hallucinations?

Brain {{c1::tumors}}
{{c1::Temporal}} lobe {{c1::epilepsy}}

What kind of speech consists of words and ideas strung together based on sounds, puns, or loose associations?

{{c1::Disorganized}} speech

Define hallucinations.

Perceptions in the absence of {{c1::external::internal/external}} stimuli
fields.Back Extra: Illusions are due to misperceptions of actual external stimuli.

fields.Text:
Define psychosis.

{{c1::Distorted}} perception of reality marked by hallucinations, delusions, and/or disorganized thought and/or speech

Define delusion.

A fixed, untrue, {{c1::idiosyncratic}} belief, persisting despite evidence against it, that is not typical of an individual's {{c1::religion}} or {{c1::culture}}

Define mood disorders.

Disorders in which an abnormal range of internal emotions/moods and loss of {{c1::control}} over them cause distress and impairment in {{c1::daily}} function

Give four examples of disorders that are classified as mood disorders.

{{c1::Major depressive}} disorder
{{c1::Bipolar}} disorder
{{c1::Dysthymic}} disorder
{{c1::Cyclothymic}} disorder

Can a patient with a mood disorder experience symptoms of psychosis, such as hallucinations or delusions?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}

What is the first-line treatment for schizophrenia?

{{c1::Atypical antipsychotics}}
fields.Back Extra: Negative symptoms often persist after treatment.

fields.Text:
How does schizophrenia affect dopaminergic activity and dendritic branching?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} dopaminergic activity
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} dendritic branching

Is schizophrenia more likely to be diagnosed in males or females?

{{c1::Males::Males/Females}}

What could be the cause of delusions, hallucinations, and catatonia lasting for 8 months with symptoms of a mood disorder?

{{c1::Schizoaffective}} disorder

Name five positive symptoms of schizophrenia.

{{c1::Delusions}}
{{c1::Hallucinations}}
{{c1::Disorganized}} speech
Evidence of {{c1::unusual}} thought processes
{{c1::Strange}} behavior

What is the most likely cause of hallucinations and delusions lasting between 1 day and 1 month?

{{c1::Brief psychotic}} disorder

How are brief psychotic disorder, schizophreniform disorder, and schizophrenia differentiated?

By {{c1::duration}} of symptoms
fields.Back Extra:
Brief psychotic disorder lasts < 1 month.
Schizophreniform disorder lasts 1 to 6 months.
Schizophrenia lasts > 6 months.

fields.Text:
For a diagnosis of schizophrenia to be made, periods of psychosis and disturbed behavior/thought leading to functional decline must last for how long?

At least {{c1::1}} month(s) during the past {{c1::6}} months or longer

Is general function impaired in a patient with delusional disorder?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}

If a delusion lasts more than 1 month without evidence of a mood disorder or other symptoms of psychosis, what is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Delusional}} disorder

How many symptoms are required to diagnose brief psychotic disorder, schizophreniform disorder, and schizophrenia?

Brief psychotic disorder → {{c1::1}} or more positive symptoms for < {{c1::1}} month
Schizophreniform disorder → {{c1::2}} or more symptoms
Schizophrenia → {{c1::2}} or more symptoms

List the five negative symptoms of schizophrenia.

{{c1::Blunted}}/{{c1::flat}} affect
{{c1::Withdrawal}} from social activity
{{c1::Avolition}}
{{c1::Anhedonia}}
{{c1::Alogia}}

Can you make a diagnosis of schizophrenia for a patient if the only symptom is auditory hallucinations for 9 months?

{{c1::No}}
fields.Back Extra:
Although common, auditory hallucinations alone cannot be used to make a diagnosis of schizophrenia.

A diagnosis requires the presence of 2 or more additional symptoms.

fields.Text:
Heavy use of which drug in adolescence is associated with incidence and worsened course of psychotic, mood, and anxiety disorders?

{{c1::Cannabis}}

What would you expect to find on brain imaging performed for a patient with schizophrenia?
