{{c1::Ventriculomegaly}}

Which personality disorder is included on the schizophrenia spectrum?

{{c1::Schizotypal}} personality disorder

What are the cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia spectrum disorders?

{{c1::Inattention}}
Decreased {{c1::working}} memory
Reduced ability to comprehend or create {{c1::plans}}

What neurochemical changes are associated with schizophrenia?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} dopaminergic activity
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} serotonergic activity

What criteria are required for a diagnosis of schizophrenia?

≥ 2 of the following active symptoms, including ≥ 1 from the first 3 symptoms:

{{c1::Delusions}}
{{c1::Hallucinations}}
{{c1::Disorganized}} speech
{{c1::Disorganized}}/{{c1::catatonic}} behavior
{{c1::Negative::Positive/Negative}} symptoms

What are the criteria for a diagnosis of schizophreniform disorder?

≥ 2 of the following symptoms:

{{c1::Delusions}}
{{c1::Hallucinations}}
{{c1::Disorganized}} speech
{{c1::Disorganized}}/{{c1::catatonic}} behavior
{{c1::Negative::Positive/Negative}} symptoms lasting for {{c1::1}} to {{c1::6}} months

In patients with schizophrenia, how does age at onset compare in males and females?

Schizophrenia presents at a(n) {{c1::younger::older/younger}} age in males when compared with females

A deficiency in which vitamin results in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome?

Vitamin {{c1::B1}} deficiency

What three symptoms are present in Korsakoff syndrome?

Irreversible {{c1::memory}} loss
{{c1::Confabulation}}
{{c1::Personality}} changes

How can symptoms of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome be precipitated in the hospital setting?

These symptoms can be precipitated in a patient with thiamine depletion by administering {{c1::dextrose}} to a patient before vitamin {{c1::B1}}

What is the triad of Wernicke encephalopathy?

{{c1::Confusion}}
{{c1::Ophthalmoplegia}}
{{c1::Ataxia}}

What are six common complications of alcohol use disorder?

{{c1::Pancreatitis}}
{{c1::Hepatitis}}
{{c1::Cirrhosis}}
{{c1::Peripheral::Central/Peripheral}} neuropathy
{{c1::Testicular}} atrophy
Vitamin {{c1::B1}} deficiency

How does naltrexone help patients with alcohol use disorder?

It reduces {{c1::cravings}}

How does disulfiram help patients with alcohol use disorder?

It conditions the patient to {{c1::abstain}} from alcohol use

Which three medications are commonly prescribed for the management of alcohol use disorder?

{{c1::Naltrexone}}
{{c1::Disulfiram}}
{{c1::Acamprosate}}

What is the treatment for Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome?

Intravenous vitamin {{c1::B1}}

What are five life-threatening effects of ecstasy intoxication?

{{c1::Tachycardia::Tachycardia/Bradycardia}}
{{c1::Hyperthermia::Hyperthermia/Hypothermia}}
{{c1::Hyponatremia::Hypernatremia/Hyponatremia}}
{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Serotonin}} syndrome

What is the treatment for alcohol withdrawal?

Longer-acting {{c1::benzodiazepines}}

How do you treat opioid withdrawal?

{{c1::Symptom}} management
{{c1::Buprenorphine}}
{{c1::Methadone}}

What are three treatment options for smoking cessation?

{{c1::Nicotine}} replacement
{{c1::Bupropion}}
{{c1::Varenicline}}

What pupillary changes can be seen with both cocaine and amphetamine toxicity?

Pupillary {{c1::dilation::dilation/constriction}}

What is the treatment for a cocaine overdose?

{{c1::Benzodiazepines}}

Do barbiturates or benzodiazepines have a higher safety margin?

{{c1::Benzodiazepines}}
fields.Back Extra: These can still cause minor respiratory depression.

fields.Text:
What life-threatening condition may develop in a patient with alcohol use disorder who has consumed no alcohol for 48 hours?

{{c1::Delirium tremens}}

What are the symptoms of barbiturate withdrawal?

{{c1::Delirium}}
{{c1::Cardiovascular}} collapse

What is the treatment for a benzodiazepine overdose?

{{c1::Flumazenil}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a competitive benzodiazepine antagonist, which is rarely used because it can precipitate seizures.

fields.Text:
What two symptoms can be present with benzodiazepine intoxication?

{{c1::Respiratory}} depression
{{c1::Ataxia}}

Intoxication with what substance may cause slurred speech, emotional lability, ataxia, coma, blackouts, and high serum GGT?

{{c1::Alcohol}}

What is the expected ratio of AST to ALT for a patient that recently consumed alcohol?

{{c1::2}}:{{c1::1}}

What are three symptoms of withdrawal from benzodiazepines?

{{c1::Sleep}} disturbance
{{c1::Depression}}
{{c1::Seizures}}

What are two cardiac manifestations of cocaine overdose?

{{c1::Angina}}
Sudden cardiac {{c1::death}}

What are two cardiovascular manifestations of amphetamine toxicity?

{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
Cardiac {{c1::arrest}} in severe intoxication

What kind of intoxication could cause acute slurred speech, disorientation, drowsiness, abnormal gait, and a perioral rash?

{{c1::Inhalant}} intoxication

Which intoxicant is the most likely cause of hyperalertness, fever, fractured teeth, and skin excoriations?

{{c1::Amphetamines}}

What is the treatment for acute alcohol intoxication?

{{c1::Supportive care}}
fields.Back Extra: This would be with antiemetics and fluids.

fields.Text:
What are three common symptoms of caffeine withdrawal?

{{c1::Flu}}-like symptoms
{{c1::Headaches}}
Lack of {{c1::concentration}}

What is the treatment for agitation and seizures secondary to methamphetamine use?

{{c1::Benzodiazepines}}

What is the treatment for marked respiratory depression for a patient taking barbituates?

Manage the patient's {{c1::symptoms}}
fields.Back Extra: Provide ventilation and increase blood pressure as needed.

fields.Text:
What class of drugs is responsible for the most drug-overdose–related deaths?

{{c1::Opioids}}

What is the treatment for opioid overdose?

{{c1::Naloxone}}

What may be present on the physical examination of a patient with chronic cocaine use?

{{c1::Perforated}} nasal septum secondary to vasoconstriction
{{c1::Ischemic necrosis}}

What is the most common presentation of acute nicotine intoxication?

{{c1::Restlessness}}

What are the three hallmarks of serotonin syndrome?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} activity
{{c1::Autonomic}} instability
Altered {{c1::mental}} status

Which medication can be used in the treatment of serotonin syndrome, and what is its mechanism?

{{c1::Cyproheptadine}}, which is a {{c1::5-HT2}} receptor antagonist

What condition can develop in a patient on a MAOI who consumes tyramine-rich foods?

{{c1::Hypertensive crisis}}

What is the treatment for a patient prescribed MAOIs undergoing a hypertensive crisis?

{{c1::Phentolamine}}

How does eating tyramine-rich foods while taking MAOIs result in hypertensive crisis?

Tyramine displaces {{c1::norepinephrine}} in the synaptic cleft → Increased {{c1::norepinephrine}} → Stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system

What are six manifestations of neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

{{c1::Myoglobinuria}}
{{c1::Fever}}
{{c1::Encephalopathy}}
{{c1::Vitals}} unstable
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} enzyme levels
Muscle {{c1::rigidity}}

What class of drugs should not be prescribed for a patient with a known family history of neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

{{c1::Antipsychotics}}

What drugs can be used to treat neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

{{c1::Dantrolene}}
{{c1::Benzodiazepines}}
{{c1::Dopamine}} agonists
fields.Back Extra: Remember to always discontinue the causative agent.

fields.Text:
In a patient experiencing alcohol withdrawal, when does delirium tremens typically arise?

{{c1::2}} to {{c1::4}} days after the last drink

What is the treatment for a patient undergoing alcohol withdrawal with seizures?

Longer-acting {{c1::benzodiazepines}}

What is the likely cause of laryngospasm requiring intubation in a patient who has started taking an antipsychotic medication?

Acute {{c1::dystonia}}

What is the treatment for lithium toxicity?

{{c1::Discontinuation}} of lithium
Hydrating aggressively with {{c1::isotonic saline}} solution

What is the treatment for a TCA overdose?

{{c1::Supportive}} treatment
Activated {{c1::charcoal}}
{{c1::Bicarbonate}}

What three symptoms may be present in a patient with acute dystonia?

Muscle {{c1::spasms}}
Muscle {{c1::stiffness}}
{{c1::Oculogyric}} crisis
fields.Back Extra: Symptoms can begin hours to days after use of a typical antipsychotic.

fields.Text:
What are three potential causes of lithium toxicity?

{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in lithium dosage
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in renal clearance
Drugs that affect {{c1::clearance}}

What two drugs can be used to treat acute dystonia?

{{c1::Diphenhydramine}}
{{c1::Benztropine}}

Which three drugs/drug classes can cause acute dystonia?

{{c1::Anticonvulsants}}
{{c1::Antipsychotics}}
{{c1::Metoclopramide}}

What are two methods of preventing serotonin syndrome?

Allow for a {{c1::washout}} period between serotonergic drugs
Avoid using {{c1::multiple}} serotonergic drugs at the same time

What are seven signs of lithium toxicity?

{{c1::Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus}}
{{c2::Nausea}}
{{c3::Vomiting}}
{{c4::Slurred}} speech
{{c5::Hyperreflexia::Hyperreflexia/Hyporeflexia}}
{{c6::Ataxia}}
{{c7::Seizures}}

What seven psychiatric drugs can contribute to serotonin syndrome?

{{c1::MAOIs}}
{{c2::SSRIs}}
{{c3::SNRIs}}
{{c4::TCAs}}
{{c5::Vortioxetine}}
{{c6::Buspirone}}
{{c7::Vilazodone}}

What are the seven symptoms of a manic episode?

{{c1::Distractibility}}
{{c1::Impulsivity}}/{{c1::indiscretion}}
{{c1::Grandiosity}}
Flight of {{c1::ideas}}
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} activity/agitation
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} sleep needs
{{c1::Talkativeness}}

For diagnosis of a manic episode, how many manic symptoms must be present and for how long?

At least {{c1::3}} symptoms for at least {{c1::1}} week(s)

Compare hypomanic and manic episodes in terms of severity.

Hypomanic episodes are {{c1::less::more/less}} intense
Hypomanic episodes do not impair {{c1::function}} or feature {{c1::psychosis}}
Hypomanic episodes do not require {{c1::hospitalization}}
Hypomanic episodes last for ≥ {{c1::4}} consecutive days

In a person with bipolar disorder, what mood can you expect between episodes of mania/hypomania and depression?

Mood generally returns to {{c1::normal}}

What disorder is present in a patient who has mild dysthymia and has been experiencing hypomanic episodes for 3 years?

{{c1::Cyclothymic}} disorder

What class of drugs are used most commonly to treat bipolar disorder?

{{c1::Mood stabilizers}}
{{c1::Atypical antipsychotics}}

How does bipolar I disorder differ from bipolar II disorder?

Bipolar I disorder includes {{c1::manic}} episodes with or without a {{c1::hypomanic}} or {{c1::depressive}} episode
Bipolar II disoder includes a {{c1::hypomanic}} episode and a {{c1::depressive}} episode, but no {{c1::manic}} episodes

What class of drugs can cause mania and increase suicide risk in patients with bipolar disorder?

{{c1::Antidepressant}}

How long are symptoms required to be present for a diagnosis of cyclothymic disorder?

{{c1::2}} or more years with symptoms present at least {{c1::50}}% of the time, with any remission lasting for {{c1::2}} months or less

What treatment options are first line for major depressive disorder?

{{c1::Cognitive behavioral}} therapy
{{c1::SSRIs}}

What are the features of major depressive disorder?

{{c1::Sleep}} disturbance
Decreased interest in {{c1::pleasurable}} activities
{{c1::Guilt}}
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} energy
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} concentration
{{c1::Appetite}}/{{c1::weight}} changes
{{c1::Psychomotor}} agitation
{{c1::Suicidal}} ideation

How long should the symptoms of anhedonia, fatigue, inattention, loss of appetite, and disturbed sleep be present for a diagnosis of a major depressive episode to be made?

Symptoms must have been present for most days for a period of {{c1::2}} weeks or longer

Which disorder is often milder than major depressive disorder with at least 2 depressive symptoms lasting at least 2 years and with remission of 2 months or less?

{{c1::Persistent depressive}} disorder

In which depressive disorder do episodes occur only during a particular season in 2 or more consecutive years?

{{c1::Major depressive}} disorder with {{c1::seasonal pattern}}

When do psychotic features occur in a patient who has major depressive disorder with psychotic features, as compared with a patient with schizoaffective disorder?

Psychotic features occur only {{c1::during}} the major depressive episode in a patient with major depressive disorder with psychotic features
A patient with schizoaffective disorder will have psychotic symptoms {{c1::independent::dependent/independent}} of a depressive episode

What is the treatment for major depressive disorder with psychotic features?

A(n) {{c1::antidepressant}} combined with a(n) {{c1::atypical antipsychotic}} or {{c1::electroconvulsive}} therapy

Define major depressive disorder with psychotic features.

Major depressive disorder accompanied by {{c1::delusions}} or {{c1::hallucinations}}

In major depressive disorder with psychotic features, hallucinations and delusions typically have what overlying theme?

They are typically mood {{c1::congruent}} with depressed mood

What are the treatment options for major depressive disorder with seasonal pattern?

{{c1::Cognitive behavior}} therapy
{{c1::SSRIs}}
{{c1::Light}} therapy

What is the treatment for atypical depression?

{{c1::SSRIs}}
{{c1::Cognitive behavioral}} therapy
{{c1::MAOIs}} (not first-line)

What symptoms differentiate atypical depression from classical depression?

{{c1::Mood}} reactivity
{{c1::Hypersomnia::Hypersomnia/Hyposomnia}}
{{c1::Overeating::Overeating/Undereating}}
{{c1::Leaden}} paralysis
{{c1::Hypersensitivity}} to rejection

Define mood reactivity, a feature of atypical depression.

Although patients are predominantly depressed, they experience transient {{c1::improvements}} in mood in the setting of positive events

What is the most common subtype of depression?

Depression with {{c1::atypical features}}

What are risk factors for postpartum psychosis?

{{c1::Bipolar}} disorder
{{c1::Psychotic}} disorder
{{c1::First::First/Second}} pregnancy
{{c1::Family}} history
Recent discontinuation of {{c1::psychotropic}} medication

Which of the peripartum mood disturbances is the only one that does not usually warrant pharmacologic therapy?

{{c1::Postpartum blues}}

What postpartum mental disorder could cause a woman to have delusions and threaten to kill herself and the baby?

{{c1::Postpartum psychosis}}

What is the treatment for major depressive disorder with peripartum onset?

{{c1::SSRIs}}
{{c1::Cognitive behavioral}} therapy

When will the symptoms of postpartum blues likely resolve?

Within {{c1::2}} weeks
fields.Back Extra: However, the patient should be followed up to assess for possible major depressive disorder with peripartum onset.

fields.Text:
What are three peripartum mood disturbances that new mothers may experience in order from highest to lowest incidence rate?

{{c1::Postpartum blues}} (50% to 85%)
{{c1::Major depressive}} disorder with {{c1::peripartum onset}} (10% to 15%)
{{c1::Postpartum psychosis}} (0.1% to 0.2%)

What is the treatment for postpartum psychosis?

Admission to inpatient {{c1::psychiatric}} unit
Administration of {{c1::atypical antipsychotics}} or {{c1::electroconvulsive}} therapy if drug therapy is ineffective

Is electroconvulsive therapy safe for pregnant patients and elderly patients?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: There are no absolute contraindications to electroconvulsive therapy.

fields.Text:
Name four clinical indications for electroconvulsive therapy.

Acute {{c1::suicidality}}
{{c1::Depression}} with {{c1::psychosis}}
Refractory {{c1::depression}}
{{c1::Catatonia}}

What is the mechanism of electroconvulsive therapy?

Electroconvulsive therapy induces {{c1::tonic-clonic}} seizures in patients under anesthesia and neuromuscular blockade

What are the adverse effects of electroconvulsive therapy?

{{c1::Headache}}
{{c1::Disorientation}}
{{c1::Anterograde}}/{{c1::retrograde}} amnesia that usually resolves within {{c1::6}} months

Do men or women attempt suicide more often?

{{c1::Women::Men/Women}} attempt suicide more often
fields.Back Extra: However, men are more likely to complete the act.

fields.Text:
What is the greatest risk factor for suicide?

Previous {{c1::attempt}}

Who is at greater risk for suicide completion?

{{c1::Men::Men/Women}}

What is the most common method of suicide in the United States?

{{c1::Firearms}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to an increased chance of suicide completion.

fields.Text:
Does family history of suicide completion affect a person's risk of suicide completion?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}

What are some of the protective factors for patients at risk for suicide completion?

Effective treatment of {{c1::comorbidities}}
Sense of {{c1::connectedness}} with others
Religious/cultural beliefs directed toward self-{{c1::preservation}}
Strong {{c1::problem-solving}} skills

What is the definition of an anxiety disorder?

When a patient experiences inappropriate {{c1::fear}} and {{c1::worry}}
fields.Back Extra: The patient's physical presentation must be incongruent with the severity of the stressor.

fields.Text:
Which three other conditions must be ruled out to make a diagnosis of anxiety disorder?

Another {{c1::psychiatric}} disorder
{{c1::Substance}} use
{{c1::Medical}} condition

What are the four polypeptide subunits that form normal adult hemoglobin?

2 {{c1::α}} subunits
2 {{c1::β}} subunits

Hemoglobin can act as a buffer for which ions?

{{c1::H+}}

Which form of hemoglobin has the lowest affinity for oxygen?

The {{c1::deoxygenated}} form

Which form of hemoglobin has the highest affinity for oxygen?

The {{c1::oxygenated}} form

What are the two conformational forms of adult hemoglobin?

{{c1::Oxygenated}}
{{c1::Deoxygenated}}

What type of oxygen-carrying molecule consists of a single polypeptide chain with a single heme moiety?

{{c1::Myoglobin}}

How does myoglobin's affinity for oxygen compare to that of hemoglobin?

Myoglobin has {{c1::greater::greater/less}} affinity for oxygen

What part of the hemoglobin molecule is represented by the red moiety marked by "X" in the diagram?



{{c1::Heme}}
fields.Back Extra: A single heme molecule is associated with each globin chain.

fields.Text:
What is the formula for oxygen delivery to the tissues?

O2 delivery to tissues = {{c1::Cardiac output}} × {{c1::O2 content of blood}}

What is the normal value of the O2 binding capacity?

{{c1::20}} mL O2/dL of blood

How many milliliters of oxygen can each gram of hemoglobin normally bind?

{{c1::1.34}} mL of oxygen

What is the normal concentration of hemoglobin in the blood?

{{c1::15}} g/dL

What is the formula for oxygen content in the blood?

O2 content = {{c1::O2 bound to hemoglobin}} + {{c1::O2 solubilized in plasma}}

What is the value of the solubility constant of oxygen?

{{c1::0.003}}

How does carbon monoxide poisoning alter oxygen content of the blood?

Hemoglobin concentration will be {{c1::normal}}
Oxygen saturation will be {{c1::decreased}}
Partial pressure of oxygen will be {{c1::normal}}
Total oxygen content will be {{c1::decreased}}

What hematologic disease presents with decreased hemoglobin concentration, normal SaO2, normal PaO2, and decreased total O2 content in the blood?

{{c1::Anemia}}

What hematological alteration has an increased hemoglobin concentration, normal SaO2, normal PaO2, and increased total O2 content in the blood.

{{c1::Polycythemia}}

How does methemoglobinemia affect the following?

Hemoglobin concentration will be {{c1::normal}}
Oxygen saturation will be {{c1::decreased}}
Partial pressure of oxygen will be {{c1::normal}}
Total oxygen content will be {{c1::decreased}}

How will cyanide toxicity affect hemoglobin concentration, oxygen saturation, partial pressure of oxygen, and total oxygen content?

All variables will be {{c1::unchanged}}
fields.Back Extra: Cyanide toxicity does not affect these variables.

fields.Text:
High altitude causes what kind of shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} shift

A patient overdoses on an opioid, and her partial pressure of CO2 is increased. How does this affect her oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve?

Shifts it to the {{c1::right::left/right}}

How does a fetus's oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve compare with an adult's oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve?

It is shifted to the {{c1::left::left/right}}
fields.Back Extra: Fetal hemoglobin has a greater affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin.

fields.Text:
Alteration in which four factors can cause an increase in hemoglobin affinity to oxygen and a left shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} carbon monoxide
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} methemoglobinemia
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} temperature

When the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve shifts to the left, how is the partial pressure of oxygen affected?

A {{c1::lower::higher/lower}} PO2 is required to saturate hemoglobin

Name six phenomenons that can decrease hemoglobin affinity to oxygen and cause a right shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve.

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} H+
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} CO2
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} pH
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} temperature
{{c1::Exercise}}
{{c1::Hypoxia}}

When the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve shifts to the left, what happens to the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen?

The affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}

When the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve shifts to the right, how is the partial pressure of oxygen affected?

A {{c1::higher::higher/lower}} PO2 is required to saturate hemoglobin

When the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve shifts to the right, what happens to the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen?

The affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}

How does the structure of myoglobin affect the shape of the oxygen-myoglobin dissociation curve?

The curve is not {{c1::sigmoidal}}
fields.Back Extra: It is monomeric and has no positive cooperativity.

fields.Text:
Why does the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve have a sigmoidal shape?

Due to {{c1::positive cooperativity}}
fields.Back Extra: Hemoglobin can bind to 4 O2 molecules, and O2 binding is easier when more O2 is bound.

fields.Text:
Which curve shown on the graph represents myoglobin?



{{c1::Solid gray}}

Which section shown on the graph represents venous blood return?



{{c1::Blue}}

Which section shown on the graph represents arterial blood?



{{c1::Pink}}

What shift will carbon monoxide poisoning or methemoglobinemia cause to the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} shift

What is the formula to calculate alveolar ventilation?

VA = ( {{c1::VT}} - {{c1::VD}} ) × {{c1::RR}}

What is the normal value for physiologic dead space?

{{c1::150}} mL/breath

What is the normal value for tidal volume?

{{c1::500}} mL/breath

What is the normal range of values for respiratory rate?

{{c1::12}} to {{c1::20}} breaths/min

What is the formula to calculate minute ventilation?

VE = {{c1::VT}} × {{c1::RR}}

What is the definition of minute ventilation?

The total volume of gas that {{c1::enters::enters/leaves}} the lungs each minute

What is the definition of alveolar ventilation?

The volume of gas that reaches {{c1::alveoli}} each minute

How does the presence of surfactant affect the compliance of the lung?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} it
fields.Back Extra: This is by decreasing surface tension.

fields.Text:
What is hysteresis in relation to the pulmonary system?

Lung inflation follows a different pressure-volume curve than lung deflation because {{c1::surface tension}} needs to be overcome during inflation

Is the lung easier or harder to fill when it has high compliance?

{{c1::Easier}} to fill

What happens to lung compliance as a healthy individual ages?

It {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} with normal aging

How does pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary edema, pneumonia, and acute respiratory distress syndrome affect lung compliance?

Lung compliance is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}

At what lung volume is the pulmonary vascular resistance at a minimum?

At {{c1::FRC}}

How is atelectasis prevented by the pressures in the lung–chest wall system?

At FRC, lung pressures are {{c1::atmospheric}}, and opposing forces of the lung and chest wall create {{c1::negative::positive/negative}} pressure in the intrapleural space

During the respiratory cycle, at the point of functional residual capacity, what is the value of the air pressure within the lungs?

The pressure within the lungs is {{c1::equal}} to atmospheric pressure

At what point in the respiratory cycle is the inward pull of the lung equal to the outward pull of the chest wall?

At {{c1::FRC}}

What is the natural movement tendency of the lungs?

The lungs tend to collapse {{c1::inward::inward/outward}}

What is the natural movement tendency of the chest wall?

The chest wall tends to spring {{c1::outward::inward/outward}}

What is the definition of lung compliance?

The change in lung volume for a given change in {{c1::pressure}}

What is the relationship between compliance and stiffness of the alveolar walls?

Compliance is {{c1::inversely}} proportional to stiffness

How does emphysema alter lung compliance?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} compliance

How is pulmonary pressure measured?

{{c1::cm H2O}}

How does pulmonary fibrosis affect the diffusion of oxygen into the blood?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} diffusion
fields.Back Extra: The thickness of the alveolar wall is increased in pulmonary fibrosis.

fields.Text:
How does emphysema affect the diffusion of oxygen into the blood?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} diffusion
fields.Back Extra: Destruction of membranes decreases the area available for gas transfer.

fields.Text:
Diseases that limit pulmonary gas diffusion are more likely to cause what?

Early {{c1::hypoxia::hypercapnia/hypoxia}}

What is the equation for diffusion of a gas across a membrane?

J = {{c1::A}} × {{c1::Dk}} × [ ( {{c1::P1}} - {{c1::P2}} ) ÷ {{c1::Δx}} ]

Under diffusion-limited conditions, where along the length of the pulmonary capillary does the gas equilibrate?

{{c1::It does not}}
fields.Back Extra: The characteristics of the gas cause it to diffuse slowly across the alveolar membrane.

fields.Text:
Under what two notable conditions is oxygen a diffusion-limited gas?

{{c1::Emphysema}}
{{c1::Fibrosis}}

What two important inhaled gases are diffusion limited?

{{c1::Carbon monoxide}}
{{c1::Oxygen}}

During perfusion-limited conditions, how can pulmonary oxygen exchange be increased?

By increasing {{c1::blood flow}}

What three gases are inhaled and limit perfusion?

{{c1::Oxygen}}
{{c1::Carbon dioxide}}
{{c1::Nitrous oxide}}

Within the lungs, a decrease in PAO2 causes what effect on the vasculature in the area?

Hypoxic {{c1::vasoconstriction::vasodilation/vasoconstriction}}
fields.Back Extra: This shifts blood away from poorly ventilated regions of the lung towards a better ventilated area.

fields.Text:
What is the normal state of resistance and compliance in pulmonary circulation?

{{c1::Low::High/Low}} resistance
{{c1::High::High/Low}} compliance

In the physiology of pulmonary circulation, what is DLCO?

The {{c1::diffusing}} capacity of carbon monoxide

In the graph shown, which line represents the diffusion of O2 in healthy lungs?



{{c1::Solid pink}}

In the graph shown, which line represents the diffusion of O2 in fibrotic lungs?



{{c1::Dashed blue}}

In the graph shown, which line represents the diffusion of CO2 in the lungs?



{{c1::Solid orange}}

In the graph shown, which line represents the diffusion of CO in the lungs?



{{c1::Solid purple}}

What is the abnormality represented by the arrows?



{{c1::Thyroglossal duct cyst}}

Why might a patient have a thyroid gland with three lobes?

The {{c1::pyramidal}} lobe of the thyroid can be a persisting remnant of the {{c1::thyroglossal duct}}

How can thyroglossal duct cysts be differentiated from pharyngeal cleft cysts on physical examination?

Thyroglossal duct cysts are {{c1::anterior}} and {{c1::move::move/do not move}} with swallowing
Pharyngeal cleft cysts are {{c1::lateral}} and {{c1::do not move::move/do not move}} with swallowing

Which germ layer gives rise to thyroid follicular cells?

{{c1::Endoderm}}

What is the embryologic origin of the thyroid gland?

The {{c1::floor}} of the primitive {{c1::pharynx}}

What is the most common location of ectopic thyroid tissue?

{{c1::Tongue}}

What syndrome might result if a lingual thyroid is removed surgically?

{{c1::Hypothyroidism}}

What is the embryologic origin of parafollicular cells?

{{c1::4th}} pharyngeal pouch

Which hormones are secreted by the anterior pituitary gland basophils?

{{c1::FSH}}
{{c1::LH}}
{{c1::ACTH}}
{{c1::TSH}}

Which parts of the hypothalamus produce ADH and oxytocin?

ADH → {{c1::Supraoptic}} nuclei
Oxytocin → {{c1::Paraventricular}} nuclei

What hormones are secreted by the anterior pituitary?

{{c1::FSH}}
{{c1::LH}}
{{c1::ACTH}}
{{c1::TSH}}
{{c1::Prolactin}}
{{c1::GH}}
{{c1::β-endorphin}}

Which pituitary hormones have a common α subunit?

{{c1::TSH}}
{{c1::LH}}
{{c1::FSH}}
{{c1::hCG}}

What hormones does the posterior pituitary secrete?

{{c1::Vasopressin}}
{{c1::Oxytocin}}

What are the embryologic origins of the anterior and posterior pituitary?

Anterior pituitary → {{c1::Rathke pouch}}
Posterior pituitary → {{c1::Neuroectoderm}}

Name the three derivatives of proopiomelanocortin that are secreted by the pituitary gland.

{{c1::β-endorphins}}
{{c1::ACTH}}
{{c1::MSH}}

Which is the only hormone secreted by the intermediate lobe of pituitary?

{{c1::MSH}}

Which subunit of pituitary hormones determines hormone specificity?

{{c1::β}} subunit

Which hormones from the anterior pituitary gland are secreted by acidophils?

{{c1::Prolactin}}
{{c1::GH}}

How are ADH and oxytocin transported to the posterior pituitary?

ADH and oxytocin are made in the {{c1::hypothalamus}} and carried via {{c1::neurophysins}} to the posterior pituitary

What are the primary regulators and secretory products of chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla?

Primary regulators are {{c1::preganglionic::preganglionic/postganglionic}} {{c1::sympathetic::sympathetic/parasympathetic}} fibers
Secretory products are {{c1::catecholamines}}

What part of the adrenal gland secretes mineralocorticoids, primarily aldosterone?

Zona {{c1::glomerulosa}}

From what embryologic tissue does the adrenal cortex arise?

{{c1::Mesoderm}}

Where is the medulla of adrenal gland derived from?

{{c1::Neural crest}}

What are the three zones of the adrenal cortex, from outermost to innermost?

{{c1::Zona glomerulosa}}
{{c1::Zona fasciculata}}
{{c1::Zona reticularis}}

What is the primary hormone produced by the zona reticularis?

{{c1::DHEA}}

Which hormone regulates aldosterone production in the zona glomerulosa?

{{c1::Angiotensin II}}

Which hormones regulate the zona fasciculata and the zona reticularis?

{{c1::ACTH}}
{{c1::CRH}}

Which part of the adrenal gland secretes glucocorticoids?

{{c1::Zona fasciculata}}

What are the three different cell types present in the endocrine pancreas and what do they release?

α endocrine cells → {{c1::Glucagon}}
β endocrine cells → {{c1::Insulin}}
δ endocrine cells → {{c1::Somatostatin}}

Where are the α, β, and δ endocrine cells located in the Islets of Langerhans?

α endocrine cells → {{c1::Peripheral}}
β endocrine cells → {{c1::Central}}
δ endocrine cells → {{c1::Interspersed}}

What would be the level of prolactin in a patient with primary hypothyroidism?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} prolactin levels
fields.Back Extra: This is due to elevated TRH.

fields.Text:
Production of which hypothalamic hormone is decreased by long-term glucocorticoid steroid use?

{{c1::CRH}}

What is the mechanism by which antipsychotics may cause galactorrhea?

{{c1::Dopamine}} antagonists, such as antipsychotics, {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} prolactin levels

Dopamine decreases secretion of which two hormones?

{{c1::TSH}}
{{c1::Prolactin}}

Which hormones stimulate and inhibit the release of GH respectively?

{{c1::GHRH}} stimulates growth hormone levels
{{c1::Somatostatin}} inhibits growth hormone levels

What is the three effects of CRH on pituitary hormone secretion?

Stimulates secretion of {{c1::ACTH}}
Stimulates secretion of {{c1::MSH}}
Stimulates secretion of {{c1::β-endorphin}}

What tumor may cause symptoms including amenorrhea, galactorrhea, osteoporosis, and hypogonadism?

{{c1::Pituitary prolactinoma}}

TRH stimulates release of which two hormones?

{{c1::TSH}}
{{c1::Prolactin}}

Which pituitary hormone is responsible for uterine contractions during labor?

{{c1::Oxytocin}}

Name a pathology where one would see inappropriately increased serum ADH levels and decreased plasma osmolality.

{{c1::SIADH}}

Why might a patient with Cushing disease have hyperpigmentation?

{{c1::MSH}} and {{c1::ACTH}} are derived from a common precursor

What are the effects of tonic and pulsed GnRH therapy?

Tonic GnRH suppresses the {{c1::hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal}} axis
Pulsed GnRH promotes {{c1::puberty}} and {{c1::fertility}}

While breastfeeding, which hormone causes milk letdown in a mother?

{{c1::Oxytocin}}

What effect does somatostatin have on pituitary hormone secretion?

Decreases {{c1::GH}} secretion
Decreases {{c1::TSH}} secretion

A patient with HIV develops HIV-associated liposdystrophy. What treatment is indicated?

{{c1::Tesamorelin}}

Apart from labor contractions and milk letdown, what role does oxytocin play in mood?

Oxytocin {{c1::regulates}} mood

What is the mechanism through which breastfeeding acts as contraception?

Breastfeeding → Increased {{c1::prolactin}} → Decreased {{c1::GnRH}} → Delays postpartum ovulation

What hormone analog is known as leuprolide?

Tonic {{c1::GnRH}} analog

Analogs of which hormone are used to treat acromegaly?

{{c1::Somatostatin}}

Which pituitary hormone is released in response to increased plasma osmolality?

{{c1::ADH}}

What are the two functions of the hormone prolactin?

Decreases {{c1::GnRH}} levels
Stimulates {{c1::lactogenesis}}

What is the difference between gigantism and acromegaly?

{{c1::Gigantism}} is growth hormone excess in children before growth plates close
{{c1::Acromegaly}} is growth hormone excess in adults after growth plates close

From what anatomic structure is GH secreted?

{{c1::Anterior pituitary}}

What are the five factors that increase GH release?

{{c1::Sleep}}
{{c1::Exercise}}
{{c1::Puberty}}
{{c1::Hypoglycemia::Hyperglycemia/Hypoglycemia}}
{{c1::Stress}}

Which three molecules decrease secretion of GH?

{{c1::Somatostatin}}
{{c1::Somatomedin}}
{{c1::Glucose}}

Which tumor is associated with tall stature, coarse facial features, and visual defects?

{{c1::Pituitary adenoma}}

What other disease, apart from gigantism/acromegaly, is a patient with growth hormone excess at risk for?

{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}
fields.Back Extra: This is from increased insulin resistance.

fields.Text:
What effect does growth hormone secretion have on insulin?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} insulin resistance

What is the treatment of acromegaly due to a pituitary adenoma?

{{c1::Somatostatin}} analogs
{{c1::Surgery}}

What are three factors that decrease GHRH secretion?

{{c1::Aging}}
{{c1::Obesity}}
{{c1::Hyperglycemia::Hyperglycemia/Hypoglycemia}}

What two factors are responsible for regulating ADH?

Plasma {{c1::osmolality}}
{{c1::Hypovolemia::Hypervolemia/Hypovolemia}}

Where is ADH synthesized, stored, and secreted?

Synthesized in the {{c1::hypothalamus}}
Stored in the {{c1::posterior pituitary}}
Secreted by the {{c1::posterior pituitary}}

What is the most appropriate hormone therapy for central diabetes insipidus and for nocturnal enuresis?

{{c1::Desmopressin}}

What is the serum ADH level in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus versus central diabetes insipidus?

{{c1::Normal}} or {{c1::increased}} in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
{{c1::Decreased}} in central diabetes insipidus

What is the mechanism of activity of ADH in the kidney?

Regulates the insertion of {{c1::aquaporin}} channels in the {{c1::principal}} cells of the renal collecting duct

What two receptors are involved in the function of ADH, and what are their functions?

V1-receptors regulate {{c1::blood pressure}}
V2-receptors regulate serum {{c1::osmolality}}

What is another name for ADH?

{{c1::Vasopressin}}

What is the defect in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?

Mutation in {{c1::V2}}-receptors in the kidney → Decreased response to {{c1::ADH}}

What class of medications inhibit prolactin release?

{{c1::Dopamine}} agonists

Prolactin is structurally homologous to which other pituitary hormone?

{{c1::GH}}
fields.Back Extra: Both are secreted by the anterior pituitary.

fields.Text:
In addition to medications, what are two physical methods by which dopamine levels can be reduced?

{{c1::Nipple}} stimulation
{{c1::Chest wall}} injury via the autonomic nervous system

What effect does estrogen have on prolactin?

Estrogen {{c1::stimulates::stimulates/inhibits}} prolactin secretion

Which hormone has a stronger effect on prolactin secretion, dopamine or TRH?

{{c1::Dopamine}}

What effect does dopamine have on prolactin secretion?

Dopamine {{c1::inhibits::stimulates/inhibits}} prolactin secretion
fields.Back Extra: This is via the tuberoinfundibular pathway of the hypothalamus.

fields.Text:
What reproductive complication can be seen in men with high prolactin levels?

Decreased {{c1::spermatogenesis}}
Decreased {{c1::libido}}

How does hypothyroidism alter prolactin levels?

Hypothyroidism increases {{c1::TRH}} → Prolactin secretion → Inhibits ovulation

Why are women less likely to become pregnant when breastfeeding?

{{c1::Prolactin}} inhibits ovulation via inhibition of {{c1::GnRH}} → Delayed postpartum ovulation

What class of medication, commonly used for mental health disorders, is associated with increased prolactin secretion?

{{c1::Antipsychotics}}
fields.Back Extra: This class of medication blocks dopamine activity, leading to increased prolactin levels.

fields.Text:
How does a baby crying stimulate lactation in the mother?

Cry of baby stimulates higher {{c1::cortical}} centers → Inhibits hypothalamic {{c1::dopamine}} → Increases prolactin levels

Where does coupling of thyroid hormones take place?

{{c1::Follicular lumen}}

Explain how iodine is prepared in the thyroid follicular lumen for use in T3/T4 production.

Iodine is {{c1::oxidized}} → Iodine is exported to the follicular lumen via {{c1::thyroid peroxidase}}

How does the thyroid gland take up iodine from the blood?

{{c1::I-}}/{{c1::Na+}} co-transporter

What are the three main functions of thyroid peroxidase?

{{c1::Oxidation}} of iodine
{{c1::Organification}} of iodine
Coupling of {{c1::MIT}} and {{c1::DIT}}

Where do free T3 and T4 exert negative feedback?

{{c1::Hypothalamus}}
{{c1::Anterior pituitary}}

What combinations of MIT and DIT are needed to make T3 and T4, respectively?

{{c1::DIT}} + {{c1::MIT}} → T3
{{c1::DIT}} + {{c1::DIT}} → T4

Where do T3 and T4 bind to exert their effects? Which of the two has greater affinity?

{{c1::T3}} has greater affinity for {{c1::nuclear}} receptors

What is the mechanism by which pregnancy and oral contraceptive pill use increase total T4 levels?

Pregnancy and oral contraceptive pill use increase {{c1::estrogen}} levels → Increased circulating {{c1::thyroxine-binding globulin}} → Increased total T3/T4

What is the mechanism by which Graves disease may arise?

{{c1::TSI}} stimulates {{c1::follicular}} cells of the thyroid → Graves disease

Describe the mechanisms by which propylthiouracil and methimazole act.

Both inhibit {{c1::thyroid peroxidase}}
Propylthiouracil also inhibits {{c1::5′-deiodinase}}

How may excess amounts of iodine lead to hypothyroid symptoms?

Temporary inhibition of {{c1::thyroid peroxidase}} by extra iodine → Reduced iodine organification → Reduced T3/T4 production
fields.Back Extra: This is known as the Wolff-Chaikoff effect.

fields.Text:
From which large precursor protein is thyroid hormone derived?

{{c1::Thyroglobulin}}

How do free T3 and T4 exert negative feedback on the anterior pituitary and the hypothalamus?

Decreases sensitivity of the anterior pituitary to {{c1::TRH}}
Decreases {{c1::TRH}} secretion from the hypothalamus

What are the catabolic effects of thyroid hormones?

Increased {{c1::glycogenolysis}}
{{c1::Lipolysis}}

What are the seven main functions of T3?

{{c1::Brain::Organ}} maturation
Bone {{c1::growth}}
{{c1::β}}-adrenergic effects in the heart
{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in basal metabolic rate
{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in blood glucose
Break down of {{c1::lipids}}
Increased {{c1::surfactant}} synthesis in babies

How do T3 and T4 affect the basal metabolic rate?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} basal metabolic rate
fields.Back Extra: This is by stimulating Na+/K+-ATPase activity, which increases oxygen consumption, respiratory rate, and body temperature.

fields.Text:
Where are T3 and T4 produced?

T3 and T4 are formed in the {{c1::follicles}} of the thyroid
Most T3 is formed via conversion from T4 to T3 by {{c1::5'-deiodinase}} in peripheral tissue

What plasma protein binds T3/T4 in the blood?

{{c1::Thyroxine-binding globulin}}

How do glucocorticoids lead to hypothyroid-like symptoms?

Glucocorticoids inhibit peripheral conversion of {{c1::T4}} to {{c1::T3}}

Other than T3 and T4, what three other hormones/substances have a negative effect on the anterior pituitary's secretion of TSH?

{{c1::Somatostatin}}
{{c1::Dopamine}}
{{c1::Glucocorticoids}}

Which factors cause a decrease in thyroxine-binding globulin?

{{c1::Nephrotic}} syndrome
{{c1::Steroid}} use

Tyrosine, freed from MIT/DIT via deiodinase in thyroid follicular epithelial cells, re-enters follicular lumens via which carrier protein?

{{c1::Thyroglobulin}}

In the thyroid follicular epithelial cells, not all MIT and DIT produce thyroid hormones. What happens to the excess molecules?

Detach from {{c1::thyroglobulin}} → Converted back into {{c1::inorganic iodine}} and {{c1::tyrosine}} via {{c1::deiodinase}}

Oxidized iodine in the follicular lumen is organified into which two molecules?

{{c1::MIT}}
{{c1::DIT}}

What medication can be given to alleviate the adrenergic symptoms of thyrotoxicosis?

{{c1::β-blockers}}

Which enzyme converts T4 to T3?

{{c1::5'-deiodinase}}

What carrier protein is required for the coupling of iodine?

{{c1::Thyroglobulin}}

Why do T3 and T4 require specific transporters to diffuse into cells?

T3 and T4 are {{c1::lipophilic}} hormones with {{c1::charged::charged/uncharged}} amino acids

Which two factors increase the concentration of rT3?

{{c1::Glucocorticoids}}
{{c1::GH}}

Which factors cause an increase in thyroxine-binding globulin?

{{c1::Pregnancy}}
{{c1::Oral contraceptive pills}} use
fields.Back Extra: This is due to an increase in estrogen.

fields.Text:
Which is the metabolically inactive byproduct of peripheral conversion of T4 to T3?

{{c1::rT3}}

What are the four common ECG findings in a patient with sick sinus syndrome?



Sinus {{c1::pauses}}
Sinus {{c1::arrest}}
{{c1::Bradycardia::Tachycardia/Bradycardia}}
{{c1::Junctional escape beats}}

What is the most likely cause of sick sinus syndrome?

{{c1::Age}}-related degeneration of the {{c1::SA node}}

A patient and several family members present with blanching skin lesions, frequent epistaxis, arteriovenous malformations, hematuria, and gastrointestinal bleeding. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome.

fields.Text:
What is the typical inheritance pattern of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What are the five common conditions in which the Kussmaul sign is seen?

{{c1::Restrictive}} cardiomyopathies
{{c1::Constrictive pericarditis}}
{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} atrial/ventricular {{c1::tumors}}
{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} heart failure
Massive {{c1::pulmonary embolism}}

What sign is associated with an increase in jugular venous pressure with inspiration?

{{c1::Kussmaul}} sign

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism associated with the Kussmaul sign?

Impaired {{c1::right::left/right}} {{c1::ventricle::atrium/ventricle}} filling → Cannot accommodate increased venous return during {{c1::inspiration::inspiration/expiration}} → Backup of blood into vena cava
fields.Back Extra: Negative intrathoracic pressure is insufficient to return blood to the right side of the heart.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism leading to syncope in patients with cardiac myxomas?

"{{c1::Ball valve}}" obstruction of the {{c1::mitral}} valve

What heart tumor is commonly associated with tuberous sclerosis?

{{c1::Rhabdomyoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the most frequent primary cardiac tumor in children.

fields.Text:
In what chambers of the heart are myxomas most commonly found?

{{c1::Atria::Atria/Ventricle}}
fields.Back Extra: This is mostly in the left atrium.

fields.Text:
What is the most common tumor found in the heart?

{{c1::Metastatic lesion}}

Gelatinous material with myxoma cells immersed in glycosaminoglycans is the histopathologic finding in which cardiac tumor?

Cardiac {{c1::myxoma}}

What is the common histologic finding of rhabdomyomas?

{{c1::Hamartomatous}} growths

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism leading to manifestation of constitutional symptoms, such as weight loss and fever, in patients with cardiac myxomas?

Excess production of {{c1::IL-6}} by the myxoma

What auscultatory finding is commonly present in patients with atrial myxomas?

A "{{c1::tumor plop}}" sound in early diastole

What is the most common primary cardiac tumor in children?

{{c1::Rhabdomyoma}}

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism of myocarditis that leads to heart failure?

{{c1::Inflammation}} of the myocardium → Enlargement of the entire heart and dilation of all chambers

What illicit recreational drug causes myocarditis?

{{c1::Cocaine}}

What histologic finding is highly indicative of viral myocarditis?

{{c1::Lymphocytic}} infiltrate with focal {{c1::necrosis}} of myocardial tissue

What are the four most common autoimmune diseases that cause myocarditis?

{{c1::Polymyositis}}/{{c1::dermatomyositis}}
{{c1::Sarcoidosis}}
{{c1::Systemic lupus erythematosus}}
{{c1::Kawasaki}} disease

What are four common symptoms seen in patients with myocarditis?

{{c1::Fever}}
{{c1::Chest}} pain
{{c1::Dyspnea}}
{{c1::Arrhythmias}}
fields.Back Extra: A characteristic symptom is a persistent tachycardia out of proportion to fever.

fields.Text:
Which spider venom causes myocarditis?

{{c1::Black widow}} venom

What are the three most common bacterial causes of myocarditis?

{{c1::Corynebacterium diphtheriae}}
{{c1::Borrelia burgdorferi}}
{{c1::Mycoplasma pneumoniae}}

What are the five most common viruses that cause myocarditis?

{{c1::HIV}}
{{c1::HHV-6}}
{{c1::Adenovirus}}
{{c1::Coxsackie B virus}}
{{c1::Parvovirus B19}}

What are the two most common parasites that cause myocarditis?

{{c1::Toxoplasma gondii}}
{{c1::Trypanosoma cruzi}}

What chemotherapeutic agent commonly used in the treatment of breast cancer causes myocarditis?

{{c1::Doxorubicin}}

What toxin contained in automobile exhaust causes myocarditis?

{{c1::Carbon monoxide}}

What are the two most common ECG findings in patients with acute pericarditis?

Diffuse ST-segment {{c1::elevation::elevation/depression}}
PR-segment {{c1::depression::elevation/depression}}

What is the most common cause of acute pericarditis?

{{c1::Idiopathic}}
fields.Back Extra: Other causes include autoimmune and connective disorders, infections, cardiac surgery, cardiovascular events, radiation, and renal failure.

fields.Text:
What physical maneuver by the patient commonly relieves the pain associated with acute pericarditis?

{{c1::Sitting up}}
Leaning {{c1::forward::forward/backward}}

What common complication of acute pericarditis is indicated by the yellow arrows?



Pericardial {{c1::effusion}}

What is the most common auscultatory finding in patients with acute pericarditis?

Pericardial {{c1::friction rub}}

Name three pharmacologic treatments for acute pericarditis.

{{c1::Colchicine}}
{{c1::NSAIDs}}
{{c1::Glucocorticoids}}

What three parts of the aorta most commonly become calcified with the characteristic "tree bark" appearance in patients with tertiary syphilis?

{{c1::Ascending::Ascending/Descending}} aortic arch
Aortic {{c1::root}}
{{c1::Thoracic::Thoracic/Abdominal}} aorta

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism associated with syphilitic heart disease?

Tertiary syphilis disrupts the aorta's {{c1::vasa vasorum}} → {{c1::Atrophy}} of the vessel wall → Dilation of the aorta and the aortic valve ring

What are the two most common cardiac complications of untreated syphilis?

Aortic valve {{c1::insufficiency}}
{{c1::Aneurysm}} of the aortic arch or ascending aorta

What are the histologic findings associated with rheumatic fever indicated by the blue and red arrows in the image called?



Red arrow → {{c1::Anitschkow}} cells
Blue arrows → {{c1::Aschoff}} bodies

How does the heart murmur of rheumatic heart disease change with time?

Early disease → {{c1::Mitral regurgitation}}
Untreated → {{c1::Mitral stenosis}}

What type of hypersensitivity reaction is responsible for rheumatic fever and what is the pathophysiologic mechanism associated with it?

Type {{c1::II}} hypersensitivity reaction in which antibodies to {{c1::M protein}} cross-react with self-antigens
fields.Back Extra: This is known as molecular mimicry.

fields.Text:
Which heart valves are preferentially affected in rheumatic heart disease?

{{c1::Mitral}} valve > {{c1::Aortic}} valve >> {{c1::Tricuspid}} valve

What antibiotic serves as both treatment and prophylaxis for rheumatic fever?

{{c1::Penicillin}}

What two antibody titers are commonly elevated in patients with rheumatic fever?

Anti-{{c1::DNase B}} titers
Anti-{{c1::streptolysin O}} titers

What are the five major criteria for the diagnosis of rheumatic fever?

{{c1::Joint}} pain
{{c1::Carditis}}
{{c1::Nodules}} in skin
{{c1::Erythema marginatum}}
{{c1::Sydenham chorea}}

What is the characteristic rash associated with rheumatic fever?

{{c1::Erythema marginatum}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an evanescent rash with ring margin.

fields.Text:
A patient has the physical exam finding shown in the image. Name this finding.



{{c1::Splinter hemorrhages}}

What 2 organisms are most commonly associated with culture-negative endocarditis?

{{c1::Coxiella burnetii}}
{{c1::Bartonella}} species

What organism is most commonly associated with prosthetic valve endocarditis?

{{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}}

What intra-abdominal malignancy is commonly found in patients with Streptococcus bovis (gallolyticus) endocarditis?

{{c1::Colon cancer}}

What signs and symptoms are commonly associated with bacterial endocarditis?

{{c1::Fever}}
{{c1::Roth}} spots
{{c1::Osler}} nodes
{{c1::Murmur}}
{{c1::Janeway}} lesions
{{c1::Anemia}}
{{c1::Nail-bed}} hemorrhage
{{c1::Emboli}}

What is the most common risk factor for tricuspid valve endocarditis?

{{c1::Intravenous drug}} use

What is the most likely source of infection in a patient who presents with a fever, glomerulonephritis, and tender, raised lesions on the finger pads?

{{c1::Cardiac valves}}
fields.Back Extra: This is suggestive of bacterial endocarditis.

fields.Text:
What are the 3 most common causes of nonbacterial endocarditis?

{{c1::Hypercoagulable}} state
{{c1::Malignancy}}
{{c1::Lupus}}

What common procedures place patients with abnormal heart valves at risk for subacute bacterial endocarditis?

{{c1::Dental}} procedures

What is the major morphologic difference between vegetations produced by Staphylococcus aureus and those produced by Streptococcus viridans?

Staphylococcus aureus → {{c1::Large}} vegetations
Streptococcus viridans → {{c1::Smaller}} vegetations

A patient presents with fever, new murmur, and the skin findings shown in the image. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Bacterial endocarditis}}

A patient has the fundoscopic exam findings shown in the image. What is the lesion indicated by the arrow?



{{c1::Roth}} spots

What 3 organisms are common causes of tricuspid endocarditis?

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
{{c1::Pseudomonas}}
{{c1::Candida}}

Which valve is most frequently involved in patients with bacterial endocarditis?

{{c1::Mitral}} valve

A patient presents with fever, new murmur, and the skin findings shown in the image, which are tender on exam. Name the lesion.



{{c1::Osler}} nodes
fields.Back Extra: This is secondary to immune complex deposition in bacterial endocarditis.

fields.Text:
What are the primary pulmonary and renal manifestations associated with bacterial endocarditis?

Septic pulmonary/arterial {{c1::emboli}}
{{c1::Glomerulonephritis}}

What type of heart valve is commonly infected by Staphylococcus aureus and what type is commonly infected by Streptococcus viridans?

Staphylococcus aureus infects {{c1::normal}} heart valves
Streptococcus viridans infects {{c1::abnormal}} or {{c1::diseased}} heart valves

Based on the finding shown in the image, how would diastolic pressures within the heart be affected?



Diastolic pressures in all four chambers would be {{c1::equilibrated}}

What are the two ECG abnormalities you would expect in patients with cardiac tamponade?

{{c1::Low::High/Low}}-voltage {{c1::QRS}} amplitude
{{c1::Electrical alternans}}

What is the triad of symptoms commonly seen in patients with cardiac tamponade?

{{c1::Hypotension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Distended}} neck veins
{{c1::Distant}} heart sounds
fields.Back Extra: This is known as Beck's triad.

fields.Text:
What is the finding of a decrease in systolic blood pressure by more than 10 mmHg during inspiration called?

{{c1::Pulsus paradoxus}}

What pathology causes compression of the heart by fluid, such as an effusion, resulting in decreased cardiac output?

Cardiac {{c1::tamponade}}

What are the most common causes of pulsus paradoxus?

{{c1::Constrictive pericarditis}}
{{c1::Obstructive::Obstructive/Restrictive}} pulmonary disease
Cardiac {{c1::tamponade}}

What diagnosis is associated with the ECG finding shown in the image?



{{c1::Pericardial effusion}}
fields.Back Extra: The ECG reveals electrical alternans, which is caused by a "swinging" movement of the heart in a large effusion.

fields.Text:
What effect do corticosteroids have on the arachidonic acid pathway?

They specifically inhibit {{c1::phospholipase A2}}

What is the mechanism of action of the medication zileuton with respect to bronchial tone?

Zileuton is a {{c1::5-lipoxygenase}} inhibitor that indirectly prevents the formation of {{c1::leukotrienes}} → Bronchial {{c1::dilation}}

Which 2 prostaglandins increase uterine tone?

{{c1::PGE2}}
{{c1::PGF2α}}

What effect do LTC4, LTD4, and LTE4 have on the bronchi and bronchioles?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} bronchial tone
{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} constriction

Which leukotriene is a neutrophil chemotactic agent?

{{c1::LTB4}}

Carboprost is a synthetic variant of which prostaglandin? What does it do?

This is a synthetic variant of {{c1::PGF2α}}
This {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} {{c1::uterine}} tone

Dinoprostone is a synthetic variant of which prostaglandin? What does it do?

This is a synthetic variant of {{c1::PGE2}}
This {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} {{c1::uterine}} tone

Alprostadil is a synthetic variant of which prostaglandin? What does it do?

This is a synthetic variant of {{c1::PGE1}}
This {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} {{c1::vascular}} tone

What is epoprostenol and how does it affect platelets and vasculature?

It is a {{c1::prostacyclin}} analog
This {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} platelet aggregation and vascular tone

Which NSAID inhibits only COX-2?

{{c1::Celecoxib}}

What type of NSAID irreversibly inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 in the arachidonic acid pathway?

{{c1::Aspirin}}

What product of the arachidonic acid cascade promotes platelet aggregation and increases vascular tone?

{{c1::TXA2}}

What does the 5-lipoxygenase pathway of the arachidonic acid pathway yield?

{{c1::Leukotrienes}}

What is the mechanism of action of the medications montelukast and zafirlukast with respect to bronchial tone?

Montelukast and zafirlukast are {{c1::leukotriene}} receptor antagonists that block the action of {{c1::leukotrienes}} → Bronchial {{c1::dilation}}

What happens to the midgut in utero during the 10th week of gestation?

Returns to the abdominal cavity and rotates around the {{c1::superior mesenteric}} artery

What happens to the midgut in utero during the 6th week of gestation?

Herniates through the {{c1::umbilical ring}}

What portion of the gastrointestinal tract is derived from the hindgut?

{{c1::Distal::Proximal/Distal}} {{c1::1}}/3 of the transverse colon to the anal canal {{c1::above::above/below}} the pectinate line

What portion of the gastrointestinal tract is derived from the midgut?

Lower part of the {{c1::duodenum}} to the {{c1::proximal::proximal/distal}} {{c1::2}}/3 of the transverse colon

What portion of the gastrointestinal tract is derived from the foregut?

The {{c1::esophagus}} to the {{c1::duodenum}} at the level of the {{c1::ampulla of Vater}}

What type of fold closure failure causes the condition shown in the image?



{{c1::Lateral}} folds failed to close properly

What structure failed to close in a patient with a congenital umbilical hernia?

{{c1::Umbilical ring}}

What is the location of the ventral wall defect shown in the image in relation to the umbilicus?



Typically to the {{c1::right::left/right}} of the umbilicus

What specific type of ventral wall defect is due to failure of caudal fold closure in utero?

{{c1::Bladder exstrophy}}

What ventral wall defects are due to failure of lateral fold closure in utero?

{{c1::Gastroschisis}}
{{c1::Omphalocele}}

What specific type of ventral wall defect is due to failure of rostral fold closure in utero?

{{c1::Sternal}} defects

What three congenital syndromes are commonly associated with omphaloceles?

Trisomy {{c1::13}}
Trisomy {{c1::18}}
{{c1::Beckwith-Wiedemann}} syndrome

What is the etiology of the ventral wall defect depicted in the image?



Failure of {{c1::lateral}} walls to migrate at the {{c1::umbilical ring}} → Omphalocele

What feature of a congenital umbilical hernia increases the likelihood of its spontaneous closure?

{{c1::Small}} size

What two congenital disorders are associated with a congenital umbilical hernia?

{{c1::Down}} syndrome
Congenital {{c1::hypothyroidism::hyperthyroidism/hypothyroidism}}

What congenital ventral wall defect presents as a skin-covered protrusion at the umbilicus that increases in size with crying?

Congenital {{c1::umbilical hernia}}

In the image, what specific pathologies do the labels A, B, and C represent compared with normal anatomy?



A → {{c1::Pure esophageal atresia}}
B → {{c1::Pure tracheoesophageal fistula}}
C → {{c1::Esophageal atresia}} with distal {{c1::tracheoesophageal fistula}}

What type of esophageal atresia presents without a gastric bubble on imaging?

{{c1::Pure esophageal atresia}}

What procedure would best confirm the likely diagnosis in a neonate with excessive drooling and vomiting during the first feeding?

Attempt to pass a {{c1::nasogastric tube}}
fields.Back Extra: In a patient with tracheoesophageal fistula, the tube will not reach the stomach.

fields.Text:
What are three initial signs and symptoms of distal tracheoesophageal fistula seen after delivery?

{{c1::Drooling}}
{{c1::Choking}}
{{c1::Vomiting}} with first feeding

Why might a newborn with a tracheoesophageal fistula become cyanotic?

Cyanosis is caused by {{c1::laryngospasm}} in an effort to avoid reflux-related aspiration

What is the most common subtype of tracheoesophageal anomaly?

{{c1::Esophageal atresia}} with a distal {{c1::tracheoesophageal fistula}}

Which two tracheoesophageal anomalies are associated with prominent gas bubbles on chest X-rays?

{{c1::Pure tracheoesophageal fistula}}
{{c1::Esophageal atresia}} with distal {{c1::tracheoesophageal fistula}}

How does a tracheoesophageal fistula usually present in utero?

With {{c1::polyhydramnios}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to an inability of the fetus to swallow amniotic fluid.

fields.Text:
Which syndrome is associated with the pathology seen in patients with the radiographic findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Down}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This newborn likely has duodenal atresia.

fields.Text:
What is the likely diagnosis of a newborn presenting with bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and the abdominal X-ray findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Duodenal atresia}}
fields.Back Extra: The X-ray shows a "double bubble" sign with a dilated stomach and proximal duodenum.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism associated with jejunal and ileal atresia?

{{c1::Mesenteric}} vessels are disrupted in utero → {{c1::Ischemic necrosis}} and {{c1::segmental}} resorption → Discontinuous bowel

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism associated with duodenal atresia?

Failure of duodenum to {{c1::recanalize}}

What radiologic finding is seen in patients with jejunal and/or ileal atresia?

{{c1::Dilated}} stomach, duodenum, and proximal jejunum with a {{c1::gasless}} colon
fields.Back Extra: This is known as the "triple bubble" sign.

fields.Text:
What metabolic manifestation is seen in patients with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?

{{c1::Hypokalemic::Hyperkalemic/Hypokalemic}}, {{c1::hypochloremic::hyperchloremic/hypochloremic}} metabolic {{c1::alkalosis::acidosis/alkalosis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to vomiting of gastric acid and resultant volume contraction.

fields.Text:
How long after birth do the symptoms of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis tend to present?

{{c1::2}} to {{c1::6}} weeks after birth

What type of vomiting is seen in infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?

{{c1::Nonbilious::Bilious/Nonbilious}} {{c1::projectile}} vomiting
fields.Back Extra: Bilious vomiting originates distal to the ligament of Treitz or the ampulla of Vater.

fields.Text:
In what newborn population is hypertrophic pyloric stenosis more likely to be seen?

{{c1::Firstborn}} {{c1::males::males/females}}

What type of antibiotics, when administered to pregnant patients, are associated with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis in newborns?

{{c1::Macrolides}}

What gastric motility issue does hypertrophy of the pylorus lead to?

Gastric {{c1::outlet obstruction}}

What is the treatment for a newborn with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?

{{c1::Pyloromyotomy}}

What physical examination finding in a newborn is suggestive of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?

{{c1::Olive}}-shaped mass palpated in the {{c1::epigastric}} region

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient presenting with vomiting and the findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Annular pancreas}}
fields.Back Extra: There is a ring of pancreatic tissue encircling the second portion of duodenum, indicated by the red arrows.

fields.Text:
What region of the embryonic gut does the spleen share its blood supply with?

{{c1::Foregut}}

What embryonic germ cell layer does the spleen arise from?

{{c1::Mesoderm}}

What symptoms might be seen in a patient with failure of fusion of the ventral and dorsal pancreatic buds?

Chronic {{c1::abdominal}} pain
{{c1::Pancreatitis}}
fields.Back Extra: The patient has pancreas divisum, which is mostly asymptomatic.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism seen in pancreas divisum?

Failure of the {{c1::ventral}} and {{c1::dorsal}} pancreatic buds to fuse during week {{c1::7}} of embryologic development

What malformation results when the abnormal rotation of the ventral pancreatic bud leads to the formation of a ring around the second part of the duodenum?

{{c1::Annular pancreas}}

What five adult pancreatic structures are derived from the dorsal pancreatic bud?

{{c1::Body}}
{{c1::Tail}}
{{c1::Isthmus}}
{{c1::Accessory::Main/Accessory}} pancreatic duct
Pancreatic {{c1::head}}

What three adult pancreatic structures are derived from the ventral pancreatic bud?

{{c1::Main::Main/Accessory}} pancreatic duct
{{c1::Uncinate process}}
Pancreatic {{c1::head}}

What part of the embryonic gut is the pancreas derived from?

{{c1::Foregut}}

Why do diaphragmatic hernias commonly occur on the left side?

The {{c1::liver::organ}} provides relative protection of the right hemidiaphragm from a diaphragmatic hernia

The contents of a hernia are at risk for what two possible complications?

{{c1::Incarceration}}
{{c1::Strangulation}}

How did the hernia in this image likely develop?



The {{c1::processus vaginalis}} did not close
fields.Back Extra: This is an indirect inguinal hernia.

fields.Text:
An infant's chest X-ray reveals loops of bowel in the thorax. Name the defect and its most common cause.



This is a {{c1::diaphragmatic hernia}}
This is a congenital defect of the {{c1::pleuroperitoneal membrane}} leading to left-sided {{c1::herniation}} of abdominal structures into the thorax

Describe the pathway of an indirect inguinal hernia.



Enters {{c1::internal::internal/external}} inguinal ring {{c1::lateral::medial/lateral}} to {{c1::inferior epigastric}} vessels → {{c1::External::Internal/External}} inguinal ring → Groin

What structure is a useful landmark for differentiating direct inguinal hernias from indirect inguinal hernias?

{{c1::Inferior epigastric}} vessels
fields.Back Extra:
Medial to inferior epigastric vessels → Direct inguinal hernias

Lateral to Inferior epigastric vessels → Indirect inguinal hernias

fields.Text:
Through which structure do both direct and indirect hernias pass?

The {{c1::external::internal/external}} inguinal ring

What developmental complication may result in the formation of an indirect inguinal hernia?

Incomplete closure of the {{c1::processus vaginalis}}

What type of hiatal hernia is displayed in the image?



{{c1::Paraesophageal}} hiatal hernia

What is a hernia?

Protrusion of the {{c1::peritoneum}} through an opening
fields.Back Extra: This is usually in a weakened area.

fields.Text:
Describe the location of a femoral hernia.

Below the {{c1::inguinal}} ligament through the femoral {{c1::canal}} below and lateral to the {{c1::pubic tubercle}}

How many layers of the spermatic fascia cover the sac of an indirect hernia?

{{c1::3}}

How many layers of spermatic fascia cover a direct inguinal hernia?

{{c1::1}}
fields.Back Extra: Only the external spermatic fascia covers a direct inguinal hernia.

fields.Text:
Which type of groin hernias are more likely to present with incarceration or strangulation?

{{c1::Femoral}} hernias

What type of hernia is displayed in the image?



{{c1::Sliding hiatal}} hernia
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as an "hourglass stomach".

fields.Text:
What are the two types of hiatal hernias and which one is more common?

{{c1::Sliding}} hiatal hernia (more common)
{{c1::Paraesophageal}} hiatal hernia

In which patient population are femoral hernias more common?

{{c1::Females::Males/Females}}

What are three signs of a complicated hernia?

{{c1::Erythema}}
{{c1::Fever}}
{{c1::Tenderness}}

Sliding hiatal hernias are associated with which condition?

{{c1::Gastroesophageal reflux}} disease

In which patient population are indirect inguinal hernias more common?

{{c1::Males::Males/Females}}

What type of hernia is shown in the image and which area in the inguinal region does it protrude from?



{{c1::Direct::Direct/Indirect}} inguinal hernia
This protrudes through the {{c1::Hesselbach triangle}}, directly through the {{c1::parietal peritoneum}}

In which patient population are direct inguinal hernias more common?

{{c1::Older::Younger/Older}} {{c1::men::men/women}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to acquired weakness of the transversalis fascia.

fields.Text:
What defect causes hiatal hernias in adults?

Laxity or defect of the {{c1::phrenoesophageal membrane}} → Herniation of the stomach through the esophageal hiatus

What are the boundaries of the Hesselbach triangle?

Lateral border of {{c1::rectus abdominis}} muscle
{{c1::Inguinal}} ligament
{{c1::Inferior epigastric}} vessels

What anatomic landmarks indicate the upper and lower limits of the inguinal ligament?

{{c1::ASIS}}
{{c1::Pubic tubercle}}

What major blood vessels and nerve pass underneath the inguinal ligament?

{{c1::External iliac}} vessels
{{c1::Femoral}} nerve

Name the region of the anterior abdominal wall surrounded by the dotted line.



{{c1::Hesselbach triangle}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as the inguinal triangle.

fields.Text:
What structures are contained in the inguinal canal?

{{c1::Internal spermatic}} vessels
{{c1::Ilioinguinal}} nerve
{{c1::Vas deferens}} in males
{{c1::Round}} ligament of the uterus in females

Which layer of the abdominal wall evaginates to form the internal inguinal ring?

{{c1::Transversalis}} fascia

The inferior epigastric vessels are branches of which vascular structures?

{{c1::External iliac}} vessels

Which artery is a continuation of the external iliac artery below the inguinal ligament?

{{c1::Femoral}} artery

Which abdominal wall layers reinforce the inguinal ligament superiorly?

{{c1::Transversalis}} fascia
{{c1::Transversus abdominis}} muscle

Relative to the inferior epigastric vessels, where do a direct and an indirect inguinal hernia present?

Direct hernia → {{c1::Medially::Medially/Laterally}}
Indirect hernia → {{c1::Laterally::Medially/Laterally}}

From what muscle layer does the external spermatic fascia of the spermatic cord originate?

{{c1::External oblique}} muscle

From which layer does the internal spermatic fascia derive?

{{c1::Transversalis}} fascia

Through what structure does a direct inguinal hernia protrude?

{{c1::Abdominal wall}}

What layers comprise the spermatic cord?

{{c1::Internal spermatic}} fascia
{{c1::Cremasteric}} muscle and fascia
{{c1::External spermatic}} fascia

Through which structure does an indirect inguinal hernia protrude?

{{c1::Internal::Internal/External}} inguinal ring

The splenorenal ligament contains what structures?

{{c1::Splenic}} artery
{{c1::Splenic}} vein
Pancreatic {{c1::tail}}

The splenorenal ligament connects which two structures?

{{c1::Spleen::Organ}}
Left {{c1::pararenal space}}

What does the gastrosplenic ligament separate?

The {{c1::greater omental sac}} and {{c1::lesser omental sac}} on the left side

The gastrosplenic ligament contains what structures?

{{c1::Short gastric}} vessels
Left {{c1::gastroepiploic}} vessels

Which two gastrointestinal ligaments are part of the greater omentum?

{{c1::Gastrocolic}} ligament
{{c1::Gastrosplenic}} ligament

The gastrocolic ligament contains what structures?

The {{c1::gastroepiploic}} arteries

The gastrocolic ligament connects which two structures?

{{c1::Transverse}} colon
{{c1::Greater curvature}} of the stomach

Which two gastrointestinal ligaments are part of the lesser omentum?

{{c1::Hepatoduodenal}} ligament
{{c1::Hepatogastric}} ligament

Which gastrointestinal ligament can be cut to access the lesser omental sac during surgery?

{{c1::Hepatogastric}} ligament

What does the hepatogastric ligament separate?

The {{c1::greater omental sac}} and {{c1::lesser omental sac}} on the right side

What vessels lie within the hepatogastric ligament?

The {{c1::gastric}} vessels

The hepatogastric ligament connects which two structures?

{{c1::Liver::Organ}}
{{c1::Lesser curvature}} of the stomach

Which structures does the omental foramen connect?

{{c1::Lesser omental sac}}
{{c1::Greater omental sac}}

Describe the Pringle maneuver and its utility in surgery.

Compression of the {{c1::hepatoduodenal}} ligament through the {{c1::omental foramen}} to control {{c1::bleeding}} from a hepatic inflow source

What structures lie within the hepatoduodenal ligament?

{{c1::Proper hepatic}} artery
{{c1::Portal}} vein
{{c1::Common bile}} duct
fields.Back Extra: This is known as the portal triad.

fields.Text:
Which two structures are connected by the hepatoduodenal ligament, a part of the lesser omentum?

{{c1::Liver::Organ}}
{{c1::Duodenum}}

The falciform, hepatoduodenal, and hepatogastric ligaments are derived from what structure?

{{c1::Ventral::Ventral/Dorsal}} {{c1::mesentery}}

The falciform ligament contains which two structures?

{{c1::Patent paraumbilical}} veins
{{c1::Ligamentum teres hepatis}}

The falciform ligament connects which two structures?

The {{c1::liver::organ}} and the {{c1::anterior::anterior/posterior}} {{c1::abdominal wall}}

The gastrocolic, gastrosplenic, and splenorenal ligaments are derived from what structure?

{{c1::Dorsal::Ventral/Dorsal}} {{c1::mesentery}}

The gastrosplenic ligament connects which two structures?

{{c1::Spleen::Organ}}
{{c1::Greater curvature}} of the stomach

List the four main layers of the gut wall, starting from the lumen.

{{c1::Mucosa}}
{{c1::Submucosa}}
{{c1::Muscularis externa}}
{{c1::Serosa}}

List the stomach, duodenum, and ileum in terms of decreasing frequency of basal electrical rhythms.

{{c1::Duodenum}} > {{c1::Ileum}} > {{c1::Stomach}}

Compare ulcers with erosions in terms of which layers of the gut wall are affected.

Ulcers extend into the {{c1::submucosa}}
Erosions are in the {{c1::mucosa}} only

What is the outermost layer of the gut called when intraperitoneal?

{{c1::Serosa}}
fields.Back Extra: It is called the adventitia when retroperitoneal.

fields.Text:
Which nerve plexus lies between the inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa?

{{c1::Myenteric}} nerve plexus
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as the Auerbach nerve plexus.

fields.Text:
If a patient were missing the submucosal nerve plexus, which gut function would be impaired?

{{c1::Secretory}} activity
fields.Back Extra: The submucosal nerve plexus is also known as the Meissner nerve plexus.

fields.Text:
List the three components of the gut wall mucosa.

{{c1::Epithelium}}
{{c1::Lamina propria}}
{{c1::Muscularis mucosa}}

What is the source of basal electric rhythm in the gastrointestinal tract?

{{c1::Interstitial}} cells of {{c1::Cajal}}

Identify the structures of the gastrointestinal tract by the labels shown in the image.



A → {{c1::Mucosa}}
B → {{c1::Submucosa}}
C → {{c1::Submucosal}} nerve plexus
D → {{c1::Myenteric}} nerve plexus
E → {{c1::Serosa}}

What are the functions of Paneth cells that are found in the crypts of Lieberkühn?

Secretion of {{c1::defensins}}
Secretion of {{c1::lysozyme}}
Secretion of {{c1::TNF}}

What are the functions of stem cells that reside in the crypts of Lieberkühn?

Replacement of {{c1::enterocytes}}
Replacement of {{c1::goblet}} cells

Which segment of the intestines contains crypts of Lieberkühn and goblet cells but no villi?

{{c1::Colon}}

Goblet cells are most highly concentrated in which area of the small intestine?

{{c1::Ileum}}

Which immunologic structures are unique to the ileum?

{{c1::Peyer patches}}

What segments of the small intestine have plicae circulares?

Distal {{c1::duodenum}}
{{c1::Jejunum}}
Proximal {{c1::ileum}}

Where are goblet cells, Paneth cells, and stem cells for enterocytes found throughout the small intestine and colon?

{{c1::Crypts of Lieberkühn}}

How do the plicare circulares in the jejunum appear?

{{c1::Feathered}} appearance with oral contrast
fields.Back Extra: They are taller, more prominent, and numerous in the jejunum than in the ileum.

fields.Text:
What submucosal glands are unique to the duodenum?

{{c1::Brunner}} glands

Gastric glands are found in which part of the digestive tract?

{{c1::Stomach}}

What type of epithelial cells normally line the esophagus?

{{c1::Nonkeratinized::Keratinized/Nonkeratinized}} {{c1::stratified::simple/stratified}} {{c1::squamous::squamous/cuboidal/columnar}} epithelium

What types of muscle are seen in the upper third and in the middle and lower two-thirds of the esophagus?

Upper third → {{c1::Striated}} muscle
Middle and lower two-thirds → {{c1::Smooth}} muscle

What histologic structures in the small intestine are an important part of the immune response?

Ileum → {{c1::Peyer patches}}
Duodenum → {{c1::Paneth}} cells

What is the function of Brunner glands?

They secrete {{c1::bicarbonate}}

The image shows a sample of tissue obtained from a portion of the stomach. Identify the structure indicated by the arrow.



{{c1::Gastric}} gland

Identify the structures indicated by the arrows in the image and indicate their usual location in the gastrointestinal tract and their function.



These are {{c1::villi}}
Found in the {{c1::small intestine}}, but not the {{c1::colon}}
Function is to increase {{c1::absorptive}} surface area

The image shows tissue obtained from an area of the ileum. Which structure is indicated by the arrow?



{{c1::Peyer patches}}

Which area of the gastrointestinal tract is shown in the image?



{{c1::Colon}}
fields.Back Extra: This is based on the lack of villi and presence of crypts of Lieberkühn and abundant goblet cells.

fields.Text:
The image shows a sample of tissue obtained from a portion of the stomach. Identify the structures indicated by the red and black arrows.



Red arrow → {{c1::Parietal}} cells
Black arrow → {{c1::Chief}} cells

Why does a ruptured abdominal aorta present with back pain rather than chest or epigastric pain?

The aorta in the abdomen is {{c1::retroperitoneal}}
fields.Back Extra: Hence, pain is referred to the dorsal aspect of the body.

fields.Text:
Which part of the esophagus is part of the retroperitoneum?

{{c1::Thoracic}} part

Which portions of the colon are retroperitoneal?

{{c1::Ascending}} colon
{{c1::Descending}} colon

Which two portions of the urinary tract are retroperitoneal?

{{c1::Kidneys}}
{{c1::Ureters}}

What part of the pancreas is not retroperitoneal?

{{c1::Tail}}

Which parts of the duodenum are retroperitoneal?

{{c1::2nd}} to {{c1::4th}} parts

Injury to retroperitoneal structures may cause what substances to accumulate in the retroperitoneal space?

{{c1::Blood}}
{{c1::Gas}}

What major vascular structures are retroperitoneal?

{{c1::Aorta}}
{{c1::Inferior vena cava}}

Identify the labeled retroperitoneal structures shown in the image.



A → {{c1::Ascending}} colon
B → {{c1::Descending}} colon
C → {{c1::Inferior vena cava}}
D → {{c1::Aorta}}
E → Right {{c1::kidney}}
F → Left {{c1::kidney}}

Arteries supplying non-gastrointestinal structures are paired and branch out which way from the aorta?

{{c1::Laterally::Medially/Laterally}}
{{c1::Posteriorly::Anteriorly/Posteriorly}}

What medical history is associated with superior mesenteric artery syndrome?

Conditions associated with reduced {{c1::mesenteric fat}}
fields.Back Extra: The patient would present with intermittent postprandial pain.

fields.Text:
Which arteries are responsible for causing superior mesenteric artery syndrome?

{{c1::Superior mesenteric}} artery
{{c1::Aorta}}
fields.Back Extra: This compress the transverse portion of the duodenum.

fields.Text:
Where is the inferior vena cava found relative to the aorta?

To the {{c1::right::left/right}}
