Unpaired arteries supplying gastrointestinal structures branch out in which direction from the aorta?

{{c1::Anteriorly::Anteriorly/Posteriorly}}

The common iliac arteries further bifurcate into which two major arteries?

{{c1::Internal iliac}} artery
{{c1::External iliac}} artery

Which three arteries does the aorta become after the bifurcation?

Left {{c1::common iliac}} artery
Right {{c1::common iliac}} artery
{{c1::Median sacral}} artery

At what level does the abdominal aorta bifurcate?

{{c1::L4}}

What anterior branch of the aorta originates at the L3 level?

{{c1::Inferior mesenteric}} artery

The paired arteries feeding the gonads originate from the abdominal aorta at which level?

{{c1::L2}}

Which branches of the aorta originate at L1?

{{c1::Superior mesenteric}} artery
{{c1::Renal}} arteries
fields.Back Extra: The inferior suprarenal arteries branch from the renal arteries.

fields.Text:
Which branches of the aorta originate at the T12 level?

{{c1::Celiac trunk}}
{{c1::Middle suprarenal}} artery
{{c1::Inferior phrenic}} artery
fields.Back Extra: The superior suprarenal artery is a branch of the inferior phrenic artery.

fields.Text:
Which arteries branching from the aorta supply the splenic flexure?

{{c1::Superior mesenteric}} artery
{{c1::Inferior mesenteric}} artery
fields.Back Extra: The splenic flexure is the watershed area between them.

fields.Text:
Which areas of the colon are particularly susceptible in cases of colonic ischemia?

{{c1::Splenic flexure}}
{{c1::Rectosigmoid}} junction

Which arteries supply the rectosigmoid junction?

Last {{c1::sigmoid}} arterial branch from the {{c1::inferior mesenteric}} artery
{{c1::Superior rectal}} artery

What vein is susceptible to compression between the superior mesenteric artery and aorta?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::renal}} vein

What vascular condition presents with abdominal pain, gross hematuria, and left-sided varicocele due to venous compression?

{{c1::Nutcracker}} syndrome

Which portion of the gut does not receive parasympathetic innervation from the vagus nerve?

{{c1::Hindgut}}
fields.Back Extra: The vagus nerve innervates the foregut and midgut, while the pelvic splanchnic nerves innervate the hindgut.

fields.Text:
At which vertebral level is the midgut's blood supply located?

{{c1::L1}}
fields.Back Extra: The midgut is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery.

fields.Text:
Which artery supplies the midgut?

{{c1::Superior mesenteric}} artery

Which structures are supplied by the celiac artery?

Lower {{c1::esophagus}} to proximal {{c1::duodenum}}
{{c1::Gallbladder}}
{{c1::Liver}}
{{c1::Spleen}}
{{c1::Pancreas}}

Where does the sympathetic innervation of the gut arise from?

{{c1::Celiac}} ganglia
{{c1::Superior mesenteric}} ganglia
{{c1::Inferior mesenteric}} ganglia

From which nerve do the foregut and midgut get their parasympathetic innervation?

{{c1::Vagus}} nerve

Which artery supplies foregut structures?

{{c1::Celiac}} artery

What artery supplies the hindgut?

{{c1::Inferior mesenteric}} artery

At what vertebral level is the body's foregut blood supply derived?

{{c1::T12}}/{{c1::L1}}
fields.Back Extra: This is from the celiac artery.

fields.Text:
At what vertebral level is the body's hindgut blood supply derived?

{{c1::L3}}
fields.Back Extra: This is from the inferior mesenteric artery.

fields.Text:
Which structure derived from the embryonic foregut is innervated by the vagus nerve but is not supplied by the celiac artery?

{{c1::Pharynx}}

What vessels supply the lesser curvature of the stomach?

Right {{c1::gastric}} artery
Left {{c1::gastric}} artery

What part of the stomach is supplied by the right and left gastroepiploic arteries?

{{c1::Greater curvature}} of the stomach

What are the three branches of the gastroduodenal artery?

Anterior {{c1::superior pancreaticoduodenal}} artery
Posterior {{c1::superior pancreaticoduodenal}} artery
Right {{c1::gastroepiploic}} artery

What are the two main branches of the common hepatic artery?

{{c1::Gastroduodenal}} artery
{{c1::Proper hepatic}} artery

What branches of the splenic artery supply the stomach?

Left {{c1::gastroepiploic}} artery
{{c1::Short gastric}} artery

Strong anastomoses exist between what arteries that branch off the celiac trunk and supply the stomach?

Left and right {{c1::gastroepiploic}} arteries
Left and right {{c1::gastric}} arteries

Which major branch of the aorta supplies the stomach?

{{c1::Celiac trunk}}
fields.Back Extra: Later branches include the gastric and gastroepiploic ateries.

fields.Text:
Name the three main branches of the celiac trunk.

{{c1::Common hepatic}} artery
{{c1::Splenic}} artery
Left {{c1::gastric}} artery

What are the three branches of the proper hepatic artery?

{{c1::Cystic}} artery
Right {{c1::hepatic}} artery
Left {{c1::hepatic}} artery

What branch of the celiac trunk gives blood supply to the esophagus?

Left {{c1::gastric}} artery

Via what pathway does blood leave the umbilicus to enter the portal circulation?

{{c1::Paraumbilical}} vein → Portal vein

Via what pathway does blood leave the umbilicus to enter the systemic circulation?

{{c1::Small epigastric}} vein

Via what pathway does blood leave the anus to enter the portal circulation?

{{c1::Superior rectal}} vein → {{c1::Inferior mesenteric}} vein → {{c1::Splenic}} vein → Portal vein

Via what pathway does blood leave the anus to enter the systemic circulation?

{{c1::Middle rectal}} vein
{{c1::Inferior rectal}} vein

A TIPS procedure can precipitate what condition?

{{c1::Hepatic encephalopathy}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is due to decreased clearance of ammonia as a result of bypassing the liver.

TIPS stands for transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt.

fields.Text:
What surgical procedure can be used to relieve portal hypertension by shunting blood from the portal to the systemic circulation?

{{c1::TIPS}}
fields.Back Extra: TIPS stands for transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt.

fields.Text:
Anastamoses between which two vessels result in anorectal varicies?

{{c1::Superior rectal}} vein
{{c1::Middle}}/{{c1::inferior}} {{c1::rectal}} vein

Which veins are responsible for the formation of caput medusae?

{{c1::Paraumbilical}} vein
{{c1::Small epigastric}} vein of the anterior abdominal wall

Via what pathway does blood leave the esophagus to enter the portal circulation?

Left {{c1::gastric}} vein → Portal vein

Anastamoses between which two vessels are responsible for esophageal varicies?

Left {{c1::gastric}} vein
{{c1::Esophageal}} vein

Via what pathway does blood leave the esophagus to enter the systemic circulation?

{{c1::Esophageal}} vein → {{c1::Azygos}} vein

What are the clinical manifestations of portal hypertension attributable to portosystemic anastomoses?

{{c1::Esophageal varices}}
{{c1::Anorectal varices}}
{{c1::Caput medusae}}

Which type of hemorrhoids are not associated with pain?

{{c1::Internal::Internal/External}} hemorrhoids
fields.Back Extra: They receive visceral innervation from the inferior hypogastric plexus and are therefore painless.

fields.Text:
What is the venous drainage system below the pectinate line?

{{c1::Inferior rectal}} vein → {{c1::Internal pudendal}} vein → {{c1::Internal iliac}} vein → {{c1::Common iliac}} vein → Inferior vena cava

What is the venous drainage system above the pectinate line?

{{c1::Superior rectal}} vein → {{c1::Inferior mesenteric}} vein → {{c1::Splenic}} vein → Portal vein

What dietary recommendations should be made for patients presenting with anal fissures?

A high-{{c1::fiber}} diet

The inferior rectal artery is a branch of what artery?

{{c1::Internal pudendal}} artery

Which nerve is responsible for the pain felt with anal fissures or thrombosed external hemorrhoids?

{{c1::Inferior rectal}} branch of the {{c1::pudendal}} nerve
fields.Back Extra: The region below the pectinate line has somatic innervation, which allows for the sensation of pain.

fields.Text:
The superior rectal artery is a branch of what artery that comes off the aorta?

{{c1::Inferior mesenteric}} artery

What are the primary locations of lymphatic drainage above and below the pectinate line?

Above → {{c1::Internal iliac}} lymph nodes
Below → {{c1::Superficial inguinal}} lymph nodes

The pectinate line is formed where which two embryologic derivatives meet?

{{c1::Endoderm}}
{{c1::Ectoderm}}

What type of hemorrhoids occur above and below the pectinate line?

Above → {{c1::Internal}} hemorrhoids
Below → {{c1::External}} hemorrhoids

What condition causes painful defecation and blood on the toilet paper due a tear in the anoderm below the pectinate line?

{{c1::Anal fissure}}

What is the structure indicated by the horizontal dotted line in the image?



{{c1::Pectinate line}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as the dentate line.

fields.Text:
What type of carcinoma is more common above the pectinate line?

{{c1::Adenocarcinoma}}

What type of carcinoma is more common below the pectinate line?

{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma

What pathophysiology is responsible for the formation of internal hemorrhoids?

Abnormal anal venous plexus {{c1::distention}}
fields.Back Extra: This is associated with chronic constipation and older age.

fields.Text:
Where are anal fissures usually located?

{{c1::Posterior::Anterior/Posterior}} midline {{c1::below::above/below}} the pectinate line

What cells within the liver are responsible for storing vitamin A when quiescent?

{{c1::Ito}} cells in the space of Disse
fields.Back Extra: These are also known as hepatic stellate cells.

fields.Text:
In this image of a liver lobule in cross-section, what are the cells indicated by the black and yellow arrows?



Black arrows → {{c1::Kupffer}} cells
Yellow arrows → {{c1::Central vein}}

Which portion of the liver is most affected in a patient with alcoholic hepatitis?

Zone {{c1::III}}

Which zone of the liver is most sensitive to metabolic toxins?

Zone {{c1::III}}

In which zone of the liver is cytochrome P-450 most highly concentrated?

Zone {{c1::III}}

What portion of the liver is affected by yellow fever?

Zone {{c1::II}}

What zone of the liver is affected first by viral hepatitis?

Zone {{c1::I}}

Which surface of hepatocytes face bile canaliculi?

{{c1::Apical}} surface

Which surface of hepatocytes face the sinusoids?

{{c1::Basolateral}} surface

Which zone of the liver is affected first by ischemia?

Zone {{c1::III}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because it is the least oxygenated zone.

fields.Text:
When activated, what do hepatic stellate cells produce?

{{c1::Extracellular matrix}}
fields.Back Extra: These are also known as Ito cells.

fields.Text:
Which cells are responsible for hepatic fibrosis?

{{c1::Ito}} cells
fields.Back Extra: These are also known as hepatic stellate cells.

fields.Text:
What structures make up the functional units of the liver?

{{c1::Lobules}} in a {{c1::hexagonal}} pattern around a {{c1::central vein}} with portal triads on edges

Which zone of the liver is the most resistant to circulatory compromise?

Zone {{c1::I}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the most oxygenated zone.

fields.Text:
What is the function of Kupffer cells of the liver?

Clearance of {{c1::bacteria}}
Clearance of {{c1::red blood}} cells that are damaged or senescent

Which zone of the liver acts on ingested toxins?

Zone {{c1::I}}

In which part of the pancreas is a tumor most likely located if a patient presents with painless jaundice and an enlarged gallbladder?

{{c1::Head}} of the pancreas

What structure do the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct form before they empty into the duodenum?

{{c1::Ampulla of Vater}}

Bile passes through what structure after the ampulla of Vater to enter the duodenum?

{{c1::Sphincter of Oddi}}

Gallstones that reach the confluence of the common bile and pancreatic ducts at the ampulla of Vater can cause what radiologic sign?

{{c1::Double duct}} sign
fields.Back Extra: This is due to blockage and dilatation of both the common bile and pancreatic ducts.

fields.Text:
Gallstones at the ampulla of Vater can cause what two acute conditions?

{{c1::Cholangitis}}
{{c1::Pancreatitis}}

A patient has right upper quadrant pain and a tender gallbladder. What does the cholangiogram reveal?



{{c1::Filling}} defects in the gallbladder and cystic duct
fields.Back Extra: This is due to an impacted gallstone in the cystic duct.

fields.Text:
What malignancy typically presents in the head of the pancreas?

{{c1::Ductal}} adenocarcinoma

Through which two ducts can pancreatic secretions travel to reach the duodenum?

{{c1::Main}} pancreatic duct
{{c1::Accessory}} pancreatic duct

What are the anatomical divisions of the pancreas?

{{c1::Head}}
{{c1::Neck}}
{{c1::Body}}
{{c1::Tail}}

What structure of the femoral triangle does not lie within the femoral sheath?

Femoral {{c1::nerve}}

What three main structures are contained within the femoral sheath?

Femoral {{c1::vein}}
Femoral {{c1::artery}}
Femoral {{c1::canal}}
fields.Back Extra: Note that the femoral nerve is not included.

fields.Text:
Name, from lateral to medial, the organization of the vasculature, lymphatics, and nerves in the femoral region.

Femoral {{c1::nerve}}
Femoral {{c1::artery}}
Femoral {{c1::vein}}
Femoral {{c1::lymphatics}}

Which structures form the superior, lateral, and medial borders of the femoral triangle?

Superior border → {{c1::Inguinal}} ligament
Lateral border → {{c1::Sartorius}} muscle
Medial border → {{c1::Adductor longus}} muscle

What structure must the intestines pass through when a femoral hernia develops?

{{c1::Femoral ring}}

What effect does vasoactive intestinal peptide have on secretion of water and electrolytes in the intestines?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} secretion of water and electrolytes

Where is vasoactive intestinal polypeptide secreted within the gastrointestinal tract?

{{c1::Parasympathetic::Sympathetic/Parasympathetic}} ganglia
fields.Back Extra: This is specifically in the gallbladder, sphincters, and small intestine.

fields.Text:
How do drugs like erythromycin increase peristalsis?

They are {{c1::motilin}} receptor agonists
fields.Back Extra: Hence, they increase production of migratory motor complexes and stimulate intestinal peristalsis.

fields.Text:
What hormone is produced by the small intestine, increases during fasting, and is involved in the production of migrating motor complexes?

{{c1::Motilin}}

What is the function of nitric oxide in the gastrointestinal tract?

Smooth muscle {{c1::relaxation::contraction/relaxation}}
fields.Back Extra: This includes relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter.

fields.Text:
Why does an oral glucose load lead to more insulin production when compared to an intravenous glucose load of the same amount?

Oral glucose stimulates glucose-dependent {{c1::insulinotropic peptide}}, which stimulates insulin release

How do fatty acids, amino acids, and oral glucose affect activity levels of K cells?

They {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} K cell activity
fields.Back Extra: This will stimulate the release of glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide.

fields.Text:
What is the exocrine regulatory effect of glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide?

Decreases secretion of {{c1::gastric acid}}

Glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide is made by which cells?

{{c1::K}} cells
fields.Back Extra:
These are found in the duodenum and jejunum.

Glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide is also called gastric inhibitory peptide.

fields.Text:
What is the endocrine regulatory effect of glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} release of insulin

What is the function of pancreatic HCO3- secretion in response to secretin?

HCO3- is secreted into the duodenum and {{c1::neutralizes}} gastric acid so that pancreatic enzymes can function

Which gastrointestinal substance causes decreased gastric acid secretion, increased pancreatic HCO3- secretion, and increased bile secretion?

{{c1::Secretin}}

Secretin is produced by which cells?

{{c1::S}} cells of the duodenum

What pathways cause pancreatic secretion in response to activation by cholecystokinin?

Neural {{c1::muscarinic}} pathways

A patient with cholelithiasis reports pain after eating. You recommend avoiding which type of food?

{{c1::Fatty}} foods
fields.Back Extra: This is because it increases cholecystokinin release, which causes gallbladder contraction.

fields.Text:
Which gastrointestinal substance decreases gastric emptying, increases gallbladder contraction, increases pancreatic secretions, and increases sphincter of Oddi relaxation?

{{c1::Cholecystokinin}}

What cells secrete cholecystokinin and where are they located?

{{c1::I}} cells located in the {{c1::duodenum}} and {{c1::jejunum}}

Octreotide, an analog of somatostatin, can be used to treat what four conditions?

{{c1::Carcinoid}} syndrome
{{c1::Acromegaly}}
{{c1::VIPoma}}
{{c1::Variceal}} bleeding

Where is ghrelin produced?

{{c1::Stomach}}

What substance in the gut lumen causes increased release of somatostatin, and what causes decreased release?

{{c1::Acid}} enhances release of somatostatin
{{c1::Vagal}} stimulation decreases release of somatostatin

Which gastrointestinal substance decreases the following:

Gallbladder contraction
Secretion of gastric acid
Secretion of pancreatic and small intestine fluids
Secretion of pepsinogen
Secretion of insulin
Secretion of glucagon

{{c1::Somatostatin}}

A patient receiving long-term therapy with omeprazole might have increased levels of which gastric hormone due to lack of negative feedback?

{{c1::Gastrin}}

Is the gastrin level increased or decreased in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is due to ectopic production of gastrin.

This is a gastrinoma.

fields.Text:
What serves as negative feedback for gastrin release?

pH < {{c1::1.5}} will inhibit gastrin secretion

What four physiologic factors stimulate gastrin release?

{{c1::Amino acids}}
{{c1::Peptides}}
Stomach {{c1::distention}}/{{c1::alkalinization}}
{{c1::Vagal}} stimulation through gastrin-releasing peptide

What are the three functions of gastrointestinal G cells?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} acid secretion
{{c1::Growth}} of the gastric mucosa
Gastric {{c1::motility}}

Where are G cells found?

{{c1::Antrum}} of the stomach
{{c1::Duodenum}}

A patient has had no desire to eat and has lost weight since his gastric bypass surgery. What hormone was affected?

{{c1::Ghrelin}}

Which gastrointestinal hormone is increased in Prader-Willi syndrome and decreased after gastric bypass surgery?

{{c1::Ghrelin}}

What hormone is released in the fasting state and increases appetite?

{{c1::Ghrelin}}

Loss of which regulatory substance is implicated in the increased lower esophageal sphincter tone of achalasia?

Loss of {{c1::nitric oxide}} secretion

Which cells produce somatostatin?

{{c1::D}} cells

What tumor could be a likely cause of watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria?

{{c1::VIPoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a non-α, non-β islet cell pancreatic tumor that releases vasoactive intestinal peptide.

fields.Text:
What stimulus decreases the secretion of vasoactive intestinal peptide?

{{c1::Adrenergic}} input

Which two stimuli increase the secretion of vasoactive intestinal peptide?

Gastrointestinal tract {{c1::distention}}
{{c1::Vagal}} stimulation

What is another name for glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide?

{{c1::Gastric inhibitory peptide}}

Where are D cells found?

{{c1::Pancreatic islets}}
{{c1::Gastrointestinal mucosa}}

How do long-term treatment with a proton pump inhibitor and presence of chronic atrophic gastritis affect gastrin levels?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} gastrin levels

Where is HCO3- usually trapped in the gastrointestinal system?

In the {{c1::mucus}} covering the gastric epithelium

What glands and cells in the gastrointestinal tract secrete bicarbonate?

{{c1::Brunner}} glands in the duodenum
{{c1::Mucosal}} cells in salivary glands, stomach, duodenum, and pancreas

Which cells secrete pepsin to aid in protein digestion?

{{c1::Chief}} cells in the stomach

Describe how pepsin is activated.

In the presence of {{c1::H+}}, {{c1::pepsinogen}} is converted to pepsin

Which substances decrease gastric acid secretion by parietal cells?

{{c1::Somatostatin}}
{{c1::Gastric inhibitory peptide}}
{{c1::Prostaglandin}}
{{c1::Secretin}}

Which substances stimulate parietal cells to release gastric acid?

{{c1::Acetylcholine}}
{{c1::Histamine}}
{{c1::Gastrin}}

What vitamin deficiency can be seen in patients with chronic gastritis or pernicious anemia?

Vitamin {{c1::B12}} deficiency
fields.Back Extra: Destruction of parietal cells in the stomach leads to a decrease in intrinsic factor, which is needed for uptake of vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum.

fields.Text:
What is the function of bicarbonate in the gastrointestinal tract?

Acid {{c1::neutralization}}

How is pepsin secretion regulated?

It is increased by {{c1::vagal}} stimulation
It is increased by local {{c1::acid}}

How is bicarbonate secretion regulated?

It is increased by {{c1::biliary}} and {{c1::pancreatic}} secretion with {{c1::secretin}}

Name the four layers of the stomach mucosa.



A → {{c1::Gastric pit}}
B → {{c1::Upper glandular}} layer
C → {{c1::Deeper glandular}} layer
D → {{c1::Muscularis mucosa}}

Which secretory cells are located in the upper glandular layer versus the deeper glandular layer of the stomach mucosa?



{{c1::Mucous::A}} cells and {{c1::parietal::B}} cells are located in the upper glandular layer
{{c1::Chief::C}} cells and {{c1::enterochromaffin::D}}-like cells are located in the deeper glandular layer

Which cells release somatostatin in the stomach?

{{c1::D}} cells in the antrum of the stomach

On which cells does gastrin act?

{{c1::Enterochromaffin}}-like cells
{{c1::Parietal}} cells

Which cells produce pepsinogen?

{{c1::Chief}} cells

HCl and intrinsic factor are released by which cells?

{{c1::Parietal}} cells in the stomach

What do enterochromaffin-like cells release in response to gastrin?

{{c1::Histamine}}
fields.Back Extra: This stimulates parietal cells to secrete HCl.

fields.Text:
What do I cells in the duodenum secrete?

{{c1::Cholecystokinin}}

What do S cells in the duodenum secrete?

{{c1::Secretin}}

What do K cells in the duodenum secrete?

{{c1::Glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide}}

What do D cells secrete in the antrum of the stomach?

{{c1::Somatostatin}}

Where are parietal cells located?

{{c1::Body}} of the stomach

Where are chief cells located?

{{c1::Body}} of the stomach

Which four gastrointestinal secretory cells receive vagal input?

{{c1::Parietal}} cells
{{c1::Chief}} cells
{{c1::D}} cells
{{c1::G}} cells

Name three secretory cells located in the antrum of the stomach.

{{c1::G}} cells
{{c1::Mucous}} cells
{{c1::D}} cells

After being converted to its active form, what does trypsin do?

Activates other {{c1::proenzymes}}
Cleaves additional {{c1::trypsinogen}} molecules into active trypsin

Which enzyme converts trypsinogen to trypsin?

{{c1::Enterokinase}}/{{c1::enteropeptidase}}
fields.Back Extra: This is found on the duodenal and jejunal mucosa.

fields.Text:
Pancreatic proteases are secreted by the pancreas in what form?

{{c1::Inactive::Active/Inactive}} form

What four proteases are secreted by the pancreas to aid in protein digestion?

{{c1::Chymotrypsin}}
{{c1::Elastase}}
{{c1::Trypsin}}
{{c1::Carboxypeptidases}}

What is the function of lipase after being secreted from the pancreas?

{{c1::Fat}} digestion

Does α-amylase need to be activated after it is secreted by the pancreas?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: It is secreted in an active form.

fields.Text:
A patient with decreased α-amylase may have impaired digestion of what type of food material?

{{c1::Starch}}

How does a low flow of pancreatic secretions affect the level of Cl- within the secretions?

Leads to {{c1::high::high/low}} levels of Cl-

Describe the tonicity of pancreatic secretions.

{{c1::Isotonic}}

How does a high flow of pancreatic secretions affect the level of HCO3- within the secretions?

Leads to {{c1::high::high/low}} levels of HCO3-

Lymphoid stem cells give rise to which type of cells?

{{c1::Lymphoblasts}}

Reticulocytes are primarily found in which part of the body?

{{c1::Bone marrow}}
fields.Back Extra: However, a small proportion is released into the blood.

fields.Text:
What cell type is derived from megakaryocytes?

{{c1::Platelets}}

What are the locations of monocytes and macrophages in the body?

Monocytes are present in the {{c1::blood}} and convert to macrophages when they migrate into {{c1::tissues}}

What are the different types of lymphocytes?

{{c1::B}}-cell lymphocytes
{{c1::T}}-cell lymphocytes
{{c1::Natural killer}} cells

The myeloid and lymphoid blood cell lineages are derived from which cell?

{{c1::Multipotent stem}} cell

The myeloid stem cell gives rise directly to which four types of cells?

{{c1::Erythroblasts}}
{{c1::Megakaryoblasts}}
{{c1::Myeloblasts}}
{{c1::Monoblasts}}

Which cell type, capable of secreting antibodies, is derived from B cells?

{{c1::Plasma}} cells

What two main types of cells do T cells differentiate into?

T-{{c1::helper}} cells
T-{{c1::cytotoxic}} cells

What type of white blood cell is shown on this peripheral blood smear?



{{c1::Neutrophils}}

A peripheral blood smear shows multiple, hypersegmented neutrophils. What lab tests will help diagnose the cause?

Vitamin {{c1::B12}} test
{{c1::Folate}} test

Which cellular structure in a neutrophil will contain proteinases, acid phosphatase, β-glucuronidase, and myeloperoxidase?

{{c1::Azurophilic granules}}
fields.Back Extra: These are also known as lysosomes.

fields.Text:
A patient is seen for a red, swollen, painful fifth finger. A blood smear reveals increased white blood cells with multilobed nuclei. What are they?

{{c1::Neutrophils}}

What neutrophil function is controlled by C5a, LTB4, IL-8, platelet-activating factor, kallikrein, 5-HETE, and N-formylmethionine?

Neutrophil {{c1::chemotaxis}}

What molecules are contained within the specific granules of neutrophils?

{{c1::Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase}}
{{c1::Lactoferrin}}
{{c1::Lysozyme}}
{{c1::Collagenase}}

An increase in the number of neutrophils indicates infection likely due to which organism?

{{c1::Bacterial}} organism

Which type of leukocyte mediates acute inflammatory responses?

{{c1::Neutrophils}}

What causes morphologic changes in neutrophils?

Acute {{c1::inflammation}}

A man with metastatic melanoma is fatigued. Neutrophil precursors and immature red blood cells are seen on his blood smear. What is happening?

{{c1::Leukoerythroblastic}} reaction
fields.Back Extra: This is either from severe anemia or an increase in neutrophilic precursors responding to melanoma invasion of the bone marrow.

fields.Text:
What is a neutrophil left shift?

{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in neutrophil precursors in peripheral blood
fields.Back Extra: This is usually from infection or inflammation.

fields.Text:
What feature of the cell type shown in the image permits easy exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide?



A {{c1::biconcave disk}} shape
fields.Back Extra: This shape yields a high surface area-to-volume ratio and facilitates rapid gas exchange.

fields.Text:
What stain would you use to evaluate RNA contained in reticulocytes, and what color would it appear?

{{c1::Wright-Giemsa}} stain
This would appear as a {{c1::bluish}} color

How long is the life span of an erythrocyte in healthy adults and in neonates?

{{c1::120}} days in healthy adults
{{c1::60}} to {{c1::90}} days in neonates

How would you describe a peripheral blood smear showing red blood cells of varying sizes and shapes?

Blood smear exhibits {{c1::anisocytosis}} and {{c1::poikilocytosis}}

Erythrocytes depend on what molecule exclusively for energy?

{{c1::Glucose}}

What anion exchange transporter allows red blood cells to carry carbon dioxide from the periphery to the lungs?

{{c1::Cl-}}/{{c1::HCO3-}} antiporter on the cell membrane

What anucleate cell is biconcave with a large surface area-to-volume ratio and lacks organelles?

{{c1::Red blood}} cell

Describe the two basic functions of an erythrocyte.

Carries O2 to {{c1::tissues}}
Carries CO2 to {{c1::lungs}}

What is erythrocytosis?

An increase in {{c1::hematocrit}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as polycythemia.

fields.Text:
What is a reticulocyte?

{{c1::Immature}} red blood cells

In the formation of a stable thrombus, fibrinogen binds platelets together via what receptor?

{{c1::Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa}}

In primary hemostasis, von Willebrand factor must bind to what platelet receptor?

{{c1::Glycoprotein Ib}}

What skin finding is typically noted in thrombocytopenic patients or those with decreased platelet function?

{{c1::Petechiae}}

What are the contents of the α granules found within platelets?

{{c1::Von Willebrand factor}}
{{c1::Fibrinogen}}
{{c1::Platelet factor 4}}
{{c1::Fibronectin}}

What are the contents of the dense granules of platelets?

{{c1::Calcium}}
{{c1::ADP}}
{{c1::Serotonin}}
{{c1::Histamine}}

What two types of granules do platelets contain?

{{c1::Dense}} granules
{{c1::α}} granules

How does endothelial injury lead to formation of a platelet plug?

{{c1::Aggregation}} of platelets and interaction with {{c1::fibrinogen}} result in formation of a platelet plug

What is the life span of a platelet?

{{c1::8}} to {{c1::10}} days

How do mature platelets form from megakaryocyte precursors?

Small fragments of {{c1::cytoplasm}} break off from megakaryocytes

What is the function of thrombopoietin?

Stimulates {{c1::megakaryocyte}} proliferation

Which organ is responsible for storing one-third of the cells indicated by the arrows in the image?



{{c1::Spleen}}

What type of immune cell is shown in this image?



{{c1::Plasma}} cell

From which cell type does multiple myeloma arise?

{{c1::Plasma}} cell

Where are plasma cells found?

{{c1::Bone marrow}}

What is the function of plasma cells?

To produce large amounts of {{c1::antibody}} specific to a particular {{c1::antigen}}

Where does the cell type shown in the image originate and mature?



T cells originate from stem cells in the {{c1::bone marrow}}
T cells mature in the {{c1::thymus}}

What is the primary cellular target of HIV?

{{c1::Th}} cells
fields.Back Extra: These are also known as CD4+ cells.

fields.Text:
What is the predominant type of lymphocyte found in the circulation?

{{c1::T}} cells
fields.Back Extra: This makes up approximately 80% of circulating lymphocytes.

fields.Text:
What costimulatory receptor, present on T cells, is required for T-cell activation?

CD{{c1::28}}

T lymphocytes mediate which type of immune response?

{{c1::Cellular}} immune response

Which CD molecule is expressed by Th cells?

CD{{c1::4}}

Cytotoxic T cells express what CD molecule and recognize what MHC?

CD{{c1::8}}
MHC {{c1::I}}

Name the three types of mature cells into which T cells differentiate.

{{c1::Cytotoxic T}} cells
{{c1::Th}} cells
{{c1::Treg}} cells

Which MHC do Th cells recognize?

MHC {{c1::II}}

Where does the cell type shown in the image originate and mature?



B cells originate in the {{c1::bone marrow}}
B cells mature in the {{c1::bone marrow}}

What happens to B cells when they encounter an antigen?

B cells differentiate into {{c1::plasma}} cells and {{c1::memory}} cells

After maturation, B lymphocytes migrate from the bone marrow to what parts of the body?

{{c1::Peripheral::Central/Peripheral}} lymphoid tissue

B cells are a part of what type of immune response?

{{c1::Humoral}} immune response
fields.Back Extra: They can function as antigen-presenting cells.

fields.Text:
What two molecules are contained in the cytoplasmic lytic granules within natural killer cells?

{{c1::Perforin}}
{{c1::Granzymes}}

What is the function of the cytoplasmic lytic granules within natural killer cells?

To induce {{c1::apoptosis}} in {{c1::target}} cells

How do natural killer cells distinguish between healthy and infected cells?

They identify cell {{c1::surface}} proteins
fields.Back Extra: This is induced by microbial infection, stress, or malignant transformation.

fields.Text:
What cells are larger than B cells and T cells and induce apoptosis in cells that do not express MHC I cell surface molecules?

{{c1::Natural killer}} cells

Natural killer cells are important in which branch of the immune system?

{{c1::Innate}} immunity

Natural killer cells are particularly important in fighting against which subset of pathogens?

{{c1::Intracellular::Intracellular/Extracellular}} pathogens

Identify the cell shown in the image.



{{c1::Natural killer}} cell

What is the major function of the cell type shown in the image?



Mediates {{c1::adaptive}} immunity
Mediates {{c1::innate}} immunity

Which blood cells appear round with densely staining nuclei and a small amount of pale cytoplasm on a peripheral blood smear?

{{c1::Lymphocytes}}

What are the three types of lymphocytes?

{{c1::B}} cells
{{c1::T}} cells
{{c1::Natural killer}} cells

A girl has anaphylaxis after eating peanuts. What four substances, released by degranulation of the cell type shown in the image, mediate this pathology?



{{c1::Histamine}}
{{c1::Tryptase}}
{{c1::Heparin}}
{{c1::Eosinophilic chemotactic}} factors

Where do mast cells bind?

{{c1::Fc}} portion of Ig{{c1::E}} binds to the mast cell membrane

What medication that targets mast cells is used for prophylaxis of asthma?

{{c1::Cromolyn sodium}}
fields.Back Extra: This stabilizes mast cell membranes and prevents degranulation.

fields.Text:
What three stimuli causes degranulation of mast cells?

Tissue {{c1::trauma}}
{{c1::C3a}}/{{c1::C5a}}
Surface Ig{{c1::E}} cross-linking by antigen

Mast cells are involved in which type of hypersensitivity reactions?

Type {{c1::I}} hypersensitivity reactions
fields.Back Extra: Mast cells mediate allergic reactions in local tissues.

fields.Text:
What other cell type do mast cells resemble, both structurally and functionally?

{{c1::Basophils}}

Mutations in which oncogene are associated with mastocytosis?

{{c1::c-KIT}} mutations

Name three drugs or agents that can elicit an IgE-independent mast cell degranulation.

{{c1::Vancomycin}}
{{c1::Opioids}}
{{c1::Radiocontrast}} dye

On autopsy, this cell is seen in a man's blood. You look for the same cell in the parenchyma of his organs, but do not find it. Why not?



{{c1::Monocytes}} are only found in the blood
fields.Back Extra: Monocytes differentiate into macrophages in the tissue.

fields.Text:
Describe the identifying features of a monocyte.

Large, {{c1::kidney}}-shaped nuclei
Extensive "{{c1::frosted glass}}" cytoplasm

A patient undergoes liver biopsy, which shows increased phagocytes with kidney-shaped nuclei. What are these cells called?

{{c1::Kupffer}} cells

A patient has septic shock due to a gram-negative organism. What receptor triggered the shock response?

The {{c1::lipid A}} component of bacterial lipopolysaccharides binds to {{c1::CD14}} on {{c1::macrophages}}

What signaling molecule activates macrophages?

{{c1::IFN-γ}}

What two roles do macrophages play in the immunologic response to extracellular pathogens?

{{c1::Phagocytoses}} bacteria, cell debris, and senescent red blood cells
Acts as an {{c1::antigen-presenting}} cell via MHC {{c1::II}}

What are the different names given to monocytes depending on the tissue they are present in?

Outside the blood → {{c1::Macrophages}}
Liver → {{c1::Kupffer}} cells
Connective tissue → {{c1::Histiocytes}}
Skin → {{c1::Langerhans}} cells
Bone → {{c1::Osteoclasts}}
Brain → {{c1::Microglial}} cells

The cell shown in the image is found exclusively in tissues. What is it?



{{c1::Macrophage}}

Which cell type is an important cellular component in granulomas?

{{c1::Macrophages}}

What molecules that are integral to its role as an antigen-presenting cell does the cell type shown in the image express on its surface?



MHC {{c1::II::I/II}}
{{c1::Fc}} receptors

How do dendritic cells process exogenous antigens?

They present these on MHC {{c1::I}} cells

What is the function of a dendritic cell?

Highly phagocytic {{c1::antigen-presenting}} cell
Links the {{c1::innate}} immune system to {{c1::adaptive}} immune system

What abnormal lab finding can be present in parasitosis, asthma, allergies, chronic adrenal insufficiency, myeloproliferative disorders, and Churg-Strauss syndrome?

{{c1::Eosinophilia}}

What do eosinophils destroy via phagocytosis?

{{c1::Antigen-antibody}} complexes

What is the function of eosinophils?

To defend against {{c1::helminthic}} infections

A patient with a parasitic infection has the findings shown on a peripheral blood smear. What protein contained within this cell is toxic to this type of infection?



{{c1::Major basic}} protein

A blood smear shows increased numbers of this cell type. What diagnosis do you consider?



{{c1::Myeloproliferative}} disorder

The intracellular contents of isolated basophils from a healthy patient are studied. Why are no leukotrienes found?

Leukotrienes are both {{c1::synthesized}} and {{c1::released}} on demand
fields.Back Extra: None will be found in storage.

fields.Text:
What three molecules are released during basophil degranulation?

{{c1::Heparin}}
{{c1::Histamine}}
{{c1::Leukotrienes}}

What is the function of basophils?

Mediate {{c1::allergic}} reactions

Besides β and γ chains, what other chains may α chains combine with to form hemoglobin?

{{c1::δ}} chains may combine with α chains to form {{c1::HbA2}}
fields.Back Extra: This variant is present in small amounts in healthy adults.

fields.Text:
Which molecule binds less avidly to fetal hemoglobin, giving it a higher affinity for oxygen?

{{c1::2,3-bisphosphoglycerate}}

Which subunits make up adult hemoglobin?

2 {{c1::α}}-globin subunits
2 {{c1::β}}-globin subunits

From week 18 of embryogenesis until adulthood, where does erythropoiesis occur?

{{c1::Bone marrow}}

How does fetal hemoglobin extract oxygen from maternal hemoglobin?

Fetal hemoglobin has a higher {{c1::affinity}} for oxygen
fields.Back Extra: This allows it to extract oxygen from maternal hemoglobin across the placenta.

fields.Text:
During weeks 10 to 28 of embryogenesis, where does erythropoiesis occur?

{{c1::Spleen}}
{{c1::Liver}}

In which organ does fetal erythropoiesis occur from week 6 until birth?

{{c1::Liver}}
fields.Back Extra: It is overlapped with the yolk sac for weeks 6 to 8.

fields.Text:
During weeks 3 to 8 of embryogenesis, where does erythropoiesis occur?

{{c1::Yolk sac}}
fields.Back Extra: It is overlapped by the liver from 6 weeks onward.

fields.Text:
Which subunits make up fetal hemoglobin?

2 {{c1::α}}-globin subunits
2 {{c1::γ}}-globin subunits

What are the two embryonic variants of hemoglobin?

Hemoglobin {{c1::ζ}}
Hemoglobin {{c1::ε}}

A patient with type O-negative blood requires a blood transfusion. Blood products from which ABO blood group may be safely given to this patient?

Only type {{c1::O}}-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} blood
fields.Back Extra: Patients with type O-negative blood who receive a blood group other than type O-negative blood will experience a hemolytic reaction.

fields.Text:
A pregnant woman is hemorrhaging, and there is no time to cross and match for a blood transfusion. What blood type do you give?

Type {{c1::O}}-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} blood
fields.Back Extra: Exposure to Rh-positive blood stimulates the formation of anti-D IgG antibodies, which may complicate future pregnancies.

fields.Text:
What ABO type of plasma is the universal donor?

A donor with type {{c1::AB}} blood
fields.Back Extra: The plasma does not have anti-A or anti-B antibodies.

fields.Text:
A patient's blood contains the A antigen. Transfusion of blood with which two ABO antigen groups produces a hemolytic reaction?

Type {{c1::B}} blood
Type {{c1::AB}} blood
fields.Back Extra: This is due to the presence of anti-B IgM antibodies in plasma.

fields.Text:
What type of reaction will occur if type AB-postive blood is mistakenly given to a patient with type B-positive blood?

{{c1::Hemolytic}} reaction
fields.Back Extra: The patient has anti-A IgM antibodies in the plasma.

fields.Text:
Which circulating antibodies can be found in the plasma of a patient with type O blood?

Ig{{c1::G}} antibodies against both A and B antigens (predominantly)
Ig{{c1::M}} antibodies against both A and B antigens

Which circulating antibodies can be found in the plasma of a patient with type A-positive blood?

Anti-{{c1::B}} Ig{{c1::M}}

A man with type AB-positive blood can receive which blood groups safely?

{{c1::All}} blood groups
fields.Back Extra: The man is a universal recipient.

fields.Text:
An Rh-negative mother is pregnant with an Rh-positive baby. What immunoglobulin must you administer to the mother during and after pregnancy?

Anti-{{c1::D}} Ig{{c1::G}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as RhoGAM.

fields.Text:
Rh-negative mothers exposed to Rh-positive blood during delivery make anti-D IgG antibodies. How does this affect subsequent pregnancies?

IgG crosses the placenta, leading to {{c1::hemolytic}} disease of the newborn in any subsequent Rh-positive fetus pregnancies

Which circulating antibodies can be found in the plasma of a patient with type B-positive blood?

Anti-{{c1::A}} Ig{{c1::M}}

A patient's blood contains the B antigen. Transfusion of blood with which two ABO antigen groups produces a hemolytic reaction?

Type {{c1::A}} blood
Type {{c1::AB}} blood
fields.Back Extra: This is due to the presence of anti-A IgM antibodies in plasma.

fields.Text:
When is anti-D IgG administered to an Rh-negative pregnant woman during an uncomplicated pregnancy?

{{c1::3rd}} trimester
Early {{c1::postpartum}} period
fields.Back Extra: This is if the fetus is Rh-positive.

fields.Text:
A type O-positive woman gives birth to a type A-positive baby. The baby has mild jaundice shortly after birth that slowly increases on investigation. What is causing this jaundice?

Mother's Ig{{c1::G}} antibodies against the {{c1::A}} antigen in the baby's blood cross the placenta → {{c1::Hemolysis}}

How does sensitization occur in an Rh-negative mother delivering an Rh-positive baby?

Maternal blood is sensitized against {{c1::Rh}} antigen → Formation of anti-{{c1::D}} Ig{{c1::G}} that crosses the placenta → Fetal red blood cells are attacked → {{c1::Hemolysis}} in the fetus in subsequent pregnancies

What maternal-fetal interaction is responsible for Rh hemolytic disease of the newborn?

Rh-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} mothers giving birth to Rh-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}} fetuses

What are the three different ways that Rh hemolytic disease of the newborn can present?

{{c1::Jaundice}} shortly after birth
{{c1::Kernicterus}}
{{c1::Hydrops fetalis}}

What maternal-fetal interaction is responsible for ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn?

Type {{c1::O}} mothers giving birth to type {{c1::A}} or {{c1::B}} fetuses

What is the treatment for ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn?

{{c1::Exchange transfusion}}
{{c1::Phototherapy}}

Can Rh hemolytic disease of the newborn occur during the first pregnancy, as a result of the pregnancy?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Only sensitization occurs during the first pregnancy.

fields.Text:
For a mother previously sensitized to Rh antigen, what happens during subsequent pregnancies?

Anti-{{c1::D}} Ig{{c1::G}} formed in the maternal blood from a prior pregnancy crosses the placenta and {{c1::hemolyzes}} fetal red blood cells

What is the mechanism by which immune response to foreign antigen is limited to avoid inflammatory damage to specific tissues?

{{c1::Immune privilege}}

What is the association between immune privilege and tissue and organ transplantation?

Transplantation of an organ or tissue with immune privilege is {{c1::less::more/less}} likely to result in allograft rejection

What process results in the β-hemolysis pattern shown in the image?



{{c1::Complete}} lysis of {{c1::red blood}} cells
fields.Back Extra: This results in a pale/clear area that surrounds colonies on blood agar.

fields.Text:
What is responsible for the brownish or greenish appearance, without peripheral clearing, around the growth of α-hemolytic bacteria on blood agar?



{{c1::Partial}} oxidation of {{c1::hemoglobin}}
fields.Back Extra: This is seen with viridans streptococci and Streptococcus pneumoniae.

fields.Text:
Name some common bacterial strains that can cause the appearance shown in the image on blood agar.



{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
{{c1::Streptococcus pyogenes}}
{{c1::Streptococcus agalactiae}}
{{c1::Listeria monocytogenes}}

How would you differentiate both Streptococcus pyogenes and Streptococcus agalactiae from Staphylococcus aureus?

Both Streptococcus pyogenes and Streptococcus agalactiae are catalase {{c1::negative::positive/negative}}
Staphylococcus aureus is catalase {{c1::positive::positive/negative}}

Which types of seizures are treated with benzodiazepines?

{{c1::Status epilepticus}}

What are the adverse effects of ethosuximide therapy?

{{c1::Fatigue}}
Gastrointestinal {{c1::distress}}
{{c1::Headache}}
{{c1::Itching}}
{{c1::Stevens-Johnson}} syndrome

What is the mechanism of action of ethosuximide?

It blocks {{c1::thalamic}} {{c1::T}}-type {{c1::Ca2+}} channels

Ethosuximide is the first-line treatment for which type of seizures?

{{c1::Absence}} seizures

What is the mechanism of action of levetiracetam?

Blocks {{c1::SV2A}} receptors
May modulate {{c1::GABA}} and {{c1::glutamate}} release
Inhibits {{c1::voltage}}-gated {{c1::Ca2+}} channels

Which types of seizures are treated with levetiracetam?

{{c1::Focal}} seizures
{{c1::Tonic-clonic}} seizures

How can the risk of lamotrigine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome be minimized?

Lamotrigine must be {{c1::titrated}} slowly

What is the mechanism of action of lamotrigine?

Blocks {{c1::voltage}}-gated {{c1::Na+}} channels
Prevents {{c1::glutamate}} release

Which types of seizures are treated with lamotrigine?

{{c1::Focal}} seizures
{{c1::Tonic-clonic}} seizures
{{c1::Absence}} seizures

Which antiepileptic drug can cause hematuria and flank pain?

{{c1::Topiramate}}

What is the mechanism of action of topiramate?

Blocks {{c1::Na+}} channels
Increases {{c1::GABA}} action

Which types of seizures are treated with topiramate?

{{c1::Focal}} seizures
{{c1::Tonic-clonic generalized}} seizures

What are the adverse effects of gabapentin therapy?

{{c1::Ataxia}}
{{c1::Sedation}}

Name three uses for gabapentin.

{{c1::Peripheral}} neuropathy
{{c1::Postherpetic neuralgia}}
{{c1::Focal}} seizures

What is the mechanism of action of gabapentin?

Inactivates {{c1::high-voltage}}-activated {{c1::Ca2+}} channels
Acts as a {{c1::GABA}} analog

What type of seizures are treated with gabapentin?

{{c1::Focal}} seizures

What is the black box warning on the vigabatrin label?

May cause permanent loss of {{c1::vision}}

What is the mechanism of action of vigabatrin?

Irreversibly inhibits {{c1::GABA transaminase}} → Increased {{c1::GABA}} concentration

Which types of seizures are treated with vigabatrin?

{{c1::Focal}} seizures

What drug, other than carbamazapine, may be responsible for elevated liver enzymes in a patient with a history of myoclonic seizures?

{{c1::Valproic acid}}

What is the mechanism of action of valproic acid?

It inactivates {{c1::Na+}} channels
Increases {{c1::GABA}} concentration by inhibiting {{c1::GABA transaminase}}

Which types of seizures are treated with valproic acid?

{{c1::Focal}} seizures
{{c1::Tonic-clonic}} seizures
{{c1::Absence generalized}} seizures

What are the adverse effects of valproic acid therapy?

{{c1::Gastrointestinal}} distress
{{c1::Hepatotoxicity}}
{{c1::Tremor}}
Weight {{c1::gain::gain/loss}}
{{c1::Pancreatitis}}
{{c1::Teratogenicity}}
{{c1::Alopecia}}
{{c1::Rash}}

Name the three antiepileptic medications that are teratogenic.

{{c1::Carbamazepine}}
{{c1::Phenytoin}}/{{c1::fosphenytoin}}
{{c1::Valproic acid}}

Which three antiepileptic drugs induce cytochrome P-450?

{{c1::Phenobarbital}}
{{c1::Phenytoin}}/{{c1::fosphenytoin}}
{{c1::Carbamazepine}}

Which four epilepsy drugs might predispose individuals to Stevens-Johnson syndrome?

{{c1::Carbamazepine}}
{{c1::Phenytoin}}
{{c1::Ethosuximide}}
{{c1::Lamotrigine}}

What is the mechanism of action of carbamazepine?

Blocks {{c1::Na+}} channels

Which types of seizures are treated with carbamazepine?

{{c1::Focal}} seizures

What drug that is used to treat trigeminal neuralgia can cause agranulocytosis, SIADH, and liver toxicity?

{{c1::Carbamazepine}}

Because of the adverse effects of carbamazepine, which tests should be routinely done to monitor patients being treated with it?

{{c1::Liver::Organ}} function tests
{{c1::Complete blood count}}

What are the risks of taking phenytoin during pregnancy?

{{c1::Fetal hydantoin}} syndrome

What adverse neurologic effects may be observed in a patient being treated with phenytoin for prevention of tonic-clonic seizures?

{{c1::Nystagmus}}
{{c1::Peripheral}} neuropathy
{{c1::Diplopia}}
{{c1::Sedation}}

Which antiepileptic drug is used primarily to treat recurrent tonic-clonic seizures and has zero-order kinetics?

{{c1::Phenytoin}}

What adverse dermatologic effect is associated with phenytoin?

{{c1::Stevens-Johnson}} syndrome

What drug can cause gingival hyperplasia, lymph node swelling, and a low international normalized ratio when taken by a patient with seizures who is receiving warfarin therapy?

{{c1::Phenytoin}}

What is the mechanism of action of phenytoin?

Blocks {{c1::Na+}} channels

Which types of seizures can be treated with phenytoin?

{{c1::Focal}} seizures
{{c1::Status epilepticus}}

What are side effects of phenobarbital?

{{c1::Tolerance}}
{{c1::Dependence}}
{{c1::Sedation}}
Cardiorespiratory {{c1::depression}}
{{c1::Cytochrome P-450}} induction

Which types of seizures are treated with phenobarbital?

{{c1::Focal}} seizures
{{c1::Tonic-clonic generalized}} seizures
{{c1::Status epilepticus}}

What drug is the first-line treatment for seizures in neonates?

{{c1::Phenobarbital}}

What black box warning is provided with lamotrigine?

It can cause {{c1::hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis}}

Topiramate can be used to prevent what condition other than seizures?

{{c1::Migraines}}

What signs and symptoms indicate phenytoin toxicity?

{{c1::Diplopia}}
{{c1::Ataxia}}
{{c1::Sedation}}

Barbiturate overdose can be fatal because of depression of which two organ systems?

{{c1::Cardiovascular}} system
{{c1::Respiratory}} system

What will happen to the anticoagulative effect of warfarin when it is combined with a barbiturate?

Barbiturates induce {{c1::cytochrome P-450}} enzymes → Warfarin will be {{c1::metabolized}} more quickly → {{c1::Efficacy}} of warfarin will decrease

What are the clinical uses of barbiturates?

Sedatives for treatment of {{c1::anxiety}}
{{c1::Seizures}}
{{c1::Insomnia}}
Induction of {{c1::anesthesia}}

What is the treatment for barbiturate overdose?

{{c1::Supportive}}

Why are barbiturates contraindicated for patients with a history of alcohol use disorder?

They have an additive {{c1::central nervous system}} depression effect when combined with alcohol
fields.Back Extra: There is no antidote for overdoses.

fields.Text:
Which class of anxiety medications is contraindicated for patients with porphyria?

{{c1::Barbiturates}}

What is the mechanism of action of barbiturates?

Increased {{c1::Cl-}} channel opening duration → Facilitation of {{c1::GABAA}} action → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} neuron firing

Thiopental and secobarbital are members of which class of drugs?

{{c1::Barbiturates}}

What is the difference between hypoxemia and hypoxia?

Hypoxemia is a state of decreased arterial {{c1::partial pressure}} of oxygen
Hypoxia is a state of decreased oxygen {{c1::delivery}} to tissue

Which three processes can lead to hypoxemia with an increased A-a gradient?

{{c1::V/Q mismatch}}
{{c1::Diffusion}} limitation
{{c1::Right}}-to-{{c1::left}} shunt

Which two processes lead to hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient?

{{c1::High::High/Low}} altitude
{{c1::Hypoventilation::Hyperventilation/Hypoventilation}}

What are five general causes of decreased oxygen delivery to tissues, otherwise known as hypoxia?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} cardiac output
{{c1::Hypoxemia}}
{{c1::Ischemia}}
{{c1::Anemia}}
{{c1::Carbon monoxide}} or {{c1::cyanide}} poisoning

What is the fate of the bicarbonate that results from the deprotonation of carbonic acid within a red blood cell?

It {{c1::leaves::enters/leaves}} the red blood cell via exchange for a {{c1::chloride}} molecule
fields.Back Extra: This is through the HCO3-/Cl- transporter via countertransport facilitated diffusion.

fields.Text:
Within a red blood cell, the carbonic acid formed from the combination of carbon dioxide and water dissociates into what two components?

{{c1::Hydrogen}} ions
{{c1::Bicarbonate}} ions

In what three forms is carbon dioxide transported from the tissues to the lungs?

{{c1::Bicarbonate}} (70%)
Bound to hemoglobin as {{c1::carbaminohemoglobin}} (21% to 25%)
{{c1::Dissolved}} CO2 (5% to 9%)

What enzyme catalyzes the conversion of carbon dioxide and water into carbonic acid?

{{c1::Carbonic anhydrase}}

Does carbaminohemoglobin have a higher or lower affinity for O2 compared with regular hemoglobin?

{{c1::Lower::Higher/Lower}} affinity
fields.Back Extra: When CO2 is bound to hemoglobin, the deoxygenated form is favored.

fields.Text:
Where does CO2 bind hemoglobin to form carbaminohemoglobin?

At the {{c1::N}}-terminus of the globin molecule
fields.Back Extra: Thus, it does not compete with oxygen at its binding site.

fields.Text:
In the lungs, how does the oxygenation of hemoglobin promote the regeneration of carbon dioxide from bicarbonate?

Oxygenation of hemoglobin causes dissociation of {{c1::H+}} from hemoglobin, which shifts the equilibrium of the reaction toward CO2
fields.Back Extra: This is known as the Haldane effect.

fields.Text:
In which part of the circulatory system would you expect red blood cells to contain a greater concentration of chloride?

{{c1::Venous}} blood

What does the respiratory quotient represent?

Ratio of {{c1::carbon dioxide}} produced to {{c1::oxygen}} consumed

What is a normal partial pressure of inspired O2 at sea level?

{{c1::150}} mmHg

What is the formula for PAO2?

PAO2 = {{c1::PIO2}} - ( {{c1::PaCO2}} ÷ {{c1::RQ}} )

By using the alveolar gas equation, what important measure of pulmonary gas diffusion can be determined?

{{c1::Alveolar-arterial gradient}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the difference between PAO2 and PaO2.

fields.Text:
What is the normal alveolar-arterial gradient?

( {{c1::Age}} / {{c1::4}} ) + {{c1::4}}
fields.Back Extra: For example, for a person younger than 40 years, the gradient should be less than 14.

fields.Text:
What adult structures in the urinary tract are derived from the metanephric mesenchyme?

{{c1::Glomerulus}} to the {{c1::distal convoluted tubule}} of the nephrons

The interaction of which two structures in the developing kidney induces differentiation and formation of the renal tubules?

{{c1::Ureteric bud}}
{{c1::Metanephric mesenchyme}}

In kidney development, at what week in embryonic development is full canalization of the metanephros complete?

Week {{c1::10}}

What adult structures in the urinary tract are derived from the ureteric bud?

{{c1::Collecting ducts}}
{{c1::Calyces}}
{{c1::Pelvises}}
{{c1::Ureters}}

What is the ureteric bud derived from?

The {{c1::caudal::cephalad/caudal}} end of the {{c1::mesonephric duct}}

When are the fetal kidneys fully developed?

At {{c1::36}} weeks of gestation

What permanent structure of the kidneys develops in the 5th week of gestation?

{{c1::Metanephros}}

What renal embryonic structure contributes to the development of ductus deferens and epididymis?

{{c1::Mesonephros}}

What fetal structure functions as the interim kidney for the 1st trimester?

{{c1::Mesonephros}}

When does the pronephros degenerate during embryonic development?

After week {{c1::4}} of development

What may occur if there is an abnormal interaction between the ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme?

Severe congenital malformation of the {{c1::kidneys}}
fields.Back Extra: Examples include renal agenesis and multicystic dysplastic kidneys.

fields.Text:
Why is the ureteropelvic junction the most common site of obstruction in the kidneys?

The ureteropelvic junction is the last structure to {{c1::canalize}}

What is the most common pathologic cause of prenatal hydronephrosis?

Congenital {{c1::ureteropelvic}} junction obstruction

How is prenatal hydronephrosis diagnosed?

It can be detected by prenatal {{c1::ultrasonography}}
fields.Back Extra: This may be either unilateral or bilateral.

fields.Text:
During which week of development is mesonephros present?

Week {{c1::4}}

What is the diagnosis if a newborn has a flattened nose, low-set ears, and retrognathia as shown?



{{c1::Potter sequence}}

By what mechanism do the physical deformities seen in Potter sequence develop?

{{c1::Oligohydramnios}} → Fetal {{c1::compression}} → Limb deformities and facial anomalies

What is the sequence of the pathogenesis causing death in a newborn with Potter sequence?

{{c1::Oligohydramnios}} → Lack of amniotic fluid {{c1::aspiration}} into fetal lungs → Pulmonary hypoplasia

What six findings are usually associated with Potter sequence?

Pulmonary {{c1::hypoplasia::hyperplasia/hypoplasia}}
{{c1::Oligohydramnios}}
{{c1::Twisted}} face
{{c1::Twisted}} skin
{{c1::Extremity}} deformities
{{c1::Renal}} failure in utero

What are four causes of Potter sequence?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney}} disease
{{c1::Bilateral::Unilateral/Bilateral}} renal {{c1::agenesis}}
Chronic placental {{c1::insufficiency}}
{{c1::Obstructive}} uropathy

What genetic abnormalities are associated with horseshoe kidney?

{{c1::Chromosomal aneuploidies}}
fields.Back Extra: Examples include Turner syndrome and trisomies 13, 18, and 21.

fields.Text:
A horseshoe kidney gets trapped beneath which artery?

{{c1::Inferior mesenteric}} artery

What is the pathophysiology behind the horseshoe kidney?

{{c1::Inferior::Superior/Inferior}} poles of both kidneys fuse → Kidneys are trapped under the {{c1::inferior mesenteric}} artery during ascension in fetal development

What complications may arise in a patient born with a horseshoe kidney?

{{c1::Infection}}
Renal {{c1::stones}}
{{c1::Hydronephrosis}}
Increased risk of renal {{c1::cancer}} (rare)

What is the term for retrograde flow of urine from the bladder to the upper urinary tract?

{{c1::Vesicoureteral reflux}}

What is a patient with vesicoureteral reflux at increased risk for?

Recurrent {{c1::urinary}} tract infections

What are common causes of primary and secondary vesicoureteral reflux?

Primary vesicoureteral reflux → Insufficient/abnormal {{c1::insertion}} of the ureter within the vesicular wall
Secondary vesicoureteral reflux → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} pressure in the bladder leading to retrograde flow

What is the most common cause of bladder outlet obstruction in male infants?

{{c1::Posterior urethral valves}}

How are posterior urethral valves diagnosed?

By detection of {{c1::bilateral::unilateral/bilateral}} {{c1::hydronephrosis}}
{{c1::Thick::Thick/Thin}}/{{c1::dilated::dilated/constricted}} bladder walls on prenatal ultrasonography

What are posterior urethral valves?

{{c1::Membrane remnants}} in the posterior urethra in males that may lead to urethral obstruction

Posterior urethral valves of the fetus can lead to what condition during pregnancy?

{{c1::Oligohydramnios}} in severe cases of obstruction

What three complications are associated with a duplex collecting system?

{{c1::Urinary}} tract infections
Ureteral {{c1::obstruction}}
{{c1::Vesicoureteral reflux}}

What are the two mechanisms by which a duplex collecting system may develop?

{{c1::Bifurcation}} of the {{c1::uteric bud}} before it enters the metanephric blastema
2 {{c1::ureteric buds}} interact with metanephric blastema

How does a duplex collecting system often present?

{{c1::Hydronephrosis}}

A bilateral multicystic dysplastic kidney can lead to what complication in utero?

{{c1::Potter sequence}}

Are multicystic dysplastic kidneys hereditary?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}

Is a multicystic dysplastic kidney usually unilateral or bilateral?

{{c1::Unilateral}}

Name two common conditions of a congenital solitary functioning kidney.

{{c1::Unilateral::Unilateral/Bilateral}} renal {{c1::agenesis}}
{{c1::Multicystic dysplastic}} kidney

What is the pathogenesis of multicystic dysplastic kidneys?

The ureteric bud develops but fails to induce differentiation of the {{c1::metanephric mesenchyme}}

What is the typical presentation for a patient with a congenital solitary functioning kidney?

The functioning kidney will be {{c1::hypertrophied::hypertrophied/hypotrophied}}
fields.Back Extra: The patient typically has no symptoms.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism through which unilateral renal agenesis occurs?

Failure of development of the {{c1::ureteric bud}} and induction of differentiation of the {{c1::metanephric mesenchyme}} → Complete lack of kidney and ureter

What is a congenital solitary functioning kidney?

The presence of {{c1::1}} functioning kidney at birth

How is a congenital solitary functioning kidney diagnosed?

Often prenatally by means of {{c1::ultrasonography}}

Name the components of the glomerular filtration barrier.



1 → {{c1::Endothelial}} cells
2 → {{c1::Basement membrane}}
3 → {{c1::Podocytes}}

Name the structures labeled as A, B, and C in the image.



A → {{c1::Macula densa}}
B → {{c1::Mesangial}} cells
C → {{c1::Juxtaglomerular}} cells

Why is the left kidney removed from the donor during living donor transplantation?

The left kidney has a {{c1::longer::longer/shorter}} renal vein than the right kidney

Which two additional veins enter the left renal vein when compared to the right renal vein?

Left {{c1::gonadal}} vein
Left {{c1::suprarenal}} vein

Which part of the kidney is most susceptible to hypoxia?

{{c1::Renal medulla}}

What is the name of the structure indicated by the label A?



{{c1::Glomerulus}}

What is the name of the structure indicated by the label B?



{{c1::Bowman space}}

What is the name of the structure indicated by the label C?



{{c1::Distal convoluted tubule}}

Name the structures that pass over the ureters in men versus women.

Women → {{c1::Uterine}} artery
Men → {{c1::Vas deferens}}

How do the structures highlighted in the image run their course to the bladder?



{{c1::Retroperitoneal::Intraperitoneal/Retroperitoneal}}
fields.Back Extra: The structures highlighted in the image are the ureters.

fields.Text:
Gynecologic procedures, such as ligation of the uterine or ovarian vessels, may damage which structure in the urinary system?

{{c1::Ureter}}
fields.Back Extra: This causes a ureteral leak or obstruction.

fields.Text:
How does the ureter run in relation to the gonadal artery?

Ureters travel {{c1::under::over/under}} gonadal arteries

How does the ureter run in relation to the common iliac artery?

Water flows {{c1::over::over/under}} the common iliac artery and {{c1::under::over/under}} the uterine artery or vas deferens

What are the three common points of ureter obstruction?

{{c1::Pelvic inlet}}
{{c1::Ureteropelvic}} junction
{{c1::Ureterovesical}} junction

How is urinary reflux prevented physiologically?

When the bladder contracts, it compresses the {{c1::intravesical ureter}} and prevents urine reflux

Which arteries supply the proximal ureter?

{{c1::Renal}} arteries

Which arteries supply the middle ureter?

{{c1::Gonadal}} artery
{{c1::Aorta}}
{{c1::Common iliac}} artery
{{c1::Internal iliac}} artery

Which arteries supply the distal ureter?

{{c1::Superior vesical}} artery
{{c1::Internal iliac}} artery

What are the 4 primary structures of the anterior eye?

{{c1::Cornea}}
{{c1::Iris}}
{{c1::Pupil}}
{{c1::Lens}}

What are the 3 main tissue layers of the eyeball?

{{c1::Sclera}} (outer)
{{c1::Choroid}} (middle)
{{c1::Retina}} (inner)

On examination of the eye, what substance of the posterior segment must the ophthalmoscope light shine through to visualize the retina?

{{c1::Vitreous humor}}

A normal retina is shown in the image. At which labeled structure does the optic nerve enter the eye?



{{c1::Optic disc}}

What structures suspend the lens at the anterior eye?

{{c1::Zonular}} fibers
fields.Back Extra: These are attached to the ciliary body.

fields.Text:
What structure regulates the size of the pupil when exposed to bright light or a dark place?

{{c1::Iris}}

A physician shines a penlight into a patient's eye. What 5 structures does the light pass through before reaching the retina?

{{c1::Cornea}}
{{c1::Anterior}} chamber
{{c1::Pupil}}
{{c1::Lens}}
{{c1::Vitreous}} chamber

A patient sustains severe cranial trauma causing the optic nerve to be severed. What 2 vascular structures might also be severed in this event?

{{c1::Central retinal}} artery
{{c1::Central retinal}} vein

A normal retina is shown in the image. Name the structures labeled A to D.



A → {{c1::Macula}}
B → {{c1::Fovea}}
C → {{c1::Optic disc}}
D → {{c1::Physiologic cup}}

Name the components of congenital CHARGE syndrome.

{{c1::Coloboma}} of the eye
{{c1::Heart}} defects
{{c1::Atresia}} of the choanae
{{c1::Restricted}} growth and development
{{c1::Genitourinary}} defects
{{c1::Ear}} defects

What congenital condition is caused by blockage of the posterior nasal opening and is associated with midface bony abnormalities?

{{c1::Choanal atresia}}

In what scenario is choanal atresia an emergency, with symptoms including upper airway obstruction, noisy breathing, and cyanosis?

{{c1::Bilateral::Unilateral/Bilateral}} choanal atresia
fields.Back Extra: Symptoms are worse with feeding and improved with crying.

fields.Text:
How is choanal atresia diagnosed and confirmed?

Diagnosed by failure to pass a {{c1::nasopharyngeal tube}}
Confirmed with {{c1::CT scan}}

Other than cilia, what cells participate in immune response and help clear the aspirated debris from the lungs?

Alveolar {{c1::macrophages}}

What type of epithelial cell is found in respiratory bronchioles?

Predominantly {{c1::cuboidal::squamous/cuboidal/columnar}} cells

Where in the respiratory tree does gas exchange occur?

{{c1::Respiratory::Conducting/Respiratory}} zone

What three anatomic areas does the respiratory zone contain?

{{c1::Respiratory bronchioles}}
{{c1::Alveolar ducts}}
{{c1::Alveoli}}

What type of muscle is found in the walls of the conducting airways?

{{c1::Smooth}} muscle
fields.Back Extra: They extend to the end of the terminal bronchioles.

fields.Text:
What two kinds of epithelium are primarily found in the bronchus, extending to the beginning of the terminal bronchioles?

{{c1::Pseudostratified::Simple/Stratified/Pseudostratified}} {{c1::ciliated::ciliated/nonciliated}} {{c1::columnar::squamous/cuboidal/columnar}} cells are found in the bronchi and early terminal bronchioles
{{c1::Cuboidal::Squamous/Cuboidal/Columnar}} cells are found in the late terminal bronchioles

Cartilage and goblet cells extend to the end of what part of the conducting zone?

{{c1::Bronchi}}

Which zone of the respiratory tree includes the anatomic dead space?

{{c1::Conducting::Conducting/Respiratory}} zone

Name the three functions of the conducting zone of the respiratory tree.

{{c1::Warms}} air
{{c1::Humidifies}} air
{{c1::Filters}} air

Which part of the conducting zone of the respiratory tree has the least airway resistance?

{{c1::Terminal bronchioles}}
fields.Back Extra: A large number of them run in parallel.

fields.Text:
Which two structures make up the small airways of the conducting zone of the respiratory tree?

{{c1::Bronchioles}}
{{c1::Terminal bronchioles}}

Which five structures make up the large airways of the conducting zone of the respiratory tree?

{{c1::Nose}}
{{c1::Pharynx}}
{{c1::Larynx}}
{{c1::Trachea}}
{{c1::Bronchi}}

Where in the respiratory tree is resistance the highest?

{{c1::Large}}-sized bronchi
{{c1::Medium}}-sized bronchi

What is the purpose of the mucociliary escalator?

It clears {{c1::mucus}} and {{c1::debris}} from the airway

Where do cilia terminate in the lungs?

{{c1::Respiratory bronchioles}}

What is the primary type of epithelium present in the alveoli?

{{c1::Simple::Simple/Stratified/Pseudostratified}} {{c1::squamous::squamous/cuboidal/columnar}} epithelium

The trachea bifurcates at what level?

{{c1::T4}}

The common carotid bifurcates at what level?

{{c1::C4}}

The abdominal aorta bifurcates at what level?

{{c1::L4}}

How does a phrenic nerve injury present on an X-ray?

As an ipsilateral elevation of the {{c1::hemidiaphragm}}

Which three nerve roots innervate the diaphragm and form the phrenic nerve?

{{c1::C3}}
{{c1::C4}}
{{c1::C5}}

Which seven important anatomic structures perforate the diaphragm? Name the vertebral levels where this occurs.

T8 → {{c1::Inferior vena cava}} and right {{c1::phrenic}} nerve
T10 → {{c2::Esophagus}} and {{c2::vagus}} nerve
T12 → {{c3::Aorta}}, {{c3::thoracic duct}}, and {{c3::azygos}} vein

A patient with carbohydrate malabsorption might undergo which test to distinguish gastrointestinal mucosal damage from other causes of malabsorption?

{{c1::D-xylose}} test
fields.Back Extra:
D-xylose is a simple sugar.

Blood and urine levels decrease with mucosal damage, but remain normal in pancreatic insufficiency.

fields.Text:
All monosaccharides are transported from the enterocytes to the blood by what transporter?

{{c1::GLUT2}}

Glucose and galactose are taken up by what transporter that is dependent on sodium ions?

{{c1::SGLT1}}

Which sugars are absorbed by enterocytes?

{{c1::Monosaccharides}}

Fructose is taken up by which transporter?

{{c1::GLUT5}}

Which monosaccharide transporters are located on the apical membrane versus the basolateral membrane of an enterocyte?



Apical membrane → {{c1::SGLT1}} and {{c1::GLUT5}}
Basolateral membrane → {{c1::GLUT2}}

Name 4 risk factors for development of pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

{{c1::Diabetes}}
Chronic {{c1::pancreatitis}}
{{c1::Cigarette}} smoking
Age > {{c1::50}} years

Which 2 tumor markers are commonly associated with pancreatic cancer?

{{c1::CA 19-9}} (more specific)
{{c1::CEA}} (less specific)

You find redness and tenderness on palpation of the extremities in a patient with pancreatic adenocarcinoma. What is this sign called?

{{c1::Trousseau}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This is also called migratory thrombophlebitis.

fields.Text:
What is the Courvoisier sign?

Obstructive {{c1::jaundice}} with a palpable, {{c1::nontender::tender/nontender}} {{c1::gallbladder}} on abdominal examination

Where is the tumor most likely located in a patient presenting with weight loss, night sweats, and painless jaundice?

{{c1::Pancreatic head}}
fields.Back Extra: The patient most likely has a pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

fields.Text:
A 72-year-old man presents with a 30 pound weight loss, painless jaundice, and palpable nontender gallbladder. What is the prognosis?

Approximately {{c1::1}} year after diagnosis
fields.Back Extra: This is a pancreatic adenocarcinoma presenting with the Courvoisier sign.

fields.Text:
A patient's pancreatic biopsy results are shown. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Pancreatic adenocarcinoma}}

How will the levels of pancreatic enzymes be affected in a patient with chronic pancreatitis?

Amylase and lipase levels may or may not be {{c1::elevated}}
fields.Back Extra: They are generally elevated in a patient with acute pancreatitis.

fields.Text:
Which vitamins are malabsorbed in a patient with pancreatic insufficiency secondary to chronic pancreatitis?

Vitamin {{c1::A}}
Vitamin {{c1::D}}
Vitamin {{c1::E}}
Vitamin {{c1::K}}

Describe the pathophysiology of chronic pancreatitis.

Chronic {{c1::inflammation}}
{{c1::Atrophy}}
{{c1::Calcification}} of the pancreas

In a patient with a history of alcoholism and chronic pancreatitis, what would steatorrhea, diabetes mellitus, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency indicate?

Pancreatic {{c1::insufficiency}}

What are the major risk factors for the development of chronic pancreatitis?

{{c1::Genetic}} predisposition
{{c1::Alcohol use}} disorder

What are the major complications of chronic pancreatitis?

Pancreatic {{c1::insufficiency}}
{{c1::Pseudocysts}}

How could acute pancreatitis lead to hypocalcemia?

Ca2+ is collected in pancreatic {{c1::soap deposits}} → Hypocalcemia

What are the potential complications/sequelae of acute pancreatitis?

{{c1::Abscess}}
{{c1::Infection}}
{{c1::Necrosis}}
{{c1::Pseudocyst}} formation
{{c1::Hemorrhage}}
{{c1::Organ}} failure
{{c1::Hypocalcemia::Hypercalcemia/Hypocalcemia}}

What enzyme has the highest specificity for acute pancreatitis?

Serum {{c1::lipase}}
fields.Back Extra: Serum amylase is also produced outside the pancreas.

fields.Text:
A 39-year-old patient with a history of gallstones has acute epigastric pain radiating to the back. What other information is needed to diagnose acute pancreatitis?

Increase in either serum {{c1::amylase}} or {{c1::lipase}} to {{c1::3}} times the upper limit of normal
{{c1::Imaging}} findings that indicate acute pancreatitis

List the causes of acute pancreatitis.

{{c1::Idiopathic}}
{{c1::Gallstones}}
{{c1::Ethanol}}
{{c1::Trauma}}
{{c1::Steroids}}
{{c1::Mumps}}
{{c1::Autoimmune}} disease
{{c1::Scorpion}} stings
{{c1::Hypercalcemia}}/{{c1::hypertriglyceridemia}}
{{c1::ERCP}}
{{c1::Drugs}}

A 42-year-old man with a history of alcoholism presents with epigastric pain radiating to his back and a markedly increased serum lipase level. What is the pathophysiology?

Activation of {{c1::pancreatic}} enzymes → {{c1::Autodigestion}} of the {{c1::pancreas}}

A patient has epigastric pain radiating to the back with the findings shown. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Acute pancreatitis}}
fields.Back Extra: The pancreas is surrounded by edema.

fields.Text:
A patient recently had acute pancreatitis and returns to the emergency department with abdominal pain. Imaging is shown. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Pseudocyst}}
fields.Back Extra: The pancreas is lined with granulation tissue, not epithelium.

fields.Text:
What is a malignant tumor of bile duct epithelium called?

{{c1::Cholangiocarcinoma}}

Risk for what condition is increased by primary sclerosing cholangitis and liver fluke infections?

{{c1::Cholangiocarcinoma}}

What could one see on imaging in a patient with cholangiocarcinoma?

Imaging may show {{c1::biliary tract}} obstruction

Describe histologic findings of cholangiocarcinoma.

Infiltrating {{c1::neoplastic}} glands associated with {{c1::desmoplastic stroma}}

What type of gallstones are shown in the image?



{{c1::Pigment}} gallstones

A patient with a porcelain gallbladder has an increased risk for what type of cancer?

{{c1::Adenocarcinoma}} of the gallbladder

What is the treatment for porcelain gallbladder, and why is it important to initiate this treatment quickly?

Prophylactic {{c1::cholecystectomy}}

This should be performed promptly because of the increased risk of gallbladder {{c1::carcinoma}}

What imaging modalities can be used to diagnose cholecystitis?

{{c1::Ultrasound}}
{{c1::Cholescintigraphy}}

How is ALP affected in choledocholithiasis?

ALP is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}

What are the causes of acalculous cholecystitis?

Gallbladder {{c1::stasis}}
{{c1::Infection}}
{{c1::Hypoperfusion}}
Observed in {{c1::critically ill}} patients

What physical exam finding is associated with inspiratory arrest on palpation of the right upper quadrant?

{{c1::Murphy}} sign

Name 3 major complications of gallstones.

{{c1::Cholecystitis}} (most common)
{{c1::Ascending cholangitis}}
Acute {{c1::pancreatitis}}

What condition can a fistula between the gallbladder and the gastrointestinal tract cause?

{{c1::Gallstone ileus}}

What are the components of the Charcot triad?

{{c1::Right upper quadrant}} pain
{{c1::Jaundice}}
{{c1::Fever}}

List the common risk factors for the formation of pigment stones.

{{c1::Crohn}} disease
{{c1::Advanced}} age
{{c1::Biliary}} infections
{{c1::Alcoholic}} cirrhosis
Chronic {{c1::hemolysis}}
{{c1::Total parenteral nutrition}}

List the common risk factors for the formation of cholesterol stones.

{{c1::Obesity}}
{{c1::Advanced}} age
{{c1::Multiparity}}
{{c1::Estrogen}} therapy
{{c1::Crohn}} disease
Rapid weight {{c1::loss::gain/loss}}
{{c1::Medications}}

Name 4 risk factors for development of cholelithiasis.

{{c1::Female}}
{{c1::Fat}}
{{c1::Fertile}}
{{c1::Forty}}

Name the hormone responsible for gallbladder contraction.

{{c1::Cholecystokinin (CCK)}}

Total parenteral nutrition is associated with the development of what type of gallstone?

{{c1::Pigment}} stones

What are the 2 types of gallstones?

{{c1::Cholesterol}} stones (80% of stones)
{{c1::Pigment}} stones (20% of stones)

This image of the gallbladder can be associated with what diagnosis?



{{c1::Calculous cholecystitis}}

In ascending cholangitis, how does the Reynolds pentad differ from the Charcot triad?

Reynolds pentad includes the Charcot triad, {{c1::shock}}, altered {{c1::mental status}}

In critically ill patients, what type of cholecystitis is most likely to arise?

{{c1::Acalculous cholecystitis}}

This image shows what gallbladder pathology?



{{c1::Porcelain}} gallbladder

What symptoms can be associated with biliary colic?

{{c1::Nausea}}
{{c1::Vomiting}}
Dull {{c1::right upper quadrant}} pain

How do black and brown pigmented gallstones differ in root cause?

Black pigmented gallstones → {{c1::Hemolysis}}
Brown pigmented gallstones → {{c1::Infection}}

What is the pathogenesis of cholesterol gallstones?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} cholesterol, {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} bile salts, and gallbladder {{c1::stasis}} → {{c1::Supersaturated}} bile with cholesterol → Cholesterol stones

What is the pathogenesis of pigment gallstones?

{{c1::Biliary tract}} infection or chronic {{c1::hemolysis}} → Increased {{c1::unconjugated::conjugated/unconjugated}} bilirubin with gallbladder {{c1::stasis}} → {{c1::Supersaturation}} of bile with {{c1::calcium bilirubinate}} → Pigment stones

Why might right upper quadrant pain associated with cholecystitis radiate to the right shoulder?

Because of irritation of the {{c1::phrenic}} nerve

What duct is impacted by a gallstone in calculous cholecystitis?

{{c1::Cystic}} duct

A gallstone ileus will show what on imaging of the biliary tree?

{{c1::Air}} in the biliary tree

What disease is associated with either the Charcot triad or the Reynolds pentad?

{{c1::Ascending cholangitis}}

What result on a HIDA scan is suggestive of cholecystitis?

Failure to visualize the {{c1::gallbladder}}

A patient with a small bowel obstruction is found to have a gallstone in the iliac fossa and air in the biliary tract on imaging. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Gallstone ileus}}

Which genes are likely mutated if appendages are in notably wrong locations?

{{c1::Hox}} genes

What genes could be mutated if there are defects in segmental organization in the cranial-caudal direction in an embryo?

{{c1::Hox}} genes

Which gene stimulates mitosis of the underlying mesoderm and promotes limb lengthening?

{{c1::FGF}} gene

What gene is responsible for proper organization along the dorsal-ventral axis?

{{c1::Wnt-7}} gene

Name two genes expressed at the apical ectodermal ridge.

{{c1::Wnt-7}} gene
{{c1::FGF}} gene
