What is the most likely abnormal finding in a newborn with a known sonic hedgehog gene mutation?

{{c1::Holoprosencephaly}}

Along what axis does the sonic hedgehog gene regulate patterning?

{{c1::Anterior-posterior}} axis

What is the gene that is expressed at the base of limb buds in a zone of polarizing activity?

{{c1::SHH}} gene

Sonic hegdehog gene plays a key role in the development of which organ system?

{{c1::Central nervous system}}

What gene codes for transcription factors?

{{c1::Hox}} genes

Which drug increases the expression of homeobox genes?

{{c1::Isotretinoin}}

In what developmental stage is the embryo when it enters the uterus?

{{c1::Morula}}

What day of development does the embryo enter the uterus?

Day {{c1::4}}

What cell is released from a follicle after ovulation?

{{c1::Secondary oocyte}}

The fetal neural plate is derived from which embryonic structure?

{{c1::Ectoderm}} overlying the {{c1::notochord}}

What structure is left behind in the ovary after an ovarian follicle ruptures?

{{c1::Corpus luteum}}

When do fetal movements start during development?

Week {{c1::6}}

During early fetal development, how do the three germ layers arise?

{{c1::Epiblast}} invaginates → Formation of the {{c1::primitive streak}} → Endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm

What process forms the trilaminar embryonic disc during embryonic development?

{{c1::Gastrulation}}

What is the chromosomal makeup of the embryo on day 1 of development in the fallopian tube?

{{c1::2N4C}}

During what day of embryogenesis does a zygote divide into a morula?

Day {{c1::4}}

During which week of development can the first male/female characteristics be distinguished in a fetus?

Week {{c1::8}}

Approximately how many weeks old is the embryo when the appearance of upper and lower limb buds is noted?

{{c1::4}} weeks

When does the embryo's heart begin to beat?

{{c1::4}} weeks

During what time is an embryo most susceptible to teratogenic effects?

Weeks {{c1::3}} to {{c1::8}}

By which week of embryogenesis does the neural tube close?

Week {{c1::4}}

From which germ layer does an embryo's neural tube form?

{{c1::Neuroectoderm}}

During what weeks of embryonic development does organogenesis occur?

Weeks {{c1::3}} to {{c1::8}}

Initial development of the notochord and primitive streak is noted. How old is the embryo?

{{c1::3}} weeks

How old is the embryo when the neural plate starts to form?

{{c1::3}} weeks

How old is the embryo when it exists as a trilaminar disc?

{{c1::3}} weeks

How many weeks old is the embryo when it exists as a bilaminar disc?

{{c1::2}} weeks

fields.Text:
At what stage of development does implantation in the uterine wall occur?

{{c1::Blastocyst}} stage

What is formed when a sperm fertilizes an ovum?

{{c1::Zygote}}

What important hormone is released around the time of blastocyst implantation?

{{c1::hCG}}

What is the chromosomal composition of a secondary oocyte?

{{c1::1N2C}}

How are developmental age and gestational age different?

Developmental age → Time since {{c1::fertilization}}
Gestational age → Time since the first day of last {{c1::menstrual period}}

From which germ layer is a Rathke pouch tumor derived?

{{c1::Surface ectoderm}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as a craniopharyngioma.

fields.Text:
What germ layer gives rise to the sweat, parotid, and mammary glands?

{{c1::Surface ectoderm}}

What germ layer gives rise to the adenohypophysis?

{{c1::Surface ectoderm}}
fields.Back Extra: This is from the Rathke pouch.

fields.Text:
What germ layer gives rise to the olfactory epithelium?

{{c1::Surface ectoderm}}

What germ layer gives rise to the epithelial linings of the oral cavity?

{{c1::Surface ectoderm}}

What germ layers give rise to the anal canal above and below the pectinate line?

Above the pectinate line → {{c1::Endoderm}}
Below the pectinate line → {{c1::Surface ectoderm}}

What germ layer gives rise to the leptomeninges?

{{c1::Neural crest}}

What germ layers give rise to the skin layers?

{{c1::Surface ectoderm}} → Epidermis
{{c1::Mesoderm}} → Dermis

What germ layer gives rise to most of the urethra?

{{c1::Endoderm}}
fields.Back Extra: This is derived from the urogenital sinus.

fields.Text:
What germ layer gives rise to the retina?

{{c1::Neural tube}}

What germ layer gives rise to the kidneys and adrenal cortex?

{{c1::Mesoderm}}

Generally speaking, what germ layer gives rise to gut tube epithelium, most of the urethra, and luminal epithelial derivatives?

{{c1::Endoderm}}

What germ layer gives rise to blood and most of the bones, muscles, connective tissues, and lymphatics in the body?

{{c1::Mesoderm}}

Generally speaking, what germ layer gives rise to cardiovascular structures?

{{c1::Mesoderm}}

What germ layers give rise to the vagina?

Proximal vagina → {{c1::Mesoderm}}
Distal vagina → {{c1::Endoderm}}

What germ layer gives rise to the aorticopulmonary septum?

{{c1::Neural crest}}

What germ layer gives rise to the spleen?

{{c1::Mesoderm}}
fields.Back Extra: This develops within the foregut mesentery.

fields.Text:
What germ layer gives rise to serous linings of body cavities?

{{c1::Mesoderm}}

What germ layer gives rise to the lens of the eye?

{{c1::Surface ectoderm}}

What is the postnatal derivative of the notochord?

{{c1::Nucleus pulposus}} of {{c1::intervertebral discs}}

The notochord induces the formation of what germ layer?

{{c1::Neuroectoderm}}

Generally speaking, from which germ layers are the central nervous system and peripheral nervous system derived?

Central nervous system → {{c1::Neural tube}}
Peripheral nervous system → {{c1::Neural crest}}

What abnormalities result from mesodermal defects?

{{c1::Vertebral}} defects
Anal {{c1::atresia}}
{{c1::Cardiac}} defects
Tracheo-esophageal {{c1::fistula}}
{{c1::Renal}} defects
{{c1::Limb}} defects

What germ layer gives rise to the spinal cord?

{{c1::Neural tube}}

What germ layer gives rise to the sensory organs of the ear?

{{c1::Surface ectoderm}}

Name the luminal epithelial derivatives that arise from endoderm.

{{c1::Eustachian tube}}
{{c2::Gallbladder}}
{{c3::Lungs}}
{{c4::Liver}}
{{c5::Pancreas}}
{{c6::Thymus}}
{{c7::Parathyroid}}
{{c8::Thyroid follicular}} cells
{{c9::Parafollicular}} cells

What germ layer gives rise to the testes and ovaries?

{{c1::Mesoderm}}

What germ layer gives rise to the tracheal cartilage?

{{c1::Mesoderm}}

What germ layer gives rise to microglia?

{{c1::Mesoderm}}

What is notably found in a Rathke pouch tumor?

{{c1::Calcium}} deposition
{{c1::Cholesterol}} deposition

What are the ten important derivatives of the neural crest?

{{c1::Enterochromaffin}} cells
{{c2::Leptomeninges}}
{{c3::Melanocytes}}
{{c4::Odontoblasts}}
{{c5::Peripheral nervous system}} ganglia
{{c6::Adrenal medulla}}
{{c7::Schwann}} cells
{{c8::Spiral}} membrane
{{c9::Endocardial cushions}}
{{c10::Skull}} bones

Which brain structures are derived from the neural tube?

{{c1::Astrocytes}}
{{c1::Central nervous system}} neurons
{{c1::Ependymal}} cells
{{c1::Neurohypophysis}}
{{c1::Oligodendrocytes}}
{{c1::Pineal}} gland

How is the tunica vaginalis formed?

{{c1::Evagination}} of the {{c1::peritoneum}}

What is the purpose of the gubernaculum in males after descent?

It anchors the {{c1::testes}} within the {{c1::scrotum}}

What two ligaments are formed from the gubernaculum in females?

{{c1::Ovarian}} ligament
{{c1::Round}} ligament of the uterus

What is the fate of the processus vaginalis in females?

It is {{c1::obliterated}}

What abnormality, detected on physical examination, may be due to persistent patent processus vaginalis in a male?

{{c1::Hydrocele}}

Where does the abnormal opening of the urethra occur in hypospadias and epispadias?

Hypospadias → Abnormal opening is on {{c1::ventral::ventral/dorsal}} surface
Epispadias → Abnormal opening is on {{c1::dorsal::ventral/dorsal}} surface

Why does epispadias occur?

Faulty {{c1::positioning}} of the {{c1::genital tubercle}}

Is epispadias or hypospadias more common?

{{c1::Hypospadias}}

What is the basis of developmental abnormality in hypospadias?

Abnormal opening of the penile {{c1::urethra}} on the {{c1::ventral::ventral/dorsal}} penis secondary to failure of the {{c1::urethral folds}} to fuse

Hypospadias is associated with what three conditions?

Inguinal {{c1::hernia}}
{{c1::Chordee}}
{{c1::Cryptorchidism}}

Hypospadias is associated with which enzyme deficiency?

{{c1::5α-reductase}} deficiency

Which abnormal condition of the bladder is associated with epispadias?

{{c1::Exstrophy}} of the bladder

Estrogen causes the labioscrotal swelling to develop into what structure in the female embryo?

{{c1::Labia majora}}

Estrogen causes the urogenital folds to develop into what structure in the female embryo?

{{c1::Labia minora}}

Dihydrotestosterone causes the labioscrotal swelling to develop into what structure in the male embryo?

{{c1::Scrotum}}

Dihydrotestosterone causes the urogenital folds to develop into what structure in the male embryo?

{{c1::Ventral::Ventral/Dorsal}} shaft of the penis

Estrogen causes the urogenital sinus to form which two structures in the female embryo?

{{c1::Greater vestibular}} glands
{{c1::Urethral}}/{{c1::paraurethral}} glands

Estrogen causes the genital tubercle to form which two structures in the female embryo?

{{c1::Glans clitoris}}
{{c1::Vestibular bulbs}}

Dihydrotestosterone causes the genital tubercle to form which three structures in the male embryo?

{{c1::Glans penis}}
{{c1::Corpus cavernosum}}
{{c1::Corpus spongiosum}}

Dihydrotestosterone causes the urogenital sinus to differentiate into which two structures in the male embryo?

{{c1::Prostate}} gland
{{c1::Bulbourethral}} gland

Which muscles form the rotator cuff?

{{c1::Supraspinatus}}
{{c1::Infraspinatus}}
{{c1::Teres minor}}
{{c1::Subscapularis}}

Which rotator cuff muscle is responsible for internal rotation and adduction of the arm?

{{c1::Subscapularis}}

Which two rotator cuff muscles are responsible for external rotation of the humerus/arm?

{{c1::Infraspinatus}}
{{c1::Teres minor}}

Which rotator cuff muscle is associated with a repeated overhand throw?

{{c1::Infraspinatus}}

Which two rotator cuff muscles are used for adduction of the humerus/arm?

{{c1::Teres minor}}
{{c1::Subscapularis}}

What is the function of the most commonly injured rotator cuff muscle?

Initial {{c1::abduction}} of the arm from {{c1::0}}° to {{c1::15}}°

Which spinal cord levels provide primary innervation for the rotator cuff?

{{c1::C5}} to {{c1::C6}}

Damage to which rotator cuff muscle is seen in the image?



{{c1::Supraspinatus}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows a tear or tendinopathy.

fields.Text:
List which nerves supply the individual rotator cuff muscles.

{{c1::Suprascapular}} nerve → Supraspinatus and infraspinatus
{{c1::Axillary}} nerve → Teres minor
{{c1::Upper subscapular}} nerve and {{c1::lower subscapular}} nerve → Subscapularis

What physical exam maneuver is used to assess for an injury to the supraspinatus muscle?

"{{c1::Empty can}}" test
fields.Back Extra: This is also called the "full can" test.

fields.Text:
Damage to the accessory nerve would affect which arm abductor muscle?

{{c1::Trapezius}}

What nerve innervates the deltoid muscle?

{{c1::Axillary}} nerve

Damage to the suprascapular nerve would affect which arm abductor muscle?

{{c1::Supraspinatus}}

Name the muscles responsible for arm movement at each of the following degrees of abduction.

0° to 15° → {{c1::Supraspinatus}}
15° to 90° → {{c1::Deltoid}}
> 90° → {{c1::Trapezius}} and {{c1::serratus anterior}}

Damage to the long thoracic nerve would affect which arm abductor muscle?

{{c1::Serratus anterior}}

Refer to the image and identify, by color, the nerves that innervate the three highlighted areas of the dorsum of the hand.



{{c1::Median}} nerve → Light blue
{{c1::Radial}} nerve → Purple
{{c1::Ulnar}} nerve → Pink

Refer to the image and identify, by color, the nerves that innervate the three highlighted areas of the palm of the hand.



{{c1::Median}} nerve → Light blue
{{c1::Radial}} nerve → Purple
{{c1::Ulnar}} nerve → Pink

Name the five major nerves that innervate the arm.

{{c1::Axillary}} nerve
{{c1::Radial}} nerve
{{c1::Musculocutaneous}} nerve
{{c1::Median}} nerve
{{c1::Ulnar}} nerve

Which nerves are commonly injured in humerus fractures, moving from proximal to distal?

{{c1::Axillary}} nerve → {{c1::Radial}} nerve → {{c1::Median}} nerve

Identify the nerve roots of each labeled nerve in the image.



Axillary nerve → {{c1::C5}} to {{c1::C6}}
Musculocutaneous nerve → {{c1::C5}} to {{c1::C7}}
Radial nerve → {{c1::C5}} to {{c1::T1}}
Median nerve → {{c1::C5}} to {{c1::T1}}
Ulnar nerve → {{c1::C8}} to {{c1::T1}}
Recurrent branch of median nerve → {{c1::C5}} to {{c1::T1}}

The thenar muscles are innervated by what branch of the median nerve?

{{c1::Recurrent}} branch of the median nerve

Which nerve injury causes loss of thumb opposition, abduction, and flexion without loss of palmar sensation?

{{c1::Recurrent}} branch of the {{c1::median}} nerve

What are the sensory effects of an ulnar nerve injury?

Decreased sensation over the {{c1::medial::medial/lateral}} 1 & 1/2 fingers
Decreased sensation of the {{c1::hypothenar eminence}}

What are the motor effects of an ulnar nerve injury?

Decreased finger {{c1::abduction}} and {{c1::adduction}}
Decreased thumb {{c1::adduction}}
Decreased {{c1::flexion::flexion/extension}} over the medial 2 fingers
Decreased {{c1::lumbrical}} action over the medial 2 fingers

Is a proximal or distal ulnar nerve injury associated with radial wrist deviation on attempted flexion?

{{c1::Proximal}} ulnar nerve injury
fields.Back Extra: This is a medial humeral epicondyle fracture.

fields.Text:
Which nerve injury is associated with a fractured hook of hamate from a fall on the outstretched hand?

Distal {{c1::ulnar}} nerve injury

Which nerve injury is associated with fractures of the humeral medial epicondyle?

Proximal {{c1::ulnar}} nerve injury

Which nerve roots give rise to the ulnar nerve?

{{c1::C8}} to {{c1::T1}}

What are the sensory effects of a proximal median nerve injury?

Reduced sensation over the {{c1::thenar eminence}}
Reduced sensation over the dorsal/palmar aspects of the {{c1::lateral::medial/lateral}} 3 1/2 fingers

Which nerve is commonly injured in association with wrist and palmar lacerations?

Injury to the {{c1::median}} nerve → Wrist lacerations
Injury to the {{c1::recurrent}} branch of the {{c1::median}} nerve → Palmar lacerations

Which nerve is compressed/injured in the setting of carpal tunnel syndrome?

{{c1::Median}} nerve

Which nerve injury is associated with a supracondylar humerus fracture?

Proximal {{c1::median}} nerve injury

What are the motor effects of a proximal radial nerve injury?

Decreased {{c1::grip}} strength
{{c1::Wrist drop}}

What are the sensory effects of a proximal radial nerve injury?

Decreased {{c1::posterior::anterior/posterior}} arm/forearm sensation
Decreased {{c1::dorsal::ventral/dorsal}} hand sensation

What are the sensory effects of a distal radial nerve injury?

Distal {{c1::paresthesias}}

What are the motor manifestations of a median nerve injury?

Loss of function of wrist {{c1::flexors::flexors/extensors}}
Loss of function of {{c1::lateral::medial/lateral}} 2 lumbricals
Loss of function of {{c1::opponens pollicis}}
Loss of function of {{c1::abductor pollicis brevis}}
Loss of function of {{c1::flexor pollicis brevis}}

Which function of the radial nerve is preserved in a midshaft fracture of the humerus?

{{c1::Tricep::Muscle}} function
{{c1::Posterior::Anterior/Posterior}} arm sensation

Which nerve injury is associated with a midshaft humerus fracture or repetitive pronation/supination?

{{c1::Radial}} nerve injury

What nerve is likely damaged in a patient who cannot flex or supinate their arm?

{{c1::Musculocutaneous}} nerve

Damage to which nerve will cause a decreased biceps reflex?

{{c1::Musculocutaneous}} nerve

Which nerve injury presents with a flattened deltoid, loss of sensation over the deltoid and lateral arm, and failure to abduct the arm from a resting position?

{{c1::Axillary}} nerve injury

Which nerve injury is associated with fracture at the surgical neck of the humerus or an anterior dislocation of the humerus?

{{c1::Axillary}} nerve injury

What is a common injury that affects the musculocutaneous nerve?

{{c1::Upper trunk compression}}

Which nerve may be damaged by compression of the axilla or by a midshaft fracture of the humerus?

{{c1::Radial}} nerve

Use the image to identify the affected nerve in the brachial plexus that presents with claw hand.



{{c1::Ulnar}} nerve
fields.Back Extra: Number 9 is affected in the image.

fields.Text:
A patient cannot flex his thumb and presents with a "Pope's blessing" deformity. Use the image to identify the affected area in the brachial plexus.



{{c1::Proximal::Proximal/Distal}} {{c1::median}} nerve
fields.Back Extra: Number 8 is affected in the image.

fields.Text:
A patient fell asleep with his arm slung over the back of a chair. On waking, he has wrist drop. Use the image to identify the affected nerve.



{{c1::Radial}} nerve
fields.Back Extra:
The patient has "Saturday night palsy".

Number 6 is affected in the image.

fields.Text:
A patient has a lesion on the humerus and reports deltoid paralysis. Use the image to identify the affected nerve.



{{c1::Axillary}} nerve
fields.Back Extra: Number 5 is affected in the image.

fields.Text:
A patient has a lesion on the long thoracic nerve and presents with a winged scapula. Where is the lesion located in the brachial plexus?

{{c1::Root}} of the brachial plexus

A patient is diagnosed with wrist drop. Use the image to identify the cord of the brachial plexus in which the lesion is located.



{{c1::Posterior}} cord
fields.Back Extra: Number 3 is affected in the image.

fields.Text:
Chest X-ray is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis? Which trunk of the brachial plexus is likely affected if this condition is symptomatic?



{{c1::Thoracic outlet}} syndrome
This is caused by compression of the {{c1::lower}} trunk of the brachial plexus
fields.Back Extra: The X-ray shows a cervical rib.

fields.Text:
What is the function and innervation of the serratus anterior muscle?

Innervated by the {{c1::long thoracic}} nerve
{{c1::Abduction}} above the horizontal position

Which nerve and muscle are injured in the patient shown below? What is the most likely diagnosis?



Nerve → {{c1::Long thoracic}} nerve
Muscle → {{c1::Serratus anterior}}
Diagnosis → {{c1::Winged scapula}}

A patient presents with lumbrical atrophy, ischemia, pain, and edema from vascular compression. Examination reveals presence of a cervical rib. What is the most likely diagnosis?

{{c1::Thoracic outlet}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This is secondary to the supernumerary cervical rib causing compression.

fields.Text:
A patient with lung cancer develops atrophy, pain, and edema in his right hand. Where is his tumor most likely invading?

{{c1::Lower}} trunk of the brachial plexus
{{c1::Subclavian}} vessels
fields.Back Extra: The patient likely has a right-sided Pancoast tumor.

fields.Text:
What brachial plexus injury is associated with forced upward flexion of the arm, like when grabbing a tree branch to break a fall or upward traction during child delivery?

{{c1::Klumpke palsy}}
fields.Back Extra: The upward force causes traction or tear of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus.

fields.Text:
Describe the expected physical exam findings in a patient with a lesion to the lower trunk of the brachial plexus.

Impaired MCP joint {{c1::flexion::flexion/extension}}
Impaired DIP/PIP joint {{c1::extension::flexion/extension}}
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by impaired lumbrical, interosseous, thenar, and hypothenar muscles leading to a total claw hand.

fields.Text:
What brachial plexus injury is associated with excessive traction on an infant's neck during delivery?

{{c1::Erb palsy}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to traction on the upper trunk of the brachial plexus.

fields.Text:
A patient has problems abducting, laterally rotating her shoulder, and flexing/supinating at the elbow. Where is the nerve injury?

{{c1::Upper}} trunk of the brachial plexus

What motor deficits would you expect in a patient with proximal median nerve damage?

Decreased {{c1::thumb}} function
Loss of {{c1::pronation::supination/pronation}}
"{{c1::Pope's blessing}}" deformity

Which 2 nerves would you expect to be affected with injury to the posterior cord of the brachial plexus? What 2 major findings would you see on exam?

{{c1::Deltoid}} paralysis → {{c2::Axillary}} nerve impairment
{{c1::Wrist drop}} → {{c2::Radial}} nerve impairment

What deficits do you expect on exam in a patient with damage to the musculocutaneous nerve?

Difficulty {{c1::flexing::flexing/extending}} the elbow
Variable sensory loss over the {{c1::lateral::medial/lateral}} forearm

What is "Saturday night palsy"?

{{c1::Wrist drop}} caused by compression of the {{c1::radial}} nerve
fields.Back Extra: This is often described by leaving arm swung over a couch or improper use of crutches.

fields.Text:
Moving proximally to distally, what are the 5 major distributions of the brachial plexus?

{{c1::Roots}} → {{c1::Trunks}} → {{c1::Divisions}} → {{c1::Cords}} → {{c1::Branches}}

What is the key toxicity attributed to cyclophosphamide?

{{c1::Hemorrhagic cystitis}}

What is the key toxicity attributed to doxorubicin, daunorubicin, and trastuzumab?

{{c1::Cardiotoxicity}}

What is the common key toxicity attributed to bleomycin and busulfan?

Pulmonary {{c1::fibrosis}}

What is the key toxicity attributed to vincristine?

{{c1::Peripheral::Central/Peripheral}} neuropathy

What are the two key common toxicities attributed to cisplatin and carboplatin?

{{c1::Nephrotoxicity}}
{{c1::Ototoxicity}}

What free radical scavenger is used to prevent the nephrotoxic effects of platinum anti-neoplastics?

{{c1::Amifostine}}

What drug is used to protect against cardiotoxic effects on anthracycline neoplastics and what is its mechanism of action?

{{c1::Dexrazoxane}} → Acts as an {{c1::iron chelator}}

What tetrahydrofolate precursor drug is used to resolve the myelosuppression associated with methotrexate use and also enhance the effects of 5-fluorouracil?

{{c1::Leucovorin}}

What drug might be used to prevent the hemorrhagic cystitis caused by cyclophosphamide or ifosfamide?

{{c1::Mesna}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a sulfydryl compound that binds the toxic metabolites of cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide.

fields.Text:
What drug might be used to prevent/treat tumor lysis syndrome?

{{c1::Rasburicase}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a recombinant uricase that increases the metabolism of uric acid to allantoin.

fields.Text:
Which two classes of antiemetics are preferred to control acute nausea and vomiting associated with chemotherapy?

{{c1::5-HT3}} receptor antagonists
{{c1::D2}} receptor antagonists

Which class of antiemetics is preferred to control delayed nausea and vomiting associated with chemotherapy?

{{c1::NK1}} receptor antagonists

What two drugs might be used to prevent/treat chemotherapy-associated neutropenia?

{{c1::Filgrastim}}
{{c1::Sargramostim}}

What drug might be used to prevent/treat chemotherapy-associated anemia?

{{c1::Epoetin-alfa}}

What cardiovascular changes occur on the left side cavities of the heart due to normal aging?

{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in the size of the left ventricular cavity
{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} of the left atrial cavity
fields.Back Extra: The interventricular septum acquires a sigmoid shape.

fields.Text:
What effect does immunosenescence due to normal aging have on immunity?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} response to new antigens

What changes due to normal aging occur with arterial compliance, aortic diameter, heart rate, and the aortic and mitral valves?

{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in arterial compliance
{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in aortic diameter
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in heart rate
{{c1::Calcified}} aortic and mitral valves

Name three gastrointestinal changes that occur due to normal aging.

{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in lower esophageal sphincter tone
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in gastric mucosal protection
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in colonic motility

What two changes occur in bone marrow due to normal aging?

{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in bone marrow mass
{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in bone marrow fat

What effect does normal aging have on adaptive immunity?

{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in naive B cells and T cells
{{c1::Preserved}} memory B cells and T cells

Name three musculoskeletal changes that occur due to normal aging.

{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in skeletal muscle mass
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in bone mass
{{c1::Thinning::Thickening/Thinning}} of joint cartilage

What two nervous system changes occur due to normal aging?

{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in brain volume
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in cerebral blood flow

How does normal aging alter eyesight, hearing, smell, and taste?

Diminished eye {{c1::accommodation}}
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in hearing
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in smell
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in taste

Name five skin changes that occur due to normal aging.

{{c1::Atrophy}} and {{c1::flattening}} of dermal-epidermal junction
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in dermal collagen
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in elastin
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in sweat glands
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in sebaceous glands

What is a cause of chronological or intrinsic aging of the skin?

Decreased synthesis capacity of dermal {{c1::fibroblasts}}

How does sun exposure contribute to aging?

{{c1::Ultraviolet rays}} degrade dermal collagen and elastin
Products of degradation accumulate in the dermis → {{c1::Solar elastosis}}

Name three renal changes that occur due to normal aging.

{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in glomerular filtration rate
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in renal blood flow
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in hormonal function

How does aging alter the male reproductive system?

Testicular {{c1::atrophy}}
Prostate {{c1::enlargement}}
{{c1::Slower::Faster/Slower}} erection/ejaculation
{{c1::Longer::Longer/Shorter}} refractory period

Name five vaginal changes that occur due to normal aging.

Vulvovaginal {{c1::atrophy}}
Vaginal {{c1::shortening::lengthening/shortening}}
Vaginal {{c1::thinning::thickening/thinning}}
Vaginal {{c1::dryness::wetness/dryness}}
{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in pH

How does aging affect libido?

Libido {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} in both genders
fields.Back Extra: It is more pronounced in females.

fields.Text:
What is the most appropriate treatment for patients infected by Zika virus?

{{c1::Supportive care}}

What is the test of choice for the diagnosis of Zika virus?

{{c1::RT-PCR}}
{{c1::Serology}}

What are three general mechanisms for Zika virus transmission?

{{c1::Aedes mosquito}} bites (most common)
{{c1::Sexual}} transmission
{{c1::Vertical}} transmission

What infectious entity causes high fever, black-colored vomitus, jaundice, hemorrhage, and backache?

{{c1::Yellow fever virus}}

What two groups act as reservoirs for the yellow fever virus?

{{c1::Monkeys}}
{{c1::Humans}}

Under what conditions are outbreaks of Zika virus more common?

{{c1::Tropical}} climates
{{c1::Subtropical}} climates

What is the vector of transmission for the dengue virus?

{{c1::Aedes mosquito}}

What are the symptoms associated with dengue hemorrhagic fever?

Dengue fever with {{c1::bleeding}} and {{c1::plasma}} leakage and extremes in {{c1::hematocrit}}

What is the transmission vector of the Chikungunya virus?

{{c1::Aedes mosquito}}

How is infection by dengue virus diagnosed?

{{c1::PCR}}
{{c1::Serology}}

How is infection with the Chikungunya virus diagnosed?

{{c1::RT-PCR}}
{{c1::Serology}}

Coinfection by what virus can occur with the dengue virus?

{{c1::Chikungunya virus}}

Of the dengue and Chikungunya viruses, which is more likely to cause severe clinical symptoms that could lead to death?

{{c1::Dengue virus}}

What are the characteristics of the vaccine against dengue virus?

{{c1::Live}}, {{c1::recombinant}} vaccine that uses {{c1::yellow fever virus}} genes into which dengue virus envelope and premembrane proteins are inserted

Describe the symptoms caused by Zika virus infection.

{{c1::Conjunctivitis}}
Low-grade {{c1::pyrexia}}
{{c1::Itchy rash}}

What are the symptoms of systemic infection by the Chikungunya virus?

{{c1::Inflammatory polyarthritis}}
{{c1::High::High/Low}} fever
{{c1::Maculopapular rash}}
{{c1::Headache}}
{{c1::Lymphadenopathy}}
fields.Back Extra: Hemorrhagic fever is uncommon compared to dengue fever.

fields.Text:
To which class of viruses does yellow fever virus belong?

{{c1::Flavivirus}}

What vaccine is recommended to prevent travelers from being infected with yellow fever virus?

{{c1::Live}}, {{c1::attenuated}} vaccine
fields.Back Extra: This is when traveling to endemic countries.

fields.Text:
What is the pathology that leads to dengue shock syndrome?

{{c1::Plasma}} leakage → Circulatory collapse

What are the six common symptoms of dengue fever?

{{c1::Fever}}
{{c1::Headache}}
{{c1::Rash}}
{{c1::Myalgia}}
{{c1::Arthralgia}}
{{c1::Neutropenia}}

What are three possible clinical conditions associated with infection by dengue virus?

{{c1::Dengue}} fever
{{c1::Dengue hemorrhagic}} fever
{{c1::Dengue shock}} syndrome

What predisposing factor significantly increases the risk of developing dengue hemorrhagic fever?

Infection with a different dengue virus {{c1::serotype}} after initial infection
fields.Back Extra: This is due to antibody-dependent enhancement of the disease.

fields.Text:
What are the clinical manifestations of infections with Zika syndrome in the affected newborn?

{{c1::Microcephaly::Macrocephaly/Microcephaly}}
{{c1::Ocular}} anomalies
{{c1::Motor}} abnormalities

What viral family is Chikungunya virus a member of?

{{c1::Alphavirus}} member of the {{c1::togavirus}} family

What might a liver biopsy reveal in a patient diagnosed with yellow fever?

{{c1::Councilman bodies}}

What is the most common mosquito-borne viral disease in the world?

{{c1::Dengue virus}}

What are the three major layers of skin, from superficial to deep?

{{c1::Epidermis}}
↓
{{c1::Dermis}}
↓
{{c1::Subcutaneous fat}}
fields.Back Extra: Subcutaneous fat includes the hypodermis and subcutis.

fields.Text:
Which layer of the epidermis contains desmosomes?

Stratum {{c1::spinosum}}

What are the five layers of the epidermis, from superficial to deep?

Stratum {{c1::corneum}}
↓
Stratum {{c1::lucidum}}
↓
Stratum {{c1::granulosum}}
↓
Stratum {{c1::spinosum}}
↓
Stratum {{c1::basalis}}

Which epithelial cell junctions are attacked by autoantibodies in bullous pemphigoid? Which epidermal layer is affected?

{{c1::Hemidesmosomes}} in the stratum {{c1::basale}}

In pemphigus vulgaris, autoantibodies are directed against what in which epithelial cell junction?

{{c1::Desmoglein-1}} and/or {{c1::desmoglein-3}} in {{c1::desmosomes}} found between two adjacent cells

Integrin proteins anchor which structures to the basolateral side of a cell? Specifically, which three structural proteins do they bind?

Integrins connect the basolateral membrane of a cell to the adjacent {{c1::basement membrane}} via binding with {{c1::collagen}}, {{c1::laminin}}, and {{c1::fibronectin}}

Which epithelial cell junction anchors keratin in basal cells to the basement membrane?

{{c1::Hemidesmosome}}

What proteins do gap junctions utilize to allow electrical and chemical communication between cells?

{{c1::Connexons}}
fields.Back Extra: These are transmembrane channel proteins with a central pore through which communication occurs.

fields.Text:
What epithelial cell junction provides structural support using intermediate filament interactions?

{{c1::Desmosomes}}

Cadherin-actin proteins depend on what ion to form an adherens junction?

{{c1::Ca2+}}

What does the cellular loss of E-cadherin promote as it relates to epithelial cell junctions?

{{c1::Metastasis}}

Which type of epithelial cell junction prevents the paracellular movement of solutes? What two proteins make up this junction?

{{c1::Tight}} junctions, which are composed of {{c1::occludins}} and {{c1::claudins}}

Electron microscopy is performed on a tissue specimen. What cell junction is present?



{{c1::Tight}} junction

What type of epithelial cell junction is connecting the actin cytoskeletons of the adjacent cells seen in this image?



{{c1::Adherens}} junction

What type of epithelial cell junction, which connects to intermediate filaments, is indicated in the image?



{{c1::Desmosomes}}

What type of epithelial cell junction, connecting to the underlying basement membrane, is shown in the image?



{{c1::Hemidesmosome}}

Instead of a middle lobe, the left lung has a space that is occupied by which organ?

{{c1::Heart}}

Which lung is the more common site for inhaled foreign bodies?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} lung
fields.Back Extra: The right bronchus is wider, more vertical, and shorter than the left bronchus.

fields.Text:
What is the anatomical position of the carina in relation to the ascending and descending aorta?

{{c1::Posterior}} to the ascending aorta
{{c1::Anteromedial}} to the descending aorta

What type of fissure is found in only the right lung?

{{c1::Horizontal}} fissure

The oblique fissure divides which two lobes in the left lung?

{{c1::Upper}} lobe
{{c1::Lower}} lobe

The oblique fissure divides which two lobes in the right lung?

{{c1::Middle}} lobe
{{c1::Lower}} lobe

Where is the pulmonary artery in relation to the bronchus within the left lung hilum?

{{c1::Superior}} to the bronchus

Where is the pulmonary artery in relation to the bronchus within the right lung hilum?

{{c1::Anterior}} to the bronchus

What structure does the left lung have that the right lung does not?

{{c1::Lingula}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the homolog of the middle lobe of the right lung.

fields.Text:
How many lobes does the left lung have?

{{c1::2}}

How many lobes does the right lung have?

{{c1::3}}

A patient chokes on a peanut while upright. Where exactly in the lungs do you expect to find the peanut?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::lower::upper/lower}} lobe

A patient chokes on a peanut while supine. Where exactly in the lungs do you expect to find the peanut?

{{c1::Superior::Superior/Inferior}} segment of the {{c1::right::left/right}} {{c1::lower::upper/lower}} lobe

A patient chokes on a peanut while lying on her right side. Where exactly in the lungs do you expect to find the peanut?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::upper::upper/lower}} lobe

What is the equation used to measure pulmonary vascular resistance using flow and the difference in pressure across the pulmonary vessels?

R = {{c1::ΔP}} ÷ {{c1::Q}}
fields.Back Extra:
R = Resistance
P = Pressure
Q = Flow

This is a modification of Ohm's law.

fields.Text:
What is the formula for pulmonary vascular resistance?

PVR = ( {{c1::Ppulm artery}} - {{c1::PL atrium}} ) ÷ {{c1::Q}}
fields.Back Extra:
Ppulm artery = Pressure in pulmonary artery
PL atrium = Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure
Q = Cardiac output

fields.Text:
What clinically measurable value can be used as a proxy for left atrial pressure?

{{c1::Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure}}

How is resistance affected by decreasing the radius of a blood vessel?

Resistance is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}

Which of the following variables will have the greatest impact on vascular resistance?

Changing the length of a vessel = {{c1::✗}}
Changing the radius of a vessel = {{c1::✓}}
Changing the viscosity of blood = {{c1::✗}}
fields.Back Extra:
R = ( 8 × η × l ) ÷ ( π × r4 )

η = Viscosity of blood
l = Vessel length
r = Vessel radius

fields.Text:
What is the formula for resistance across a blood vessel or vascular system?

R = ( {{c1::8}} × {{c1::η}} × {{c1::l}} ) ÷ ( {{c1::π}} × {{c1::r4}} )
fields.Back Extra:
η = Viscosity of blood
l = Vessel length
r = Vessel radius

fields.Text:
What term is used to define the energy depleted, or the consumed O2 by respiratory muscles, in order to produce a sufficient ventilation to meet the body's metabolic demand?

{{c1::Work of breathing}}

Which two factors does breathing work need to overcome in order to occur?

{{c1::Elastic recoil}}
{{c1::Airway resistance}}

Which two variables can determine the work of breathing?

{{c1::Respiratory rate}}
{{c1::Tidal volume}}

How do restrictive diseases alter the work of breathing?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} respiratory rate
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} tidal volume

How does obstructive disease alter the work of breathing?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} respiratory rate
{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} tidal volume

Which four reproductive organs drain into the internal iliac lymph nodes?

{{c1::Prostate}}
{{c1::Corpus cavernosum}}
{{c1::Cervix}}
{{c1::Proximal::Proximal/Distal}} vagina

Which lymph nodes drain the glans penis or clitoris?

{{c1::Deep inguinal}} lymph nodes

Which female reproductive organs drain fluid to the external iliac lymph nodes?

{{c1::Body}} of the uterus
{{c1::Cervix}}
{{c1::Superior::Superior/Inferior}} part of the bladder

Is the right or left testis a more common location for a varicocele?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} testis
fields.Back Extra: Flow is less laminar there, so venous pressure is increased.

fields.Text:
Which lymph nodes provide lymphatic drainage from the distal vagina, vulva, scrotum, and distal anus?

{{c1::Superficial inguinal}} lymph nodes

Which lymph nodes provide lymphatic drainage from the testes, ovaries, and fundus of the uterus?

{{c1::Para-aortic}} lymph nodes

Which gonadal vein drains through the renal vein and into the inferior vena cava?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} gonadal vein

Which gonadal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} gonadal vein

What ligament connects the ovaries to the lateral pelvic wall?

{{c1::Suspensory}} ligament of the ovaries
fields.Back Extra: This is also called the infundibulopelvic ligament.

fields.Text:
Which ligament contains the uterine vessels?

{{c1::Cardinal}} ligament
fields.Back Extra: This is also called the transverse cervical ligament.

fields.Text:
What ligament connects the uterine horn to the labia majora?

{{c1::Round}} ligament of the uterus

What ligament connects the medial pole of the ovary to the uterine horn?

{{c1::Ovarian}} ligament

What three structures are contained within the broad ligament of the uterus?

{{c1::Round}} ligaments of the uterus
{{c1::Fallopian tubes}}
{{c1::Ovaries}}

The round ligament travels above which artery?

Artery of {{c1::Sampson}}

What are the three components of the broad ligament?

{{c1::Mesovarium}}
{{c1::Mesometrium}}
{{c1::Mesosalpinx}}

Which ligament contains the ovarian vessels?

{{c1::Infundibulopelvic}} ligament

What ligament connects the cervix to the side wall of the pelvis?

{{c1::Cardinal}} ligament
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as the transverse cervical ligament.

fields.Text:
The ureter is at risk of injury during ligation of which two vessels during oophorectomy and hysterectomy?

Oophorectomy → {{c1::Ovarian}} vessels
Hysterectomy → {{c1::Uterine}} vessels

Which two structures of the uterus and ovaries are derivatives of gubernaculum?

{{c1::Ovarian}} ligament
{{c1::Round}} ligament of the uterus

Which three structures are connected to pelvic side wall through the broad ligament?

{{c1::Ovaries}}
{{c1::Fallopian tubes}}
{{c1::Uterus}}

Through which canal does the round ligament of the uterus travel?

{{c1::Inguinal}} canal

Why does ligation of ovarian vessels during oophorectomy pose a risk to the ureter?

The {{c1::retroperitoneal}} course of the ureter positions it near the ovarian vessels

What anticoagulant is safe for use during pregnancy?

{{c1::Heparin}}

The fetus is at increased risk for what disorders when a pregnant patient is taking warfarin?

{{c1::Optic}} nerve atrophy
{{c1::Bone}}/{{c1::cartilage}} deformities
Fetal cerebral {{c1::hemorrhage}}

What effect can maternal consumption of fish containing high levels of methylmercury have on a fetus?

{{c1::Neurotoxicity}}

What type of birth defect is associated with the use of folate antagonists during pregnancy?

{{c1::Neural tube}} defects

Name four antiepileptic agents that should be avoided in pregnancy because of their teratogenicity.

{{c1::Carbamazepine}}
{{c1::Phenytoin}}
{{c1::Valproate}}
{{c1::Phenobarbital}}

What medication must be prescribed for a pregnant patient if she takes antiepileptic drugs?

High-dose {{c1::folate}}

How do nicotine and carbon monoxide exposure in utero increase the risk for low birth weight?

Nicotine causes {{c1::vasoconstriction::vasodilation/vasoconstriction}}
Carbon monoxide impairs {{c1::oxygen}} delivery
fields.Back Extra: Smoking is the leading cause of low birth weight in developed countries.

fields.Text:
Use of which medication during pregnancy may cause aplasia cutis congenita in a newborn?

{{c1::Methimazole}}

What birth defects are associated with radiation exposure in utero?

{{c1::Microcephaly::Macrocephaly/Microcephaly}}
{{c1::Intellectual}} disability

A pregnant patient with poor diabetic control has increased risk for what disorders in her child?

{{c1::Cardiac}} defects
{{c1::Caudal regression}} syndrome
{{c1::Neural tube}} defects
{{c1::Macrosomia::Macrosomia/Microsomia}}
{{c1::Polycythemia}}
Neonatal {{c1::hypoglycemia::hyperglycemia/hypoglycemia}}
Neonatal {{c1::respiratory distress}} syndrome

What cardiac anomaly is associated with lithium exposure in utero?

{{c1::Ebstein}} anomaly

What birth defects might occur when a patient takes antiepileptic drugs during pregnancy?

{{c1::Cardiac}} defects
{{c1::Neural tube}} defects
{{c1::Cleft palate}}
{{c1::Skeletal}} abnormalities

An infant exposed to aminoglycoside antibiotics in utero should be tested for what defect?

{{c1::Hearing}} loss

What fetal abnormalities can occur if a pregnant patient receives chemotherapy with alkylating agents?

Multiple anomalies, including absence of the {{c1::digits}}

An infant with discolored erupting teeth may have been exposed to which antibiotic in utero?

{{c1::Tetracyclines}}

What teratogen may cause "flipper limbs" due to in utero exposure?

{{c1::Thalidomide}}
fields.Back Extra: The defect is known as phocomelia or micromelia.

fields.Text:
What birth defects might occur if a pregnant patient takes isotretinoin?

{{c1::Craniofacial}} defects
{{c1::Central nervous system}} defects
{{c1::Thymic}} defects
{{c1::Cardiac}} defects

What teratogenic effects can iodine excess and deficiency have on a fetus?

Excess iodine → Congenital {{c1::goiter}}
Iodine deficiency → {{c1::Cretinism}}

What are the consequences of tobacco use during pregnancy?

{{c1::Low::High/Low}} birth weight
{{c1::Preterm}} labor
{{c1::Placental}} problems
Intrauterine growth {{c1::retardation}}
{{c1::Attention-deficit hyperactivity}} disorder
Increased risk of {{c1::sudden infant death}} syndrome

What other condition is a female fetus at risk for when exposed to a drug that increases her risk of vaginal clear cell adenoma?

Congenital {{c1::Müllerian}} anomalies

What four effects are likely to result from a patient's use of cocaine during pregnancy?

Placental {{c1::abruption}}
{{c1::Preterm}} delivery
{{c1::Low::High/Low}} birth weight
Intrauterine growth {{c1::retardation}}

Use of an ACE inhibitor can damage which organ in the fetus?

{{c1::Kidney}}
fields.Back Extra: This can also lead to oligohydramnios and hypocalvaria.

fields.Text:
A woman abuses alcohol during her pregnancy. What might you expect to see in her child?

{{c1::Fetal alcohol}} syndrome

Will organogenesis be affected if a fetus is exposed to a teratogen after 8 weeks of pregnancy?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Growth and function will be affected, but not organogenesis.

fields.Text:
What embryonic process is occurring when the fetus is most susceptible to teratogens?

{{c1::Organogenesis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is between the 3rd and 8th weeks of pregnancy.

fields.Text:
What is the likely effect on development when a 2-week-old embryo is exposed to an unknown teratogen?

Embryonal {{c1::demise}}
{{c1::No abnormalities}}
fields.Back Extra: There will be an all-or-none effect before week 3.

fields.Text:
What teratogenic effect is expected with the use of fluoroquinolones during pregnancy?

{{c1::Cartilage}} damage

How can birth defects from exposure to X-rays be minimized in pregnant patients?

{{c1::Lead shielding}}

Which animal source has high concentrations of methylmercury?

{{c1::Top::Top/Bottom}}-predator {{c1::fish}}
fields.Back Extra: Some examples would include the king mackerel, shark, swordfish, and tilefish.

fields.Text:
Which type of morphogenesis error occurs as a result of an intrinsic development defect during the embryonic period?

{{c1::Malformation}}

What type of morphogenesis error can cause the Potter sequence secondary to oligohydramnios?

{{c1::Sequence}} error
fields.Back Extra: Abnormalities can result from a single primary embryologic event.

fields.Text:
Why does amniotic band syndrome occur with a disruption–type error in organ morphogenesis?

It is due to the {{c1::secondary::primary/secondary}} breakdown of a tissue with normal developmental potential

What type of error in morphogenesis results in incomplete development of a fetal organ in the presence of its primordial tissue?

{{c1::Hypoplasia::Hyperplasia/Hypoplasia}}

What type of morphogenetic error results in failure of organ development in the presence of primordial tissue?

{{c1::Aplasia}}

What type of morphogenesis error results in the lack of an organ because of the absence of primordial tissue?

{{c1::Agenesis}}

What type of morphogenesis error can result in congenital torticollis?

{{c1::Deformation}}

What does extrinsic mechanical distortion during the fetal period result in?

{{c1::Deformation}}

Why does holoprosencephaly develop with a field defect–type error of organ morphogenesis?

It is caused by the development of {{c1::tissue}} disturbances in a {{c1::contiguous}} physical space

Use of what substance by the mother during pregnancy led to development of the facial features of the infant shown in the image?



{{c1::Alcohol}}

What is the mechanism of development of the characteristic features of fetal alcohol syndrome?



Impaired {{c1::migration}} of {{c1::neuronal}} and {{c1::glial}} cells

What conditions characterize the most severe form of fetal alcohol syndrome?

Heart-lung {{c1::fistulas}}
{{c1::Holoprosencephaly}}

What limb abnormality is associated with fetal alcohol syndrome?

Limb {{c1::dislocation}}

What condition associated with substance use by a pregnant woman is a leading preventable cause of intellectual disability in the United States?

{{c1::Fetal alcohol}} syndrome

What craniofacial findings are characteristic of fetal alcohol syndrome?

{{c1::Microcephaly::Macrocephaly/Microcephaly}}
Small palpebral {{c1::fissures}}
Smooth {{c1::philtrum}}
{{c1::Thin::Thick/Thin}} vermillion border

What congenital abnormalities are seen in fetal alcohol syndrome?

Prenatal and postnatal {{c1::developmental}} delay
{{c1::Microcephaly::Macrocephaly/Microcephaly}}
Limb {{c1::dislocation}}
{{c1::Facial}} abnormalities
{{c1::Heart::Organ}} defects

What syndrome is an infant at risk for post partum if the mother was taking short-acting opiates throughout the pregnancy?

{{c1::Neonatal abstinence}} syndrome

What findings are present in a newborn with neonatal abstinence syndrome?

Uncoordinated {{c1::sucking}} reflexes
{{c1::High::High/Low}}-pitched crying
{{c1::Irritability}}
{{c1::Tremors}}
{{c1::Sneezing}}
{{c1::Tachypnea::Tachypnea/Bradypnea}}
{{c1::Diarrhea}}

What is the general recommendation for screening of substance abuse in pregnant patients?

{{c1::Universal}} screening

What is the treatment for a pregnant woman with a history of opiate abuse?

{{c1::Methadone}}
{{c1::Buprenorphine}}
{{c1::Morphine}}

What systems are involved in neonatal abstinence syndrome?

{{c1::Central nervous }} system
{{c1::Autonomic nervous}} system
{{c1::Gastrointestinal}} system

What are the inner and outer layers of the placenta?

Inner layer → {{c1::Cytotrophoblast}}
Outer layer → {{c1::Syncytiotrophoblast}}

In the placental chorionic villi, what is able to pass from the maternal circulation to the fetal circulation?

{{c1::Oxygen}}
{{c2::Water}}
{{c3::Electrolytes}}
{{c4::Nutrients}}
{{c5::Hormones}}
Ig{{c6::G}}
Certain {{c7::drugs}}
{{c8::Viruses}}

In the maternal circulation, which vessels carry oxygen-rich blood to the lacunae? Which vessels remove oxygen-poor blood?

Oxygen-rich blood → Endometrial {{c1::arteries::arteries/veins}}
Oxygen-poor blood → Endometrial {{c1::veins::arteries/veins}}

Fetal blood within arteries and veins is exposed to maternal blood in the lacunae within what structure?

{{c1::Chorionic villus}}

In the umbilical cord, which vascular structure carries oxygen-rich blood from the mother to the fetus?

Umbilical {{c1::vein::artery/vein}}

What waste products diffuse from the fetal circulation into the maternal circulation via the placenta?

{{c1::CO2}}
{{c1::H2O}}
{{c1::Hormones}}
{{c1::Urea}}

In the umbilical cord, what vascular structures carry oxygen-poor blood from the fetus to the mother?

Umbilical {{c1::arteries::arteries/veins}}

Which structure separates the amniotic cavity from the lacunae containing maternal blood?

{{c1::Chorion}}

Why is there a decreased chance of attack by the maternal immune system on the placenta?

Lack of {{c1::MHC I}} expression

Which layer of the placenta is mitotically active?

{{c1::Inner::Inner/Outer}} layer

What is the primary site of nutrient and gas exchange between the mother and the fetus?

{{c1::Placenta}}

What hormone stimulates the corpus luteum to secrete progesterone during the 1st trimester of pregnancy?

{{c1::hCG}}

The decidua basalis is derived from what?

{{c1::Endometrium}}

Which layer of the placenta synthesizes hormones, such as hCG?

{{c1::Outer::Inner/Outer}} layer

What are five fetal and maternal disorders associated with polyhydramnios?

Fetal esophageal/duodenal {{c1::atresia}}
{{c1::Anencephaly}}
Fetal {{c1::anemia}}
Multiple {{c1::gestations}}
{{c1::Diabetes}} in pregnant patients

What fetal syndrome is associated with severe oligohydramnios?

{{c1::Potter sequence}}

Name three congenital conditions that cause oligohydramnios.

Bilateral renal {{c1::agenesis}}
{{c1::Posterior::Anterior/Posterior}} urethral valves (males)
{{c1::Placental}} insufficiency
fields.Back Extra: They all lead to the inability to excrete urine.

fields.Text:
What term describes the expected amniotic fluid level if a fetus is unable to excrete urine?

{{c1::Oligohydramnios}}

Why do fetal malformations, such as esophageal/duodenal atresia or anencephaly, result in polyhydramnios?

Decreased ability of the fetus to {{c1::swallow}} amniotic fluid → {{c1::High::High/Low}} amniotic fluid levels in the sac

How is amniotic fluid cleared?

Fetal {{c1::swallowing}}
Intramembranous {{c1::absorption}}

From what sources is amniotic fluid derived?

Fetal {{c1::urine}}
Fetal {{c1::lung liquid}}

What important structure forms in the zygote around the 12th day after fertilization?

{{c1::Embryonic disc}}

After fertilization, what are the major zygotic stages before formation of the embryonic disc?

Fertilized egg → {{c1::2}}-cell stage → {{c1::Morula}} → {{c1::Blastocyst}} → Formed embryonic disc

What percentage of twins are dizygotic versus monozygotic?

Dizygotic → ∼{{c1::66}}%
Monozygotic → ∼{{c1::33}}%

For monozygotic twins, what determines both the chorionicity and the amnionicity?

{{c1::Timing}} of splitting

A blastocyst split just before embryonic disc formation results in what type of twin pregnancy?

{{c1::Monozygotic::Monozygotic/Dizygotic}}, {{c1::monochorionic::monochorionic/dichorionic}}, {{c1::monoamniotic::monoamniotic/diamniotic}} twins

A patient has monozygotic, dichorionic, diamniotic twins. Between what two stages of the zygote did splitting occur?

Between the {{c1::2}}-cell stage and the {{c1::morula}} stage

A morula is split just before becoming a blastocyst. What type of twin pregnancy will result?

{{c1::Monozygotic::Monozygotic/Dizygotic}}, {{c1::monochorionic::monochorionic/dichorionic}}, {{c1::diamniotic::monoamniotic/diamniotic}} twins

From how many eggs and sperm do monozygotic twins arise?

{{c1::1}} egg
{{c1::1}} sperm

From how many eggs and sperm do dizygotic twins arise?

{{c1::2}} eggs
{{c1::2}} sperm

How many chorions and amniotic sacs should be present in a pregnant patient with dizygotic twins?

{{c1::2}} chorions
{{c1::2}} amniotic sacs

What two mechanisms cause an embryonic disc to undergo conjoined, monochorionic, monoamniotic twinning?

{{c1::Splitting}}
{{c1::Axis duplication}}

What type of twin pregnancy is expected to arise when a zygote splits on day 14 after fertilization?

{{c1::Conjoined}}, {{c1::monochorionic::monochorionic/dichorionic}}, {{c1::monoamniotic::monoamniotic/diamniotic}} twins

What type of gestation may lead to twin-twin transfusion syndrome?

{{c1::Monochorionic::Monochorionic/Dichorionic}} twin gestation

Why is there net blood flow from one twin to the other in twin-twin transfusion syndrome?

This is a result of {{c1::unbalanced}} vascular connections between twins in a shared placenta

In twin-twin transfusion syndrome, what happens to the levels of blood volume and amniotic fluid in the donor twin and the recipient twin?

Donor twin → {{c1::Hypovolemia::Hypervolemia/Hypovolemia}} and {{c1::oligohydramnios::oligohydramnios/polyhydramnios}}
Recipient twin → {{c1::Hypervolemia::Hypervolemia/Hypovolemia}} and {{c1::polyhydramnios::oligohydramnios/polyhydramnios}}

What are two complications of an anomaly that results from the failure of the urachus to involute?

{{c1::Malignancy}}
{{c1::Infection}}

What is the pathophysiology behind the defect shown?



Partial closure of the {{c1::vitelline duct}} with the patent portion attached to the {{c1::ileum}}

In fetal development, into which part of the fetus does the allantois extend?

{{c1::Urogenital sinus}}

What is the pathophysiology of the defect represented in the image?



Partial failure of the urachus to {{c1::obliterate}} → Fluid-filled cavity between the {{c1::umbilicus}} and {{c1::bladder}}

What happens to the urinary bladder of a newborn with vesicourachal diverticulum?

{{c1::Outpouching}} of the bladder
fields.Back Extra: This is a result of a slight failure of the urachus to obliterate.

fields.Text:
What causes a leakage of urine in a patent urachus in a newborn?

Total failure of the urachus to {{c1::obliterate}}

What is the pathogenesis of the disease represented in the image where a newborn presents with meconium discharge from his umbilicus?



Failure of the {{c1::vitelline duct}} to {{c1::close::open/close}}

An 8-month-old child presents with abdominal pain and bloody stool. Exploratory laparotomy reveals the findings shown in the image. What might be seen on histology?



{{c1::Heterotopic gastric mucosa}}
{{c1::Pancreatic}} tissue

When does the vitelline duct become obliterated?

{{c1::7th}} week

Which two structures are connected by the vitelline duct?

The vitelline duct connects the {{c1::yolk sac}} to the {{c1::midgut lumen}}

What structure in the embryo gives rise to the allantois?

{{c1::Hindgut}}

What structure connects the fetal bladder with the umbilicus and removes nitrogenous waste?

{{c1::Urachus}}

Normally, how many umbilical arteries and veins are present?

{{c1::2}} umbilical arteries
{{c1::1}} umbilical vein

The umbilical vein drains into the inferior vena cava via which structures?

{{c1::Liver::Organ}}
{{c1::Ductus venosus}}

Umbilical vessels are derived from which fetal structure?

{{c1::Allantois}}

Why is it important to inspect the umbilical cord for vascular abnormalities after delivery?

{{c1::Congenital}} anomalies
{{c1::Chromosomal}} anomalies
fields.Back Extra: This is associated with a single umbilical artery.

fields.Text:
Does the umbilical vein carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?

{{c1::Oxygenated}} blood

The umbilical arteries shunt deoxygenated blood to the placenta out of which arteries in the fetus?

Fetal {{c1::internal iliac}} arteries

Do the umbilical arteries carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?

{{c1::Deoxygenated}} blood

What structure represents the remains of the urachus?

{{c1::Median umbilical ligament}}
fields.Back Extra: This is covered by the median umbilical fold of the peritoneum.

fields.Text:
What is the vitelline duct also known as?

{{c1::Omphalomesenteric}} duct

Name three anomalies that result from failure of the urachus to obliterate.

Total failure → {{c1::Patent urachus}}
Partial failure → {{c1::Urachal cyst}}
Slight failure → {{c1::Vesicourachal diverticulum}}

Name three anomalies that result from failure of the vitelline duct to obliterate.

Total failure → {{c1::Patent vitelline duct}}
Partial failure → {{c1::Vitelline duct cyst}}
Slight failure → {{c1::Meckel diverticulum}}

The risk for volvulus is increased in which vitelline duct anomaly?

{{c1::Vitelline duct cyst}}

What happens to the ileum of a patient with Meckel diverticulum?

{{c1::Outpouching}} of the ileum
fields.Back Extra: This is a result of a slight failure of the vitelline duct to obliterate.

fields.Text:
How does a urachal cyst present clinically?

{{c1::Painful::Painful/Painless}} mass {{c1::below::above/below}} the umbilicus when it becomes infected

What are the components of the pharyngeal apparatus?

Pharyngeal {{c1::clefts}}
Pharyngeal {{c1::arches}}
Pharyngeal {{c1::pouches}}

Pharyngeal pouches are derived from which germ layer?

{{c1::Endoderm}}

From which two embryologic structures are the pharyngeal arches derived?

Muscles and arteries → {{c1::Mesoderm}}
Bones and cartilages → {{c1::Neural crest}}

From which primary germ layer are pharyngeal clefts derived?

{{c1::Ectoderm}}

Where is the pharyngeal cleft cyst expected to be found on the neck?

It is typically seen in the {{c1::lateral::medial/lateral}} neck as a mass, {{c1::anterior::anterior/posterior}} to the sternocleidomastoid muscle

The 2nd through 4th pharyngeal clefts are obliterated through the proliferation of which structure?

{{c1::2nd}} pharyngeal arch {{c1::mesenchyme}}

The 2nd through 4th pharyngeal clefts initially develop into what structures?

Temporary {{c1::cervical sinuses}}

The external auditory meatus derives from which pharyngeal cleft?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal cleft

What pathology may arise with failure of pharyngeal cleft sinus obliteration?

Pharyngeal cleft {{c1::cyst}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a persistent cervical sinus.

fields.Text:
How can you differentiate a pharyngeal cleft cyst and a thyroglossal duct cyst?

A pharyngeal cleft cyst {{c1::will not::will/will not}} move with swallowing
A thyroglossal duct cyst {{c1::will::will/will not}} move with swallowing

The mandibular process is a derivative of which pharyngeal arch subset?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subsets are the lesser and greater horns of the hyoid bone derived?

The lesser horn is derived from the {{c1::2nd}} pharyngeal arch
The greater horn is derived from the {{c1::3rd}} pharyngeal arch

Cranial nerve IX is a derivative of which pharyngeal arch subset?

{{c1::3rd}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subset is cranial nerve V3 derived?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal arch

The anterior belly of the digastric muscle is derived from which pharyngeal arch?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal arch
fields.Back Extra: The posterior belly of the digastric muscle is derived from 2nd arch.

fields.Text:
From which pharyngeal arch subset is the zygomatic bone derived?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subset is the sphenomandibular ligament derived?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal arch

The ossicles of the middle ear are derived from which subsets of pharyngeal arches?

The malleus and incus arise from the {{c1::1st}} pharyngeal arch
The stapes arises from the {{c1::2nd}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subset is the recurrent/inferior laryngeal branch of cranial nerve X derived?

{{c1::6th}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subset is the maxillary process derived?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subset is the mylohyoid muscle derived?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subset are most pharyngeal constrictor muscles derived?

{{c1::4th}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subset are most of the intrinsic muscles of the larynx derived?

{{c1::6th}} pharyngeal arch
fields.Back Extra:
All the intrinsic muscles of the larynx, except the cricothyroid, are derived from the 6th pharyngeal arch.

The cricothyroid is derived from the 4th pharyngeal arch.

fields.Text:
From which pharyngeal arch subset is the tensor tympani muscle derived?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subset is the superior laryngeal branch of cranial nerve X derived?

{{c1::4th}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subset is the anterior two-thirds of the tongue derived?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subset is cranial nerve VII derived?

{{c1::2nd}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subset are the muscles of facial expression derived?

{{c1::2nd}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subset is the levator veli palatini muscle derived?

{{c1::4th}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subset is Meckel cartilage derived?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subsets is the posterior one-third of the tongue derived?

{{c1::3rd}} pharyngeal arch
{{c1::4th}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subset are the muscles of mastication derived?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal arch

What are the cartilaginous derivatives from the 2nd pharyngeal arch?

{{c1::Stylohyoid}} ligament
{{c1::Styloid process}}
{{c1::Stapes}}
{{c1::Lesser::Greater/Lesser}} horn of the hyoid
fields.Back Extra: These cartilaginous derivatives are known as Reichert cartilage.

fields.Text:
What are the characteristic findings of the Pierre Robin sequence?

{{c1::Micrognathia::Macrognathia/Micrognathia}}
{{c1::Cleft palate}}
{{c1::Glossoptosis}}
Airway {{c1::obstruction}}

How are sensory and motor neurons derived during the development of the pharyngeal arches?

Sensory neurons are derived from the {{c1::neural crest}}
Motor neurons are derived from the {{c1::neuroectoderm}}
fields.Back Extra: They grow into the pharyngeal arches during development, but are not derived from the pharyngeal arches.

fields.Text:
Which muscles are derived from the 2nd pharyngeal arch?

Muscles of {{c1::facial expression}}
{{c1::Stapedius}}
{{c1::Stylohyoid}}
{{c1::Platysma}}
{{c1::Posterior::Anterior/Posterior}} belly of the digastric muscle

Which cartilages are derived from the 4th and 6th pharyngeal arches?

{{c1::Arytenoid}}
{{c1::Cricoid}}
{{c1::Corniculate}}
{{c1::Cuneiform}}
{{c1::Thyroid}}

What structure is derived from the 5th pharyngeal arch?

{{c1::None}}
fields.Back Extra: The 5th pharyngeal arch does not make any major developmental contributions.

fields.Text:
From which pharyngeal arch subset is the stylopharyngeus muscle derived?

{{c1::3rd}} pharyngeal arch

From which pharyngeal arch subset is the tensor veli palatini muscle derived?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal arch

What are the common findings associated with Treacher Collins syndrome?

{{c1::Craniofacial}} abnormalities
{{c1::Airway}} compromise
{{c1::Hearing}} loss

Dysfunction of which structure results in Treacher Collins syndrome?

Dysfunction of the {{c1::neural crest}}
fields.Back Extra: The inheritance pattern of this syndrome is autosomal dominant.

fields.Text:
Name the muscles of mastication that are derived from the 1st pharyngeal arch.

{{c1::Temporalis}}
{{c1::Masseter}}
{{c1::Lateral pterygoid}}
{{c1::Medial pterygoid}}

Pierre Robin sequence and Treacher Collins syndrome can be caused by abnormal development of which two pharyngeal arches?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal arch
{{c1::2nd}} pharyngeal arch

What is noteworthy about the final position of structures derived from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch?

They end up {{c1::inferior::superior/inferior}} to structures derived from the {{c1::4th}} pharyngeal pouch anatomically

Which structures are derived from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch?

Ventral wings → {{c1::Thymus}}
Dorsal wings → {{c1::Inferior::Superior/Inferior}} {{c1::parathyroids}}

From which structure are middle ear cavities and mastoid air cells derived?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal pouch

The superior parathyroids are derived from which pharyngeal pouch?

{{c1::Dorsal::Ventral/Dorsal}} wings of the {{c1::4th}} pharyngeal pouch
fields.Back Extra: The inferior parathyroids are derived from dorsal wings of the 3rd pharyngeal pouch.

fields.Text:
From which pharyngeal pouch are the parafollicular cells of the thyroid derived?

{{c1::Ventral::Ventral/Dorsal}} wings of the {{c1::4th}} pharyngeal pouch

Eustachian tubes are derived from which pharyngeal pouch?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal pouch

The epithelial lining of the palatine tonsil is derived from which pharyngeal pouch?

{{c1::2nd}} pharyngeal pouch

The ultimopharyngeal body is derived from which pharyngeal pouch?

{{c1::4th}} pharyngeal pouch

The endoderm-lined structures of the ear are derived from which pharyngeal pouch?

{{c1::1st}} pharyngeal pouch

Although cleft lip and cleft palate have two distinct origins, can they occur in the same patient?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}

Failure of which process can lead to cleft lip?

Fusion of the {{c1::intermaxillary segment}} with the {{c1::maxillary process}}
fields.Back Extra: This involves the formation of the primary palate.

fields.Text:
Failure of which three processes can lead to cleft palate?

Fusion of the two lateral {{c1::palatine shelves}}
Fusion of the lateral {{c1::palatine shelf}} with the {{c1::nasal septum}}
Fusion of the lateral {{c1::palatine shelf}} with the {{c1::primary ​​​​​palate}}
fields.Back Extra: This involves the formation of the secondary palate.

fields.Text:
What three female internal structures are derived from the paramesonephric duct?

{{c1::Fallopian tubes}}
{{c1::Uterus}}
{{c1::Upper::Upper/Lower}} portion of the vagina
fields.Back Extra: The lower portion of the vagina is derived from the urogenital sinus.

fields.Text:
What four male internal structures are derived from the mesonephric duct?

{{c1::Seminal vesicles}}
{{c1::Epididymis}}
{{c1::Ejaculatory duct}}
{{c1::Ductus deferens}}

Which duct develops in male development?

{{c1::Mesonephric}} duct
fields.Back Extra: The paramesonephric duct degenerates, except the appendix testis.

fields.Text:
A woman with fully developed secondary sexual characteristics has primary amenorrhea. What is her most likely diagnosis?

{{c1::Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: In this syndrome, the uterus does not develop.

fields.Text:
What embryologic structure becomes the lower part of the vagina?

{{c1::Urogenital sinus}}

Which cells produce Müllerian inhibitory factor in males?

{{c1::Sertoli}} cells
fields.Back Extra: This is also called antimullerian hormone.

fields.Text:
In male development, the mesonephric duct develops into all genitourinary internal structures except for which structure?

{{c1::Prostate}}
fields.Back Extra: The prostate develops after stimulation by dihydrotestosterone.

fields.Text:
Which gene on what chromosome encodes testis-determining factor?

{{c1::SRY}} gene on the {{c1::Y::X/Y}} chromosome

In female development, which duct develops?

{{c1::Paramesonephric}} duct
fields.Back Extra: The mesonephric duct degenerates, except for the Gartner duct.

fields.Text:
Is male or female development the default fetal development?

{{c1::Female}}

What class of hormones stimulates the development of the mesonephric ducts in males?

{{c1::Androgens}}
fields.Back Extra: These are secreted by Leydig cells.

fields.Text:
What are the mesonephric and paramesonephric ducts also known as?

Mesonephric duct → {{c1::Wolffian}} duct
Paramesonephric duct → {{c1::Müllerian}} duct

Why do females with Müllerian agenesis have primary amenorrhea?

Lack of {{c1::uterine}} development

What is the function of Müllerian inhibitory factor in males?

{{c1::Inhibits::Stimulates/Inhibits}} the formation of the {{c1::Müllerian}} duct

What factor in male development determines testes development?

{{c1::Testis-determining}} factor

Deficiency of which hormone is responsible for the absence of external female genitalia?

{{c1::Estrogen}}
fields.Back Extra: This is secreted by the ovaries.

fields.Text:
Impaired hormone release by which cells can be blamed for the impaired development of male internal genitalia?

{{c1::Leydig}} cells
fields.Back Extra: Leydig cells produce testosterone, which are required for differentiation of the Wolffian duct into male internal genitalia.

fields.Text:
The SRY gene is located on which chromosome?

{{c1::Y::X/Y}} chromosome

What is the function of dihydrotestosterone in male sexual differentiation?

Promotes the development of the undifferentiated {{c1::gonads}} into the male {{c1::external::internal/external}} genitalia

What is the function of 5α-reductase?

Converts {{c1::testosterone}} to {{c1::dihydrotestosterone}}

Absence of which hormone may be the cause of improper degeneration of the paramesonephric duct?

{{c1::Müllerian inhibitory}} factor

What internal and external genitalia will be seen in a male with 5α-reductase deficiency?

{{c1::Male::Male/Female}} internal genitalia
{{c1::Ambiguous}} external genitalia until puberty

What features will be seen in a male who lacks Müllerian inhibitory factor?

{{c1::Male}} and {{c1::female}} internal genitalia
{{c1::Male::Male/Female}} external genitalia

Testosterone leads to development of which secondary sexual characteristics?

{{c1::Facial}} hair
{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in penis size and length
{{c1::Growth spurt}} in males
{{c1::Pubic}} and {{c1::axillary}} hair in both sexes

Testosterone action on the mesonephric duct leads to development of which internal male genitalia?

{{c1::Seminal vesicles}}
{{c1::Epididymis}}
{{c1::Ejaculatory ducts}}
{{c1::Ductus deferens}}

What is the treatment of the condition depicted in this X-ray of the uterus?



{{c1::Septoplasty}}

What may be the abnormality seen in this X-ray of the uterus?



{{c1::Uterus didelphys}}

What is the pathogenesis of the disorder depicted in this X-ray of the uterus?



{{c1::Incomplete}} fusion of the {{c1::Müllerian}} ducts

How does septate uterus occur?

Incomplete {{c1::resorption}} of the septum

How does uterus didelphys occur?

{{c1::Complete}} failure of fusion of the {{c1::Müllerian}} ducts

A 16-year-old girl is noted to have a double uterus, cervix, and vagina on ultrasound exam. What is the likely diagnosis?

{{c1::Uterus didelphys}}

What are two complications associated with Müllerian duct anomalies?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} fertility
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} risk of complicated pregnancy

In adnexal torsion, the ovary twists around which two ligaments?

{{c1::Infundibulopelvic}} ligament
{{c1::Ovarian}} ligament

Why does the ovary become edematous in adnexal torsion?

Ovarian vessels within the infundibulopelvic ligament are {{c1::compressed}} → Blockage of lymphatic and venous outflow with persistent arterial {{c1::perfusion}}

What condition is ovarian torsion commonly associated with?

Ovarian {{c1::masses}}

What are the three signs and symptoms of ovarian torsion?

{{c1::Nausea}}/{{c1::vomiting}}
Acute {{c1::pelvic}} pain
{{c1::Adnexal mass}}

What can lead to local hemorrhage and necrosis in the ovary of a patient with a diagnosis of adnexal torsion?

Complete blockage of {{c1::arterial::arterial/venous}} inflow → Ovarian {{c1::edema}}

In what condition do the pelvic organs herniate to or beyond the vaginal walls or apex?

{{c1::Pelvic organ prolapse}}

Name three factors associated with increased risk for pelvic organ prolapse.

Increased {{c1::age}}
{{c1::Obesity}}
{{c1::Multiparity}}

What are the common presenting findings of pelvic organ prolapse?

Pelvic {{c1::pressure}}
Urinary {{c1::frequency}}
{{c1::Constipation}}
{{c1::Sexual}} dysfunction
Tissue {{c1::protrusion}} from the vagina

How is pelvic organ prolapse classified according to compartments of the pelvis?

{{c1::Anterior}} compartment prolapse
{{c1::Posterior}} compartment prolapse
{{c1::Apical}} compartment prolapse
fields.Back Extra: Uterine procidentia is used to describe herniation through all three compartments.

fields.Text:
Which organ is prolapsed in anterior compartment prolapse?

{{c1::Bladder}}

Which organs are prolapsed in posterior compartment prolapse?

{{c1::Small bowel}}
{{c1::Rectum}}

Which organs are prolapsed in apical compartment prolapse?

{{c1::Cervix}}
{{c1::Uterus}}
{{c1::Vaginal vault}}

Which compartment of the pelvis is most commonly involved in cases of pelvic organ prolapse?

{{c1::Anterior}} compartment

What type of epithelium lines the outer surface of the ovaries?

{{c1::Simple::Simple/Stratified}} {{c1::cuboidal::squamous/cuboidal/columnar}} epithelium

What type of epithelium lines the uterus in the proliferative phase versus the secretory phase?

Proliferative phase → {{c1::Simple::Simple/Stratified}} {{c1::columnar::squamous/cuboidal/columnar}} epithelium with {{c1::long tubular}} glands
Secretory phase → {{c1::Coiled}} glands

What types of epithelium line the endocervix and ectocervix?

Endocervix → {{c1::Simple::Simple/Stratified}} {{c1::columnar::squamous/cuboidal/columnar}} epithelium
Ectocervix → {{c1::Stratified::Simple/Stratified}} {{c1::squamous::squamous/cuboidal/columnar}}, {{c1::nonkeratinized::keratinized/nonkeratinized}} epithelium

What type of epithelium lines the vagina?

{{c1::Stratified::Simple/Stratified}} {{c1::squamous::squamous/cuboidal/columnar}}, {{c1::nonkeratinized::keratinized/nonkeratinized}} epithelium

Which female reproductive structure is lined by ciliated simple columnar epithelium?

{{c1::Fallopian tubes}}

What is the area of greatest risk for cervical cancer in the female reproductive tract?

{{c1::Transformation}} zone
fields.Back Extra: This involves the squamocolumnar junction, where the ectocervix meets the endocervix.

fields.Text:
What type of epithelium lines the vulva?

{{c1::Stratified::Simple/Stratified}} {{c1::squamous::squamous/cuboidal/columnar}} epithelium

Name the area in the image indicated by the arrow.



The {{c1::transformation}} zone of the {{c1::cervix}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as the squamocolumnar junction.

fields.Text:
List, in order, the structures through which sperm must travel to complete ejaculation.

{{c1::Seminiferous tubules}} → {{c1::Epididymis}} → {{c1::Vas deferens}} → {{c1::Ejaculatory ducts}} → {{c1::Urethra}} → {{c1::Penis}}

What part of the urethra is prone to injury in perineal straddle injuries?

{{c1::Bulbar}} urethra

What part of the urethra is disrupted in a pelvic fracture, causing posterior urethral injury?

{{c1::Bulbomembranous}} junction
fields.Back Extra: This is the weakest part of the urethra.

fields.Text:
Where would urine leak in a male patient with a perineal straddle injury?

{{c1::Buck fascia}} is torn → Urine escapes into the {{c1::perineal}} space
fields.Back Extra: This is an anterior urethral injury.

fields.Text:
What type of urethral injury could cause urine to leak into the retropubic space?

{{c1::Posterior::Anterior/Posterior}} urethral injury

What could cause blood at the urethral meatus in a patient with a pelvic fracture?

Urethral {{c1::injury}}

What part of the urethra is most likely injured if a rectal exam reveals a high riding prostrate?

{{c1::Posterior::Anterior/Posterior}} part of the urethra

In what type of genitourinary trauma is urinary catheterization relatively contraindicated?

{{c1::Urethral}} injury

Disruption of the bulbar urethra in anterior urethral injury leads to what condition?

{{c1::Scrotal hematoma}}

What kind of genitourinary injury can occur as a result of direct blows or rib fractures?

{{c1::Renal}} injury

How do patients with a renal injury present?

{{c1::Bruises}}
{{c1::Flank}} pain
{{c1::Hematuria}}

Why do BUN and serum creatinine levels increase in a patient with a bladder injury?

Absorption of urine into the {{c1::blood}} from {{c1::intraperitoneal}} urine accumulation → High BUN and serum creatinine levels

Which parts of the bladder are prone to injury with a pelvic fracture?

{{c1::Anterior::Anterior/Posterior}} bladder wall
{{c1::Anterior::Anterior/Posterior}} bladder neck

Which two genitourinary injuries cause urine leakage into the retropubic space?

Injury to the {{c1::anterior::anterior/posterior}} bladder wall or neck
Injury to the {{c1::posterior::anterior/posterior}} urethra

Which part of the autonomic nervous system mediates emission during the male sexual response?

{{c1::Sympathetic::Sympathetic/Parasympathetic}} nervous system

How does norepinephrine exert an antierectile effect on the penis?

Norepinephrine causes vascular smooth muscle {{c1::contraction::contraction/relaxation}} through {{c1::Ca2+}} influx → {{c1::Vasoconstriction::Vasodilation/Vasoconstriction}}

Name the drug class that acts on the nitric oxide pathway to treat erectile dysfunction.

{{c1::PDE-5}} inhibitors reduce {{c1::cGMP}} breakdown → Vascular smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation

How does nitric oxide mediate penile erection?

Nitric oxide causes {{c1::relaxation::contraction/relaxation}} of vascular smooth muscle through {{c1::cGMP}} production → Increased penile blood flow

Which part of the autonomic nervous system mediates erection of the penis?

{{c1::Parasympathetic::Sympathetic/Parasympathetic}} nervous system

What spinal nerves are responsible for expulsion during the male sexual response?

{{c1::Visceral}} nerves
{{c1::Somatic}} nerves

What hormone, produced by Sertoli cells, provides negative feedback to the anterior pituitary?

{{c1::Inhibin B}}

Leydig cells are the homolog of what female cells?

{{c1::Theca interna}} cells

What is the function of aromatase in Sertoli cells?

Converts {{c1::testosterone}} and {{c1::androstenedione}} to {{c1::estrogen}}

What hormones do Sertoli and Leydig cells respond to?

Sertoli cells → {{c1::FSH}}
Leydig cells → {{c1::LH}}

Sertoli cells are the homolog of what female cells?

{{c1::Granulosa}} cells

Which cells in the seminiferous tubules contain aromatase?

{{c1::Sertoli}} cells

In the testes, where are spermatogonia, Sertoli cells, and Leydig cells found?

Spermatogonia line the {{c1::seminiferous tubules}}
Sertoli cells line the {{c1::seminiferous tubules}}
Leydig cells → {{c1::Interstitium}}

What type of cell provides most of the support and nourishment for the developing spermatozoa and regulates spermatogenesis?

{{c1::Sertoli}} cells

How do Sertoli cells and Leydig cells respond to changes in temperature?

Sertoli cells {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} sperm production and inhibin B release with increased temperature
Leydig cells are {{c1::unaffected}}

What type of cell is probably defective if a man is unable to produce primary spermatocytes and maintain a sperm pool?

{{c1::Spermatogonia}}

How is the blood-testis barrier formed?
