{{c1::Tight}} junctions between adjacent {{c1::Sertoli}} cells

What three hormones/proteins do Sertoli cells produce?

{{c1::Androgen}}-binding protein
{{c1::Inhibin B}}
{{c1::Müllerian inhibiting}} factor

In men, what cells secrete testosterone?

{{c1::Leydig}} cells

What are the names for the germ cells, non-germ cells, and endocrine cells found in/around the seminiferous tubules?

Germ cells → {{c1::Spermatogonia}}
Non-germ cells → {{c1::Sertoli}} cells
Endocrine cells → {{c1::Leydig}} cells

What are the two important functions of Sertoli cells in relation to spermatocytes?

{{c1::Nourish}} and {{c1::support}} developing spermatozoa
{{c1::Regulate}} spermatogenesis

What is the function of the blood-testis barrier?

Isolates {{c1::gametes}} from the immune system → Prevents an {{c1::autoimmune}} attack

Which protein, secreted by Sertoli cells, maintains local levels of testosterone?

{{c1::Androgen}}-binding protein

What is the definition of off-label drug use?

Treating a disease by using a drug in a form, group, or dosage not approved by the {{c1::FDA}}

Name two reasons to consider off-label drug use.

Treatment of a disease with no {{c1::approved}} drug therapies
Trial of {{c1::alternative}} treatment after failure of {{c1::approved}} treatment for a disease

What is the demographic transition that occurs as a country moves into higher levels of development?

Birth and mortality rates {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} {{c1::unequally::equally/unequally}}
fields.Back Extra: This changes the population's age distribution.

fields.Text:
When birth rate increases more than mortality rate increases, what demographic transition can be expected in terms of the life expectancy and population growth?

Life expectancy will be {{c1::shorter::longer/shorter}}
Population growth will {{c1::grow::grow/decline}}

When birth rate and mortality rate decrease to a similar degree, what demographic transition can be expected in terms of the life expectancy and population growth?

Life expectancy will be {{c1::longer::longer/shorter}}
Population growth will be {{c1::stable::stable/unstable}}

When birth rate decreases more than mortality rate decreases, what demographic transition can be expected in terms of the life expectancy and population growth?

Life expectancy will be {{c1::longer::longer/shorter}}
Population growth will {{c1::decline::grow/decline}}

What information is displayed in a Kaplan-Meier curve?



"{{c1::Time-to-event}}" data
fields.Back Extra: This is often used to graph mortality data.

fields.Text:
How is probability of survival related to event probability?

Survival probability = {{c1::1}} - {{c1::Event probability}}

What is statistical significance?

It is defined by the likelihood of results being due to {{c1::chance}}
fields.Back Extra: A higher statistical significance indicates a lower likelihood that the results are due to chance.

fields.Text:
What is clinical significance?

A measure of effect on {{c1::outcomes}} of treatment
fields.Back Extra: A higher clinical significance indicates a greater impact on patient outcomes.

fields.Text:
Is a study with a high statistical significance guaranteed to have a high clinical significance?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Although there is a high statistical significance, the intervention being studied may not have a significant impact on clinical outcomes.

fields.Text:
Who is in charge of medical decision-making if a patient's ventilator-assisted support information is absent?

{{c1::Surrogate}} decision-makers
fields.Back Extra: This is either patient determined or legally determined.

fields.Text:
What steps are necessary if the decision is made to withhold or withdraw life support from a patient?

{{c1::Palliative}} care
{{c1::Chaplain}} services
Family {{c1::emotional support}}
fields.Back Extra: This is via primary care physician discussions.

fields.Text:
What kind of gifts should physicians politely decline to accept?

Inappropriately {{c1::expensive}} or {{c1::large::large/small}} gifts
Gifts that may cause {{c1::financial}} or {{c1::emotional}} distress to the patient
Any gift that might negatively affect the {{c1::quality of care}}

When deciding not to accept a gift from a patient, what is the recommended way to politely decline?

With {{c1::gratitude}} while politely saying that the gift must be declined and {{c1::assuring}} the patient that this will not affect their care or relationship with the physician in any way

How would you begin discussing a patient's problem when taking a culturally inclusive history?

Ask the patient to describe, in their {{c1::own}} way, the problem, why they {{c1::think}} they have it, and what makes it {{c1::better}} or {{c1::worse}}
fields.Back Extra: You should be aware of spiritual, community, and family issues.

fields.Text:
How do you prepare a culturally inclusive medical treatment plan?

Ask if the patient has {{c1::concerns}} or {{c1::suggestions}} regarding the treatment plan
fields.Back Extra: Aim to include their cultural beliefs and practices in the treatment plan.

fields.Text:
How could you address cultural barriers to medical care?

Ask if anything would {{c1::prevent}} them from seeking standard medical care
Ask about ways to maintain a good {{c1::physician-patient relationship}}

Why do pulses remain palpable in cholesterol emboli syndrome?

{{c1::Larger::Larger/Smaller}} arteries are {{c1::unaffected}}

What are five consequences of the microembolization of cholesterol displaced from atherosclerotic plaques in large arteries?

{{c1::Livedo reticularis}}
Digital {{c1::ischemia}}
Acute {{c1::renal}} failure
{{c1::Cerebrovascular}} accident
Gut {{c1::ischemia}}

What is another name for nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis?

{{c1::Marantic}} endocarditis

Vegetations in nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis usually arise on which valves of the heart?

{{c1::Mitral}} valve
{{c1::Aortic}} valve

What is nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis associated with?

{{c1::Hypercoagulable}} state observed in advanced malignancy
fields.Back Extra: This is seen especially in pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

fields.Text:
What are the major changes in preload, afterload, and cardiac output in the setting of distributive shock?

Preload {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
Cardiac output increases in patients with {{c1::sepsis}} or {{c1::anaphylaxis}}
Cardiac output decreases in patients with a {{c1::central nervous system}} injury
Afterload {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}

What are the major changes in preload, afterload, and cardiac output in an individual experiencing cardiogenic shock?

Preload {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}
Cardiac output {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
Afterload {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}

What are the major changes in preload, afterload, and cardiac output in the setting of obstructive shock?

Preload {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}
Cardiac output {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
Afterload {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}

What are the major changes in preload, afterload, and cardiac output in an individual experiencing hypovolemic shock?

Preload significantly {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
Cardiac output {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
Afterload {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}

Which three subtypes of shock lead to cold, clammy skin?

{{c1::Hypovolemic}} shock
{{c1::Cardiogenic}} shock
{{c1::Obstructive}} shock

What are three common causes of distributive shock?

{{c1::Anaphylaxis}}
{{c1::Central nervous system}} injury
{{c1::Sepsis}}

What are four common causes of cardiogenic shock?

Heart {{c1::failure}}
{{c1::Vascular}} dysfunction
{{c1::Arrhythmias}}
Acute {{c1::myocardial infarction}}

What are three common causes of hypovolemic shock?

{{c1::Dehydration}}
{{c1::Hemorrhage}}
{{c1::Burns}}

What are three common causes of obstructive shock?

Pulmonary {{c1::embolism}}
{{c1::Tension pneumothorax}}
Cardiac {{c1::tamponade}}

What is the main characteristic of high-output heart failure?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} cardiac output

What are the 6 causes of high-output heart failure?

Advanced {{c1::cirrhosis}}
Severe {{c1::anemia}}
{{c1::Hyperthyroidism}}
Severe {{c1::obesity}}
{{c1::Wet beriberi}}
{{c1::Paget disease of bone}}

What kind of heart failure can present with both pulmonary and systemic venous congestion?

{{c1::High-output}} heart failure

What 2 medications provide only symptomatic relief in patients with heart failure?

{{c1::Thiazide}}
{{c1::Loop diuretics}}

What 2 medications, used in combination, both relieve symptoms of heart failure and lower associated mortality in select patients?

{{c1::Hydralazine}}
{{c1::Nitrates}}

What is the role of the RAAS in the symptomatic presentation of edema in heart failure?

Activation of RAAS → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} circulating volume due to {{c1::Na+}} and {{c1::H2O}} reabsorption in the kidneys → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} preload → Edema

What happens to EF and EDV in the setting of diastolic dysfunction?

EF is {{c1::preserved}}
EDV is {{c1::normal}}

What is the effect of increased pulmonary venous pressure, causing fluid transudation into the lungs in patients with heart failure?

{{c1::Pulmonary edema}}

What common symptom associated with heart failure is caused by increased venous return from redistribution of blood and reabsorption of peripheral edema?

{{c1::Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea}}

Medications in what 4 drug classes are prescribed to reduce mortality in patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction?

{{c1::ACE}} inhibitors
{{c1::Angiotensin II}} receptor antagonists
{{c1::β-blockers}}
{{c1::Aldosterone}} receptor antagonists

What is the most common cause of right-sided heart failure in the absence of left-sided heart failure?

{{c1::Cor pulmonale}} due to {{c1::COPD}}

What is the most common cause of right-sided heart failure?

{{c1::Left-sided}} heart failure

What is the major histologic finding in the lungs of patients with left-sided heart failure?

{{c1::Hemosiderin-laden macrophages}}
fields.Back Extra: These are also known as "heart failure" cells.

fields.Text:
What is the major effect of right-sided heart failure on liver function?

{{c1::Hepatomegaly}}
{{c1::Cirrhosis}} (rare)

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism leading to orthopnea in patients with left-sided heart failure?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} venous return to the heart in the {{c1::supine}} position → Pulmonary vascular congestion and shortness of breath

What type of heart failure is associated with decreased contractility, reduced ejection fraction, and increased ventricular end-diastolic volume?

{{c1::Systolic}} heart failure

What are the 4 most common physical exam findings in patients with heart failure?

{{c1::Jugular venous distention}}
{{c1::Pitting edema}}
{{c1::S3}} heart sound
{{c1::Rales}}

What are the 3 physical exam findings most suggestive of right-sided heart failure?

{{c1::Peripheral edema}}
{{c1::Jugular venous distention}}
{{c1::Hepatomegaly}}

What side of the heart is primarily affected in a patient with worsening dyspnea, pitting edema, jugular venous distention, and hepatomegaly in the absence of pulmonary rales?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} side

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism leading to the physical exam finding shown in a patient with known right-sided heart failure?



{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} venous pressure → Fluid {{c1::transudation}} into tissues

β-blockers are used to treat heart failure except in which situation?

{{c1::Acute decompensated}} heart failure

What is the most likely diagnosis based on the pathologic specimen shown in the image?



{{c1::Dilated}} cardiomyopathy

What is the most common cardiomyopathy seen in young athletes with syncope, a family history of sudden cardiac death, and signs of heart failure?

{{c1::Hypertrophic}} cardiomyopathy
fields.Back Extra: This can cause ventricular arrhythmias during exercise.

fields.Text:
What is the mode of inheritance of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What is the major difference between the myocardial cellular structures seen in dilated cardiomyopathy and those seen in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?

Dilated cardiomyopathy → Sarcomeres are added in {{c1::series}}
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy → Sarcomeres are added in {{c1::parallel}}

Endomyocardial fibrosis with prominent eosinophilic infiltrate is associated with which type of endocarditis?

{{c1::Löffler}} endocarditis

What are the 6 causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy?

Postradiation {{c1::fibrosis}}
{{c1::Löffler}} endocarditis
Endocardial {{c1::fibroelastosis}}
{{c1::Amyloidosis}}
{{c1::Sarcoidosis}}
{{c1::Hemochromatosis}}

Which cardiomyopathy is commonly associated with Friedreich ataxia?

{{c1::Hypertrophic}} cardiomyopathy

What 2 common cardiomyopathies present with diastolic dysfunction?

{{c1::Restrictive}} cardiomyopathy
{{c1::Hypertrophic}} cardiomyopathy

Which restrictive cardiomyopathy will demonstrate pathologic appearance of thick fibroelastic tissue in the endocardium?

Endocardial {{c1::fibroelastosis}}

Which extra heart sounds are present in dilated cardiomyopathy?

{{c1::Systolic::Systolic/Diastolic}} {{c1::regurgitant}} murmur
{{c1::S3}}

What are 2 common medications for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?

{{c1::β-blockers}}
{{c1::Nondihydropyridine Ca2+ channel}} blockers

What are 2 common non-pharmaceutical treatments for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?

Cessation of high-{{c1::intensity}} sports
Placement of implantable {{c1::cardioverter defibrillator}} if risk is high

What is the most likely diagnosis based on the pathologic specimen shown in the image?



{{c1::Hypertrophic}} cardiomyopathy

What is the major pathophysiologic mechanism associated with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy?

Hypertrophied {{c1::interventricular septum}} obstructs the outflow tract of the {{c1::left}} side of the heart → {{c1::Dyspnea}} and {{c1::syncope}}

What congenital hematologic disorder can cause both dilated cardiomyopathy and restrictive cardiomyopathy?

{{c1::Hemochromatosis}}

What 7 medications are commonly used to treat dilated cardiomyopathy?

{{c1::ACE}} inhibitors
{{c1::Angiotensin II}} receptor blockers
{{c1::Mineralocorticoid}} receptor blockers
{{c1::Diuretics}}
{{c1::Sacubitril}}
{{c1::β-blockers}}
{{c1::Digoxin}}

What chemotherapeutic agent commonly used in the treatment of breast cancer could lead to dilated cardiomyopathy?

{{c1::Doxorubicin}}

What type of ventricular hypertrophy is seen in patients with long-standing hypertension?

{{c1::Concentric}} {{c1::left::left/right}} ventricular hypertrophy

What type of cardiomyopathy is commonly associated with periods of intense emotional stress?

{{c1::Takotsubo}} cardiomyopathy
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as broken heart syndrome.

fields.Text:
What is the most common gene mutation associated with familial dilated cardiomyopathy?

{{c1::TTN}} gene
fields.Back Extra: This encodes the sarcomere protein called titin.

fields.Text:
What type of ventricular hypertrophy is seen in patients with Friedrich ataxia?

{{c1::Concentric}} {{c1::left::left/right}} ventricular hypertrophy

In addition to drug therapy, what is the most important step in the management of a STEMI?

{{c1::Reperfusion}} therapy

What are two medications for immediate symptom control in patients with unstable angina?

{{c1::Nitroglycerin}}
{{c1::Morphine}}

What are the five initial treatments that should be administered to patients with unstable angina or NSTEMI?

{{c1::Anticoagulation}}
{{c1::Antiplatelet}} therapy
{{c1::β-blockers}}
{{c1::Statins}}
{{c1::ACE}} inhibitors

Which myocardial infarction complication is associated with fibrosis and causes a dyskinetic, outward bulge during contraction?

{{c1::True ventricular aneurysm}}
fields.Back Extra: This could arise 2 weeks to several months after a myocardial infarction.

fields.Text:
What cell-mediated damage often leads to interventricular septal rupture 3 to 5 days after a myocardial infarction?

{{c1::Macrophage}}-mediated degradation

What is the most likely cause of a friction rub detected on auscultation of a patient who had a myocardial infarction 6 weeks ago?

{{c1::Postcardiac injury}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra:
This is also known as Dressler syndrome.

This is an autoimmune reaction resulting in fibrinous pericarditis several weeks after a myocardial infarction.

fields.Text:
What is the most likely cause of a friction rub detected on auscultation of a patient who had a myocardial infarction 2 days ago?

{{c1::Peri-infarction pericarditis}}
fields.Back Extra: This occurs 1 to 3 days after a myocardial infarction.

fields.Text:
What is the most likely cause of death in a patient experiencing a myocardial infarction within the first 24 hours after the onset of symptoms?

Cardiac {{c1::arrhythmia}}

How many days after a myocardial infarction is a ventricular free wall rupture likely to develop?

{{c1::5}} to {{c1::14}} days

What changes in oxygen saturation in the heart chambers would be expected after an intraventricular septal rupture following myocardial infarction?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} oxygen saturation and pressure in the {{c1::right::left/right}} ventricle from {{c1::left}}-to-{{c1::right}} shunting

What is an anatomical risk factor for posteromedial papillary muscle rupture after a myocardial infarction?

A {{c1::single}} blood supply from the {{c1::posterior descending}} artery increases risk of rupture

What is the finding indicated by the yellow arrow in the image, which usually occurs 3 to 14 days after a myocardial infarction?



{{c1::Ventricular pseudoaneurysm}}

What finding can be seen on this autopsy specimen obtained 1 to 2 weeks after a myocardial infarction?



{{c1::Ventricular free wall rupture}}

What are two protective factors that reduce the risk of ventricular free wall rupture after a myocardial infarction?

Previous {{c1::myocardial infarction}}
{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} ventricular {{c1::hypertrophy::hypertrophy/hypotrophy}}

What 3 underlying cardiac conditions are commonly associated with sudden cardiac death?

Hereditary {{c1::ion}} channelopathies
{{c1::Hypertrophic}} or {{c1::dilated}} cardiomyopathy
{{c1::Coronary artery}} disease

What pathophysiologic mechanism leads to most myocardial infarctions?

Acute {{c1::thrombosis}} from ruptured {{c1::coronary}} artery {{c1::atherosclerotic}} plaques

What are 3 treatments for vasospastic angina?

{{c1::Nitrates}}
{{c1::Calcium}} channel blockers
{{c1::Smoking}} cessation

How would an ECG help determine whether a myocardial infarction is transmural or subendocardial?

A transmural MI is associated with ST {{c1::elevations}}
A subendocardial MI is associated with ST {{c1::depressions}}

What ECG changes are typically seen with unstable angina?

ST {{c1::depression}}
{{c1::T}}-wave {{c1::inversion}}

What ECG changes are associated with stable angina compared with those seen with vasospastic angina?

Stable angina → ST {{c1::depressions}}
Vasospastic angina → Transient ST {{c1::elevations}} even at rest

What is pathophysiologic mechanism leading to chronic ischemic heart disease?

Chronic ischemic {{c1::myocardial}} damage → {{c1::Congestive}} heart failure over many years

What is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death?

Lethal {{c1::arrhythmia}}

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism that leads to coronary steal syndrome?

{{c1::Vasodilator}} dilates vessels unaffected by coronary stenosis → Blood is shunted to {{c1::well}}-perfused areas → Blood is stolen from {{c1::poorly}} perfused tissue

How do the symptoms of unstable angina differ from those of stable angina?

Unstable angina → Chest pain occurs with {{c1::increasing}} frequency or intensity and at {{c1::rest}}
Stable angina → Chest pain occurs on {{c1::exertion}} and resolves with {{c1::rest}} or {{c1::nitroglycerin}}

What are 3 common triggers of vasospastic angina?

{{c1::Alcohol}}
{{c1::Cocaine}}
{{c1::Triptans}}

What are the typical symptoms of stable angina?

Chest pain occurring with {{c1::exertion}} that is relieved by {{c1::rest}} and/or {{c1::nitroglycerin}}

What is an appropriate prophylactic treatment for sudden cardiac death?

{{c1::Implantable cardioverter defibrillator}}
fields.Back Extra: This can prevent sudden cardiac death due to a lethal arrhythmia.

fields.Text:
What is the underlying pathophysiologic mechanism leading to stable angina?

{{c1::Atherosclerosis}}

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism leading to Prinzmetal angina?

{{c1::Coronary}} artery {{c1::spasm}}

What is the definition of myocardial hibernation?

Potentially {{c1::reversible::reversible/irreversible}} {{c1::left::left/right}} ventricular systolic dysfunction in the presence of chronic {{c1::ischemia}}

What is the definition of myocardial stunning?

Transient {{c1::left::left/right}} ventricular systolic dysfunction following a brief period of acute {{c1::ischemia}}

What condition is seen in this ECG?



{{c1::Premature atrial contraction}}

What condition is seen in this ECG?



{{c1::Premature ventricular contraction}}

Why might caffeine cause premature atrial contraction?

Increases {{c1::adrenergic}} drive

Risk of which diseases are increased in patients with premature atrial contraction?

{{c1::Atrial fibrillation}}
{{c1::Atrial flutter}}

How does premature ventricular contraction affect stroke volume?

Stroke volume {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} due to {{c1::shorter::longer/shorter}} filling time in {{c1::diastole::systole/diastole}}

What changes to stroke volume occur in patients with premature ventricular contractions?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} stroke volume
fields.Back Extra: This is due to a shortened diastolic filing time.

fields.Text:
What is the most common cause of premature atrial contractions?

Increased {{c1::adrenergic}} drive

What ECG findings are typically seen in a patient with Brugada syndrome?

ST-segment {{c1::elevations::elevations/depressions}} in leads V{{c1::1}} to V{{c1::2}}
{{c1::Pseudo-right::Pseudo-left/Pseudo-right}} bundle branch block

What device can be used in patients with Brugada syndrome to help to prevent sudden cardiac death?

{{c1::Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator}}

What is the inheritance pattern of Brugada syndrome?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What is the genetic mutation associated with Brugada syndrome?

{{c1::Loss::Gain/Loss}} of function mutation affecting {{c1::sodium}} channels

What are the two most common congenital long QT syndromes?

{{c1::Romano-Ward}} syndrome
{{c1::Jervell and Lange-Nielsen}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: These are both due to K+ channel loss of function mutations.

fields.Text:
What are the inheritance patterns of Jervell and Lange-Neilsen syndrome and Romano-Ward syndrome?

Jervell and Lange-Neilsen syndrome → {{c1::Autosomal recessive}} pattern
Romano-Ward syndrome → {{c1::Autosomal dominant}} pattern

How can you distinguish Romano-Ward syndrome from Jervell and Lange-Nielson syndrome based on clinical features?

Both are congenital long QT syndromes, but Jervell and Lange-Nielson syndrome also presents with sensorineural {{c1::deafness}}

What gene mutation leads to congenital long QT syndrome?

Mutations in {{c1::KCNQ1}}
fields.Back Extra: This leads to a loss of function mutation of potassium channels.

fields.Text:
What inflammatory cell type and tissue type are seen within the affected myocardium 1 week after a myocardial infarction?

{{c1::Macrophages}}
{{c1::Granulation}} tissue forming at the margins

What inflammatory cell type is predominantly seen within the affected myocardium 1 to 3 days after a myocardial infarction?

{{c1::Neutrophils}}

What are 4 chronic complications of a myocardial infarction?

Heart {{c1::failure}}
{{c1::Arrhythmias}}
{{c1::Dressler}} syndrome
{{c1::True ventricular aneurysm}}

How many days after a myocardial infarction will the gross appearance of heart tissue show a hyperemic border and yellow-brown softening centrally at the area of infarct?

{{c1::3}} to {{c1::14}} days

What is the gross appearance of the heart 24 hours after a myocardial infarction?

{{c1::Dark}} and {{c1::mottled}} in the region of the infarct

Which complication after a myocardial infarction can cause cardiac tamponade?

{{c1::Free wall rupture}}

After a myocardial infarction, how long does it take for contracted scars to completely form?

A gray-white scar will appear after {{c1::2}} weeks to {{c1::several}} months

What are 3 complications of a myocardial infarction seen within the first 24 hours?

{{c1::Ventricular arrhythmias}}
{{c1::Cardiogenic shock}}
Heart {{c1::failure}}

How long after a myocardial infarction, do wavy fibers, early coagulative necrosis with edema and hemorrhage, and reperfusion injury with hypercontraction of myofibrils appear?

{{c1::0}} to {{c1::24}} hours

What 4 complications may occur 3 to 14 days after a myocardial infarction?

{{c1::Papillary}} muscle rupture
{{c1::Interventricular septal}} rupture
{{c1::Free wall}} rupture
{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} ventricular pseudoaneurysm

Compare the time courses of early and extensive coagulative necrosis after a myocardial infarction.

Early coagulative necrosis occurs {{c1::4}} to {{c1::24}} hours after an MI
Extensive coagulative necrosis occurs {{c1::1}} to {{c1::3}} days after an MI

A patient presents with retrosternal pain radiating to his left arm and jaw with associated dyspnea, nausea, and diaphoresis. What serious condition is likely causing his symptoms?

{{c1::Myocardial infarction}}

Which 3 coronary arteries are most likely to be occluded during a myocardial infarction?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::anterior}} descending > {{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::coronary}} artery > {{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::circumflex}} artery

What complication is typically seen 1 to 3 days after a myocardial infarction?

{{c1::Fibrinous pericarditis}}

What is the mechanism underlying reperfusion injury 0 to 24 hours after a myocardial infarction?

Generation of {{c1::free radicals}} and increased {{c1::calcium}} influx → Hypercontraction of {{c1::myofibrils}}

How many days after a myocardial infarction will diffuse hyperemia develop in the region of the infarct?

{{c1::1}} to {{c1::3}} days

Which complication after a myocardial infarction can cause mitral regurgitation?

{{c1::Papillary}} muscle rupture

Which complication after a myocardial infarction can cause a left-to-right shunt?

{{c1::Interventricular septal}} rupture due to structural degradation by {{c1::macrophages}}

What complication can be seen with a left ventricular pseudoaneurysm compared with a true ventricular aneurysm?

Left ventricular pseudoaneurysm increases risk for {{c1::rupture}}
True aneurysm increases risk for {{c1::mural thrombus}}

What pathogen causes a red, inflamed eye, similar to that shown in the image, without any pus or thick discharge?



{{c1::Adenovirus}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is viral conjunctivitis, also known as "pink eye".

This is the most common cause of inflammation of the conjunctiva.

fields.Text:
What is the cause of red, irritated eye, with watery discharge and preauricular lymphadenopathy?

{{c1::Viral}} conjunctivitis

What causes unilateral red, painful eye oozing pus?

{{c1::Bacterial}} conjunctivitis

What is associated with bilateral eye redness itching and tearing lasting several weeks?

{{c1::Allergic}} conjunctivitis

What is the prognosis of viral conjuctivitis?

It will most likely resolve {{c1::without::with/without}} treatment

During what time of pregnancy does the ectoderm differentiate into the neural tube and neural crest and establish the dorsal-ventral axis?

The {{c1::first}} trimester, days {{c1::18}} to {{c1::21}}

The nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc in adults is derived from what structure?

{{c1::Notochord}}

Is the basal plate dorsal or ventral? Does it contain motor or sensory neurons?

The basal plate is {{c1::ventral::ventral/dorsal}}
It gives rise to {{c1::motor::motor/sensory}} neurons

Is the alar plate dorsal or ventral? Does it contain motor or sensory neurons?

The alar plate is {{c1::dorsal::ventral/dorsal}}
It gives rise to {{c1::sensory::motor/sensory}} neurons

What two structures are derived from the neural plate?

{{c1::Neural crest}}
{{c1::Neural tube}}

The notochord induces overlying ectoderm to differentiate into neuroectoderm. These cells then go on to form what structure?

{{c1::Neural plate}}

The notochord induces overlying ectoderm to differentiate into what line of cells?

{{c1::Neuroectoderm}}

In neural development, what regulates the alar plate?

{{c1::TGF-β}}, specifically induced by {{c1::bone morphogenetic}} protein

In neural development, what gene regulates the basal plate?

{{c1::SHH}} gene

What does the myelencephalon become in the developing brain? Specify the walls and cavities.

Walls → {{c1::Medulla}}
Cavities → {{c1::Lower::Upper/Lower}} part of the {{c1::fourth ventricle}}

What does the metencephalon become in the developing brain? Specify the walls and cavities.

Walls → {{c1::Pons}} and {{c1::cerebellum}}
Cavities → {{c1::Upper::Upper/Lower}} part of the {{c1::fourth ventricle}}

What does the telencephalon become in the adult brain? Specify the walls and cavities.

Walls → {{c1::Cerebral hemispheres}} and {{c1::basal ganglia}}
Cavities → {{c1::Lateral ventricles}}

The rhombencephalon divides into what two secondary vesicles?

{{c1::Metencephalon}}
{{c1::Myelencephalon}}

What structure does the mesencephalon eventually give rise to in the adult brain? What is the associated cavity?

{{c1::Midbrain}}
The associated cavity is the {{c1::cerebral aqueduct}}

What are the adult derivatives of the diencephalon in the developing brain? Specify the walls and cavities.

Walls → {{c1::Thalamus}}, {{c1::hypothalamus}}, and {{c1::retina}}
Cavities → {{c1::Third ventricle}}

The prosencephalon later divides into what two secondary vesicles?

{{c1::Telencephalon}}
{{c1::Diencephalon}}

What are the three primary vesicles of the developing brain?

Forebrain → {{c1::Prosencephalon}}
Midbrain → {{c1::Mesencephalon}}
Hindbrain → {{c1::Rhombencephalon}}

Central nervous system neurons are derived from what embryologic structure?

{{c1::Neuroepithelia}}

Schwann cells, peripheral nervous system neurons and ganglia, adrenal medulla, autonomic ganglia, and melanocytes are all derived from what group of cells?

{{c1::Neural crest}}

From which embryonic layer do microglia originate?

{{c1::Mesoderm}}

The neuroepithelia give rise to what four cell types?

{{c1::Astrocytes}}
{{c1::Ependymal}} cells
{{c1::Oligodendrocytes}}
{{c1::Central nervous system}} neurons

What cranial nerves mediate somatosensation in the posterior third of the tongue?

Cranial nerve {{c1::IX}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::X}}

What cranial nerve mediates somatosensation in the anterior 2/3 of the tongue?

Cranial nerve {{c1::V3}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.

fields.Text:
What cranial nerve mediates taste in the posterior third of the tongue?

Cranial nerve {{c1::IX}}

What cranial nerve mediates taste in the anterior 2/3 of the tongue?

Cranial nerve {{c1::VII}}

What part of the tongue is formed by the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal arches?

{{c1::Posterior::Anterior/Posterior}} {{c1::1}}/3

What part of the tongue is formed by the 1st pharyngeal arch?

{{c1::Anterior::Anterior/Posterior}} {{c1::2}}/3

Which tongue muscle elevates the posterior part of the tongue during swallowing?

{{c1::Palatoglossus}}
fields.Back Extra: This is innervated by cranial nerve X.

fields.Text:
Which tongue muscle protrudes the tongue?

{{c1::Genioglossus}}
fields.Back Extra: This is innervated by cranial nerve XII.

fields.Text:
Which tongue muscle draws the sides of the tongue upward into a "U" shape to form a trough for swallowing?

{{c1::Styloglossus}}
fields.Back Extra: This is innervated by cranial nerve XII.

fields.Text:
Which muscle retracts and depresses the tongue? Which cranial nerve innervates this muscle?

{{c1::Hyoglossus}}, which is innervated by cranial nerve {{c1::XII}}

Which cranial nerves convey pain sensation from the tongue? Specify regions of the tongue.

Cranial nerve {{c1::V3}} → Anterior 2/3
Cranial nerve {{c1::IX}} → Posterior 1/3
Cranial nerve {{c1::X}} → Extreme posterior area

Which brainstem nucleus moderates the nerves carrying taste sensation from the tongue?

{{c1::Solitary}} nucleus
fields.Back Extra: This moderates taste-sensing fibers from cranial nerves VII, IX, and X.

fields.Text:
Which cranial nerves supply motor innervation to the tongue?

Palatoglossus → Cranial nerve {{c1::X}}
Hyoglossus → Cranial nerve {{c1::XII}}
Genioglossus → Cranial nerve {{c1::XII}}
Styloglossus → Cranial nerve {{c1::XII}}

An MRI of the cervical spine shows fluid in the spinal cord and ectopic cerebellar tonsils. What is the diagnosis?



Chiari type {{c1::I}} malformation with {{c1::syringomyelia}}

Which two congenital malformations are commonly associated with syringomyelia?

Chiari type {{c1::I}} malformation
{{c1::Scoliosis}}

Why does fine touch sensation remain intact with syringomyelia?

The {{c1::dorsal::ventral/dorsal}} columns do not border the {{c1::central canal}}, which is {{c1::dilated}} in syringomyelia

What spinal cord tract is affected first in syringomyelia and how does this affect sensation of the extremities?

{{c1::Spinothalamic}} tract is affected first
Fibers cross the {{c1::anterior white commissure}} and are compressed by the syrinx in the cervical cord → Loss of {{c1::pain}} and {{c1::temperature}} sensation in both arms

Syringomyelia is often congenital. What are two acquired causes of syringomyelia?

{{c1::Trauma}}
{{c1::Tumors}}

What are the spinal regions most often affected by syringomyelia in descending order?

{{c1::Cervical}} > {{c1::Thoracic}} >> {{c1::Lumbar}}

What 4 medications are safe to use in the treatment of hypertension during pregnancy?

{{c1::Nifedipine}}
{{c1::Methyldopa}}
{{c1::Labetalol}}
{{c1::Hydralazine}}

What 5 classes of antihypertensive medications are best for use in treatment of patients with diabetes mellitus?

{{c1::ACE}} inhibitors
{{c1::Angiotensin II}} receptor blockers
{{c1::Ca2+}} channel blockers
{{c1::Thiazide}} diuretics
{{c1::β-blockers}}

Which class of antihypertensives must be used with caution in patients with decompensated heart failure and should not be used in cardiogenic shock?

{{c1::β-blockers}}

What are the 5 most common classes of medications indicated for the treatment of hypertension with heart failure?

{{c1::ACE}} inhibitors
{{c1::Angiotensin II}} receptor blockers
{{c1::Aldosterone}} antagonists
{{c1::Diuretics}}
{{c1::β-blockers}}

What are the 4 most common classes of medications indicated for treatment of primary essential hypertension?

{{c1::Dihydropyridine Ca2+}} channel blockers
{{c1::ACE}} inhibitors
{{c1::Angiotensin II}} receptor blockers
{{c1::Thiazide}} diuretics

What 2 classes of antihypertensive medications should be avoided in the treatment of patients with asthma?

{{c1::Nonselective::Selective/Nonselective}} {{c1::β-blockers}}
{{c1::ACE}} inhibitors

What 4 classes of medications are used in the treatment of hypertension in patients with asthma?

Cardioselective {{c1::β-blockers}}
{{c1::Angiotensin II}} receptor blockers
{{c1::Thiazide}} diuretics
{{c1::Ca2+}} channel blockers

What antihypertensive agent can mask symptoms of hypoglycemia in patients with diabetes?

{{c1::β-blockers}}

What drug class can be augmented with sacubitril to treat heart failure?

{{c1::Angiotensin II}} receptor blockers

What are the 3 most common cardiovascular agents that activate the natriuretic peptide receptor?

{{c1::ANP}}
{{c1::BNP}}
{{c1::Nesiritide}}

What 2 common neurotransmitters act on Gi to inhibit the effect of adenylate cyclase?

{{c1::Epinephrine}}
{{c1::Norepinephrine}}

What specific type of channel is blocked by drugs such as amlodipine, nicardipine, and nifedipine?

{{c1::L}}-type {{c1::voltage}}-gated {{c1::Ca2+}} channels

What are the 5 most common Gs-protein agonists that act on smooth muscle?

{{c1::Epinephrine}}
{{c1::Prostaglandins}}
{{c1::Prostacyclin}}
{{c1::Fenoldopam}}
{{c1::Adenosine}}

What is the major mechanism of action of Gs-protein agonists in smooth muscle cells?

Gs protein stimulation increases {{c1::adenylate cyclase}} activity → Converts {{c1::AMP}} to {{c1::cAMP}} → Activates {{c1::PKA}} → Inhibits {{c1::PLB}} → Cytosolic {{c1::Ca2+}} increases → Inhibits smooth muscle relaxation

What is the major effect of the Ca2+-calmodulin complex on myosin light-chain kinase and on smooth muscle?

{{c1::Stimulates::Stimulates/Inhibits}} myosin light-chain kinase → Myosin {{c1::phosphorylation}} → {{c1::Contraction::Contraction/Relaxation}} of smooth muscle

Name a drug that acts by the following mechanism:

Inhibits PDE-3 → cAMP accumulates → Activates PKA → Inhibits PLB → Cytosolic Ca2+ increases → Inhibits smooth muscle relaxation

{{c1::Milrinone}}

What 2 substances act on myosin light-chain phosphatase?

{{c1::Rho kinase}} inhibits myosin light-chain phosphatase
{{c1::cGMP}} stimulates myosin light-chain phosphatase

Name the drug class that acts via the following mechanism:

Activates guanylyl cyclase to produce cGMP → Stimulates myosin light-chain phosphatase → Smooth muscle relaxation

{{c1::Nitrates}}

What are 6 common substances that stimulate the release of nitric oxide from endothelial cells?

{{c1::Acetylcholine}}
{{c1::α2-agonists}}
{{c1::Bradykinin}}
{{c1::Cytokines}}
{{c1::Histamine}}
{{c1::Serotonin}}

What is the mechanism of action that allows Ca2+ to increase the production of nitric oxide from endothelial cells?

Ca2+ stimulates {{c1::nitric oxide synthase}} → Conversion of {{c1::L-arginine}} to nitric oxide → {{c1::Diffusion}} into smooth muscle cells

What is the mechanism of action of natriuretic peptide agonists?

Stimulation of natriuretic peptide receptor → Activation of {{c1::guanylyl cyclase}} to produce {{c1::cGMP}} → Stimulation of {{c1::myosin light-chain phosphatase}} → Smooth muscle relaxation

Name 4 common cardiovascular agents that act as Gq agonists.

{{c1::Epinephrine}} and {{c1::norepinephrine}}
{{c1::Endothelin-1}}
{{c1::Angiotensin II}}
{{c1::Vasopressin}}

What are the 2 mechanisms of action by which Gq agonists promote muscle contraction?

Activation of {{c1::Rho kinase}} → Inhibition of {{c1::MLC phosphatase}} and activation of {{c1::IP3}} →  Release of Ca2+ by {{c1::sarcoplasmic reticulum}} → Activation of {{c1::MLC kinase}} by Ca2+-calmodulin complex

What are the three most common adverse effects of ivabradine?

{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Bradycardia::Tachycardia/Bradycardia}}
{{c1::Luminous}} phenomena

What are the two main indications for prescribing ivabradine?

Chronic {{c1::stable angina}} with contraindications for β-blockers
Chronic {{c1::heart failure with reduced ejection fraction}}

What is ivabradine's mechanism of action?

Ivabradine selectively inhibits "{{c1::funny}}" {{c1::Na+}} channels → {{c1::Prolonged}} slow depolarization phase

What is the most common endocrine-related adverse effect associated with the administration of verapamil?

{{c1::Hyperprolactinemia}}

What is the relative activity of the following Ca2+ channel blockers on vascular smooth muscle?

Amlodipine {{c1::=}} Nifedipine {{c1::>}} Diltiazem {{c1::>}} Verapamil

What Ca2+ channel blocker is prescribed for a patient who has had a subarachnoid hemorrhage and why?

{{c1::Nimodipine}} is prescribed to prevent subsequent {{c1::cerebral vasospasm}}

What are the 3 most common clinical indications for the use of nondihydropyridine Ca2+ channel blockers?

{{c1::Angina}}
{{c1::Hypertension}}
{{c1::Atrial fibrillation}} or {{c1::atrial flutter}}

What are the 3 most common adverse effects associated specifically with dihydropyridine Ca2+ channel blockers?

{{c1::Flushing}}
{{c1::Dizziness}}
Peripheral {{c1::edema}}

What are the 2 major Ca2+ channel blockers used for the management of hypertensive urgency or emergency?

{{c1::Clevidipine}}
{{c1::Nicardipine}}

What is the primary mechanism of action of Ca2+ channel blockers?

They decrease contractility by blocking {{c1::voltage}}-dependent {{c1::L}}-type Ca2+ channels in cardiac and smooth muscle

What are the 3 most common clinical uses for dihydropyridine Ca2+ channel blockers except nimodipine?

{{c1::Angina}}
{{c1::Hypertension}}
{{c1::Raynaud}} phenomenon

Which class of calcium channel blockers acts on vascular smooth muscle?

{{c1::Dihydropyridines}}

What are the 3 most common adverse effects seen specifically with nondihydropyridine Ca2+ channel blockers?

Cardiac {{c1::depression}}
{{c1::Atrioventricular block}}
{{c1::Constipation}}

Name the 2 nondihydropyridine Ca2+ channel blockers.

{{c1::Verapamil}}
{{c1::Diltiazem}}

What adverse effect is common to both dihydropyridine and nondihydropyridine Ca2+ channel blockers?

{{c1::Gingival hyperplasia}}

What are the 3 most common clinical indications for hydralazine?

Severe {{c1::hypertension}}
{{c1::Hypertension}} in {{c1::pregnancy}}
Heart {{c1::failure}}

How can you prevent the compensatory tachycardia that is associated with hydralazine?

It is coadministered with a {{c1::β-blocker}}

What is the major reason hydralazine is contraindicated for patients with coronary artery disease or angina?

It causes {{c1::reflex tachycardia}}

What is hydralazine's mechanism of action?

Increases {{c1::cGMP}} → Smooth muscle {{c1::relaxation}}
Vasodilates arterioles {{c1::more::more/less}} than veins → {{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in afterload

What are the 5 most common adverse effects associated with hydralazine therapy?

Drug-induced {{c1::lupus}}
{{c1::Headache}}
{{c1::Angina}}
{{c1::Compensatory tachycardia}}
Fluid {{c1::retention}}

What is the mechanism of action of fenoldopam?

{{c1::Dopamine D1}} receptor agonist → Reduces {{c1::blood pressure}} and increases {{c1::natriuresis}}

What is the mechanism of action of nitroprusside?

Increases {{c1::cGMP}} by directly releasing {{c1::nitric oxide}}

What adverse effect can occur with the use of nitroprusside?

{{c1::Cyanide}} toxicity
fields.Back Extra: This is because the drug releases cyanide.

fields.Text:
What 5 medications can be used in the treatment of hypertensive emergency?

{{c1::Clevidipine}}
{{c1::Fenoldopam}}
{{c1::Labetalol}}
{{c1::Nicardipine}}
{{c1::Nitroprusside}}

In which vessels does fenoldopam exert its effects?

{{c1::Coronary}} vessels
{{c1::Peripheral}} vessels
{{c1::Renal}} vessels
{{c1::Splanchnic}} vessels

What are the 3 major contraindications to administration of nitrates?

{{c1::Hypertrophic}} cardiomyopathy
{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::ventricular::atrial/ventricular}} infarction
Concurrent treatment with a {{c1::PDE-5}} inhibitor

What medication can treat reflex tachycardia caused by nitrates?

{{c1::β-blockers}}

Why might sublingual nitroglycerin cause palpitations?

The {{c1::hypotensive}} effect of nitroglycerin causes a reflex tachycardia

What is an explanation for a factory worker's symptoms of headache, lightheadedness, and tachycardia on return to work after a weekend off?

Industrial nitric oxide {{c1::tolerance}} develops during the week and is lost on the weekends
fields.Back Extra: "Monday disease" is due to industrial nitrate exposure.

fields.Text:
What are the 5 most common adverse effects of nitrates?

{{c1::Methemoglobinemia}}
{{c1::Reflex tachycardia}}
{{c1::Hypotension}}
{{c1::Headache}}
{{c1::Flushing}}

What are 3 main indications for the use of nitrates?

{{c1::Acute coronary}} syndrome
{{c1::Angina}}
Pulmonary {{c1::edema}}

What is the mechanism of action of nitrates?

Increase in nitric oxide → Increase in {{c1::cGMP}} → {{c1::Relaxation::Contraction/Relaxation}} of vascular smooth muscle and vasodilation of {{c1::more::more/less}} veins than arteries → Decrease in {{c1::preload}}

What are the 3 nitrates commonly used to treat pulmonary edema, angina, or acute coronary syndrome?

{{c1::Nitroglycerin}}
{{c1::Isosorbide dinitrate}}
{{c1::Isosorbide mononitrate}}

What is the major effect of β-blockers on ejection time?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} ejection time

What antianginal therapy reduces blood pressure, contractility, heart rate, and MVO2?

{{c1::β-blockers}}

What is the major effect of nitrates on heart rate and heart contractility?

{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in heart rate
{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in heart contractility

Which antianginal therapy decreases end-diastolic volume, blood pressure, ejection time, and MVO2?

{{c1::Nitrates}}

Which Ca2+ channel blocker has an effect most similar to that of a β-blocker?

{{c1::Verapamil}}

Which β-blockers should be used with caution in patients with angina?

{{c1::Pindolol}}
{{c1::Acebutolol}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because they are partial β-agonists.

fields.Text:
What is the primary goal of antianginal therapy?

Reduction of {{c1::MVO2}} by decreasing 1 or more determinants of {{c1::MVO2}}
fields.Back Extra: The determinants include blood pressure, heart rate, end-diastolic volume, and contractility.

fields.Text:
What major effects are observed when combining a nitrate with a β-blocker?

{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in blood pressure
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in MVO2

What is ranolazine used to treat?

{{c1::Refractory angina}}

What is the mechanism of action of ranolazine?

Inhibition of the {{c1::late}} phase of the inward {{c1::Na+}} current → Decrease in {{c1::diastolic::systolic/diastolic}} wall tension and {{c1::oxygen}} consumption
fields.Back Extra: It does not affect heart rate or blood pressure.

fields.Text:
What is the primary clinical use of sacubitril?

Used in combination with {{c1::valsartan}} to treat {{c1::heart failure with reduced ejection fraction}}

What is the mechanism of action of sacubitril?

Inhibits {{c1::neprilysin}} → Prevents breakdown of bradykinin, substance P, natriuretic peptides, and angiotensin II → {{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} vasodilation and {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} extracellular fluid volume

What are the five most common adverse effects associated with sacubitril therapy?

{{c1::Cough}}
{{c1::Dizziness}}
{{c1::Hypotension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Hyperkalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
{{c1::Angioedema}} if taken with an ACE inhibitor

What major adverse effects may a person being treated with PCSK9 inhibitors experience?

{{c1::Myalgias}}
Neurocognitive effects including {{c1::delirium}} and {{c1::dementia}}

What is the mechanism of action of alirocumab and evolocumab?

Inhibits {{c1::PCSK9}} → Decreases {{c1::LDL}}-receptor degradation → Increases the amount of {{c1::LDL}} cleared from the blood

Which class of lipid-lowering agents is most commonly associated with hepatotoxicity?

{{c1::HMG-CoA reductase}} inhibitors

What is the main mechanism of action of ezetimibe?

Prevention of {{c1::cholesterol}} absorption at the {{c1::brush border}} of the small intestine to decrease {{c1::LDL}} levels

How do bile acid resins lower lipid levels?

Prevents intestinal {{c1::reabsorption}} of bile acids → Liver synthesizes more from {{c1::cholesterol}} stores

What is the mechanism of action of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors?

Inhibition of the conversion of HMG-CoA to {{c1::mevalonate}}

What is the major mechanism of action of fibrates?

Activation of {{c1::PPAR-α}} → Increase in {{c1::LPL}} → Increase in {{c1::TG}} clearance
Activation of {{c1::PPAR-α}} → Increase in {{c1::HDL}} synthesis

What are the 2 major mechanisms of action of niacin?

Inhibition of {{c1::lipolysis}} by blocking hormone-sensitive {{c1::lipase}} in adipose tissue
Reduction of hepatic synthesis of {{c1::VLDL}}

Which class of lipid-lowering agents is commonly associated with diarrhea?

{{c1::Ezetimibe}}
{{c1::Bile acid resins}}

What adverse effects can occur in patients taking bile acid resins?

Decreased {{c1::absorption}} of fat-soluble vitamins and other drugs
{{c1::Gastrointestinal}} disturbance

Which 2 classes of lipid-lowering agents are most effective at lowering LDL levels?

{{c1::HMG-CoA reductase}} inhibitors
{{c1::PCSK9}} inhibitors

How do fibrates cause the development of cholesterol gallstones?

Via inhibition of cholesterol {{c1::7α-hydroxylase}}

What class of lipid-lowering agents has the greatest effect in decreasing triglycerides?

{{c1::Fibrates}}

Which class of lipid-lowering agents reduces mortality in patients with coronary artery disease?

{{c1::HMG-CoA reductase}} inhibitors

What drug class includes cholestyramine, colesevelam, and colestipol?

{{c1::Bile acid resins}}

What 3 adverse effects are commonly associated with niacin therapy?

Facial {{c1::flushing}}
{{c1::Hyperglycemia}}
{{c1::Hyperuricemia}}

Which lipid-lowering agent has the greatest effect in increasing HDL levels?

{{c1::Niacin}}

What are the major effects of omega-3 fatty acids and fish oils on LDL, HDL, and triglyceride levels?

{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in HDL levels
{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in LDL levels
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in triglyceride levels at high doses

What is the mechanism of action of fish oils and marine omega-3 fatty acids?

Decreases the activity of {{c1::triglyceride}}-synthesizing enzymes
Decreases delivery of free {{c1::fatty acids}} to the liver

What are the 2 adverse effects commonly associated with fish oils and marine omega-3 fatty acids?

{{c1::Nausea}}
{{c1::Fish}}-like taste

What mediates facial flushing due to niacin therapy, and how can the flushing be reduced?

Facial flushing is due to {{c1::prostaglandins}}
Facial flushing can be reduced with {{c1::NSAIDs}} or long-term {{c1::niacin}} use

What 2 lipid-lowering medications are commonly associated with myopathy?

{{c1::HMG-CoA reductase}} inhibitors
{{c1::Fibrates}}

What effects do HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors have on intrahepatic cholesterol, LDL receptors, and LDL catabolism?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} intrahepatic cholesterol
{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} LDL receptor recycling
{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} LDL catabolism

How do extracellular potassium levels affect the risk of digoxin toxicity?

{{c1::Hypokalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}} allows increased binding of digoxin at the {{c1::K+}}-binding site located on the {{c1::Na+/K+-ATPase}} → Digoxin toxicity

What are the 4 common treatments for digoxin toxicity?

Slow normalization of {{c1::K+}} levels
Cardiac {{c1::pacer}}
Anti-digoxin {{c1::Fab}} fragments
{{c1::Mg2+}}

What is the main action of digoxin that aids in treatment of atrial fibrillation?

Depresses {{c1::SA}} node activity
Slows {{c1::AV}} node conduction

What are the 2 mechanisms of action of digoxin?

Directly inhibits {{c1::Na+/K+-ATPase}} pump
Indirectly inhibits {{c1::Na+}}/{{c1::Ca2+}} exchanger

What are the 5 most common adverse effects of digoxin therapy?

Blurry {{c1::yellow}} vision
{{c1::Cholinergic}} effects
{{c1::AV block}}
{{c1::Arrhythmias}}
{{c1::Hyperkalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}

What 4 common factors may predispose a patient to digoxin toxicity?

{{c1::Renal}} failure
{{c1::Hypokalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
Medications that displace digoxin from {{c1::tissue-binding}} sites
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} clearance

What is the main action of digoxin that aids in treatment of heart failure?

It increases {{c1::contractility}}

What class of antiarrhythmics causes the changes represented by the dark blue line in the myocardial action potential shown?



Class {{c1::IC}}

What class of antiarrhythmics causes the changes represented by the dark blue line in the myocardial action potential shown?



Class {{c1::IB}}

What class of antiarrhythmics causes the changes represented by the dark blue line in the myocardial action potential shown?



Class {{c1::IA}}

Which phase of the cardiac action potential represents inward Na+ current?

Phase {{c1::0}}

Which subtype of class I antiarrhythmics possesses some K+ channel blocking effects?

Class {{c1::IA}}

Which 2 types of tissues have no change in their effective refractory period when exposed to class IC antiarrhythmics?

{{c1::Purkinje}} tissue
{{c1::Ventricular}} tissue

Which 2 antiarrhythmics belong to class IC?

{{c1::Flecainide}}
{{c1::Propafenone}}

What 3 types of arrhythmias are class IC antiarrhythmics typically used to treat?

{{c1::Supraventricular tachycardia}}
{{c1::Atrial fibrillation}}
{{c1::Refractory ventricular tachycardia}} only as a last resort

Which 2 organ systems can be adversely affected by class IB antiarrhythmics?

{{c1::Cardiovascular}} system
{{c1::CNS}}

What types of arrhythmias are class IB antiarrhythmics typically used to treat?

Acute {{c1::ventricular}} arrhythmias, especially after a myocardial infarction
{{c1::Digitalis}}-induced arrhythmias

What type of tissue do class IB antiarrhythmics preferentially act on?

Depolarized or ischemic {{c1::ventricular}} tissue
Depolarized or ischemic {{c1::Purkinje}} tissue

Which class IA antiarrhythmic causes heart failure?

{{c1::Disopyramide}}

Why are Na+ channel blocker antiarrhythmics described as state dependent?

Faster heart rates → Na+ block effect {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}
Slower heart rates → Na+ block effect {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}

Which Na+ channel-blocking antiarrhythmic class is contraindicated after a myocardial infarction?

Class {{c1::IC}}

What parts of the conduction pathway do class IC antiarrhythmics primarily act on?

They prolong the effective refractory period in the {{c1::AV}} node and {{c1::accessory bypass}} tracts

How do the different subclasses of class I antiarrhythmics compare in their impact on action potential duration?

Class IA → {{c1::Lengthens}} it
Class IB → {{c1::Shortens}} it
Class IC → {{c1::Minimal}} effect on it

What class I antiarrhythmic causes cinchonism?

{{c1::Quinidine}}

Which class I antiarrhythmic is associated with a reversible systemic lupus erythematous-like syndrome?

{{c1::Procainamide}}

Which ion channel is targeted by class I antiarrhythmics?

{{c1::Na+}}

What effect do class IA antiarrhythmics have on the effective refractory period?

They {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} the duration of the effective refractory period

Which 3 antiarrhythmics belong to class IA?

{{c1::Quinidine}}
{{c1::Procainamide}}
{{c1::Disopyramide}}

Which 3 antiarrhythmics belong to class IB?

{{c1::Lidocaine}}
{{c1::Phenytoin}}
{{c1::Mexilitene}}

What is the difference regarding Na+ channel blocking properties among class IA, IB, and IC antiarrhythmics?

Class IA → {{c1::Moderate::Strong/Moderate/Weak}} blocking
Class IB → {{c1::Weak::Strong/Moderate/Weak}} blocking
Class IC → {{c1::Strong::Strong/Moderate/Weak}} blocking

What is the clinical use for disopyramide?

{{c1::Atrial}} arrhythmias
{{c1::Ventricular}} arrhythmias
fields.Back Extra: This is especially used for either reentrant or ectopic supraventricular tachycardia and ventricular tachycardia.

fields.Text:
What effect do class IC antiarrhythmics have on the effective refractory period in the AV node and accessory bypass tracts?

They {{c1::prolong}} the effective refractory period

What adverse effects are common to all class IA antiarrhythmics?

{{c1::Torsades de pointes}}
{{c1::Thrombocytopenia}}

What sexual side effect is commonly seen in those taking β-blockers?

{{c1::Impotence}}

Which β-blocker should be avoided in patients with vasospastic angina?

{{c1::Propranolol}}
fields.Back Extra: This can exacerbate vasospasm in patients with vasospastic angina.

fields.Text:
Why is treatment with β-blockers risky for a patient with diabetes?

β-blockers may mask the signs of {{c1::hypoglycemia}}

Which β-blocker can cause dyslipidemia?

{{c1::Metoprolol}}

What common CNS side effects do β-blockers have?

{{c1::Sedation}}
{{c1::Sleep}} alteration

What adverse pulmonary effects are commonly associated with β-blockers?

Exacerbation of {{c1::chronic obstructive pulmonary}} disease
Exacerbation of {{c1::asthma}}

Which part of the cardiac conduction system is particularly sensitive to β-blockers?

{{c1::AV}} node

What is the effect of class II antiarrhythmics on the PR interval?

They {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} the PR interval by prolonging {{c1::repolarization}}

What is the effect of β-blockers on the SA and AV node?

They {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} SA and AV nodal activity by decreasing {{c1::cAMP}} and decreasing {{c1::Ca2+}} currents

Which class II antiarrhythmic has the shortest duration of action?

{{c1::Esmolol}}

What is the common treatment regimen for β-blocker overdose/toxicity?

{{c1::Glucagon}}
{{c1::Atropine}}
{{c1::Saline}}

Why should β-blockers be used with caution in the treatment of pheochromocytoma and in patients who have recently used cocaine?

β-blockers may cause unopposed {{c1::α1}}-agonism if given alone

Which β-blockers can be considered for patients being treated for a pheochromocytoma?

{{c1::Carvedilol}}
{{c1::Labetalol}}

Which class of antiarrhythmics causes the changes to the pacemaker cell action potential indicated by the dark blue line shown?



Class {{c1::II}} antiarrhythmics

Which antiarrhythmic drug is lipophilic and has the effects of antiarrhythmic classes I, II, III, and IV?

{{c1::Amiodarone}}

Which class of antiarrhythmics leads to the cell action potential changes shown?



Class {{c1::III}} antiarrhythmics

What lab tests are required to be done regularly for patients taking amiodarone?

{{c1::Pulmonary}} function tests
{{c1::Liver}} function tests
{{c1::Thyroid}} function tests

Why must thyroid function be monitored regularly in a patient taking amiodarone?

Amiodarone has an {{c1::iodine}} component and can cause {{c1::hyperthyroidism}} or {{c1::hypothyroidism}}

What are the 3 most common adverse cardiovascular effects caused by amiodarone?

Heart {{c1::block}}
{{c1::Bradycardia::Tachycardia/Bradycardia}}
Heart {{c1::failure}}

What are the hapten-related side effects of amiodarone therapy?

Blue/gray skin deposits that may result in {{c1::photodermatitis}}
{{c1::Corneal}} deposits

How do class III antiarrhythmics affect the action potential, the effective refractory period, and the QT interval?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} the duration of the action potential
{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} the effective refractory period
{{c1::Prolongs}} the QT interval

What are the 4 typical class III antiarrhythmic drugs?

{{c1::Amiodarone}}
{{c1::Ibutilide}}
{{c1::Dofetilide}}
{{c1::Sotalol}}

Which 2 class III antiarrhythmics are used in the management of ventricular tachycardia?

{{c1::Amiodarone}}
{{c1::Sotalol}}

What are the 3 most common uses for class III antiarrhythmics?

{{c1::Atrial fibrillation}}
{{c1::Atrial flutter}}
{{c1::Ventricular tachycardia}}

What is the major adverse effect of ibutilide therapy?

{{c1::Torsades de pointes}}

What are the 2 most common adverse effects of sotalol therapy?

Excessive {{c1::β}} blockade
{{c1::Torsades de pointes}}

Why are class IV antiarrhythmics prescribed for patients with atrial fibrillation?

{{c1::Rate}} control

What are the 4 most common adverse effects of verapamil and diltiazem?

{{c1::Flushing}}
{{c1::Constipation}}
{{c1::Edema}}
{{c1::Cardiovascular}} abnormalities

How do diltiazem and verapamil affect conduction velocity, the effective refractory period, and ECG findings?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} conduction velocity
{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} the effective refractory period
{{c1::Prolongs}} the PR interval

Which 2 Ca2+ channel blockers are typically used as antiarrhythmics?

{{c1::Verapamil}}
{{c1::Diltiazem}}

What are the 2 clinical uses of class IV antiarrhythmics?

Prevention of {{c1::nodal}} arrhythmias
{{c1::Rate}} control in patients with atrial fibrillation

What 2 substances may blunt the effects of adenosine?

{{c1::Caffeine}}
{{c1::Theophylline}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because they are both adenosine receptor blockers.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of adenosine?

Increases {{c1::K+}} outflow → {{c1::Hyperpolarization}} of the cell and decreased intracellular {{c1::Ca2+}} → Decreased {{c1::AV}} node conduction

What is the clinical benefit of adenosine's short half life?

{{c1::Rapid}} onset of action
Quick abortion of {{c1::SVT}} by induction of a {{c1::short}}-lasting heart block

What 2 cardiac pathologies are treated with magnesium administration?

{{c1::Torsades de pointes}}
{{c1::Digoxin}} toxicity

What drug is indicated if carotid sinus massage fails in the management of SVT?

{{c1::Adenosine}}

What are the 6 common adverse effects of adenosine therapy?

{{c1::Flushing}}
{{c1::Chest}} pain
{{c1::Bronchospasm}}
{{c1::Dyspnea}}
{{c1::Hypotension}}
Sense of {{c1::impending doom}}

What diagnosis is indicated by this ECG tracing?



{{c1::Mobitz type I}} atrioventricular block

What is the treatment for the arrhythmia shown in the ECG below?



{{c1::Pacemaker placement}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a Mobitz type II atrioventricular block.

fields.Text:
What type of atrioventricular block is characterized by a prolonged PR interval that does not change in length?

{{c1::First-degree}} atrioventricular block

What ECG findings are seen in third-degree heart block?

P waves and QRS complexes are present, but not {{c1::rhythmically}} associated
fields.Back Extra: The atria and ventricles beat independently.

fields.Text:
What is the most common cardiac complication of Lyme disease?

{{c1::Third-degree}} atrioventricular block

Which subtype of second-degree heart block is more likely to progress to third-degree heart block?

{{c1::Mobitz type II}} atrioventricular block

What arrhythmia is characterized by progressive lengthening of the PR interval?

{{c1::Mobitz type I}} atrioventricular block

What ECG finding is seen in first-degree atrioventricular conduction block?

{{c1::PR interval}} is prolonged to more than {{c1::200}} milliseconds

Does a first-degree atrioventricular conduction block cause symptoms?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra:
A first-degree atrioventricular block is asymptomatic and benign.

This condition does not require treatment.

fields.Text:
Which type of conduction block is seen in this ECG?



{{c1::Mobitz type I}} atrioventricular block

Does a Mobitz type I atrioventricular block require treatment?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}

Which type of conduction block is seen in this ECG?



{{c1::Mobitz type II}} atrioventricular block

Which second-degree atrioventricular conduction block often suggests a structural abnormality, such as ischemia or fibrosis, and may progress to third-degree atrioventricular block?

{{c1::Mobitz type II}} atrioventricular block

Which two types of AV conduction blocks are usually treated with a pacemaker?

{{c1::Mobitz type II}} atrioventricular block
{{c1::Third-degree}} atrioventricular block

What ECG findings are seen in a third-degree atrioventricular block?

{{c1::Dissociation}} of P waves and QRS complexes
fields.Back Extra: This is due to the independent activities of the atria and ventricles.

fields.Text:
On ECG, do the PP intervals and RR intervals change or remain constant in a third-degree atrioventricular block?

PP intervals {{c1::remain constant::remain constant/change}}
RR intervals {{c1::remain constant::remain constant/change}}

Which type of atrioventricular conduction block may be caused by Lyme disease?

{{c1::Third-degree}} atrioventricular block

What are two common causes of bundle branch blocks?

{{c1::Ischemia}}
{{c1::Degenerative}} causes

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism of a bundle branch block?

Affected ventricle depolarizes via slower {{c1::myocyte}}-to-{{c1::myocyte}} conduction from the unaffected ventricle, which depolarizes via the faster {{c1::His-Purkinje}} system

What ECG abnormality is shown in the image?



{{c1::Torsades de pointes}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that is characterized by sinusoidal waves of different sizes.

fields.Text:
What is a dangerous sequela of torsades de pointes?

{{c1::Ventricular fibrillation}}

What arrhythmia is fatal without immediate CPR and intervention?

{{c1::Ventricular fibrillation}}

What three electrolyte abnormalities can lead to torsades de pointes?

{{c1::Hypokalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
{{c1::Hypomagnesemia::Hypermagnesemia/Hypomagnesemia}}
{{c1::Hypocalcemia::Hypercalcemia/Hypocalcemia}}

Which arrhythmia, with a high risk for sudden cardiac death, can produce the following on an ECG?

Regular rhythm
Heart rate > 100 beats per minute
QRS duration > 120 milliseconds

{{c1::Ventricular tachycardia}}

Which wide complex tachycardia produces a disorganized rhythm without any discernable waves on ECG?

{{c1::Ventricular fibrillation}}

How is ventricular fibrillation managed?

Immediate {{c1::CPR}}
{{c1::Defibrillation}}

Which classes of antiarrhythmics can prolong the QT interval?

Class {{c1::IA}}
Class {{c1::III}}

Which three antibiotics/antifungals can prolong the QT interval?

{{c1::Macrolides}}
{{c1::Fluoroquinolones}}
{{c1::Fluconazole}}

Which classes of antidepressants can prolong the QT interval?

{{c1::TCAs}}

Which analgesic and antiemetic drugs can prolong the QT interval?

{{c1::Opioids}}
{{c1::Ondansetron}}

Which class of diuretics can prolong the QT interval?

{{c1::Thiazide diuretics}}

What is the ECG characteristic that predisposes a patient to torsades de pointes?

{{c1::Prolonged QT interval}}

What is the pharmacologic treatment for torsades de pointes?

{{c1::Magnesium sulfate}}

What are the nine common drug classes that increase the risk of developing the arrhythmia shown in the ECG in the image?



{{c1::Antiarrhythmics}}
{{c1::Antibiotics}}
{{c1::Antipsychotics}}
{{c1::Antidepressants}}
{{c1::Diuretics}}
{{c1::Antiemetics}}
{{c1::Antifungals}}
{{c1::Protease}} inhibitors
{{c1::Opioids}}

What is the mechanism of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome?

{{c1::Bundle of Kent}} allows conduction from the atria to the ventricles and bypasses the {{c1::AV node}}

What does this ECG depict?



{{c1::Atrial fibrillation}}

Why does atrial flutter present with sawtooth waves on ECG?

It yields a {{c1::rapid}} sequence of identical {{c1::consecutive}} atrial depolarization waves

What cardiovascular pathology are patients with atrial fibrillation predisposed to?

{{c1::Thromboembolic}} events

The ECG findings shown are associated with which syndrome?



{{c1::Wolff-Parkinson-White}} syndrome

Left untreated, what is the major risk associated with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome?

Development of a {{c1::reentry}} circuit → {{c1::Supraventricular tachycardia}}

What region is targeted by catheter ablation in the arrhythmia shown in the ECG below?



The region between the {{c1::tricuspid annulus}} and the {{c1::inferior vena cava}}

What is the pathophysiology of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia?

A {{c1::reentry}} tract between the atrium and ventricle
fields.Back Extra: The most common location is within the AV node.

fields.Text:
What are four possible treatments for paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia?

{{c1::Vagal}} maneuvers
Intravenous {{c1::adenosine}}
Electrical {{c1::cardioversion}} if hemodynamically unstable
{{c1::Catheter ablation}} of the reentry tract (definitive treatment)

What arrhythmia commonly presents with the sudden onset of diaphoresis, lightheadedness, and palpitations?

{{c1::Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a narrow QRS complex tachycardia.

fields.Text:
Which arrhythmia produces an irregularly irregular rate and rhythm without identifiable P waves on ECG?

{{c1::Atrial fibrillation}}

Atrial fibrillation increases the risk of which neurologic condition?

{{c1::Stroke}}

Name five options for the treatment of atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter.

{{c1::Rate}} control
{{c1::Rhythm}} control
{{c1::Cardioversion}}
{{c1::Ablation}} of pulmonary vein ostia or left atrial appendage
{{c1::Anticoagulation}} based on risk of stroke

Where are ablations commonly performed in the treatment of atrial fibrillation and in the treatment of atrial flutter?

Atrial fibrillation → {{c1::Pulmonary vein ostia}} and {{c1::left atrial appendage}}
Atrial flutter → Region between the {{c1::inferior vena cava}} and the {{c1::tricuspid annulus}}

Which arrhythmia produces a sawtooth pattern of P waves with a regular RR interval on ECG due to identical atrial depolarizations in succession?

{{c1::Atrial flutter}}

What arrhythmia is characterized by an irregularly irregular rate and rhythm with at least three distinct P wave morphologies?

{{c1::Multifocal atrial tachycardia}}

Which arrhythmia is commonly seen in patients with pneumonia, heart failure, and/or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?

{{c1::Multifocal atrial tachycardia}}

What is the most common type of ventricular preexcitation syndrome?

{{c1::Wolff-Parkinson-White}} syndrome

What is the definitive mechanism of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia?

{{c1::Catheter ablation}} of the reentry tract

What is the management of an individual with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia who is hemodynamically unstable?

Electrical {{c1::cardioversion}}

What is the characteristic ECG finding of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome?

{{c1::Delta}} wave

What is the first-line management of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome?

{{c1::Procainamide}}

ECG for a patient with chest pain shows ST elevation in leads V7 – V9 and ST depression with tall R waves in leads V1 – V3. Which vessel is occluded?

{{c1::Posterior descending}} artery

ECG for a patient with chest pain shows ST elevations in leads I and aVL. Which vessel is occluded?

{{c1::Left circumflex}} artery

ECG for a patient with chest pain shows ST elevations in leads V3 and V4. Which vessel is occluded?

{{c1::Distal::Proximal/Distal}} {{c1::left anterior descending}} artery

ECG for a patient with chest pain shows ST elevations in leads V5 and V6. Occlusion of which two vessels could cause this ECG finding?

{{c1::Left circumflex}} artery
{{c1::Left anterior descending}} artery

ECG in a patient with chest pain shows ST elevations in leads V1 and V2. Which vessel is occluded?

{{c1::Left anterior descending}} artery

ECG for a patient with chest pain shows ST elevations in leads II, III, and aVF. Which vessel is occluded?

{{c1::Right coronary}} artery

Describe the time course of CK-MB elevation after an acute myocardial infarction.

Rises {{c1::6}} to {{c1::12}} hours after a myocardial infarction
Peaks at {{c1::16}} to {{c1::24}} hours
Returns to normal after {{c1::48}} hours

What might pathologic Q waves or poor R wave progression on ECG indicate?

Old or evolving {{c1::transmural infarct}}

Where else can CK-MB be found other than the myocardium?

{{c1::Skeletal}} muscle

Which protein marker is the most specific during the early stages of myocardial infarction?

{{c1::Troponin I}}

How long after the onset of a myocardial infarction does the troponin I level become abnormal, and for how long does it remain elevated?

Rises {{c1::4}} hours after a myocardial infarction
Peaks at {{c1::24}} hours
Remains elevated for {{c1::7}} to {{c1::10}} days

What is the current gold standard for diagnosing a myocardial infarction in the first 6 hours?

{{c1::ECG}}

Which cardiac biomarker can be used to detect reinfarction after an acute myocardial infarction and why?

The {{c1::CK-MB}} level usually returns to normal after {{c1::48}} hours

What might hyperacute T waves or T-wave inversions on ECG signify?

An evolving {{c1::myocardial infarction}}

What ST-segment changes would you expect to see on an ECG in a transmural infarct and a subendocardial infarct?

Transmural infarct → ST {{c1::elevation::elevation/depression}}
Subendocardial infarct → ST {{c1::depression::elevation/depression}}

What is the mechanism of action of α-glucosidase inhibitors?

Inhibition of intestinal {{c1::brush-border}} α-glucosidases → Delay in carbohydrate {{c1::hydrolysis}} and glucose {{c1::absorption}} → Reduced postprandial hyperglycemia

What class of drugs used to treat diabetes includes acarbose and miglitol?

{{c1::α-glucosidase}} inhibitors

What are two common adverse effects of acarbose?

{{c1::Gastrointestinal}} disturbances
{{c1::Bloating}}

Which class of drugs used to treat diabetes is associated with potential dehydration, urinary tract infections, and vulvovaginal yeast infections?

{{c1::SGLT-2}} inhibitors
fields.Back Extra: These inhibitors cause glucosuria, which leads to an increased risk for infection.

fields.Text:
Which class of drugs used to treat diabetes includes canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin?

{{c1::SGLT-2}} inhibitors
fields.Back Extra: These inhibitors are active in the proximal convoluted tubule in the kidney.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of pramlintide in the setting of type 2 diabetes?

Pramlintide is an {{c1::amylin}} analog → Decreases both gastic {{c1::emptying}} and release of {{c1::glucagon}}

Which class of drugs used to treat diabetes is associated with increased satiety, respiratory infections, and urinary tract infections, but does not affect weight?

{{c1::DPP-4}} inhibitors

Which class of drugs used to treat diabetes is associated with pancreatitis, nausea, vomiting, increased satiety, and weight loss?

{{c1::GLP-1}} analogs

What class of drugs used to treat diabetes do exenatide and liraglutide belong to?

{{c1::GLP-1}} analogs

What mechanism of action is shared by GLP-1 analogs and DPP-4 inhibitors?

GLP-1 analogs bind to {{c1::GLP-1}} receptors and DPP-4 inhibitors prevent {{c1::inactivation}} of native {{c1::GLP-1}} → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} glucose-induced insulin secretion, {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} glucagon, and {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} gastric emptying

What class of drugs used to treat diabetes do nateglinide and repaglinide belong to?

{{c1::Meglitinides}}

What class of drugs used to treat diabetes do linagliptin, saxagliptin, and sitagliptin belong to?

{{c1::DPP-4}} inhibitors

What thiazolidinedione is associated with an increased risk of myocardial infarction?

{{c1::Rosiglitazone}}

What medication used to treat diabetes is associated with increased satiety, nausea, and hypoglycemia?

{{c1::Pramlintide}}

Which class of drugs used to treat type 2 diabetes is associated with edema, weight gain, heart failure, and an increased risk of fractures?

{{c1::Thiazolidinediones}}

What 2 classes of drugs used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes act to increase insulin sensitivity?

{{c1::Thiazolidinediones}}
{{c1::Biguanides}}

What is the mechanism of action of the thiazolidinediones?

Activation of {{c1::PPAR-γ}} → Increase in both {{c1::insulin}} sensitivity and {{c1::adiponectin}} levels → Regulation of {{c1::fatty acid}} storage and {{c1::glucose}} metabolism

What class of drugs do pioglitazone and rosiglitazone belong to?

{{c1::Thiazolidinediones}}

What are the 2 major side effects associated with all sulfonylureas and meglitinides?

Weight {{c1::gain::gain/loss}}
{{c1::Hypoglycemia::Hyperglycemia/Hypoglycemia}}

What is the mechanism of action of sulfonylureas and meglitinides?

Closure of {{c1::K+}} channels in pancreatic {{c1::β}} cell membranes  → Cell {{c1::depolarization}} → {{c1::Ca2+}} influx → Increased {{c1::insulin}} release

Which drug class used in the management of type 2 diabetes leads to a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol ingestion?

{{c1::First}}-generation {{c1::sulfonylureas}}

What is the mechanism of action of biguanides in the liver and peripheral tissues?

Inhibits {{c1::mGPD}} → Inhibition of hepatic {{c1::gluconeogenesis}} and the action of {{c1::glucagon}}
Increases peripheral {{c1::glucose}} uptake
Increases {{c1::glycolysis}}

What medication used in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus is associated with gastrointestinal upset, weight loss, and vitamin B12 deficiency?

{{c1::Metformin}}

What medication used in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus may cause lactic acidosis, particularly in a patient with renal impairment?

{{c1::Metformin}}

Which insulin preparation is preferred in the management of diabetic ketoacidosis?

{{c1::Short}}-acting insulin

What is the mechanism of action of insulin in liver tissue?

Increases storage of {{c1::glucose}} as {{c1::glycogen}}

What intrinsic signaling system does the insulin receptor possess?

{{c1::Tyrosine kinase}} activity

What 3 insulin preparations are rapid-acting?

{{c1::Lispro}}
{{c1::Aspart}}
{{c1::Glulisine}}

What are the 4 common adverse effects associated with insulin therapy?

{{c1::Hypoglycemic}} risk
{{c1::Lipodystrophy}}
Weight {{c1::gain::gain/loss}}
{{c1::Hypersensitivity}} reactions (rare)

What is the basic treatment strategy for gestational diabetes mellitus?

{{c1::Lifestyle}} modification followed by {{c1::insulin}}

What is the primary treatment strategy for type 1 diabetes mellitus?

{{c1::Insulin}} replacement

Which drugs used in the treatment of diabetes mellitus reduce glucose reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule?

{{c1::SGLT-2}} inhibitors

How long does it take for rapid-acting insulin to reach peak activity?

{{c1::1}} hour

What insulin preparation is classified as short-acting?

{{c1::Regular insulin}}

What insulin preparation is classified as intermediate-acting?

{{c1::Insulin NPH}}

What 2 insulin preparations are classified as long-acting?

{{c1::Detemir}}
{{c1::Glargine}}

What is the mechanism of action of insulin in muscle tissue?

Increases synthesis of {{c1::glycogen}} and {{c1::protein}}

What is the mechanism of action of insulin in fat cells?

Increases storage of {{c1::triglycerides}}

What is the mechanism of action of insulin in cell membranes?

Increases the uptake of {{c1::potassium}}

What is a contraindication for acarbose administration?

{{c1::Renal}} insufficiency

How long does it take short-acting insulin to reach peak activity?

{{c1::2}} to {{c1::3}} hours

How long does it take for intermediate-acting insulin to reach peak activity?

{{c1::4}} to {{c1::10}} hours

How long does it take long-acting insulin to reach peak activity?

{{c1::No significant peak}}
fields.Back Extra: It is more of a plateau.

fields.Text:
Which antithyroid medication is preferred for use during the first trimester of pregnancy?

{{c1::Propylthiouracil}}

What are the 4 adverse effects associated with the use of thionamides?

{{c1::Aplastic}} anemia
{{c1::Hepatotoxicity}}
Skin {{c1::rash}}
{{c1::Agranulocytosis}} (rare)

What is the teratogenic effect of methimazole?

{{c1::Aplasia cutis}}

What additional mechanism of action does propylthiouracil possess when compared with methimazole?

Blocks {{c1::5'-deiodinase}} → Decreases peripheral {{c1::T4}} to {{c1::T3}} conversion

What is the common mechanism of action of methimazole and propylthiouracil?

Inhibition of {{c1::thyroid}} hormone synthesis by blockade of {{c1::thyroid peroxidase}} → Inhibition of oxidation and organification/coupling of {{c1::iodine}}

Which class of drugs do propylthiouracil and methimazole belong to?

{{c1::Thionamides}}

What is preferred over thionamides for the treatment of Graves ophthalmopathy?

{{c1::Corticosteroids}}

Which thionamide has been associated with ANCA-positive vasculitis?

{{c1::Propylthiouracil}}

Which antithyroid medication is preferred for use during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy?

{{c1::Methimazole}}

Why might levothyroxine or liothyronine be abused?

Weight {{c1::loss::gain/loss}}

What are 4 common adverse effects of thyroid hormone replacement therapy?

{{c1::Arrhythmias}}
{{c1::Heat}} intolerance
{{c1::Tachycardia}}
{{c1::Tremors}}
