What 2 medications are typically used as thyroid hormone replacements in hypothyroidism?

{{c1::Levothyroxine}}
{{c1::Liothyronine}}

What are 3 ways to differentiate levothyroxine abuse from endogenous hyperthyroidism via diagnostic tests?

Detection of {{c1::TSH receptor}} antibodies
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} thyroid blood flow on ultrasound exam
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} uptake of radioactive iodine

What drug class do sodium polystyrene sulfonate, patiromer, and zirconium cyclosilicate belong to?

{{c1::Cation exchange resins}}

What is the mechanism of action of the cation exchange resins?

Binding of {{c1::K+}} in the {{c1::colon}} in exchange for alternative cations → Increased {{c1::K+}} excretion in the feces

What are cation exchange resins used to treat?

{{c1::Hyperkalemia}}

What are the 2 most common adverse effects associated with cation exchange resins?

{{c1::Gastrointestinal}} upset
{{c1::Hypokalemia}}

What 4 conditions are treated with desmopressin?

{{c1::Central diabetes insipidus}}
{{c1::Von Willebrand}} disease
{{c1::Hemophilia A}}
Sleep {{c1::enuresis}}

What is the mechanism of action of octreotide?

Octreotide is a {{c1::somatostatin}} analog that binds {{c1::somatostatin}} receptors

What are 2 uses of oxytocin because of its effects on the uterus?

Induce {{c1::labor}}
Control uterine {{c1::hemorrhage}}

What 2 pathologies is growth hormone often used to treat?

{{c1::Growth hormone}} deficiency
{{c1::Turner}} syndrome

What is the mechanism of action of desmopressin?

It is a {{c1::centrally}} and {{c1::peripherally}} acting synthetic {{c1::antidiuretic}} hormone analog

What condition can be treated with drugs that block the vasopressin-2 receptor?

{{c1::SIADH}}

What medication other than the "vaptans" is effective in treating SIADH?

{{c1::Demeclocycline}}

What drug from the tetracycline antibiotic class acts as an antidiuretic hormone antagonist?

{{c1::Demeclocycline}}

What drug can exert its effects in various conditions such as carcinoid syndrome, gastrinoma, glucagonoma, and esophageal varices?

{{c1::Octreotide}}

What drug may be prescribed to combat excess growth hormone for a patient with acromegaly?

{{c1::Octreotide}}

What are 3 common adverse effects of fludrocortisone?

{{c1::Edema}}
{{c1::Heart}} failure exacerbation
{{c1::Hyperpigmentation}}

What is the drug of choice for mineralocorticoid replacement in the setting of primary adrenal insufficiency?

{{c1::Fludrocortisone}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a synthetic analog of aldosterone with glucocorticoid effects.

fields.Text:
What endogenous hormone is fludrocortisone a synthetic analog of?

{{c1::Aldosterone}}

What is the mechanism of action of cinacalcet?

Increases {{c1::CaSR}} sensitivity to circulating {{c1::Ca2+}} → Decreases release of {{c1::PTH}}

What are the 3 common clinical uses of cinacalcet?

{{c1::Parathyroid}} carcinoma
{{c1::Secondary hyperparathyroidism}} in patients with CKD
{{c1::Hypercalcemia}} in patients with primary hyperparathyroidism

What is the typical side effect of cinacalcet therapy?

{{c1::Hypocalcemia}}

What is the mechanism of action of sevelamer?

{{c1::Phosphate}} binds within the gastrointestinal tract → Prevents {{c1::absorption}} of {{c1::phosphate}}

What are the 2 most common adverse effects of sevelamer?

Low serum {{c1::phosphate}}
{{c1::Gastrointestinal}} upset

What condition is sevelamer used to treat?

{{c1::Hyperphosphatemia}} in patients with chronic kidney disease

Which carpal bone can be felt in the anatomic snuff box?



{{c1::Scaphoid}} bone

What type of injury to the wrist could lead to acute carpal tunnel syndrome?

A dislocation of the {{c1::lunate}} bone may cause {{c1::median}} nerve impingement

What is the most commonly fractured carpal bone and how is it typically injured?

The {{c1::scaphoid}} bone is commonly injured by a fall on an {{c1::outstreched}} hand

Name all the carpal bones.

{{c1::Scaphoid}}
{{c1::Lunate}}
{{c1::Triquetrum}}
{{c1::Pisiform}}
{{c1::Hamate}}
{{c1::Capitate}}
{{c1::Trapezoid}}
{{c1::Trapezium}}

Why are scaphoid fractures at higher risk for avascular necrosis and nonunion?

The scaphoid bone receives a {{c1::retrograde}} blood supply from the {{c1::radial}} artery

Fracture of which carpal bone is associated with ulnar syndrome?

{{c1::Hook}} of the {{c1::hamate}} bone

What are the 3 muscles of the hypothenar compartment?

{{c1::Opponens digiti minimi}}
{{c1::Abductor digiti minimi}}
{{c1::Flexor digiti minimi brevis}}

What are the 3 muscles of the thenar hand compartment?

{{c1::Opponens pollicis}}
{{c1::Abductor pollicis brevis}}
{{c1::Flexor pollicis brevis}}

Which nerve would be affected if the dorsal and palmar interossei lost their respective functions?

{{c1::Ulnar}} nerve

What are the functions of the lumbricals?

{{c1::Flex::Flex/Extend}} at the MCP joint
{{c1::Extend::Flex/Extend}} at the PIP and DIP joints

The lumbricals are innervated by which nerves?

1st and 2nd lumbricals → {{c1::Median}} nerve
3rd and 4th lumbricals → {{c1::Ulnar}} nerve

What is the name of the region on the palmar surface highlighted in red?



{{c1::Hypothenar eminence}}

What is the name of the region on the palmar surface highlighted in teal?



{{c1::Thenar eminence}}

What type of lesions manifest as clawing of the hands?

{{c1::Distal::Proximal/Distal}} lesions of the {{c1::median}} or {{c1::ulnar}} nerves

What action will reveal an "ulnar claw" deformity?

{{c1::Extension::Flexion/Extension}} of the fingers from rest

Name the hand deformity shown, which occurs when making a fist, and its cause.



"{{c1::OK gesture}}" → Lesion in the {{c1::proximal::proximal/distal}} portion of the {{c1::ulnar}} nerve

Name the hand deformity shown, which occurs on extending the fingers at rest, and its cause.



"{{c1::Median claw}}" → Lesion in the {{c1::distal::proximal/distal}} portion of the {{c1::median}} nerve

Name the hand deformity shown, which occurs on making a fist, and its cause.



"{{c1::Hand of benediction}}" → Lesion in the {{c1::proximal::proximal/distal}} area of the {{c1::median}} nerve

Name the hand deformity shown, which is exacerbated on extending the fingers, and its cause.



"{{c1::Ulnar claw}}" → Lesion in the {{c1::distal::proximal/distal}} portion of the {{c1::ulnar}} nerve

What action will reveal a "hand of benediction" deformity?

Making a {{c1::fist}}

What action will reveal a "median claw" deformity?

{{c1::Extending::Flexing/Extending}} the fingers at rest

What action will reveal an "OK gesture" deformity?

Making a {{c1::fist}}

Describe the function of the lumbrical muscles of the hand.

{{c1::Flexion::Flexion/Extension}} of the MCP joint
{{c1::Extension::Flexion/Extension}} of the DIP and PIP joints
fields.Back Extra: This allows a neutral resting position.

fields.Text:
Generally speaking, for distortions of the hand caused by nerve injuries, which subtype has deficits that are less pronounced?

{{c1::Proximal::Proximal/Distal}} lesions

Which 5 muscles are primarily involved in external rotation of the hips?

{{c1::Obturator internus}}
{{c1::Obturator externus}}
{{c1::Piriformis}}
{{c1::Iliopsoas}}
{{c1::Gluteus maximus}}

Which 3 muscles are involved with internal rotation of the hip?

{{c1::Tensor fascia latae}}
{{c1::Gluteus medius}}
{{c1::Gluteus minimus}}

Which 5 muscles are involved in flexing the hips?

{{c1::Pectineus}}
{{c1::Sartorius}}
{{c1::Iliopsoas}}
{{c1::Rectus femoris}}
{{c1::Tensor fascia lata}}

Which 4 muscles are the extensors of the hips?

{{c1::Semitendinosus}}
{{c1::Semimembranosus}}
{{c1::Gluteus maximus}}
{{c1::Long::Long/Short}} head of the {{c1::biceps femoris}}

Which 3 muscles are involved in adduction of the hip?

{{c1::Adductor brevis}}
{{c1::Adductor longus}}
{{c1::Adductor magnus}}

Which 2 muscles work to abduct the hip?

{{c1::Gluteus medius}}
{{c1::Gluteus minimus}}

Identify the nerve that leads to the condition shown in the image.



{{c1::Superior gluteal}} nerve

Pelvic surgery is associated with an increased risk of injury to which nerve?

{{c1::Obturator}} nerve

Injury to which nerve presents with reduced sensation in the perineum and can cause urinary and/or fecal incontinence?

{{c1::Pudendal}} nerve

Injury to which nerve is associated with difficulty rising from a seat or climbing stairs?

{{c1::Inferior gluteal}} nerve

Injury to which nerve is associated with decreased medial thigh sensation and weakness of adduction?

{{c1::Obturator}} nerve

Tight clothing, obesity, prolonged pelvic procedures, and pregnancy all increase risk of compression and damage to which lower extremity nerve?

{{c1::Lateral femoral cutaneous}} nerve

Which 2 nerve injuries are commonly associated with posterior hip dislocations?

{{c1::Inferior gluteal}} nerve
{{c1::Sciatic}} nerve

How does a genitofemoral nerve injury present in female patients?

Loss of sensation in the {{c1::labia majora}}
Loss of sensation in the {{c1::medial::medial/lateral}} {{c1::thigh}}

To avoid injuring the superior gluteal nerve when giving an IM injection in the buttocks, in what area should the shot be given?

{{c1::Superolateral}} quadrant, especially the {{c1::anterolateral}} area

How does a genitofemoral nerve injury present in male patients?

Sensation is lost in the {{c1::scrotum}}
Sensation is lost in the {{c1::medial::medial/lateral}} {{c1::thigh}}
{{c1::Cremasteric}} reflex is absent

How is the superior gluteal nerve commonly injured?

{{c1::Iatrogenic}} injury during {{c1::IM injection}}

Compression of which nerve causes numbness, tingling, and burning pain in the anterolateral thigh?

{{c1::Lateral femoral cutaneous}} nerve

Injury to which nerve presents as burning/tingling pain radiating from an abdominal surgical incision to the inguinal/suprapubic region?

{{c1::Iliohypogastric}} nerve

When is the iliohypogastric nerve commonly injured?

{{c1::Abdominal surgery}}

Name the roots of the femoral nerve.

{{c1::L2}} to {{c1::L4}}

Name the roots of the obturator nerve.

{{c1::L2}} to {{c1::L4}}

The tibial nerve may be damaged distally in the setting of which condition?

{{c1::Tarsal tunnel}} syndrome

Name the roots of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.

{{c1::L2}} to {{c1::L3}}

Injury to which nerve is associated with knee trauma and Baker cysts?

{{c1::Tibial}} nerve

Injury to which nerve presents with an inverted foot and the inability to dorsiflex or evert the foot?

{{c1::Common peroneal}} nerve

Injury to which nerve presents with an everted foot and the inability to invert or plantarflex the foot?

{{c1::Tibial}} nerve

What are the sensory deficits seen with injury to the common peroneal nerve?

Loss of sensation on the {{c1::dorsal::ventral/dorsal}} foot

Lateral leg compression and fibular neck fractures are associated with damage to which nerve?

{{c1::Common peroneal}} nerve

What lower extremity nerve injury presents as "foot drop" with a steppage gait on physical exam?

{{c1::Common peroneal}} nerve injury

Name the roots of the genitofemoral nerve.

{{c1::L1}} to {{c1::L2}}

What does the sciatic nerve split into?

{{c1::Common peroneal}} nerve
{{c1::Tibial}} nerve

Name the roots of the iliohypogastric nerve.

{{c1::T12}} to {{c1::L1}}

Stretch injury to which nerve is associated with childbirth, horseback riding, and prolonged cycling?

{{c1::Pudendal}} nerve

What nerve is likely injured if a patient with a pelvic fracture has both a decrease in leg extension and a diminished patellar reflex?

{{c1::Femoral}} nerve

What landmark may be used to identify a site of injection when giving a pudendal nerve block?

{{c1::Ischial spine}}

Damage to which lower extremity nerve is associated with laparoscopic surgery?

{{c1::Genitofemoral}} nerve

Damage to which lower extremity nerve is most often associated with a spinal disc herniation?

{{c1::Sciatic}} nerve

Name the roots of the inferior gluteal nerve.

{{c1::L5}} to {{c1::S2}}

Name the roots of the pudendal nerve.

{{c1::S2}} to {{c1::S4}}

Knee pain and a "popping" sound on internal rotation of the tibia and application of varus force to a patient's foot with the knee flexed indicates what likely diagnosis?

{{c1::Lateral meniscus}} tear

What maneuver requires tibial internal and external rotation with applied varus and valgus force on examination of a patient's knee?

{{c1::McMurray}} test
fields.Back Extra:
A lateral meniscal tear is assessed via internal rotation and varus force.

A medial meniscal tear is assessed via external rotation and valgus force.

fields.Text:
What constitutes a positive posterior drawer sign?

Increased {{c1::posterior::anterior/posterior}} gliding of the tibia when the knee is bent at {{c1::90}}°

What constitutes a positive anterior drawer sign?

Increased {{c1::anterior::anterior/posterior}} gliding of the tibia when the knee is bent at {{c1::90}}°

What is the difference between the Lachman test and the anterior drawer sign?

Anterior drawer sign assesses anterior gliding of the tibia with the knee at {{c1::90}}°
Lachman test assesses anterior gliding of the tibia with the knee at {{c1::30}}°
fields.Back Extra: The Lachman test is more sensitive.

fields.Text:
Which ligament is injured if extending a patient's knee and applying a valgus force reveals medial space widening of the tibia?

{{c1::Medial collateral}} ligament

Which ligament is injured if extending a patient's knee and applying a varus force reveals lateral space widening of the tibia?

{{c1::Lateral collateral}} ligament

Knee pain and a "popping" sound on external rotation of the tibia and application of valgus force to a patient's foot with the knee flexed likely indicates what diagnosis?

{{c1::Medial meniscal}} tear

What are the 2 attachment points of the ACL?

{{c1::Lateral::Medial/Lateral}} femoral condyle
{{c1::Anterior::Anterior/Posterior}} tibia

What are the 2 attachment points of the PCL?

{{c1::Medial::Medial/Lateral}} femoral condyle
{{c1::Posterior::Anterior/Posterior}} tibia

What ligament is involved in the most common ankle sprain?

{{c1::Anterior talofibular}} ligament

What is the most common high ankle sprain?

{{c1::Anterior inferior tibiofibular}} ligament

What unusual movement typically causes anterior talofibular strains?

{{c1::Supination::Supination/Pronation}} of the foot

Lumbar disc herniation at which level presents with a decreased patellar reflex and weak knee extension?

{{c1::L3}} to {{c1::L4}} compresses the {{c1::L4}} nerve root

Lumbar disc herniation at which level presents with dorsiflexion weakness and trouble walking on the heels?

{{c1::L4}} to {{c1::L5}} compresses the {{c1::L5}} nerve root

Lumbar disc herniation at which level presents with plantarflexion weakness, decreased Achilles tendon reflex, and trouble walking on the toes?

{{c1::L5}} to {{c1::S1}} compresses the {{c1::S1}} nerve root

Why are lumbar disc herniations more likely to occur posterolaterally as opposed to anteriorly?

The posterior longitudinal ligament is {{c1::thin::thick/thin}} along the midline of vertebral bodies
The anterior longitudinal ligament is {{c1::thick::thick/thin}} along the midline of vertebral bodies

If a patient has an L3 to L4 disc herniation, which nerve roots are impaired by this lesion?

{{c1::L4}} nerve roots

Define lumbosacral radiculopathy.

{{c1::Weakness}} and {{c1::paresthesia}} related to specific lumbosacral nerves
fields.Back Extra: This is usually due to intervertebral disc herniation.

fields.Text:
What nerve and artery are at risk for damage with trauma to the medial malleolus?

{{c1::Tibial}} nerve
{{c1::Posterior tibial}} artery

What major nerve and artery are at risk for damage with trauma to the popliteal fossa?

{{c1::Tibial}} nerve
{{c1::Popliteal}} artery

Which artery and nerve are likely damaged with a distal humerus or cubital fossa fracture?

{{c1::Brachial}} artery
{{c1::Median}} nerve

Which nerve and artery are likely damaged with a midshaft humerus fracture?

{{c1::Radial}} nerve
{{c1::Deep brachial}} artery

Which nerve and artery would you expect to see injured with a fracture at the surgical neck of the humerus?

{{c1::Axillary}} nerve
{{c1::Posterior circumflex}} artery

With which artery does the long thoracic nerve travel in the axillary region?

{{c1::Lateral thoracic}} artery

What happens when ATP binds to a myosin head that is attached to the actin filament?

{{c1::Release}} of the myosin head
fields.Back Extra: Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP puts myosin in a cocked position for the next contraction cycle.

fields.Text:
Reuptake of calcium by what receptors leads to muscle relaxation?

{{c1::SERCA}}

During skeletal muscle contraction, which bands of the sarcomere decrease in length?

{{c1::H}} band between the Z lines
{{c1::I}} band between the Z lines
fields.Back Extra: The A band is always the same length.

fields.Text:
During the power stroke, what happens to myosin?

Myosin releases {{c1::ADP}} and becomes {{c1::displaced}} on the thin {{c1::actin}} filament

What is the role of troponin C in muscle contraction?

Binds to intracellular {{c1::Ca2+}} → {{c1::Conformational}} change that moves tropomyosin out of the myosin-binding sites on {{c1::actin}}

What is released by activation of the mechanically coupled ryanodine receptor from the sarcoplasmic reticulum?

{{c1::Ca2+}} ions

Ryanodine receptors are coupled with which receptors on the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane?

{{c1::Dihydropyridine}} receptors

Where are ryanodine receptors of muscles located?

{{c1::Sarcoplasmic reticulum}}

As an action potential travels over the whole muscle cell, it goes down into invaginations in the membrane. What are these invaginations called?

{{c1::T-tubules}}
fields.Back Extra: These travel deep into the muscle, allowing for coordinated contraction.

fields.Text:
After presynaptic neuron neurotransmitter release, postsynaptic acetylcholine binding leads to the depolarization of which membrane for muscle contraction?

{{c1::Motor end plate}} of the muscle cell

What opens the presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, inducing the release of acetylcholine into the synaptic space?

{{c1::Action potential}}

At the presynaptic membrane of a neuromuscular junction, influx of which ion into the axon triggers the release of acetylcholine?

{{c1::Ca2+}}

What are T-tubules, and what is their function in the muscle?

T-tubules are extensions of muscle {{c1::plasma membrane}} in contact with the {{c1::sarcoplasmic reticulum}} → Coordinated {{c1::contraction}} of {{c1::striated}} muscles

During muscle contraction, which of the muscle bands remains the same length?

{{c1::A}} band

As the myosin head binds to the active site forming a crossbridge, what happens to the ADP and Pi complex in the myosin head?

Pi is {{c1::released}} → Starts the {{c1::power stroke}}

Release of calcium into the cytoplasm from which calcium-binding protein of the sarcoplasmic reticulum triggers muscle contraction?

{{c1::Calsequestrin}}

Osmotic demyelination syndrome is also referred to by what name?

{{c1::Central pontine myelinolysis}}

What are five treatments for SIADH?

{{c1::Fluid}} restriction (first-line)
{{c1::Hypertonic::Hypertonic/Hypotonic}} saline
{{c1::Salt}} tablets
{{c1::Diuretics}}
{{c1::ADH}} antagonists

In a patient with known SIADH, what happens to the ANP and BNP levels?

ANP {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}
BNP {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}
fields.Back Extra: This is to promote urinary sodium secretion.

fields.Text:
Why is there euvolemia in a patient with SIADH?

SIADH {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} aldosterone and {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} both ANP and BNP → Urinary sodium excretion

In SIADH, how does urine osmolality compare to serum osmolality?

Urine osmolality is {{c1::greater::greater/less}} than serum osmolality

Which type of lung cancer is commonly associated with SIADH?

{{c1::Small cell}} lung cancer

A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is found to have hyponatremia with high urine osmolality and low serum osmolality. What is the likely diagnosis?

{{c1::SIADH}}
fields.Back Extra: This can be caused by pulmonary disease.

fields.Text:
What are the common causes of SIADH?

{{c1::Head}} trauma
{{c1::Central nervous system}} disease
{{c1::Ectopic}} ADH production
{{c1::Exogenous}} hormones
{{c1::Lung::Organ}} disorders
{{c1::Drugs}}

In a patient with hyponatremia due to SIADH, why is it important to monitor Na+ levels closely during treatment?

Sodium correction should be undertaken at a {{c1::slow::fast/slow}} pace to avoid {{c1::osmotic demyelination}} syndrome

Very low sodium levels can result in what two neurologic complications?

Cerebral {{c1::edema}}
{{c1::Seizures}}

What volume status and sodium balance do you expect in SIADH secretion?

{{c1::Euvolemic::Hypervolemic/Euvolemic/Hypovolemic}} {{c1::hyponatremia::hypernatremia/hyponatremia}}

List four possible causes of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

{{c1::Hereditary}}
{{c1::Drugs}}
{{c1::Hypercalcemia::Hypercalcemia/Hypocalcemia}}
{{c1::Hypokalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}

List two possible causes of central diabetes insipidus.

{{c1::Idiopathic}} injury
{{c1::Brain}} injury

What are two common clinical manifestations of diabetes insipidus?

{{c1::Thirst}}
{{c1::Polyuria}}

What are the two main categories of diabetes insipidus?

{{c1::Central}}
{{c1::Nephrogenic}}

What test is useful in differentiating primary polydipsia from central/nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?

{{c1::Water}} restriction
fields.Back Extra: This will occur for 2 to 3 hours with hourly measurements of urine volume, urine osmolality, serum osmolality, and plasma sodium.

fields.Text:
What lifestyle change can be used to manage central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?

Central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus can be treated with {{c1::hydration}}
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus requires avoidance of the {{c1::offending}} agent and dietary {{c1::salt}} restriction

How are ADH levels affected in central versus nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?

Central diabetes insipidus has {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} ADH levels
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus has normal or {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} ADH levels

In a patient with central diabetes insipidus, at what serum osmolality and sodium level would you administer desmopressin as treatment?

Serum osmolality > {{c1::295}} to {{c1::300}} mOsm/kg
Na+ ≥ {{c1::145}} mEq/L

What test can differentiate between central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?

Administration of {{c1::desmopressin}}

In central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, what values would you expect for serum osmolality and urine osmolality?

Serum osmolality is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}
Urine osmolality is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}

List three pharmacologic agents used to treat nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

{{c1::Hydrochlorothiazide}}
{{c1::Indomethacin}}
{{c1::Amiloride}}

What is the treatment for hypopituitarism?

{{c1::Hormone replacement}} therapy

A man with a radiation-treated glioblastoma multiforme always feels cold. He reports decreased libido. Exam is notable for poor skin turgor and thin hair. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Hypopituitarism}}
fields.Back Extra: This is likely secondary to prior radiation.

fields.Text:
A patient with a known pituitary adenoma presents with sudden onset of severe headache and double vision and becomes hypotensive. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Pituitary apoplexy}}

An obese woman spontaneously develops central hypothyroidism and amenorrhea. What is the cause of her hormone deficiencies?

{{c1::Empty sella}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by idiopathic atrophy or compression of the pituitary gland.

fields.Text:
What process in pregnancy makes the pituitary more susceptible to hypoperfusion and thus Sheehan syndrome?

Pregnancy-induced pituitary {{c1::growth}}

A woman who had a severe hemorrhage during her recent delivery cannot breastfeed her newborn and feels cold all the time. What is this disease?

{{c1::Sheehan}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This is an ischemic infarction of the pituitary gland after postpartum bleeding.

fields.Text:
Identify a neuropathologic condition often seen in young, obese women that is associated with empty sella syndrome.

{{c1::Idiopathic intracranial hypertension}}

What is the definitive treatment for acromegaly?

{{c1::Surgical resection}} of the {{c1::pituitary adenoma}}

What are three pharmacologic treatment options for acromegaly?

{{c1::Pegvisomant}}
{{c1::Octreotide}}
{{c1::Dopamine}} agonists

What are three ways to diagnose acromegaly?

Lack of suppression of serum {{c1::GH}} after oral glucose tolerance tests
{{c1::Pituitary mass}} on MRI
Increased serum {{c1::IGF-1}}

What is the clinical implication of excess GH in children?

It causes {{c1::gigantism}} with increased {{c1::linear}} bone growth

What is the most common cause of death in gigantism and acromegaly?

{{c1::Heart::Organ}} failure

What endocrine disease typically presents with an enlarged tongue with deep furrows, coarsening of facial features with age, deep voice, and frontal bossing?

{{c1::Acromegaly}}

How is glucose regulation affected in acromegaly?

Glucose tolerance is impaired due to insulin {{c1::resistance}}

The patient shown in the image has noted difficulty speaking due to tongue enlargement. Based on this symptom and the physical exam findings shown, what is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Acromegaly}}

What is the term for swelling in the face and periorbital region, commonly associated with hypothyroidism?

{{c1::Myxedema}}

What thyroid lab findings do you expect in a patient with hypothyroidism?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} TSH levels (if primary)
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} free T3 levels
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} free T4 levels

What type of thyroid disease presents with fatigue, dry skin, brittle hair, myxedema, and slow reflexes?

{{c1::Hypothyroidism}}

What are the gastrointestinal findings in hypothyroidism?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} gastrointestinal motility
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} appetite

What lab values do you expect in hyperthyroidism?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} TSH levels
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} free T3 levels
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} free T4 levels

What may be seen on the shins of patients with hyperthyroidism?

{{c1::Pretibial myxedema}}
fields.Back Extra: This is in the setting of Graves disease.

fields.Text:
What type of thyroid disorder is associated with bradycardia and dyspnea on exertion?

{{c1::Hypothyroidism}}

How does hypothyroidism affect the skin and the hair?

It causes {{c1::dry}}, {{c1::cool}} skin
It causes {{c1::coarse}}, {{c1::brittle}} hair with {{c1::diffuse alopecia}}

What is the mechanism by which hypothyroidism leads to hypercholesterolemia?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} {{c1::LDL}} receptor expression

How do you distinguish hypothyroid myopathy from thyrotoxic myopathy, given that both present with proximal muscle weakness?

Hypothyroid myopathy is associated with {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} TSH levels and {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} creatinine kinase levels

How does hypothyroidism affect cholesterol levels?

It causes {{c1::hypercholesterolemia::hypercholesterolemia/hypocholesterolemia}}

A 52-year-old patient with hypothyroidism is noted to have puffy facies and water retention. What is the mechanism underlying these findings?

Deposition of {{c1::glycosaminoglycans}} in the {{c1::interstitial}} space → Water retention and edema

What is the mechanism of weight loss in hyperthyroidism?

Metabolic rate is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} due to increased synthesis of {{c1::Na+/K+-ATPase}}

What is the mechanism underlying lid lag/retraction in patients with hyperthyroidism?

Increased {{c1::sympathetic::sympathetic/parasympathetic}} stimulation of the levator palpebrae superioris and superior tarsal muscle

Why do patients with hyperthyroidism exhibit an increased rate of osteoporosis and fractures?

{{c1::T3}} stimulates bone {{c1::resorption}} directly

What is the mechanism behind fine tremors in patients with hyperthyroidism?

Increased {{c1::β}}-adrenergic activity due to increases in the number and sensitivity of {{c1::β}}-adrenergic receptors

How are libido and fertility affected in patients with hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} libido
{{c1::Infertility}}

What is the cause of hyponatremia seen in hypothyroidism?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} free water clearance

How does hypothyroidism affect the reproductive system?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} libido
Abnormal uterine {{c1::bleeding}}
{{c1::Infertility}}

What type of thyroid disorder is associated with tachycardia, dyspnea, palpitations, chest pain, arrhythmias, and systolic hypertension?

{{c1::Hyperthyroidism::Hyperthyroidism/Hypothyroidism}}

What is the finding associated with thyroid disease shown in this image?



{{c1::Onycholysis}}

What is myoedema, which is found in patients with hypothyroidism?

A {{c1::small::large/small}} {{c1::lump}} arising on the surface of a {{c1::muscle}} after it has been struck with a {{c1::hammer}}

How does hyperthyroidism affect the skin and the hair?

It causes {{c1::warm}}, {{c1::moist}} skin
It causes {{c1::thin::thick/thin}} hair

1α-hydroxylase catalyzes what reaction pertaining to vitamin D?

{{c1::25-OH}} D3 → {{c1::1,25-(OH)2}} D3

Calcitriol works primarily on the bones and intestines. How does it affect Ca2+/PO43- processing in each?

Bones → Promotes Ca2+/PO43- {{c1::release}}
Intestines → Promotes Ca2+/PO43- {{c1::absorption}}

Name two malignancies that commonly increase the secretion of PTHrP.

{{c1::Renal cell}} carcinoma
{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma of the {{c1::lung}}

Which three stimuli will promote PTH synthesis via direct stimulation?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} ionized Ca2+
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PO43-
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} 1,25-(OH)2 D3

How do PTH and phosphate levels promote the production of active vitamin D?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PTH and {{c1::low::high/low}} PO43- levels both stimulate {{c1::1α-hydroxylase}} to produce {{c1::1,25-(OH)2}} D3 in the proximal convoluted tubule of the kidneys

How does the Mg2+ level affect PTH secretion?

A moderately low Mg2+ level can {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} PTH secretion
An extremely low Mg2+ level can {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} PTH secretion

How does PTH alter Ca2+ and PO43- in the kidneys?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} Ca2+ reabsorption
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} PO43- reabsorption

What is the mechanism by which some malignancies can alter the serum phosphate level?

Some cancers secrete {{c1::PTHrP}} → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} PO43- reabsorption

What is the mechanism by which a RANK-L inhibitor lowers the serum Ca2+ level?

Inhibiting RANK-L prevents {{c1::osteoclast}} stimulation → Decreased Ca2+ levels

In what pattern must parathyroid hormone be administered to stimulate bone formation?

{{c1::Intermittently}} administered

How can alcohol abuse, diuretics, diarrhea, or aminoglycoside use affect PTH secretion?

They all decrease {{c1::Mg2+}} levels
fields.Back Extra:
Mildly low Mg2+ levels increase PTH.

Severely low Mg2+ levels decrease PTH.

fields.Text:
How does PTH affect Ca2+ and PO43- absorption in the intestines?

It {{c1::promotes}} intestinal Ca2+ and  PO43- absorption

What serum and urinary findings do you see in a patient with increased PTH secretion?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} serum Ca2+
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} serum PO43-
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} urine PO43-

Which cells normally produce PTH?

{{c1::Chief}} cells of the parathyroid glands

What is the primary function of PTH?

Increases the free {{c1::Ca2+}} level in the blood

How does PTH affect Ca2+ and PO43- in bone?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} release of Ca2+
{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} release of PO43-

Which form of calcium has an effect on PTH levels?

{{c1::Ionized}} Ca2+ is a significant regulator of PTH secretion

What is the relationship between alkalosis and levels of Ca2+?

An increase in pH allows albumin to bind to {{c1::more::more/less}} Ca2+ → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} free Ca2+

In what three forms is Ca2+ found in plasma?

{{c1::Ionized}} (~ 45%)
Bound to {{c1::albumin}} (∼ 40%)
Bound to {{c1::anions::cations/anions}} (∼ 15%)

Does change in albumin concentration have an effect on PTH secretion?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}

Which vitamin is absorbed in the terminal ileum along with bile salts?

Vitamin {{c1::B12}}

Patients with a history of bariatric surgery, small bowel disease, or resected bowel are at risk for what types of deficiencies?

{{c1::Vitamin}} deficiency
{{c1::Mineral}} deficiency
fields.Back Extra: Vitamin B12 deficiency is common after terminal ileum resection.

fields.Text:
In which part of the gastrointestinal tract is folate absorbed?

{{c1::Small bowel}}

In what part of the small intestine is iron primarily absorbed in its ionized form?

{{c1::Duodenum}}

What does vitamin B12 bind to after it is released from animal protein by pepsin and HCl in the stomach?

{{c1::Salivary R-protein}}

What does vitamin B12 bind to after it is released from salivary R-protein by pancreatic protease in the duodenum?

{{c1::Intrinsic}} factor

Where in the cell do steroid hormones bind to their receptors?

{{c1::Cytoplasm}}
{{c1::Nucleus}}

Increased levels of what hormone in women can lead to increased sex hormone–binding globulin levels?

Increased levels of {{c1::estrogen}}

Why does decreased sex hormone–binding globulin in women lead to hirsutism?

Decreased sex hormone–binding globulin → Increased free {{c1::testosterone}} → Hirsutism

Why does increased sex hormone–binding globulin in men lead to gynecomastia?

Increased sex hormone–binding globulin → Decreased free {{c1::testosterone}} → Gynecomastia

Why do steroid hormones circulate bound to specific binding globulins?

Steroid hormones are {{c1::lipophilic}} → Specific binding globulins increase their {{c1::solubility}}

The following hormones use which signaling pathway?

GnRH
Oxytocin
ADH
TRH
Histamine
Angiotensin II
Gastrin

{{c1::IP3}} signaling pathway

The following endocrine hormones use which signaling pathway?

Progesterone
Estrogen
Testosterone
Cortisol
Aldosterone
T3
T4
Vitamin D

{{c1::Intracellular receptor}} signaling pathway

The following hormones use which signaling pathway?

BNP
ANP
EDRF

{{c1::cGMP}} signaling pathway

The following hormones use which signaling pathway?

IGF-1
FGF
PDGF
EGF
TGF-β
Insulin

{{c1::Receptor tyrosine kinase}} signaling pathway
fields.Back Extra: This also involves the MAPK pathway.

fields.Text:
What type of signaling pathway of endocrine hormones do acidophils and cytokines use?

{{c1::Nonreceptor tyrosine kinase}} via the {{c1::JAK/STAT}} pathway

ADH can bind to either the V1-receptor or V2-receptor. Which signaling pathway does it use for each receptor?

V1-receptor activates the {{c1::IP3}} pathway
V2-receptor acts on the {{c1::cAMP}} pathway

The following hormones use which signaling pathway?

G-CSF
Erythropoietin
Thrombopoietin
Prolactin
Immunomodulators
GH

{{c1::Nonreceptor tyrosine kinase}} signaling pathway
fields.Back Extra: This also involves the JAK/STAT pathway.

fields.Text:
Which cellular signaling pathway utilized by endocrine hormones typically leads to vasodilation and/or diuresis?

{{c1::cGMP}}

The following hormones use which signaling pathway?

FSH
LH
ACTH
TSH
CRH
hCG
ADH
MSH
PTH
Calcitonin
Histamine
Glucagon
GHRH

{{c1::cAMP}} signaling pathway

What is the mechanism behind appetite enhancement during states of sleep deprivation or fasting?

Increased {{c1::ghrelin}} production
Decreased {{c1::leptin}} production

In patients with Prader-Willi syndrome, increased production of which hormone accounts for increased appetite?

{{c1::Ghrelin}}

By what mechanism does marijuana cause appetite enhancement?

Endocannabinoids stimulate receptors in the {{c1::hypothalamus}} and {{c1::nucleus accumbens}}

How is the level of leptin altered in people who are obese?

Leptin is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} due to high adipose tissue
fields.Back Extra: However, they are resistant to leptin's anorexigenic effect.

fields.Text:
What are the functions of ghrelin?

Ghrelin stimulates {{c1::hunger}}

Mutation of which appetite-regulating hormone can result in central obesity?

{{c1::Leptin}}

What areas of the brain do ghrelin and leptin act on?

Ghrelin acts on the {{c1::lateral hypothalamus}}
Leptin affects the {{c1::ventromedial hypothalamus}}

Where is leptin produced?

{{c1::Adipose}} tissue

Why do steroids cause neutrophilia?

Steroids inhibit white blood cell {{c1::adhesion}} → Neutrophilia

What provides the stimulus for cortisol secretion?

Hypothalamic {{c1::CRH}} stimulates release of pituitary {{c1::ACTH}}

Why should a patient with a prescription for a high-dose steroid undergo a PPD test before starting to take the medication?

{{c1::Tuberculosis}} or {{c1::candidiasis}} reactivation can occur due to decreased {{c1::IL-2}} production

What causes hypokalemia and hypernatremia in a patient on high-dose steroids?

At high concentrations, {{c1::cortisol}} can bind to and act as an agonist on {{c1::aldosterone}} receptors, mimicking {{c1::hyperaldosteronism::hyperaldosteronism/hypoaldosteronism}}

How is chronic stress associated with recurrent illnesses?

Chronic stress can lead to prolonged {{c1::cortisol}} secretion and {{c1::cortisol}} resistance → Impairment of immunocompetency

How is the natural mechanism for cortisol regulation affected in a patient receiving long-term steroid therapy?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} CRH
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} ACTH
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} endogenous cortisol secretion

Why do you provide a calcium and/or vitamin D supplement to a patient receiving long-term steroid therapy?

Steroids suppress {{c1::osteoblast}} activity
fields.Back Extra: This results in decreased bone formation and increased risk for osteoporosis.

fields.Text:
What is the cause of hyperglycemia in a patient who takes steroids frequently?

Steroids increase {{c1::insulin}} resistance

How do steroids affect leukotriene and prostaglandin to block inflammation?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} leukotriene production
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} prostaglandin production

Decreased activity of which cells causes striae in patients on steroids?

{{c1::Fibroblasts}}

In what form is cortisol found in the bloodstream?

Bound to {{c1::corticosteroid-binding globulin}}

By what mechanism does cortisol increase blood pressure?

Upregulates {{c1::α1}}-receptors on arterioles → Increased sensitivity to {{c1::norepinephrine}} and {{c1::epinephrine}}

By what mechanism does chronic stress increase cortisol levels?

Stress stimulates the hypothalamus to release {{c1::CRH}}

What ion stimulates the secretion of calcitonin?

Increased serum {{c1::Ca2+}} levels

How is calcitonin involved in Ca2+ homeostasis?

It {{c1::is not::is/is not}} important in normal Ca2+ homeostasis
fields.Back Extra: It opposes the action of PTH.

fields.Text:
What cells secrete calcitonin?

{{c1::Parafollicular}} cells
fields.Back Extra: These are also known as C cells of the thyroid.

fields.Text:
What is the function of calcitonin?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} bone resorption

After consuming a large meal, what will blood measurements of glucagon activity show?

Glucagon activity will be {{c1::low::high/low}}
fields.Back Extra: It is inhibited by both hyperglycemia and insulin.

fields.Text:
What effect will octreotide, used to treat acromegaly, have on glucagon?

It will {{c1::inhibit::stimulate/inhibit}} glucagon secretion

Glucagon promotes catabolism by inducing which four metabolic pathways?

{{c1::Ketogenesis}}
{{c1::Glycogenolysis}}
{{c1::Gluconeogenesis}}
{{c1::Lipolysis}}

What metabolic state results in secretion of glucagon?

{{c1::Hypoglycemia::Hyperglycemia/Hypoglycemia}}

Which hormone maintains homeostasis in blood glucose levels during states of fasting?

{{c1::Glucagon}}

Which cells produce glucagon?

{{c1::α}} cells of the pancreas

Cleavage of which part of the proinsulin molecule will lead to a functional molecule of insulin?

{{c1::C-peptide}}

Why is blood glucose lowered when a patient takes oral glucose as compared with intravenous injection of glucose?

Insulin response is increased because {{c1::incretins}} are released after oral glucose intake

Spermatocytes use GLUT5 for insulin-independent transport of what molecule?

{{c1::Fructose}}

Why is glucose more efficiently transferred into cells after exercise?

Exercise induces increased {{c1::GLUT4}} expression on striated skeletal muscles

What fuel does the brain use during starvation, and why can't red blood cells do the same?

{{c1::Ketone bodies}} are used by the brain during starvation
Red blood cells lack {{c1::mitochondria}} for {{c1::aerobic::aerobic/anaerobic}} metabolism

What diabetic medication closes K+ channels in islet β-cells to cause insulin release?

{{c1::Sulfonylureas}}

How does insulin affect muscle protein synthesis?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} muscle protein synthesis

How does insulin affect triglyceride synthesis?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} triglyceride synthesis

How does insulin affect glycogen synthesis and glucagon release?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} glycogen synthesis
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} glucagon release

How does insulin affect lipolysis in adipose tissue?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} lipolysis

What is the effect of insulin on electrolyte and amino acid transport?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} Na+ retention by the kidneys
Shifts K+ and amino acids {{c1::into::into/out of}} cells

What GLUT receptors are present in the placenta and the brain?

{{c1::GLUT1}}
{{c1::GLUT3}}

Which GLUT receptor requires insulin for transport?

{{c1::GLUT4}}

Which GLUT receptor is used by β-cells, the liver, kidneys, and gastrointestinal tract?

{{c1::GLUT2}}

How does the intake of glucose in the β-cells of the pancreas stimulate insulin release?

Glucose enters β-cells to make {{c1::ATP}} → {{c1::K+}} channels closes → Cell depolarizes → Influx of {{c1::Ca2+}} → Insulin release

Why do the brain, cornea, placenta, and red blood cells not require insulin for glucose transport into cells?

Glucose is taken up in these organs by {{c1::GLUT1}}

Where is preproinsulin synthesized in pancreatic β-cells?

{{c1::Rough endoplasmic reticulum}}

What could be the cause of high insulin and C-peptide levels in a patient with a negative sulfonylurea assay?

{{c1::Insulinoma}}

How does an excess of exogenous insulin affect insulin and C-peptide levels?

Insulin will be {{c1::increased}}
C-peptide will be {{c1::normal}}

How does overdosing on glyburide affect insulin and C-peptide levels?

Insulin will be {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}
C-peptide levels will be {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}

Which GLUT receptor is bidirectional?

{{c1::GLUT2}}

After insulin binding, tyrosine phosphorylation results in activation of the PI3K pathway. What downstream glucose transporter is affected?

{{c1::GLUT4}}

Where is GLUT4 insulin receptor expressed?

{{c1::Adipose}} tissue
{{c1::Striated}} muscle

Between glucose and insulin, which one crosses the placenta?

{{c1::Glucose}}

After insulin binding, tyrosine phosphorylation results in activation of the RAS/MAPK pathway. What are the two downstream effects?

Cell {{c1::growth}}
{{c1::DNA}} synthesis

Through which transporter is glucose taken up into islet β-cells and the liver?

{{c1::GLUT2}} transporter

What two pathways are activated by tyrosine phosphorylation by insulin?

{{c1::RAS/MAPK}} pathway
{{c1::PI3K}} pathway

In subjects with 17α-hydroxylase deficiency, do XX subjects have male or female internal anatomy?

XX subjects have both internal and external {{c1::female::male/female}} anatomy
fields.Back Extra: However, there is no secondary sexual development.

fields.Text:
In individuals with 17α-hydroxylase deficiency, what is the anatomical presentation of those with an XY genotype?

{{c1::Ambiguous}} external genitalia
{{c1::Undescended}} testes

What levels of aldosterone, cortisol, K+, and sex hormones do you expect in patient with 17α-hydroxylase deficiency?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} aldosterone
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} cortisol
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} K+
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} sex hormones

What stimulates aldosterone synthase to convert corticosterone into aldosterone?

{{c1::Angiotensin II}}

Which congenital adrenal enzyme deficiencies are characterized by bilaterally enlarged adrenal glands and skin hyperpigmentation?

{{c1::All of them}}
fields.Back Extra: Decreased cortisol → Increased ACTH and MSH production

fields.Text:
Which enzyme catalyzes the conversion of testosterone to DHT?

{{c1::5α-reductase}}

What are the effects of ACTH and ketoconazole on cholesterol desmolase–mediated conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone?

ACTH {{c1::activates::activates/blocks}} cholesterol desmolase
Ketoconazole {{c1::blocks::activates/blocks}} cholesterol desmolase

The enzyme aromatase creates estrone and estradiol from which two precursors?

Estrone → {{c1::Androstenedione}}
Estradiol → {{c1::Testosterone}}

Where in the adrenal cortex does cortisol synthesis occur?

Zona {{c1::fasciculata}}

Where in the adrenal cortex is aldosterone produced?

Zona {{c1::glomerulosa}}

What enzyme converts corticosterone into aldosterone?

{{c1::Aldosterone synthase}}

What enzyme catalyzes the transformation of 11-deoxycortisol into cortisol?

{{c1::11β-hydroxylase}}

What enzyme catalyzes the transformation of progesterone into 17-hydroxyprogesterone?

{{c1::17α-hydroxylase}}

What is the mechanism of action of finasteride?

Finasteride inhibits {{c1::5α-reductase}}

How do aromatase inhibitors help in treating estrogen receptor–positive breast cancer?

Blocks conversion of androstenedione to {{c1::estrone}} and conversion of testosterone to {{c1::estradiol}} → Lowers estrogen levels

Why does inhibition of 17α-hydroxylase result in bilateral adrenal enlargement?

Inhibition of 17α-hydroxylase blocks {{c1::cortisol}} synthesis → Secondarily increases {{c1::ACTH}} levels

In which congenital adrenal hyperplasia does blood pressure increase?

{{c1::17α-hydroxylase}} deficiency
{{c1::11β-hydroxylase}} deficiency

Progesterone can be acted on by one of two enzymes in the adrenal cortex. What are they, and what are their respective products?

{{c1::17α-hydroxylase}} can convert progesterone to {{c2::17-hydroxyprogesterone}}
{{c1::21-hydroxylase}} can convert progesterone to {{c2::11-deoxycorticosterone}}

After cholesterol becomes pregnenolone, it can be acted on by one of two enzymes. What are they, and what are their respective products?

{{c1::17α-hydroxylase}} can convert pregnenolone to {{c2::17-hydroxypregnenolone}}
{{c1::3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase}} can convert pregnenolone to {{c2::progesterone}}

How do the levels of cortisol and mineralocorticoids change in patients with 21-hydroxylase deficiency?

Cortisol levels {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}}
Mineralcorticoid levels {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to decreased enzyme availability.

fields.Text:
Why do patients with a 11β-hydroxylase deficiency have hypertension despite having hypoaldosteronism?

Patients have increased {{c1::11-deoxycorticosterone}}

What is the most common form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia?

{{c1::21-hydroxylase}} deficiency

Which congenital adrenal hyperplasia manifests with salt wasting during infancy and precocious puberty?

{{c1::21-hydroxylase}} deficiency

Metyrapone is used in the diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency. What is its mechanism of action?

Blocks {{c1::11β-hydroxylase}} → Inhibits conversion of {{c1::11-deoxycortisol}} into cortisol

Where in the adrenal cortex are androgens synthesized?

Zona {{c1::reticularis}}

What would be the phenotype of an XX genotype with 21-hydroxylase deficiency?

{{c1::Virilization}}

How are sex hormones impacted in 21-hydroxylase deficiency?

Sex hormones are {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}

How does the level of 17-hydroxyprogesterone change in a patient with 21-hydroxylase deficiency?

The level of 17-hydroxyprogesterone is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}

What two enzymes catalyze the transformation of pregnenolone into DHEA?

{{c1::17α-hydroxylase}}
{{c1::17,20-lyase}}

What two enzymes catalyze the transformation of progesterone into androstenedione?

{{c1::17α-hydroxylase}}
{{c1::17,20-lyase}}

What are two clinical indications for minoxidil therapy?

Androgenetic {{c1::alopecia}}
Severe refractory {{c1::hypertension::hypertension/hypotension}}

What is the mechanism of action of minoxidil?

Direct arteriolar {{c1::vasodilation::vasoconstriction/vasodilation}} → Increased {{c1::follicle}} stimulation

Why does tamsulosin relax the smooth muscles of the prostate, but not the systemic vasculature?

Tamsulosin is selective for {{c1::α1A/D}}-receptors

What drug inhibits smooth muscle contraction in patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia?

{{c1::Tamsulosin}}

What two drugs can you prescribe to decrease androgenic symptoms associated with polycystic ovarian syndrome?

{{c1::Ketoconazole}}
{{c1::Spironolactone}}

What condition is treated with flutamide, bicalutamide, apalutamide, and enzalutamide?

{{c1::Prostate}} cancer

What two adverse effects are common to both ketoconazole and spironolactone?

{{c1::Gynecomastia}}
{{c1::Amenorrhea}}

Name two drugs that function as antiandrogens by interfering with steroid synthesis.

{{c1::Ketoconazole}}
{{c1::Spironolactone}}

What is the mechanism of action of flutamide and bicalutamide?

{{c1::Nonsteroidal::Steroidal/Nonsteroidal}} competitive {{c1::androgen}} receptor antagonists

Which antiandrogen can be used to treat benign prostatic hyperplasia and male-pattern baldness?

{{c1::Finasteride}}

What is the mechanism of action of finasteride?

Decreases the conversion of {{c1::testosterone}} to {{c1::dihydrotestosterone}}

What are two adverse effects of finasteride therapy?

{{c1::Gynecomastia}}
{{c1::Sexual}} dysfunction

What screening test should be done in a patient who is receiving long-term testosterone therapy?

Serum {{c1::lipid}} panel

What general exam finding would you expect in a male patient using exogenous testosterone?

Testicular {{c1::atrophy}}

How is testosterone useful for patients who have sustained burns?

Stimulates {{c1::anabolism::anabolism/catabolism}} → Promotes recovery from burns and severe injuries

How can testosterone be used to treat hormonal deficiencies?

Promotes development of {{c1::secondary::primary/secondary}} {{c1::sexual}} characteristics in patients with {{c1::hypogonadism::hypergonadism/hypogonadism}}

How would prescribing an adolescent exogenous testosterone affect his adult height?

Exogenous testosterone → Premature closure of {{c1::epiphyseal}} plates

What is the mechanism of action of danazol?

Partial {{c1::agonist::agonist/antagonist}} at {{c1::androgen}} receptors

Name three adverse effects of danazol therapy related to its androgenic effects.

{{c1::Acne}}
{{c1::Hirsutism}}
{{c1::Masculinization}}

What two medical conditions are treated with danazol?

{{c1::Endometriosis}}
Hereditary {{c1::angioedema}}

Name an adverse neurologic effect of danazol.

Idiopathic {{c1::intracranial}} {{c1::hypertension::hypertension/hypotension}}

What are the effects of the β2-agonist terbutaline during labor?

{{c1::Relaxes::Contracts/Relaxes}} the uterus
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} contraction frequency during labor

Why are tocolytics used in preterm labor?

Decreases {{c1::contraction}} frequency
fields.Back Extra: This allows time for promoting fetal lung maturity by steroids or transfer to an appropriate care facility.

fields.Text:
Name three tocolytics and their drug classes.

{{c1::Indomethacin}} → {{c2::NSAID}}
{{c1::Terbutaline}} → {{c2::β2}}-agonist
{{c1::Nifedipine}} → {{c2::Ca2+}} channel blocker

How does a copper intrauterine device work?

Produces a local {{c1::inflammatory}} reaction that is {{c1::toxic}} to sperm and ova → Prevents fertilization and implantation

What is a contraindication for placing a copper intrauterine device?

Active pelvic {{c1::infection}}

What are three adverse effects of a copper intrauterine device?

{{c1::Longer::Longer/Shorter}} menses
{{c1::Dysmenorrhea}}
Risk of {{c1::pelvic inflammatory}} disease

What is the most effective form of emergency contraception?

{{c1::Copper}}-containing intrauterine device

Aside from preventing ovulation, how else do progestins prevent pregnancy?

{{c1::Thickens::Thickens/Thins}} cervical mucus
Inhibits {{c1::endometrial}} proliferation

What is the mechanism of action by which combined oral contraceptives prevent ovulation?

Inhibits {{c1::LH}} and {{c1::FSH}} → Blocks {{c1::estrogen}} and {{c1::LH surges}}

What are three forms of combined contraception delivery?

{{c1::Pills}}
{{c1::Patch}}
Vaginal {{c1::ring}}

What are the five contraindications of combined oral contraception?

{{c1::Smoking}} if over 35 years of age
Increased risk of {{c1::cardiovascular}} disease
{{c1::Migraines}}
{{c1::Liver::Organ}} disease
{{c1::Breast}} cancer

What are the adverse effects of combined contraceptives?

{{c1::Breakthrough}} menstrual bleeding
Breast {{c1::tenderness}}
{{c1::Hepatic}} adenomas
Venous {{c1::thromboembolism}}

What combination of antiprogestin and prostaglandin is used for termination of pregnancy?

{{c1::Mifepristone}}
{{c1::Misoprostol}}

What is the mechanism of action of mifepristone and ulipristal?

Competitively inhibit {{c1::progestins}} at {{c1::progesterone}} receptors

Which antiprogestin can be used for emergency contraception?

{{c1::Ulipristal}}

How is progesterone administered?

{{c1::Pill}}
{{c1::Implant}}
{{c1::Depot}} injection
{{c1::Intrauterine}} device

What does bleeding on withdrawal of progestin during a progestin challenge represent?

Rules out chronic {{c1::anovulation}} without {{c1::estrogen}}
Rules out {{c1::anatomic}} defects

Name three clinical indications for progestins.

{{c1::Contraception}}
Abnormal uterine {{c1::bleeding}}
{{c1::Endometrial}} cancer

What effect do progestins have on the endometrium?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} endometrial lining growth
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} vascularization
{{c1::Thickening::Thickening/Thinning}} of the cervical mucus

What drug class do levonorgestrel, medroxyprogesterone, etonogestrel, norethindrone, and megestrol belong to?

{{c1::Progestins}}

What benefit does hormone replacement therapy have for bones?

Increases {{c1::estrogen}} → Decreases {{c1::osteoclast}} activity

Why is progesterone/progestin added to a patient's estrogen replacement regimen?

To decrease the risk of {{c1::endometrial}} cancer

What are two indications for hormone replacement therapy?

Prevention of {{c1::menopausal}} symptoms
{{c1::Osteoporosis}}

Increased risk of what adverse events is associated with hormone replacement therapy where estrogen is combined with progesterone?

{{c1::Cardiovascular}} adverse events

What is the mechanism of action of the aromatase inhibitors?

Inhibits {{c1::peripheral::central/peripheral}} conversion of {{c1::androgens}} to {{c1::estrogen}}

Anastrozole, letrozole, and exemestane belong to what drug class?

{{c1::Aromatase}} inhibitors

What are aromatase inhibitors indicated for?

{{c1::Estrogen}} receptor-positive {{c1::breast}} cancer in {{c1::postmenopausal}} women

What are the major adverse effects of clomiphene?

{{c1::Hot flashes}}
Multiple simultaneous {{c1::pregnancies}}
Ovarian {{c1::enlargement}}
{{c1::Visual}} disturbances

How is raloxifene safer compared to tamoxifen?

Raloxifene does not increase the risk of {{c1::endometrial}} cancer when compared to tamoxifen

Which SERM reduces the resorption of bone and is used to treat osteoporosis?

{{c1::Raloxifene}}
fields.Back Extra: This acts as an estrogen receptor agonist in bone and reduces bone resorption.

fields.Text:
What are the two major adverse effects of tamoxifen?

{{c1::Endometrial}} cancer
Increase in {{c1::thromboembolic}} events (especially in smokers)

What are tamoxifen's effects on the breast, bone, and endometrium?

{{c1::Antagonist::Agonist/Antagonist}} on breast tissue
{{c1::Agonist::Agonist/Antagonist}} on bone
Partial {{c1::agonist::agonist/antagonist}} on endometrial tissue

What is the primary clinical use for clomiphene?

{{c1::Infertility}} due to {{c1::anovulation}}

Describe the mechanism by which clomiphene acts on the hypothalamus to increase ovulation.

Binds to {{c1::estrogen}} receptors in the hypothalamus → Blocks {{c1::negative::positive/negative}} feedback of LH and FSH → {{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} release of LH and FSH → Promotes ovulation

What is tamoxifen primarily used to treat?

{{c1::Estrogen}} and/or {{c1::progesterone}} receptor-positive {{c1::breast}} cancer

How is the action of raloxifene different from that of tamoxifen?

Tamoxifen is a partial {{c1::agonist::agonist/antagonist}} at the uterus
Raloxifene is an {{c1::antagonist::agonist/antagonist}} at the uterus

What option may be recommended in a female patient with history of deep venous thrombosis desiring birth control?

{{c1::Non-estrogen::Estrogen/Non-estrogen}} birth control methods

What three contraindications should be screened for before prescribing estrogen therapy?

Estrogen receptor-positive {{c1::breast}} cancer
History of {{c1::deep venous thrombosis}}
Tobacco use in women over {{c1::35}} years of age

What is the adverse effect of using diethylstilbesterol?

{{c1::Clear cell}} adenoma of the vagina in females exposed in utero

Why should estrogens be given with progesterone when possible?

Risk of {{c1::endometrial}} cancer increases without progesterone

Name four conditions in women that are treated with estrogen.

{{c1::Hypogonadism::Hypergonadism/Hypogonadism}}
{{c1::Ovarian}} failure
{{c1::Menstrual}} abnormalities
Postmenopausal {{c1::hormone}} deficiency

What is the mechanism of action of ethinyl estradiol, diethylstilbestrol, and mestranol?

Binds to {{c1::estrogen}} receptors → Acts as an {{c1::agonist::agonist/antagonist}}

What treatment is indicated for irregular menses?

{{c1::Combined oral contraceptive pills}}

What may make degarelix a better option than leuprolide for the treatment of prostate cancer?

No tumor {{c1::flare}}

How does degarelix work?

{{c1::GnRH}} antagonist

What are the two main adverse effects of degarelix?

{{c1::Hot flashes}}
{{c1::Hepatotoxicity}}

What is degarelix typically used to treat?

{{c1::Prostate}} cancer

Why do patients treated with leuprolide sometimes experience a "tumor flare" during treatment?

Temporarily acts as a {{c1::GnRH}} agonist before {{c1::downregulating::upregulating/downregulating}} the receptor when given in a continuous fashion

Leuprolide is an analog of what hormone?

{{c1::GnRH}}

Is leuprolide given in a pulsatile or continuous fashion to treat infertility?

{{c1::Pulsatile}}
fields.Back Extra: It will act as a GnRH agonist.

fields.Text:
Continuous administration of leuprolide is used to treat what conditions?

Uterine {{c1::fibroids}}
{{c1::Endometriosis}}
{{c1::Prostate}} cancer
{{c1::Precocious}} puberty

How does leuprolide work when given in continuous versus pulsatile fashion?

Acts as a GnRH {{c1::antagonist::agonist/antagonist}} when administered continuously
Acts as a GnRH {{c1::agonist::agonist/antagonist}} when administered in a pulsatile manner

What are three adverse hormonal effects of leuprolide?

Decreased {{c1::libido}}
{{c1::Hypogonadism::Hypergonadism/Hypogonadism}}
{{c1::Erectile}} dysfunction

What two hormones are decreased due to the antagonistic effect of goserelin and leuprolide?

{{c1::FSH}}
{{c1::LH}}

Aromatase is responsible for the generation of which forms of estrogen?

{{c1::Estradiol}}
{{c1::Estrone}}

Name three antiandrogenic drugs that function by preventing androgens from binding to their specific receptors.

{{c1::Flutamide}}
{{c1::Cyproterone}}
{{c1::Spironolactone}}

What drug is useful for lowering dihydrotestosterone levels?

{{c1::Finasteride}}

How do tamoxifen and raloxifene modulate the effects of estrogen?

Binds to {{c1::estrogen}} receptors → Blocks or stimulates {{c1::gene expression}} in {{c1::estrogen}}-responsive cells

Which two drugs inhibit CYP450c17, an enzyme that is important for synthesis of androgens?

{{c1::Ketoconazole}}
{{c1::Danazol}}

Leydig cells are stimulated by which hormone to produce testosterone?

{{c1::LH}}

How do GnRH agonists influence LH and FSH release from the anterior pituitary?

Pulsatile administration → {{c1::Agonists::Agonists/Antagonists}}
Continuous administration → {{c1::Antagonists::Agonists/Antagonists}}

How do LH and FSH levels change with the administration of clomiphene?

LH levels {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}}
FSH levels {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}}
fields.Back Extra: It prevents normal feedback inhibition of GnRH.

fields.Text:
Where is GnRH synthesized and released from?

Synthesized in the {{c1::hypothalamus}}
Released from the {{c1::anterior pituitary}}

At what organ level do oral contraceptives influence the action of reproductive hormones?

{{c1::Ovaries}}

Which two drugs directly inhibit the ovaries to reduce levels of androgens and estrogens?

{{c1::Oral contraceptives}}
{{c1::Danazol}}

What levels of estrogen, LH, and FSH are found in a patient with Turner syndrome?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} estrogen levels
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} LH levels
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} FSH levels

What causes the short stature in females with Turner syndrome?

{{c1::SHOX}} gene
fields.Back Extra: This can be prevented with growth hormone therapy.

fields.Text:
Describe the genitalia of a patient with ovotesticular disorder of sex development.

{{c1::Ambiguous}} genitalia

What is the most common mutation behind sex chromosome disorders?

{{c1::Aneuploidy}} caused by {{c1::meiotic nondisjunction}}

How is fertility affected by an XYY karyotype?

Fertility {{c1::is not::is/is not}} affected

Is male or female gonadal tissue more prevalent in individuals with ovotesticular disorder of sex development?

{{c1::Female::Male/Female}} tissue

What is commonly found on biopsy of the genitals of patients with both (46,XX) and (46,XY) chromosomes?

The presence of {{c1::ovotestis}}
fields.Back Extra: The condition is known as ovotesticular disorder and was formerly called true hermaphroditism.

fields.Text:
What developmental disorder is associated with double Y males?

{{c1::Autism spectrum}} disorders

What are two interventions that can be used to help a woman with Turner syndrome become pregnant?

{{c1::In vitro fertilization}}
Administration of exogenous {{c1::progesterone}} and {{c1::estradiol-17β}}

Describe how a female with Turner syndrome can exhibit genetic mosaicism.

{{c1::Mitosis}} errors occur after formation of the {{c1::zygote}} → Loss of the {{c1::sex}} chromosome in some cells

What is the most common cause of primary amenorrhea?

{{c1::Turner}} syndrome

What will an ovarian biopsy show in a patient with Turner syndrome?

Ovarian {{c1::dysgenesis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as a streak ovary.

fields.Text:
What two cardiovascular abnormalites are associated with Turner syndrome?

{{c1::Bicuspid}} aortic valve
{{c1::Coarctation}} of the aorta

What is unique about menarche and menopause in females with Turner syndrome?

Menopause occurs {{c1::before::before/after}} menarche

How many Barr bodies are seen when the cells of a patient with Turner syndrome are examined under the microscope?

{{c1::0}}

A tall boy is noted to have testicular atrophy, gynecomastia, long extremities, and an eunuchoid body shape. What may intelligence testing reveal?

Developmental {{c1::delay}}

In XXY males, how are the levels of testosterone and estrogen affected?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} testosterone levels
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} estrogen levels
fields.Back Extra: Abnormal Leydig cell function causes decreased testosterone, resulting in increased LH and estrogen.

fields.Text:
What mechanism causes elevated FSH levels in Klinefelter syndrome?

Dysgenesis of the {{c1::seminiferous tubules}} → Reduced {{c1::inhibin B}} production → Increased FSH production

Testicular atrophy and infertility in a tall male patient with eunuchoid proportions may indicate which disorder of sex chromosomes?

{{c1::Klinefelter}} syndrome

What is the clinical significance of a Barr body in a male patient?

Indicates {{c1::Klinefelter}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: A Barr body is an inactivated X chromosome.

fields.Text:
Patients with Turner syndrome with (45,X/46,XY) mosaicism have an increased risk for development of what type of tumor?

{{c1::Gonadoblastoma}}

In patients with Turner syndrome due to a meiosis error, in which gamete does the error typically occur?

{{c1::Paternal::Maternal/Paternal}} gamete

What are two possible conditions that cause 46,XX disorder of sex development?

Congenital {{c1::adrenal hyperplasia}}
Exogenous {{c1::androgen}} exposure in utero

What is the diagnosis when a patient has ovaries but the external genitalia are virilized or ambiguous?

{{c1::46}},{{c1::XX}} disorder of sex development

What is the most common cause of 46,XY disorder of sex development?

{{c1::Androgen insensitivity}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as testicular feminization.

fields.Text:
What internal and external sex organs are present in a patient with 46,XY disorder of sex development?

Presence of {{c1::testes}}
{{c1::Female::Male/Female}} or {{c1::ambiguous}} external genitalia
fields.Back Extra: This is most commonly caused by androgen insensitivity syndrome.

fields.Text:
What are two conditions that can result in the presence of a uterus but lack of breasts in a female?

{{c1::Hypogonadotropic::Hypergonadotropic/Hypogonadotropic}} {{c1::hypogonadism::hypergonadism/hypogonadism}}
{{c1::Hypergonadotropic::Hypergonadotropic/Hypogonadotropic}} {{c1::hypogonadism::hypergonadism/hypogonadism}}

What disorder causes the absence of a uterus but the presence of breasts in a genotypic female?

{{c1::Uterovaginal agenesis}}

A male presents with breasts but no uterus. What disorder of sex development does he have?

{{c1::Androgen insensitivity}} in a genotypic male

What is the mechanism of primary dysmenorrhea?

Excessive uterine {{c1::contractions}} → Decrease in {{c1::blood}} loss → Ischemic pain

What is the treatment for primary dysmenorrhea?

{{c1::NSAIDs}}
{{c1::Acetaminophen}}
{{c1::Hormonal contraceptives}}

What molecules mediate primary dysmenorrhea?

{{c1::Prostaglandins}}

What is the most common ovarian mass in young women?

{{c1::Follicular}} cyst

What type of ovarian cysts are associated with choriocarcinoma and hydatidiform moles?

{{c1::Theca lutein}} cysts

What type of ovarian cyst is most likely to form in the presence of increased hCG stimulation?

{{c1::Theca lutein}} cyst

What ovarian mass is associated with hyperestrogenism and endometrial hyperplasia in young females?

{{c1::Follicular}} cyst

Compare the mechanism of formation of a follicular cyst with that of a theca lutein cyst.

Follicular cysts are caused by failure of a(n) {{c1::mature::mature/immature}} follicle to {{c1::rupture}} and {{c1::ovulate}}
Theca lutein cysts are due to overstimulation by {{c1::hCG}}

How is a corpus luteal cyst formed?

Failure of corpus luteum to {{c1::involute}} after {{c1::ovulation}}

What is the usual clinical course of follicular and corpus luteal cysts?

Usually resolves {{c1::spontaneously}}

What benign ovarian tumor presents as a large, multiloculated mass, lined by mucus-secreting epithelium?

{{c1::Mucinous cystadenoma}}

Name the condition in which an ovarian tumor presents with a slowly enlarging collection of mucinous material in the peritoneum.

{{c1::Pseudomyxoma peritonei}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to a mucinous cystadenoma.

fields.Text:
On microscopic examination, how do findings of an immature teratoma differ from those of a mature teratoma?

An immature teratoma contains {{c1::fetal}} tissue, particularly {{c1::neuroectodermal}} tissue
A mature teratoma contains tissue from all 3 {{c1::germ}} layers

Which ovarian tumor is very aggressive and appears as a yellow, solid, and friable hemorrhagic mass on gross pathologic exam?

{{c1::Yolk sac}} tumor
fields.Back Extra: This is also called an endodermal sinus.

fields.Text:
Describe the histologic findings of a yolk sac tumor.



{{c1::Schiller-Duval bodies}} resemble glomeruli
fields.Back Extra:
Yolk sac tumors present with increased α-fetoprotein levels.

Yolk sac tumors occur in children and young females.

fields.Text:
What neoplasm is associated with the biopsy findings in the image, showing sheets of uniform "fried egg" cells?



{{c1::Dysgerminoma}}

What is the most common malignant ovarian tumor in adolescents?

{{c1::Dysgerminoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is equivalent to the male seminoma, but rarer.

fields.Text:
What common malignant ovarian neoplasm has psamomma bodies on histology?

{{c1::Serous}} carcinoma

Name four generalized symptoms and findings you would expect to see in a patient with an ovarian neoplasm.

{{c1::Adnexal}} mass
Bowel {{c1::obstruction}}
Abdominal {{c1::distention}}
Pleural {{c1::effusion}}

Can CA 125 be used for screening for ovarian cancer?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: It is a general marker for ovarian neoplasia used to monitor disease progression, but it is not good for screening.

fields.Text:
Which benign ovarian neoplasm is lined by a fallopian tube-like epithelium?

{{c1::Serous cystadenoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the most common ovarian neoplasm.

fields.Text:
What is the malignant potential of a mature cystic teratoma?

Risk of malignant transformation is {{c1::rare}}
fields.Back Extra: If it occurs, squamous cell carcinoma usually develops.

fields.Text:
What is the classic triad of Meigs syndrome?

{{c1::Ascites}}
Ovarian {{c1::fibroma}}
Pleural {{c1::effusion}}

Microscopic analysis of tissue from an ovarian mass reveals bundles of spindle-shaped fibroblasts. Is this a benign neoplasm?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a fibroma of the ovary.

fields.Text:
What benign ovarian neoplasm has bladder-like epithelium with "coffee bean" nuclei on hematoxylin and eosin stain?

{{c1::Brenner}} tumor

What serum marker is used to monitor response to therapy and relapse in patients with epithelial ovarian cancer?

{{c1::CA 125}}

What benign sex cord stromal ovarian tumor may present with an increased estrogen level and abnormal uterine bleeding in postmenopausal women?

{{c1::Thecoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This produces estrogen and causes endometrial hyperplasia and bleeding.

fields.Text:
What are four protective factors that decrease a woman's risk for developing ovarian neoplasms?

Previous {{c1::pregnancy}}
Use of {{c1::oral contraceptives pills}}
Tubal {{c1::ligation}}
History of {{c1::breastfeeding}}

What are four risk factors for ovarian cancer?

Advanced {{c1::age}}
Increased number of lifetime {{c1::ovulations}}
{{c1::Endometriosis}}
{{c1::Genetic}} predisposition

What hormones can be produced by granulosa cell tumors?

{{c1::Estrogen}}
{{c1::Progesterone}}

What are the three main cell types that can give rise to ovarian neoplasms?

{{c1::Surface epithelium}}
{{c1::Germ}} cells
{{c1::Sex cord stromal}} cells

What type of germ cell tumor may cause hyperthyroidism?

{{c1::Struma ovarii}}
fields.Back Extra: Functional thyroid tissue within a monodermal teratoma can cause symptoms of hyperthyroidism.

fields.Text:
What is the most common germ cell ovarian tumor in girls and women of reproductive age?

{{c1::Mature cystic teratoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as a dermoid cyst.

fields.Text:
What sex cord stromal tumor may present with abnormal uterine bleeding, endometrial hyperplasia, and breast tenderness with the histologic findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Granulosa cell}} tumor

What is seen on gross examination of a Brenner tumor?

An {{c1::encapsulated}} solid mass with a {{c1::pale yellow-tan::color}} appearance

What tumor is shown in the image?



{{c1::Mature cystic teratoma}} with all 3 germ layers

Name the histologic finding of eosinophilic fluid collections surrounded by granulosa cells, resembling primordial follicles.

{{c1::Call-Exner bodies}}

What hormone may be produced by a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor?

{{c1::Androgen}}

In what age range are most epithelial ovarian tumors diagnosed?

{{c1::Postmenopausal}} women
Over {{c1::55}} years of age

Dysgerminomas, teratomas, and yolk sac tumors are all examples of what category of ovarian neoplasms?

{{c1::Germ cell}} tumors

Describe the three ways in which a germ cell tumor may differentiate.

May remain {{c1::undifferentiated}}
Form {{c1::extra-embryonic}} structures
Form {{c1::somatic}} structures

What does the embryonic sex cord differentiate into in females versus males?

Females → {{c1::Theca}} cells and {{c1::granulosa}} cells
Males → {{c1::Sertoli}} cells and {{c1::Leydig}} cells of the seminiferous tubules

What is the primary reason that testosterone levels are normal in those with cryptorchidism?

{{c1::Leydig}} cell function is unaffected by the {{c1::higher::higher/lower}} testicular temperature seen in cryptorchidism

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism associated with the reduced fertility seen in those with cryptorchidism?

Impaired {{c1::spermatogenesis}}

What are the two most common complications seen in patients with cryptorchidism?

Increased risk of {{c1::infertility}}
{{c1::Germ cell}} tumors

What are the expected levels of inhibin B, FSH, LH, and testosterone in patients with cryptorchidism?

{{c1::Decreased}} inhibin B levels
{{c1::Increased}} FSH levels
{{c1::Increased}} LH levels
{{c1::Normal}} testosterone levels if cryptorchidism is unilateral
{{c1::Decreased}} testosterone levels if cryptorchidism is bilateral

What is the major risk factor for the development of cryptorchidism?

{{c1::Prematurity}}

What is the primary treatment method for patients with cryptorchidism?

Most cases resolve {{c1::spontaneously}}
If testicles have not descended by 2 years of age, {{c1::orchiopexy}} may be performed

What is the definition of testicular torsion?

{{c1::Rotation}} of the testicle around the {{c1::spermatic cord}} and {{c1::vascular pedicle}}

In what age group is testicular torsion most commonly seen?

{{c1::12}} to {{c1::18}} years of age

Why must bilateral orchiopexy be performed in patients with testicular torsion?

The unaffected testis is at an increased risk for {{c1::torsion}}

What two major physical examination findings are typically found in a patient with testicular torsion?

{{c1::High::High/Low}}-riding testis
Absent {{c1::cremasteric}} reflex

What is the major treatment strategy for patients with testicular torsion?

{{c1::Orchiopexy}} within 6 hours
{{c1::Manual detorsion}} if surgery is unavailable within this timeframe

What is the most common cause of the development of testicular torsion?

Congenital inadequate fixation of the testis to the {{c1::tunica vaginalis}} → {{c1::Horizontal::Horizontal/Vertical}} positioning of the testis
fields.Back Extra: This is known as the "bell clapper" deformity.

fields.Text:
What are two major treatment options for patients with a varicocele?

Surgical {{c1::ligation}}
{{c1::Embolization}} if it is associated with infertility or pain

What is the major reason varicoceles are more common on the left side of the body?

The left {{c1::gonadal}} vein drains into the left {{c1::renal}} vein → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} venous pressure
fields.Back Extra: This is a path of higher resistance.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism associated with the development of a varicocele?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} venous pressure → Dilation of the {{c1::pampiniform plexus}}

What are two major ways to clinically diagnose a varicocele?

{{c1::Ultrasound}}
Performance of a {{c1::standing::standing/sitting}} clinical exam with the {{c1::Valsalva}} maneuver → {{c1::Distention}} on visual inspection and the "{{c1::bag of worms}}" finding on palpation

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism by which the pathology leads to infertility?



{{c1::Temperature}} increase in the scrotum impairs {{c1::spermatogenesis}}

What are the two major indications for intervention in a patient with a varicocele?

{{c1::Pain}}
{{c1::Infertility}}

What is the significance of a patient with a right-sided varicocele that does not resolve when the patient lies supine?

Indicates {{c1::inferior vena cava}} obstruction

What are the four most common locations of extragonadal germ cell tumors found in adults?

{{c1::Mediastinum}}
{{c1::Retroperitoneum}}
{{c1::Pineal}} region
{{c1::Suprasellar}} region
fields.Back Extra: They are generally in midline locations.

fields.Text:
What is the most common extragonadal germ cell tumor seen in infants and young children?

{{c1::Sacrococcygeal teratoma}}

What is the natural disease course of a congenital hydrocele?

Most resolve spontaneously by {{c1::1}} year(s) of age

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism associated with the development of a spermatocele?

Cyst due to the {{c1::dilation::constriction/dilation}} of an {{c1::epididymal duct}} or {{c1::rete testis}}

What are the three most common causes of an acquired hydrocele?

{{c1::Trauma}}
{{c1::Infection}}
{{c1::Tumor}}
fields.Back Extra: These can cause fluid to collect in the scrotum.

fields.Text:
What is the most common cause of scrotal swelling in an infant?

Incomplete obliteration of the {{c1::processus vaginalis}} → Congenital hydrocele

How can transillumination help to determine whether a scrotal mass is benign or malignant?

Benign masses {{c1::can::can/cannot}} be transilluminated
Malignant masses {{c1::cannot::can/cannot}} be transilluminated

What is the difference in the mechanisms behind development of communicating and noncommunicating hydroceles?

Communicating hydroceles are {{c1::congenital}}
Noncommunicating hydroceles are {{c1::acquired}}

What is the equivalent of a seminoma in female patients?

{{c1::Ovarian dysgerminoma}}

What tumor subtype is least likely in a male infant with a testicular mass?

{{c1::Seminomas}}
fields.Back Extra: They do not occur in infancy.

fields.Text:
What pathophysiologic mechanism leads to the development of hyperthyroidism and gynecomastia in patients with choriocarcinomas?

Increased {{c1::hCG}} produced by the tumor

Which testicular germ cell tumor typically metastasizes to the lungs and brain?

{{c1::Choriocarcinoma}}

Which two conditions are commonly associated with increased risk of the development of testicular germ cell tumors in young men?

{{c1::Cryptorchidism}}
{{c1::Klinefelter}} syndrome

What germ cell tumor presents as a firm, painless swelling in the testicle and is yellow and mucinous on gross examination?

{{c1::Yolk sac}} tumor
fields.Back Extra: This is also called an endodermal sinus tumor.

fields.Text:
What germ cell tumor demonstrates Schiller-Duval bodies and an increased α-​​​​​​fetoprotein level in children?

{{c1::Yolk sac}} tumor
