fields.Back Extra: This is also called an endodermal sinus tumor.

fields.Text:
What germ cell tumor presents as a hemorrhagic, necrotic testicular mass, often with mixed glandular/papillary morphology?

{{c1::Embryonal}} carcinoma

How does the prognosis of an embryonal carcinoma compare with that of a seminoma?

Prognosis of an embryonal carcinoma is {{c1::worse::better/worse}}

What malignant painful testicular germ cell tumor typically demonstrates glandular/papillary histopathology and is typically mixed with other tumor types?

{{c1::Embryonal}} carcinoma

What is the most common type of testicular tumor?

{{c1::Seminoma}}

What is the malignancy potential of mature teratomas in men?

Mature teratomas may be {{c1::malignant::benign/malignant}} in men

What painless testicular mass typically demonstrates lobules of large cells with a "fried egg" appearance on pathologic examination?

{{c1::Seminoma}}

Are germ cell tumors of the testicle usually benign or malignant?

{{c1::Malignant}}
fields.Back Extra: Teratomas in children are usually benign.

fields.Text:
What germ cell tumor typically demonstrates disordered syncytiotrophoblasts and cytotrophoblasts on biopsy?

{{c1::Choriocarcinoma}}

Which type of testicular tumor is most common?

{{c1::Germ::Germ/Non-germ}} cell tumors make up 95% of testicular tumors
fields.Back Extra: Non-germ cell tumors account for the remaining 5% of testicular tumors.

fields.Text:
Which testicular non-germ cell tumors tend to be malignant?

{{c1::Testicular}} lymphoma

What are Sertoli cell tumors derived from?

{{c1::Sex cord stroma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also called an androblastoma.

fields.Text:
What is the most common testicular cancer among older men?

{{c1::Testicular}} lymphoma
fields.Back Extra: It is not a primary tumor, but arises when the lymphoma metastasizes to the testes.

fields.Text:
What color are Leydig cell tumors typically on gross examination?

{{c1::Golden brown}}

What symptom would be expected to be seen in an adult with a testicular Leydig cell tumor?

{{c1::Gynecomastia}} in men
fields.Back Extra: This is due to an overproduction of androgens and estrogens.

fields.Text:
What symptom would you expect to see in a child with a testicular Leydig cell tumor?

{{c1::Precocious}} puberty in boys
fields.Back Extra: This is due to an overproduction of estrogens and androgens.

fields.Text:
What are the eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions found on histologic examination of a Leydig cell tumor called?

{{c1::Reinke crystals}}

What structure does sex cord stroma normally develop into?

Boys → {{c1::Leydig}} cells and {{c1::Sertoli}} cells
Girls → {{c1::Theca}} cells and {{c1::granulosa}} cells

What is the major function of the cells from which testicular germ cell tumors arise?

They normally produce {{c1::sperm}}

Which hormone levels are typically increased in patients with a teratoma?

{{c1::None}}
fields.Back Extra: Hormone levels are not used as a marker for teratoma.

fields.Text:
What four germ cell tumors typically present with high β-hCG levels?

{{c1::Choriocarcinoma}}
{{c1::Embryonal}} carcinoma
{{c1::Seminoma}}
{{c1::Yolk sac}} tumor

Which hormone is significantly increased in patients with choriocarcinoma?

{{c1::β-hCG}}

Which type of germ cell tumor is associated with elevated levels of PLAP?

{{c1::Seminoma}}

Which two hormones are typically elevated in patients with a yolk sac tumor?

{{c1::α-fetoprotein}} is significantly increased
{{c1::β-hCG}} may be increased

Which two hormones are typically elevated in patients with an embryonal carcinoma?

{{c1::β-hCG}} is elevated
{{c1::α-fetoprotein}} could be elevated in the mixed type

What is the major complication of mumps orchitis?

Increased risk of {{c1::infertility}}

What are the two most common causes of epididymitis and orchitis in young men?

{{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}}
{{c1::Neisseria gonorrhoeae}}

What two organisms are typically responsible for epididymitis and orchitis in elderly men?

{{c1::Escherichia coli}}
{{c1::Pseudomonas}}
fields.Back Extra: They are associated with urinary tract infections and benign prostatic hyperplasia.

fields.Text:
What are the typical microscopic findings in the testicular tissue of a patient with autoimmune orchitis?

{{c1::Granulomas}} involving {{c1::seminiferous tubules}}

What major physical examination finding differentiates epididymitis from orchitis?

{{c1::Prehn}} sign is seen in epididymitis

What disease involves the inflammation of the testis presenting with testicular pain and swelling?

{{c1::Orchitis}}

What is the risk of the development of malignancy in patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia?

{{c1::Negligent}}

Which lobes of the prostate are typically affected in benign prostatic hyperplasia?

{{c1::Lateral}} lobe
{{c1::Middle}} lobe
fields.Back Extra: Hypertrophy causes compression of the urethra → Difficulty stopping/starting urine stream

fields.Text:
What is the typical age range for the presentation of benign prostatic hyperplasia?

Over {{c1::50}} years of age

What characteristic findings are expected on the digital rectal exam of a patient with benign prostatic hyperplasia?

{{c1::Smooth::Smooth/Rough}}, {{c1::elastic::elastic/inelastic}}, {{c1::firm}} nodular enlargement of the prostate

What are the four common complications associated with benign prostatic hyperplasia?

{{c1::Hydronephrosis}}
{{c1::Distention}} of the bladder
{{c1::Hypertrophy::Hypertrophy/Hypotrophy}} of the bladder
{{c1::Urinary}} tract infections

What mechanism is responsible for α1-antagonists aiding in the treatment of prostatic hyperplasia?

α1-antagonists {{c1::relax::constrict/relax}} prostate smooth muscle

What benign pathology often leads to increased frequency of urination, nocturia, and difficulty starting and stopping the urinary stream in elderly males?

{{c1::Benign prostatic hyperplasia}}

What is the next step in the management of benign prostatic hyperplasia after the failure of medical therapy?

Surgical {{c1::resection}}

What mechanism is responsible for finasteride being effective in the management of benign prostatic hyperplasia?

Finasteride is a {{c1::5α-reductase}} inhibitor → Decreased conversion of {{c1::testosterone}} to {{c1::dihydrotestosterone}} → Decreased prostatic growth

What mechanism is responsible for tadalafil being effective in the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia?

As a {{c1::PDE-5}} inhibitor, tadalafil {{c1::relaxes::constricts/relaxes}} vascular smooth muscle

What is the major difference between the causes of acute prostatitis and chronic prostatitis?

Acute prostatitis is usually {{c1::bacterial}}
Chronic prostatitis may be secondary to previous {{c1::infection}}, {{c1::chemical}} irritation, or {{c1::nerve}} problems

What two bacteria are commonly found in young men with acute prostatitis?

{{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}}
{{c1::Neisseria gonorrhoeae}}

What organism is most commonly implicated in bacterial prostatitis in older men?

{{c1::Escherichia coli}}

What is likely to be seen on the prostate exam in a patient with prostatitis?

{{c1::Tender::Tender/Nontender}}, {{c1::warm}}, and {{c1::enlarged}} prostate

In which lobe of the prostate gland is prostatic adenocarcinoma typically found?

{{c1::Posterior}} lobe
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as the peripheral zone of the prostate gland.

fields.Text:
What is the most common way to diagnose prostatic adenocarcinoma in a patient?

Measurement of {{c1::PSA}} followed by {{c1::needle core biopsy}} of the prostate

What two serum markers may indicate the presence of osteoblastic metastases of prostatic adenocarcinoma?

Increased serum {{c1::ALP}}
Increased serum {{c1::PSA}}

In what age group is prostatic adenocarcinoma most common?

{{c1::Men::Men/Women}} over {{c1::50}} years of age

What are the two most useful tumor markers seen in patients with prostatic adenocarcinoma?

{{c1::PAP}}
{{c1::PSA}}

What is the pathway by which prostatic carcinoma commonly metastasizes to the lumbar spine?

Via the {{c1::Batson venous plexus}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as the vertebral venous plexus.

fields.Text:
What histologic grading scale is typically used in prostatic adenocarcinoma?

{{c1::Gleason}} grade
fields.Back Extra: This is based on glandular architecture and closely correlates with metastatic potential.

fields.Text:
What is the major treatment for the patient with the physical examination shown?



{{c1::Collagenase}} injections
{{c1::Surgery}} once curvature stabilizes

What is the major difference between Peyronie disease and penile fracture?

Penile fracture involves rupture of the {{c1::corpora cavernosa}} from forced bending
Peyronie disease is an abnormal curvature from {{c1::fibrous plaques}}

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism associated with Peyronie disease?

Accumulation of {{c1::fibrous plaques}} within the {{c1::tunica albuginea}} → Abnormal curvature of the penis

Which in situ lesion that is a precursor of squamous cell carcinoma of the penis typically presents with leukoplakia?

{{c1::Bowen}} disease

Which three geographic regions have the highest prevalence of penile squamous cell carcinoma?

{{c1::South America}}
{{c1::Asia}}
{{c1::Africa}}

What are three major treatment options for patients with ischemic priapism?

Intracavernosal {{c1::phenylephrine}}
Corporal {{c1::aspiration}}
Surgical {{c1::decompression}} to prevent ischemia

What are the two major medications that can cause ischemic priapism?

{{c1::Sildenafil}}
{{c1::Trazodone}}
fields.Back Extra: It can cause a painful sustained erection that lasts over 4 hours.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism of ischemic priapism associated with sickle cell disease?

Abnormally shaped or sickled red blood cells block venous drainage of the {{c1::corpus cavernosum}} → Venous {{c1::pooling}} → Priapism

Which precursor in situ lesion of squamous cell carcinoma of the penis presents with the findings shown?



{{c1::Erythroplasia of Queyrat}}

What penile carcinoma in situ presents as reddish papules?

{{c1::Bowenoid papulosis}}

What causes the increase in LH found in patients with polycystic ovarian syndrome?

{{c1::Pituitary}} and/or {{c1::hypothalamic}} dysfunction resulting from {{c1::hyperinsulinemia::hyperinsulinemia/hypoinsulinemia}} and/or {{c1::insulin}} resistance

What treatments can regulate the menstrual cycle of a patient with polycystic ovarian syndrome?

Weight {{c1::loss::gain/loss}}
{{c1::Oral contraceptives pills}}

A patient with polycystic ovarian syndrome is at increased risk for what type of cancer?

{{c1::Endometrial}} cancer
fields.Back Extra: This is secondary to unopposed estrogen from repeated anovulatory cycles.

fields.Text:
How does polycystic ovarian syndrome affect LH, FSH, and androgen levels?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} LH levels
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} FSH levels
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} androgen levels

What is the cause of the increased serum testosterone level in a patient with polycystic ovarian syndrome?

Deranged {{c1::steroid}} synthesis by {{c1::theca}} cells due to a {{c1::high::high/low}} LH/FSH ratio → Hyperandrogenism

What is a common cause of amenorrhea/oligomenorrhea that presents with hirsutism, acne, and decreased fertility?

{{c1::Polycystic ovarian}} syndrome

What three medications will treat hirsutism in a patient with polycystic ovarian syndrome?

{{c1::Spironolactone}}
{{c1::Flutamide}}
{{c1::Finasteride}}

What medication may be used to induce ovulation in a patient with polycystic ovarian syndrome who wishes to become pregnant?

{{c1::Clomiphene}}

What are three common comorbid conditions associated with polycystic ovarian syndrome?

{{c1::Type 2 diabetes mellitus}}
{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Obesity}}

How is polycystic ovarian syndrome diagnosed?

Presence of two or more of {{c1::cystic}} or {{c1::enlarged}} ovaries on ultrasound
{{c1::Oligoovulation}} or {{c1::anovulation}}
{{c1::Hyperandrogenism::Hyperandrogenism/Hypoandrogenism}}

What lab abnormalities would be seen in an individual who is suspected of using steroids?

{{c1::High::High/Low}} testosterone levels
{{c1::Low::High/Low}} LH levels

What would be the expected levels of testosterone and LH in a patient with insensitive androgen receptors?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} testosterone levels
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} LH levels

What sex hormone disorder is suspected in a male patient with a low testosterone level and a high LH level?

{{c1::Primary hypergonadotropic hypogonadism}}

What sex hormone disorder is suspected in a male patient with low testosterone and LH levels?

{{c1::Secondary hypogonadotropic hypogonadism}}

How do levels of testosterone and LH distinguish primary hypogonadism from secondary hypogonadism?

Primary hypogonadism → {{c1::Low::High/Low}} testosterone level and {{c1::high::high/low}} LH level
Secondary hypogonadism → {{c1::Low::High/Low}} testosterone level and {{c1::low::high/low}} LH level

What lab test helps distinguish an insensitivity in the androgen receptor from a testosterone-secreting tumor in a patient with elevated testosterone levels?

{{c1::LH}} level
fields.Back Extra: This will be high in a patient with an insensitive androgen receptor and low in a patient with a testosterone-secreting tumor.

fields.Text:
What physical characteristics can we find in a female patient with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism?

{{c1::Uterus}}
No {{c1::breasts}}

What is the difference between hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and müllerian agenesis in female patients?

Patients with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism have a {{c1::uterus}} and no {{c1::breasts}}
Patients with Müllerian agenesis have {{c1::breasts}} and no {{c1::uterus}}

What physical characteristics can we find in patients with androgen insensitivity?

No {{c1::uterus}}
{{c1::Breasts}}

A pregnant patient has evidence of virilization during her pregnancy. Fetal androgens are detected in her blood. What is the diagnosis?

Placental {{c1::aromatase}} deficiency in her fetus
fields.Back Extra: Fetal androgens can cross the placenta and cause maternal virilization.

fields.Text:
A female infant (46,XX) has masculinized genitalia and increased serum testosterone and androstenedione. What is the diagnosis?

Placental {{c1::aromatase}} deficiency
fields.Back Extra: There is an inability to synthesize estrogens from androgens.

fields.Text:
Why is it important to surgically remove the testes in patients with androgen insensitivity syndrome?

To prevent {{c1::malignancy}}

What is the karyotype of a patient with androgen insensitivity syndrome?

({{c1::46}},{{c1::XY}})

What hormone levels distinguish androgen insensitivity syndrome from sex chromosome disorders?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} testosterone levels
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} estrogen levels
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} LH levels
fields.Back Extra: This is not the case with sex chromosome disorders.

fields.Text:
Pelvic exam of a normal-appearing girl reveals a blind-pouch vagina without a palpable uterus and a small, mobile mass in the labia majora. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Androgen insensitivity}} syndrome

What hormone prevents development of the uterus and fallopian tubes?

{{c1::Anti-Müllerian}} hormone from the testes

What are Paget cells?

{{c1::Intraepithelial adenocarcinoma}} cells

What type of noninvasive breast carcinoma demonstrates cells with high-grade nuclei, extensive central necrosis, and dystrophic calcification?



{{c1::Comedocarcinoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a subtype of ductal carcinoma in situ.

fields.Text:
Which invasive breast cancer typically presents without a palpable mass?

{{c1::Inflammatory}} breast cancer

What are the two subtypes of invasive breast carcinoma?

{{c1::Mucinous}}
{{c1::Tubular}}

What type of breast cancer is associated with multiple lesions in the same location and is frequently found in both breasts?

Invasive {{c1::lobular}} carcinoma

What type of invasive carcinoma demonstrates decreased E-cadherin expression leading to an orderly row of cells in "single file" as seen in the image?



Invasive {{c1::lobular}} carcinoma

What must be considered if appropriate antibiotic therapy for suspected mastitis is unsuccessful?

A possible diagnosis of {{c1::inflammatory}} breast cancer
fields.Back Extra: It is often mistaken for mastitis or Paget disease.

fields.Text:
What is an early sign of ductal carcinoma in situ on mammography?

{{c1::Microcalcifications}}

Which invasive breast cancer presents as large, anaplastic cells growing in sheets with lymphocytes and plasma cells?

{{c1::Medullary}} carcinoma

Members of which racial group in the United States are at increased risk for triple-negative breast cancer?

{{c1::Black}} individuals

What type of invasive breast cancer may demonstrate a desmoplastic stroma with small, glandular, duct-like cells on histologic examination?

Invasive {{c1::ductal}} carcinoma

Why is postmenopausal obesity a risk factor for breast cancer?

{{c1::Androstenedione}} is converted to {{c1::estrone}} in adipose tissue
fields.Back Extra: This serves as a major source of estrogen in postmenopausal women.

fields.Text:
What are six nonmodifiable risk factors for breast cancer in women?

{{c1::Aging}}
{{c1::Race}}
History of {{c1::atypical hyperplasia}}
{{c1::Family history}} of breast cancer
{{c1::BRCA1}}/{{c1::BRCA2}} mutations
{{c1::High::High/Low}} total number of menstrual cycles

In which quadrant of the breast will malignant masses most often be found?

{{c1::Upper::Upper/Lower}} {{c1::outer::inner/outer}} quadrant of the breast

What is the single most important prognostic factor in early-stage breast cancer?

{{c1::Axillary}} lymph node involvement

What is the prognostic implication of a malignant breast tumor that is negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2?

{{c1::Poor}} prognosis

What three tumor markers are commonly used for prognosis and to guide therapy in breast cancer?

{{c1::Estrogen}} receptor
{{c1::Progesterone}} receptor
{{c1::HER2}}

From which part of the breast do malignant tumors most commonly arise?

{{c1::Terminal duct lobular unit}}

Which noninvasive breast carcinoma demonstrates ductal lumen filling and engorgement of blood vessels as seen on biopsy?



{{c1::Ductal carcinoma in situ}}

What type of breast cancer can present with breast pain and warm, swollen, erythematous skin around exaggerated hair follicles?



{{c1::Inflammatory}} breast carcinoma

What noninvasive breast carcinoma demonstrates eczematous patches over the nipple and areolar skin as shown in the image?



{{c1::Paget}} disease
fields.Back Extra: The underlying ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive breast cancer extends up the lactiferous ducts and into the skin surrounding the nipple.

fields.Text:
What is the underlying mechanism that causes the peau d’orange appearance often seen in patients with inflammatory breast carcinoma?

Cancer invades the dermal {{c1::lymphatics}} → Pain, redness, and swelling of the skin around exaggerated {{c1::hair follicles}}

What are two risk factors for breast cancer in men?

{{c1::Klinefelter}} syndrome
{{c1::BRCA2}} mutation

What are the five modifiable risk factors for breast cancer in women?

Increased {{c1::estrogen}} exposure
Postmenopausal {{c1::obesity}}
Absence of {{c1::breastfeeding}}
{{c1::Later::Early/Later}} age at first pregnancy
{{c1::Alcohol}} consumption

Which noninvasive type of breast cancer is associated with an increased risk of cancer in both breasts versus only the breast in which it is found?

{{c1::Lobular carcinoma in situ}}

Why is skin dimpling a negative prognostic factor in breast cancers?

Dimpling is caused by invasion of {{c1::pectoral}} muscles, {{c1::deep::superficial/deep}} fascia, and {{c1::Cooper}} ligaments
fields.Back Extra: This indicates a more invasive cancer.

fields.Text:
Which benign breast disease is the most common cause of nipple discharge in females?

{{c1::Intraductal papilloma}}
fields.Back Extra: This may cause serous or bloody discharge.

fields.Text:
What might be seen on biopsy of fat necrosis of the breast?

Necrotic {{c1::fat}}
{{c1::Giant}} cells

What is the treatment for lactational mastitis?

{{c1::Antibiotics}}
Recommendation for continued {{c1::breastfeeding}}

What is the most common causative agent of lactational mastitis?

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}

When is gynecomastia physiologic in males?

Newborns, adolescents, and elderly men may have physiologic breast enlargement due to an increased {{c1::estrogen}}/{{c1::androgen}} ratio at these times

Which hormone influences the size and tenderness of fibroadenomas?

{{c1::Estrogen}}

What congestive heart failure medication can cause bilateral breast enlargement?

{{c1::Spironolactone}}

What are three nonpharmacologic causes of gynecomastia in an adult male?

{{c1::Testicular}} tumors
{{c1::Cirrhosis}}
{{c1::Hypogonadism::Hypergonadism/Hypogonadism}}

What is the likely diagnosis for a woman who presents with a painless breast lump following trauma to her chest?

{{c1::Fat necrosis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a benign process that occurs after an injury to the breast.

fields.Text:
What large, bulky mass in a woman's breast has the characteristic biopsy findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Phyllodes}} tumor
fields.Back Extra: This is indicated by the "leaf-like" projections.

fields.Text:
What benign breast condition presents with generalized pain in both breasts that worsens a few days before a patient's period?

{{c1::Fibrocystic}} breast changes

Where does epithelial hyperplasia occur in a patient with proliferative fibrocystic changes in the breast?

{{c1::Terminal ductal}} epithelium
{{c1::Lobular}} epithelium
fields.Back Extra: It often grows into the lumen of the duct.

fields.Text:
What proliferative fibrocystic breast change is described as stromal fibrosis and acini with calcifications on histologic exam?

{{c1::Sclerosing adenosis}}

What benign breast disease presents with simple fluid-filled cysts, papillary apocrine metaplasia, and stromal fibrosis?

{{c1::Fibrocystic}} changes in the breast
fields.Back Extra: This is a condition that is not associated with increased cancer risk.

fields.Text:
Does intraductal papilloma carry an increased risk of cancer?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: It is associated with a slightly increased risk.

fields.Text:
At what age do phyllodes tumors most commonly arise?

{{c1::40}} years of age

Which benign breast tumor that is small, well-defined, and composed of fibrous tissue and glands occurs most commonly in women less than 35 years of age?

{{c1::Fibroadenoma}}

What benign, fibroepithelial breast tumor is typically found beneath the areola and within the lactiferous ducts?

{{c1::Intraductal papilloma}}

What are the three major benign breast tumors found in women?

{{c1::Fibroadenomas}}
{{c1::Intraductal papillomas}}
{{c1::Phyllodes}} tumors

Where does lobular carcinoma most commonly manifest in the breast?

{{c1::Terminal duct lobular unit}}

What parts of the breast are affected in Paget disease?

{{c1::Lactiferous}} ducts
{{c1::Major}} ducts

What two breast pathologies arise in the stroma?

{{c1::Fibroadenomas}}
{{c1::Phyllodes}} tumor

Name the most common location for ductal carcinoma in situ or ductal carcinoma in the breast.

{{c1::Terminal duct lobular unit}}

Where in the breast do fibrocystic changes manifest?

{{c1::Terminal duct lobular unit}}

What is the most common location for a breast abscess or mastitis?

{{c1::Lactiferous}} ducts
{{c1::Major}} ducts

What are the five pharmaceutical treatments for endometriosis?

{{c1::Oral contraceptive pills}}
{{c1::NSAIDs}}
{{c1::Danazol}}
{{c1::GnRH}} agonists
{{c1::Progestins}}

Name three theories that explain the ectopic implantation of endometrial tissue in patients with endometriosis.

{{c1::Retrograde::Anterograde/Retrograde}} menstrual flow
{{c1::Metaplastic}} transformation of mulitpotent cells
Transportation of endometrial tissue by way of the {{c1::lymphatic}} system

What condition may present as infertility with severe pain during menstruation, intercourse, and defecation?

{{c1::Endometriosis}}

What are the blood-filled cysts in the ovaries shown in the image called?



{{c1::Endometriomas}}
fields.Back Extra:
These are also known as "chocolate cysts".

This is associated with endometriosis.

fields.Text:
What condition should you suspect in a postmenopausal woman who reports irregular vaginal bleeding?

{{c1::Endometrial}} carcinoma
fields.Back Extra: Postmenopausal bleeding is considered to be indicative of cancer until proven otherwise.

fields.Text:
What syndrome is characterized by adhesions and/or fibrosis of the endometrium and is associated with previous dilation and curettage?

{{c1::Asherman}} syndrome

What is the risk of a leiomyoma progressing to leiomyosarcoma?

Malignant transformation to leiomyosarcoma is {{c1::rare}}

What are the three major unwanted/concerning effects of leiomyomas?

Abnormal uterine {{c1::bleeding}}
{{c1::Iron deficiency}} anemia
{{c1::Miscarriage}} due to abnormal uterine shape
fields.Back Extra: Leiomyomas do not carry a high risk of malignant transformation.

fields.Text:
Why will leiomyomas grow during pregnancy and shrink during menopause?

Leiomyomas are {{c1::estrogen}} sensitive

What is the most common benign smooth muscle tumor in females that often presents with multiple discrete tumors?

{{c1::Leiomyomas}}

What is the major risk factor for endometrial hyperplasia?

Increased {{c1::estrogen}} exposure

What are the histologic signs that can predict the risk of progression of endometrial hyperplasia to endometrial carcinoma?

Presence of {{c1::nuclear atypia}} (greatest risk factor)
{{c1::Complex::Simple/Complex}} gland architecture

What is the treatment for adenomyosis?

Administration of {{c1::GnRH}} agonists
{{c1::Hysterectomy}}
{{c1::Excision}} of organized adenomyoma

What is the underlying pathophysiology of adenomyosis?

Hyperplasia of the endometrial {{c1::basalis}} layer → Extension of glandular tissue into the surrounding uterine {{c1::myometrium}}

What infectious uterine condition is associated with retained products of conception following delivery, abortion, miscarriage, or presence of a foreign body?

{{c1::Endometritis}}
fields.Back Extra: Retained tissue acts as nidus for infection by bacteria from the gastrointestinal tract or vagina.

fields.Text:
What uterine tumor demonstrates a whorled pattern of smooth muscle bundles with well-demarcated borders, as shown in the image?



{{c1::Leiomyoma}}

What is the most common tumor in women, as shown in the image?



{{c1::Leiomyoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a type of benign smooth muscle tumor that often presents as multiple discrete tumors.

fields.Text:
Name the disease that presents with abnormal bleeding in a postmenopausal woman and the uterine biopsy findings shown.



{{c1::Endometrial}} carcinoma

What do you expect to see on histologic exam of a biopsy specimen obtained from a patient with chronic endometritis?

{{c1::Plasma}} cells

What uterine condition may present with yellow-brown "powder burn" lesions in the peritoneum visualized on laparoscopy?

{{c1::Endometriosis}}

Which subtype of endometrial carcinoma shows abnormally arranged endometrial glands on histology?

{{c1::Endometrioid}} endometrial carcinoma

Which subtype of endometrial carcinoma is defined by formation of papillae, tufts, and psammoma bodies on histology?

{{c1::Serous}} endometrial carcinoma

What uterine tumor demonstrates proliferation of myometrial smooth muscle tissue with areas of necrosis on histologic exam?

{{c1::Leiomyosarcoma}}

What is the major pathogenic event associated with endometrioid endometrial carcinoma?

Increased {{c1::estrogen}} exposure
Loss of {{c1::PTEN}} or {{c1::mismatch repair}} proteins

Severe calorie restriction, energy expenditure, and stress can result in what type of amenorrhea?

{{c1::Functional hypothalamic}} amenorrhea
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as exercise-induced amenorrhea.

fields.Text:
What are the findings of the "female athlete triad"?

Decreased {{c1::calorie}} availability or excessive {{c1::exercise}}
{{c1::Menstrual}} dysfunction
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} bone mineral density

In functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, what changes occur in levels of cortisol and leptin?

Cortisol level is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} due to stress and excessive exercise
Leptin level is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} due to a decrease in fat

Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea results in what changes in FSH, LH, and estrogen?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} FSH
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} LH
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} estrogen
fields.Back Extra: This is due to a lack of pulsatile GnRH release.

fields.Text:
Female patients engaging in competitive athletics may experience what abnormality in the menstrual cycle?

{{c1::Anovulation}}
fields.Back Extra: This leads to a lack of menstruation.

fields.Text:
What might cause anovulation in a 30-year-old woman with hot flashes, irregular menstrual cycles, and dyspareunia?

{{c1::Premature ovarian}} failure

Name two causes of anovulation, other than pregnancy, that are due to increased levels of circulating estrogens.

{{c1::Polycystic ovarian}} syndrome
{{c1::Obesity}}

Name four endocrine disorders not directly related to the production of FSH, LH, or estrogen that may cause anovulation.

{{c1::Thyroid::Organ}} disorders
{{c1::Cushing}} syndrome
{{c1::Adrenal}} insufficiency
{{c1::Hyperprolactinemia::Hyperprolactinemia/Hypoprolactinemia}}

What condition that results from a chromosomal abnormality may be a cause of anovulation?

{{c1::Turner}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This is due to the presence of streak ovaries and lack of estrogen production.

fields.Text:
A female patient with an eating disorder may experience what abnormality in the menstrual cycle?

{{c1::Anovulation}}
fields.Back Extra: This leads to a lack of menstruation.

fields.Text:
What would you expect to see on ovarian biopsy of a patient with premature ovarian failure?

{{c1::Atresia}} of the ovarian follicles

How are estrogen, FSH, and LH levels affected in primary ovarian insufficiency?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} estrogen level
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} FSH level
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} LH level

What distinguishes primary ovarian insufficiency from menopause?

Menopause occurs {{c1::after::before/after}} the age of 40
Primary ovarian failure occurs {{c1::before::before/after}} the age of 40

What screening test is necessary for a patient with primary ovarian insufficiency?

{{c1::Karyotype}} screening for {{c1::chromosomal}} abnormalities

What method can be used to diagnose cervical cancer after an abnormal Pap smear result has been reported?

{{c1::Colposcopy}}
{{c1::Biopsy}} of abnormal tissue

What is the cellular mechanism by which carcinogenic HPV strains lead to cervical cancer?

HPV-{{c1::16}} and HPV-{{c1::18}} express both the {{c2::E6}} gene, which inhibits {{c3::TP53}}, and the {{c2::E7}} gene, which inhibits {{c3::pRb}}

What are the two major chemical risk factors for cervical dysplasia?

{{c1::Diethylstilbestrol}} exposure
{{c1::Smoking}}

Describe the three levels of classification for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia.

Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia 1 is {{c1::mild}} dysplasia
Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia 2 is {{c1::moderate}} dysplasia
Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia 3 is {{c1::severe}}, {{c1::full}}-thickness, {{c1::irreversible::reversible/irreversible}} dysplasia or {{c1::carcinoma in situ}}

What is the mechanism by which invasive cervical carcinoma can result in renal failure?

{{c1::Lateral::Medial/Lateral}} invasion obstructs the {{c1::ureters}} → {{c1::Hydronephrosis}} → Renal failure

Describe the histologic findings from a Pap smear shown in the image.



The image shows {{c1::koilocytes}}
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by HPV infection.

fields.Text:
What are the two carcinogenic strains of HPV?

HPV-{{c1::16}}
HPV-{{c1::18}}

Where does cervical dysplasia typically first manifest?

{{c1::Basal}} layer of the {{c1::squamocolumnar junction}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as the transformation zone.

fields.Text:
What are the two medical conditions that increase the risk of cervical dysplasia?

{{c1::HPV}} infection
{{c1::Immunocompromised}} state

What are the two major behavioral risk factors for developing cervical dysplasia?

{{c1::Early::Early/Late}} coitarche
{{c1::Multiple}} sexual partners

Does 5α-reductase deficiency occur in males, females, or both?

{{c1::Males}}

What is the inheritance pattern of 5α-reductase deficiency?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What chemical reaction is hindered in patients with 5α-reductase deficiency?

Conversion of {{c1::testosterone}} to {{c1::dihydrotestosterone}}

How are the levels of testosterone, estrogen, and LH altered in patients with 5α-reductase deficiency?

{{c1::Normal}} testosterone levels
{{c1::Normal}} estrogen levels
{{c1::Normal}} or {{c1::increased}} LH levels

What are the genital manifestations of 5α-reductase deficiency in genetic males?

{{c1::Atypical}} genitalia until puberty
Internal genitalia are {{c1::normal}}
fields.Back Extra: When puberty is reached, an increase in testosterone causes masculinization.

fields.Text:
What might be expected on sperm testing of a man with Kallman syndrome?

{{c1::Low::High/Low}} sperm count

What are two reproductive complications of Kallmann syndrome in a female patient?

{{c1::Amenorrhea}}
{{c1::Infertility}}

What condition typically presents with amenorrhea and anosmia in a young female?

{{c1::Kallmann}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This is a form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

fields.Text:
What is the pathogenesis of Kallman syndrome?

Defective {{c1::migration}} of neurons and subsequent failure of {{c1::olfactory bulbs}} to develop → Decreased production of {{c1::GnRH}} in the hypothalamus

What vaginal tumor is histologically described as having desmin-positive, spindle-shaped cells?

{{c1::Sarcoma botryoides}}

What condition presents with a clear, grape-like polypoid mass emerging from the vagina?

{{c1::Sarcoma botryoides}}

Exposure in utero to what drug is usually responsible for clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina?

{{c1::Diethylstilbestrol}}

What vaginal cancer develops secondary to cervical carcinoma?

Vaginal {{c1::squamous cell}} carcinoma

Sarcoma botryoides usually affects females of what age group?

{{c1::Under::Over/Under}} {{c1::4}} years of age

Name the diagnosis associated with amenorrhea, cyclic abdominal pain, and a blue mass extruding from the vagina presenting in a pubescent female.

{{c1::Imperforate hymen}}

What is the pathophysiology underlying an imperforate hymen?

Failure of the {{c1::central::central/peripheral}} part of the hymen to {{c1::degenerate}} → Vaginal mucus {{c1::accumulation}} at birth → Self-resolving {{c1::bulge}} at the introitus

What sign of imperforate hymen is present at birth?

{{c1::Accumulation}} of vaginal mucus → Self-resolving {{c1::bulge}} in the introitus

What are the three diagnostic criteria for preeclampsia?

After {{c1::20}} weeks' gestation
Finding of new {{c1::hypertension::hypertension/hypotension}}
Either {{c1::proteinuria}} or {{c1::end-organ}} dysfunction

What are two serious complications of HELLP syndrome?

Rupture of a {{c1::hepatic subcapsular hematoma}}
{{c1::Disseminated intravascular coagulation}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to release of tissue factor from the injured placenta.

fields.Text:
What does onset of preeclampsia before 20 weeks of gestation suggest?

{{c1::Molar pregnancy}}

What are six possible complications associated with preeclampsia?

Placental {{c1::abruption}}
{{c1::Renal}} failure
Pulmonary {{c1::edema}}
{{c1::Coagulopathy}}
Development of {{c1::eclampsia}}
{{c1::HELLP}} syndrome

What are three treatment options for eclampsia?

{{c1::Antihypertensive}} agents
Intravenous {{c1::magnesium sulfate}}
Immediate {{c1::delivery}}

What is the recommendation regarding delivery for a patient with gestational hypertension?

Deliver at {{c1::37}} to {{c1::39}} weeks

What drugs can be used to treat gestational hypertension?

{{c1::Hydralazine}}
{{c1::α-methyldopa}}
{{c1::Labetalol}}
{{c1::Nifedipine}}

What three sequelae of eclampsia can result in maternal death?

{{c1::Stroke}}
Intracranial {{c1::hemorrhage}}
{{c1::Acute respiratory distress}} syndrome

What is thought to be the etiology of preeclampsia?

Abnormal placental {{c1::spiral}} arteries → Maternal {{c1::endothelial}} dysfunction, {{c1::vasoconstriction::vasoconstriction/vasodilation}}, and {{c1::ischemia}}

What is the treatment for HELLP syndrome?

Immediate {{c1::delivery}}

What is the treatment for preeclampsia?

{{c1::Antihypertensive}} agents and intravenous {{c1::magnesium sulfate}} for seizure prevention
{{c1::Delivery}} of the fetus (definitive treatment)

Name some preexisting maternal conditions that are associated with an increased risk of developing preeclampsia.

History of {{c1::preeclampsia}}
{{c1::Multifetal}} gestation
Chronic {{c1::hypertension::hypertension/hypotension}}
Chronic {{c1::renal}} disease
{{c1::Diabetes}}
{{c1::Autoimmune}} disorders
{{c1::Obesity}}
Over {{c1::35}} years of age

During pregnancy, when can gestational hypertension or preeclampsia be diagnosed?

After {{c1::20}} weeks' gestation

What drug is used for prophylaxis of preeclampsia?

{{c1::Aspirin}}

A newborn has the defect shown in the diagram. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Myelomeningocele}}
fields.Back Extra: Both the spinal cord and meninges herniate through a vertebral defect.

fields.Text:
A newborn has the defect shown in the diagram. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Spina bifida occulta}}
fields.Back Extra: There is a defect in the bony vertebral column with no myelomeningocele herniation.

fields.Text:
An infant has the spinal cord anatomy shown in the image. What kind of neural tube defect is this?



{{c1::Meningocele}}
fields.Back Extra: There is herniation of the meninges, but not of the spinal cord itself.

fields.Text:
A fetus with anencephaly develops polyhydramnios. What is the mechanism?

Amniotic fluid {{c1::accumulates}} due to the lack of a {{c1::swallowing center}} in the brain

A fetal malformation of the anterior neural tube causing agenesis of the forebrain and calvarium is called what?

{{c1::Anencephaly}}

What is the relation of the meninges and spinal cord in a meningocele?

The {{c1::spinal cord}} is within the canal
Only the {{c1::meninges}} herniate through the bony defect

What is the relation of the meninges and spinal cord in a meningomyelocele?

Both the spinal cord and meninges {{c1::herniate}} through the bony defect

What condition is associated with a dimple and small tufts of hair above the gluteal cleft in a newborn?

{{c1::Spina bifida occulta}}

In a fetus with spina bifida occulta, how would α-fetoprotein and acetylcholinesterase in amniotic fluid be affected?

{{c1::Normal}} α-fetoprotein
{{c1::Increased}} acetylcholinesterase in amniotic fluid

Why is acetylcholinesterase elevated in amniotic fluid of a fetus with a myeloschisis?

Fetal acetylcholinesterase flows {{c1::out of::into/out of}} the defect in the spinal cord and {{c1::into::into/out of}} the amniotic fluid

What two maternal conditions can increase the risk of neural tube defects?

{{c1::Folate}} deficiency
{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}

How can a woman reduce the risk of neural tube defects for her fetus?

{{c1::Folate}} supplementation
fields.Back Extra: This is to avoid low levels of folic acid before conception and during pregnancy.

fields.Text:
The neural tube typically fuses by the 4th week of gestation. If fusion fails, what type of defect remains?

A persistent connection between the {{c1::spinal canal}} and {{c1::amniotic cavity}}

When must the neural tube fuse in order to avoid neural tube defects?

By the {{c1::4th}} week of gestation/development

A newborn has the finding shown on MRI. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Holoprosencephaly}}

At what time during embryonic development does the brain divide into separate hemispheres?

Typically during weeks {{c1::3}} to {{c1::4}}

A baby is born with one midline eye. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Cyclopia}}

What syndromes are associated with holoprosencephaly?

{{c1::Patau}} syndrome
{{c1::Fetal alcohol}} syndrome

Holoprosencephaly may be related to what genetic mutation?

{{c1::SHH}} mutations

"Smooth brain" lacking sulci and gyri due to the failure of neuronal migration is referred to as what?

{{c1::Lissencephaly}}

Lissencephaly is associated with which other neurologic abnormalities?

{{c1::Microcephaly::Macrocephaly/Microcephaly}}
{{c1::Hydrocephalus}}
{{c1::Ventriculomegaly}}

What is the mechanism that leads to holoprosencephaly?

Failure of the {{c1::prosencephalon}} to separate into two cerebral hemispheres

What are two additional malformations associated with the malformation shown in the image?



{{c1::Noncommunicating}} hydrocephalus
{{c1::Spina bifida}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows a Dandy-Walker malformation.

fields.Text:
What is the red arrow pointing to in this MRI obtained from an infant with Dandy-Walker malformation?



Enlarged {{c1::4th ventricle}}
fields.Back Extra: This fills the enlarged posterior fossa due to agenesis of the cerebellar vermis.

fields.Text:
What structures herniates through the foramen magnum in a Chiari II malformation?

{{c1::Cerebellum}}
{{c1::Medulla}}

What kind of hydrocephalus results due to Chiari II malformation?

{{c1::Noncommunicating}} hydrocephalus

The MRI findings shown in the image in conjunction with dull occipital headaches, ataxia, and loss of pain sensation in both arms of an adult indicate what?



Chiari {{c1::I}} malformation with {{c1::syringomyelia}}
fields.Back Extra: This is more likely to present in adulthood, in contrast to Chiari II malformation.

fields.Text:
Absence of the cerebellar vermis and cystic dilation of the 4th ventricle filling the enlarged posterior fossa are characteristic of what malformation?

{{c1::Dandy-Walker}} malformation

What two abnormalities are typically associated with Chiari II malformations?

Lumbosacral {{c1::meningomyelocele}}
Aqueductal {{c1::stenosis}}

Which Chiari malformation is more severe and presents early in life with stridor, apnea, limpness, and dysphagia?

Chiari {{c1::II}} malformation

What is the mechanism of action of imiquimod?

Imiquimod is a topical {{c1::antitumor immune response modifier}} → Binds to {{c1::TLR-7}} on macrophages, dendritic cells, and monocytes to activate them

Name 2 conditions for which imiquimod is indicated.

{{c1::Anogential warts}}
{{c1::Actinic keratosis}}

Name 3 possible local side effects of imiquimod.

{{c1::Burning}} pain at the site of application
{{c1::Rashes}}
{{c1::Itching}}

What is the treatment for acetaminophen overdose and how does it work?

{{c1::N-acetylcysteine}} regenerates {{c1::glutathione}} depleted by {{c1::NAPQI}} in the overdose → Prevents buildup of toxic metabolites

What byproduct of acetaminophen metabolism can lead to a depletion of glutathione, a buildup of toxic tissue byproducts, and hepatic necrosis with an overdose?

{{c1::NAPQI}}

Acetaminophen has antipyretic and analgesic effects, but lacks what property that is common to NSAIDs?

{{c1::Anti-inflammatory}} effects

What is the mechanism of action of acetaminophen? Where is it most effective?

Acetaminophen is a {{c1::reversible::reversible/irreversible}} {{c1::cyclooxygenase}} inhibitor that is most effective in the {{c1::CNS}}

In an aspirin overdose, damage to which cranial nerve causes tinnitus?

Cranial nerve {{c1::VIII}}

Tinnitus, respiratory alkalosis, and gastric ulceration are all adverse effects of long-term or excessive use of what medication?

{{c1::Aspirin}}

Why should you avoid administering aspirin to children? What should be given instead?

Aspirin administered to children with a viral illness can cause {{c1::Reye}} syndrome
{{c1::Acetaminophen}} should be given instead

What are 3 adverse effects of long-term aspirin use?

{{c1::Interstitial nephritis}}
Acute {{c1::kidney::organ}} injury
Gastrointestinal {{c1::bleeding}}

What dose of aspirin can you prescribe to help relieve fever and pain?

{{c1::Intermediate}} dose

At what dose does aspirin begin to work as an antiplatelet agent?

{{c1::Low}} dose

How does aspirin affect PT, PTT, and bleeding time?

{{c1::Normal}} PT
{{c1::Normal}} PTT
{{c1::Increased}} bleeding time

Describe the acid-base status expected in a patient experiencing an aspirin overdose.

Toxic doses cause {{c1::respiratory alkalosis}} early, but transitions to {{c1::mixed metabolic acidosis-respiratory alkalosis}}

What is the mechanism of action of aspirin?

{{c1::Irreversible::Reversible/Irreversible}} inhibition of {{c1::COX-1}} and {{c1::COX-2}} via {{c1::covalent acetylation}}

What dose of aspirin is best for an anti-inflammatory effect?

{{c1::High}} dose

Patients with what 2 medical conditions are most likely to have an allergic reaction to aspirin?

{{c1::Asthma}}
Nasal {{c1::polyps}}

What is the treatment for an aspirin overdose?

{{c1::Sodium bicarbonate}}

What is an adverse effect of selective COX-2 inhibitors?

Increased risk of {{c1::thrombosis}}

What common allergy precludes patients from using COX-2 inhibitors?

{{c1::Sulfa}} allergy

For which 2 diseases are COX-2 inhibitors indicated?

{{c1::Osteoarthritis}}
{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}

How do the mechanism of action and gastrointestinal effects of celecoxib differ from those of other NSAIDs?

Celecoxib selectively and reversibly inhibits COX-{{c1::2}} and spares COX-{{c1::1}} → Provides a {{c1::protective}} effect on gastric mucosa

How do TNF-α inhibitors lead to reactivation of latent tuberculosis infections?

Inhibition of TNF will stop {{c1::granuloma}} formation and stabilization → Predisposes reactivation

What are 4 diseases that are managed with anti-TNF-α monoclonal antibodies?

{{c1::Ankylosing spondylitis}}
{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}
{{c1::Psoriasis}}
{{c1::Inflammatory bowel}} disease

What is the mechanism of action of golimumab, certolizumab, adalimumab, and infliximab?

Inhibition of {{c1::TNF-α}}

What are 3 diseases that etanercept is indicated for?

{{c1::Psoriasis}}
{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}
{{c1::Ankylosing spondylitis}}

What is the mechanism of action of etanercept?

Acts as a decoy receptor for {{c1::TNF-α}} and {{c1::IgG1 Fc}}

TNF-α inhibitor use may cause a patient to experience a new rash and myalgias. What is the diagnosis?

Drug-induced {{c1::lupus}}

Which 2 medications can precipitate uric acid renal stones in patients with gout?

{{c1::Probenecid}}
{{c1::Aspirin}}

How should penicillin dosing be adjusted with probenecid use and why?

The penicillin dose should be {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} because probenecid inhibits the {{c1::secretion}} of penicillin by the {{c1::kidneys::organ}}

How can probenecid use lead to a kidney stone?

Probenecid blocks reabsorption of {{c1::uric acid}} in the proximal convoluted tubule → Increased risk for the development of {{c1::uric acid calculi}}

What is the mechanism of action of allopurinol?

It is a competitive {{c1::xanthine oxidase}} inhibitor → Decreases the conversion of {{c1::hypoxanthine}} and {{c1::xanthine}} into {{c1::urate}}

Allopurinol increases serum levels of which 2 drugs if taken concurrently?

{{c1::Azathioprine}}
{{c1::6-mercaptopurine}}

What is the mechanism of action of pegloticase?

It is a recombinant {{c1::uricase}} that catalyzes the metabolism of {{c1::uric acid}} to {{c1::allantoin}}

Why is allopurinol used in lymphoma and leukemia treatment?

Allopurinol blocks {{c1::urate}} production
fields.Back Extra: Chemotherapy results in tumor lysis, which releases purines and causes urate nephropathy.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of colchicine?

It binds and stabilizes {{c1::tubulin}} to stop {{c1::microtubules}} from polymerizing → Prevents {{c1::chemotaxis}} and {{c1::degranulation}} of neutrophils

What 3 medications are indicated for an acute gout flare?

{{c1::NSAIDs}}
{{c1::Glucocorticoids}}
{{c1::Colchicine}}

How does aspirin contribute to gout?

{{c1::Low}} dose aspirin decreases {{c1::uric acid}} clearance → Increases risk of gout flares

What is the mechanism of action of febuxostat?

Inhibits {{c1::xanthine oxidase}}

What 4 drugs can be used to prevent flares in patients with chronic gout?

{{c1::Allopurinol}}
{{c1::Pegloticase}}
{{c1::Febuxostat}}
{{c1::Probenecid}}

Which drug used for acute gout has gastrointestinal and neuromyopathic adverse effects?

{{c1::Colchicine}}

Teriparatide may increase the risk for which electrolyte derangement?

Transient {{c1::hypercalcemia}}

What is the mechanism of action of teriparatide when administered in a pulsatile fashion?

It is a recombinant {{c1::parathyroid}} analog that increases {{c1::osteoblast}} activity → Increases {{c1::bone}} growth

Teriparatide may increase the risk of osteosarcoma and should therefore be avoided in what 2 groups of patients?

Patients with {{c1::Paget disease of bone}}
Patients with an unexplained increase in {{c1::ALP}}

What disease is teriparatide used to treat and what effect does it have on bone growth/resorption?

Teriparatide is used to treat {{c1::osteoporosis}}
Teriparatide causes an {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} in bone growth

How can esophagitis be avoided with bisphosphonate use?

By taking bisphosphonates with {{c1::water}} and staying {{c1::upright}} for at least {{c1::30}} minutes afterward

What are 3 major adverse effects of bisphosphonates?

Atypical femoral {{c1::stress fractures}}
Jaw {{c1::osteonecrosis}}
{{c1::Esophagitis}}

Aside from osteoporosis, what are 4 other clinical indications for use of bisphosphonates?

{{c1::Hypercalcemia}}
{{c1::Metastatic bone}} disease
{{c1::Paget disease of bone}}
{{c1::Osteogenesis imperfecta}}

What is the mechanism of bisphosphonates?

They are {{c1::pyrophosphate}} analogs that bind to {{c1::hydroxyapatite}} in bone and inhibit the activity of {{c1::osteoclasts}}

What are 4 adverse effects of leflunomide?

{{c1::Teratogenicity}}
{{c1::Hepatotoxicity}}
{{c1::Diarrhea}}
{{c1::Hypertension}}

What diseases are indications for use of leflunomide?

{{c1::Psoriatic arthritis}}
{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}

How does leflunomide's inhibition of the enzyme dihydroorotate dehydrogenase help in treating inflammatory conditions?

Inhibition of dihydroorotate dehydrogenase stops {{c1::pyrimidine}} synthesis → Suppresses {{c1::T}}-cell proliferation

What enzyme does leflunomide reversibly inhibit?

{{c1::Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase}}

How can NSAIDs lead to gastric ulcers and renal ischemia?

NSAIDs inhibit the formation of {{c1::prostaglandins}}
fields.Back Extra: Prostaglandins help protect the gastric mucosa and vasodilate the afferent arterioles.

fields.Text:
Which NSAID is indicated for patent ductus arteriosus in a newborn?

{{c1::Indomethacin}}

What is the mechanism of action of NSAIDs?

{{c1::Reversible::Reversible/Irreversible}} inhibition of {{c1::COX-1}} and {{c1::COX-2}} → Blocks {{c1::prostaglandin}} synthesis

To which class of drugs do ibuprofen, indomethacin, naproxen, ketorolac, diclofenac, meloxicam, and piroxicam belong?

{{c1::NSAIDs}}

What are potential renal side effect of NSAIDs?

{{c1::Interstitial nephritis}}
Renal {{c1::ischemia}}

What are glands that produce substances other than hormones called?

{{c1::Exocrine}} glands

What are three subtypes of exocrine glands?

{{c1::Merocrine}} glands
{{c1::Apocrine}} glands
{{c1::Holocrine}} glands

What are examples of the gland subtype shown in the diagram that release substances via secretory vesicles?



{{c1::Salivary}} glands
{{c1::Sweat}} glands

What are examples of the gland subtype shown in the diagram that release substances via a pinched portion of cells?



{{c1::Mammary}} glands

What are examples of the gland subtype shown in the diagram that release substances via disintegration of cells?



{{c1::Sebaceous}} glands

What is the dermatologic term for the lesion on the infant's face shown in the image?



{{c1::Crust}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is a dry exudate.

The image shows an infant with impetigo.

fields.Text:
What is the dermatologic term for the lesion shown in the image?



{{c1::Scale}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows flaking of the stratum corneum in a squamous cell carcinoma of the skin.

fields.Text:
What is the dermatologic term for the lesion shown in the image?



{{c1::Wheals}}

What is the dermatologic term for the lesion shown in the image?



{{c1::Pustule}}

What is the dermatologic term for the lesion shown in the image?



{{c1::Bulla}}

What is the dermatologic term for the lesions shown in the image?



{{c1::Vesicles}}

What is the dermatologic term for the lesion shown in the image?



{{c1::Plaque}}

What is the dermatologic term for the lesion shown in the image?



{{c1::Papule}}

What is the dermatologic term for the lesion shown in the image?



{{c1::Patch}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows a large birthmark.

fields.Text:
What is the dermatologic term for the lesion shown in the image?



{{c1::Macule}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows a labial macule.

fields.Text:
What is the difference between vesicles and bullae?

{{c1::Vesicles}} are < 1 centimeter
{{c1::Bullae}} are > 1 centimeter

What is the difference between a papule and plaque?

{{c1::Papule}} is < 1 centimeter
{{c1::Plaque}} is > 1 centimeter

What is the difference between a macule and a papule?

Macule is {{c1::flat}}
Papule is {{c1::raised}}

What is the difference between a macule and a patch?

{{c1::Macule}} is < 1 centimeter
{{c1::Patch}} is > 1 centimeter

Which epidermal layer is thickened in acanthosis nigricans?

Stratum {{c1::spinosum}}

A male patient with pemphigus vulgaris reports that his skin splits open at the slightest touch. What is the microscopic term for this lesion?

{{c1::Acantholysis}}

What is the term for a collection of edematous fluid in the epidermal space?

{{c1::Spongiosis}}

What is the microscopic dermatologic term for increased thickness of the stratum granulosum?

{{c1::Hypergranulosis}}

What is the microscopic dermatologic term for a thickened stratum corneum?

{{c1::Hyperkeratosis}}

A thickened stratum corneum with retention of nuclei is indicative of which disease process?

{{c1::Psoriasis}}

What is the microscopic term for retained nuclei in the stratum corneum?

{{c1::Parakeratosis}}

What pathophysiologic change underlies this skin condition?



Decreased numbers of {{c1::melanocytes}} via an {{c1::autoimmune}} mechanism

What is the hyperpigmentation shown in the image called?



{{c1::Melasma}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is a hyperpigmentation associated with pregnancy and oral contraceptive pill use.

This is also known as the "mask of pregnancy".

fields.Text:
A teenager comes to your office to establish care. She has an increased risk for which cancer?



{{c1::Skin}} cancer

Decreased tyrosinase activity results in which dermatologic disorder? What else can cause this disease?

{{c1::Albinism}}, which may also be caused by defective {{c1::tyrosine}} transport in {{c1::melanocytes}}

What are three risk factors for the development of melasma?

{{c1::Oral contraceptive pill}} use
{{c1::Pregnancy}}
{{c1::Dark::Light/Dark}} complexion

What changes are seen in melanocytes and melanin production in patients with albinism?

Melanocyte production is {{c1::normal}}
Melanin production is {{c1::decreased}}

What genetic condition causes patchy dipigmentation of hair, skin, and irises and may be associated with deafness?

{{c1::Waardenburg}} syndrome

What is the pathogenesis of Waardenburg syndrome?

Waardenburg syndrome is caused by abnormalities in the differentiation of {{c1::neural crest}} cells to {{c1::melanocytes}}

What is the medical term for "cradle cap", consisting of erythmatous plaques with greasy yellow scaling, on the scalp of an infant?

{{c1::Seborrheic dermatitis}}

Seborrheic dermatitis is associated with which neurologic disease?

{{c1::Parkinson}} disease

Which fungal species might be associated with seborrheic dermatitis?

{{c1::Malassezia}} species

What are two treatment options for seborrheic dermatitis?

Topical {{c1::antifungal}} agents
{{c1::Corticosteroids}}

Greasy, yellow scales and erythmatous plaques are characteristic of which disease process?



{{c1::Seborrheic dermatitis}}

Which three areas of the body are the most common sites of seborrheic dermatitis?

{{c1::Face}}
{{c1::Scalp}}
{{c1::Periocular}} area

What kind of gland is involved in the development of seborrheic dermatitis?

{{c1::Sebaceous}} glands

What is the lesion, which is completely asymptomatic, shown in the image called?



{{c1::Intradermal nevus}}

What type of hypersensitivity caused this reaction in response to topical neomycin?



Type {{c1::IV}} hypersensitivity

Which immunoglobulin is likely elevated in an individual with multiple food allergies and atopic dermatitis, as seen in the image?



Ig{{c1::E}}

Mutations in what gene can predispose a young child to atopic dermatitis, as seen in the image?



{{c1::Filaggrin}} gene

Which immunologic cells are responsible for the reaction shown in the image, which occurred after consumption of peanuts?



{{c1::Mast}} cells
fields.Back Extra:
Degranulation of mast cells promotes wheal formation.

The image shows urticaria.

fields.Text:
Based on the image, what is this patient's diagnosis?



{{c1::Condyloma acuminatum}}
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by low-risk HPV strains.

fields.Text:
The rapid appearance of greasy lesions all over the body is referred to as what telling sign? What is this sign indicative of?



{{c1::Leser-Trélat}} sign can indicate an underlying {{c1::malignancy}}

What is the arrow pointing to on this skin leison, and what is it characteristic of?



A {{c1::horn cyst}} is characteristic of {{c1::seborrheic keratosis}}

Outbreaks of pimples on the face and flushing with alcohol consumption in the absence of comedones are indicative of what common skin disorder?



{{c1::Rosacea}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an inflammatory skin condition with erythematous pustules and papules, but without comedones.

fields.Text:
Scratching off a scale causes pinpoint bleeding as shown in the image. What is the term for this bleeding?



{{c1::Auspitz}} sign

A biopsy specimen obtained from the lesions shown in the image reveals nucleated cells in the stratum corneum. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Psoriasis}}
fields.Back Extra: The presence of nucleated cells in the stratum corneum is called parakeratosis.

fields.Text:
Colonization by which bacteria may cause the skin findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Cutibacterium acnes}}

How do increased levels of androgen and sebum production affect acne?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} outbreaks
{{c1::Worsens::Improves/Worsens}} acne

What is a commonly used term for urticaria?

{{c1::Hives}}

How does urticaria arise?

Wheals form due to {{c1::mast}} cell degranulation after exposure to an {{c1::allergen}} → Lymphocytic channel dilation and dermal edema

Benign seborrheic keratoses are most likely to arise on which three areas of the body?

{{c1::Head}}
{{c1::Trunk}}
{{c1::Extremities}}

What are three treatment options for acne?

{{c1::Benzoyl peroxide}}
{{c1::Antibiotics}}
{{c1::Retinoids}}

Melanocytic nevi can be classified as intradermal or junctional. How do you tell the difference?

Intradermal nevi are {{c1::papular}}
Junctional nevi present as {{c1::macules}}

What skin condition presents with painful, pruritic, hyperpigmented papules after shaving and occurs primarily in Black males?

{{c1::Pseudofolliculitis barbae}}
fields.Back Extra: These are also known as razor bumps.

fields.Text:
Name three conditions associated with eczema.

{{c1::Asthma}}
{{c1::Food}} allergies
Allergic {{c1::rhinitis}}

What are three changes to the epidermis in psoriasis?

{{c1::Parakeratotic}} scaling
{{c1::Acanthosis}}
Decrease in stratum {{c1::granulosum}}

Munro microabscesses are a characterisric finding in which dermatologic disease?

{{c1::Psoriasis}}

Bulbous deformation of the nose in patients with rosacea is referred to as what?

{{c1::Rhinophyma}}

What type of hypersensitivity is atopic dermatitis?

Type {{c1::I}} hypersensitivity reaction

The nail shown in the image is warped due to a painful red-blue spot under the nail bed. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Glomus}} tumor
fields.Back Extra: This is derived from a proliferation of modified smooth muscle cells of the thermoregulatory glomus body.

fields.Text:
What is the diagnosis for this lesion that has been growing since birth?



{{c1::Strawberry}} hemangioma
fields.Back Extra: This grows rapidly in the first few weeks of life, then regresses spontaneously by 5 to 8 years of age.

fields.Text:
What is the diagnosis for this bright red lesion that bleeds frequently and occurs in pregnant women?



{{c1::Pyogenic}} granuloma
fields.Back Extra: This is a benign hemangioma of the skin that is associated with pregnancy and trauma.

fields.Text:
What type of lesion is displayed in the image and how do such lesions change with age?



A {{c1::cherry}} hemangioma {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} in frequency with age and {{c1::does not::does/does not}} regress

What are the diagnosis and prognosis for this rash, which occurred after a cat scratch in an HIV-positive patient with a low CD4+ count?



{{c1::Bacillary}} angiomatosis is a {{c1::benign::benign/malignant}} condition with a {{c1::good}} prognosis

Which vascular tumor is associated with vinyl chloride and arsenic exposure?

{{c1::Hepatic}} angiosarcoma

In which three areas of the body do angiosarcomas usually appear?

{{c1::Head}}
{{c1::Neck}}
{{c1::Breasts}}

A breast cancer survivor develops postmastectomy lymphedema. What malignancy is she at an increased risk for due to this postoperative complication?

{{c1::Angiosarcoma}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is a highly aggressive rare blood vessel malignancy associated with postmastectomy lymphedema.

This is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome.

fields.Text:
In what four locations is Kaposi sarcoma most likely to arise in the body?

{{c1::Mouth}}
{{c1::Skin}}
{{c1::Respiratory}} tract
{{c1::Gastrointestinal}} tract

What two viruses are associated with the development of Kaposi sarcoma?

{{c1::HHV-8}}
{{c1::HIV}}

Patients with AIDS and low CD4+ counts can develop bacillary angiomatosis or Kaposi sarcoma. What are the differences in the biopsy findings for each?

Bacillary angiomatosis → {{c1::Neutrophilic}} infiltrate
Kaposi sarcoma → {{c1::Lymphocytic}} infiltrate

What is the prognosis for a patient diagnosed with angiosarcoma? What makes this malignancy so difficult to treat?

The prognosis is {{c1::poor}}
It is {{c1::aggressive}} and difficult to {{c1::resect}}
fields.Back Extra: This is often due to a delay in diagnosis.

fields.Text:
Which three populations are at increased risk for developing Kaposi sarcoma?

Older {{c1::Eastern European}} {{c1::men::men/women}}
Recipients of {{c1::organ transplants}}
Patients with {{c1::AIDS}}

What germ cell does Kaposi sarcoma arise from?

{{c1::Endothelium}}

Herpes virus infection causing a painful blister on a finger is referred to as what?



Herpetic {{c1::whitlow}}

What positive sign is shown in the image that is characterized by skin that sloughs off on stroking?



Positive {{c1::Nikolsky}} sign
fields.Back Extra: There is separation of the epidermis on stroking of skin.

fields.Text:
What organisms cause this surgical emergency with bullous purple skin changes and crepitus on examination?



{{c1::Streptococcus pyogenes}}
{{c1::Anaerobic::Aerobic/Anaerobic}} bacteria

What is shown in the image and what is the most likely causative pathogen?



The image shows an {{c1::abscess}} containing a walled-off collection of {{c1::pus}}, most likely caused by {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} infection

What layers of the skin would be involved in the skin infection shown in the image, which occurred 1 week after a break in the skin?



{{c1::Deeper}} dermis
{{c1::Subcutaneous}} layers

A well-demarcated lesion with involvement of upper dermis and superficial lymphatics is likely caused by what?



{{c1::Streptococcus pyogenes}}
fields.Back Extra:
The image shows erysipelas.

This is characterized by a well-defined, raised demarcation between healthy and infected skin.

fields.Text:
What pathogen is most likely responsible for the contagious rash shown in the image?



{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}

What pathogen is responsible for this nonscrapable lesion in an HIV-positive male patient?



{{c1::Epstein-Barr virus}}

What virus most likely caused the lesions shown in the image?



{{c1::Poxvirus}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows the characteristic umbilicated papules of molluscum contagiosum.

fields.Text:
What two pathogenic organisms are most likely responsible for the contagious rash shown in the image?



{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
{{c1::Streptococcus pyogenes}}

How can staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome be distinguished from toxic epidermal necrosis on biopsy?

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome → Exotoxin destroys {{c1::keratinocyte}} attachments only in stratum {{c1::granulosum}}
Toxic epidermal necrosis → Exotoxin destroys {{c1::epidermal}}-{{c1::dermal}} junction

What populations are at risk for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome?

Adults and children with {{c1::renal}} insufficiency
{{c1::Newborns}}

Compare the potential for malignancy associated with hairy leukoplakia versus other forms of leukoplakia.

Hairy leukoplakia is {{c1::benign}}
Leukoplakia is a {{c1::premalignant}} condition

What groups of patients are susceptible to hairy leukoplakia?

{{c1::Immunocompromised}} patients

A patient with AIDS has a lesion on the tongue that cannot be scraped off. Is the lesion painful?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}

How can you differentiate hairy leukoplakia from oral thrush?

Leukoplakia {{c1::cannot::can/cannot}} be scraped off
Oral thrush {{c1::can::can/cannot}} be scraped off

A patient who is taking immunosupressants has a generalized vesicular rash and a positive result for VZV on PCR. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Disseminated zoster}}
fields.Back Extra: Patients usually present with dermatomal vesicles in reactivation, but distribution can be diffused in the immunocompromised.

fields.Text:
What childhood infection predisposes adults to development of a painful rash that follows a dermatomal distribution?

{{c1::Varicella}}

What three skin conditions are caused by HSV-1 and HSV-2?

Herpes {{c1::genitalis}}​​​
Herpes {{c1::labialis}}
Herpetic {{c1::whitlow}}

Molluscum contagiosum classically presents with what type of skin lesion?

{{c1::Umbilicated papule}}

Honey-colored crusting is a finding associated with which superficial skin infection?

{{c1::Impetigo}}

What causes the violaceous color of bullae and surrounding skin in an infection by "flesh-eating bacteria"?

Skin {{c1::necrosis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a finding of necrotizing fascitis, a surgical emergency.

fields.Text:
What type of skin cancer may appear on a sun-exposed area as a nonhealing ulcer, similar to the lesion shown in the image?



{{c1::Basal cell}} carcinoma

What is the skin lesion in this image?



{{c1::Basal cell}} carcinoma

A patient with the lesion shown in the image is found to have an activating BRAF kinase mutation. What is the likely diagnosis?



{{c1::Acral lentiginous}} melanoma

What tumor marker is associated with melanoma?

{{c1::S-100}}

What is the primary treatment for melanoma?

{{c1::Wide::Wide/Narrow}}-margin {{c1::excision}}

What type of melanoma is shown in the image?



{{c1::Superficial spreading}} melanoma

What condition does the histologic pattern shown in the image represent?



{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma

What type of lesion is a common precursor of squamous cell carcinoma?



{{c1::Actinic keratosis}}

In what four areas of the body does squamous cell carcinoma most commonly occur?



{{c1::Face}}
{{c1::Lower::Upper/Lower}} lip
{{c1::Ears}}
{{c1::Hands}}

Which skin cancer type has a high risk of metastasis?

{{c1::Melanoma}}

What medical therapy may be beneficial for a patient with metastatic melanoma and a BRAF V600E mutation?

{{c1::Vemurafenib}}

List the ABCDEs of melanoma.

{{c1::Asymmetry}}
{{c1::Border}} irregularity
{{c1::Color}} variation
Diameter > {{c1::6}} mm
{{c1::Evolution}} over time

Relative to the upper and lower lips, where are basal cell and squamous cell carcinomas commonly found?

Basal cell carcinoma → {{c1::Above::Above/Below}} upper lip
Squamous cell carcinoma → {{c1::Below::Above/Below}} lower lip

A noncancerous, rapidly growing, dome-shaped nodule filled with keratin in middle-aged or elderly individuals describes what skin lesion?



{{c1::Keratoacanthoma}}

What are the common forms of skin cancer?

{{c1::Basal cell}} carcinoma (most common)
{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma (2nd most common)

List the four big risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma.

Excessive {{c1::sun}} exposure
{{c1::Immunosuppression}}
Chronic nonhealing {{c1::wounds}}
Exposure to {{c1::arsenic}}

Which skin cancer develops cells that are histologically described as having "palisading" or aligned nuclei?

{{c1::Basal cell}} carcinoma

What one factor strongly predisposes to skin cancer?

{{c1::Sun}} exposure

What factor best predicts the prognosis of melanoma?

{{c1::Depth}} of invasion

What skin cancer does a keratoacanthoma resemble?

{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma

What does the rule of 9's measure?

Extent of a {{c1::burn}} injury estimated by the percentage of involved body {{c1::surface area}}

What percentage of body surface area is accounted for by each leg?

{{c1::18}}% each

What percentage of body surface area is accounted for by each arm?

{{c1::9}}% each

What percentage of body surface area is accounted for by the torso?

{{c1::9}}% front
{{c1::9}}% back

A woman having full-thickness burns covering both legs, the perineum, and the entire left arm has what percent of her body surface area involved in the injury?

{{c1::46}}%

Are superficial partial-thickness burns or deep partial-thickness burns painful?

{{c1::Superficial}} partial-thickness burns
fields.Back Extra: A deep partial-thickness burn is painless with only the perception of pressure.

fields.Text:
How deep is a burn described as "inelastic, white, leathery, and dry", which does not blanch with pressure and has associated sensation of deep pressure only?

{{c1::Full-thickness}} burn
{{c1::Deeper injury}} burn

Which burn classification would a simple sunburn fall under?

{{c1::Superficial}} burn

Which skin layers are involved in a superficial burn?

{{c1::Epidermis}}

What would be seen on a KOH preparation of a sample taken from the lesion shown in the image?



{{c1::Branching septate hyphae}}

Which cutaneous mycosis presents with pruritic lesions on the extremities?



{{c1::Tinea corporis}}
fields.Back Extra: Note the patches with central clearing in the image.

fields.Text:
Which cutaneous mycosis presents in the inguinal area?



{{c1::Tinea cruris}}

Which cutaneous mycosis presents with foot discoloration as shown in the image?



{{c1::Tinea pedis}}

What cutaneous mycosis presents as alopecia and scaling, as shown in the image?



{{c1::Tinea capitis}}

Describe the mechanism behind tinea versicolor causing skin hypopigmentation.

{{c1::Lipid}} degradation by {{c1::Malassezia}} species produces acids that inhibit {{c1::tyrosinase}} → Hypopigmentation
fields.Back Extra: Tyrosinase is involved in the synthesis of melanin.

fields.Text:
Which cutaneous mycosis presents as multiple erythematous scaling rings with central clearing?

{{c1::Tinea corporis}}

What part of the body is affected in a patient with a tinea unguium infection?

{{c1::Nails}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as onychomycosis.

fields.Text:
What are the three different varieties/distributions of tinea pedis?

{{c1::Moccasin}} distribution
{{c1::Vesicular}} type
{{c1::Interdigital}} (most common)

What class of organisms causes tinea pedis, tinea cruris, tinea corporis, tinea capitis, and tinea unguium?

{{c1::Dermatophytes}}

Which cutaneous mycosis can present as hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules?

{{c1::Tinea versicolor}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is caused by Malassezia species.

An inflammatory response can produce hyperpigmented or pink patches.

fields.Text:
What characteristic pattern would be seen on microscopic examination of a specimen obtained from the lesion shown in the image?



"{{c1::Spaghetti and meatballs}}" pattern

What organism is shown in this image?



{{c1::Malassezia}} species
fields.Back Extra: The image shows a "spaghetti and meatballs" appearance on microscopy.

fields.Text:
What causes the hyperpigmentation and/or pink patches seen in tinea versicolor?

An {{c1::inflammatory}} response

What is the treatment for tinea versicolor?

{{c1::Selenium sulfide}}
Topical and/or oral {{c1::antifungal}} medications

How can tinea corporis be acquired?

Contact with infected {{c1::pets}}
Contact with {{c1::farm}} animals

Nikolsky-negative blisters with the immunofluorescence findings shown on biopsy indicate what condition?



{{c1::Bullous pemphigoid}}
fields.Back Extra: There is a linear pattern at the epidermal-dermal junction.

fields.Text:
What are the blisters shown in the image filled with?



{{c1::Eosinophils}}

Nikolsky-positive blisters with the immunofluorescence findings shown on biopsy indicate what condition?



{{c1::Pemphigus vulgaris}}
fields.Back Extra: The immunofluorescence shows a reticular pattern forming around epithelial cells.

fields.Text:
Patients with bullous pemphigoid develop IgG antibodies against which antigen?

{{c1::Hemidesmosomes}}

Patients with pemphigus vulgaris develop IgG antibodies against which antigen?

{{c1::Desmoglein-1}}
{{c1::Desmoglein-3}}

Which autoimmune blistering skin disorder affects the oral mucosa?

{{c1::Pemphigus vulgaris}}

What is the phenomenon of epidermal separation on stroking a lesion with large, flaccid bullae called?

Positive {{c1::Nikolsky}} sign

What physical exam finding can differentiate pemphigus vulgaris from bullous pemphigoid?

{{c1::Nikolsky}} sign

What type of hypersensitivity reaction occurs in pemphigus vulgaris and bullous pemphigoid?

Type {{c1::II}} hypersensitivity reaction

A skin biopsy specimen showing "tombstoning" and acantholysis on an H&E stain indicates which autoimmune skin blistering condition?

{{c1::Pemphigous vulgaris}}

What is the inheritance pattern of epidermolysis bullosa simplex?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

How may the pathophysiology of epidermolysis bullosa simplex be explained?

Defect in {{c1::keratin}} filament assembly → {{c1::Cytoskeleton}} disruption → Epithelial fragility

What skin biopsy finding is expected in a child presenting with blisters on palms and soles?

{{c1::Intraepidermal cleavage}}

The lesions shown in the image are characteristic of what skin disorder?



{{c1::Eythema multiforme}}

How would a man with frequent bouts of diarrhea and a rash on his elbow like that shown in the image be treated?



{{c1::Dapsone}}
{{c1::Gluten}}-free diet
fields.Back Extra: The image shows dermatitis herpetiformis secondary to celiac disease.

fields.Text:
How is the characteristic sign shown in the image described?



{{c1::Sloughing}} of skin at {{c1::dermal}} junction
fields.Back Extra: This is known as the Nikolsky sign.

fields.Text:
What is the diagnosis for the patient shown in the image who has diffuse sloughing of the skin of over 30% of the body after taking a new medication?



{{c1::Toxic epidermal necrolysis}}

Describe the risk of mortality for a patient who has recently taken phenytoin and presents with fever and the skin signs shown in the image.



{{c1::High::High/Low}}

A patient presents with fever, eye crusting, and sloughing of the skin on less than 10% of the body after taking a new drug. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Stevens-Johnson}} syndrome

What blistering skin disorder is most commonly associated with celiac disease?

{{c1::Dermatitis herpetiformis}}

In a patient with the classic targetoid lesions of erythema multiforme, it is important to consider what other severe conditions?

{{c1::Stevens-Johnson}} syndrome
{{c1::Toxic epidermal necrolysis}}

What blistering skin disorder involves bullae, necrosis, and skin sloughing that affects between 10% and 30% of the body?

{{c1::Stevens-Johnson}} syndrome
{{c1::Toxic epidermal necrolysis}}

List two general causes of erythema multiforme.

{{c1::Drugs}}
{{c1::Infections}}

How does a biopsy specimen obtained from a patient with dermatitis herpetiformis appear on immunofluorescence?

Ig{{c1::A}} deposits are seen at the tips of dermal {{c1::papillae}}

What areas are frequently involved in dermatitis herpetiformis?

{{c1::Elbows}}
{{c1::Knees}}
{{c1::Buttocks}}

What is the underlying cause of venous ulcers?

Chronic venous {{c1::insufficiency}}

A shallow, exudative ulcer over the ankle malleolus in the presence of mild pain is likely which type of ulcer?

{{c1::Venous}} ulcer

An extremely painful ulcer on the anterior shin in the absence of pulses is indicative of what type of lower extremity ulcer?

{{c1::Arterial}} ulcer

A patient with diabetes mellitus and associated peripheral neuropathy is most likely to develop what type of lower extremity ulcer?

{{c1::Neuropathic}} ulcer

What underlying disease results in an arterial ulcer of the lower extremities?

{{c1::Peripheral artery}} disease

A venous ulcer may be associated with what additional signs?

{{c1::Telangiectasias}}
{{c1::Varicose}} veins
{{c1::Stasis dermatitis}}

What is the cause of the rough, erythematous papules shown?



{{c1::Sun}} exposure

What predicts the risk of progression to squamous cell carcinoma in actinic keratosis?



Degree of epithelial {{c1::dysplasia}}

What two clinical conditions are associated with acanthosis nigricans?

{{c1::Visceral}} malignancy
{{c1::Insulin}} resistance

What histologic finding is seen in a patient presenting with acanthosis nigricans?



Epidermal {{c1::hyperplasia::hyperplasia/hypoplasia}}

Name the scaly, erythematous rash that develops over the back and lasts 6 to 8 weeks.



{{c1::Pityriasis rosea}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows a "Christmas tree" distribution.

fields.Text:
What is the treatment for the lesions shown in the image, which are characterized as multiple plaques with collarette scales?



{{c1::None}}
fields.Back Extra:
The condition is self-resolving.

The image shows a herald patch of pityriasis rosea.

fields.Text:
What underlying infection should be suspected in a patient with a pruritic papular rash like the one shown in the image?



{{c1::Hepatitis C}}
fields.Back Extra: It is associated with lichen planus.

fields.Text:
What two fungal infections are associated with the painful inflammatory lesions of subcutaneous fat shown in the image?



{{c1::Coccidioidomycosis}}
{{c1::Histoplasmosis}}

A patient with Streptococcus pyogenes infection has lesions on the shins. How do you classify them?



{{c1::Erythema nodosum}}

A patient with lichen planus has white reticular lines on her oral mucosa. What is it known as?

{{c1::Wickham striae}}

What type of UV radiation predominantly causes photoaging and tanning?

{{c1::UVA}}

How does UV irradiation affect the skin at a cellular level?

UV irradiation → {{c1::DNA}} mutation → {{c1::Apoptosis}} of keratinocytes
