What two autoimmune disorders may cause erythema nodosum?

{{c1::Inflammatory bowel}} disease
{{c1::Sarcoidosis}}

What type of UV radiation typically causes sunburn?

{{c1::UVB}}

What gastrointestinal manifestations are associated with the disease most likely characterized by the skin findings shown in the image?



Esophageal {{c1::dysmotility}}
{{c1::Reflux}}

Name the skin finding associated with anti-centromere antibodies shown in the image.



{{c1::Calcinosis cutis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is likely due to CREST syndrome.

fields.Text:
What renal manifestation is associated with the disease most likely characterized by the skin findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Scleroderma renal crisis}}

Where do skin lesions appear in limited scleroderma or CREST syndrome?

{{c1::Fingers}}
{{c1::Face}}

What does the CREST acronym stand for?

{{c1::Calcinosis cutis}}
{{c1::Anti-centromere}} antibody
{{c1::Raynaud}} phenomenon
Esophageal {{c1::dysmotility}}
{{c1::Sclerodactyly}}
{{c1::Telangiectasia}}

What are the 2 types of scleroderma? Which has a more benign clinical course?

{{c1::Diffuse}} scleroderma
{{c1::Limited}} scleroderma (more benign)

Widespread skin involvement, early visceral involvement, and rapid progression are indicative of what type of scleroderma?

{{c1::Diffuse}} scleroderma

What condition involves autoimmunity, noninflammatory vasculopathy, and excessive fibrosis and collagen deposition?

{{c1::Scleroderma}}

Which 2 antibodies are associated with diffuse scleroderma?

{{c1::Anti-Scl-70}} antibody
{{c1::Anti-RNA polymerase III}} antibody

What 2 lung pathologies are associated with scleroderma?

{{c1::Interstitial fibrosis}}
Pulmonary {{c1::hypertension}}

A patient's fingers change color with cold temperatures or stress. What is the pathophysiology?



{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} blood flow to the skin as a result of {{c1::vasospasm}} of arterioles

Describe the sequence of skin color changes that occur in Raynaud phenomenon.

{{c1::White}} → {{c1::Blue}} → {{c1::Red}}

Raynaud disease occurs most often in which 2 parts of the body?

{{c1::Fingers}}
{{c1::Toes}}

What drug class would be prescribed to treat Raynaud disease or syndrome?

{{c1::Calcium}} channel blockers

Name 2 common triggers for the digital vasospasm seen in Raynaud disease/syndrome.

{{c1::Stress}}
{{c1::Cold}}

What is the key difference between Raynaud disease and Raynaud syndrome?

Raynaud {{c1::disease}} → Idiopathic and primary
Raynaud {{c1::syndrome}} → Associated with another disease process

What 3 diseases are commonly associated with Raynaud syndrome?

{{c1::SLE}}
{{c1::Mixed connective tissue}} disease
{{c1::CREST}} syndrome

How is myasthenia gravis treated?

{{c1::Acetylcholinesterase}} inhibitors

What changes in deep tendon reflexes are expected in myasthenia gravis versus Lambert-Eaton syndrome?

Myasthenia gravis → {{c1::Spared reflexes}}
Lambert-Eaton syndrome → {{c1::Hyporeflexia}}

Would myasthenia gravis and Lambert-Eaton syndrome both improve with acetylcholinesterase inhibitor use?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Only symptoms of myasthenia gravis are reversed with the use of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.

fields.Text:
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is associated with what malignancy?

{{c1::Small cell lung}} cancer

Proximal muscle weakness and autonomic symptoms are associated with which neuromuscular junction disease?

{{c1::Lambert-Eaton myasthenic}} syndrome

What is the pathophysiology of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome?

Autoantibodies to {{c1::presynaptic::presynaptic/postsynaptic}} {{c1::Ca2+}} channels → Decreased {{c1::acetylcholine}} release

Name the 2 ophthalmic manifestations that can present in a patient diagnosed with myasthenia gravis.

{{c1::Ptosis}}
{{c1::Diplopia}}

How does repetitive muscle activity affect patients with myasthenia gravis versus those with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome?

Myasthenia gravis → {{c1::Worsens::Improves/Worsens}} with muscle use
Lambert-Eaton syndrome → {{c1::Improves::Improves/Worsens}} with muscle use

What is the pathophysiology of myasthenia gravis?

Autoantibodies bind to {{c1::postsynaptic::presynaptic/postsynaptic}} {{c1::acetylcholine}} receptors

In patients with myasthenia gravis, involvement of which muscle groups results in symptoms of dyspnea and dysphagia?

{{c1::Respiratory}} muscle involvement causes dyspnea
{{c1::Bulbar}} muscle involvement causes dysphagia

What oncologic pathology is associated with myasthenia gravis?

{{c1::Thymoma}}
{{c1::Thymic}} hyperplasia

Repetitive flexion activity at the elbow can lead to which injury?

{{c1::Medial epicondylitis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as golfer's elbow.

fields.Text:
Repetitive extension activity at the elbow can lead to which injury?

{{c1::Lateral epicondylitis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as tennis elbow.

fields.Text:
What are the common causes of clavicle fractures?

Direct trauma to the {{c1::shoulder}}
Fall on an {{c1::outstretched}} hand

Where is the weakest portion of the clavicle and thus most likely to fracture?

The junction between the {{c1::middle third}} segment and {{c1::lateral third}} segment
fields.Back Extra: The middle third segment is the most common site of fracture overall.

fields.Text:
What fracture presents with shoulder drop, medial arm rotation, and a shortened clavicle?

{{c1::Clavicle}} fracture
fields.Back Extra: The arm rotation is due to tension from the pectoralis major.

fields.Text:
Fracture of which bone is shown in the image?



{{c1::Clavicle}}

What is the pathophysiology of carpal tunnel syndrome?

{{c1::Median}} nerve is trapped between {{c1::transverse carpal}} ligament and {{c1::carpal}} bones → Nerve {{c1::compression}} → Pain, paresthesia, and numbness in {{c1::median}} nerve distribution

Where can atrophy be seen in carpal tunnel syndrome?

{{c1::Thenar eminence}}

Tingling during the Phalen maneuver and a positive Tinel sign suggest what diagnosis?

{{c1::Carpal tunnel}} syndrome

What is Guyon canal syndrome and with what sport is it commonly associated?

Compression of {{c1::ulnar}} nerve at the wrist
Associated with {{c1::cycling}}

What is the most common cause of the fracture shown in the image?



Direct blow with a {{c1::closed::open/closed}} {{c1::fist}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows a metacarpal neck fracture.

fields.Text:
Which metacarpal is the most commonly fractured in a metacarpal neck fracture?

{{c1::5th}} metacarpal

What condition in the wrist or hand is common to pregnancy, diabetes, hypothyroidism, dialysis-associated amyloidosis, and acromegaly?

{{c1::Carpal tunnel}} syndrome

Why is sensation spared in carpal tunnel syndrome?

{{c1::Palmar cutaneous}} branch of the {{c1::median}} nerve enters the hand outside of the carpal tunnel

What fracture or dislocation may cause Guyon canal syndrome?

{{c1::Hook}} of the {{c1::hamate}} bone

What are 2 common origins of an iliopsoas abscess?

{{c1::Blood}}
{{c1::Adjacent}} structures

Name 2 organisms commonly associated with iliopsoas abscesses.

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} (most common)
{{c1::Tuberculosis}}

What is the most likely diagnosis in an immunocompromised patient with fever, flank pain with bulging, inguinal mass, a positive psoas sign, and leukocytosis?

{{c1::Iliopsoas abscess}}

What imaging finding is seen with iliopsoas abscesses?

{{c1::Focal}} {{c1::hypodensity::hyperdensity/hypodensity}} within the iliopsoas muscle on CT or MRI

How is an iliopsoas abscess treated?

{{c1::Antibiotics}}
{{c1::Drainage}}

What are the swellings shown in the image?



{{c1::Bouchard nodes}}

What is the hand deformity shown in the image? What disease is it associated with?



This is a {{c1::swan neck}}
This is characteristic of {{c1::rheumatoid arthritis}}

What are the swellings shown in the image?



{{c1::Heberden nodes}}

What hand deformity is shown in the image? What disease is it associated with?



This is a {{c1::boutonniere}}
This is characteristic of {{c1::rheumatoid arthritis}}

How does osteoarthritis develop?

Mechanical {{c1::wear}} and {{c1::tear}} → Destruction of {{c1::articular}} cartilage → {{c1::Inflammation}} with inadequate repair

Which articular pathology is characterized by inflammatory synovial fluid?

{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}

What joint disease is associated with juxta-articular osteopenia, soft tissue swelling, erosions, subchondral cysts, and symmetric joint space narrowing?

{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}

What is Caplan syndrome?

{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}} in the presence of {{c1::pneumoconiosis}} and {{c1::rheumatoid nodules}}

What is Felty syndrome?

{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}} with {{c1::neutropenia}} and {{c1::splenomegaly}}

What are rheumatoid nodules?

Areas of {{c1::fibrinoid necrosis}} with {{c1::palisading histiocytes}}
fields.Back Extra: These are found in subcutaneous tissue and the lungs.

fields.Text:
What joint disease is associated with osteophyte formation, asymmetric joint space narrowing, cysts, and subchondral sclerosis?

{{c1::Osteoarthritis}}

Name the first-line pharmacologic treatments for acute and chronic rheumatoid arthritis.

Acute → {{c1::Corticosteroids}} and {{c1::NSAIDs}}
Chronic → {{c1::Disease-modifying}} agents and {{c1::biologic}} agents

What class of drugs, used to treat rheumatoid arthritis, do methotrexate and sulfasalazine belong to?

{{c1::Disease-modifying}} agents

HLA-DR4 is associated with which arthritis?

{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis::Rheumatoid arthritis/Osteoarthritis}}

What joint disease presents with pain in the morning that improves with use?

{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}

Name 1 lifestyle and 3 pharmacologic treatment options for osteoarthritis.

Lifetyle option → {{c1::Activity}} modification
Pharmacologic options → {{c1::NSAIDs}}, {{c1::acetaminophen}}, and intra-articular {{c1::glucocorticoids}}

Is rheumatoid arthritis more prevalent in females or males?

{{c1::Females::Males/Females}}

What are the sensitive and specific antibodies used to diagnose rheumatoid arthritis?

Sensitive antibody → {{c1::Rheumatoid factor}}
Specific antibody → {{c1::Anti-CCP}} antibody

If a patient with arthritis has DIP joint or 1st CMC joint involvement, what kind of arthritis do you suspect?

{{c1::Osteoarthritis}}

If a patient with arthritis has MCP joint involvement, what kind of arthritis do you suspect?

{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}

Why is the presentation of osteoarthritis in the knees sometimes described as "bowlegged"?

Cartilage loss typically begins at the {{c1::medial::medial/lateral}} aspect of the knees

What systemic symptoms are seen in osteoarthritis?

{{c1::None}}

Symmetric joint space narrowing suggests what type of articular pathology?

{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}

Asymmetric joint space narrowing suggests what type of articular pathology?

{{c1::Osteoarthritis}}

What joint disease presents with pain after use that improves with rest?

{{c1::Osteoarthritis}}

Name 4 major risk factors for osteoarthritis.

{{c1::Age}}
{{c1::Obesity}}
{{c1::Joint}} trauma
{{c1::Female::Male/Female}} sex

What articular pathology is caused by autoimmune inflammation with granulation tissue proliferation and pannus formation?

{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}

Name the finding shown in the image and the disease with which it is classically associated.



{{c1::Tophus}}, which is associated with {{c1::gout}}

Joint aspirate under polarized light is shown in the image. What is the likely diagnosis?



{{c1::Gout}}

What type of meal usually precipitates an acute gout attack?

A large meal of {{c1::purine}}-rich foods
{{c1::Alcohol}}

What is podagra?

A painful, swollen {{c1::MTP}} joint of the {{c1::big toe}}
fields.Back Extra: This is classically seen in acute gout flares.

fields.Text:
What drugs can be prescribed as long-term treatment for gout to prevent acute flare-ups?

{{c1::Xanthine oxidase}} inhibitors

What are the 3 treatment options for an acute gout attack?

{{c1::NSAIDs}} (first line)
{{c1::Glucocorticoids}}
{{c1::Colchicine}}

Are serum uric acid levels always elevated during gout flares?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}

Describe the appearance of a monosodium urate crystal on microscopic examination.

{{c1::Needle}} shaped with {{c1::no birefringence::birefringence/no birefringence}} under polarized light
fields.Back Extra: It is blue under perpendicular light and yellow under parallel light.

fields.Text:
Describe the general cause of gout attacks associated with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and tumor lysis syndrome.

Overproduction of {{c1::uric acid}}

Describe the general cause of gout attacks associated with renal failure and use of thiazide diuretics.

Underexcretion of {{c1::uric acid}}

Is gout more common among male patients or female patients?

{{c1::Male::Male/Female}} patients

Does gout typically present in a symmetric or asymmetric joint distribution?

{{c1::Asymmetric}} distribution

What type of diuretic increases the risk of a gout attack?

{{c1::Thiazide}} diuretic
fields.Back Extra: It blocks excretion of uric acid.

fields.Text:
Gout is caused by precipitation of what crystals in joint spaces?

{{c1::Monosodium urate}} crystals

Name 4 risk factors that can precipitate an acute gout attack that do not involve the patient's diet.

{{c1::Surgery}}
{{c1::Trauma}}
{{c1::Diuresis}}
{{c1::Dehydration}}

How does alcohol use increase the risk for an acute gout flare?

Alcohol metabolites compete with {{c1::uric acid}} for excretion sites in the kidney → Decreased excretion of {{c1::uric acid}}

What is the strongest risk factor for gout?

{{c1::Hyperuricemia}}

What is a popliteal cyst?

Popliteal fluid collection occurring in the {{c1::gastrocnemius}}-{{c1::semimembranous}} bursa commonly communicating with the {{c1::synovial}} space

What condition may cause inflammation anterior to the kneecap, as seen in the image?



{{c1::Prepatellar bursitis}}

What is the most common meniscal injury associated with ACL and MCL injury?

{{c1::Lateral::Medial/Lateral}} meniscus injury

Which 3 structures are involved in the "unhappy triad" knee injury?

{{c1::ACL}}
{{c1::MCL}}
{{c1::Medial meniscus}}

Under what conditions does an "unhappy triad" knee injury commonly occur?

{{c1::Contact}} sports
{{c1::Laterally::Medially/Laterally}} directed force applied to a {{c1::planted}} foot

Baker cysts are typically associated with what group of conditions?

Chronic {{c1::joint}} diseases

Presentation of a poorly healing foot in an adult male with a history of tobacco smoking indicates what likely diagnosis and treatment?



{{c1::Buerger}} disease
Treatment is to stop {{c1::smoking}}

What disease is characterized by headaches, skin lesions, and the angiogram findings shown in the image? What is the most appropriate treatment?



This is {{c1::polyarteritis nodosa}}
Treatment is {{c1::glucocorticoids}} and {{c1::cyclophosphamide}}

What finding on a temporal artery biopsy specimen confirms a diagnosis of giant cell arteritis?



{{c1::Focal granulomatous inflammation}}

Findings on biopsy of a skin nodule alongside asthma, foot/wrist drop, purpura, and sinusitis indicate what likely diagnosis?



{{c1::Churg-Strauss}} syndrome

What dangerous vascular consequence is mostly feared in Kawasaki disease?

{{c1::Coronary}} artery {{c1::aneurysm}}
fields.Back Extra: Thrombosis or rupture can be lethal.

fields.Text:
What types of arteries are most commonly affected in giant cell arteritis?

{{c1::Large}} arteries
fields.Back Extra: They usually are branches of the carotid artery.

fields.Text:
All ANCA-positive vasculitides affect vessels of which size?

{{c1::Small}} vessels

How is a suspected case of giant cell arteritis initially managed and why?

{{c1::High::High/Low}}-dose {{c1::steroids}} are administered first to prevent {{c1::blindness}}, followed by biopsy to confirm diagnosis

Polymyalgia rheumatica is associated with which type of large-vessel vasculitis?

{{c1::Giant cell arteritis}}

Which MPO-ANCA/p-ANCA-positive vasculitis is a granulomatous vasculitis with eosinophilia and elevated serum IgE levels?

{{c1::Churg-Strauss}} syndrome

Unilateral headache, jaw claudication, temporal artery tenderness, and anterior optic neuropathy are associated with which vasculitis?

{{c1::Giant cell arteritis}}

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis have similar presentations. How can you differentiate these 2 vasculitides?

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis → Nasopharynx {{c1::involved::involved/not involved}}, granulomas {{c1::present::present/not present}}, and positive for {{c1::c}}-ANCA
Microscopic polyangiitis → Nasopharynx {{c1::not involved::involved/not involved}}, granulomas {{c1::not present::present/not present}}, and positive for {{c1::p}}-ANCA

What lab test may help to establish the diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis?

{{c1::PR3}}-ANCA
{{c1::c}}-ANCA

Which vasculitis presents with necrotizing granulomas in the lungs and upper airway, necrotizing glomerulonephritis, and focal necrotizing vasculitis?

{{c1::Granulomatosis with polyangiitis}}

What vasculitis is indicated by MPO-ANCA/p-ANCA positivity, but no nasopharyngeal involvement?

{{c1::Microscopic polyangiitis}}

Which vasculitis is described as segmental thrombosing vasculitis affecting nerves and veins?

{{c1::Buerger}} disease

Intermittent claudication, superficial nodular phlebitis, gangrene, and digit autoamputation in the presence of Raynaud phenomenon are indicative of which vasculitis?

{{c1::Buerger}} disease

Fever along with which 5 clinical findings are associated with Kawasaki disease?

Bilateral nonexudative bulbar {{c1::conjunctivitis}}
{{c1::Rash}}
Cervical {{c1::adenopathy}}
{{c1::Strawberry}} tongue
{{c1::Hand-foot}} changes

Polyarteritis nodosa is usually found in individuals of what demographic?

{{c1::Middle}}-aged {{c1::males::males/females}}

Polyarteritis nodosa is strongly associated with which infectious disease?

{{c1::Hepatitis B}}

Which medium-vessel vasculitis presents with different stages of arterial wall transmural inflammation and fibrinoid necrosis?

{{c1::Polyarteritis nodosa}}

Which vasculitis is associated with granulomatous thickening, increased ESR, and narrowing of aortic arch and proximal great vessels?



{{c1::Takayasu arteritis}}

What classic triad of symptoms is associated with the most common childhood systemic vasculitis?



{{c1::Hinge}} pain
{{c1::Stomach}} pain
Palpable {{c1::purpura}} on legs and buttocks

What disease presents with fever, arthralgia, skin nodules, weak upper extremity pulses, and visual changes?

{{c1::Takayasu arteritis}}

Which viral illness is most closely associated with mixed cryoglobulinemia?

{{c1::HCV}}

Behçet syndrome has a high incidence in which demographic?

{{c1::Turkish}} descent
{{c1::Eastern Mediterranean}} descent

A presentation of genital ulcerations, uveitis, erythema nodosum, and recurrent aphthous ulcers is indicative of what vasculitis?

{{c1::Behçet}} syndrome

Kawasaki disease presents most commonly in which demographic?

{{c1::Asian}} children younger than {{c1::4}} years of age

What are the 2 most appropriate treatments for granulomatosis with polyangiitis?

{{c1::Glucocorticoids}}
{{c1::Rituximab}} or {{c1::cyclophosphamide}}

What type of vasculitis is microscopic polyangiitis and which organs are affected?

This is {{c1::necrotizing}} vasculitis
Commonly involves {{c1::kidneys}}, {{c1::lungs}}, and {{c1::skin}}

What is the pathophysiology of mixed cryoglobulinemia?

Deposition of mixed Ig{{c1::G}} and Ig{{c1::M}} immune complexes → Precipitate in the {{c1::cold}}

Which 2 viruses can precipitate Behçet syndrome?

{{c1::HSV}}
{{c1::Parvovirus}}

Which infections can cause cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis?

{{c1::HCV}}
{{c1::HIV}}

Which serotype is most closely associated with Behçet syndrome?

{{c1::HLA-B51}}

What is the pathophysiology of cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis?

A {{c1::leukocytoclastic}} vasculitis mediated by an {{c1::immune}} complex

Giant cell arteritis most commonly affects which demographic?

{{c1::Women::Men/Women}} older than {{c1::50}} years of age

Based on the staining pattern in the biopsy specimen shown, what type of antibody do you identify, and what diagnosis do you suspect?



Staining pattern is consistent with {{c1::PR3-ANCA}}/{{c1::c-ANCA}}
Most commonly associated with {{c1::granulomatosis with polyangiitis}}

Based on the staining pattern in the biopsy specimen shown, what type of antibody do you identify, and what diagnosis do you suspect?



Staining pattern is consistent with {{c1::MPO-ANCA}}/{{c1::p-ANCA}}
Most commonly seen with {{c1::microscopic polyangiitis}} and {{c1::eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis}}

What is the treatment for Kawasaki disease?

IV {{c1::immunoglobulin}}
{{c1::Aspirin}}

What is the treatment for Takayasu arteritis?

{{c1::Glucocorticoids}}

Which vasculitis is associated with IgA nephropathy?

{{c1::IgA vasculitis}}

What is the treatment for immunoglobulin A vasculitis?

{{c1::Supportive care}}
Possibly {{c1::glucocorticoids}}

What type of vasculature is not affected in polyarteritis nodosa?

{{c1::Pulmonary}} arteries

Takayasu vasculitis presents most commonly in which demographic?

{{c1::Asian}} {{c1::females::males/females}} younger than {{c1::40}} years of age

What are the upper respiratory tract symptoms seen in patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis?

{{c1::Otitis media}}
{{c1::Mastoiditis}}
Chronic {{c1::sinusitis}}
{{c1::Perforation}} of nasal septum

What are the lower respiratory tract symptoms seen in patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis?

{{c1::Cough}}
{{c1::Hemoptysis}}
{{c1::Dyspnea}}

Which vasculitis is associated with penicillin, cephalosporins, phenytoin, or allopurinol use and presents with palpable purpura, but no visceral involvement?

{{c1::Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis}}

What disease is caused by blunt muscle trauma leading to heterotropic ossification of skeletal muscle?

{{c1::Myositis ossificans}}

How will a patient with myositis ossificans present?

With a {{c1::painful::painful/painless}}, soft tissue {{c1::mass}} likely found in the {{c1::quadriceps}}
Possibly a recent history of {{c1::trauma}}

What does imaging show in the setting of myositis ossificans?

A {{c1::mass}} in soft tissue with "{{c1::eggshell calcifications}}"

On histologic exam, what condition, commonly mistaken for a sarcoma, shows metaplastic bone surrounding a proliferation of fibroblasts within soft tissue?

{{c1::Myositis ossificans}}

Both dermatomyositis and polymyositis cause proximal muscle weakness. What presenting symptoms differentiate the two?

Dermatomyositis presents with {{c1::skin}} findings

In a patient with dermatomyositis, what is the name for the pathology shown in the image?



"{{c1::Shawl and face}}" rash

In a patient with dermatomyositis, what is the name for the pathology shown in the image?



{{c1::Heliotrope}} rash

In a patient with dermatomyositis, what is the name for the pathology shown in the image?



{{c1::Gottron papules}}

What antibodies may be specifically elevated in patients with polymyositis and dermatomyositis?

{{c1::Anti-Jo-1}} antibodies
{{c1::Anti-SRP}} antibodies
{{c1::Anti-Mi-2}} antibodies

What would be seen on a muscle biopsy specimen obtained from a patient with polymyositis?

CD{{c1::8}}+ {{c1::T}} cells
fields.Back Extra: These cause endomysial inflammation of skeletal myofibers.

fields.Text:
Polymyositis generally causes progressive muscle weakness of which muscle groups?

{{c1::Proximal::Proximal/Distal}} muscle groups

What would be seen on a muscle biopsy specimen obtained from a patient with dermatomyositis?

CD{{c1::4}}+ {{c1::T}} cells
fields.Back Extra: These cause perimysial inflammation and atrophy.

fields.Text:
What primary bone tumor presents with the histologic findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Ewing}} sarcoma
fields.Back Extra: The image shows anaplastic small blue cells of neuroectodermal origin resembling lymphocytes.

fields.Text:
What is the finding shown in the image called?  What tumor is it associated with?



The finding is call {{c1::Codman triangle}}
This is associated with an {{c1::osteosarcoma}}

What primary bone tumor is shown in the image? Describe its composition.



This is a benign {{c1::osteochondroma}}
Consists of a {{c1::bony}} core with {{c1::cartilaginous}} cap

What is the finding shown in the image? What tumor is this associated with?



The finding is a "{{c1::sunburst pattern}}"
It is associated with an {{c1::osteosarcoma}}

Which locally aggressive primary bone tumor has this characteristic appearance on X-ray?



{{c1::Giant cell}} tumor

Which age group is at highest risk for development of a primary giant cell tumor of bone?

{{c1::Adults}} that are {{c1::20}} to {{c1::40}} years old

Which bone tumor is indicated by an "onion skin" periosteal reaction seen on an X-ray?

{{c1::Ewing}} sarcoma

What bone tumor is more common in White males younger than 15 years old?

{{c1::Ewing}} sarcoma

Codman triangle and sunburst pattern are pathognomic X-ray findings associated with which cancer?

{{c1::Osteosarcoma}}

Paget disease of bone increases the risk for which malignant bone tumor?

{{c1::Osteosarcoma}}

What is the treatment for osteosarcoma?

{{c1::Surgical resection}}
{{c1::Chemotherapy}}

Name 2 genetic conditions commonly associated with osteosarcoma.

{{c1::Li-Fraumeni}} syndrome
{{c1::Familial retinoblastoma}}

In what demographic does the incidence of primary osteosarcoma peak?

{{c1::Men::Men/Women}} younger than {{c1::20}} years old

What bone tumor is characterized by a "soap bubble" appearance on X-ray?

{{c1::Giant cell}} tumor

What benign primary bone tumor consists of a projected bony growth covered by a cartilagenous cap?

{{c1::Osteochondroma}}

Are osteochondromas likely to transform into malignancy?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}

What is the most common benign bone tumor?

{{c1::Osteochondroma}}

What bone tumor is more commonly located on the surface of facial bones?

{{c1::Osteoma}}

What bone tumor is associated with Gardner syndrome?

{{c1::Osteoma}}

A bony mass less than 2 cm with a radiolucent osteoid core presents with bone pain that increases at night and is relieved with NSAIDs. This describes which primary bone tumor?

{{c1::Osteoid osteoma}}

Which primary bone tumor arises in vertebrae?

{{c1::Osteoblastoma}}

Which primary bone tumor has histology similar to that of osteoid osteoma?

{{c1::Osteoblastoma}}
fields.Back Extra: It is unresponsive to NSAIDs and is usually larger than 2 cm.

fields.Text:
Which primary bone tumor arises in the medulla of small bones in the hands and feet?

{{c1::Chondroma}}

What is the name of a benign tumor of cartilage?

{{c1::Chondroma}}

Which tumor arises from the medulla of the pelvis, proximal femur, and humerus?

{{c1::Chondrosarcoma}}

Malignant chondrocytes are observed in which bone tumor?

{{c1::Chondrosarcoma}}

What tumor is characterized by neoplastic mononuclear cells and osteoclast-like giant cells on histologic exam?

{{c1::Giant cell}} tumor

What tumor is characterized by pleomorphic cells that produce osteoids on histologic exam?

{{c1::Osteosarcoma}}

Which malignant bone tumor presents as an enlarging mass that produces pain or occurrence of pathologic fractures?

{{c1::Osteosarcoma}}

Name 2 conditions that present with a morphology similar to that of Ewing sarcoma.

{{c1::Lymphoma}}
Chronic {{c1::osteomyelitis}}

What is the most common malignancy of the bone?

{{c1::Metastatic}} disease is more common than primary bone tumors

Which benign bone tumors are more common in boys?

{{c1::Osteochondroma}}
{{c1::Osteoma}}
{{c1::Osteoid osteoma}}
{{c1::Osteoblastoma}}

What primary bone tumor is shown in the image? Is it benign or malignant?



{{c1::Benign::Benign/Malignant}} {{c1::osteoid osteoma}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows a small bony mass with a radiolucent core in the cortex of a long bone.

fields.Text:
What bone tumor is associated with the mutation t(11;22)?

{{c1::Ewing}} sarcoma

What is meant by the "fibro fog" experienced by patients diagnosed with fibromyalgia?

{{c1::Cognitive}} disturbances

What are the classic physical exam findings in a patient with fibromyalgia?

Chronic {{c1::pain}} with "{{c1::tender points}}" and {{c1::stiffness}}

Name 1 lifestyle and 2 pharmacologic treatment approaches to fibromyalgia.

Lifestyle option → Regular {{c1::exercise}}
Pharmacologic options → {{c1::Antidepressants}} and/or a drug that targets {{c1::neuropathic}} pain

Members of what demographic are most commonly diagnosed with fibromyalgia?

{{c1::Females::Males/Females}} that are {{c1::20}} to {{c1::50}} years old

What is the treatment for polymyalgia rheumatica?

{{c1::Low::High/Low}}-dose {{c1::glucocorticoids}}

Is polymyalgia rheumatica associated with pain, muscle weakness, or both?

{{c1::Pain}}

What other autoimmune condition is associated with polymyalgia rheumatica?

{{c1::Giant cell arteritis}}

Polymyalgia rheumatica most commonly affects which age group?

{{c1::Females::Males/Females}} older than {{c1::50}} years old

What are the expected ESR, CRP levels, and creatine kinase levels with a diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica?

{{c1::Increased}} ESR
{{c1::Increased}} CRP levels
{{c1::Normal}} creatine kinase levels

What autoimmune disease presents with pain and stiffness in proximal muscles, fever, malaise, and weight loss?

{{c1::Polymyalgia rheumatica}}

A child has a puffy face, protruding tongue, and hypotonia. What is this condition?



{{c1::Cretinism}}

What is the natural clinical course for most cases of Hashimoto thyroiditis?

Initial period of {{c1::hyperthyroidism}} due to follicular rupture followed by {{c1::hypothyroidism}}

A patient has a fixed, painless goiter that is rock-hard. Histology shows inflammatory infiltrates within fibrous tissue. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Riedel thyroiditis}}

A patient has a thyroid biopsy shown in the image below. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Hashimoto thyroiditis}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows Hürthle cells and lymphoid aggregates with germinal centers.

fields.Text:
A patient with hypothyroidism who recently emigrated from the Himalayas has an enlarged thyroid. What is the likely cause of his hypothyroidism?



{{c1::Iodine}} deficiency

What is the Wolff-Chaikoff effect?

{{c1::Downregulation::Upregulation/Downregulation}} of the thyroid gland in response to {{c1::high::high/low}} iodine levels

A patient with bipolar disorder notes an enlarging mass over her anterior neck and the signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism. What is the most likely cause?

Adverse effect of {{c1::lithium}}

What is the clinical presentation of de Quervain thyroiditis?

De Quervain thyroiditis presents with a {{c1::flu}}-like illness → Transient {{c1::hyperthyroidism}} → {{c1::Euthyroid}} state → Self-limited {{c1::hypothyroidism}}

In de Quervain thyroiditis, what do you see on thyroid biopsy?

{{c1::Granulomatous inflammation}}

What is the treatment for subacute granulomatous thyroiditis?

{{c1::None}}
fields.Back Extra: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis is a self-limited condition.

fields.Text:
What six findings suggest cretinism in a newborn?

{{c1::Pot}}-bellied
{{c1::Pale}}
{{c1::Puffy}}-faced
{{c1::Protruding}} umbilicus
{{c1::Protuberant}} tongue
{{c1::Poor}} brain development

What are two causes of congenital hypothyroidism?

{{c1::Thyroid dysgenesis}} (most common)
{{c1::Dyshormonogenesis}} in iodine-sufficient regions

What two antibodies are commonly implicated in Hashimoto thyroiditis?

{{c1::Antithyroid peroxidase}} antibody
{{c1::Antithyroglobulin}} antibody

What is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions?

{{c1::Hashimoto thyroiditis}}

Which HLA variants are associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis?

{{c1::HLA-DR3}}

A postpartum female has episodes of sweating and palpitations. More recently, she has had fatigue and lethargy. Thyroid exam is normal. What is the diagnosis?

Postpartum {{c1::thyroiditis}}

What is the treatment for postpartum thyroiditis?

{{c1::None}}

What is the histological finding in postpartum thyroiditis?

{{c1::Lymphocytic}} infiltrate
Occasional {{c1::germinal center}} formation

A diagnosis of Hashimoto thyroiditis raises a patient's risk for what type of cancer?

{{c1::Non-Hodgkin}} lymphoma
fields.Back Extra: This is typically of B-cell origin.

fields.Text:
What is euthyroid sick syndrome?

{{c1::Decreased}} T3
{{c1::Normal}} or {{c1::decreased}} T4
{{c1::Normal}} TSH
fields.Back Extra: This is seen in critical non-thyroidal illness.

fields.Text:
How is a secretin stimulation test used to diagnose Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} gastrin levels after administration of secretin

What inherited syndrome is associated with gastrinomas?

{{c1::Multiple endocrine neoplasia}} type {{c1::1}}

Multiple and recurrent duodenal and jejunal ulcers indicate what endocrine disorder?

{{c1::Zollinger-Ellison}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by a gastrin-secreting tumor.

fields.Text:
What hormone is overproduced in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?

{{c1::Gastrin}}

What two symptoms are commonly associated with a gastrinoma?

{{c1::Abdominal}} pain
{{c1::Diarrhea}}

In what two locations are gastrinomas usually found?

{{c1::Pancreas}}
{{c1::Duodenum}}

What finding in this histology image is characteristic of a carcinoid tumor?



Cells arranged in a {{c1::rosette}}

What percentage of carcinoid tumors metastasize?

{{c1::33}}%

What are treatment options for carcinoid syndrome?

{{c1::Octreotide}}
{{c1::Telotristat}}
{{c1::Surgical}} resection

What cardiac complications can occur in carcinoid syndrome?

{{c1::Tricuspid regurgitation}}
{{c1::Pulmonic stenosis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to right-sided valvular disease.

fields.Text:
Why would a patient with a carcinoid tumor limited to the small bowel suddenly develop wheezing and diarrhea?

The tumor has {{c1::metastasized}}
fields.Back Extra: This allows serotonin to reach systemic circulation.

fields.Text:
What endocrine tumor is associated with niacin deficiency?

{{c1::Carcinoid tumors}}

Describe the metabolism of 5-HT in the liver and lungs.

{{c1::First}}-pass metabolism in the liver
{{c1::MAO}} breakdown in the lungs

Name the 2 histologic neuroendocrine markers associated with carcinoid syndrome.

{{c1::Chromogranin A}}
{{c1::Synaptophysin}}

At what 2 sites do carcinoid tumors most commonly arise?

{{c1::Intestines}}
{{c1::Lungs}}

What cell line do carcinoid tumors arise from and what do they secrete?

Carcinoid tumors originate from {{c1::neuroendocrine}} cells and secrete {{c1::5-HT}}

Increased urinary 5-HIAA suggests what endocrine tumor?

{{c1::Carcinoid tumor}}

What is a tumor of pancreatic α cells?

{{c1::Glucagonoma}}

What are the 6 D's that describe symptoms of a glucagonoma?

{{c1::Dermatitis}}
{{c1::Diarrhea}}
{{c1::Diabetes}}
{{c1::Declining}} weight
{{c1::DVT}}
{{c1::Depression}}

Insulinomas are associated with which inherited syndrome?

{{c1::MEN1}}

What lab test result can you use to distinguish an insulinoma from exogenous insulin use?

{{c1::C-peptide}} level
fields.Back Extra: It is increased in an insulinoma and decreased with exogenous insulin.

fields.Text:
Define the Whipple triad of insulinomas.

Low blood {{c1::glucose}}
{{c1::Hypoglycemia}} symptoms
Symptom resolution after {{c1::glucose}} normalization

What is a tumor of pancreatic β cells?

{{c1::Insulinoma}}

What pancreatic tumor may present with new-onset diabetes, gallstones, achlorhydria, and steatorrhea?

{{c1::Somatostatinoma}}

Overproduction of somatostatin by a somatostatinoma will decrease the level of which 6 hormones?

{{c1::Cholecystokinin}}
{{c1::Glucagon}}
{{c1::Secretin}}
{{c1::Insulin}}
{{c1::Gastrin}}
{{c1::GIP}}

What is a tumor of pancreatic δ cells?

{{c1::Somatostatinoma}}

What pancreatic tumor is necrolytic migratory erythema associated with?

{{c1::Glucagonoma}}

What are the treatment options for pancreatic islet cell tumors?

{{c1::Octreotide}} may be used for symptomatic relief in glucagonoma and somatostatinoma
{{c1::Surgical resection}} is needed for all 3 types of tumors

How would physical exam findings help you differentiate a thyroid adenoma from Graves disease?

Graves disease presents with {{c1::smooth}} and {{c1::diffuse}} thyroid enlargement
Thyroid adenomas are {{c1::nodular}}

Name four differential diagnoses for a smooth, diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland on physical exam.

{{c1::Graves}} disease
{{c1::Hashimoto thyroiditis}}
{{c1::TSH}}-secreting {{c1::pituitary adenoma}}
{{c1::Iodine}} deficiency

A 40-year-old woman has protruding eyes and a diffuse goiter. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Graves}} disease

A biopsy specimen obtained from an enlarged thyroid shows focal patches of hyperfunctioning, colloid-enlarged follicular cells. T3 and T4 levels are increased. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Toxic multinodular goiter}}

A patient has weight loss and palpitations. Thyroid biopsy shows tall, crowded follicular epithelial cells and scalloped colloid. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Graves}} disease

Graves disease is associated with which two human leukocyte antigens?

{{c1::HLA-DR3}}
{{c1::HLA-B8}}

What is the Jod-Basedow phenomenon?

{{c1::Hyperthyroidism::Hyperthyroidism/Hypothyroidism}} induced by iodine repletion in patients with iodine deficiency and partially autonomous thyroid tissue

What is the treatment of thyroid storm?

{{c1::β-blockers}}
{{c1::Propylthiouracil}}
{{c1::Corticosteroids}}
{{c1::Potassium iodide}}

What is the hepatic laboratory finding seen in thyroid storm?

Thyroid storm may present with a(n) {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} in liver function tests

A patient with Graves disease hospitalized with a bacterial infection suddenly develops ventricular fibrillation. What happened?

{{c1::Thyroid storm}}
fields.Back Extra: This occurs when hyperthyroidism is improperly treated in the setting of stressors.

fields.Text:
A patient with multinodular goiter is found to have focal patches of high radioactive iodine uptake. What is the likelihood that it is malignant?

These are {{c1::hot}} nodules, which are {{c1::rarely}} malignant

A patient with elevated T3 and T4 levels is diagnosed with a toxic multinodular goiter. What is the expected TSH level?

{{c1::Normal}}
fields.Back Extra: TSH receptors are mutated 60% of the time in toxic multinodular goiter.

fields.Text:
Graves disease is associated with what type of hypersensitivity reaction?

Type {{c1::II}} hypersensitivity reaction

In Graves disease, what causes the exophthalmos?

Activation of {{c1::T}} cells → {{c1::Lymphocytic}} infiltration of retroorbital space → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} cytokines → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} fibroblast secretion of hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} osmotic muscle swelling, muscle inflammation, and adipocyte count → Exophthalmos

Which two muscle findings would be found in the retroorbital space in a patient with Graves disease?

{{c1::Osmotic}} muscle {{c1::swelling}}
Muscle {{c1::inflammation}}

What antibodies are seen in Graves disease?

Ig{{c1::G}} against {{c1::TSH receptors}}

Graves disease is caused by IgG autoantibodies stimulating TSH receptors. What two cell types do these autoantibodies pathologically react with?

{{c1::Dermal fibroblasts}}
{{c1::Orbital fibroblasts}}

What is the most likely cause of death in a patient with thyroid storm?

{{c1::Tachyarrhythmia}}

A patient feels a lump in the throat. Results of thyroid biopsy are shown in the image. What findings are demonstrated on the histology slide?



{{c1::Follicular}} histology with absence of {{c1::capsular}} or {{c1::vascular}} invasion
fields.Back Extra: This is most commonly seen in thyroid adenomas.

fields.Text:
What is the difference between the histology of thyroid follicular adenomas and follicular carcinomas?

Follicular carcinoma demonstrates the presence of {{c1::capsular}} or {{c1::vascular}} invasion

What are the functional thyroid effects of a thyroid adenoma?

Most thyroid adenomas are {{c1::nonfunctional}}
fields.Back Extra: They very rarely cause hyperthyroidism by autonomous thyroid hormone production.

fields.Text:
List the order in which hemoglobin molecules move from cathode to anode, starting with the molecule that moves the farthest.

Hemoglobin {{c1::A}} → Hemoglobin {{c1::F}} → Hemoglobin {{c1::S}} → Hemoglobin {{c1::C}}

What type of mutation causes a more positive charge in hemoglobin S and hemoglobin C compared with hemoglobin A?

{{c1::Missense}} mutation

Which hemoglobin type travels farthest on gel electrophoresis?

Hemoglobin {{c1::A}}
fields.Back Extra: It is the most negatively charged hemoglobin type.

fields.Text:
Which row in the hemoglobin electrophoresis pattern shown in the image is most likely to correspond to that of a healthy newborn?



Row {{c1::2}}

Which row in the hemoglobin electrophoresis pattern shown in the image is most likely to correspond to that of a healthy adult?



Row {{c1::1}}

Row 3 in the hemoglobin electrophoresis pattern shown in the image corresponds to the hemoglobin type of which patients?



Patients with the {{c1::sickle cell}} trait

Row 4 in the hemoglobin electrophoresis pattern shown in the image corresponds to the hemoglobin type of which patients?



Patients with {{c1::sickle cell}} disease

What is the direction of movement of hemoglobin on an electrophoresis gel plate?

{{c1::Negatively::Positively/Negatively}} charged {{c1::cathode::cathode/anode}} → {{c1::Positively::Positively/Negatively}} charged {{c1::anode::cathode/anode}}

What changes in the amino acid sequence of hemoglobin result in hemoglobin C and S?

Hemoglobin S → {{c1::Valine}} replaces glutamic acid
Hemoglobin C → {{c1::Lysine}} replaces glutamic acid

Which four coagulation factors are activated by factor IIa to exert positive feedback on the coagulation cascade to promote more thrombosis?

Factor {{c1::V}}
Factor {{c1::VIII}}
Factor {{c1::XI}}
Factor {{c1::XIII}}

Name four agents that can block factor Xa in the coagulation cascade.

{{c1::Low-molecular-weight heparin}}
{{c1::Heparin}}
{{c1::Direct::Direct/Indirect}} factor {{c1::Xa}} inhibitors
{{c1::Fondaparinux}}

What will an assay measuring factor XIIIa activity show in a patient who has started taking argatroban?

{{c1::Low::High/Low}} activity

What is the mechanism of action of the antifibrinolytics?

Inhibition of {{c1::tPA}}

Name four thrombolytics that can convert plasminogen into plasmin.

{{c1::Alteplase}}
{{c1::Reteplase}}
{{c1::Tenecteplase}}
{{c1::Streptokinase}}

How does alteplase carry out fibrinolysis?

Activates {{c1::tPA}}

Which anticoagulants act on factor IIa?

{{c1::Heparin}}
{{c1::Low-molecular-weight heparin}}
{{c1::Direct::Direct/Indirect}} {{c1::thrombin}} inhibitors

What inheritance pattern is illustrated by both hemophilia A and B?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

What is the inheritance pattern of hemophilia C?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What accounts for elevated bradykinin activity in a person starting to take an ACE inhibitor?

ACE normally {{c1::inactivates::activates/inactivates}} bradykinin

What does factor XIII require to stabilize the fibrin mesh?

{{c1::Ca2+}}

What are two stimuli for the conversion of factor X to factor Xa?

Extrinsic → Factor {{c1::VIIa}}
Intrinsic → Factor {{c1::IXa}} with factor {{c1::VIIIa}} as a cofactor

Name four initiators of the intrinsic coagulation pathway.

{{c1::High-molecular-weight kinin}}
{{c1::Collagen}}
{{c1::Basement membrane}}
Activated {{c1::platelets}}

Which five reactions in the coagulation cascade require both Ca2+ and phospholipid surface as cofactors?

Conversion of factor VII → {{c1::VIIa}}
Conversion of factor IX → {{c1::IXa}}
Conversion of factor X → {{c1::Xa}}
Conversion of factor II → {{c1::IIa}}
Formation of {{c1::fibrin mesh}}

What is the end result of the coagulation cascade?

Conversion of {{c1::fibrinogen}} to {{c1::fibrin}} to form {{c1::fibrin mesh}}

Which coagulation factors are common to both the intrinsic and extrinsic coagulation pathways?

Factor {{c1::I}}
Factor {{c1::II}}
Factor {{c1::V}}
Factor {{c1::X}}
Factor {{c1::XIII}}

Which coagulation factors are specific to the extrinsic coagulation pathway?

Factor {{c1::VII}}
{{c1::Thromboplastin}}

Which coagulation factors are specific to the intrinsic coagulation pathway?

Factor {{c1::VIII}}
Factor {{c1::IX}}
Factor {{c1::XI}}
Factor {{c1::XII}}

What are the effects of the kinin cascade, mediated by bradykinin?

Increased {{c1::vasodilation::vasodilation/vasoconstriction}}
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} vascular permeability
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} pain

What is the product of interaction of plasmin and fibrin clots?

{{c1::Fibrin degradation}} products

Name two reactions initiated by high-molecular-weight kininogen.

{{c1::Kinin}} cascade
{{c1::Coagulation}} cascade

What is the role of C1-esterase inhibitor in the coagulation and kinin pathways?

Inhibits factors {{c1::XIIa}} and {{c1::XIa}} in the intrinsic pathway
Inhibits {{c1::kallikrein}} in the kinin cascade

How does hereditary angioedema occur?

{{c1::C1-esterase}} inhibitor deficiency → Disinhibits {{c1::kallikrein}} → Increased {{c1::bradykinin}}

Name two agents that block the conversion of plasminogen into plasmin.

{{c1::Aminocaproic acid}}
{{c1::Tranexamic acid}}

Which coagulation factors will be affected in vitamin K deficiency?

Factor {{c1::II}}
Factor {{c1::VII}}
Factor {{c1::IX}}
Factor {{c1::X}}
Protein {{c1::C}}
Protein {{c1::S}}

What anomaly in the coagulation cascade causes thrombosis in a patient with factor V Leiden mutation?

Production of a factor V that resists activated protein {{c1::C}} inhibition

What medication may reduce brain damage in acute thrombotic stroke if given within 3 to 4.5 hours of onset?

{{c1::tPA}}

What is tPA used for clinically?

{{c1::Thrombolytic}}

What is the role of protein S in anticoagulation?

Protein S is a cofactor for protein {{c1::C}}
Inactivates factors {{c1::Va}} and {{c1::VIIIa}}

Name the three endogenous factors that promote anticoagulation.

{{c1::Antithrombin III}}
Protein {{c1::C}}
Protein {{c1::S}}

Why is vitamin K administration necessary for neonates soon after birth?

They lack enteric {{c1::bacteria}} that produce vitamin K

What is the mechanism of action of warfarin?

Inhibition of vitamin {{c1::K}} {{c1::epoxide reductase}}

What is the mechanism of action of heparin?

Enhancement of {{c1::antithrombin III}} activity

What two medications can be administered to reverse the inhibitory effect of warfarin?

Vitamin {{c1::K}} (slow reversal)
{{c1::Fresh frozen plasma}} or {{c1::prothrombin complex concentrate}} (immediate reversal)

Which coagulation factor has the shortest half life?

Factor {{c1::VII}}

Which coagulation factor has the longest half life?

Factor {{c1::II}}

Activated forms of which factors are susceptible to inhibition by antithrombin?

Factor {{c1::II}}
Factor {{c1::VII}}
Factor {{c1::IX}}
Factor {{c1::X}}
Factor {{c1::XI}}
Factor {{c1::XII}}

What are the two principal targets of antithrombin?

{{c1::Thrombin}}
Factor {{c1::Xa}}

Which enzyme is responsible for converting inactive vitamin K-dependent factors to their active forms?

{{c1::γ-glutamyl carboxylase}}

What is the first step in the protein C pathway?

{{c1::Thrombin-thrombomodulin}} complex activates protein C

How does activated protein C proceed to inactivate factors Va and VIIIa?

Requires protein {{c1::S}} to cleave factors Va and VIIIa

After a platelet plug forms and bleeding ceases, what step in hemostasis begins to ensure its stability?

{{c1::Coagulation}} cascade

In a patient who is taking aspirin, which prevents TXA2 synthesis, what will happen to the stability of a platelet plug?

It will be {{c1::destabilized}}

Which phase of platelet plug formation will be most impaired if platelets are unable to release ADP?

{{c1::Adhesion}}

Which two anti-aggregation factors are released by endothelial cells to increase blood flow and decrease platelet aggregation?

{{c1::PGI2}}
{{c1::NO}}

Which pro-aggregation factor reduces blood flow and increases platelet aggregation?

{{c1::TXA2}}

What happens after platelet activation of GpIIb/IIIa receptors by ADP?

{{c1::Fibrinogen}} binds GpIIb/IIIa receptors and {{c1::links}} platelets together

After von Willebrand factor binds to collagen, how do platelets respond?

Platelets bind to von Willebrand factor → {{c1::Conformational}} changes → Releases {{c1::ADP}}, {{c1::Ca2+}}, {{c1::TXA2}}

In the process of platelet plug formation, what binds to exposed collagen after injury?

{{c1::Von Willebrand factor}}

What happens in response to injury to endothelial cells in the process of platelet plug formation?

Transient {{c1::vasoconstriction::vasodilation/vasoconstriction}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is a neural stimulation reflex.

Endothelin is released from damaged cells.

fields.Text:
What happens during the activation of platelets after ADP binds to P2Y12 receptors?

Induction of {{c1::GpIIb/IIIa}} at platelet surface

What are the five events of platelet plug formation?

{{c1::Injury}} → {{c1::Exposure}} → {{c1::Adhesion}} → {{c1::Activation}} → {{c1::Aggregation}}

What are the two sources of von Willebrand factor?

{{c1::α-granules}} of platelets
{{c1::Weibel-Palade bodies}} of endothelial cells

For a patient with a deficiency of GpIIb/IIIa receptors, what will the results of a ristocetin cofactor assay be?

{{c1::Normal}}

What two disorders are associated with a lack of agglutination on a ristocetin cofactor assay?

{{c1::von Willebrand}} disease
{{c1::Bernard-Soulier}} syndrome

What is the pathophysiology of Glanzmann thrombasthenia?

Deficiency of {{c1::GpIIb/IIIa}}

What is the pathology in Bernard-Soulier syndrome?

{{c1::GpIb}} receptor deficiency

Which molecule, found on the surface of vascular endothelial cells, is a cofactor in activating protein C?

{{c1::Thrombin-thrombomodulin}} complex

Name the five mediators of thrombus formation or degradation that are found in the vascular endothelial cell.

{{c1::Von Willebrand factor}}
Factor {{c1::VIII}}
{{c1::Thromboplastin}}
{{c1::tPA}}
{{c1::PGI2}}

Which stage of platelet plug formation is affected by ticlopidine?

{{c1::ADP}}-induced expression of {{c1::GpIIb/IIIa}}

What is the mechanism of action of aspirin in preventing clot formation?

Inhibition of {{c1::TXA2}}

How do the functions of GpIb and GpIIb/IIIa on the platelet surface differ?

GpIb binds to {{c1::von Willebrand factor}}
GpIIb/IIIa binds to {{c1::fibrinogen}}

What is the mechanism of action of abciximab?

Direct inhibition of {{c1::GpIIb/IIIa}}
fields.Back Extra: Eptifibatide and tirofiban act this way as well.

fields.Text:
Which coagulation factor is carried by von Willebrand factor?

Factor {{c1::VIII}}

How is ADP-induced expression of GpIIb/IIIa inhibited by drugs such as clopidogrel, ticagrelor, and prasugrel?

Inhibition of {{c1::P2Y12}} receptor

{{c1::Antiglobulin}} test

{{c1::Viral}} infections

Which cell is abundantly seen in mixed cellularity Hodgkin lymphoma?

{{c1::Eosinophils}}

What is the most common type of Hodgkin lymphoma?

{{c1::Nodular sclerosis}} Hodgkin lymphoma

Name four subtypes of Hodgkin lymphoma.

{{c1::Nodular sclerosing}}
{{c1::Lymphocytic depleted}}
{{c1::Lymphocytic rich}}
{{c1::Mixed cellularity}}

Which subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma has the best and worst prognosis?

Best prognosis → {{c1::Lymphocyte rich}}
Worst prognosis → {{c1::Lymphocyte depleted}}

Describe the appearance of a Reed-Sternberg cell under the microscope.

"{{c1::Owl-eyes}}" appearance

What is the CD profile of the cell type shown?



CD{{c1::15}}+
CD{{c1::30}}+

Which two subtypes of Hodgkin lymphoma are seen in immunocompromised patients?

{{c1::Mixed cellularity}}
{{c1::Lymphocyte depleted}}

How is the histologic appearance of Burkitt lymphoma, as shown in the image, described?



"{{c1::Starry sky}}" appearance

What viral illness may lead to a mass lesion in a patient with HIV/AIDS, as shown in the image?



{{c1::Epstein-Barr virus}}

What infectious cause of ring-enhancing lesions in a patient with HIV/AIDS must primary central nervous system lymphoma be distinguished from?

{{c1::Toxoplasmosis}}

In Burkitt lymphoma, where do lesions occur in different epidemiological forms?

{{c1::Jaw}} lesions in the endemic form in Africa
{{c1::Pelvic}} and/or {{c1::abdominal}} lesions in the sporadic form

What translocation is associated with follicular lymphoma?

t({{c1::14}};{{c1::18}})

How do adults with primary central nervous system lymphoma present?

{{c1::Confusion}}
{{c1::Memory}} loss
{{c1::Seizures}}

What is the typical prognosis for a patient with follicular lymphoma?

{{c1::Indolent}} course

Which virus is associated with adult T-cell lymphoma?

{{c1::HTLV}}

What personal history is associated with adult T-cell lymphoma?

Intravenous {{c1::drug abuse}}

What translocation is associated with mantle cell lymphoma?

t({{c1::11}};{{c1::14}})

What may be the histopathological finding of a skin biopsy in a patient with Mycosis fungoides as shown?



Atypical CD{{c1::4}}+ cells exhibiting "{{c1::cerebriform}}" nuclei
{{c1::Pautrier microabscess}}

Which non-Hodgkin lymphoma subtype is associated with an (11;18) translocation?

{{c1::Marginal zone}} lymphoma

What conditions are associated with the development of marginal zone lymphoma?

Chronic {{c1::inflammatory}} conditions

Which non-Hodgkin lymphoma has an aggressive late stage presentation?

{{c1::Mantle cell}} lymphoma

Which variant of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is most commonly associated with HIV/AIDS?

{{c1::Primary central nervous system}} lymphoma

What genetic mutations is seen in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma?

Mutation in {{c1::BCL-2}}
Mutation in {{c1::BCL-6}}

Which non-Hodgkin lymphoma of mature B-cell origin is most common in adults?

{{c1::Diffuse large B-cell}} lymphoma

What electrolyte abnormality is seen in adult T-cell lymphoma?

{{c1::Hypercalcemia::Hypercalcemia/Hypocalcemia}}
fields.Back Extra: This is secondary to lytic bone lesions.

fields.Text:
Name two non-Hodgkin lymphoma subtypes that are associated with mature T cells.

{{c1::Adult T-cell}} lymphoma
{{c1::Mycosis fungoides}}
fields.Back Extra: Mycosis fungoides can progress to Sézary syndrome.

fields.Text:
Which infectious agent is associated with Burkitt lymphoma?

{{c1::Epstein-Barr virus}}

What is the genetic basis of Burkitt lymphoma?

t({{c1::8}};{{c1::14}})

Which condition may mycosis fungoides progress to?

{{c1::Sézary}} syndrome

What population age is associated with Burkitt lymphoma?

{{c1::Adolescents}}
{{c1::Younger::Older/Younger}} adults

What is the end function of Bcl-2?

Inhibits {{c1::apoptosis}}

What three geographic regions are associated with adult T-cell lymphoma?

{{c1::Japan}}
{{c1::West Africa}}
{{c1::Caribbean}}

Which gender group is more often affected by mantle cell lymphoma?

{{c1::Males::Males/Females}}

How does disease location differ between leukemia and lymphoma?

Leukemia → Neoplasms involve {{c1::bone marrow}}, while cells involve {{c1::blood}}
Lymphoma → Discrete {{c1::lymph node}} tumors

Of TTP and HUS, which is more commonly seen in females?

{{c1::TTP}} is typically seen in females
fields.Back Extra: HUS is typically seen in children.

fields.Text:
What is the etiology of HUS?

{{c1::Shiga toxin}}-producing {{c1::Escherichia coli}} infection

Describe the pathophysiology of TTP.

Inhibition or deficiency of {{c1::ADAMTS13}} → Decreased degradation of {{c1::vWF}} multimers → Increased large {{c1::vWF}} multimers → Increased platelet {{c1::adhesion}} and {{c1::aggregation}} → Microthrombi

What is the triad seen in both TTP and HUS?

{{c1::Thrombocytopenia}}
Acute {{c1::kidney}} injury
{{c1::Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia}}

How do you differentiate between TTP and HUS based on clinical symptoms/signs?

HUS presents with {{c1::bloody diarrhea}}
TTP presents with {{c1::neurologic}} symptoms and {{c1::fever}}

How do you differentiate TTP and HUS from DIC?

PT and PTT is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} in DIC

How is TTP treated?

{{c1::Plasmapheresis}}
{{c1::Steroids}}
{{c1::Rituximab}}

How is HUS managed?

{{c1::Supportive care}}

What lab findings help diagnose von Willebrand disease?

{{c1::Increased}} bleeding time
{{c1::Increased}} PTT
{{c1::Negative::Positive/Negative}} platelet aggregation

What are the coagulation-related lab findings for DIC?

{{c1::Decreased}} platelet count
{{c1::Decreased}} fibrinogen
{{c1::Increased}} bleeding time
{{c1::Increased}} PT
{{c1::Increased}} PTT
{{c1::Increased}} fibrin degradation products

How is a bleeding state brought about in DIC?

Deficiency in {{c1::clotting factors}} → Widespread activation of {{c1::clotting}} → Decreased ability to form future {{c1::clots}}

Which factor of the coagulation pathway does vWF carry/protect?

Factor {{c1::VIII}}

What mixed platelet and coagulation disorder can result from snake bites, trauma, acute pancreatitis, malignancy, nephrotic syndrome, and most commonly sepsis from gram-negative bacteria?

{{c1::DIC}}

What is the most common inherited bleeding disorder?

{{c1::von Willebrand}} disease

How is platelet plug formation defective in von Willebrand disease?

Decreased {{c1::vWF}} available for {{c1::platelet}}-to-{{c1::vWF}} {{c1::adhesion}}

What is the mechanism of desmopressin treatment for von Willebrand disease?

Releases {{c1::vWF}} stored in {{c1::endothelium}}

What is the inheritance pattern of von Willebrand disease?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What are three common complications in patients with factor V Leiden?

{{c1::Cerebral vein thrombosis}}
{{c1::DVT}}
Recurrent {{c1::pregnancy}} loss

What are the roles of protein C and protein S?

Inactivate factors {{c1::Va}} and {{c1::VIIIa}}

What is a complication of warfarin administration in the setting of protein C or S deficiency?

Warfarin-induced {{c1::skin necrosis}}

Which hereditary thrombophilia can cause a diminished increase in PTT after standard heparin dosing?

{{c1::Antithrombin III}} deficiency

In what two disease states can antithrombin deficiency be acquired?

{{c1::Renal}} failure
{{c1::Nephrotic}} syndrome

What mutation in the prothrombin gene would lead to increased production of venous clots?

{{c1::Point}} mutation in the {{c1::3}}′ untranslated region

What is the pathogenesis of factor V Leiden?

Mutated factor V is unable to be degraded by protein {{c1::C}} → {{c1::Hypercoagulable}} state

How does antithrombin deficiency affect a patient's PT, PTT, and thrombin time?

{{c1::No direct effect}}

What is the mode of inheritance of hereditary thrombophilias?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What hemodynamic state is created with deficiency of proteins C and S?

{{c1::Hypercoagulable}} state

In what two conditions is the transfusion of fresh frozen plasma warranted to reverse a coagulopathy?

{{c1::Cirrhosis}}
Situations requiring immediate {{c1::anticoagulation}} reversal

By how much will a unit of transfused platelets increase the platelet count?

{{c1::5000}} platelets/mm3

What is a physiologic benefit of packed RBC transfusion?

Increased {{c1::hemoglobin}}
Increased {{c1::O2}} carrying capacity of blood

Name any five risks associated with blood transfusion.

Transfusion {{c1::reaction}}
{{c1::Infection}} transmission
{{c1::Hypocalcemia}}
{{c1::Hyperkalemia}}
{{c1::Iron}} overload

What transfusion therapy is used to treat fibrinogen and factor VIII deficiencies?

{{c1::Cryoprecipitate}}

What may be the cause of numbness and tingling in fingers and toes after receiving multiple blood transfusions during surgery?

{{c1::Citrate}}

Name two clinical situations warranting platelet transfusion.

{{c1::Thrombocytopenia}}
{{c1::Qualitative}} platelet defects

What are the contents of PCC?

Factor {{c1::II}}
Factor {{c1::VII}}
Factor {{c1::IX}}
Factor {{c1::X}}
Protein {{c1::C}}
Protein {{c1::S}}

What are the contents of FFP?

All {{c1::coagulation factors}}
{{c1::Plasma}} proteins

Name two indications of packed RBC transfusion.

Acute {{c1::blood}} loss
Severe {{c1::anemia}}

What are two treatments for acute iron poisoning?

Gastric {{c1::lavage}}
{{c1::Chelation}}

What is a common cause of acute iron poisoning in children?

Accidental consumption of adult {{c1::iron tablets}}

What are two mechanisms of iron poisoning?

Cell death from {{c1::free radical}} formation
{{c1::Peroxidation}} of membrane lipids

What are six complications of chronic iron poisoning?

{{c1::Cardiomyopathy}}
{{c1::Cirrhosis}}
{{c1::Arthropathy}}
{{c1::Hypogonadism::Hypergonadism/Hypogonadism}}
{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}
Skin {{c1::pigmentation}}

What are two treatments for chronic iron poisoning?

{{c1::Chelation}}
{{c1::Phlebotomy}} for patients without anemia

What lab finding may indicate acute iron poisoning in a child?

{{c1::Anion gap metabolic acidosis}}

What abdominal X-ray finding may be present in a child who ingested iron tablets?

{{c1::Radiopaque}} pills

What are the two most common causes of chronic iron poisoning?

Primary cause → {{c1::Hereditary}}
Secondary cause → {{c1::Hemochromatosis}}

What is the finding shown in the image?



{{c1::Basophilic stippling}}
fields.Back Extra: This is observed in lead poisoning.

fields.Text:
What is the defective enzyme in acute intermittent porphyria?

{{c1::Porphobilinogen deaminase}}

What are two common environmental sources of lead poisoning in adults?

{{c1::Batteries}}
{{c1::Ammunition}}

What are the differences in neurologic symptoms between adults and children with lead poisoning?

{{c1::Adults::Adults/Children}} → Headache, memory loss, and peripheral neuropathy
{{c1::Children::Adults/Children}} → Mental deterioration

X-linked sideroblastic anemia results from a defect in which enzyme involved in heme synthesis?

{{c1::Aminolevulinic acid synthase}}

Acute intermittent porphyria leads to accumulation of which two heme precursors?

{{c1::Porphobilinogen}}
{{c1::Aminolevulinic acid}}

Lead poisoning leads to the accumulation of what two heme precursors in the blood?

{{c1::Protoporphyrin}}
{{c1::Aminolevulinic acid}}

What are two causes of porphyria cutanea tarda?

{{c1::Familial}}
{{c1::Hepatitis C}} infection

What exacerbates porphyria cutanea tarda?

{{c1::Alcohol}} consumption

What type of porphyria presents with blistering skin, hyperpigmentation, photosensitivity, and tea-colored urine?

{{c1::Porphyria cutanea tarda}}

What enzyme catalyzes the conversion of protoporphyrin to heme?

{{c1::Ferrochelatase}}

Which enzyme is affected in porphyria cutanea tarda?

{{c1::Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase}}

What is the inheritance mode of acute intermittent porphyria?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What's the function of aminolevulinic acid dehydratase in heme synthesis?

Converts {{c1::aminolevulinic acid}} to {{c1::porphobilinogen}}

What are three treatments for porphyria cutanea tarda?

{{c1::Phlebotomy}}
Avoidance of {{c1::sun}}
{{c1::Antimalarials}}

What type of porphyria presents with abdominal pain, wine-colored urine, polyneuropathy, and psychological disturbances?

{{c1::Acute intermittent porphyria}}

What two enzymes involved in heme synthesis are inhibited by lead?

{{c1::Ferrochelatase}}
{{c1::Aminolevulinic acid dehydratase}}

Name two possible treatments for acute intermittent porphyria.

{{c1::Glucose}}
{{c1::Hemin}}

Which step in heme synthesis requires iron?

Conversion of {{c1::protoporphyrin}} to {{c1::heme}}

How does heme provide feedback for its own synthesis?

Heme inhibits {{c1::aminolevulinic acid synthase}}

What are the characteristic findings in a bone marrow specimen obtained from a patient with lead poisoning?

{{c1::Ringed sideroblasts}}

What common change in leukocyte count is noted with HIV, DiGeorge syndrome, severe combined immunodeficiency, and systemic lupus erythematosus?

{{c1::Lymphopenia}}

{{c1::Sepsis}}
{{c1::Aplastic}} anemia
{{c1::Radiation}}
{{c1::Drugs}}
{{c1::Systemic lupus erythematosus}}

Inhibition of neutrophil {{c1::adhesion}} molecule activation → Prevents {{c1::migration}} out of vasculature

Absolute eosinophil count < {{c1::30}} cells/mm3

What is the criteria for lymphopenia?

Absolute lymphocyte count < {{c1::1500}} cells/mm3

What is the criteria for neutropenia?

Absolute neutrophil count < {{c1::1500}} cells/mm3

What are two causes of eosinopenia?

{{c1::Cushing}} syndrome
{{c1::Corticosteroid}} use

Name two conditions that cause macroangiopathic hemolytic anemia.

Presence of {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}}

{{c1::Mechanical}} damage to red blood cells

What three conditions can present with hemolytic anemia resulting from cold agglutinin?

{{c1::Mycoplasma pneumoniae}} infection
{{c1::Mononucleosis}}
{{c1::Chronic lymphocytic}} leukemia

Name three conditions associated with warm agglutinin autoimmune hemolysis.

{{c1::Systemic lupus erythematosus}}
{{c1::Chronic lymphocytic}} leukemia
{{c1::Drug}} reactions

What is the pathogenesis of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia?

Red blood cells are damaged on passage through {{c1::narrowed}} or {{c1::obstructed}} vessels

Name three forms of treatment for warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

{{c1::Steroids}}
{{c1::Rituximab}}
{{c1::Splenectomy}}

How does cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia lead to painful, blue fingers and toes?

Ig{{c1::M}} + {{c1::Complement}} → Red blood cell {{c1::agglutination}} upon cold exposure → Painful, blue fingers and toes

Name two forms of treatment for cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

{{c1::Rituximab}}
{{c1::Cold}} avoidance

Name two infections that cause anemia by destruction of red blood cells.

{{c1::Malaria}}
{{c1::Babesiosis}}

Name four conditions in which microangiopathic hemolytic anemia is seen.

{{c1::HELLP}} syndrome
{{c1::Disseminated intravascular coagulation}}
{{c1::Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura}}/{{c1::Hemolytic uremic}} syndrome
{{c1::Systemic lupus erythematosus}}

{{c1::Extravascular}} space
{{c1::Intravascular}} space
fields.Back Extra: The crescent-shaped red blood cells in the image indicate sickle cell anemia.

fields.Text:
What renal complication can sickle cell anemia cause?

{{c1::Renal papillary necrosis}}

What potential complication can occur if a child with sickle cell anemia has a parvovirus B19 infection?

{{c1::Aplastic crisis}}

What test can help confirm the diagnosis of sickle cell anemia?

{{c1::Hemoglobin electrophoresis}}

Which organism is likely to cause osteomyelitis in a patient with sickle cell anemia?

{{c1::Salmonella}}

What causes the appearance of Howell-Jolly bodies in patients with sickle cell anemia?

{{c1::Autosplenectomy}}

What manifestation of sickle cell anemia is also seen in patients with thalassemias?

"{{c1::Crew cut}}" appearance on skull X-ray
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by marrow expansion resulting from increased erythropoiesis.

fields.Text:
What two treatment options are available for patients with sickle cell anemia?

{{c1::Hydroxyurea}}
{{c1::Hydration}}

What evolutionary advantage may explain the prevalence of sickle cell trait in the African American population?

Resistance to {{c1::malaria}}

What is the pathogenesis of sickle cell anemia?

{{c1::Low::High/Low}} oxygen, {{c1::high::high/low}} altitude, or {{c1::acidosis::acidosis/alkalosis}} → Sickling → Anemia and vaso-occlusive disease

What mutation causes sickle cell anemia?

{{c1::Point}} mutation in the {{c1::β-globin}} gene
fields.Back Extra: This mutation converts glutamic acid to valine.

fields.Text:
Why is a newborn with sickle cell anemia initially asymptomatic?

Presence of {{c1::HbF}}

What may be the cause of reddish urine passed by a patient with known aplastic anemia?

{{c1::Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria}}

What is the triad associated with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?

Coombs-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} hemolytic anemia
{{c1::Pancytopenia}}
{{c1::Venous thrombosis}}

What is the mechanism of hemolysis in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?

{{c1::Complement}}-mediated {{c1::intravascular::intravascular/extravascular}} hemolysis due to acquired {{c1::PIGA}} mutation → Affects decay-accelerating factor (CD55)

What is the treatment of choice for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?

{{c1::Eculizumab}}

What will a blood smear obtained from a patient with homozygous HbC disease show?

{{c1::Target}} cells
{{c1::Hemoglobin crystals}} inside red blood cells

A patient has a combined HbS and HbC mutation. How will this affect disease severity as compared with HbSS disease?

An HbSC mutation results in a {{c1::milder}} form of disease when compared with an HbSS mutation

What mutation produces HbC, and what type of hemolytic anemia does it cause?

{{c1::β-globin chain}} mutation → {{c1::Extravascular::Intravascular/Extravascular}} hemolysis
fields.Back Extra: This mutation converts glutamic acid to lysine.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiology of pyruvate kinase deficiency?

Pyruvate kinase defect→ Decreased ATP → {{c1::Rigid}} red blood cells → {{c1::Extravascular::Intravascular/Extravascular}} hemolysis
Increased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate → Decreased hemoglobin affinity for O2

How does pyruvate kinase deficiency commonly present?

{{c1::Hemolytic anemia}} in newborns

What is the inheritance pattern for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency?

{{c1::X-linked recessive}}

Where does hemolysis occur in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency who are exposed to oxidants?

{{c1::Extravascular}} space
{{c1::Intravascular}} space

Name three examples of oxidative stress that lead to glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.

{{c1::Antimalarials}}
{{c1::Sulfa}} drugs
{{c1::Fava beans}}

What findings on a peripheral blood smear would aid in the diagnosis of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency?

{{c1::Heinz bodies}}
{{c1::Bite}} cells

In glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, what underlying pathophysiology is behind the anemia?

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency → Decreased {{c1::NADPH}} → Decreased {{c1::glutathione}} → Increased susceptibility of red blood cells to {{c1::oxidative}} stressors→ Hemolysis

What is the best treatment for hereditary spherocytosis?

{{c1::Splenectomy}}

What are the red blood cell indices that define hereditary spherocytosis?

{{c1::Normal}} or {{c1::decreased}} mean corpuscular volume
{{c1::Increased}} mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration
{{c1::Increased}} red blood cell count

Defects in what four proteins are responsible for the red blood cell morphology seen in hereditary spherocytosis?

{{c1::Ankyrin}}
{{c1::Spectrin}}
{{c1::Band 3}}
{{c1::Protein 4.2}}

What two lab tests can confirm hereditary spherocytosis?

{{c1::Osmotic fragility}} test
{{c1::EMA binding}} test

Which organ is most responsible for development of anemia in patients with hereditary spherocytosis?

{{c1::Spleen}}

Name two conditions associated with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.

{{c1::Acute::Acute/Chronic}} leukemias
{{c1::Aplastic}} anemia

What specific life-threatening venous thrombotic event is associated with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinura?

{{c1::Budd-Chiari}} syndrome

What are five indicators of a vaso-occlusive crisis in a patient with sickle cell anemia?

{{c1::Dactylitis}}
{{c1::Priapism}}
{{c1::Acute chest}} syndrome
{{c1::Avascular necrosis}}
{{c1::Stroke}}

What may be the cause of back pain and hemoglobinuria in a patient after consumption of fava beans?

{{c1::Oxidative}} stress in {{c1::glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase}} deficiency

What lab investigation helps to confirm a diagnosis of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?

Absence of {{c1::CD55}}/{{c1::CD59}} on red blood cells as determined by flow cytometry

What may be seen in the blood smear of a newborn with pyruvate kinase deficiency?

{{c1::Burr}} cells

What is the most likely diagnosis after examination of the bone marrow sample shown in the image?



{{c1::Aplastic}} anemia

What type of anemia is seen in a patient with Fanconi anemia?

{{c1::Aplastic}} anemia secondary to {{c1::bone marrow}} failure

What two immunosuppresive agents may be used in the treatment of aplastic anemia?

{{c1::Cyclosporine}}
{{c1::Antithymocyte globulin}}

What is the pathophysiology behind the nonhemolytic, normocytic anemia seen in chronic kidney disease?

Failure of/decrease in {{c1::erythropoietin}} production

Use of benzene, chloramphenicol, antimetabolites, and alkylating agents can lead to which type of anemia?

{{c1::Aplastic}} anemia

What are five treatments for aplastic anemia?

{{c1::Removal}} of causative factor
{{c1::Immunosuppressive}} regimens
Red blood cell and platelet {{c1::transfusions}}
Bone marrow {{c1::allografts}}
Bone marrow-{{c1::stimulating}} agents

What are five causes of aplastic anemia?

{{c1::Viruses}}
{{c1::Fanconi}} anemia
{{c1::Radiation}}
{{c1::Idiopathic}}
{{c1::Drugs}}

How are iron levels, ferritin levels, and total iron-binding capacity affected in a patient with anemia of chronic disease?

Iron level is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}
Ferritin level is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}
Total iron-binding capacity is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}

What is the pathophysiology behind anemia of chronic disease?

Inflammation → Increased {{c1::hepcidin}} level → Decreased release of {{c1::iron}} from macrophages → Decreased {{c1::iron}} absorption from the gut

What findings on bone marrow aspiration indicate a diagnosis of aplastic anemia?

Bone marrow {{c1::hypocellularity::hypercellularity/hypocellularity}} with {{c1::fatty}} infiltration

What are three treatments for anemia of chronic disease?

Address the underlying cause of {{c1::inflammation}}
Careful use of blood {{c1::transfusions}}
{{c1::Erythropoiesis}}-stimulating medications

How are reticulocyte counts and erythropoietin levels affected in patients with aplastic anemia?

Reticulocyte count is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}
Erythropoietin levels are {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}

What are four conditions associated with anemia of chronic disease?

Chronic {{c1::infections}}
Chronic {{c1::kidney::organ}} disease
{{c1::Neoplastic}} disorders
{{c1::Autoimmune}} diseases

What molecule does hepcidin bind to on intestinal mucosal cells and macrophages to inhibit iron transport?

{{c1::Ferroportin}}

How does anemia of chronic disease affect the size of red blood cells?

RBCs are {{c1::normocytic::macrocytic/normocytic/microcytic}}, but may become {{c1::microcytic::macrocytic/normocytic/microcytic}}

How is the size of red blood cells affected in patients with Fanconi anemia?

Red blood cells may be {{c1::normocytic::macrocytic/normocytic/microcytic}} or {{c1::macrocytic::macrocytic/normocytic/microcytic}}

How is aplastic anemia distinguished from an aplastic crisis?

Aplastic anemia presents with {{c1::anemia}}, {{c1::leukopenia}}, and {{c1::thrombocytopenia}}
Aplastic crisis presents with {{c1::anemia}} alone

A patient presenting with fatigue, purpura, pallor, mucosal bleeding, malaise, and petechiae might have what underlying condition?

{{c1::Aplastic}} anemia

What type of hemolysis is seen in hereditary spherocytosis and autoimmune hemolytic anemia?

{{c1::Extravascular::Intravascular/Extravascular}} hemolysis

What type of hemolysis occurs with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, mechanical destruction, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia?

{{c1::Intravascular::Intravascular/Extravascular}} hemolysis

What type of hemolytic anemia presents with the following:

High lactate dehydrogenase
High unconjugated bilirubin
High peripheral reticulocytes in blood
High urobilinogen in urine

{{c1::Extravascular::Intravascular/Extravascular}} hemolytic anemia

What type of hemolytic anemia presents with the following:

Low haptoglobin
High lactate dehydrogenase
High unconjugated bilirubin
High schistocytes
High reticulocytes

{{c1::Intravascular::Intravascular/Extravascular}} hemolytic anemia

How are normocytic, normochromic hemolytic anemias classified?

According to {{c1::cause}} and by {{c1::location}}

What pathology can arise secondary to hemolytic anemias in the gallbladder?

{{c1::Pigmented gallstones}}

What is the mechanism of extravascular hemolysis?

{{c1::Macrophages}} in {{c1::spleen::organ}} clear red blood cells

What congenital cause of anemia can present with craniofacial abnormalities, triphalangeal thumbs, short stature, and upper extremity deformities?

{{c1::Diamond-Blackfan anemia}}

What is the disease mechanism in Diamond-Blackfan anemia?

{{c1::Intrinsic}} defect in {{c1::erythroid progenitor}} cells → Rapid-onset anemia

What will hemoglobin electrophoresis show in the case of Diamond-Blackfan syndrome?

Increased percent of {{c1::HbF}}

What was the Schilling test historically used for?

To find the cause of vitamin {{c1::B12}} deficiency
fields.Back Extra: It distinguishes dietary insufficiency from malabsorption.

fields.Text:
What is the likely cause of a patient presenting with a macrocytic anemia years after a gastrectomy procedure?

Vitamin {{c1::B12}} deficiency

Which three medications can cause folate deficiency and a resulting macrocytic anemia?

{{c1::Methotrexate}}
{{c1::Trimethoprim}}
{{c1::Phenytoin}}

Levels of which compound help to differentiate vitamin B12 deficiency from folate deficiency?

{{c1::Methylmalonic acid}}

Name three causes of nonmegaloblastic macrocytic anemia.

{{c1::Alcoholism}}
{{c1::Liver}} disease
{{c1::Diamond-Blackfan anemia}}

Why does anemia due to insufficient intake of vitamin B12 take several years to develop?

Liver can store vitamin B12 for up to {{c1::3}} to {{c1::4}} years

How is orotic aciduria treated?

{{c1::Uridine monophosphate}}
{{c1::Uridine triacetate}}

What is the likely diagnosis in a child with failure to thrive, developmental delay, megaloblastic anemia unresponsive to vitamin B12/folate supplementation, and a normal ammonia level?

{{c1::Orotic aciduria}}

What is the inheritance pattern of orotic aciduria?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

How does nonmegaloblastic macrocytic anemia differ from megaloblastic macrocytic anemia?

{{c1::DNA synthesis}} in megaloblastic macrocytic anemia is dysfunctional
fields.Back Extra: This dysfunction is not observed in nonmegaloblastic macrocytic anemia.

fields.Text:
What are two neurological symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency?

{{c1::Reversible::Reversible/Irreversible}} {{c1::dementia}}
{{c1::Subacute combined degeneration}}

Why is there an increased demand for folate during pregnancy?

Required for fetal {{c1::neural tube}} development

How do homocysteine levels compare in vitamin B12 and folate deficiency?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} in vitamin B12 deficiency
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} in folate deficiency

What disease results from a congenital deficiency of pyrimidine synthesis leading to low UMP synthase activity?

{{c1::Orotic aciduria}}

Why is MCV increased in megaloblastic macrocytic anemias?

{{c1::DNA synthesis}} defect → {{c1::Nucleus}} taking longer to mature than cytoplasm → Excess cytoplasm

What two vitamins would you like to test for in a patient with macrocytic anemia whose peripheral blood smear is shown?



Vitamin {{c1::B9}}
Vitamin {{c1::B12}}

What would a blood smear of a patient with nonmegaloblastic anemia reveal?

RBC {{c1::macrocytosis}} {{c1::without::with/without}} hypersegmented neutrophils

What will be the result of folate supplementation in a patient with vitamin B12 deficiency?

Corrects {{c1::anemia}}
Worsens {{c1::neurologic}} symptoms

What is the congenital form of pure red cell aplasia?

{{c1::Diamond-Blackfan anemia}}

Why do hemolytic states have an increased demand for folate?
