Folate is needed to {{c1::replenish}} hemolyzed blood in hemolytic anemia

What are the expected findings of iron studies in a patient with hemochromatosis?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} transferrin
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} serum iron
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} ferritin
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} transferrin saturation

What are the expected findings of iron studies in a patient with iron deficiency anemia?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} serum iron
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} ferritin
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} transferrin
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} transferrin saturation

What are the expected findings of iron studies in a patient with anemia of chronic disease?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} serum iron
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} transferrin
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} ferritin
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} or normal transferrin saturation

What are the expected findings of iron studies in a pregnant patient or one actively using oral contraceptive pills?

Normal serum iron
Normal ferritin
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} transferrin
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} transferrin saturation

What is the evolutionary theory behind the origin of anemia of chronic disease?

Sequestering iron in {{c1::macrophages}} may prevent {{c1::pathogens}} from acquiring iron for survival

What is the relationship between transferrin and total iron-binding capacity?

Total iron-binding capacity is a(n) {{c1::indirect::direct/indirect}} measure of transferrin

What is the role of ferritin in the body?

Primary iron {{c1::storage}} protein

A patient with a history of alcohol use disorder is pale and has high iron levels, high ferritin levels, normal total iron-binding capacity, and the bone marrow smear shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?



{{c1::Sideroblastic anemia}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows ringed sideroblasts with iron-laden mitochondria in bone marrow.

fields.Text:
What is the X-ray finding shown in the image called?



{{c1::Lead line}} on the {{c1::metaphyses}} of long bones

What is the possible long-term adverse effect of treatment for β-thalassemia major?

Multiple blood transfusions may cause secondary {{c1::hemochromatosis}}

What laboratory findings are diagnostic of β-thalassemia minor?

Increased {{c1::HbA2}} fraction on electrophoresis

Name two common places where the risk of exposure to lead is increased.

Children → Old houses with {{c1::chipped paint}}
Adults → {{c1::Workplace}}

A patient with β-thalassemia major has an increased risk of aplastic crisis due to what infection?

{{c1::Parvovirus B19}}

What are three treatment options for lead poisoning?

{{c1::EDTA}}
{{c1::Dimercaprol}}
Chelation with {{c1::succimer}}

What is the consequence of inhibition of aminolevulinate dehydratase and ferrochelatase in red blood cells?

Decrease in the synthesis of {{c1::heme}}
Increase in red blood cell {{c1::protoporphyrin}}
fields.Back Extra: This is seen in lead poisoning.

fields.Text:
Why does β-thalassemia major become symptomatic only after 6 months of age?

{{c1::Hemoglobin F}} is protective in newborns
{{c1::Hemoglobin F}} levels decrease after 6 months of age

What disease results from deletion of one α-globin gene?

{{c1::α-thalassemia minima}}
fields.Back Extra: This is typically clinically silent without anemia.

fields.Text:
Name five reversible causes of sideroblastic anemia.

{{c1::Alcohol}} use (most common)
Vitamin {{c1::B6}} deficiency
{{c1::Copper}} deficiency
{{c1::Lead}} poisoning
{{c1::Drugs}}

What disease results from deletions of two α-globin genes?

{{c1::α-thalessemia minor}}

What is the best treatment for sideroblastic anemia?

{{c1::Pyridoxine}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is also known as vitamin B6.

This is a cofactor for aminolevulinic acid synthase.

fields.Text:
What causes hereditary sideroblastic anemia?

Defect in the {{c1::aminolevulinic acid synthase}} gene

What type of heavy metal poisoning can present with Burton lines, erythrocyte stippling, abdominal pain, sideroblastic anemia, and wrist/foot drop?

{{c1::Lead}} poisoning

What disease presents with tongue inflammation and atrophy, dysphagia with solids, and an iron deficiency anemia?

{{c1::Plummer-Vinson}} syndrome

What is the cause of basophilic stippling associated with lead poisoning?

Lead disrupts {{c1::rRNA}} degradation → Red blood cells retain aggregates of {{c1::rRNA}} to form basophilic stippling

What is the most likely cause of the anemia shown in the peripheral blood smear in the image?



{{c1::Iron}} deficiency

What is the clinical outcome for an individual who is a hemoglobin S and/or β-thalassemia heterozygote?

{{c1::Mild}} to {{c1::moderate}} sickle cell anemia
fields.Back Extra: This varies with the level of β-chain production.

fields.Text:
What condition results from deletions of three of the four α-globin genes?

{{c1::Hemoglobin H}} disease

What two physical examination findings may be seen in a patient diagnosed with β-thalessemia major?

{{c1::Hepatosplenomegaly}}
{{c1::Skeletal}} deformities

What is the consequence of the mutation associated with β-thalassemia minor?

Underproduction of β-chain → Mild {{c1::microcytic anemia}}

What cause of microcytic, hypochromic anemia has a higher prevalence among individuals of Mediterranean descent?

{{c1::β-thalassemia}}

What are five causes of iron deficiency?

Chronic {{c1::bleeding}}
{{c1::Absorption}} disorders
{{c1::Malnutrition}}
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} demand
{{c1::Gastrointestinal}} surgery

Hemoglobin H disease generally results in what type of anemia?

Moderate to severe {{c1::microcytic hypochromic}} anemia

What is the inheritance pattern of hereditary sideroblastic anemia?

{{c1::X-linked}}

What type of anemia can present with low iron/ferritin, high total iron-binding capacity, high red blood cell distribution width, microcytosis, hypochromasia, and central pallor?

{{c1::Iron deficiency}} anemia

How does iron deficiency cause anemia?

Iron deficiency impairs {{c1::heme}} synthesis

A patient presenting with fatigue, koilonychia, pica, and conjunctival pallor might have what underlying condition?

{{c1::Iron deficiency anemia}}

On which chromosome is the α-globin gene present?

Chromosome {{c1::16}}

On which chromosome is the β-globin gene present?

Chromosome {{c1::11}}

Which mutations result in β-thalassemia?

{{c1::Point}} mutations in splice sites and promoter sequences for β-globin

What is the prognosis for patients with no α-globin chain?

{{c1::Lethal}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is incompatible with life.

This is hemoglobin Barts disease.

fields.Text:
What will an X-ray of the skull of a patient with β-thalessemia show?

"{{c1::Crew-cut}}" appearance
fields.Back Extra: This is due to marrow expansion.

fields.Text:
What is β-thalessemia major also known as?

{{c1::Cooley anemia}}

In which two layers of the gastrointestinal tract are Peyer patches found?

{{c1::Lamina propria}}
{{c1::Submucosa}} of the ileum

After being secreted by B cells in Peyer patches, IgA functions to bind what?

{{c1::Intraluminal}} antigens

What do B cells that are present in Peyer patches secrete after they have differentiated into plasma cells?

Ig{{c1::A}}

What is the main function of M cells that reside in Peyer patches?

M cells sample and present {{c1::antigens}} from the gut lumen to {{c1::immune}} cells

What component does IgA receive before it is transported across the epithelium into the gut?

{{c1::Protective secretory}} component

What is the mechanism by which bile exerts antimicrobial activity?

{{c1::Membrane}} disruption

What enzyme is responsible for the rate-limiting step of bile acid synthesis?

{{c1::Cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase}}

What are the six components of bile?

{{c1::Bile salts}}
{{c1::Cholesterol}}
{{c1::Phospholipids}}
{{c1::Bilirubin}}
{{c1::Ions}}
{{c1::Water}}

Which amino acids are conjugated to bile acids to make them water soluble?

{{c1::Glycine}}
{{c1::Taurine}}

How does decreased absorption of enteric bile salts at the distal ileum lead to calcium oxalate kidney stones?

Calcium binds unabsorbed {{c1::fat}} instead of oxalate in the gut → Free oxalate is absorbed in the gut → Increased frequency of calcium oxalate kidney stones

What is the mechanism behind bile acid diarrhea?

Decreased bile salt absorption in the {{c1::distal::proximal/distal}} {{c1::ileum}} → Decreased {{c1::fat}} absorption → Diarrhea

What nutrients are digested and absorbed with the help of bile?

{{c1::Lipids}}
{{c1::Fat}}-soluble {{c1::vitamins}}

What fluid is primarily responsible for bilirubin and cholesterol excretion?

{{c1::Bile}}

Which enzyme catalyzes bilirubin conjugation?

{{c1::UDP-glucuronosyltransferase}}

In an experiment, tagged urobilinogen in the gut can be expected to be later found in which organ?

{{c1::Liver}}

A patient with an inability to deposit conjugated bilirubin in the gut will see what characteristic change in his or her stools?

Stools will be {{c1::pale}} due to loss of {{c1::brown}} coloration
fields.Back Extra: Without conjugated bilirubin, urobilinogen, which normally becomes brown-colored stercobilin, won't be formed.

fields.Text:
Of the 20% of urobilinogen that goes to the kidneys and liver, how much enters the enterohepatic circulation and how much is excreted renally?

{{c1::90}}% enters the enterohepatic circulation
{{c1::10}}% is excreted as urobilin in urine via the kidneys

How much of urobilinogen is excreted as stercobilin in feces?

{{c1::80}}% as stercobilin
fields.Back Extra: This gives stool its brown color.

fields.Text:
Why would a patient taking antibiotics have urine that is paler than usual?

Antibiotics wipe out gut {{c1::bacteria}} → Impaired conversion of {{c1::bilirubin}} to {{c1::urobilinogen}} → Impaired conversion of {{c1::urobilinogen}} to {{c1::urobilin}}, which gives urine its yellow color

If exposed to conjugated bilirubin, colonic bacteria will produce what?

{{c1::Urobilinogen}}

What gives urine its yellow color?

{{c1::Urobilin}}
fields.Back Extra: This is one of the forms in which bile is excreted from the body.

fields.Text:
To what is bilirubin bound as it travels through the circulation?

{{c1::Albumin}}
fields.Back Extra: This is as an unconjugated bilirubin-albumin complex.

fields.Text:
How is bilirubin ultimately excreted from the body?

{{c1::Conjugated::Conjugated/Unconjugated}} bilirubin is deposited in bile → Bile is excreted in stool as {{c1::stercobilin}} or in urine as {{c1::urobilin}}

What is the essential structural difference between direct and indirect bilirubin?

Direct bilirubin is conjugated with {{c1::glucuronic acid}} and is water {{c1::soluble::soluble/insoluble}}
Indirect bilirubin is not conjugated and is water {{c1::insoluble::soluble/insoluble}}

How is unconjugated bilirubin removed from blood?

It is conjugated with {{c1::glucuronate}} in the liver and is excreted in {{c1::bile}}

Describe how heme becomes bilirubin.

{{c1::Heme oxygenase}} metabolizes heme to {{c1::biliverdin}} → {{c1::Biliverdin}} is reduced to bilirubin

What are the three fates of urobilinogen?

Excreted in {{c1::feces}}
Excreted in {{c1::urine}}
Recycled via {{c1::enterohepatic circulation}}

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with long-standing choledocholithiasis and a recent ERCP showing bile duct fibrosis who presents with fever and RUQ pain?

{{c1::Secondary biliary cirrhosis}} complicated by {{c1::ascending cholangitis}}

Which immunoglobulin is elevated in patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis and primary biliary cholangitis?

{{c1::IgM}}

What biliary tract disease does a patient with Hashimoto thyroiditis and celiac disease presenting with jaundice likely have?

{{c1::Primary biliary cholangitis}}

What are the expected conjugated bilirubin, cholesterol, ALP, and GGT levels in a patient with secondary biliary cirrhosis?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} conjugated bilirubin levels
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} cholesterol levels
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} ALP levels
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} GGT levels

Which antibodies are classically associated with patients with primary biliary cholangitis?

{{c1::Antimitochondrial}} antibodies

What would a liver biopsy show if performed for a patient with Hashimoto thyroiditis who presents with diffuse itching and elevated antimitochondrial antibodies?

{{c1::Lymphocytic}} infiltrate, with or without {{c1::granulomas}}
Destruction of {{c1::lobular bile ducts}}
fields.Back Extra: The patient has primary biliary cholangitis.

fields.Text:
What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with known ulcerative colitis presenting with jaundice, pale stools, and an ERCP showing beading of bile ducts?

{{c1::Primary sclerosing cholangitis}}

What are the typical pathologic changes seen in patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis?

Concentric "{{c1::onion skin}}" bile duct fibrosis → Alternating {{c1::dilation}} and {{c1::strictures}} with "{{c1::beading}}" of intrahepatic/extrahepatic ducts on ERCP or MRCP

What 2 cancers are patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis at elevated risk of developing?

{{c1::Cholangiocarcinoma}}
{{c1::Gallbladder}} cancer

What is the likely diagnosis in a middle-aged man with ulcerative colitis presenting with RUQ pain and weight loss?

{{c1::Primary sclerosing cholangitis}}
fields.Back Extra: He may have associated cholangiocarcinoma or gallbladder cancer.

fields.Text:
What is the first-line treatment for primary biliary cholangitis?

{{c1::Ursodiol}}

A 55-year-old man presents with a painless swelling on his cheek, which is found to consist of chondromyxoid stroma and epithelium. Image shows biopsy findings. What is the likely diagnosis?



{{c1::Pleomorphic adenoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the most common salivary gland tumor.

fields.Text:
Name two histologic components of the most common malignant salivary gland tumor.

{{c1::Mucinous}} components
{{c1::Squamous}} components

Pleomorphic adenomas typically consist of what two types of tissue?

{{c1::Chondromyxoid stroma}}
{{c1::Epithelium}}

A long-time smoker has a benign cystic tumor in one of his salivary glands that contains several germinal centers. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Warthin}} tumor

In which three major salivary glands can sialolithiasis occur?

{{c1::Sublingual}} salivary gland
{{c1::Submandibular}} salivary gland
{{c1::Parotid}} salivary gland

Name two presenting symptoms of sialolithiasis.

{{c1::Swelling}} in the affected gland
Recurrent {{c1::preprandial}}/{{c1::periprandial}} pain

A patient presents with recurrent jaw pain around mealtimes. In the image of the oral cavity, what is indicated by the arrow?



{{c1::Sialolithiasis}}

Under what conditions can a pleomorphic adenoma recur?

If it was not completely {{c1::excised}}
If it {{c1::ruptured}} during surgery

What are the most common presenting symptoms of a salivary gland tumor?

{{c1::Painless::Painful/Painless}} swelling and mass
fields.Back Extra: Facial paralysis or pain suggests malignant involvement.

fields.Text:
What are some common causes of sialadenitis?

{{c1::Infection}}
{{c1::Obstruction}}
{{c1::Immune}}-mediated diseases like {{c1::Sjögren}} syndrome

What is the most common malignancy of the oral cavity?

{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma

What are the most common causes of oral squamous cell carcinoma?

{{c1::Alcohol}}
{{c1::Tobacco}}
{{c1::HPV-16}}

How does squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity present?

{{c1::Nonhealing::Healing/Nonhealing}} ulcer
{{c1::Irregular::Regular/Irregular}} margins
{{c1::Raised}} borders
fields.Back Extra: It can also present as leukoplakia and erythroplakia.

fields.Text:
What is the presentation of aphthous ulcers or canker sores?

{{c1::Painful::Painful/Painless}}, shallow, round to oval ulcers covered by {{c1::yellowish::color}} exudate

Name some conditions that can cause recurrent aphthous stomatitis.

{{c1::Celiac}} disease
{{c1::Behçet}} syndrome
{{c1::HIV}} infection
{{c1::Inflammatory bowel}} disease
{{c1::Systemic lupus erythematosus}}

What is achalasia?

Failure of the {{c1::lower::upper/lower}} esophageal sphincter to relax due to degeneration of {{c1::inhibitory}} neurons in the {{c1::myenteric plexus}} of the esophageal wall

What is a common presenting symptom of achalasia?

Progressive {{c1::dysphagia}} to both {{c1::solids}} and {{c1::liquids}}

Name two secondary causes of achalasia.

{{c1::Chagas}} disease from {{c1::Trypanosoma cruzi}} infection
Extraesophageal {{c1::malignancies}}

Which motility disorder increases the risk for esophageal cancer?

{{c1::Achalasia}}

What is the cause of the abnormal findings on barium swallow shown in the image?



{{c1::Achalasia}}
fields.Back Extra:
The image shows a dilated esophagus with distal stenosis.

This is also known as "bird's beak".

fields.Text:
What are the manometry findings in a patient with achalasia?

Absent or uncoordinated {{c1::peristalsis}}
{{c1::High::High/Low}} lower esophageal sphincter resting pressure

What neurotransmitters are implicated in achalasia?

Achalasia results from degeneration of {{c1::inhibitory}} neurons that contain {{c1::nitric oxide}} and {{c1::vasoactive intestinal peptide}}

What are some treatment options for achalasia?

{{c1::Surgery}}
{{c1::Endoscopic}} procedures

How can a patient with β-thalassemia major develop hemochromatosis?

Secondary to long-term {{c1::transfusion}} therapy

What would be the expected ferritin, serum iron, TIBC, and transferrin saturation in a patient with hemochromatosis?

{{c1::High::High/Low}} ferritin
{{c1::High::High/Low}} serum iron
{{c1::Low::High/Low}} TIBC
{{c1::High::High/Low}} transferrin saturation

What are the 2 accepted treatment options for hemochromatosis?

Repeated {{c1::phlebotomy}}
Iron chelation with {{c1::deferoxamine}}, {{c1::deferasirox}}, or {{c1::deferiprone}}

What MRI findings would be expected for a patient with hemochromatosis?

{{c1::Hemosiderin}} deposits in the {{c1::liver}}

What is the inheritance pattern of hemochromatosis?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

Why does hemochromatosis typically present later in women than in men?

Iron is lost via {{c1::menses}}
fields.Back Extra: This stalls the accumulation of iron in organs.

fields.Text:
What is the most common cause of death in patients with hemochromatosis?

{{c1::Hepatocellular carcinoma}}

What arthrocentesis findings are expected for a patient with hemochromatosis?

{{c1::Calcium pyrophosphate}} deposition, especially at {{c1::MCP}} joints

What gene is typically mutated in hemochromatosis?

{{c1::HFE}} gene on chromosome {{c1::6}}

What stain was used to reveal the histologic findings seen in the image, which shows a liver biopsy specimen from a patient with hemochromatosis?



{{c1::Prussian blue}} stain

How does a mutation of the HFE gene cause hemochromatosis?

Leads to abnormal {{c1::hepcidin}} production
Increased intestinal {{c1::absorption}}

What is the classic triad of signs/symptoms in patients with hemochromatosis?

{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}
Skin {{c1::pigmentation}}
{{c1::Cirrhosis}}

What 2 cardiac pathologies are most commonly associated with hemochromatosis?

{{c1::Restrictive}} cardiomyopathy
{{c1::Dilated}} cardiomyopathy

How does hemochromatosis affect a patient's reproductive organs?

It can cause {{c1::hypogonadism}}

What esophageal pathology is depicted by the image?



Esophageal {{c1::perforation}}

In which part of the esophagus are esophageal varices typically found?

The {{c1::lower::upper/lower}} {{c1::1}}/3 of the esophagus
fields.Back Extra: This is secondary to portal hypertension.

fields.Text:
The endoscopic image depicts what type of esophageal pathology?



Esophageal {{c1::varices}}

What is the underlying pathophysiology of acid reflux and dysphagia associated with CREST syndrome?

{{c1::Atrophy}} of esophageal smooth muscle → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} lower esophageal sphincter pressure and {{c1::dysmotility}} in distal esophagus → Acid reflux and dysphagia

Plummer-Vinson syndrome is characterized by what triad of findings/symptoms?

{{c1::Dysphagia}}
{{c1::Iron deficiency}} anemia
Esophageal {{c1::webs}}
fields.Back Extra: This is associated with an increased risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

fields.Text:
Describe Mallory-Weiss syndrome.

Partial {{c1::thickness::thickness/thinness}}, {{c1::longitudinal}} lacerations of the {{c1::gastroesophageal junction}} mucosa/submucosa
fields.Back Extra:
This is due to severe vomiting.

This is common in patients with history of alcoholism or bulimia.

fields.Text:
What manometry finding is associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease?

Transient {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} in lower esophageal sphincter tone

What symptoms are associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease?

{{c1::Heartburn}}
{{c1::Regurgitation}}
{{c1::Dysphagia}}
{{c1::Hoarseness}}
Chronic {{c1::cough}}

How can you differentiate esophageal ulcers caused by HSV-1 from those caused by cytomegalovirus?

HSV-1 causes {{c1::punched-out}} ulcers
Cytomegalovirus causes {{c1::linear}} ulcers

What are the four main causes of esophagitis?

Infection in {{c1::immunocompromised}} individuals
{{c1::Reflux}}
Ingestion of {{c1::caustic}} substances
{{c1::Pills}}

Ingestion of caustic compounds, chronic acid reflux, and esophagitis can lead to what esophageal pathology?

Esophageal {{c1::strictures}}

Esophageal rings and linear furrows are endoscopic findings associated with what esophageal pathology?

{{c1::Eosinophilic esophagitis}}

A biopsy specimen of the esophagus showing infiltration of eosinophils is associated with what disease?

{{c1::Eosinophilic esophagitis}}

What medications can cause pill-induced esophagitis?

{{c1::Bisphosphonates}}
{{c1::Tetracycline}}
{{c1::NSAIDs}}
{{c1::Potassium chloride}}
{{c1::Iron}}

What syndrome is defined as a transmural distal esophageal rupture due to violent retching?

{{c1::Boerhaave}} syndrome

What esophageal pathology is associated with crepitus in the neck region or chest wall?

Esophageal {{c1::perforation}}

What are some causes of noniatrogenic esophageal perforation?

Spontaneous {{c1::rupture}}
{{c1::Trauma}}
{{c1::Malignancy}}
{{c1::Foreign body}} ingestion

What is the most common cause of esophageal perforation?

Inadvertent puncture during esophageal {{c1::instrumentation}}

How do lower esophageal sphincter pressures change with gastroesophageal reflux disease, scleroderma, and diffuse esophageal spasm, respectively?

Gastroesophageal reflux disease → Transient {{c1::decreases}}
Scleroderma → {{c1::Decreased}}
Diffuse esophageal spasm → {{c1::Normal}}

A barium swallow revealing the pattern shown in the image is associated with what pathology?



{{c1::Distal esophageal spasm}}
fields.Back Extra:
This may reveal a "corkscrew" esophagus.

This was formerly called diffuse esophageal spasm.

fields.Text:
What are pharmacologic treatment options for distal esophageal spasm?

{{c1::Nitrates}}
{{c1::Calcium}} channel blockers

What symptoms does a patient with distal esophageal spasm have?

{{c1::Dysphagia}}
{{c1::Angina}}-like chest pain

What manometric findings are diagnostic of distal esophageal spasms?

{{c1::Spontaneous}} and {{c1::nonperistaltic}} contractions of the esophagus
{{c1::Normal}} lower esophageal sphincter pressure

What is the likely diagnosis when the finding shown in the image is seen on upper endoscopy of an immunocompromised patient?



{{c1::Candida esophagitis}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows the classic white pseudomembrane appearance.

fields.Text:
Esophageal varices are common in patients with what condition?

Patients with {{c1::cirrhosis}}
fields.Back Extra: This may be a source of life-threatening hematemesis.

fields.Text:
Name three complications that can arise due to gastroesophageal reflux disease.

{{c1::Strictures}}
{{c1::Erosive esophagitis}}
{{c1::Barrett esophagus}}

What type of anemia is typically associated with Wilson disease?

{{c1::Hemolytic anemia}}

What are the copper deposits in the eye of a patient with Wilson disease called?



{{c1::Kayser-Fleischer rings}}

What are the 4 major organs affected by excessive copper deposition in those with Wilson disease?

{{c1::Liver}}
{{c1::Brain}}
{{c1::Kidneys}}
{{c1::Corneas}}

Why is serum ceruloplasmin decreased in patients with Wilson disease?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} copper incorporation into {{c1::apoceruloplasmin}}
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} copper excretion into bile

What is the preferred treatment for a 32-year-old man presenting with cirrhosis, depression, and parkinsonian symptoms whose father had similar symptoms at age 28?

Chelation with {{c1::penicillamine}} or {{c1::trientine}}
Oral {{c1::zinc}}
fields.Back Extra:
The patient has Wilson disease.

A liver transplant is performed in acute liver failure related to Wilson disease.

fields.Text:
What gene is mutated in patients with Wilson disease?

{{c1::ATP7B}} gene

What is the inheritance pattern of Wilson disease?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

The image represents what gastrointestinal anomaly that occurs during fetal development?



{{c1::Malrotation}} with {{c1::Ladd bands}}

Malrotation of the gut as shown in this X-ray is due to improper rotation of what fetal structure during development?



{{c1::Midgut}}
fields.Back Extra: The small bowel is clumped on the right side of the abdomen.

fields.Text:
What 2 complications could be seen with malrotation of the bowel?

{{c1::Volvulus}}
Duodenal {{c1::obstruction}}

Name the condition associated with a proximal bowel segment telescoping into a distal segment.

{{c1::Intussusception}}

What is the cause of intermittent, severe abdominal pain in intussusception?

{{c1::Vascular}} compromise
Small bowel {{c1::obstruction}}

What are 2 common pathologic lead points for intussusception in children?

Small bowel wall {{c1::hematoma}}
{{c1::Meckel diverticulum}}

What is the most common pathologic lead point for intussusception in adults?

Intraluminal {{c1::tumor}}

What is the pathophysiology behind increased risk of intussusception following a viral infection or administration of the rotavirus vaccine?

{{c1::Peyer patch}} {{c1::hypertrophy::hypertrophy/atrophy}} creates a lead point

What part of the gastrointestinal tract is commonly affected in intussusception?

{{c1::Ileocecal}} junction

Intussusception is most common in which age group?

{{c1::Infants}}

Describe the appearance of stool in intussusception.

{{c1::Bloody::Bloody/Nonbloody}} "{{c1::currant jelly}}” stools

What finding on physical exam of the abdomen may be detected in patients with intussusception?

{{c1::Sausage}}-shaped mass on palpation of the {{c1::right::left/right}} side of the abdomen

A child presents with recent-onset severe abdominal pain that is episodic. He is drawing his legs up to his chest repeatedly. Ultrasound of his abdomen is shown. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Intussusception}}
fields.Back Extra: The ultrasound image of the intestines shows a classic target sign.

fields.Text:
What physical maneuver may help relieve the pain associated with intussusception?

Drawing {{c1::legs}} up to the {{c1::chest}}

What is the diagnosis based on this abdominal X-ray?



{{c1::Sigmoid volvulus}}
fields.Back Extra: The X-ray shows the classic coffee bean sign.

fields.Text:
Which portion of the bowel is most likely to be involved in a volvulus in infants and children as compared with adults?

Infants/children → {{c1::Midgut}}
Adults → {{c1::Sigmoid colon}}

What is a volvulus?

The {{c1::twisting}} of a portion of {{c1::bowel}} around its {{c1::mesentery}}
fields.Back Extra: This can result in obstruction and infarction of the involved bowel.

fields.Text:
What preexisting condition increases the risk of gastric volvulus?

{{c1::Anatomic}} abnormalities

What may occur if you attempt to place a nasogatric tube in a patient with a gastric volvulus?

Inability to {{c1::pass}} the nasogastric tube

What loss of function mutations are associated with Hirschsprung disease?

Loss of function mutations in {{c1::RET}}

What will be found proximal to the diseased segment of bowel in Hirschsprung disease?

{{c1::Dilated}} portion of bowel creating a "{{c1::transition zone}}"

There is an increased risk for Hirschsprung disease in individuals with what genetic syndrome?

{{c1::Down}} syndrome

What is the mechanism that causes Hirschsprung disease?

Failure of {{c1::neural crest}} cell migration → Absence of {{c1::ganglion}} cells and {{c1::enteric nervous plexuses}} in distal segment of colon

What would a rectal suction biopsy show to indicate a diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease?

Absence of {{c1::ganglion}} cells

What symptoms occur in a newborn with Hirschsprung disease?

Abdominal {{c1::distention}}
{{c1::Bilious emesis}}
Failure to pass {{c1::meconium}} within 48 hours

What may a digital rectal exam reveal in Hirschsprung disease?

{{c1::Squirt}} sign → {{c1::Empty}} rectum

The absence of which 2 nerve plexus result in the disease shown in the image below?



{{c1::Auerbach}} plexus
{{c1::Meissner}} plexus

In patients with Hirschspring disease, which enzyme is increased in hypertrophied nerve fibers of the lamina propria?

{{c1::Acetylcholinesterase}}

Persistance of what structure leads to the pathology shown in the image?



Persistance of the {{c1::vitelline}} duct leads to {{c1::Meckel diverticulum}}

What is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract?

{{c1::Meckel diverticulum}}

By what age do Meckel diverticula typically present?

Commonly by {{c1::2}} years of age

In approximately what percentage of the population can Meckel diverticula be found?

{{c1::2}}%

How far are Meckel diverticula typically located from the ileocecal valve?

{{c1::2}} feet

Approximately what size is a typical Meckel diverticulum?

{{c1::2}} inches long

What type of tissue may be present in a Meckel diverticulum?

{{c1::Pancreatic}} tissue
{{c1::Ectopic}} acid-secreting gastric mucosa

What is the diagnostic test for Meckel diverticulum?

{{c1::99mTc-pertechnetate}} scan
fields.Back Extra: It is used for assessing uptake by heterotopic gastric mucosa.

fields.Text:
What kind of diverticulum is a Meckel diverticulum?

{{c1::True::True/False}} diverticulum

What 4 complications can occur with Meckel diverticulum?

{{c1::Hematochezia}}
{{c1::Intussusception}}
{{c1::Volvulus}}
Obstruction near the terminal {{c1::ileum}}

In which sex is Meckel diverticulum more common?

{{c1::Two}} times as likely in {{c1::males::males/females}}

In what age and sex group is Zenker diverticulum most common?

{{c1::Elderly}} {{c1::men::men/women}}

What are the expected presenting symptoms of Zenker diverticulum?

{{c1::Halitosis}}
{{c1::Aspiration}}
{{c1::Dysphagia}}
{{c1::Gurgling}}
Neck {{c1::mass}}

What is the pathophysiology of Zenker diverticulum?

Esophageal {{c1::dysmotility}} → {{c1::Herniation}} of mucosa at the {{c1::Killian triangle}}
fields.Back Extra: The herniation occurs between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor.

fields.Text:
Identify labels A, B, and C, shown on this diagram of a Zenker diverticulum.



A → {{c1::Thyropharyngeus}} muscle
B → {{c1::Killian triangle}}
C → {{c1::Cricopharyngeus}} muscle

Is Zenker diverticulum a true or false diverticulum?

{{c1::False::True/False}} diverticulum

Barrett esophagus leads to increased risk of what cancer?

{{c1::Adenocarcinoma}} of the esophagus

A biopsy specimen from a patient with a history of reflux is shown in the image. Describe the histologic findings.



Replacement of {{c1::nonkeratinized::keratinized/nonkeratinized}} {{c1::stratified::simple/stratified}} squamous epithelium with {{c1::nonciliated::ciliated/nonciliated}} {{c1::columnar::simple/cuboidal/columnar}} epithelium with {{c1::goblet}} cells

A patient with chronic reflux esophagitis undergoes a workup. Findings on endoscopy are shown. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Barrett esophagus}}

Barrett esophagus is an example of what kind of pathologic aberration to the normal tissue histology?

{{c1::Metaplasia}}

Achalasia increases the risk for which type of cancer in the esophagus?

{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma

A patient with a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease now has dysphagia to solids and liquids as well as weight loss. What is the likely diagnosis?

Esophageal {{c1::adenocarcinoma}}

A patient with esophageal strictures from consuming caustic substances is at increased risk for what type of cancer?

{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma of the esophagus

A smoker presents with dysphagia that progressed from solids to liquids and unintentional weight loss in the past few months. What is the likely diagnosis?

Esophageal {{c1::cancer}}
fields.Back Extra: This may either be an adenocarcinoma or a squamous cell carcinoma.

fields.Text:
Consumption of alcohol or hot liquids and the presence of caustic strictures are risk factors for what type of cancer?

{{c1::Squamous cell}} cancer of the esophagus

What traits of esophageal cancer typically give it a poorer prognosis compared with that of other cancer types?

Aggressive course due to the lack of {{c1::serosa}} in the esophageal wall → Allows rapid {{c1::extension}}
fields.Back Extra: Advanced disease at presentation leads to a poor prognosis.

fields.Text:
Compare the part of the esophagus affected in squamous cell carcinoma with the part affected in adenocarcinoma.

Squamous cell carcinoma → {{c1::Upper::Upper/Lower}} {{c1::2}}/3 of the esophagus
Adenocarcinoma → {{c1::Lower::Upper/Lower}} {{c1::1}}/3 of the esophagus

What pathologic findings would be seen in a liver biopsy specimen obtained from a nonsmoker who presents with shortness of breath and elevated liver enzyme levels?

{{c1::PAS}}-positive {{c1::globules}} within hepatocytes
fields.Back Extra: The patient likely has α1-antitrypsin deficiency.

fields.Text:
What mechanism is responsible for the development of lung disease in patients with α1-antitrypsin deficiency?

Decreased α1-antitrypsin → Uninhibited {{c1::elastase}} in the alveoli → Decreased {{c1::elastic}} tissue → {{c1::Panacinar emphysema}}

A young patient presents with dyspnea and has abnormal liver enzyme levels and liver biopsy findings shown in the image. What is the inheritance pattern of the likely diagnosis?



{{c1::Codominant trait}}

What are the major cellular effects in individuals with α1-antitrypsin deficiency?

{{c1::Misfolded}} gene product protein aggregates in hepatocellular {{c1::endoplasmic reticulum}} → {{c1::Cirrhosis}}
fields.Back Extra: PAS-positive globules are seen in liver biopsy specimen.

fields.Text:
Colonic angiodysplasia is most common in which age group?

{{c1::Elderly}}

What is the diagnosis for a premature infant with the abdominal X-ray shown?



{{c1::Necrotizing enterocolitis}}

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with hematochezia and tortuous dilation of vessels in the colon seen on colonoscopy?

{{c1::Angiodysplasia}}

What diagnosis is classically associated with abdominal pain out of proportion to physical examination findings?

{{c1::Acute mesenteric ischemia}}
fields.Back Extra: The pain is due to bowel necrosis.

fields.Text:
What are 3 possible complications of necrotizing enterocolitis?

{{c1::Pneumoperitoneum}}
{{c1::Pneumatosis intestinalis}}
{{c1::Portal venous gas}}

Which patients are most at risk for necrotizing enterocolitis?

{{c1::Premature}} neonates
Neonates who are {{c1::formula fed}}
fields.Back Extra: There is decreased immunity in these patients.

fields.Text:
What may cause small bowel obstruction in newborns?

{{c1::Meconium plug}}

What are the treatment options for ileus?

{{c1::Electrolyte}} correction
Bowel {{c1::rest}}
{{c1::Cholinergic}} drugs to stimulate intestinal motility

What disorder causes intestinal hypomotility without intestinal obstruction?

{{c1::Ileus}}

How is gastrointestinal motility affected by abdominal surgeries, use of opiates, hypokalemia, and/or sepsis?

These factors may all cause {{c1::ileus}}

What are the 3 most common causes of small bowel obstruction?

{{c1::Adhesions}}
{{c1::Tumors}}
{{c1::Hernias}}

What might the stool produced by a patient with acute mesenteric ischemia look like?

{{c1::Red::Color}} "{{c1::currant jelly}}" stools

Where is angiodysplasia typically found in the gastrointestinal tract?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} side of the colon

What are 2 common symptoms of colonic ischemia?

{{c1::Cramping}} abdominal pain, which is followed by {{c1::hematochezia}}

Which age group is typically affected by colonic ischemia?

{{c1::Elderly}}

Where does colonic ischemia commonly occur?

{{c1::Splenic flexure}}
{{c1::Rectosigmoid junction}}

What disease causes postprandial pain in the epigastric region with associated food aversion and weight loss?

{{c1::Chronic mesenteric ischemia}}

Which artery is often blocked in patients with acute mesenteric ischemia?

{{c1::Superior mesenteric}} artery via {{c1::embolic occlusion}}
fields.Back Extra: Superior mesenteric artery occlusion leads to blocked intestinal blood flow and bowel necrosis.

fields.Text:
Angiodysplasia is associated with which other medical conditions?

End-stage {{c1::renal}} disease
{{c1::Aortic stenosis}}
{{c1::von Willebrand}} disease

What locations of the gastrointestinal tract are most commonly involved in necrotizing enterocolitis?

Terminal {{c1::ileum}}
Proximal {{c1::colon}}

What can sometimes be found on abdominal imaging in individuals with colonic ischemia?

{{c1::Thumbprint}} sign
fields.Back Extra: This is the result of either mucosal edema or hemorrhage.

fields.Text:
What is the source of pain in patients with chronic mesenteric ischemia?

Artherosclerosis of the following arteries:

{{c1::Superior mesenteric}} artery
{{c1::Inferior mesenteric}} artery
{{c1::Celiac}} artery

What are 3 complications of small bowel obstruction?

{{c1::Ischemia}}
{{c1::Necrosis}}
{{c1::Perforation}}
fields.Back Extra: These complications are caused by compromised blood flow to the bowel due to bowel dilation/strangulation.

fields.Text:
What is the diagnosis in a patient with sudden-onset abdominal pain, vomiting, and abdominal distension with air-fluid levels seen on upright abdominal X-ray?

{{c1::Small bowel obstruction}}

How is small bowel obstruction managed?

Volume {{c1::resuscitation}}
Gastrointestinal {{c1::decompression}}
Bowel {{c1::rest}}

Describe the size of the bowel proximal and distal to a small bowel obstruction.

Intestinal {{c1::dilation::dilation/decompression}} proximal to the obstruction
Intestinal {{c1::decompression::dilation/decompression}} distal to the obstruction

What genes are typically silenced/mutated in serrated polyps?

Defect may silence {{c1::mismatch repair}} gene expression → Creates {{c1::microsatellite}} instability and promotes mutations in {{c1::BRAF}}

A biopsy specimen from which type of colonic polyp is likely to reveal crypts in a "saw-tooth" pattern?

{{c1::Serrated polyps}}

Testing of which genes may help determine malignant potential of adenomatous polyps?

{{c1::APC}}
{{c1::KRAS}}

List the 3 adenomatous polyp subtypes in order of their potential for malignant transformation.

{{c1::Tubular}} adenomas (lowest)
{{c1::Tubulovillous}} adenomas
{{c1::Villous}} adenomas (highest)

What types of polyps are potentially malignant?

{{c1::Adenomatous polyps}}
{{c1::Serrated polyps}}

Hamartomatous colonic polyps are associated with which 2 polyposis syndromes?

{{c1::Peutz-Jeghers}} syndrome
{{c1::Juvenile polyposis}}
fields.Back Extra: These polyps consist of normal tissue with distorted architecture.

fields.Text:
In which part of the colon do hyperplastic polyps tend to arise?

{{c1::Rectosigmoid}} area

What 5 types of polyps are generally nonneoplastic?

{{c1::Hamartomatous polyps}}
{{c1::Mucosal polyps}}
{{c1::Submucosal polyps}}
{{c1::Hyperplastic polyps}}
{{c1::Inflammatory pseudopolyps}}

What is the most common type of polyps?

{{c1::Hyperplastic polyps}}

What type of polyps arise due to mucosal erosion in inflammatory bowel disease?

{{c1::Inflammatory pseudopolyps}}

Lipomas, leiomyomas, and fibromas are classified as what type of colonic polyps?

{{c1::Submucosal polyps}}

What type of polyps can occasionally evolve into serrated polyps and more advanced lesions?

{{c1::Hyperplastic polyps}}

What is the likely diagnosis based on the findings shown in this histologic image of a colonic polyp?



{{c1::Villous polyp}}

What is the likely diagnosis based on the findings shown in this histologic image of a colonic polyp?



{{c1::Tubular polyp}}

What is the malignant potential of serrated polyps?

{{c1::Neoplastic}}
fields.Back Extra: They contribute to up to 20% of cases of sporadic colorectal cancer.

fields.Text:
What is the likely prognosis of a solitary hamartomatous polyp?

It {{c1::does not::does/does not}} have significant risk of transformation to carcinoma

What phenotype is characteristic of serrated polyps?

{{c1::CpG island methylator}} phenotype

During a colonoscopy, how are any discovered colonic polyps grossly characterized?

By their degree of {{c1::protrusion}} into the colonic lumen
fields.Back Extra: They can be flat, sessile, or pedunculated.

fields.Text:
What 4 medical conditions are often associated with the onset of Budd-Chiari syndrome?

{{c1::Polycythemia vera}}
{{c1::Pregnancy}}
{{c1::Hypercoagulable}} states
{{c1::Hepatocellular carcinoma}}

Which histologic liver region is likely to become congested and necrotic in Budd-Chiari syndrome?

{{c1::Centrilobular}} region

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient presenting with heart failure without JVD, hepatocellular carcinoma, ascites, hepatomegaly, and abdominal pain?

{{c1::Budd-Chiari}} syndrome secondary to {{c1::hepatocellular carcinoma}}
fields.Back Extra: Right-sided heart failure may also cause congestive hepatopathy, but the patient would have JVD.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism associated with Budd-Chiari syndrome?

Hepatic venous outflow {{c1::obstruction}} → {{c1::Centrilobular}} congestion and necrosis

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient presenting with pruritus after warm showers, fatigue, headache, abdominal pain, and ascites?

{{c1::Budd-Chiari}} syndrome secondary to {{c1::polycythemia vera}}
fields.Back Extra: Polycythemia vera leads to a hypercoagulable state resulting in thrombosis of the hepatic veins.

fields.Text:
What are the 3 hereditary conditions that commonly lead to cirrhosis and thereby hepatocellular carcinoma?

{{c1::Hemochromatosis}}
{{c1::Wilson}} disease
{{c1::α1-antitrypsin}} deficiency

What 2 imaging tools are used to confirm the diagnosis when an ultrasound exam shows results suggestive of hepatocellular carcinoma?

{{c1::Contrast CT}}
{{c1::MRI}}

What imaging tool is typically used in screening for hepatocellular carcinoma?

Liver {{c1::ultrasound}}

What carcinogen associated with Aspergillus can lead to hepatocellular carcinoma?

{{c1::Aflatoxin}}

What are the 3 most common physical exam findings in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma?

{{c1::Jaundice}}
Tender {{c1::hepatomegaly}}
{{c1::Anorexia}}

What 2 viral diseases are commonly associated with an increased risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma?

{{c1::Hepatitis B}}
{{c1::Hepatitis C}}

What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient with multiple hepatic tumors, iron deficiency anemia, and an unintentional weight loss of 40 pounds?

{{c1::Colon cancer}} with {{c1::metastases}} to the {{c1::liver}}

What is the most likely diagnosis of a liver mass in a man who has worked for 30 years at a polyvinyl chloride pipe manufacturing facility?

{{c1::Hepatic angiosarcoma}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is due to vinyl chloride exposure from polyvinyl chloride pipes.

Exposure to arsenic is also a risk factor.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism by which hepatic adenomas can directly result in the death of a patient?

Spontaneous {{c1::rupture}} → {{c1::Hemorrhagic shock}}

What is the likely diagnosis for a woman taking oral contraceptives who has a liver mass detected on imaging?

{{c1::Hepatic adenoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a rare benign liver tumor often related to use of oral contraceptives or anabolic steroids.

fields.Text:
What role does a biopsy have in the workup of a patient with an MRI showing a likely cavernous hemangioma?

It should be {{c1::avoided}}
fields.Back Extra: A biopsy is contraindicated because a cavernous hemangioma is a highly vascular tumor with increased risk of hemorrhage.

fields.Text:
What is the most common benign liver tumor?

{{c1::Cavernous hemangioma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to venous malformations.

fields.Text:
What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with the autopsy specimen shown in the image, severe liver enzyme derangements, and an elevated α-fetoprotein level?



{{c1::Hepatocellular carcinoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the most common primary malignant tumor of the liver in adults.

fields.Text:
What is the likely diagnosis for a 40-year-old patient with the liver biopsy findings shown in the image and no symptoms?



{{c1::Cavernous hemangioma}}

How does hepatocellular carcinoma metastasize?

Spreads {{c1::hematogenously}}

Which liver tumor is typically caused by a hyperplastic reaction of hepatocytes to an aberrant dystrophic artery?

{{c1::Focal nodular hyperplasia}}

Which viral infection can lead to hepatocellular carcinoma without first causing underlying cirrhosis?

{{c1::Hepatitis B}} infection

What drug can be used to treat type II Crigler-Najjar syndrome?

{{c1::Phenobarbital}}

What is meant by the term kernicterus?

Deposition of {{c1::unconjugated bilirubin}} in the {{c1::brain}}

How does conjugated bilirubin differ from its unconjugated form in terms of solubility?

Conjugated bilirubin {{c1::is::is/is not}} water soluble
Unconjugated bilirubin {{c1::is not::is/is not}} water soluble

What enzyme converts unconjugated bilirubin into conjugated bilirubin within hepatocytes?

{{c1::UDP-glucuronosyltransferase}}

What is the mechanism by which unconjugated bilirubin is transported into the bloodstream?

By being bound to {{c1::albumin}}

What protein when degraded forms unconjugated bilirubin?

{{c1::Hemoglobin}}

What is the pathophysiologic mechanism seen in patients with Gilbert syndrome?

Mildly {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugation → Increased {{c1::unconjugated::conjugated/unconjugated}} hyperbilirubinemia from stress, illness, or fasting

What is the typical prognosis for patients with Gilbert syndrome?

{{c1::Excellent}}

What hereditary hyperbilirubinemia is associated with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and a grossly black liver?

{{c1::Dubin-Johnson}} syndrome

What pathophysiologic mechanism leads to the characteristic grossly black liver seen in patients with Dubin-Johnson syndrome?

Impaired excretion of {{c1::epinephrine}} metabolites

What hereditary hyperbilirubinemia leads to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and a normal liver on gross presentation?

{{c1::Rotor}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This is similar to Dubin-Johnson syndrome, but milder in presentation and without a grossly black liver.

fields.Text:
What is the pattern of inheritance seen in all hereditary hyperbilirubinemias?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What are the 3 major treatment options for patients with type I Crigler-Najjar syndrome?

{{c1::Plasmapheresis}}
{{c1::Phototherapy}}
Liver {{c1::transplant}}

What is the major mechanism by which phototherapy helps to treat type I Crigler-Najjar syndrome?

Increases {{c1::polarity}} and {{c1::water solubility}} → Allows excretion of {{c1::unconjugated::conjugated/unconjugated}} bilirubin

When in life does type I Crigler-Najjar syndrome typically present?

{{c1::Early::Early/Late}} in life
fields.Back Extra: Neurologic signs may not present until later in life.

fields.Text:
What are the 3 critical steps in bilirubin metabolism?

Bilirubin {{c1::uptake}}
{{c1::Conjugation}}
Intracellular {{c1::transport}}/{{c1::excretion}} in bile

When does biliary atresia typically present in newborns?

After {{c1::2}} weeks of life

What are the 4 common presenting symptoms of biliary atresia?

Persistent {{c1::jaundice}} after 2 weeks of life
{{c1::Darkening}} urine
{{c1::Hepatomegaly}}
{{c1::Acholic}} stools

What are the histopathologic findings associated with biliary atresia?

{{c1::Fibro-obliterative}} destruction of bile ducts → {{c1::Cholestasis}}

What is the most common reason for pediatric liver transplantation?

{{c1::Biliary atresia}}

What laboratory findings are commonly seen with biliary atresia?

Increased {{c1::direct::direct/indirect}} bilirubin
Increased {{c1::GGT}}

Why is excess unconjugated bilirubin harmful to neonates?

Excess unconjugated bilirubin can cause {{c1::kernicterus}}

What is the treatment for exaggerated forms of benign neonatal hyperbilirubinemia?

{{c1::Phototherapy}}
fields.Back Extra: Non-UV light isomerizes unconjugated bilirubin to a water-soluble form.

fields.Text:
What are the 3 major pathophysiologic mechanisms associated with benign neonatal hyperbilirubinemia?

Increased fetal {{c1::RBC}} turnover
Decreased activity of {{c1::UDP-glucuronosyltransferase}}
{{c1::Sterile}} neonatal gut

When does benign neonatal hyperbilirubinemia occur?

After first {{c1::24}} hours of life in nearly all infants
fields.Back Extra: This typically resolves without treatment in 1 to 2 weeks.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiology of breastfeeding failure jaundice?

Insufficient breast milk intake → Decreased elimination of {{c1::bilirubin}} in stool → Increased {{c1::bile}} in enterohepatic circulation

What is the pathophysiology of breast milk jaundice?

Increased {{c1::β-glucuronidase}} in breast milk → Increased {{c1::deconjugation::conjugation/deconjugation}} of bilirubin → Increased {{c1::bile}} in enterohepatic circulation

What are the 2 major causes of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to bile excretion defects?

{{c1::Dubin-Johnson}} syndrome
{{c1::Rotor}} syndrome

What are the 2 major causes of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia secondary to intrinsic biliary tract disease?

{{c1::Primary sclerosing cholangitis}}
{{c1::Primary biliary cholangitis}}

What type of hyperbilirubinemia is typically seen in patients with pancreatic or liver cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, or liver flukes?

{{c1::Conjugated::Conjugated/Unconjugated}} hyperbilirubinemia associated with biliary tract obstruction

What type of hyperbilirubinemia is typically seen in patients with hemolytic diseases, physiologic jaundice, Crigler-Najjar syndrome, and Gilbert syndrome?

{{c1::Unconjugated::Conjugated/Unconjugated}} hyperbilirubinemia

What lysosomal enzyme is responsible for bilirubin deconjugation?

{{c1::β-glucuronidase}}
fields.Back Extra: This is found in intestinal brush borders and breast milk.

fields.Text:
What 3 broad pathophysiologic mechanisms lead to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia?

Biliary {{c1::obstruction}}
{{c1::Intrinsic biliary tract}} disease
Bile {{c1::excretion}} defects

What type of hyperbilirubinemia is seen in patients with cirrhosis and hepatitis?

{{c1::Mixed}} hyperbilirubinemia

What is the definition of jaundice?

Abnormal {{c1::yellowing}} of the skin and/or sclera caused by deposition of {{c1::bilirubin}}

What is the mechanism by which jaundice develops?

{{c1::Hyperbilirubinemia}} secondary to increased {{c1::production}} or decreased {{c1::clearance}}

What are the 4 most common causes of elevated bilirubin levels?

{{c1::Hemolysis}}
{{c1::Obstruction}} of bile ducts
{{c1::Tumor}}
{{c1::Liver::Organ}} disease

What is the mechanism of action of lactulose in the treatment of hepatic encephalopathy?

Increased {{c1::ammonium}} production from {{c1::ammonia}} in the gastrointestinal tract → {{c1::Ammonium}} eliminated in feces

What mechanism explains why hepatic encephalopathy develops after a patient undergoes TIPS procedure?

Bypassed hepatic blood flow → Decreased removal of {{c1::NH3}}

What is the mechanism of action of rifaximin in the treatment of hepatic encephalopathy?

Decreases the amount of {{c1::NH3}}-producing gut bacteria

What are the 2 common pharmacologic treatments for patients with hepatic encephalopathy?

{{c1::Rifaximin}}
{{c1::Lactulose}}

What is the mechanism by which gastrointestinal bleeding, constipation, or infection leads to hepatic encephalopathy?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} {{c1::ammonia}} production and absorption

What is the mechanism by which renal failure, diuretic use, or TIPS procedure leads to hepatic encephalopathy?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} {{c1::ammonia}} removal

What chemical compound in excess primarily leads to hepatic encephalopathy?

{{c1::Ammonia}}

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient presenting with elevated transaminases and a liver biopsy showing periportal and portal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate?

{{c1::Autoimmune hepatitis}}

What are 3 common symptoms reported by patients with autoimmune hepatitis?

{{c1::Nausea}}
{{c1::Pruritus}}
{{c1::Fatigue}}

Which autoimmune markers are typically positive in patients with autoimmune hepatitis?

{{c1::Anti-smooth muscle}} antibodies
{{c1::Anti-liver/kidney microsomal-1}} antibodies

What type of cancer is a 40-year-old woman with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease at risk for?

{{c1::Cirrhosis}} and subsequent {{c1::hepatocellular carcinoma}}

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with metabolic syndrome and the liver biopsy findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Nonalcoholic fatty liver}} disease
fields.Back Extra: The image shows fatty infiltration of hepatocytes and cellular ballooning, which can lead to necrosis.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease?

{{c1::Obesity}} → Fatty infiltration of hepatocytes → Cellular “{{c1::ballooning}}” → {{c1::Necrosis}}

For what disease is aspirin used as a first-line treatment in children?

{{c1::Kawasaki}} disease
fields.Back Extra: Treatment of children with aspirin is otherwise avoided because of aspirin's association with Reye syndrome.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism associated with the aspirin toxicity seen in Reye syndrome?

Aspirin metabolites decrease {{c1::β-oxidation}} by {{c1::reversible::reversible/irreversible}} inhibition of {{c1::mitochondrial}} enzymes

Which 2 viruses, when treated with aspirin in children, are typically associated with the development of Reye syndrome?

{{c1::VZV}}
{{c1::Influenza}}

What pathologic findings will be seen on autopsy in a patient who developed encephalopathy and elevated liver enzymes after receiving aspirin while recovering from the flu?

Microvesicular {{c1::fatty}} changes in the liver

A child with a viral infection who accidentally receives aspirin is at risk for development of what syndrome?

{{c1::Reye}} syndrome

What will examination of the ankles of a patient with alcohol use disorder who has jaundice and foul-smelling breath reveal?

{{c1::Peripheral edema}}

What are the 4 hematologic anomalies that commonly arise in patients with liver disease?

{{c1::Anemia}}
{{c1::Coagulation}} disorders
{{c1::Thrombocytopenia}}
{{c1::Splenomegaly}}

What is the term for the coarse, flapping tremor of the hands in a patient with cirrhosis?

{{c1::Asterixis}}

What leads to the gynecomastia and testicular atrophy seen in men with cirrhosis?

{{c1::Hyperestrogenism}}

What is the term for the proliferation of visibly dilated capillaries within the skin in patients with cirrhosis?

{{c1::Spider angiomas}}

What is the term for the noticeably musty breath of a patient with cirrhosis?

{{c1::Fetor hepaticus}}

What is the cause of confusion, a flapping tremor, and an elevated ammonia level in a patient with cirrhosis?

Development of {{c1::hepatic encephalopathy}}

What are the 2 direct consequences of portal hypertension?

Formation of esophageal and gastric {{c1::varices}} → {{c1::Hematemesis}} and {{c1::melena}}

What is the most common cause of portal hypertension in developed countries?

{{c1::Cirrhosis}}

What cutaneous findings in a patient with cirrhosis are due to increased estrogen levels?

{{c1::Spider angiomas}}
{{c1::Palmar erythema}}

The presence of cirrhosis increases the risk for development of what cancer?

{{c1::Hepatocellular carcinoma}}

What are the common causes of cirrhosis?

Chronic {{c1::alcohol}} use
Chronic {{c1::viral}} hepatitis
{{c1::Nonalcoholic fatty liver}} disease
{{c1::Autoimmune}} hepatitis
{{c1::Biliary}} disease
{{c1::Genetic}} and {{c1::metabolic}} disorders

What cells typically cause the bridging fibrosis seen in cirrhosis?

{{c1::Stellate}} cells

What are the major histopathologic changes seen in patients with cirrhosis?

{{c1::Diffuse bridging fibrosis}}
{{c1::Regenerative nodules}} disrupting normal liver architecture

What is the most likely tumor type shown in the image of the liver of a patient with chronic untreated hepatitis C?



{{c1::Hepatocellular carcinoma}}

What common and potentially fatal bacterial infection are patients with cirrhosis at risk of developing?

{{c1::Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also called primary bacterial peritonitis.

fields.Text:
What is the most appropriate first-line antibiotic to administer to a patient with cirrhosis who presents with fever, chills, and diffuse abdominal pain?

{{c1::Third}}-generation {{c1::cephalosporin}}
fields.Back Extra: The patient likely has spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

fields.Text:
Which organisms are usually responsible for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?

Gram-{{c1::negative::positive/negative}} organisms
Gram-{{c1::positive::positive/negative}} {{c1::streptococci}} (less common)

What method can be used to definitively diagnose spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?

{{c1::Paracentesis}} with an ascitic fluid ANC > {{c1::250}} cells/mm3

What are the common presentations of patients with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?

{{c1::Ileus}}
Abdominal {{c1::pain}}
{{c1::Fevers}}
{{c1::Chills}}
Worsening {{c1::encephalopathy}}

What do the inclusion bodies indicated by the arrow in the image, often seen in those with alcoholic hepatitis, represent?



{{c1::Mallory bodies}}
fields.Back Extra: These are intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions from remnants of destroyed keratin filaments.

fields.Text:
What pathologic findings would be seen in a liver biopsy specimen obtained from a patient with a history of alcoholism, jaundice, hypoalbuminemia, and an elevated INR?

{{c1::Sclerosis}} around {{c1::central vein}}

What liver biopsy findings would be seen in an individual with a long history of heavy alcohol use and dull RUQ pain?

{{c1::Mallory bodies}}
{{c1::Necrotic}} hepatocytes with {{c1::neutrophilic}} infiltrate
fields.Back Extra: This is most likely alcoholic hepatitis.

fields.Text:
What does alcohol cessation lead to in patients with hepatic steatosis?

Possible {{c1::reversal}} of the hepatic steatosis

What pathologic features are seen in a liver biopsy specimen obtained from a patient with hepatic steatosis?

{{c1::Macrovesicular::Macrovesicular/Microvesicular}} {{c1::fatty}} change

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient whose liver biopsy specimen shows regenerative nodules surrounded by fibrous bands?

{{c1::Alcoholic cirrhosis}}
fields.Back Extra: The patient may have portal hypertension and end-stage liver disease.

fields.Text:
What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with elevated liver enzymes and the findings on liver biopsy shown in the image?



{{c1::Hepatic steatosis}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows macrovesicular fatty change.

fields.Text:
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism of diffuse petechiae and purpura in a patient with cirrhosis due to chronic hepatitis C?

{{c1::Thrombocytopenia}} secondary to decreased synthesis of {{c1::thrombopoietin}}
Liver and splenic {{c1::sequestration}} of platelets

Why is PT increased in advanced liver disease?

Production of clotting factors is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}

Why is albumin decreased in advanced liver disease?

{{c1::Biosynthetic}} function of the liver is decreased

How will bilirubin levels be affected in a patient with severe liver dysfunction?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} bilirubin levels

What is the next most appropriate step in determining the cause of elevated ALP found incidentally in an asymptomatic patient?

Measure {{c1::GGT}}
fields.Back Extra: This is to distinguish biliary obstruction/infiltration from bone disease.

fields.Text:
What are the 3 major causes of an elevated ALP level?

Biliary tree {{c1::obstruction}}
{{c1::Infiltrative}} biliary disorders
{{c1::Bone}} disease

What is the likely pattern of aminotransferases that will be seen in a patient with chronic hepatic C presenting with ascites and spider angiomata?

AST {{c1::>::</>}} ALT

How will the relationship of AST to ALT be affected in a patient with alcohol use disorder who reports acute RUQ pain and jaundice?

AST {{c1::>::</>}} ALT

What aminotransferase pattern is consistent with a diagnosis of acute hepatitis B infection?

ALT {{c1::>::</>}} AST

What 2 hepatic enzymes are typically elevated in patients with injury to hepatocytes?

{{c1::ALT}}
{{c1::AST}}

What must be included in the differential diagnosis for a patient with aminotransferase levels greater than 1000 U/L?

{{c1::Drug}}-induced liver injury
Acute {{c1::viral}} hepatitis
{{c1::Autoimmune}} hepatitis
{{c1::Ischemic}} hepatitis

What are the 2 pathways that commonly lead to the development of colorectal cancer?

{{c1::Chromosomal}} instability pathway
{{c1::Microsatellite}} instability pathway

What genetic event is responsible for transforming a colonic adenoma to a colonic adenocarcinoma?

Loss of {{c1::tumor suppressor}} genes → Increased {{c1::tumorigenesis}}

What gene is responsible for transforming a normal colon to a colon at risk?

{{c1::APC}} gene
fields.Back Extra: Loss of function of the APC gene leads to decreased intercellular adhesion and increased proliferation.

fields.Text:
Which pathway implicated in the formation of colorectal cancer involves mutations or methylations of mismatch repair genes?

{{c1::Microsatellite}} instability pathway
fields.Back Extra: This leads to the serrated polyp pathway of carcinogenesis.

fields.Text:
Which genes are mutated in the final stage of the malignant transformation of colonic epithelial cells?

{{c1::TP53}}
{{c1::DCC}}

Which gene mutation leads to colonic adenoma formation?

{{c1::KRAS}} mutation

Which gene is likely mutated in a patient presenting with hundreds of colonic polyps with concomitant colorectal cancer?

{{c1::APC}} gene
fields.Back Extra: Loss of function causes increased proliferation and decreased intercellular adhesion.

fields.Text:
What is the typical sequence of events that leads to most sporadic colorectal cancers?

Loss of {{c1::APC}} gene → {{c1::KRAS}} mutation → Loss of {{c1::tumor suppressor}} genes

Which class of drugs may be chemopreventive in the formation of colorectal cancer?

{{c1::NSAIDs}}
fields.Back Extra: Overexpression of COX-2 has been linked to colorectal cancer.

fields.Text:
What type of colorectal cancer forms via the serrated polyp pathway?

{{c1::Sporadic colorectal cancer}}

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient reporting vague abdominal pain and unintentional weight loss who has the findings on barium enema shown in the image?



{{c1::Colorectal cancer}}
fields.Back Extra:
The patient needs a full colonoscopy.

The X-ray shows an "apple core" lesion.

fields.Text:
What can be offered as screening alternatives to a patient who is "scared of colonoscopies"?

{{c1::FOBT}}
{{c1::FIT}}
fields.Back Extra: CEA levels are used for monitoring recurrence, not for screening.

fields.Text:
Which nonspecific serum tumor marker is used to monitor for recurrence in a patient with colorectal cancer after resection?

{{c1::CEA}}

When should a 40-year-old patient have a colonoscopy if family history includes diagnosis of colon cancer in the father at 50 years of age?

At {{c1::40}} years of age

What is the first-line method for screening individuals with an average risk of colon cancer?

{{c1::Colonoscopy}}
fields.Back Extra: This starts at 45 years of age.

fields.Text:
What lab finding in adults suggests a possible diagnosis of colon cancer?

{{c1::Iron deficiency anemia}} in males and postmenopausal women

Why might you want to perform a colonoscopy on a patient presenting with fevers, hypotension, a new murmur, and blood cultures growing Streptococcus bovis?

Streptococcus bovis bacteremia or endocarditis may be associated with {{c1::colorectal cancer}}

What signs and symptoms are commonly seen in patients with colorectal cancer of the descending colon?

{{c1::Colicky}} pain
Presence of infiltrating {{c1::mass}}
Partial {{c1::obstruction}}
{{c1::Hematochezia}}

What symptoms and signs are commonly seen in patients with colorectal cancer of the ascending colon?

{{c1::Iron deficiency anemia}}
Weight {{c1::loss::gain/loss}}
{{c1::Exophytic}} mass

What are the 3 major locations of colorectal cancer in descending order?

{{c1::Rectosigmoid junction}}
{{c1::Ascending colon}}
{{c1::Descending colon}}

What are the 6 most common risk factors for the development of colorectal cancer?

{{c1::Adenomatous polyps}}
{{c1::Serrated polyps}}
{{c1::IBD}}
{{c1::Familial cancer}} syndromes
{{c1::Tobacco}} use
Diet rich in {{c1::processed meat}} and low in {{c1::fiber}}

What percentage of patients with colorectal cancer have a family history of the disease?

Approximately {{c1::25}}%

What are the classic presenting symptoms of right-sided colon cancers?

{{c1::Occult bleeding}}
fields.Back Extra: This can lead to iron deficiency anemia.

fields.Text:
What are the classic presenting symptoms of left-sided colon cancers?

{{c1::Hematochezia}}
{{c1::Obstruction}}
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} stool caliber due to the {{c1::narrower}} lumen

How does a diagnosis of IBD alter the colorectal cancer screening regimen?

Patients with IBD require {{c1::more::more/less}} frequent screening than the general population
fields.Back Extra: This begins 8 years after the initial diagnosis.

fields.Text:
In what percentage of patients will Lynch syndrome progress to colorectal cancer?

Approximately {{c1::80}}%

What part of the colon is always involved in Lynch syndrome?

{{c1::Proximal::Proximal/Distal}} colon

Describe the pathophysiology of Lynch syndrome.

Mutation in {{c1::mismatch repair}} genes → {{c1::Microsatellite}} instability

What cancers is Lynch syndrome associated with?

{{c1::Colorectal cancer}}
{{c1::Endometrial cancer}}
{{c1::Ovarian cancer}}
{{c1::Skin cancer}}

What is the inheritance pattern for Lynch syndrome?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What is the mode of inheritance of Peutz-Jeghers syndome?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What syndrome includes malignant CNS tumors and familial adenomatous polyposis or Lynch syndrome?

{{c1::Turcot}} syndrome

What 4 conditions occur in patients with Gardner syndrome?

{{c1::Familial adenomatous polyposis}}
Osseous or soft tissue {{c1::tumors}}
Congenital {{c1::hypertrophy}} of retinal pigment epithelium
{{c1::Impacted}} or {{c1::supernumerary}} teeth

What findings do you expect on a colonoscopy performed for a patient with familial adenomatous polyposis?

{{c1::Thousands}} of polyps

What is the specific genetic mutation and inheritance pattern of familial adenomatous polyposis?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}} mutation of {{c1::APC}} gene

What percentage of patients with familial adenomatous polyposis develop colorectal cancer?

{{c1::100}}%

What is the inheritance pattern of juvenile polyposis syndrome?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What condition causes multiple polyps in the colon, stomach, and small bowel in a young child?

{{c1::Juvenile polyposis}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This usually presents in children less than 5 years of age.

fields.Text:
What disease causes multiple gastrointestinal tract hamartomas and hyperpigmented macules on the hands, mouth, lips, and genitalia?

{{c1::Peutz-Jeghers}} syndrome

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome increases risk for which cancers?

{{c1::Breast}} cancer
{{c1::GI}} cancers

A patient with juvenile polyposis syndrome has an increased risk for development of which cancer?

{{c1::Colorectal}} cancer

What treatment for familial adenomatous polyposis can reduce the risk of developing cancer?

Prophylactic {{c1::colectomy}}

PAS staining of an intestinal biopsy specimen obtained from a patient with Whipple disease would show what?

{{c1::Foamy macrophages}} in intestinal lamina propria and mesenteric nodes

What disease causes cardiac symptoms, arthralgias, and neurologic symptoms and later progresses to include diarrhea or steatorrhea?

{{c1::Whipple}} disease

What organism causes Whipple disease?

{{c1::Tropheryma whipplei}}

Tropical sprue can cause what type of anemia?

{{c1::Megaloblastic anemia}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to folate deficiency and, later, vitamin B12 deficiency.

fields.Text:
Unlike celiac sprue, tropical sprue can be treated with which class of drugs?

{{c1::Antibiotics}}

Pancreatic insufficiency causes malabsorption of which macronutrients?

{{c1::Fat}}
{{c1::Fat}}-soluble vitamins
Vitamin {{c1::B12}}

Why is the stool pH in patients with lactose intolerance low?

Bacteria in the colon {{c1::ferment}} the lactose that is not {{c1::absorbed}}

The result of a lactose hydrogen breath test is positive if post-lactose breath hydrogen rises how much above baseline?

More than {{c1::20}} ppm

What type of diarrhea is seen in patients with lactase deficiency?

{{c1::Osmotic}} diarrhea

How would villi appear on an intestinal biopsy specimen obtained from a patient with lactose intolerance?

{{c1::Normal}}
fields.Back Extra: This is unless the lactase deficiency is caused by injury to the villi.

fields.Text:
What is the treatment for celiac disease?

{{c1::Gluten}}-free diet

Celiac disease causes malabsorption and steatorrhea due to involvement of which parts of the bowel?

Distal {{c1::duodenum}}
Proximal {{c1::jejunum}}

What results of a D-xylose test would you expect in celiac disease compared with pancreatic insufficiency?

Celiac disease → {{c1::Abnormal::Normal/Abnormal}} D-xylose test result
Pancreatic insufficiency → {{c1::Normal::Normal/Abnormal}} D-xylose test result

What 3 antibodies are associated with celiac disease?

{{c1::Anti-endomysial}} antibodies
{{c1::Anti-deamidated gliadin peptide}} antibodies
{{c1::IgA tTG}} antibodies

What histologic findings are seen in patients with celiac disease?

Villous {{c1::atrophy}}
Crypt {{c1::hyperplasia}}
Intraepithelial {{c1::lymphocytosis}}

Patients with celiac disease have an increased risk for what malignancy?

{{c1::T-cell lymphoma}}

What is the name of the rash that can be associated with celiac disease?

{{c1::Dermatitis herpetiformis}}

Celiac disease is associated with autoimmune-mediated intolerance to what protein found in wheat and rye?

{{c1::Gluten}} protein
fields.Back Extra: Celiac disease is also known as gluten-sensitive enteropathy or celiac sprue.

fields.Text:
What fecal finding can be used in screening for malabsorption syndromes?

Fecal {{c1::fat}}

What are general signs and symptoms that are associated with malabsorption syndromes?

{{c1::Diarrhea}}
{{c1::Weakness}}
{{c1::Steatorrhea}}
Weight {{c1::loss::gain/loss}}
{{c1::Vitamin}} and {{c1::mineral}} deficiencies

How is duodenal pH affected in pancreatic insufficiency?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} pH due to decreased {{c1::bicarbonate}} secretion

How is fecal elastase affected in pancreatic insufficiency?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}}

What are 3 common causes of pancreatic insufficiency?

Chronic {{c1::pancreatitis}}
{{c1::Cystic fibrosis}}
Obstruction due to {{c1::cancer}}

Which parts of the intestine are affected in tropical sprue?

{{c1::Duodenum}}
{{c1::Jejunum}}
fields.Back Extra: The ileum may be affected over time.

fields.Text:
Celiac disease is associated with which 2 HLA subtypes?

HLA-{{c1::DQ2}}
HLA-{{c1::DQ8}}

How does celiac disease affect bone density?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} bone density

Tropical sprue is typically seen in what patient populations?

Residents of or visitors to {{c1::tropical}} areas

Patients of which demographics more commonly develop Whipple disease?

{{c1::Older::Younger/Older}} {{c1::males::males/females}}

An upper gastrointestinal bleed typically occurs in what section of the gastrointestinal tract?

{{c1::Proximal::Proximal/Distal}} to the {{c1::ligament of Treitz}}

How does an upper gastrointestinal bleed typically present?

{{c1::Hematemesis}}
{{c1::Melena}}

A lower gastrointestinal bleed typically occurs in what section of the gastrointestinal tract?

{{c1::Distal::Proximal/Distal}} to the {{c1::ligament of Treitz}}

How does a lower gastrointestinal bleed typically present?

{{c1::Hematochezia}}

What are the common causes of lower gastrointestinal bleeding?

{{c1::Angiodysplasia}}
{{c1::Inflammatory bowel}} disease
{{c1::Diverticulosis}}
{{c1::Hemorrhoids}}
Anal {{c1::fissure}}
{{c1::Cancer}}

The intestinal friable mucosa shown is found in which inflammatory bowel disease?



{{c1::Ulcerative colitis::Crohn disease/Ulcerative colitis}}

The image shows what common barium swallow X-ray finding in Crohn disease?



{{c1::String}} sign
fields.Back Extra: This is due to bowel wall thickening.

fields.Text:
What part of the bowel does Crohn disease commonly affect?

Terminal {{c1::ileum}}
{{c1::Colon}}

Which inflammatory bowel disease causes continuous colonic lesions with crypt abscesses/ulcers and always involves the rectum?

{{c1::Ulcerative colitis::Crohn disease/Ulcerative colitis}}

Which inflammatory bowel disease has creeping fat, skip lesions, cobblestone mucosa, linear ulcers, bowel wall thickening, fissures, and rectal sparing?

{{c1::Crohn disease::Crohn disease/Ulcerative colitis}}

What are the treatment options for ulcerative colitis?

{{c1::5-aminosalicyclic}} preparations
{{c1::Infliximab}}
{{c1::6-mercaptopurine}}
{{c1::Colectomy}}

Which inflammatory bowel disease is associated with gallstones and calcium oxalate kidney stones?

{{c1::Crohn disease::Crohn disease/Ulcerative colitis}}

Which autoantibodies are associated with ulcerative colitis?

{{c1::p-ANCA}}
{{c1::MPO-ANCA}}

Primary sclerosing cholangitis is associated with which inflammatory bowel disease?

{{c1::Ulcerative colitis::Crohn disease/Ulcerative colitis}}

Name 4 complications specific to Crohn disease.

{{c1::Strictures}}
{{c1::Phlegmons}} and/or {{c1::abscesses}}
{{c1::Fistulas}}
{{c1::Perianal}} disease

Name 4 major extraintestinal manifestations common to both ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease.

{{c1::Rashes}}
Oral {{c1::ulcerations}}
Eye {{c1::inflammation}}
{{c1::Arthritis}}

What is the diagnosis for transmural colonic inflammation with noncaseating granulomas and lymphoid aggregates?

{{c1::Crohn disease::Crohn disease/Ulcerative colitis}}

In ulcerative colitis, what causes the "lead pipe" appearance on imaging?

Loss of {{c1::haustra}}

Toxic megacolon, fulminant colitis, and perforation are complications that are most commonly associated with which inflammatory bowel disease?

{{c1::Ulcerative colitis::Crohn disease/Ulcerative colitis}}

Which antibodies are associated with Crohn disease?

{{c1::Anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae}} antibodies

Recurrent urinary tract infections and pneumaturia may indicate what complication of Crohn disease?

{{c1::Enterovesical fistulae}}

Name 4 treatment options for Crohn disease.

{{c1::Azathioprine}}
{{c1::Glucocorticoids}}
{{c1::Antibiotics}}
{{c1::Biologics}}

Name 2 gastrointestinal complications common to both Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.

{{c1::Malabsorption}} and/or {{c1::malnutrition}}
Colorectal {{c1::cancer}}

How does the diarrhea in Crohn disease differ from that of ulcerative colitis?

{{c1::Crohn disease::Crohn disease/Ulcerative colitis}} → Diarrhea may or may not be bloody
{{c1::Ulcerative colitis::Crohn disease/Ulcerative colitis}} → Bloody diarrhea

How does the depth of intestinal inflammation of Crohn disease compare with that of ulcerative colitis?

{{c1::Crohn disease::Crohn disease/Ulcerative colitis}} → Transmural inflammation
{{c1::Ulcerative colitis::Crohn disease/Ulcerative colitis}} → Mucosal and submucosal inflammation

What test can be used to monitor disease activity in patients with IBD and to distinguish IBD from noninflammatory diseases?

{{c1::Fecal calprotectin}}

A patient has hypercalcemia, high parathyroid hormone, and hypocalciuria. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia}}

What is the cellular defect that results in familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia?

Defective {{c1::G}}-coupled {{c1::Ca2+}}-sensing receptor on parathyroid and kidney cells → Lack of {{c1::PTH}} suppression

What mutation is associated with medullary carcinoma of the thyroid?

{{c1::RET}} mutation

A biopsy of a thyroid nodule shows sheets of cells with amyloid that stain in Congo red. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Medullary}} carcinoma of the thyroid

A patient undergoes a fine needle aspiration of a thyroid nodule that reveals "Orphan Annie" eyes, psammoma bodies, and nuclear grooves. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Papillary}} carcinoma

What are three risk factors, including genetic mutations, for papillary carcinoma of the thyroid?

Childhood {{c1::irradiation}}
{{c1::RET}}/{{c1::PTC}} rearrangements
{{c1::BRAF}} mutations

What hormone does medullary carcinoma of the thyroid typically produce?

{{c1::Calcitonin}}

Mutations in the RAS gene are associated with which subtype of thyroid cancer?

{{c1::Follicular}} carcinoma

How does follicular thyroid carcinoma typically disseminate?

{{c1::Hematogenously}}

A patient discovers a thyroid mass. Biopsy shows uniform follicles. How does the pathologist know whether this mass is benign or malignant?

{{c1::Invasion}} of the thyroid capsule suggests a more malignant follicular carcinoma

A patient with thyroid cancer opts for a total thyroidectomy. Weeks later, paresthesias and hyper-reflexia develop. What happened?

Inadvertent removal of all the {{c1::parathyroid}} glands with resultant {{c1::hypocalcemia::hypercalcemia/hypocalcemia}}

A surgeon injures a nerve during ligation of the inferior thyroid artery in a thyroidectomy. What nerve is most likely affected?

{{c1::Recurrent laryngeal}} nerve

How is thyroid cancer typically diagnosed and treated?

Diagnosed with {{c1::fine needle aspiration}}
Treated with {{c1::thyroidectomy}}

Place the following thyroid cancers in order from best to worst prognosis.

Best prognosis → {{c1::Papillary}} carcinoma
Good prognosis → {{c1::Follicular}} carcinoma
Worst prognosis → {{c1::Undifferentiated/anaplastic}} carcinoma

Which thyroid cancer is associated with PAX8–PPAR-γ translocations?

{{c1::Follicular}} carcinoma

A professional singer lost tenor after a thyroidectomy for thyroid carcinoma. What nerve was injured during surgery?

{{c1::Superior laryngeal}} nerve
fields.Back Extra: This occurred during ligation of the superior thyroid vascular pedicle.

fields.Text:
What genetic mutation is undifferentiated/anaplastic carcinoma of the thyroid associated with?

{{c1::TP53}} mutation

During surgical resection of thyroid cancer in a patient, the recurrent laryngeal nerve is accidentally cut. What symptoms will the patient present with after surgery?

{{c1::Dysphagia}}
{{c1::Dysphonia}}

Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid originates from which cells?

{{c1::Parafollicular C}} cells
