A patient with a high level of PTH is found to have a low level of Ca2+. What are 3 possible causes of these lab findings?

Vitamin {{c1::D}} deficiency
Low {{c1::Ca2+}} intake
Chronic {{c1::renal}} failure

A patient diagnosed with hyperparathyroidism is found to have a high level of Ca2+. What are three possible causes of this lab finding?

Parathyroid {{c1::hyperplasia}}
Parathyroid {{c1::carcinoma}}
Parathyroid {{c1::adenoma}}

A patient with hypercalcemia has a low level of PTH. What are 3 possible causes of these lab findings?

Excessive {{c1::Ca2+}} intake
{{c1::Malignancy}}
High vitamin {{c1::D}} levels

A patient has low levels of both PTH and Ca2+. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Primary hypoparathyroidism}}

What are 2 common causes of primary hypoparathyroidism?

{{c1::Surgical resection}}
{{c1::Autoimmune}} disease

What lab values would you expect to see in a patient with vitamin D deficiency?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} Ca2+
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} PO43-
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PTH

What lab values would you expect to see in a patient with hypoparathyroidism?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} Ca2+
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PO43-
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} PTH

What lab values would you expect to see in a patient with secondary hyperparathyroidism?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} Ca2+
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PO43-
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PTH

What lab values would you expect to see in a patient with pseudohypoparathyroidism?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} Ca2+
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PO43-
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PTH

What lab values would you expect to see in a patient with hyperphosphatemia?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} Ca2+
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PO43-
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PTH

What is the genetic defect that leads to paternally transmitted pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism?

Defective {{c1::Gs}} protein {{c1::α}}-subunit
fields.Back Extra: This is without end-organ resistance to PTH.

fields.Text:
What is the genetic defect that leads to pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A?

{{c1::GNAS1}}-inactivating mutation
fields.Back Extra: This results in a defective Gs protein α-subunit.

fields.Text:
What lab values would you expect to see in maternally inherited pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PTH
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} Ca2+
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PO43-

What is the mechanism of the electrolyte abnormality seen in pseudohypoparathyroidism 1A?

{{c1::Kidney}} and {{c1::bone}} do not respond to PTH → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} Ca2+ and {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} PO43-

Describe the Chvostek sign seen in patients with hypoparathyroidism.

Muscle {{c1::contracts::contracts/relaxes}} with {{c1::facial}} nerve tap

What are 3 classic findings in hypoparathyroidism?

{{c1::Hypocalcemia}}
{{c1::Tetany}}
{{c1::Hyperphosphatemia}}

List 3 causes of hypoparathyroidism.

Injury to {{c1::parathyroid}} glands or their {{c1::blood}} supply
{{c1::DiGeorge}} syndrome
{{c1::Autoimmune}} destruction

What is the inheritance pattern of pseudohypoparathyroidism and pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

Describe the Trousseau sign seen in patients with hypoparathyroidism.

Occlusion of {{c1::brachial}} artery with BP cuff → Carpal {{c1::spasm}}

What lab values would you expect to see in paternally inherited pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism?

{{c1::Normal}} PTH
{{c1::Normal}} Ca2+
{{c1::Normal}} PO43-

In which subtype of hyperparathyroidism do you typically see osteitis fibrosa cystica?

{{c1::Primary}} hyperparathyroidism
fields.Back Extra: This may also be seen in secondary hyperparathyroidism.

fields.Text:
A man with a parathyroid adenoma has thigh pain and gets a biopsy of the painful area. What do you expect the biopsy to reveal?



{{c1::Brown::Color}} {{c1::fibrous}} tissue containing {{c1::osteoclasts}} and deposited {{c1::hemosiderin}} from hemorrhages

What lab finding can distinguish secondary hyperparathyroidism due to CKD from that of other causes?

CKD presents with {{c1::hypocalcemia}} and {{c1::hyperphosphatemia}}

What is tertiary hyperparathyroidism?

{{c1::Autonomous}} hyperparathyroidism → Very high PTH and high Ca2+
fields.Back Extra: This is seen with chronic kidney disease.

fields.Text:
If a patient has bone lesions because of renal osteodystrophy, what is the mechanism underlying the formation of the lesions?

Kidney disease → {{c1::Secondary}} and {{c1::tertiary}} hyperparathyroidism that affects the bones → Lesion formation

What abnormal lab findings are seen in secondary hyperparathyroidism?

{{c1::Hypocalcemia::Hypercalcemia/Hypocalcemia}}
{{c1::Hyperphosphatemia::Hyperphosphatemia/Hypophosphatemia}}
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} ALP
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PTH

What is the most common cause of secondary hyperparathyroidism?

{{c1::CKD}} → Hypovitaminosis {{c1::D}} and {{c1::hyperphosphatemia::hyperphosphatemia/hypophosphatemia}}

What are the classic signs and symptoms of hyperparathyroidism?

"{{c1::Stones}}"
"{{c1::Thrones}}"
"{{c1::Bones}}"
"{{c1::Groans}}"
"{{c1::Psychiatric}} overtones"

What lab findings are seen in primary hyperparathyroidism?

{{c1::Hypercalcemia::Hypercalcemia/Hypocalcemia}}
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PTH

What are two common causes of primary hyperparathyroidism?

Parathyroid {{c1::adenoma}}
Parathyroid {{c1::hyperplasia}}

Explain the pathophysiology behind the skin/mucosal findings shown in the image.



Increased {{c1::MSH}} in {{c1::Addison}} disease → Increased {{c1::melanin}} synthesis → Skin/mucosal hyperpigmentation

On physical exam, how can you differentiate primary from secondary/tertiary adrenal insufficiency?

Primary adrenal insufficiency causes skin/mucosal {{c1::hyperpigmentation}}

How are K+ levels affected in secondary and tertiary adrenal insufficiency?

{{c1::Normal}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to intact aldosterone synthesis.

fields.Text:
Steroids are tapered slowly before discontinuation to avoid development of what condition?

{{c1::Tertiary adrenal insufficiency}}

What are the most common causes of Addison disease in resource-rich and resource-limited countries?

Resource-rich countries → {{c1::Autoimmune adrenalitis}}
Resource-limited countries → {{c1::Tuberculosis}}

What is Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome?

{{c1::Bilateral::Unilateral/Bilateral}} adrenal {{c1::hemorrhage}} in a patient with {{c1::sepsis}} → {{c1::Acute pimary adrenal insufficiency}}

What electrolyte abnormalities and acid-base status are expected with primary adrenal insufficiency?

{{c1::Metabolic acidosis}} with {{c1::hyperkalemia::hyperkalemia/hypokalemia}} and {{c1::hyponatremia::hypernatremia/hyponatremia}}

What type of adrenal insufficiency correlates with lab findings of low cortisol and normal or low ACTH levels?

{{c1::Secondary}} adrenal insufficiency
{{c1::Tertiary}} adrenal insufficiency

What type of adrenal insufficiency correlates with lab findings of low cortisol and high ACTH levels?

{{c1::Primary}} adrenal insufficiency

What 2 tests should be initially ordered to diagnose adrenal insufficiency?

Measurement of morning serum {{c1::cortisol}}
{{c1::ACTH}} stimulation test

What is the treatment for adrenal insufficiency?

{{c1::Glucocorticoid}} with or without replacement of {{c1::mineralocorticoid}}

Low levels of which 2 hormones cause fatigue, muscle aches, orthostatic hypotension, weight loss, and sugar or salt cravings in patients with adrenal insufficiency?

{{c1::Glucocorticoids}}
{{c1::Mineralocorticoids}}

Name the most common causes of secondary and tertiary adrenal insufficiency.

Secondary adrenal insufficiency → {{c1::Pituitary}} pathology
Tertiary adrenal insufficiency → Abrupt cessation of long-term {{c1::glucocortiocid}} use

What commonly precipitates an addisonian crisis?

An unusual {{c1::stressor}} that increases requirement for {{c1::glucocorticoids}} in patients with adrenal insufficiency or patients taking glucocorticoids

What are 2 physical exam findings seen in patients with primary adrenal insufficiency?

{{c1::Hypotension}}
Skin/mucosal {{c1::hyperpigmentation}}

What signs/symptoms are characteristic of acute adrenal insufficiency?

{{c1::Nausea}}
{{c1::Vomiting}}
Acute {{c1::abdominal}} pain
Altered {{c1::mental}} status
{{c1::Shock}}

What urinary products would you expect to be elevated in a patient with a neuroblastoma?

{{c1::HVA}}
{{c1::VMA}}

What finding in this histology slide is commonly seen in neuroblastoma?



{{c1::Homer-Wright rosettes}}

What oncogene is commonly amplified in neuroblastomas?

{{c1::N-myc}} oncogene

Which 2 markers do neuroblastomas typically stain positive for?

{{c1::NSE}}
{{c1::Bombesin}}

What do you expect blood pressure measurements to show in a child newly diagnosed with a neuroblastoma?

{{c1::Normal}} blood pressure
fields.Back Extra: Patients with neuroblastoma are less likely to develop hypertension than those with pheochromocytoma.

fields.Text:
What condition is associated with opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome?

{{c1::Neuroblastoma}}

Where in the body can a neuroblastoma develop?

Any location along the {{c1::sympathetic chain}}

Neuroblastomas originate from which embryonic cell line?

{{c1::Neural crest}} cells

What is the most common presentation of a neuroblastoma?

{{c1::Distension}} of the abdomen
Firm, irregular mass that {{c1::can::can/can not}} cross the midline in a child

How can you differentiate a neuroblastoma and a nephroblastoma on physical examination?

A neuroblastoma is {{c1::irregular::smooth/irregular}} and crosses the {{c1::midline}}
A nephroblastoma is {{c1::smooth::smooth/irregular}} and {{c1::unilateral::unilateral/bilateral}}

What is the most common medullary adrenal tumor in children?

{{c1::Neuroblastoma}}

Describe the mechanism that causes a patient with severe hyperglycemia to vomit.

{{c1::Ketogenesis}}, {{c1::ketonemia}}, and {{c1::ketonuria}} induce vomiting

What 3 direct effects on cellular metabolism can a diabetic insulin deficiency create?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} tissue glucose uptake with {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} protein catabolism
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} lipolysis

Why might a patient with ketoacidosis hyperventilate?

The respiratory system compensates for {{c1::anion gap metabolic acidosis}} with hyperventilation
fields.Back Extra: This is known as Kussmaul respiration.

fields.Text:
What 2 processes lead to anion gap metabolic acidosis in patients with hyperglycemia?

Increased {{c1::ketogenesis}}
Increased serum {{c1::lactate}} due to hypovolemia from {{c1::osmotic diuresis}}

What causes ketonemia and ketonuria in a patient with hyperglycemia?

Increased {{c1::lipolysis}} due to {{c1::insulin}} deficiency in diabetes mellitus

How can untreated hyperglycemia ultimately lead to coma and death?

{{c1::Hypovolemia}} from {{c1::osmotic diuresis}} → {{c1::Circulation}} failure and poor tissue {{c1::perfusion}} → Coma and death

Why do patients with diabetes experience polydipsia?

Hyperglycemia and excess glycosuria cause {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} plasma osmolality → Increased {{c1::thirst}} response

On random plasma glucose testing, what cutoff level and exam finding are required for a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?

Plasma glucose level ≥ {{c1::200}} mg/dL
Symptoms of {{c1::hyperglycemia}}

What 3 tests may be used to diagnose diabetes mellitus?

{{c1::Oral glucose tolerance}} test
{{c1::Fasting plasma glucose}} test
{{c1::HbA1c}} test

What are the cutoff levels needed to indicate a positive result for diabetes mellitus?

HbA1c ≥ {{c1::6.5}}%
Fasting plasma glucose ≥ {{c1::126}} mg/dL
2-hour oral glucose tolerance test ≥ {{c1::200}} mg/dL

Why does sorbitol accumulate in the lens, retina, and Schwann cells in a patient with diabetes?

These cell lines lack {{c1::sorbitol dehydrogenase}}

In a patient with diabetes, what causes sensory and autonomic nerve damage?

{{c1::Osmotic}} damage to the {{c1::PNS}}

What is the most common cause of death among people with chronic diabetes mellitus?

{{c1::Myocardial infarction}}
fields.Back Extra: This is related to large vessel atherosclerosis.

fields.Text:
How long does a patient need to fast before checking their fasting plasma glucose level?

Typically for more than {{c1::8}} hours

What lab test might help identify the early stages of diabetic nephropathy?

Urine dipstick test for {{c1::microalbuminuria}}

Which antihypertensive agents are recommended to prevent progressive proteinuria in patients with diabetes?

{{c1::ACE}} inhibitors
{{c1::ARBs}}

Describe the pathophysiologic progression of diabetic nephropathy to chronic kidney disease.

Basement membrane {{c1::thickening::thickening/thinning}} and protein {{c1::leakage}} → {{c1::Nodular glomerulosclerosis}} and progressive {{c1::proteinuria}}

What is the consequence of small vessel disease in individuals with chronic diabetes mellitus in the retina?

Retinal {{c1::hemorrhages}}
Vessel {{c1::proliferation}}
{{c1::Microaneurysms}}
{{c1::Exudates}}

What is the consequence of nonenzymatic glycation in small vessels in the setting of chronic diabetes mellitus?

Diffuse {{c1::thickening::thickening/thinning}} of the blood vessel basement membrane

When uncontrolled, which type of diabetes will classically present acutely with diabetic ketoacidosis?

Type {{c1::1}} diabetes

What does the HbA1c value signify?

The average blood {{c1::glucose}} in the preceding {{c1::3}} months
fields.Back Extra: This is influenced by RBC turnover.

fields.Text:
Unopposed secretion of which 2 hormones may cause secondary diabetes mellitus?

{{c1::Epinephrine}}
{{c1::GH}}

Patients receiving what long-term pharmacologic therapy may develop diabetes mellitus over time?

{{c1::Glucocorticoid}} therapy

When uncontrolled, which type of diabetes will classically present acutely with a hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state?

Type {{c1::2}} diabetes

Polyphagia, polyuria, polydipsia, and unintentional weight loss represent the classic presentation of which endocrine disease?

{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}

Which macrovascular pathologies are related to nonenzymatic glycation of blood vessel walls in patients with diabetes mellitus?

{{c1::Large::Large/Small}} vessel atherosclerosis
{{c1::Peripheral vascular occlusive}} disease
{{c1::Coronary artery}} disease
{{c1::Cerebrovascular}} disease
{{c1::Gangrene}}

In the setting of diabetes mellitus, osmotic damage to the lens increases the risk for what complication?

{{c1::Cataracts}}

What is the genetic predisposition to type 1 diabetes mellitus versus type 2 diabetes mellitus?

Type 1 diabetes mellitus → {{c1::Weak::Strong/Weak}} genetic predisposition
Type 2 diabetes mellitus → {{c1::Strong::Strong/Weak}} genetic predisposition

Compare types 1 and 2 diabetes mellitus in terms of the number of β-cells in the pancreatic islets and histology of the islets.

Type 1 diabetes mellitus → {{c1::Less::More/Less}} cells with {{c1::leukocytic}} infiltrates
Type 2 diabetes mellitus → Demonstrates {{c1::IAPP}} deposits

Compare types 1 and 2 diabetes mellitus in terms of glucose intolerance and the risk of ketoacidosis.

Type 1 diabetes mellitus → Shows {{c1::severe}} glucose intolerance and ketoacidosis is {{c1::common::common/rare}}
Type 2 diabetes mellitus → Shows {{c1::mild to moderate}} glucose intolerance and ketoacidosis is {{c1::rare::common/rare}}

Which HLAs are associated with type 1 diabetes mellitus?

HLA-{{c1::DR4}}
HLA-{{c1::DR3}}

Is obesity more commonly associated with type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus?

Type {{c1::2}} diabetes mellitus

Describe the need for insulin therapy, degree of insulin sensitivity, and serum insulin level in type 1 diabetes mellitus.

Insulin {{c1::always}} needed
{{c1::High::High/Low}} insulin sensitivity
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} serum insulin level

What is the underlying etiology of type 1 diabetes mellitus?

{{c1::Autoimmune}} {{c1::T::B/T}}-cell–mediated destruction of pancreatic {{c1::β}} cells

Describe the need for insulin therapy, degree of insulin sensitivity, and serum insulin level in type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Insulin {{c1::sometimes}} needed
{{c1::Low::High/Low}} insulin sensitivity
Serum insulin level is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} initially and later {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}

What life-threatening neurologic, cardiac, and infectious complications are associated with diabetic ketoacidosis?

Neurologic → {{c1::Cerebral edema}}
Cardiac → {{c1::Arrhythmias}}
Infectious → {{c1::Mucormycosis}}

In diabetic ketoacidosis, what changes are noted in K+ levels in the following locations?

{{c1::Low::High/Low}} intracellular K+ levels
{{c1::High::High/Low}} and normal serum K+ levels
{{c1::High::High/Low}} urinary K+ levels
{{c1::Low::High/Low}} total body K+ levels

How do the following lab values change in diabetic ketoacidosis?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} glucose
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} pH
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} bicarbonate
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} ketone levels
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} WBC count

What is the cause of the fruity breath odor in diabetic ketoacidosis?

Exhalation of {{c1::acetone}}

Describe Kussmaul respirations.

{{c1::Deep::Deep/Shallow}}, {{c1::rapid::rapid/slow}} breathing
fields.Back Extra: This is characteristic of diabetic ketoacidosis.

fields.Text:
A patient with diabetes presents with delirium, abdominal pain, fruity breath, and evidence of dehydration. What is the most likely diagnosis?

{{c1::Diabetic ketoacidosis}}

Which 2 specific ketone bodies are increased in the serum of a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis?

{{c1::β-hydroxybutyrate}}
{{c1::Acetoacetate}}

What are 2 common causes of diabetic ketoacidosis?

Noncompliance with {{c1::insulin}} therapy
Increased need for {{c1::insulin}} due to metabolic stress

What changes are seen in glucose level, serum osmolality, pH, and ketones in a hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state?

{{c1::Increased}} glucose
{{c1::Increased}} serum osmolality
{{c1::Normal}} pH
{{c1::No}} ketones produced

What 2 neurologic symptoms might you be concerned about in a patient presenting in a hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state?

{{c1::Seizures}}
{{c1::Focal}} neurologic deficits

Why is a hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state more common in elderly patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus?

They are less able to sustain {{c1::oral}} intake of {{c1::fluids}} in the setting of hyperglycemia and/or osmotic diuresis

What is the sequence of events that typically leads to a hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state?

Severe {{c1::hyperglycemia}} → Excessive {{c1::osmotic diuresis}} → Dehydration and {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} serum osmolality

How can you differentiate diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state based on levels of insulin and ketones?

Diabetic ketoacidosis → Insulin is {{c1::deficient::present/deficient}} and ketones are {{c1::present::present/deficient}}
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state → Insulin is {{c1::present::present/deficient}} and ketones are {{c1::deficient::present/deficient}}

What happens to K+ levels in a hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state?

Serum K+ level is normal or {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}
Intracellular K+ level is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}

What are 4 general treatments for a hyperglycemic emergency?

IV {{c1::fluids}}
{{c1::K+}}
IV {{c1::insulin}}
{{c1::Glucose}} (as needed)

Name 3 major risk factors for hypoglycemia in patients with diabetes mellitus.

High doses of {{c1::insulin}} or {{c1::insulin}} secretagogues
Excess {{c1::exercise}}
Inadequate intake of {{c1::food}}

Name 2 neuroglycopenic symptoms of hypoglycemia in a patient with diabetes.

{{c1::Seizures}}
Altered {{c1::mental}} status

What are 3 ways to treat hypoglycemia in a patient with diabetes?

Administer {{c1::simple carbohydrates}}
IV {{c1::dextrose}}
IM {{c1::glucagon}}

What is hypoglycemia awareness?

Patient's ability to recognize {{c1::low::high/low}} blood sugar by recognizing the {{c1::neurogenic}} symptoms of hypoglycemia

What condition causes neuroglycopenic symptoms to occur without preceding neurogenic symptoms in patients with diabetes experiencing hypoglycemia?

{{c1::Hypoglycemia unawareness}}
fields.Back Extra: This occurs in patients with a blunted autonomic response.

fields.Text:
What are 2 common presenting symptoms of Nelson syndrome?

{{c1::Hyperpigmentation}}
{{c1::Mass effect}} symptoms

What complication occurs if both adrenal glands are excised as treatment for refractory Cushing disease?

{{c1::Nelson}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This is an enlargement of an existing ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma.

fields.Text:
Describe the treatment course for Nelson syndrome.

{{c1::Transsphenoidal resection}} of the pituitary adenoma, followed by postoperative pituitary {{c1::irradiation}} of the residual tumor

What physical exam finding in Cushing syndrome does the image depict?



{{c1::Abdominal striae}}

What physical exam finding is shown in the image?



{{c1::Moon facies}}

A CRH stimulation test shows increases in ACTH and cortisol. What diagnosis is suggested?

{{c1::Cushing}} disease

To confirm that a patient has Cushing disease after suppression with a high-dose dexamethasone test, what do you order?

{{c1::MRI}} of the {{c1::pituitary}} gland

What would a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test do to ACTH in Cushing disease?

{{c1::Suppress}} ACTH

When a patient is found to have ectopic ACTH secretion causing Cushing syndrome, what diagnostic test can done to confirm the diagnosis?

{{c1::CT}} of the abdomen, pelvis, and chest
fields.Back Extra: This is to look for a source of ectopic secretion.

fields.Text:
What happens to ACTH levels during a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test in a patient with ectopic ACTH production from small cell lung cancer?

There will be {{c1::no suppression::suppression/no suppression}} of ACTH

A patient with suspected Cushing syndrome has low ACTH levels and does not take steroids. What diagnostic test should be ordered next?

{{c1::CT}} of chest, abdomen, and pelvis
fields.Back Extra: This is to confirm the presence of an adrenal tumor.

fields.Text:
A 24-hour urine test reveals a high free cortisol level in a patient suspected of having Cushing syndrome. What diagnostic test should be ordered next?

Measurement of serum {{c1::ACTH}}

What will administration of CRH do to ACTH and cortisol levels in a patient with ectopic ACTH production?

{{c1::Normal}} ACTH levels
{{c1::Normal}} cortisol levels

Name 3 screening tests for Cushing syndrome.

{{c1::24-hour urinalysis}} showing increased free cortisol
Increased late-night {{c1::salivary}} cortisol
Overnight {{c1::low::high/low}}-dose {{c1::dexamethasone}} test showing no suppression

What are the most common causes of exogenous and endogenous Cushing syndrome?

{{c1::Steroid}} use → Most common exogenous cause
{{c1::Cushing}} disease → Most common endogenous cause

What is the difference between Cushing syndrome and Cushing disease?

Cushing syndrome is caused by an increase in {{c1::cortisol}} levels from various causes
Cushing disease is caused by an {{c1::ACTH}}-producing {{c1::pituitary adenoma}}

Describe the appearance of the adrenals on abdominal imaging of a patient with Cushing disease.

{{c1::Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia}}

What are 2 possible mechanisms of increased cortisol with increased ACTH levels in Cushing syndrome?

{{c1::ACTH}}-producing {{c1::pituitary adenoma}}
Paraneoplastic {{c1::ACTH}} production

In a patient with Cushing syndrome due to unilateral adrenal carcinoma, what will a CT scan of the unaffected adrenal gland show?

Uninvolved adrenal gland may show {{c1::atrophy}}

What are 2 causes of increased serum cortisol with a low ACTH level?

Exogenous {{c1::glucocorticoids}} (most common)
{{c1::Adrenal}} overproduction of cortisol

What is a finding of Cushing syndrome that is specific to children?

{{c1::Growth}} restriction

Besides elevated cortisol, what 2 other elevated lab findings are associated with Cushing syndrome?

{{c1::Hypercholesterolemia}}
{{c1::Hyperglycemia}}

Name 2 pathologic causes of primary hyperaldosteronism.

{{c1::Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia}}
{{c1::Conn}} syndrome

What K+ levels would you expect in a patient with hyperaldosteronism?

Normal or {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} K+ levels

Name 3 pathologic causes of secondary hyperaldosteronism.

{{c1::Renovascular hypertension}}
{{c1::Edema}}
{{c1::Juxtaglomerular}} cell tumors

What physical exam finding might help you differentiate primary hyperaldosteronism from secondary hyperaldosteronism?

Primary hyperaldosteronism does not cause {{c1::edema}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to an intact aldosterone escape mechanism.

fields.Text:
In primary hyperaldosteronism, what are the typical serum measurements of renin and aldosterone?

Renin is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}
Aldosterone is {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}

From where in the body is aldosterone secreted?

{{c1::Adrenal}} glands

Which form of hyperaldosteronism is associated with treatment-resistant hypertension?

{{c1::Primary}} hyperaldosteronism

Does hyperaldosteronism cause metabolic alkalosis or acidosis?

Metabolic {{c1::alkalosis}}

What vital sign will likely be abnormal in hyperaldosteronism?

{{c1::Blood pressure}}

What enzyme is common to all neuroendocrine tumors?

{{c1::APUD}}

What is an example of a neuroendocrine tumor in the adrenal glands?

{{c1::Pheochromocytoma}}

What is an example of a neuroendocrine tumor in the lungs?

{{c1::Small cell carcinoma}}

What is an example of a neuroendocrine tumor in the thyroid?

{{c1::Medullary carcinoma}}

What type of tumor can secrete products, such as chromogranin A, synaptophysin, NSE, serotonin, calcitonin, and histamine?

{{c1::Neuroendocrine}} tumors

Name 2 examples of neuroendocrine tumors that arise in the gastrointestinal tract.

{{c1::Carcinoid}} tumor
{{c1::Gastrinoma}}

Name 2 examples of neuroendocrine tumors that arise in the pancreas.

{{c1::Glucagonoma}}
{{c1::Insulinoma}}

What are the treatment options for neuroendocrine tumors?

{{c1::Somatostatin}} analogs
{{c1::Surgical resection}}

In adults, what is the most common tumor of the adrenal medulla?

{{c1::Pheochromocytoma}}

When managing a pheochromocytoma, why must administration of an α-antagonist precede administration of a β-blocker and surgical resection?

To prevent {{c1::hypertensive crisis}}

Which 4 hormones are commonly secreted by a pheochromocytoma?

{{c1::Epinephrine}}
{{c1::Norepinephrine}}
{{c1::Dopamine}}
{{c1::Erythropoietin}}

What is the best irreversible α-antagonist to use for pheochromocytoma management?

{{c1::Phenoxybenzamine}}

What will be elevated on urine and blood analysis of a patient with pheochromocytoma?

Increased {{c1::catecholamines}} in serum and urine
Increased {{c1::metanephrines}} in serum and urine

What are 5 common episodic hyperadrenergic symptoms associated with pheochromocytoma?

{{c1::Pressure}}
{{c1::Pain}}
{{c1::Perspiration}}
{{c1::Palpitations}}
{{c1::Pallor}}

Name 2 places in the pelvis where an extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma would likely be found.

{{c1::Organ of Zuckerkandl}}
{{c1::Bladder}} wall

List the 5 components of the pheochromocytoma rule of 10's.

10% {{c1::malignant}}
10% {{c1::bilateral}}
10% {{c1::extra-adrenal}}
10% {{c1::calcify}}
10% {{c1::kids}}

List 3 genetic conditions that are associated with pheochromocytomas.

{{c1::Neurofibromitosis type 1}}
{{c1::von-Hippel Lindau}} syndrome
{{c1::MEN 2A/2B}}

Which 3 histologic stains will show positive results for a pheochromocytoma?

{{c1::Chromogranin}}
{{c1::Synaptophysin}}
{{c1::NSE}}

What cell line is a pheochromocytoma derived from?

{{c1::Chromaffin}} cells
fields.Back Extra: These are derived from neural crest cells.

fields.Text:
Which variant of MEN causes a marfanoid habitus?

MEN type {{c1::2B}} syndrome

What 3 tumors are associated with MEN type 2B syndrome?

{{c1::Mucosal neuromas}}
{{c1::Medullary thyroid carcinoma}}
{{c1::Pheochromocytoma}}

Which MEN syndrome is associated with parathyroid adenomas, and which is associated with parathyroid hyperplasia?

MEN type {{c1::1}} syndrome is associated with parathyroid adenomas
MEN type {{c1::2A}} syndrome is associated with parathyroid hyperplasia

What gene mutation is seen in MEN type 2A/2B syndrome, and what does it encode?

A mutation in the {{c1::RET}} gene on chromosome {{c1::10}}, encoding a {{c1::receptor tyrosine kinase}}

Which MEN syndromes present with increased catecholamines and increased calcitonin on labs?

MEN type {{c1::2A}} syndrome
MEN type {{c1::2B}} syndrome

What 3 abnormalities are associated with MEN type 2A syndrome?

{{c1::Medullary thyroid carcinoma}}
{{c1::Pheochromocytoma}}
Parathyroid {{c1::hyperplasia}}

Which multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome is associated with angiofibromas, collagenomas, and meningiomas?

MEN type {{c1::1}} syndrome

MEN type 1 syndrome is associated with a mutation of which gene?

{{c1::MEN1}} on chromosome {{c1::11}}

Name 4 pancreatic endocrine tumors seen in MEN type 1 syndrome.

{{c1::Insulinoma}}
{{c1::Zollinger-Ellison}} syndrome
{{c1::VIPoma}}
{{c1::Glucagonoma}}

MEN type 1 syndrome is associated with tumors in what 3 locations?

{{c1::Parathyroid}}
{{c1::Pituitary}}
{{c1::Pancreas}}

What is the inheritance pattern of all MEN syndromes?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

What prophylactic surgery should patients with MEN type 2A syndrome have?

Prophylactic {{c1::thyroidectomy}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to an association with medullary thyroid cancer.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of antacids?

Antacids work in the stomach lumen and neutralize the {{c1::H+}} secreted by {{c1::parietal}} cells

By what two mechanisms does the vagus nerve stimulate gastric acid secretion?

Release of {{c1::acetylcholine}} → Stimulates M3 receptors on parietal cells
Release of {{c1::GRP}} → Stimulates G cells to release gastrin

Where does somatostatin act to decrease HCl secretion?

Somatostatin acts on {{c1::parietal}} cells of the stomach → Inhibits {{c1::gastric acid}} secretion

Atropine acts on which cell type in the stomach and acts at which receptors?

{{c1::Parietal}} cells via inhibition of {{c1::M3}} receptors

H2 blockers act on which stomach cell type?

{{c1::Parietal}} cells

Proton pump inhibitors work on pumps that exchange which two ions?

{{c1::H+}}
{{c1::K+}}
fields.Back Extra: Proton pump inhibitors inhibit the ATPase that acts to transport H+ out of the parietal cell and K+ into the cell.

fields.Text:
Acetylcholine and gastrin increase acid production via which messenger?

{{c1::Gq}} protein → Increased {{c1::IP3}} and {{c1::Ca2+}} intracellularly

Histamine increases acid production via which messenger?

{{c1::Gs}} protein → Increased {{c1::cAMP}}

What is the alkaline tide?

{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in blood pH after secretion of {{c1::gastric acid}}

Somatostatin and prostaglandins decrease acid production via inhibition of which messenger?

{{c1::cAMP}}

What two cell types are stimulated by gastrin?

{{c1::Parietal}} cells
{{c1::Enterochromaffin-like}} cells

What drug can be used to treat acute variceal bleeding, VIPoma, carcinoid tumors, and acromegaly?

{{c1::Octreotide}}

What is the mechanism of action of octreotide?

Analog of {{c1::somatostatin}} → Prevents secretion of splanchnic {{c1::vasodilatory}} hormones

Name common adverse effects of octreotide.

Increased risk of {{c1::cholelithiasis}} due to inhibition of cholecystokinin
{{c1::Nausea}}
{{c1::Cramps}}
{{c1::Steatorrhea}}

What 2 conditions can be treated with sulfasalazine?

{{c1::Ulcerative colitis}}
{{c1::Crohn}} disease

Name 4 adverse effects of sulfasalazine.

Reversible {{c1::oligospermia}}
{{c1::Nausea}}
{{c1::Malaise}}
{{c1::Sulfonamide}} toxicity

What specifically activates sulfasalazine in the gut?

{{c1::Colonic bacteria}}

What 2 drugs make up sulfasalazine?

{{c1::Sulfapyridine}}
{{c1::5-aminosalicylic acid}}

What medication prescribed for weight loss inhibits gastric and pancreatic lipase to reduce dietary fat absorption?

{{c1::Orlistat}}

What are the adverse effects of orlistat?

{{c1::Steatorrhea}}
{{c1::Abdominal}} pain
Bowel {{c1::urgency}}
{{c1::Flatulence}}
{{c1::Frequent::Frequent/Infrequent}} bowel movements
Decreased absorption of {{c1::fat}}-soluble vitamins

What is the effect of H2-blockers on parietal cells?

{{c1::Reversible::Reversible/Irreversible}} inhibition of H2-receptors in parietal cells → Decreased {{c1::gastric acid}} secretion

What class of drugs do cimetidine, famotidine, and nizatidine belong to?

{{c1::H2}}-blockers

Which H2-blocker can cause antiandrogenic effects including impotence, gynecomastia, low libido, and elevated prolactin release?

{{c1::Cimetidine}}

Which H2-blocker used to treat gastritis can cause headaches, dizziness, and confusion?

{{c1::Cimetidine}}
fields.Back Extra: It is able to cross the blood-brain barrier and placenta.

fields.Text:
Which H2-blocker can decrease the renal excretion of creatinine?

{{c1::Cimetidine}}

Which H2-blocker should you avoid prescribing for patients taking multiple medications?

{{c1::Cimetidine}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because it causes inhibition of cytochrome P-450 and may alter the metabolism of other drugs.

fields.Text:
Name the common clinical uses of H2-receptor blockers.

{{c1::Gastritis}}
{{c1::Peptic ulcers}}
Mild esophageal {{c1::reflux}}

What infectious adverse effects can occur in patients taking proton pump inhibitors?

{{c1::Clostridioides difficile}} infection
{{c1::Pneumonia}}

Absorption of which vitamin and electrolytes can be impaired in patients taking proton pump inhibitors?

Vitamin {{c1::B12}}
{{c1::Mg2+}}
{{c1::Ca2+}}

Name six conditions for which proton pump inhibitors are used as treatment or prophylaxis.

{{c1::Peptic ulcers}}
Esophageal {{c1::reflux}}
{{c1::Gastritis}}
{{c1::Zollinger-Ellison}} syndrome
{{c1::Helicobacter pylori}} infection
Prophylaxis for {{c1::stress ulcers}}

What is the mechanism of action of proton pump inhibitors?

{{c1::Irreversible::Reversible/Irreversible}} inhibiton of {{c1::H+/K+-ATPase}} located in the {{c1::parietal}} cells of the stomach

What renal pathology can result from proton pump inhibitor use?

Acute {{c1::interstitial nephritis}}

Which antacid can chelate and reduce the effectiveness of other medications such as tetracycline?

{{c1::Calcium carbonate}}

What is the common electrolyte abnormality that all antacids can cause?

{{c1::Hypokalemia}}

What adverse effect might overusing calcium carbonate for self-treatment of GERD lead to?

{{c1::Hypercalcemia}}
Increased {{c1::rebound acid}}

Diarrhea, hypotension, hyporeflexia, cardiac arrest, and hypokalemia are adverse effects of which antacid?

{{c1::Magnesium hydroxide}}

What could lead to constipation, proximal muscle weakness, and seizures in a patient taking antacids to treat GERD?

{{c1::Aluminum hydroxide}}

Name 3 compounds commonly used as antacids.

{{c1::Aluminum hydroxide}}
{{c1::Calcium carbonate}}
{{c1::Magnesium hydroxide}}

How might antacids interact with other medications?

Antacids can interfere with the {{c1::absorption}}, {{c1::bioavailability}}, or {{c1::urinary excretion}} of other medications
fields.Back Extra: This is by affecting gastric/urinary pH and slowing gastric emptying.

fields.Text:
Name 3 conditions that can be treated with bismuth.

{{c1::Peptic ulcers}}
{{c1::Traveler's}} diarrhea
{{c1::Helicobacter pylori}} infection

Which 2 drugs bind to ulcer bases, serving to provide physical protection and promoting bicarbonate secretion to reestablish a pH gradient in the mucous layer?

{{c1::Bismuth}}
{{c1::Sucralfate}}

Sucralfate works best in what type of environment, and what drugs are not administered with sucralfate for this reason?

{{c1::Acidic}} environment
{{c1::PPIs}} and {{c1::H2}} blockers are not administered with sucralfate

Name 1 adverse effect of misoprostol and 1 contraindication to treatment with this drug.

It can cause {{c1::diarrhea}}
It is contraindicated in patients with {{c1::childbearing}} potential

Which drug can be used to protect against NSAID-induced peptic ulcers and to induce labor via cervical ripening?

{{c1::Misoprostol}}

What is the mechanism of action of misoprostol in gastric acid synthesis?

Synthetic {{c1::PGE1}} analog → {{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} production and secretion of gastric mucus barrier and {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} acid production

Why does loperamide have a low addictive potential?

It has poor {{c1::CNS}} penetration

Which μ-opioid receptor agonist can be used to treat diarrhea?

{{c1::Loperamide}}
fields.Back Extra: It acts to slow gut motility.

fields.Text:
What are the adverse effects of loperamide?

{{c1::Constipation}}
{{c1::Nausea}}

What is the mechanism of action of lactulose in treating hepatic encephalopathy?

Lactulose is broken down by gut {{c1::microbiota}} into {{c1::lactic acid}} and {{c1::acetic acid}} → Excretes nitrogen as {{c1::NH4+}} by trapping it in the colon

What is the mechanism of action of osmotic laxatives?

Creation of an {{c1::osmotic load}} to draw water {{c1::into::into/out of}} the gastrointestinal lumen

Magnesium hydroxide, magnesium citrate, polyethylene glycol, and lactulose all belong to which class of medications?

{{c1::Osmotic laxatives}}

What is the mechanism of action of stimulant laxatives such as senna and bisacodyl?

Stimulation of enteric {{c1::nerves}} → Colonic contraction

What is the mechanism of action of bulk-forming laxatives such as psyllium and methylcellulose?

Soluble {{c1::fibers}} help draw water into the gut lumen → Creates viscous fluid and promotes {{c1::peristalsis}}

What are the adverse effects of osmotic laxatives?

{{c1::Diarrhea}}
{{c1::Dehydration}}
fields.Back Extra: Patients with bulimia may abuse these.

fields.Text:
What adverse effect can occur with bulk-forming laxatives?

{{c1::Bloating}}

What is the mechanism of action of an emollient laxative such as docusate?

Acts as a {{c1::surfactant}} → Decreases {{c1::surface tension}} of stool → Increases incorporation of water into stool

What is the mechanism of action of lubiprostone?

Activates {{c1::chloride}} channels → {{c1::Increases::Increases.Decreases}} intestinal secretion of fluids

Name four common adverse effects of ondansetron and granisetron.

{{c1::Serotonin}} syndrome
Prolonged {{c1::QT}} interval
{{c1::Constipation}}
{{c1::Headache}}

Ondansetron and granisetron are used to control vomiting primarily in which settings?

{{c1::Surgery}}
{{c1::Chemotherapy}}
{{c1::Radiotherapy}}

What is the mechanism of action of ondansetron and granisetron?

{{c1::5-HT3}}-receptor antagonists
Acts peripherally to decrease {{c1::vagal}} stimulation

Which antiemetic is used for treating diabetic gastroparesis?

{{c1::Metoclopramide}}

Which antiemetic drugs can cause gastrointestinal distress, extrapyramidal symptoms, hyperprolactinemia, depression, anxiety, and drowsiness?

{{c1::Metoclopramide}}
{{c1::Prochloroperazine}}

What is the mechanism of action of the antiemetics metoclopramide and prochloroperazine?

{{c1::D2}}-receptor antagonists
Metoclopramide also {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} lower esophageal sphincter tone and gastric {{c1::emptying}}

What is the main indication for aprepitant?

{{c1::Chemotherapy}}-induced nausea and vomiting

What is the mechanism of action of aprepitant and fosaprepitant?

{{c1::NK1}} receptor antagonists

Where do antiemetics act in the brain?

{{c1::Chemoreceptor trigger}} zone, located in the {{c1::area postrema}}

Ménétrier disease is considered to be a precursor for what pathology?

{{c1::Malignancy}}

What gross and histologic changes are seen in Ménétrier disease?

{{c1::Hyperplasia::Hyperplasia/Hypoplasia}} of the gastric mucosa → {{c1::Hypertrophied::Hypertrophied/Hypotrophied}} rugae and parietal cell {{c1::atrophy}}

What changes occur to mucus and acid production in Ménétrier disease?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} mucus production
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} acid production

Why does edema occur with Ménétrier disease?

Due to {{c1::protein}} loss

What five signs and symptoms are commonly present in patients with Ménétrier disease?

{{c1::Epigastric}} pain
{{c1::Anorexia}}
{{c1::Vomiting}}
Weight {{c1::loss::gain/loss}}
{{c1::Edema}}

What is the pathophysiology of NSAID-induced acute gastritis?

NSAIDs reduce {{c1::PGE2}} → Decreased gastric mucosa protection

Which parts of the stomach are affected in autoimmune chronic gastritis?

{{c1::Body}}
{{c1::Fundus}}

Which part of the stomach does chronic gastritis caused by Helicobacter pylori affect?

Affects the {{c1::antrum}} initially and then spreads to the {{c1::body}} of the stomach

What is the most common cause of chronic gastritis?

{{c1::Helicobacter pylori}} infection

Helicobacter pylori infection causes an increased risk for what two diseases?

{{c1::Peptic ulcer}} disease
{{c1::MALT}} lymphoma

Why is there increased risk of gastric cancer in patients with chronic gastritis?

Chronic gastritis leads to intestinal {{c1::metaplasia}}

In a patient with chronic gastritis, which hormone is increased due to hypochlorhydria?

{{c1::Gastrin}}

How can brain injury cause acute gastritis?

Cushing ulcers are caused by increased {{c1::vagal}} stimulation → Increased {{c1::acetylcholine}} → Increased acid production

How can burns cause acute gastritis?

Curling ulcers caused by burns → {{c1::Hypovolemia::Hypervolemia/Hypovolemia}} and mucosal {{c1::ischemia}}

What are two common risk factors that predispose a patient to the development of acute gastritis?

Excessive {{c1::alcohol}} use
Long-term use of {{c1::NSAIDs}}

How would you differentiate acute gastritis from chronic gastritis on pathologic examination?

Acute gastritis is typically {{c1::erosive}}
Chronic gastritis is defined by mucosal {{c1::inflammation}} with {{c1::atrophy}} and intestinal {{c1::metaplasia}}

What is the pathophysiology of autoimmune gastritis?

Autoantibodies to {{c1::H+/K+-ATPase}} on parietal cells and {{c1::intrinsic factor}}

Autoimmune gastritis increases the risk for what type of anemia?

{{c1::Pernicious}} anemia

Describe the histologic appearance of a Krukenberg tumor.

{{c1::Signet ring}} cells that secrete {{c1::mucin}}

What is the name of the tumor associated with gastric cancer metastases to bilateral ovaries?

{{c1::Krukenberg}} tumor

What are Sister Mary Joseph nodules?

{{c1::Subcutaneous periumbilical}} metastasis from gastric cancer

What are Virchow nodes?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::supraclavicular}} nodes involved in metastasis from gastric cancer

What is linitis plastica?

{{c1::Diffuse}} type of {{c1::gastric}} cancer in which the walls of the stomach have {{c1::thickened::thickened/thinned}} and become {{c1::leathery}}

Name common risk factors for intestinal-type gastric cancer.

{{c1::Helicobacter pylori}} infection
{{c1::Nitrosamines}} in diet
{{c1::Smoking}}
Chronic {{c1::gastritis}}
{{c1::Achlorhydria}}

Where are intestinal types of gastric cancer most commonly located in the stomach?

{{c1::Lesser curvature}}

What two skin manifestations might be seen with gastric cancer?

{{c1::Leser-Trélat}} sign
{{c1::Acanthosis nigricans}}

What is the most common type of gastric cancer?

{{c1::Adenocarcinoma}}

Describe the gross appearance of an intestinal type of gastric cancer.

It appears similar to an {{c1::ulcer}} with {{c1::raised}} margins

What abdominal signs and symptoms are associated with gastric cancer?

{{c1::Abdominal}} pain
Early {{c1::satiety}}
{{c1::Obstruction}}
Weight {{c1::loss::gain/loss}}

What type of cells are shown in the image and what pathology are they associated with?



{{c1::Signet-ring}} cells are associated with {{c1::diffuse}} gastric cancer

What is a Blumer shelf, and what does this finding typically indicate?

A palpable {{c1::mass}} on digital rectal exam
Presence of this sign raises concern for {{c1::metastasis}} to the {{c1::rectouterine pouch}}

Where does gastric cancer tend to metastasize?

{{c1::Lymph nodes}}
{{c1::Liver::Organ}}
fields.Back Extra: Gastric cancer is aggressive and spreads early.

fields.Text:
What is a common genetic cause that underlies the development of the diffuse type of gastric cancer?

{{c1::E-cadherin}} mutations

Which type of peptic ulcer disease puts a patient at greater risk for cancer?

{{c1::Gastric}} ulcer

What is the pathophysiology of duodenal ulcers?

{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in mucosal protection
{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in gastric acid secretion

Which type of gastrointestinal ulcer is associated with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?

{{c1::Duodenal}} ulcer

Which type of gastrointestinal ulcer is associated with pain that decreases after meals, which may result in weight gain?

{{c1::Duodenal}} ulcer

What is the pathophysiology of gastric ulcers?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} mucosal protection against the effects of gastric acid

Which type of gastrointestinal ulcer is associated with NSAID use?

{{c1::Gastric}} ulcer

Is Helicobacter pylori infection more frequently associated with gastric ulcers or duodenal ulcers?

{{c1::Duodenal}} ulcers
fields.Back Extra: Helicobacter pylori is implicated in 90% of duodenal ulcers and 70% of gastric ulcers.

fields.Text:
Which type of gastrointestinal ulcer can cause pain after eating and result in weight loss?

{{c1::Gastric}} ulcers

Which two regions of the gastrointestinal tract are affected by peptic ulcer disease?

{{c1::Stomach}}
{{c1::Duodenum}}

How should you rule out malignancy in a patient with a gastric ulcer?

By obtaining a {{c1::biopsy}} specimen from the {{c1::margins}} of the ulcer for histopathologic examination

What diagnosis and associated complication are shown in this image?



{{c1::Diverticulitis}} with {{c1::perforation}}

While performing a colonoscopy of the sigmoid colon, you observe the findings shown. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Diverticulum}}

What is the management for uncomplicated and complicated diverticulitis?

Uncomplicated diverticulitis → {{c1::Supportive care}}
Complicated diverticulitis → {{c1::Antibiotics}}

What are the 4 most common potential complications of diverticulitis?

{{c1::Perforation}}
{{c1::Abscess}} formation
{{c1::Fistula}}
{{c1::Obstruction}}

Diverticulitis classically causes pain in what region of the abdomen?

{{c1::LLQ}} pain

In patients with diverticulosis, where in the gastrointestinal tract are diverticula most likely found?

{{c1::Sigmoid colon}}

What is the etiology of diverticulosis?

Increased intraluminal {{c1::pressure}} combined with {{c1::focal weakness}} of the colonic wall

What gastrointestinal pathology tends to occur at locations where vasa recta perforate the muscularis externa?

{{c1::False diverticulum}}

What is the difference between a true diverticulum and a false diverticulum?

True diverticulum contains {{c1::3}} layers
False diverticulum contains {{c1::2}} layers

What is a diverticulum?

A {{c1::blind pouch}} protruding from the alimentary tract that communicates with the {{c1::lumen}} of the gut

What 2 complications may be seen with diverticulosis?

Diverticular {{c1::bleeding}}
{{c1::Diverticulitis}}

Which foods consumed in large amounts put patients at risk for the development of diverticulosis?

{{c1::Red meat}}
Foods with high total {{c1::fat}} content
Foods with a low {{c1::fiber}} content

What is microscopic colitis?

Colonic {{c1::inflammation}} → Chronic {{c1::watery}} diarrhea

Which gender is more likely to develop microscopic colitis?

{{c1::Females}}

What is the likely diagnosis if colonic histology shows a thickened subepithelial collagen band or intraepithelial lymphocytes and inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria?

{{c1::Microscopic colitis}}

Are there any characteristic signs of microscopic colitis on endoscopy?

{{c1::No}}
fields.Back Extra: The mucosa of the colon appears normal.

fields.Text:
A 34-year-old man presents with nausea and vomiting. A CT scan of the abdomen is shown. What is the treatment?



{{c1::Appendectomy}}

What is the cause of appendicitis in adults versus children?

Adults → {{c1::Obstruction}} due to a {{c1::fecalith}}
Children → {{c1::Lymphoid hyperplasia}}

What signs would you check for on physical exam to help confirm a diagnosis of suspected acute appendicitis?

{{c1::Psoas}} sign
{{c1::Obturator}} sign
{{c1::Rovsing}} sign

What is the location and significance of the McBurney point?

The McBurney point is located 1/{{c1::3}} of the distance from the {{c1::right::left/right}} {{c1::ASIS}} to the {{c1::umbilicus}}
Pain at this point is concerning for {{c1::appendicitis}}

What is the mechanism that underlies the development of abdominal pain in acute appendicitis in the context of appendiceal obstruction?

Closed-loop {{c1::obstruction}} → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} intraluminal pressure → Stimulation of {{c1::T8}} to {{c1::T10}} visceral afferents→ Diffuse {{c1::periumbilical}} pain → Inflammation of serosa and irritation of parietal peritoneum

What do you expect a colonoscopy to show in irritable bowel syndrome?

No {{c1::structural}} abnormalities

What disease causes recurrent abdominal pain associated with ≥ 2 of the following?

Changes in stool frequency
Changes in stool consistency
Pain related to defecation

{{c1::Irritable bowel}} syndrome

What are the 3 subtypes of irritable bowel syndrome?

{{c1::Constipation}}-predominant
{{c1::Diarrhea}}-predominant
{{c1::Mixed}}

What is the first-line treatment for irritable bowel syndrome?

{{c1::Lifestyle}} modification
Changes in {{c1::diet}}

In which patient population is irritable bowel syndrome most common?

{{c1::Middle}}-aged {{c1::women::men/women}}

What 2 conditions are associated with irritable bowel syndrome?

{{c1::Mood}} disorders
{{c1::Fibromyalgia}}

A patient with peptic ulcer disease presents with pain in the shoulder and the chest X-ray shown. What is the explanation for the presence of shoulder pain?



Free {{c1::air}} under the diaphragm → Shoulder pain via irritation of the {{c1::phrenic}} nerve

In what location do perforations from ulcers typically occur?

{{c1::Duodenum}}

Where are obstructions due to peptic ulcers likely to occur?

{{c1::Pyloric channel}}
{{c1::Duodenum}}

Are duodenal ulcer perforations more likely to occur anteriorly or posteriorly?

{{c1::Anteriorly}}
fields.Back Extra: Free air in the anterior abdominal cavity can cause pneumoperitoneum.

fields.Text:
Which artery is most likely to hemorrhage with a ruptured duodenal ulcer on the posterior wall of the duodenum?

{{c1::Gastroduodenal}} artery

Which artery is most likely to hemorrhage with a ruptured gastric ulcer on the lesser curvature of the stomach?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::gastric}} artery

What is the most common complication associated with peptic ulcers?

{{c1::Hemorrhage}}

How does a Bartholin abscess develop?

Blocked Bartholin gland forms a cyst → {{c1::Infection}}, {{c1::inflammation}}, and {{c1::fluid}} accumulation → Abscess formation

In what population do Bartholin cysts usually occur?

{{c1::Females::Males/Females}} of {{c1::reproductive}} age

What non-neoplastic vulvar pathology presents with porcelain-white plaques with red/violet borders and skin fragility with erosions?

{{c1::Lichen sclerosus}}

Who is most at risk for development of vulvar lichen sclerosus?

{{c1::Prepubertal}} females
{{c1::Perimenopausal}}/{{c1::postmenopausal}} females

What is the pathophysiology underlying lichen sclerosus?

{{c1::Thinning::Thickening/Thinning}} of the epidermis
{{c1::Fibrosis}}/{{c1::sclerosis}} of the dermis

What non-neoplastic vulvar pathology is described as leathery, thick vulvar skin with enhanced skin markings due to scratching?

{{c1::Lichen simplex chronicus}}

What is the pathophysiology underlying lichen simplex chronicus?

{{c1::Hyperplasia::Hyperplasia/Hypoplasia}} of the vulvar squamous epithelium
fields.Back Extra: This is typically secondary to chronic irritation/scratching.

fields.Text:
What are three risk factors for developing HPV-related vulvar carcinoma?

{{c1::High::High/Low}}-risk HPV exposure
Multiple {{c1::partners}}
Early {{c1::coitarche}}

Describe the common cause of vulvar carcinoma not caused by HPV.

Long-standing {{c1::lichen sclerosus}} in an elderly female → Chronic itching and subsequent development of squamous cell carcinoma

Which two HPV types are high risk for causing the pathology shown in the image?



HPV type {{c1::16}}
HPV type {{c1::18}}

How is vulvar carcinoma differentiated from other causes of leukoplakia?

{{c1::Biopsy}} is often required to identify a carcinoma from squamous epithelial lining

What intraepithelial adenocarcinoma in situ presents as shown in the image?



{{c1::Extramammary Paget}} disease

What diagnosis presents with vulvar pain and the exam findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Bartholin cyst}}

What is the prognosis of extramammary Paget disease?

{{c1::Low::High/Low}} risk of underlying carcinoma
{{c1::Good}} prognosis

Does squamous cell carcinoma develop from lichen sclerosus or lichen simplex chronicus?

{{c1::Lichen sclerosus}}

List the types of gynecologic tumors, in order, from highest to lowest incidence in the United States.

{{c1::Endometrial}} > {{c1::Ovarian}} > {{c1::Cervical}}

List the types of gynecologic tumors, in order, from best to worst prognosis.

{{c1::Cervical}} > {{c1::Endometrial}} > {{c1::Ovarian}}

List the types of gynecologic tumors, in order, from youngest to oldest typical age at onset.

{{c1::Cervical}} < {{c1::Endometrial}} < {{c1::Ovarian}}

Why is cervical cancer more common in other countries as compared with the United States?

Due to lack of {{c1::screening}} and {{c1::HPV}} vaccination

What is the mechanism of supine hypotensive syndrome in pregnancy?

Supine position → Compression of the {{c1::abdominal aorta}} and {{c1::inferior vena cava}} by a gravid uterus → Decreased venous return and hypotension
fields.Back Extra: This is also called aortocaval compression syndrome.

fields.Text:
What is the most concerning complication of supine hypotensive syndrome?

{{c1::Pregnancy}} loss
fields.Back Extra: This is due to decreased placental perfusion.

fields.Text:
What position relieves supine hypotensive syndrome?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::lateral decubitus}} position

What is vasa previa?

Condition in which fetal vessels run over or are close to the {{c1::cervical os}}

What condition presents as abdominal pain without vaginal bleeding in a pregnant female? Fetal heart tracings will show bradycardia.

{{c1::Abruptio placentae}}
fields.Back Extra: This can present with a concealed hemorrhage.

fields.Text:
What is the condition shown?



{{c1::Abruptio placentae}}

In a patient with placenta percreta, the placenta can become attached to which two other organs? What symptom may develop as a result?

The placenta can become attached to the {{c1::rectum}} and {{c1::bladder}} → {{c1::Hematuria}} may develop

What is the difference between placenta accreta, increta, and percreta?

Placenta accreta → Placenta {{c1::attaches}} to myometrium without penetration
Placenta increta → Placenta {{c1::penetrates}} into myometrium
Placenta percreta → Placenta {{c1::invades}} myometrium and enters uterine serosa

Describe the velamentous umbilical cord insertion that is frequently associated with vasa previa.

The umbilical cord inserts into the {{c1::chorioamniotic membrane}} instead of the placenta → Fetal vessels travel to the placenta unprotected by {{c1::Wharton jelly}}

How does abruptio placentae present?

{{c1::Abrupt}}, {{c1::painful::painful/painless}} bleeding in the {{c1::3rd}} trimester
fields.Back Extra: This may lead to disseminated intravascular coagulation, maternal shock, and/or fetal distress.

fields.Text:
What condition should be considered in a pregnant patient with membrane rupture, painless vaginal bleeding, and a fetal heart rate indicating bradycardia?

{{c1::Vasa previa}}

Name some risk factors that may predispose to placental abruption.

Maternal {{c1::hypertension::hypertension/hypotension}}
{{c1::Preeclampsia}}
{{c1::Smoking}}
{{c1::Cocaine}} use
Abdominal {{c1::trauma}}

A pregnant patient presents with sudden lower abdominal pain. An hCG level is checked and is lower than expected. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Ectopic pregnancy}}

Name four risk factors for placenta accreta, increta, and percreta.

Advanced {{c1::age}}
{{c1::Multiparity}}
{{c1::Placenta previa}}
Prior {{c1::C-section}} or other uterine surgery involving the {{c1::myometrium}}

Name two risk factors for placenta previa.

{{c1::Multiparity}}
Prior {{c1::C-section}}

What are three possible causes of postpartum hemorrhage and failure to complete the 3rd stage of delivery?

{{c1::Placenta accreta}}
{{c1::Placenta increta}}
{{c1::Placenta percreta}}

Name two risk factors associated with uterine rupture.

Prior {{c1::C-section}}
Abdominal {{c1::trauma}}

How does uterine rupture present?

{{c1::Painful::Painful/Painless}} vaginal bleeding
Fetal {{c1::heart rate}} abnormalities
{{c1::Palpable}} fetal parts
Loss of {{c1::fetal station}}

If treatment of postpartum hemorrhage with uterine massage and oxytocin is not successful, what two arteries may be ligated to stop the bleeding?

{{c1::Uterine}} artery
{{c1::Internal iliac}} artery
fields.Back Extra: Fertility will be preserved because the ovarian arteries provide collateral circulation.

fields.Text:
What is the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide?

{{c1::Postpartum hemorrhage}}

Name four causes of postpartum hemorrhage.

Uterine {{c1::tone}}
Uterine {{c1::trauma}}
Uterine {{c1::tissue}}
{{c1::Thrombin}}

How is postpartum hemorrhage treated?

Uterine {{c1::massage}}
{{c1::Oxytocin}}

How is fertility preserved if the internal iliac arteries are ligated to stop postpartum hemorrhage?

{{c1::Ovarian}} arteries provide {{c1::collateral circulation}}

What type of imaging is used to confirm an ectopic pregnancy?

{{c1::Ultrasonography}}
fields.Back Extra: This can reveal an extraovarian mass.

fields.Text:
An image obtained during laparotomy is shown. What is indicated by the arrow?



{{c1::Ectopic pregnancy}}
fields.Back Extra: Note the developing pregnancy over the fallopian tube.

fields.Text:
What is the most common site of an ectopic pregnancy?

{{c1::Ampulla}} of the fallopian tube

Name four risk factors for an ectopic pregnancy.

Antagonist to the {{c1::estrogen}} receptor in the {{c1::breast}}
Partial agonist in the {{c1::bone}} and {{c1::endometrium}}

{{c1::Direct::Direct/Indirect}} inhibition of {{c1::thrombin}}

What is the mechanism of action of rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban?

{{c1::Direct::Direct/Indirect}} inhibition of factor {{c1::Xa}}

What is the major adverse effect associated with direct factor Xa inhibitors and direct thrombin inhibitors?

{{c1::Bleeding}}

What are the common indications for the direct factor Xa inhibitors?

Treatment and prophylaxis for {{c1::DVT}} and {{c1::PE}}
Prophylaxis for {{c1::stroke}} in patients with atrial fibrillation

Which of the direct thrombin inhibitors can be given orally?

{{c1::Dabigatran}}

What is the mechanism that causes a patient to experience the skin findings shown in the image when treated with warfarin?



Skin/tissue {{c1::necrosis}} due to {{c1::microthrombi}} in small vessels
fields.Back Extra: This is the result of a transient hypercoagulable state when warfarin is initiated.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of warfarin?

Inhibition of vitamin {{c1::K}} {{c1::epoxide reductase}} → Inhibition of {{c1::γ-carboxylation}} of factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S

What treatments can reverse warfarin?

{{c1::FFP}} or {{c1::PCC}} for rapid reversal
Vitamin {{c1::K}} for slow reversal

To achieve anticoagulation, why is heparin used when warfarin is initiated?

Heparin "{{c1::bridge}}" is needed for the initial transient {{c1::hypercoagulable}} state caused by warfarin

A patient receiving long-term warfarin needs which weekly labs to determine if they are within therapeutic range?

{{c1::PT}} and {{c1::INR}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to the effect of warfarin on the extrinsic pathway of coagulation.

fields.Text:
Polymorphism in what gene affects the metabolism of warfarin?

{{c1::VKORC1}} gene

List three adverse effects of warfarin.

{{c1::Teratogenic}} effects
{{c1::Bleeding}}
Skin/tissue {{c1::necrosis}}

What is the mechanism that causes a patient to experience an initial hypercoagulable state when treated with warfarin?

Protein C has a {{c1::shorter::longer/shorter}} half-life than factors II and X
fields.Back Extra: Thus, protein C is depleted before factors II and X are depleted.

fields.Text:
Which hepatic enzyme is responsible for metabolism of warfarin and is implicated in warfarin drug-drug interactions?

{{c1::Cytochrome P-450}}

Can warfarin be given to a pregnant woman?

{{c1::No}}
fields.Back Extra: It can cross the placenta and is teratogenic.

fields.Text:
What is muscle fiber type grouping?

Growth of a {{c1::single}} muscle fiber type in a {{c1::larger::larger/smaller}} area

Where does muscle fiber type grouping commonly occur?

When {{c1::denervated}} muscle fibers undergo {{c1::reinnervation}} in areas of {{c1::peripheral}} nerve damage

Resistance training and sprinting condition which type of muscle fiber?

Type {{c1::II}} muscle fibers

Name the predominant metabolic process used by type II muscle fibers to create energy.

{{c1::Anaerobic glycolysis}}

Endurance training conditions which type of muscle fiber?

Type {{c1::I}} muscle fibers

Which type of muscle fibers have a higher concentration of myoglobin and mitochondria?

Type {{c1::I}} muscle fibers

Name the predominant metabolic process used by type I muscle fibers to create energy.

{{c1::Oxidative phosphorylation}}

How do you divide type I and II muscle fibers on the basis of contraction velocity and fiber color?

Type I muscle fibers → {{c1::Red::Color}} {{c1::slow::fast/slow}}-twicth muscle fibers
Type II muscle fibers → {{c1::White::Color}} {{c1::fast::fast/slow}}-twitch muscle fibers

How does estrogen deficiency lead to osteoporosis?

Excess cycles of bone {{c1::remodeling}} and {{c1::resorption}} occur → Increased risk of osteoporosis

How does estrogen affect bone during puberty?

It causes the {{c1::epiphyseal}} plates to close

What effect does estrogen exert on osteoblasts and osteoclasts?

{{c1::Inhibits::Induces/Inhibits}} apoptosis in osteoblasts
{{c1::Induces::Induces/Inhibits}} apoptosis in osteoclasts

Which hormone is likely chronically elevated in a patient with osteitis fibrosa cystica?

{{c1::PTH}}
fields.Back Extra: This leads to excess bone catabolism.

fields.Text:
What effect does PTH exert on osteoblasts and osteoclasts at low, intermittent levels?

{{c1::Anabolic::Anabolic/Catabolic}} effect on osteoblasts {{c1::directly::directly/indirectly}}
{{c1::Anabolic::Anabolic/Catabolic}} effect on osteoclasts {{c1::indirectly::directly/indirectly}}

Osteoclasts originate from which precursor cells?

Osteoclasts are derived from the fusion of {{c1::monocyte}} and {{c1::macrophage}} lineage precursors

Osteoclasts produce what 2 secretions to dissolve/resorb bone?

{{c1::H+}}
{{c1::Collagenases}}

What 3 cell markers can measure the activity of osteoblasts?

{{c1::Osteocalcin}}
Bone {{c1::ALP}}
Propeptides of type {{c1::1}} procollagen

At what pH do bone formation and resorption occur?

Osteoblasts form bone in {{c1::alkaline::acidic/alkaline}} conditions
Osteoclasts create an {{c1::acidic::acidic/alkaline}} environment for bone resorption

Which type of bone cells work by secreting collagen and catalyzing mineralization using ALP?

{{c1::Osteoblasts}}

Osteoblasts differentiate from which stem cell line?

{{c1::Mesenchymal}} stem cells in the {{c1::periosteum}}

Which receptors are involved in the activation of osteoclasts and what activates them?

{{c1::RANK}} receptors on osteoclasts
{{c1::RANKL}}, which is expressed on osteoblasts, stimulates {{c1::RANK}} receptors to activate osteoclasts

How might osteoprotegerin decrease osteoclast activity?

Prevents {{c1::RANK}}-{{c1::RANKL}} interaction by binding to {{c1::RANKL}} → Decreased osteoclast activation

In membranous ossification, what is the role of cartilage in the formation of woven bone?

Woven bone is formed directly {{c1::without::with/without}} cartilage and is later remodeled to {{c1::lamellar}} bone

In achondroplasia, which type of ossification is defective?

{{c1::Endochondral}} ossification

What bone type will be seen in a pathologic lesion in a patient with Paget disease?

{{c1::Woven}} bone

What type of bone is formed by healed fractures?

{{c1::Woven}} bone

What role do osteoclasts and osteoblasts play in endochondral ossification?

They replace the cartilaginous model with {{c1::woven}} bone and later remodel it into {{c1::lamellar}} bone

Which bones are formed by membranous ossification?

{{c1::Calvarium}}
{{c1::Face}}
{{c1::Clavicle}}

Which bones are formed by endochondral ossification?

{{c1::Axial}} skeleton
{{c1::Appendicular}} skeleton
{{c1::Base}} of the {{c1::skull}}

What are sensory receptors that transmit information about muscle dynamics called?

Muscle {{c1::proprioceptors}}

What are the 2 main types of muscle proprioceptors?

{{c1::Golgi tendon organs}}
Muscle {{c1::stretch}} receptors

Where are muscle stretch receptors located?

{{c1::Body}} of the muscles

What is the function of the Golgi tendon organ, a muscle proprioceptor?

Senses {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} tension and {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} the tension on the muscle and tendon

Where is the Golgi tendon organ located?

{{c1::Tendon}} of the muscle

What is the function of muscle stretch receptors?

They sense {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} muscle stretch and act to protect the muscle from {{c1::overstretching}}
fields.Back Extra: It is also responsible for deep tendon reflexes.

fields.Text:
Describe the muscle stretch receptor activation pathway.

Increased length and speed of stretch via {{c1::DRG}} → Activation of {{c1::inhibitory}} interneuron and {{c1::α motor}} neuron → {{c1::Inhibition::Activation/Inhibition}} of antagonist muscle and {{c1::activation::activation/inhibition}} of agonist muscle

Describe the Golgi tendon organ activation pathway.

Increased muscle tension detected via {{c1::DRG}} → {{c1::Inhibitory}} interneuron activated → {{c1::Agonist::Agonist/Antagonist}} muscle inhibited → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} tension

What type of sensory axons innervate Golgi tendon organs?

Type {{c1::Ib}} sensory axons

What type of sensory axons innervate muscle stretch receptors?

Type {{c1::Ia}} sensory axons
Type {{c1::II}} sensory axons

How do molecules such as acetylcholine and bradykinin induce smooth muscle cell relaxation?

They bind to {{c1::endothelial}} cell receptors → Increased {{c1::Ca2+}} → Activation of {{c1::NO synthase}} → {{c1::NO}} diffuses in smooth muscle → Relaxation

Nitric oxide in smooth muscle cells is derived from which amino acid generated in the endothelial cells?

{{c1::L-arginine}}

In smooth muscle relaxation, how does NO activate MLCP?

NO increases the conversion of {{c1::GTP}} into {{c1::cGMP}} → Activation of MLCP

What is the difference in function between MLCK and MLCP?

MLCK → Muscle {{c1::contraction::contraction/relaxation}}
MLCP → Muscle {{c1::relaxation::contraction/relaxation}}

How does smooth muscle respond to intracellular Ca2+ versus NO?

Ca2+ → {{c1::Contraction::Contraction/Relaxation}}
NO → {{c1::Relaxation::Contraction/Relaxation}}

What are the steps in smooth muscle contraction that follow calmodulin binding to Ca2+?

Activation of {{c1::MLCK}} → {{c1::Phosphorylation}} of myosin → Contraction

In smooth muscle, Ca2+ binds to which molecule after entering the cell to initiate contraction?

{{c1::Calmodulin}}

An action potential reaching a smooth muscle cell must activate what type of channel to promote Ca2+ influx into the cell?

{{c1::L}}-type {{c1::voltage}}-gated {{c1::Ca2+}} channel

Name the 2 mechanisms by which myofibrils and myonuclei undergo atrophy.

Myofibrils are removed via the {{c1::ubiquitin-proteasome}} system
Myonuclei undergo selective {{c1::apoptosis}}

Name the 2 mechanisms by which myofibrils and myonuclei undergo hypertrophy.

Myofibrils increase by the addition of {{c1::sarcomeres}} in parallel
Myonuclei increase via fusion of {{c1::satellite}} cells

What role do muscle satellite cells have in skeletal muscle adaptation/repair?

Fusion of satellite cells leads to {{c1::hypertrophy}} of myonuclei and also helps repair damaged {{c1::myofibrils}}

What is the appropriate treatment for a patient with antiphospholipid syndrome?

Systemic {{c1::anticoagulation}}

What disease may cause prolonged PTT that is not corrected by addition of plasma?

{{c1::Antiphospholipid}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This is due to a lupus anticoagulant.

fields.Text:
What can cause VDRL/RPR false-positive test results in a patient with antiphospholipid syndrome?

{{c1::Anticardiolipin}} antibodies

Name 3 antibodies that may be used in the diagnosis of antiphospholipid syndrome if a patient has an abnormal clotting history.

{{c1::Anticardiolipin}} antibodies
{{c1::Lupus anticoagulant}} antibodies
{{c1::Anti-β2 glycoprotein I}} antibodies

Antiphospholipid syndrome may present as a primary or secondary autoimmune diagnosis. Which disease is associated with the secondary form?

{{c1::SLE}}

How would you describe the rash on a patient with SLE shown in the image?



{{c1::Discoid}}

What condition is classically associated with the rash shown in the image?



{{c1::SLE}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows a malar rash.

fields.Text:
Deficiency of which proteins leads to a decrease in clearance of immune complexes in a patient with SLE?

Deficiency of early {{c1::complement}} proteins

Name the 3 most common causes of death associated with SLE.

{{c1::Kidney::Organ}} disease (most common)
Accelerated {{c1::coronary artery}} disease
{{c1::Infections}}

Which antibody, if present in a pregnant woman with SLE, increases the risk of her newborn developing neonatal lupus?

{{c1::Anti-SSA}} antibodies

What cardiac pathology is associated with SLE?

{{c1::Libman-Sacks endocarditis}}

What populations are most commonly affected by SLE?

{{c1::Female::Male/Female}} patients of {{c1::reproductive}} age
{{c1::Black}}, {{c1::Caribbean}}, {{c1::Asian}}, and {{c1::Hispanic}} individuals living in the United States

Which 4 serologic findings can be positive in patients with SLE?

{{c1::Antinuclear}} antibodies
{{c1::Anti-dsDNA}} antibodies
{{c1::Anti-Smith}} antibodies
{{c1::Antiphospholipid}} antibodies

Describe the pathophysiologic effects SLE can have on the renal system.

Deposition of {{c1::DNA}}-{{c1::anti-DNA}} immune complexes in glomerulus → {{c1::Proteinuria}} and {{c1::hematuria}}

What neurologic disorders can manifest in SLE?

{{c1::Psychosis}}
{{c1::Seizures}}

What autoimmune disease classically presents in a young woman with relapsing/remitting rash, joint pain, and unexplained fever?

{{c1::SLE}}

What 2 types of hypersensitivity reactions are associated with SLE?

Type {{c1::III}} hypersensitivity reaction (most common)
Type {{c1::II}} hypersensitivity reaction

Name the 4 features associated with neonatal lupus.

Congenital {{c1::heart block}}
Periorbital/diffuse {{c1::rash}}
{{c1::Transaminitis}}
{{c1::Cytopenias}}

Which disease presents with features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis with a positive titer of anti-U1 RNP antibodies?

{{c1::Mixed connective tissue}} disease

What glomerular disease is most common and severe in patients with SLE?

{{c1::Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis}}

What hematologic abnormality is characteristic of SLE?

{{c1::Cytopenias}}

Where are ulcers commonly seen in patients with SLE?

{{c1::Mouth}}
{{c1::Nose}}
{{c1::Pharynx}}

What disease is associated with the findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Ankylosing spondylitis}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows a bamboo spine due to vertebral fusion.

fields.Text:
What disease presents with asymmetric arthritis, dactylitis, and the skin findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Psoriatic arthritis}}

What finding can be seen in this X-ray of a patient diagnosed with psoriatic arthritis?



"{{c1::Pencil-in-cup}}" deformity of DIP joint

Patients with inflammatory bowel disease are most likely to have which form of arthritis?

{{c1::Seronegative spondyloarthritis}}

What is the classic triad of reactive arthritis?

{{c1::Conjunctivitis}}
{{c1::Urethritis}}
{{c1::Arthritis}}

Is psoriatic arthritis symmetric or asymmetric?

{{c1::Asymmetric}}

In what demographic group is ankylosing spondylitis most commonly diagnosed?

{{c1::Males::Males/Females}} between {{c1::20}} to {{c1::40}} years of age

What 6 pathogens are associated with reactive arthritis?

{{c1::Shigella}}
{{c1::Campylobacter}}
{{c1::Escherichia coli}}
{{c1::Salmonella}}
{{c1::Chlamydia}}
{{c1::Yersinia}}

What are the major subtypes of seronegative spondyloarthritis?

{{c1::Psoriatic arthritis}}
{{c1::Ankylosing spondylitis}}
{{c1::Inflammatory bowel}} disease
{{c1::Reactive arthritis}}

In seronegative spondyloarthropathies, there is a strong association with which HLA?

HLA-{{c1::B27}}

How will the pattern of joint stiffness caused by an inflammatory arthritis change over the day?

It will be {{c1::severe::better/severe}} in the morning and {{c1::improve::improve/worsen}} with physical activity

What does the term "seronegative spondyloarthritis" mean?

{{c1::Autoimmune}} arthropathy is present, but serology for {{c1::rheumatoid factor}} is negative

Chondrocalcinosis is seen on a knee X-ray. What does this term mean, and what disease process does it suggest?

Cartilage calcification, likely due to {{c1::calcium pyrophosphate deposition}} disease

Examination of joint aspirate reveals the findings shown in the image. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Calcium pyrophosphate deposition}} disease

Hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, and a history of joint trauma are all associated with increased risk of what joint crystal deposition disease?

{{c1::Calcium pyrophosphate deposition}} disease

What treatment would you prescribe as a prophylactic therapy for calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease?

{{c1::Colchicine}}

What is the treatment for an acute episode of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease?

{{c1::Colchicine}}
{{c1::Glucocorticoids}}
{{c1::NSAIDs}}

Describe the acute presentation of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease.

Acute {{c1::inflammation}}, {{c1::pain}}, and {{c1::swelling}} of a large joint

People of what age are predisposed to calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease?

Older than {{c1::50}} years of age
fields.Back Extra: This disease affects both sexes equally.

fields.Text:
What disease is characterized by deposition of pyrophosphate crystals in the joint space?

{{c1::Calcium pyrophosphate deposition}} disease

What is the term for chronic joint degeneration caused by calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease?

{{c1::Pseudo-osteoarthritis}}

A salivary gland biopsy specimen obtained from a patient reporting dry mouth is shown in the image. What do the findings in the image demonstrate?



{{c1::Lymphocytic}} infiltrates

What autoimmune disease is associated with the findings on oral exam shown in the image?



{{c1::Sjögren}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: The image shows mucosal atrophy and fissuring of the tongue.

fields.Text:
Name a common oral complication of the dry mouth symptoms associated with Sjögren syndrome.

{{c1::Dental caries}}

Sjögren syndrome carries an increased risk of developing what malignancy?

{{c1::MALT}} lymphoma
fields.Back Extra: This may present as a parotid enlargement.

fields.Text:
Sjögren syndrome is associated with destruction of what types of glands?

{{c1::Exocrine}} glands

Which other autoimmune diseases are commonly associated with Sjögren syndrome?

{{c1::SLE}}
{{c1::Systemic sclerosis}}
{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}

Which 4 serologic findings are characteristic of Sjögren syndrome?

{{c1::Antinuclear}} antibodies
{{c1::Rheumatoid factor}} antibodies
{{c1::Anti-SSA}} antibodies
{{c1::Anti-SSB}} antibodies

What autoimmune disease commonly presents in middle-aged women with xerostomia, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, and inflammatory joint pain?

{{c1::Sjögren}} syndrome

What test can confirm a diagnosis of Sjögren syndrome?

Biopsy of the {{c1::labial salivary}} gland
fields.Back Extra: Findings of focal lymphocytic sialadenitis confirm Sjögren syndrome.

fields.Text:
At what age does systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis present?

In children younger than {{c1::16}} years of age

What are the abnormal CBC findings associated with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis?

{{c1::Anemia}}
{{c1::Leukocytosis}}
{{c1::Thrombocytosis}}

What pathology presents in children with daily spiking fevers, arthritis, and a salmon-pink macular rash?

{{c1::Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis}}

What 4 treatment options are available for systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis?

{{c1::NSAIDs}}
{{c1::Methotrexate}}
{{c1::TNF}} inhibitors
{{c1::Steroids}}

Which inflammatory markers might be increased in systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis?

{{c1::ESR}}
{{c1::CRP}}

What eye pathology may be associated with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis?

{{c1::Anterior uveitis}}

What signs and symptoms are classically associated with disseminated gonococcal arthritis?

{{c1::Purulent}} arthritis
Triad of {{c1::tenosynovitis}}, {{c1::dermatitis}}, and {{c1::polyarthralgia}}

Name the 3 organisms that most commonly cause septic arthritis.

{{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}
{{c1::Streptococcus}}
{{c1::Neisseria gonorrhoeae}}

What synovial fluid findings are characteristic of septic arthritis?

Synovial fluid in septic arthritis is {{c1::purulent}} with a WBC count > {{c1::50,000}} mm3

Describe the 3 major physical exam findings associated with septic arthritis.

{{c1::Redness}}, {{c1::swelling}}, and {{c1::pain}} around the affected joint

Why do patients with granulomatous diseases develop hypercalcemia?

Due to {{c1::hypervitaminosis D}} induced by the disease

What are some causes of primary hyperparathyroidism?

Parathyroid {{c1::hyperplasia}}
Parathyroid {{c1::adenoma}}/{{c1::carcinoma}}
{{c1::Idiopathic}}

What are 2 distinguishing histologic characteristics of the bones in patients with long-term osteitis fibrosa cystica?

"{{c1::Brown tumors}}" caused by fibrous replacement of bone
Subperiosteal {{c1::thinning::thickening/thinning}}

What bone density disease classically has no laboratory abnormalities?

{{c1::Osteoporosis}}

What disease is correlated with secondary hyperparathyroidism?

Chronic {{c1::kidney::organ}} disease
Vitamin {{c1::D}} overproduction

What bone diseases are characterized by increased ALP?

{{c1::Paget disease of bone}}
{{c1::Osteitis fibrosa cystica}}
{{c1::Osteomalacia}} or {{c1::rickets}}

What bone disease is characterized by decreased PTH?

{{c1::Hypervitaminosis D}}

What bone diseases are characterized by increased serum Ca2+?

{{c1::Hypervitaminosis D}}
{{c1::Primary hyperparathyroidism}}

What bone diseases are characterized by increased serum PO43-?

{{c1::Secondary hyperparathyroidism}}
{{c1::Hypervitaminosis D}}
