What hematologic disease is associated with hip pain and the X-ray findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Sickle cell}} disease
fields.Back Extra: It is associated with avascular necrosis of bone.

fields.Text:
What is the most common site for avascular necrosis of bone?

{{c1::Femoral head}}
fields.Back Extra: This results from insufficiency of the medial circumflex femoral artery.

fields.Text:
What are some common causes of avascular necrosis?

{{c1::Glucocorticoids}}
{{c1::Alcohol}} overuse
{{c1::Sickle cell}} disease
{{c1::Trauma}}
{{c1::SLE}}
{{c1::Caisson}} disease
{{c1::Legg-Calvé-Perthes}} disease
{{c1::Gaucher}} disease
{{c1::Slipped capital femoral epiphysis}}

What is the most common cause of short-limbed dwarfism?

{{c1::Achondroplasia}}

In achondroplasia, why are the head and torso unaffected?

The skull is formed by {{c1::membranous}} ossification, which is unaffected in achondroplasia

In achondroplasia, what pathway/gene is pathologically activated? What process is inhibited?

{{c1::FGFR3}} is constitutively activated → Inhibition of {{c1::chondrocyte}} proliferation

In achondroplasia, what type of bone ossification is impaired?

Impaired {{c1::endochondral}} ossification → Failed {{c1::longitudinal}} bone growth → Short limbs

Most cases of achondroplasia occur due to sporadic mutation. What risk factor increases the chance of this disease?

Mutation is associated with increased {{c1::paternal::paternal/maternal}} age

Name the inheritance pattern of achondroplasia.

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}} with full penetrance

What conditions, other than trauma, can increase the risk for fractures like that shown in the image?



{{c1::Anorexia}}
{{c1::Multiple myeloma}}
{{c1::Hyperparathyroidism}}
{{c1::Hyperthyroidism}}
{{c1::Malabsorption}} syndromes

Name the first-line treatment for osteoporosis.

{{c1::Bisphosphonates}}

What is the mechanism of action of the drug denosumab?

Denosumab is a {{c1::monoclonal}} antibody that antagonizes {{c1::RANKL}}

Name 5 drug classes commonly associated with development of osteoporosis.

{{c1::Steroids}}
{{c1::Alcohol}}
{{c1::Anticonvulsants}}
{{c1::Thyroid}} replacement therapy
{{c1::Anticoagulants}}

Describe the lab values associated with osteoporosis.

{{c1::Normal}} Ca2+ levels
{{c1::Normal}} PO43- levels

What are the conditions that need to be met for a diagnosis of osteoporosis?

T-score of ≤ {{c1::-2.5}} on DEXA scan
{{c1::Fragility fracture}} in the hip or vetebra

What 4 fractures, following minimal trauma, are classically seen in osteoporosis?

{{c1::Femoral neck}}
{{c1::Vertebrae}}
Distal {{c1::radius}}
{{c1::Hip}}

Name the nonpharmacologic prophylactic treatments for osteoporosis.

Regular {{c1::weight-bearing}} exercise
Adequate {{c1::Ca2+}} and vitamin {{c1::D}} intake throughout adulthood

What types of bone does osteoporosis affect?

{{c1::Trabecular}} bone
{{c1::Cortical}} bone

At what age is a one-time screening for osteoporosis recommended for women?

{{c1::65}} years of age or older

What hormone impairment is associated with the development of osteoporosis?

Decreased {{c1::estrogen}} levels
fields.Back Extra: This is commonly observed in postmenopausal women.

fields.Text:
Describe the pathophysiologic process for the development of osteoporosis.

Increased bone {{c1::resorption}}
fields.Back Extra: There is an increase in the number and activity of osteoclasts.

fields.Text:
This X-ray shows a "bone-in-bone" or "stone bone" appearance. This is indicative of what bone pathology?



{{c1::Osteopetrosis}}

What is the curative treatment for osteopetrosis?

{{c1::Bone marrow transplant}}
fields.Back Extra: This provides normal monocytic precursors that differentiate into osteoclasts.

fields.Text:
What neurologic lesions may result from osteopetrosis?

Cranial nerve {{c1::impingement}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::palsies}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to a narrowed foramina in the skull, which disturbs the nerve.

fields.Text:
What are the hematologic consequences of osteopetrosis?

{{c1::Pancytopenia}}
Increased extramedullary {{c1::hematopoiesis}}

Describe the pathophysiology behind osteopetrosis.

{{c1::Carbonic anhydrase II}} mutation → Decreased {{c1::osteoclast}} generation of acidic environment → Impaired bone {{c1::resorption}} → Dense, fragile bones

What enzyme mutation most commonly causes osteopetrosis?

{{c1::Carbonic anhydrase II}} mutation

Identify the structures indicated by the arrows.



"{{c1::Rachitic rosary}}"
fields.Back Extra: These are bead-like bumps on the costochondral junctions.

fields.Text:
What is another name for genu varum, and with what disease is it associated?

{{c1::Bow legs}}, which are associated with {{c1::rickets}}

What long bone X-ray findings are associated with vitamin D deficiency in adults and children?

Adults → {{c1::Osteopenia}} and {{c1::pseudofractures}}
Children → Epiphyseal {{c1::widening::widening/narrowing}} and metaphyseal {{c1::cupping}}/{{c1::fraying}}

What is the pathophysiology of osteomalacia?

Low vitamin {{c1::D}} → Low serum {{c1::Ca2+}} levels → Increased secretion of {{c1::PTH}} and secondary lowering of {{c1::PO43-}} levels

How are ALP levels affected in a patient with rickets or osteomalacia?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to osteoblast hyperactivity.

fields.Text:
Where does defective mineralization occur in osteomalacia and rickets?

Osteomalacia → In {{c1::osteoid}}
Rickets → In cartilaginous {{c1::growth plates}}

What is craniotabes, and what disease is it associated with?

{{c1::Soft}} skull, which is associated with {{c1::rickets}}

What is the most common cause of osteomalacia/rickets?

Vitamin {{c1::D}} deficiency

What is the difference between osteomalacia and rickets?

Osteomalacia occurs in {{c1::adults::children/adults}}
Rickets is the term for the {{c1::childhood::childhood/adulthood}} form

What bone pathology is characterized by increased hat size and hearing loss?

{{c1::Osteitis deformans}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also called Paget disease of bone.

fields.Text:
What bone disorder is associated with chalk-stick fractures in long bones?

{{c1::Osteitis deformans}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as Paget disease of bone.

fields.Text:
Osteitis deformans increases the risk for what bone cancer?

{{c1::Osteosarcoma}}

What is the first-line treatment for osteitis deformans?

{{c1::Bisphosphonates}}

What are the 4 main stages of osteitis deformans?

{{c1::Lytic}}
{{c1::Mixed}}
{{c1::Sclerotic}}
{{c1::Quiescent}}

How do levels of Ca2+, PO43-, PTH, and ALP present in patients with osteitis deformans?

{{c1::Normal}} Ca2+ levels
{{c1::Normal}} PO43- levels
{{c1::Normal}} PTH levels
{{c1::Increased}} ALP levels

What causes high-output heart failure in patients with Paget disease of bone?

Pathologic bone {{c1::remodeling}} → {{c1::Atrioventricular shunt}} formation → Increased blood flow and cardiac output

On histologic exam, a mosaic pattern of woven and lamellar bone is observed. What bone disease does this finding indicate?

{{c1::Osteitis deformans}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as Paget disease of bone.

fields.Text:
What is the underlying pathophysiology of Paget disease of bone?

Increased {{c1::osteoblastic}} and {{c1::osteoclastic}} activity → {{c1::Poor}}-quality bone formation

What cells predominate in the lytic and sclerotic phases of Paget disease of bone?

{{c1::Osteoclasts}} in the lytic phase
{{c1::Osteoblasts}} in the sclerotic phase

What is the underlying cause of the head CT findings shown in the image?



Skull thickening due to {{c1::osteitis deformans}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as Paget disease of bone.

fields.Text:
What is the incomplete fracture shown in the image called?



{{c1::Greenstick}} fracture
fields.Back Extra: This extends only partway through the bone.

fields.Text:
A greenstick fracture typically results from which situations?

{{c1::Bending}} stress in an immature pediatric bone

What condition is caused by an axial force on bone, leading to bone cortex buckling on the side of the compression as shown in the image?



{{c1::Torus}} fracture

Which side of the bone is affected in a greenstick fracture as compared to a torus fracture?

Greenstick fracture → {{c1::Tension}} side of the bone is fractured
Torus fracture → {{c1::Compression}} side of the bone buckles

How is developmental dysplasia of the hip diagnosed on physical exam, and what imaging modality is used to confirm the diagnosis?

{{c1::Barlow}} and {{c1::Ortolani}} maneuvers
Confirmed via {{c1::ultrasound}}
fields.Back Extra: These maneuvers of the newborn hip reveal a "clunk".

fields.Text:
What pediatric condition presents more commonly in males with insidious hip pain, a limp, and potentially normal X-ray findings?

{{c1::Legg-Calvé-Perthes}} disease

What pediatric condition commonly presents in obese adolescents with hip/knee pain, a change in gait, and an X-ray showing epiphysis displacement from the femoral neck?

{{c1::Slipped capital femoral epiphysis}}

What condition is commonly known as "nursemaid's elbow"?

{{c1::Radial head subluxation}}
fields.Back Extra: It is common in children less than 5 years of age and may be caused by a sudden pull on the arm.

fields.Text:
Describe the pathophysiology of slipped capital femoral epiphysis.

Increased {{c1::axial}} force on the femoral head → {{c1::Displacement}} of the epiphysis relative to the femoral neck

Which pediatric condition is caused by idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head?

{{c1::Legg-Calvé-Perthes}} disease

What pediatric condition presents in female athletes with anterior knee pain worsened by bearing weight with knee flexion or sitting for extended periods of time?

{{c1::Patellofemoral}} syndrome

What condition presents as worsening anterior knee pain in young athletes due to repeated strain and avulsion of the secondary ossification center of the proximal tibial tubercle?

{{c1::Osgood-Schlatter}} disease

Describe the pathophysiology of radial head subluxation and the typical arm positioning after the injury occurs.

Sudden {{c1::pull}} of arm → Immature {{c1::annular}} ligaments slip over the head of the radius
The arm is typically held in a {{c1::flexed::flexed/extended}} and {{c1::pronated::supinated/pronated}} position

What is a major risk factor for developmental dysplasia of the hip?

{{c1::Breech}} presentation at birth

What is the pathophysiology underlying medial tibial stress syndrome?

Diffuse shin tenderness in runners due to bone {{c1::resorption}} exceeding bone {{c1::formation}} in the tibial cortex

Name the "5 Ps" associated with compartment syndrome.

{{c1::Pain}}
{{c1::Pallor}}
{{c1::Paresthesia}}
{{c1::Pulselessness}}
{{c1::Paralysis}}

Reperfusion injury, animal venom, and long bone fractures are all associated with what orthopedic emergency?

{{c1::Compartment}} syndrome

Describe the pathophysiology of limb compartment syndrome.

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} fascial compartment pressure → Venous outflow obstruction → Arteriolar collapse → {{c1::Anoxia}}, {{c1::necrosis}}, and {{c1::rhabdomyolysis}} → Acute tubular necrosis

What common musculoskeletal condition presents with heel pain and tenderness that is worse in the morning or after inactivity?

{{c1::Plantar fasciitis}}

Which physical exam maneuver can produce pain at the radial styloid when the thumb tendons are stretched, and what diagnosis does this suggest?

{{c1::Finkelstein}} test
The likely diagnosis is {{c1::De Quervain tenosynovitis}}

What condition commonly presents as a fluid-filled swelling over a tendon sheath on the dorsal wrist and often spontaneously resolves?

{{c1::Ganglion cyst}}

How do ganglion cysts form?

{{c1::Herniation}} of dense connective tissue
fields.Back Extra: This is commonly over the dorsal wrist tendon sheath.

fields.Text:
Name 2 signs of irreversible nerve and muscle damage in a patient with limb compartment syndrome.

{{c1::Motor}} deficits on physical exam
Increased serum {{c1::creatine kinase}} concentration

What is the pathophysiology underlying iliotibial band syndrome?

{{c1::Overuse}} injury due to friction of the iliotibial band moving across the {{c1::lateral::medial/lateral}} {{c1::femoral epicondyle}}

What musculoskeletal condition is commonly found in new parents and also associated with golf, racquet sports, and "thumb texting"?

{{c1::De Quervain tenosynovitis}}

What group of disorders is characterized by constant unilateral facial pain that worsens with movement, otalgias, headaches, and jaw dysfunction?

{{c1::Temporomandibular}} disorders

What is the pathophysiology of costochondritis?

Costochondral or costosternal junction {{c1::inflammation}}
fields.Back Extra: This is typically due to minor trauma.

fields.Text:
What are the symptoms of costochondritis, and how are they managed?

Symptoms include {{c1::focal}} tenderness to palpation and {{c1::pleuritic}} chest pain
They are managed with {{c1::analgesia}} and {{c1::stretching}}

What condition is caused by thickening of the tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis?

{{c1::De Quervain tenosynovitis}}

What condition causes fibroblast proliferation and superficial palmar fascia thickening, often involving the base of the fourth and fifth fingers?

{{c1::Dupuytren contracture}}

What types of activity and aspects of foot anatomy are associated with plantar fasciitis?

Activity → {{c1::Jumping}} and prolonged {{c1::standing}}
Aspects → {{c1::Flat}} feet and heel {{c1::spurs}}

What shape are the lenses needed to correct vision in astigmatism?

{{c1::Cylindrical}} lenses

What pathologic abnormality is present in the eye with astigmatism?

Abnormal {{c1::curvature}} of the cornea → Different {{c1::refractive}} powers to arise at different {{c1::axes}}

What kind of lenses are needed to correct myopic vision?

{{c1::Concave}} lenses

Where is light focused with respect to the retina in myopia?

{{c1::In front of::In front of/Behind}} the retina
fields.Back Extra:
The eye is too long for the refractive power of the cornea and lens.

People with myopia are said to be "nearsighted".

fields.Text:
What kind of lenses are needed to correct vision in hyperopia?

{{c1::Convex}} lenses

Where is light focused with respect to the retina in hyperopia?

{{c1::Behind::In front of/Behind}} the retina
fields.Back Extra:
In hyperopia, the eye is too short for the refractive power of the cornea and lens.

People with hyperopia are said to be "farsighted".

fields.Text:
What is the cause of presbyopia?

{{c1::Aging}} causes impaired accommodation due to reduced lens {{c1::elasticity}}

What kind of glasses are needed to correct vision in presbyopia?

{{c1::Reading}} glasses
{{c1::Magnifiers}}

What causes painless, often bilateral, opacification of the lens?



{{c1::Cataract}}

What are the 8 risk factors of acquired cataract?

{{c1::Aging}}
{{c1::Smoking}}
Excessive {{c1::sunlight}}
{{c1::Alcohol}} overuse
{{c1::Trauma}}
{{c1::Infection}}
{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}
Prolonged {{c1::glucocorticoid}} use

What are the 8 risk factors of congenital cataract?

{{c1::Trisomies}}
Classic {{c1::galactosemia}}
{{c1::Galactokinase}} deficiency
{{c1::Marfan}} syndrome
{{c1::Alport}} syndrome
{{c1::Neurofibromatosis}} type {{c1::2}}
{{c1::Myotonic dystrophy}}
{{c1::TORCH}} infections

What is the treatment for cataracts?

{{c1::Surgical removal}} of lens followed by replacement with an {{c1::artificial}} lens

Name the components of the anterior segment of the eye that are involved in aqueous humor circulation.

{{c1::Ciliary body}}
{{c1::Iris}}
{{c1::Trabecular}} meshwork
{{c1::Canal of Schlemm}}
{{c1::Episcleral}} vessels

What receptors are responsible for mydriasis?

{{c1::α1}}-receptors
fields.Back Extra: Noradrenaline binds to the α1-receptors of the dilator pupillae muscles, leading to mydriasis.

fields.Text:
How do cholinergic agonists cause miosis?

Cholinergic agonists activate {{c1::M3}} receptors on the {{c1::sphincter pupillae}} muscles → Miosis

What drug class can be used to increase aqueous humor drainage via the uvea and sclera in patients with open-angle glaucoma?

{{c1::Prostaglandin}} agonists

What drug class can be used to increase drainage of aqueous humor via the trabecular meshwork in patients with open-angle glaucoma?

{{c1::M3}} agonists

What are the two main pathways whereby aqueous humor drains from the anterior chamber?

{{c1::Trabecular}} outflow
{{c1::Uveoscleral}} outflow

What 3 drug classes can be used to reduce production of aqueous humor in patients with open-angle glaucoma?

{{c1::α2}}-agonists
{{c1::β}}-blockers
{{c1::Carbonic anhydrase}} inhibitors

What structure in the anterior eye produces aqueous humor?

{{c1::Nonpigmented::Pigmented/Nonpigmented}} epithelium on the ciliary body

Where is the lens of the eye located?

It is suspended from the {{c1::ciliary body}} by {{c1::zonule}} fibers
fields.Back Extra: This is in between the posterior and the vitreous chambers.

fields.Text:
How does the ciliary body help in accommodation of the lens to near and far objects?

{{c1::Muscular}} fibers in the ciliary body change the {{c1::shape}} of the lens to allow for accommodation

Name 2 conditions in which bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia is seen.

{{c1::Multiple sclerosis}}
{{c1::Stroke}}

In patients with internuclear ophthalmoplegia, which side will have an adduction failure and which side will have nystagmus?

{{c1::Ipsilateral::Ipsilateral/Contralateral}} adduction failure
Nystagmus in {{c1::opposite::same/opposite}} side

Why is internuclear ophthalmoplegia common in diseases that affect myelin?

Because of the extensive myelination of the {{c1::medial longitudinal fasciculus}}

What is the directional term in internuclear ophthalmoplegia referring to?

The eye that is unable to {{c1::adduct}}

If on left lateral gaze, the left eye has nystagmus, the right eye fails to move, and convergence is normal, what is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}}-sided {{c1::internuclear ophthalmoplegia}}

If the right eye is unable to adduct while an individual is trying to look left horizontally, where is the lesion?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::medial longitudinal fasciculus}}

What is the most common presentation of cavernous sinus syndrome?

Variable {{c1::ophthalmoplegia}}
Reduced {{c1::corneal}} sensation
{{c1::Horner}} syndrome
Occasionally reduced {{c1::maxillary}} sensation

Which arteries pass through the cavernous sinus?

{{c1::Internal carotid}} arteries

What 3 underlying conditions may cause cavernous sinus syndrome?

{{c1::Pituitary}} tumors
Carotid-cavernous {{c1::fistulae}}
Cavernous sinus {{c1::thrombosis}}

Which 5 cranial nerves may be endangered when a cavernous sinus thrombosis forms?

Cranial nerve {{c1::III}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::IV}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::V1}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::V2}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::VI}}

What is the pathway of blood from the eye and superficial cortex to the greater venous system?

This is via the {{c1::cavernous sinus}} to the {{c1::internal jugular}} vein

The cavernous sinus is a collection of venous sinuses surrounding what structure?

{{c1::Pituitary}} gland
fields.Back Extra: This sits in the sella turcica.

fields.Text:
A patient has a stroke resulting in loss of the entire left visual field except for the macula. Which vessel was likely involved?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::posterior cerebral}} artery

A patient has a distal right middle cerebral artery stroke affecting branches to the temporal lobe. What deficit may be found on visual field testing?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::upper quadrantanopia}}
fields.Back Extra: This occurs if the right Meyer loop is affected.

fields.Text:
Where is the lesion in a patient with lower quadrantanopia?

{{c1::Dorsal::Ventral/Dorsal}} {{c1::optic radiation}}
fields.Back Extra: This travels through the internal capsule through the parietal lobe.

fields.Text:
Where is the lesion in a patient with left upper quadrantanopia?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::temporal}} lesion
fields.Back Extra: The Meyer loop will loop around the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle.

fields.Text:
What is the likely cause of central loss of vision in a 75-year-old patient?

{{c1::Central scotoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This likely results from macular degeneration in the eye.

fields.Text:
What deficit may visual field testing reveal in a person who has a distal left middle cerebral artery stroke affecting branches to the parietal lobe?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::lower quadrantanopia}}
fields.Back Extra: This occurs if the left dorsal optic radiation is affected.

fields.Text:
What lesion is expected if a visual field defect as shown in number 3 on the image is present?



{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::optic tract}} lesion

What happens to an image when it hits the primary visual cortex?

{{c1::Upside down}}
Left-right {{c1::reversed}}

What structure in the optic pathway may be affected by a pituitary lesion?

{{c1::Optic chiasm}}

A right middle cerebral artery stroke may cause which 2 defects in the visual field?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::upper quadrantanopia}}
{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::lower quadrantanopia}}

A patient presents with the finding shown when looking to the right. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} cranial nerve {{c1::VI}} palsy/damage
fields.Back Extra: The affected eye is unable to abduct and is displaced medially in the primary position of gaze.

fields.Text:
A patient presents with the finding shown when looking to the left. Which cranial nerve is dysfunctional?



{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} cranial nerve {{c1::IV}}
fields.Back Extra: The eyes move upward, particularly with a contralateral gaze.

fields.Text:
A patient's right eye is stuck in the position shown. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Oculomotor}} nerve palsy

A patient has the findings shown when asked to look to the right. What specific ocular movement is impaired in this patient and in which eye?



{{c1::Abduction}} in the {{c1::right::left/right}} eye
fields.Back Extra: This is due to right cranial nerve VI palsy.

fields.Text:
Why are the motor fibers of cranial nerve III affected first in vascular injury?

The vasculature supplying cranial nerve III runs along the {{c1::periphery}} of the nerve, therefore {{c1::deeper}} motor fibers are affected first

What is the most likely etiology of cranial nerve III injury if the gaze is normal, but pupillary light reflex is diminished unilaterally?

Compression of the {{c1::outer}} fibers of cranial nerve III interfere with {{c1::parasympathetic}} output

What is the etiology of the cranial nerve III injury if the gaze is fixed in a "down and out" position, but the light reflex is preserved?

{{c1::Vascular}} disease → {{c1::Hypoxia}} to {{c1::interior}} fibers

What is the pathophysiology of a persistently dilated pupil?

Interruption of cranial nerve III {{c1::parasympathetic}} fibers → Unopposed {{c1::sympathetic}} stimulation

A patient's right eye is stuck in a "down and out" position due to a cranial nerve injury. What are 3 commonly associated findings you would also expect to note?

{{c1::Ptosis}}
Diminished/absent {{c1::pupillary light}} reflex
{{c1::Mydriasis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is likely a cranial nerve III injury.

fields.Text:
What are the 5 common causes of cranial nerve III damage?

{{c1::Ischemia}}
{{c1::Uncal}} herniation
{{c1::Cavernous sinus}} thrombosis
{{c1::Posterior communicating}} artery aneurysm
{{c1::Midbrain}} stroke

Damage to cranial nerve III due to uncal herniation is associated with what symptom?

{{c1::Coma}}

Damage to cranial nerve III via a cavernous sinus thrombosis is associated with what other symptoms?

{{c1::Proptosis}}
Involvement of cranial nerves {{c1::IV}}, {{c1::V1}}, {{c1::V2}}, and {{c1::VI}}

Damage to cranial nerve III via a midbrain stroke is associated with what symptom?

{{c1::Contralateral::Ipsilateral/Contralateral}} {{c1::hemiplegia}}

What eye position is best for testing the function of the superior oblique muscle?

When the eye is {{c1::adducted::adducted/abducted}}, the function of the superior oblique muscle can be tested by asking the patient to look {{c1::down::up/down}}
fields.Back Extra: The superior oblique muscle depresses the adducted eye.

fields.Text:
Which extraocular muscle is responsible for gazing upward and laterally?

{{c1::Superior rectus}} muscle
fields.Back Extra: This is innervated by cranial nerve III.

fields.Text:
Which extraocular muscle is responsible for gazing towards the temple?

{{c1::Lateral rectus}} muscle
fields.Back Extra: This is innervated by cranial nerve VI.

fields.Text:
Which extraocular muscle is responsible for gazing downwards and laterally?

{{c1::Inferior rectus}} muscle
fields.Back Extra: This is innervated by cranial nerve III.

fields.Text:
Which extraocular muscle is responsible for gazing upwards and medially?

{{c1::Inferior oblique}} muscle
fields.Back Extra: This is innervated by cranial nerve III.

fields.Text:
Which extraocular muscle helps in adduction of the eyeball?

{{c1::Medial rectus}} muscle
fields.Back Extra: This is innervated by cranial nerve III.

fields.Text:
How does the "chemical formula" mnemonic LR6SO4R3 help you remember the innervation of the extraocular muscles?

Cranial nerve {{c1::VI}} innervates the lateral rectus muscle
Cranial nerve {{c1::IV}} innervates the superior oblique muscle
Cranial nerve {{c1::III}} innervates the rest

Weakness of which extraocular muscle causes double vision on downward gaze and on tilting the head to the left?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}}-sided {{c1::superior oblique}} muscle
fields.Back Extra: This is indicated by an inability to intort the eye when tilting the head to the affected side.

fields.Text:
What extraocular muscle is paralyzed in trochlear nerve palsy?

{{c1::Superior oblique}} muscle
fields.Back Extra: This abducts, intorts, and depresses the eye while adducted.

fields.Text:
What extraocular muscle is paralyzed in abducens nerve palsy?

{{c1::Lateral rectus}} muscle

What nerve may be injured with a traumatic blowout fracture of the orbital floor?

{{c1::Infraorbital}} nerve

Name the 4 ocular muscles innervated by cranial nerve III.

{{c1::Superior rectus}} muscle
{{c1::Inferior oblique}} muscle
{{c1::Inferior rectus}} muscle
{{c1::Medial rectus}} muscle

Name the muscle that passes through the trochlea in the eye.



{{c1::Superior oblique}} muscle

What pathology of the retina presents with central scotomas in older individuals?

{{c1::Age}}-related {{c1::macular degeneration}}

Which type of age-related macular degeneration presents with gradual diminution of vision with subretinal drusen in fundoscopy?



{{c1::Dry}} type
fields.Back Extra: This is more common than the wet type.

fields.Text:
Which type of age-related macular degeneration presents with metamorphopsia and rapid diminution of vision?

{{c1::Wet}} type
fields.Back Extra: This is due to bleeding secondary to neovascularization of the choroid.

fields.Text:
What retinal pathology presents with vision loss with fundoscopic findings of macular edema, microaneurysms, cotton wool spots, hemorrhages, and hard exudates?



{{c1::Nonproliferative::Proliferative/Nonproliferative}} {{c1::diabetic}} retinopathy

What is the mechanism of vision loss in proliferative diabetic retinopathy?

Chronic hyperglycemia → Increased {{c1::permeability}} and {{c1::occlusion}} of retinal vessels → Chronic {{c1::hypoxia}} → Retinal {{c1::neovascularization}} → Vitreous {{c1::hemorrhage}} and tractional retinal detachment

What retina pathology causes vision loss and arteriovenous nicking, microaneurysms, hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and macular star on fundoscopy?



{{c1::Hypertensive}} retinopathy

What finding in fundoscopy indicates hypertensive emergency?

{{c1::Papilledema}}

What is the pathophysiological mechanism of development of hypertensive retinopathy?

Chronic hypertension → {{c1::Spasm}}, {{c1::sclerosis}}, and {{c1::fibrinoid necrosis}} of retinal vessels

What are the 2 common causes of retinal artery occlusion?

{{c1::Embolism}}
{{c1::Giant cell arteritis}}

What retina pathology presents with acute onset, painless monocular vision loss, and cloudy retina with a "cherry-red" spot on fovea and identifiable retinal emboli on fundoscopy?



{{c1::Retinal}} artery {{c1::occlusion}}

What are the 3 fundoscopic findings of retinal vein occlusion?



Retinal {{c1::hemorrhage}}
Venous {{c1::engorgement}}
Retinal {{c1::edema}}

What is the cause of central retinal vein occlusion?

{{c1::Primary thrombosis}}

What is the likely cause of branch retinal vein occlusion?

{{c1::Secondary thrombosis}} at arteriovenous crossings

What causes the degeneration of photoreceptors in retinal detachment?

Separation of {{c1::neurosensory}} retina from underlying retinal {{c1::pigment}} epithelium → Loss of {{c1::choroidal}} blood supply → {{c1::Hypoxia}} → Degeneration of photoreceptors

What are the 3 causes of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment?

Retinal {{c1::tears}}
{{c1::Posterior::Anterior/Posterior}} vitreous detachment
{{c1::Trauma}}

Which type of retinal detachment is associated with advanced age and high myopia?

{{c1::Rhegmatogenous}} retinal detachment
fields.Back Extra: This is due to posterior vitreous detachment.

fields.Text:
What are the 2 types of nonrhegmatogenous retinal detachment?

{{c1::Tractional}}
{{c1::Exudative}}

What are the 3 symptoms of retinal detachment?

{{c1::Floaters}}
{{c1::Flashes}} of light
{{c1::Painless::Painful/Painless}} monocular vision loss

What are the 2 fundoscopic findings of retinal detachment?



Change in vessel {{c1::direction}}
{{c1::Wrinkling}} of detached retina

Is retinal detachment a surgical emergency?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}

What group of inherited dystrophies causes progressive degeneration of photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelium and is associated with abetalipoproteinemia?

{{c1::Retinitis pigmentosa}}

What are the 2 early symptoms of retinitis pigmentosa?

{{c1::Night blindness}}
{{c1::Peripheral}} vision loss

What are the fundoscopic findings in retinitis pigmentosa?



Optic disc {{c1::pallor}}
Retinal vessel {{c1::attenuation}}
Retinal pigmentation with bone {{c1::spicule}}-shaped deposits

What could be the pathophysiological mechanism of development of optic disc swelling?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} intracranial pressure → Impaired {{c1::axoplasmic}} flow in {{c1::optic}} nerve

Describe the characteristic fundoscopic finding of papilledema.



{{c1::Elevated}} optic disc with {{c1::blurred}} margins

Sounds of different frequencies produce vibrations in different regions of the basilar membrane. What is the term for this concept?

{{c1::Tonotopy}}

Which region of the basilar membrane is damaged in a patient experiencing low-frequency hearing loss?

{{c1::Apex}} of the {{c1::cochlea}} near the helicotrema

Which region of the basilar membrane is damaged in a patient experiencing high-frequency hearing loss?

{{c1::Base}} of the {{c1::cochlea}}

How does the inner ear transfer sound to the brainstem?

Basilar membrane transduces {{c1::vibrations}} through specialized {{c1::hair}} cells that transmit signals → {{c1::Auditory}} nerve signaling → Brainstem

What structure makes up the inner ear?

{{c1::Cochlea}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a snail-shaped, fluid-filled structure.

fields.Text:
How does the middle ear transfer sound to the inner ear?

{{c1::Ossicles}} conduct and amplify sound from the {{c1::tympanic membrane}} to the inner ear

What three bones are found in the middle ear?

{{c1::Malleus}}
{{c1::Incus}}
{{c1::Stapes}}

How does the outer ear transfer sound to the middle ear?

By {{c1::vibration}} of the {{c1::tympanic membrane}}

What three structures make up the outer ear?

{{c1::Pinna}}
{{c1::Auditory canal}}
{{c1::Tympanic membrane}}

What is the most common pathogen associated with otitis externa?

{{c1::Pseudomonas}}

What pathology of the ear is associated with water exposure, occlusion, and trauma of the ear canal?

{{c1::Otitis externa}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as "swimmer's ear".

fields.Text:
What are the four clinical features of otitis externa?

{{c1::Otalgia}}
{{c1::Discharge}}
{{c1::Pruritus}}
{{c1::Hearing}} loss

What is a dreaded complication of otitis externa in older patients with diabetes?

{{c1::Malignant}} otitis externa
fields.Back Extra: This is an invasive otitis externa with osteomyelitis.

fields.Text:
What are the clinical findings of malignant otitis externa?

{{c1::Otalgia}}
{{c1::Otorrhea}}
{{c1::Granulation}} tissue in ear canal
fields.Back Extra: This may lead to cranial nerve palsies.

fields.Text:
What are the 3 common pathogens associated with otitis media?

{{c1::Hemophilus influenzae}}
{{c1::Streptococcus pneumoniae}}
{{c1::Moraxella catarrhalis}}

Dysfunction of what anatomical structure is associated with increased risk of developing otitis media?

{{c1::Eustachian tube}}
fields.Back Extra: This dysfunction promotes overgrowth of bacterial colonizers of the upper respiratory tract.

fields.Text:
What are the clinical features of otitis media?

{{c1::Fever}}
{{c1::Otalgia}}
{{c1::Hearing}} loss
{{c1::Bulging}} erythematous tympanic membrane that may rupture

What complication presenting with erythema and swelling of the postauricular region might arise after an unresolved acute otitis media infection?

{{c1::Mastoiditis}}

What is a dreaded complication of mastoiditis?

{{c1::Brain abscess}}

A patient has the following findings. What type of hearing loss is this?

Weber test → Localization to the right ear
Right ear → Bone conduction > Air conduction

{{c1::Conductive}} hearing loss in the {{c1::right::left/right}} ear

A patient has sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear. What will the Weber and Rinne tests show?

Weber test → Localization to the {{c1::left::left/right}} ear
Rinne test → Air conduction {{c1::>::</>}} Bone conduction

A patient's audiogram demonstrates conductive hearing loss in the right ear. What will the Weber and Rinne tests show?

Weber test → Localization to the {{c1::right::left/right}} ear
Rinne test → Bone conduction {{c1::>::</>}} Air conduction

What is the position of the tuning fork when the Weber test is performed?

{{c1::Vertex}} of the skull

Where is the tuning fork positioned when the Rinne test is performed?

{{c1::Ear}} for air conduction
{{c1::Mastoid process}} for bone conduction

What type of sound is decreased in a patient with conductive hearing loss?

{{c1::Background}} noise

What type of sound is decreased in a patient with sensorineural hearing loss?

{{c1::All}} sounds

A patient has the following findings. What type of hearing loss is this?

Weber test → Localization to the right ear
Right ear → Air conduction > Bone conduction

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}}-sided {{c1::sensorineural}} hearing loss

Is central or peripheral vertigo more common?

{{c1::Peripheral}} vertigo

What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient with history of malignancy with a sensation of "room spinning", diplopia, and vertical nystagmus?

{{c1::Metastasis}}
fields.Back Extra: Metastasis to the central nervous system may invade the brain stem or cerebellum and produce central vertigo.

fields.Text:
What do you see on positional testing of vertigo in a patient with stroke compromising the vestibular nuclei?

Immediate {{c1::nystagmus}} in any direction

Where is the pathology located in peripheral vertigo?

{{c1::Inner ear}}

What is the diagnosis when a patient experiences a sensation of spinning while stationary?

{{c1::Vertigo}}

What is the classic triad seen in Ménière disease?

{{c1::Sensorineural}} hearing loss
{{c1::Tinnitus}}
{{c1::Vertigo}}

What is the pathology in Ménière disease?

{{c1::Endolymphatic hydrops}} → Increased {{c1::endolymph}} within the inner ear

Where are the lesions found in patients with diseases that cause central vertigo?

{{c1::Brainstem}}
{{c1::Cerebellum}}

What are three common causes of central vertigo?

{{c1::Demyelinating}} disease
Stroke affecting the {{c1::vestibular nuclei}}
Tumor in the {{c1::posterior fossa}}

On otoscopy, a patient has the finding shown in the image. What is the likely diagnosis?



{{c1::Cholesteatoma}}

Describe the pathology of cholesteatoma.

Abnormal growth of {{c1::keratinized::keratinized/nonkeratinized}} {{c1::squamous::squamous/cuboidal/columnar}} epithelium in the middle ear

What is the most common presenting feature of cholesteatoma?

{{c1::Painless::Painful/Painless}} {{c1::otorrhea}}

How does conductive hearing loss occur in cholesteatoma?

It results from {{c1::erosion}} of the ossicles

Is cholesteatoma congenital or acquired or both?

{{c1::Both}}

Why is the ability to hear high-frequency tones lost first in presbycusis?

The destruction of {{c1::hair}} cells occurs at the {{c1::base}} of the cochlea
fields.Back Extra: Low-frequency hearing may be better preserved.

fields.Text:
Which type of hearing loss may involve early loss of high-frequency sound perception?

{{c1::Presbycusis}}

What is the likely mechanism of hearing loss after extremely loud noise exposure?

Rupture of the {{c1::tympanic membrane}}

The ability to hear which frequencies are lost first in noise-induced hearing loss?

{{c1::High::High/Low}} frequencies

What structure is damaged in noise-induced hearing loss?

{{c1::Stereociliated}} cells in the {{c1::organ of Corti}}
fields.Back Extra: Sudden extremely loud noises can rupture the tympanic membrane.

fields.Text:
What is the main function of the pineal gland?

{{c1::Melatonin}} secretion

What actions may be affected if the superior colliculus is damaged?

{{c1::Direct}} eye movements in response to objects of interest
{{c1::Reactions}} to stimuli

Which one of the two colliculi transmits the auditory pathway?

{{c1::Inferior::Superior/Inferior}} colliculus

Which four cranial nerves have their nuclei in the medial aspect of the brainstem?

Cranial nerve {{c1::III}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::IV}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::VI}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::XII}}

Which four cranial nerves exit above the pons?

Cranial nerve {{c1::I}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::II}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::III}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::IV}}

Which four cranial nerves exit from the pons?

Cranial nerve {{c1::V}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::VI}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::VII}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::VIII}}

Which four cranial nerves arise from the medulla?

Cranial nerve {{c1::IX}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::X}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::XI}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::XII}}

Until what value of PCO2 does CPP rise linearly with PCO2 and then plateau?

Until PCO2 > {{c1::90}} mmHg

How is CPP affected by hypoxia?

CPP {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} with hypoxia while PO2 is below {{c1::50}} mmHg
fields.Back Extra: Above 50 mmHg, CPP plateaus despite changes in PO2.

fields.Text:
What are the 2 main determinants of CPP?

{{c1::MAP}}
{{c1::ICP}}
fields.Back Extra:
MAP must be greater than ICP to maintain CPP.

CPP = MAP - ICP

fields.Text:
What bedside intervention can decrease ICP in patients with acute cerebral edema?

Therapeutic {{c1::hyperventilation}}

If a patient's CPP remains at 0 mmHg, what is the patient's brain function?

Brain {{c1::death}}
fields.Back Extra: Essential findings are coma, absent brainstem reflexes, and apnea.

fields.Text:
What effect does hyperventilation have on ICP?

Hyperventilation {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} ICP
fields.Back Extra: Increased respiration lowers PCO2, decreasing cerebral perfusion through vasoconstriction.

fields.Text:
Which blood gas has the greatest impact on cerebral perfusion at baseline?

{{c1::Carbon dioxide}}

How do MAP, ICP, and CPP relate to each other mathematically?

{{c1::CPP}} = {{c1::MAP}} - {{c1::ICP}}

Which region of the body is most controlled by the most lateral aspect of the motor cortex?

{{c1::Face}}

Which region of the body is most controlled by the medial segments of the motor cortex?

{{c1::Trunk}}
{{c1::Lower::Upper/Lower}} limbs

Why do some areas of the body appear larger and distorted in the homunculus?

Body regions that are richly {{c1::innervated}} have higher {{c1::cortical}} representation and thus appear larger

What is a topographic visual representation of the sensory and motor areas in the cerebral cortex organized by body region called?

{{c1::Homunculus}}

Generally speaking, which parts of the homunculus would be impaired by an infarction of the middle cerebral artery?

{{c1::Face}}
{{c1::Neck}}
{{c1::Arms}}
{{c1::Hands}}

Generally speaking, which parts of the homunculus would be impaired by an infarction of the anterior cerebral artery?

{{c1::Trunk}}
{{c1::Lower::Upper/Lower}} extremities
{{c1::Genitals}}

An anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery watershed infarct will result in what symptoms?

{{c1::Proximal::Proximal/Distal}} upper and lower {{c1::extremity}} weakness

Which 2 areas of the cortex are at greatest risk for ischemia in a patient with severe hypotension?

Junction of the {{c1::anterior cerebral}} artery and {{c1::middle cerebral}} artery
Junction of the {{c1::posterior cerebral}} artery and {{c1::middle cerebral}} artery

Where is the internal border watershed zone located in the cortex?

Between the {{c1::superficial}} and {{c1::deep}} vascular territories of the {{c1::middle cerebral}} artery

Infarction in watershed areas of the brain usually occurs due to what pathologic process?

Severe {{c1::hypoperfusion}}

A posterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery watershed infarct will result in what symptoms?

{{c1::Higher::Higher/Lower}}-order {{c1::visual}} dysfunction

Regarding metastatic tumor spread, what significance do brain watershed areas carry?

Common locations for brain {{c1::metastases}} to arise

In the image shown, identify the yellow, teal, and purple circulations within the brain.



Yellow → {{c1::Anterior cerebral}} artery
Teal → {{c1::Middle cerebral}} artery
Purple → {{c1::Posterior cerebral}} artery

In the image, what perfuses the green, yellow, and purple areas?



Green area → {{c1::Middle cerebral}} arteries
Yellow area → {{c1::Anterior cerebral}} arteries
Purple area → {{c1::Posterior cerebral}} arteries

From which major vessels in the upper thorax do the left and right common carotid arteries originate?

The left common carotid artery originates directly from the {{c1::aortic arch}}
The right common carotid artery originates from the {{c1::brachiocephalic}} artery

From which major vessel in the upper thorax do the vertebral arteries originate?

{{c1::Subclavian}} arteries

What vessels do the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, posterior inferior cerebellar artery, and superior cerebellar artery stem from?

Anterior inferior cerebellar artery → {{c1::Inferior basilar}} artery
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery → {{c1::Vertebral}} artery
Superior cerebellar artery → {{c1::Superior basilar}} artery

What are the major branches of the aortic arch, from proximal to distal, that contribute to cerebral circulation?

{{c1::Brachiocephalic}} artery
{{c1::Common carotid}} artery
{{c1::Subclavian}} artery

Which branches off the basilar artery perfuse the pons?

{{c1::Pontine perforating}} branches
fields.Back Extra: This stems from the basilar artery over the pons.

fields.Text:
From which larger artery does the anterior choroidal artery originate?

{{c1::Internal carotid}} artery

From which larger arteries does the anterior spinal artery originate?

{{c1::Superior vertebral}} arteries

What 3 arteries of the cerebral circulation supply the cerebellum?

{{c1::Superior cerebellar}} artery
{{c1::Anterior inferior cerebellar}} artery
{{c1::Posterior inferior cerebellar}} artery

Which artery links the anterior and posterior circulations of the brain?

{{c1::Posterior communicating}} artery

The major branches of the posterior circulation of the circle of Willis stem from which artery?

{{c1::Basilar}} artery

The major branches of the anterior circulation of the brainstem are from which artery?

{{c1::Internal carotid}} artery

Which pair of arteries meet to form the basilar artery?

{{c1::Vertebral}} arteries

In which vessel in the circle of Willis would an aneurysm affect vision through mass effect?

{{c1::Anterior communicating}} artery
fields.Back Extra: This is due to its proximity to the optic chiasm/nerves.

fields.Text:
What are the 3 main arteries that branch from the internal carotid artery in the Circle of Wills?

{{c1::Anterior cerebral}} artery
{{c1::Middle cerebral}} artery
{{c1::Posterior communicating}} artery

Which 3 major blood vessels comprise the posterior circulation of the brain?

{{c1::Vertebral}} arteries
{{c1::Basilar}} artery
{{c1::Posterior cerebral}} arteries

From which larger artery do the lenticulostriate arteries originate?

{{c1::Middle cerebral}} artery

Name the numbered structures in this diagram.



1 → {{c1::Superior sagittal}} sinus
2 → {{c1::Confluence}} of the sinuses
3 → {{c1::Transverse}} sinus
4 → {{c1::Sigmoid}} sinus
5 → {{c1::Internal jugular}} vein

What are the presenting signs/symptoms of venous sinus thrombosis?

{{c1::Headaches}}
{{c1::Papilledema}}
{{c1::Seizures}}
{{c1::Focal}} neurologic deficits
fields.Back Extra:
This is due to an increase in ICP.

This may also lead to venous hemorrhage.

fields.Text:
What general risk factor predisposes patients to venous sinus thromboses?

{{c1::Hypercoagulability}}

Through which aperture does blood leave the skull to enter the internal jugular veins?

{{c1::Jugular foramen}}

What structures reabsorb the CSF into the venous system?

{{c1::Arachnoid granulations}}
fields.Back Extra: This lines the superior sagittal sinus.

fields.Text:
Which sinus is the primary site of CSF return?

{{c1::Superior sagittal}} sinus

The straight sinus receives drainage from which 2 key vascular structures?

{{c1::Inferior sagittal}} sinus
{{c1::Great cerebral}} vein of {{c1::Galen}}

What are the 2 major venous structures that communicate with the cavernous sinus?

{{c1::Superior ophthalmic}} vein
{{c1::Sphenoparietal}} sinus

Through which layers of the meninges does the venous system of the brain run?

{{c1::Periosteal}} layer of the dura mater
{{c1::Meningeal}} layer of the dura mater

What 3 sinuses converge at the confluence of the sinuses?

{{c1::Superior sagittal}} sinus
{{c1::Straight}} sinus
{{c1::Occipital}} sinus

What is a dangerous complication of venous sinus thromboses?

Venous {{c1::hemorrhage}}

Along with the blood from the cerebral veins, what extra fluid do dural venous sinuses receive?

{{c1::CSF}} from the {{c1::arachnoid granulations}}

Which structure produces cerebrospinal fluid in the brain?

{{c1::Choroid plexus}}

Where is the choroid plexus located?

{{c1::Lateral ventricle}}
{{c1::Third ventricle}}
{{c1::Fourth ventricle}}

How does cerebrospinal fluid drain from the 4th ventricle into the subarachnoid space?

Laterally → {{c1::Foramina of Luschka}}
Medially → {{c1::Foramen of Magendie}}

What connects the 3rd and 4th ventricles of the brain?

{{c1::Cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius}}

What connects the lateral and 3rd ventricles of the brain?

{{c1::Interventricular foramina of Monro}}

How is cerebral spinal fluid circulated?

Choroid plexus in the lateral, 3rd, and 4th ventricles → Subarachnoid space via {{c1::foramina of Luschka}} and {{c1::foramen of Magendie}} → Reabsorbed via {{c1::arachnoid granulations}} → Dural venous sinuses

Lesion in which cranial nerve may cause weakness in shrugging the shoulder?

Cranial nerve {{c1::XI}}

Lesion in which cranial nerve, and on what side, may deviate the uvula to the right?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} cranial nerve {{c1::X}}
fields.Back Extra: The uvula deviates away from the lesion as the weakened side collapses.

fields.Text:
Lesion of which cranial nerve, and on what side, may deviate the jaw to the right?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} cranial nerve {{c1::V}}
fields.Back Extra: The jaw deviates toward the same side as the lesion due to unopposed force from the opposite pterygoid muscle.

fields.Text:
In which direction will the tongue deviate with a lesion of the right hypoglossal nerve?

Toward the {{c1::right::left/right}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to weakened tongue muscles on affected side.

fields.Text:
What could be the clinical manifestation of a right cranial nerve XI lesion?

Weakness turning the head to the {{c1::left::left/right}} side
fields.Back Extra: The sternocleidomastoid muscle is innervated by the spinal accessory nerve and turns the head to the contralateral side.

fields.Text:
What is the first clinical sign of Friedreich ataxia most commonly seen in children?

{{c1::Kyphoscoliosis}}

Which cellular organelles are dysfunctional in Friedreich ataxia?

{{c1::Mitochondria}}

What protein is dysfunctional in Friedreich ataxia?

{{c1::Frataxin}}
fields.Back Extra: This is an iron-binding protein that functions to sequester usable iron in the mitochondria.

fields.Text:
A child with Friedreich ataxia needs monitoring for what endocrine disease?

{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}

For what lethal complication should a patient with Friedreich ataxia be frequently monitored?

{{c1::Hypertrophic}} cardiomyopathy
fields.Back Extra: This is the most common cause of death in patients with Friedreich ataxia.

fields.Text:
What can be observed while a patient with Friedreich ataxia is walking?

{{c1::Staggering}} gait
Frequent {{c1::falls}}

Which region of the nervous system is affected in Friedreich ataxia?

{{c1::Spinal cord}}
fields.Back Extra: It involves the lateral corticospinal tract, spinocerebellar tract, dorsal columns, and dorsal root ganglia.

fields.Text:
What genetic abnormality causes Friedreich ataxia?

Autosomal recessive trinucleotide repeat disorder ({{c1::GAA}})n on chromosome {{c1::9}} in the gene encoding {{c1::frataxin}}

In a patient with Friedreich ataxia, what tract symptoms are apparent due to degeneration of the spinocerebellar tract and dorsal columns?

Spinocerebellar tract → {{c1::Ataxia}}
Dorsal columns → Decreased sense of {{c1::vibration}}/{{c1::proprioception }}

In a patient with Friedreich ataxia, what tract symptoms are apparent due to degeneration of the lateral corticospinal tracts and dorsal root ganglia?

Lateral corticospinal tracts → {{c1::Spastic paralysis}}
Dorsal root ganglia → Loss of {{c1::deep tendon reflexes}}

What could be seen on an eye exam of a patient with Friedreich ataxia?

{{c1::Nystagmus}}

What 2 changes could be seen in the extremities of a patient with Friedreich ataxia?

{{c1::Pes cavus}}
{{c1::Hammer}} toes

What ipsilateral sensory deficits are expected with hemisection of the spinal cord?

Ipsilateral loss of all {{c1::sensation}} at the level of the lesion
Ipsilateral loss of the sensations of {{c1::proprioception}}, {{c1::vibration}}, and {{c1::light}} touch below the level of the lesion

What contralateral deficits below the level of the lesion are expected in a patient with Brown-Séquard syndrome?

Contralateral loss of sensation of {{c1::temperature}}, {{c1::pain}}, and {{c1::crude}} touch
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by spinothalamic tract damage.

fields.Text:
What sympathetic facial defect may be associated with hemisection of the spinal cord above T1?

{{c1::Ipsilateral::Ipsilateral/Contralateral}} {{c1::Horner}} syndrome

In Brown-Séquard syndrome, ipsilateral deficits below the level of the lesion are caused by damage to which 2 tracts?

{{c1::Corticospinal}} tract
{{c1::Dorsal column}}

What spinal cord pathology will cause the pattern of neurologic findings shown?



{{c1::Brown-Séquard}} syndrome, with {{c1::hemisection}} of the spinal cord on the patient's {{c1::right::left/right}} side

Are UMN or LMN affected in spinal muscular atrophy?

{{c1::LMN}}
fields.Back Extra: Degeneration occurs at the anterior horns of the spinal cord.

fields.Text:
What congenital brain malformation is associated with syringomyelia?

{{c1::Chiari I malformation}}

What three spinal tracts are affected in an individual with severe vitamin B12 deficiency?

{{c1::Spinocerebellar}} tracts
{{c1::Lateral corticospinal}} tracts
{{c1::Dorsal columns}}

What 4 neurologic symptoms might develop if a person follows a strict vegan diet and has low B12 levels on routine blood tests?

{{c1::Paresthesia}}
{{c1::Ataxic}} gait
Impaired {{c1::position}}/{{c1::vibration}} sense
{{c1::UMN::UMN/LMN}} symptoms

What are the characteristic signs and symptoms of tabes dorsalis secondary to tertiary syphilis?

Progressive {{c1::sensory ataxia}}
Positive {{c1::Romberg}} sign
Absence of {{c1::deep tendon reflexes}}
fields.Back Extra: This is usually associated with shooting pain, Charcot joints, and Argyll Robertson pupils.

fields.Text:
What is the other name for spinal muscular atrophy type 1?

{{c1::Werdnig-Hoffmann}} disease

What tracts and CNS regions are degenerated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis?

UMN → {{c1::Corticobulbar}} tract and {{c1::corticospinal}} tract
LMN → {{c1::Medullary}} region and {{c1::spinal cord}} region

Which neural functions are not affected by amyotrophic lateral sclerosis?

{{c1::Sensory}} function
{{c1::Bladder}}/{{c1::bowel}} function

What drug may extend the lifespan of a patient with a defect in superoxide dismutase 1?

{{c1::Riluzole}}

What symptoms can distinguish spinal muscular atrophy from poliomyelitis?

{{c1::Symmetric::Symmetric/Asymmetric}} weakness is observed with spinal muscular atrophy
{{c1::Asymmetric::Symmetric/Asymmetric}} weakness is seen with poliomyelitis

Where in the spinal cord does degeneration occur in Werdnig-Hoffmann disease?

{{c1::Anterior horn}}
fields.Back Extra: This contains the cell bodies of LMNs.

fields.Text:
By what mode of inheritance would a neonate develop marked hypotonia and tongue fasciculations with normal karyotyping?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}
fields.Back Extra: This is likely spinal muscular atrophy.

fields.Text:
What symptoms of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis result from LMN deficits due to anterior horn cell involvement?

{{c1::Bulbar}} palsy
{{c1::Fasciculations}}
{{c1::Flaccid}} limb weakness
{{c1::Atrophy}} of muscles

What symptoms of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis are due to UMN deficits?

{{c1::Pseudobulbar}} palsy
{{c1::Spastic}} limb weakness
{{c1::Hyperreflexia}}
{{c1::Clonus}}

What surgery can result in accidental complete occlusion of the anterior spinal artery?

{{c1::Aortic aneurysm}} repair

What is the usual disease course of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis?

{{c1::Fatal}}
fields.Back Extra: This is most often from respiratory failure.

fields.Text:
Which tracts are spared in a case of anterior spinal artery occlusion?

{{c1::Dorsal columns}}
{{c1::Lissauer}} tract

Which thoracic spinal cord levels are watershed areas?

{{c1::Midthoracic::Region}} {{c1::anterior spinal}} artery territory

Why does a patient with tabes dorsalis have poor coordination?

{{c1::Dorsal column}} and {{c1::dorsal root}} degeneration/demyelination → Progressive {{c1::sensory}} ataxia

What are the classical features of syringomyelia?

{{c1::Symmetric::Symmetric/Asymmetric}}, {{c1::bilateral::unilateral/bilateral}} loss of {{c1::pain}}/{{c1::temperature}} sensation in a {{c1::cape}}-like distribution

What order neurons are damaged in syringomyelia?

{{c1::2nd}}-order neurons

What pathology presents with acute onset UMN deficits below lesion, LMN deficits at lesion, loss of temperature/pain sensation below lesion, and sparing of dorsal column functions?

{{c1::Complete occlusion}} of the {{c1::anterior spinal}} artery

What pathology usually results in cauda equina syndrome?

Intervertebral disc {{c1::herniation}}
{{c1::Tumor}}

Cauda equina syndrome results from compression of the spinal roots at what level?

At or below {{c1::L2}}

How does cauda equina syndrome usually present?

{{c1::Radicular}} pain
Absent {{c1::knee}} and {{c1::ankle}} reflexes
{{c1::Saddle}} anesthesia
Loss of {{c1::bladder}} and {{c1::anal sphincter}} control

What gene defect is implicated in the pathology underlying spinal muscular atrophy?

Mutation of the {{c1::SMN1}} gene
fields.Back Extra: This leads to a defective snRNP assembly.

fields.Text:
Where is the lesion located if a 1-month-old infant has positive Babinski signs bilaterally?

{{c1::No}} lesion
fields.Back Extra:
A positive Babinski sign is normal in infants.

Most primitive reflexes are gradually lost in the first year of life.

fields.Text:
What four exam findings do you expect in a patient with a LMN lesion that are not seen in a patient with an UMN lesion?

{{c1::Atrophy}}
{{c1::Flaccid}} paralysis
{{c1::Fasciculations}}
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} reflexes/tone

What four exam findings do you expect in a patient with an UMN lesion that are not seen in a patient with a LMN lesion?

Positive {{c1::Babinski}} sign
{{c1::Spastic}} paresis
{{c1::Clasp knife}} spasticity
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} reflexes/tone

Are UMN or LMN lesions associated with weakness?

{{c1::Both}}

A patient with herniation of a structure has Duret hemorrhages identified at autopsy. At which number in the diagram shown did herniation occur?



{{c1::2}}
fields.Back Extra: This shows a transtentorial herniation with caudal displacement of the brainstem.

fields.Text:
A patient with herniation of a structure has compression of the anterior cerebral artery. At which number in the diagram shown has herniation occurred?



{{c1::1}}
fields.Back Extra: This shows a cingulate herniation under the falx cerebri.

fields.Text:
A patient with herniation of a posterior fossa structure is in a coma. At which number in the diagram shown has herniation likely occurred?



{{c1::4}}
fields.Back Extra: This shows a herniation of a cerebellar tonsil through the foramen magnum.

fields.Text:
A patient is found to have a blown pupil and unilateral weakness. At which number in the diagram shown has herniation likely occurred?



{{c1::3}}
fields.Back Extra: This shows an uncal herniation past the tentorium cerebelli.

fields.Text:
Identify the herniations labeled 1 through 4 in the image.



1 → {{c1::Cingulate}} herniation under the falx cerebri
2 → {{c1::Central/downward transtentorial}} herniation
3 → {{c1::Uncal transtentorial}} herniation
4 → {{c1::Cerebellar tonsil}} herniation into foramen magnum

Downward transtentorial herniation causes displacement of what structure?

{{c1::Brainstem}} in a {{c1::caudal}} direction
fields.Back Extra: This can lead to fatal Duret hemorrhages due to rupture of the paramedian basilar artery branches.

fields.Text:
A head CT shows right-sided uncal herniation. What structure is being compressed, causing weakness?

{{c1::Kernohan notch}}

What clinical findings would be observed in patient with early uncal herniation?

Contralateral {{c1::hemiparesis}}
Ipsilateral {{c1::blown pupil}}
fields.Back Extra: Late findings include coma and Kernohan phenomenon.

fields.Text:
Acute paralysis and sensory loss are present in the left leg after severe head trauma. What kind of herniation has likely occurred?

{{c1::Cingulate}} herniation under the {{c1::falx cerebri}}
fields.Back Extra: This compresses the anterior cerebral artery.

fields.Text:
Which lobe is affected if uncal herniation occurs?

{{c1::Medial temporal}} lobe

A cingulate herniation could compress which structure?

{{c1::Anterior cerebral}} artery

"Startle myoclonus" with dementia and ataxia is classic for which neurodegenerative disorder?

{{c1::Creutzfeldt-Jakob}} disease

What are the five reversible causes of dementia?

{{c1::Depression}}
{{c1::Hypothyroidism}}
Vitamin {{c1::B12}} deficiency
{{c1::Neurosyphilis}}
{{c1::Normal}} pressure hydrocephalus

Autopsy of a patient with a rapidly progressive, fatal dementia reveals the microscopic findings shown in the image. How is this disease usually transmitted?



By {{c1::contaminated}} materials

Which lobes degenerate in Pick disease?

{{c1::Frontotemporal}} lobe

What is the difference in presentation between Lewy body dementia and dementia secondary to Parkinson disease?

Lewy body dementia → Cognitive and motor symptom onset are {{c1::<::</>}} 1 year apart
Dementia secondary to Parkinson disease → Cognitive and motor symptom onset are {{c1::>::</>}} 1 year apart

What are Lewy bodies?



Intracellular {{c1::eosinophilic}} inclusions composed of {{c1::α-synuclein}}
fields.Back Extra: This is seen in Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia.

fields.Text:
What histologic findings might be present in a brain tissue specimen obtained from a patient with resting tremor, memory loss, and visual hallucinations?

{{c1::Lewy bodies}}
fields.Back Extra:
These are primarily found in cortical regions.

This is Lewy body dementia.

fields.Text:
What forms the inclusions in frontotemporal dementia?



{{c1::Hyperphosphorylated tau}}
{{c1::Ubiquitinated TDP-43}}

How does frontotemporal dementia usually present?

Early changes in {{c1::personality}} and {{c1::behavior}}
{{c1::Aphasia}}
fields.Back Extra: This may be associated with movement disorders.

fields.Text:
How does the extracellular β-amyloid core, shown in the image, form in the gray matter of a patient with Alzheimer disease?



Senile plaques from the cleavage of {{c1::APP}} to {{c1::amyloid-β}} form the extracellular β-amyloid core

Which histopathologic finding in the image correlates with the degree of dementia in Alzheimer disease?



{{c1::Neurofibrillary tangles}}
fields.Back Extra: The number of tangles correlates with the degree of dementia.

fields.Text:
How does being homozygous for the apolipoprotein E2 allele affect the risk of Alzheimer disease?

Risk is {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}}
fields.Back Extra: The ApoE4 isoform increases the risk of sporadic Alzheimer disease, while the ApoE2 isoform is protective.

fields.Text:
What serious complication is associated with amyloid angiopathy in a patient with a history of Alzheimer disease?

{{c1::Intracranial intraparenchymal hemorrhage}}

The proteins APP, presenilin-1, and presenilin-2 are associated with the familial form of what type of dementia?

{{c1::Alzheimer}} disease

What gross changes are seen in the brain of a patient with Alzheimer disease?



Widespread {{c1::cortical}} atrophy
fields.Back Extra: This is especially in the hippocampus with narrowing of the gyri and widening of the sulci.

fields.Text:
Which neurotransmitter decreases in a patient with Alzheimer disease?

{{c1::Acetylcholine}}

Why are patients with Down syndrome at higher risk of developing Alzheimer disease?

{{c1::APP}} is located on chromosome {{c1::21}}

What are the 2 most common causes of dementia in the elderly?

{{c1::Alzheimer}} disease (most common)
{{c1::Vascular dementia}}

What changes in the neurotransmitters are seen in Huntington disease?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} dopamine
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} GABA
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} acetylcholine

In Huntington disease, what mechanism is primarily responsible for neuronal cell death?

Excessive {{c1::NMDA}}-receptor binding → {{c1::Glutamate}} excitotoxicity

At what age do symptoms of Huntington disease usually manifest?

{{c1::20}} to {{c1::50}} years of age

How is Huntington disease inherited?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant::Inheritance pattern}} trinucleotide ({{c1::CAG}})n repeat in the {{c1::HTT}} gene on chromosome {{c1::4}}

What gross brain findings are present in a patient with Huntington disease?



Atrophy of {{c1::putamen}} and {{c1::caudate}}
{{c1::Ex vacuo ventriculomegaly}}

What causes the histologic findings in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease?



Prion proteins misfold to {{c1::PrPsc}} → {{c1::Protease}}-resistant {{c1::β-pleated sheets}}

What EEG and CSF findings may help diagnose Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease?

EEG → Periodic {{c1::sharp}} waves
CSF → Increased level of {{c1::14-3-3}} protein

In a patient with Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, what changes would be found at autopsy?

{{c1::Spongiform cortical}} changes

Which substance is metabolized in the body to a toxic product that damages the substantia nigra and may result in Parkinson disease?

{{c1::MPTP}}
fields.Back Extra: This is metabolized to MPP+, which is toxic to the substantia nigra.

fields.Text:
What form of dementia results from multiple arterial infarcts and/or chronic ischemia?

{{c1::Vascular}} dementia

Which form of dementia results from loss of dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta?



{{c1::Parkinson}} disease

What pattern of progression is classically seen in vascular dementia?

{{c1::Step-wise}} decline in cognitive function
{{c1::Late::Early/Late}}-onset memory loss

What psychiatric disorder should be ruled out before a diagnosis of dementia is made?

{{c1::Depression}}

Where are infarcts commonly located in vascular dementia?

{{c1::Cortex}}
{{c1::Subcortex}}

What disease causes deposition of neurofibrillatory tangles in the brain and intracellular eosinophilic proteinaceous rods in the hippocampus?

{{c1::Alzheimer}} disease
fields.Back Extra: The eosinophilic rods are Hirano bodies.

fields.Text:
What gross and histologic findings are seen in HIV-associated dementia?

Gross findings → Diffuse {{c1::gray::white/gray}} matter and {{c1::subcortical}} atrophy
Histologic findings → {{c1::Microglial}} nodules with {{c1::multinucleated giant}} cells

What findings are seen in an individual with subcortical dysfunction associated with advanced HIV infection?

{{c1::Cognitive}} deficits
{{c1::Gait}} disturbances
{{c1::Irritability}}
{{c1::Depressed}} mood

Where is the lesion in the central nervous system of a comatose patient whose upper limbs are in flexion and lower limbs are in extension?

{{c1::Above::Above/Below}} the {{c1::red nucleus}}
fields.Back Extra: This is decorticate posturing with overactive rubrospinal and vestibulospinal tracts.

fields.Text:
Where is the lesion in the central nervous system of a comatose patient whose upper and lower limbs are in extension?

Between the {{c1::red nuclei}} and {{c1::vestibular nuclei}}
fields.Back Extra: This is decerebrate posturing with an overactive vestibulospinal tract.

fields.Text:
Between decorticate and decerebrate posturing, which has the worse prognosis?



{{c1::Decerebrate}} posturing

What is the other name for idiopathic intracranial hypertension?

{{c1::Pseudotumor cerebri}}

What imaging changes are expected in idiopathic intracranial hypertension?

{{c1::None}}
fields.Back Extra: Findings on imaging are typically normal.

fields.Text:
What are the risk factors for developing idiopathic intracranial hypertension?

{{c1::Female::Male/Female}} sex
{{c1::Tetracyclines}}
{{c1::Obesity}}
Vitamin {{c1::A}} excess
{{c1::Danazol}}

What clinical findings are expected in a patient with idiopathic intracranial hypertension?

{{c1::Headache}}
{{c1::Tinnitus}}
{{c1::Diplopia}}
{{c1::Papilledema}}
fields.Back Extra: There will be no changes in mental status.

fields.Text:
What causes papilledema in patients with idiopathic intracranial hypertension?

Impaired {{c1::optic}} nerve {{c1::axoplasmic}} flow secondary to {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} intracranial pressure

What findings are expected on visual field testing in a patient with idiopathic intracranial hypertension?

Peripheral {{c1::constriction}}
{{c1::Enlarged}} blind spot

What treatments can be provided for a patient with idiopathic intracranial hypertension?

Initial treatment → Weight {{c1::loss::gain/loss}} and {{c1::acetazolamide}}
Refractory cases → {{c1::Invasive}} procedures

What would a lumbar puncture reveal in a patient with idiopathic intracranial hypertension?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} opening pressure with {{c1::relief}} of symptoms
fields.Back Extra: The cerebrospinal fluid itself would be normal.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of capsaicin?

Capsaicin stimulates and desensitizes {{c1::nociceptive}} fibers → Reduced {{c1::substance P}} release → Reduced {{c1::pain}}

Name a substance that is naturally found in hot peppers and is used for neuropathic and musculoskeletal pain.

{{c1::Capsaicin}}

What tissue gave rise to this malignant mass in the posterior fossa in a boy with histologic findings as shown?



{{c1::Primitive neuroectoderm}} gives rise to {{c1::medulloblastoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This features Homer-Wright rosettes and small blue cells.

fields.Text:
What tissue gives rise to a suprasellar mass in a child with the histologic features shown?



{{c1::Rathke pouch remnants}}
fields.Back Extra: Calcification and cholesterol crystals in a "motor oil"–like fluid within the tumor are characteristic of craniopharyngioma.

fields.Text:
What is the prognosis for a child with hydrocephalus due to a tumor that most commonly obstructs the 4th ventricle, as shown on MRI?



Generally {{c1::poor}}
fields.Back Extra: Ependymomas are typically aggressive and malignant at the time of diagnosis.

fields.Text:
A young boy has a cerebellar tumor with the histologic findings shown. From what part of the brain was the biopsy specimen most likely obtained?



{{c1::Posterior fossa}}
fields.Back Extra: This is where pilocytic astrocytomas most commonly arise.

fields.Text:
What is the prognosis of this GFAP-positive posterior fossa tumor with cystic and solid components?



{{c1::Good}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is because the tumor is benign.

This is a pilocytic astrocytoma.

fields.Text:
What complications are likely to arise from this primitive neuroectodermal tumor that is compressing the fourth ventricle in a child?



{{c1::Noncommunicating hydrocephalus}}
"{{c1::Drop metastases}}" to the spinal cord

The image shows biopsy findings from a malignant brain tumor in a child. What does the biopsy specimen show?



{{c1::Homer-Wright rosettes}}
{{c1::Small blue}} cells

MRI of the brain of a child with obstructive hydrocephalus is shown. What characteristic findings will histologic exam of the mass likely reveal?



{{c1::Perivascular pseudorosettes}}
{{c1::Rod}}-shaped {{c1::blepharoplasts}} near the nucleus
fields.Back Extra: This is an ependymoma, which most commonly arises in the 4th ventricle.

fields.Text:
Where in the brain is this tumor with the following histological findings and hydrocephalus?



{{c1::4th ventricle}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is the most common site of an ependymoma.

Note the characteristic perivascular pseudorosettes.

fields.Text:
Calcifications are common in what highly recurring primary brain tumor of children?



{{c1::Craniopharyngioma}}

What stain may be positive in a benign supratentorial tumor with both cystic and solid components?

{{c1::GFAP}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is a marker for glial cells.

This is positive in a pilocytic astrocytoma, which may be supratentorial.

fields.Text:
Histologically, what other type of neoplasm does a pineal gland tumor resemble?

{{c1::Germ cell}} tumor

What childhood supratentorial tumor is often confused with a pituitary adenoma due to similar presenting symptoms?

{{c1::Craniopharyngioma}}
fields.Back Extra: Both this and a pituitary adenoma may present with bitemporal hemianopia.

fields.Text:
What is the most common childhood supratentorial tumor?

{{c1::Craniopharyngioma}}

What is the embryonic origin of craniopharyngioma?

{{c1::Remnants}} of {{c1::Rathke pouch}}

How does a pineal gland tumor result in Parinaud syndrome?

A tumor of the pineal gland causes {{c1::compression}} of the {{c1::tectum}} → {{c1::Vertical gaze}} palsy

How can a pineal gland tumor cause obstructive hydrocephalus?

By compressing the {{c1::cerebral aqueduct}}

How can a pineal gland tumor cause precocious puberty?

Through {{c1::β-hCG}} production

What is the cellular origin of an ependymoma?

{{c1::Ependymal}} cells

Which posterior fossa structure does a medulloblastoma most commonly involve?

{{c1::Cerebellum}}

What is the most common primary brain tumor in childhood?

{{c1::Pilocytic astrocytoma}}

A child has a well-circumscribed cystic and solid mass in the posterior fossa as shown in the image. What are the cells of origin?



{{c1::Astrocytes}}

What three symptoms are associated with a medulloblastoma?

{{c1::Headaches}}
{{c1::Papilledema}}
Truncal {{c1::ataxia}}

Which immunohistochemical cell marker can be used to identify medulloblastoma tumors?

{{c1::Synaptophysin}}

What is the most common malignant brain tumor in childhood?

{{c1::Medulloblastoma}}

Bilateral masses positive for S-100 tumor marker are resected from the cerebellopontine angles. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Neurofibromatosis}} type {{c1::II}}
fields.Back Extra: This is associated with bilateral vestibular schwannomas.

fields.Text:
Histologic findings of an adult primary brain tumor are shown in the image. Staining for S-100 is positive. What are the cells of origin?



{{c1::Schwann}} cells

What is this mass shown on an MRI that causes right-sided tinnitus and hearing loss?



{{c1::Vestibular schwannoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is usually found at the cerebellopontine angle and localized to cranial nerve VIII in the internal acoustic meatus.

fields.Text:
Describe the histologic findings seen with glioblastoma multiforme.



{{c1::GFAP}} positive
"{{c1::Pseudopalisading}}" pleomorphic tumor cells of {{c1::astrocyte}} origin bordering central areas of necrosis, hemorrhage, and/or microvascular proliferation

The biopsy specimen obtained from a brain tumor in an adult shows "fried egg" cells, "chicken-wire" capillaries, and calcifications. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Oligodendroglioma}}

A patient with polycythemia has a mass revealed on MRI. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Hemangioblastoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This can lead to secondary polycythemia due to production of erythropoietin.

fields.Text:
What tissue gives rise to a cerebellar mass that has the histological findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Blood vessels}}
fields.Back Extra: The histologic findings suggest a hemangioblastoma, which is associated with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome when retinal angiomas are present.

fields.Text:
What is the most common hormone secreted by a pituitary adenoma?



{{c1::Prolactin}}

A patient has the MRI findings shown. From what cell type does this tumor arise?



{{c1::Arachnoid}} cells

What blood work might you order to confirm the pathology that caused the following change in the field of vision?



Measurement of {{c1::pituitary hormone}} levels
fields.Back Extra: A pituitary adenoma, causing pressure on the optic chiasm, may be responsible for the change in the field of vision.

fields.Text:
What syndrome causes bilateral renal cell carcinomas, pheochromocytoma, and a brain mass with the histological findings shown in the image?



{{c1::von Hippel-Lindau}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: The image shows findings indicative of a hemangioblastoma, which is found with retinal angiomas in patients with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome.

fields.Text:
A slow-growing frontal lobe mass is biopsied and found to be a rare tumor. What would one see on histopathologic exam?



"{{c1::Fried egg}}" cells
"{{c1::Chicken-wire}}" capillary pattern

What visual symptoms are expected in a patient with a large suprasellar mass like that shown in the image?



{{c1::Bitemporal hemianopia}}
fields.Back Extra: Mass effect from a pituitary adenoma can compress the optic chiasm.

fields.Text:
Where would a rare, slow-growing adult brain tumor of oligodendrocyte origin most likely be found?

{{c1::Frontal}} lobe

What could be the cause of new onset of seizures and paresis of the right leg along with MRI findings of an extra-axial brain mass with a dural attachment/tail?

{{c1::Meningioma}}
fields.Back Extra: This may produce seizures and/or focal neurologic deficits.

fields.Text:
What complication is suspected in a patient with history of a pituitary mass presenting with a severe headache and acute adrenal insufficiency?

{{c1::Pituitary apoplexy}}
fields.Back Extra: In this complication, a pituitary adenoma causes internal hemorrhage.

fields.Text:
An intracranial tumor that causes a buffalo hump, moon facies, and abdominal striae originates from what cell type?

{{c1::Corticotrophs}}
fields.Back Extra: These become hyperplastic in ACTH-secreting pituitary adenomas.

fields.Text:
Which two benign adult primary brain tumors are treated via resection or stereotactic radiosurgery?

{{c1::Meningiomas}}
{{c1::Schwannomas}}

How long do patients typically survive with a highly malignant tumor extending across corpus callosum?

{{c1::1}} year is the median survival

Tumors arising from what cells cause enlarged hands and feet and coarse facies?

{{c1::Somatotrophs}}

What are 2 general ways in which pituitary adenomas present?

{{c1::Silent}}
{{c1::Hormone}} producing

What is glioblastoma multiforme also known as?

Grade {{c1::IV}} {{c1::astrocytoma}}

What cellular origins of pituitary adenoma can be identified via the hormones they produce?

Commonly → {{c1::Lactotrophs}}, {{c1::somatotrophs}}, and {{c1::corticotrophs}}
Rarely → {{c1::Thyrotrophs}} and {{c1::gonadotrophs}}

Hyperplasia of a single type of endocrine cells in the pituitary leads to what type of tumor?

{{c1::Pituitary adenoma}}

What treatment options can you offer to a patient who has a pituitary adenoma?

{{c1::Dopamine}} agonists
{{c1::Transsphenoidal}} resection

What cranial nerves are most commonly involved in schwannomas?

CN {{c1::V}}
CN {{c1::VII}}
CN {{c1::VIII}}

What histopathologic features are characteristic of a glioblastoma?

"{{c1::Pseudopalisading}}" pleomorphic tumor cells that border central areas of necrosis, hemorrhage, and/or microvascular proliferation

When is glioblastoma multiforme also referred to as "butterfly glioma"?

When it crosses the {{c1::corpus callosum}}

What features are characteristic of hemangioblastoma on histopathologic examination?

{{c1::Closely}} arranged, {{c1::thin::thick/thin}}-walled capillaries
Minimal intervening {{c1::parenchyma}}

A patient with a pituitary adenoma has the visual field findings shown in the lower image. What type of hemianopia is this?



{{c1::Bitemporal hemianopia}}

What histopathologic findings are characteristic of meningioma?



{{c1::Spindle}} cells arranged in a {{c1::concentric}}, {{c1::whorled}} pattern
{{c1::Psammoma bodies}}

How will a prolactinoma present differently in men and women?

Women → Causes decreased {{c1::bone}} density, {{c1::galactorrhea}}, and {{c1::amenorrhea}}
Men → Causes {{c2::gynecomastia}}, decreased {{c2::libido}}, and {{c2::infertility}}

What tumor marker and genetic amplification are associated with glioblastoma?

{{c1::GFAP}} tumor marker because of its {{c1::astrocyte}} origin
{{c1::EGFR}} amplification

Which movement disorder explains "flapping" of the wrists bilaterally with forced extension?

{{c1::Asterixis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is classically seen in patients with hepatic injury that produces metabolic derangement.

fields.Text:
What movement disorder presents with restlessness and a persistent, annoying urge to move in a patient being treated for schizophrenia?

{{c1::Akathisia}}
fields.Back Extra: This can be seen with neuroleptic use or as an adverse effect of Parkinson disease treatment.

fields.Text:
Which tremor, which is usually familial, worsens with movement or during episodes of anxiety?

{{c1::Essential}} tremor

What disease is classically associated with a unilateral "pill-rolling" tremor?

{{c1::Parkinson}} disease

What are the 2 common treatment modalities for essential tremor?

{{c1::Nonselective::Selective/Nonselective}} {{c1::β-blocker}}
{{c1::Primidone}}

In a person with intention tremor, where is the lesion located?

{{c1::Cerebellum}}

How does an intention tremor present?

A {{c1::slow::fast/slow}}, {{c1::zigzag}} motion when pointing or extending toward a target

How does alcohol affect essential tremor?

Alcohol {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}} essential tremor amplitude
