fields.Back Extra: Affected individuals often use it to self-medicate.

fields.Text:
What movement disorder would present as a sustained twisting of the neck, especially in patients who recently started taking haloperidol?

{{c1::Dystonia}}

A hiccup is categorized as what type of movement disorder?

{{c1::Myoclonus}}

What movement disorder, seen in Huntington disease, manifests as a slow, writhing, snake-like movement of fingers?

{{c1::Athetosis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by a lesion in the basal ganglia.

fields.Text:
What movement disorder presents with sudden, jerky, purposeless movements, appearing like dancing?

{{c1::Huntington}} disease

Sudden, jerky, purposeless movements or slow, writhing movements are characteristic of lesions in which part of the brain?

{{c1::Basal ganglia}}

What toxin can be used to treat dystonia?

{{c1::Botulinum}} toxin

What characteristic lesion on neuroimaging confirms the diagnosis of hemiballismus?

A {{c1::contralateral::ipsilateral/contralateral}} {{c1::subthalamic nucleus}} lesion caused by a lacunar stroke

Where is the lesion located in Parkinson disease?

{{c1::Substantia nigra}}

What syndrome causes a persistent urge to move the legs, especially at night?

{{c1::Restless leg}} syndrome

What drugs can be used to treat restless legs syndrome?

{{c1::Dopamine}} agonists

Name two conditions commonly associated with restless leg syndrome.

{{c1::Iron}} deficiency
Chronic {{c1::kidney}} disease

What movement disorder is typically seen in Creutzfeldt-Jackob disease?

{{c1::Myoclonus}}

What are the skin lesions shown in the image?



{{c1::Neurofibromas}}
fields.Back Extra: These are neurocutaneous lesions characteristic of neurofibromatosis type I.

fields.Text:
What gene mutation causes tuberous sclerosis?



{{c1::TSC1}} mutation on chromosome {{c1::9}}
{{c1::TSC2}} mutation on chromosome {{c1::16}}
fields.Back Extra:
The image shows ash-leaf spots.

This is tuberous sclerosis.

fields.Text:
Focal neurologic signs seen in patients with neurofibromatosis type I are usually due to what lesion?

{{c1::Meningioma}}

What mutation, on which chromosome, causes the syndrome that presents with optic glioma and the findings shown?



Mutation of the {{c1::NF1}} gene on chromosome {{c1::17}}

What is the lesion shown in the image, seen on the skin of patients with neurofibromatosis type I, called?



{{c1::Café-au-lait spot}}

What neurocutaneous disorder presents with the findings shown and cardiac rhabdomyoma?



{{c1::Tuberous sclerosis}}

What are the common presenting features in a patient with neurofibromatosis type I?

{{c1::Café-au-lait}} spots
{{c1::Intellectual}} disability
Cutaneous {{c1::neurofibromas}}
{{c1::Lisch}} nodules
Optic {{c1::gliomas}}
{{c1::Pheochromocytoma}}
{{c1::Seizures}}
{{c1::Focal}} neurologic signs
{{c1::Bone}} lesions

What are four common findings in patients with neurofibromatosis type II?

{{c1::Bilateral vestibular schwannomas}}
Juvenile {{c1::cataracts}}
{{c1::Ependymomas}}
{{c1::Meningiomas}}

What mutation causes neurofibromatosis type II?

{{c1::NF2}} tumor suppressor gene on chromosome {{c1::22}}

Which bony lesion is common in patients with neurofibromatosis type I?

{{c1::Sphenoid dysplasia}}

Why does glaucoma commonly affect patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome?

Episcleral {{c1::hemangiomas}} → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} intraocular pressure → Early-onset glaucoma

What pathology results in Sturge-Weber syndrome?

{{c1::Somatic mosaicism}} of an activating mutation in 1 copy of the {{c1::GNAQ}} gene → Abnormal development of {{c1::neural crest}} derivatives

A patient has a family history of angiomatosis, renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and hemangioblastoma. What disease is present in this family?

{{c1::Von Hippel-Lindau}} disease

What are 4 common cutaneous manifestations of tuberous sclerosis?

{{c1::Angiofibromas}}
{{c1::Ash-leaf}} spots
{{c1::Shagreen}} patches
Ungual {{c1::fibromas}}

Which sporadic neurocutaneous disorder is characterized by "port-wine stain" birthmarks as shown in the image and ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomata with calcifications?



{{c1::Sturge-Weber}} syndrome

What is the mode of inheritance of Sturge-Weber syndrome?

{{c1::Congenital}}, {{c1::noninherited::inherited/noninherited}} disorder
fields.Back Extra: The mutation that causes this disorder is somatic.

fields.Text:
What are the modes of inheritance of tuberous sclerosis, neurofibromatosis type I and II, and von Hippel-Lindau disease?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}

Increases in incidence of subependymal giant cell astrocytomas and ungual fibromas are seen with which neurocutaneous disorder?

{{c1::Tuberous sclerosis}}

What is the other name for neurofibromatosis type I?

{{c1::von Recklinghausen}} disease

What is the role of pVHL?

pVHL ubiquitinates {{c1::hypoxia-inducible factor 1a}}

What are the common sites for hemangioblastoma in von Hippel-Lindau disease?

{{c1::Retina}}
{{c1::Brainstem}}
{{c1::Cerebellum}}
{{c1::Spine}}

How do hemangioblastomas present histopathologically?

High {{c1::vascularity}} with {{c1::hyperchromatic}} nuclei

What neurologic consequence may occur if the blood sodium level of a hypernatremic patient decreases too quickly?

Cerebral {{c1::edema}}/{{c1::herniation}}

What is the cause of axonal demyelination in osmotic demyelination syndrome?

{{c1::Rapid}} osmotic changes

What is the most common subtype of Guillain-Barré syndrome?

{{c1::Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy}}

Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy results in destruction of what cell type?

{{c1::Schwann}} cells

The most common type of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is caused by what gene abnormality?

{{c1::PMP22}} gene duplication
fields.Back Extra: The most common type of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is CMT1A.

fields.Text:
What symptoms are commonly seen in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease?

{{c1::Foot}} deformities
{{c1::Sensory}} deficits
{{c1::Lower::Upper/Lower}} extremity weakness

Which areas of the brain are most commonly affected in a patient with secondary reactivation of latent JC virus?

{{c1::Parietal}} area
{{c1::Occipital}} area

What population is particularly susceptible to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy?

Severely {{c1::immunocompromised}} patients

Which group of hereditary nerve disorders is marked by defective production of peripheral nerve or myelin sheath proteins?

{{c1::Charcot-Marie-Tooth}} disease

Describe the pathogenesis of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.

Demyelination of the {{c1::CNS}} due to destruction of {{c1::oligodendrocytes}}, secondary to reactivation of a latent {{c1::JC virus}} infection

What two drugs increase the risk of JC virus reactivation?

{{c1::Natalizumab}}
{{c1::Rituximab}}

What disease process is responsible for development of rapidly progressive memory loss and aphasia in an immunocompromised patient who tests positive for JC virus?

{{c1::Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy}}

What is the other name for osmotic demyelination syndrome?

{{c1::Central pontine myelinolysis}}

What are the symptoms of osmotic demyelination syndrome?

Acute {{c1::paralysis}}
{{c1::Diplopia}}
{{c1::Dysphagia}}
{{c1::Dysarthria}}
Loss of {{c1::consciousness}}
fields.Back Extra: This can be a cause of "locked-in-syndrome".

fields.Text:
What infections have been associated with acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy?

{{c1::Viral}} infections
fields.Back Extra: There is no definitive causal link to any pathogen.

fields.Text:
How does acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy occur?

{{c1::Autoimmune}} destruction of {{c1::Schwann}} cells via inflammation and demyelination of motor fibers, sensory fibers, and peripheral nerves
fields.Back Extra: This is likely due to molecular mimicry.

fields.Text:
What type of paralysis occurs in acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy?

{{c1::Symmetric::Symmetric/Asymmetric}} {{c1::ascending::ascending/descending}} muscle weakness/paralysis
Depressed/absent {{c1::deep tendon reflexes}}

Other than muscle weakness, what neural abnormalities may be seen in a patient with acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy?

{{c1::Facial}} paralysis
{{c1::Respiratory}} failure
{{c1::Sensory}} or {{c1::autonomic}} abnormalities

What is the prognosis of acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy?

Most patients survive with {{c1::good}} functional recovery

What are the classical cerebrospinal fluid findings in acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy?

{{c1::Albuminocytologic dissociation}}

How do you treat acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy?

{{c1::Respiratory}} support
{{c1::Plasma}} exchange
IV {{c1::immunoglobulins}}
fields.Back Extra: There is no role for steroid use.

fields.Text:
How does acute disseminated encephalomyelitis usually present?

{{c1::Rapidly}} progressive multifocal neurologic symptoms
Altered {{c1::mental}} status
fields.Back Extra: This occurs after infection or vaccination and is caused by multifocal inflammation and demyelination.

fields.Text:
Where does axonal demyelination take place in osmotic demyelination syndrome?



{{c1::Pontine white matter}}

What treatment options are available for spasticity in a patient with multiple sclerosis?

{{c1::Baclofen}}
{{c1::GABAB}}-receptor agonists

How would you treat a neurogenic bladder in a patient with multiple sclerosis?

{{c1::Catheterization}}
Use of {{c1::muscarinic}} antagonists

What three disease-modifying therapies can be used to stop relapses and halt/slow progression of multiple sclerosis?

{{c1::β-interferon}}
{{c1::Glatiramer}}
{{c1::Natalizumab}}

Is the course of multiple sclerosis usually rapidly progressive, chronic, insidious, or relapsing and remitting?

{{c1::Relapsing and remitting}}
fields.Back Extra: Flares of disease activity may occur and subside with time and treatment.

fields.Text:
What MRI findings are characteristic of multiple sclerosis?



{{c1::Periventricular plaques}}
Multiple {{c1::white::white/gray}} matter lesions disseminated in time and space

What symptoms indicate spinal cord involvement in patients with multiple sclerosis?

{{c1::Paraparesis}}
{{c1::Neurogenic}} bladder
Sensory manifestations in the {{c1::trunk}}
Sensory manifestations in 1 or more {{c1::extremities}}
Electric shock-like sensations along cervical spine during neck {{c1::flexion::flexion/extension}}

What symptoms would manifest if a patient with multiple sclerosis had pyramidal tract demyelination?

{{c1::Weakness}}
{{c1::Spasticity}}

What demographic group is most likely to be affected by multiple sclerosis?

{{c1::White::Race}} {{c1::women::men/women}} in their 20s and 30s
fields.Back Extra: The risk of multiple sclerosis increases with distance from the equator and with low serum vitamin D levels.

fields.Text:
Describe the findings in a patient with multiple sclerosis presenting with acute optic neuritis.

{{c1::Painful::Painful/Painless}} {{c1::unilateral::unilateral/bilateral}} vision loss with {{c1::Marcus Gunn pupil}}

How does a hot bath or exercise affect a patient with multiple sclerosis?

Symptoms {{c1::worsen}} as a result of increased body temperature

What CSF test findings suggest a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis?

Increased Ig{{c1::G}} level in CSF
{{c1::Myelin basic protein}} in CSF
{{c1::Oligoclonal}} bands in CSF

Describe the pathogenesis of multiple sclerosis.

{{c1::Autoimmune}} inflammation and demyelination in the {{c1::CNS}} → {{c1::Axonal}} damage

What 3 symptoms are classically associated with normal pressure hydrocephalus?

Urinary {{c1::incontinence}}
{{c1::Gait}} apraxia
{{c1::Cognitive}} dysfunction

A patient presents with the brain MRI shown. He has symptoms related to stretching of the corona radiata. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Normal pressure hydrocephalus}}

A patient with advanced Alzheimer disease presents with the MRI findings shown. What will a measurement of the patient's ICP reveal?



ICP will be {{c1::normal}}
fields.Back Extra: This patient has ex vacuo ventriculomegaly due to atrophy of brain tissue.

fields.Text:
What kind of hydrocephalus is likely with the brain MRI finding shown in the image?



{{c1::Noncommunicating hydrocephalus}}
fields.Back Extra: This involves structural blockage of cerebrospinal fluid flow.

fields.Text:
What is the classic gait pattern seen in a patient with enlarged ventricles on brain imaging, urinary incontinence, and cognitive impairment?

{{c1::Magnetic}} gait
fields.Back Extra: This is characteristic of normal pressure hydrocephalus.

fields.Text:
What conditions are associated with ex vacuo ventriculomegaly?

{{c1::Neurodegenerative}} disorders that cause brain {{c1::atrophy}}

Aqueductal stenosis causes what type of hydrocephalus?

{{c1::Noncommunicating hydrocephalus}}
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by a structural blockage of cerebrospinal fluid circulation within the ventricular system.

fields.Text:
In a patient with normal pressure hydrocephalus, on lumbar puncture, what will the opening pressure measurement be?

{{c1::Normal}}

What will a head CT show in an older adult who presents with urinary incontinence, cognitive dysfunction, and gait apraxia?

{{c1::Ventricular}} expansion → Distortion of the fibers of the {{c1::corona radiata}} without an increase in {{c1::subarachnoid space}} volume

What is the mechanism by which meningitis can cause a communicating hydrocephalus and subsequent papilledema, herniation, and increased ICP?

Arachnoid {{c1::scarring}} after meningitis → Limited CSF {{c1::absorption}} via arachnoid {{c1::granulations}}

How can the symptoms of normal pressure hydrocephalus be reversed?

CSF drainage via {{c1::lumbar puncture}}
CSF {{c1::shunt}} placement

What are the 3 common causes of noncommunicating hydrocephalus?

Blockage of the {{c1::foramen of Monro}} by a colloid cyst
Stenosis of the {{c1::aqueduct of Sylvius}}
{{c1::Tumor}}

What is hydrocephalus?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} CSF volume → Ventricular {{c1::dilation}} with/without {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} ICP

What are the classic features of a migraine?

Severe {{c1::unilateral::unilateral/bilateral}} {{c1::throbbing}} pain
{{c1::Nausea}}
{{c1::Photophobia}}
{{c1::Phonophobia}}

What are 5 common causes of secondary headaches?

{{c1::Subarachnoid hemorrhage}}
{{c1::Neoplasm}}
{{c1::Meningitis}}
{{c1::Hydrocephalus}}
{{c1::Giant cell arteritis}}

How can you differentiate a cluster headache from trigeminal neuralgia?

{{c1::Duration}}
fields.Back Extra: Cluster headaches last longer, while the pain of trigeminal neuralgia typically lasts for a few seconds or minutes.

fields.Text:
What is the first-line treatment for trigeminal neuralgia?

{{c1::Carbamazepine}}

What is the likely cause of sharp, shooting pains that travel down the jaw for several seconds when eating ice cream?

{{c1::Trigeminal neuralgia}}

What diagnosis must be ruled out with sudden onset of the "worst headache" of a patient's life?

{{c1::Subarachnoid hemorrhage}}
fields.Back Extra: This must be carefully differentiated from other types of headaches so that it can be treated immediately.

fields.Text:
Which type of headaches are more common in males than in females?

{{c1::Cluster}} headaches

What two treatments may be offered for tension headaches?



Acute pain → {{c1::Analgesics}}
Chronic pain → {{c1::Amitriptyline}} and prophylactic {{c1::behavioral}} therapy

What is the likely type of headache lasting 45 minutes with constant, bilateral "band-like" pain, but no photophobia or aura?

{{c1::Tension}} headaches

Irritation of which 3 cranial structures may be implicated in migraine pathogenesis?

{{c1::Meninges}}
CN {{c1::V}}
{{c1::Blood vessels}}

What is the likely cause of a pulsating headache lasting 24 hours, which is distributed as shown in the image?



{{c1::Migraine}}

What are 7 measures that may be prescribed as prophylaxis for migraine?

{{c1::Lifestyle}} changes
{{c1::β}}-blockers
{{c1::Amitriptyline}}
{{c1::Topiramate}}
{{c1::Valproate}}
{{c1::Botulinum}} toxin
Anti-{{c1::CGRP}} monoclonal antibodies

What four classes of drugs can be used to treat an acute migraine?

{{c1::Analgesics}}
{{c1::Triptans}}
{{c1::Ergots}}
{{c1::Antiemetics}}

What is the role of verapamil in the treatment of cluster headaches?

{{c1::Prophylactic}} treatment

What is the likely type of headache with a short lasting, excruciating pain, distributed as shown in the image?



{{c1::Cluster}} headache

Describe the typical pattern of pain episodes in trigeminal neuralgia.

Pain is usually {{c1::unilateral::unilateral/bilateral}}, {{c1::shooting}}/{{c1::shock}}-like over CN V distribution
Episodes often {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} in intensity and frequency over time
fields.Back Extra: This initially lasts a few seconds to minutes.

fields.Text:
Headaches in general are caused by irritation of what structures in the head?

{{c1::Dura}}
Cranial {{c1::nerves}}
{{c1::Extracranial}} structures

What are 2 therapeutic options used to treat acute cluster headaches?

Inhaled {{c1::oxygen}}
{{c1::Sumatriptan}}

What neurochemicals are involved in the pathogenesis of migraine?

Vasoactive neuropeptides such as {{c1::substance P}} and {{c1::calcitonin gene-related peptide}}

What 3 actions can trigger trigeminal neuralgia?

{{c1::Talking}}
{{c1::Chewing}}
{{c1::Touching}} certain areas of the face

What are the five most common causes of seizures in children less than 18 years old?

{{c1::Genetic}} disorders
{{c1::Infections}}
{{c1::Trauma}}
{{c1::Congenital}} abnormalities
{{c1::Metabolic}} derangement

What are the five most common causes of seizures in adults older than 65 years?

{{c1::Stroke}}
{{c1::Tumor}}
{{c1::Trauma}}
{{c1::Metabolic}} derangement
{{c1::Infection}}

What are the four most common causes of seizures in adults ages 18 to 65?

{{c1::Tumor}}
{{c1::Trauma}}
{{c1::Stroke}}
{{c1::Infection}}

What common seizure type is not classified as epilepsy?

{{c1::Febrile}} seizures

Which type of seizure is commonly mistaken for fainting?

{{c1::Atonic}} seizure

How would a tonic seizure manifest?

Sudden generalized {{c1::stiffening}}

What type of generalized seizure features rapid, repetitive jerking movements of all extremities without loss of consciousness?

{{c1::Myoclonic}} seizure

What classic EEG pattern is seen during an absence seizure?

{{c1::3}} Hz {{c1::spike-and-wave}} discharges

What type of seizure will result in alternating stiffening and jerking movements of all limbs?

{{c1::Tonic-clonic}} seizure
fields.Back Extra: This is a type of generalized seizure.

fields.Text:
How does neuronal firing during a seizure differ from normal brain activity?

Neuronal firing is {{c1::synchronized}} and {{c1::high::high/low}}-frequency during a seizure

From which part of the brain do partial seizures most commonly originate?

{{c1::Medial temporal}} lobe

What do you call a disorder of recurrent, unprovoked seizures?

{{c1::Epilepsy}}

What are the 2 types of partial seizures?

{{c1::Simple}} partial seizure
{{c1::Complex}} partial seizure

What are the 5 common types of generalized seizures?

{{c1::Absence}}
{{c1::Myoclonic}}
{{c1::Tonic-clonic}}
{{c1::Tonic}}
{{c1::Atonic}}

A person has abnormal body movements with loss of consciousness for approximately 10 minutes. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Status epilepticus}}

What is the difference between partial and generalized seizures?

Partial seizures affect a {{c1::single}} area of the brain
Generalized seizures are {{c1::diffuse}} across the brain

What are 3 common consequences of tonic-clonic seizures?

Postictal {{c1::confusion}}
Tongue {{c1::biting}}
Urinary {{c1::incontinence}}

What type of seizure is associated with brief and frequent episodes of blank stares?

{{c1::Absence}} seizure

What can trigger an absence seizure?

{{c1::Hyperventilation}}

A patient presents with evidence of a large stroke. What artery is likely occluded by a thrombus?



{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::middle cerebral}} artery

What kind of necrosis would be found in the brain at autopsy if a patient died of stroke?

{{c1::Liquefactive}} necrosis

What is the most common cause of thrombotic stroke?

{{c1::Atherosclerotic plaque}} rupture

How would an echocardiogram with bubble study benefit a patient who has a new ischemic stroke and a history of DVT?

This procedure can rule out a {{c1::patent foramen ovale}} or {{c1::atrial septal}} defect

For what type of stroke is a patient at risk if he develops sudden hypotension while undergoing cardiac surgery?

{{c1::Hypoxic}} stroke
fields.Back Extra: It is common in cardiovascular surgeries and typically affects watershed areas.

fields.Text:
What are 3 methods of decreasing future stroke risk in a patient with history of stroke?

{{c1::Antiplatelet}} therapy
Management of {{c1::comorbidities}}
Control of {{c1::blood pressure}}, blood {{c1::glucose}}, {{c1::lipid}} levels

What is the treatment available for emergent stroke?

{{c1::tPA}}
{{c1::Thrombectomy}}
fields.Back Extra: If a stroke occurred in the past 3 to 4.5 hours, tPA can be given to a patient who has no contraindications.

fields.Text:
A patient develops an acute right facial palsy. Function returns 10 minutes later. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Transient ischemic attack}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a brief, reversible period of neurologic dysfunction from focal ischemia with no MRI findings.

fields.Text:
What are the 3 most common types of ischemic stroke?

{{c1::Embolic}}
{{c1::Thrombotic}}
{{c1::Hypoxic}}

Which treatment would benefit a patient with occlusion of a large vessel in cerebral circulation?

{{c1::Thrombectomy}}

After a stroke, how long do ischemic changes to the brain take to appear on a CT scan image?

{{c1::6}} to {{c1::24}} hours
fields.Back Extra: A noncontrast CT is obtained to rule out hemorrhage before therapy is started.

fields.Text:
What imaging modality would be most sensitive in diagnosing an ischemic stroke within 30 minutes of onset?

{{c1::Diffusion-weighted MRI}}
fields.Back Extra:
This can detect ischemia within 3 to 30 minutes of onset.

A CT scan would be indicated first to rule out hemorrhage.

fields.Text:
Why does a patient with suspected stroke need CT scan imaging before initiation of therapy?

To exclude {{c1::hemorrhage}} before the administration of {{c1::tPA}}

How long would it take for a glial scar to appear in an area of ischemic stroke?

More than {{c1::2}} weeks

What are the histologic features of brain tissue obtained from a patient who had an ischemic stroke within the past 12 to 24 hours?

{{c1::Red}} neurons with {{c1::eosinophilic}} cytoplasm

What are the histologic features of brain tissue obtained from a patient who had an ischemic stroke 4 days ago?

An infiltrate of {{c1::macrophages}} is most often seen 3 to 5 days after an ischemic injury

What are the histologic features of brain tissue obtained from a patient who had an ischemic stroke 2 days ago?

{{c1::Necrosis}}
{{c1::Neutrophilic}} infiltrate
fields.Back Extra: This is most likely to be seen 24 to 72 hours after an ischemic event.

fields.Text:
What four regions of the brain are most vulnerable to ischemic injury?

{{c1::Hippocampus}}
{{c1::Neocortex}}
{{c1::Cerebellum}}
{{c1::Watershed}} areas

After how many minutes of hypoxia does irreversible brain damage begin?

{{c1::5}} minutes

What are 4 major risk factors/conditions associated with an embolic ischemic stroke?

{{c1::Atrial fibrillation}}
Infective {{c1::endocarditis}}
{{c1::Carotid}} artery stenosis
{{c1::DVT}} with {{c1::patent foramen ovale}}

Where does the fluid accumulate in cerebral edema?

Brain {{c1::parenchyma}}

What are the three causes of cytotoxic cerebral edema?

Early {{c1::ischemia}}
{{c1::SIADH}}
{{c1::Hyperammonemia}}
fields.Back Extra: This results in an intracellular accumulation of fluids due to osmotic shift.

fields.Text:
What are the five causes of vasogenic cerebral edema?

Late {{c1::ischemia}}
{{c1::Trauma}}
{{c1::Inflammation}}
{{c1::Hemorrhage}}
{{c1::Tumors}}
fields.Back Extra: This results in a disruption of the blood-brain barrier and an accumulation of extracellular fluid.

fields.Text:
In a patient presenting with the MRI findings shown, what neurologic deficits would you expect to see on your assessment?



{{c1::Right::Left/Right}}-sided {{c1::dysmetria}}/{{c1::ataxia}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a right cerebellar infarction.

fields.Text:
In a patient presenting with the MRI findings shown, what neurologic deficits would you expect to see on your assessment?



{{c1::Left::Left/Right}}-sided {{c1::paralysis}} with no {{c1::cortical}} signs
fields.Back Extra: The patient has a right-sided lacunar infarct.

fields.Text:
In a patient presenting with the MRI findings shown, what neurologic deficits would you expect to see on your assessment?



{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::upper::upper/lower}} limb and {{c1::facial}} sensory loss and paresis
Variable {{c1::aphasia}} and {{c1::visual}} deficits
fields.Back Extra: Patient has had a left-sided middle cerebral artery stroke.

fields.Text:
In a patient presenting with the MRI findings shown, what neurologic deficits would you expect to see on your assessment?



{{c1::Right::Left/Right}}-sided {{c1::homonymous hemianopia}} with {{c1::macular sparing}}
{{c1::Alexia}} without {{c1::agraphia}} if dominant hemisphere is involved
fields.Back Extra: The patient has a left posterior cerebral artery stroke.

fields.Text:
What cerebellar peduncles are supplied by the anterior inferior cerebellar artery and posterior inferior cerebellar artery?

Anterior inferior cerebellar artery → {{c1::Middle}} and {{c1::inferior}}
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery → {{c1::Inferior }}
fields.Back Extra: Infarcts in either distribution may produce cerebellar symptoms.

fields.Text:
What symptom is especially characteristic of an infarct in the anterior inferior cerebellar artery and why?

{{c1::Ipsilateral::Ipsilateral/Contralateral}} {{c1::facial droop}} and loss of taste from {{c1::anterior::anterior/posterior}} {{c1::2}}/3 of tongue due to infarction of the {{c1::facial nucleus}}

A patient presents with vertigo, nystagmus, loss of sensation, dysmetria, hearing loss, and a unilateral facial droop. What artery is affected?

{{c1::Anterior inferior cerebellar}} artery
fields.Back Extra: This supplies the lateral pons and middle and inferior cerebellar peduncles.

fields.Text:
A patient presents with vertigo, nystagmus, loss of sensation, dysmetria, hearing loss, and a unilateral facial droop. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Lateral pontine}} syndrome

What brainstem reflex is classically impaired in Wallenberg syndrome?

{{c1::Gag}} reflex
fields.Back Extra: This is mediated by cranial nerves IX and X.

fields.Text:
What symptom is especially characteristic of an infarct in the posterior inferior cerebellar artery and why?

{{c1::Hoarseness}}/{{c1::dysphagia}} due to infarct of the {{c1::nucleus ambiguus}}

A patient presents with vertigo, reduced arm and face sensation, dysphagia, Horner syndrome, and ataxia. Which artery is affected?

{{c1::Posterior inferior cerebellar}} artery
fields.Back Extra: This supplies the lateral medulla and inferior cerebellar peduncle.

fields.Text:
A patient presents with vertigo, reduced pain and temperature sensation in contralateral arm, ipsilateral Horner syndrome, and ataxia. His facial nerve is unaffected. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Lateral medullary}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as Wallenberg syndrome.

fields.Text:
What are the brain regions affected in anterior inferior cerebellar artery stroke?

{{c1::Facial}} nerve nucleus
{{c1::Vestibular}} nuclei
{{c1::Spinothalamic}} tract
{{c1::Spinal trigeminal}} nuclei
{{c1::Middle}} and {{c1::inferior}} cerebellar peduncles
{{c1::Labyrinthine}} artery
{{c1::Sympathetic}} fibers

A patient has right-sided weakness, right proprioceptive loss, and a left-deviating tongue. Which artery is involved?

{{c1::Paramedian}} branches of the {{c1::anterior spinal}} artery
{{c1::Vertebral}} arteries

A patient has right-sided weakness, right proprioceptive loss, and a left-deviating tongue. Where is the lesion?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::medial medulla}}

A patient presents with fluent but nonsensical speech. She cannot follow commands or repeat phrases. What visual field defect is likely present?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::superior quadrantanopia}}
fields.Back Extra:
This is due to involvement of the inferior optic radiation in the left temporal lobe.

This is likely a middle cerebral artery stroke.

fields.Text:
What symptoms are characteristically absent in a patient with a lacunar infarct?

{{c1::Cortical}} signs
fields.Back Extra: Lacunar strokes are subcortical by definition.

fields.Text:
What mechanism underlies the development of a lacunar infarct in patients with hypertension?

{{c1::Hyaline arteriosclerosis}} of the {{c1::lenticulostriate}} arteries secondary to chronic hypertension

What neurologic deficits do you expect to see in a patient with a lacunar infarct?

{{c1::Paralysis}} {{c1::contralateral::ipsilateral/contralateral}} to the lesion with no {{c1::cortical}} signs

What regions of the brain are most likely affected in a patient with a lacunar infarct?

{{c1::Striatum}}
{{c1::Internal capsule}}
fields.Back Extra: These are supplied by the lenticulostriate arteries.

fields.Text:
A patient has acute-onset left leg weakness, loss of left leg sensation, and urinary incontinence. Where is the stroke most likely located?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::anterior cerebral}} artery distribution
fields.Back Extra: This supplies the medial aspects of the primary somatosensory and motor cortices.

fields.Text:
What artery is likely occluded in a patient with locked-in syndrome?

{{c1::Basilar}} artery
fields.Back Extra: This supplies most of the pons and is often compromised in locked-in syndrome.

fields.Text:
Sparing of which structure allows consciousness to be preserved in a patient who has had a basilar artery stroke?

{{c1::Reticular activating system}}

A patient loses sensation and strength in her right arm and face. She has broken speech and is visibly frustrated. In which arterial territory is the stroke located?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::middle cerebral}} artery distribution

A patient suddenly loses the right visual field of each eye but retains some of the center field. What artery was affected?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::posterior cerebral}} artery

A patient loses sensation and strength in the left arm and lower face and has evidence of neglect on the left side as well. Where is the stroke located?

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::middle cerebral}} artery distribution

What brain region is affected by a posterior inferior cerebellar artery stroke?

{{c1::Lateral medulla}}

A patient presents with left-sided facial droop, left-sided hearing loss, and vertigo. Infarct of which artery caused hearing loss and vertigo?

{{c1::Labyrinthine}} artery
fields.Back Extra: This is a branch of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery.

fields.Text:
What type of intracranial hemorrhage is likely to be seen in patients with systemic hypertension, amyloid angiopathy, vasculitis, a vascular malformation, or reperfusion injury?

{{c1::Intraparenchymal hemorrhage}}

What diagnosis do you give a patient presenting with the CT scan findings shown?



{{c1::Intraparenchymal hemorrhage}}

In a patient who has an epidural hematoma, what bony region is likely fractured in the skull and why?

The {{c1::pterion}}, which is the {{c1::thinnest}} area of the lateral skull

What type of hemorrhage is seen on this CT scan?



{{c1::Epidural hematoma}}

What diagnosis do you give a patient presenting with the CT scan findings shown?



{{c1::Subarachnoid hemorrhage}}
fields.Back Extra: There is blood in the basal cisterns.

fields.Text:
What type of intracranial hemorrhage is shown by the blue arrows in the image?



"{{c1::Acute on chronic}}" {{c1::subdural hematoma}}

What type of intracranial hemorrhage is indicated by the red arrow in the image?



{{c1::Acute::Acute/Chronic}} {{c1::subdural hematoma}}

Rupture of which artery is most often implicated in an epidural hematoma?

{{c1::Middle meningeal}} artery
fields.Back Extra: This is a branch of the maxillary artery.

fields.Text:
Where are intraparenchymal hypertensive hemorrhages most likely to occur?

{{c1::Lenticulostriate}} vessels in the {{c1::putamen}} of the {{c1::basal ganglia}}
fields.Back Extra: This is followed by the thalamus, pons, and cerebellum.

fields.Text:
What are 2 key predisposing factors for subdural hematomas?

{{c1::Trauma}}
Cerebral {{c1::atrophy}}
fields.Back Extra: This causes retraction of the parenchyma and "stretches" bridging veins.

fields.Text:
What is the likely cause of altered mental status in a patient from a nursing home who had several falls and has a crescent-shaped hemorrhage on CT?

{{c1::Subdural hematoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the result of shearing injury from the falls.

fields.Text:
What are 2 complications of epidural hematoma expansion?

{{c1::Transtentorial herniation}}
Cranial nerve {{c1::III}} palsy

A patient is struck on the side of the head by a baseball bat. He appears fine initially but becomes obtunded 30 minutes later. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Epidural hematoma}}
fields.Back Extra: The patient had a classic lucid interval followed by hematoma expansion.

fields.Text:
What 2 vascular anomalies can result in subarachnoid hemorrhage?

Rupture of {{c1::saccular aneurysm}}
{{c1::Arteriovenous}} malformation

What type of intracranial hemorrhage presents with "the worst headache of my life" and a spinal tap showing xanthochromia?

{{c1::Subarachnoid hemorrhage}}

What 2 kinds of hydrocephalus is a patient at risk for after a subarachnoid hemorrhage?

{{c1::Obstructive}} hydrocephalus → Blood clogs a foramen or aqueduct
{{c1::Communicating}} hydrocephalus → Arachnoid granulations are blocked

What medication can prevent vasospasm after a subarachnoid hemorrhage?

{{c1::Nimodipine}}

What complication commonly occurs in the first 3 to 10 days after the development of a subarachnoid hemorrhage?

{{c1::Ischemic infarct}}
fields.Back Extra: This occurs secondary to vasospasm due to blood breakdown.

fields.Text:
What type of hematoma would you expect to see on a CT scan of the head of a baby who is shaken by a frustrated mother and shortly afterward becomes obtunded?

{{c1::Subdural hematoma}}
fields.Back Extra: This is produced by the shearing of sensitive bridging veins within the immature skull.

fields.Text:
What is the most likely underlying cause of recurrent cortical intraparenchymal hemorrhages in different lobes in an elderly male with Alzheimer disease?

{{c1::Amyloid angiopathy}}
fields.Back Extra: This leads to recurrent lobar hemorrhagic strokes in the elderly.

fields.Text:
What type of intracranial hematoma crosses suture lines?

{{c1::Subdural hematoma}}

Which structure does neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage originate from?

{{c1::Germinal matrix}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a highly vascularized zone within the subventricular zone.

fields.Text:
Why are premature and low-birth-weight infants at higher risk for intraventricular hemorrhage?

Reduced {{c1::glial}} fiber support
Impaired {{c1::blood pressure}} autoregulation

A coronal transcranial sonogram of a premature infant is shown. What is the diagnosis?



{{c1::Neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage}}

What term describes pain caused by ordinarily painless stimuli?

{{c1::Allodynia}}

Where are lesions that give rise to central poststroke pain syndrome located?

{{c1::Thalamus}}

What can lead to pain, even with the slightest touch, years after a person experiences sensory deficits in an arm and leg after a stroke?

{{c1::Central poststroke pain}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: It presents with early paresthesias and evolves into allodynia and dysesthesia in 10% of patients who have had a stroke.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of developing phantom limb pain?

{{c1::Reorganization}} of primary {{c1::somatosensory}} cortex

What does phantom limb pain feel like?

{{c1::Aching}}, {{c1::burning}}, or {{c1::electric shock}}-like pain in a limb that is no longer present after amputation

On which part of the nephron do thiazides diuretics act?

{{c1::Distal convoluted tubule}}
fields.Back Extra: This is located in the cortex.

fields.Text:
How permeable to H2O is the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle?

{{c1::Impermeable}} to H2O

What are the main electrolytes/molecules reabsorbed at the proximal convoluted tubule?

{{c1::Na+}}
{{c1::Sugars}}
{{c1::Amino acids}}
{{c1::HCO3-}}

Which part of the nephron is freely permeable to H2O, but not to electrolytes?

{{c1::Thin::Thick/Thin}} {{c1::descending::ascending/descending}} limb of the loop of Henle

Where are Ca2+ and Mg2+ reabsorbed by the nephron?

The {{c1::cortical}} portion of the {{c1::thick::thick/thin}} {{c1::ascending::ascending/descending}} limb of the loop of Henle

On which segments of the nephron does mannitol exert its major diuretic effects?

{{c1::Proximal convoluted tubule}}
Portion of {{c1::medullary}} part of the {{c1::descending::ascending/descending}} limb of the loop of Henle

What are the main electrolytes absorbed and secreted by the site of the nephron on which K+-sparing diuretics act?

Reabsorbed → {{c1::Na+}}
Secreted → {{c1::K+}} and {{c1::H+}}
fields.Back Extra: They act on the cortical collecting duct.

fields.Text:
On which segments of the nephron does acetazolamide exert its major diuretic effects?

{{c1::Proximal convoluted tubule}}
{{c1::Cortical}} part of the {{c1::descending::ascending/descending}} limb of the loop of Henle

On which part of the nephron do loop diuretics act?

{{c1::Ascending::Ascending/Descending}} limb of the loop of Henle
fields.Back Extra: This is in both the cortex and medulla.

fields.Text:
What are the adverse effects of mannitol?

{{c1::Dehydration}}
Pulmonary {{c1::edema}}
{{c1::Hypernatremia}} or {{c1::hyponatremia}}

What is the mechanism of action of mannitol?

Increases serum {{c1::osmolality}} → Fluid shift from {{c1::interstitium}} to {{c1::intravascular space}} →  {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} urine flow →  {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} intracranial/intraocular pressure

What are two contraindications to mannitol use?

{{c1::Anuria}}
{{c1::Heart::Organ}} failure

Name two clinical uses for mannitol.

Elevated {{c1::intracranial}}/{{c1::intraocular}} pressure
Drug {{c1::overdoses}}

What adverse effects can occur with aliskiren?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} glomerular filtration rate
{{c1::Hypotension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Angioedema}}
{{c1::Hyperkalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}

How does aliskiren affect angiotensinogen, angiotensin I, and angiotensin II levels?

Angiotensinogen {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}
Angiotensin I {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
Angiotensin II {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}

What is the mechanism of aliskiren?

Direct {{c1::renin}} inhibition → Blocks conversion of {{c1::angiotensinogen}} to {{c1::angiotensin I}}

Name relative contraindications to aliskiren use.

Relative contraindication → Current treatment with {{c1::ACE}} inhibitors or {{c1::angiotensin II}} receptor blockers
Full contraindication → {{c1::Pregnancy}}

What is the clinical use for aliskiren?

{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}

Name some clinical indications for acetazolamide.

{{c1::Altitude sickness}}
{{c1::Glaucoma}}
Idiopathic intracranial {{c1::hypertension::hypertension/hypotension}}
Metabolic {{c1::alkalosis::acidosis/alkalosis}}

How does acetazolamide increase calcium phosphate stone formation?

Acetazolamide {{c1::alkalinizes}} urine → Decreases solubility at {{c1::high::high/low}} pH

What is the mechanism of action of acetazolamide?

{{c1::Carbonic anhydrase}} inhibitor → Self-limited {{c1::NaHCO3}} diuresis and reduction in total body {{c1::HCO3-}} stores

What are the common adverse effects associated with acetazolamide?

{{c1::Hypokalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
Formation of {{c1::calcium phosphate}} stones
{{c1::Paresthesias}}
{{c1::NH3}} toxicity
{{c1::Sulfa}} allergy
Proximal {{c1::renal tubular acidosis}}

In what part of the nephron does acetazolamide act?

{{c1::Proximal convoluted tubule}}

What type of drug allergy is acetazolamide associated with?

{{c1::Sulfa}} allergy

Which class of diuretics acts on the boxed part of the nephron in the image?



{{c1::Loop diuretics}}

What is the most concerning toxicity of ethacrynic acid, especially as compared with other loop diuretics?

Ethacrynic acid is much more {{c1::ototoxic}} than the sulfonamide loop diuretics

How do loop diuretics dilate the afferent arterioles?

By stimulating {{c1::PGE}} release

When would ethacrynic acid be used in place of furosemide or other loop diuretics?

Diuresis in patients allergic to {{c1::sulfa}} drugs
fields.Back Extra: Ethacrynic acid is a nonsulfonamide drug.

fields.Text:
Name eight toxicities associated with use of loop diuretics.

{{c1::Ototoxicity}}
{{c1::Hypokalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
{{c1::Hypomagnesemia::Hypermagnesemia/Hypomagnesemia}}
{{c1::Dehydration}}
{{c1::Sulfa}} allergy
Metabolic {{c1::alkalosis::acidosis/alkalosis}}
{{c1::Nephritis}}
{{c1::Gout}}

What is the effect of the loop diuretic furosemide on Ca2+ handling in the kidney nephron?

Furosemide {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} Ca2+ excretion

What is the mechanism of action of loop diuretics?

Inhibits cotransporters in the {{c1::thick::thick/thin}} {{c1::ascending::ascending/descending}} limb of the loop of Henle
Abolishes medullary {{c1::hypertonicity::hypertonicity/hypotonicity}} → Prevents {{c1::urine}} concentration
Increased {{c1::PGE}} release

What are general clinical uses for loop diuretics?

{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Edematous}} states
{{c1::Hypercalcemia::Hypercalcemia/Hypocalcemia}}

How do loop diuretics and thiazide diuretics differ in their effect on serum calcium?

Loop diuretics {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} serum Ca2+
Thiazide diuretics {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} serum Ca2+

NSAIDs have an inhibitory effect on what aspect of loop diuretic activity?

They inhibit {{c1::PGE}}-induced afferent arteriole vasodilation

How does hydrochlorothiazide reduce levels of Ca2+ in the urine?

Increases {{c1::distal convoluted tubule}} reabsorption of Ca2+

Why should treatment of hypertension with hydrochlorothiazide be avoided for a patient with gout and diabetes?

Hydrochlorothiazide increases levels of both {{c1::uric acid}} and {{c1::glucose}}
fields.Back Extra: This may worsen gout and diabetes.

fields.Text:
What acid-base abnormality is associated with thiazide diuretic use?

{{c1::Hypokalemic::Hyperkalemic/Hypokalemic}} metabolic {{c1::alkalosis::acidosis/alkalosis}}

Serum levels of which substances are increased as a result of the effects of thiazide diuretics such as metolazone?

{{c1::Glucose}}
{{c1::Lipids}}
{{c1::Uric acid}}
{{c1::Calcium}}

What is the mechanism of action of thiazide diuretics?

Reduces the {{c1::diluting}} capacity of the kidney nephron by inhibiting {{c1::NaCl}} reabsorption in the early {{c1::distal convoluted tubule}}

What are clinical uses for thiazide diuretics?

{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Heart::Organ}} failure
Idiopathic {{c1::hypercalciuria::hypercalciuria/hypocalciuria}}
{{c1::Osteoporosis}}
Nephrogenic {{c1::diabetes insipidus}}

Thiazide diuretics cannot be prescribed for patients with which allergy?

{{c1::Sulfa}} allergy

Hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, metolazone are examples of drugs of which class?

{{c1::Thiazide diuretics}}

Which class of diuretics acts on the boxed part of the nephron in the diagram shown?



{{c1::Thiazide diuretics}}

What clinical manifestation can be caused by the endocrine effects of spironolactone therapy, especially in male patients?

{{c1::Gynecomastia}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to antiandrogen effects.

fields.Text:
What electrolyte change would you be most worried about in a patient taking amiloride or spironolactone?

{{c1::Hyperkalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}

Name some clinical uses of K+-sparing diuretics.

{{c1::Potassium}} depletion
{{c1::Hyperaldosteronism::Hyperaldosteronism/Hypoaldosteronism}}
Nephrogenic {{c1::diabetes insipidus}}
{{c1::Heart::Organ}} failure
Hepatic {{c1::ascites}}
{{c1::Antiandrogen}}

What is the mechanism of action of triamterene and amiloride?

Blocks {{c1::Na+}} channels in the cortical {{c1::collecting tubule}}

What are the mechanisms of action of spironolactone and eplerenone?

Competitively antagonize the {{c1::aldosterone}} receptor in the cortical {{c1::collecting tubule}}

Name four potassium-sparing diuretics that act on the cortical collecting tubule.

{{c1::Spironolactone}}
{{c1::Eplerenone}}
{{c1::Amiloride}}
{{c1::Triamterene}}

What class of diuretics acts on the boxed part of the nephron in the diagram?



{{c1::Potassium-sparing diuretics}}

What are the common adverse effects associated with use of potassium-sparing diuretics?

{{c1::Hyperkalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
{{c1::Endocrine}} abnormalities
Metabolic {{c1::acidosis::acidosis/alkalosis}}

How does a low K+ state lead to alkalemia and paradoxical aciduria?

{{c1::H+}}, rather than K+, is exchanged for {{c1::Na+}} at the cortical collecting tubule

By what mechanism, involving all cells, does K+ loss lead to alkalemia?

K+ exits all cells in exchange for {{c1::H+}} entering cells to maintain plasma concentration of {{c1::K+}}

All diuretics cause what changes to serum and urine sodium?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} serum sodium
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} urine sodium
fields.Back Extra: The strength varies based on potency of diuretic effect.

fields.Text:
What mechanism underlies volume contraction alkalosis?

Volume contraction increases {{c1::angiotensin II}} → Increased {{c1::Na+}}/{{c1::H+}} exchange in the proximal convoluted tubule and {{c1::HCO3-}} reabsorption

What is the effect on urinary Ca2+ excretion of loop diuretics and thiazide diuretics?

Loop diuretics {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} Ca2+ in urine
Thiazide diuretics {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} Ca2+ in urine

What happens to blood pH with overuse of loop and thiazide diuretics?

Loop diuretics and thiazide diuretics {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} blood pH

How does a loop diuretic affect K+ levels in the serum and urine?

{{c1::Lowers::Raises/Lowers}} serum K+ levels
{{c1::Raises::Raises/Lowers}} urine K+ levels

How does acetazolamide cause acidemia?

Causes the kidney to decrease {{c1::HCO3-}} reabsorption → Decreased body pH → Acidemia

What is the mechanism by which K+-sparing diuretics cause acidemia?

{{c1::Aldosterone}} blockade prevents {{c1::K+}} and {{c1::H+}} secretion

Why are ACE inhibitors contraindicated for patients with C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency?

ACE inhibitors must be avoided to prevent the adverse effect of {{c1::angioedema}}

How does an ACE inhibitor slow diabetic nephropathy?

ACE inhibitors {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}} intraglomerular pressure → Slows glomerular basement membrane {{c1::thickening::thickening/thinning}}

What are some clinical uses for ACE inhibitors?

{{c1::Proteinuria}}
{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Heart::Organ}} failure
{{c1::Diabetic}} nephropathy
Prevention of {{c1::heart::organ}} remodeling from chronic hypertension

Why might patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis develop renal failure when taking an ACE inhibitor?

ACE inhibitors lower {{c1::angiotensin II}} levels
fields.Back Extra: These patients are dependent on angiotensin II to maintain their glomerular filtration rate.

fields.Text:
Why are ACE inhibitors contraindicated in pregnancy?

They are {{c1::teratogens}}
May cause fetal {{c1::renal}} malformations

How would you expect creatinine levels to change immediately after administration of an ACE inhibitor?

Transient {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} of creatinine levels
fields.Back Extra: There would be a decrease in efferent arteriole pressure.

fields.Text:
Which electrolyte abnormality can cause arrhythmias in patients taking captopril?

{{c1::Hyperkalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}

How can an ACE inhibitor cause cough and/or angioedema?

By preventing inactivation of {{c1::bradykinin}}

What medication replacement would you suggest for a patient experiencing a dry cough while taking lisinopril?

{{c1::Angiotensin II}} receptor blocker
fields.Back Extra: It is less likely to cause coughing as a side effect.

fields.Text:
Why does a high serum renin level occur when ACE inhibitors are administered?

Loss of {{c1::negative::positive/negative}} feedback

What is the mechanism of action of a drug such as lisinopril?

Lisinopril is an {{c1::ACE}} inhibitor → Inhibits {{c1::ACE}} → Decreased {{c1::angiotensin II}} → Reduced blood pressure

What adverse effects can occur with ACE inhibitors?

{{c1::Cough}}
{{c1::Angioedema}}
{{c1::Teratogenicity}}
Increased {{c1::creatinine}} levels
{{c1::Hyperkalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
{{c1::Hypotension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}

Name some clinical indications for angiotensin II receptor blockers.

{{c1::Heart::Organ}} failure
{{c1::Proteinuria}}
{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
Chronic kidney disease with intolerance to {{c1::ACE}} inhibitors

What are the adverse effects of angiotensin II receptor blockers?

{{c1::Hyperkalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
Decreased {{c1::renal}} function
{{c1::Hypotension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Teratogenicity}}

How do angiotensin II receptor blockers affect levels of renin, angiotensin I, and angiotensin II?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} renin levels
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} angiotensin I levels
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} angiotensin II levels

What is the mechanism of action of candesartan?

Selectively blocks binding of {{c1::angiotensin II}} to {{c1::AT1}} receptor

How do serum levels of angiotensin II differ with ACE inhibitors when compared with angiotensin II receptor blockers?

ACE inhibitors → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} angiotensin II levels
Angiotensin II receptor blockers → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} angiotensin II levels

What type of psychotherapy utilizes empathy to help individuals during a difficult time to maintain hope or optimism?

{{c1::Supportive}} therapy

What type of psychotherapy focuses on improving an individual's relationships and communication skills?

{{c1::Interpersonal}} therapy

What type of psychotherapy teaches patients to identify and change reactions to stimuli/maladaptive behaviors?

{{c1::Behavioral}} therapy

What type of psychotherapy teaches patients to develop constructive coping mechanisms, decrease maladaptive coping behaviors, and recognize distorted thought processes?

{{c1::Congnitive behavioral}} therapy

Which therapy is used in borderline personality disorder and depression?

{{c1::Dialectical behavioral}} therapy

What form of interviewing explores and resolves ambivalence and is used in substance use disorder and weight loss?

{{c1::Motivational}} interviewing

Which medication class is typically used to treat patients experiencing withdrawal from alcohol?

{{c1::Benzodiazepines}}

What is the treatment for social anxiety disorder?

{{c1::SSRIs}}
{{c1::Venlafaxine}}

What is the treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder and the associated nightmares?

{{c1::SSRIs}}
{{c1::Venlafaxine}}
{{c1::Prazosin}} (nightmares)

What is the treatment for attention-deficient hyperactivity disorder?

{{c1::Stimulants}}

What is the treatment of choice for Tourette syndrome?

{{c1::Antipsychotics}}
{{c1::Tetrabenazine}}

What is the treatment for schizophrenia?

{{c1::Atypical antipsychotics}}

What medications are preferred for treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder?

{{c1::SSRIs}}
{{c1::Venlafaxine}}
{{c1::Clomipramine}}

What three medication classes are used for the treatment of panic disorder?

{{c1::SSRIs}}
{{c1::Venlafaxine}}
{{c1::Benzodiazepines}}

What is the first-line drug class for major depressive disorder?

{{c1::SSRIs}}

What are the two first-line drug classes for generalized anxiety disorder?

{{c1::SSRIs}}
{{c1::SNRIs}}

What is the first-line drug class for bulimia nervosa?

{{c1::SSRIs}}

What medications are used for bipolar disorder?

{{c1::Mood stabilizers}}

Which two drug classes are indicated in performance-only social anxiety disorder?

{{c1::β-blockers}}
{{c1::Benzodiazepines}}

The following adverse effects may be present in a patient being treated by which class of central nervous system drugs?

Nervousness
Hypertension
Insomnia
Agitation
Anxiety
Anorexia
Tachycardia
Tics
Bruxism
Weight loss

{{c1::Stimulants}}

What three conditions can central nervous system stimulants be used to treat?

{{c1::Binge-eating}} disorder
{{c1::Attention-deficit hyperactivity}} disorder
{{c1::Narcolepsy}}

What is the mechanism of action of central nervous system stimulants?

They increase {{c1::catecholamine}} release at the synaptic cleft

What are four central nervous system stimulants?

{{c1::Dextroamphetamine}}
{{c1::Methylphenidate}}
{{c1::Lisdexamfetamine}}
{{c1::Methamphetamine}}

Name four high-potency typical antipsychotics.

{{c1::Haloperidol}}
{{c1::Trifluoperazine}}
{{c1::Pimozide}}
{{c1::Fluphenazine}}

Which drug class can cause neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

{{c1::Antipsychotics}}

What could be the cause of a prolonged QT interval in a patient treated for schizophrenia?

The use of typical or atypical {{c1::antipsychotics}}

What is the reason for the long half-life of antipsychotics?

They are {{c1::lipid}} soluble and stored in {{c1::fat}}
fields.Back Extra: Hence, they are slowly eliminated from the body.

fields.Text:
Put the following extrapyramidal symptoms in the order in which they occur.

Tardive dyskinesia
Akathisia
Dystonia
Bradykinesia

Hours to days → {{c1::Dystonia}}
Days to months → {{c1::Akathisia}} and/or {{c1::bradykinesia}}
Months to years → {{c1::Tardive dyskinesia}}

What are the adverse effects of higher potency antipsychotics such as haloperidol, trifluoperazine, and fluphenazine?

{{c1::Neurologic}} effects

What are the ophthalmologic adverse effects of chlorpromazine?

{{c1::Corneal deposits}}

Which two typical antipsychotics are considered low-potency drugs?

{{c1::Chlorpromazine}}
{{c1::Thioridazine}}

A patient treated with antipsychotics develops difficulty sitting still and paces frequently. What is the adverse effect?

{{c1::Akathisia}}

Through what mechanism do atypical antipsychotics cause dry mouth, constipation, and sedation?

{{c1::Antimuscarinic}} effects
{{c1::Antihistaminic}} effects

By what mechanism do typical antipsychotics cause hypotension?

{{c1::α1}}-blockade

What extrapyramidal adverse effect of antipsychotics is irreversible?

{{c1::Tardive dyskinesia}}

What adverse effect of antipsychotic medications involves sluggishness in initiating purposeful movement days to months after the drug is taken?

{{c1::Bradykinesia}}

What is the treatment for acute dystonia?

{{c1::Benztropine}}
{{c1::Diphenhydramine}}

Describe the mechanism by which antipsychotics cause galactorrhea.

Antipsychotics antagonize {{c1::dopamine}} receptors → Disinhibition of {{c1::prolactin}} → Hyperprolactinemia and galactorrhea

In what two scenarios can treatment with clozapine be considered?

Treatment-resistant {{c1::psychotic}} disorders
Persistent {{c1::suicidality}}

Which two antipsychotic medications have the highest risk for metabolic disturbances?

{{c1::Clozapine}}
{{c1::Olanzapine}}

What blood test should be ordered when a patient is given a new prescription for clozapine?

{{c1::Complete blood cell count}}
fields.Back Extra: This is to monitor absolute neutrophil count because clozapine can cause agranulocytosis.

fields.Text:
What are four clinical uses for antipsychotics apart form schizophrenia?

{{c1::Bipolar}} disorder
{{c1::Obsessive-compulsive}} disorder
{{c1::Huntington}} disease
{{c1::Tourette}} syndrome

How do typical and atypical antipsychotics differ in their ability to target positive and negative symptoms of scizhophrenia?

{{c1::Typical::Typical/Atypical}} antipsychotics treat positive symptoms
{{c1::Atypical::Typical/Atypical}} antipsychotics can treat both positive and negative symptoms

What are the ophthalmologic adverse effects of thioridazine?

{{c1::Retinal deposits}}

How is the mechanism of action of aripiprazole unique in comparison with other antipsychotics?

Aripiprazole is a {{c1::D2}} partial agonist

What major receptors are affected by antipsychotic medications?

{{c1::D2}} receptors are blocked by antipsychotics → Increased {{c1::cAMP}}

What is the treatment for akathisia?

{{c1::β-blockers}}
{{c1::Benztropine}}
{{c1::Benzodiazepines}}

What is the treatment for parkinsonism induced by antipsychotics?

{{c1::Benztropine}}
{{c1::Amantadine}}

Between typical and atypical antipsychotics, which class has a greater affinity for the dopamine receptor?

{{c1::Typical}} antipsychotics
fields.Back Extra: This is why they have an increased risk for hyperprolactinemia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and extrapyramidal symptoms.

fields.Text:
What are four treatments for tardive dyskinesia?

{{c1::Benzodiazepines}}
{{c1::Botulinum}} toxin injections
{{c1::Valbenazine}}
{{c1::Deutetrabenazine}}

What adverse effects are more common with low-potency typical antipsychotics?

{{c1::Antihistaminic}} effects
Anti-{{c1::α1}}-adrenergic effects
{{c1::Antimuscarinic}} effects

What is the normal range for serum osmolality?

{{c1::275}} to {{c1::295}} mOsm/kg H2O

What fluid compartment can radiolabeled albumin measure?

{{c1::Plasma}} volume

What is the 60-40-20 rule for the average person?

60% total body {{c1::water}}
40% {{c1::intracellular}} fluid
20% {{c1::extracellular}} fluid

In which fluid compartment is the concentration of K+ higher?

{{c1::Intracellular}}

What is the total blood volume of an average 70 kg man?

~ {{c1::6}} L
fields.Back Extra:
Total blood volume = Plasma volume + Red blood cell volume

Total blood volume = 3.5 L + 2.8 L

Total blood volume = ~ 6 L

fields.Text:
In a person who weighs 70 kg, what percentage of mass is water?

{{c1::60}}%

What percentage of extracellular fluid is plasma versus interstitial?

Plasma → {{c1::25}}% extracellular fluid
Interstitial → {{c1::75}}% extracellular fluid

What fraction of total body water is extracellular versus intracellular?

Extracellular → {{c1::1}}/3 total body water
Intracellular → {{c1::2}}/3 total body water

In a 70 kg patient, what percentage of the total blood volume is hematocrit?

{{c1::45}}%

The body's intracellular fluid is mainly composed of what three electrolytes?

{{c1::Mg2+}}
{{c1::K+}}
{{c1::Organic phosphates}}

The body's extracellular fluid is mainly composed of what three electrolytes?

{{c1::HCO3-}}
{{c1::Na+}}
{{c1::Cl-}}

What fluid compartment can inulin or mannitol measure?

{{c1::Extracellular}} volume

How is plasma volume calculated in relation to total blood volume and hematocrit?

Plasma volume = {{c1::TBV}} × ( {{c1::1}} - {{c1::Hct}} )

What do podocyte foot processes in the glomerular filtration barrier interpose with to form a size barrier?

Glomerular {{c1::basement membrane}}

What polysaccharide is contained in the renal glomerular basement membrane?

{{c1::Heparan sulfate}}

The glomerular slit diaphragm filters by what parameter?

By {{c1::size}}
fields.Back Extra: It prevents molecules that are over 40 nm to 50 nm from entering.

fields.Text:
The glomerular fenestrated capillary endothelium filters plasma by what parameter?

By {{c1::size}}
fields.Back Extra: It prevents molecules or blood cells that are over 100 nm from entering.

fields.Text:
Which layers of the glomerulus filter by preventing negatively charged molecules, such as albumin, from entering?

{{c1::All}} layers
fields.Back Extra: This is because they all contain negatively charged glycoproteins.

fields.Text:
What are the three components of the glomerular filtration barrier?

{{c1::Fenestrated capillary endothelium}}
{{c1::Basement membrane}}
{{c1::Visceral epithelial}} layer

What is the function of the glomerular filtration barrier?

It filters plasma according to {{c1::size}} and {{c1::charge}} selectively

What is the arrow pointing to in this image of the glomerular filtration barrier?



{{c1::Endothelial cell pore}}

What type of collagen is mainly present in the glomerular basement membrane?

Type {{c1::IV}} collagen

Which cells secrete renin?

{{c1::Juxtaglomerular}} cells

What effects does angiotensin II exert on proximal convoluted tubules?

Increased {{c1::Na+}}/{{c1::H+}} activity on the proximal convoluted tubules → Increased reabsorption of {{c1::HCO3-}}, {{c1::Na+}}, and {{c1::H2O}}

Besides maintaining blood pressure and blood volume, what are two additional physiologic functions of angiotensin II?

Helps regulate {{c1::baroreceptor}} function
Limits {{c1::reflex bradycardia}}

What two peptides involved in the renal-angiotensin-aldosterone system promote natriuresis and dilate renal afferent arterioles?

{{c1::ANP}}
{{c1::BNP}}

How does aldosterone secretion from the adrenal glands create favorable conditions for salt retention?

Acts on renal principal cells to increase {{c1::K+}} conductance, {{c1::Na+/K+ ATPase}}, and {{c1::ENaC}} activity → Increased Na+ reabsorption

What two hormones derived from cardiac tissue inhibit the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system in response to volume overload?

Atria → {{c1::ANP}}
Ventricles → {{c1::BNP}}

How will serum levels of aldosterone and ADH be affected in a patient with hemorrhagic shock?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} aldosterone
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} ADH
fields.Back Extra: This is because they rise in states of severe volume depletion.

fields.Text:
Angiotensin II stimulates release of aldosterone from where?

{{c1::Adrenal}} glands

What are three conditions that lead to increased plasma renin levels?

Decreased {{c1::blood pressure}} detected by renal baroreceptors in afferent arteriole
Decreased delivery of {{c1::NaCl}} to macula densa cells
Increased renal {{c1::sympathetic::sympathetic/parasympathetic}} tone

From which cells is ACE derived and what are its two primary functions?

{{c1::Vascular endothelial}} cells in the lungs and kidneys
ACE cleaves {{c1::angiotensin I}} into {{c1::angiotensin II}} and participates in {{c1::bradykinin}} breakdown

In which organ is the angiotensinogen of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system pathway first synthesized?

{{c1::Liver}}

Angiotensin II acts on the hypothalamus, resulting in what physiologic change?

Increased {{c1::thirst}}

By what mechanism do both ANP and BNP help to decrease blood volume?

ANP and BNP relax vascular smooth muscle via {{c1::cGMP}} → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} GFR → Decreased {{c1::renin}} levels
fields.Back Extra: ANP and BNP also dilate afferent arterioles to increase natriuresis.

fields.Text:
What does ADH primarily regulate and by what mechanism?

Serum {{c1::osmolality}} via {{c1::reabsorption}} of water in the collecting ducts

In addition to water, ADH stimulates reabsorption of what molecule within collecting ducts?

{{c1::Urea}}

What stimulates aldosterone release?

{{c1::Angiotensin II}} stimulation during {{c1::hypovolemic::hypervolemic/hypovolemic}} states and {{c1::hyperkalemia::hyperkalemia/hypokalemia}}

What two cell types in the nephron does aldosterone act on?

{{c1::Principal}} cells
{{c1::α-intercalated}} cells

What is the result of aldosterone binding to receptors on α-intercalated cells?

Increased {{c1::H+ ATPase}} activity

What is the effect of aldosterone binding to receptors on principal cells?

Increased {{c1::Na+/K+-ATPase}} and {{c1::ENaC}} activity → {{c1::Na+}} reabsorption and {{c1::K+}} secretion

On which cell type in the nephron does ADH exert its function?

{{c1::Principal}} cells of collecting ducts → Increased {{c1::aquaporins}} → Increased {{c1::water}} reabsorption

In what tissues does ACE catalyze the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II?

{{c1::Lungs}}

Angiotensin II acts on the adrenal cortex, resulting in what change?

Increased {{c1::aldosterone}} release

Angiotensin II acts on the posterior pituitary, resulting in what change?

Increased {{c1::ADH}} release

Which form of renal tubular acidosis increases the risk of hypophosphatemic rickets in Fanconi syndrome?

Renal tubular acidosis type {{c1::2}}

How would heparin, cyclosporine, NSAIDs, and ACE inhibitors lead to renal tubular acidosis?

Decreased production of {{c1::aldosterone}} → Renal tubular acidosis type {{c1::4}}

Identify the two broad categories of disorders that lead to renal tubular acidosis type 4.

Low {{c1::aldosterone}} production
Resistance to {{c1::aldosterone}}

Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, multiple myeloma, and Fanconi syndrome can cause which type of renal tubular acidosis?

Renal tubular acidosis type {{c1::2}}

Amphotericin B, analgesic nephropathy, systemic lupus erythematosus, and obstruction of the urinary tract can cause which type of renal tubular acidosis?

Renal tubular acidosis type {{c1::1}}

What are the K+ imbalances in renal tubular acidosis types 1, 2, and 4?

Type 1 cause {{c1::hypokalemia::hyperkalemia/hypokalemia}}
Type 2 cause {{c1::hypokalemia::hyperkalemia/hypokalemia}}
Type 4 cause {{c1::hyperkalemia::hyperkalemia/hypokalemia}}

What is the urine pH in renal tubular acidosis type 2?

pH {{c1::<::</>}} 5.5 when plasma HCO3- is below reduced resorption threshold
pH {{c1::>::</>}} 5.5 when it exceeds resorptive threshold

What is the mechanism behind the metabolic acidosis in renal tubular acidosis type 1?

{{c1::α-intercalated}} cells are unable to secrete {{c1::H+}} → Impairment of the formation of {{c1::HCO3-}}

What is the mechanism behind the metabolic acidosis in renal tubular acidosis type 4?

Hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance → {{c1::Hyperkalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}} and decreased proximal convoluted tubule {{c1::NH3}} synthesis → Decreased urinary {{c1::NH4+}} excretion

What is the mechanism behind the metabolic acidosis in renal tubular acidosis type 2?

Defect in proximal convoluted tubule {{c1::HCO3-}} reabsorption → Increased excretion of {{c1::HCO3-}}

What are the typical urine pH readings for renal tubular acidoses types 1 and 4?

Type 1 urine pH {{c1::>::</>}} 5.5
Type 4 urine pH is variable but usually {{c1::<::</>}} 5.5

In renal tubular acidosis type 2, what compensatory mechanism of the kidney may acidify the urine, and what is the net result on body acid-base status?

Urine can be acidified by {{c1::α-intercalated}} cells in the collecting duct
Net result is metabolic {{c1::acidosis::acidosis/alkalosis}}

Potassium-sparing diuretics, nephropathy due to obstruction, and TMP-SMX can cause which type of renal tubular acidosis?

Renal tubular acidosis type {{c1::4}}
fields.Back Extra: They all can cause aldosterone resistance.

fields.Text:
Calcium phosphate kidney stones are associated with which renal tubular acidosis?

Renal tubular acidosis type {{c1::1}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to increased urine pH and increased bone turnover.

fields.Text:
Classify hyperaldosteronism, Bartter syndrome, and Gitelman syndrome into saline-responsive or saline-resistant metabolic alkalosis.

Saline-{{c1::resistant}} metabolic alkalosis

Classify recent loop/thiazide diuretics, vomiting, and antacids into the saline-responsive or saline-resistant metabolic alkalosis.

Saline-{{c1::responsive}} metabolic alkalosis

What helps to differentiate metabolic acidosis into saline-resistant and saline-responsive?

Urine Cl- > {{c1::20}} mEq/L indicates saline resistant

What is the initial acid-base imbalance seen with aspirin overdose?

{{c1::Respiratory alkalosis}}

What are the possible causes of metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap?

{{c1::Glycols}}
{{c2::Oxoproline}}
{{c3::Lactic acidosis}}
{{c4::D-lactate}}
{{c5::Methanol}}
{{c6::Aspirin}} (late effect)
{{c7::Renal}} failure
{{c8::Ketones}}

What mechanisms or disease states can lead to respiratory acidosis?

{{c1::Hypoventilation::Hyperventilation/Hypoventilation}} due to airway obstruction
Acute or chronic {{c1::lung::organ}} disease
{{c1::Sedatives}}
{{c1::Opioids}}
Weakened respiratory {{c1::muscles}}

What are the possible conditions that can cause a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis?

{{c1::Hyperchloremia::Hyperchloremia/Hypochloremia}} and/or {{c1::hyperalimentation::hyperalimentation/hypoalimentation}}
{{c2::Addison}} disease
{{c3::Renal tubular acidosis}}
{{c4::Diarrhea}}
{{c5::Acetazolamide}}
{{c6::Spironolactone}}
{{c7::Saline}} infusion

What is the normal value for an anion gap?

{{c1::8}} to {{c1::12}} mEq/L

What is the main cause of respiratory alkalosis?

{{c1::Hyperventilation::Hyperventilation/Hypoventilation}}
{{c1::Hypoxemia}}
Pulmonary {{c1::emboli}}
{{c1::Salicylates}} (early)
{{c1::Tumors}}

Which acid-base abnormality would you expect with hyperventilation?

{{c1::Respiratory alkalosis}}

What primary acid-base disturbance is present when arterial pH is < 7.35 and PCO2 is < 44 mmHg?

{{c1::Metabolic acidosis}}

What is the formula for calculating the anion gap?

Anion gap = {{c1::Na+}} - ( {{c1::Cl-}} + {{c1::HCO3-}} )

What primary acid-base disturbance is present when arterial pH is > 7.45 and PCO2 is < 36 mmHg?

{{c1::Respiratory alkalosis}}

What type of acid-base imbalance develops after initial respiratory alkalosis in the later stages of aspirin overdose?

{{c1::Metabolic acidosis}}

What primary acid-base disturbance is present when arterial pH is < 7.35 and PCO2 is > 44 mmHg?

{{c1::Respiratory acidosis}}

What primary acid-base disturbance is present when arterial pH is < 7.35, HCO3- is < 20 mEq/L, and the anion gap is > 12 mEq/L?

{{c1::Increased anion gap metabolic acidosis}}

What primary acid-base disturbance is present when arterial pH is < 7.35, HCO3- is < 20 mEq/L, and the anion gap is 8 to 12 mEq/L?

{{c1::Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis}}

In performing a workup for acid-base status on a patient, what is the first test that should be ordered?

{{c1::Arterial blood gas pH}}
fields.Back Extra:
A pH < 7.35 indicates acidemia.

A pH > 7.45 indicates alkalemia.

fields.Text:
What primary acid-base disturbance is present when arterial pH is < 7.35 and HCO3- is < 20 mEq/L?

{{c1::Metabolic acidosis}}

What primary acid-base disturbance is present when arterial pH is > 7.45 and HCO3- is > 28 mEq/L?

{{c1::Metabolic alkalosis}}

What is the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for pH calculation?

pH = {{c1::6.1}} + log ( [ {{c1::HCO3-}} ] / {{c1::0.03}} {{c1::PCO2}} )

How do respiratory and metabolic acid-base disorders differ in their primary alterations?

Metabolic disorders are primarily driven by {{c1::HCO3-}}
Respiratory disorders are primarily driven by {{c1::PCO2}}

How is the expected compensatory change in PCO2 calculated in metabolic acidosis?

Winters formula → PCO2 = {{c1::1.5}} × [ {{c1::HCO3-}} ] + {{c1::8}} ± {{c1::2}}

Describe the PCO2 status, HCO3- status, and compensatory response of respiratory alkalosis.

{{c1::Hyperventilation::Hyperventilation/Hypoventilation}} → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} PCO2 with delayed compensatory renal HCO3- excretion into urine

Describe the PCO2 status, HCO3- status, and compensatory response of respiratory acidosis.

{{c1::Hypoventilation::Hyperventilation/Hypoventilation}} → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} PCO2 → Delayed compensatory {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} in renal reabsorption of HCO3-

Describe the PCO2 status, HCO3- status, and compensatory response of metabolic alkalosis.

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} HCO3- → Immediate compensatory {{c1::hypoventilation::hyperventilation/hypoventilation}} and {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} PCO2

Describe the PCO2 status, HCO3- status, and compensatory response of metabolic acidosis.

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} HCO3- → Immediate compensatory {{c1::hyperventilation::hyperventilation/hypoventilation}} and {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} PCO2

What does it indicate if the predicted PCO2 is less than the measured PCO2 in a patient with metabolic acidosis?

There is a concomitant respiratory {{c1::acidosis::acidosis/alkalosis}}

What does it indicate if the predicted PCO2 is greater than the measured PCO2 in a patient with metabolic acidosis?

There is a concomitant respiratory {{c1::alkalosis::acidosis/alkalosis}}

What is the mechanism of injury in diffuse axonal injury?

Traumatic {{c1::shearing}} forces from rapid brain {{c1::acceleration}} and/or {{c1::deceleration}}

This brain MRI is from a patient who presented in a coma after a serious motor vehicle accident. What are the arrows pointing to?



Multiple {{c1::lesions}} that involve {{c1::white matter}} tracts
fields.Back Extra: This is likely caused by diffuse axonal injury.

fields.Text:
What are the most common consequences of diffuse axonal injury?

Severe neurologic injury → {{c1::Coma}} or persistent {{c1::vegetative}} state

How does insight in patients with receptive aphasia differ from insight in patients with expressive aphasia?

Insight {{c1::is not::is/is not}} intact in patients with receptive aphasia
Insight {{c1::is::is/is not}} intact in patients with expressive aphasia

What term describes a speech disorder caused by a cortical language deficit resulting in problems with production or processing of language?

{{c1::Aphasia}}

What term describes a speech disorder caused by a motor deficit?

{{c1::Dysarthria}}

What structures of the brain are damaged in global aphasia?

{{c1::Wernicke}} area
{{c1::Broca}} area

What aphasia type presents with inability to follow commands, repeat phrases, or speak fluently?

{{c1::Global}} aphasia

Which area of the cerebral cortex is injured in Wernicke aphasia?

The {{c1::superior temporal}} gyrus of the {{c1::temporal}} lobe

What aphasia presents with spoken but completely unrelated phrases?

{{c1::Wernicke}} aphasia

Which area of the cerebral cortex is injured in Broca's aphasia?

The {{c1::inferior frontal}} gyrus of the {{c1::frontal}} lobe

What type of aphasia is seen in a patient after a stroke if they can understand speech but cannot repeat words or talk fluently?

{{c1::Broca}} aphasia

Which area of the cerebral cortex is injured in conduction aphasia?

{{c1::Arcuate fasciculus}}

What type of aphasia presents with lack of repitition, but with normal speech?

{{c1::Conduction}} aphasia

Which cerebral hemisphere is usually involved in patients with aphasia?

{{c1::Dominant}} cerebral hemisphere
fields.Back Extra: This is typically the left cerebral hemisphere.

fields.Text:
What clinical findings do you expect in a patient with a berry aneurysm in the posterior communicating artery?

{{c1::Ipsilateral::Ipsilateral/Contralateral}} cranial nerve {{c1::III}} compression → {{c1::Mydriasis}}
fields.Back Extra: There may also be a "down-and-out" eye and ptosis.

fields.Text:
Aneurysmal rupture of which vessel would lead to sensory deficits and contralateral upper extremity and lower facial hemiparesis?

{{c1::Middle cerebral}} artery

What mechanism underlies aneurysm formation?

Weakening of the {{c1::arterial wall}} → Abnormal {{c1::dilation}}

What chronic condition is most often associated with Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms?

{{c1::Hypertension}}

What is the most common presenting symptom of cerebral aneurysmal rupture and a consequent subarachnoid hemorrhage?

"{{c1::Thunderclap headache}}"
"{{c1::Worst headache of my life}}"
fields.Back Extra: This is may be followed by focal deficits.

fields.Text:
What are three important risk factors for aneurysm formation?

{{c1::Hypertension}}
{{c1::Advanced}} age
{{c1::Smoking}}

What 2 congenital diseases are often associated with berry aneurysms?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney}} disease
{{c1::Ehlers-Danlos}} syndrome

How do Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms typically appear on a conventional angiogram?

They are {{c1::not visible}} on angiographic studies

Where are Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms most commonly located?

In the small vessels of the {{c1::basal ganglia}} and {{c1::thalamus}}

What symptoms would most likely occur if an anterior communicating artery aneurysm was compressing surrounding structures?

{{c1::Bitemporal hemianopia}}
Visual {{c1::acuity}}

What symptoms are present when a saccular aneurysm ruptures?

{{c1::Subarachnoid hemorrhage}} → Severe {{c1::headache}} and {{c1::focal}} neurologic deficits

Where is a saccular aneurysm most likely to be located?

At the junction of the {{c1::anterior communicating}} artery and {{c1::anterior cerebral}} artery in the circle of Willis

What homeostatic function in disrupted in heat stroke?

The body's ability to {{c1::dissipate heat}}

What are five common complications of heat stroke?

{{c1::CNS}} dysfunction
{{c1::ARDS}}
{{c1::Rhabdomyolysis}}
Acute {{c1::kidney}} injury
{{c1::DIC}}

What therapeutic options can be used in the treatment of febrile seizures?

{{c1::Acetaminophen}}
{{c1::Ibuprofen}}
{{c1::Antibiotic}} therapy (if indicated)

How would you treat a patient with a heat stroke?

Rapid external {{c1::cooling}}
{{c1::Electrolyte}} correction
{{c1::Rehydration}}

What are the potential complications of high fever in children?

{{c1::Febrile seizures}}

What is the minium required temperature to diagnose a heat stroke?

A temperature greater than {{c1::40}} °C or {{c1::104}} °F

What 3 neurons may be compromised in a patient who has Horner syndrome?

First neuron → Extending from the {{c1::hypothalamus}} to the {{c1::spinal cord}}
Second neuron → {{c1::Stellate}} ganglia
Third neuron → {{c1::Superior cervical}} ganglia

A patient has an isolated spinal cord injury at the level of T2. What abnormal findings do you expect on an ophthalmologic exam?

{{c1::None}}
fields.Back Extra: This lesion is just below the synapse of the 1st and 2nd sympathetic chain neurons, so the eye will not be affected.

fields.Text:
A patient with carotid artery dissection has anhidrosis of the lower face only. Where is the dissection most likely found?

{{c1::External carotid}} artery

What is the classic triad of findings associated with Horner syndrome?

{{c1::Ptosis}}
Ipsilateral {{c1::anhidrosis}} and {{c1::flushing}}
{{c1::Miosis}}

A patient with carotid dissection has ipsilateral pain, miosis, and ptosis, but no anhidrosis. Which order neuron in the affected pathway has been interrupted?

{{c1::Third}}-order neuron

Which order neuron in the oculosympathetic pathway is interrupted in Horner syndrome due to a Pancoast tumor?

{{c1::Second}}-order neuron

What facial syndrome may occur as a result of spinal cord lesions above T1 or a Pancoast tumor at the stellate ganglion?

{{c1::Horner}} syndrome

Give 3 examples of lesions that affect the first neuron in Horner syndrome.

{{c1::Pontine}} hemorrhage
{{c1::Lateral medullary}} syndrome
Spinal cord lesion above {{c1::T1}}

Which cranial nerve carries the innervation to pupillary dilators?

{{c1::Ophthalmic}} division of the trigeminal nerve
Later, it is innervated by the {{c1::long ciliary}} nerve

At what level is the superior cervical ganglion located?

{{c1::C2}}

Name the 4 parts of the face innervated by the sympathetic chain.

{{c1::Sweat}} glands of forehead
{{c1::Smooth}} muscle of eyelid
Pupillary {{c1::dilators}}
{{c1::Sweat}} glands of face

What 2 sympathetic chain synapses may be compromised in a patient who has Horner syndrome?

{{c1::Lateral horn}}
{{c1::Superior cervical}} ganglion
