What could be the cause of severe frontal headache, seeing halos around lights, and painful eyes?



Acute {{c1::closed}}-angle glaucoma

Which variant of glaucoma is considered an ophthalmologic emergency?

Acute {{c1::closed}}-angle glaucoma

How will the pupil of the affected eye look in acute closed-angle glaucoma?

{{c1::Fixed}}
{{c1::Mid-dilated}}

What is the most likely cause of optic disc atrophy and cupping in older patients?

{{c1::Open}}-angle glaucoma

Is closed-angle glaucoma painful?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}

Is open-angle glaucoma painful?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}

What is the mechanism of development of acute angle-closure glaucoma by epinephrine?

Epinephrine causes {{c1::mydriasis}} → Pushes the iris {{c1::forward}} → {{c1::Outflow}} obstruction

What is the mechanism of development of secondary open-angle glaucoma?

{{c1::White blood}} cells, {{c1::red blood}} cells, or {{c1::retinal}} elements block trabecular meshwork

Tonometry shows a patient has increased intraocular pressure. Slit lamp shows retinal changes. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Glaucoma}}

In a patient with glaucoma, describe 2 main findings you would expect on fundoscopic exam.

Optic disc {{c1::atrophy}} with {{c1::cupping}}

What type of medications are contraindicated in closed-angle glaucoma?

{{c1::Mydriatics}}

What is the mechanism of primary closed-angle glaucoma?

{{c1::Forward}} movement of lens against central iris → Obstruction of {{c1::aqueous}} flow → Buildup of fluid pushes iris against {{c1::cornea}}

What is the mechanism of secondary closed-angle glaucoma?

{{c1::Hypoxia}} from retinal disease → {{c1::Vasoproliferation}} in the iris that contracts the angle

In case of a defect in the left ciliary ganglion, when light is shone on the left eye only, how do both eyes' pupils respond?



Left eye → {{c1::No change}}
Right eye → {{c1::Constricts}}
fields.Back Extra: The left ciliary ganglion only controls left eye constriction.

fields.Text:
A physician shines a light into a healthy patient's pupil. What will happen to the other pupil?

The other pupil will {{c1::constrict}}
fields.Back Extra: This demonstrates a direct and consensual pupillary light reflex.

fields.Text:
Apart from the pupillary dilator muscles, what 2 other structures are innervated by sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion?

{{c1::Smooth}} muscles of the eyelids
{{c1::Sweat}} glands of the forehead and face

What brainstem structure might have been damaged in a patient with a midbrain stroke who presents with mydriasis?

{{c1::Edinger-Westphal}} nucleus
fields.Back Extra: This carries 1st-order parasympathetic neurons projecting to the ciliary ganglion.

fields.Text:
Where are the 3 neuron cell bodies in the pathway regulating mydriasis?

1st neuron → {{c1::Hypothalamus}}
2nd neuron → {{c1::Ciliospinal center of Budge}}
3rd neuron → {{c1::Internal carotid plexus}}

Where are the 2 neuron cell bodies in the pathway regulating miosis?

1st neuron → From the {{c1::Edinger-Westphal}} nucleus to the {{c1::ciliary}} ganglion
2nd neuron → From the {{c1::ciliary}} ganglion to the {{c1::sphincter pupillae}}

Which ciliary nerves cause pupillary constriction?

{{c1::Short::Long/Short}} ciliary nerves

Which ciliary nerves increase the pupil diameter?

{{c1::Long::Long/Short}} ciliary nerves

What's the term used to refer to dilation of the pupil?

{{c1::Mydriasis}}

When light is shone in the eye, where does the signal go via cranial nerve II?



Light in the retina sends a signal via cranial nerve II to the {{c1::pretectal}} nuclei in the midbrain

Name the blanked out structure in the image that represents the origin of the 4th neuron in the pupillary light reflex.



{{c1::Ciliary}} ganglion

Which nerve connects the Edinger-Westphal nucleus to the ciliary ganglion in the pupillary light reflex pathway?



{{c1::Occulomotor}} nerve

Where are the pretectal nuclei located?

{{c1::Midbrain}}

What will a swinging flashlight test show if the left optic nerve is severed?

Left eye → Both pupils {{c1::dilate}}
Right eye → Both pupils {{c1::constrict}}

A patient has decreased pupillary constriction when light is shone into the left eye only. Damage to what neurologic structure typically causes this?

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::optic}} nerve

What exam technique can be used to test for Marcus Gunn pupil?

{{c1::Swinging flashlight}} test

What is a Marcus Gunn pupil?

Impaired conduction of light signal along the injured {{c1::optic}} nerve → Bilateral {{c1::dilation}} when light is shone in the affected eye

What is another name for Marcus Gunn pupil?

{{c1::Relative afferent pupillary defect}}

What eye pathology associated with rheumatoid arthritis causes this finding in the eye?



{{c1::Uveitis}}
fields.Back Extra: This causes conjunctival redness and hypopyon.

fields.Text:
Based on location in the eye, what are the different types of uveitis?

{{c1::Anterior::Anterior/Posterior}} uveitis → Iritis
{{c1::Posterior::Anterior/Posterior}} uveitis → Choroiditis and retinitis

What 4 underlying systemic inflammatory disorders may be associated with chronic relapsing uveitis?

{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}
{{c1::Sarcoidosis}}
{{c1::Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis}}
{{c1::HLA-B27}}-associated conditions

What 2 underlying conditions do you suspect in a child with the physical exam findings shown?



Congenital {{c1::cataracts}}
{{c1::Retinoblastoma}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows leukocoria in a child's left eye.

fields.Text:
What is leukocoria?

Loss of the {{c1::red reflex}} on eye examination

What are 2 adverse ocular effects of cholinomimetic therapy for glaucoma?

{{c1::Cyclospasm}}
{{c1::Miosis}}

What are 2 side effects of prostaglandin analogs used in the treatment of glaucoma?

{{c1::Eyelash}} growth
{{c1::Darkening}} of iris

Name 2 indirect cholinomimetics for the treatment of glaucoma.

{{c1::Echothiophate}}
{{c1::Physostigmine}}

Name 2 direct cholinomimetics for the treatment of glaucoma.

{{c1::Carbachol}}
{{c1::Pilocarpine}}

What type of cholinomimetic would be administered to a patient with severe eye pain caused by blockage of aqueous humor outflow?

A {{c1::direct::direct/indirect}} cholinomimetic, specifically {{c1::pilocarpine}}

Of the drugs epinephrine, timolol, and acetazolamide, which can cause pupillary or vision changes?

{{c1::Epinephrine}}

Which drugs used in the treatment of glaucoma can cause darkening of the iris?

{{c1::Latanoprost}}
{{c1::Bimatoprost}}

What is the mechanism of action of prostaglandin analogs in the treatment of glaucoma?

Increases {{c1::aqueous humor}} outflow via the {{c1::uveoscleral}} pathway

Name two prostaglandin analogs used to treat glaucoma.

{{c1::Bimatoprost}}
{{c1::Latanoprost}}

What is the mechanism of action of cholinomimetics in the treatment of glaucoma?

Increases {{c1::aqueous humor}} outflow by contracting {{c1::ciliary}} muscle and opening {{c1::trabecular meshwork}}

What is the mechanism of action of acetazolamide in the treatment of glaucoma?

Decreases {{c1::aqueous humor}} synthesis by inhibiting {{c1::carbonic anhydrase}} in the ciliary body

What is the mechanism of action of β-blockers in the treatment of glaucoma?

They decrease {{c1::aqueous humor}} synthesis

What 3 β-blockers are commonly used to treat glaucoma?

{{c1::Timolol}}
{{c1::Betaxolol}}
{{c1::Carteolol}}

Which drug used for glaucoma treatment may cause a foreign body sensation and ocular pruritus?

{{c1::Brimonidine}}

Which α-agonist is contraindicated for closed-angle glaucoma?

{{c1::Epinephrine}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because it has mydriatic effects.

fields.Text:
How does brimonidine work in the treatment of glaucoma?

Decreases {{c1::aqueous humor}} synthesis → Decreased {{c1::intraocular pressure}}

How does epinephrine work in the treatment of glaucoma?

Inhibits {{c1::aqueous humor}} synthesis via {{c1::vasoconstriction}} to decrease {{c1::intraocular pressure}}

Name the five classes of drugs used to treat glaucoma.

{{c1::β-blockers}}
{{c1::α-agonists}}
{{c1::Diuretics}}
{{c1::Prostaglandins}}
{{c1::Cholinomimetics}}

Which two drug classes used for glaucoma increase outflow of aqueous humor via the uveoscleral pathway?

{{c1::α-agonists}}
{{c1::Prostaglandins}}

What is the general indication for butorphanol or nalbuphine?

Severe {{c1::pain}}
fields.Back Extra: These drugs may be used in labor.

fields.Text:
What is the key risk associated with high doses of butorphanol or nalbuphine?

{{c1::Overdose}} cannot be easily reversed with naloxone

What adverse effect may occur with butorphanol or nalbuphine when combined with a full opioid agonist?

{{c1::Opioid withdrawal}} symptoms

What is the mechanism of action of nalbuphine and butorphanol?

{{c1::κ-opioid}} receptor full agonist
{{c1::μ-opioid}} receptor partial agonist
fields.Back Extra: It causes less respiratory depression than full opioid agonists.

fields.Text:
How does the respiratory depression caused by butorphanol or nalbuphine compare to that caused by full opioid agonists?

{{c1::Less::More/Less}} respiratory depression occurs with butorphanol or nalbuphine

Which antidepressants are contraindicated for patients who are taking tramadol and why?

{{c1::SSRIs}}, {{c1::SNRIs}}, and {{c1::MAO}} inhibitors are contraindicated due to the risk of {{c1::serotonin}} syndrome

What 3 kinds of adverse effects may occur with tramadol?

{{c1::Opioid}}-like adverse effects
Lowering of {{c1::seizure}} threshold
{{c1::Serotonin}} syndrome

What is the mechanism of action of tramadol?

Weak {{c1::opioid}} agonist
Inhibits the reuptake of {{c1::norepinephrine}} and {{c1::serotonin}}

Which opioid causes mydriasis?

{{c1::Meperidine}}

What drug may be used to prevent relapse of oxycodone abuse?

{{c1::Naltrexone}}

What drug is used to reverse opiod intoxication?

{{c1::Naloxone}}

Patients with a history of opioid use disorder will not develop tolerance to what 2 adverse effects?

{{c1::Miosis}}
{{c1::Constipation}}

Opioid toxicity can be caused by overactivity at which 3 receptors?

Excessive binding at {{c1::μ}}, {{c1::δ}}, and {{c1::κ}} receptors

Which opioid drugs may be used for opioid replacement therapy?

{{c1::Methadone}}
Combination of {{c1::buprenorphine}} and {{c1::naloxone}}

Which 2 opioid drugs can be used to treat diarrhea?

{{c1::Loperamide}}
{{c1::Diphenoxylate}}

Release of which 5 neurotransmitters is inhibited by opioid analgesics?

{{c1::Acetylcholine}}
{{c1::Norepinephrine}}
{{c1::Serotonin}}
{{c1::Glutamate}}
{{c1::Substance P}}

Which opioid receptors are bound most avidly by dynorphin?

{{c1::κ}}-receptors

Which opioid receptors are bound most avidly by enkephalin?

{{c1::δ}}-receptors

Which opioid receptors are bound most avidly by β-endorphin?

{{c1::μ}}-receptors

What is the mechanism of action of opioid analgesics?

Stimulation of opioid receptors to open postsynaptic {{c1::K+}} channels and close presynaptic {{c1::Ca2+}} channels → Inhibition of {{c1::synaptic transmission}}

Butorphanol and diphenoxylate belong to what drug class?

{{c1::Opioid analgesics}}

Opioid use can result in depression of which 2 organ systems?

{{c1::Central nervous}} system
{{c1::Respiratory}} system

What are 4 common gastrointestinal effects of opioid use?

{{c1::Constipation}}
{{c1::Nausea}}
{{c1::Vomiting}}
{{c1::Sphincter of Oddi}} spasm

A patient who presents with opioid intoxication will have what ocular finding?

{{c1::Miosis}}

Name the opioid analgesics that act as full agonists at the opioid receptor.

{{c1::Heroin}}
{{c1::Meperidine}}
{{c1::Methadone}}
{{c1::Morphine}}
{{c1::Codeine}}
{{c1::Fentanyl}}

Name an opioid medication that acts as a partial agonist at the opioid receptor.

{{c1::Buprenorphine}}

Name 3 opioid analgesics that act as mixed agonists/antagonists at the opioid receptor.

{{c1::Butorphanol}}
{{c1::Nalbuphine}}
{{c1::Pentazocine}}

Name 3 opioid analgesics that act as antagonists at the opioid receptor.

{{c1::Methylnaltrexone}}
{{c1::Naloxone}}
{{c1::Naltrexone}}

What is the mechanism of action of dantrolene?

Blocks the release of {{c1::Ca2+}} from the sarcoplasmic reticulum by inhibiting the {{c1::ryanodine}} receptor

What medication is used to treat malignant hyperthermia caused by succinylcholine?

{{c1::Dantrolene}}

Name 3 conditions for which baclofen is used.

{{c1::Dystonia}}
Muscle {{c1::spasticity}}
{{c1::Multiple sclerosis}}

What is the mechanism of action of baclofen?

Baclofen activates {{c1::GABAB}} receptors at the spinal cord level to {{c1::relax}} muscles

What are 2 adverse effects of the skeletal muscle relaxant cyclobenzaprine?

{{c1::Anticholinergic}} effects
{{c1::Sedation}}

Where does cyclobenzaprine primarily act?

{{c1::CNS}}, mainly targeting the {{c1::brainstem}}

Cyclobenzaprine is commonly prescribed for what clinical condition?

Muscle {{c1::spasms}}

What centrally acting antispasmodic works by acting as an agonist on α2-receptors?

{{c1::Tizanidine}}

What are the 2 clinical indications for dantrolene therapy?

{{c1::Malignant hyperthermia}}
{{c1::Neuroleptic malignant}} syndrome

By what mechanism does the antidote of a nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drug work?

Inhibition of {{c1::cholinesterase}}

Compare the actions of depolarizing and nondepolarizing neuromuscular drugs on target receptors.

Depolarizing drugs are {{c1::agonists}} for acetylcholine receptors
Nondepolarizing drugs are competitive {{c1::antagonists}} for acetylcholine

Name 6 nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs.

{{c1::Tubocurarine}}
{{c1::Atracurium}}
{{c1::Cisatracurium}}
{{c1::Pancuronium}}
{{c1::Vecuronium}}
{{c1::Rocuronium}}

What agent may reverse phase II of succinylcholine?

{{c1::Cholinesterase}} inhibitors

Phase I depolarization by succinylcholine is potentiated by which class of inhibitors?

{{c1::Cholinesterase}} inhibitors

What 3 complications are associated with succinylcholine?

{{c1::Hyperkalemia}}
{{c1::Hypercalcemia}}
{{c1::Malignant hyperthermia}}

What is the mechanism of action of succinylcholine?

Strong {{c1::acetylcholine}} receptor agonist
Causes sustained {{c1::depolarization}} and prevents muscle {{c1::contraction}}

Neuromuscular blocking drugs used for paralysis during surgery or mechanical ventilation are selective for what type of nicotinic receptors?

{{c1::Nm}} receptors

Why should neostigmine be administered with atropine or glycopyrrolate for blockade reversal?

To prevent adverse {{c1::muscarinic}} effects

Which local anesthetics may cause methemoglobinemia?

{{c1::Benzocaine}}
{{c1::Prilocaine}}

Which infrequently used local anesthetic is a commonly abused street drug that may cause cardiac arrhythmias or hypertension?

{{c1::Cocaine}}

Which amide, used in local anesthesia, may cause CNS excitation and severe cardiovascular toxicity?

{{c1::Bupivacaine}}

What are 2 clinical uses for amide and ester anesthetics?

Minor {{c1::surgical}} procedures
{{c1::Spinal}} anesthesia

Why would more anesthetic be necessary with an infected wound than with a fresh wound?

Alkaline anesthetics are {{c1::charged}} in infected tissue
They cannot {{c1::penetrate}} the membrane effectively

Which drug is commonly mixed with local anesthetics to enhance their action, decrease bleeding, and decrease systemic concentration?

{{c1::Epinephrine}}

How does the local anesthetic lidocaine reach its site of action?

Lidocaine penetrates the cell membrane in an {{c1::uncharged::charged/uncharged}} form, then binds the {{c1::Na+}} channel in a {{c1::charged::charged/uncharged}} form

What is the mechanism of action of a local anesthetic on a nerve cell?

Blocks {{c1::voltage}}-gated {{c1::Na+}} channels binding to specific receptors within the channels

Lidocaine, mepivacaine, bupivacaine, prilocaine, and ropivacaine are classified as which type of local anesthetics?

{{c1::Amides}}

Procaine, tetracaine, benzocaine, and chloroprocaine are classified as which type of local anesthetics?

{{c1::Esters}}

What is the order of loss of sensation after administration of local anesthetics?

{{c1::Pain}} → {{c1::Temperature}} → {{c1::Touch}} → {{c1::Pressure}}

In what 3 common situations is propofol used?

{{c1::Sedation}} in the ICU
Rapid {{c1::anesthesia}} induction
{{c1::Short::Long/Short}} procedures

What is the mechanism of action of propofol?

It potentiates {{c1::GABAA}}

What is the mechanism of action of ketamine?

{{c1::NMDA}} receptor antagonist

What are 3 common adverse effects of ketamine?

{{c1::Disorientation}}
{{c1::Hallucinations}}
{{c1::Vivid}} dreams

What are 3 common adverse effects of midazolam?

Postoperative {{c1::respiratory}} depression
{{c1::Hypotension}}
{{c1::Anterograde}} amnesia

What are the physiologic characteristics that terminate the effects of thiopental?

Rapid {{c1::redistribution}} into {{c1::tissue}} and {{c1::fat}}

What are the 2 common uses of midazolam as an anesthetic agent?

{{c1::Sedation}} for procedures
Anesthesia {{c1::induction}}

What type of anesthesia is induced by use of ketamine?

{{c1::Dissociative}} anesthesia

Which autonomic nervous system activity is increased when ketamine is used during induction of anesthesia?

{{c1::Sympathetic}} activity

What are 2 common adverse effects of propofol?

{{c1::Respiratory}} depression
{{c1::Hypotension}}

What are 3 adverse effects of sumatriptan therapy?

Mild {{c1::paresthesias}}
{{c1::Coronary}} vasospasm
{{c1::Serotonin}} syndrome

What are the clinical uses of sumatriptan?

Acute {{c1::migraine}}
{{c1::Cluster headaches}}

Why is sumatriptan contraindicated for a patient who has a history of vasospastic angina and/or coronary artery disease?

Causes {{c1::coronary vasospasm}}

Which drug can be used to treat cluster headaches in a patient with Horner syndrome?

{{c1::Sumatriptan}}

What is the mechanism of action of sumatriptan?

{{c1::5-HT1B/1D}} agonist
Inhibits {{c1::trigeminal}} nerve activation
Prevents {{c1::vasoactive peptide}} release
Induces {{c1::vasoconstriction}}

Why are nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics advisable for insomnia treatment?

{{c1::Short::Long/Short}} duration
Fewer {{c1::amnestic}} effects and moderate day-after psychomotor {{c1::depression}}
Lower risk of {{c1::dependence}}
Less {{c1::sleep cycle}} disturbance

What are the adverse effects of nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics?

{{c1::Ataxia}}
{{c1::Confusion}}
{{c1::Headaches}}

What is the main clinical use for nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics?

Treating {{c1::insomnia}}

What is the mechanism of action of nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics?

Acts via the {{c1::benzodiazepine-1}} subtype of the {{c1::GABA}} receptor

Name 3 nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics.

{{c1::Zaleplon}}
{{c1::Zolpidem}}
{{c1::Eszopiclone}}

What are the primary benefits of suvorexant compared with a benzodiazepine?

Low risk of physical {{c1::dependence}}
Low risk of {{c1::abuse}}

What are 3 contraindications for suvorexant use?

{{c1::Narcolepsy}}
{{c1::Liver::Organ}} disease
Ongoing treatment with agents that are strong {{c1::CYP3A4}} inhibitors

What are 3 common adverse effects of suvorexant therapy?

{{c1::Headache}}
{{c1::CNS}} depression
Abnormal {{c1::sleep}}-related activities

What is the mechanism of action of suvorexant?

It antagonizes {{c1::orexin}} receptors

What advantage does ramelteon have in the treatment of insomnia as compared with benzodiazepines?

No risk of physical {{c1::dependence}}

What are 4 possible common adverse effects of ramelteon therapy?

{{c1::Headache}}
{{c1::Dizziness}}
{{c1::Fatigue}}
{{c1::Nausea}}

What is the mechanism of action of ramelteon?

{{c1::Melatonin}} agonist that binds to {{c1::MT1}} and {{c1::MT2}} receptors

What agent can be used to reverse the effects of the nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics?

{{c1::Flumazenil}}

What is the concerning potential adverse effect of flumazenil?

{{c1::Seizures}}

How does the risk of respiratory depression and coma compare between triazolam and phenobarbital?

Triazolam carries less risk of {{c1::respiratory}} depression and {{c1::coma}}

What are the adverse effects of lorazepam and diazepam?

{{c1::Dependence}}
Additive {{c1::CNS}} depression with {{c1::alcohol}}

Which three benzodiazepines are safe to give to patients with severe liver disease?

{{c1::Lorazepam}}
{{c1::Oxazepam}}
{{c1::Temazepam}}

To which receptor do benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and alcohol all bind?

{{c1::GABAA}} receptor

What is the antidote for a benzodiazepine overdose?

{{c1::Flumazenil}}

Compare the mechanism of action by which benzodiazepines facilitate GABAA with that of barbiturates.

Benzodiazepines increase the {{c1::frequency}} of  Cl- channel opening
Barbiturates increase the {{c1::duration}} of Cl- channel opening

What is the risk of using benzodiazepines with short half-lives?

Higher {{c1::addictive}} potential

Which four benzodiazepines have short half-lives?

{{c1::Alprazolam}}
{{c1::Triazolam}}
{{c1::Oxazepam}}
{{c1::Midazolam}}

Chlordiazepoxide and alprazolam are members of which class of drugs?

{{c1::Benzodiazepines}}

Which 3 benzodiazepines can be used to treat status epilepticus?

{{c1::Lorazepam}}
{{c1::Diazepam}}
{{c1::Midazolam}}

What 3 drugs act as direct dopamine agonists?

{{c1::Bromocriptine}}
{{c1::Pramipexole}}
{{c1::Ropinirole}}

What are the 2 subclasses of direct dopamine agonists?

{{c1::Ergots}}
{{c1::Non-ergots}}

What is the pathophysiology of Parkinson disease?

{{c1::Dopaminergic}} neuron loss
Excess {{c1::cholinergic}} activity

Which 2 medications reduce the tremor and rigidity of Parkinson disease but not the bradykinesia?

{{c1::Benztropine}}
{{c1::Trihexyphenidyl}}

Which 2 antimuscarinic drugs are prescribed for patients with Parkinson disease?

{{c1::Benztropine}}
{{c1::Trihexyphenidyl}}

What enzyme is inhibited by selegiline and rasagiline to increase available dopamine within the central nervous system?

{{c1::MAO-B}}

Where in the neurons do centrally acting Parkinson drugs act to inhibit dopamine breakdown?

{{c1::Presynaptic}} terminals of the {{c1::substantia nigra}} neurons

What is the peripheral mechanism of action of entacapone?

Inhibits {{c1::COMT}} → Prevents peripheral {{c1::L-DOPA}} degradation to {{c1::3-O-methyldopa}}

How does carbidopa attenuate the adverse effects of increased peripheral dopamine?

Inhibits {{c1::DOPA decarboxylase}}

Name 2 COMT inhibitors that prevent the breakdown of L-DOPA in the peripheral nervous system.

{{c1::Entacapone}}
{{c1::Tolcapone}}

Peripheral inhibition of COMT with entacapone prevents breakdown of L-DOPA into which metabolite?

{{c1::3-O-methyldopa}}

What enzyme is inhibited by entacapone?

{{c1::COMT}}

What enzyme converts L-DOPA to dopamine?

{{c1::DOPA decarboxylase}}

How do Parkinson drugs that increase L-DOPA availability work?

Act peripherally to prevent {{c1::breakdown}} of L-DOPA and increase the amount that passes through the {{c1::blood-brain barrier}} for conversion to {{c1::dopamine}}

What are the 2 mechanisms of action of amantadine in the treatment of Parkinson disease?

Promoting release of {{c1::dopamine}} from presynaptic neurons
Inhibiting {{c1::dopamine}} reuptake by presynaptic neurons

What 3 manifestations characterize amantadine toxicity?

{{c1::Ataxia}}
{{c1::Livedo reticularis}}
Peripheral {{c1::edema}}

What are the adverse effects of non-ergot dopamine agonist therapy?

{{c1::Hallucinations}}
{{c1::Confusion}}
{{c1::Impulse control}} disorders
Postural {{c1::hypotension}}
{{c1::Nausea}}
{{c1::Edema}}
{{c1::Sleepiness}}

Entacapone is typically used in conjunction with what other drug?

{{c1::Levodopa}}

Of the COMT inhibitors, which works both inside and outside the CNS?

{{c1::Tolcapone}}

Which drug used in Parkinson disease therapy is prescribed to reduce levodopa-induced dyskinesias?

{{c1::Amantadine}}

What is the "on-off" phenomenon due to long-term use of L-DOPA?

Improved {{c1::mobility}} during "on" periods
Impaired {{c1::motor}} function during "off" periods

Which medication is a peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitor that is given with L-DOPA to increase its bioavailability in the brain?

{{c1::Carbidopa}}

Which drug crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase in the CNS?

{{c1::L-DOPA}}

Name 1 PNS and 2 CNS adverse effects of levodopa.

PNS → {{c1::Postural hypotension}}
CNS → {{c1::Nausea}} and {{c1::hallucinations}}

The combination of carbidopa/levodopa is indicated for what disease?

{{c1::Parkinson}} disease

What is the mechanism of action of tetrabenazine?

Inhibition of {{c1::VMAT}} → Limits {{c1::dopamine}} vesicle packaging and release

What are 2 clinical indications for tetrabenazine?

{{c1::Chorea}} from {{c1::Huntington}} disease
{{c1::Tardive dyskinesia}}

What is the treatment for ALS that increases survival?

{{c1::Riluzole}}

How does riluzole work?

Decreases neuron {{c1::glutamate}} excitotoxicity

What are 3 adverse effects of donepezil?

{{c1::Dizziness}}
{{c1::Nausea}}
{{c1::Insomnia}}

What are 3 adverse effects of memantine?

{{c1::Dizziness}}
{{c1::Confusion}}
{{c1::Hallucinations}}

Memantine helps prevent what Ca2+-mediated process in Alzheimer disease?

{{c1::Excitotoxicity}} of neurons

Which drug, used for Alzheimer disease, acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist?

{{c1::Memantine}}

What drugs, used in the treatment of Alzheimer disease, inhibit acetylcholinesterase?

{{c1::Donepezil}}
{{c1::Rivastigmine}}
{{c1::Galantamine}}

What is the clinical indication for memantine therapy?

Moderate to advanced {{c1::dementia}}

What is the main contraindication for use of the first-line drug for Alzheimer disease?

{{c1::Cardiac conduction}} abnormalities

An anesthetic with high solubility in lipids and blood shows what kind of induction and potency?

{{c1::Slow}} induction
{{c1::High}} potency

An anesthetic that has low solubility in blood and lipids shows what kind of induction and potency?

{{c1::Fast}} induction
{{c1::Low}} potency

How does the minimum alveolar concentration of an anesthetic relate to potency?

The lower the minimum alveolar concentration, the {{c1::greater}} the potency

In anesthesia, how is minimal alveolar concentration defined?

{{c1::50}}% of subjects stop moving in response to {{c1::noxious}} stimulus

How do general anesthetics get across the blood-brain barrier?

{{c1::Lipid}} soluble
{{c1::Actively}} transported

What are the characteristics of an anaesthetic agent with low solubility in blood?

{{c1::Rapid}} induction
{{c1::Rapid}} recovery

What is the inheritance pattern of malignant hyperthermia susceptibility? What receptor is affected?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}} with variable penetrance mutations in the {{c1::ryanodine}} receptor

How are cerebral blood flow and cerebral metabolism affected when an inhaled anesthetic is administered?

Cerebral blood flow {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}
Cerebral metabolic demand {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}

Which anesthetic class can cause malignant hyperthermia, myocardial depression, and a decrease in cerebral metabolic demand?

{{c1::Inhaled anesthetics}}

Which anesthetic causes side effects due to release of trapped gas in body cavities?

{{c1::N2O}}

Which inhaled anesthetic should be avoided in a patient with a history of seizures?

{{c1::Enflurane}}

Which inhaled anesthetic agent causes increased blood urea nitrogen and creatinine levels?

{{c1::Methoxyflurane}}

Which inhaled anesthetic agent causes increased liver enzyme levels?

{{c1::Halothane}}

Desflurane, halothane, enflurane, isoflurane, sevoflurane, methoxyflurane, and N2O are all classified as what kind of anesthetic?

{{c1::Inhaled anesthetics}}

What are the clinical features indicating malignant hyperthermia after induction of anesthesia?

{{c1::Hyperthermia}} with severe muscle {{c1::contractions}}

What receptor type does dantrolene antagonize?

{{c1::Ryanodine}} receptors

Why does lithium require close monitoring of serum levels?

Lithium has a {{c1::narrow::wide/narrow}} therapeutic window

What are four common side effects of lithium use?

{{c1::Hypothyroidism::Hyperthyroidism/Hypothyroidism}}
{{c1::Ebstein}} anomaly
{{c1::Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus}}
{{c1::Tremor}}

What is the mechanism of lithium reabsorption in the kidney?

It is reabsorbed at the proximal convoluted tubule along with {{c1::Na+}} through {{c1::Na+}} channels

How does lithium adversely affect the thyroid?

{{c1::Hypothyroidism}}
{{c1::Hyperthyroidism}}

What teratogenic congenital cardiac defect is caused by lithium use in pregnancy?

{{c1::Ebstein}} anomaly

What is the mechanism by which lithium causes polyuria?

Lithium inhibits {{c1::ADH}} function at the level of the kidney → {{c1::Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus}}

What is the clinical use of lithium?

{{c1::Mood stabilizer}} in bipolar disorder
fields.Back Extra: Lithium can prevent relapse and manage acute manic episodes.

fields.Text:
What three drug classes are often implicated in affecting lithium clearance?

{{c1::ACE}} inhibitors
{{c1::Thiazide diuretics}}
{{c1::NSAIDs}}

Which organ almost exclusively excretes lithium?

{{c1::Kidneys}}

How does lithium affect calcium levels?

Lithium causes mild {{c1::hypercalcemia::hypercalcemia/hypocalcemia}}

What is the primary clinical indication for prescribing buspirone?

{{c1::Generalized anxiety}} disorder

What is the mechanism of action of buspirone?

{{c1::5-HT1A}} receptor partial agoinst

How long after a patient starts taking buspirone does it begin to take effect?

{{c1::1}} to {{c1::2}} weeks

What is the advantage of buspirone when compared with other anti-anxiety medications such as benzodiazepines and barbiturates?

Buspirone does not cause {{c1::tolerance}}, {{c1::sedation}}, or {{c1::addiction}}
Buspirone does not interact with {{c1::alcohol}}

What is the mechanism of action of mirtazapine?

Mirtazapine inhibits the {{c1::α2}}-adrenergic receptor
fields.Back Extra: The α2-adrenergic receptor increases norepinephrine release.

fields.Text:
What changes in neurotransmitter levels are expected when a patient takes a MAOI?

Blockage of {{c1::monoamine oxidase}} → Increased levels of {{c1::serotonin}}, {{c1::norepinephrine}}, and {{c1::dopamine}}
fields.Back Extra: Monoamine oxidase breaks down serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine into metabolites.

fields.Text:
Which three classes of antidepressants act by inhibiting norepinephrine reuptake?

{{c1::TCAs}}
{{c1::SNRIs}}
{{c1::Bupropion}}

Which four classes of antidepressants act by inhibiting the reuptake of serotonin?

{{c1::TCAs}}
{{c1::Trazodone}}
{{c1::SSRIs}}
{{c1::SNRIs}}

Before prescribing SSRIs, you should inform the patient of what five possible adverse effects?

{{c1::Gastrointestinal}} upset
{{c1::Sexual}} dysfunction
{{c1::SIADH}}
{{c1::Mania}} if there is underlying bipolar disorder
{{c1::Serotonin}} syndrome

How much time does it take for SSRIs to show appreciable effect?

{{c1::4}} to {{c1::8}} weeks

What class of drugs can be used to treat bulimia, premature ejaculation, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder?

{{c1::SSRIs}}

What is the mechanism of action of SSRIs?

Inhibition of serotonin {{c1::reuptake}}

What is the benefit of the use of SSRIs over TCAs?

SSRIs have fewer {{c1::side effects}}

What are five common side effects of SNRIs?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} blood pressure
{{c1::Stimulant}} effects
{{c1::Nausea}}
{{c1::Sexual}} dysfunction
{{c1::Sedation}}

What antidepressant drug class can be used for fibromyalgia?

{{c1::SNRIs}}

Which drug class is indicated in the treatment of depression and generalized anxiety disorder and can also be used for diabetic neuropathy?

{{c1::SNRIs}}

What is the mechanism of action of SNRIs?

Inhibition of serotonin {{c1::reuptake}}
Inhibition of norepinephrine {{c1::reuptake}}

Name five SNRIs.

{{c1::Duloxetine}}
{{c1::Venlafaxine}}
{{c1::Desvenlafaxine}}
{{c1::Levomilnacipran}}
{{c1::Milnacipran}}

In addition to depression and generalized anxiety, venlafaxine is indicated for which four psychiatric conditions?

{{c1::Social anxiety}} disorder
{{c1::Obsessive-compulsive}} disorder
{{c1::Post-traumatic stress}} disorder
{{c1::Panic}} disorder

How do TCAs affect ECG intervals?

They prolong the {{c1::QT}} interval

Why are TCAs avoided in elderly patients?

Because of {{c1::anticholinergic}} effects
fields.Back Extra: They may cause confusion and hallucinations.

fields.Text:
What are the 5 major adverse effects of a tricyclic antidepressant overdose?

{{c1::Convulsions}}
{{c1::Coma}}
{{c1::Cardiotoxicity}}
{{c1::Hyperpyrexia}}
{{c1::Respiratory}} depression

Tricyclic antidepressants such as amitryptyline and doxepin block the reuptake of which two neurotransmitters?

{{c1::Serotonin}}
{{c1::Norepinephrine}}

Which TCA can be used to treat obsessive-compulsive disorder?

{{c1::Clomipramine}}

How do you prevent cardiac arrhythmias in a patient with TCA toxicity?

IV {{c1::sodium bicarbonate}}

What antidepressant is a treatment option for patients with noctural enuresis?

{{c1::Imipramine}}
fields.Back Extra: Adverse effects may limit its use.

fields.Text:
Which TCA is better tolerated by elderly patients?

{{c1::Nortriptyline}}

What are 6 common indications for TCAs?

{{c1::Major depressive}} disorder
Chronic {{c1::neuropathic}} pain
{{c1::Obsessive-compulsive}} disorder
Peripheral {{c1::neuropathy}}
{{c1::Bedwetting}}
{{c1::Migraine}} prevention

Which MAO inhibitor is used to treat Parkinson disease?

{{c1::Selegiline}}

What is the mechanism of action of MAO inhibitors?

Inhibition of MOA prevents breakdown of {{c1::serotonin}}, {{c1::norepinephrine}}, and {{c1::dopamine}} → Increased levels of these {{c1::amine}} neurotransmitters

What are the 4 MAO inhibitors?

{{c1::Phenelzine}}
{{c1::Isocarboxazid}}
{{c1::Tranylcypromine}}
{{c1::Selegiline}}

What 7 medications should be avoided by a patient taking MAO inhibitors because of the increased risk of serotonin syndrome?

{{c1::Dextromethorphan}}
{{c1::Pseudoephedrine}}
{{c1::Linezolid}}
{{c1::SSRIs}}
{{c1::TCAs}}
{{c1::Meperidine}}
{{c1::St. John’s wort}}

What foods should be avoided by a patient who takes a MAO inhibitor?

Foods with a high {{c1::tyramine}} content
fields.Back Extra:
This includes wine and cheese.

Tyramine can cause a hypertensive crisis in patients taking a MAO inhibitor.

fields.Text:
How long should a patient wait after discontinuation of an MAO inhibitor to begin taking another serotonergic drug or stop dietary restrictions?

{{c1::2}} weeks

What are 3 clinical uses of MAO inhibitors?

{{c1::Atypical::Typical/Atypical}} {{c1::depression}}
{{c1::Parkinson}} disease
{{c1::Anxiety}}

What are the 4 side effects vortioxetine?

{{c1::Nausea}} (common)
{{c1::Anticholinergic}} effects
{{c1::Sleep}} disturbances
{{c1::Sexual}} dysfunction
fields.Back Extra: May cause serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic agents.

fields.Text:
What is the major adverse effect of varenicline?

{{c1::Sleep}} disturbance

What is the mechanism of action of varenicline?

Partial agonist at the {{c1::nicotinic acetylcholine}} receptor

Which atypical antidepressant has stimulant properties and a lower risk of sexual side effects and weight gain?

{{c1::Bupropion}}

Why is trazodone primarily used for insomnia and not depression?

Trazodone causes {{c1::sedation}}, which is desirable in the treatment of insomnia
fields.Back Extra: Very high doses of trazodone are needed for antidepressant effects.

fields.Text:
What is the mechanism of action of mirtazapine?

It antagonizes {{c1::H1}}, {{c1::α2}}, {{c1::5-HT2}}, and {{c1::5-HT3}} receptors

What are 4 common side effects of mirtazapine?

Weight {{c1::gain::gain/loss}}
Increased {{c1::appetite}}
{{c1::Sedation}}
{{c1::Dry mouth}}

What is the mechanism of action of trazodone?

Trazadone blocks {{c1::5-HT2}}, {{c1::H1}}, and {{c1::α1-adrenergic}} receptors
Weakly inhibits {{c1::serotonin reuptake}}

What is the mechanism of action of vortioxetine?

{{c1::5-HT}} reuptake inhibitor
{{c1::5-HT3}} receptor antagonist
{{c1::5-HT1A}} receptor agonist

What is the mechanism of action of bupropion?

Inhibits reuptake of {{c1::norepinephrine}}
Inhibits reuptake of {{c1::dopamine}}

What are the 4 major side effects of trazodone?

{{c1::Postural hypotension}}
{{c1::Nausea}}
{{c1::Sedation}}
{{c1::Priapism}}

What is the mechanism of action of vilazodone?

Partial agonist at {{c1::5-HT1A}} receptors
{{c1::5-HT3}} receptor antagonist

Which 2 atypical antidepressants are used for smoking cessation?

{{c1::Bupropion}}
{{c1::Varenicline}}

Which atypical antidepressant may be suitable for an underweight patient?

{{c1::Mirtazapine}}

Intravenous drug use increases a patient's risk for which diseases?

Infectious diseases including {{c1::HBV}}, {{c1::HIV}}, and {{c1::HCV}}
{{c1::Abscesses}}
{{c1::Right::Left/Right}}-sided infective {{c1::endocarditis}}
{{c1::Bacteremia}}

How is methadone used in the treatment of patients with substance use disorder?

Methadone is a long-acting {{c1::opioid}} that is used for {{c1::detoxification}} from heroin and long-term {{c1::maintenance}} therapy

How is naltrexone used in the treatment of patients with substance use disorder and what is its mechanism of action?

It is used to prevent {{c1::relapse}} after {{c1::opioid detoxification}}
It is a long-acting oral {{c1::opioid antagonist}}

What treatment should be administered to an unresponsive patient when an opioid overdose is suspected?

{{c1::Naloxone}}

What is the mechanism of action of buprenorphine and how is it used in the treatment of patients with substance use disorder?

Partial {{c1::opioid}} agonist
It is administered in the form of a sublingual film for {{c1::maintenance}} therapy and suppression of {{c1::withdrawal}}

What adverse effect may occur when buprenorphine is taken shortly after a full opioid agonist by an opioid-dependent individual?

Precipitation of {{c1::withdrawal}} symptoms
fields.Back Extra: This is because buprenorphine is a partial opiod agonist.

fields.Text:
Apart from opioid detoxification, what are the other uses for naltexone?

Weight {{c1::loss::gain/loss}}
Cessation of {{c1::alcohol}} or {{c1::nicotine}} use

What are the criteria for a diagnosis of panic disorder?

{{c1::Panic attack}} followed by history of  ≥ {{c1::1}} month of {{c1::1}} or more of the following criteria:

{{c1::Fear}} of new attacks
{{c1::Worry}} about consequences of attacks
Changed {{c1::behavior}} due to attacks

What is the treatment for panic disorder?

{{c1::Cognitive behavioral}} therapy
{{c1::SSRIs}}
{{c1::Venlafaxine}}
fields.Back Extra: Benzodiazepines may be used for acute episodes.

fields.Text:
Is panic disorder genetic?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}

What disorder causes recurrent episodes of intense fear, nausea, paresthesias, and depersonalization for short periods?

{{c1::Panic}} disorder

How does panic disorder affect the risk for suicide?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} sucide risk

What are the treatment options for performance-type social anxiety disorder?

{{c1::β-blockers}}
{{c1::Benzodiazepines}}

What disorder is agoraphobia commonly associated with?

{{c1::Panic}} disorder

What is the fear of leaving the house, using public transportation, and being in big crowds or open spaces known as?

{{c1::Agoraphobia}}

Which therapies can be prescribed for social anxiety disorder?

{{c1::SSRIs}}
{{c1::Venlafaxine}}
{{c1::Cognitive behavioral}} therapy

How do phobias differ from normal fears?

Fear present in pathologic phobias is {{c1::excessive}} and {{c1::persistent}} for over {{c1::6}} months

Do individuals with a phobia recognize their excessive fear?

{{c1::Yes::Yes/No}}

What is the treatment for a patient with a phobia?

{{c1::Cognitive behavioral}} therapy
{{c1::Exposure}} therapy

What disorder could cause an exaggerated fear of social situations?

{{c1::Social anxiety}} disorder

What is the definition of performance-type social anxiety disorder?

Anxiety restricted to {{c1::public speaking}} or {{c1::performing}}

What are the treatment options for agoraphobia?

{{c1::Cognitive behavioral}} therapy
{{c1::SSRIs}}

What are seven of the most common symptoms associated with generalized anxiety disorder?

Excessive {{c1::anxiety}}
{{c1::Sleep}} problems
{{c1::Restlessness}}
{{c1::Fatigue}}
Difficulty {{c1::concentrating}}
{{c1::Irritability}}
Muscle {{c1::tension}}

By definition, the symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder must be present for how long to be clinically significant?

On most days for {{c1::6}} months or longer

What disorder is characterized by excessive anxiety and worry about various aspects of daily life for 6 months or longer?

{{c1::Generalized anxiety}} disorder

What are three first-line treatment options available for generalized anxiety disorder?

{{c1::Cognitive behavioral}} therapy
{{c1::SSRIs}}
{{c1::SNRIs}}

How do the criteria for a diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder in adults compare with the criteria for a diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder in children?

Adults → ≥ {{c1::3}} symptoms of generalized anxiety
Children → ≥ {{c1::1}} symptoms of generalized anxiety

What are three second-line treatment options for generalized anxiety disorder?

{{c1::Buspirone}}
{{c1::TCAs}}
{{c1::Benzodiazepines}}

What is the definition of body dysmorphic disorder?

A preoccupation with slight/imagined defects in {{c1::appearance}} → Significant distress and {{c1::appearance}}-related compulsions
fields.Back Extra: This is often seen with eating disorders.

fields.Text:
What psychologic disorder is associated with Tourette syndrome?

{{c1::Obsessive-compulsive}} disorder

What four treatment methods can be used to treat obsessive-compulsive disorder?

First-line → {{c1::Cognitive behavioral}} therapy and {{c1::SSRIs}}
Second-line → {{c1::Venlafaxine}} and {{c1::clomipramine}}

In the context of obsessive-compulsive disorder, how do you define obsessions?

Obsessions are {{c1::intrusive}}, recurring thoughts/feelings that cause extreme {{c1::anxiety}}

What is the treatment for body dysmorphic disorder?

{{c1::Cognitive behavioral}} therapy

In the context of obsessive-compulsive disorder, how do you define compulsions?

Compulsions are {{c1::repetitive}} actions that provide {{c1::relief}}

In patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder, how does their perception of their illness differ from patients with obsessive-compulsive personality disorder?

The behavior of obsessive-compulsive disorder is ego-{{c1::dystonic}}
The behavior of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is ego-{{c1::syntonic}}

What is the definition of trichotillomania?

Compulsive pulling out of one’s own {{c1::hair}} despite attempts to stop → Significant distress

What physical signs suggest that an individual has trichotillomania?

Patients may have {{c1::bald}} patches or areas of {{c1::thinning}} hair, usually on the {{c1::scalp}}
fields.Back Extra: Bald patches can be found on any part of the body.

fields.Text:
Which age groups are affected most by trichotillomania?

Incidence is highest in {{c1::children}}
fields.Back Extra: However, it is seen in all age groups.

fields.Text:
What is the treatment for trichotillomania?

{{c1::Psychotherapy}}

How would you describe the hair shafts of a patient with trichotillomania?

Hair shafts have {{c1::different::similar/different}} lengths

How long must symptoms be present for a diagnosis of delusional disorder to be made?

> {{c1::1}} month(s)

How long must symptoms persist for a diagnosis of brief psychotic disorder?

< {{c1::1}} month(s)

Compare the duration of symptoms in major depressive disorder, dysthymia, and cyclothymia.

Symptoms of major depressive disorder last ≥ {{c1::2}} weeks
Dysthymia and cyclothymia are diagnosed in adults after symptoms last > {{c1::2}} years

After how many months of anxiety-related symptoms can the diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder be made?

> {{c1::6}} months

After how many months of symptoms can the diagnosis of panic disorder be made?

> {{c1::1}} month(s)

How long must a child exhibit symptoms of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder for a diagnosis to be made?

> {{c1::6}} months

How many months of symptoms are necessary for a narcolepsy diagnosis?

> {{c1::3}} months

How long must symptoms be present in a child for a diagnosis of oppositional defiant disorder to be made?

> {{c1::6}} months

How long must symptoms be present for the diagnosis of tic disorder be made?

> {{c1::1}} year(s)

How long must symptoms be present for the diagnosis of a phobia be made?

> {{c1::6}} months

Compare the duration of symptoms in adjustment disorder versus generalized anxiety disorder.

Symptoms persisting {{c1::<::</>}} {{c1::6}} months indicate adjustment disorder
Symptoms persisting {{c1::>::</>}} {{c1::6}} months indicate generalized anxiety disorder

Compare the duration of symptoms in acute stress disorder versus post-traumatic stress disorder.

Acute stress disorder → Symptoms persist {{c1::<::</>}} {{c1::1}} month(s)
Post-traumatic stress disorder → Symptoms persist {{c1::>::</>}} {{c1::1}} month(s)

How long must symptoms be present for a diagnosis of schizophreniform disorder to be made?

Symptoms must be present for {{c1::1}} to {{c1::6}} months

How long must symptoms be present for a diagnosis of schizophrenia to be made?

> {{c1::6}} months

How long must symptoms be present for a diagnosis of selective mutism be made?

> {{c1::1}} month(s)

How long must symptoms be present before a diagnosis of separation anxiety can be made?

> {{c1::4}} weeks

How long must symptoms be present before a diagnosis of disruptive mood dysregulation can be made?

> {{c1::1}} year(s)

How long must symptoms persist for a diagnosis of specific learning childhood disorder?

> {{c1::6}} months

What is the definition of personality disorder?

{{c1::Inflexible::Flexible/Inflexible}} and {{c1::maladaptive}} pattern of behavior that is pervasive in their life → Distress and/or impaired function

What is the definition of personality trait?

A personality trait is an enduring pattern in which a person processes and relates to his/her {{c1::environment}} and his/her {{c1::role}} in it

What are the three clusters of personality disorders?

Cluster A → "{{c1::Weird}}"
Cluster B → "{{c1::Wild}}"
Cluster C → "{{c1::Worried}}"

What are four common characteristics of schizotypal personality disorder?

{{c1::Odd}} beliefs
Interpersonal {{c1::awkwardness}}
{{c1::Magical}} thinking
{{c1::Eccentric}} appearance

What three characteristics are common with schizoid personality disorder?

Limited {{c1::emotional}} expression
Indifferent to the {{c1::opinion}} of others
Prefers {{c1::solitary}} activities

What are the three cluster A personality disorders?

{{c1::Paranoid}} personality disorder
{{c1::Schizoid}} personality disorder
{{c1::Schizotypal}} personality disorder

What personality disorder could cause a person who has fragile self-esteem to demonstrate entitlement, grandiosity, and defensiveness and lack empathy?

{{c1::Narcissistic}} personality disorder

What personality disorder could cause a person to engage in impulsive and self-mutilating behavior, express emotional emptiness, and have unstable moods and relationships?

{{c1::Borderline}} personality disorder

Cluster B personality disorders are genetically associated with what two other disorders?

{{c1::Substance}} abuse
{{c1::Mood}} disorders

What personality disorder could cause a person to be shallow and sexually provocative, seek attention, and use dramatic speech and emotional expression?

{{c1::Histrionic}} personality disorder

What is the minimum age a patient must be to be diagnosed with antisocial personality disorder?

≥ {{c1::18}} years of age
fields.Back Extra: In patients less than 18 years of age, the diagnosis is conduct disorder.

fields.Text:
What personality disorder could cause individuals to be hostile, impulsive, manipulative, and unremorseful when they disregard the rights of others?

{{c1::Antisocial}} personality disorder

What three characteristics do cluster B personality disorders share?

{{c1::Dramatic}} behavior
{{c1::Emotional}} behavior
{{c1::Erratic}} behavior

What personality disorder could cause an individual to have low self-confidence, often remain in abusive relationships, and constantly seek support from others?

{{c1::Dependent}} personality disorder

What personality disorder could cause a person to be preoccupied with perfectionism, order, and control and experience pleasure in doing so?

{{c1::Obsessive-compulsive}} personality disorder

What are the three cluster C personality disorders?

{{c1::Avoidant}} personality disorder
{{c1::Obsessive-compulsive}} personality disorder
{{c1::Dependent}} personality disorder

What category of disorders is cluster C personality disorders associated with?

{{c1::Anxiety}} disorders

What is a major defense mechanism for a patient with borderline personality disorder?

{{c1::Splitting}}

In what age group do personality disorders usually present?

Before or during early {{c1::adulthood}}

What common characteristics could be observed in an individual with paranoid personality disorder?

Pervasive {{c1::distrust}}
{{c1::Hypervigilance::Hypervigilance/Hypovigilance}}
{{c1::Suspiciousness}}
Very {{c1::cynical}} view of the world

What two characteristics are common to all cluster A personality disorders?

{{c1::Odd}}/{{c1::eccentric}} behavior
Inability to maintain meaningful {{c1::social}} relationships

Cluster A personality disorders have a genetic association with which other psychiatric disorder?

{{c1::Schizophrenia}}

What are the four cluster B personality disorders?

{{c1::Antisocial}} personality disorder
{{c1::Borderline}} personality disorder
{{c1::Histrionic}} personality disorder
{{c1::Narcissistic}} personality disorder

Is antisocial personality disorder more common in males or females?

{{c1::Males::Males/Females}}

What personality disorder could cause a person to be hypersensitive to rejection, timid, and socially inhibited and express feelings of inadequacy yet desire relationships?

{{c1::Avoidant}} personality disorder

Which cluster A personality disorder is considered part of the schizophrenia spectrum?

{{c1::Schizotypal}} personality disorder

What is the treatment for borderline personality disorder?

{{c1::Dialectical behavioral}} therapy

What four symptoms would you expect in a patient with post-traumatic stress disorder?

Persistent {{c1::hyperarousal::hyperarousal/hypoarousal}}
{{c1::Avoidance}} of trauma-related stimuli
{{c1::Re-experiencing}} of event
Distress lasting > {{c1::1}} month(s)

What is the treatment for acute stress disorder?

{{c1::Cognitive behavioral}} therapy

What are the three first-line treatments for post-traumatic stress disorder?

{{c1::Cognitive behavioral}} therapy
{{c1::SSRIs}}
{{c1::Venlafaxine}}

How long must symptoms be present for a diagnosis of acute stress disorder versus post-traumatic stress disorder?

Acute stress disorder → Symptoms persist for {{c1::3}} days to {{c1::1}} month(s)
Post-traumatic stress disorder → Symptoms persist > {{c1::1}} month(s)

What is the definition of adjustment disorder?

A patient experiences emotional and/or behavioral symptoms within {{c1::3}} months of an identified {{c1::psychosocial}} stressor with symptoms lasting less than {{c1::6}} months

What is the treatment for adjustment disorder?

{{c1::Cognitive behavioral}} therapy
fields.Back Extra: Anxiolytics and antidepressants may be used in some cases.

fields.Text:
What is the treatment for nightmares in a patient with post-traumatic stress disorder?

{{c1::Prazosin}}

Exposure to what types of experiences may result in post-traumatic stress disorder?

{{c1::Direct::Direct/Indirect}} experience
Discovering that a loved one has experienced {{c1::traumatic}} events
fields.Back Extra: Examples of traumatic events include serious injury, sexual trauma, and witnessing death.

fields.Text:
How can you determine whether a person is malingering or has factitious disorder?

Factitious disorder → Gains are {{c1::primary::primary/secondary}}
Malingering → Gains are {{c1::secondary::primary/secondary}}

Which disorder is intentional and the patient's complaints stop after something is gained?

{{c1::Malingering}}

Which disorder occurs when a patient consciously fakes, exaggerates, or reports a disorder with goal of attaining a secondary gain?

{{c1::Malingering}}

How does malingering affect a patient's compliance with treatment and follow-up?

Compliance with treatment or follow-up is often {{c1::poor}}

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient who has hallucinations just before falling asleep and on awakening and a decreased hypocretin in cerebrospinal fluid?

{{c1::Narcolepsy}} with {{c1::hypnagogic}}/{{c1::hypnopompic}} hallucinations

What two classes of drugs are used to treat narcolepsy?

{{c1::Stimulants}} during the day
{{c1::Sodium oxybate}} at night

What neurochemical changes are found in patients with narcolepsy?

Decreased production of {{c1::orexin}} in the lateral hypothalamus
{{c1::Sleep-wake}} cycle dysregulated

What is the definition of cataplexy?

Loss of all {{c1::muscle}} tone as a result of a strong {{c1::emotional}} stimulus

What are three conditions associated with narcolepsy?

{{c1::Hypnagogic}}/{{c1::hypnopompic}} hallucinations
Sleep {{c1::paralysis}}
{{c1::Cataplexy}}

What criteria must a patient meet for a diagnosis of narcolepsy?

Excessive daytime {{c1::sleepiness}} with repeated episodes of quick and overwhelming {{c1::sleepiness}} at least {{c1::3}} times per week for the past {{c1::3}} months

What nonpharmacologic treatment is available for narcolepsy?

Good {{c1::sleep hygiene}}

Aside from the dangerous effects on health, how can a substance use disorder harm a person and their social life?

Recurrent use in {{c1::physically}} dangerous situations
Significant {{c1::energy}} expended in obtaining/using/recovering from the substance
Problems with {{c1::work}}/{{c1::school}}

What could cause a person to always use more drugs than intended despite knowing the dangers and trying to cut down on use?

{{c1::Substance use}} disorder

What is the definition of gambling disorder?

Persistent, recurrent, problematic gambling that cannot be better explained as a {{c1::manic}} episode

What is the treatment of gambling disorder?

{{c1::Psychotherapy}}

What is the definition of the relapse phase of the transtheoretical model of change?

Patient falls back to {{c1::previous}} behavior
fields.Back Extra: This does not occur in all patients.

fields.Text:
What is the definition of the maintenance phase of the transtheoretical model of change?

Patient has {{c1::sustained}} their behavior and integrated it into their {{c1::lifestyle}} and personal {{c1::identity}}

What is the definition of the action/willpower phase of the transtheoretical model of change?

Patient actively {{c1::executes}} a plan to change their behavior

What is the definition of the preparation phase of the transtheoretical model of change?

Patient {{c1::acknowledges}} a problem and {{c1::plans}} for behavior change
fields.Back Extra: The patient must also commit to the behavior change.

fields.Text:
What is the definition of the contemplation phase of the transtheoretical model of change?

Patient {{c1::acknowledges}} a problem exists, but is not {{c1::ready}} to change their behavior

What is the definition of the precontemplation phase of the transtheoretical model of change?

Patient {{c1::denies}} a problem and its consequences

What are the six stages of the transtheoretical model of change?

{{c1::Precontemplation}}
{{c1::Contemplation}}
{{c1::Preparation/determination}}
{{c1::Action/willpower}}
{{c1::Maintenance}}
{{c1::Relapse}}

What are three motivational strategies for the precontemplation stage of the transtheoretical model of change?

Remind the patient that the {{c1::physician}} is available for them
Remind the patient of their own {{c1::priorities}} when explaining risks
Encourage the patient to be {{c1::introspective}}

What are two motivational strategies for the contemplation stage of the transtheoretical model of change?

Suggest different ways to {{c1::support}} behavioral change
Discuss the {{c1::pros}} and {{c1::cons}} of behavior change to support the healthy behavior

What are three motivational strategies for the preparation/determination stage of the transtheoretical model of change?

{{c1::Encourage}} the first steps of change
Promote {{c1::expectations}} for good results
Ensure the patient is aware of {{c1::resources}} to help planning

What are two motivational strategies for the action/willpower stage of the transtheoretical model of change?

Assist with strategies to {{c1::cope}} with situations that trigger old behaviors
Promote {{c1::self-efficacy}}

What are three motivational strategies for the maintenance stage of the transtheoretical model of change?

{{c1::Reinforce}} good habits
{{c1::Positive::Positive/Negative}} reinforcement for good behavior
Decrease {{c1::relapse}} risk

What are two motivational strategies for the relapse stage of the transtheoretical model of change?

{{c1::Encourage}} the patient to return to good habits
Provide {{c1::reassurance}} that goals are achievable

What is the first-line treatment for someone diagnosed with enuresis?

{{c1::Behavioral}} modifications
{{c1::Positive::Positive/Negative}} reinforcement

For nocturnal urinary incontinence refractory to behavioral modifications, what are two treatment options?

Bedwetting {{c1::alarm}}
Oral {{c1::desmopressin}}

How long must symptoms of nighttime incontinence last for a diagnosis of enuresis to be made?

≥ {{c1::2}} times per week for ≥ {{c1::3}} months

How old does a person have to be for a diagnosis of enuresis to be made?

> {{c1::5}} years

Name three electrolyte disturbances that occur in refeeding syndrome in patients with anorexia.

{{c1::Hypokalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
{{c1::Hypophosphatemia::Hyperphosphatemia/Hypophosphatemia}}
{{c1::Hypomagnesemia::Hypermagnesemia/Hypomagnesemia}}

In anorexia nervosa, what three symptoms or diseases may present due to disruption of the endocrine symptom?

{{c1::Hypothyroidism::Hyperthyroidism/Hypothyroidism}}
{{c1::Amenorrhea}}
{{c1::Osteoporosis}}

Compare the body weight profiles of patients with anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa.

Anorexia nervosa → {{c1::Low}} BMI
Bulimia nervosa → {{c1::Normal}} BMI or {{c1::overweight}}

What is the treatment for pica?

First-line treatment → {{c1::Nutritional}} rehabilitation and {{c1::psychotherapy}}
Second-line treatment → {{c1::SSRIs}}

What population of patients does pica typically affect?

{{c1::Children}}
{{c1::Pregnant}} women

What four comorbidities is pica associated with?

{{c1::Iron deficiency}} anemia
{{c1::Developmental}} disabilities
{{c1::Malnutrition}}
{{c1::Emotional}} trauma

What is the definition of anorexia nervosa?

Intense fear of {{c1::gaining::gaining/losing}} weight, distortion of body image, and overvaluation of {{c1::thinness}} → Calorie {{c1::restriction}}, extreme weight {{c1::loss::gain/loss}}, and inappropriately {{c1::low::high/low}} BMI

Which eating disorder involves recurrent purging behaviors or binge eating for ≥ 3 months?

{{c1::Anorexia nervosa}}, {{c1::binge-eating/purging}} type

Which eating disorder involves dieting, fasting, and/or exercising excessively without purging or binge eating for ≥ 3 months?

{{c1::Anorexia nervosa}}, {{c1::restricting}} type

Describe the mechanism of refeeding syndrome and three potential complications in a patient with anorexia.

Sudden increase in calorie intake → Increase in {{c1::insulin}} → {{c1::Hypophosphatemia::Hyperphosphatemia/Hypophosphatemia}}, {{c1::hypokalemia::hyperkalemia/hypokalemia}}, and {{c1::hypomagnesemia::hypermagnesemia/hypomagnesemia}} → Rhabdomyolysis, seizures, and cardiac complications

What is the definition of pica?

Recurring consumption of {{c1::nonfood}} items, not considered normal for an individual's culture or developmental stage, for {{c1::1}} month(s) or longer

What four findings may be seen in a patient with bulimia nervosa?

{{c1::Erosion}} of enamel on teeth
Metabolic {{c1::alkalosis::acidosis/alkalosis}}
{{c1::Electrolyte}} disturbances
{{c1::Dorsal::Ventral/Dorsal}} hand {{c1::calluses}} caused by induction of vomiting

What treatment options are available for binge-eating disorder?

{{c1::Psychotherapy}} (first-line treatment)
{{c1::SSRIs}}
{{c1::Lisdexamfetamine}}

Why is bupropion contraindicated for patients with bulimia nervosa?

Elevated risk of {{c1::seizures}}

Why might a doctor order an endoscopy for a patient with bulimia nervosa?

To check for {{c1::tears}} in the {{c1::lower::upper/lower}} part of the esophagus

Which enzyme would increase as a result of parotid gland hypertrophy in patients with bulimia nervosa?

Serum {{c1::amylase}}

What are the two types of anorexia nervosa?

{{c1::Binge-eating/purging}} type
{{c1::Restricting}} type

What three treatment options are available for patients with anorexia nervosa?

{{c1::Psychotherapy}}
{{c1::Nutritional}} rehabilitation
{{c1::Olanzapine}}

What is the treatment for bulimia nervosa?

{{c1::Antidepressants}}
{{c1::Nutritional}} rehabilitation
{{c1::Psychotherapy}}

How may body hair be altered in anorexia nervosa?

Development of {{c1::soft}} hair on the arms and legs
fields.Back Extra: This is similar to a fetus or newborn, which is called lanugo.

fields.Text:
What are three common triggers for sleep terror disorders?

{{c1::Fever}}
{{c1::Emotional}} stress
Lack of {{c1::sleep}}

What waveform is seen on an EEG performed for a patient with sleep terror disorder?

{{c1::Slow}} waves
fields.Back Extra:
This indicates deep sleep.

This is stage N3.

fields.Text:
What is the definition of sleep terror disorder?

Episodes of inconsolable {{c1::terror}} accompanied by {{c1::screaming}} in the middle of the night

In which population are sleep terror disorders most common?

{{c1::Children}}

Which sleep stage do sleep terror disorders occur in?

Stage {{c1::N3}} {{c1::non-REM::REM/non-REM}} sleep
fields.Back Extra:
This indicates deep sleep.

There will be no memory of the waking episode.

fields.Text:
Is a patient with sleep terror disorder likely to remember the arousal episodes the next morning?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}
fields.Back Extra: Patients have no memory of the episode as it occurs during non-REM sleep.

fields.Text:
What are the four broad categories of sexual dysfunction?

{{c1::Desire}}
{{c1::Arousal}}
{{c1::Orgasmic}}
{{c1::Pain}}

What five causes should you include in the differential for any sexual dysfunction disorder?

{{c1::Psychological}}
{{c1::Endocrine}}
{{c1::Neurogenic}}
Insufficient {{c1::blood flow}}
{{c1::Substances}}

What is the definition of transgender?

When a patient lives their life as a {{c1::different::similar/different}} gender than what was assigned at {{c1::birth}}
fields.Back Extra: Medical intervention may be undergone to align physical appearance to gender identity.

fields.Text:
What is definition of gender dysphoria?

A difference between the way an individual {{c1::experiences}} gender and the gender assigned at {{c1::birth}}
fields.Back Extra: This lasts for over 6 months and causes persistent distress.

fields.Text:
Is gender nonconformity a mental disorder?

{{c1::No::Yes/No}}

At what age does gender identity develop?

About {{c1::3}} years old

In what disorder is "la belle indifférence" seen?

{{c1::Conversion}} disorder

How does a somatic symptom disorder differ from malingering?

Malingering → {{c1::Conscious::Conscious/Unconscious}} actions with goal of obtaining specific gain
Somatic symptom disorder → {{c1::Unconscious::Conscious/Unconscious}} symptoms and {{c1::unconscious::conscious/unconscious}} motivation

What is a somatic symptom disorder?

One or more {{c1::physical}} complaints that last for {{c1::1}} month(s) to {{c1::several}} years
fields.Back Extra:
This may occur with a medical illness.

This is associated with anxiety about symptoms.

fields.Text:
Patients with what disorder demonstrate anxiety about having a disease, despite lack of symptoms, multiple evaluations showing no evidence, and many attempts at reassurance?

{{c1::Illness anxiety}} disorder

What form of somatic symptoms and related disorders presents with unexplained loss of motor or sensory function following an acute stressor?

{{c1::Conversion}} disorder

Identify the three groups in which conversion disorder is most common.

{{c1::Females::Males/Females}}
{{c1::Adolescents}}
{{c1::Younger::Older/Younger}} adults

What treatment options are available for somatic symptom disorder?

{{c1::Regular}} visits with the same {{c1::physician}} along with {{c1::psychotherapy}}

What is another name for conversion disorder?

{{c1::Functional neurologic symptom}} disorder

How do the somatic symptoms seen in somatic symptom disorder compare with those of illness anxiety disorder?

Somatic symptom disorder → ≥ {{c1::1}} bodily complaint lasting from {{c1::months}} to {{c1::years}}
Illness anxiety disorder → {{c1::Few}} or {{c1::no}} somatic symptoms

Which disorder is a form of abuse in which caregivers cause or fabricate illness to assume the sick role by proxy?

{{c1::Factitious}} disorder imposed on {{c1::another::self/another}}

How does factitious disorder imposed on self differ from malingering regarding willingness to undergo testing and procedures?

Patients with factitious disorder imposed on self are {{c1::willing}} to undergo tests and procedures
Patients with malingering often {{c1::avoid}} treatment

What is the primary goal of a patient with a factitious disorder?

To get {{c1::sympathy}} and medical {{c1::attention}} by means of the sick role

If a parent or caregiver directly causes an illness in a child or other individual or fabricates symptoms to obtain treatment, what is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Factitious}} disorder imposed on {{c1::another::self/another}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a form of child abuse.

fields.Text:
What are the two types of factitious disorders?

Factitious disorder imposed on {{c1::self}}
Factitious disorder imposed on {{c1::another}}

In which two population groups is factitous disorder imposed on self more common?

{{c1::Healthcare}} workers
{{c1::Women::Men/Women}}

How does a renin-secreting tumor affect blood pressure, plasma renin, aldosterone, serum Mg2+, and urine Ca2+?

{{c1::Increased}} blood pressure
{{c1::Increased}} plasma renin
{{c1::Increased}} aldosterone
{{c1::Normal}} serum Mg2+
{{c1::Normal}} urine Ca2+

How does primary hyperaldosteronism affect blood pressure, plasma renin, aldosterone, serum Mg2+, and urine Ca2+?

{{c1::Increased}} blood pressure
{{c1::Decreased}} plasma renin
{{c1::Increased}} aldosterone
{{c1::Normal}} serum Mg2+
{{c1::Normal}} urine Ca2+

How does SIADH affect blood pressure, plasma renin, aldosterone, serum Mg2+, and urine Ca2+?

{{c1::Normal}} or {{c1::increased}} blood pressure
{{c1::Decreased}} plasma renin
{{c1::Decreased}} aldosterone
{{c1::Normal}} serum Mg2+
{{c1::Normal}} urine Ca2+

How does Liddle syndrome affect blood pressure, plasma renin, aldosterone, serum Mg2+, and urine Ca2+?

{{c1::Increased}} blood pressure
{{c1::Decreased}} plasma renin
{{c1::Decreased}} aldosterone
{{c1::Normal}} serum Mg2+
{{c1::Normal}} urine Ca2+

How does Gitelman syndrome affect blood pressure, plasma renin, aldosterone, serum Mg2+, and urine Ca2+?

{{c1::Normal}} blood pressure
{{c1::Increased}} plasma renin
{{c1::Increased}} aldosterone
{{c1::Decreased}} serum Mg2+
{{c1::Decreased}} urine Ca2+

How does Bartter syndrome affect blood pressure, plasma renin, aldosterone, serum Mg2+, and urine Ca2+?

{{c1::Normal}} blood pressure
{{c1::Increased}} plasma renin
{{c1::Increased}} aldosterone
{{c1::Increased}} urine Ca2+
{{c1::Normal}} serum Mg2+

How do Bartter and Gitelman syndrome differ in terms of their effects on urine Ca2+?

Bartter syndrome → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} urine Ca2+
Gitelman syndrome → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} urine Ca2+

How do Liddle syndrome and primary hyperaldosteronism differ in terms of their effects on aldosterone?

Liddle syndrome → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} aldosterone
Primary hyperaldosteronism → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} aldosterone

What other electrolyte disturbances can occur with a Mg2+ level < 1.0 mEq/L?

{{c1::Hypokalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
{{c1::Hypocalcemia::Hypercalcemia/Hypocalcemia}}

Describe five symptoms/signs of hypocalcemia.

{{c1::Seizures}}
{{c1::Tetany}}
{{c1::Spasm}}
{{c1::Twitching}}
{{c1::QT}} interval prolongation

What physical exam finding is associated with hypermagnesemia?

Diminshed {{c1::deep tendon}} reflexes
{{c1::Hypotension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}

What are clinical manifestations of hypercalcemia?

Renal {{c1::stones}}
{{c1::Bone}} pain
{{c1::Abdominal}} pain
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} urinary frequency
{{c1::Anxiety}} or altered {{c1::mental}} status

What two ECG findings are associated with hyperkalemia?

Peaked {{c1::T}} waves
Widened {{c1::QRS}} complexes

What clinical findings are associated with low phosphate levels?

{{c1::Bone}} loss
{{c1::Rickets}} in children
{{c1::Osteomalacia}} in adults

What are two ECG findings associated with hypokalemia?

{{c1::U}} waves
Flattened {{c1::T}} waves

What symptoms/signs can be seen in a patient with hypernatremia?

{{c1::Stupor}}
{{c1::Irritability}}
{{c1::Coma}}

What symptoms/signs can be seen in a patient with hyponatremia?

{{c1::Malaise}}
{{c1::Stupor}}
{{c1::Nausea}}
{{c1::Seizures}}
{{c1::Coma}}

What laboratory finding is associated with high phosphate levels?

{{c1::Hypocalcemia::Hypercalcemia/Hypocalcemia}}

What serious cardiac abnormality can be precipitated by hypomagnesemia?

{{c1::Torsades de pointes}}

How would you expect K+ levels to change in a patient with cells undergoing lysis?

K+ levels would {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to release from cells.

fields.Text:
How might you expect treatment with succinylcholine to affect serum K+ levels?

{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in K+ levels would be expected

How do insulin and β-adrenergic agonists lower serum K+?

They increase {{c1::Na+/K+-ATPase}} activity to {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} K+ shift intracellularly

What would you expect the serum K+ level to be in a patient who overdoses on insulin?

{{c1::Low::High/Low}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because insulin drives K+ into cells.

fields.Text:
Name four ways hypokalemia is caused by promoting a shift of K+ into cells.

{{c1::β}}-adrenergic agonists
{{c1::Alkalosis::Acidosis/Alkalosis}}
{{c1::Hypo::Hyper/Hypo}}-osmolarity
{{c1::Insulin}}

Name seven ways hyperkalemia is caused by promoting a shift of K+ out of cells.

{{c1::Digoxin}}
{{c1::Hyper::Hyper/Hypo}}-osmolarity
{{c1::Lysis}} of cells
{{c1::Acidosis::Acidosis/Alkalosis}}
{{c1::β-blocker}}
High blood {{c1::sugar}}
{{c1::Succinylcholine}}

Which two parts of the kidney are affected by PTH?

{{c1::Proximal convoluted tubule}}
{{c1::Distal convoluted tubule}}

What effect does ADH exert on the number of aquaporins and H2O reabsorption in the nephron collecting tubules?

ADH binds to receptors on {{c1::principal}} cells → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} number of aquaporins and {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} reabsorption of H2O

What are the effects of 1,25-(OH)2 vitamin D3 in the gut in response to the action of PTH in the kidneys?

Increased absorption of {{c1::Ca2+}} and {{c1::PO43-}}

How does angiotensin II affect the glomerular filtration rate and the filtration fraction?

Angiotensin II causes {{c1::constriction::constriction/dilation}} of efferent arterioles → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} glomerular filtration rate and filtration fraction

What are the main effects of aldosterone on the electrolytes of the kidneys?

Increased secretion of {{c1::K+}} and {{c1::H+}}
Increased reabsorption of {{c1::Na+}}

What is a major difference between the actions of angiotensin II and ANP on Na+ in the kidneys?

Angiotensin II increases Na+ {{c1::reabsorption}}
ANP increases Na+ {{c1::filtration}}

On what segment of the nephron does aldosterone primarily exert its effects?

{{c1::Collecting duct}}

What is the effect of ANP on the kidney's glomerular filtration rate and Na+ excretion?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} glomerular filtration rate and {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} Na+ filtration → Net {{c1::loss::gain/loss}} of Na+ and volume

Which four parts of the kidney are directly and indirectly affected by angiotensin II?

{{c1::Efferent::Afferent/Efferent}} arteriole
{{c1::Proximal convoluted tubule}}
{{c1::Ascending::Ascending/Descending}} loop of Henle
{{c1::Distal convoluted tubule}}

ADH primarily acts on which cells in the kidney?

{{c1::Principal}} cells of collecting duct

ANP is secreted in response to what physiologic change?

Increased {{c1::atrial pressure}}

What effects does PTH have on calcium and phosphate at the distal and proximal convoluted tubules?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} PO43- reabsorption at the proximal convoluted tubule
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} Ca2+ reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule

In response to what physiologic changes is the PTH secreted?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} plasma [Ca2+]
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} plasma [PO43-]
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} plasma 1,25-(OH)2 vitamin D3

What is ADH secreted in response to?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} plasma osmolarity
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} blood volume

Aldosterone is secreted in response to what physiologic changes?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} blood volume
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} plasma [K+]

What is angiotensin II secreted in response to?

Decrease in {{c1::blood pressure}}

What is the net effect of angiotensin II when it acts on the kidney?

Preserves renal function by {{c1::increasing::increasing/decreasing}} the filtration fraction in low-volume states and maintaining circulating volume by increasing {{c1::Na+}} reabsorption

How does ADH assist in maximizing the corticocapillary osmotic gradient?

ADH increases reabsorption of {{c1::urea}} in the collecting ducts

Where in the nephron does the conversion of 25-OH vitamin D3 to 1,25-(OH)2 vitamin D3 take place?

{{c1::Proximal convoluted tubule}}

What effect would the administration of NSAIDs have on patients with low renal blood flow states?

Inhibition of {{c1::prostaglandin}} synthesis by NSAIDs → {{c1::Constriction::Constriction/Dilation}} of afferent arterioles and {{c1::decreased::increased/decreased}} glomerular filtration rate → Possible acute kidney injury

What hormone released by the kidneys induces red blood cell proliferation in bone marrow?

{{c1::Erythropoietin}}

What enzyme from the kidneys is activated by PTH?

{{c1::1α-hydroxylase}}

Which hormone is secreted by the kidneys in response to hypoxia?

{{c1::Erythropoietin}} is released by the {{c1::interstitial}} cells of the renal peritubular capillaries

Name four key hormones/enzymes released by the kidneys that contribute to its endocrine function.

{{c1::Calciferol}}
{{c1::Prostaglandins}}
{{c1::Erythropoietin}}
{{c1::Dopamine}}

How does paracrine secretion of prostaglandins affect renal blood flow?

Causes {{c1::dilation::constriction/dilation}} of afferent arterioles → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} renal blood flow

Which nephron cells secrete dopamine and what is the effect?

{{c1::Proximal convoluted tubule}} cells to promote {{c1::natriuresis}}

What effect does dopamine have on renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate at low doses?

{{c1::Dilates::Constricts/Dilates}} afferent/efferent arterioles and interlobular arteries → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} renal blood flow and minor or no effect on glomerular filtration rate

What is the effect of dopamine at high doses?

Acts as a {{c1::vasoconstrictor::vasoconstrictor/vasodilator}}

What conversion does 1α-hydroxylase mediate in the kidneys?

{{c1::Calcidiol}} to {{c1::calcitriol}}

Why are patients with chronic kidney disease often anemic?

{{c1::Erythropoietin}} release is compromised in chronic kidney disease

What adverse effect can erythropoietin supplementation cause?

{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}

What is the active form of vitamin D that is produced in the kidneys?

{{c1::Calcitriol}}

How do β-blockers lower renin levels?

β-blockers inhibit {{c1::β1}}-receptors of the {{c1::juxtaglomerular apparatus}}

What are the effects of renin release by the juxtaglomerular cells on blood pressure and glomerular filtration rate?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} blood pressure
{{c1::Maintenance}} of glomerular filtration rate

Name three triggers of renin release by the juxtaglomerular cells.

{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in renal blood pressure
Reduced delivery of {{c1::NaCl}} to the distal tubule
Increase in {{c1::sympathetic::sympathetic/parasympathetic}} tone

What effect will decreased NaCl delivery to the distal convoluted tubule have on the macula densa cells and juxtaglomerular apparatus?

Increased release of {{c1::renin}} → Efferent arteriole {{c1::vasoconstriction::vasodilation/vasoconstriction}} → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} glomerular filtration rate

Juxtaglomerular cells in the juxtaglomerular apparatus are modified smooth muscle cells of what arteriole of the glomerular vasculature?

{{c1::Afferent::Afferent/Efferent}} arteriole

What are the three types of cellular structures that make up the juxtaglomerular apparatus?

{{c1::Juxtaglomerular}} cells
{{c1::Mesangial}} cells
{{c1::Macula densa}}

What is the function of the macula densa in the juxtaglomerular apparatus?

Senses {{c1::NaCl}} located at the {{c1::distal convoluted tubule}}

Under what condition will the TF/P ratio of a solute be > 1?

When the solute is reabsorbed {{c1::less::more/less}} quickly than H2O
When the solute is {{c1::secreted}}

How do the concentrations of Na+ and Cl- compare as they move distally through the proximal tubule in the TF/P ratio curve?

Distally → Cl- concentration {{c1::plateaus}} and {{c1::parallels}} Na+
Proximally → Relative concentration of Cl- {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} when compared to Na+

What changes in the concentration of inulin occur along the proximal tubule and why?

The concentration of inulin {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} due to increased {{c1::H2O}} reabsorption along the proximal tubule

Is a solute being secreted or reabsorbed if the slope of a solute on the TF/P ratio curve decreases along the length of the proximal tubule?

{{c1::Reabsorbed}}

Reabsorption of which electrolyte drives H2O reabsorption, nearly matching total osmolarity throughout the length of the proximal convuluted tubule?

{{c1::Na+}}

Why does the slope of certain solutes like Na+, K+, and Cl- remain constant along the length of the proximal tubule in the TF/P ratio curve?



These solutes and water are being {{c1::reabsorbed}} at the {{c1::same}} rate → Constant concentration

Which three substances have a TF/P ratio < 1?

{{c1::HCO3-}}
{{c1::Amino acids}}
{{c1::Glucose}}

Which two electrolytes have a TF/P ratio = 1?

{{c1::Na+}}
{{c1::K+}}

Which two substances have a TF/P ratio greater than inulin?

{{c1::PAH}}
{{c1::Creatinine}}

In a patient taking acetazolamide, what change in urine pH would you expect?

It will become {{c1::alkalotic}}

In the early distal convoluted tubule, which ions diffuse from the urine into the blood as a result of transporter activity?

{{c1::Na+}}
{{c1::Cl-}}

In terms of ion processing, what are the two main functions of β-intercalated cells in the renal collecting tubule?

Secrete {{c1::HCO3-}} into the urine in exchange for {{c1::Cl-}}
Promote {{c1::H+}} release into the blood
