In terms of ion processing, what are the two main functions of α-intercalated cells in the renal collecting tubule?

Secretes {{c1::H+}} into the urine in exchange for {{c1::K+}}
Promotes {{c1::HCO3-}} release into the blood in exchange for {{c1::Cl-}}

What is the effect of PTH on the early distal convoluted tubule?

Increased {{c1::Ca2+}}/{{c1::Na+}} exchange → Increased {{c1::Ca2+}} reabsorption

What percentage of Na+ and water is reabsorbed in the early proximal convoluted tubule?

{{c1::65}}% to {{c1::80}}%

What indirectly induces the paracellular absorption of Mg2+ and Ca2+ at the thick ascending loop of Henle?

{{c1::Positive::Positive/Negative}} lumen potential generated by {{c1::K+}} back leak

What hormone inhibits the Na+/PO43- cotransporter in the early proximal convoluted tubule?

{{c1::PTH}}

What is the mechanism by which aldosterone influences electrolyte management within renal collecting tubules?

Aldosterone acts on {{c1::mineralocorticoid}} receptors on both {{c1::principal}} cells and {{c1::α-intercalated}} cells

What happens to the osmolarity of urine as it passes through the early distal convoluted tubule?

Increased {{c1::hypotonicity::hypertonicity/hypotonicity}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to the membrane impermeability to water.

fields.Text:
What happens to the osmolarity of urine as it passes through the thick ascending loop of Henle?

Becomes increasingly {{c1::hypotonic::hypertonic/hypotonic}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because the membrane is impermeable to water.

fields.Text:
What is the pathway by which ADH acts in the collecting tubule to increase water reabsorption?

ADH acts at {{c1::V2}} receptors on basal side of {{c1::principal}} cells → Increased {{c1::aquaporin}} channels on apical side

What type of cell in the collecting tubule of a nephron is responsible for Na+/K+ exchange and the reabsorption of H2O?

{{c1::Principal}} cell

On which segment of the kidney nephron do the hormones aldosterone and ADH act?

{{c1::Collecting tubules}}

What is the effect of acetazolamide on the proximal convoluted tubule?

Inhibits {{c1::carbonic anhydrase}} → Decreased conversion of {{c1::H2CO3}} to {{c1::CO2}} and {{c1::H2O}} → Decreased {{c1::HCO3-}} intracellular absorption

What is the effect of angiotensin II on the proximal convoluted tubule?

Increased {{c1::Na+}}/{{c1::H+}} exchange → Increased {{c1::Na+}}, {{c1::H2O}}, and {{c1::HCO3-}} reabsorption

What is the tonicity of the reabsorption of glucose, amino acids, HCO3-, Na+, Cl-, K+, PO43-, and H2O in the proximal tubule?

{{c1::Isotonic}}

Where are all amino acids and glucose and most HCO3-, Na+, Cl-, K+, PO43-, H2O, and uric acid reabsorbed?

Early {{c1::proximal convoluted tubule}}

What substance is secreted into the lumen of the renal early proximal convoluted tubule to provide a buffer for H+ ions and allow greater renal secretion of H+?

{{c1::Ammonia}}

How does urine osmolarity change in the thin descending loop of Henle?

Becomes {{c1::hypertonic::hypertonic/hypotonic}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because the thin descending loop is impermeable to Na+ while passively reabsorbing H2O due to medullary hypertonicity.

fields.Text:
Which portion of the loop of Henle is permeable to H2O?

{{c1::Thin::Thick/Thin}} {{c1::descending::ascending/descending}} portion
{{c1::Proximal convoluted tubule}}

Which portion of the loop of Henle is impermeable to H2O?

{{c1::Thick::Thick/Thin}} {{c1::ascending::ascending/descending}} portion
{{c1::Distal convoluted tubule}}

Which three ions are actively taken up from the urine by the thick ascending loop of Henle?

{{c1::Cl-}}
{{c1::Na+}}
{{c1::K+}}

What percentage of Na+ is reabsorbed in the thick ascending loop of Henle?

{{c1::10}}% to {{c1::20}}%

What percentage of Na+ is reabsorbed in the early distal convoluted tubule?

{{c1::5}}% to {{c1::10}}%

What percentage of Na+ is reabsorbed in the collecting tubule?

{{c1::3}}% to {{c1::5}}%

How do thiazide diuretics affect the distal convoluted tubule?

Inhibits {{c1::Na+}} and {{c1::Cl-}} reabsorption from the lumen

How do loop diuretics affect the thick ascending loop of Henle?

Inhibits {{c1::Na+}}, {{c1::K+}}, and 2 {{c1::Cl-}} reabsorption from the lumen

How do amiloride and triamterene affect the collecting tubule?

Both inhibit {{c1::Na+}} reabsorption from the lumen to {{c1::principal}} cells

What is the mechanism of action of potassium-sparing diuretics?

Inhibits {{c1::aldosterone}} receptors in the collecting tubule's {{c1::principal}} cells and {{c1::α-intercalated}} cells → Decreased K+ secretion into urine

What effect does aldosterone have on cellular transports in principal cells of the renal collecting tubule?

Increases apical {{c1::K+}} conductance, {{c1::Na+}}/{{c1::K+}} pump activity, and {{c1::ENaC}} activity → Lumen {{c1::negativity::positivity/negativity}} → Increased {{c1::K+}} secretion

How do SGLT-2 inhibitors work on the nephron to help treat hyperglycemia in patients with diabetes?

Inhibits {{c1::Na+}}/{{c1::glucose}} cotransporters in the proximal convoluted tubule → Glucose {{c1::excretion}} → Decreased blood glucose levels

What part of the nephron contains a brush border?

Early {{c1::proximal convoluted tubule}}

What effect does aldosterone have on cellular transports in α-intercalated cells of the renal collecting tubule?

Lumen negativity → Increased {{c1::H+ ATPase}} activity → Increased {{c1::H+}} secretion → Increased {{c1::HCO3-}}/{{c1::Cl-}} exchanger activity

Each portion of the nephron shares a basolateral membrane that excretes and absorbs solutes from blood except for which section of the nephron?

{{c1::Distal convoluted tubule}}

The symptoms of Bartter syndrome and Gitelman resemble what iatrogenic conditions?

Bartter syndrome resembles chronic use of {{c1::loop}} diuretics
Gitelman syndrome resembles chronic use of {{c1::thiazide}} diuretics

What is the inheritance pattern of Liddle syndrome?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the only renal tubular defect with an autosomal dominant inheritance.

fields.Text:
What is the inheritance pattern of Bartter syndrome?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What are the prominent serum and urine electrolyte abnormalities seen in Gitelman syndrome?

{{c1::Hypokalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
{{c1::Hypomagnesemia::Hypermagnesemia/Hypomagnesemia}}
Metabolic {{c1::alkalosis::acidosis/alkalosis}}
{{c1::Hypocalciuria::Hypercalciuria/Hypocalciuria}}

What are five possible causes of Fanconi syndrome?

{{c1::Hereditary}} defects
{{c1::Multiple myeloma}}
{{c1::Ischemia}}
{{c1::Lead}} poisoning
{{c1::Drugs}}

Liddle syndrome is caused by decreased Na+ channel degradation leading to increased Na+ reabsorption in which region of the nephron?

{{c1::Collecting tubules}}

What is the treatment of choice for Liddle syndrome?

{{c1::Amiloride}}

Gitelman syndrome is caused by what pathology?

Defect in reabsorption of {{c1::NaCl}} in the {{c1::distal convoluted tubule}}

Which cotransporter is defective in Bartter syndrome?

{{c1::Na+}}/{{c1::K+}}/2{{c1::Cl-}} cotransporter

What is the pathophysiology of Fanconi syndrome?

Generalized {{c1::reabsorption}} defect in the {{c1::proximal convoluted tubule}} → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} excretion

Which renal tubular defect can present similarly to hyperaldosteronism, but with nearly undetectable aldosterone?

{{c1::Liddle}} syndrome

What three serum and urine electrolyte abnormalities are seen in patients with Bartter syndrome?

{{c1::Hypokalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
{{c1::Hypercalciuria::Hypercalciuria/Hypocalciuria}}
Metabolic {{c1::alkalosis::acidosis/alkalosis}}

Ifosfamide, cisplatin, tenofovir, or expired tetracyclines can cause which renal tubular defects?

{{c1::Fanconi}} syndrome

What is the inheritance pattern of Gitelman syndrome?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What is the defect in Liddle syndrome?

{{c1::Gain-of-function}} mutation → Decreased {{c1::Na+}} channel degradation → Greater reabsorption of {{c1::Na+}} in the collecting tubules

Besides genetic inheritance, how can SAME be acquired and why?

Ingestion of {{c1::glycyrrhetinic acid}} → Inhibition of {{c1::11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase}} activity

What are the prominent serum electrolyte abnormalities seen in SAME?

{{c1::Hypokalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
Metabolic {{c1::alkalosis::acidosis/alkalosis}}
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} serum aldosterone

What enzyme is deficient or inhibited in SAME?

{{c1::11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase}}

What is the pathophysiology that results in metabolic and electrolyte derangement in SAME?

{{c1::11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase}} deficiency → Increased {{c1::cortisol}} → Increased {{c1::mineralocorticoid}} receptor activity

What is the treatment for SAME?

{{c1::Potassium-sparing diuretics}}
Exogenous {{c1::corticosteroids}}

What is the pattern of inheritance for congenital SAME?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

Name the five syndromes caused by renal tubular defects and the part of the nephron affected by each.



Proximal convoluted tubule → {{c1::Fanconi}} syndrome
Thick ascending loop of Henle → {{c1::Bartter}} syndrome
Distal convoluted tubule → {{c1::Gitelman}} syndrome
Collecting tubules → {{c1::Liddle}} syndrome
Collecting tubules → {{c1::SAME}}

What are the clinical differences between Bartter syndrome and Gitelman syndrome?

Gitelman syndrome presents with {{c1::hypomagnesemia::hypermagnesemia/hypomagnesemia}} in addition to other electrolyte and metabolic derangement, but is {{c1::less::more/less}} severe than Bartter syndrome

In the graph shown, what does "splay" refer to?



{{c1::Nephron heterogeneity}}
fields.Back Extra: This is represented by the portion of the titration curve between the threshold and Tm.

fields.Text:
In the graph shown, what is Tm?



The level of glucose at which the glucose transporters are fully {{c1::saturated}}

What is the mechanism of action of SGLT2 inhibitors?

SGLT2 inhibitors permit {{c1::glucosuria}} at plasma concentrations below {{c1::200}} mg/dL

What is the splay phenomenon in terms of glucose clearance?

Full {{c1::saturation}} of glucose transporters is reached {{c1::gradually}} instead of sharply

Why can pregnant women have glucosuria but not have diabetes?

Normal pregnancy is associated with {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} GFR → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} filtration → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} glucose threshold  → Glucosuria at normal plasma glucose levels

At what rate are proximal tubule transporters fully saturated for glucose?

At approximately {{c1::375}} mg/min

When plasma glucose levels exceed 200 mg/dL, what finding may be seen on urinalysis?

{{c1::Glucosuria}}

In the nephron, what happens to glucose in the proximal convoluted tubule?

Glucose is fully {{c1::reabsorbed}} in the proximal convoluted tubule for blood glucose levels < {{c1::200}} mg/dL

What is considered the normal plasma level of glucose?

{{c1::60}} mg/dL to {{c1::120}} mg/dL

What kind of transporter reabsorbs glucose in the proximal convoluted tubule of the renal system?

{{c1::Na+}}/{{c1::glucose}} cotransporter

How do you calculate net filtration pressure via hydrostatic and oncotic pressure of the Bowman space and glomerular capsule?

Net filtration pressure = ( {{c1::PGC}} + {{c1::πBS}} ) - ( {{c1::PBS}} + {{c1::πGC}} )

How does angiotensin II affect renal plasma flow, glomerular filtration rate, and filtration fraction?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} RPF
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} GFR
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} FF

How do prostaglandins affect renal plasma flow, glomerular filtration rate, and filtration fraction?

{{c1::Increased}} RPF
{{c1::Increased}} GFR
{{c1::Normal}} FF

How does angiotensin II affect the efferent arterioles?

{{c1::Constricts::Dilates/Constricts}} efferent arteriole

How do ACE inhibitors affect filtration fraction?

ACE inhibitors block {{c1::angiotensin II}} → Efferent arteriole {{c1::constriction::dilation/constriction}} → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} filtration fraction

How do NSAIDs affect renal afferent arterioles?

NSAIDs block prostaglandins' {{c1::dilatory::dilatory/constrictive}} effect on afferent arterioles → {{c1::Constriction::Dilation/Constriction}} of afferent arterioles

What effect do prostaglandins have on afferent arterioles?

{{c1::Dilate::Dilate/Constrict}} afferent arterioles

The clearance of which substance best estimates renal plasma flow?

{{c1::PAH}}

The clearance of which substance can be used to estimate the GFR?

{{c1::Creatinine}}

In terms of filtration in the glomerulus, what is the equation for filtered load?

Filtered load = {{c1::GFR}} × {{c1::Plasma concentration}}

What is the expected renal filtration fraction in a healthy individual?

{{c1::20}}%

What is the formula for calculating the filtration fraction for a given molecule?

FF = {{c1::GFR}} / {{c1::RPF}}

Calculate the reabsorption rate if the filtered load is 30 mg/min, and the excretion rate is 20 mg/min.

{{c1::10}} mg/min
fields.Back Extra:
Reabsorption rate = Filtered load - Excreted rate

Reabsorption rate = 30 mg/min - 20 mg/min

Reabsorption rate = 10 mg/min

fields.Text:
Calculate the secretion rate when the filtered load is 100 mg/min, and the excretion rate is 200 mg/min.

{{c1::100}} mg/min
fields.Back Extra:
Secretion rate = Excreted rate - Filtered load

Secretion rate = 200 mg/min - 100 mg/min

Secretion rate =100 mg/min

fields.Text:
What formula is used to calculate the excretion rate for a given molecule?

Excretion rate = {{c1::V}} × {{c1::Ux}}
fields.Back Extra:
V = Urine flow rate

Ux = Urine concentration

fields.Text:
What formula is used to calculate the filtered load for a given molecule?

Filtered load = {{c1::GFR}} × {{c1::Px}}

What is the equation for fractional excretion of sodium?

FeNa = Na+ {{c1::excreted}} / Na+ {{c1::filtered}}
FeNa = ( {{c2::V}} × {{c2::UNa}} ) / ( {{c2::GFR}} × {{c2::PNa}} )
FeNa = ( {{c3::PCr}} × {{c3::UNa}} ) / ( {{c3::UCr}} × {{c3::PNa}} )

In what way is the effective renal plasma flow a flawed estimate of renal plasma flow?

Effective renal plasma flow slightly {{c1::underestimates}} renal plasma flow

What is the formula for estimating renal blood flow if the renal plasma flow is known?

RBF = {{c1::RPF}} ÷ ( {{c1::1}} - {{c1::Hct}} )

What is the formula for estimating the effective renal plasma flow using PAH?

eRPF = {{c1::UPAH}} × {{c1::V}} / {{c1::PPAH}}

The clearance of which substance is used to estimate renal plasma flow?

{{c1::PAH}}

What percentage of cardiac output is typically allocated to renal blood flow?

{{c1::20}}% to {{c1::25}}%
fields.Back Extra: This remains constant due to autoregulation.

fields.Text:
What two autoregulatory mechanisms help maintain constant renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate?

{{c1::Myogenic}}
{{c1::Tubuloglomerular}}

How does the myogenic reflex decrease the renal blood flow in case of increased arterial pressure?

Increased arterial pressure → {{c1::Stretch}} of afferent arteriole → Mechanical activation of vascular smooth muscle →  {{c1::Vasoconstriction::Vasodilation/Vasoconstriction}} of the afferent arteriole → Decreased renal blood flow

What stimulates the paracrine-driven vasoconstriction of the afferent arteriole to decrease the renal blood flow?

Increased {{c1::NaCl}} or {{c1::tonicity}} of the filtrate sensed by macula densa cells → Paracrine-driven vasoconstriction of the afferent arteriole → Decreased renal blood flow

What two parameters does the autoregulatory mechanism help to maintain in spite of changes in renal perfusion pressure?

{{c1::RBF}}
{{c1::GFR}}

Describe the effects of dehydration on GFR, RPF, and FF.

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} GFR
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} RPF
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} FF

Describe the effects of ureter constriction on GFR, RPF, and FF.

{{c1::Decreased}} GFR
{{c1::Decreased}} FF
{{c1::Normal}} RPF

Describe the effects of reduced plasma protein concentration on GFR, RPF, and FF.

{{c1::Increased}} GFR
{{c1::Increased}} FF
{{c1::Normal}} RPF

Describe the effects of elevated plasma protein concentration on GFR, RPF, and FF.

{{c1::Decreased}} GFR
{{c1::Decreased}} FF
{{c1::Normal}} RPF

Describe the effects of efferent arteriole constriction on GFR, RPF, and FF.

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} GFR
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} FF
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} RPF

Describe the effects of afferent arteriole constriction on GFR, RPF, and FF.

{{c1::Decreased}} GFR
{{c1::Decreased}} RPF
{{c1::Normal}} FF

Unlike inulin, why does creatinine clearance slightly overestimate the GFR?

Creatinine is {{c1::moderately}} secreted by renal tubules

What is the value for the normal GFR?

≈ {{c1::100}} mL/min

Which substance can be used to accurately calculate the GFR and why?

{{c1::Inulin}}, as it is freely {{c1::filtered}} and neither {{c1::secreted}} nor {{c1::reabsorbed}}

What is the unit of measurement for GFR?

{{c1::mL/min}}

Which formula calculates the GFR by relating the glomerular capillary and Bowman space pressures?

GFR = {{c1::Kf }} × [ ( {{c1::PGC}} - {{c1::PBS}} ) - ( {{c1::πGC}} - {{c1::πBS}} ) ]

What formula is used to calculate the GFR in relation to inulin?

GFR = Cinulin = {{c1::Uinulin}} × {{c1::V}} / {{c1::Pinulin}}

If a patient's renal clearance is greater than the GFR of substance X, is there net tubular reabsorption or secretion of substance X?

Net tubular {{c1::secretion}}

If a patient's renal clearance is below the GFR, is there net tubular reabsorption or secretion?

Net tubular {{c1::reabsorption}}
Not {{c1::freely}} filtered

What is the formula for calculating the renal clearance of substance X?

Cx = ( {{c1::Ux}} × {{c1::V}} ) / {{c1::Px}}

With what unit of measurement is renal clearance expressed?

{{c1::mL/min}}

What is the volume of plasma from which a substance is completely cleared in the urine per unit time called?

{{c1::Renal clearance}}

What type of cast is shown in the image?



{{c1::Hyaline}} cast
fields.Back Extra: These are nonspecific and may be a normal finding with dehydration, exercise, or diuretic use.

fields.Text:
What two pathologies are often associated with the casts seen in the image?



{{c1::Hypertensive emergency}}
{{c1::Glomerulonephritis}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows red blood cell casts.

fields.Text:
What three renal pathologies are often associated with the casts seen in the image?



Acute {{c1::pyelonephritis}}
Tubulointerstitial {{c1::inflammation}}
{{c1::Transplant rejection}}
fields.Back Extra: The image shows white blood cell casts.

fields.Text:
How are hyaline casts formed?

Via the solidification of {{c1::Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein}}
fields.Back Extra: These are secreted by renal tubular cells.

fields.Text:
What type of casts will microscopy most likely show in the urine from a patient with 3.8 grams of protein detected on a 24-hour urine collection?

{{c1::Fatty}} casts
fields.Back Extra: These are found in nephrotic syndrome.

fields.Text:
What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with colicky flank pain, hematuria, and the findings of red blood cells and oxalate crystals on urinalysis?

{{c1::Kidney stones}}

What two regions of the renal system may be involved when there are casts present in the urine?

{{c1::Glomeruli}}
{{c1::Renal tubules}}

Pyuria without casts on microscopic exam of urine is a classic sign of what pathology?

Acute {{c1::cystitis}}

What type of casts would be seen in the urine of a patient with chronic kidney disease or end-stage renal disease?

{{c1::Waxy}} casts

What underlying pathology is likely in a smoker with painless hematuria and the finding of red blood cells without casts on microscopic exam of the urine?

{{c1::Bladder}} cancer

What pathology is most commonly associated with the type of cast shown in the image?



{{c1::Acute tubular necrosis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is associated with granular casts.

fields.Text:
What type of cast is described as having a "Maltese cross" sign and what is it associated with?

{{c1::Fatty}} casts are associated with {{c1::nephrotic}} syndrome

A renal biopsy finding of hypercellular glomeruli is consistent with which type of glomerular disease?

{{c1::Proliferative}}

What percentage of the glomeruli need to be involved for a disorder to be classified as diffuse?

More than {{c1::50}}% of the glomeruli are involved in diffuse disorders

Are lupus nephritis and diabetic nephropathy considered primary or secondary glomerular diseases? Why?

{{c1::Secondary::Primary/Secondary}} glomerular disease
Both are {{c1::systemic}} diseases that affect the glomeruli as part of the disease course

Is minimal change disease an example of primary or secondary glomerular disease?

{{c1::Primary}} glomerular disease
fields.Back Extra: It is an intrinsic renal disorder that specifically affects the glomeruli.

fields.Text:
The thickening of the glomerular basement membrane on microscopic examination is consistent with what type of glomerular disorder?

{{c1::Membranous}}

Which two types of nephrotic syndromes are always the result of a systemic process?

{{c1::Diabetic glomerulonephropathy}}
{{c1::Amyloidosis}}

What two consequences of nephrotic syndrome lead to an increased risk of infection?

Loss of Ig{{c1::G}} in the urine
{{c1::Soft tissue}} compromise from edema → Hypoalbuminemia

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with significant facial edema, a known deep vein thrombosis in the left lower leg, and proteinuria?

{{c1::Nephrotic}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: Loss of albumin leads to edema while the loss of antithrombin III creates a hypercoagulable state.

fields.Text:
What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with oliguria, hematuria with red blood cell casts, and hypertension?

{{c1::Nephritic}} syndrome

What is the cutoff, in grams per day, for urine protein excretion that characterizes nephrotic syndrome?

> {{c1::3.5}} grams/day

In which syndrome does severe glomerular basement membrane damage and an impaired charge barrier lead to hematuria with red blood cell casts and massive proteinuria?

{{c1::Nephritic-nephrotic}} syndrome

What are the two glomerular disorders that most commonly present with both nephritic and nephrotic features?

{{c1::Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis}}
{{c1::Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis}}

In which syndrome does podocyte injury cause impairment in the charge barrier that leads to proteinuria?

{{c1::Nephrotic}} syndrome

In which syndrome does glomerular inflammation cause damage to the glomerular basement membrane resulting in hematuria?

{{c1::Nephritic}} syndrome

What kind of casts may be found in the urine of a patient with nephrotic syndrome?

{{c1::Fatty}} casts

What two infections should be suspected in a patient with subendothelial deposits seen on electron microscopy and the findings on PAS staining shown in the image?



{{c1::Hepatitis B}}
{{c1::Hepatitis C}}
fields.Back Extra: This is type I membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, which features splitting of glomerular basement membrane and "tram-track" appearance on pathology.

fields.Text:
What is the likely prognosis for a pediatric patient presenting with hematuria weeks after impetigo and the immunofluorescent findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis}} resolves {{c1::spontaneously}} in most children
fields.Back Extra: Note the “lumpy-bumpy” appearance of glomerular basement membrane and mesangium.

fields.Text:
What is the likely prognosis for a patient presenting with hematuria, hypertension, red blood cell casts, and the light microscopy findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Poor}}
fields.Back Extra: Renal function rapidly deteriorates over days to weeks in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

fields.Text:
What is the immunofluorescence pattern associated with acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?

A "{{c1::starry sky}}" or "{{c1::lumpy-bumpy}}" granular appearance
fields.Back Extra: This is due to deposition of IgG, IgM, and C3.

fields.Text:
What are the three classic clinical features of Alport syndrome?

{{c1::Eye}} problems
{{c1::Glomerulonephritis}}
Sensorineural {{c1::deafness}}

What is the serum C3 level likely to be in a patient with hematuria, proteinuria, and intramembranous immune complex deposits on a kidney biopsy specimen?

The C3 level will be {{c1::low::high/low}} in {{c1::type II membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis}}

What are the most common electron microscopy findings associated with type I versus type II membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis?

Type I membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis → Associated with {{c1::subendothelial immune complex}} deposits
Type II membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis → Associated with {{c1::intramembranous}} deposits

What is the typical inheritance pattern of the disease that shows a "basket-weave" pattern on electron microscopy in a patient with hearing loss, retinopathy, and hematuria?

{{c1::X-linked dominant}}

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with chronic hepatitis B if a renal biopsy specimen shows subendothelial immune complex deposits?

{{c1::Type I membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis}}

How does C3 nephritic factor produce type II membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis?

C3 nephritic factor is an Ig{{c1::G}} autoantibody that stabilizes {{c1::C3 convertase}} → Persistent {{c1::complement}} activation and {{c1::deposition}} in the glomerular membrane

What two syndromes may have progressed to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis in a patient with a granular immunofluorescence pattern seen on a renal biopsy specimen?

{{c1::Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis}}
{{c1::Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis}}

What is the treatment for Goodpasture syndrome?

{{c1::Plasmapheresis}}
fields.Back Extra: This removes circulating antibodies specific for the alveolar and glomerular basement membranes.

fields.Text:
Where would you expect to find immune complexes in a renal biopsy specimen obtained from a patient with IgA nephropathy?

Immune complex deposits would be found with IgA in the {{c1::mesangium}}

What is the likely cause of episodic hematuria with red blood cell casts detected in the urine immediately after a gastrointestinal infection?

{{c1::Berger}} disease
fields.Back Extra:
This is also known as IgA nephropathy.

This is a renal manifestation of Henoch-Schönlein purpura.

fields.Text:
What type of renal pathology is most likely present in a woman with a malar rash and the light microscopy findings seen on a kidney biopsy specimen?



{{c1::Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis}}

What is the key laboratory difference between granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis?

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis → Positive for {{c1::PR3}}-ANCA and {{c1::c}}-ANCA
Microscopic polyangiitis → Positive for {{c1::MPO}}-ANCA and {{c1::p}}-ANCA

What is seen on immunofluorescence staining of a renal biopsy specimen obtained from a patient with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with antibodies for PR3-ANCA and c-ANCA?

{{c1::Negative::Positive/Negative}} immunofluorescence
{{c1::Pauci-immune}} pattern

Findings of glomerular crescents and monocytes, macrophages, and parietal cells on light microscopy suggest what nephritic syndrome?

{{c1::Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis}}

What demographic is most frequently affected by acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?

{{c1::Children}}
fields.Back Extra: They are more likely to experience spontaneous recovery.

fields.Text:
What is the pathogenesis of the disease seen in a patient with hematuria, hemoptysis, and a linear pattern on immunofluorescence staining of a renal biopsy specimen?

Antibodies target glomerular and alveolar {{c1::basement membranes}} in {{c1::Goodpasture}} syndrome

What type of hypersensitivity reaction is involved in the disease process leading to production of cola-colored urine weeks after a streptococcal skin infection?

Type {{c1::III}} hypersensitivity reaction

Which nephritic syndrome is associated with subendothelial IgG-based immune complexes, often with C3 deposition on electron microscopy?

{{c1::Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis}}

What mechanism is responsible for the "basket-weave" pattern observed on electron microscopy of renal biopsy specimens from patients with Alport syndrome?

A mutation in type {{c1::IV}} collagen → Thinning and splitting of the glomerular basement membrane

What is a complication of the condition seen in an adult with "dark urine" weeks after a "sore throat" and a renal biopsy notable for subepithelial "humps" on electron microscopy?

Progression to renal {{c1::insufficiency}}
fields.Back Extra: This may occur in adults who develop poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

fields.Text:
How quickly can crescentic glomerulonephritis cause renal insufficiency?

Within {{c1::days}} to {{c1::weeks}}

What is the sequence whereby squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder may develop?

Chronic bladder {{c1::irritation}} produces squamous {{c1::metaplasia}} → Eventually gives rise to dysplasia and carcinoma

A patient from Egypt presents with painless hematuria. He recalls recently being treated for a parasitic infection. What is the likely diagnosis?

{{c1::Squamous cell}} carcinoma of the bladder
fields.Back Extra: This is associated with Schistosoma haematobium infection.

fields.Text:
What are the key risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder?

{{c1::Schistosoma haematobium}} infection
Chronic {{c1::cystitis}}
Chronic {{c1::nephrolithiasis}}
{{c1::Smoking}}
fields.Back Extra: All of these produce chronic bladder irritation.

fields.Text:
What diagnosis is suggested by the cystoscopic findings in the image of a dye industry worker who developed painless hematuria?



{{c1::Transitional cell}} carcinoma

What four key environmental exposures are associated with the development of transitional cell carcinoma?

{{c1::Phenacetin}}
{{c1::Smoking}}
{{c1::Aromatic amines}}
{{c1::Cyclophosphamide}}

What chemotherapeutic agent is known to dramatically increase the risk for transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder?

{{c1::Cyclophosphamide}}

What is another name for transitional cell carcinoma?

{{c1::Urothelial}} carcinoma

What are the four regions of the urinary tract in which transitional cell carcinoma may develop?

{{c1::Bladder}}
{{c1::Ureters}}
Renal {{c1::calyces}}
Renal {{c1::pelvis}}

What are the components of WAGR complex?

{{c1::Wilms}} tumor
{{c1::Aniridia}}
{{c1::Genitourinary}} malformations
Range of {{c1::development}} delays

What mutation is the likely cause of nephroblastoma in a child with Beckwith-Wideman syndrome?

A loss-of-function mutation in the {{c1::WT2}} tumor suppressor gene

What are the three clinical manifestations of Denys-Drash syndrome?

{{c1::Wilms}} tumor
{{c1::Diffuse mesangial sclerosis}}
Dysgenesis of {{c1::gonads}}

Which malignancy contains embryonic glomerular structures and may be a component of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome?

{{c1::Wilms}} tumor

What is the most common renal malignancy of early childhood?

{{c1::Wilms}} tumor

What are the three most common symptoms associated with nephroblastoma?

{{c1::Hematuria}}
Large, palpable, {{c1::unilateral::unilateral/bilateral}} {{c1::flank mass}}
Possible {{c1::hypertension::hypertension/hypotension}}

What genetic abnormality is likely present in Denys-Drash syndrome?

Loss-of-function mutation in the {{c1::WT1}} tumor suppressor gene

What clinical features comprise Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome?

{{c1::Wilms}} tumor
{{c1::Macroglossia::Macroglossia/Microglossia}}
{{c1::Organomegaly}}
{{c1::Hemihyperplasia::Hemihyperplasia/Hemihypoplasia}}
{{c1::Omphalocele}}

What three syndromes are associated with nephroblastoma?

{{c1::WAGR}} complex
{{c1::Denys-Drash}} syndrome
{{c1::Beckwith-Wiedemann}} syndrome

What is the diagnosis for a man with longstanding benign prostatic hyperplasia, urinary retention, and the renal ultrasound findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Hydronephrosis}}
fields.Back Extra: Note the distention/dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces.

fields.Text:
Where does distention/dilatation generally occur in hydronephrosis?

{{c1::Proximal::Proximal/Distal}} to the site of pathology
fields.Back Extra: This is commonly observed in the renal pelvis and calyces.

fields.Text:
What are three common causes of hydronephrosis?

Urinary tract {{c1::obstruction}}
Retroperitoneal {{c1::fibrosis}}
{{c1::Vesicoureteral reflux}}

Hydronephrosis is associated with a rising serum creatinine level in which two situations?

{{c1::Bilateral::Unilateral/Bilateral}} obstruction
Obstruction of a solitary {{c1::kidney::organ}}

What is a possible complication of renal compression in untreated hydronephrosis?

{{c1::Atrophy}} of renal cortex and medulla → Eventual {{c1::failure}} of the affected kidney

What are four risk factors for the disease process with sloughing of necrotic tissue shown in the image?



{{c1::Sickle cell}} disease/trait
Acute {{c1::pyelonephritis}}
{{c1::Analgesics}}
{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}

What is the presentation on urinalysis of renal papillary necrosis?

Gross {{c1::hematuria}}

What are two common triggers for acute renal papillary necrosis?

{{c1::Immune}} stimulus
Recent {{c1::infection}}

What is the likely diagnosis in a patient with urinary incontinence with lifting and episodes of increased urgency?

{{c1::Mixed}} incontinence
fields.Back Extra: This includes features of both stress and urgency incontinence.

fields.Text:
What would be an effective pharmacotherapy for urgency incontinence?

{{c1::Antimuscarinics}}
{{c1::Mirabegron}}

What is the only type of urinary incontinence for which Kegel exercises are not useful?

{{c1::Overflow}} incontinence

What are the four main types of incontinence?

{{c1::Stress}}
{{c1::Urgency}}
{{c1::Mixed}}
{{c1::Overflow}}

What are the two key treatments for a patient with severe benign prostatic hyperplasia who reports intermittent urinary incontinence?

{{c1::Catheterization}}
{{c1::α-blockers}}

What is the primary mechanism behind urgency incontinence?

{{c1::Overactive}} bladder → Urinary {{c1::leakage}} with the urge to void {{c1::immediately}}

What are three factors associated with an increased risk of stress incontinence?

{{c1::Vaginal}} delivery
{{c1::Prostate}} surgery
{{c1::Obesity}}

What are three possible treatments for stress incontinence?

Weight {{c1::loss::gain/loss}}
{{c1::Kegel}} exercises to strengthen pelvic floor muscles
{{c1::Pessaries}}

What are three conditions that may increase the risk of overflow incontinence?

Bladder outlet {{c1::obstruction}}
{{c1::Neurogenic}} bladder
{{c1::Polyuria}}

What test finding is often diagnostic for overflow incontinence?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} postvoid residual on {{c1::catheterization}} or {{c1::ultrasound}}

What are two common mechanisms that produce urinary outlet incompetence in patients with stress incontinence?

{{c1::Intrinsic sphincter}} deficiency
Urethral {{c1::hypermobility::hypermobility/hypomobility}}

What underlying medical problem is often associated with urgency incontinence?

Urinary tract {{c1::infection}}

Describe the mechanism causing leakage of urine in stress incontinence.

{{c1::Incompetence}} of the bladder outlet → Leaking with {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} intra-abdominal pressure

What clinical test may be diagnostic for stress incontinence?

Positive {{c1::bladder stress}} test

What are two non-pharmacological therapies for urgency incontinence?

Bladder {{c1::training}}
{{c1::Kegel}} exercises

What is the mechanism by which overflow incontinence occurs?

Incomplete bladder {{c1::emptying}} → Leakage with {{c1::overfilling}}

What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient with hepatitis B, edema, frothy urine, and the renal biopsy findings shown?



{{c1::Membranous nephropathy}}
fields.Back Extra: Note the diffuse glomerular basement membrane and capillary thickening.

fields.Text:
What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient with diabetes, nephropathy, edema, frothy urine, and the renal biopsy findings shown?



{{c1::Diabetic glomerulonephropathy}}
fields.Back Extra: The arrows in the image point to Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions.

fields.Text:
A patient with HIV infection and a history of heroin use presents with edema and frothy urine. Renal biopsy findings are shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?



{{c1::Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis}}
fields.Back Extra: The arrows indicate segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis.

fields.Text:
What are the expected light microscopy findings on a kidney biopsy specimen obtained from a patient with systemic amyloidosis presenting with nephrotic syndrome?

{{c1::Apple-green birefringence}} on {{c1::Congo red}} staining

In diabetic glomerulonephropathy, how does hyperglycemia lead to pathologic changes in renal tissue?

Hyperglycemia → Nonenzymatic {{c1::glycation}} of proteins, mesangial {{c1::expansion}}, and {{c1::thickening::thickening/thinning}} of the glomerular basement membrane

Which nephrotic syndrome is associated with HIV infection, interferon treatment, and sickle cell disease?

{{c1::Secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis}}

Which type of nephrotic syndrome may be caused by antibodies to phospholipase A2 receptors?

{{c1::Primary membranous nephropathy}}

What are the typical responses of primary minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, and membranous nephropathy to steroid therapy?

Primary minimal change disease → {{c1::Excellent}} response
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis → {{c1::Inconsistent}} response
Membranous nephropathy → {{c1::Poor}} response

What is the pathophysiology behind lymphoma and its association with minimal change disease?

{{c1::Cytokine}}-mediated damage to the kidneys

Which type of nephrotic syndrome is characterized by diffuse capillary and glomerular basement membrane thickening seen on light microscopy?

{{c1::Membranous nephropathy}}

What is the first-line treatment for minimal change disease?

{{c1::Corticosteroids}}

What are the two characteristic findings of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis on light microscopy?

Segmental {{c1::sclerosis}}
{{c1::Hyalinosis}} of glomeruli

Which type of nephrotic syndrome is characterized pathologically by a granular pattern on immunofluorescence staining?

{{c1::Membranous nephropathy}}

What are the three hallmark findings of diabetic glomerulonephropathy on light microscopy?

{{c1::Eosinophilic}} nodular glomerulosclerosis
Mesangial {{c1::expansion}}
Glomerular basement membrane {{c1::thickening::thickening/thinning}}

What is the hallmark laboratory finding in a patient with nephrotic syndrome?

Massive {{c1::proteinuria}}

Which nephrotic syndrome typically presents with a "spike-and-dome" appearance with subepithelial deposits on electron microscopy?

{{c1::Membranous nephropathy}}

What is the likely diagnosis for a child with a recent history of viral upper respiratory infection presenting with edema, frothy urine, and the renal biopsy findings shown?



{{c1::Minimal change}} disease
fields.Back Extra: The arrows indicate effacement of the podocyte foot processes.

fields.Text:
What is the most common pathologic finding on immunofluorescence in minimal change disease?

Immunofluorescence is {{c1::negative::positive/negative}}

What immunofluorescence findings are typically associated with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis?

Immunofluorescence is often {{c1::negative::positive/negative}}, although it may be {{c1::positive::positive/negative}} for nonspecific focal deposits of IgM, C3, and C1

What is the single most common cause of end-stage renal disease in the United States?

{{c1::Diabetes}} with progression to {{c1::diabetic glomerulonephropathy}}

What pathologic change leads to glomerulosclerosis in diabetic glomerulonephropathy?

{{c1::Hyperfiltration::Hyperfiltration/Hypofiltration}} produces glomerulosclerosis

What organ is most commonly involved in systemic amyloidosis?

{{c1::Kidney}}

What are the "4 I's" of minimal change disease?

{{c1::Idiopathic}} (primary)
{{c1::Infection}}
{{c1::Immunization}}
{{c1::Immune}} stimulus

What diagnosis is associated with the findings on microscopic examination of urine shown in the image?



{{c1::Uric acid}} kidney stones
fields.Back Extra: This is associated with rhomboid or rosette urine crystals.

fields.Text:
What are two treatment options for uric acid kidney stones?

{{c1::Allopurinol}}
Urine {{c1::alkalinization}}

What are the four most common renal stones, in descending order of prevalence?

{{c1::Calcium}} (80%)
{{c1::Ammonium magnesium phosphate}} (15%)
{{c1::Uric acid}} (5%)
{{c1::Cystine}}

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient who presents with colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, hematuria, and unilateral flank tenderness?

{{c1::Kidney stone}}

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with a history of tophaceous gout who experiences flank pain and hematuria with no noted radiographic abnormalities?

{{c1::Uric acid}} kidney stones
fields.Back Extra:
These are not visible on X-ray films.

They may be minimally visualized with either CT or ultrasound.

fields.Text:
What type of kidney stones can result from overuse of vitamin C supplements?

{{c1::Calcium oxalate}} kidney stones

What are two treatments for calcium phosphate kidney stones?

Low-{{c1::sodium}} diet
Administration of {{c1::thiazide diuretics}}

Which two types of kidney stones tend to form at a high urine pH?

{{c1::Ammonium magnesium phosphate}} kidney stones
{{c1::Calcium phosphate}} kidney stones

What are the three possible treatments for cystine stones in a patient with hereditary cystinuria?

Low-{{c1::sodium}} diet
Urine {{c1::alkalinization}}
{{c1::Chelating}} agents if refractory

What diagnosis is associated with the findings on microscopic examination of urine shown in the image?



{{c1::Calcium oxalate}} kidney stones

What are the three main treatment options for calcium oxalate kidney stones?

{{c1::Citrate}}
{{c1::Thiazides}}
Low-{{c1::sodium}} diet

What are the two major components of treatment for ammonium magnesium phosphate kidney stones?

Resolution of underlying {{c1::infections}}
{{c1::Surgical extraction}} of stones

What inherited mutation results in recurrent cystine kidney stones?

Loss-of-function mutation in {{c1::cystine-reabsorbing}} proximal convoluted tubule transporter → Cystinuria

What is the inheritance pattern of hereditary cystine stones?

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

What is demonstrated in the renal CT scan shown?



{{c1::Staghorn calculus}}
fields.Back Extra: It is visible in the left kidney.

fields.Text:
Which three types of kidney stones are clearly radiopaque on plain X-ray films?

{{c1::Calcium oxalate}} kidney stones
{{c1::Calcium phosphate}} kidney stones
{{c1::Ammonium magnesium phosphate}} kidney stones

What urine crystal shape is associated with cystine kidney stones?

{{c1::Hexagonal}}

What three situations increase the risk of precipitation of uric acid stones in a patient with hyperuricemia or increased cell turnover?

{{c1::Acidic}} pH
{{c1::Low::High/Low}} urine volume
{{c1::Arid}} climates

What action is most useful in both treating and preventing kidney stones?

{{c1::Fluid}} intake

What urine crystal shape is associated with calcium phosphate stones?

{{c1::Wedge}}-shaped {{c1::prisms}}

What type of urine crystal shape is associated with calcium oxalate stones?

{{c1::Envelope}}-shaped
{{c1::Dumbell}}-shaped

Which three types of kidney stones tend to form at low urine pH?

{{c1::Uric acid}} kidney stones
{{c1::Cystine}} kidney stones
{{c1::Calcium oxalate}} kidney stones
fields.Back Extra: Hypocitraturia is associated with low pH.

fields.Text:
What amino acids would you expect to find at high concentrations in a patient with hereditary cystinuria?

{{c1::Cystine}}
{{c1::Ornithine}}
{{c1::Lysine}}
{{c1::Arginine}}

Which two types of kidney stones are commonly associated with staghorn calculi?

{{c1::Ammonium magnesium phosphate}} kidney stones (most common)
{{c1::Cystine}} kidney stones

What are the relative serum and urine calcium levels in patients with calcium kidney stones?

Serum calcium levels are {{c1::normal}}
Urine calcium levels are {{c1::increased}}

What three organisms can cause urinary tract infections associated with kidney stones and the urine microscopic findings shown?



{{c1::Proteus mirabilis}}
{{c1::Staphylococcus saprophyticus}}
{{c1::Klebsiella}}
fields.Back Extra: Note the coffin-lid crystals of ammonium magnesium phosphate stones.

fields.Text:
What is the likely diagnosis for a child with flank pain and a positive sodium cyanide nitroprusside test result?

{{c1::Hereditary cystinuria}}
fields.Back Extra: This leads to the formation of cystine stones.

fields.Text:
What four conditions may promote the formation of calcium oxalate stones?

{{c1::Hypocitraturia::Hypercitraturia/Hypocitraturia}}
{{c1::Malabsorption}}
Ingestion of {{c1::ethylene glycol}}
Overuse of vitamin {{c1::C}}

Diffuse cortical necrosis is thought to be related to a combination of which two pathologic processes?

{{c1::Disseminated intravascular coagulation}}
{{c1::Vasospasm}}

Obstetric catastrophes and septic shock are both associated with which serious renal pathology?

{{c1::Diffuse cortical necrosis}}

What is acute, generalized cortical infarction of both kidneys known as?

{{c1::Diffuse cortical necrosis}}

How does the glomerular filtration rate change in a patient with intrinsic renal failure?

Glomerular filtration rate {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the result of fluid backflow caused by obstructing necrotic debris in the tubules.

fields.Text:
What are the expected values for urine osmolality, urine Na+, FENa, and BUN/Cr ratio in intrinsic renal failure?

Urine osmolality < {{c1::350}} mOsm/kg
Urine Na+ > {{c1::40}} mEq/L
FENa > {{c1::2}}%
BUN/Cr ratio < {{c1::15}}

What are the expected values for urine osmolality, urine Na+, FENa, and BUN/Cr ratio in prerenal azotemia?

Urine osmolality > {{c1::500}} mOsm/kg
Urine Na+ < {{c1::20}} mEq/L
FENa < {{c1::1}}%
BUN/Cr ratio > {{c1::20}}

What is the BUN/Cr ratio in a patient with intrinsic renal failure?

{{c1::<::</>}} {{c1::15}}
fields.Back Extra: This is because the kidneys do not reabsorb urea, leading to a reduced BUN/Cr ratio.

fields.Text:
What are four potential causes of postrenal outflow obstruction?

Urinary tract {{c1::stones}}
{{c1::Benign prostatic hyperplasia}}
{{c1::Congenital}} anomalies
{{c1::Neoplasia}}

Name two causes of acute intrinsic renal failure that affect the tubules and interstitium.

Acute {{c1::tubular necrosis}}
Acute {{c1::interstitial nephritis}}

What is the classic urinalysis finding in a patient with intrinsic renal failure?

{{c1::Granular}} casts
fields.Back Extra: These are also known as muddy casts.

fields.Text:
Why does the BUN/Cr ratio increase in patients who have low renal blood flow?

Decreased renal blood flow → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} glomerular filtration rate → Reabsorption of {{c1::urea}}, but not {{c1::creatinine}} → Inflated BUN/Cr ratio

In patients experiencing dehydration and hypotension, the kidney promotes resorption of which three compounds?

{{c1::Na+}}
{{c1::H2O}}
{{c1::Urea}}

What type of acute kidney injury is likely seen in a trauma patient with hypotension, a BUN level of 45, and a creatinine level of 1.5?

{{c1::Prerenal azotemia}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to decreased renal blood flow, as the BUN/Cr ratio is greater than 20.

fields.Text:
What are the differences in urine osmolality and urine Na+ findings seen in prerenal azotemia and intrinsic renal failure?

{{c1::Higher::Higher/Lower}} urine osmolality and {{c1::lower::higher/lower}} urine Na+ in prerenal azotemia

What are the three general types and the respective causes of acute kidney injury?

{{c1::Prerenal azotemia}} → Reduced {{c2::renal blood flow}}
{{c1::Intrinsic renal failure}} → Tubular {{c2::necrosis}}
{{c1::Postrenal azotemia}} → Outflow {{c2::obstruction}}

In a patient with a urine osmolality < 350, urine Na+ > 40, FENa > 2%, BUN/Cr > 15, and postvoid residual urine of 125 mL, what type of acute kidney injury is the likely cause?

{{c1::Postrenal azotemia}}
fields.Back Extra: The key is the postvoid residual value, which should be near 0 normally.

fields.Text:
What cause of intrinsic renal failure may affect the glomerulus?

{{c1::Acute glomerulonephritis}}

What kind of acute kidney injury is associated with vasculitides, malignant hypertension, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, and hemolytic uremic syndrome?

{{c1::Intrinsic renal failure}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to the destruction of the renal vasculature.

fields.Text:
What are four organisms commonly associated with urinary tract infections?

{{c1::Esherichia coli}} (most common)
{{c1::Staphylococcus saprophyticus}}
{{c1::Proteus mirabilis}}
{{c1::Klebsiella}}

What are five key risk factors for acute cystitis?

{{c1::Female::Male/Female}} sex
{{c1::Sexual intercourse}}
{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}
Impaired bladder {{c1::emptying}}
{{c1::Indwelling catheters}}

What organism is the second most common cause of acute cystitis in young, sexually active women?

{{c1::Staphylococcus saprophyticus}}
fields.Back Extra: Escherichia coli is the most common cause.

fields.Text:
What organism is likely to cause urinary urgency, dysuria, suprapubic pain, and ammonia-like odor of a patient's urine?

{{c1::Proteus mirabilis}}

What two organisms should be suspected as the cause of acute cystitis in a patient with a finding of sterile pyuria?

{{c1::Neisseria gonorrhoeae}}
{{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}}

What finding on urinalysis distinguishes gram-negative bacteria from gram-positive bacteria?

The presence of {{c1::nitrites}} indicates the presence of gram-negative bacteria

What organism is the most common cause of acute cystitis?

{{c1::Escherichia coli}}

What are two common antibiotics used to treat acute simple cystitis?

{{c1::Nitrofurantoin}}
{{c1::TMP-SMX}}

What is the classic CT finding associated with acute pyelonephritis shown in the image?



{{c1::Striated parenchymal enhancement}}

What is a common histologic finding in kidneys affected by chronic pyelonephritis?



{{c1::Eosinophilic}} casts resembling {{c1::thyroid}} tissue

What finding on urinalysis suggests acute pyelonephritis?

{{c1::White blood}} cells with/without white blood cell casts

What disease process is indicated by the findings in the renal biopsy specimen shown in the image?



Acute {{c1::pyelonephritis}}
fields.Back Extra: Note the neutrophils invading the interstitium of the renal cortex.

fields.Text:
What form of chronic pyelonephritis is associated with a history of Proteus infection?

{{c1::Xanthogranulomatous}} pyelonephritis

What disease manifests renally as coarse, asymmetric corticomedullary scarring and blunting of calyces?

Chronic {{c1::pyelonephritis}}

What two conditions commonly lead to chronic pyelonephritis because they predispose individuals to infection?

{{c1::Vesicoureteral reflux}}
Chronic obstruction by {{c1::kidney stones}}

What is the likely diagnosis for a patient with fever, chills, nausea, and costovertebral angle tenderness on examination?

Acute {{c1::pyelonephritis}}

What organism most commonly produces the condition demonstrated by the renal biopsy findings shown?



{{c1::Escherichia coli}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the most common pathogen responsible for an ascending urinary tract infection leading to acute pyelonephritis.

fields.Text:
What type of urinary tract infection is most associated with the development of xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis?

{{c1::Proteus}} infection

What are two common mechanisms for development of acute pyelonephritis?

{{c1::Ascending::Ascending/Descending}} urinary tract infection
{{c1::Hematogenous}} spread of bacteria to the kidney

What are five risk factors for acute pyelonephritis?

Urinary tract {{c1::obstruction}}
{{c1::Indwelling urinary catheters}}
{{c1::Vesicoureteral reflux}}
{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}
{{c1::Pregnancy}}

What is the general treatment for the condition seen in a patient with fever, chills, nausea, and the CT findings shown?



{{c1::Antibiotics}} are the treatment for acute {{c1::pyelonephritis}}

What kidney disease demonstrates eosinophils on urinalysis and interstitial inflammation on renal biopsy and can be triggered by rifampin?

{{c1::Acute interstitial nephritis}}

What are the classic urinalysis findings in a patient with acute interstitial nephritis?

{{c1::Pyuria}} with {{c1::eosinophils}}

Name seven types of drugs that are associated with acute interstitial nephritis.

{{c1::Diuretics}}
{{c1::NSAIDs}}
{{c1::Penicillins}}
{{c1::Cephalosporins}}
{{c1::Proton pump}} inhibitors
{{c1::Rifampin}}
{{c1::Sulfa}} drugs

A patient with a history of long-term NSAID use presents with fever, rash, hematuria, and costovertebral angle tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Drug-induced {{c1::interstitial nephritis}}

What three autoimmune diseases are associated with interstitial nephritis?

{{c1::Systemic lupus erythematosis}}
{{c1::Sjögren}} syndrome
{{c1::Sarcoidosis}}

What systemic infection may cause acute interstitial nephritis?

{{c1::Mycoplasma}} infection

How do drugs incite the inflammatory response that occurs in tubulointerstitial nephritis?

They act as {{c1::haptens}} and induce an acute {{c1::hypersensitivity}} reaction

What happens to the patient's FENa in nephrotoxic acute tubular necrosis?

FENa is likely {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}}

What three lab abnormalities may be seen during the first 3 weeks after acute tubular necrosis with urine sediment findings shown in the image?



{{c1::Hyperkalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
Metabolic {{c1::acidosis::acidosis/alkalosis}}
{{c1::Uremia}}

What type of casts do you expect to see on urinalysis performed for a patient with acute tubular necrosis?

{{c1::Granular}} casts

What are the three classic phases of acute tubular necrosis?

{{c1::Inciting}} event
{{c1::Maintenance}} phase
{{c1::Recovery}} phase

In the recovery phase of acute tubular necrosis, what lab abnormalities can be expected?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} BUN levels
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} serum creatinine levels
{{c1::Hypokalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
Renal {{c1::wasting}} of other electrolytes and minerals

What would likely happen to a patient's serum K+ levels in the maintenance phase of acute tubular necrosis?

{{c1::Hyperkalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to an inability to excrete K+.

fields.Text:
How much urine will a patient in the recovery phase of acute tubular necrosis produce?

{{c1::Excessive}} amount

How much urine will a patient in the maintenance phase of acute tubular necrosis typically produce?

{{c1::Minimal}} amount

What are the two main types of acute tubular necrosis?

{{c1::Ischemic}}
{{c1::Nephrotoxic}}

What is the likely cause of muddy brown casts in urine obtained from a patient with sepsis, hypotension, and oliguria?

Decreased {{c1::renal blood flow}}
fields.Back Extra: This is ischemic acute tubular necrosis.

fields.Text:
What is the usual prognosis of acute tubular necrosis?

{{c1::Spontaneously}} resolves

What two segments of the nephron are most susceptible to ischemic acute tubular necrosis?

{{c1::Proximal convoluted tubule}}
{{c1::Thick::Thick/Thin}} {{c1::ascending::ascending/descending}} limb of the loop of Henle

What is the most common cause of acute kidney injury in hospitalized patients?

{{c1::Acute tubular necrosis}}

How long may it take for kidneys to start recovering in sepsis-associated acute tubular necrosis?

{{c1::1}} to {{c1::3}} weeks

Which segment of the nephron is most susceptible to nephrotoxic acute tubular necrosis?

{{c1::Proximal convoluted tubule}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the first region to come into contact with the filtered nephrotoxins.

fields.Text:
What disorder would you suspect in a patient presenting with nausea/anorexia, asterixis, encephalopathy, pericarditis, and platelet dysfunction?

{{c1::Uremia}}
fields.Back Extra: Check the BUN/Cr ratio for suspected renal failure.

fields.Text:
What are three complications of excess Na+ and H2O retention in a patient with renal failure?

{{c1::Congestive heart}} failure
{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
Pulmonary {{c1::edema}}

What is the likely cause of anemia in a patient with chronic renal failure?

Decrease in {{c1::erythropoietin}} production by the diseased kidneys

What are the two main forms of renal failure?

{{c1::Acute}}
{{c1::Chronic}}

In renal failure, what may happen to serum potassium?

Serum potassium {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}

How does renal failure lead to the retention of nitrogenous wastes and electrolyte disturbances?

Decreased renal {{c1::filtration}} → Impairs nitrogenous waste {{c1::clearance}} and {{c1::regulation}} of serum electrolyte levels

What are eight key clinical consequences of renal failure?

Metabolic {{c1::acidosis::acidosis/alkalosis}}
{{c1::Dyslipidemia}}
{{c1::Hyperkalemia::Hyperkalemia/Hypokalemia}}
{{c1::Uremia}}
{{c1::Na+}}/{{c1::H2O}} retention
{{c1::Growth}} retardation and {{c1::developmental}} delay
{{c1::Erythropoietin}} deficiency
Renal {{c1::osteodystrophy}}

What measured value defines the stages of chronic renal failure?

{{c1::Glomerular filtration rate}}

Why is the phosphate level normal in patients with early stages of chronic kidney disease?

Increase in the level of {{c1::FGF23}} → Increased renal {{c1::excretion}} of phosphate

How does elevation of calcium levels occur in renal osteodystrophy?

Poorly managed {{c1::secondary hyperparathyroidism}} in renal osteodystrophy → {{c1::Tertiary hyperparathyroidism}} → Increased serum calcium levels

What are the two ways that hypocalcemia occurs in patients with renal osteodystrophy?

High serum {{c1::phosphate}} binds to calcium → Tissue deposits → Decreased serum calcium
Decreased {{c1::1,25-(OH)2 vitamin D3}} → Decreased intestinal calcium absorption

Which part of the bone is most affected by renal osteodystrophy?

{{c1::Subperiosteal}} region

An X-ray obtained from a patient with end-stage renal disease shows subperiosteal bone thinning. Labs are notable for low vitamin D, hypocalcemia, and hyperphosphatemia. What is the diagnosis?

{{c1::Renal osteodystrophy}}
fields.Back Extra: In this case, it is associated with secondary hyperparathyroidism.

fields.Text:
Renal osteodystrophy may progress as a result of a failure in which step in vitamin D processing?

Vitamin D {{c1::hydroxylation}}
fields.Back Extra: This is usually secondary to chronic kidney disease.

fields.Text:
How are the serum levels of calcium and phosphate affected in renal osteodystrophy?

{{c1::Hypocalcemia::Hypercalcemia/Hypocalcemia}}
{{c1::Hyperphosphatemia::Hyperphosphatemia/Hypophosphatemia}}

What is the likely prognosis of a patient with a renal tumor presenting as gross findings of well-circumscribed mass with central scar?



{{c1::Excellent}}
fields.Back Extra: This is a renal oncocytoma arising from the collecting ducts.

fields.Text:
What is the most common treatment for a suspected renal oncocytoma?

{{c1::Surgical resection}}

What are the three classic symptoms produced by a renal oncocytoma?

{{c1::Flank}} pain
Abdominal {{c1::mass}}
Painless {{c1::hematuria}}

How can a renal oncocytoma be distinguished histologically from the chromophobe subtype of renal cell carcinoma?

Abundant {{c1::mitochondria}} without {{c1::perinuclear}} clearing

What accounts for the unique color of renal cell carcinoma in this gross specimen?



Renal cell carcinoma often appears {{c1::golden-yellow}} due to its increased {{c1::lipid}} content

What disease does this histopathological specimen represent in a 60-year-old patient with hematuria and weight loss?



{{c1::Renal cell}} carcinoma
fields.Back Extra: This appears most commonly as polygonal clear cells filled with accumulated lipids and carbohydrates.

fields.Text:
In what demographic is renal cell carcinoma most common?

{{c1::Men::Men/Women}} aged {{c1::50}} to {{c1::70}} years

What are two risk factors for developing renal cell carcinoma?

{{c1::Smoking}}
{{c1::Obesity}}

Renal cell carcinoma is typically resistant to which two modalities of treatment?

{{c1::Chemotherapy}}
{{c1::Radiotherapy}}

What is the usual treatment for metastatic renal cell carcinoma?

{{c1::Immunotherapy}}
Targeted {{c1::molecular}} therapies

What is the most common subtype of renal cell carcinoma?

{{c1::Clear cell}} type

How might a left-sided varicocele occur in a male with left-sided renal cell carcinoma?

Invasion of the left {{c1::renal}} vein by the tumor may also obstruct the left {{c1::testicular}} vein

What genetic disorder is most associated with hereditary renal cell carcinoma?

{{c1::Von Hippel-Lindau}} syndrome

What is the most effective treatment for localized renal cell carcinoma?

{{c1::Surgery}}
{{c1::Ablation}}

What is the most common mechanism of metastasis in renal cell carcinoma?

Invasion of the {{c1::renal}} vein and {{c1::inferior vena cava}} with subsequent hematogenous spread, often metastasizing to {{c1::lung}} and {{c1::bone}}

What could be the cause of hyperviscosity syndrome developing in a smoker with hematuria, weight loss, and a palpable flank mass?

{{c1::Renal cell}} carcinoma producing excess {{c1::erythropoietin}} → Polycythemia

Renal cell carcinoma is a malignancy of which specific cell type?

{{c1::Proximal convoluted tubule}} cells
fields.Back Extra: They become filled with lipids and carbohydrates.

fields.Text:
What genetic anomaly is renal cell carcinoma most commonly associated with?

Gene deletion on chromosome {{c1::3}}
fields.Back Extra: This is associated with sporadic renal cell carcinoma and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome.

fields.Text:
What are the four hormones that may be ectopically secreted by renal cell carcinoma to produce paraneoplastic syndromes?

{{c1::PTHrP}}
Ectopic {{c1::erythropoietin}}
{{c1::ACTH}}
{{c1::Renin}}

What is the most common primary renal malignancy?

{{c1::Renal cell}} carcinoma

What are the two main causes of renal artery stenosis?

{{c1::Fibromuscular dysplasia}}
{{c1::Atherosclerotic}} plaques

What happens to renin levels, as determined by renal venous sampling, in patients with unilateral renal artery stenosis?

Affected kidney → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} renin levels
Unaffected kidney → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} renin levels

When do you expect the creatinine level to rise suddenly in a patient with bilateral renal artery stenosis?

When the patient begins taking an {{c1::ACE}} inhibitor, {{c1::angiotensin}} receptor blocker, or {{c1::renin}} inhibitor
fields.Back Extra: They interfere with RAAS-mediated renal perfusion.

fields.Text:
What underlying pathology is most likely in an adult with refractory secondary hypertension?

{{c1::Renovascular}} disease

Where would you expect to see stenosis on angiography in an old smoker with resistant hypertension and bruit over the left flank?

Within the {{c1::proximal::proximal/distal}} third of the left {{c1::renal}} artery
fields.Back Extra: This is a classic presentation of renal artery stenosis due to a high atherosclerotic plaque burden.

fields.Text:
Where would you expect to see stenosis on angiography in an otherwise healthy 36-year-old woman presenting with resistant hypertension and a bruit over the right flank?

Within the {{c1::distal::proximal/distal}} {{c1::2}}/3 or {{c1::segmental}} branches of the right {{c1::renal}} artery
fields.Back Extra: This is a classic presentation of renal artery stenosis due to fibromuscular dysplasia.

fields.Text:
What are the common presenting features of renovascular disease?

Severe/refractory {{c1::hypertension::hypertension/hypotension}}
Flash pulmonary {{c1::edema}}
{{c1::Bruit}} in the epigastrium or flank

What is the general mechanism whereby renovascular disease may produce hypertension?

Diminished renal perfusion upregulates {{c1::renin}} and {{c1::angiotensin}} release → Increased blood pressure

What is the general definition of renovascular disease?

Renal impairment caused by {{c1::ischemia}} from {{c1::renal artery stenosis}} or {{c1::microvascular}} disease

What is the likely cause of this appearance of the kidneys in an autopsy of an adult?



{{c1::Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney}} disease
fields.Back Extra: This presents with numerous cortical and medullary cysts that ultimately destroy the renal parenchyma.

fields.Text:
What is the likely diagnosis in an infant with the following imaging findings, hematemesis, and family history of death due to renal failure?



{{c1::Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney}} disease

A patient has a cyst in the left renal cortex that appears thin walled and filled with ultrafiltrate as shown in the image. What is the likely diagnosis?



{{c1::Simple renal cyst}}

What is the ideal management for asymptomatic complex renal cysts that are septate, enhancing with contrast or with solid components in imaging?

{{c1::Follow-up}}
{{c1::Removal}}, due to the possibility of {{c1::renal cell}} carcinoma

What is the prognosis of a patient with medullary cystic kidney disease?

{{c1::Poor}}

What two mutations may cause autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease?

Mutation in {{c1::PKD1}} (85%)
Mutation in {{c1::PKD2}} (15%)

Why is autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease often fatal in the neonatal period?

Due to the {{c1::Potter sequence}}
fields.Back Extra: This may be caused by significant renal failure in utero.

fields.Text:
What kind of liver disease is associated with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease?

Congenital {{c1::hepatic fibrosis}}
fields.Back Extra: This may lead to portal hypertension and liver cirrhosis.

fields.Text:
What are the most common complications in patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease?

Chronic {{c1::kidney::organ}} disease
{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}

What are the characteristic clinical features of medullary cystic kidney disease?

Progressive renal {{c1::insufficiency}} and tubulointerstitial {{c1::fibrosis}}
{{c1::Dilute}} urine
{{c1::Small::Large/Small}} kidneys on ultrasound

What are the four common systemic associations of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease?

{{c1::Benign hepatic cysts}}
{{c1::Berry aneurysms}}
{{c1::Mitral valve prolapse}}
{{c1::Diverticulosis}}

What might neuroimaging reveal in a patient with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease?

{{c1::Berry aneurysms}}

When should a patient with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease be given a prescription for an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker?

If {{c1::hypertension::hypertension/hypotension}} or {{c1::proteinuria}} develops

Where in the nephron does cystic dilation occur in patients with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease?

{{c1::Collecting ducts}}

Why do simple renal cysts typically appear anechoic on ultrasound?

They are filled with {{c1::ultrafiltrate}}

What are five signs and symptoms of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease?

{{c1::Hematuria}}
{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}}
{{c1::Flank}} pain
Urinary tract {{c1::infections}}
{{c1::Progressive}} renal failure

What are three key complications of autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease in children who survive the neonatal period?

{{c1::Progressive}} renal insufficiency
{{c1::Systemic}} hypertension
{{c1::Portal}} hypertension

What is the most common type of renal mass overall?

{{c1::Simple renal cysts}}

The absence of how many sexual characteristics is classified as delayed puberty?

The absence of {{c1::2}} sexual characteristics
fields.Back Extra: This is by age 13 in males and age 14 in females.

fields.Text:
What are the two main causes of delayed puberty?

{{c1::Hypergonadotropic::Hypergonadotropic/Hypogonadotropic}} {{c1::hypogonadism::hypergonadism/hypogonadism}}
{{c1::Hypogonadotropic::Hypergonadotropic/Hypogonadotropic}} {{c1::hypogonadism::hypergonadism/hypogonadism}}

What are three causes of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism?

Constitutional delay of {{c1::growth}} and {{c1::puberty}}
{{c1::Kallmann}} syndrome
{{c1::Central nervous system}} lesions

What are three causes of hypergonadotropic hypogonadism?

{{c1::Klinefelter}} syndrome
{{c1::Turner}} syndrome
{{c1::Gonadal}} injury

Precocious puberty can be diagnosed if secondary sexual characteristics develop before what age?

{{c1::8}} years for girls
{{c1::9}} years for boys

What mechanism causes short stature in children affected by precocious puberty?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} sex hormone exposure or production → Early skeletal {{c1::maturation}} → Premature closure of the {{c1::epiphyseal}} plates

What is the difference in the mechanism of disease for central and peripheral precocious puberty?

Central precocious puberty → Increased {{c1::GnRH}} secretion
Peripheral precocious puberty → Increased {{c1::sex hormone}} production independent of {{c1::GnRH}}

What are two causes of central precocious puberty?

{{c1::Idiopathic}}
Central nervous system {{c1::tumors}}

What are two possible oncologic causes of peripheral precoious puberty?

{{c1::Estrogen-secreting ovarian}} tumor
{{c1::Leydig}} cell tumor

What are two congenital conditions that may cause peripheral precocious puberty?

Congenital {{c1::adrenal hyperplasia}}
{{c1::McCune-Albright}} syndrome

What are the two main types of precocious puberty?

{{c1::Central}} precocious puberty
{{c1::Peripheral}} precocious puberty

At what Tanner stage and average age will males begin to notice testicular enlargement and females notice a pubic mound?

Tanner stage {{c1::II}} → {{c1::8}} to {{c1::11.5}} years old

During what two Tanner stages and at what average age does the penis begin to grow?

Lengthen in Tanner stage {{c1::III}} → {{c1::11.5}} to {{c1::13}} years old
Widen in Tanner stage {{c1::IV}} → {{c1::13}} to {{c1::15}} years old

At what Tanner stage and average age does coarse hair spread across the pubis but spare the thighs?

Tanner stage {{c1::IV}} → {{c1::13}} to {{c1::15}} years old

At what Tanner stage and average age will pubic hair begin to appear and breast buds begin to form?

Tanner stage {{c1::II}} → {{c1::8}} to {{c1::11.5}} years old

At what Tanner stage and average age does coarsening of pubic hair begin?

Tanner stage {{c1::III}} → {{c1::11.5}} to {{c1::13}} years old

At what Tanner stage and average age do the female breasts contour and the areolae flatten?

Tanner stage {{c1::V}} → > {{c1::15}} years old

What is the earliest detectable secondary sexual characteristic in male and in females?

Females → {{c1::Breast bud}}
Males → {{c1::Testicular}} enlargement

What two processes occur during spermiogenesis?

Spermatids lose their {{c1::cytoplasmic}} contents and gain an {{c1::acrosomal cap}} to form mature spermatozoa

Where does spermatogenesis occur?

{{c1::Seminiferous tubules}}

What kind of barrier must the spermatogonia cross during the replication stage of spermatogenesis?

{{c1::Tight}} junctions of the {{c1::blood-testis}} barrier

When does spermatogenesis begin in a male?

{{c1::Puberty}}

Which condition is associated with impaired tail mobility of the sperm?

{{c1::Kartagener}} syndrome → Infertility
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as ciliary dyskinesia.

fields.Text:
Differentiation of sperm occurs via meiosis I and meiosis II. Which sperm subtypes are involved in each?

Meiosis I → {{c1::Primary spermatocyte}} to {{c1::secondary spermatocyte}}
Meiosis II → {{c1::Secondary spermatocyte}} to {{c1::spermatid}}

What is the genetic makeup of a mature spermatozoon?

It is {{c1::haploid::diploid/haploid}} with {{c1::23}} single chromatids and a sex of {{c1::X}} or {{c1::Y}}

What is the genetic makeup of a spermatid?

It is {{c1::haploid::diploid/haploid}} with {{c1::23}} single chromatids and a sex of {{c1::X}} or {{c1::Y}}

What is the genetic makeup of a secondary spermatocyte?

It is {{c1::haploid::diploid/haploid}} with {{c1::23}} sister chromatids and a sex of {{c1::X-X}} or {{c1::Y-Y}}

What is the genetic makeup of a primary spermatocyte?

It is {{c1::diploid::diploid/haploid}} with {{c1::46}} sister chromatids and a sex of {{c1::X-X}} or {{c1::Y-Y}}

What is the genetic makeup of a spermatogonium?

It is {{c1::diploid::diploid/haploid}} with {{c1::46}} single chromosomes and a sex of {{c1::X-Y}}

What is the order of development of a spermatozoan from a spermatogonium?

Spermatogonium → {{c1::Primary spermatocyte}} → {{c1::Secondary spermatocyte}} → {{c1::Spermatid}} → Spermatozoan

How long do mature spermatids take to develop?

{{c1::2}} months

In cystic fibrosis, what is the cause of infertility?

Absent {{c1::vas deferens}}

When does hCG typically peak during pregnancy?

At {{c1::8}} to {{c1::10}} weeks' gestation

When is hCG first detectable in the blood and urine of a pregnant patient?

Blood → Detectable {{c1::1}} week(s) after fertilization
Urine → Detectable {{c1::2}} week(s) after fertilization

What is the difference between embryonic/developmental age and gestational age?

Gestational age is calculated from the {{c1::last menstrual period}}
Embryonic age is determined from the {{c1::date of conception}}

What cell type secretes hCG shortly after conception?

{{c1::Syncytiotrophoblasts}}

When does implantation occur in relation to ovulation?

{{c1::1}} week(s) after ovulation
{{c1::6}} day(s) after fertilization

When does fertilization occur in relation to ovulation?

Within {{c1::1}} day(s) of ovulation

Where is the most common area of fertilization in the female reproductive tract?

{{c1::Ampulla}} of the fallopian tube

Define abnormal uterine bleeding.

Heavy {{c1::menstrual}} bleeding
{{c1::Intermenstrual}} bleeding

What are four structural causes of abnormal uterine bleeding?

{{c1::Polyp}}
{{c1::Adenomyosis}}
{{c1::Leiomyoma}}
{{c1::Malignancy}}

What are four nonstructural causes of abnormal uterine bleeding?

{{c1::Coagulopathy}}
{{c1::Ovulatory}}
{{c1::Endometrial}}
{{c1::Iatrogenic}}
Not yet classified

What hormone is produced by the theca cells?

{{c1::Androstenedione}}

To which three receptors is estrogen known to provide upregulation?

{{c1::Estrogen}} receptors
{{c1::LH}} receptors
{{c1::Progesterone}} receptors

During pregnancy, what happens to the levels of endogenous estrogens?

{{c1::50}}-fold increase in estradiol and estrone
{{c1::1000}}-fold increase in estriol

An increase in which variant of estrogen is an indicator of fetal well-being during pregnancy?

{{c1::Estriol}}

Where are estrogen receptors located in a cell?

{{c1::Cytoplasm}}
fields.Back Extra: The receptors translocate to the nucleus once estrogen binds to it.

fields.Text:
What is the effect of estrogen on prolactin secretion?

Estrogen {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}} prolactin secretion

How does estrogen affect FSH and LH levels?

Estrogen provides {{c1::negative::positive/negative}} feedback on FSH and LH secretion except near ovulation
Estrogen provides {{c1::positive::positive/negative}} feedback for the LH surge

What are the two effects of estrogen on the plasma lipid profile?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} HDL
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} LDL

What is the effect of estrogen on the synthesis of proteins in the body?

Increased synthesis of {{c1::sex hormone-binding globulin}} and {{c1::transport}} proteins

What are the two roles of estrogen in physical development during puberty?

Development of {{c1::breasts}} and external/internal {{c1::genitalia}}
Female {{c1::fat}} distribution

What three effects does estrogen have on the uterus and ovaries?

Stimulates {{c1::follicle}} growth
Stimulates {{c1::endometrial}} proliferation
Increases myometrial {{c1::excitability}}

What is the effect of LH in theca cells?

LH promotes the conversion of {{c1::cholesterol}} to {{c1::androgens}}
fields.Back Extra: This is via the enzyme desmolase.

fields.Text:
What major hormone is produced by granulosa cells?

{{c1::Estrogen}}
fields.Back Extra: This is via the conversion of androgens by the enzyme aromatase.

fields.Text:
Rank the following three forms of estrogen in order of most to least potent:

Estradiol
Estriol
Estrone

{{c1::Estradiol}} > {{c1::Estrone}} > {{c1::Estriol}}

Name three places in the female body where estrogen can be produced.

{{c1::Ovaries}}
{{c1::Placenta}}
{{c1::Adipose}} tissue

During the menstrual cycle, regression of the corpus luteum leads to what event?

{{c1::Menstruation}}

Is the corpus luteum present during the follicular or luteal phase of the menstrual cycle?

{{c1::Luteal}} phase
fields.Back Extra: The corpus luteum is formed from the ruptured follicle and produces progesterone.

fields.Text:
In relation to ovulation, when does the estrogen level peak?

{{c1::Before::Before/After}} ovulation

In relation to ovulation, when does the progesterone level peak?

{{c1::After::Before/After}} ovulation

How long does the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle typically last?

Follicular phase can {{c1::vary}} in length
fields.Back Extra: This accounts for the differences in menstrual cycle lengths.

fields.Text:
How long does the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle typically last?

The luteal phase has a fixed duration of {{c1::14}} days

What hormone stimulates endometrial proliferation during the menstrual cycle?

{{c1::Estrogen}}

Which part of the menstrual cycle has the fastest follicular growth?

{{c1::2nd}} week of the {{c1::follicular}} phase

Which hormone is essential in maintaining the endometrium and supporting implantation during the beginning of pregnancy?

{{c1::Progesterone}}

List the following events of the menstrual cycle in order:

Progesterone produced by corpus luteum
LH surge
Menstruation
Ovulation
Increase in estrogen
Progesterone declines

1 → {{c1::Increase in estrogen}}
2 → {{c1::LH surge}}
3 → {{c1::Ovulation}}
4 → {{c1::Progesterone produced by corpus luteum}}
5 → {{c1::Progesterone declines}}
6 → {{c1::Menstruation}}

What effect does progesterone have on uterine smooth muscle?

It {{c1::relaxes::contracts/relaxes}} uterine smooth muscle

What is the effect of progesterone on cervical mucus?

Progesterone {{c1::thickens::thickens/thins}} cervical mucus
fields.Back Extra: This is to prevent sperm entry into the uterus.

fields.Text:
What effect does progesterone have on pregnancy?

Progesterone {{c1::maintains}} the pregnancy

Progesterone causes what two changes in the endometrium?

{{c1::Spiral}} artery development
Stimulation of endometrial {{c1::glandular}} secretions

Name the four sources of progesterone.

{{c1::Corpus luteum}}
{{c1::Placenta}}
{{c1::Adrenal cortex}}
{{c1::Testes}}

How does progesterone affect myometrial excitability during pregnancy?

{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} myometrial excitability → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} frequency and intensity of contractions during pregnancy

What effect does progesterone exert on body temperature?

{{c1::Increases::Increases/Decreases}} body temperature

What is the significance of decreased progesterone expression after delivery of a newborn?

Drop in progesterone level disinhibits {{c1::prolactin}} → Increase in {{c1::lactation}}

What does the elevation in the progesterone level during a menstrual cycle indicate?

Progesterone elevation indicates that {{c1::ovulation}} has occurred

What effects does progesterone have on FSH, LH, and estrogen?

{{c1::Inhibits::Stimulates/Inhibits}} release of FSH
{{c1::Inhibits::Stimulates/Inhibits}} release of LH
