{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} estrogen receptor expressivity

What are the two main causes of low birth weight in newborns?

{{c1::Prematurity}}
Intrauterine {{c1::growth}} restriction

What is the definition of low birth weight?

Less than {{c1::2500}} grams

An infant with low birth weight is at increased risk for what poorly understood condition?

{{c1::Sudden infant death}} syndrome
fields.Back Extra: The risk of overall mortality is also increased.

fields.Text:
When are Apgar scores assessed in a newborn?

{{c1::1}} minute(s) after delivery
{{c1::5}} minute(s) after delivery

What is the expected range of the Apgar score for a healthy infant?

{{c1::7}} to {{c1::10}}

In the Apgar scoring system for newborns, how many points are possible for each of the five criteria?

{{c1::0}} to {{c1::2}} points

What is a potential sequela of an Apgar score that remains low in a newborn for a prolonged period?

Long-term {{c1::neurologic}} damage

What are the five criteria for assessing the Apgar score?

{{c1::Appearance}}
{{c1::Pulse}}
{{c1::Grimace}}
{{c1::Activity}}
{{c1::Respiration}}

What is the function of human placental lactogen in relation to insulin?

Increases insulin {{c1::production}} and {{c1::resistance}}

Which cell type produces human placental lactogen?

{{c1::Syncytiotrophoblasts}} of the placenta

What is another name for human placental lactogen?

{{c1::Chorionic somatomammotropin}}

What are the potential risks of elevated human placental lactogen?

{{c1::Gestational diabetes}}
fields.Back Extra: This can occur if maternal pancreatic function cannot overcome the insulin resistance.

fields.Text:
What two things can happen to the first polar body?

{{c1::Degenerates}}
Gives rise to {{c1::2}} polar bodies

In which stage of oogenesis does a secondary oocyte become an ovum and polar body?

{{c1::Meiosis II}}

What stage of oogenesis begins with an oogonium and ends with a primary oocyte?

{{c1::Replication}}

What cell types are present at the end of meiosis II during oogenesis, when arrested at metaphase II?

{{c1::Secondary oocyte}}
{{c1::Polar body}}

During the process of oogenesis, what cell type begins meiosis I?

{{c1::Primary oocyte}}
fields.Back Extra: It becomes a secondary oocyte at the end of meiosis I.

fields.Text:
What is the genetic makeup of an ovum?

{{c1::Haploid::Diploid/Haploid}} with {{c1::23}} single chromatids

What is the genetic makeup of a secondary oocyte?

{{c1::Haploid::Diploid/Haploid}} with {{c1::46}} sister chromatids

What is the genetic makeup of an oogonium?

{{c1::Diploid::Diploid/Haploid}} with {{c1::46}} single chromosomes

What type of oocyte is released on day 14 of the menstrual cycle, and what happens if it is not fertilized?

{{c1::Secondary oocyte}}
It {{c1::degenerates}} if fertilization does not occur within 1 day

In what stage of meiosis II is a secondary oocyte arrested between ovulation and fertilization?

{{c1::Metaphase II}}

What is the genetic makeup of a primary oocyte?

{{c1::Diploid::Diploid/Haploid}} with {{c1::46}} sister chromatids

In what stage of meiosis I is a primary oocyte arrested between fetal life and ovulation?

{{c1::Prophase I}}

When does a primary oocyte begin and complete meiosis I?

Meiosis I begins during {{c1::fetal life}} and is completed just before {{c1::ovulation}}

In preparation for ovulation, increased estrogen leads to increased GnRH receptor expression in which organ?

{{c1::Anterior pituitary}}

What hormone causes a woman's temperature to rise during ovulation?

{{c1::Progesterone}}

What causes LH to surge during ovulation?

{{c1::Estrogen}} causes the LH surge
fields.Back Extra: This leads to the rupture of an ovarian follicle and ovulation.

fields.Text:
What causes transient midcycle ovulatory pain?

Fallopian tube {{c1::contraction::contraction/relaxation}} or follicular {{c1::rupture}} → {{c1::Peritoneal}} irritation
fields.Back Extra:
This can mimic appendicitis.

This is known as Mittelschmerz.

fields.Text:
Pain during ovulation can mimic which medical emergency?

Acute {{c1::appendicitis}}

How is typical ovulation pain described?

{{c1::Unilateral::Unilateral/Bilateral}}
{{c1::Mild}}

What is the underlying physiologic mechanism of peripheral edema in pregnancy?

{{c1::Hemodilution}} due to increased blood volume → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} capillary oncotic pressure → Peripheral edema

Which three transport proteins are secreted at higher levels during pregnancy?

{{c1::Cortisol}}-binding globulin
{{c1::Sex hormone}}-binding globulin
{{c1::Thyroxine}}-binding globulin

What physiologic change in pregnancy predisposes a patient to gastroesophageal reflux disease?

{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} lower esophageal sphincter tone

What physiologic changes predispose to gallstones in pregnancy?

Gallbladder stasis caused by {{c1::estrogen}} and {{c1::progesterone}}

What musculoskeletal changes will be seen in the joints of pregnant patients?

Increased joint {{c1::laxity}}
fields.Back Extra: This is to facilitate fetal descent.

fields.Text:
List three possible dermatologic changes in pregnancy that are caused by hyperpigmentation.

Darkening of {{c1::areolae}}
{{c1::Melasma}}
{{c1::Linea nigra}}

List three possible dermatologic findings in pregnancy that are caused by vascular changes.

Palmar {{c1::erythema}}
{{c1::Spider angiomas}}
{{c1::Varicosities}}

Describe the physiologic change in pregnancy that predisposes to pyelonephritis.

Ureter and renal pelvis {{c1::dilation::dilation/constriction}} → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} stasis → Resultant infection

How does the glomerular filtration rate change during pregnancy?

{{c1::Vasodilation::Vasodilation/Vasoconstriction}} → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} renal plasma flow → {{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} glomerular filtration rate

What are the three major mechanisms of increased cardiac output during pregnancy?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} heart rate (major contributor)
{{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} systemic vascular resistance
{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} blood volume

What physiologic respiratory change should be expected in pregnancy?

Chronic {{c1::hyperventilation::hyperventilation/hypoventilation}} helps to eliminate excess fetal {{c1::CO2}}

What is the pathophysiology of anemia in pregnancy?

{{c1::Increased::Increased/Decreased}} plasma volume and {{c1::increased::increased/decreased}} red blood cell mass → Dilutional anemia

What is the purpose of the hypercoagulable state that occurs during pregnancy?

The hypercoagulable state helps reduce {{c1::blood loss}} at the time of delivery

How do insulin resistance and hypoglycemia affect a pregnant patient and her child?

Insulin resistance and hypoglycemia → {{c1::Mobilization}} of fat stores to reserve {{c1::glucose}} and {{c1::amino acids}} for the fetus

What organ is the major source of androstenedione?

{{c1::Adrenals}}

Testosterone influences the differentiation of all internal male genitalia except for which organ?

{{c1::Prostate}}

Which androgen is responsible for differentiation of the epididymis, vas deferens, internal genitalia, and seminal vesicles?

{{c1::Testosterone}}

What hormone causes epiphyseal plate closure?

{{c1::Estrogen}}

What is the mechanism by which anabolic-androgenic steroid use cause infertility?

Exogenous testosterone inhibits the {{c1::hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal}} axis → {{c1::Decreased::Increased/Decreased}} intratesticular testosterone → Azoospermia and decreased sperm count

Name four ways testosterone affects male puberty.

Growth {{c1::spurt}}
{{c1::Deepening}} of the voice
Increased {{c1::libido}}
Closure of {{c1::epiphyseal}} plates

Which enzyme converts testosterone and androstenedione to estrogen in men?

{{c1::Aromatase}} in adipose tissue and testes

What medication inhibits 5α-reductase conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone?

{{c1::Finasteride}}

Which androgen may affect balding, prostate growth, and sebaceous gland activity in older men?

{{c1::Dihydrotestosterone}}

What is the major source of dihydrotestosterone and testosterone in men?

{{c1::Testes}}

Rank these three androgens in order, from most to least potent:

Androstenedione
Dihydrotestosterone
Testosterone

{{c1::Dihydrotestosterone}} > {{c1::Testosterone}} > {{c1::Androstenedione}}

What three physical exam findings suggest a diagnosis of anabolic steroid abuse in men?

{{c1::Acne}}
{{c1::Gynecomastia}}
{{c1::Small}} testes

How are women affected by anabolic steroid use?

They experience physical signs of {{c1::virilization}}
fields.Back Extra: These signs include hirsutism, breast atrophy, acne, and male pattern baldness.

fields.Text:
What is the cause of the decreased level of estrogen in a woman experiencing menopause?

{{c1::Age}}-linked decline in the number of {{c1::ovarian follicles}}

What are five clinical and pathologic manifestations of menopause?

{{c1::Hot flashes}}
{{c1::Atrophy}} of the vagina
{{c1::Osteoporosis}}
{{c1::Coronary artery}} disease
{{c1::Sleep}} disturbances

Menopause before age 40 suggests what likely diagnosis?

{{c1::Primary ovarian insufficiency}}
fields.Back Extra: This is also known as premature ovarian failure.

fields.Text:
What is the main source of estrogen after menopause?

The peripheral conversion of {{c1::androgens}} into {{c1::estrone}}

What is the average age for the onset of menopause in nonsmokers?

{{c1::51}} years old

What laboratory test can you use to confirm menopause?

Measurement of {{c1::FSH}}
fields.Back Extra: Increased level of FSH indicates menopause.

fields.Text:
In menopause, what changes occur in estrogen, LH, FSH, and GnRH levels?

Estrogen levels {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}}
LH levels {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}}
FSH levels {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}}
GnRH levels {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}}

How can menopause be diagnosed clinically?

Amenorrhea for {{c1::12}} months
fields.Back Extra: This is usually preceded by 4 to 5 years of abnormal menstrual cycles.

fields.Text:
What are two functions of oxytocin in the perinatal period?

Increases milk {{c1::letdown}}
Promotes uterine {{c1::contraction::contraction/relaxation}}

What two nutritional supplements should be provided for an exclusively breastfed infant?

Vitamin {{c1::D}}
{{c1::Iron}}

What are two benefits of breastfeeding for a mother?

Decreased risk of {{c1::ovarian}}/{{c1::breast}} cancer
Facilitation of {{c1::bonding}} with the infant

Breastfeeding in infancy reduces the risk of what five conditions?

{{c1::Infections}}
{{c1::Asthma}}
{{c1::Allergies}}
{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}
{{c1::Obesity}}

Why is breast milk considered the ideal nutrition for infants who are less than 6 months of age?

Breast milk contains maternal {{c1::immunoglobulins}} that confer passive immunity, {{c1::lymphocytes}}, and {{c1::macrophages}}

Why is suckling necessary to maintain milk production?

Suckling stimulates nerves that induce {{c1::oxytocin}} and {{c1::prolactin}} secretion

What are two functions of prolactin in the perinatal period?

Induces/maintains {{c1::lactation}}
{{c1::Decreases::Increases/Decreases}} reproductive function

What process induces lactation after delivery of an infant?

Rapid decrease in {{c1::progesterone}} and {{c1::estrogen}} → Disinhibition of {{c1::prolactin}} → Induction of lactation

How does hCG affect the thyroid status in pregnant women with thyroid disease?

An increased level of hCG can cause {{c1::hyperthyroidism::hyperthyroidism/hypothyroidism}}
fields.Back Extra: hCG has a structure similar to that of TSH.

fields.Text:
Name three disorders that could result in low hCG levels for gestational age.

{{c1::Ectopic}} pregnancy
{{c1::Patau}} syndrome
{{c1::Edwards}} syndrome

Does a pregnancy test detect the α or β subunit of hCG? Why is this important?

It detects the {{c1::β}} subunit
The {{c1::α}} subunit is structurally identical to LH, FSH, and TSH → Makes it less specific

What is the source of hCG, estriol, and progesterone during the 2nd and 3rd trimesters?

{{c1::Placenta}}

What is the role of hCG in the 1st trimester of pregnancy?

By acting like {{c1::LH}}, hCG prevents spontaneous {{c1::abortion}} by maintaining the {{c1::corpus luteum}}

Name three disorders that could cause abnormally high hCG levels for gestational age.

{{c1::Choriocarcinoma}}
{{c1::Down}} syndrome
{{c1::Hydatidiform moles}}
fields.Back Extra: Increased hCG is also seen in multiple gestations.

fields.Text:
Are the symptoms and motivation of malingering intentional or unconscious?

Malingering symptoms → {{c1::Intentional}}
Malingering motivation → {{c1::Intentional}}

Are the symptoms and motivation of factitious disorder intentional or unconscious?

Factitious disorder symptoms → {{c1::Intentional}}
Factitious disorder motivation → {{c1::Unconscious}}

Are the symptoms and motivation of somatic symptom disorders intentional or unconscious?

Somatic symptom disorders symptoms → {{c1::Unconscious}}
Somatic symptom disorders motivation → {{c1::Unconscious}}

How does blood flow obstruction alter the V/Q ratio?

V/Q ratio would approach {{c1::infinity}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to impaired perfusion.

fields.Text:
How does airway obstruction alter the V/Q ratio?

V/Q ratio = {{c1::0}}
fields.Back Extra: Complete airway obstruction creates a shunt that does not allow gas exchange.

fields.Text:
Where in the lungs do microorganisms that flourish in high O2 thrive?

{{c1::Apex}}
fields.Back Extra: Zone 1 in the lungs is a higher-oxygen environment that allows aerobic organisms to thrive.

fields.Text:
Exercise results in what change to the V/Q ratio?

V/Q ratio approaches {{c1::1}}
fields.Back Extra: Vasodilation of the apical capillaries of the lung increases gas exchange to meet the metabolic demands of exercise.

fields.Text:
Where are ventilation and perfusion greater, at the base or at the apex of the lung?

{{c1::Base}} of the lung

Within which zone of the lung does the V/Q ratio equal approximately 3?

Zone {{c1::1}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the apex of the lungs.

fields.Text:
What is the ideal V/Q ratio for gas exchange?

V/Q ratio = {{c1::1}}
fields.Back Extra: Adequate gas exchange occurs at a state in which ventilation is matched to perfusion.

fields.Text:
What happens to the relationship between PA, Pa, and Pv in zone 1 as shown in the diagram?



{{c1::PA}} ≥ {{c1::Pa}} > {{c1::Pv}}
fields.Back Extra: Zone 1 is associated with decreased perfusion relative to ventilation.

fields.Text:
What happens to the relationship between PA, Pa, and Pv in zone 2 as shown in the diagram?



{{c1::Pa}} > {{c1::PA}} > {{c1::Pv}}
fields.Back Extra: The V/Q ratio is approximately equal to 1.

fields.Text:
What happens to the relationship between PA, Pa, and Pv in zone 3 as shown in the diagram?



{{c1::Pa}} > {{c1::Pv}} > {{c1::PA}}
fields.Back Extra: Zone 3 is associated with increased perfusion relative to ventilation.

fields.Text:
What ABO type of plasma can be given to a patient with type O blood?

{{c1::Any}} type of plasma
fields.Back Extra: These patients have no antigens to be recognized by the antibodies in plasma.

fields.Text:
How do bacteria facilitate nutrient transport and generate ATP when they lack membrane bound organelles?

Their processes are carried out by enzymes embedded in the bacterial {{c1::cytoplasmic}} membrane

Peptidoglycan is an important sugar structure unique to bacteria that is cross-linked by what important enzyme?

{{c1::Transpeptidase}}
fields.Back Extra: Transpeptidase is the inhibition target of many antibiotics, including the penicillins.

fields.Text:
What fungi will positively stain with silver?

{{c1::Coccidiodes}}
{{c1::Pneumocystis jiroveci}}
{{c1::Aspergillus fumigatus}}

What bacteria can be stained with silver?

{{c1::Legionella}}
{{c1::Helicobacter pylori}}
{{c1::Bartonella henselae}}

What staining technique is the first-line lab test for bacterial identification?

{{c1::Gram}} stain

What are the components of Thayer-Martin agar?

{{c1::Vancomycin}} → Inhibits gram-positive organisms
{{c1::Trimethoprim}} and {{c1::colistin}} → Inhibits gram-negative organisms, except for Neisseria
{{c1::Nystatin}} → Inhibits fungi

What are the components of Regan-Lowe medium?

{{c1::Charcoal}}
{{c1::Blood}}
{{c1::Antibiotics}}

Which class of bacteria, known for having a foul smell and being difficult to culture, produces CO2 and H2 gas in tissues?

{{c1::Anaerobes::Aerobes/Anaerobes}}

What organ is responsible for opsonizing and eliminating encapsulated bacteria?

{{c1::Spleen}}

What enzyme do Bordetella, Helicobacter pylori, Burkholderia cepacia, Nocardia, Pseudomonas, Listeria, Aspergillus, Candida, Escherichia coli, Serratia, and Staphylococci have in common?

They all have {{c1::catalase}}

What are the common pathogenic spore-forming organisms?

{{c1::Bacillus anthracis}}
{{c1::Bacillus cereus}}
{{c1::Clostridium botulinum}}
{{c1::Clostridium difficile}}
{{c1::Clostridium perfringens}}
{{c1::Clostridium tetani}}

What factor of bacteria is a major determinant of virulence?

{{c1::Capsular}} polysaccharides
fields.Back Extra: They act as a barrier to phagocytosis and complement-mediated lysis.

fields.Text:
What is the action of the Staphylococcus aureus virulence factor protein A?

Prevents {{c1::opsonization}} and {{c1::phagocytosis}} by binding to the {{c2::Fc}} region of Ig{{c2::G}}

The autoimmune response in acute rheumatic fever is provoked by which phenomenon?

{{c1::Molecular mimicry}}
fields.Back Extra: M protein expresses sequence homology with cardiac myosin and tropomyosin.

fields.Text:
What happens to the heart rate after administration of phenylephrine?

The heart rate {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
fields.Back Extra: This is due to reflex bradycardia.

fields.Text:
A patient is given phenylephrine, and the blood pressure response is shown in the image. What would happen to the patient's mean arterial pressure if she were treated with phentolamine before phenylephrine?



The patient would have a smaller {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} in mean arterial pressure
fields.Back Extra: The pressor effect of phenylephrine is suppressed by an α-blockade.

fields.Text:
The blood pressure response after administration of epinephrine is shown in the image. How would the mean arterial pressure differ if phentolamine were given before epinephrine?



Mean arterial pressure would {{c1::decrease::increase/decrease}}

A patient's heart rate response after administration of epinephrine is shown. How would the heart rate response curve differ if phentolamine were given before epinephrine?



Amplitude of the curve would be {{c1::higher::higher/lower}}
fields.Back Extra: The curve would not return to baseline.

fields.Text:
Among isoproterenol, epinephrine, and norepinephrine, which of the following has the greatest impact on the heart rate?

{{c1::Isoproterenol}} > {{c1::Epinephrine}} > {{c1::Norepinephrine}}

Among isoproterenol, epinephrine, and norepinephrine, which of the following has the greatest impact on the mean arterial pressure?

{{c1::Norepinephrine}} > {{c1::Epinephrine}} > {{c1::Isoproterenol}}

Among isoproterenol, epinephrine, and norepinephrine, which of the following has the greatest impact on the pulse pressure?

{{c1::Isoproterenol}} > {{c1::Epinephrine}} = {{c1::Norepinephrine}}

What classes of antiarrhythmics can cause torsades de pointes?

Class {{c1::IA}}
Class {{c1::III}}

What receptor and muscle mediates mydriasis?

{{c1::α1}} receptor
{{c1::Radial::Radial/Sphincter}} muscle

What receptor and muscle mediates miosis?

{{c1::M3}} receptor
{{c1::Sphincter::Radial/Sphincter}} muscle

What type of study assesses frequency of disease and risk-associated factors to examine prevalence of disease?

{{c1::Cross-sectional}} study

What type of study compares a group of people with a known exposure to a group without the exposure to assess whether exposure is associated with disease development?

{{c1::Cohort}} study

What type of study reports findings in individuals with the same diagnosis, treatment, or outcome without proving an association between risk factors and disease?

{{c1::Case series}}

What type of study compares frequency of disease and risk-related factors in different populations?

{{c1::Ecological}} study

What is the ecological fallacy of ecological studies?

{{c1::Population}} data do not necessarily apply to individuals

Which two types of clinical trial analyses carry an increased risk of bias?

{{c1::Per-protocol}} analysis
{{c1::As-treated}} analysis

What is an as-treated analysis in a clinical trial?

All subjects are evaluated based on the {{c1::treatment}} they received

Which phases of a clinical trial are randomized, controlled, and anonymized?

Phase {{c1::II}}
Phase {{c1::III}}

Which phases of a clinical trial are open-label?

Phase {{c1::0}}
Phase {{c1::I}}
Phase {{c1::IV}}

What does it mean if a new drug has a higher number needed to harm?

The new drug is a {{c1::safer}} treatment

How do you calculate the number of patients who must be exposed to a risk factor for a disease in order for 1 patient to be harmed?

NNH = {{c1::1}} / {{c1::AR}}

What is the relative risk in a study showing that a disease develops in 5 of 10 people with a given exposure versus 1 of 10 of people without that exposure?

RR = {{c1::5}}
fields.Back Extra:
RR = Risk of disease in exposed / Risk of disease in unexposed
RR = 0.5 / 0.1
RR = 5

fields.Text:
What formula is used to calculate the case fatality rate for a given disease?

CFR% = ( {{c1::Deaths}} / {{c1::Cases}} ) × {{c1::100}}

How is the attack rate for a disease calculated?

Attack rate = People who become {{c1::ill}} / Total people {{c1::exposed}}

How is relative risk reduction calculated?

RRR = {{c1::1}} - {{c1::RR}}

What is the meaning of an odds ratio > 1?

Odds of exposure are {{c1::higher::higher/lower}} in cases than in controls

What is the meaning of an odds ratio < 1?

Odds of exposure are {{c1::higher::higher/lower}} in controls than in cases

What is the definition of the positive likelihood ratio?

The likelihood of a {{c1::positive::positive/negative}} test result in a patient with a disease versus the likelihood of a {{c1::positive::positive/negative}} test result in a patient without the disease

For what type of disease will the receiver operating characteristic curve be flipped?

Diseases identified by {{c1::low::high/low}} laboratory values
fields.Back Extra: An example of this is anemia.

fields.Text:
For diseases diagnosed based on low laboratory values, what happens to the false-positive and false-negative rates when the diagnostic cutoff is lowered?

False-positive rate {{c1::decreases::increases/decreases}}
False-negative rate {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}

What term describes a difference in exposure-related outcomes in subgroups stratified by a given factor?

{{c1::Effect modification}}
fields.Back Extra: There is a difference in associations between exposure and outcome in subgroups when they are stratified by another factor.

fields.Text:
Which measure of central tendency is best to use for skewed data?

{{c1::Median}}

In a positively skewed distribution, where do the tail and the mean fall in relation to the peak?

The tail and the mean fall to the {{c1::right::left/right}} of the peak

In a negatively skewed distribution, where do the tail and the mean fall in relation to the peak?

The tail and the mean fall to the {{c1::left::left/right}} of the peak

What happens to the statistical significance level as α increases?

The statistical significance level {{c1::increases::increases/decreases}}

What does β represent in statistical hypothesis testing?

The probability of making a type {{c1::II::I/II}} error

How should you identify a patient's name and pronouns during a patient-centered interview?

{{c1::Ask}} the patient what name and pronouns they prefer
fields.Back Extra: Be sure to address the patient by the name and pronouns they provide.

fields.Text:
Why should you ask a patient with a disability whether assistance is needed before assisting them?

Individuals with disabilities, like most people, value their {{c1::independence}}

What types of language may people with disabilities use to self-identify?

{{c1::Person-first}} language
{{c1::Identity-first}} language
fields.Back Extra: The clinician should confirm with patients which language they prefer.

fields.Text:
How should you communicate with a patient who speaks little or no English in an emergency situation?

Use any available {{c1::tools}}
fields.Back Extra: Examples include friends or family, interpreter applications, or sketches.

fields.Text:
Monitoring hemoglobin A1C to guide treatment and prevent complications is what level of disease prevention?

{{c1::Tertiary}} disease prevention

Due to the ongoing pandemic, COVID-19 has been added as one of the most common causes of death in which age group?

> {{c1::65}} years of age

What neurological complication can occur due to both cutaneous and pulmonary anthrax?

{{c1::Hemorrhagic meningitis}}

Age → {{c2::Young adult}} or {{c2::older adult}}
{{c3::Depression}}
Previous {{c4::attempt}}
{{c5::Ethanol}}/{{c5::drug}} use
{{c6::Rational}} thinking loss
{{c7::Sickness}}

No {{c9::social support}}
Stated {{c10::intent}}

GH is released in {{c1::pulses}} in response to {{c1::GHRH}}

The {{c1::distal::proximal/distal}} end of the respiratory {{c1::diverticulum}}

C3 and C4 → {{c1::Trapezius ridge}}
C5 → {{c1::Shoulder}}

PIO2 = {{c1::FIO2}} × ( {{c1::PB}} - {{c1::PH2O}} )

{{c1::Normal}} perfusion in areas of no ventilation

{{c1::Chocolate}}-colored blood
{{c1::Cyanosis}} that is not improved with administration of supplemental oxygen

Interlobular artery → {{c1::Afferent::Afferent/Efferent}} arteriole → {{c1::Glomerulus}} → {{c1::Efferent::Afferent/Efferent}} arteriole → {{c1::Peritubular capillaries}} → Interlobular vein

In what populations infected with tuberculosis is its reactivation most likely to occur?

{{c1::Immunocompromised}} individuals

Who are the high-risk patients for progression of cellulitis to necrotizing fasciitis in Vibrio vulnificus infection?

Those with {{c1::liver::organ}} diseases

DNA {{c1::methylation}}
{{c1::Noncoding}} RNA

What is the term for changing gene expression without a change in underlying DNA sequence?

{{c1::Epigenetics}}
fields.Back Extra: The changes can be inherited mitotically or meiotically.

Capping → {{c1::Cotranscriptional::Cotranscriptional/Posttranscriptional}}
Polyadenylation → {{c1::Posttranscriptional::Cotranscriptional/Posttranscriptional}}

{{c1::AG}} at the end

{{c1::Release}} factors

{{c1::16S RNA}} in the ribosomal subunit

{{c1::Non-motile::Motile/Non-motile}} cilia

Unbalanced translocations can result in {{c1::miscarriage}}, {{c1::stillbirth}}, and chromosomal {{c1::imbalances}}

It is a potent vasopressor that can {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} organ perfusion during septic shock

Mydriasis

What are the classic electron microscopic findings in patients with mesothelioma?

{{c1::Polygonal tumor}} cells with {{c1::microvilli}}, {{c1::desmosomes}}, and {{c1::tonofilaments}}

The failure of the septum primum and septum secundum to fuse after birth gives rise to which congenital heart defect?

{{c1::Patent foramen ovale}}

{{c1::Left::Left/Right}} {{c1::ventricle::atrium/ventricle}} → 2/3 of the inferior cardiac surface
{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::ventricle::atrium/ventricle}} → 1/3 of the inferior cardiac surface

Which blood vessel runs in the left atrioventricular groove and drains into the right atrium?

{{c1::Coronary sinus}}

{{c1::Coronary sinus}}

What five treatment options are commonly recommended in patients with obstructive sleep apnea?

Weight {{c1::loss::gain/loss}}

{{c1::Dental}} devices

Invasive {{c1::tubes}}

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::lower::upper/lower}} lobe

{{c1::Right::Left/Right}} {{c1::upper::upper/lower}} lobe

{{c1::Gastric acid}}-mediated inflammation

{{c1::Mastocytosis}}
fields.Back Extra: This is caused by proliferation of mast cells in the skin and/or extracutaneous organs.

Membrane defect → {{c1::Hereditary spherocytosis}} and {{c1::paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria}}
Enzyme defect → {{c2::Pyruvate kinase}} deficiency and {{c2::glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase}} deficiency
Hemoglobinopathy → {{c3::Sickle cell}} disease and {{c3::hemoglobin C}} disease

High values indicate {{c1::compensatory::compensatory/noncompensatory}} red blood cell production
Low values indicate {{c1::inadequate::adequate/inadequate}} response to correct anemia

{{c1::RPR}}

pH > {{c1::4.5}}

Why are autosomal monosomies usually incompatible with life?

There is a high risk for expression of {{c1::recessive}} traits of the affected chromosome

{{c1::Down}} syndrome > {{c1::Edwards}} syndrome > {{c1::Patau}} syndrome

What type of hernia is commonly seen in patients with Down syndrome?

{{c1::Umbilical}} hernia
fields.Back Extra: This is due to incomplete closure of the umbilical ring.

Why is Down syndrome associated with early-onset Alzheimer disease?

Chromosome 21 codes for {{c1::amyloid precursor}} protein
fields.Back Extra: Mutations of amyloid precursor protein can lead to early-onset Alzheimer disease.

fields.Text:

{{c1::Patau}} syndrome

What are the clinical manifestations of fragile X syndrome when there is a premutation?

{{c1::Ataxia}}
{{c1::Tremor}}
{{c1::Primary ovarian}} insufficiency

{{c1::Self-mutilation}}

What type of tissues are typically affected in mitochondrial diseases?

Those with increased {{c1::energy}} requirements

{{c1::Oxidative phosphorylation}}

{{c1::MELAS}}
{{c1::MERRF}}

Mitochondrial {{c1::crystalline inclusions}}

Leber hereditary optic neuropathy typically presents in what part of the population?

{{c1::Teens}}
{{c1::Young::Young/Older}} adults
fields.Back Extra: Males are more commonly affected than females.

Mutations in complex {{c1::I}} of the electron transport chain → Neuronal death in {{c1::retina}} and {{c1::optic}} nerve → Subacute permanent bilateral vision loss

What accompanying symptoms can be seen in a patient who has from vision loss due to Leber hereditary optic neuropathy?

Features of {{c1::neurologic}} dysfunction

Sudden release of bacterial antigens by the host in response to administration of {{c1::antibiotics}} → {{c1::Flu}}-like symptoms

{{c1::Autosomal recessive}}

{{c1::Enzymes}}

{{c1::Prader-Willi}} syndrome

{{c1::Prader-Willi}} syndrome

{{c1::p}} + {{c1::q}} = 1

What is the equation relating frequencies of genotypes in a population exhibiting Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?

{{c1::p2}} + ( {{c1::2}} × {{c1::p}} × {{c1::q}} ) + {{c1::q2}} = 1

{{c1::Cystic}} duct

{{c1::None}}

Eradication of infestation is necessary.

{{c1::Cimex lectularius}}

{{c1::Enveloped::Enveloped/Nonenveloped}} virus with {{c1::helical}} capsid

{{c1::Epstein-Barr virus}}

{{c1::Bunyavirus}}

What are the commonly used treatment modalities against SARS-CoV-2 infection?

Supplemental {{c1::oxygen}}
{{c1::Supportive care}}

How does corticosteroid administration affect eosinophil and lymphocyte counts?

Eosinopenia due to {{c1::sequestration}} in lymph nodes
Lymphopenia due to {{c1::apoptosis}} of lymphocytes

Name the four potential fates of pyruvate and indicate which are important, irreversible points of regulation.

{{c1::Lactate}} → Reversible
{{c1::Alanine}} → Reversible
{{c1::Acetyl-CoA}} → Irreversible
{{c1::Oxaloacetate}} → Irreversible

In what osteomyelitis cases are X-rays useful?

{{c1::Chronic::Acute/Chronic}} osteomyelitis

What drug should be added to meningitis empirical treatment if Listeria infection is suspected?

{{c1::Ampicillin}}

What is the mechanism of action of carbapenems?

They inhibit {{c1::cell wall}} synthesis by binding to {{c1::penicillin-binding}} protein → Cell death

Which two antibiotics can be used against multidrug-resistant strains of gram-negative bacteria?

{{c1::Polymyxin B}}
{{c1::Colistin}}

How do you treat pericarditis due to uremia?

{{c1::Dialysis}}

Rheumatic fever is a result of pharyngeal infection with what organism?

Group {{c1::A}} streptococci

What is the name of the phenomenon observed when a population undergoes a sharp reduction in population size, resulting in new allele frequencies?

{{c1::Bottleneck effect}}

What is the name of the phenomenon by which alleles that increase a species' fitness are more likely to be passed down to offspring?

{{c1::Natural selection}}

What is the name of the phenomenon by which a dramatic change in allele frequency occurs by change, and not through natural selection?

{{c1::Genetic drift}}

What is the term used to describe a transient loss of consciousness caused by a period of decreased cerebral blood flow?

{{c1::Syncope}}

Which subtype of reflex syncope presents with the common faint?

{{c1::Vasovagal}} syncope

Which subtype of reflex syncope occurs due to triggers such as coughing, sneezing, swallowing, defacation, or micturition?

{{c1::Situational}} syncope

Which type of reflex syncope results from an exaggerated response to carotid sinus baroreceptor stimulation?

{{c1::Carotid sinus hypersensitivity}}

Which form of syncope can be caused by drugs, hypovolemia, and autonomic dysfunction?

{{c1::Orthostatic}} syncope

Which form of syncope can be caused by arrhythmias or structural heart defects?

{{c1::Cardiac}} syncope

What changes on ECG can be seen with the use of azoles?

{{c1::QT interval prolongation}}

What four dietary supplements should be added to a vegetarian/vegan diet?

Vitamin {{c1::B2}}
Vitamin {{c1::B12}}
Vitamin {{c1::D}}
{{c1::Iron}}

High consumption of egg whites can predispose to which vitamin deficiency?

Vitamin {{c1::B7}}
fields.Back Extra: Egg whites contain avidin, which binds to biotin and prevents its absorption.

fields.Text:
Consumption of untreated corn is associated with which vitamin deficiency?

Vitamin {{c1::B3}}

How do nicotine replacement therapies such as long-acting nicotine patches or short-acting gum and lozenges assist with smoking cessation?

Binds to {{c1::nicotinic acetylcholine}} receptors to relieve withdrawal symptoms

Which adverse effects can be caused by nicotine replacement therapy?

Oral {{c1::irritation}}
{{c1::Headaches}}

Which smoking cessation drug acts as a partial agonist at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors to decrease withdrawal and effects on the reward system?

{{c1::Varenicline}}

Name two common side effects of varenicline.

{{c1::Sleep}} disturbances
{{c1::Gastrointestinal}} discomfort

What is the pathophysiology of constrictive pericarditis?

Pericardial {{c1::fibrosis}} +/– {{c1::calcification}} → Limited space for expansion → Decreased ventricular filling

Which type of inflammation is associated with constrictive pericarditis?

{{c1::Chronic::Acute/Chronic}} inflammation

What are five common causes of constrictive pericarditis?

{{c1::Idiopathic}}
{{c1::Viral}} infections
Cardiac {{c1::surgery}}
Thoracic {{c1::radiation}} (late)
{{c1::Tuberculosis}} in resource-limited countries

What happens to end diastolic volume, cardiac output, and venous return in constrictive pericarditis?

End diastolic volume → {{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}}
Cardiac output → {{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}}
Venous return → {{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}}

What are the common signs and symptoms associated with constrictive pericarditis?

{{c1::Dyspnea}}
Jugular venous {{c1::distention}}
Peripheral {{c1::edema}}
{{c1::Pulsus paradoxus}}
{{c1::Kussmaul}} sign
Pericardial {{c1::knock}}

Which condition in infants after birth is due to increased pulmonary vasculature resistance and causes respiratory distress and cyanosis?

{{c1::Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn}}

Name two risk factors for persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn.

{{c1::Meconium aspiration}}
Neonatal {{c1::pneumonia}}

How does persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn affect blood flow in the infant?

Causes {{c1::right::left/right}}-to-{{c1::left::left/right}} shunting
fields.Back Extra: This is via the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale.

fields.Text:
How does preductal oxygen saturation compare to postductal oxygen saturation in neonates with persistant pulmonary hypertension of the newborn?

Preductal oxygen saturation is {{c1::higher::higher/lower}} than postductal oxygen saturation

Which condition is caused by narrowing of the aorta near the insertion of the ductus arteriosus?

{{c1::Coarction of the aorta}}

Which congenital disease of the aorta is associated with Turner syndrome and bicuspid aortic valve?

{{c1::Coarction of the aorta}}

What physical exam findings can be seen in the upper extremities and lower extremities of patients with coarction of the aorta?

{{c1::Hypertension::Hypertension/Hypotension}} in upper extremities
{{c1::Weak::Strong/Weak}} and {{c1::delayed}} pulses in lower extremities
fields.Back Extra: The delayed pulses are specifically known as brachiofemoral delay.

fields.Text:
As patients with coarction of the aorta age, what chest X-ray finding develops due to enlargement of intercostal arteries?

{{c1::Rib notching}}
fields.Back Extra: Collateral circulation causes intercostal arteries to enlarge and erode into the ribs.

fields.Text:
Name four complications from coarction of the aorta.

Aortic {{c1::rupture}}
{{c1::Heart failure}}
{{c1::Infective endocarditis}}
{{c1::Cerebral hemorrhage}}

What is the pathophysiologic cause of cranial nerve V compression in trigeminal neuralgia?

Usually caused by an aberrant {{c1::vascular loop}}

What is the probable diagnosis of a patient presenting with unilateral, electric-shock-like pain that lasts seconds?

{{c1::Trigeminal neuralgia}}

What drug is the first-line treatment for trigeminal neuralgia?

{{c1::Carbamazepine}}

What are the two most common risk factors for the development of cerebral palsy?

{{c1::Prematurity}}
{{c1::Low::High/Low}} birth weight

What childhood movement disorder is associated with the development of periventricular leukomalacia?

{{c1::Cerebral palsy}}
fields.Back Extra: This is the most common movement disorder in children.

fields.Text:
What type of motor neuron signs are characteristic of cerebral palsy?

{{c1::Upper::Upper/Lower}} motor neuron signs

What are three therapeutic options available for children with cerebral palsy?

{{c1::Botox}} injections
Muscle {{c1::relaxants}}
Selective dorsal {{c1::rhizotomy}}

What syndrome is associated with uncomfortable sensations in the legs, usually relieved by movement?

{{c1::Restless legs}} syndrome

What three underlying conditions are usually associated with restless legs syndrome?

{{c1::Iron deficiency}} anemia
{{c1::Chronic kidney}} disease
{{c1::Diabetes mellitus}}

In what part of the day do symptoms of restless legs syndrome most commonly appear?

{{c1::Evening}}
{{c1::Night}}

What are two treatment options for restless legs syndrome?

{{c1::Dopamine}} agonists
{{c1::Gabapentinoids}}

What disease is classically associated with a unilateral "pill rolling" tremor at rest?

{{c1::Parkinson}} disease

What are the characteristic symptoms of Parkinson disease?

{{c1::Tremor}}
{{c1::Rigidity}}
{{c1::Akinesia}}
{{c1::Postural}} instability

Which form of dementia results from loss of dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta?

{{c1::Parkinson}} disease

What intracellular eosinophilic inclusions composed of α-synuclein are seen in Parkinson disease?

{{c1::Lewy bodies}}

Atrophy of the sections highlighted in this image is consistent with what disease?



{{c1::Huntington}} disease

What features does Huntington disease usually present with?

{{c1::Chorea}}
{{c1::Athetosis}}
{{c1::Depression}}
{{c1::Aggression}}
{{c1::Dementia}}

How is Huntington disease inherited?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}} inheritance

At what age do symptoms of Huntington disease usually manifest?

Typically between the ages of {{c1::30}} and {{c1::50}} years

In Huntington disease, what mechanism is primarily responsible for neuronal cell death?

{{c1::NMDA}}-receptor binding causing {{c1::glutamate}} excitotoxicity

What changes in the neurotransmitters are seen in Huntington disease?

{{c1::Increase::Increase/Decrease}} in dopamine
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in GABA
{{c1::Decrease::Increase/Decrease}} in acetylcholine

What are the two most common causes of dementia in the elderly?

{{c1::Alzheimer}} disease (most common)
{{c1::Vascular dementia}}

Superior colliculus → Letter {{c1::A}}

Level → {{c1::Midbrain}}

Level → {{c1::Midbrain}}

Identify the level of the brainstem as well as which letter represents the red nucleus.



Level → {{c1::Midbrain}}
Red nucleus → Letter {{c1::F}}

Identify the level of the brainstem as well as which letter represents the substantia nigra.



Level → {{c1::Midbrain}}
Substantia nigra → Letter {{c1::G}}

Level → {{c1::Pons}}

Cranial nerve V → Letter {{c1::D}}

Corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts → Letter {{c1::E}}

Identify the level of the brainstem as well as which letter represents the superior cerebellar peduncle.

Superior cerebellar peduncle → Letter {{c1::F}}

Locus ceruleus → Letter {{c1::G}}

Medial lemniscus pathway → Letter {{c1::H}}

Inferior cerebellar peduncle → Letter {{c1::A}}

Level → {{c1::Medulla}}
Medial longitudinal fasciculus → Letter {{c1::B}}

Nucleus ambiguus → Letter {{c1::C}}

Level → {{c1::Medulla}}
Inferior olivary nucleus → Letter {{c1::D}}

Identify the level of the brainstem as well as which letter represents the cerebral pyramid.

Cerebral pyramid → Letter {{c1::E}}

Level → {{c1::Medulla}}
Cranial nerve XII → Letter {{c1::F}}

Dorsal motor nucleus → Letter {{c1::G}}

Identify the level of the brainstem as well as which letter represents the nucleus tractus solitarius.

Nucleus tractus solitarius → Letter {{c1::H}}

Identify the level of the brainstem as well as which letter represents the fibers of cranial nerve X.



Level → {{c1::Medulla}}
Fibers of cranial nerve X → Letter {{c1::I}}

Identify the level of the brainstem as well as which letter represents the medial lemniscus pathway.



Level → {{c1::Medulla}}
Medial lemniscus pathway → Letter {{c1::J}}

What is the inheritance pattern and affected genes that cause susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia?

{{c1::Autosomal dominant}} mutations in the {{c2::ryanodine}} receptor ({{c2::RYR1}}) or the {{c3::dihydropyridine}} receptor ({{c3::DHPR}})

What is the treatment for malignant hyperthermia?

{{c1::Dantrolene}}
fields.Back Extra: This acts as an antagonist at the ryanodine receptor.

fields.Text:
What condition causes hyperthermia, severe muscle contractions and rigidity, tachycardia, hypercapnia, and rhabdomyolysis after induction of anesthesia?

{{c1::Malignant hyperthermia}}

What can trigger malignant hyperthermia?

Administration of {{c1::succinylcholine}} or potent inhaled {{c1::anesthetics}} in patients who are susceptible to malignant hyperthermia

What causes the sustained muscle contractions seen in malignant hyperthermia?

Excessive release of {{c1::Ca2+}} from the {{c1::sarcoplasmic reticulum}}

Which is the most common intraocular malignancy in children?

{{c1::Retinoblastoma}}

What is the chromosomal basis of pathogenesis of retinoblastoma?

Mutations in both {{c1::RB1}} tumor suppressor genes on chromosome {{c1::13}}
fields.Back Extra: This ordinarily restricts G1→ S phase progression.

fields.Text:
What are the clnical findings associated with retinoblastoma?

{{c1::Leukocoria}}
{{c1::Strabismus}}
{{c1::Nystagmus}}
{{c1::Redness}} of eye

Which is the most common type of strabismus in children?

{{c1::Esotropia}}

Name 3 complications of strabismus.

{{c1::Amblyopia}}
{{c1::Diplopia}}
Associated adverse {{c1::psychosocial}} impact

What is the pathophysiology of amblyopia?

Decreased visual {{c1::acuity}} due to maldevelopment of visual {{c1::cortex}} secondary to abnormal visual experience early in life

What cardiac abnormality is commonly found in patients with cri-du-chat syndrome?

{{c1::Ventricular septal}} defect

What is CRISPR/Cas9 derived from?

{{c1::Bacteria}}
